[Page 98]

2. Surat al-Baqarah

This is the well-known name. In the Sahih, it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "This is the station of the one upon whom Surat al-Baqarah was revealed." This contradicts what has been narrated prohibiting such a usage. It must therefore be said that this refers to the surah in which al-Baqarah is mentioned, and likewise for all the surahs of the Qur'an. For this reason the majority permitted it without disapproval. It is possible to reconcile the two by saying that it was disliked at the beginning of Islam because of the mockery of the disbelievers, and then, after its light had shone forth, the prohibition was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one), so it spread without objection. A hadith also came as an explanation of its permissibility. Some of the discussion on this has already preceded.

Khalid ibn Ma'dan used to call it "the tent-pole of the Qur'an" (fustat al-Qur'an). It is mentioned in a marfu' hadith in Musnad al-Firdaws, and this is due to its greatness and because it contains rulings that are not mentioned in other surahs, to the extent that some shaykhs said: "In it are a thousand commands, a thousand prohibitions and a thousand reports." It was said: "And in it are fifteen parables." For this reason Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, spent eight years learning it. A hadith in al-Mustadrak calls it "the hump of the Qur'an" (sanam al-Qur'an), and the hump of everything is its highest part, and perhaps it is also for this reason.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Which surah of the Qur'an is the best?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Surat al-Baqarah." Then he said: "And which verse is the best?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The Verse of the Throne."

It is a Madinan surah. Its verses number two hundred and eighty-seven according to the well-known count, and it was said: two hundred and eighty-six. In it is the last verse revealed, which is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾. It was revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage, on the Day of Sacrifice. This does not take it out of being Madinan, as is well known.

The connection (munasabah) between it and Surat al-Fatihah is that al-Fatihah includes the explanation of lordship (rububiyyah) first, servitude ('ubudiyyah) second, and the seeking of guidance toward religious aims and certain objectives third. Likewise, Surat al-Baqarah includes the explanation of knowledge of the Lord first, as in ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ and similar expressions; then the acts of worship and what relates to them second; and finally the seeking of what is needed in this world and the next. Also, at the end of al-Fatihah is the request for guidance, and at the beginning of al-Baqarah there is an allusion to that in His saying: ﴿guidance for the God-conscious﴾.

Since the Exalted began al-Fatihah with an outward matter, and since behind every outward thing there is an inward one, He began this surah with what is hidden in its secret and whose matter is concealed except from whomever Allah, the Exalted, wills. So He, glorified and exalted, said: "In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾"

These, and the other utterances by which one spells out letters (such as ba ta tha), are names whose referents are the simple letters from which the word is composed, because they truly fit the agreed definition of a noun and the properties agreed upon for it apply to each of them. It is reported from al-Khalil that he asked his companions: "How do you pronounce the ba in daraba and the kaf in laka?" They said: "ba, kaf." He said: "You have only brought the name, not the letter." [Page 99] I, however, say: "bah – kah."

It is also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever recites a letter of the Book of Allah, the Exalted, will have a good deed for it, and a good deed is worth ten like it. I do not say that "Alif Lam Mim" is a letter, but Alif is a letter, Lam is a letter, and Mim is a letter.'" So what is meant by "letter" here is not the technical sense, since that is a later convention, but the linguistic meaning, namely one of the letters that form words. Thus the meaning of "Alif is a letter", etc., is the name of Alif, and so on. Perhaps the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) named that a letter by the name of its referent, so this is a real meaning for it. What has been said, that he called it a letter metaphorically because it is the name of the letter, and the use of one of two mutually implying things for the other is a well-known metaphor, is nothing. If by "Alam" [in the verse] the opening of Surat al-Fil is meant, then its referent is also meant, and the good deeds would be thirty. The purpose of the negation is to remove the suspicion that "letter" in "whoever recites a letter" means a word. If what is meant is something like what is here, then its referent itself is meant, and the number of good deeds would then be ninety. The purpose of the new sentence (istinaf) is to remove the suspicion that "letter" means an independent sentence, as in al-Ibanah of Abu Nasr ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The last letter with which Jibril presented to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was: ﴿Alif. Lam. Mim.﴾ ﴿This is the Book; there is no doubt in it; a guidance for the God-conscious﴾."

The meaning is: I do not say that the whole group of the three names is a letter, but the referent of each of them is a letter. He did not mention those letters in terms of their being parts, such as saying "the alif of a letter" and "the lam of a letter", to indicate that what counts in the number of good deeds are the letters that are read, which are the referents, whether they are parts of those names or of other words, and not in terms of their being parts of those names. So the number of good deeds in something like "daraba" is thirty.

The summary is that the letters mentioned, in terms of their being the referents of those names, are parts of all words when read in isolation, and in terms of their being parts of those names, they are not read in isolation except when those names are read. What counts for the number of good deeds is the first consideration, not the second. This was mentioned by some verifiers. Furthermore, in this naming they observed a subtle point: they made the referent the beginning of each name for it, as Ibn Jinni said, so that when one pronounces it, the referent is the first thing to strike the hearing. Do you not see that when you say "jim", its first letter is jim, and when you say "alif", its first letter is alif, which you pronounced as a hamzah? When the one who spells could not begin with the alif, which is a quiescent prolonged vowel, he supported it with a lam before it, which is vocalized, so that it could be begun. So they said: "la, ka" (for alif, as in "lam-alif", they say "la" then "ka" [i.e., lā kamā]), not "lam alif" as the teachers say, which is an error. The lam was singled out for this support because they reached the lam through its sister in definition [i.e., the lam of the definite article], so it is as if they intended a kind of counter-balance. Thus alif is the first letter of the alphabet, which in reality is the form of the hamzah. This is similar, in putting a word to express meaning, to the basmalah (saying "bismillah"), the hamdalah (saying "al-hamdu lillah"), the hawqalah (saying "la hawla wa la quwwata illa billah"), and the naht (coining a compound word) that the grammarians call naht.

The rule for the names of letters is that their last part is quiescent unless they are governed (ma'mulah) by something. Are they mu'rab (inflected by i'rab, the grammatical case endings) or mabni (indeclinable)? Or neither? The disagreement is based on the disagreement over the definition of the inflected and the indeclinable, so the disagreement is verbal. People have various views on what they are fond of. The discussion is fully covered in our grammar books.

Much has been said about the beginnings of the surahs. The view on which the majority agreed, which is the position of Sibawayh and others among the earlier scholars, is that they are names for the surahs, and they were named by them to indicate that they are words of known composition. If they were not a revelation from Allah, the Exalted, their power would not have fallen short of challenging them. This is like how they named the father of Harithah ibn Lam al-Ta'i "Lam", the copper "Sad", and the mountain "Qaf".

It was argued that if they did not convey meaning, addressing with them would be like addressing with meaningless sounds, or speaking Zanji (a foreign language) to an Arab, and the whole Qur'an would not be a clarification and guidance, and the challenge (tahaddi, the challenge to produce something similar) could not be made with it. And if they do convey meaning, then either what is meant by them is the surahs that they begin, on the basis that they are their titles, according to that indication, or something else. The second is invalid, because either what is meant is what they were set for in the language of the Arabs, which obviously is not so, or something other than that, which is invalid because the Qur'an was revealed in clear Arabic speech, [Page 100] so it is not to be interpreted by something not in their language.

This was objected to with several points. First, we find many surahs beginning with "Alif Lam Mim" and "Ha Mim", and the purpose of a name is to remove confusion. Second, if they were names, they would be mentioned and well known by them, but their fame is contrary to that, like Surat al-Baqarah and Al 'Imran. Third, the Arabs did not go beyond what they named with a compound of two names, such as Ba'labakk, and no one of them named with a compound of three, four, or five names. So the claim that they are names of surahs is a departure from their language. Fourth, it leads to the unity of the name and the named. Fifth, these expressions are included within the surahs, and the part of a thing is prior to the thing in rank, while the name of a thing is posterior to it, so it would follow that it is both prior and posterior at once, which is impossible.

The first was answered by what is answered regarding shared proper names: they are not of a single imposition. The second was answered by the fact that it has been narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Ya-Sin is the heart of the Qur'an," and "Whoever recites Ha Mim will be protected until morning," and in the Sunan: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prostrated in (Sad)." When it is established for some, it is established for all, since there is no difference. Moreover, the fame of one of two proper names does not harm the proper-nounhood of the other. How many a named thing is not known by its name except after searching, because it is famous for something else, like Abu Hurayrah and Dhu al-Yadayn? And the lack of fame of some of them is because it is shared, so it was left out because it needs an addition, like "Alif Lam Mim" here. The third was answered by the fact that naming by three names, for example, is only forbidden when they are compounded and made one name. But when they are scattered like the names of numbers, it is not forbidden, because it falls under naming by what should be quoted (hikayah).

Naming with three words has indeed occurred, such as "Shab Qarnaha", "Sarra man ra'a", and "Darabjard". Sibawayh explained naming by a sentence, by a line of poetry, and by a group of names of letters of the alphabet. The fourth was answered by the fact that this naming is naming a compound by a single word, and the single word is not the compound, so there is no unity. Do you not see that they made the name of the letter composed of it and something else, like "Sad", so they are different in essence and attribute? The fifth was answered by the fact that the precedence of what is prior with respect to one aspect and its posteriority with respect to another is not impossible. The part is prior in terms of its essence and posterior in terms of its description, which is nominality (ismiyyah), so there is no problem.

Some said: that they are names of the disjointed letters is closer to verification, because it is clear, there is no metaphor in it, it is sound from what can be objected to in others, and because it is the established matter. It also better suits the subtleties of the revelation, because it indicates the miraculousness (i'jaz) intentionally. Sharing among proper names from a single imposer returns, by contradiction, to what is the very aim of proper-nounhood. The words of Sibawayh and others are not explicit on this, because it is possible that they meant that they run in the manner of names, as they say: "I recited: Banat Su'ad," and "Say: He is Allah, the One," meaning what begins with that. When its running on the tongues prevailed, they became like the dominant proper names, so they were mentioned in the chapter on proper names and the rules of proper names were applied to them. Moreover, what was mentioned in the third objection is something unavoidable, since the absence of naming by three, four, or five names in the speech of the Arabs is beyond doubt, and what is reported from Sibawayh is merely an analogy needing proof, as al-Sayyid al-Sanad mentioned.

Beyond these two opinions are other views, the mention of which I fear would cause tedium. What is most likely is that the verification of this is a hidden knowledge and a concealed secret, which scholars have been unable to grasp, as Ibn 'Abbas said, and whose reach the horses of imagination have fallen short of attaining. For this reason al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Every book has a secret, and the secret of the Qur'an is the beginnings of the surahs." Al-Sha'bi said: "It is the secret of Allah, so do not seek it."

"Between lovers there is a secret that neither speech nor pen can reveal to the creation."

**[Page 101]**

After the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, none knows it except the inheriting saints (al-awliya' al-warathah), for they know it from that Presence (al-hadrah), and the letters may speak to them of what is within them, just as they spoke to one who had the pebbles glorify Allah in his palm, and the lizard (al-dabb) and the gazelle (al-zaby) spoke to him, as this is established from the narration of our forefathers, the People of the House, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with them. Indeed, whenever the servant gathers the fruit of the tree of drawing near through voluntary acts (qurb al-nawafil), he knows it, and other things besides, by the knowledge of Allah the Exalted, from which not even the weight of an atom in the earth or in the heavens is hidden. As for what the one presenting the objection mentioned earlier, that if they did not convey meaning, the address with them would be like address with the meaningless (al-muhmal), and so on: it is meaningless speech, however great its speaker may be. For if he intends to make all people understand, we do not grant that this exists in the world of knowledge (al-'alamiyyah). If he intends to make the one addressed by them understand, who here is the Messenger ﷺ, then this is something no believer doubts. And if he intends a group of people, then how wonderful, for the people of spiritual taste (arbab al-dhawq) know them, and they are many among the Muhammadans, and praise be to Allah.

*Stars of a sky: whenever a star falls, another star appears to which its stars return.*

The ignorance of people like us of their intended meaning does no harm. For among the acts we have been charged with are some whose wisdom we do not know, such as throwing the pebbles (ramy al-jamarat), the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah, the ramal (the quick pace in tawaf) and the idtiba' (the uncovering of the right shoulder). Obedience in such matters is more indicative of perfect submission and the utmost surrender. So why should it not be permissible that He who is not questioned about what He does, may His majesty be exalted, command us with words whose meaning we have not grasped, the purpose being the manifestation of the perfect submission of the one commanded to the one commanding, and the utmost surrender and compliance to the Wise, the Powerful?

*If he said, in bewilderment: "Stand upon the coals of the ghada wood," I would stand, obeying, and not hesitate.*

Furthermore, there is another benefit in it: when a person comprehends the meaning and encompasses it, its impact falls away from the heart. But when he does not grasp its intended purpose, while being certain that the speaker is wise, his heart remains inclined toward it forever, turning toward it perpetually, reflecting upon it, and his mind, with its forefront and its wings, flies back to its nest. The gate of obligation is the occupation of the inner self with the remembrance of the Beloved and reflection upon Him and upon His speech. So it is not far-fetched that Allah the Exalted knows that for the servant to remain with his mind turned toward it, his thought occupied with it forever, there is a great benefit and a mighty favor from Him upon him, through which he may perhaps rise to the enclosures of holiness (haza'ir al-quds) and the landmarks of intimacy (ma'alim al-uns). The beginning of love is imagination. And this does not contradict the Qur'an being "Arabic, clear" (Qur'an 12:2 type statement), for it is so in relation to the one you know.

As for the challenge (al-tahaddi), it is not in all its parts, and that the beginning of the surah should be something to be challenged with is not granted by one who disagrees. Among the wonders of these openings (fawatih) is that they constitute half of the letters of the alphabet according to one view, and they occur in twenty-nine surahs, the number of all the letters according to another view, and they include half of their categories: the whispered (al-mahmusah) and the voiced (al-majhurah), the hard (al-shadidah) and the closed (al-mutbaqah), the raised (al-mustaliyah) and the lowered (al-munkhafidah), and the letters of qalqalah (echoing letters). The Greatest Shaykh (Ibn 'Arabi), may Allah sanctify his secret, spoke about the secret of the number of their letters with repetition, the number of their letters without repetition, their totality across the surahs, their singular occurrence in (Sad), (Qaf) and (Nun), their dual occurrence in (Ya Sin) and (Ta Ha) and their like, and their gathering in groups of three or more, and why they reached five letters, and why some of them are connected and some disconnected. He, may Allah sanctify his secret, said in his Futuhat, may Allah the Exalted restore to us from the good of His breezes what he attained:

Know that the beginnings of the unknown surahs are not understood in their reality except by the people of intelligible forms (ahl al-suwar al-ma'qulah). He, blessed and exalted, made them twenty-nine surahs, which is the completion of the form: *"And the moon—We have determined for it stations"* (Qur'an 36:39). The twenty-ninth is the pole (al-qutb) upon which the sphere (al-falak) stands, and it is the cause of its existence, and it is the surah of Al 'Imran: *"Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah"* (Qur'an 3:1-2). Had it not been for that, the twenty-eight would not be established. Their total, counting repeated letters, is seventy-eight letters. The eight is the true meaning of *bid'* (a few), and he said: "Faith has *bid'* (a few) and seventy" (the hadith: "Faith has over seventy branches"). These letters are seventy-eight, so a servant does not perfect the secrets of faith until he knows the realities of these letters in their surahs. Just as, if he knows them without repetition, he knows the indication of Allah in them to the reality of origination (al-ijad), and the Eternal, glorified and exalted, is singular in His eternal attributes. So He sent them in His Qur'an as fourteen single, undetermined letters. He made the eight for knowledge of the Essence, and the seven for the attributes from us, and He made the four for the composed natures, so there came twelve existing letters. This human being is from this sphere, and from another sphere composed of eleven, and of ten, and of nine, and of eight, until it reaches the sphere of two, and it never dissolves into oneness, for that is what the Real, glorified be He, has singled out. Then He, exalted, made its first letter the alif in writing and the hamzah in pronunciation, and its last the nun. The alif is for the existence of the Essence in its perfection, for it does not require a vowel (haraka). The nun is for the existence of the half of the world, which is the world of composition, and that is the half of the circle of the sphere visible to us. The other half is the intelligible nun upon it, which, if it appeared to the senses and moved to the world of spirit, would be an encompassing circle. But He concealed this spiritual nun, through which is the perfection of existence, and the visible dot of the nun was made to indicate it. Thus the alif is complete in all its aspects, and the nun is deficient. The sun is complete and the moon is deficient, for it is effacement (mahw), so the quality of its light is borrowed, and that is the trust (amanah) which it carried. In proportion to its effacement and eclipse is its affirmation and manifestation, three for three. The three is the setting of the spiritual divine moon in the Presence of Oneness (al-hadrah al-ahadiyyah), and three is the rising of the spiritual divine moon in the Lordly Presence (al-hadrah al-rabbaniyyah). Between them, in going out and returning, step by step, it never fails. Then He, glorified and exalted, placed these letters in ranks: some connected, some disconnected, some single, and dual and plural. Then He drew attention to the fact that in every connection there is a disconnection, but not in every disconnection is there a connection. Every connection indicates a separation, but not every separation indicates a connection. Connection and separation are in the plural and the non-plural, and separation alone is in the very distinction. What He made singular of these is an indication of the annihilation of the servant's trace in eternity, or what He affirmed is an indication of the existence of the trace of servanthood in the present, and what He gathered is an indication of eternity through the endless sources. Singularity is for the eternal sea, plurality is for the everlasting sea, and the dual is for the Muhammadan human isthmus (al-barzakh al-muhammadi al-insani). The alif in what we are discussing is an indication of Unity (al-tawhid), the mim is an indication of the Kingdom that does not perish, and the lam between them is a intermediary, so that there may be a bond between them. Look at the line upon which the writing falls from the lam: you will find the alif its origin ends there, and you will find the mim begins its growth from it. Then you descend from the best form, which is the position of the line, to the lowest of the lowest, the end of the definition of the mim. The descent of the alif to the line is like His saying: "Our Lord descends to the lowest heaven" (hadith: "Our Lord descends to the lowest heaven"). That is the first world of composition, for it is the heaven of Adam, peace be upon him, and next to it is the sphere of fire. Therefore it descended to the beginning of the line. He, glorified and exalted, descended from the station of Oneness to the station of the creation of the Vicegerent, a descent of sanctity and transcendence, not a descent of likeness and resemblance. The lam was an intermediary, and it is the substitute for the Originator and the originated, and it is the Power (al-qudrah) through which the world came into being. So it resembled the alif in descending to the beginning of the line. And since it is composed of the Originator and the originated, He, glorified and exalted, is not described as having power over Himself; rather He is powerful over His creation, so the aspect of power was directed toward creation, and it must be connected to them. And since its reality is not completed by reaching the line, so that it would be on the same level as the alif, its reality demanded descending beneath the line or upon it, as the mim descended. So it descended to bring it into existence, but it could not descend in its own form, so only the mim came into being from it. It descended as a half-circle until it reached the line from a direction other than that from which it had descended. So it became a half of a sensible sphere, seeking the other half of an intelligible sphere, and from the two of them came a complete sphere. So the whole world came into being in six days, kinds from the first day, Sunday, to the last day, Friday. The day of Saturday remained for the transition from station to station and from state to state. So (Alif-Lam-Mim) became an encompassing sphere, behind which is the knowledge of the Essence, the Attributes, the Acts, and the Things Done. Whoever reads them with this truth is present with the All, for the All, with the All, to the end of what he said.

He mentioned in the book (The Night Journey to the Furthest Station, al-Isra' ila al-maqam al-asra) what points to subtle thoughts and hidden secrets built upon the numbers of the letters, which are three thousand, five hundred and thirty-two. The first detail is from Noah to the rising of Yuh (Jesus), then to the end of the composition in which the Word and the Spirit descended. So after its number, you multiply it, add it, subtract from it by casting out (tarh), and place it, and there appears to you the completion of the Law, until the breaking of nature. Among what is used as support for this is what Izz ibn Abd al-Salam narrated: that Ali, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him, extracted the battle of Mu'awiyah from (Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf). And Abu al-Hakam Abd al-Salam ibn Barrajan, in his tafsir, extracted the conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) in the year 583 AH from the words of the Exalted: *"Alif-Lam-Mim. The Romans have been defeated"* (Qur'an 30:1-2). The Shaykh, may Allah sanctify his secret, mentioned how to extract that by a method other than the one he mentioned. It is this: you take the number of (Alif-Lam-Mim) by the small jummal (al-jummal al-saghir, the reckoning by unit values), which is eight, and you add it to the eight of the bid' in the verse, so it becomes sixteen. You remove the one of the alif for the root (al-ussi), leaving fifteen, and you hold that aside. Then you return to the operation in that by the large jummal (al-jummal al-kabir, the reckoning by the value of letters), which is by unit-value, and you multiply the eight of the bid' by seventy-one, and you make all that years. The product comes to five hundred and sixty-eight years. You add to it the fifteen you had set aside, so it becomes five hundred and eighty-three years, and that is the time of the conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis, according to the reading "ghalabat" (they were defeated) with the ghayn and lam vowelled as fatha, and "sa-yughlabun" (they will be defeated) with the ya' vowelled with damma and the lam with fatha. End.

When you know that these openings are the greatest secret, the mighty sea, and the most complete light...

*Clarity without water, subtlety without air, light without fire, spirit without body.*

**[Part 3 of 3]**

(Know well) that everything people have said about these letters is but a sip from the seas of their meanings. Whoever claims to have exhausted them has done so out of his own deficiency, and whoever claims to have brought much has done so out of the weakness of his light. The gnostic (al-'arif) says that all that has been said about them is contained within the shell of their benefits, and all that has been written about them is mixed into the abyss of their benefits. So if you wish, say: just as these letters contain those secrets, each letter of them points to one of the names of the Exalted. If you wish, say: He brought them in this way as a waking call and a striking of the staff for those who challenged with the Qur'an. If you wish, say: they came thus so that the opening of what is recited to them would stand alone with a kind of strangeness, as a model for the various forms of inimitability (i'jaz) found in the remainder. The pronunciation of the most precious letters within the flow of speech, even when at the edge of the thyme plant, is accessible to both the elite and the common people. But pronouncing their names can only be achieved by one who has studied and written. As for one who has never come near this at all, he is rarer than the eggs of the 'anuq bird and more distant than the Pleiades' hold (al-'Ayyuq). This is especially so when it is in a wondrous style and a strange method, pointing to a secret hidden upon a unique path, such that the minds of intelligent people are bewildered by it and the intellects of the mighty are unable to grasp it. If you wish, say: in them is an attraction for the attention of minds, and a bridle for every unruly unbeliever when the Qur'an is revealed, because when they hear what they do not understand from this wondrous style, they abandon their noise, and their motives are stirred to look into the matter of the connection between these letters of the alphabet, which came disconnected, and the words adjacent to them, hoping that perhaps speech will come explaining that ambiguity and clarifying that difficulty. In this is the averting of much evil from their obstinacy, their arrogance, and their idle talk, which was then appearing from them. And in this is a mercy from Him, exalted is He, to the believers, and a favour to those who seek insight. If you wish, say: some of their compounds, in the meaning that the people of God, exalted is He, understand from them, may be correctly applied to Him, glory be to Him. Thus what is reported from Ali, may God honour his face, that he said, "O Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad, and O Ha Mim 'Ayn Sin Qaf," is applied to its literal sense. And if you refuse, then say, the intended meaning is "O You who sent them down." And if you wish, say something other than that. Speak of the sea, and there is no blame.

I have in this matter some subtleties, and glory be to the One whose speech's secrets are endless. He, glory be to Him, indicated by the beginning of the Opening (al-Fatiha), where He brought it clearly, His manifest name, and by the beginning of Surat al-Baqara, His hidden name. He is "the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward" (Q. 57:3). By placing the First (al-Awwal) first, He indicated that the outward is prior, and with it is the general scope of the prophetic mission. (We judge by the outward, and God takes care of the inward secrets.) Also, in the First there is an indication of the station of unification (maqam al-jam'), and in the Second there is an allusion to separation after unification. Also, opening this surah with the ambiguous and then following it with the clear has the most complete correspondence with the story of the cow (al-baqara), after which the surah is named: ﴿And [recall] when you killed a soul and disputed over it, but Allah was to bring forth that which you were concealing﴾ (Q. 2:72). Also, in the letters there is an allusion to three things: the alif indicates the Sharia, the lam the Tariqa (the mystical path), and the mim the Haqiqa (the ultimate reality). There the servant becomes like a circle whose end is the beginning itself, and this is the station of annihilation (fana') in God, exalted is He, completely. Also, the alif is from the furthest part of the throat, the lam from the tip of the tongue, which is the middle of the places of articulation, and the mim from the lips, which is its last. Thus by them He indicates that the beginning of the servant's remembrance, its middle, and its end are not proper except to God, Mighty and Majestic. Also, in this there is an indication of the secret of trinity: the alif points to God, exalted is He; the lam to Gabriel; and the mim to Muhammad (ﷺ). Ja'far al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him, said: "In the alif there are six attributes from the attributes of God, exalted is He: the beginning (ibtida'), and God, exalted is He, is the First; the uprightness (istiwa'), and God, exalted is He, is the Just who does not oppress; the singularity (infirad), and God, exalted is He, is the Single; the non-connection to a letter, and He, glory be to Him, is separate from His creation; the need of the letters for it while it has no need of them, and you are the poor towards God and God is the Rich; and its meaning is companionship (al-ulfa), and with God is harmony (al-i'tilaf)." And secrets remain, and what secrets! A zealous gnostic guards them from strangers.

Among the curiosities: some of the Shi'a took comfort in these letters for the caliphate of the Commander Ali, may God honour his face, for if the repeated letters are removed from them, what remains is what can be extracted to form: "The path of Ali is the truth, we hold to it." But you, O Sunni, may take comfort in them for your own position, for after the removal, what remains can be extracted to form what is addressed to the Shi'ite, reminding him of what has been reported concerning the Companions, may God be pleased with them all. It is: "The advice has reached your ear." This is like what they mentioned letter by letter. And if you wish, you can say: "Your path is sound with the Sunna," and this is more fitting and more subtle. In sum, the wonders of these openings never run out, nor can counting enumerate them.

Everyone claims union with Layla,
but Layla does not admit that to them.

People have differed over their i'rab (grammatical case-inflection), in accordance with the differing of their sayings about them. If they are made names for the surahs, for example, they have a share of i'rab in the nominative, accusative, and genitive. The nominative is on the basis that they are the predicate of an omitted subject, or a subject whose predicate is omitted. The accusative is by the implied verb of oath, or a verb suitable to the context. The accusative by implying the verb of oath is permitted in what follows a genitive with the conjunction "waw," as in ﴿Qaf. By the Qur'an﴾ (Q. 50:1), although this requires a disagreement between the two conjoined elements in case, if the waw is taken as a conjunction, and the gathering of two oaths upon one thing, if the waw is taken as an oath particle. This is disliked, as al-Khalil and Sibawayh said, because the element conjoined to is in a position where the genitive occurs, so the conjunction is to the position (al-'atf 'ala al-mahall). The answer is understood to be of the same kind as what follows if the waw is for oath, or no estimation is needed, and one answer suffices, since there is no barrier to making one of the two oaths emphasize the other without conjunction. Or it is said: since both emphasize one thing, which is the answer, that is permitted. There is no convincing reason for the disliking. As for "If error has a father, then imitation is its father," the genitive is by implying the oath particle. Ibn Hisham's saying that this is a mistake, because that is specific according to the Basrans to the name of God, glory be to Him, and because there is no answer to the oath in Surat al-Baqara and similar, and it is not correct to make what follows an answer, and the lam has been omitted as in his saying:

By the Lord of the high heavens and their constellations,
and the earth and what is in it, what is decreed will come to pass.

Because that, despite its rarity, is restricted to the lengthening of the oath, is a mistake not hidden from a novice, since our school is Kufan, and following the Basran is not obligatory. Often one dispenses with the answer by what indicates it, and what is sworn to is the content of what follows, and this is a close indication. This is expressly stated in al-Tashil (Ibn Malik's work) and its commentaries. And the principle of lengthening is not binding; rather it is the most common, as Ibn Malik expressly stated.

Then whatever of these openings is single, like (Sad), or of the same weight as it, like (Ha Mim) in the pattern of Qabil, the i'rab can apply to it either verbally or by position, by being made quiescent as a quotation of its earlier state, and its i'rab is supposed. It is non-declinable for being a proper name and feminine. Whatever differs from these two, such as ﴿Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad﴾ (Q. 19:1), is quoted only and nothing else. Quotation of these names is permitted although they are specific to proper names transferred from sentences, like Ta'abbaṭa Sharran, for preserving their forms which indicate their transfer to being proper names. And in words which became names of themselves, like "daraba" as a past-tense verb, for preserving the homogeneity with the named thing, in indicating that they were not transferred from their original completely, because through their frequent use they are counted as settled, this state became as if it were the origin. So when they were made names, quoting them in that firm form was permitted, as an indication that there is in them a mark of attention to the origin, which is the separate letters spelled out. The purpose is awakening and the striking of the staff. Thus the permission of quotation is restricted to these names as names of the surahs; otherwise quotation is not permitted. So it is in the Noble Marginal Glosses of al-Sharifiyya. And the agreement of the grammarians that individual words are quoted after "min" and "ayy," the interrogative ones, and without them, as in their saying "da'na man tamratan" (leave aside who the two dates are), contradicts the claim of restriction which he related, as is not hidden. If they are left in their meanings, recited in a list, they are not inflected, for lack of a trigger and an operator. Likewise, if they are considered parts (of words), according to the correct view, or extra for separation, for example. Yes, if they are estimated as composed of these letters, they are in the place of nominative as explained above. If they are made the object of an oath, each word of them is in the accusative or genitive according to the two dialects in "by God, I will certainly do" (Allahi la-af'alanna). Is that whole combination like (Alif Lam Mim) and (Ha Mim), or is it for the alif and the ha as in the example "the pomegranate is sweet sour" (al-rummanu hulwun hamidun)? There is a difference, and the apparent is the first. Some permitted the nominative by beginning, with the predicate being an omitted oath phrase. Al-Radi's explicit statement that this is specific to when the subject is clearly an oath makes it not accepted. Some made the accusative in some specific cases, restricted to when no obstacle prevents it, as in ﴿Sad. By the Qur'an﴾ (Q. 38:1). Then the genitive is necessary because of the requirement of disagreement between the two conjoined elements, and the gathering of the two oaths then. There is in this what has preceded, so do not be heedless. Other views remain built upon views, which I do not think will be hidden from you, if you have comprehensive knowledge of what we have put before you. So reflect.

Regarding whether these openings are verses, there is a difference. The Kufans said: (Alif Lam Mim) is a verse wherever it occurs, and likewise (Alif Lam Mim Sad), (Ta Sin Mim), and their siblings, (Ta Ha), (Ya Sin), (Ha Mim) and its siblings, and (Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad) is a verse, and (Ha Mim) (Ayn Sin Qaf) are two verses. As for (Alif Lam Ra) and its five siblings, they are not verses. Likewise (Ta Sin) and (Sad), (Qaf), (Nun). The Basrans said: none of that is a verse. In al-Murshid it is said that the openings in all the surahs are verses according to the Kufans without distinction, but this is nothing, like the saying of some that (Alif Lam Mim) in Al 'Imran is not a verse.

[Page 105]

﴿Dhalika al-Kitab la rayba fihi hudan lil-muttaqin﴾ ("That is the Book; there is no doubt in it, a guidance for the God-conscious"). This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, a new sentence beginning a discourse), or it is connected to what precedes it. There are possibilities on which they have dwelt at length, but the Book of God, exalted is He, is to be interpreted in the best of interpretations, the furthest from artificial strain, and the most acceptable in the Arabic language. The demonstrative *dhalika* ("that") refers to the Book promised to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We will send down upon you a heavy word﴾, as al-Wahidi said. Or it refers to the Book as spoken through Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they used to seek victory against those who disbelieved﴾, the verse. This is supported by what is related from Ka'b: "Upon you is the Qur'an, for it is the understanding of intellect, the light of wisdom, the springs of knowledge, and the most recent of books in its covenant with God." He also said in the Torah: "O Muhammad, I shall send down to you a new Torah, by which I shall open blind eyes, deaf ears, and veiled hearts," as stated by more than one scholar. Or the reference is to what is before us. The demonstrative with *dhalika* serves to magnify, and the placement of a rank-distance (*bu'd rutbi*) in the position of a literal distance is as in His saying: ﴿That is the one about whom you blamed me﴾, as chosen by al-Sakkaki in *al-Miftah* (Miftah al-Ulum). Or, because it descended from the station of lordship and came into our presence, it became distant; and whoever gives something to another, or delivers it to him, or considers its arrival, refers to it with that (distant demonstrative), because by its separation from its source it is distant, or it is in the status of distance. It has been said: "Everything that is not in your hands is distant."

Since this meaning could not be achieved in His saying: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down﴾, because that refers to what is with Him, glorified is He, it did not use that (distant form) despite the distance of rank. This mention ("this") has the letters of disjunction at the beginning (in the first verse), which are used to split letters, and this applies only in our case; and their absence in the second verse. Therefore the two situations differed and the two demonstratives diverged, as al-Suhayli said. This is, for some people, a verification; and it guides you to what is in it. In my view there is a subtle consideration. Some scholars went further and explained the distance as follows: the Qur'an is an utterance, and it belongs to the category of flowing accidents that are not fixed; so whatever of it exists perishes and vanishes, becomes past, and is hidden from the senses; and what is like that is in the status of the distant. It was also said: the forms of distant and near may alternate, as in His saying, exalted is He, concerning the story of Jesus, peace be upon him: ﴿That We recite to you﴾, then He said, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, this is the true narrative﴾, and it has parallels in the noble Book. Al-Jurjani related this from a group, and they recited:

*I say to him while the spear bends its shaft: "Be light; indeed I am that."*

This is not definitive, since it is possible that the intended meaning is: "Indeed I am that one about whom you were told and heard." The statement of Imam al-Razi, that *dhalika* is for the distant by custom and not by linguistic convention, so applying it here according to linguistic convention rather than customary usage, contradicts what we understand from the books of the masters of Arabic grammar. Above every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing. As for the claim that the reference is to the Torah and the Gospel, as related from Ikrimah: if a sound hadith has been transmitted about it, we accept it and strain to accommodate it; otherwise we cast it aside. Not every possibility is appropriate. The strangest view we have seen regarding the reference is that it refers to the Straight Path in al-Fatihah, as if when they asked for guidance to it, it was said to them: "That is the path you asked to be guided to; it is the Book." If you accept this, the connection of Surat al-Baqarah with Surat al-Hamd will be clear in the most complete manner, and the reference will be to what has been previously mentioned. What is pleasing to hear is that it refers to the Qur'an. The reason for the distance is what the author of *al-Miftah* mentioned, and a light of nearness shines upon it. The criterion for demonstrative nouns is the sensory indication, which can only be connected to a perceived, witnessed object. If they are used to refer to what cannot be perceived by the senses, such as: ﴿That is God, your Lord﴾, or to a sensible object not witnessed, such as: "that Paradise," then this is making it as if witnessed, and treating the intellectual indication as the sensory one, as in al-Radi. So the indication here is not free of subtlety. As for the statement of some: "When the demonstrative noun is accompanied by a description, it need not be sensory," and they (the people) are sensory, and the Book is like the writing, the verbal noun of *kataba*; it is used for the written thing, as *libas* (clothing) means the worn thing. Writing, as al-Raghib said, is joining one piece of leather to another by sewing; in common usage it is joining letters to one another. The essence of writing (*kitaba*) is ordering by script, and it may also be said of what is joined by utterance. Therefore each is used metaphorically for the other. That is why it is called "the Book of God," even though it is not a book (in the physical sense). The word *kitab* here is either kept as a verbal noun, and that which is written is named by it as an intensification; or it means the object, and it is applied to the arranged (speech) as an expression before its letters are arranged in the script of which it is composed, naming it by what it will become, with suitable connection. As for the statement of the Imam: that the derivation of *kitab* is from *katabtu al-shay'* when you gather it, and the battalion (*katibah*) was named for its gathering, so the Book was named *kitab* because it is like a battalion against armies of doubts, or because all knowledge is gathered in it, or because God imposed obligations on creation through it, it is an eclectic statement whose flaws are not hidden. The word *kitab*, like the Qur'an, is applied to the whole collection sent down upon the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, and to a commonly known portion of it, and to the whole and the part. Here one does not need what has been said to resolve the well-known fallacy of the "deaf root" (*al-jidhr al-asamm*), and I see no harm in it if you need it. The definite article in *al-kitab* is for the reality (*lil-haqiqah*), like it in "you are the man." The meaning is: that is the perfect Book, worthy of being specifically named "the Book," due to its extreme superiority over the rest of its kind in possessing the perfections of the genus, so that it is as if the other heavenly books were excluded from it in comparison. Ibn Usfur said: every *lam* that comes after the demonstrative noun, or *ayyu* in address, or *idha* of sudden occurrence, is for the mental presence of the referent (*lil-'ahd al-huduri*). It is read: "The sending down of the Book." *Al-Rayb* is doubt. Its origin is the verbal noun of *rabani al-shay'*, when the thing causes unease (*al-ribah*) in you; *ribah* is restlessness of the soul. From it comes "the vicissitudes of time" (*rayb al-zaman*) for its calamities. So it is a term transferred from restlessness to something resembling it. It is also used for what stirs in the heart of the causes of anger. The statement of Imam al-Razi, that these two may return to the meaning of doubt, because what is feared from events is probable and therefore like what is doubted, and likewise what stirs in the heart, since it is not certain, and not certain of its rejection, so that *al-manun* (fate) is from *rayb*, or something doubted, and what stirs in the heart of the causes of anger against the disbelievers, for example, is something about which there is no doubt, or about which there is doubt. Abu Zayd distinguished between *rabani* and *arabani*: one says, "a matter has troubled me (*rabani min fulan amr*)" when you are certain of it with doubt, and when you think ill of it without being certain, you say "*arabani*." On this is the verse of Bashshar:

*Your brother, if you doubt him, says, "He only stirred suspicion,"*
*and if you rebuke him, his side softens.*

Some distinguish between *rayb* and *shakk* (doubt) in that *rayb* is doubt accompanied by suspicion. Al-Raghib said: *shakk* is the soul standing between two opposites, in such a way that neither is preferred over the other by any sign; *mirya* is hesitation regarding the two opposites; seeking a sign is from *maraa al-darra*, that is, wiping the udder to make it yield milk; and *rayb* is to imagine something and then to have it revealed as other than what was imagined. Al-Jawli said: *shakk* is said of what both beliefs are equal in, or are not equal, but neither has reached the level of manifest clarity on which affairs are built; and *rayb* is for what has not reached the degree of certainty, even if it appears in some manner of appearance. For this reason ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾ is apt here, to indicate that no *rayb* arises in it, let alone *shakk*. God, glorified is He, negated *rayb* from it despite the multitude of the doubters (may God not increase them), in the sense that it is of such exalted rank and radiant proof that no intelligent person will doubt, after reflection, that it is a revelation from God, exalted is He. It does not mean that no one doubts it at all so that it would be invalid, requiring a reinterpretation that the existence of doubt among some is treated as nonexistence because of what removes it. It has also been said: it is elliptical, as if He said: "there is no cause of doubt in it," because the causes that produce doubt in speech are obscurity, complication, contradiction, and baseless claims without proof, and all of this is absent from the Book of God, exalted is He. It has been said: its meaning is a prohibition, though its wording is a statement, meaning: "do not doubt it," in the manner of ﴿So there shall be no obscenity, nor wickedness﴾. It has been said: its meaning is "there is no doubt in it for the God-conscious," so the adverbial phrase is a description, and *lil-muttaqin* is the predicate; and *huda* is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the pronoun in the genitive, meaning: there is no doubt present in it for the God-conscious while it is guiding; this is a necessary circumstance, so it conveys the negation of doubt at all times and in all conditions, and the restriction serves as evidence for the negation of doubt. The *la* is for negating the attribution of the predicate to the subject, not for negating the restriction of the subject, so it does not turn toward it, lest the meaning be disrupted. Yet this is a view of little benefit, and the prevailing use of the adverbial phrase after this *la* is that it is a predicate. He, glorified is He, did not say "*la fihi rayb*" (there is in it no doubt) in the manner of ﴿in them there is no intoxication﴾, because fronting indicates something that distances from the intended meaning, namely that another book in which there is doubt exists. It is as in the verse where the intent was to praise the wine of Paradise over the wines of this world, that it does not confuse the intellects as they do, so there is no defect in it as there is in others; so said al-Zamakhshari. Some did not distinguish between "there is no man in the house" and "there is no man in the house," to the point that Abu Hayyan denied that fronting the predicate here implies exclusivity; and this is not worth considering. Sulaym Abu al-Sha'tha' read: *la raybun fihi* with *raf'* (nominative), and this, because it is the opposite of *rayb fihi*, is possibly an affirmation of an instance, and its negation conveys its absence, so it does not imply totality, as in the well-known reading. For this reason one may say: "there is no man in the house, but two men," but not: "there is no man in it, but two men." So the *la* is for generality of negation, not for negation of generality. Stopping at *fihi* is the well-known practice, and on it the Book itself is guidance; this has been repeated in the revelation. From Nafi' and 'Asim, stopping is at ﴿la rayb﴾; and there is no doubt about deleting the predicate. Al-Zajjaj went to making ﴿la rayb﴾ mean "truly," so stopping on it is complete, but it is still lesser than the first. Ibn Kathir read *fihi* with the *ya* joined to the *ha* in pronunciation, and likewise every pronoun *ha* preceded by a silent *ya*; if a silent letter other than *ya* precedes it, he joins it with *waw*. Hafs agreed with him in ﴿fihi muhanan﴾ and ﴿mulaqihi﴾ and ﴿sa-usliihi﴾. The rest do not lengthen it, and when the letter before the *ha* is vowelled, they lengthen it. Al-Zuhri and Ibn Jundub read the *ha* of pronominal suffixes with *damma* throughout the Qur'an, according to the original form. *Al-huda* in origin is the verbal noun of *hada*, or a substitute for the verbal noun; both are in Sibawayh's speech. Few verbal nouns come in this pattern, such as *al-tuqa*, *al-sura*, and *al-buka* in one dialect, with shortened vowel, and *luqan*, as al-Shatibi said, and he recited:

*They claimed that your meeting is forbearance, but I added nothing,*
*by the praise of Him who gave you forbearance nor intellect.*

[Page 106]

The intended meaning of "guidance" (hudan) here is the active participle, in one of the familiar senses of such nouns. It is feminine according to Ibn 'Atiyyah, and masculine according to al-Lihyani. The Banu Asad use it as feminine, as al-Farra' stated. It is therefore like "hidayah" (guidance, a verbal noun), whose meaning has already been explained. In al-Kashshaf, guidance is "the indication that leads to the desired goal." Three arguments are cited for this definition.

The first is that its opposite is misguidance, as in His words: ﴿Surely we are either on guidance or in manifest error﴾. Misguidance means failure and not reaching the desired goal. If reaching the goal were not part of the concept of guidance, the two would not be opposites, since they could coexist.

The second is that one says "mahdiyy" (guided) as a term of praise, like "muhtadi" (one who is guided). Someone who receives indication without being guided is not called this. It is therefore known that arrival (at the goal) is included in its concept.

The third is that "ihtada" (he was guided) is the intransitive form (mutawa'ah) of "hada" (he guided), and an intransitive form cannot have a meaning contrary to its root. Consider, for example, "kasarahu fa-inkasara" (he broke it, so it broke).

There is discussion on this. Firstly, what is mentioned in opposition to misguidance is the intransitive guidance, in the sense of "being guided," used either metaphorically or as a homonym. Our discussion concerns the transitive form, whose opposite is "idlal" (causing to go astray), so the argument does not apply. It may be interpreted as indication of something that does not lead to the goal and does not make one astray. Moreover, if guidance is explained as indication of whatever has the nature of leading to the goal, whether it actually leads or not, and misguidance, as its contrary by way of contradiction (ta-qabul al-ijab wa-al-salb), is explained as the absence of that unrestricted indication, then the absence of arrival would follow. This is because the negation of unrestricted indication entails the negation of restricted indication, since negation of the more general entails negation of the more specific. Hence there is nothing in this opposition that favours the claim.

Secondly, we do not accept that misguidance means failure. Rather, it is deviation from the path that leads to the goal. Guidance is then indication of the path that leads. It is true that failure to reach the goal is necessary for misguidance, but the necessary condition may be more general.

Thirdly, the fact that the participle "mahdiyy" is used only of the guided does not require that arrival be included in the concept of guidance, since a participle may become specialised in one individual of the concept from which it is derived.

Fourthly, we do not accept that "ihtada" is the intransitive form of "hada." Rather, it is of the type "amarahu fa-ta'mara" (he ordered him, so he obeyed), where a second act follows that differs from the first. The meaning of "hadahu fa-ihtada" is that he indicated to him the path that leads and he took it. The proof is that one says "hadahu fa-lam yahtadi" (he guided him, but he was not guided). Moreover, a group of respected scholars held that the existence of the verb does not necessarily entail the existence of its intransitive form in every case. In al-Mukhtar it is stated: "It is not necessary for the intransitive form to agree with its root, though it is necessary in other cases." This is supported by His words: ﴿And We send not the signs except as a warning﴾ together with His words: ﴿And We warn them, but it only increases them in transgression﴾. Here warning occurred without fear. One does not say "kasartuhu fa-ma inkasara" (I broke it, but it did not break). The difference between the two is explained in detail in 'Arus al-Afrah.

Fifthly, what he mentioned is opposed by the case where guidance exists but there is no arrival at the goal. Part of this has already been mentioned. For this reason, scholars differ on whether the word is literal (haqiqah) in unrestricted indication and metaphorical (majaz) in other senses, or the reverse, or whether it is a homonym (mushtarak) between them, or whether it is coined for a common shared quality. Each view has been held by a group.

It has been said that what is mentioned in the words of the Ash'ariyyah is that their preferred view is what was mentioned in al-Kashshaf, while among the Mu'tazilah it is what we have mentioned. The well-known view is the reverse. The reconciliation is that the statement of the Ash'ariyyah concerns the legal (shar'i) meaning, while the well-known view is based on the linguistic or customary meaning. However, this is undermined by the fact that the author of al-Kashshaf, despite his rigid adherence to Mu'tazilism, chose what he chose, and the apparent meaning in the Qur'an is the legal meaning. Therefore, for the one who seeks success, the more apparent reconciliation is the reverse of this. The truth according to the People of Truth is that guidance is a homonym between the two meanings mentioned and the meaning of not causing destruction. By this, much of the dispute and controversy is resolved.

"Al-muttaqin" (the God-fearing) is the plural of "muttaqin," the active participle of "waqahu, fa-ittaqa" (he protected him, so he guarded himself). Its first radical is waw, not ta'. Wiqayah (protection) linguistically means safeguarding in general. Legally it means a person safeguarding himself from what harms him in the Hereafter. The levels are many, corresponding to the many levels of harm. The first is guarding against shirk (associating partners with God). The second is guarding against major sins, among which is persisting in minor sins. The third is what is indicated by what al-Tirmidhi related from him (ﷺ): "A servant does not reach the level of being among the God-fearing until he leaves what is not harmful for fear of what is harmful." At this level, leaving minor sins is required. Hence it has been said:

Leave sins, both great and small, for that is taqwa (God-consciousness).
Act like one who walks over thorny ground, watchful of every step.
Do not belittle any small sin, for mountains are made of pebbles.

At this level, the expressions of the great scholars differ. It has been said: taqwa is that God does not see you where He has forbidden you, and does not miss you where He has commanded you. It has been said: detachment from power and strength. It has been said: purification from everything that distracts the heart from the Truth. In this field the spirits of lovers have raced, and the bodies of travellers have perished, until one of them said:

If any thought of other than You were to cross my mind even by inadvertence, I would judge myself an apostate.

The guidance of the Clear Book includes all the people of these levels together. If by its being guidance for the God-fearing is meant its guiding them to attain the first level, then the meaning of "the God-fearing" is those approaching it, metaphorically, since attaining what is already attained is impossible. This is preferred over the explicit expression for brevity, and the opening of the noble surah with mention of His friends and the exaltation of their rank is consistent with this. The approach is considered relative to the time of the attribution of guidance, so it does not contradict the good sequence with "those who believe," because that is, as has been said, relative to the time of establishing that attribution, as one says: "He was killed as a slain man," "He was buried in such a place." Perhaps the estimated sense is: "they are those who..." in answer to "who are the God-fearing?" Taking the whole to be approaching (mushārafah) is rejected by the context.

It may be said that "al-muttaqin" is a metaphor by approach, and the qualifier is a reinforcement without approach, which is not metaphorical, as is usual in such cases. Or we say it is in the manner of our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), the intercessor on the Day of Gathering, so there is no difficulty.

If by it is meant guiding them to attain one of the last two levels, then if by "the God-fearing" are meant the people of the first level, the literal sense is fixed. If by them are meant the people of one of the last two levels, the metaphor is fixed, because arrival at them is achieved only through His guidance that raises them in rank. The same applies to the situation between the second and third levels. If guidance is meant as guiding to attain the third level, then if by "the God-fearing" are meant the people of the second level, the literal sense is fixed. If by them are meant the people of the third level, the metaphor is fixed. The word "guidance" is literal in all these cases.

As for if by its being guidance for them is meant establishing them in what they are upon and guiding them to increase in it, on condition that the concept of increase is included in the meaning used, then it is necessarily metaphorical. The word "the God-fearing" is literal in every case. This is what Our Master, the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, verified. From this it is known that the objection is refuted, which said: if guidance is explained as indication that leads, then "guidance for the God-fearing" requires that it indicate the attainment of what is attained, as if it were said: "an indication that leads to the sought goal for those who have arrived at it." And if guidance is explained as indication of what leads, there is another problem, since the one who is guided to his goal would have his indication of what leads him to it be pointless. The refutation is clear. However, some verifiers have concluded that it is more apparent that there is no need for metaphor here. When it is said: "Weapons are protection for the one who seeks protection, and wealth is independence for the independent," meaning the cause of his independence and protection, it does not follow that the weapon and the wealth are two causes of protection and independence that are new and other than what they are. Therefore what we are dealing with does not need interpretation and is not metaphor at all, since the God-fearing is truly guided by this guidance. Scholars of Arabic grammar and the principles of jurisprudence have differed on whether the derived descriptive (al-wasf al-mushtaqq) is literal for the present time or for the future, and whether the intended time is that of the attribution or of the speaking without intermediary between them. What the verifiers hold is that it refers to the time of attribution. Al-Subki and al-Kirmani held that "Whoever kills a slain man, then he has his spoils" is literal, and they judged in error the one who said it is metaphorical. It cannot be said that there is no benefit in affirming killing to one who was killed by it, because the eloquent speaker, through the aid of the intellectual indication, intends that the killing attributed to him was issued by this slayer and not by others. It is as if it were said: no one else shared in it, so his spoils belong to him and not to another. From here, in our case, the meaning has been made: there is no guidance for the God-fearing except by the Book of God, Most High, whose light of guidance shines and whose proof of indication gleams. When a judgement is attached to a demonstrative noun described in a way, such as "I pressed this vinegar," for example, there are in reality two attachments: the attachment of the earlier judgement to the very thing indicated, and the attachment of the indication. What is considered is the time of the indication, not the time of the earlier judgement. So if it is correct to apply the name "vinegar" to the thing indicated and for it to be characterised by vinegarness at the time of the indication, regardless of the earlier judgement, it is literal; otherwise, it is metaphorical. Understand and reflect.

Then the presence in it of what is concise (mujmal) and ambiguous (mutashabih) does not detract from its being guidance, because being guidance does not require that its guidance be by consideration of every part of it. It is permissible that it contain what is a trial for people of intellect among the learned, by things that minds and understandings cannot reach, or because that cannot be separated from explaining its intended meaning, as the Shafi'is held. So after its clarification, it is guidance. That its guidance depends on something does not harm it, just as it depends in one view on prior faith in God, Most High, and His Messenger (ﷺ). The Imam has stated that whatever the validity of the Qur'an as proof depends on, the Qur'an cannot be guidance in that matter, such as knowledge of God's essence and attributes and knowledge of prophethood, lest circularity (dawr) follow. Except that it may be guidance in confirming what is in the intellects and in relying upon it. Some have held that the Qur'an in itself is guidance in everything, even knowledge of God, Most High, for one who reflects on its rational evidence and certain proofs, as the apparent sense of His words suggests: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down, a guidance for mankind﴾. The restriction to the God-fearing here, on our interpretation of guidance, is for praise of them, to make clear that they are the ones who were guided and benefited from it, as He, Most High, said: ﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾, although His warning (ﷺ) is general, and others are not included. ﴿And when you recite the Qur'an, We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter a hidden barrier﴾. ﴿And it increases the wrongdoers only in loss﴾. As for the view that the estimated meaning is "guidance for the God-fearing and the disbelievers," and that it was omitted because "the God-fearing" indicates it, in the manner of ﴿garments that protect you from heat﴾, this is not worth considering.

This is so, and the coherence in these sentences and verses is not hidden. "Alif-Lam-Mim" indicated what it indicated. "That is the Book" affirmed part of its indication, that it is the perfect Book, such that no other may rightly be called a book in its genre, that is, the domain of challenge and guidance. "There is no doubt in it" is like an emphasis on one of the two pillars. "A guidance for the God-fearing" is like an emphasis on the other pillar.

Its summary: it is the one deserving to be challenged with, for the perfection of its composition in the domain of eloquence (balagha), its perfection in itself, and in what its purpose is. It has also been said, on the reading of it as a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as if it were asked: "What is the matter with it that it became miraculous?" So it was answered: "It is perfect, reaching the utmost perfection in wording and meaning," and this is the meaning of ﴿That is the Book﴾. Then it was asked about what the restriction (ikhtisas) implies, by it being the perfect Book, so it was answered: "No doubt hovers around it." Then, when it was demanded to be shown the proof for that, it argued by its being ﴿guidance for those who are mindful of God﴾, because of the evident fact that it includes the religious and worldly benefits and the interests of this life and the next, such that no one denies it except one who obstinately opposes himself and contradicts his reason and his senses. It may also be said: miraculousness entails the utmost perfection, and the utmost perfection of eloquent speech lies in its remoteness from doubt and suspicion, owing to the manifestness of its truth, and that necessarily calls for guiding and directing (to it). If the unity of the meanings is considered in terms of their outcome, the second is a confirmation of the first, and therefore the conjunction is omitted. If, however, it is considered that the first necessitates what follows it, since it is necessarily entailed after sincere reflection, then the first (is related to the second) by its entailing what comes after it, and its being in its strength makes it, relative to it, in the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because of the connection and the necessary relation between them. Its pattern is thus the pattern of ﴿her beauty﴾ in "the slave-girl pleased me, her beauty," and the conjunction is omitted at that point because of the strong connection between these sentences. In it there are also also refined subtleties and surpassing excellences, the greatness of whose worth is not hidden from one who has reflected on what we have mentioned.

﴿Those who believe in the unseen, establish the prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them﴾ is a description of the God-conscious (al-muttaqun) mentioned before it. If by taqwa (God-consciousness) is meant its first level, the description is restrictive (mukhassisa). If its second level is meant, it is revelatory (kashifa). If its third level is meant, it is laudatory (madiha).

In Sharh al-Miftah al-Sharifi: "Taking the muttaqi in its sharia meaning, namely one who performs the obligations and abstains from the sins, then if the addressee is ignorant of that meaning the description is revelatory, and if he is aware of it, the description is laudatory. If it is taken in a meaning close to its linguistic sense, the description is restrictive." It is affirmed that the relative clause is disjoined (mafsul), with the intent of informing about it with what follows, affirming it of what precedes. Even if it is understood implicitly, it is as if it were said explicitly, though it is not construed as such. This is sufficient for the connection. The resumption (istinaf) is either grammatical (nahwi) or explanatory (bayani), as if it were said: "What is the case with the God-conscious that they have been singled out for this guidance?" The pause on "al-muttaqin" is complete according to this view, and good according to the first view.

Iman (faith) in the linguistic sense is tasdiq (affirmation), that is, submitting to the judgment of the informant, accepting it, and deeming it true. It is a form (if'al) from amn (security), as if the basic meaning of "he believed in him" is that he made him secure from denial and opposition. It takes the preposition lam, as in the Almighty's saying: ﴿Shall we believe you when the lowest have followed you?﴾ (26:111), and the preposition ba', as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Faith is that you believe in God..." the hadith. They said: the first is according to its implication of the meaning of submission (idh'an), and the second according to its implication of the meaning of acknowledgment (i'tiraf), indicating that affirmation is not considered unless it is accompanied by acknowledgment.

It is sometimes used in the meaning of trust (wuthuq), in that the one who trusts becomes one who has security, and this is also a customary literal meaning, as in al-Asas. The apparent wording of al-Kashshaf indicates its figurative usage.

In the sharia, it is affirmation of what is known by necessity to have been brought by the Prophet (ﷺ): in detail regarding what is known in detail, and in summary regarding what is known in summary. This is the view of the majority of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun). However, they differed as to whether the criterion for the otherworldly rulings is merely this meaning, or together with verbal confession (iqrar). Al-Ash'ari and his followers held that merely this meaning is sufficient, because it is the intended meaning, and confession is only so that its existence may be known, since it is an inner matter, and rulings apply to it. So whoever affirms in his heart, and abandons confession while being able to do it, is a believer in the sharia between himself and God Most High, and his abode is Paradise.

But Ibn al-Humam mentioned that the adherents of this view agreed that it is necessary to believe that whenever confession is demanded of him, he will perform it. If he is asked and does not confess, then it is disbelief of obstinacy (kufr 'inad).

Our Imam Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, and most of his followers, held that confession, and what is in its ruling like the sign of a mute, is indispensable. So the affirmer mentioned does not become a believer with a faith that entails the otherworldly rulings, like one who prays out of showing off, for his prayer does not benefit him. Perhaps this is because God Most High condemned the obstinate more than He condemned the ignorant who fall short. The opponent may hold that the condemnation is for verbal denial, and there is no doubt that it is a sign of denial, or for inner denial, which is denial itself. The outcome of this is the denial of the occurrence of affirmation in the obstinate, for it is the opposite of denial. What occurs to him is only ma'rifa (knowledge), which is the opposite of ignorance and unawareness. They agreed that this knowledge lies outside linguistic affirmation, which is what is considered in faith.

Yes, they differed as to whether it is included in conception (tasawwur) or in logical affirmation (tasdiq mantiqi). Al-Allama al-Thani held the former, and that it is permissible for the image resulting from a complete declarative relation to be a conception, and that logical affirmation is itself linguistic affirmation. Therefore their leader explained it in Persian books as (bakr wedan), and in Arabic as what is contrary to denial and rejection, and this is exactly the linguistic meaning. This is supported by what al-Sayyid al-Sanad reported in the margin of the commentary on al-Talkhis: that the logician only clarifies what is in custom and language. However, it is objected that the meaning expressed as (bakr widin) is a certainty, and al-Allama stated this in al-Maqasid. Therefore, in the matter of faith, affirmation reaching the degree of firm conviction and submission suffices, although logical affirmation by agreement encompasses the conjectural. For they divide knowledge in the more general sense into conception and affirmation, a division that is exhaustive, as a means of demonstrating the need for logic with all its parts, among which is dialectical syllogism composed of the well-known and the accepted, and among which is rhetorical syllogism composed of the probable, and poetic syllogism composed of imaginings. So if logical affirmation were not general, the need for these parts would not be established, and this is evident.

Sadr al-Shari'a held the latter view, for the image resulting from a complete declarative relation is certainly an affirmation. If it is acquired with intention and choice in such a way that it entails submission and acceptance, then it is a linguistic affirmation. If it is not so, like one whose gaze falls on something and he knows that it is a wall, for example, then it is certain knowledge, and not a linguistic affirmation. So linguistic affirmation according to him is more specific than logical affirmation.

The Karramiyya held that faith in the sharia is merely the tongue's confession of the two testimonies (shahadatayn) and nothing else. The Kharijites, al-'Allaf, and 'Abd al-Jabbar of the Mu'tazila held that every act of obedience is faith, whether obligatory or supererogatory. Al-Jubba'i and his son and most of the Mu'tazila of Basra held that it is the obligatory acts of obedience only, not the supererogatory among them. Al-Qalanisi of the People of the Sunna, and al-Najjar of the Mu'tazila, and this is the view of most of the people of hadith, held that it is knowledge in the heart, confession with the tongue, and action with the limbs.

It was said: the secret of this disagreement is the disagreement over whether the responsible agent is the spirit alone, or the body alone, or both together. The truth is that the source of every view is an evidence that prompted its holder to adopt it. The clearest of these views is that it is affirmation. Therefore the chief of the believers, 'Ali, may God ennoble his face, said: "Faith is knowledge, knowledge is submission, and submission is affirmation."

This view is supported by the saying of the Most High: ﴿Those, He has written faith in their hearts﴾ (58:22), and His saying: ﴿Faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ (49:14), and His saying: ﴿while his heart is at rest with faith﴾ (16:106), and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O God, make my heart firm upon Your religion." In these and countless similar texts, He attributed it to the heart, which indicates that it is an act of the heart, and it is nothing other than affirmation. For it has not been explained in the sharia with any other meaning, so there is no transfer of meaning (naql). Otherwise, the address with faith would be an address with what is not understood. Also, because it contradicts the original sense, so one does not turn to it without evidence. The possibility that the texts intend linguistic faith, which has the heart as its locus, and not sharia faith, so that confession or something else might be part of its meaning, is answered by the fact that faith is among the sharia-transferred terms according to the particular object (mutaʿallaq). Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ), may God exalt him and grant him peace, clarified its object rather than its meaning, saying: "That you believe in God and His angels..." the hadith.

So it is figurative in the linguistic meaning in the speech of the Lawgiver, and the basic rule in usage is that it is literal. Also, the conjunction of actions with faith occurs, as in the saying of the Most High: ﴿Indeed those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ (18:107), and a part is not conjoined to its whole.
