The descent of the angels and the Spirit on one of the two views is by way of interpreting it as exit, for a rhetorical consideration. Restricting it to supererogatory acts, on the basis of their being excluded, is contrary to the apparent meaning, and the apparent meaning suffices as proof.

Also, faith was made a condition for the validity of actions, as in the saying of the Most High: ﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer﴾ (20:112), together with the certainty that the conditioned does not enter into the condition, because it is impossible to make a thing a condition for itself, since a part of a condition is a condition.

Also, faith was affirmed of one who abandons some actions, as in the saying of the Most High: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight﴾ (49:9), even though a thing is not realized without its pillar. Also, what we have mentioned is closer to the original rule, for there is no difference between them except by consideration of the particular object, as is not hidden.

The opponent has raised several objections as reductio. The first: if faith were the expression of affirmation, it would not differ, whereas the faith of the Messenger (ﷺ) is not similar to the faith of the common people, nor even of the elite. The second: transgression (fusuq) contradicts faith and does not coexist with it, by the explicit text: ﴿But God has made faith beloved to you and adorned it in your hearts, and made disbelief and transgression hateful to you﴾ (49:7). Had it meant affirmation, its coexistence with it would not be impossible. The third: committing a major sin is among what is incompatible with it, by the saying of the Most High: ﴿And He is ever merciful to the believers﴾ (33:43), together with His saying concerning the offender: ﴿Let not pity for them overtake you﴾ (24:2). Had it meant affirmation, it would not be incompatible. The fourth: the believer is not disgraced, by the saying of the Most High: ﴿The day God will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believe with him﴾ (66:8). And the Most High said concerning highway robbers: ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾ (5:33). So they are not believers, although they affirm. The fifth: one who is able to perform the Hajj and abandons it without excuse is a disbeliever, by the saying of the Most High: ﴿And due to God from the people is the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way to it. And whoever disbelieves, indeed God is free of need from the worlds﴾ (3:97), although he affirms. The sixth: one who does not rule by what God has revealed is an affirmer, although he is a disbeliever by the explicit text: ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ (5:44). The seventh: the adulterer is likewise, by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), may God exalt him and grant him peace: "The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer," and likewise one who deliberately abandons the prayer without excuse, and the like. The eighth: one who belittles a prophet, for example, is an affirmer although he is a disbeliever by consensus. The ninth: performing the obligations is the religion, by the saying of the Most High: ﴿And they were not commanded except to worship God, sincere to Him in religion, inclining to truth, and to establish prayer and give zakat; and that is the upright religion﴾ (98:5). And religion is Islam, by the saying of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, the religion with God is Islam﴾ (3:19). And Islam is faith, for if it were other than it, it would not be accepted from one who seeks it, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ (3:85). The tenth: if it were affirmation, the responsible agent would not be described by it in the true sense except at the time of its occurrence from him, as in all other acts. Yet the sleeper and the heedless are described by it by consensus, although affirmation does not remain in them. The eleventh: it would follow that one who affirms the divinity of other than God, glorified is He, is a believer, and this is contrary to consensus. The twelfth: God Most High described some of the believers in Him, Mighty and Majestic, as associators, saying: ﴿And most of them do not believe in God except that they are associators﴾ (12:106). Had it been affirmation, its coexistence with association would be impossible.

We grant that it is affirmation, but what prevents it from being verbal affirmation, as the Karramiyya said? How, when the people of language understand from affirmation nothing but verbal affirmation?

The first objection is answered by saying that affirmation is of one kind. Even if we grant that there is no increase or decrease in it, whether from the Prophet or from one of us, it is still not impossible that there be variation between the two faiths, due to the intervening of acts and strength between the successive instances of renewed faith, and the paucity or abundance of their intervening, or due to the arising of doubts and skeptical objections, or their absence. And to the Most Perfect of the Perfect Prophet, may God exalt him and grant him peace.

And for the wasp and the falcon alike, at the time of flight, there are wings and beating,
but between what the falcon catches and what the wasp catches, there is a difference.

As for the second, the verse contains nothing indicating that transgression does not coexist with faith. For if it were said: "He made knowledge beloved to you and made hateful to you..."

[p. 113]

[Page 113 continues]

...the verb *fusuq* (wickedness) does not indicate a contradiction between knowledge and wickedness. That *kufr* (disbelief) is the opposite of *iman* (faith) is not derived from the verse itself, but from outside it. Even if we grant that the verse indicates what you have mentioned, it is opposed by what indicates the opposite, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing﴾, for this indicates that wrongdoing can coexist with faith in some cases.

As for the third objection, we do not grant that committing a major sin contradicts faith. ﴿And let not compassion for them take hold of you in the religion of Allah﴾ means: let not pity move you to drop the limits (*hudud*) of Allah, exalted is He, once they have become obligatory.

As for the fourth objection, what was cited of the two verses contains no proof, because the verse negating disgrace only negates it in the Hereafter for the believers in general, or for the Companions of the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. The verse of the thief indicates disgrace in this world. Contradicting disgrace on the Day of Resurrection with faith does not require contradicting it with faith in this world.

As for the fifth objection, we do not grant that one who abandons the Hajj without an excuse is a disbeliever. ﴿And whoever disbelieves﴾ is the start of a new sentence, or what is meant is one who does not affirm the rites of the Hajj and denies them, and affirmation is not conceivable alongside that.

As for the sixth objection, the meaning of ﴿whoever does not judge﴾ in the verse is: whoever does not affirm, or whoever does not judge by anything that Allah has sent down, or what is meant by it is the Torah, by the indication of the preceding context.

As for the seventh objection, it is possible to say: the meaning of "the adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer" is: safe from the punishment of Allah, i.e., if he commits it, God forbid, let him fear His punishment, glorified and exalted is He, and not feel secure from His plan. Or what is meant is: he does not commit adultery while considering it lawful, while being a believer. Or: he does not commit it while he is upon the attributes of the believer, namely avoiding what is forbidden. This interpretation is preferable to contradicting the linguistic conventions, because it is more common than them, and the same applies to the similar cases.

As for the eighth objection, we do not deny that major sins can coexist with faith by reason, but the community (*ummah*) is in consensus on the disbelief of one who treats it lightly, so we know, by revealed evidence, the absence of affirmation when contempt is present, for example.

The combination of acting by the linguistic convention and the consensus of the community on the declaration of disbelief is preferable to nullifying one of them.

As for the ninth objection, the verse has distinguished between religion and performing the obligations by the conjunction (*ʿatf*), and this, apparently, is evidence of difference. Even if we grant that religion is performing the obligations, and that religion is Islam, we do not grant that Islam is faith. What is meant by "other than Islam" in the verse is not what is different from it in concept; otherwise it would follow that prayer and zakat, for example, would not be accepted. Rather, what is meant is what is different from it in reference, so it is possible that Islam is more general. This is like when you say: "Whoever seeks other than the sacred knowledge (*al-ʿilm al-shariʿi*) has erred." You do not judge the one who seeks speech as having erred. It is evident that censuring the less general does not necessitate censuring the more specific. Your saying "other than animal" is blameworthy, but that does not necessitate that the human is blameworthy.

As for the tenth objection, it is a shared imposition. Whatever your answer is, it is our answer, with this addition: we say that affirmation remains in the heart during sleep and heedlessness, and what is absent is its occurrence (its coming into being), and sleep is opposed to the initial perception of things, not to the continuation of the perception that occurred while awake. Even if we grant that, the Lawgiver has made the established state, which nothing opposed to it has befallen, as if it were continuing, so that the believer is the name of one who believed at present or in the past, and nothing befell him that is a sign of denial.

As for the eleventh objection, the non-naming of one who affirms the divinity of other than Allah as a believer is only because of the specificity of the object of faith in the Sacred Law. Calling him a believer is valid according to the linguistic convention, but not valid according to the legal usage.

As for the twelfth objection, faith is the opposite of shirk by consensus, and what they mentioned is binding on every school. We say: faith there is linguistic, because in the legal sense, affirmation of everything known to have been brought by him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is required, as has preceded. So the polytheist who affirms only some things is not a believer except in the linguistic sense and not the legal one, because he has violated monotheism (*tawhid*), and the verse points to this.

Their saying, "The people of language do not understand..." etc., is a mere claim that proof does not support. Yes, there is no doubt that one who professes only with the tongue is called a believer linguistically, because the evidence of faith, which is the inner affirmation of the heart, is present in him, just as "angry" and "happy" are applied in their true sense because the indications of them are present, from the effects that necessarily accompany anger and happiness. The rulings of faith apply to him outwardly, and there is no dispute about that. The dispute is only about whether he is a believer in the sight of Allah, exalted is He, and of the Prophet, and those after him, just as they used to rule on the faith of one who uttered the two testimonies, and they used to rule on the disbelief of the hypocrite. This indicates that mere utterance by the tongue does not suffice for faith.

[Page 114]

This is something that two rams should not butt heads over. Perhaps for this reason al-Raqqashi and al-Qattan required the agreement of the heart with knowledge in the first case, and acquired affirmation by choice in the second. The Karramiyya said: whoever conceals denial and displays submission, even if he is a believer linguistically and legally, because the spoken word that the term "faith" was established to signify has been realized, yet that person deserves eternal abiding in the Fire, because the meaning of that word, which is the intended purpose for considering its signification, is not realized.

Having surveyed the opinions on this matter, what has become clear to me is that there is no harm in what the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-salih*) held: that the word *iman* is established for the common element between affirmation and deeds, so its application to affirmation alone, and to the whole of affirmation and deeds, is literal, just as in a specific tree, according to custom, what is considered is the common element between its trunk and the whole of its trunk together with its branches and leaves. So the tree is not described as nonexistent as long as the trunk remains. Affirmation is like the root of the tree, and deeds are like its branches and limbs. As long as the root remains, faith remains.

It has been reported in the authentic collection: "Faith has seventy-some branches, the highest of which is the saying 'There is no god but Allah,' and the lowest of which is removing harm from the road."

Close to this is the saying of one who said: deeds are external effects outside faith, causing it, and the word *iman* is applied to them figuratively. There is no real contradiction between the two positions, except that applying the term to them is literal according to the first and figurative according to the second, and this is a verbal question. What is understood from *iman* here is affirmation, as is not hidden.

"Al-ghayb" (the unseen) is a verbal noun placed in the position of a descriptive adjective, and it is "ghaʾib" (absent) for emphasis, by making it as if it were the thing itself. Making it mean the passive participle (*maf'ul*) is rejected, as in al-Bahr: *al-ghayb* is the verbal noun of *ghaba*, which is intransitive, and no passive participle is formed from it. Making it an explanation by meaning, because the absent one is absent by himself, is forced without need. Or it is a *fayʿal* lightened like *qil* and *mayt*. In al-Bahr: one should not claim this except for what has been heard both lightened and heavy.

Some have explained it here as what does not fall under the senses and is not required by the immediacy of reason. Among it is what no proof has been established for, and which only the Subtle, the All-Aware, glorified and exalted is He, knows, such as the knowledge of divine decree, for example. Among it is what a proof has been established for, such as the Truth, exalted is He, and His sublime attributes. For this is unseen, but whoever Allah, exalted is He, has given light knows it according to the measure of that light. This is why you find people varying in it. The awliya' (saints), may Allah benefit us through them, have the greatest share of it.

From here it has been said: the unseen is the witnessing of the All through the eye of the Truth. A servant may be granted nearness through supererogatory acts (*qurb al-nawafil*), so that the Truth, glorified is He, becomes his sight with which he sees, and his hearing with which he hears. He may ascend from that to nearness through obligatory acts (*qurb al-fara'id*), so that he becomes light. There, the unseen becomes witnessed by him, and what is lost to us becomes present with Him. Yet despite this, I do not permit anyone who has reached that station to be described as "he knows the unseen." ﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾.

Say to the one slain by love: you have fulfilled his right,
And to the claimant: far is it, the kohl is not the kohl.

The people differed about the intended meaning of the term here, with various opinions, until the Shi'a claimed that it refers to the Qa'im (the awaited Imam), and they hesitated to establish proof for that. What the heart inclines to is what the Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, reported in the hadith of Jibril, peace be upon him: that it is Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and the decree, its good and its evil. This is because the faith required by the Sacred Law is that, especially since two attributes have been added after it. That this entails applying "the unseen" to Him, glorified is He, implicitly, and that the unseen and the absent are what is permissible to be present, and absence is not harmful, since there is in it no specific application to Him, glorified is He. This is not from the category of naming. Moreover, we do not grant that "the unseen" is used only for what is permissible to be present.

Some scholars distinguished between *al-ghayb* and *al-ghaʾib*. They say: Allah is *ghayb* and is not *ghaʾib*, and by *ghaʾib* they mean what does not see you and you do not see, and by *ghayb* what you do not see. It is not far-fetched to say that this is by way of prevalence (*taghlib*), so that the faith of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, in him, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, is included, since he is not unseen in relation to them. Or it may be said: faith in him, upon him be prayer and peace, returns to faith in his messengership, for example, since there is no meaning to faith

[Page 115]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 3 (part 3 of 5):

…by Himself, free from any particular modes (ḥaythiyyāt), and His message is an unseen matter for which evidence has been set up, just as it has been set up for us, even though we differ in that we know it through report (khabar) and direct observation (mu'āyanah). Or it may be that the attribution of something to some of them is ascribed to all of them metaphorically, as in "the sons of So-and-so killed So-and-so." Or the meaning is that they believe in the unseen just as they believe in the seen, so that the witnessed and the non-witnessed are equal to them.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani chose that the meaning is that these pious ones believe in the unseen, that is, while you are absent from them, just as they believe when you are present, and not like the hypocrites, "who, when they meet those who believe, say, 'We believe,' but when they are alone with their devils they say, 'Indeed, we are with you; we were only mocking.'" So it is in the sense of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is so that he (Yusuf's master) may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾.

It is also possible to say: during the absence of the one believed in. In the Sunan of al-Darimi, it is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that al-Harith ibn Qays said to him: "We hope, with Allah, for the reward for what you have preceded us in, namely seeing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Ibn Mas'ud said: "We hope, with Allah, for your faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) though you did not see him. The affair of Muhammad (ﷺ) was clear to anyone who saw him. By Him besides whom there is no god, no one is better than one who has faith in the unseen." Then he recited: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim. That is the Book, there is no doubt in it, a guidance for the pious﴾ up to His saying: ﴿the successful﴾.

It does not follow from preferring one faith over another, in the respect in which it is preferred, that it is preferred in every respect, nor that the one who has one of them is preferred over the one who has the other. Excellence (al-afḍaliyyah) varies according to relations and considerations, and something may be found in the lesser that is not found in the greater. Would that Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, had calmed the anguish of al-Harith with what was related from him (ﷺ) in a marfu' report: "How excellent are a people who will come after you, who will believe in me though they have not seen me." How rich he was, may Allah be pleased with him, in what he answered with, since the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, are excluded from this generality in this verse, as his recitation of it, citing it as evidence, indicates. Some scholars have said this, but I do not incline to it.

It has been said: the meaning of "the unseen" is the heart, that is, they believe with their hearts, not like those who say with their mouths what is not in their hearts. The bā' (in bihi/bi-l-ghayb) is for transitivity according to the first view, for accompaniment according to the second and third, and for instrumentality according to the fourth.

Abu Ja'far and Asim, in the narration of al-A'sha from Abu Bakr, read ﴿yu'minūna﴾ without the hamzah, and likewise every silent hamzah. Indeed, they may omit many moving hamzahs too, such as ﴿lā yu'ākhidhukum﴾ and ﴿yu'ayyidu bi-naṣrihi﴾. The detailed account of Abu Ja'far's school is long. As for Abu 'Amr, he omits every silent hamzah unless its silence is a sign of the jazm (apocope), as in "yuhayyi' lakum" and "wa-nabbi'hum," and ﴿iqra' kitābaka﴾, for he does not omit the hamzah in these. It is also related from him that he keeps the hamzah in the silent ones. As for Nafi', he omits every silent and moving hamzah when it is the first radical of the verb, such as (yu'minūna) and (lā yu'ākhidhukum). The readings of al-Kisa'i and Hamzah differ, and each has a school whose account is long.

(wa-yuqīmūna) is from iqāmah (establishing). It is said: "I established the thing, iqāmah," when you fulfilled its right. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿You are not on anything until you establish the Torah and the Gospel﴾, that is, until you fulfil their rights through knowledge and action.

As for the meaning of "they establish the prayer": they make its pillars upright, by performing it completely with all its obligations and required elements, or with them together with its courtesies and recommended practices, from "aqāma al-'ūd" when he straightened the stick. Or they persevere in it and are constant, from "qāmati al-sūq" when the market was brisk, and "aqamtuhā" when you made it brisk. Or they exert themselves to perform it without lapse or slackness, from their saying "qāma bi-l-amr" and "aqāmahu" when he applied himself earnestly to it. Or they perform it and do it, and this is expressed by iqāmah because standing is part of its pillars. These are four aspects.

In the discussion of the first two of them there is a metaphor of the derivative kind (isti'ārah tab'iyyah), and in the last two there is a metonymic-type figurative usage (majāz mursal). The explanation of the first is that one likens the making upright of the pillars to straightening the stick by removing its crookedness, so it becomes "qawīm" (straight), by analogy with "qā'im" (standing). Then the word "iqāmah" is borrowed from the levelling of physical bodies, which has become literal for them, to the levelling of meanings, such as making the pillars of the prayer conform to what is due to them.

It has been said that iqāmah in the sense of levelling is literal both for physical objects and for meanings, and that taqwīm in meanings, like "religion" and "school," is more common, so there is no need for metaphor. This is not without problems, for figurativeness is that about which there is no doubt in either knowledge or transmission, and that usage is a well-known metaphor, or a conventional literal usage.

The explanation of the second is that the market's brisk trade is like a person's standing in good condition and complete prominence. So standing is used for this, and iqāmah for making it brisk. Then it is borrowed from this for constancy, for each of the two makes its object desired, competed for, and directed toward. This is a subtle meaning that only the elite grasp, although it involves a certain stretch of metaphor. Perhaps for this reason al-Tibi inclined to the view that in this aspect there is an allusive metonymy (kināyah talwīḥiyyah), in that he expressed constancy by iqāmah, for establishing the prayer in the first sense indicates that it is something desired. Neglecting it indicates its being cheapened, just as when a market is seen standing, it shows that its goods are in demand, and that demand implies that desires are directed to them, which requires continuity, unlike when it is not standing.

The explanation of the third is that standing to an affair indicates attention to its matter, and this entails exertion, so "standing" is used for its concomitant. It may be said that "qāma bi-l-amr" means that one applied oneself to it and discharged its duty without delay or shortfall, as if one stood up for it by oneself. And "aqāmahu" means he raised it on his shoulder entirely. Then it is valid that there may be in it an allegorical metaphor (isti'ārah tamthiliyyah), or an implicit metaphor (makniyyah), or an explicit metaphor (taṣrīḥiyyah). It may also be a metonymic-type figurative usage (majāz mursal), because whoever stands up for a matter on the feet of advancing, and lifts it on the shoulder of diligence, has exerted his utmost effort in it.

The explanation of the fourth is that performance (adā') here means doing the prayer, and the qualification is external. He expressed it by iqāmah through the relation of necessity (ʿalāqat al-lūzūm), since performing the prayer and bringing it into being in its entirety necessarily involves the act of standing, which is iqāmah, because doing a thing is doing its parts; or through the partial relation (al-ʿalāqah al-juz'iyyah), since iqāmah is a part or a part of the general act. It is also possible that there is a metaphor (isti'ārah) on account of the resemblance of performance to iqāmah, in that each of them is an act connected to the prayer.

Many have inclined to prefer the first of these aspects, because it is the most apparent, closest to the literal, and most beneficial. This is related from the interpreter of the Qur'an, Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, as Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related it through several chains from him. Perhaps this came from him by way of a directive from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or as a way of interpreting the speech of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, in its best interpretation, since it suits the arrangement of complete guidance and comprehensive, perfect success, and it contains great praise and abundant commendation. It is not far-fetched to say that it entails what is in the last aspects too, and the last is specified, as is said concerning the hadith: "I have been commanded to fight people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and they establish the prayer and give the zakat. When they do that, they have secured from me their blood and their property, except by right of Islam." This does not harm the preponderance of the first in the ancient speech, for it would be said, if that were meant: "they pray" (yuṣallūna). Deviating from the shorter and clearer without benefit is not fitting in any speech, let alone the most eloquent speech. Every situation has its speech, so understand.

"Ṣalāh" (prayer) originally, according to some, means supplication (du'ā'). From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "If one of you is invited to a meal, let him accept, and if he is fasting, let him pray (fa-l-yuṣalli)." In the terminology of the religious law (ahl al-sharʿ) it is used for the actual acts with their pillars, because it is supplication by the three tongues: of the state, of the act, and of speech. It is well known in the principles of jurisprudence (uṣūl al-fiqh) that the Mu'tazilah hold that these and similar terms are newly invented legal literal meanings (ḥaqā'iq mukhtara'ah shar'iyyah), because they are transferred from linguistic meanings. Our Qadi Abu Bakr holds that they are well-known linguistic figurative usages that did not become literal meanings. The majority of our companions hold that they are legal literal meanings derived from linguistic meanings.

Abu 'Ali, and al-Suhayli preferred it, said: prayer comes from the two ṣalawān, which are two veins in the back, because the first thing observed of its states is the moving of these two for bowing (rukū'). Ibn Jinni found this commendable. The one who supplicates is called muṣalli (one who prays) by analogy, in his humility, with one who bows and prostrates. It was also said: prayer is taken from that because it came second to faith, so it was likened to the muṣallī horse, the one that comes alongside the two ṣalawān of the leader.

The Imam (al-Razi) denied the derivation from the two ṣalawān, on the basis that ṣalāh is among the most famous words, so deriving it from something not well-known is extremely remote. I almost agree with him, although it may be said that lack of popularity does not impair the transmission. It has also been said that it comes from ṣallaytu al-'aṣā, when you straighten the stick with the fire (al-ṣalā), so the one who prays seeks, as it were, to straighten his outward and inward being, just as one tries to straighten a piece of wood by holding it over the fire. It is of the form fa'alah.
