[Page 117]

with a fatha on the ʿayn according to the well-known reading, though some allowed its sukūn, in which case the vowel of the ʿayn is transposed from the lām. The codices agreed on writing a waw in place of the alif in مِشْكَوَةٍ (mishkawa), نَجاةٍ (najāh, written as najawa), مَناةٍ (manāh, written as manawa), صَلاةٍ (ṣalāh, written as ṣalawa), زَكاةٍ (zakāh, written as zakawa), and حَياةٍ (ḥayāh, written as ḥayawa), where they occur in the singular, indefinite, and with the definite article. They also agreed on writing the alif in the construct form, as in صَلاتِي (ṣalātī). In some of the ʿUthmānic codices the alif was omitted. They agreed on writing the plural with a waw, following the pronunciation. Al-Juʿbarī said: The reason for writing the waw is to indicate that the original form of the letter is a waw that was converted into an alif. This is a following (itbāʿ) of the emphatic pronunciation (tafkhīm). This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Qutayba: "Some of the Arabs incline the alif toward the waw." I did not adopt this as the explanation because it does not occur in the Great Qur'an or in the speech of the eloquent.

By ṣalāh here is meant the obligatory prayer, namely the five daily prayers, as stated by Muqātil. Or it means the obligatory and the supererogatory prayers, as stated by the majority of scholars. The first view is the one transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. The Imam (al-Rāzī) claimed that this is the intended meaning, because it is what success (falāḥ) is attached to. When the Prophet (ﷺ) explained to the Bedouin the description of the obligatory prayer, the man said: "By Allah, I will not add to it or take away from it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The Bedouin has succeeded, if he is truthful."

(And the provision) — ar-rizq, with a fatha, linguistically means giving that which an animal benefits from. It was said that it includes other things as well, such as plants. With a kasra, al-rizq is a noun derived from it, and according to one view it is also a verbal noun. It was said: the root meaning of ar-rizq is "portion" (al-ḥaẓẓ). It is used to mean that which is provided and benefited from, to mean ownership, and to mean gratitude among the tribe of Azd. The theologians differed about its meaning in the sharīʿa. According to the Ashʿarites, the reliable definition is: whatever Allah, Exalted is He, drives to an animal so that it benefits from it, whether it is lawful or unlawful, whether it is food, drink, clothing, or something else. The well-known view is that it is a name for what Allah drives to an animal so that it may nourish itself with it. On the first definition, it follows that loaned goods (al-ʿawārī) are provision, because they are among the things Allah drove to the animal and it benefited from them. Calling them provision afterward is by custom, as is well known. It also follows that a person eats the provision of another, because the other may benefit from it by eating. However, the verse agrees with this, since the benefit may come from spending on others. This differs from the second definition, since what is nourished by cannot be spent unless one says that applying the term provision to what is spent is a metaphor, because it is about to be consumed.

The Muʿtazilites explained it, in the well-known view, sometimes as what Allah gives His servant and enables him to dispose of, and sometimes as what Allah gives for his subsistence and survival specifically. Since the attribution to Allah is taken into account in its meaning, and since there is no provider except Allah, glorified is He, and since the servant deserves blame and punishment for eating what is unlawful, and since what is attributed to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is not, in their view, ugly, nor is its perpetrator deserving of blame or punishment, they said: provision is the lawful, and the unlawful is not provision. Al-Jaṣṣāṣ from among us (the Ḥanafīs) went to this view in his book Aḥkām al-Qur'ān. But in our view, everything is from Him, by Him, and to Him: "Say: all is from Allah" (Qur'an 4:78). "There is no power nor strength except by Allah" and "to Allah are all matters returned." Blame and punishment are for the wrongful handling of causes by choice. Indeed, courtesy is the best capital of the believer, so it is not proper to attribute to Him, glorified is He, except the more excellent, and the most excellent, as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: "And when I am ill, it is He who cures me" (Qur'an 26:80). And He, exalted, said: "Those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger" (Qur'an 1:7). So the unlawful is provision in reality, but we are courteous in attributing it to Him, glorified is He.

The evidence that provision includes the unlawful is what Ibn Māja, Abū Nuʿaym, and al-Daylamī transmitted from the hadith of Ṣafwān ibn Umayya, who said: "ʿAmr ibn Qurra came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Allah has decreed misery upon me. I think I will not be provided for except from my drum with my palm. So permit me to be wealthy without indecency.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'No permission for you, no honour, no blessing. You have lied, O enemy of Allah! Allah, Exalted, has provided you with lawful, good provision, but you chose what Allah, Exalted, forbade you from His provision, instead of what Allah made lawful for you from His lawful things.'"

To take it as a figure of speech (al-mushākala), like saying that the Prophet's words (ﷺ) "you chose" etc. may allow the meaning that it is provision for those for whom it is lawful, so that the argument falls because of this possibility, is very contrary to the apparent meaning. Such a possibility, if it were to undermine the argument, would leave no evidence on the face of the earth. Challenging the chain of transmission without any basis is not accepted, and this is the seat of Thurayyā, as is well known. The argument for this matter, as al-Bayḍāwī and others did, is that if the unlawful were not provision, then the one who ate it all his life would not be provided for, and this is not so, because of the verse: "There is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah" (Qur'an 11:6). This is not a sound argument, because the Muʿtazilites may refuse to restrict provision to food, and suffice with mere benefit rather than actual benefiting, or even with the capacity for it. The argument would only be complete if it were assumed that this person did not benefit from anything lawful from the time of his birth until his death, not a single suckling from a breast, nor a single sip of permissible water, nor a single glance at a beloved, nor a single attaining of a goal, indeed not even the ability to do any of that at all. Custom dictates that this does not exist, and the basis of refutation must be established. Moreover, even if we assume its existence, they would say: that is not forbidden for him, and "whoever is forced, neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him" (Qur'an 2:173). Also, they can object with the one who lived a day, for example, then died before taking anything lawful or unlawful. Our answer to them will be their answer to us. Furthermore, the verse does not indicate that Allah delivers to each person everything he benefits from, since reality contradicts that. Rather, it indicates that He, glorified and exalted is He, drives the provision and enables the benefiting from it. So if a turning from the lawful to the unlawful occurs, this does not harm the reality of His being the Provider, exalted is He.

Also, it may be said: the meaning of the verse is "there is no creature characterized by being provided for," so the case of consumption does not enter, and thus its exit does no harm. Just as fish do not enter the statement, "every creature slaughtered with a knife," meaning every creature characterized as slaughtered, the characterization applies only to what is slaughtered. So this is not a valid proof. The better argument is consensus before the emergence of the Muʿtazilites, that whoever ate the unlawful all his life was provided with that unlawful all his life. The apparent texts also testify that provision is divided into good and bad, and these suffice in a matter like this. The principle on which the restriction is built has been abandoned by the People of the Sunna, leaving it a level plain.

(And spending) — al-infāq, from infād (exhaustion). It is said: anfaqtu al-shayʾ and anfadtuhu with the same meaning, and the hamza is for transitivity. The root meaning indicates going out and departing, and from it come nāfaqa (hypocrisy), al-nāfiqāʾ (the hole in a lizard's burrow), and nafaqa (a tunnel). The reason the object was placed first is to highlight what Allah has entrusted to the servant, or because it precedes the spending in external reality, and for the harmony of the verse endings. The provision here means the lawful, because it is in the context of describing the God-fearing, and there is no praise in spending the unlawful. It was said: The statement of the jurists does not contradict this: if a person comes into possession of property whose owner he does not know, he should give it in charity, and if he later finds its owner, he pays its value or its equivalent to him. This spending is rewarded, because when he did it by the permission of the Lawgiver he deserved praise. Since he did not know its owner, he had the right to dispose of it, the liability was transferred to his ownership, and the prohibition changed to its price. Moreover, there has been disagreement about the case where one does good with property seized unlawfully whose owner is known, as Ibn al-Qayyim mentioned in Badāʾiʿ al-Fawāʾid. Ibn ʿAqīl held that there is no reward for the usurper in it, because he is sinful, nor for the owner of the property, because he has no intention, and there is no reward without intention. Rather, it is taken from the good deeds of the usurper in proportion to his property. It was also said that it is a benefit that resulted from his property and came from it, and such a thing is rewarded, like a righteous child for whom one is rewarded even if one did not intend it. It is understood from the words of some (and it is very strange) that the usurper is also rewarded if he spends it on good, even though he transgressed and his good deeds are taken in retribution for his taking, because if he had committed immorality with it, he would be punished twice: once for the usurpation and once for the immorality. So if he does good with it, he should be rewarded for it. "Whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it" and "whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it" (Qur'an 99:7–8). This is not contradicted by the Prophet's (ﷺ) statement: "Allah does not accept charity from ill-gotten gains (ghulūl)," nor his statement: "Allah is good and accepts only what is good," because the outcome of what was mentioned is that the reward is for the very act of shifting from spending in disobedience to spending on what is itself obedience, not for charity itself with unlawful property qua unlawful. The distinction is subtle and is not reached except by divine guidance.

It has been disputed what spending means here. It was said, and this is the preferable view: spending wealth in the paths of good, or giving from the apparent and hidden blessings, and knowledge that is not taught, like a treasure from which nothing is spent. From Ibn ʿAbbās: zakāh. From him and from Ibn Masʿūd: maintenance of dependents. From al-Ḍaḥḥāk: voluntary charity before the obligation of zakāh, or spending in jihad. Perhaps these views are examples of what is spent, about which there is no disagreement, and some scholars made them into disagreements. They preferred that it is the obligatory zakāh, because it is mentioned alongside its sister, the prayer, in many places in the Qur'an. In that case the partitive min is something whose secret one should not ask about, since obligatory zakāh is not the whole of wealth. If the intended meaning of spending is its general sense, then the purpose of including the partitive is to indicate that spending part of the wealth suffices for the spender to be characterized by guidance and success, and it does not depend on spending all of it. The statement of our master al-Bayḍāwī, following al-Zamakhsharī, that it is for restraint from the forbidden extravagance and is specific to one who has not endured poverty and swallowed the bitterness of need, otherwise Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him, gave all his wealth in charity and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not deny it to him, because he knew his patience and knew what was in his heart. For this reason, when it was said to al-Ḥasan ibn Sahl, "There is no good in extravagance," he said, "There is no extravagance in good." It was also said: the point of including the partitive min is that provision is more general than the lawful and the unlawful, so it was included to indicate that the spending that counts is that which comes from the lawful, and that is a part of provision.

(And what) in the verse is either a relative pronoun, or a verbal (masdariyya) particle, or a descriptive (mawṣūfa) particle. The first is preferable, in which case the returning pronoun is omitted. An objection was raised: if it is taken as connected, it would require the connection of two pronouns of equal rank, and separation in such a case is obligatory. If it is taken as separate, its omission is not permitted, because they required mentioning the separate pronoun, giving the reason that it is separated only for a purpose, and if it were omitted, the indication would be lost. The answer for each option: For the first, since the two pronouns differ in number (plural and singular), their connection is permitted, even if they are of equal rank, as in the verse of the poet:

"For your face in beneficence there is expansiveness and radiance;
I am the one who follows the noblest of fathers."

And it also follows that whoever forbids its deletion when it is spoken must forbid it when it is implied, since the verbal ugliness is removed. As for the second point, what may not be deleted is only that which is separated for a semantic purpose, such as restriction (*hasr*), not in every case. This is what Ibn Hisham said in *al-Jami' al-Saghir*, and more than one scholar has alluded to it. The word *min* was written joined to *ma* with its nun deleted, because the preposition and its object are like one thing, and the nun had been deleted in pronunciation, so its deletion in the script was appropriate. This was stated in *al-Bahr*.

He, glorified is He, made the relative clauses (*silat*) of *alladhina* (those who) into imperfect verbs, and He did not make the relative pronoun (*mawsul*) *al-* so that it would be joined to an active participle (*ism al-fa'il*). This is because the imperfect verb, as some have mentioned, indicates renewal and occurrence, together with the continuous renewed sense (*istimrar tajaddudi*) it carries here. These qualities are renewed in the God-fearing, whereas the active participle, according to them, does not have this sense.

He arranged these in this order because deeds are either of the heart, the greatest of which is the firm belief in the reality of monotheism (*tawhid*), prophethood, and the afterlife, for without it deeds are like a mirage in a bare plain which the thirsty one takes for water. Or they are physical, and their foundation is prayer (*salah*), because it distinguishes between disbelief and Islam. It is the pillar of the religion, the ladder of the monotheists, and the mother from which all other goods and acts of righteousness branch out. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer." God has also applied the term faith (*iman*) to it, as a group of exegetes have said, in His saying: ﴿And God would not let your faith go to waste﴾ (2:143). Or they are financial, namely spending for the sake of God, the Exalted, and when this is present it is known that one is steadfast in faith. These three are different in rank, so He, glorified and exalted is He, arranged them placing first the more important, then the more binding, because faith is obligatory for the responsible person at every moment, prayer at most times, and spending in some circumstances. So understand this, and may God guide you.

﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you, and who are certain of the Hereafter﴾ is coordinated with the first relative clause, separated and joined in turn. It is reported from Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are the believers among the People of the Book (Ahl al-Kitab). Since coordination ordinarily implies that belief in each of the two revelations is independent, this description applies to them in particular, because the belief of others in what was sent down before is only general and follows from their belief in the Qur'an, especially in a context of praise. The verses and hadiths indicate that the People of the Book receive a double reward on account of this, and by this they differ from those who came before them. It has also been said that the difference lies in the fact that the first belief is by reason and the second is by transmission, or that the first is in the unseen and the second is in what they recognized, just as they recognize their sons. Then ﴿those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ refers to the first group, because their belief comes purely from divine guidance, and ﴿and those are the successful﴾ refers to the second, for their attainment of what they were awaiting. Or it may be that the first group, taken collectively, had some associationism (shirk) among them, whereas these did not associate partners with Allah and did not deny. It has also been said that the difference is one of generality and specificity, like His saying ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend﴾. The specification here after the generalization serves to indicate their superiority in that they are given their reward twice. Something may be found in the lesser that is not found in the greater, and in this there is encouragement for the People of the Book to enter Islam. Some have said that these first ones are the same persons, and that the insertion of the conjunction is applicable to names and attributes in terms of the difference of concepts. It may be by waw, fa, and thumma: by waw (and) for the simultaneous combination, by fa (then) for immediate sequence, and by thumma (then) for sequence with interval, reflecting the successive transitions between states. The plurality derived from the waw here falls among the meanings of the attributes understood from the two coordinated terms. The belief accompanying the first is general and by reason, while that accompanying the second is detailed and by transmission. The repetition of the relative pronoun serves to draw attention to the difference between the two categories and the divergence of the two paths. It may also be coordinated with ﴿the God-fearing﴾ without a separation of the relative clause, because separating it would entail placing an extraneous element between the subject and its predicate, and between the conjunct and what it is conjoined to. The difference between the two conjuncts is considered in that what is meant by the thing conjoined to is those Arabs who believed but were not People of the Book, and what is meant by the conjunct is those People of the Book who believed in him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Some verifying scholars have preferred the possibility that these are the first group, and that the conjunction of the waw between the attributes is because belief in the two revelations is shared by all believers without exception. There is therefore no basis for restricting it to believing People of the Book. The mention of the revelations separately does not indicate that belief in each is independent, for He has mentioned the earlier scriptures separately in His saying ﴿Say: We believe in God and in what has been sent down to us and what was sent down to Abraham﴾, and belief in them individually was not required. Also, the People of the Book were not believers in all that was sent down before, because the Jews did not believe in the Gospel, and their religion is abrogated (naskh, the annulment of a ruling by a later one) by it. And the attributes previously mentioned apply to whoever among the People of the Book believed, so restricting them to others is arbitrary. Making the statement a case of coordinating the specific with the general does not suit the context.

I answer: first, the understanding that emerges from the context is belief in independence, especially in a context of praise, and to this refers what has come down that they will be given their reward twice. The address in the verse is to the Muslims, telling them to say it all at once, and belief and believer are not repeated in it, so it is not a counterexample. Second, the belief of the People of the Book in every revelation is considered with regard to all of them: the Jews' belief included the Qur'an and the Torah, and the Christians' belief included the Gospel as well. This suffices to account for what is reported about those who witnessed the descent of revelation, and one should not turn away from it when it can be interpreted. That the understood meaning is that the ruling applies to each one individually, if granted, does not refute it. Nor does it refute that the Jews who believed in the time of our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, had not believed in the Torah before that; otherwise they would have become Christians, because in it is the prophethood of Jesus, just as in it is the prophethood of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. For it has come in it: "God came from Mount Sinai, and appeared from Seir, and shone forth from Paran." Seir is Jerusalem, where Jesus appeared, and Paran is the mountains of Mecca, which were the place of manifestation of the Chosen One, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. We say: they believed in the Torah, but they interpreted what in it pointed to the prophethood of the Messiah, peace be upon him. Some of them denied his prophethood outright and attributed to him what they attributed, and far be it from him; these are the majority. Others, like the Ananiyya, said: he was one of the sincere friends of Allah, the Exalted, who knew the rulings of the Torah, and he was not a prophet. These are few, differing from the rest of the Jews regarding the Sabbath and the festivals, and they limit themselves to eating birds, gazelles, fish, and locusts. This belief, although it does not benefit in salvation from the Fire, does reduce evil compared with disbelief in the Torah and outright denial of it together with disbelief in Jesus, peace be upon him. They may perhaps be praised with regard to the basic belief in it, even if they are blamed on another account. It seems that for this reason the jizya (poll tax) is accepted from them, and they were not made fodder for the swords absolutely. The claim that they were praised after their belief in the Qur'an for belief in the Torah, with regard to their ancestors who were in the time of Moses, peace be upon him, for they believed in it with correct belief in its proper manner, just as they were blamed for what their fathers did in his time, as many verses indicate, is nothing, for there is no sense in their being given two rewards then. The difference between the two chapters is clear. Furthermore, the abrogation that the one who preferred this view claimed is contrary to what al-Shahrastani and others mentioned, that the Gospel did not explain rulings nor contain lawful and unlawful matters, but consisted of symbols, parables, and admonitions, and that the rulings were referred to the Torah. The Messiah said: "I have not come to abolish the Torah, but to fulfill it." This is contrary to what the apparent meanings require, and its verification will come, Allah willing, Exalted is He. Third, the attributes' applicability to those of the People of the Book who believe does not harm us, for they are explicitly mentioned in the first and implicitly in the second. Fourth, we do not concede that that coordination does not suit the context, for the subtleties of coordinating the specific with the general are not hidden in their abundance from people of understanding. So leave what has passed and take what pleases you. In my view, after all this, the objection is masculine and the answer is feminine, but the narration compelled that. Perhaps the people of Mecca know its mountain paths better, and above every possessor of knowledge is One All-Knowing. Moreover, reflective understanding may support it, as has been said, on the basis that repeating the relative pronoun and describing it with belief in the two revelations, despite its being shared among all believers, and the inclusion of belief in what was sent down to you within belief in what was sent down before you, requires that it refers to those who have a particular connection to the revelation, namely the believers among the People of the Book, since they were addressed specifically to believe in the Qur'an, as He said: ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾, believing in the books independently in general, unlike the rest of the believers. Then, what is understood from People of the Book is the People of the Torah and the Gospel, and restricting it to the People of the Gospel alone is not supported by transmission or reason. Of them, forty-two believed, who came with Ja'far from the land of Abyssinia, and eight from Syria. And the sending down (inzal) means conveying and delivering, and it is not required that it be from above, contrary to whoever claimed so, as in ﴿But when it descends into their courtyard﴾, meaning arrives and alights. The sending down of divine books has been discussed in the introductions, where you will find what leads you to its ways. It has been mentioned that the meaning of the sending down of the Qur'an is that Gabriel heard the speech of Allah, the Exalted, as Allah willed, and descended with it, or that He made it appear in the Preserved Tablet in writing, and the angel memorized it. Some of the early scholars went so far as to say that it is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters which we affirm without inquiring into its modality. The philosophers said: the souls of the prophets, peace be upon them, are holy, and so they are strong enough to connect with the higher assembly, and forms are imprinted upon them that pass to the imaginative faculty and the common sense, and so they see as one who witnesses; this is revelation. Sometimes they rise higher and hear speech that is arranged, and it is likely that the sending down of books is of this kind. In my view, this may apply to possessors of holy souls and human spirits, but the matter of prophethood is beyond that, and how far is the Pleiades from the hand of the one who reaches for it.

The two verbs of sending down are in the passive voice, and al-Nakha'i, Abu Haywa, and Yazid ibn Qutayb read them in the active voice. It is read irregularly: "bima unazzilla ilayka" with the lam doubled. The reason for this is that he made the lam of unzila quiescent, then deleted the hamza of ila and transferred its kasra to the lam, so the two like letters met and were assimilated. The subject of the verb is said to be Allah, and it is said to be Gabriel, peace be upon him. In al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is said that there is in it a shift (iltifat), because of the preceding "of what We have provided for them," for it changed from the first-person plural pronoun to the third-person pronoun. Had it followed the first, it would have been: "bima anzalna ilayka, wa ma anzalna min qablika." Glorified is He, He used the past verb as the relative clause of the first ma, although what is meant by the thing sent down is all of it, because the context demands that, and because of the context's connection with it in the arrangement of complete guidance and success upon it, and because it is in contrast to what was sent down before, and because "they believe" implies continuity. All of it had not been sent down at the time this verse was revealed, for two reasons. The first is that this is a dominance (taghlib) of what has been sent down over what has not been sent down, and so it is of the type of applying the part to the whole. The second is that all of the thing sent down is likened to something that has descended in the certainty of its occurrence, because part of it has descended and part of it will surely descend. So the sending down of its whole becomes analogous to the sending down of that thing which has descended, and the past form of the verb for sending it down is borrowed for the sending down of the whole. This is what the one who is recognized as expert in the fine points of the matter (the one about whom knowledge is tied when mentioned) has verified. Yet in it there is a great perplexity. Less problematic than this is that the past tense is used here for the sake of parallelism (mushakala), since what has not yet occurred accompanies what has occurred. Still less problematic than all of that is that the actual meaning of the past is intended, and belief in the future is indicated by the evidence of the text. As for what is said, that belief in what will be sent down is not obligatory except that taking it to mean all of it is more complete, and so it is limited to that, there is no basis for it, for there is no doubt that the believer is obliged to believe in what has been sent down, and that everything that will be sent down is true, even if its detailed specification is not obligatory. The scholars have mentioned that belief in the divine books in general is a communal obligation (fard 'ayn), and belief in the Qur'an in detail, which one is required to follow in its details, is a collective obligation (fard kifaya), for if it were an individual obligation it would lead to hardship and difficulty, and religion is ease, not hardship. This is something about which there is no doubt. So much so that al-Dawwani said: it is obligatory as a collective duty to detail the foundational proofs such that one can thereby remove doubts, silence the obstinate, and guide those seeking guidance. The jurists have mentioned that in every stage of a journey of shortening the prayer there must be a person characterized by this quality, called the one appointed for defense (al-manṣub lil-dhabb), and it is forbidden for the imam to leave these places empty of such a person, just as it is forbidden to leave them empty of the scholar of the rulings that the common people need. It has been said: there must be such a person in every region. It has been said: it suffices that there be one in all the inhabited Islamic lands. Perhaps this descent to a lower level is due to the descent of the matter, and the scarcity of religious scholars in this age of the world.

It has become a desolate waste, and its people have departed,
and what wore away its remnants has worn away Labad as well.

To Allah the Exalted I complain, and to Him I resort.

To Allah I complain: there is a need in the heart
that the days pass over while it remains as it is.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 4 (part 2 of 2):

(And the Hereafter) is the feminine of *al-akhir*, the active participle of *akhara* (the triliteral form), meaning *ta'akhkhara* (to come later), even though this verb is not used. Similarly, *al-akhar* with a fatha on the kha' is its superlative form. The word is originally an adjective, as in *al-dar al-akhira* (the Final Abode), and *yunshi'u al-nash'ah al-akhirah* (He brings into being the final creation). Then it became dominant, like *al-dunya* (the world). A dominant adjective may be used as a description without the dominant noun, so one does not say *qayd adham* (a dark-colored shackle), because this would entail a redundant repetition in meaning. Although *adham* derives from *duhma* (darkness), people use it without thinking of its original sense at all. Understand this. The word *dar* (abode) may also be attached to it, as in His saying ﴿and the Abode of the Hereafter﴾, meaning the abode of the final life. It may also be contrasted with *al-ula* (the first), as in His saying, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿To Him belongs praise in the first and in the last﴾. The meaning here is either the final abode or the final creation. The majority read with the sukun on the lam of the definite article and keep the hamza that follows it as a glottal stop (*li-l-qat'*). Warsh omits the hamza, moving its vowel onto the lam.

(And certainty) (*al-iqan*) is the establishing of a thing's reality, like its stillness and clarity. It is said: *yaqana al-ma'* (the water became certain) when it became still and what lies beneath it became visible. *Al-iqan* and *al-yaqin* have the same meaning, contrary to those who have erred regarding this. Al-Jawhari said: *al-yaqin* is knowledge and the removal of doubt. From it one says *yaqintu* (with kasra) *yaqinan*, and *ayqantu* and *istayqantu* all have the same meaning. Al-Wahidi and a group of scholars held that it is what arises from reflection and inference, so the self-evident is not described by it, nor is God's knowledge.

Imam al-Nasafi and some other scholars held that it is knowledge that does not admit its opposite. The Truth, glorified and exalted is He, is not described by it because there is no revelatory stipulation (*tawqif*) for this. Others held that it is knowledge of a thing after its possessor had been doubtful about it, whether it is necessary (*daruri*) or inferential (*istidlali*). Al-Raghib mentioned that *al-yaqin* is a quality of knowledge that is higher than *al-ma'rifah* (recognition), *al-dirayah* (understanding), and their like. One says *'ilm yaqin* (certain knowledge), but one does not say *ma'rifat yaqin*. It is the tranquility of the soul together with the firmness of the judgment. In *al-Ihya'* (the Revival of the Religious Sciences), and the heart inclines to it, it is held that *al-yaqin* is shared between two meanings. The first is the absence of doubt, so it applies to everything without doubt, whether it is obtained through reflection, sense perception, innate intellectual disposition, mass transmission (*tawatur*), or proof. This does not vary. The second is what the jurists, the Sufis, and many scholars have explicitly stated. It is that in which one does not consider the possibility or doubt, but rather its dominance over the heart, to the point that one says: so-and-so has weak certainty regarding death and strong certainty regarding the affirmation of provision. Thus everything that dominates the heart and takes hold of it is certainty. The variation of this is evident.

The majority read (they are certain) with a silent waw after the ya', which is substituted from it (*mubdalah minha*), because the verb is from *aqana*. Al-Numayri read with a silent hamza in place of the waw. It was common among them that when a waw takes a non-accidental damma, as detailed in Arabic grammar, it may be substituted by a hamza, as is said of *wujuh*, the plural of *wajh* (face), which becomes *ajuh*. Perhaps the substitution here is due to its proximity to the damma, so it was given the ruling of the damma. The neighbor may be held accountable for the wrongdoing of the neighbor.

God, glorified is He, distinguished between belief in what was sent down and belief in the Hereafter. He did not say: *wa-bi-l-akhirah hum yu'minun* (and in the Hereafter they believe), to avoid the burden of repetition, or because of the abundance of the strange matters related to the Hereafter, and what is prepared therein of reward and punishment, and the details of the types of bliss and torment, and the nature of the inhabitants of each, which is contrary to the worldly nature, along with affirming the bodily resurrection (*al-ma'ad al-jismani*) in whatever form it takes, and other things that are stranger than belief in the revealed Book. Many people have denied it. The Torah and the Gospel, as we have them, are devoid of its details. In the first, according to what is in the commentary on *al-Tawali'*, there is no mention of bodily resurrection. It is mentioned only in the books of Ezekiel (*Hizqiel*) and Isaiah (*Ash'ya'*). What is mentioned in the Gospel is only spiritual resurrection. So it was fitting that this important and strange matter, about which the minds of many were bewildered in affirming it, and which they rushed to deny as moths rush into fire, should be paired with (certainty), which is the very same thing, to show the completeness of praise and to display the utmost of commendation.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase (*al-majrur*) indicates that their certainty is restricted to the reality of the Hereafter and does not extend beyond it to something contrary to its reality, such as what the Jews claim, for example. They said: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who were Jews﴾, and ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few countable days﴾. They claimed that they delight in the breeze and the spirits, since that is not from the Hereafter at all. In the construction of (they are certain) upon (they), there is an indication that the belief of their opponents regarding the Hereafter is pure ignorance and empty imagination, and they have no share of certainty, neither in shade nor in shelter.

[Page 123]

[Page 123]

﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾. Apparently this is a clause in the nominative position, serving as a predicate. If the first relative pronoun (ﷺ, "those who") is treated as a separate clause in most of the possibilities concerning the second, and its separation follows accordingly, then the predicative sense belongs to it, since the thing conjoined is not cut off from what it is conjoined to. If it is treated as a relative clause, and the second relative refers to a group among those mentioned before it, and that group is treated as a separate clause, then the statement is about it. Mentioning the particular after the general may be done by way of joining the two in the preceding ruling, namely ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾. It may also be done by singling it out with the ruling apart from the general. In that case, the clause composed of the second relative and the predicate clause is conjoined to the clause ﴿guidance for the God-fearing﴾, whose subjects are described as ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾, and the first clause. Although the first clause is intended to praise the Book, and the second is intended to praise those described as believing in all the books, their praise is only by virtue of their belief in that Book. So the two are suitably connected in conveying its praise. The purpose of making the praise an intended goal in itself is to encourage those like them, and it is said that it implicitly addresses those who do not share their qualities. The specification drawn from the conjoined clause, measured against those who do not possess their attributes, does not contradict what is drawn from the clause conjoined to, namely that guidance is established for the God-fearing absolutely. Yes, this aspect is not in eloquence on the level of separating the first relative. Therefore the first is preferable. In accordance with this, the clause indicates an answer to a question, either about the ruling, meaning: do the God-fearing deserve what has been established for them of being singled out for guidance? Or about the cause, as if it were said: what is the cause of their being singled out? Or about both matters together, meaning: are they worthy of that, and what is the reason for it that they should be so? So it is answered that these people, because of their being characterized by the attributes mentioned, are able to attain the perfect guidance which their Lord, exalted is He, granted them through His Book. It is known that the cause is specific to them, so they deserve to be singled out. Thus the answer includes the required ruling together with a summary of its requirement. Adding the consequence of guidance reinforces the emphasis contained in the indefiniteness of ﴿guidance﴾, or it confirms the ruling by the proof that also follows. For this reason, emphasis on the attribution is dispensed with. Or the nominal clause is emphatic. It may be said: he explained the answer, arranging upon it its two effects, namely guidance and success, because that leads more directly to knowledge of the cause. In that case there is no need for emphasis. The matter according to the third assumption is clear. Treating the clause as indicating an answer, on the supposition of joining the first and separating the second, is something whose rejection from the domain of acceptance is not hidden. If the first is joined and the second conjoined, this clause is a grammatical resumption (istinaf nahwi), and the separation is for complete connection, since it is like the result of the preceding attributes. Or it is an explanatory resumption (bayani), and the separation is because it is like a connected clause. It is as if a questioner says: what is it for those described by these attributes that they are singled out for guidance? So it is answered that the cause of their being singled out is that He, glorified is He, decreed in eternity their happiness and their guidance. Their nature is then stamped with guidance, and the happy one is happy in his mother's womb. This is especially so when the success of the Hereafter is added to it, which is the greatest of aims. Or it is said: the answer is by explaining what their name comprises in summary of the qualities of perfection, and clarifying what it requires of the result, meaning: those whose affairs are such are worthy of what is greater than that. This method is pursued at times by repeating the one from whom the discourse was resumed, as in: "I did good to Zayd; Zayd deserves kindness." At other times by repeating his attribute, as in: "I did good to Zayd, your old friend; he is fit for that." The latter is more eloquent because it contains a statement of the cause of the ruling. The use of the demonstrative here has the position of repeating the described with its mentioned attributes, together with what it implies of his complete distinction by them, and his being placed among those visible matters for that, along with an indication of the remoteness of his station and the loftiness of his rank. Furthermore, taking ﴿ulaika﴾ alone as the predicate, with ﴿upon guidance﴾ as a circumstantial clause, is a remote possibility, as is taking it as an apposition to ﴿those who﴾ and the adverbial phrase as the predicate. The reason they wrote a waw in ﴿ulaika﴾ is to distinguish it from ﴿ilaika﴾ (to you) with its preposition and object, as it is said. It is also said that since it refers to a masculine plural and is indeclinable and different from the common forms of plurals, it is compensated in general by writing a letter which occurs in the plural in some verses. Among the well-known sayings is: "Turn away the questioner even with a burnt hoof." In His words, exalted is He, ﴿upon guidance﴾ there is a figurative metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya tab'iyya), in that it likens the state of those people, which is their being empowered by guidance, their firm establishment upon it, and their holding fast to it, to the state of one who mounts a thing and rides it. Then the word for elevation, which is used for the likened thing, is borrowed for the state which is the omitted likened item. Al-Sa'd took this view, but al-Sayyid denied that the figurative metaphor and the subordinate metaphor can be combined, because its being subordinate requires that each of the two sides be a single meaning, since particle meanings are single, and its being figurative requires that both be abstracted from multiple matters, and that entails its composition.

He, may his secret be sanctified, put forward three aspects in the verse. The first is that it is a single subordinate metaphor, in that he likened the God-fearing's holding fast to guidance to the rider's elevation over his mount in firmness and stability, so the particle designated for elevation is borrowed for it. The second is that he likens a form abstracted from the God-fearing, guidance, and his holding fast to it, to a form abstracted from the rider and the mount, and his elevation over it. Then there is a figurative metaphor in which each of its two sides is composed. But among the expressions that correspond to the likened item, only the word ﴿upon﴾ is stated, for its meaning is the core of that form, and what is other than it is subordinate to it and is considered within implied expressions, even if they are not stated in the structure of the speech. So there is no metaphor at all in ﴿upon﴾; rather it remains as it was before the metaphor, as when all those expressions are explicitly stated. The third is that he likens guidance to the mount by way of metaphor through implication (isti'ara bi'l-kinaya), and the word ﴿upon﴾ is made a clue to it, the reverse of the first aspect.

This disagreement between the two shaykhs on this question is something that travelers have carried and assemblies have been convened over, and treatises have been written about it. The first meeting between them took place in the assembly of Timur, and the arbiter was Nu'man al-Khwarazmi, the Mu'tazili. He ruled, and it is apparent that it was for some reason in favor of Sayyid al-Sanad. Scholars to this day are of two camps on this matter, and they continue to differ about it. Yet most are with al-Sa'd. They answered al-Sayyid's objection by saying that abstracting something from multiple matters occurs in various ways. It may come from the totality of those matters, like an conventional unity. It may come from one matter in relation to another, like relations of attribution. It may come partly from one matter and partly from another. In the first two cases, its composition is not required, but rather the multiplicity of its sources. In that case, it is permissible that the particle meaning, since it is a relational matter like elevation, be a state abstracted from multiple matters, so because it applies to the particle it is subordinate. And because each of the two sides is a relational state abstracted from multiple matters, it is figurative. Perhaps the people's choice, in defining the figurative metaphor, of the term "abstraction" rather than "composition" guides the fair-minded to the fact that composition is not a condition on its two sides; otherwise the clearer term would have been "composition." I have expanded the discussion on this and mentioned what is for and against it in my book "The Iraqi Answers to the Iranian Questions." This much is sufficient here.

In the indefiniteness of ﴿guidance﴾ there is an indication of its greatness, so no one knows its reality and measure except the Subtle, the All-Aware. The Lord is mentioned although guidance comes only from Him, glorified is He, as an emphasis of that by attributing it to Him, exalted is His majesty. There is clear appropriateness in this: since He is their Lord, it fits that He prepares for them the means of both happinesses and bestows upon them the good of both abodes. There may be an omitted attribute, meaning ﴿upon guidance﴾ means a guidance, and omitting the attribute is permissible when the meaning is understood. It is said: the nunation may indicate singularity, meaning upon one guidance, since there is no guidance except the guidance that was sent down to him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, because it abrogates what came before it. ﴿From﴾ (min) is for the beginning of the limit, or for partitive sense, with an omitted noun, meaning "from the guidance of their Lord." The meaning of this being from Him, glorified is He, is that He is the one who grants them success and pours upon them from the seas of His kindness and generosity, even if ordinary causes and apparent intermediaries intervene there. Moreover, those intermediaries may be removed from between them, so the dawn of direct vision shines for one who has two eyes.

Ibn Harmaz read ﴿min rabbihum﴾ with a dammah on the ha'. Likewise all the ha's of masculine and feminine plurals, according to the original, without observing a preceding kasra or ya'. The noon was assimilated into the ra' without nasalization by the majority, and this is the practice. Many of the reciters' authorities held that it is assimilation with nasalization, and they narrated it from Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub. Abu 'Awn, from Qalun, and Abu Hatim, from Ya'qub, made the noon clear. These variants also apply to the noon and tanwin when they meet a lam.

﴿And those are the successful.﴾ Al-falah (success) means attaining the desired goal and prevailing in gaining it. Its root meaning is splitting and cutting. Sharing in the sense of splitting are words that share its first and middle radicals, such as fala, falaqa, and faladha. Repeating the demonstrative (ism al-isharah, the demonstrative noun) indicates that those who possess these qualities deserve, on that basis, independent firmness in guidance and sole claim to success, and that each of the two is exclusive to them. Were it not for this repetition, it could be understood that they alone possess the two together, which would suggest that each one is found in others when taken separately. The conjunction is placed between the two sentences because they stand between full connection and full disconnection. Although they are related, they differ in concept and existence: guidance is in this world and success is in the next, and each is intended in its own right. For this reason they differ from His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Those are like livestock; rather, they are further astray. Those are the heedless.﴾ There the second sentence emphasizes the first, since the comparison with livestock has no meaning except as an intensification of heedlessness, so there is no room for conjoining the two. The pronoun ﴿هم﴾ may be a separating pronoun (fasl, a pronoun placed between subject and predicate to mark the predicate and affirm the relation), or an apposition (badal). In that case al-muflihun is the predicate of ﴿أولئك﴾. Or it may be a subject (mubtada'), with al-muflihun as its predicate, and the whole clause the predicate of ﴿أولئك﴾. This sentence necessarily carries the meaning of restriction (hasr), as is evident. Many have stated that the lam in al-muflihun is the definite article, on the basis that what is intended is the constancy of success. In that case it is among the words where nominal character predominates, or it has been assimilated to the attributive adjective (sifah mushabbahah). The lam may be for the external known reference (al-'ahd al-kharji), to indicate that the God-conscious (al-muttaqin) are those of whom it has reached you that they are successful in the hereafter. The separating pronoun is either for restriction, or merely to affirm the attribution. There is no difficulty in restriction being reversed (qalban), or specifying (ta'yinan), or even individual (ifradan). Or the lam is for the genus, so the sentence points to what every person knows of this concept. If restriction is intended, the separating pronoun serves to affirm the attribution and also to affirm exclusivity. If identity is intended, it serves merely to affirm the attribution.

The Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij have clung to this verse to argue for the eternal punishment of one who abandons an obligation, since restricting the genus of success to those described entails the negation of success for one who abandons prayer and zakat, and so he will be eternally punished. This argument is weaker than a spider's web, and it cannot serve as evidence, because success means avoiding entry (into punishment), or because the negation of complete success, as the context requires, is what is meant, and the context does not require its absolute negation. There is also no need to interpret the God-conscious as those who avoid shirk, so that the sinner may be included among them, because the indication is not directed at them alone, and so this profits nothing, just as the description being praiseworthy does not profit, as is evident.

Here there is a subtle secret: at the opening of His noble Book, He, glorified and exalted, related the servant's praise of his Creator on account of His beneficence toward him, and it ascended in its levels. Then here the Creator praised His servant on account of His guidance to him, and it ascended in its levels, in a single style. So glorified is a glorious God who has bestowed great favor, given abundantly, and been thanked little. To Him belongs grace without counting, and to Him belongs praise without limit.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 6 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾ This is a resumed statement (kalam mustaʾnaf) that distinguishes the condition of the disbelievers, the misguided, the obstinate and the insolent, [a statement] that was driven along right after the explanation of the wondrous conditions of their opposites, who are characterised by the attributes of perfection and who attain their aims both in the present and in the final outcome. It was not conjoined to what precedes it by the conjunction of one story to another story, because the purpose of that is to explain that the Book is characterised by utmost perfection in guidance, establishing that it is certainty with no room for doubt about it. From this also [comes] the explanation that the disbelievers are characterised by persistence in disbelief and misguidance, to the extent that warning does not benefit them. And the view that both [verses] are driven to explain the state of the Book, and that it is guidance for one group but not guidance for others from which no benefit is gained, because the fact that it is not guidance for them is understood secondarily, not intended primarily. Moreover, benefiting from it is an attribute of perfection for it, which supports what preceded regarding the magnification of its status and the elevation of its station, unlike the absence of benefit. It was also said: the omission of the conjunction is because it is another resumed statement, as if it were said a second time: what is the matter with the others that they were not guided by it? So it was answered: because of their aversion, and the loss of their readiness, the call of the Book to faith has not taken effect on them. But this is not correct, because once it is established that those specific attributes are the ones that necessitate [this], no basis remains for this question. More strange than this is the imagination that the omission [of the conjunction] is due to complete connection, supposing that the explanation of the rebellion of the disbelievers confirms that the Book is perfect in guidance. Yes, it is possible, though remotely, that the basis of the question is that one says: if the Book were perfect, it would be guidance for the disbelievers too; so it is answered that its not guiding them is due to their rebellion and obstinacy, not to any deficiency in the Book.

"The star: the eyes find its sight small, and the tail belongs to the glance, not to the star, in terms of smallness."

The conjunction in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the righteous are surely in bliss﴾ ﴿And indeed, the wicked are surely in the Blazing Fire﴾ is because the common factor is unified, since the first sentence is driven to explain the reward of the good, and the second to mention the recompense of the wicked, together with the rhyming and antithesis found in both. Opposition and what resembles it has been counted as a common factor that requires conjunction, because the mind places two opposites in the position of two correlatives, so one strives to join them in the mind, to the extent that they said: the opposite comes to mind alongside its opposite more readily than similar things do.

The sentence is introduced by "inna" to give emphasis to its content, and answers are often introduced by it, because the questioner, being hesitant, is suited to emphasis. The definiteness of the relative pronoun is either for a specific referent, and what is meant are those who were addressed by the Prophet ﷺ with warning in his time and who persisted in their disbelief, or it is for the category, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿like the likeness of one who shouts to what hears nothing﴾ and as in the verse of the poet:
He strives, when I build, to demolish my righteous [works], *** and he who builds is not like one whose nature is demolition.

Then it is general, but the intellect restricts it to those other than the persistent ones, and the report of what was mentioned is an indicator of this. Or the specifier is the return of a specific pronoun to it from the predicate, not the predicate itself. The scholars of legal theory (usuliyyun) have mentioned three opinions regarding the case in which a specific pronoun returns to a general term: it is said that it specifies it, it is said that it does not, and it is said that the matter is suspended. They illustrated this with His words, exalted is He: ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾, since the pronoun in "their husbands" refers only to the revocable divorcees. As for what some of the great exegetes mentioned, that the specifier here is the predicate, it was objected that determining the subject by the meaning of the predicate contradicts what has been established, that the subject must be determined for the addressee before the predicate is mentioned; so if the determination of the subject depended on the predicate, circularity would follow.

Kufr (disbelief), with a dammah, is the opposite of iman (faith). Its original source, from which it is taken, is kufr with a fatha, a verbal noun meaning covering. It is said: kafara yakfuru, from the pattern of qatala. What is in al-Sihah that it is from the pattern of daraba is therefore apparently incorrect, even though the Qamus did not draw attention to it. Its usage became common in the sense of concealing blessings specifically, and in opposition to faith, because in it there is concealment of the truth and of the overflowing bounties of existence. The theologians have found it difficult to define legal disbelief that is not derivative, and they differed in defining it according to their differences in defining faith. However, what the Shafi'is rely upon,

Page 127

may God have mercy on them, is that it is denial of what is known to have been brought by the Messenger ﷺ, of matters that are so widely known that both the elite and the common people recognise them. Therefore one who rejects a consensus in general does not become a disbeliever; rather, whoever rejects a consensus for which there is a text, and which is among the manifest matters that all people share in knowing, such as prayer and the prohibition of wine, [is a disbeliever]. And whoever rejects a consensus that only the elite know, such as the entitlement of a son's daughter to a sixth alongside a daughter of the loins, is not a disbeliever. And whoever rejects a consensus that is manifest but has no text regarding it, there is disagreement over ruling him a disbeliever. As for our masters, the Hanafis, may God be pleased with them, they did not stipulate for takfir anything other than certainty of the established matter to which the denial relates, without requiring that knowledge of it reach the level of necessity. This is a grave matter, and perhaps for this reason Ibn al-Humam said: it must be understood as applying when the denier knows with certainty that it is established, because the basis of takfir is denial or contempt. It is not objected against taking denial into the definition that the people of the law have ruled some acts and statements to be disbelief which are not, when apparent, a denial by their doer, because they explicitly stated that they are not disbelief but only indicate it; the indicator is thus placed in the position of what it indicates, as a protection for the sanctity of the religion and a safeguard for the law of the Lord of the Messengers ﷺ. Some of the forbidden things that desire of the soul prompts are not like this, so the converse does not fail, with regard to sin other than disbelief. Thus the distinctive dress of the disbelievers, for example, is not in reality disbelief, as our master Imam al-Razi and others said; yet they disbelieved by it because it is a manifest sign of an inner matter, namely denial, since the apparent state is that one who believes in the Messenger ﷺ does not adopt it. So when one adopts it, this indicates non-belief. This holds when no evidence exists that negates that indication. For this reason some verifiers said: wearing the distinctive dress of the disbelievers is mockery of them and jesting, and is not disbelief. Our master al-Shihab said: it is not far-fetched when evidence is present. I say: when evidence points to a purpose other than mockery and jesting, there is no disbelief in it either, as some who claim knowledge today suppose, and it has no place in any of this, neither in the caravan nor in the company. Then, denial here means rejection. It is not objected that one who is in doubt, or who is empty of both affirmation and denial, is not an affirmer, nor a rejecter, and that this is a view of an intermediate position between two positions; this is false according to the people of the Sunnah, because it is possible that the disbelief of the doubter and of the empty one exists, since their abstaining from affirmation while having the means, and their complete abandonment of works, is evidence, as stated by al-Salkuti, of denial, just as uttering the words of testimony is evidence of affirmation. It was also said: here it is from ankartu al-shay', meaning I was ignorant of it, so there is no objection either. But it may be replied that ignorance of a thing is the opposite of knowledge, so the one who knows but does not affirm, such as the rabbis of the Jews, would have to be an intermediary, and the difficulty remains as it was. In al-Mawaqif, disbelief is defined as the non-affirmation of the Messenger ﷺ in some of what is known with necessity to have been brought by him. Perhaps he also holds that some acts and statements take the place of non-affirmation. Objection was raised to taking necessity in the definition, that what is established by consensus may leave the category of the necessary, and likewise the innocence of Aisha, may God be pleased with her, was established by the Qur'an, and its verbal proofs do not necessarily produce knowledge, so it too leaves the category of the necessary.

It is answered that the departure of what is established by consensus from the necessary is denied, and verbal indication produces knowledge when combined with indicators, and these exist in the innocence of Aisha, may God be pleased with her. Our companions, may God be pleased with them, have counted in the chapter on takfir many things which, I do not see, necessitate takfir, and expulsion from the religion is a matter that nothing resembles, so caution should be exercised in this chapter as far as possible. The saying of Ibn al-Humam: "Be gentle with people," and in Abkar al-Afkar in this discussion there is what is cause for wonder. I do not desire length without benefit, nor excess without merit.

The Mu'tazilah used this verse and similar ones to argue that the speech of God, glorified and exalted, is created, because the truthfulness of a report in the past tense of this kind requires that the reported matter precede it, namely the temporal relation, and everything preceded by time is created. It is answered that the precedence of the reported matter requires that His eternal speech relate to the reported matter, so what necessarily follows is the precedence of the reported matter over the relation and its occurrence, and this does not entail the creation of speech, just as in His knowledge, exalted is He, of the occurrence of things, there is a relation that occurs while He is not created. Or it is said that His essence, exalted is He, and His attributes

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 6 (part 2 of 3):

Since (Allah) is not temporal, all times are equally present to Him as all places are, so every category of them is present to Him in its own rank. The variation in expressions is with regard to the temporal addressee, in observance of wisdom in the matter of conveying meaning. It has been said other than this, which would take long to mention. We have mentioned in the Fourth Benefit what is useful to you to mention here, so reflect on it.

(Sawa'un) is an ism al-masdar (verbal noun) meaning "equality (istiwa')," and it is not dualized or pluralized. They have dispensed with its dual by using the dual of sayy (equal) except in rare cases. It was originally a masdar, as al-Radi said. It is in the nominative as the predicate of inna, and what follows it is raised by it as its agent. It is as if it were said: "Indeed, those who disbelieved, your warning them and not warning them is equal to them." Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "The two matters are equal," and then he clarified the two matters with His words, glorified is He: ﴿Whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾. Or it is the predicate of what follows it, meaning: your warning and its absence are equal (siyyan). This is the well-known usage among students in such cases.

Several objections have been raised against this. The first: a verb is not attributed to it. The second: it nullifies the front position of the interrogative. The third: the hamza and am are both placed for one of two matters, and whatever indicates equality is attributed only to a plural subject; hence one says "istawa wujuduhu wa 'adamuhu" (his existence and his non-existence were equal), and one does not say "aw 'adamuhu" (or his non-existence). The fourth: if it is a predicate, then it should not be permissible to front it, due to the confusion of the subject with the agent.

The answer to the first is that this is of the type of speech in which the aspect of wording is abandoned in favor of the aspect of meaning, and the Arabs in some of their speech lean toward meanings quite clearly. Among this is: "La ta'kul al-samaka wa tashrab al-laban" (do not eat the fish and drink the milk), meaning: eating fish and drinking milk are not possible for you. If it were taken according to its outward form, it would require coordinating a noun in the accusative with a verb, or rather a single word with a sentence that has no place in i'rab. The claim of al-Baydawi (may Allah whiten the forehead of his affairs) that the word is used for part of its meaning, namely the event, metaphorically, which is why the predication about it is valid, just as it is permissible to predicate about what is meant by the mere wording itself, like "daraba" (he struck), a past verb with an open ba' over what is in it, is not feasible when the two balanced items or one of them, after the hamza of equalization, is a nominal sentence, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿It is equal for you whether you call them or you are silent﴾. Leaning toward meaning also enters into this, although it does not necessarily entail departing from the literal sense.

Ibn Jinni has transmitted from Abu 'Ali that he said: "A compound sentence of subject and predicate takes the place of a verb in the accusative with 'anna' when it is in the accusative and the view is taken that it is so, and the opinion in it is toward the school of the masdar, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Is there any of what your right hands possess, partners in what We have provided you, so that you are equal therein?﴾ and as in His words, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Does he have knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾ Do you not see that the fa' is the answer to the interrogative, and it turns the verb after it into the accusative by an implied 'an', and the accusative verb is necessarily a masdar, to the point that it is as if he said: 'Does he have knowledge of the unseen, then his seeing?' and 'Is there a partnership between you, then equality?'"

As for the second and third, the answer is that the hamza and am have stripped away the meaning of interrogation about one of two matters, and since they are equal in the knowledge of the questioner, they are made equal in the attachment of the ruling to both of them. For this reason it has been said that they are used figuratively to mean the coordinating waw, which indicates the joining of its two coordinated items in some relation, without consideration of precedence or subsequence. Then, this meaning, although intended, is not considered in the title of the subject after composition, just as the meaning of the coordinator is not considered. Therefore one says in the translation here only: "The warning and its absence are equal," without regard to "equality," so that it might be said: if the estimate of the subject is "the two equal," then placing sawa' upon it is superfluous, and it is answered by what has been answered.

The Imam al-Aqsara'i has said: "If you warn them, etc.," it moved from the intention being one of them to the intention being both of them, and this is the meaning of the equality present in it. As for the ruling of equality in the non-benefit, it is not obtained except from His words: ﴿It is equal for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾. It is mentioned that he found a similar statement from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, and the words of Mawla al-Fanari revolve around this same sanctuary. Some verifiers have gone to the view that the two were originally for interrogation about one of two matters, and they are equal in the knowledge of the questioner. That equality has departed here when the interrogation has been stripped from them, and the equality in knowledge remains; this is the meaning of the statement of the one who said: "The hamza and am are both stripped for the meaning of equality," so the result in what we are dealing with is that the two equal items are equal in your knowledge, equal in the futility of benefit. This, despite its artificiality, is dispensed with by what we have mentioned. Similar to it is what al-'Amili mentioned: that the completion of their meaning is both equality and interrogation together, so they were stripped of the meaning of interrogation, and what remained is equality. And because the ruling of equality is repeated with one meaning, emphasis is achieved, as if it were said: "Equal is the warning and its absence is equal," and this is far from the courtyard of verification, as is not hidden. The phrase of the grammarians about "stripping" may imply that there is a metonymy in which the whole is used for its part, but the verified view is that it is either a metaphor or used for a necessary implication of its meaning.

Then, the well-known view is that it is not permissible to coordinate after sawa' with aw if the hamza of equalization is present, to the point that in al-Mughni it is said: "It is a solecism of the jurists." In the commentary on the Book by al-Sirafi: "Sawa' when followed by the alif of interrogation requires am, as in: sawa'un 'alayya aqamta am qa'adta (it is equal to me whether you stood or sat). When one of two nouns is coordinated after it onto another, it is coordinated with waw only, such as: sawa'un 'indi Zayd wa 'Amr (it is equal to me, Zayd and 'Amr). When after it there are two verbs without interrogation, one of them is coordinated onto the other with aw, as in your saying: sawa'un 'alayya qumta aw qa'adta (it is equal to me whether you stood or sat). If after it there are two masdars, such as: sawa'un 'alayya qiyamuka wa qu'uduka (it is equal to me your standing and your sitting), then you may coordinate with waw and with aw." The verbs were preceded by no interrogation because of what that carries of the meaning of conditionality: the example's estimate is: "If you stand or sit, then they are equal to me." The apparent point of this is the exposition of the usages of the Arabs with sawa', and nothing of that is related as irregular. Thus the recitation of Ibn Muhaysin, via al-Za'farani: (sawa'un 'alayhim anzartahum aw lam tunzirhum) is irregular only in transmission, not in usage, as the statement of Ibn Hisham indicates. Understand this position, for many people have erred in it, generation after generation.

As for the fourth, the answer is that the grammarians have explicitly restricted that [fronting] to a verbal predicate, not to a descriptive one, as in: Zayd qama (Zayd stood). So the confusion of subject with agent does not prevent fronting in that case. If it is not prohibited in the clear case of a descriptive predicate, then its non-prohibition here is more fitting, according to what has been said.

He, glorified is He, deviated from the masdar and did not come with it in its original form for two reasons: a verbal reason, which is the good placement of the hamza and am, since they are originally for interrogation, and interrogation is more suited to the verb; and a semantic reason, which is the suggestion of renewal, in view of the apparent form of the expression. In this there is an indication that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, initiated that and brought it into existence, so he discharged the trust and conveyed the message. They did not believe because of the precedence of wretchedness and the attainment of decree, not because of any shortcoming on his part, far be it from him. So although it conveys despair, in it is consolation for him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace.

(Ala) here is considered according to the basic sense of its meaning, because equality is transitive with ala, as in His words: ﴿He istawa ala the Throne﴾. It has been said that it means "inda" (with). In al-Mughni: "ala" is used purely to denote location, and most exegetes take it so. The view that it is here for harm, as in "du'a' 'alayhi" (a curse upon him), is no valid claim, because sawa' is used with ala absolutely, as one says: "My affection is lasting, equal to me whether you visit or do not visit." Al-Inzar is warning in general, or notifying, and it is used most often for warning of the punishment of Allah, and it is transitive to two objects, as in His words: ﴿We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ and ﴿Say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt﴾. So the second object here is omitted, that is, the punishment, apparent and implied, and it was judged good not to estimate it, so that it is general. In al-Bahr: inzar is informing together with threat, within a period sufficient for guarding against the one threatened. If it is not sufficient, then it is notification and information, not warning.

He, glorified is He, did not mention glad tidings, because it is understood by way of the indication of the text, since warning has a stronger effect on the heart and more impact. So when it does not benefit, glad tidings of non-benefit are more fitting. It has been said: there is no place for glad tidings here, because the disbeliever is not fit for them.

His words, mighty is the Speaker: ﴿They will not believe﴾ may be an explanation of the generality of what precedes it, of what contains the equality, and disbelief, and the non-benefit of warning in the past, apparently, with silence about continuation; and ﴿They will not believe﴾ indicates it and clarifies it. So there is no need to say that this is with regard to the concept of the wording, apart from its being a report about the persistent ones. Then it has no place in i'rab, as is the case with explanatory sentences. According to al-Shalawbin, it has a place, because it is a badal (appositive) in his view. It is also possible that it is a circumstantial clause emphasizing what precedes it, and the qualified element is the pronoun in (alayhim) or (andharta-hum). This is not like "Zayd abuka 'atufan" (Zayd, your father, kind), because the conditions that this type requires are absent here, and that

page 130

...that it be a substitute (*badal*). It may be a *badal ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion), since the non-benefit of what has been mentioned includes the lack of faith. Or it may be a *badal kull* (substitution of the whole), because He specified them according to their final state. Or it may be a second predicate after a predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they do not believe." Or it may be the predicate of *inna*, with the sentence before it being an *i'tiraD* (parenthetical insertion). In *al-Tashil* it is said: the parenthetical insertion is that which conveys emphasis, and here it is like the cause of the judgement, because it indicates the hardness of their hearts and their being unaffected by the warning. This requires the lack of faith. Since the subject indicates the lack of faith in the past, and the predicate is taken to mean its continuation in the future, the supposition that there is no benefit in the report is dispelled. Making the sentence a supplication is far-fetched, and even more far-fetched is what is reported: that one pauses at "*am lam tunzir*" (or not), and begins with "*hum la yu'minun*" as a subject and predicate. Rather, this should not be paid any attention.

Al-Jahdari recited *(sawa')* with the hamza lightened, according to the dialect of the Hijaz. So it is possible that he changed the *waw* (into a clear vowel), and it is possible that he made the hamza *bayna bayn* (an intermediate sound between hamza and *waw*). It is reported from al-Khalil that he recited *(suw' 'alayhim)* with a *damma* on the *sin* and a *waw* after it. This is then a departure from the meaning of equality to abuse and ugliness, and in that case it has no grammatical connection with what follows, as in *al-Bahr*.

The Kufans, Ibn Dhakwan, and it is the dialect of the Banu Tamim, recited *(a-andhartahum)* with both hamzas pronounced in full, which is the original form. The people of the Hijaz do not permit joining the two for the sake of lightening. So Ibn Kathir... (the two Haramayn, Abu 'Amr and Hisham) recited with the first hamza pronounced in full and the second lightened. Except that Abu 'Amr, Qalun, Isma'il ibn Ja'far from Nafi', and Hisham insert an *alif* between them, while Ibn Kathir does not insert it. It is also reported that Hisham pronounced both in full with an *alif* inserted between them, and this is the recitation of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Abi Ishaq. It is reported from Warsh, like Ibn Kathir and like Qalun, that the second hamza is replaced by an *alif*, so that two consecutive unvowelled letters meet in a way outside their usual limit according to the Basrans. Al-Zamakhshari claimed that this is a grammatical error (*lahn*) and a departure from the speech of the Arabs in two respects. The first is the joining of two unvowelled letters beyond their limit.
