The second is that the method for lightening a hamza that is vowelled and preceded by an open vowel is by the intermediate sound (*tashil bayn bayn*), not by changing it into an *alif*, since that is the method for an unvowelled hamza. But what they said is the view of the Basrans, while the Kufans permitted joining beyond the limit that the Basrans permitted. This recitation belongs to the category of *ada'* (the manner of delivery). The transmission of the Egyptians from Warsh and the people of Baghdad transmit the intermediate lightening, as is analogical. So criticism of it is not criticism of what belongs to the seven mutawatir (widely transmitted) readings. However, the Mu'tazili erred in manners in his expression. Those who held that obligation can be imposed with what is impossible in itself have argued by this verse and similar ones, on the basis that the relative pronoun is intended to refer to specific people. The gist of the argument is that He, glorified and exalted, informed that they do not believe, and commanded them to believe, and this is impossible. For if it were possible, the supposition of its occurrence would not entail an impossibility. But it does entail one, since if they believed, His report would turn into a lie. Their faith would include the belief that they do not believe, because this is something the Prophet (ﷺ) brought. And their belief that they do not believe is a branch of their being characterized by non-belief, so it would entail their being characterized by belief and non-belief together, and two opposites would be combined. Both of these, the reversal of His report into a lie and the combination of opposites, are impossible, and whatever entails the impossible is impossible. It was answered that their faith is not part of what is in dispute, because it is something possible in itself, and by His, glorified and exalted, informing of their non-belief it does not leave the category of possibility. At most it becomes impossible through something external. The entailment of its occurrence in a lie or in the combination of opposites is only in relation to that. For His informing of the occurrence or non-occurrence of a thing does not negate the power to do it, nor does it take it out of intrinsic possibility, since reversal is impossible. It only negates its non-occurrence or its occurrence, so it becomes impossible through something external. What is necessary for the possible is that the supposition of its occurrence does not entail an impossibility considered in itself. As for considering its impossibility through something external, it may entail what is impossible in itself, like the entailment of the non-existence of the first effect for the non-existence of the Necessary Being. It has been said, to explain the impossibility of their believing that they do not believe, that it is an obligation to two contradictories, because affirming in a report that they do not affirm him in anything entails that they do not affirm him in that. And the obligation to a thing is an obligation to its necessary consequences. This is countered by denial, especially since the consequences are negative.

It has also been said: because their affirming, in that they do not affirm him, entails that they do not affirm him, and what its existence entails for its non-existence is impossible. It was rejected by saying that this entailment may be possible due to its being impossible through something external, as in what we are discussing. It has also been said: because a person's acceptance of something contrary to what he finds in himself is impossible. It was objected that God may not create in them the knowledge of affirming him, so they affirm him in that they do not affirm him. Yes, it is contrary to custom, but it is not impossible in itself. Thus it has been said. And the discussion is not free of something further, and what a thing it is, while the investigation is long. Its full treatment here is like the obligation of what cannot be borne, and it will come to you, God willing, in the most complete form.

Then the benefit of the warning after knowing that it does not produce results is to bring out the secret of what knowledge has preceded, following what is known, of obedience and refusal in those who are obligated, "so that people will have no argument against God after the messengers" (Q. 4:165). For if God had brought everyone initially into His abode, which knowledge had preceded as being their abode, then the state of those who are punished among them would be what God described in His words: "And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: Our Lord, why did You not send us a messenger so that we might follow Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced" (Q. 20:134). So He sent messengers as bearers of good news and warners, in order to bring out what is in their capacity of obedience and refusal. "That he who perishes might perish by clear proof, and he who lives might live by clear proof" (Q. 8:42). For the reminder benefits the believers, and the proof is established against the others, since after the reminder and the conveyance of the message, the motives toward obedience and refusal are stirred according to the eternal capacity. Thus the act or the omission follows from the prior will, which follows knowledge of what is known and eternally established. Thus benefit and harm follow from it, namely reward and punishment. The proof is established against the unbeliever because what he refrains from doing after the call has reached him and the miracle has appeared, namely faith, if it were impossible in itself absolutely, would never have occurred from anyone. But it has occurred. So it is known that its non-occurrence from him was due to refusal arising from his eternal capacity, by his evil choice. And even if his refusal was by God's creation, God's act follows His will, which follows His knowledge, which follows what is known. And what is known, in terms of its eternal established reality, is not made. So knowledge relates to it as it is, in its non-made established reality, which is what its eternal capacity requires. Then will relates to specifying what knowledge has preceded from the requirement of its eternal capacity, and power brings it out in conformity with will. He, exalted, said: "He gave everything its creation" (Q. 20:50). Therefore He said: "Say: To God belongs the conclusive argument. Had He willed, He would have guided you all" (Q. 6:149). But He did not will it, since knowledge had not preceded it, because knowledge is revealing what is known and what is in its capacity. The one known as ready for guidance, in himself, revealed him as he is in accepting it. And the one ready for misguidance is related to as he is in not accepting it. So He willed only what knowledge had preceded of the requirements of capacity, and power brought forth only what God willed. Thus it is valid that to God belongs the conclusive argument, glorified is He, when it is disputed, because God has "given everything its creation" and what its capacity requires, and has not withheld anything from it. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever finds good should praise God," for God is gracious in bringing into existence and is under no obligation. "And whoever finds otherwise, let him blame no one but himself," because He did not bring forth His power in His generosity and mercy except by what wisdom requires, of the matter in which there is no good for him, except because it is the requirement of his capacity. So praise is to God in every state, and we seek refuge in Him from the conditions of the people of deviation and error.

As for His, glorified is He, saying "It is the same for them" and not "for you," it is because warning and its absence are not the same to the Prophet (ﷺ), due to the excellence of the warning that is obligatory for him, over its abandonment. If the relative pronoun is intended to mean specific people, on the basis that it is a definite by prior reference, as has passed, then there is in it a miracle, since He informed of the unseen, namely that those people would die in disbelief, as it happened.

[p. 132]

﴿God has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering; and theirs is a great punishment﴾ is a demonstration *lammi* (a demonstration from the cause to the effect, *propter quid*) for the preceding ruling, just as ﴿It is all the same for them﴾ and what follows, if it is taken as a parenthetical clause, is a demonstration *inni* (a demonstration from the effect to the cause, *quia*). So the sealing and the covering are caused by disbelief itself, while the commission of sins is a cause for persistence in not believing. Alternatively, [the clause is a demonstration] for the equality of warning and not warning. The separation [of this clause from what precedes] is because it answers a question about the cause of the ruling.

*Al-khatm* (sealing) means marking with a seal or the like, and the resulting impression. It is used figuratively at times for making something secure and preventing it, by analogy with the prevention achieved by sealing books and doors. At other times it is used for producing one effect from another, by analogy with the impression that results. And at other times it is understood to include reaching the end, as in *khatamtu al-Qur'an* (I completed the Qur'an).

*Al-ghishawa* (covering), according to the reading of the Seven [Readers], is with a *kasra* on the *ghayn*, from *ghashshahu*, meaning he covered it. Abu 'Ali [al-Farisi] said: "No verb from it has been heard except a *ya'i* verb, so the *waw* [in *ghashwa*] is, in his view, a substitution for a *ya'*." Or it may be said that it has two roots. *Fi'ala* (the pattern *fi'ala/fi'āla*) is, according to al-Zajjaj, for what contains something, like *al-liffa* (wrapping), and from it come the names of crafts like *al-khiyata* (sewing), because they contain what is in them; and likewise what takes control of something, like *al-khilafa* (caliphate). According to al-Raghib [al-Isfahani], it is for what is done with the act, like *al-laff* (wrapping) in *al-liffa*. If it is used for something other than that, it is by way of analogy. Some distinguished between nouns with the feminine *ha'* and those without it: the first is a name for what something is done with, like an instrument, as in *hizām* (belt) and *imām*; the second is for what contains a thing and encompasses it.

The literalists (*al-Zahiriyyun*) took the sealing and the covering in their literal sense, and they committed the modality (*al-kayfiyya*) to the knowledge of the One who has no modality, glorified is He. It is narrated from Mujahid that he said: "When the servant commits a sin, a [mark] is gathered from the heart like this," and he gathered his little finger; "then when he sins again, it is gathered like this," and he gathered his ring finger; and so on up to the thumb. Then he said: "This is the sealing, the stamping and the rust (*al-rayn*)." But it is, to me, unintelligible.

What the muhaqqiqun (the careful scholars) held is that *al-khatm* is borrowed from striking a seal upon things like vessels, to produce a state in the heart and the hearing that prevents the truth from reaching them, just as the imprint of a seal prevents those vessels from receiving what is poised to be poured into them. This is then a metaphor of a perceptible thing for an intelligible thing, with a rational common ground, namely the encompassing of preventing the receptive recipient from receiving what it ought to receive. Then *khatama* (he sealed) was derived from *al-khatm*, so there is a verbal (*tasrihiyya*) metaphor here, of the derivative kind (*tab'iyya*).

As for *al-ghishawa*, it has been borrowed from its original meaning for a state in their eyes that makes them unable to perceive the signs, and the common ground is what has been mentioned. So there is a verbal metaphor here, either original or derivative, if you interpret *al-ghishawa* as a derived noun, or if you make it a noun of instrument, as some have said.

It is also possible that there is in the sentence an allegorical metaphor (*isti'āra tamthiliyya*), by saying: the state of their hearts, their hearing and their eyes, together with the newly formed condition in them that prevents them from benefiting from them, is likened to the state of things prepared for being benefited from in important interests, while they are prevented from that by sealing and covering. Then the expression that indicates the thing likened to is borrowed for the thing being likened, so each of the two sides of the comparison becomes a composite. The common ground is the non-benefit from what was prepared for it, due to an accidental obstacle that can occur in it, like the original obstacle. It is an intellectual matter abstracted from that preparation.

Furthermore, the attribution of the sealing to Him, mighty and majestic, is in terms of creation. The blame and the censure to which the verse points are in terms of its being caused by what the disbelievers acquired of sins, as is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, God has set a seal upon them for their disbelief﴾. Otherwise, censure and blame would be problematic if it were not their own action. So said the commentators of the People of the Sunna, all of them to the last of them, as far as I know. The Mu'tazilites, when they saw that the verse implies that He, glorified is He, prevents the acceptance and hearing of the truth by sealing, which is an ugly thing that cannot proceed from Him, exalted is He, according to their principle, they imposed on the verse interpretations. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned a number of them, to the point that he said: "The Satan is the seal in reality, or the disbeliever. But since God, glorified and exalted is He, is the one who empowered him or enabled him, the sealing is attributed to Him, as it is attributed to the cause, like: 'The emir built the city,' and 'a milch camel' (*naqa halub*)."

I say: The quiddities of possible things are known to Him, glorified is He, from eternity. They are distinct in themselves with an essential distinction that is not made by Him, because the knowledge of them depends on that distinction. And they have essential predispositions (*isti'dadat*), also not made by Him, varying in their demands. The divine knowledge is related to them, revealing them as they are in themselves, with the variation of their predispositions, which are among the keys of the Unseen that none knows but He, and with the variation in the demands of those predispositions. When the divine knowledge relates to them as they are, in what their predisposition requires of choosing one of the two sides, good or evil, the divine will relates to that very thing which the servant has chosen according to his predisposition. So his will, after the relation of the divine will, becomes the will of God, exalted is He. Thus his eternal choice, according to his predisposition, follows the knowledge, which follows the will, out of regard for wisdom. And his choice in what he continually does is subject to the eternal will related to his choice of what he has chosen. So the servants are driven to do what proceeds from them by their choice, not by compulsion or coercion. And they are not compelled in their eternal choice, because it precedes in rank the knowledge that precedes the will. Compulsion follows the will, which follows the knowledge, which follows the known, which here is their eternal choice. So it is impossible that it should follow what is later than it by many ranks.

Thus there is nothing that God, exalted is He, brings forth according to the requirement of wisdom and bestows upon possible things, except that it is what they seek by the tongue of their predisposition. He did not deprive them, glorified is He, of anything of that, as His saying, exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Who gave everything its creation﴾, that is, what is established for it in eternity from what its non-made predisposition requires. Although the existent forms that come into being are made. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He inspired it with its wickedness and its piety﴾, that is, the two established for it in reality. And all of it, insofar as He created it, is good, because it emerges by the requirement of wisdom from an absolute Maker against whom there is no judge. For this reason He, mighty is His majesty, said: ﴿He made good everything He created﴾ and ﴿You see no disproportion in the creation of the Merciful﴾, that is, insofar as it is ascribed to Him and emanates from Him, even if it varies in another respect, and differs when some of it is ascribed to some other.

Accordingly, the sealing from Him, glorified and exalted is He, is then a sign of the equality of their predisposition, established in His eternal, non-made knowledge. Rather, this sealing, which is one of the requirements of the predisposition, was not from God, exalted is He, except that He brought it into existence and manifested His decree in accordance with what He knew of them from eternity, where there is no making. And He did not wrong them, exalted is He, in its manifestation, since it is of His attribute, glorified is He, to bestow existence upon receptacles according to their receptivities, as wisdom requires. But they themselves were wronging themselves, since they were by their essence predisposed to that. Then it becomes clear that the attribution of the sealing to Him, exalted is He, in terms of bringing into existence, is literal truth. And blame is fitting for them because of it, insofar as it indicates the badness of the predisposition and the ugliness of what their essences contained in that opposition: ﴿And the good land brings forth its plants by the permission of its Lord, while that which is bad brings forth only scanty [growth]﴾.

As for what the commentators mentioned, that the attribution of the sealing to Him, exalted is He, is in terms of creation, this is granted, and we have no dispute about it. And as for their saying that the blame is in terms of its being caused by what the disbelievers acquired, etc., we say concerning this: If by *kasb* (acquisition) they mean what has become widespread among the Ash'aris, namely that the act is concomitant with the servant's power without having any influence on it at all, and that the only influential one is God, exalted is He, then this, together with its contradiction to the meaning of acquisition, and its being like ﴿a mirage in a lowland plain, which the thirsty one takes to be water, until when he comes to it he finds it to be nothing﴾, does not heal the sick nor quench the thirst. For the opponent may say: What sense is there in blaming the servant for something in which his power has no part at all, except as the part of a withered hand in what healthy hands do? And at that point what Sahib ibn 'Abbad said on this subject becomes applicable: "How can God command the servant to believe, when He has prevented him from it; and forbid him from disbelief, when He has driven him to it? How does He turn him away from belief and then say: ﴿How are they turned away?﴾; He creates falsehood in them and then says: ﴿How are they deluded?﴾; He produces disbelief in them and then says: 'Why do you disbelieve?'; He creates in them the confusing of truth with falsehood and then says: ﴿Why do you confuse the truth with falsehood?﴾; He turns them away from the path and then says: 'Why do you turn [others] away from the path of God?'; He comes between them and faith and then says: ﴿And what would it harm them if they had believed?﴾; He leads them astray from right guidance and then says: 'Where are you going?'; He misguides them from religion until they turn away and then says: ﴿Why are they turning away from the Reminder?﴾!"

If they answer that God may do what He wills, and that those who object have no standing to object to Him: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they are questioned﴾, we say to them: This is a word of truth by which falsehood is intended, a garden of truthfulness, but you have no gain from it. For His being not questioned about what He does is only because He is wise, who does not do what He would be questioned about. And if you say that the created power has no effect on what it is powerful over, just as knowledge has no effect on what it knows, then the obligation of the servant to his acts is like the obligation to make for himself colors and perceptions. This is a departure from the limit of moderation into the adoption of falsehood and absurdity, and in it is the abolition of the great laws and the rejection of what came from the Prophets, upon them be blessings and peace.

And if they mean by *kasb* the act of the servant independently, that which he wills even if God does not will it, then this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilites, and in it is departure from what the community's predecessors (*salaf*) walked upon, and plunging into the pits of error, and treading the deserts of ruin.

*Like poetry that, if divided among the women, would leave none of them dowered except by divorce.*

But if they mean by it the acquisition by the servant through his created power, according to his eternal predisposition, which is effective, not independently, but by the permission of God, exalted is He, of the voluntary acts with which his will is concerned, that will following the will of God, exalted is He, as we have indicated, then the will is excellent and how good is the course on this path! Its elucidation will come, God willing, exalted is He, and the establishment of proofs for its soundness, and the removal of harm from its way. Yet our Ash'aris today do not perceive it, and they indeed think they are doing well, while evil is what they were doing.

*There is no one in these abodes, a companion in longing, with whom we may converse about the tale of Najd, nor a friend with whom we may keep pace.*

[p. 135 begins mid-passage; the page markers are kept as they appear in the source.]

As for what the Mu'tazilah have said, especially their great scholar al-Zamakhshari, this is not the first blind camel-step they have taken, nor the first pit of desires into which they have been cast down. How often have they descended from the platform of faith in the text to the lowest depths of interpreting it, seeking discord and fulfilling the trial that was written for them. How often have they found the sweet waters of the Sunnah unpalatable, and gone down to the scalding water of innovation, to the places of torment. The doubt that circles here around the forbidden enclosure is that if the acts of servants were created by Allah the Exalted, He would not have forbidden them to His servants, nor punished them for them, and the proof of Allah the Exalted against them would not stand. This doubt is weaker than a spider's web, and indeed the weakest of houses. You already know its answer from what we have set forth for you, and let it be in your mind. Moreover, we return and say: if they base this implication, as they indeed do, on the principle of the goodness and ugliness (of acts), and say: punishing a person, for instance, for the act of another is ugly in the visible world, especially if it comes from the agent himself, so this must be extended to the unseen, then it is said: it is also ugly in the visible world for a person to enable his servant to commit abominations and vices, before his eyes and within his hearing, and then punish him for that while having the power to deter him and to turn him away from them from the beginning. And you say: the power by which the servant creates abominations for himself is created by Allah the Exalted, with His knowledge, may He be glorified and exalted, that the servant creates by it that for himself. This is like giving a sharp sword to a wicked man whom one knows will use it to cut off the road and take captive the sacred women, and that is certainly ugly in the visible world. If they say: there is a wisdom which Allah the Exalted has kept to Himself, which distinguishes between the Unseen and the visible, so that such enabling is good from the Unseen but is not good in the visible, (we reply, by way of concession and agreement with some people): what prevents those acts from being created by Allah the Exalted, and His punishing the servant for them for a benefit and a wisdom which He has kept to Himself, as you have just finished saying, exactly like one feather matching another? Moreover, that the seal in reality is by Satan is something not even Satan would undertake. Do you not hear how he said: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all﴾? So there is no power and no strength except with Allah. Let this amount suffice for this station, and there remains for the reed-pen, if Allah the Exalted wills, a further passage, upon every branch a warbling in the finest station.

(And "the hearts," ﴿qulub﴾) is the plural of qalb (heart). Originally it is a verbal noun, and the name was given to the cone-shaped organ placed in the left cavity of the chest, which is the place where the human subtle essence shines. It is also applied to the subtle, luminous, lordly essence itself, which knows, and which is the descent-point of the divine lights, and by it a human being becomes human, and by it he becomes ready to acquire commands and to avoid prohibitions. It is an essence produced from the spiritual spirit, and the philosophers call it the rational soul. Because it is the target of the arrows of majesty and gentleness, the locus of beauty and splendour, the source of expansion and contraction, the origin of effacement and sobriety, and the spring of praiseworthy character traits and blameworthy states, and because it rarely settles in one state and rarely persists in one manner, it was named qalb (from qalaba, to turn over). It is continually turning over in His affair, and being turned over by the decree and measure of Allah.

In a hadith: "The heart is like a feather in a desert land, which the winds turn over." The poet has also said:

"The heart was named 'heart' because of its turning,
So beware for the heart of a heart and of transformation."

And calling the familiar bodily organ "heart," if you look closely, is only because of the turning of that shining subtle essence upon it, since it is the principal organ, the source of the innate heat that sustains the whole body. Its soundness and corruption are used as a figure for the soundness and corruption of that subtle essence, because of the connection between them, the reality of which none knows except Allah the Exalted. Perhaps for this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed it is the heart." Many people have held that this piece of flesh is the place of knowledge. It has been said that it is in the brain, and it has been said that it is shared between them. This is built upon the affirmation of the inner senses, and the discussion of them is well known. Whoever reflects will find that he has perceived that between the brain and the heart there is a spiritual bond and a secret mutual relation, which no one denies who has a heart, or who gives ear while being present. But knowing the reality of this is as difficult as it is unattainable, and pointing to the essence of what lies there is hard for the masters of realities and the people of subtleties. Whoever knows himself knows his Lord, and inability to grasp the grasping is itself a grasping.

The word ﴿sam'﴾ (hearing) is the verbal noun of sami'a, sam'an and sama'an. It is applied to a power deposited in the nerve that is spread out or extends into the ear, by which sounds are perceived. It is sometimes used to refer to the ear itself and sometimes to the act, as in ﴿Indeed, they are removed from hearing﴾. And ﴿abṣār﴾ (sights) is the plural of baṣar, which originally means the perception and sensing of the eye. Then it was used figuratively for the power deposited at the junction of the two hollow nerves that connect the brain to the two eyeballs, which by its nature perceives colours and shapes in a detail known in its proper place, and also figuratively for the eye which is its locus. This became so common that it became the literal meaning in common usage, because it comes to mind first. It suits the ﴿ghishāwah﴾ (covering), since that is attached to the eyes, and what suits the covering also suits the sealing.

The reason why Allah the Exalted placed the sealing before the hearts here is that the verse is an affirmation of the absence of faith, so it was fitting to mention the hearts first, since they are the locus of faith, while hearing and sight are paths and instruments for it. This is different from His saying: ﴿and has sealed over his hearing and his heart﴾, for that is directed toward indifference to admonitions, and therefore the closing phrase is ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾. Thus the more suitable order there is to mention hearing first. Allah, whose majesty is great, repeated the preposition so that it would be more indicative of the intensity of the sealing in both places. For whatever is placed in a chest, when its chest is sealed and its house is sealed, is stronger in preventing access to it. And it is more evident in independence, because repeating the preposition requires taking into account the meaning of the transitive verb governed by it, so that it is as though it were mentioned twice. This is why they say: "I passed by Zayd and 'Amr" indicates one passing, while "I passed by Zayd and by 'Amr" indicates two passings. Although conjunction is in effect a repetition, it is not as clearly equal to it in conveying meaning, because it carries a possibility of ambiguity.

He made ﴿sam'﴾ (hearing) singular although it is in fact plural. The principle of arrangement by parallelism and matching would require that it follow the pattern of the other two, for brevity and variety, together with an indication of a subtle point: that the objects perceived by hearing are of one kind, while the objects perceived by the other two are different. Eloquent speakers often take such things into account. It has also been said that the singularity of the word indicates the singularity of what it names, namely the sense faculty, and the singularity of the faculty indicates the paucity of what it perceives at first glance, so there is an implicit meaning, and a similar sort of implication is sufficient in ordinary usage. From this one may recognise the reason for the plural ﴿qulub﴾ (hearts) alongside the plural ﴿abṣār﴾ (sights) being fewer in number, although the usage of the jurists is that the plural is used for all of them. Moreover, hearing rarely strikes the ear (in the sense of rarely being used), and from this comes the reading of Ibn Abi Ablah in the non-canonical readings: ﴿and upon their hearings﴾. He cited as evidence for it the verse:

"She said, without intending the speech of obscenity:
'Enough! You have reached my hearing!'"

The view that it is singular for the sake of avoiding confusion, as in the verse:

"Eat from the middle of your bellies, that you may be chaste,
For your time is a time of hunger,"

is not worth anything, and neither is the view that it is singular because it is originally a verbal noun and verbal nouns are not pluralised, so it was observed as such. For what has been mentioned is a justifying factor, not a preferring one. In my view what is closer to this is to posit an elided genitive, such as ﴿and the faculties of their hearing﴾. The readers have agreed on stopping at ﴿their hearing﴾, and this apparent stop indicates that it has no connection with what follows, so it is conjoined to ﴿upon their hearts﴾. This is preferable to saying that it is itself, and that what is conjoined to it, is a fronted predicate for ﴿a covering﴾, or two governing elements in a relation of competition, though the verse may allow that, because the parallel to it is fixed in the verse ﴿and has sealed over his hearing and his heart﴾, and the Qur'an explains one part by another. Also, hearing, like the heart, perceives what it perceives from all directions, so it was fitting that it be joined with sealing, which prevents from all of them, even if sealing specifically falls on one side, though it is not restricted to that.

Since the perception of sight normally occurs only by facing and direct opposition, the impediment was made to be what prevents that, namely the covering, because it is generally of that kind, like the cover of a saddle. This suffices for the subtle points, and it does not harm it that the covering wraps around all sides like a garment. As for what is in al-Kashshaf, that the covering is well known in diseases of the eye, and therefore it is more suited to sight without needing what they have strained to, the examination of the linguistic meaning by someone who has no covering over his sight reveals its state. Perhaps the reason for putting hearing before sight is that it shares with the heart the capacity to act in the six directions, just as the heart does, and not sight. From here it has been said that hearing is superior to sight. The truth is that each of the senses is necessary in its place, and whoever loses one sense loses a kind of knowledge. Preferring some over others is a lengthy digression without any profit.

It has been read with imala of ﴿abṣārihim﴾ (their sights). The reason for imala here, although the ṣād is an emphatic letter which is contrary to it because the emphatic letters require the lowering of sound, is the harmony with the kasra, and it is taken into account on the rā' rather than other letters, because of the fitness of imala with thinness. The well-known view among the grammarians of Arabic is that this is because of the strength of the rā', lest the rā' be trilled, since trilling is harmful to correct articulation, to the extent that I heard from some Shafi'is that whoever repeats the rā' in the takbir of the iḥram, his prayer is not valid. But the responsibility for that lies with the transmitter.

The majority hold that ﴿upon their sights﴾ is the fronted predicate of ﴿a covering﴾, and fronting is what validates beginning with an indefinite noun, although there is a conformity of the sentence before it, because the fronting of the component about which the judgment is made is what is involved, and here it is so. So in the verse there are two declarative sentences: a verbal one, indicating renewal, and a nominal one, indicating permanence, so that it is as though the covering were innate in them. That the two sentences are supplicatory is nothing. In the fronting of the verbal sentence there is an indication that this has already occurred and is finished.

Al-Mufaddal, Abu Haywah, and Isma'il ibn Muslim read ﴿a covering﴾ in the accusative. It has been said that it is in the accusative because of an elided preposition. Abu Hayyan said: it may be a verbal noun derived from the meaning of "sealed," because its meaning is "covered and concealed," as though it were said "a covering," as an emphasis. In that case, their hearts, their hearing, and their sights are sealed and covered. It has been said also that it may be the object of "sealed," and the adverbial phrases are circumstantial, meaning: the sealing of a covering that is upon these things, so that it cannot be dealt with by lifting or removal. In each case there is what is not hidden. The reading in the nominative is therefore preferable.

It has also been read with a ḍamma on the ghayn and nominative; with a fatḥa on the ghayn and accusative; ﴿ghishwah﴾ with a kasra on the unpointed letter in the nominative, and with a fatḥa in both nominative and accusative; ﴿ghashyah﴾ with fatḥa and nominative; and ﴿ʿashāwah﴾ with a fatḥa on the unmarked letter and nominative. It was also permitted to read it with kasra and accusative from

[Page 138 begins mid-passage]

with the fatḥah and short vowel (*qaṣr*), meaning sight by day rather than by night. The meaning is that they see with the sight of heedlessness, not the sight of reflection. Or it means that they do not see the signs of God Most High in the darkness of their disbelief; were that darkness to lift, they would see them.

Al-Raghib said: *al-'ashā* is a darkness that afflicts the eye, and *'ashā 'an kadhā* means he became blind to such-and-such. God Most High says: ﴿And whoever turns blindly away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ (43:36). The meaning in this sense is then clear. The tanwīn (nunation) in *ghishāwah* indicates a type of covering different from what people are familiar with. It may also be for emphasis, meaning: a covering, what a covering! Some have expressly taken it to signify both type and emphasis together, just as it has been taken to signify both multiplicity and emphasis together in God's words: ﴿So messengers have indeed been denied﴾ (35:4).

The *lām* in *lahum* is the lām of entitlement (*lām al-istiḥqāq*), as in ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾ (2:114). In *al-Mughni* (Ibn Hisham): the lām of entitlement is the one that falls between a meaning and an entity, and here too it is so, except that the predicate has been placed first for stylistic preference, because the subject is an indefinite noun qualified by an adjective. Had it been placed after, it would have been permissible, as in *ajalun musammā ʿindahu* (a term appointed with Him). It may also be, as has been said, that its being placed first is for restriction: no one shall punish with their punishment, and no one shall bind with their bond. As for the lām being for benefit, and it being used here for mockery, this has no basis, because the lām of benefit occurs only in opposition to *ʿalā* ("against") in supplication and what is close to it, and no one trustworthy has said it here. One does not say ʿalayhimu al-ʿadhāb (the punishment is upon them).

The apparent view is that the sentence is brought to explain their persistence: that their faculties have been sealed, and that wretchedness has been sealed upon them. It is coordinated with what precedes it, and is neither a fresh sentence (*isti'nāf*) nor a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). Al-Sakalkuti said: it is coordinated with *alladhīna kafarū* ("those who disbelieve"), the common element being that the preceding describes their state while this describes what they deserve. Or it is coordinated with the predicate of *inna* (indeed), the common element being sharing in the subject together with the harmony of the concepts of the two predicates. The purpose of this is to repel what might be imagined, namely that they do not deserve punishment for their disbelief, because being sealed and covered by God Most High is not a fitting excuse, as is not hidden.

The word *ʿadhāb* (punishment) originally means persistence, and then it was extended so that every persistent pain is called by it. From it they derived *ʿadhdhabtuhu*, meaning I kept the pain continuously upon him. This is what Abu Hayyan reported, and from al-Khalil, and many inclined to it, that its root is prevention: *ʿadhaba al-faras* means the horse refused fodder, and from it *al-ʿadhb* (sweet water) because it prevents thirst. Then it was extended and applied to every painful, arduous thing absolutely, even if it does not prevent or deter. For this reason it is more general than *nakāl* (exemplary punishment), since *nakāl* is what deters, like *ʿiqāb* (retribution). It has been said: *ʿiqāb* is what one is requited with, as in the Hereafter.

The explanation covers the punishment of children, animals and others. Al-Sajawandi restricted *ʿadhāb* to the infliction of pain upon a living being together with humiliation; so the causing of pain to children and animals is not a punishment in his view. It has been said that *ʿadhāb* is originally derived from *taʿdhīb*, and then was used for infliction of pain absolutely. The origin of *taʿdhīb*, as is said, is repeatedly striking with the tip of the whip. Al-Raghib said: its origin is from *ʿadhb* (sweetness), so *ʿadhdhabtuhu* means I removed the sweetness of his life, on the pattern of *marradtuhu* (I made him ill) and *qadhdhaytuhu* (I afflicted him).

The indefiniteness in it is for type: for them in the Hereafter there is a kind of punishment unfamiliar in the punishments of this world. Taking it to be for magnification requires taking what is derived from the qualifier as emphasis, and there is no need for this.

*Al-ʿaẓīm* means the great. It has been said that it is above *al-kabīr* (the big), because the big is opposed by the small, and the magnificent is opposed by the contemptible, and the contemptible is below the small. So the small and the contemptible are both base, and the contemptible is the more base of the two; the magnificent and the big are both noble, and the magnificent is the more noble of the two. Thus describing punishment with *ʿaẓīm* is more powerful in inspiring awe than describing it with *kabīr*, as many have mentioned, among those whose excellence is widely known, since the custom is that the most base is opposed by the most noble, and the base by the noble. What is imagined, that the opposite of the more specific is more general, is not to be heeded here.

Yes, it is problematic for the claim that *ʿaẓīm* is above *kabīr* that He, may His majesty be exalted, said in the sacred hadith: "Greatness (*al-kibriyāʾ*) is My cloak, and majesty (*al-ʿaẓamah*) is My waistwrap." Here He, glory be to Him, placed greatness in the position of the cloak and majesty in the position of the waistwrap. It is known that the cloak is higher than the waistwrap, so the attribute of greatness (*kibr*) must be higher than majesty. It may be said that *al-kabīr* is great in His essence, whether or not others regard Him as great; but majesty is an expression of His being such that others regard Him as majestic. On this basis the first attribute is essential and nobler than the second.

It is possible to answer this with a remote answer: what they have mentioned applies only when *al-kabīr* and *al-ʿaẓīm* are used of other than God Most High, or when the speech is free of any indication requiring the reverse. Or it may be said that He, glory be to Him, made majesty, which is nobler than greatness, a waistwrap, because few know Him, may His majesty be exalted, under this title in relation to those who know Him under the title of greatness. Because those few were few, it was a waistwrap; because these are many, it was a cloak. Glory be to the Great, the Magnificent.

[Page 139 begins]

Al-Raghib mentioned that the original sense of *ʿaẓuma al-rajulu* was that his bones became large (*kabura ʿaẓmuhu*), then it was borrowed for every big thing and given its standing, whether sensible or intelligible, whether a meaning or a physical entity. When *al-ʿaẓīm* is used of physical things, its basic usage is for connected parts, while *al-kabīr* is used of separated parts. *Al-ʿaẓīm* may also be used of separated things, meaning *kabīr*, as in "a great army" (*jaysun ʿaẓīm*). The magnitude of a punishment relative to a lesser punishment involves an interval of slackening (*futūr*), and by this interval two punishments can be differentiated, as two blacks may be, one blacker than the other, and something other than black may intervene between them.

The Muslims have held that it is good (*ḥasan*) for God Most High to punish disbelievers, and this verse and similar ones are true evidence for that. Some said that it is not good, and they cited rational proofs founded on the rational goodness and badness of acts (*al-ḥusn wa'l-qubḥ al-ʿaqliyyān*: the doctrine that reason itself can determine that acts are good or bad). They said: punishment is harm devoid of benefit, since He, glory be to Him, is exalted above benefiting from anything, while the servant is harmed by it. Even if we grant that He benefits, God Most High is able to deliver the benefit to him without punishment, and harm devoid of benefit is manifestly ugly. Also, the disbeliever shows nothing but disobedience, so when he is made subject to obligation, punishment follows; and what leads to harm without benefit is ugly. Then either it is said there is no obligation, or there is obligation without punishment. Also, He is the creator of the motive to disobedience, so it is ugly to punish for it.

They also said: granted that we concede punishment, whence comes the claim of its perpetuity? And the most hard-hearted of people, if someone who has greatly wronged him and whom he punishes and persists against is taken, everyone blames him; and it is said to him: either kill him and relieve him, or pardon him. If this is ugly from a human who delights in vengeance, how would perpetuity befit the Self-Sufficient, who is free of all needs?

Also, whoever repents of disbelief, even after a time, God Most High accepts his repentance. Do you think that this great generosity is abandoned in the Hereafter, or that the minds of those who are punished are stripped away so that they do not repent? Or would it be fitting for Him to say in this world, "Call upon Me, I will answer you," and in the Hereafter not to answer their supplication except with, ﴿Remain in it in disgrace, and do not speak to Me﴾ (23:108)?

* * *

What remains is holding to the verbal evidences, and these do not produce certainty, so they do not oppose the rational proofs that do. Moreover, we claim that the threats of punishment regarding disbelievers are conditional upon the absence of pardon, even if this condition is not stated explicitly, as whoever permitted pardon for the sinful said regarding those threats. Furthermore, it is possible that those sentences are supplicatory, or that they are informative, but informing about deserving the occurrence and not about the occurrence itself. This is the summary of what has been said on this subject. Imam al-Razi expanded the discussion on it, but did not follow it with anything that would soothe the heart and cool the liver. That is a trait I recognise from Akhzam (a familiar, recurring disposition). By my life, these are doubts that have taken hold in the hearts of many people, becoming for them the slinking whisperer, so they cast off the bond of obligation and deviated from the upright religion. For the firmly established believers they are like the creaking of a door, or like the buzzing of a fly.

I say, and my success is only through God; in Him I trust, and to Him I turn: the negation of punishment absolutely is something that none of those who believe in God Most High and the Last Day has said, even the Magians, though they have reached the furthest extremes of delirium. For their wise men, far from reason, claimed that Iblis, may he be cursed, remained in darkness, apart from the authority of God Most High, then kept crawling until he saw the light, and leapt, and so came under the authority of God Most High, and calamities and evils were introduced with him. So God Most High made this world a net for him, and he fell into it, so he could no longer return to his realm. He remained imprisoned, struck by calamities. Whoever God gives life, He causes to die; whoever He makes healthy, He makes sick; whoever He makes joyful, He saddens. Each day his dominion diminishes, and when the Resurrection comes and his strength is gone, God Most High will cast him into the air, and will call the people of the religions to account, and will requite them for their obedience to Satan and their disobedience to Him.

Indeed, it is well known from them that worldly pains are ugly in themselves, and are never good in any respect; so they issue from the darkness and not from the light. The falsity of this doctrine is more manifest than fire on a mountain-top. Even if we grant that some people say this, it is rejected. Most of the proofs cited in this subject are founded on the rational goodness and badness of acts, and Ahl al-Sunnah wa'l-Jamaʿah (the Sunni community of orthodoxy) denied both, and established proofs for their falsity. The prevalence of that in the books of kalām (theology) makes its transmission here idle talk.

Moreover, we say: God Most High has two attributes, of gentleness (*luṭf*) and of subjugation (*qahr*). It is obligatory in wisdom that the King, especially the King of kings, be such, since each of them is among the attributes of perfection, and neither can stand in for the other. Whoever denies this has been obstinate. Such a thing has been praised in human experience, as has been said:

"Your one hand is one whose good is hoped for, and the other is one that enrages your enemies."

[Page 140 marker omitted]

When God, glory be to Him, looked upon what He knows of the eternal quiddities (*mahiyyat*, the essential realities of things) and the fixed entities (*a'yan thabitah*), and saw among them those who were predisposed to good and sought it by the tongue of their predisposition, and those who were predisposed to evil and sought it likewise, He bestowed upon each, in accordance with His wisdom, what they were predisposed to, and gave them what they had asked of Him. Then He imposed obligations upon them, encouraged them, and warned them, in completion of His favour and in manifestation of the proof. For had He punished him and displayed in him the attribute of His subjugation before warning him, it might well have been said: ﴿Why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced?﴾ Thus punishment, even though it brings Him, glory be to Him, no benefit in the familiar sense, is nevertheless one of the effects of subjugation (*qahr*), and the placing of a group in the path of subjugation is necessary in His wisdom, exalted is He. Whatever His wisdom and perfection require is good. And if you wish, say: the two attributes of gentleness (*lutf*) and subjugation are among the consequences of His essence, which is in the utmost perfection, and they have objects of relation in reality, predisposed to them from eternity by a predisposition that is not created. God, glory be to Him, knew from eternity the relations and the related objects, so they manifested in accordance with what He knew. Had they not manifested thus, the reversal of realities would follow, and that is impossible. Therefore faith and disbelief are, in reality, not a true cause and a complete reason for bliss and punishment; rather they are signs of them, to which wisdom and mercy called. This is the meaning of what is related in the authentic collection: "Act, for each is made easy for that for which he was created." As for one who was, in God's knowledge, among the people of happiness whose essence is predisposed to it, he will be made easy, in accordance with mercy, for the deeds of the people of happiness, because it is His way to overflow upon receptacles according to their capacities. As for one who was, from eternity and in the eternal knowledge, among the people of misery, which was established for his quiddity, not created, from eternity, he will be made easy, in accordance with subjugation, for the deeds of the people of misery. In this the favour becomes manifest and the proof is complete.

The words of God, exalted is He, ﴿Had He willed, He would have guided you all﴾ are not an objection to this, because the negation of guidance is due to the negation of will. Undoubtedly will follows knowledge, and knowledge follows the establishment of the known in reality, as His words, exalted is He, concerning the impossible non-existent that is not established in itself, indicate: ﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth?﴾ Where guidance has no establishment in itself, knowledge has no relation to it, and where there is no relation there is no will. So the cause of the negation of bringing guidance into existence is the negation of will, and the cause of the negation of will is the fixed non-existence of guidance in itself. The matter thus returns to this: the cause of the negation of bringing guidance into existence is its absence in reality and its not being fixed in eternal knowledge. ﴿And had God known any good in them, He would have made them hear﴾.

When this is impressed upon the page of your mind, we say: their claim that harm devoid of benefit is ugly is self-evidently ugly and is nothing, because that harm is one of the effects of subjugation, which follows the Most Holy Essence. Whenever it is void of subjugation, He, exalted is His dignity, is far above what the wrongdoers say, like the one-handed man who has only one hand. Rather, whoever his intellect treats justly knows that the absence of the attribute of subjugation undermines lordship, strips away the garment of majesty, and lowers the station of sovereignty, for then He would not be feared, the order would be disrupted, and the bonds of this arrangement would come apart. Moreover, this objection requires the absence of suffering for animals in this world, especially cattle and children, who receive from these pains no benefit at all, neither immediately nor later, although we observe the occurrence of such things more than the stars of the sky. So whatever their answer is concerning these pains from Him, exalted is He, in this world, though He gains nothing from them in any way, that is our answer concerning punishment in the other world.

As for their saying that the unbeliever shows nothing but disobedience, so his obligation, once it occurs, entails punishment, etc.: in reply, the unbeliever, in God's knowledge, according to his predisposition, is passionately attached to the Fire, as iron is attached to a magnet. Even if some one turns away from it, turning away from Paradise as darkness turns away from light, if he becomes attached to it, then whether he is obligated or not, he must be punished therein. But the obligation serves to bring out what lies in his predisposition of refusal, in order to manifest the proof, while unbelief is merely a sign.

﴿God did not wrong them, but they were wronging themselves﴾.

[Page 140 marker omitted]

As for their saying that He, glory be to Him, is the Creator of the motive to disobedience, this is granted, but He created it and manifested it in accordance with what the essential predisposition called for, and the power has no role except in bringing it into existence. What ugliness is there in giving a thing what it asked for by the tongue of its predisposition, even if that harms it? Nor does it follow for God, exalted is He, by reason, that He must abandon the requirement of His wisdom and nullify the status of His lordship, while His knowledge does not relate to anything contrary to what that predisposition required.

As for their saying: "Suppose we grant the punishment, whence comes its perpetuity, etc.?" We say: perpetuity arises from the corruption of the essence and the ugliness of the attributes, which are established in them from eternity and manifest eternally through refusal after obligation, with regard to wisdom. This corruption abides in them as long as the essential wisdom of God and their essences endure, as His words, exalted is He, guide you to this: ﴿And if they were returned, they would revert to what they were forbidden﴾. An effect endures as long as its cause endures. Or it may be said: punishment, which in reality is distance from God, is necessarily tied to unbelief, and the necessary cannot be separated from the necessitated. Also, unbelief, when the proof is manifest in the souls and the horizons, concerning One whose greatness is boundless and whose majesty is unlimited, is a matter whose ugliness the scope of thought cannot encompass. Even if He, glory be to Him, is not harmed by it, the divine jealousy (*ghayrah ilahiyyah*) does not accept it, even though the eternal power overflows it in accordance with predisposition by the requirement of wisdom. Such a thing calls for everlasting punishment and endless chastisement, and a thing's like is drawn to it.

This should not be compared with the example it set forth, for where is the lowliness of dust compared with the majesty of the Lord of lords? The source of the two questions is not one and the same spring.

As for their saying: "Whoever repents of unbelief, even after a while, God repents toward him. Do you think that this great generosity will vanish in the Hereafter, or that the minds of those punished will be taken away, so they will not repent, etc.?" In reply: whoever repents of unbelief has replaced the ugly with its opposite, and God, glory be to Him, has manifested the requirement of His essence and His quiddity, which He knew. Then there is an ugly unbelief that has passed away and a good faith that is established. Along with this faith comes regret for that unbelief, in an abode where the making up for what was missed and regret for slips are of benefit. So unbelief becomes, through this faith, as though it had never been anything worth mentioning, since the ugly is exchanged for the good, and regret remains, which is the pillar of repentance, as gain. Moreover, the appearance of faith after unbelief is a sign of the nobility of the essence in itself and its purity in its being known. "Deeds are judged by their endings." So there is no wonder in God, exalted is He, forgiving him out of bounty and generosity. God's mercy, though it encompasses all things in some of its aspects, has specific regard for the God-fearing in another aspect, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿My mercy encompasses all things, so I will prescribe it for those who fear God﴾. It is like His presence, glory be to Him, which is not described in modes: do you not hear His words, once: ﴿There is no secret conversation among three but that He is their fourth, nor among five but that He is their sixth, nor fewer than that or more but that He is with them wherever they are﴾; and at another time: ﴿Indeed, God is with those who fear Him and those who are doers of good﴾; and at another: ﴿Indeed, God is with us﴾; and at yet another: ﴿Indeed, my Lord is with me﴾.

That mercy has a wider circle than wrath does not contradict this, as indicated by ﴿The Most Merciful, established on the Throne﴾, nor does it mean that the punished unbelievers outnumber the blessed believers, as His words, exalted is He, imply: ﴿But most of mankind do not believe﴾. Likewise the hadith about the resurrection (*ba'th*), because this multitude is in relation to the children of Adam, who are few in relation to the angels, the houris, and the youths: ﴿None knows the hosts of your Lord but He﴾; ﴿He creates what you do not know﴾. So the people of mercy will be more numerous than the people of wrath. Moreover, the people of the Fire are shown mercy even in their punishment. What is with God is of everything without end. Some evil is lighter than other evil, and they differ in punishment. Between the punishment of each rank and another is the distance between heaven and earth, even if each of its inhabitants thinks he is the most severely punished. But the matter in reality is not so; rather, some of them find pleasure in their punishment from certain aspects, while others do not. Yes, among them is one whose punishment is pure, with no pleasure in it for him, yet even so they loathe themselves, knowing that it was they who had made themselves ready for this, so there overflowed upon them what overflowed from the side of the overflowing Source, as His words, exalted is He, indicate: ﴿The hatred of God for you is greater than your hatred of yourselves﴾. Whoever among them is heedless of this, Iblis, may he be cursed, reminds him of it, as God relates of him: ﴿So do not blame me, but blame yourselves﴾. Repentance does not benefit them there as it benefits them here, because the two abodes have differed, the two groups have been distinguished, and the term set for [repentance] has come to an end

[Page 141 marker omitted]

by the requirement of the divine wisdom. We have seen in what is witnessed that medicine has a specific time for its benefit, and if that time is exceeded it may cause harm. Among the unbelievers is one who knows that the time has passed and that period has ended, and that repentance was only in the worldly abode. That is why he says: ﴿My Lord, send me back, that I may do righteousness in what I have left behind﴾. Since this was the request of one who knows from one aspect and is ignorant from another, God, exalted is He, answered him: ﴿No! It is merely a word he speaks﴾. He was not harsh with him as He was harsh with those who said: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾, since the latter spoke out of pure ignorance. So He answered them: ﴿Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me﴾. When the request differed, the answer differed. Not every supplication is answered, as is not hidden from people of understanding.

As for their saying: "The proof by verbal evidence remains, and it does not yield certainty, so it does not oppose rational proofs which yield certainty": the reply is that if they mean these rational proofs yield certainty, then you know their state, that they are like a mirage in a level plain. Would that they yielded even conjecture. If they mean rational proofs in general, these are not among them. Moreover, the view that verbal proofs do not yield certainty is the position of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school) and the majority of the Ash'ariyyah (followers of al-Ash'ari). The truth is that they may yield certainty when accompanied by witnessed or mass-transmitted indicators that establish the absence of possibilities. From the truthfulness of the speaker one knows the absence of a rational contrary, for when the meaning is determined and was intended by him, if there were a rational contrary, it would follow that he lied. Yes, there is room for examination regarding whether verbal proofs yield certainty in rational matters, because their yielding certainty depends on whether the certainty that there is no rational contrary is attained by them alone and by considering them, together with the truthfulness of the speaker, and whether the indicator that is witnessed or transmitted by mass transmission has any role in that certainty. Whether that certainty is attained by them alone, and whether the indicator has a role in it, is something whose affirmation or negation cannot be decided. Therefore their yielding certainty in rational matters is a matter for consideration and reflection.

If you say: when the truthfulness of the speaker is held as certain, it follows that certainty about the absence of a contrary in rational matters follows, just as it follows in legal matters; otherwise his speech would allow the possibility of lying in both, and so there is no difference between them.

I say: Some of the verifying scholars answered that what is meant by the revealed matters (*sharʿiyyāt*, matters known only through revelation) is things whose existence or non-existence the intellect judges to be possible, with no means of access to them except revelation. By the rational matters (*ʿaqliyyāt*, matters known through reason) is meant what is not so. In that case, it is possible that some of them are among the impossible things. Because of this possibility, certainty may not be reached that there is no rational counter-evidence against the transmitted proof in rational matters, even though certainty is reached in revealed matters. This differs from rational proofs in rational matters, for these by themselves yield certainty that there is no counter-evidence, because they are composed of premises whose soundness is known by immediate intuition, or whose entailment is known by immediate intuition from what is known to be sound by immediate intuition. In that case, it is impossible that anything should exist that contradicts them, because the judgments of immediate intuition do not, in reality, conflict at all.

That said, the eminent Rumi scholar said: Here there is a well-known discussion, namely that the meaning of "no rational counter-evidence in revealed matters" is the truthfulness of the speaker. This also holds in rational matters. And what the intellect does not judge to be possible or impossible in existence or non-existence does not necessarily belong to the impossibilities, since its possibility may be hidden from the intellect. Therefore, every matter that is known to have been spoken by the Law should be understood in this sense, lest its falsehood be entailed and the intellect's certainty of its truth be nullified. So the truth is that transmitted evidence yields certainty in rational matters as well. There is no escape except by saying that what is meant is that considering the proofs themselves and the indications in revealed matters yields certainty that there is no counter-evidence, because the truthful speaker's intention is certainly conveyed. In rational matters, whether his speech conveys certainty of there being no counter-evidence is a matter for examination, on the basis that his conveying of intention is merely probable. End of quotation.

The Greatest Shaykh, may Allah sanctify his secret, held that transmitted evidence takes precedence over rational evidence. In the seventy-second chapter after four hundred of the *Futuhat*, he said:

*We relied on the report, and so we became people of understanding,*
*and there is no knowledge in what does not come from the report.*

He, may Allah sanctify his secret, also said in the three hundred and fifty-eighth chapter:

*How can reason be evidence, when what reason built*
*has been demolished by unveiling?*
*So the soul's salvation lies in the Law, so do not be*
*a person who saw and then was deprived.*
*Page 142*
*Hold fast to the Law in unveiling, for*
*servants who were preserved have won the good.*
*Neglect thought and do not concern yourself with it,*
*and leave it like meat in a pot.*
*Thought has a station, so rely on it,*
*and in it you will be a person who is shown mercy.*
*Every knowledge that the Law testifies to*
*is knowledge in which you should hold fast.*
*And if reason contradicts it, then say:*
*keep to your own station, where you have a foothold.*

This is supported by what is related from al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Reason has a limit at which it ends, just as sight has a limit at which it ends." Imam al-Ghazali said: "Do not consider it unlikely, O you who secludes himself in the world of reason, that beyond reason there is another stage in which things appear that do not appear in reason, just as you should not consider it unlikely that reason is a stage beyond discernment and sense perception, in which worlds and wonders are revealed that sense perception falls short of," and so on to the end of what he said. Thus, in what we are discussing, there are countless matters in the Qur'an and in the mass-transmitted Sunnah that indicate eternal abiding in the Fire, and in the punishment there is a clear indication with no ambiguity. To interpret all of them by mere doubts is weaker than spider's web. To turn away from them to the claim that there is no punishment or no eternal abiding in it is not appropriate, especially in times like these in which people are as you see. Moreover, these interpretations are utterly feeble. For how can the reality of supplication be conceived from the Lord of the earth and heaven? Or how can the conditional clause be understood after considering His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾? Or how can it be accepted that the report concerns entitlement rather than actual occurrence, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Every time it dies down, We increase for them the blaze﴾ and ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We replace them with other skins﴾? Glory be to You, this is a tremendous slander.

As for what is related from some of the righteous predecessors, and likewise from our master the Greatest Shaykh, and from those who followed his path among the Sufi masters, may Allah be pleased with them, regarding the view that there is no eternal abiding, that is based on another school of thought and a manifestation that has not been unveiled to us. Most of them built their speech on technical terms, symbols and allusions, between us and understanding of which stand worldly obstacles and soul-bound attachments. Perhaps the view of whoever says there is no eternal abiding, from among those who have not followed the path of the people of spiritual wayfaring, is based on the non-eternal abiding of a group of the people of the Fire, namely the sinners who committed what is less than disbelief. And if the term "disbelief" is applied to them, it is understood in another sense, just as it was understood in another sense in the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him (ﷺ): "Whoever abandons the prayer has disbelieved."

Moreover, the Shaykh, may Allah sanctify his secret, many times explicitly stated eternal abiding in his books. He said in his *ʿAqida Sughra*, at the beginning of the *Futuhat*: "Perpetuity for the people of the Fire in the Fire is a truth." And in the fourth chapter after sixty, on the discussion of the slaughter of death and the caller's proclamation: "O people of the Fire, abiding forever, with no exit," the text of which is: "The people of the Fire will be seized with the greatest grief because of that. Then the gates of the Fire will be shut with a closing that has no opening after it, and the Fire will close in upon its people, and some of them will enter into others, so that their crushing within it will be greatest, and its upper part will return to its lower part and its lower part to its upper part. People and jinn will be seen in it like pieces of meat in a pot under which is a great fire, boiling like boiling water, so they revolve among creation, high and low: ﴿Every time it dies down, We increase for them the blaze﴾." Shaykh ʿAbd al-Karim al-Jili mentioned in his book called *al-Insan al-Kabir*, and in a commentary on the chapter of Secrets from the *Futuhat*: "The people of the Sufis mean by 'the people of the Fire will come out of it' only the sinners among the monotheists, not the disbelievers." He said: "Beware of taking the words of Shaykh Muhyi al-Din or others among the Sufis, in their saying about the end of the term of the sinners in the Fire being over the disbelievers, for that is a lie and an error. And when speech admits a correct meaning, it must be taken in that sense." End of quotation.

Yes, the Shaykh said, may Allah sanctify his secret, in his commentary on the Opening Chapter in the *Futuhat*: "When the wall falls, the Trumpet is shattered, the rivers mingle, the two seas meet, and the barrier is removed, punishment becomes bliss, Hell becomes Paradise, and there is no punishment and no chastisement, only bliss and security by direct witnessing," and so on. This and similar statements are to be understood in a correct sense known to the people of spiritual taste, which does not contradict what the decisive texts have come with. The most that occurs to people like us about it is that it refers to the dwelling of the sinners of this community in the Fire, in which the Almighty places His foot, and manifests Himself with the attribute of subjugation over the Fire, so that it says, "Enough, enough," and cannot bear His manifestation, so it subsides. And it is not far-fetched that it will afterward join Paradise. Beware of taking its outward meaning, given your condition. Whenever you find something like this from one of the people of Allah, the Exalted, accept it from them in the meaning they intended, which you do not know, nor do I, and not in the meaning that arises in your intellect clouded by illusions. By Allah, the matter lies beyond that. Holding to the outward meanings of these expressions that deny eternal abiding in punishment, and interpreting the texts that indicate eternal abiding in the Fire by saying that abiding in it does not entail abiding in punishment, since enjoyment may occur in it and punishment may turn into sweetness, leads to negating the legal rulings, nullifying prophethood, and opening a door that cannot be shut. And if your soul beautifies this to you, we will go back and forth with you in argument, and we will bring against you armies of proofs you cannot withstand. Victory is only from Allah, and it is incumbent upon us to aid the believers. Do not let it occur to you in illusion that eternal abiding entails the finitude of manifestations, for Allah, the Exalted, is Allah, and every day He is in a matter. So take what I have given you and be among the thankful. I do not think you will find this verification from anyone other than us. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

[Page 143]

This verse and what follows it, up to the end of the story, are coordinated with the story of ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾. Each of the two coordinated passages is addressed to a specific purpose, although both contain a great deal of condemnation of the people of misguidance. This verse and the thirteen verses that follow it were brought to condemn the hypocrites (munafiqun), who concealed disbelief and displayed Islam. Outwardly, they are greater in sin than the rest of the disbelievers, as indicated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest level of the Fire﴾. The word al-nas (people) is, according to Sibawayh and the majority of scholars, originally unas, which is either a plural or a collective noun (ism jam') for insan (human being). Its first radical has been dropped for lightness, so its pattern is fu'al. Its original form is supported by insan, uns, and anasi. Its shortened and full forms are both permissible when it is indefinite. When it is definite with the article al-, the shortened form is more common. Whoever uses the definite form restricts it to affliction. Using the full form is permissible but rare, as in the line:

"Indeed, the fates (death) come upon the people who feel secure."

It is derived from al-uns, the opposite of loneliness, because of man's companionship with his own kind, since he is civil by nature. For this reason it is said:

"Man is named only for his inclination to companionship, and the heart only because it turns about."

It may also be derived from anasa, meaning "he saw," and Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿He perceived a fire from the side of the mount﴾. It also came to mean "he heard" and "he knew." It was named this because it is apparent and perceptible. Al-Sakkaki held that it is a complete noun whose middle radical is waw, from nawasa, meaning "he moved," as shown by its diminutive form nuwayس. Its pattern is therefore fa'l. In al-Kashshaf it is stated that it is a diminutive form that comes with a meaning different from its enlarged form, like unaysiyan and ruwayjil. It has also been said that it derives from nasiya (to forget with the heart), because of Allah's words about Adam, peace be upon him: ﴿So he forgot, and We found in him no resolve﴾. This is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Its pattern in this case is fal'. It is generally used only for the children of Adam. Ibn Khalawayh reported from some Arabs: "unas from the jinn." Abu Hayyan said: "This is metaphorical." If it is derived from nawasa, then applying it to the jinn is clearly valid, especially if we say that nawas means the swinging of a thing in the air. Salama ibn Asim asserted that both nas and unas are independent roots. The lam (al-) in it is either for the genus (jins) or for a specific known referent (ahd khariji). If it is the first, then the phrase is "from an indefinite qualified noun." If it is the second, then it is a relative clause, intending by it Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and his followers. Ibn Hisham and a group of scholars allowed that it may be a relative clause on the assumption of genus, and a qualified noun on the assumption of a known referent. This is because some of the genus may be determined in some respect, and some of those determined may be unknown in terms of some state of theirs, like the people of a neighborhood among whom there is a murderer whose identity is not known. If the individual is known, then there is no basis for specification according to these scholars. It has been said that specification is more appropriate, because the definite by the article of genus, owing to its lack of time-specification, is close to the indefinite, and part of the indefinite is indefinite. Thus it fits the qualified form for correspondence. The matter is the opposite with a known referent. On this pattern, ﴿Among the believers are men﴾ and ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾ were revealed. This is because in the first the genus is intended, while in the second the antecedent of the pronoun is a specific group of the hypocrites. Since the verse contains a meaningful division, for Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the believers, then the disbelievers, then followed with the hypocrites, it becomes like a verbal division. Dividing people into believer, disbeliever, and hypocrite, and including the information about the one who says he is among the people, has a benefit. You may also interpret it to mean: whoever among the hypocrites conceals himself is known to us, and were it not that concealment is generous, I would have exposed him. This is also beneficial and hints at some threat. It has been said that the meaning of their being from the people is that they have no attribute distinguishing them except the human form. Or the intent is to alert that the mentioned attributes contradict humanity, so one is astonished at them. Or the point of the benefit is existence, meaning that they exist among them. Or they are from the people and not from the jinn, since there is no hypocrisy among the jinn. Or the intent by "the people" is the Muslims, and the meaning is that they are counted as Muslims or treated as Muslims in what is due to them and what is upon them. Some of these views contain much strain and artificiality, but every fallen thing has a picker-up. Abu Hayyan chose here that min be a relative pronoun, claiming that it is only a qualifying particle when it occurs in a place that is mostly specific to the indefinite, and that otherwise it is rare, to the extent that al-Sakkaki, despite his high standing, denied it. There is no concealing what is in this. The objection to the intention of the known referent, namely how the hypocrites can be included absolutely among the persistent disbelievers who are judged to have a seal upon them, and that ﴿And among the people﴾ and the verse came as a counterpart, because ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ is an explanation of the third category, the wavering one, is not valid. This is because by the hypocrites are meant those among them who are determined, sealed with disbelief, as indicated by ﴿Deaf, dumb, and blind, so they do not return﴾, not all hypocrites. Also, their specification with the mixture of deception and mockery alongside disbelief does not preclude their being included among the persistent disbelievers. By this consideration they became a third category. So the division is binary in reality and tripartite in terms of consideration.
