In the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿says﴾ and ﴿We believed﴾, there is consideration of the word min and its meaning. Had he considered only the first, he would have said "I believed." Had he considered only the second, he would have said "they say." Since both were considered, it is good to consider the wording first, since it is prior in external existence to meaning, and the singular is prior to the plural. Had the order been reversed, it would have been permissible. Ibn Atiyya claimed that it is not permissible to shift from plural to singular, but the verse of the poet refutes it:

"I am not one who shrinks back or submits when the enemy's cavalry confronts him."

He restricted the object of belief to Allah and the Last Day, even though they used to believe with their mouths in everything the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought. This is because these two are the greatest intended goal of faith, since whoever believes in Allah in a manner befitting the majesty of His essence, believes in His books, His messengers, and His laws. Whoever knows that the return is to Him prepares for it by righteous deeds. This implies a claim to possessing faith in both its ends, the origin and the return, and what is known by reason and revelation, and this includes belief in prophethood. Alternatively, the specification of these two in mention is to indicate that they conceal disbelief in matters in which they are not hypocrites in general, because the people, as is well known, were Jews, and they were sincere in the basic faith in Allah and the Last Day according to their own opinion. Yet they were hypocritical regarding the manner of belief in these two, and they saw the believers' belief in them as being like their own. How, then, about what they intend by pure hypocrisy, in which they are not believers at all, such as the prophethood of our Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the Qur'an? Or they intended, by specifying belief in these two, to imply non-belief in the Seal of the Messengers, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and what he conveyed. In that is a statement of their greater wickedness. If the real meaning of this were intended, it would not be faith, because acknowledging what the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought is necessary. How much more so when it is deception and confusion. It has also been said that since their aim was to exaggerate the purity of their Islam, by saying that they had abandoned the beliefs they held concerning origin and return and acknowledged that they had been in error, they specified their faith with these, because they had been professing all the other fundamentals. As for prophethood, believing in it contains no acknowledgment of that. Also, abandoning what is firmly fixed in the heart and what is refused by the rejection of belief in him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is among the established matters. So they did not address it, to indicate that it is one of the matters about which there is no doubt that they believed in it after believing what is even more severe for them. Taking ﴿by Allah and the Last Day﴾ as an oath by them on faith is extremely crude, and far cruder is interpreting it as an oath by Him, the Exalted, on their non-belief, as in: ﴿They did not believe, and they are not believers﴾. Therefore the preposition bi must be the complement of the verb of belief. It was repeated for the sake of exaggeration in deception and confusion, by showing that their faith is detailed, emphatic, and strong. The Last Day may be intended as the eternal time from the Gathering without end, or what Allah, the Exalted, determined from it until each of the believers and disbelievers settles in what has been prepared for him. It was called "last" because it is the last of the limited times. The first is more fitting, because the application of "day" to it is common in the Qur'an, whether literal or metaphorical. Also, belief in it includes belief in the second, since the second is included in it without the reverse. Indeed, the term "day" in lexical usage more appropriately refers to the second, because of its being bounded. In any case, it differs from what people understand: customarily, "day" is from sunrise to sunset; by the Shari'ah, according to the sound view, from true dawn to sunset; and technically, from midday to midday. The matter goes beyond that, and there will be a continuation of this later. In His saying, glorified is He, ﴿And they are not believers﴾, in placing the subject first and the particle of negation at the beginning, there is a rejection of the claim of those hypocrites in the most eloquent manner. This is because their inclusion in the ranks of believers is a necessary consequence of the real existence of faith in them, and the negation of the necessary consequence is the strongest evidence for the negation of the thing necessitating it. Exaggeration has been made in negating the necessary consequence by indicating its persistent absence, which requires the non-occurrence of the necessitating thing at all. This negation was also emphasized by the bi. This is the reason for turning away from the response "they believed," which would correspond to the beginning of the speech. Some scholars interpret the statement as restrictive: when the disbelievers saw themselves as like the believers in true faith and claimed agreement with them, it was said in response: ﴿And they are not believers﴾ in restriction of the specific type (qasr al-ifrad). Taste rejects this, and the use of the attribute indicates generality, that they have no share of faith at all. It may be restricted by what its predecessor was restricted by, since it falls in its response. However, the negation of the absolute necessarily implies the negation of the restricted, so it is more eloquent and emphatic.

In this verse there is evidence that whoever does not affirm with his heart is not a believer. As for whether one who professes with his tongue, while nothing in his heart agrees with or contradicts it, is not a believer, this is not established here, because there is a contradiction in the hypocrite here, since he is among those sealed upon the heart, or because Allah, the Exalted, called him a liar. That is only because the inner affirmation does not correspond to the outer profession, so it is said. Some scholars examined this more closely, claiming that whoever makes faith the mere verbal profession, whether he requires absence of denial and rejection or requires that it be the profession of the two testimonies, and does not consider sufficient such a statement as "I believed in Allah and the Last Day," because the basis is the utterance of both, as occurs in the authentic reports, even stipulated the saying of "I bear witness," the name specific to Allah, the Exalted, and the name of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Therefore there is no proof in this verse at all against the doctrine of the Karramiyya (a sect holding that faith is verbal profession alone). So let it be pondered.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 9 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive only themselves, and they are not aware.﴾

The root of *khad'* (deception, pronounced with a fatha or kasra on the kha') is concealment and creating a false impression. Some say that with a kasra it is a verbal noun (*ism masdar*). From the same root come *makhda'* (an inner chamber or storeroom) and *akhda'an* (two hidden veins in the place where cupping is applied). *Khada'a al-dabb* means the lizard hid and concealed itself. The word is also used for displaying what gives an appearance of safety, and for nullifying what would require harm to another, or for escaping from it, as al-Imam (al-Razi) stated. Al-Sayyid (al-Sharif al-Jurjani) said: it is to make one's companion imagine the opposite of what one intends, of harm, so that one inflicts it upon him. In *al-Kashf*, the verification is that *khad'* is an act-attribute (*sifah fi'liyyah*) subsisting in the soul after the mind has assembled premises by means of which one reaches, by a route that is reprehensible according to the law, reason or custom, the drawing of a benefit, whether gaining some good for oneself or inflicting some harm on another, while both the means and the end are concealed from the one toward whom the intention is directed. In such a way that this gain or infliction cannot be achieved without it, or if it could be achieved, it would entail the loss of another aim according to his perception. On this basis, the saying "war is deception" (*al-harbu khud'ah*) is metaphorical, and its oddity is not hidden.

*Mukhada'ah* is a *mufa'alah* form, and what is known about it is that each party does to the other the same as what the other does to him. Thus here it requires that from each of Allah, the believers and the hypocrites there should proceed an act that is directed at the other. The apparent meaning of this is problematic, because Allah, glorified is He, neither deceives nor is deceived. As for the verification: He is free of all need of any gain, infliction, or drawing of benefit for Himself, and He is also exalted above contrivance and the assembling of premises. Moreover, He is far too majestic to let the deficiency of being affected, and the obvious imperfection in it, come near the veils of His majesty. As for what al-Sayyid mentioned: He, great is His majesty, is greater than that anything hidden be concealed from Him, or that any harm reach Him. How then could the hypocrites deceive Him, and bring into His knowledge the opposite of what they want of harm, and inflict it upon Him, when they, being People of the Book, know the impossibility of that? A sensible person does not intend what he knows to be impossible. As for His not being deceived: although it is permissible in our view that He, glorified, cause the imaginations of the hypocrites to be misled into the opposite of what He wants of harms, so that they are deceived and then He inflicts it upon them, it is impossible to attribute this to Him, because it suggests that it arises only from inability to confront and from displaying what is concealed. This is what is customarily understood from the term, as in *al-Intisaf* (of Ibn al-Munir). For this reason the phrase is qualified in its explanation, with a sense of fear or shame from open confrontation. As for the believers: although it is permissible that they deceive, it is unlikely that they intend to deceive the hypocrites, because that is not praiseworthy but blameworthy and reprehensible, and it is the most similar thing to hypocrisy, and they are free of it. Moreover, the deception that is praised is *al-takhada'* (feigning), in the sense of displaying being affected while not being affected, out of nobility, as the Prophet (ﷺ) indicated with his saying: "The believer is gullible and noble." It is not the deception that indicates foolishness. For this reason A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with them both, said of Umar: "He was too intelligent to be deceived, and too virtuous to deceive." It may be answered that the form of their conduct toward Allah, the Exalted, in that they feign faith while they are disbelievers; and the form of Allah's conduct toward them, in that He commanded that the rulings of Muslims be applied to them, while they are in His sight in the lowest abyss; and the form of the believers' conduct toward them, in that they obeyed Allah's command concerning them and applied that to them, resemble the image of deception. Therefore in the sentence there is either a metaphor by *isti'arah tab'iyyah* (a verbal metaphor extended from a root) in the word *yukhadi'una* alone, or a *tamthiliyyah* (an allegorical image) in the whole sentence. And since the initiation of the act in the *mufa'alah* form comes explicitly from the side of the subject, and the object's being one who brings a similar act is implied by the flow of the discourse, it is good to introduce this in the context of blame, when the act is explicitly attributed to them. That the context requires mentioning only their state, as the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, our master, stated, does not undermine this fine point. Or it may be answered, as has been said, that what is meant is deception of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the act is placed upon other than the one it is directed at, because of the connection between them, which is the caliphate. So there is a *majaz 'aqli* (rational metaphor) in the act-attribution (*nisbah iqa'iyyah*). This is evident according to the view of those who are satisfied with a connection between what belongs to someone and what is other than what belongs to him. But according to the view of those who require that the act be connected to something other than its own subject by being among its objects, then it is not evident. Moreover, the difficulty remains that there is no deception from the Messenger and the believers, and there is no room for deception to be literal from one side and metaphorical from the other, because the word is one. It seems that the answerer either holds that it is permissible to combine the literal and the metaphorical, or does not hold that the emission of deception from the Messenger and the believers is impossible, so that they may achieve what they want of exalting the religion and the interests of the Muslims. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, and Abu Haywah read *yakhda'una*. The answer to what this entails is the answer to what has already been required. And it has come to pass that *fa'ala* has the meaning of *fa'ala*, as in "Allah pardoned me" (*ʿafani Allahu*) and "I punished the thief" (*ʿaqabtu al-lisa*). So there is no remoteness in taking the majority reading in this way. The choice of the *mufa'alah* form is to express intensification either in manner, since when an act is contested in it, it is carried out intensively, or in quantity, as in practice and habitual performance, since they were persistent in deception. The phrase "and they deceive" (*wa-yukhadi'una*) is either an explanatory clause (*bayan*) for "they say" (*yaqulu*), not as a coordinating conjunction, since explanatory apposition does not apply to sentences according to the grammarians, although the discourse of the rhetoricians may suggest it. Or it is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), as if it had been said: "Why do they claim faith while they are liars, and what has it benefited them?" So it was said: "They deceive..." etc. In the final result this is like the first, though the first is likely the more preferable. Abu Hayyan permitted this sentence to be a substitute for the relative clause of "who" (*man*) as a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*), or a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the concealed pronoun in "says," meaning "deceiving." Abu al-Baqa permitted that it be a circumstantial clause from the concealed pronoun in "believers." Perhaps the negation is directed at the accompaniment, not at the circumstance itself, as in "Zayd did not come to me while the dawn had risen," and "Allah would not punish them while you are among them, and Allah would not punish them while they seek forgiveness." Moreover, the circumstance and what resembles it in such a case may be made a qualifier of the negation, not of the negated thing, as they have established in "I did not exaggerate" (*lam ubaligh*), briefly as an approximation. Making the sentence a description of the believers is forbidden because of the negation and the qualifier. A circumstance is not like a description, so there is no wonder in permitting one and forbidding the other, as Abu Hayyan imagined in his *Bahr*. Yes, there is surprise at the sentence being an explanation of the surprise at their being among the people, as is not hidden. Furthermore, the purpose of deceiving these people, for those whom they deceived, is like the purpose of their hypocrisy, exactly alike: they intended to exalt themselves in the eyes of the believers, to get a look at their secrets in order to divulge them, to lift killing from themselves, or to impose the poll-tax upon them, to win a share of the spoils, and similar things. The fruit of the deception of those whom they deceived, if it was a divine wisdom and religious interests, may lead, if abandoned, to countless corruptions and unnumbered dangers. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr (the two Haramayn) read *wa-ma yukadi'una*, and the rest of the seven read *wa-ma yakhda'una*. Al-Jarud and Abu Taluyt read *wa-ma yukhda'una* with a damma on the yaʾ, in the passive voice. Some read *wa-ma yukhada'una* with a fatha on the dal, also in the passive. Qatadah and al-Ijli read *wa-ma yukhaddi'una*, from *khadda'a* (intensive form), in the active voice. Some read with a fatha on the yaʾ, the kha' and a shaddah on the dal with a kasra. Apart from the first two readings, the rest are irregular (*shadhdhah*). Upon the first two, *anfusahum* is in the accusative as a pure object, or as an agent in meaning. As for the reading with the passive voice, it is either by omitting the preposition, meaning "in their own souls," or "against their own souls," or as a specification (*tamyiz*) according to the view of the Kufans, or as an analogy to the object according to the claim of some, or as an object by including in the verb the meaning of "they diminish," for example.

It is not problematic on the reading *yukadi'una* that how can the restriction of deception to themselves be valid, which would require negating it from Allah and the believers, when it has already been affirmed at the beginning? And since deception is only in appearance between two parties, how can one deceive himself? We say: what is meant is that the circle of deception returns to them, and its harm reverts to them. So the deception here is the first deception, and the restriction is in terms of its harm being returned to themselves. Thus the expression signifying it is a metaphor or a metonymy (*kinayah*) for the confinement of its harm to them. Or we make the word "deception" a *majaz mursal* (a metonymy of the general relation) for its harm in the second degree. That it is a metaphor in relation to the first, as al-Sa'd (al-Taftazani) said, is not evident. It may be said: they deceived themselves when they beguiled themselves with that, and it deceived them when it told them of empty hopes. So the meaning of deception is other than the first, and the deceiver and the deceived are different in consideration. On this basis, deception is a metaphor for suggesting falsehood and presenting it in the form of truth. Taking it in its literal meaning is remote. That this is an abstraction (*tajrid*), like the saying of the poet:

"You have no horse with you to give, nor wealth; so let speech give bliss if the state does not give bliss."

This is not accepted by sound taste, like the claim that the discourse is hyperbole in the impossibility of their deceiving Allah and the believers, because, as is not hidden, the deceiver's deceiving himself is impossible, so his deceiving Him is impossible. Allah's being deceived is impossible because of His knowledge, and the believers because of their being informed by Allah's information. Or it is a metonymy for their opposition and enmity toward Allah and His beloved ones being a dealing with themselves, because Allah and the believers benefit them as they benefit themselves. Some make the expression of deception here by way of *mushakalah* (a figure of association, using a word for the sake of a related word), while both the associating and the associated are metaphors, and each acts according to his own disposition.

(The self, *nafs*) is the reality of a thing and its essence. It is not restricted to bodies, as in His saying: "He has prescribed for Himself mercy" and "Allah warns you of Himself." It is applied to the subtle vaporous substance carrying the power of life, sensation and voluntary motion. The philosophers call it the animal spirit (*al-ruh al-hayawaniyyah*). Its first organ that it inhabits is the heart, since it is the first thing created according to the prevalent view, and from it it flows to the brain, the liver and the rest of the organs. It does not follow from this that it is the origin of the nerves, since it is possible that the organ receiving the influx may be the origin of the instrument of reception. It has been said that it is the brain, since it is the origin, but there is no definitive proof of this, as is stated in al-Razi's commentary on the *Qanun* (of Ibn Sina). It is also often applied to the immaterial substance connected to the body by way of management and disposition. This is the divine spirit (*al-ruh al-amriyyah*), which is intended in the saying: "Whoever knows his self knows his Lord." It is called the rational soul (*al-nafs al-natiqah*), and its names differ according to the variety of its attributes. The organ most favored by the illumination of its spiritual lights is also the heart, and for this nobility it is sometimes called a self. Some call opinion (*ra'y*) by it. In the verse, according to what has been said, the apparent meaning is the first sense, since the intention is to show that the harm of their deception returns to themselves and does not pass beyond them to others. But this is not definitively fixed, as is not hidden. It is applied to other meanings which you will hear, together with the verification of this discussion, God willing, Exalted is He.

The clause ﴿and they do not perceive﴾ is either a new sentence or is conjoined to ﴿and they deceive none but themselves﴾. The object of (yash'uruna, they perceive) is omitted, meaning: "and they do not perceive that they are deceiving them (themselves)." Or it means: "God knows what they conceal and what they disclose." Or it means: God informed His Prophet (ﷺ) of their deception and lying, as this is narrated from Ibn Abbas. Or it means the ruin of their own selves and their casting themselves into everlasting wretchedness through their disbelief and hypocrisy, as is narrated from Zayd. Or the meaning is: they perceive nothing at all. It is also possible, as in al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit), that ﴿and they do not perceive﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: "and they deceive none but themselves while not perceiving that, and had they perceived, they would not have deceived." Shu'ur (perception, shu'ur) is apprehension through the five outward senses, and it may also mean knowledge. Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) said: "I perceived such-and-such" is used in two ways. One is derived from touching hair (mass al-sha'r), and it is expressed as touch, from which the term mashaʻir (the senses) is derived. So when it is said, "So-and-so does not perceive," this is more emphatic in censure than saying he does not hear or see, because the sense of touch is more general than the senses of hearing and sight. The other usage is: "I perceived such-and-such," meaning I apprehended something subtle, from the saying "I reached its hair (sha'arahu)," like "I reached its ear (adhantuhu)" and "I reached its head (ra'astuhu)." This points to the saying, "So-and-so splits the hair (yashuqqu al-sha'r)," when his gaze is penetrating, and from it the word poet (sha'ir) is taken, for one who grasps the subtleties of meanings. End of quotation. The verse may bear the negation of shu'ur in the sense of knowledge, so that the meaning of ﴿they do not perceive﴾ is "they do not know," which occurs frequently in this sense, and the appended phrase contains a kind of allusion to it. It may also bear negation in the sense of perception through the senses, so that the object of the verb is treated as a sensible matter that is hidden only from one who lacks the senses. Negating this is the utmost censure, because one who does not perceive the self-evident sensible has a rank lower than that of beasts; they are like cattle, rather they are more astray. Perhaps this is preferable, because it contains mockery of them, along with indicating the negation of knowledge by the stronger means. It is also more fitting with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and over their sight is a veil﴾, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 10 (part 1 of 2):

﴿In their hearts is a sickness, so Allah has increased their sickness. And for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie.﴾ The word al-maraḍ (sickness) is pronounced with a fatha on the ra', as the majority read it, and with a sukun on the ra', as al-Asma'i reported from Abu 'Amr. According to what the lexicographers (ahl al-lughah) held, it is a condition that departs from the natural temperament and is actually harmful. In the terminology of the physicians, it is the opposite of health (ṣiḥḥah), which is the condition from which actions proceed in a sound manner, and by "actions" is meant what is commonly understood: these are either natural, such as growth; or animal, such as sensation; or psychological, such as quickness of thought. Thus the squint and the hunchback are, for example, a sickness according to the physicians but not according to the lexicographers. The word maraḍ may also be used in the lexical sense for its effect, which is pain, as stated by a group of trustworthy scholars; and for darkness, as in the verse:

In a night that was sick on every side,
so that neither star nor moon could be perceived.

It is also used for the weakness and lethargy of the heart, as stated by more than one scholar. It is used figuratively for whatever befalls a person and impairs the perfection of his soul, such as hatred, heedlessness, corrupt belief, envy, and other impediments to perfections, which resemble the disorder of the body, preventing pleasures and leading to spiritual ruin, which is greater than physical ruin. What is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and the rest of the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih) is to take sickness in the verse in its figurative meaning. There is no doubt that the hearts of the hypocrites were filled with those vices which prevented them from what they were prevented from, and brought them down to the lowest level of the Fire. Some hold that there is no obstacle to also taking sickness in its literal meaning, which is darkness: "And whomever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light" (24:40); "And those who disbelieve, their allies are the ṭāghūt, who bring them out of the light into the darknesses" (2:257). Likewise it may be taken in the sense of pain, for in the hearts of those people there is great pain through the might of Islam and the complete order of its affairs. The verse on this reading is open to both meanings. The establishment of a preventive indicator (qarīnah) against the figurative meaning is required only for specifying it, not for admitting it. When a figurative sense contains a point of rhetoric, it equals the literal sense, so it is possible to apply both, considering both originality and the rhetorical point. However, an objection arises here: pain in general is not the literal meaning of sickness; rather its literal meaning is pain caused by bad temperament, and this is absent in the hypocrites. The claim that their condition leads to it is extremely weak. Moreover, if their hearts were diseased, their bodies would be so too, or death would have hastened to them. The prophetic hadith and the medical canon support this. As for the hadith, it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, in the body there is a lump of flesh..." (the full hadith). As for the medical canon, the sages, after explaining the anatomy of the heart, said: If a thick matter gets into it, and it penetrates it and its covering, or one of them, death hastens its owner; and if it does not penetrate, life endures for a brief period, and there is no way for life to continue with a diseased heart. Therefore, in both reason and transmission, it is better to take it in its figurative meaning, which includes cowardice and feebleness. This has entered the hearts of the hypocrites when they witnessed from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers what they witnessed. The tanwin (indefiniteness) indicates that it is a type different from the sicknesses commonly known among people. It was not put in the plural as "hearts" was, because enumerating the locations logically indicates enumerating what resides in them, so the plural of the locations sufficed for the plural of the illness. The first clause is either a resumed statement explaining the cause of their deception and their hypocrisy, or it confirms what is conveyed by "and they are not believers," namely the continuance of their unbelief, or it gives its cause, as if it were said: "What is wrong with them that they do not believe?" He said: "In their hearts is a sickness that prevents it." Or it confirms their lack of awareness, although the way of His saying "and they are not aware" is the way of interjection (i'tirāḍ) according to what has been said. The clause "so Allah has increased their sickness" is either a supplicatory clause (du'a'iyyah) interposed between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, and an interposed clause may be accompanied by "fa" as in the verse:

Know that the knowledge of a man benefits him
that it will come whenever it is decreed.

As stated in al-Talwih and others, citing the grammarians. Or it is an informative clause conjoined to the first. The conjunction of a past verb to a nominal clause is for a rhetorical point: if it is meant in the first that this has not ceased to be fresh and tender until the time of the report, and in the second that this is a cause for the increase of their certain sickness, since were it not for the defilement of their nature, they would have increased in healing through what Allah the Exalted has bestowed on the believers. This does not repeat with His saying "and He extends for them in their transgression," because there is a difference between the increase of sickness and the increase of transgression. Moreover, there is no obstacle to an increase of emphasis despite the distance. Also, if the supplication is not current on the tongues of the servants, or is not intended merely as abuse and disparagement, it becomes a command from Him, glorified is He, and thus returns to what the informative sentence amounts to. The increase of their sickness by Allah the Exalted is either by intensifying their envy through the increase of Allah the Exalted's blessings upon His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the believers; or by the darkness of their hearts through the renewal of their disbelief by what He sends down little by little of the signs and the Wise Reminder, so they are in darknesses, some above others; or by increasing their fear and terror, which results in leaving off openly declaring their disbelief, because of Allah the Exalted's support of Islam and raising its banners over the banners of honor and esteem; or by magnifying the pain through increasing sorrows and kindling the fires of anxieties.

Grief wears down souls with emaciation,
and whitens the forelock of the youth and makes him old.

This occurs through Allah the Exalted's continually renewed obligations upon them, and their performing them while disbelieving in them; and through the Prophet ﷺ's imposing certain matters upon them, and their failure to comply with him, which brings what they dislike, namely his blame and bad opinion of them; so they grieve whether they act or refrain. Attributing the increase to Allah the Exalted is literal, even if it is explained as nature (ṭab'), for He, glorified is He, is the true agent through causes and without them, and nothing is ugly from Him. Some made the attribution figurative in some respects, perhaps a Mu'tazili lapse. Some went further and said: the attribution is figurative whatever the sickness is, and it was interpreted to mean that there is no one here who actually increases their sickness, according to the opinion of Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir that in figurative attribution it is not necessary that the verb have an agent to whom the attribution is literal, like:

His face increases him in beauty
when you increase your gaze at it.

So reflect. He, glorified is He, transferred the increase to them and not to the hearts, so He did not say "fa-zādahā" (He increased it), either by taking the liberty of omitting the possessive noun, i.e., "so Allah increased their hearts in sickness," or as an allusion that the sickness of the heart is a sickness for the whole body, or as a symbol that the heart is the rational soul, for without it a human would not be human. The repetition of "sickness" in indefinite form is because it differs from the first, since the increase differs from what is increased upon. The claim of one who asserted that it is a case of placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun is a delusion. The indefinite form is for magnification. "Alim" is a form (fa'il) from pain, in the sense of mufil (causing pain), like "samī'" in the sense of "musmi'" (causing to hear). According to al-Zamakhshari's view that it derives from the triliteral alima, it is like wajī', and attributing it to "punishment" is a figurative usage on the pattern of "his fortune was great" (jadda jiddu-hu). He did not establish the form fa'il in the sense of mufil. In the verse "Originator of the heavens" (2:117), it is taken as a adjective of quality (al-sifah al-mushabbahah), i.e., "its heavens are wondrous." And "samī'" in the verse:

Is it from Raihanah, the caller, the hearing one, that sleeplessness troubles me, and my companions are asleep?

is in the sense of "sāmi'" (hearing), i.e., is it from Raihanah, a caller from my heart who hears the call of its caller, according to what follows it, for most anxiety and sleeplessness come from the callings and thoughts of the self. On this basis, explaining it as "mu'lim," an active participle, is an exposition of the resulting meaning. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "Everything in the Qur'an that is 'alīm is painful (mūji')." Two kinds of punishment have been combined for the hypocrites: "great" and "painful," and that is for the specification by mention here, and the inclusion together with the disbelievers there. It has been said: this clause is interposed to explain the threat for hypocrisy and deception. The bā' is either causal or substitutive. "Mā" is either a verbal-masdar (maṣdariyyah) construction, interpreted with a masdar of "kāna" if "kāna" is used, or with a masdar derived from the predicate, such as "al-kadhib" (lying); or it is a relative (mawṣūlah), and Abu al-Baqa' preferred this, on the ground that the implied pronoun refers to what was mentioned in al-Bahr, that it is not necessary that there be an implied element there. Whoever reads "yakdhibūn" with light stress, namely the Kufans, then the verb is intransitive. Whoever reads it with heavy stress, like Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr, then the object is omitted because the meaning is understood, and the estimate is "by their lying to the Prophet ﷺ regarding what he brought." It may be that the intensive form has the sense of the light form, for emphasis in the mode (kayf), as they say: "bāna al-shay'" and "bayyana," and "ṣadaqa" and "ṣaddaqa." The doubling may also be for increase in quantity, as in "mawwattat al-ibil" (the camels died in quantity). It may also be from "kadhaba al-waḥsh" when it runs and stops to look at what is behind it, and that is the state of the bewildered, which is the state of the hypocrite. In that case there is a derived, figurative, illustrative metaphor in the speech. This meaning is supported by the Prophet ﷺ's saying: "The likeness of the hypocrite is like the likeness of a stray sheep between two flocks: it goes to this one once and to that one once." The prepositional phrase is an attribute of "punishment," not of "painful," as Abu al-Baqa' said, because the principle regarding an attribute is that it is not itself described. Lying is informing about a thing with a relation or a subject contrary to

...the reality of the matter according to us, and according to al-Nazzam in belief, and according to al-Jahiz in both. Every desirable aim that can be reached by either truth or falsehood is treated as follows: lying about it is forbidden, since there is no need for it. If it can be reached only by lying, then lying about it is permitted, provided that achieving that aim is permitted, and obligatory if achieving it is obligatory. The Hadith explicitly permits lying in three situations: in war, in reconciling people, and when a man lies to his wife to please her. This is not an exhaustive list. For this reason it was permitted to prompt those who had confessed to offences punishable by prescribed penalties (hudud) to retract their confession. Therefore one should weigh the harm of lying against the harm that results from telling the truth. If the harm in telling the truth is greater, then lying is permitted for him. If the reverse is the case, or if he is in doubt, lying is forbidden to him. Accordingly, what the Imam al-Baydawi, may God pardon him, said, that lying is entirely forbidden, is likely something he said in error.

In the verse there is an exhortation to the believers to maintain the truthfulness and affirmation they already have. When the believer hears that punishment is the consequence of lying, but not of hypocrisy (nifaq), which is itself [a form of lying], he imagines in himself the gravity of the name of lying and conceives its ugliness, and so he restrains himself from it with the greatest restraint. This is evident on the reading with lightening (qira'at al-takhfif), and it is also possible on the other readings, because attributing truthfulness to lying is itself lying, and likewise its frequency. Although the final meaning is strained, it has been said that the word (yukadhdhibun) is derived from the transitive form (kadhdhaba), as if he were calling his own opinion a lie, and so he stops to examine it. However, since this usage became common in this sense, and since the state of the hypocrite resembles this, it became permissible to borrow it for that state. Thus that exhortation is possible, though from a far distance.

The Hadith of intercession, narrated from Ibrahim, peace be upon him, in which he says: "I am not fit for it, for I told three lies," does not contradict the prohibition of lying in some of its forms. He meant, as in the narration of Ahmad: "I am sick" and "Rather, the largest of them did it," and his saying to the king in reply to his question about his wife Sarah: "She is my sister," when the king wanted to seize her. It was part of political strategy to target married women, other than those whose husbands consented. If these were forbidden lies, then where is his infallibility (ismah), and he is the father of the prophets! And if they were not such, then he reported on the Day of Resurrection something contrary to reality, and far be it from him. For what is understood from that statement is: "I have sinned, so I am ashamed to intercede," and would one be ashamed of something that contains no sin?

Because of the strength of this doubt, al-Razi firmly asserted that the narration is false, in order to protect the reputation of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. We say: these were indirect statements (ma'arid), and there is an alternative to lying in them. They came from the master of those possessing infallibility, ﷺ, such as his saying in the Hadith of the Hijra. Calling them lies is by way of metaphor, because of the shared outward form. They are therefore truthful indirect statements, as you will see in the best manner, God willing, in its proper place. However, since they were based on gentleness of disposition toward enemies, and someone like him, whom God has undertaken to protect, is fitting for open confrontation, he deviated from what was more fitting for his station. For this, he counted that act in that station as a sin, and called it a lie because it has the form of a lie. What happened to our Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, of this kind did not occur in such a station that would make him ashamed of it. Thus, for every station there is a fitting speech.

Furthermore, if they were actual lies with no harm in them, and no reason for shame, how could that be, when the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "Every one of them was only a lie by which he argued for the religion of God, the Exalted"? Therefore they are among the permissible lies. However, since the station of intercession is the praiseworthy station reserved for the Beloved, not the Friend, he displayed shame in order to avert it by what he thought would necessitate that, while it did not necessitate it. In this there is humility, display of inability, and repelling with what is better, which is obvious. So it is as if he said: "I am not secure from reproach for a permissible lie, so how could I intercede for you in this station?" So let this be noted.

Then, the use of present-tense verbs in reporting past actions with the defective past verbs is a widespread matter, like (asbaha yaqulu kadha) and (kadat tazighu qulubu fariqin minhum). Its meaning is that in the past it was continuous and renewing, through the succession of similar cases, the passing of time, and the future, relative to the time of the judgment. Continuity has been counted among the meanings of (kana). So there is no difficulty in "bima kanu yakdhibun" (because of what they used to lie), since (kana) indicates the attribution of lying to them in the past, while (yakdhibun) indicates its attribution in the present and future. The time in these two differs. The answer to this is that (kana) indicates continuity across all times, and (yukadhdhibun) indicates renewing continuity that enters all times, with its complications, which God the Exalted is sufficient to dispense with.

Hamza inclined (fa-zadahum) in ten verbs, and Ibn Dhakwan agreed with him in the inclination of (ja'a) and (sha'a), and he added these, while there is a difference of report from him regarding (zada) other than these. The inclination (imalah) is for the Tamim tribe, while the emphatic pronunciation (tafkhim) is for the Hijaz. Abu Hayyan versified these ten, saying:

Ten verbs are inclined by Hamza:
ja'a, sha'a, dak, ran, and completed by
zada, khaba, tab, khafa together, and ha, and zagha,
except al-Ahzab with its sad, so no.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 11:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth," they say, "We are only reformers."﴾ There is a difference of opinion regarding this clause. It was said that it is conjoined (ma'tufah, grammatically coordinated) to "they lie," because it is closer, and so that it also conveys that their corruption is a cause of the punishment, and to indicate that the attribute of corruption is to be avoided just as lying is to be avoided. The way in which it conveys that corruption is a cause of the punishment is that it falls within the scope of the relative clause (silah) of the relative pronoun, which serves as the cause. For the meaning of their words, ﴿We are only reformers﴾, is a denial of the claim that what is attributed to them is reform, and this is obstinacy and persistence in corruption, and persistence in that is corruption and sin. This is the view that al-Zamakhshari inclined toward, and it is based on the absence of any need for a pronoun in the clause referring back to "ma" (what). For a subordinate element tolerates what a principal element does not tolerate. Otherwise the sense would be: "And for them is a painful punishment because of what they used to do when it was said to them," etc., and this is not coherent. It seems that whoever takes "ma" to be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah) makes the connection with "kana" (was), since its connection to a conditional sentence is not known. Yes, it may be objected that the words of Allah, the Exalted, ﴿We are only reformers﴾, are a lie, so the meaning reverts to deserving punishment for lying, and conjoining an explanation (ʿatf al-tafsir) is something that taste and usage reject. For this reason it was said that this conjunction is sound according to one of the possibilities of the reading "yukadhdhibuna" (with the shaddah), so that it may be a cause for combining their condemnation for lying and for denying (the truth). As for the objection of our master, the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, that this kind of causal explanation should be by attributes whose causality is clear and whose ascription to the described party is accepted as established, needing no clarification because the hearer is well aware of their being attributed to him, or because they were mentioned explicitly or by implication before. There is no doubt that this conditional clause is not known to be attributed to them in any way that would merit its inclusion in the category of causal explanation. What is wrong with this is not hidden from one who reflects carefully. It was also said: it is conjoined to "they say" (yaqulu), for it is free from the awkwardness that the conjunction involves, and so that the verses then follow the pattern of enumerating their vices, and their conveying that they are characterized by each of those attributes independently and intentionally, and their indicating that the punishment befalls them because of their lying, which is the least of their states; so consider what the rest of them would be. And because this past tense, by virtue of "idhā" (when), is future in sense, the conjunction is fine. But in this there is the point that the outcome of this clause is lying, as has been indicated, so it is not different from what precedes it. Even if a difference is granted by consideration and by adding the restrictions, it is still part of the relative clause or the qualifier, and both require that it not be independent. Also, that this lying is the least of their states is not accepted by anyone who has even a little intellect. Moreover, the interposition of an explanation and a resumptive sentence, even if it is not foreign, between the parts of the relative clause or qualifier is not free from being objectionable. So what I incline to and rely on, rather than these two matters, is what the meticulous scholar in al-Kashf (al-Kashf) chose, and close to it is the statement of Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr: that it is conjoined to His words, ﴿And among the people is one who says﴾, to explain their state in claiming faith, and their lying in it first, and then to explain their state in their immersion in their falsehood, and seeing ugliness as beauty and corruption as reform, second. The conjunction is to be understood as conveying the totality of their states, and even if it entails conjoining a verbal sentence to a nominal sentence, that is preferable according to the context and the pattern of enumerating vices. As for what was said against it, that it is not something to be counted on, though it was supposed that it is more complete in conveying these meanings, that is because it does not indicate that this attribute and what follows it are included in the story of the hypocrites and the explanation of their states, for then it would not be good for the pronouns in them to refer back to them, as the soundness of disposition attests for anyone who has even a little familiarity with the methods of speech. That statement is outside the bounds of fairness, as the soundness of disposition free from the disease of partisanship and bias attests. For the return of the pronouns is a link tying the attributes to them, and the flow of the discourse calls for this. Indeed, in one narrative there may come a resumptive sentence without a conjunction. So if the resumption does not contradict it at all, how can the conjunction to its first, resumed part contradict it? The conjunction only requires a difference of states, not a difference of stories and their people. As for what Ibn Jarir reported from Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, that the people of this verse have not yet come, the intent is not that it is specific to other people, as the apparent meaning suggests, but rather that it is not restricted to those among the hypocrites, even though it was revealed concerning them, for the specificity of the cause does not contradict the generality of the wording. Then, the speaker to the hypocrites in the time of revelation of these words was either the Prophet ﷺ conveying from Allah, the Exalted, who informed him of their hypocrisy; or the Prophet, may the blessings and peace be upon him, was informed of this about them and did not affirm it, so he advised them, and they answered him with what they answered; or some of the believers who suspected them and perceived by the light of faith within them; or some of those to whom they used to propose corruption, who would not accept it from them for some reason, so he turned into an admonisher to them, saying: "Do not cause corruption." Corruption is a deviation from the state of balance and uprightness, and its opposite is reform. The meaning is: do not do what leads to corruption, which here is disbelief, as Ibn Abbas said; or sins, as Abu al-Aliyah said; or hypocrisy by which they associated with the disbelievers, thereby informing them of the secrets of the believers. For all of these lead, even if through intermediaries, to the ruin of the earth, the scarcity of good, the removal of blessing, and the cessation of benefits. And if the speaker was one of those to whom they used to propose corruption, and he would not accept it from one who shared their disbelief, then corruption is taken to mean the stirring up of wars and strife, which causes the loss of uprightness and the occupation of people with one another, so that the tilth and the offspring are destroyed. Perhaps the prohibition of this is due to cowardice, or to reflection on the outcome, and to relieving the soul of what harm outweighs its benefit, which the shrewd tend toward. Moreover, at that time many of the disbelievers had in their minds the hope of achieving what would spare them fighting, namely that some harm would befall the believers. ﴿But Allah refuses except to perfect His light﴾. And the flaws in this view are not hidden, and the earth here means its kind, or the illuminated city (Madinah). To take it as the whole earth is nothing, for the definiteness of a singular noun conveys the inclusion of its individuals, not its parts. Unless one considers every patch of land an earth, but then there remains no sense in taking it as all-encompassing with respect to the realization of the judgment in one single instance. And the mention of the earth is not merely for emphasis; rather, in it there is an alert that corruption occurs in a dwelling owned by a benefactor who settled you in it and granted you its blessings.

And the most hateful of Allah's creatures is one who spends the night disobeying the One who spends the night turning in His bounties.

("Innama") is for restriction (hasr), as some grammarians and the scholars of the principles of jurisprudence held. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr chose that restriction is understood from the context and is not indicated by the form itself. The view that it is composed of "ma" (the negative particle) followed by "inna" (which is for affirmation), so that it conveys restriction, is a weak statement issuing from one who lacks knowledge of grammar. The meaning of ﴿We are only reformers﴾ is that they are confined to pure reform, which has no resemblance to any aspect of corruption, and this has become so clear that one should not doubt it. The restriction is either restriction of singularity (qasr ifrad) or restriction by reversal (qasr qalb). This either arises from double ignorance, so that they took corruption to be reform and persisted in it, and they were arrogant with great arrogance.

Judgment is passed upon a man in the days of his trial, until he sees as good what is not good.

Or it proceeds in accordance with their habit of lying and saying with their mouths what is not in their hearts. Hisham and al-Kisa'i read "qila" (it was said) with ishmam al-damm (a partial rounding of the vowel toward u), so that it indicates the underlying waw that was converted. "Quwl" (with pure damm and a sukun on the waw) is a dialect of Hudhayl, but it was not read with it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 12:

﴿Unquestionably, they are the corrupters, but they do not perceive.﴾ This is a rebuttal of their stated claim in the most emphatic manner. It takes the form of a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), which results in the ruling becoming more firmly fixed in the mind of the listener, along with the affirmation and confirmation of the ruling. This is through (bi-anna, and alla), based on their being composed of the interrogative hamza of denial (al-hamza al-istifhamiyya al-inkariyya), which carries the meaning of the negating (wa-la) particle. Thus it is a negation, and it conveys affirmation by a demonstrative method more eloquent than other methods. Because it conveys confirmation, as Nasir al-Din said: a sentence rarely comes after it except when it is introduced by that which is used with the oath (kana, the lam, and the particle of prohibition). What most scholars have accepted is that it is simple (basita), not because it enters upon an emphatic (anna al-mushaddada) and the negating particle does not enter upon it, since it could be said that its original ruling is nullified after composition. Rather, it is because the original state is simplicity. The claim "rarely comes after it, etc." is not entirely sound, how so, since it has entered upon rubba and hayyadha, and the vocative ya, in: "Unquestionably, many a day that is good for you from both of them," and "Unquestionably, how excellent is Hind, and the land in which is Hind," and "Unquestionably, O Qays and al-Dahhak, go forth." He added to that the definiteness of the predicate (ta'rif al-khabar), and the placing of the separator (tawassut al-fasl). By his words "but they do not perceive" he indicated, in a certain way, that their being corrupters has become manifest like something sensed by the senses, even if they do not grasp it. Here the Exalted used the corrective conjunction (istidrak), and did not use it after the deception, because in that case nothing preceded the deception that could be taken to imply perception, a supposition that would require it to be followed by a lifting of the matter. This is unlike the present case, for when they were forbidden from the corruption they had engaged in, which is not hidden from people of intellect, they answered by claiming that they were the opposite of it. Then the Exalted informed them of their corruption, and they were deserving of knowing it, while in fact they did not. So it was a fitting place for the corrective conjunction. As for what is said, that there is no blame on one who corrupts without knowing, and that blame attaches only to one who corrupts with knowledge, it is refuted by the fact that the one who is negligent in knowledge while able to acquire it is blameworthy without doubt, and indeed it may be said that he is in a worse state than others. All of this is on the assumption that the object of "they do not perceive" is omitted and understood as "that they are corrupters." It is also possible to understand that the consequence of that corruption returns to them, or that "We know that they are corrupters," and that "Unquestionably, they are the corrupters" serves to convey a necessary implication of the information, based on the premise that they know the information and deny it, as is their constant habit. This is less likely if the hypocrites were People of the Book. It is also possible that the object is not intended to be omitted, and this is more forceful in censure, and it contains further consolation for him (ﷺ), since one who is from among the people of ignorance should not be concerned by the opposition of the scholar. In the Ta'wilat of 'Alam al-Huda (Abu Mansur al-Maturidi), this verse is an argument against the Mu'tazila in that moral obligation (taklif) does not apply without knowledge of what one is obligated to, and that proof does not bind without recognition. For God the Exalted informed that what they did of hypocrisy was corruption on their part despite the absence of knowledge. Had the reality of knowledge been a condition for obligation, and they had no knowledge of it, their conduct would not have been corruption, because corruption is the commission of what is forbidden. If the prohibition against hypocrisy was not binding upon them, their action would not have been corruption. Since it was corruption, this shows that obligation depends on the existence of the instrument of knowledge and the ability to acquire knowledge, not on the reality of knowledge itself, and so it is a proof against them. This question is a branch of the question of whether capability is concurrent with the act or not. You know that, while the possibility of its existence remains, reasoning from inability is set aside.

﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed"﴾. This alludes to *al-tahliya* (adornment) with the unpointed *ḥāʾ* (حاء مهملة), just as ﴿do not spread corruption﴾ alludes to *al-takhliya* (clearing away) with the dotted *khāʾ* (خاء معجمة). For this reason the former was placed first. There is nothing here that indicates that deeds are part of the perfection of faith or of its essence, as has been said, because the consideration of abstaining from corruption is due to its indicating denial, which contradicts faith. The object of belief (*al-mu'min bihi*) has been omitted because it is evident, or the meaning is: "Perform faith." The *kāf* (ك) is in the accusative position. Most grammarians make it an adjective (*naʿt*) of an omitted verbal noun (*maṣdar*), meaning: "a faith like the faith of the people." Sibawayh, however, does not permit the omission of the modified noun and the placing of the adjective in its position in this context. He makes it accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) from the implied verbal noun understood from the verb. It was not made to depend on *āminū* (آمنوا), and the adverbial phrase is *laghw* (redundant), on the basis that the *kāf* does not function in that way. *Mā* (ما) is either a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyya*) or a restrictive particle (*kāffa*). It was not made a relative pronoun (*mawṣūla*) because of the artificiality this involves. The meaning according to the verbal-noun reading is: "Believe with a faith similar to the faith of the people." According to the restrictive reading it is: "Realize your faith as the faith of the people was realized," which means that it should be accompanied by sincerity, pure of any admixture of hypocrisy. By "the people" is meant the Messenger (ﷺ) and those believers with him in general, as Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. They are "in the sight of the eminent" (*nuṣb ʿayn ulī al-ghayn*), and the attention of their thoughts is drawn to them through their contemplation. Their mention has already occurred, because they enter at the first level into "those who believe." So the reference is external (*ʿahd kharijī*), or external by mention (*kharijī dhikrā*), or it refers to those among their own kind who believed, such as ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, as a number of the senior Companions have said. Or the intended ones are the perfect in humanity, whose peers are regarded as among the animals in lacking the discernment between truth and falsehood. So the *lām* (ال) is either for the genus or for totality (*istighrāq*).

The verse has been cited as evidence that the verbal affirmation of faith is faith, since otherwise the restriction would have no effect. That it is for encouragement (*targhīb*) is refuted by their introduction of the comparison in their reply and the response to it. Also, it is possible to counter it with the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And they are not believers﴾. There is no disagreement about the permissibility of applying the term faith to verbal affirmation, but insofar as it is an expression of what is in the heart, it stands in its place. The dispute is only about whether it is the name of faith in itself, and whether the Lawgiver established it for that while disregarding what is in the heart, as is explained to you in its proper place. When hypocrites were asked to believe, this indicates the acceptance of the repentance of the heretic (*zindīq*).

*"If he is not her, or if he is her, then he is her brother; his mother has nourished him with her milk."*

Yes, if he is known for heresy, calling others to it, and does not repent before being apprehended, he is to be killed like the sorcerer, and his repentance is not accepted, as a group of the verifying scholars (*muḥaqqiqūn*) has ruled.

﴿They said, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?"﴾ They meant that this would never happen at all. The interrogative *hamza* (همزة) is for rejecting and nullifying. By "the foolish" they meant either those earlier people, or the whole species. The noble and intelligent of those are included in it according to their corrupt assumption, at the first level. Whoever went to the view that the *lām* is for a dominant attribute, as in *al-ʿAyyūq* (the star name), is far off the mark, because this attribute did not dominate particular people unless it is claimed that it dominated among themselves. ﴿May Allah fight them; how are they deluded?﴾ Foolishness (*safah*) is lightness, agitation, and disturbance, and it has become common for deficiency of reason and judgment. They called them foolish out of their own ignorance, since they busied themselves with what, in their opinion, is useless. It is possible that this was from the posture of defiance (*tajallud*), out of fear of mockery, if "the people" is interpreted as those among them who believed. The Jews are a people of slander. Many scholars have found this verse problematic, in that if the speakers are the believers, as is apparent, and the responders are the hypocrites, then they would have to be displaying disbelief when they met the believers, so where is the hypocrisy, which is what is understood from the context and the setting? It has been answered that this reply was among themselves, and Allah related it about them and refuted it against them. A reply is not only what is said face to face. It has become widespread among later scholars to apply the word "reply" to the refutation of the words of earlier scholars, despite the distance of time, without objection. It has also been said: "*idhā*" (إذا) here means "if" (*law*), to confirm their concealment of disbelief and that they are in a state requiring that if they were told such a thing they would say such a thing, as has been said of a similar construction in the line: "And when I blame him, I blame him alone." It has been said that it occurred in the presence of the Muslims but as a private whispering among them, and the One who knows secrets and private conversations made it manifest. It has also been said that it occurred in the presence of those among the believers who did not disclose their secret, for kinship or some interest. Our master, the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, mentioned that the truth from which there is no escape is that their statement, even if it was made in the presence of the advisors, does not require that they be open rejecters. It is a refined kind of disbelief and an ancient art of hypocrisy, because it is a statement that is open to the meaning of polytheism, as he mentioned in his commentary, and to the good meaning of being understood as claiming faith like the faith of the people, and denying what they were accused of, namely hypocrisy, in the sense: "Shall we believe as the foolish and the insane believe, whose faith is not counted, even if they believed? Nor shall we believe as the people believe until you order us to do so." They addressed this to the advisors mockingly, showing off, intending the last meaning, while they relied on the first. The Law looks at the outward, and with Allah, Exalted, is knowledge of the hidden. For this reason the believers were silent, and Allah, Glorified be He, returned upon them what they had concealed. So the statement is a metonymy (*kināya*) for the perfection of their faith. Let there be in the heart of that metonymy a sting, so it accords with their saying: ﴿And hear, without being heard﴾, in its openness to both evil and good. For this reason it was forbidden. May Allah, Exalted, have mercy on him, made His saying in relating about them ﴿We are only reformers﴾ belong to this category as well. Our master al-Shihab al-Khafaji inclined to this and claimed that it was from the products of his own thought. In my view it is nothing, because ﴿Shall we believe?﴾ is a denial of the action in the present, and their saying ﴿as the foolish have believed﴾ in the past tense is explicit

in attributing foolishness to the believers because of their faith. So there is no equivocation (*tawriya*) and no hypocrisy. Perhaps when he saw the past tense he added to the explanation of the meaning "if they had believed," and I do not know where he got it from.

*"And the perfume-seller cannot repair what time has spoiled."*

So the easiest of those aspects is some of them. As for his statement that bringing out what one of the two interlocutors said in private, in the context of what occurred between them in the setting of dialogue, is something for which there is no precedent in speech, let alone something in the position of inimitability, its problem is not hidden to anyone who has looked into people's dialogues, ancient and modern. ﴿And Allah speaks the truth, and He guides to the way﴾.

﴿Surely they are the foolish, but they do not know﴾. This is a refutation and a most grievous charge of ignorance, as indicated earlier. Glorified and Exalted is He, why did He say here "they do not know," and there "they do not perceive"? Because what is affirmed for them there is corruption, which is perceived with slight reflection and does not require much thought. So He negated from them what is perceived by the senses, as an exaggeration in declaring them ignorant. What is affirmed here is foolishness, and what is introduced with it is the command to believe, and that requires complete reflection which leads to faith and assent. What was commanded did not occur from them, so the negation of knowledge from them is appropriate. Also, foolishness is lightness of reason, and ignorance of matters according to what has been said, so the negation of knowledge is most appropriate to it. This is based on the apparent reading of the object (*maf'ūl*), and on a reading other than the apparent one it is not apparent, so reflect.

Then know that when two *hamzas* meet, the first vowelled with *ḍamma* and the second with *fatḥa*, from two words such as *al-sufahāʾ* and *alā*, there are several ways of pronouncing them. Making both *hamzas* fully articulated is the reading of the Kufans and Ibn ʿĀmir. Making the first fully articulated and softening the second by changing it into a *wāw* is the reading of the two Ḥaramayn (Mecca and Medina) and Abū ʿAmr. Softening the first by placing it between *hamza* and *wāw*, with the second fully articulated, or softening the first and changing the second into a *wāw*. A group permitted making both *hamzas* intermediate (*bayn bayn*), and others prohibited it.
