﴿When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe."﴾ This describes the habitual conduct of the hypocrites: when they encounter the believers, they ward them off from themselves by saying "We believe," mocking them. One should not suppose that this repeats the beginning of the story, because it is a display of their malice and deceit, and an uncovering of their extreme depravity and their claim to be like the believers in genuine faith, and that they surround the believers from both sides. Moreover, even if this were not the case, one should not suppose a repetition either, because the meaning is: "Among the people is one who utters faith in hypocrisy, for the sake of deception, and that utterance occurs when meeting the believers." This is not repetition at all, because it includes restriction and additional clarification, and because they added mockery to deception, and they utter this only when there is need. As for the view that what is meant by "We believe" in the first instance is the report of the creation of faith, and here the report of the creation of sincere faith, which the Imam (al-Imam) approved, and I do not follow him in this, and his support for it on the grounds that verbal affirmation was already known from them and did not need clarification, whereas what was doubtful was the sincerity of the heart, so that this must be intended, is refuted by reflection by one with discernment, in what we have set out.

The liqa' (meeting, encountering) is approaching a person closely; it is one of fourteen verbal nouns of the verb laqiya. Abu Hanifa and Ibn al-Samayqa' read ﴿لاقَوْا﴾ (laqaw), and in al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit) it is taken to have the meaning of the bare verb. The omission of the object in "We believe" is said to be for the sake of the restriction stated before it, "in Allah and the Last Day." It is also said that what is meant is "We believe in what you have believed." One who said that they meant belief in Musa (ﷺ) alone, to the exclusion of others, and that they omitted it as an equivocation and a concealment, is far off the mark. Here, in my view, nothing has been established concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse. As for what al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, our master the Mufti of the Ottoman lands (Mawlana Mufti al-Diyar al-Rumiyya), and others mentioned, it comes through al-Suddi al-Saghir, who is a liar, and that chain is a chain of lies, not a chain of gold. The signs of fabrication are evident in what they related, so it is not relied upon, nor is it to be turned to in any way.

﴿And when they go apart to their shayatin (devils)﴾. The verb khalaw is from "khalawtu bihi" and "khalawtu ilayhi," meaning that you were alone with him. Or it is from their saying in the proverb: "Seek the matter, and let go of blame (khalak dhamm)," meaning: leave you, pass by you, and go on from you. From this comes ﴿Certainly, precedents have passed before you﴾. According to the second sense, the first object here is omitted because the purpose does not depend on it, meaning: when they leave them (khallawhum). Its transitivity to the second object by "ila" (to) is because passing away from something implies reaching another. The possibility that it is from "khalawtu bihi," meaning "I mocked him," gives the meaning of the verse as: when they end the mockery with them and speak it. This is not appropriate for the speech of the Lord of Might, though al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and others mention it, because khala in the sense of "mocked" has not occurred explicitly in the speech of any trustworthy source. The saying "So-and-so was alone with so-and-so's honour, playing with it" is not explicit, since khala may be in its literal sense, or in the sense of "gained control over him," as has been said. The indicator of mockery is "yaʿbathu bihi" (plays with him). Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl claimed that "ila" here means "maʿa" (with), but there is no evidence for this, just as the claim that it means "bi" (with). Moreover, Sibawayh and al-Khalil do not hold that one particle substitutes for another. Yes, indeed, khalwa, as in al-Taj (Taj al-Arus), is used with ila, bi and maʿa with one meaning. It is understood from al-Raghib's speech that the original meaning of khuluww is the emptiness of a place or space from an occupier, and likewise of time, and it does not mean passing away. If it is meant in that sense, it is a metaphor, while the apparent sense of others' speech is that it is literal. Two weak meanings overcome a strong one.

What is meant by "shayatinihim" (their devils) is those who used to command them to deny, from among the Jews, as Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said, or their soothsayers (kahana), as al-Dahhak and a group said. They were named so because of their rebelliousness and their making evil seem fine and good seem ugly. Or it is because their companions, the devils, are, if they are interpreted as soothsayers. There were many of them in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), such as Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf from the Banu Qurayza, Abu Burda from the Banu Aslam, ʿAbd al-Dar in Juhayna, ʿAwf ibn ʿAmir in the Banu Asad, and Ibn al-Sawda in Syria.

To interpret it as the devils of the jinn, as al-Kalbi said, is something that does not stir in my heart. The word shayatin is a broken plural (jamʿ taksir). Treating it as a sound plural, as in one of the irregular readings (tanazzalat bihi al-shayatun), is a very strange dialect. Its singular is shaytan. According to the Basrans, it is on the pattern fayʿal, so its nun is original, from shatana, meaning "he went far," because of its distance from obeying the command. This is shown by tashayṭana (he acted as a devil). Otherwise it would have dropped out. The possibility that it is taken from al-shaytan rather than from its own root, on the grounds that the meaning is "he did his action," is contrary to the apparent sense. According to the Kufans, its pattern is faʿlan, its nun is extra, from shaṭa yashiṭu, meaning he perished, or became void, or burned with anger. The feminine is shaytana.

In al-Bahr he recited:
"She is the mature she-camel, the great one, nothing other than her,
and a she-devil whose eyelids have gone mad because of her."

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that the shaytan is every rebel among the jinn, humans and beasts.

﴿They say, "We are indeed with you"﴾. That is, a moral companionship, which is their equality with them in the Jewish belief, and it is the mother of evils. He used the nominal sentence indicating occurrence with the omission of emphasis in what is directed to the believers who deny what they are upon, or who rebel. He used the affirmative nominal sentence with emphasis in what is directed to their devils, who are not like that, because in the first case they are seeking to claim the creation of faith, and they did not here look to the denial of anyone, and its hesitation is an appearance that they are at a level in which there should be no hesitation about their faith, so that they might emphasize, perhaps their aim would be fulfilled by that in their own view. In the second, they intend to convey steadfastness, to repel what stirs in the thoughts of their devils concerning mixing with the believers and addressing them with faith. It is said that emphasis, as it can be to remove denial and doubt, can also be to show the sincerity of desire, and its omission, as it can be for the absence of such, can be for the speaker's lack of concern. So for desire they emphasized, and for its absence they omitted. Or because if they said, "We are believers," it would be a claim to the perfection of faith and its steadfastness, and that does not find acceptance among the believers, given what they are upon of gravity and sharpness of intellect, whereas their devils are not like that. In my view, the first reason is correct, since the words of the Exalted about them, as reported, refute the last two: ﴿We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah﴾. Unless it is said that they displayed desire there and feigned indifference to lack of acceptance for some purpose or other, and circumstances vary, and the obstacles are many. For this reason it is said that they did so for dissimulation, deception, and the claim that they are like the believers in faith, in order that the rulings of the believers be applied to them and that they be spared from war. They emphasized with "bi" in what came before, where they said: ﴿in Allah and the Last Day﴾. The claim that the difference between the verse of testimony and the verse of faith here is clear, because if they had said, "We are indeed believers," they would be committing themselves to two things: his (ﷺ) prophethood and the obligation of their belief in it. This is unlike the verse of testimony, for it includes commitment to the first only. The absence of desire for two things does not necessarily entail its absence in one of them, which is clearly weak for the fair-minded, as is not hidden.

The majority read ﴿maʿakum﴾ (with you) with a moving ʿayn (the letter ʿayn with a vowel). It was read irregularly with a sukun on it, and that is the dialect of Rabiʿa and Ghanm.

﴿We are only mockers﴾. Al-istihza' (mockery) is contempt and ridicule. The form istafʿala here has the meaning of faʿala: one says hazi'tu bihi and istahzi'tu bihi with one meaning, like istaʿjaba and ʿajiba. Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali mentioned that mockery is belittling and disdain, and pointing out faults and defects in a way that provokes laughter, and this may be by imitating in deed and speech, and by gesture and signalling. They meant "mocking the believers." The root of this word is lightness. One says: his she-camel tahza' with him, meaning she hastens and is light. The statement of al-Razi, that it is an expression of showing agreement while nullifying what is in the category of evil in the way of mockery, does not agree with the language or custom.

The sentence is either a resumptive sentence (istinaf, a new sentence), as if the devils said to them, when they said "We are indeed with you": "If that is so, why do you agree with the believers?" and they answered with this. Or it is an apposition to "We are indeed with you." Is it a badal ishtimal (inclusive apposition), or a badal kull (total apposition), or badal baʿd (partial apposition)? This is disputed. As for the first, since this sentence conveys what the first conveys, namely steadfastness in Judaism, because the one who mocks a thing persists in its opposite, plus an addition, which is the magnification of unbelief, which serves to remove the suspicion of mixing and their obstinacy in unbelief, it is an inclusive apposition.

As for the second, and al-Sa'd (al-Taftazani) said this: it is because of equality in truthfulness, and it does not require equality in the meaning conveyed. As for the third, it is because their being with them is general in companionship, encompassing mockery, ridicule and other things. Or it is an emphasis of what precedes it, such that one says: their claim "We are indeed with you" is steadfastness in unbelief, and "We are only mockers" entails rejecting Islam, and its negation serves to confirm steadfastness in it, since lifting the contradictory of a thing is an emphasis of its firmness, lest the lifting of both contradictories follow. Or it is said: it entails: "We are indeed with you, we are in fact making the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) suppose faith," so that mocking them and their religion becomes an emphasis in view of that implied consequence. The best of these views according to the scholars is the resumptive sentence, were it not for what al-Shaykh (ʿAbd al-Qahir al-Jurjani) mentioned in Dala'il al-I'jaz, that the function of innama (only) is to come with a statement that the addressee does not ignore and does not dispute its truth, for this requires that presupposing a question here is a less preferred matter. Perhaps the matter in this is easy.

It was read ﴿mustahziʾun﴾ (mocking, with a hamza) with the hamza lightened, and with it changed to a vowelled yāʾ, and some drop the yāʾ, so the zāy is vowelled.

﴿Allah mocks them﴾. The People of Hadith and a group of the interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) understood the mockery (istihza') attributed to Almighty God in its literal sense, even though "the one who mocks" (al-mustahzi') is not among His names, glorified is He. They said: it is belittling (al-tahqir) in a manner that is part of His dignity, such that whoever becomes aware of it marvels at it and laughs, and there is no impossibility in such a thing occurring from Him, exalted is His dignity. He forbade analogizing the Unseen (al-ghaib) to the seen (al-shahid). Most people, however, held that He cannot be described with it in its literal sense, because it implies confirming the one mocked in the ignorance he has. The requirement of wisdom and mercy is that He show him the truth. If he believes that He is not characterized by what he is mocked for, then it is a play (la'ib) that does not befit His majesty (kibriya'). Accordingly, the verse is interpreted in one of these ways: either mockery means its recompense (jaza'uhu), because of the resemblance in measure between the act and its recompense, the strong association between them, and a kind of causal relation, together with the presence of the mushakala (reciprocity of expression) which beautifies the phrase here. Thus there is a metaphor by sequence (isti'arah tab'iyyah) or a free metaphor (majaz mursal) in the speech. Or it means the infliction of humiliation and disgrace, and this is a metaphor for what is in the position of its end (ghaya), so it is the use of the effect (musabbab) for the cause (sabab) with respect to conception (tasawwur), and the reverse with respect to existence (wujud). Or He makes Allah, exalted and sanctified, like one who mocks them by way of the implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyya), and attributing mockery to Him is by imagination (takhyil). Many a thing is valid as a consequence (tab'an) but not valid intentionally (qasdan). He, glorified is He, may apply to His holy essence whatever He wills, to make His servants understand. It may also be said that the verse follows the mode of figurative representation (tamthil), and the meaning is that He treats them, glorified is He, as one who mocks is treated: in this world, by applying the rulings of Islam to them and leading them gradually (istidraj) from where they do not know; and in the Hereafter, by opening for one of them a door to Paradise, so it is said: "Come, come," and he comes with his distress and grief, but when he arrives, it is shut in his face. Then another door is opened for him, and it is said: "Come, come," and he comes with his distress and grief, and when he reaches it, it is shut in his face. So it continues until a man is opened a door and it is said: "Come, come," but he does not come to it. This has been related with a mursal chain which is of good chain (jayyid al-isnad), concerning those who mock people.

He, glorified is He, ascribed the mockery to Himself, beginning the sentence with the mention of Himself, to draw attention to the fact that the mockery of the hypocrites (munafiqin) is the most eloquent mockery, with which their mockery carries no weight, since it issues from One whose knowledge and power vanish in comparison with His knowledge and power. And He, exalted is He, suffices His believing servants, and avenges them. How greatly they are in need of confronting the hypocrites, in order to magnify their status, since they were mocked only in Him, and no one is more jealous than Allah, glorified is He. He left out the conjunction (ʿatf) because it is the original form (al-asl), and there is nothing in the preceding sentence to which this statement can validly be conjoined except with strain and remoteness. It has been said: the speech is delivered in a way that answers the question about how Allah, exalted is He, treats them in response to their treatment of the believers. Their saying ﴿We are only mockers﴾ indicates that what is related of their vileness is of such a kind that it calls for the manifestation of Allah's jealousy, and each one asks about the manner of His vengeance upon them. The words of some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) suggest that if this statement had been introduced with a conjunction, even on an ellipsed element suited to the context, such as "they are mockers at the believers," it would have indicated that this was in return for their mockery, and would not indicate that Allah, exalted is He, has made the believers absolutely independent of confronting them, nor that He has absolutely undertaken to requite them; rather, it would imply restricting His undertaking to this particular recompense. Also, because Allah's mockery is at a place far removed from their mockery, to the point that there is no correspondence between the two, the conjunction would be like conjoining two unrelated matters. Some have arranged the two benefits we mentioned, deriving from attributing it to Him, on the basis of a new sentence (isti'naf), claiming that if it were conjoined, even by supposition, to an assumed element such as "the believers are mockers at them, and Allah mocks them," both benefits would be lost. This is it. Perhaps what we have mentioned is safer from idle talk (qil wa qal) and further from places of doubt. So ponder this.

He, glorified is He, departed from "Allah is a mocker of them" (Allahu mustahzi'un bihim), which would correspond to their saying, to His saying "Allah mocks them" (Allahu yastahzi'u bihim), because it indicates renewal and continuity (al-tajaddud al-istimrari), and this is more eloquent than the stability of continuance (al-istimrar al-thubuti) which the nominal sentence indicates, because when a trial continues it may become light, and the soul grows accustomed to it, as it has been said:

"I was created for a thousand [years]; were I to return to youth, I would part from my white hair, with a heart in pain, weeping."

The inflictions of Allah, exalted is He, upon them and the descent of verses concerning them were a matter renewed and continuous. ﴿Do they not see that they are tested once or twice every year?﴾ ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down against them, informing them of what is in their hearts﴾ ﴿Say: "Mock on; surely Allah will bring forth what you fear"﴾. This is a kind of the lesser punishment (al-adhab al-adna), and the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe, if they only knew. He mentioned the object of mockery explicitly here, so that the mockery directed at them would be explicit. The hypocrites, in what is related of them, left it out, out of fear that it would reach the believers, so they kept the wording ambiguous, so that they would have room for denial if they were called to account. Thus Allah, exalted is He, made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest, and His word is the highest.

﴿And He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾ is conjoined to His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿mocks them﴾, serving as an explanation of it according to one opinion. The verb madda (to extend) and amadda have the same meaning, namely, to add to something what strengthens it and increases it. It has been said: madda means to increase in kind, and amadda means to increase in what is not of the same kind. It has also been said: madda is used for evil and amadda for good, the reverse of wa'ada and aw'ada. When amadda is used for evil, it is perhaps of the type of ﴿So give them good news of a painful punishment﴾. This root has been used in two meanings: one of them is what we have mentioned, and the second is granting respite (al-imhal), from which comes "extending the lifespan" (madd al-'umr). What applies here is the first and not the second, for two reasons. The first is that it has been related from Ibn Kathir, outside the seven readers, as (yumiddahum) with a ḍamma from the derived form (al-mazid), and this has not been heard in the second sense. The second is that the first is transitive by itself, while the other is transitive by the preposition lam, and omission and attachment (of the preposition) contradict the original form, so it is not resorted to without a reason. Thus the meaning of "He extends them in their transgression" is that He increases them and strengthens them in it. Al-Baydawi and others took this view. The truth is that granting respite is possible here too, and al-Zajjaj and Ibn Kaysan held this view. Both opinions are open to objection, for each of the two forms has been reported, in the view of the lexicographers who are relied upon, both as triliteral and as derived, both transitive by itself and by the preposition lam, and both derive from one root, and their meanings return to increase, whether in quantity or in quality. In the Sihah it is said: "Allah extended his life (madda Allahu fi 'umrihi)" and "He extended him in his error (maddahu fi ghayyihi)," meaning He granted him respite and prolonged it for him.

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that the extension of Allah, exalted is He, in their transgression is the enabling of them to disobedience. From Ibn 'Abbas it is granting respite (al-imla'). Ascribing extension to Allah, exalted is He, in whatever sense, is in the view of the People of Truth (ahl al-haqq) a reality, since He, glorified and exalted is He, is the originator of things, the sole creator of them according to what wisdom requires, and the preparednesses (al-isti'dadat) have raised their palms to Him. Ascribing it to other than Him, glorified and exalted is He, in His saying, exalted is His dignity: ﴿and their brothers extend them in error﴾, is like ascribing the taking of souls (tawaffi) to the angel in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The angel of death who is charged with you will take you﴾, together with His saying, exalted and glorified is He: ﴿Allah takes the souls﴾. The Mu'tazila held that increase in transgression and strengthening in it is among the things whose ascription to Him, exalted is He, literally is impossible, and they interpreted the verse according to other meanings. We have already presented what weakens their doctrine, so let us set it aside here with what it contains.

"Transgression" (al-tughyan) with a ḍamma on the ṭa' is the well-known form, and Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read it with a kasra on it. Both are dialectal forms of it, and both have been heard as the verbal noun of liqa' (meeting). Al-Kisa'i inclined it. Its origin is going beyond the place where you stand. Whoever neglects what has been designated of the legal standing-points (al-mawaqif al-shar'iyya) and rational knowledge (al-ma'arif al-'aqliyya), and does not observe them, has transgressed. From this is "the water transgressed," that is, it went beyond its known limit. Its being attributed to them is because it is their act, issuing from them by their powers, which are effective by the permission of Allah, exalted is He. So the particularization which the attribution indicates is only in this respect, not in respect of location or attributes, since that is known and needs no attribution, nor in respect of origination (al-ijad) independently without dependence on the permission of the Doer for what He wills; for that is a consideration with dust upon it, indeed dust with no consideration at all. So do not let the bluster and clamor of al-Zamakhshari dismay you. It may be that the particularization is to indicate that the transgression of others is beside theirs, like nothing, given their claim to be specially connected with it. This is not a deviation from the norms of eloquence.

(Al-'Amah) is wandering and bewilderment (al-taraddud wa al-tahayyur), and it is used specifically of opinion, while blindness (al-'ama) is used of both opinion and sight. Thus between them there is a general and specific relation in usage, even if they differ in original imposition, and blindness is said to be restricted to sight. Its origin is the absence of signs on the road, which are set up to guide, made of stones, dust and the like, and these are the landmarks (al-manar). It is said: 'amiha ya'mahu like ta'iba ya'tabu, 'amahan and 'amahanan; so he is 'amih, 'amih, and 'amha'. Thus the meaning of ya'mahun according to this is "they wander and are bewildered." This is the view of a group of exegetes. It has also been said: al-'amah is blindness regarding right guidance. Ibn Qutayba said: it is that one bows his head and so does not see what comes ahead. Thus the meaning is "they are blind regarding their guidance, or they bow their heads and do not see." This seems closer to the truth, because the hypocrites were not wavering in disbelief; rather, they were persistent in it, believing it to be the truth and all else to be falsehood. Unless it is said: the wandering and bewilderment were in another matter, not in disbelief.

The clause ﴿wandering blindly﴾ is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), either from the pronoun in "yamuddu-hum" or from the pronoun in "tughyanihim," since the latter is a verbal noun (masdar) with an agent (fa'il) attached to it. "In their transgression" may be connected either to "yamuddu-hum" or to "ya'mahun." It was permissible, contrary to the case where "in their transgression" and "wandering" are two circumstantial clauses, for both to be circumstances of the pronoun in "yamuddu-hum,"

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 16:**

﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance.﴾ This refers to the hypocrites mentioned earlier, who combined the blameworthy qualities: claiming to be righteous while being corrupters, attributing foolishness to the believers while being the fools themselves, and mocking while being the ones mocked. Because of their remoteness in evil and their wretched state, He pointed to them with a demonstrative that indicates distance. The discourse here may be placed in the position of ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾, for the hearer, after hearing their description and these qualities being attributed to them, seems to ask: From where did these conditions come to these people? It is answered that those who are remote in this way dared to commit them only because they bought error in exchange for guidance, so that their transaction was lost, they lost the guidance to the straight path, and they fell into the bewilderment of confusion and error. It has also been said that it is a summation and comprehensive statement of all that preceded of the reality of their condition, or a justification for their deserving the most eloquent mockery and the extension in transgression. Or it confirms His statement, ﴿And He extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾. In it is the restriction of the predicate to the subject, since the definiteness of the relative pronoun for the category is like the definiteness of the generic *al-* (the generic definite article), and this is figurative in view of their perfection in that buying.

(Page 161)

Although the other disbelievers share with them in that, by gathering those hideous vices and grievous traits, on the basis of this consideration it is correct to specify them with it. *Ḍalāla* (error) is deviation from the aim, and *hudā* (guidance) is turning toward it. Both are also used for deviating from the correct position in religion and remaining firm upon it. *Ishtirā'* (buying), like *shirā'*, is the exchange of a commodity for a price, that is, taking it in return for that price. Some scholars consider it one of the words with opposite meanings (*al-aḍdād*), because the two contracting parties exchange the price and the goods, so each of the two counter-values is bought from one side and sold from the other. It is also used figuratively for taking something by giving what is in one's hand, whether each of the two is a tangible object or an abstract meaning. Outwardly, this requires that what plays the role of the price, which is guidance, was already present for these people, and there is no doubt that they were far from it. As for saying that *ishtirā'* is a metaphor for choosing, since the buyer of a thing prefers it, it is as if He, exalted is He, said: "Choose error over guidance." And since the exchange is intended, the particle *bi* (with) is used, on the basis that it has been said that agreement in meaning does not require agreement in the construction. This interpretation is not refuted by its being inconsistent with the *tarshīḥ* (the supporting metaphor that follows), as the Mufti of the Ottoman lands claimed, because the said *tarshīḥ* is satisfied by the presence of the word *ishtirā'*, even if the intended meaning is not supported, as is customary in such cases. Or it may be said: what is in the place of the price is not guidance itself, but the complete capacity for it, through the combining of causes and the taking of the premises that lead to it, by way of *isti'āra* (metaphor), as if it were guidance itself, by the common feature of being followed by benefit. There is no doubt that this was present for those hypocrites through the marvelous signs they witnessed, the overpowering miracles, the great guidance, sincere counsel and instruction, but they rejected all of that and fell into the abysses of destruction. Or it may be said: the intended guidance is innate guidance, which was in fact present for them, since every child is born upon the natural disposition (*fiṭra*). As for the statement of the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, that taking guidance as the original disposition present in everyone is refuted by the fact that losing it is not peculiar to these people; and if it is taken to mean complete loss reaching the point of sealing, which is peculiar to them, then the loss of it alone is not as shameful as its loss together with the supporting textual and rational proofs. Moreover, that would lead to the conclusion that what was explained from the beginning of the surah up to here is wasted. This is a statement arising from heedlessness of the meaning of the demonstrative, for it requires that they be considered together with all the qualities previously mentioned. The meaning is that those characterized by the aforementioned hypocrisy are the ones who wasted the natural disposition most severely, by Judaizing their fathers; then, after they attained it, they lost it through hypocrisy, together with urging others to preserve it and offering counsel verbally and similar things that are not found in others, as the definite reference indicates. Or it may be said: this is a translation (*tarjama*) of another of their crimes, and the intended guidance is what they had of affirming the mission of the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and the truth of his religion through what they found with them in the Torah. For this reason they used to seek victory through him, invoke his sanctity, and threaten the disbelievers with his coming. ﴿But when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it; so the curse of God is upon the disbelievers.﴾ As for taking guidance to mean what was outwardly apparent among them of uttering the testimony, establishing prayer, giving zakat, fasting, and fighting, this is something that one guided to the right path would not approve. What we have mentioned, that ﴿those﴾ refers to the hypocrites, is what most exegetes adopted, and it is what is transmitted from Mujahid, and it is what the noble structure of the verse requires, and I hold it. It is also reported from Qatada that they are the People of the Book in general, and from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with them, that they are the disbelievers in general. All of these, in my view, are far-fetched. Perhaps the intent of whoever said that is that the verse, by the outward sense of its meaning, applies to those they had in mind, not that the verse was revealed concerning them. Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Ishaq read *ishtaraw al-ḍalāla* with a kasra (*ishtaraw*), because that is the original form in joining two unvowelled letters. Abu al-Simak read *ishtaraw* with a fatha, following the preceding vowel. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i inclined the *alif* of *al-hudā* (imala), which is the dialect of the Banu Tamim, while non-inclination is the dialect of Quraysh.

﴿So their commerce did not profit, nor were they guided.﴾ It is coordinated with the relative clause (*ṣila*). He used the *fa'* (so) to indicate that the negation of profit follows the buying immediately, and that with the very act of buying the absence of profit is established. Some claimed that the *fa'* entered because the sentence has the meaning of a conditional, owing to the relative pronoun, so it is like the example: "He who enters the house, for him is a dirham." This is not correct, because the relative pronoun here is not the subject as in the example; rather it is a predicate about "those." What follows the *fa'* is not a predicate but is coordinated with the relative clause, so it is part of the relative clause. It is not permissible that "those" be the subject and "who" a subject, with "so their commerce did not profit" as the predicate of the second, and that predicate together with its predicate be a predicate of the first, because there is no connecting pronoun in the second sentence, and because the meaning of the relative clause is established. When the relative clause is past in meaning, the *fa'* does not enter the predicate of its relative pronoun. Nor is it permissible for "those" to be the subject and "who" a substitute for it, with the sentence being the predicate, because the *fa'* enters the predicate only when the relative pronoun is general, and what is substituted from a specified item is specified. So the correct view is what we have mentioned, and the meaning of the verse is only that, as in *al-Baḥr* (the Ocean commentary). Commerce (*tijāra*) is the disposal of capital seeking profit. There is hardly any original *tā'* followed by a *jīm* except in *nataja*, *tajira*, *rataja*, and *irtaja*. As for *tujāh* and the like, their root is a *wāw*. Profit (*ribḥ*) is the attainment of increase over the capital, and it has spread to mean excess over it. *Al-muhtadī* is the active participle of *ihtadā*, the reflexive of *hadā*, and the *ifta'ala* form is only reflexive from a transitive verb. As for the line of poetry:

*Until, when Suhayl rose in the pre-dawn, like the blaze of the fire-kindler scattering sparks*

the *ifta'ala* in it has the meaning of *fa'ala*: one says *shāla yashūl* and *ishtāla yashtāl* with the same meaning. In the verse there is *tarshīḥ* (supporting metaphor) for the figurative use you have heard before it. The primary aim is to depict their loss by the forfeiture of the benefits that follow from guidance, which are like profit, and the waste of guidance, which is like the capital, in the image of a merchant's loss who misses profit and wastes his capital, until it is, by way of the representative metaphor (*isti'āra tamthīliyya*), an exaggeration in their being made losers and falling into the most shameful loss which the people of insight shun. Attributing profit to commerce, when it belongs to its owners, is a metaphor by association. In a context of blame, he expressed by the negation of profit the notion of loss, because the failure to gain profit necessarily implies it in some degree, and at least the amount of effort expended. The benefit of the metaphor by implication (*kināya*) is the explicit affirmation that the purpose of commerce is absent while its opposite is present, unlike if it were said: "their commerce lost," in which case one would not suppose that negating one of two opposites necessarily establishes the other when there is no intermediate state between them. An intermediate state exists here, for a merchant may neither profit nor lose. It has been said that this holds when the locus accepts all of them, as in real commerce; but if it accepts only two of them, then the negation of one is an affirmation of the other. Profit and loss in religion have no intermediate state between them. Moreover, the context here clearly indicates loss, by His statement, ﴿and they were not guided﴾. Many have taken it as a metaphor by implication for the waste of capital, for if a merchant is not guided in the ways of commerce, many calamities befall his wealth. The metaphor by implication was chosen as a way of afflicting them by declaring them ignorant and foolish. It is possible, though remote, that the negation here is like the line: "On a broad road whose landmark cannot be followed," meaning there is no landmark to follow, so it is as if He said: there is no commerce and no profit. Apparently, ﴿and they were not guided﴾ is coordinated with "did not profit," for closeness, for suitability, and because it follows from the figurative meaning. By supplying the object of guidance, namely the ways of guidance, the supposition is dispelled that the absence of guidance was already understood from what came before, which would make it a repetition of what has passed. This is either for completeness and precaution, like the line:

*So may the cloud's rain water your abodes, unspoiled by it, with a steady downpour*

or for the sake of ornamentation (*ta'nīm*), like the line:

*As if the eyes of the wild beasts around our tents and our saddles were the unpierced bead.*

The noble Sharif, may his secret be sanctified, said: coordination with "bought error in exchange for guidance" is preferable, because coordinating it with "did not profit" requires that it be ordered after what precedes by the *fa'*, so it would necessarily come later, whereas the matter is the reverse. Unless it is said that the ordering is by way of the judgment and the report. In reply: if it were coordinated with "bought," the more apparent thing would be to place it first, since placing it later creates an ambiguity; and in that case the better course is to omit the coordination as a precaution, as was mentioned in such a line as:

(Page 163)

*And Salma thinks that I seek in exchange for her another, whom I see wandering in error.*

Moreover, there is a closeness in meaning between "they bought…" and "and they were not…" that prevents the goodness of coordination, as is not hidden from one who has not corrupted his sound natural disposition. It has also been permitted that the clause be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). The wretchedness of its condition is not hidden from one whose discernment is sound. Ibn Abi 'Abla read *tijārātuhum* in the plural, and the reason is that each one of them has a commerce. The reason for the singular in the reading of the majority is that the meaning is understood, with the indication that their commercial dealings, though many, belong to one market, and they are partners in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 17 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾ is a sentence that confirms the preceding sentence about the story of the hypocrites, narrated up to this point. Therefore it is not joined by a conjunction to what precedes it. Since that story runs, with its metaphors and figurative expressions, in the manner of descriptive attributes that uncover the reality of the hypocrites and explain their conditions, he followed it with an explanation depicting that reality and bringing it forth in the form of something witnessed, through the coining of a parable (ḍarb al-mathal), as a completion of the exposition. The coining of parables has a standing that cannot be concealed, and a light that cannot be extinguished. It lifts the veils from the faces of realities, unveils the face of subtle matters, brings the imagined into the appearance of certainty, and makes the absent seem present. Sometimes the meanings that are intended to be conveyed are purely intelligible, so the imagination (al-wahm) contends with the intellect in grasping them until it prevents them from joining what is in the intellect. So through the coining of parables they come forth in the appearance of the sensible, and the imagination assists the intellect in grasping them. There the darkness of illusions is dispelled, and the clamor of dispute is lifted. ﴿And these parables We set forth for the people, that perhaps they may reflect﴾. It has been said: the more likely view is to make it an elucidation of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Those are the ones who have bought﴾ and so on, and there is no difficulty in that. Taking it as a new sentence (isti'nāf) is remote, especially since parables are coined for disclosure and clarification. The word mathal, with two fatahs, is like mathal with a kasra and a sukun. The mathīl, originally, is the equal and the like. The distinction (between them) is one I do not accept. It seems to be derived from al-muthūl, which is standing upright, and from it is the hadith: "Whoever desires that people stand up for him (yatamaththala lahu al-nās qiyāman), let him take his seat in the Fire." Then it was applied to eloquent speech that is widespread and good, comprising either a comparison without a like (tashbīh bilā shabīh), or a striking figurative expression of the dramatic kind (istiʿāra ra'iqa tamthīliyya) and others, or wisdom and beneficial admonition, or a beautiful allusion (kināya badī'a), or an arrangement from the comprehensive concise words (jawāmiʿ al-kalim). It is not required that it be a compound metaphor, contrary to whoever has thought so. Rather, it is not required that it be a figure of speech at all. These are the proverbs of the Arabs, which have been singled out for compilations, and many works have been written on them. Among them, much is used in its literal meaning. And because it is unique in its category, and its quotation is intended, they did not permit altering it, since the intended purpose would be lost. Explaining it as "a saying circulated, whose coinage is likened to its source" is refuted by the parables of the Qur'an, because God, exalted is He, initiated them, and they had no prior source. Except that it may be said: this is a new terminology, or that the majority of proverbs are of that kind. Then it was borrowed for every situation, story, or attribute that has significance and is strange. From this is ﴿And to God belongs the highest likeness﴾, ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾. And here the intended meaning is mathal, not the tamthīl indicated by the kāf. The meaning is: their condition, which is wondrous in its nature, is like the condition of one who kindled a fire, and so on, as will be uncovered in its aspect, God willing. So the kāf is a particle of comparison, related to an omitted predicate of the subject. Ibn ʿAṭiyya claimed that it is a noun, like it in the verse of al-Aʿshā:
Will they desist, when he who forbids the reckless will not forbid them, as the spear-thrust in which the oil and the twisted cord go (i.e., are spilled)?
This is the view of Ibn al-Ḥasan, and it is not good except in poetic necessity, and the claim of an additional element (ziyāda), as in His saying: "So become like ﴿chewed-up stalks﴾," is an added ignorance. As for the one placed in the position of "those who" (alladhī wuḍiʿa mawḍiʿ alladhīna), if the pronoun in "with their light" refers to it, then it is well; otherwise it remains on its apparent meaning, since there is no harm in likening the condition of a group to the condition of one individual. Here the placement of the singular in the place of the plural is permissible, though the majority have prohibited it, and did not permit placing the singular participle in place of the plural participles, because this is contrary to other cases, due to a particularity that required it. For it was only placed so that it could be used to describe definite items by means of clauses, and since it is not intended for its own sake, they were lenient with it. And because it, together with its relative clause, is like a single thing, and the plural marker does not occur in the middle, therefore they did not attach it to it. They used it for what is general, like man and ma, and alladhīna is not a plural of it; rather it is a noun placed with an added element to increase the meaning, and its explicit mention is intended. For this reason it is not defined by particles as others are, according to the most eloquent view. And because it has lengthened by its relative clause, it deserves lightening, to the point that it was exaggerated, until it was restricted to the lām in forms like the active participle. This was said by al-Qāḍī and others, and it is not free of difficulty, especially the last view. What is reported from some grammarians, that the nūn of alladhīna may be omitted, is not accepted by the scholars of verification. Even if it is granted, it requires the return of a plural pronoun to it, as in His saying: ﴿And you plunged as those who plunged﴾ according to one view, and the saying of the poet:
O Lord of ʿĪsā, do not bless anyone, among those who stood or sat, except the one who stood at the edges of the palm-fiber rope.
The singular pronoun, we have not heard it from one who is trusted. Perhaps this is because the omitted is like the pronounced. The proper view is to say that it looks to what is in alladhī of general generic meaning, since there is no doubt that it does not refer to a particular kindler, nor to all the individual kindlers. The relative pronoun is like the definite article al-, and what applies to it applies to it. The noun of genus, although its form is singular, may be treated as plural, as in ﴿Above them are garments of green silk﴾, and their saying: "the yellow dinar" and "the white dirham." Or it may be said: there is an implied noun modifying it, singular in form but plural in meaning, like "company" (fawj) and "group" (farīq). Thus the arrangement is good, and the pronoun in "kindled" (istawqada) is considered with the form of the noun modified, and in "their light" with its meaning. And istawqadū means awqadū (they kindled), for Abū Zayd related: awqada and istawqada have the same meaning, like ajāba and istajāba. Al-Akhfash also said this. To take istiqād as meaning "seeking fuel," which is the blazing of the fire, as al-Bayḍāwī did, requires an omission. The meaning then is: they sought fire and asked for it, so they kindled it. When it lit up, because lighting does not result from seeking, but from kindling. Fire is a subtle, luminous, burning substance. Its derivation is from nāra yanūru nūran, meaning to flee, because in it, as you observe, there is movement and agitation in seeking the center. That this is a mistake of the senses, as it were, is a mistake of perception. Indeed, an objection was raised against the definition: lighting is not considered part of its essence, and it does not include what is established in the judicial books, that the original fire, where the ether is, is transparent and has no color. The same is said about burning. The answer is that the assignment of names is to the actual things as they are perceived, or to the mental meanings derived from them. As for considering their necessary properties and essential attributes, that is the task of one who wishes to stand on their realities, and that is beyond the capacity of most people. People perceive from the fire that is with them the lighting and burning, and they make these the most distinctive of its attributes. Definition is for what is commonly known. The absence of burning due to an impediment does not harm. Moreover, the claim that the fire beneath the sphere is guiding and non-burning, though some people assert it, was refuted by the Shaykh. The burning of meteors is for one who denies burning. More strange than this is the denial of the fire that is with the ether, and close to it is the saying that it is nothing but very hot air. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ read "like the example of those who" in the plural. This reading is very problematic. The most we have found in explaining it is that the singular pronoun is by way of the habitual confusion (tawahhum) known in the speech of the Arabs, as if he uttered man alladhī for it in both form and meaning, just as he jazama with alladhī by way of confusion with the conditional, in the saying:
Thus is he who oppresses people unjustly; the consequences of what he did will befall him despite himself.
Or he was content with the singular in place of the plural, as the apparent singular is used in place of it. So it is like his saying:
And among us in the desert is a clan who guard it, swift to the summoner, great are their hindquarters.
That is, "their hindquarters." Or the subject of istawqada refers to the active participle understood from the verb, as in His saying: ﴿Then it appeared to them, after they had seen the signs﴾ according to one view. The returning pronoun is then omitted contrary to analogy, that is, "for them." Or there is no returning pronoun in the first clause, being satisfied with the pronoun in the second clause joined by fa, and in inversion there is something of everything. ﴿So when it lit up what was around it, God took away their light﴾. Lamma is a particle of occurrence for occurrence, or of necessity for necessity, as Sibawayh expressly stated, or a temporal adverb meaning "when" or "since." The lighting is the making

صفحة 165

[Page 165]

...the thing shining and radiant. Or *ishrāq* (shining forth) and *farṭ al-ināra* (excessive illumination). *Aḍā'a* is used both transitively and intransitively. On the first use, *mā* is either a relative pronoun (*mawṣūla*) or a descriptive (*mawṣūfa*), the adverbial phrase is either a complement (*ṣila*) or a qualifier (*ṣifa*), and *mā* is the direct object (*maf'ūl*), with the subject being the pronoun referring to the fire. On the second use, *mā* is likewise a relative or descriptive, but it is the subject (*fā'il*), and its verb is feminine because it is interpreted as a feminine noun, as with places and directions. Alternatively, the subject is the pronoun referring to the fire, and *mā* is superfluous (*zā'ida*), or *mā* is in the accusative position as an adverb of place (*ẓarfiyya*). There is no requirement to state *fī* (in) here, as some have imagined, because the correct view is that when the relative or descriptive *mā* is used as an adverb, what is meant by it is the places surrounding the one who kindles the fire, which are the six directions. These are among the things put in the accusative as adverbs by a consistent analogy, so what is expressed by them is likewise in the accusative. The most preferable of these views is that *aḍā'at* is transitive and *mā* is a relative pronoun, for then there is no need to interpret the sentence according to its meaning, nor to resort to a usage that is rarely employed, especially the superfluous *mā* here. To the point that they have stated that it has not been heard here, nor preserved from the speech of the Arabs: *jalastumā majlisan ḥasanan* ("you two sat a good sitting") or *qumtumā yawma al-jumu'a* ("you two stood on Friday"). Alas, from where did al-Zamakhsharī take this, and how did al-Bayḍāwī follow him?!

If the subject is the pronoun referring to the fire and the verb is intransitive, then the attribution is to the cause. This is because the fire itself did not come into existence around the one kindling it, but its light existed, so the shining forth of its light around him was made as though it were the shining forth of the fire itself, as has been said. This is based on the principle that when an adverbial phrase is attached to an intransitive verb that has a transitive effect, the adverbial relation must be established both for the effect and for the agent. Therefore, for the shining forth of this in that, there must be the shining forth and the one who shines being in it. This is like when an adverbial phrase is attached to an intransitive verb, as in *qāma Zaydun fi al-dār* ("Zayd stood in the house"), for Zayd and the standing are both in it, essentially and derivatively. Al-Zamakhsharī inclined to this view. Some people, however, were satisfied with the existence of the effect in it, even if the agent itself did not exist in it in its own essence, as in transitive verbs. Thus, "the sun shone upon the earth" is literal according to this view, and figurative according to the first.

*Ḥawla* is an adverb of place, which is inseparably used as an adverb and in construct (*iḍāfa*), and it may be dualized and pluralized, so one says *ḥawlayhi*, *aḥwālahu*, and *ḥawāla mithlihi*. It is dualized as *ḥawālay*. We have not found its plural in the lexicographical books available to us. Do not say *ḥawālihi* with a kasra on the *lām*, as in the *Ṣiḥāḥ*. Perhaps the dual and plural forms, together with what is understood from some books, that *ḥawl* and likewise *ḥawāl* mean "the sides," which are all-encompassing, are not literal. It has been said that it is according to the division of the circle, as indicated by al-Mawlā ʿĀṣim Efendi in his Turkish translation of the *Qāmūs*, but there is room for reflection on this. The original root of this structure is that it is used for circling and encompassing, like *al-ḥawl* for the year, since it revolves from one season or day to its like. When it necessarily involved movement and change, it was used with that sense, like "transformation." The meaning of *ḥawāla* (transfer), although it is obscure in examples like *ḥawl* in the sense of "strength," has also been said to originally mean the change of a thing and its separation.

*(Wa-dhahaba)* etc. is the response to *lammā* ("when"). The causal relation is figurative, because when the removal of light followed the illumination without delay, it was treated as if it were a cause for it. Moreover, for a condition, mere dependence is sufficient, as in: *in kāna lī mālun ḥajjtu* ("if I have wealth, I will perform the pilgrimage"). The removal depends upon the illumination. The pronoun in *bi-nūrihim* ("with their light") refers to the one (*alladhī*) or to its descriptive antecedent, and its plurality is due to what was mentioned before. He chose "light" over "fire" because it is the greatest of its benefits, and it is the more fitting for the context, both in what precedes and what follows. It has been said that the sentence is resumptive, as a response to what is said about them, and their condition is likened to that, or it is an explanatory substitute for the sentence of the parable. The pronoun refers to the hypocrites. The response to *lammā* is omitted, meaning: their fire went out, so they remained bewildered. Similar to it is *fa-lammā dhahabū bihi* ("So when they took him away"). Its omission is for brevity and for the security against confusion. What is in this will not be hidden from one who has even a little fairness, though many have accepted it. The speech of Allah, the Subtle, the All-Aware, is too exalted for such obscurity. The attribution of the verb to Him, exalted is He, is literal, for He is the Absolute Doer, in whose hand is the management of all affairs, directly and indirectly. No one may object to the Wise about anything. Taking the fire to mean a fire that Allah does not approve of kindling, whether it is figurative, like the fire of strife and enmity toward Islam, or literal, kindled by the misguided for corruption or mischief, then it is fitting for the Wise to extinguish it. Otherwise, a figurative meaning would have to be resorted to, which none has called for except the Mu'tazilites, and the kindling of the fire of misguidance and misleading.

It is transitive by the preposition *bi-* rather than by the hamza, because of what is in the famous proverb: *dhahaba bi-al-shay'* ("he took away the thing") implies that he kept it with him and held it from returning to its original state, while *adhhabahu* does not carry this meaning. So although *bā'* and hamza share the meaning of transitivity, it is not far-fetched that the author of the *Maʿānī* considers the original meanings of hamza and *bā'*, namely removal, accompaniment, and attachment. There is an undeniable subtlety in the verse, especially since the agent is Allah, the Mighty, the Powerful, to whom none can return what He has taken, nor release what He has withheld. Abū al-ʿAbbās mentioned that *dhahabtu bi-Zaydin* implies that the speaker went away together with Zayd, unlike *adhhabtuhu*. Perhaps he means that the verse is metaphorical for the intensity of seizing, such that it cannot be returned. Or it may be that Allah described Himself with "going away" in a sense fitting to Him, just as He described Himself with "coming" in His saying: *wa-jā'a rabbuka* ("and your Lord comes"), in its apparent meaning. Sībawayh held that *bā'* has the meaning of hamza, so both are merely for transitivity in his view, without difference. Therefore, they are not combined.

Light is the source and origin of radiance, as the Arabs' usage indicates, since they attributed radiance to it, as Waraqa ibn Nawfal said: "And a radiance of light appears in the lands." Al-ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

"When you appeared, the earth was lit up,
and the horizons glowed with your light."

For this reason, Allah referred to it as light rather than radiance. He indicated the negation of radiance, which is what the apparent sense requires, by negating light and removing it, because light is its root, and when the root is negated, the branch is negated. What we have mentioned is what the verifying scholars of the language have endorsed. From this we learn the reason why the Muhammadan law is described as light in His saying: *qad jā'akum mina Allāhi nūrun wa-kitābun mubīn* ("There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book"), and the law of Moses is described as radiance in His saying: *wa-laqad ātaynā Mūsā wa-Hārūna al-furqāna wa-ḍiyā'an wa-dhikran lil-muttaqīn* ("And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a radiance and a reminder for the God-conscious"). In this is an indication of the station of our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, who combines and distinguishes, and of his superiority over his brother Moses, peace be upon him, who came only with distinction. Also, for the difference between the Beloved and the one who spoke with Allah:

"Every sign the noble messengers brought,
from His light did they connect to them."

Similarly, the reason for describing prayer as forbidding indecency and wrongdoing with light, and patience with radiance, in the hadith of Muslim, is clear. It is known from this that light is stronger than radiance, so it is said, though it has been objected that the description of what our Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was given has been described as radiance just as what Moses, peace be upon him, was given has been described as light. This is what the words of al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, in *al-Futūḥāt* indicate, so reflect. Some people have held that radiance is stronger than light, based on His saying: *ja'ala al-shamsa ḍiyā'an wa-al-qamara nūran* ("He made the sun a radiance and the moon a light"). According to this view, the expression *dhahaba Allāhu bi-nūrihim* ("Allah took away their light") rather than *dhahaba Allāhu bi-ḍaw'ihim* ("Allah took away their radiance") serves to exclude the possibility of removing the excess in radiance while leaving what is called light, whereas the purpose is the complete removal of light.

Some have mentioned that both radiance and light are applied to what the other is applied to, so they are like synonyms, and the difference arises from usage or convention, not from the original root and language. From here the philosophers said: radiance is what belongs to a thing from itself, and light is what belongs to it from another. Radiance is used for what has heat in it literally, like that in the sun, or figuratively, like what was mentioned about what was given to Moses, peace be upon him, of what has hardship and great burden. From this is the hadith: "Patience is a radiance" (*al-ṣabru ḍiyā'*), and it is known that it is like its name. Light is used for what is not like that, like that in the moon, and in what the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, brought of the easy, tolerant, white law. From this is the hadith: "Prayer is light" (*al-ṣalāt nūr*), and there is no doubt that it is the coolness of the eyes and the relief of the heart. To this the hadith indicates: "And the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer," and "Relieve us, O Bilal." Light is also used for what appears in darkness, as in the hadith: "The people were in darkness, so Allah spread upon them from His light," and the poet's words:

"We spent the night while the life of the night was in its full vigor,
and it had, by the light of the full moon, a grey-streaked branch."

Radiance is not like this. And there are other things that will not be hidden from one who investigates. What the heart inclines to is that radiance is applied to strong light, and to the spreading ray of light. In the first sense, it is stronger, and in the second, weaker. For every situation there is a manner of speech, and for every rank there is an expression. The eloquent is not restricted in choosing one of the two terms in some contexts, for a subtle reason he has considered and a relevance he has noticed. The verse about the sun does not indicate that radiance is stronger than light wherever it occurs, for Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth (*Allāhu nūru al-samāwāti wa-al-arḍ*), and to Allah belongs the highest likeness (*wa-lillāhi al-mathal al-a'lā*). The application of light to pure essences, rather than radiance, is widespread. Perhaps this is because the notion of accidentality comes to mind more quickly from radiance than from light. It is well established that light is an accident and a quality distinct from color. The view that it is an expression of the appearance of color, or that it consists of tiny particles that separate from the luminous body and join the illuminated one, has been clearly shown to be false in the books of philosophy, even though some philosophers held each of these views.

Furthermore, the use of light here rather than radiance may have a secret other than what has come to people's minds, namely that it is more fitting to the condition of the hypocrites, who were deprived of benefiting from and being illuminated by what came from Allah, which He called light in His saying: *qad jā'akum mina Allāhi nūrun wa-kitāb* ("There has come to you from Allah a light and a Book"). It is as though Allah, exalted is His affair, withheld light from them and deprived them of benefiting from it. He did not call it radiance, so that this indication could be achieved. If He had said here, "Allah took away their radiance," He would have clothed it in garments of His names and poured upon it of the lights of His favors. So He is the most complete manifestation and the adorned mantle. Furthermore, the attribution of light to them is due to the slightest connection, for it truly belongs to the fire. But since they benefited from it, it is correct to attribute it to them.

Ibn al-Samayqaʿ and Ibn Abī ʿAbla read *fa-lammā ḍā'at* with a triliteral verb, and its explanation is known from what has preceded. The Yemeni reader read *adhhaba Allāhu nūrahum* ("Allah took away their light"), and in this there is support for Sībawayh's view.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 17 (part 3 of 3):

﴿And He left them in darkness, not seeing.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with His saying, ﴿Allah took away their light﴾, and it is more complete in conveying the intended meaning. From it is derived the affirmation of the complete absence of light, following from the mention of darkness (ẓulumah). The plural form, the indefinite form, the statement ﴿not seeing﴾, and making the waw a circumstantial waw (wāw al-ḥāl) with the implied qad, all have their effect. However, this implies that the darkness existed before the light was taken away and together with it, and that is not the intended meaning. Tark (leaving) in the well-known usage means casting something aside, like leaving a staff from one's hand, or letting it be, whether perceptible or otherwise, even if it is not in one's hand, like leaving one's homeland and religion. Al-Raghib said: "Tark of a thing is abandoning it, deliberately and by choice, or by compulsion and necessity." It is understood from al-Misbah that it is literally used for departing from perceptible things, and then it was used figuratively for meanings. Whether the verb is among the nawasikh (verbs that govern two objects, such as ṣayyara, "to make") by being construed to include the sense of ṣayyara, or not, is disputed. All of this is possible here. According to the first view, (hum) is its first object, (fī ẓulumātin) is its second object, and (lā yubṣirūn) is an attribute of (ẓulumāt), with the implied fīhā, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the hidden pronoun, or from (hum). It is not permissible for (fī ẓulumātin) to be a circumstantial clause and (lā yubṣirūn) a second object, because the original state of a predicate is that it is not emphatic, although some have permitted it. According to the second view, (hum) is its object, and (fī ẓulumātin lā yubṣirūn) are two synonymous circumstantial clauses of the object, or overlapping ones: the first is from the object, and the second from the pronoun in it. (Fī ẓulumātin) is connected to (tarakahum), and (lā yubṣirūn) is a circumstantial clause. The darkness, in the well-known usage, is the absence of light from that which by its nature should be illuminated. So the opposition between it and light is an opposition of privation and possession (taqābul al-ʿadam wa-al-malakah). It has been objected that darkness is a perceptible quality, and nothing of privation is like that. It has also been objected that darkness is created, as His saying indicates, ﴿and He made the darknesses and the light﴾, and what is created must be existent. The first objection is answered by denying the minor premise: when we close our eyes we see nothing at all, and likewise when we open our eyes in darkness. The second objection is answered also by denial: the Creator who creates the existent also creates a specific privation, such as blindness, and what is incompatible with being created is pure privation. It has been said that darkness is a quality that prevents seeing, so the opposition is contrariety (taqābul al-taḍād). It has been objected that if it were a quality, the state of one in a dark cave and one outside would not differ in seeing and not seeing. It may be said that the intended meaning is that it is a quality preventing the seeing of what is within it, and thus the objection is removed. It may even be preferred over that view, because it may apply to the original darkness that preceded the existence of the world, though not to the quality. It has been said that the opposition between light and darkness is the opposition of affirmation and negation (taqābul al-ījāb wa-al-salb). The plural ẓulumāt is either because of their multiplicity in reality, whether the plural pronoun refers to those who kindled the fire or to the hypocrites, or because, although in reality it is one darkness, it is so intense that the plural form is used for it as an intensification, as they say: "One lord is worth a thousand." Or because, since each one has a darkness specific to him, it is pluralized on that basis. So they said. Among the subtle points is that wherever darkness occurs in the Qur'an it occurs in the plural, and wherever light occurs it occurs in the singular. Perhaps the reason is that darkness, though little, is considered abundant, and light, though abundant, is considered sufficient as long as it does not harm. Also, these two are often used to refer to disbelief and faith, and a little disbelief is much, while much faith is little. So one should not rely on a little of the former, nor be content with much of the latter. Also, the source of darkness in this sense is the hearts of the disbelievers: ﴿You think them united, while their hearts are divided﴾. The place where light rises in this sense is the hearts of the believers, which are like the heart of one man. Also, the light that is bestowed is the existence that is attributed, and it is one with no multiplicity in it, as His saying indicates: ﴿Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth﴾, whereas in darkness such a thing is not seen. Also, the root meaning of darkness revolves around prevention, so it is derived from their saying: "What prevented you (ma ẓalamaka) from doing such-and-such?", i.e., what prevented you. In Mutallathat Ibn al-Sayyid: "ẓalm," with a fatḥah on the ẓāʾ, is the figure of every thing that blocks the sight of the viewer. It is said: "I met him at the first ẓalm," i.e., the first figure that blocks my sight, and "I visited him while the night was ẓalm," i.e., preventing visitation. So it was called ẓulumah because it blocks in the well-known sense and prevents seeing. Therefore, because of the multiplicity of obstacles it is pluralized, and no such consideration was taken in the root meaning of light, so it was not pluralized. The darkness is indefinite here and was not made a genitive of their pronoun as light was, for the sake of brevity of expression and sufficiency with what the meaning indicates. The sense of place (ẓarfiyyah) is figurative, however you explain darkness according to some opinions. ﴿Not seeing﴾ is treated as intransitive, since the object is omitted and forgotten, and because there is no intention to a particular object over another, so it conveys generality. Al-Jumhur read (fī ẓulumātin) with a ḍammah on the lām. Al-Hasan and Abu al-Simak read it with a sukūn, and a group read it with a fatḥah. All of them are plurals of ẓulmah. A group claimed that ẓulumātin with a fatḥah is the plural of ẓulam, which is the plural of ẓulmah, so it is a plural of a plural. Shifting to the fatḥah for lightness, given that it is heard in similar forms, is easier than claiming a plural of a plural, since that is not analogical and there is no definitive evidence for it. Al-Yamani read (fī ẓulmatin). The verse also contains an allusion to the likeness of the utterance of the testimony of faith on the tongues of those mentioned, and adorning themselves with the adornment of the believers, and the like, which prevents their being killed and brings them worldly benefits, such as security and spoils, while they are not sincere in what they displayed, in hypocrisy that harms religion, by kindling a bright fire to benefit from it, which Allah extinguished, so the winds and rains blew upon them and made its kindler in darkness and regret. It is also possible that when they were described as having bought misguidance in exchange for guidance, this was followed by this illustration, to liken their guidance which they sold to the bright fire, and the surroundings of the one who kindled it, and the misguidance which they bought, and Allah sealed their hearts with it by Allah's taking away their light and leaving them in darkness. The interpretation transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, as Ibn Jarir reported from him, is that this is a parable for the faith that they displayed, to gather its fruits with a fire of far-shining lights kindled for benefit and insight, and for the departure of its effect and the obliteration of its light by their destruction, and the exposure of their state by Allah's extinguishing it and taking away its light. The likeness contains other aspects. (Among the inner Qur'anic meanings mentioned by our masters the Sufis, may Allah benefit us through them): the verse is like one who enters the path of the saints by imitation and not by realization, so he acts outwardly and does not find the sweetness of the inner, so he abandons the works after losing the states. Or it is like one who kindles the fires of claims while having no reality, so his outward appearance shines with fame and acceptance, then Allah exposes his hypocrisy among the people until they finally cast him off, and he finds no escape from disgrace on the day when secrets are tested. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq said: This is a parable that Allah struck for one who did not correct the states of the will, and rose from those states through claims to the states of the great. The states of his will would have shone upon him had he corrected them by adhering to their etiquettes. But when he mixed them with claims, Allah took away those lights from him, and he remained in the darkness of his claims, unable to see the way out of them. We ask Allah for pardon and well-being, and we seek refuge in Him from returning to disorder after order.

[Page 168]

﴿Deaf, dumb, blind; so they will not return.﴾ The attributes (ṣifāt) are broken plurals (jumūʿ kathrah) on the pattern fuʿl (فُعْل). This is the regular analogical pattern (qiyās) for the plural of faʿlāʾ and afʿal when the two adjectives are either opposites, like aḥmar and ḥamrāʾ, or stand alone because of a natural impediment in creation, like ghurl and ruthq. If the adjective is shared between masculine and feminine but the two forms were not used in the pattern of aḥmar and ḥamrāʾ, like rajulun alīyun and imraʾah ʿajzāʾ, then the pattern is transmitted through usage (samāʿī).

Ṣamam (deafness) is an ailment of the ear that prevents hearing. The physicians said it is when the ear canal (ṣimākh) is created without a cavity containing still air, through whose vibration sound is heard, or when there is a cavity but the nerve does not convey the power of sensation. If it conveys it with difficulty, they call it ṭaraṣ (partial deafness). Its root is from hardness or blocking, and from this comes their saying qanāh ṣammāʾ (a solid, closed reed) and ṣummimat al-qārūrah (the bottle was sealed).

Bukm are the mute, the dumb, in form and meaning. It is an ailment of the tongue that prevents speech. It was said that the abkam is one born mute. It was also said that he is one who understands nothing and is not guided to what is right, and then it is an ailment of the heart, not of the tongue.

ʿAmā (blindness) is the absence of sight in what should naturally see. It was also said to be darkness in the eye that prevents perceiving visible things. It is applied to lack of insight (baṣīrah) metaphorically according to some and literally according to others.

These are predicates (akhbār) of an omitted subject, namely the pronoun referring to the hypocrites, or they are a single predicate. The meaning returns to their not accepting the truth. Although they have hearing ears, eloquent tongues and seeing eyes, since they did not lend an ear to the truth, and their tongues refused to speak all of it, and they did not perceive the proofs of guidance set up in the horizons and in the souls, they were described with what they were described with, of deafness, dumbness and blindness, in the manner of his saying:

I am blind when my neighbour appears, until the curtain (khidr) screens my neighbour,
And I am deaf to what was between us, my ear, and in its hearing is heaviness.

This is, according to the verifiers (al-muḥaqqiqūn), an eloquent simile (tashbīh balīgh), because mentioning both parts (ṭarafān), the subject and the object of comparison, in judgement and in intention, prevents metaphor (istiʿārah) in their view. Some said it is a metaphor, and others said both are permissible. This is a settled matter, and there is little benefit in establishing it here. However, they raised a point here: there is no dispute that the implied meaning is "they are deaf," and so on, but the borrowed-for (mustaʿār lahu) is not mentioned at that time, because the verse is to explain the states of the hypocrites' inner perceptions for themselves. So in these attributes there is an explicit indirect metaphor (istiʿārah tabaʿiyyah muṣarraḥah). Unless it is said that the comparison of the hypocrites' persons with the persons of deaf individuals is derived from the comparison of their state with deafness, so the intention to establish this derived element is stronger and more eloquent. It is as if the resemblance between the two states extended to the two persons, so the verse is taken as this comparison with regard to emphasis (rināyat al-mubālaghah).

Or it may be said, and this is perhaps preferable, that the implied (muqaddar) pronoun "hum" refers to the hypocrites whose states, attributes and exposure through them have been mentioned, until they became a proverb. It is as if it were said: "These, who are characterized by what you see, are deaf." The borrowed-for is what the pronoun contains, which was made an expression for those characterized by what has passed, and the borrowed is what contains deafness and its two siblings from his saying "deaf," and so on. Thus the hidden thing is revealed. This is not very far-fetched.

The verse is a summary (fadhlakah) and conclusion of what preceded it, since it is known from his saying "they do not perceive" and "they do not see" that they are deaf and blind, and from their denying that they speak the truth that they are like the mute, and from their not being guided that they do not return. He mentioned deafness first because, if it is innate, it entails muteness. He delayed blindness because, as it was said, it includes blindness of the heart arising from the paths of perceptible things and the outer senses. In this sense it is later, because it is pure intellectual meaning. If it were placed in the middle, it would fall between the staff and its bark. If it were placed first, it would give the impression that it is connected to "they do not see," or the order would be according to the state of the one being illustrated, since he first hears the call to the truth, then responds and acknowledges, then reflects and gains insight.

Similar sentences occur sometimes with fa' (then), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We appointed for Moses thirty nights and completed them with ten, so the appointed time of his Lord was completed as forty nights.﴾ And other times without it, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So a fast of three days during the Ḥajj and seven when you return; those are ten complete.﴾ This is because what precedes it entails it and includes it potentially, so it is treated as united with it, and the conjunction is omitted. Its distinctness from it, and its being subsequent to it as offspring and branch to its root, requires attachment with fa', which is the common and well-known usage. Some people make the verse part of the illustration (tatimmat al-tamthīl), so then no figurative extension (tajawwuz) is needed, and the supposition (farḍ) suffices for it, even if it is customarily impossible, as in his saying:

Banners of ruby, spread over spears of emerald.

So it is supposed here that deafness, dumbness and blindness occur to those who fall into that severe, enveloping darkness. It was said: it is not far-fetched that the senses are lost for one who falls into frightening, terrible darkness, since that may lead to death, let alone that. What supports that it is a completion of the illustration is the reading of Ibn Masʿūd and Ḥafṣah, Mother of the Believers, may God be pleased with them, (ṣummān wa bukman wa ʿumyan) with the accusative case.
