The adjectives then may be a second object of (tarakahum), with (fī ẓulumāt) connected to it, or in the position of a circumstantial phrase. (Lā yubṣirūn) is a circumstantial clause, or in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the object of (tarakahum), transitive to two objects or one. Or it is in the accusative by an omitted verb, meaning "I mean, I mean." The view that they are in the accusative as a circumstantial state of the pronoun in (lā yubṣirūn) is an error regarding the circumstance. Close to it in censure is the one who puts them in the accusative for dispraise (dhamm), since that is only good where the previously mentioned noun is named. As for making this sentence, in the well-known reading, a supplication (duʿāʾiyyah), with an indication of what happens in the Hereafter from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, dumb and deaf﴾, we ask God, exalted is He, for pardon and well-being from committing the like of it, and we seek refuge in Him from the blindness and ignorance of its speaker. The view that the sentence (lā yarjiʿūn) is similar, and even more calamitous and bitter, is that its complement (mutaʿallaq) is omitted, meaning: they will not return to guidance after they have sold it, or from misguidance after they have bought it. Or nothing is supposed, and it is left absolute.

The first two possibilities are based on the view that the aspect of comparison in the illustration is derived from ﴿Those are the ones who bought﴾, and so on. The last is based on the assumption that it is from ﴿God took away their light﴾, and so on, meaning that after the illumination they stumbled, they wandered in darkness and became entangled in bewilderment. Here the meaning is that they are like the bewildered who remain rigid in their places, not moving, and not knowing whether to advance or retreat. How can they return to where they began, when the blind does not see a path, the mute does not ask about it, and the deaf does not hear a voice from the direction of his return so that he may be guided by it? The fa' indicates that their possession of what was previously mentioned is the cause of their bewilderment and confinement, however they may be.

(And from the inner dimensions) they are deaf, the ears of their spirits, to the voices of union and the realities of the inspiration of nearness; mute, regarding the explanation of the causes of their inner states to the physicians of the hearts, in wonder; blind, regarding the vision of the lights of the beauty of the Truth in the countenance of His friends. My master al-Junayd, may his secret be sanctified, said: "They are deaf to understanding what they heard, mute about expressing what they knew, and blind to the insight regarding that to which they were called."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 19 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Or like a downpour from the sky﴾. This begins a second illustration of their condition, following the previous one, and a clarification of every fine and grand detail within it. They are the leaders of disbelief, who excelled in it and sought shelter in the shadows of misguidance after they had flown to it on the two wings of hypocrisy, both its forward and its hidden feathers. It is therefore fitting that the tent of illustrations be pitched in the wasteland of explaining their vile states, and that the ropes of elaboration be extended in describing their deeds, so that it may be a further warning for them and a punishment upon punishment. Every speech that has a share of eloquence and a portion of forcefulness and skill must give its due to each of the two positions, elaboration and brevity. What, then, can be said about a speech that has reached the highest peak of eloquence, skill and inimitability? In this illustration, He (glorified be He) has censured them for the details of their crimes, which have no equal. It is conjoined to ﴿the one who kindled a fire﴾, and the structure becomes "like the likeness of people of a downpour", so that the referent of the plural pronoun appears later, and the conjoined element is harmonized with the element it is conjoined to and with the thing being likened. The particle (or), according to the scholars of verification, indicates one of two matters. In a declarative statement it produces doubt and ambiguity, and the detail depends on the speaker's considerations. In an imperative statement it produces permission and choice in the same way, and then there is no need to posit homonymy (ishtirak, a word having two meanings equally) or the distinction between literal (haqiqa) and figurative (majaz) usage.

Some scholars say that it is originally established for equality in doubt, and it was understood as one instance of the literal meaning. Then it was extended, so that it came to denote equality without doubt, as in the case under discussion, according to one opinion. The meaning is: illustrate with whichever of the two stories you wish, for they are equal in illustration, and there is no harm if you illustrate with both together. Although the second comparison is more eloquent, since it indicates the extreme of bewilderment, the intensity of the matter, and its dreadfulness, it has therefore been placed later, so that it progresses from the lesser to the greater.

Some have claimed that (or) here means (and), and that the two verses contain a single illustration. It has also been said that it means (but), and that it is for ambiguity. All of these are worthless. Yes, Abu Hayyan chose that it is for detailing, and it seems that whoever looked at their state among them compares it to the state of the one who kindled the fire, and among them is one who compares it to the state of the people of the downpour, claiming that permission and likewise choice occur only in imperative statements or what has their meaning. This is his statement, and it is not hidden from one who considers its meaning and verifies what it means that what we are dealing with falls under the second category. Moreover, the claim of exclusivity is something on which the elite have not agreed. Ibn Malik mentioned that most occurrences of (or) for permission in comparison are like ﴿so it is like stones, or harder in hardness﴾, and the estimation is like ﴿so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or nearer﴾.

The (ṣayyib) in the well-known usage is rain, from (ṣāba yaṣūbu), when it descends. This is what is related here from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, Qatadah, 'Ata' and others, may God be pleased with them. It is also applied to the cloud, as in the verse:

*Until it erased them, a downpour whose drops reached far and wide, a pouring, pelting one.*

Its measure is (fayʿil) with a kasra on the ʿayn according to the Basrans, and it is one of the patterns specific to the weak-middle roots, except for the rare (ṣayqal) with a kasra on the qaf, which is a woman's proper name. The Baghdadis pronounce the ʿayn with a fatha, and that is an opinion one should stop one's ears against. Close to it is the view of the Kufans that its origin is (faʿīl) like (ṭawīl), and it was inverted. Is it a collective noun, or an adjective meaning "descending" or "caused to descend"? There are two views, the first being the more famous, and most of its counterparts in pattern follow the second.

It has been read as (ṣāʾib), and (ṣayyib) is more intensive than it. The indefiniteness in it is for classification and for magnification. The (samā') is everything above you, such as a roof and the like. It is what is known to the elite of the earth, and what is seen to the common folk. Its origin is the waw, from (sumuw) (elevation), and it is feminine, though it may also be masculine, as in the verse:

*If the sky had raised to Him a people, we would have joined the sky along with the clouds.*

The feminine ending (tāʾ) may be attached to it, and then the waw is sound, as Abu Hayyan said, because the word was built upon it. So one says (samāwa), and it is pluralized as (samāwāt), (asmiya), and (samāʾiyy). All of these, as in al-Bahr, are rare, because it is a collective noun, and its analogical form is that it should not be pluralized. Its plural by the suffixes (-āt) and (-ān) lacks the conditions of what is pluralized by them analogically. Its plural on the pattern (afʿila) is not among the analogical plurals of the feminine, and on the pattern (faʿāʾil) it is not analogical for (faʿāl).

The meaning of "the sky" here is the horizon, and the definite article is for totality, not for the mental known reference, as occurs to some minds. It therefore indicates that the clouds take hold of all the horizons, which conveys the strength of the calamity, together with the preparation of darkness that it contains. For this purpose He mentioned it. In my view, the mention may also be for terror, and as an indication that what harms them comes from above their heads, which is more effective in harming, as His exalted words indicate: ﴿Boiling water is poured over their heads﴾. We often find that a person takes more care to protect his head than the rest of his limbs, to the extent that the wealthiest of people takes a shawl for that purpose. Sight and direct experience are the strongest witnesses to what we have said.

(Min), here, is for the beginning of the point of origin. It has been said that it may be partitive, with an omitted noun, that is "from the rains of the sky", but this is worthless. Some have claimed that the verse refutes what is said, namely that rain comes from vapours rising from below. This claim comes from the vapours of ignorance, for the verse contains only the statement that the rain comes from this direction, and this does not contradict what has been mentioned. How could it, when observation attests to it? For someone who reached the level of mass-transmission has related to me that they witnessed, while standing on towering mountains, a cloud raining below them, and they witnessed streams of vapours rising from the direction of the mountains, which gathered into cloud and then rained. So beware of turning toward the flashing of a deceptive speech, and do not suppose that this is knowledge; ignorance in it is more correct.

Then, taking (ṣayyib) here to mean the cloud, although it is possible, is distant, like the distance of the cloud, and likewise taking (samā') to mean it. ﴿In it are darkness, thunder and lightning﴾, that is, with it are those things, as in His exalted words: ﴿Enter into nations﴾. When you take (fī) as locative, as is common in the words of the exegetes, it becomes necessary to interpret the relation required by locativity as any relation at all, including causation, adjacency and others. Thus in that meaning there are three darknesses: the darkness of its density due to its succession, the darkness of its cloud together with the darkness of night, which the taste perceives from His exalted words: ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾. Likewise, in it there is thunder and lightning, because they are in its place of origin and the place from which it pours. It has been said that (fī) is here in the sense of "with", and this, as al-Shihab said, is a delusion arising from lack of reflection. If the (ṣayyib) is meant as the cloud, the matter of locativity is more evident, and the darknesses then are the darkness of blackness and enclosure together with the darkness of night. The pluralization of "darkness" is significant on both interpretations. "Thunder" and "lightning" were not pluralized, although they were pluralized in the language of the Arabs. With this, the intensification increases and correspondence with "darkness" and "thunderbolts" is achieved, because these two are verbal nouns in origin. If the two are meant as the specific phenomena here, as is apparent, then the basic principle of a verbal noun is that it is not pluralized. Had they been pluralized, it would have indicated plurality of kinds, as in the conjoined element; but each of thunder and lightning is a single kind.

Al-Shihab mentioned, claiming that it is one of the matters illuminated by the flashes of guidance in the darknesses of thoughts, a secret subtlety in their singularity here. It is that thunder, as has been transmitted in the hadith and as custom has established, drives the cloud from one place to another. If it were plural, the cloud would not be enveloping, and so the intensity of its darkness would be lessened. Likewise lightning: if its flashing were frequent, the darkness would not be complete, as His exalted words indicate: ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾. Thus their singularity is required here.

In my view, and this is among the lights of the care that shine upon the horizons of secrets, since "light" is not pluralized in any verse of the Qur'an for the reason already mentioned, lightning was not pluralized either, since it is not far from it, as His words "Whenever it lights up for them" guide you. Thunder accompanies it, so its rays are reflected upon it.

*Do you not see the lowly sheet of cloud approaching, with its mouth as the lines of the mushaf when it has become a neighbour?*

As for the nominative of (ẓulumāt), it is either the subject of the locative adverb relying on the described noun, or the inchoative with the adverb as its predicate. Making the adverb a circumstantial element of an indefinite noun specified by it, with (ẓulumāt) as its agent, is not free of the darkness of distance, as is not hidden.

As for the thunder and lightning, there are various opinions. The one relied upon is that the first is the sound of the angel's driving-cry, who is entrusted with the cloud, and the second is the gleam of his whips, which are of fire. What is well known among the philosophers is that when the sun shines upon dry land, it dissolves from it fiery parts mixed with earthly parts. From these is composed smoke, which mixes with the vapour. This happens because of the heavenly heat when it acts upon the moisture. Both rise together to the cold layer, and a cloud forms there. The smoke becomes enclosed within it, and it seeks to ascend if it remains in its hot nature, or to descend if it becomes heavy and cold. Whatever the case, it tears the cloud with its violence, and thunder arises from this. Sometimes, because of the intensity of its movement and its friction, a shining fire ignites; this is lightning if it is subtle, and a thunderbolt if it is thick. Sometimes lightning is the cause of thunder, for the burning smoke is extinguished in the cloud, and a sound is heard from its extinguishing, as when we extinguish a fire before us. Thunder and lightning occur together, but lightning is seen immediately, because sight requires only facing without obstruction, while thunder is heard afterward, because hearing occurs only when the undulation of air reaches the hearing faculty, and that requires time. So they have said.

It may occur to your mind that this is near, and you do not know what to do with what has come from the presence of the one who was carried by night, without thunder or lightning, upon the back of the Buraq, and ascended to the Lord of the Ascents, where there is no time and no place. He returned, and he was the most knowledgeable of God's creation in all respects, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. So I, by the strength of the One whose strength is mighty, and by the grace of the One whose bounty has overwhelmed me, shall make available to you what removes the veil from the eye and reveals the secret of the all-comprehensive words that were given to the lord of both worlds, may God's blessings and peace be upon him.

I say: It is established among the masters of wisdom and prophecy, from what they have witnessed through their spiritual observations in their solitary retreats and spiritual exercises, and likewise among all the godly sages of Islam, the Persians, and others, that every corporeal kind, whether spheres, stars, simple elements, or their compounds, has a lord. This lord is a light free from matter, self-subsisting, governing it, and preserving it. It is the one who causes growth, nourishes, and generates in plants, animals, and humans. This is because the diverse activities found in plants and animals cannot proceed from a simple power that has no awareness, and the same applies to ourselves; otherwise we would be aware of them. So all these activities come from the lords, and toward those lords. The Great Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, pointed to this in his saying: "Indeed, for everything there is an angel," and further: "Every drop of rain descends with an angel." He also said: "The angel of the mountains and the angel of the seas came to me." Aflatun (Plato) related about himself that he stripped off the dark veils of the soul and the bodily attachments, and witnessed them. Our master, Shaykh Sadr al-Din al-Qunawi, may God sanctify his secret, mentioned in his commentary on the Fatiha that there is no form except that it has a spirit. The people of God, may He be exalted, have spoken at length on this matter. Once you know this, it is not far-fetched to say that by the angel entrusted with the clouds in explaining the thunder, the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace, meant this governing, preserving lord. By its driving, he meant its governance of it according to its preparedness and receptivity. By the sound of that driving, he meant what occurs when the vapors are split, which that governance requires. By the "makhariq" in explaining lightning, he meant the instrument through which the splitting is produced. The word "makhariq" is the plural of "mikhraq," which originally means a cloth that is wrapped up and with which children strike one another. There is no doubt that, as we have established, it is fire kindled by the intensity of motion and friction. So it appears as you see. Since we have opened this door for you, you are able to interpret much of what has come in this manner, including the saying that thunder is the speech of the angel and lightning is his laughter, even though outwardly it is something that is laughed at. I have not seen anyone who succeeded in this and was granted success, or who verified and was verified. God, may He be exalted, is the Granter of success, He is sufficient for me, and the best Guardian.

﴿يَجْعَلُونَ أصابِعَهم في آذانِهِمْ مِنَ الصَّواعِقِ حَذَرَ المَوْتِ﴾ [They put their fingers in their ears because of the thunderbolts, fearing death]. The pronouns refer to the known omitted antecedent mentioned earlier. The Qur'an often shifts in this way, as in His saying: ﴿And how many a town We destroyed, and Our punishment came upon it by night, or while they were resting at midday﴾.

This clause is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new independent clause) with no place in the i'rab (grammatical analysis). It answers a question arising from the discourse, as if it were said while describing their terrifying condition: "What do they do amid that severity?" So He said: "They put..." etc. Some scholars allowed other possibilities, such as that it occupies a genitive position as a description of the omitted noun. It was also permitted for it and for "yakadu" (it nearly...) to be a description of "sayyib" (downpour) with an interpretation, such as "they cannot bear it." It was also permitted to be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) from a pronoun in it, with the returning pronoun omitted or the lam acting in its place, meaning "its thunderbolts." The word "ja'l" (putting, making) originally means placing. "Asabi'" is the plural of "isba'" (finger). In it there are nine dialectal forms, arising from multiplying the three states of the hamza by the same states of the ba'. They also reported a tenth form: "usbu'" with a dammah, which is feminine, and likewise all its names are feminine, except "ibham" (the thumb). Some of the Banu Asad treat it as masculine, but the feminine usage is better. In the verse there is an intensification of their extreme astonishment and complete bewilderment, as mentioned in al-Fara'id in several aspects. First, the attribution of "putting" to all the fingers, though it is actually attributed to only some of them, namely the fingertips. Second, regarding the thumb among the fingers, the customary practice is to insert the index finger; so they, out of extreme astonishment, insert whichever finger it is and do not follow the usual course. Third, in mentioning "putting" in place of "inserting," since placing something in something indicates more strongly that the second encloses the first than inserting it into it does. Is this a linguistic metaphor (majaz lughawi), by naming the whole with the name of its part, or is it a figurative stretch in the "putting," or is it a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), in which "putting" is attributed to the fingers while it belongs to the fingertips? There is disagreement about this. The well-known view is the first, and it is the view of the majority. Ibn Malik and a group held the last view, thinking that the intensity of avoiding hearing the thunderbolt can only be expressed this way. They did not rely on the mind's immediate understanding that all of them were inserted into the ear before looking, because of the context. It has also been said that there is no metaphor here at all, since attributing some actions to a thing with parts that can be divided suffices with its being associated with some of its parts, as one says: "I entered the city," "I came on Thursday night," and "I wiped with the handkerchief." This is a literal usage, though the entering, coming, and wiping only occur in part of the city, the night, and the handkerchief. It is not hidden that such usage is not literal without qualification, and the difference between it and what we are discussing is evident.

["min" (from) here is causal (ta'liliyyah), functioning like the lam in the object of purpose (maf'ul lah). It introduces the motivating cause that comes first and the goal that comes later. It is connected to "yaj'aluna" (they put). Connecting it to "death" is far-fetched.] The meaning is: they put (their fingers) because of the thunderbolts. "Sawa'iq" is the plural of "sa'iqah" (thunderbolt), and there is no irregularity here. The apparent view is that originally it is an adjective derived from "sa'q," which is a shriek, and its ta' marks the feminine if you treat it as a description of a feminine noun, or it marks intensification if you do not, as in "rawiyah" (one who narrates a great deal), or it marks transfer from adjective to noun, as in "haqiqah" (reality). It has also been said that it is a verbal noun, like "al-'afiyah" and "al-'aqibah." It is a name for every terrifying thing that is heard or seen. The well-known meaning is a violent thunderclap accompanied by a piece of fire that passes through nothing without consuming it, and it may be accompanied by a stone or iron body. Stopping the ears only benefits on the first meaning, but the second meaning may also be intended, and the speech then contains an indication of another intensification of their extreme astonishment, in that they imagine that something that does not benefit is beneficial. al-Hasan read "min al-sawaqi'" (with qaf), which is the dialect of the Banu Tamim, as in the poem:

*Did you not see that the criminals were struck*
*by thunderbolts? Nay, they are beyond thunderbolts.*

This is not a case of metathesis (qalb), according to the more correct view, since the sign of metathesis is that one of the two forms is superior to the other in some respect of morphology, and here the two forms are equal in morphology.

[The phrase] "hadhar al-mawt" (fearing death) is in the accusative as a reason for "yaj'aluna" (they put). If "min al-sawa'iq" is considered in meaning as the object of purpose, then there are two types, an accusative and a genitive. The claim that conjunction is obligatory in such a case is not accepted, contrary to whoever asserted it. There is no obstacle to its being a cause of the verb together with its own cause, just as "min al-sawa'iq" is a cause of the verb itself. The object of purpose is said to come in definite form, though rarely, as in the poem:

*I overlook the faults of the noble, saving them,*
*and turn away from the reviling of the base, out of generosity.*

To take it as an absolute object of an omitted verb, meaning "they fear a fear of death," is far-fetched. Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Abi Layla read "hidhar" (instead of "hadhar"). It means the same as "hadhar," intense fear. Death, in the well-known view, is the cessation of life in what is characterized by it actually. Using it for the prior non-existence mentioned in His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿And you were dead, and He gave you life﴾, is a metaphor. This is not refuted by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He created death﴾, because "creation" there means determining and specifying the measure in a certain way, and that can be predicated of both existence and non-existence, since non-existence also has a duration and a determined measure with Him, may He be exalted. It has also been said that the intended meaning of the creation of death is originating its causes. It has also been said that it is non-existence absolutely, even though it is not created, except that the cancellation of attributes is created, because there is an aspect of actual realization in it, in that the receptivity of the substrate is considered part of its concept, and this is an existential matter. So it is permissible to consider the relation of creation and origination in view of that. The verifying scholars of the People of the Sunnah affirmed that death is an existential attribute created as the opposite of life. For this reason it becomes manifest, as in the hadith: "On the day when meanings are embodied, as the people of God, may He be exalted, have said, in the form of a white-horned ram" and it becomes pure non-existence when it is slaughtered with the knife of life, whose duration never ends.

﴿And God encompasses the disbelievers﴾, meaning they cannot escape Him, just as the encompassed cannot escape the encompassing. His encompassing them, may He be exalted, is therefore a metaphor, by likening the state of His complete power, which nothing escapes from being within, to the encompassing of an encompasser over the encompassed in such a way that nothing escapes it. In the encompassing there is therefore a subsidiary metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah). If one likens His state, and to Him belongs the highest likeness, with them to the state of the encompasser with the encompassed, by likening a configuration abstracted from several matters to a similar configuration, then there is a representational metaphor (isti'arah tamthiliyyah) in which no changes are made to its individual words, except that the main element has been stated explicitly and the rest left implicit. Understand this.

Abu 'Ali permitted that "muhit" (encompassing) could mean "destroying," as in His saying: ﴿and his sin has encompassed him﴾, or "knowing with the knowledge of recompense," as in His saying: ﴿and He encompasses what is with them﴾. All of this is apparent. The people of witnessing have a discourse beyond this, which is "encompassing from behind." The "wa" here is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), neither conjunctive nor circumstantial. The sentence is inserted between two sentences of a single story, and it completes the intended purpose of the parable [p. 174] with what it conveys of intensification, because the "disbelievers" is placed in the position of a pronoun and expressed in this way to indicate that those afflicted by the downpour deserve that punishment because of their disbelief. The speech is thus in the manner of His saying: ﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is like a wind in which there is a biting cold, which strikes the tilth of a people who have wronged themselves, and destroys it﴾. The comparison with the tilth of such a people is clearly beautiful, because destruction arising from wrath is more severe and more eloquent. In it there is also an indication that what they did, stopping their ears with their fingers, will avail them nothing, and that destruction has encompassed them, and that caution does not avert decree, and what can human planning do against divine decree? The parenthetical clause has been made part of the states of the likened thing, on the basis that the intended "disbelievers" are the hypocrites, and for them there is no escape from the punishment of both abodes. He placed it between the states of the likened thing (the wind-and-tilth comparison) to show the complete care for the likened subject and to draw attention to the intensity of the connection, which sound taste would reject.

﴿يَكادُ البَرْقُ يَخْطَفُ أبْصارَهُمْ﴾ [The lightning nearly snatches away their sight.] This is another resumptive clause (isti'naf) that explains the preceding statement, as if it were asked: "What is their condition with that lightning?" So it was said: "It nearly snatches…" Al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's Al-Bahr al-Muhit) says: It is possible that this phrase is in a genitive position, modifying the omitted antecedent (dhawi) in what preceded. (Yakādu) is the present tense of (kāda), one of the verbs of approximation (af'al al-muqarabah). It indicates that the event is close to occurring but has not occurred. The first (the closeness) is because its causes exist; the second (the non-occurrence) is due to an obstacle, or the absence of a condition, as customary usage requires. The well-known view is that if it is negated, it becomes affirmative, and if it is affirmed, it becomes negative. They made riddles of this. Abu Hayyan did not accept this view, and he held the correct position that it is like other verbs: its negation is a negation and its affirmation is an affirmation.

The alif-lam in (al-barq) is for a previously known referent, pointing back to what preceded. Some say it is indefinite. It has also been said that it refers to the lightning that accompanies the thunderbolts, i.e., its flash, and that is as you see. The attribution of the snatching (khatf), which originally means taking swiftly or seizing, to the lightning is of the same type as attributing burning to fire. Its verification will come, God willing, shortly. The common construction for the predicate of (kāda) is a present-tense verb not preceded by the future-indicating masdariyyah particle (an). The present tense is used because it indicates the immediacy appropriate to nearness, as if, due to its extreme nearness, the event has already occurred. As for its not being preceded by (an), this is because (an) contradicts what is intended. Examples include: "Wa ubtu ila fahmin" (I returned to understanding), "Wa ma kidtu ayiban" (I was nearly not returning), "Kada al-faqru an yakuna kufran" (Poverty nearly becomes disbelief), and "Qad kada min tuli al-bila an yumahhisa" (Wear and tear had nearly purified it). These are rare.

Mujahid, Ali ibn al-Husayn, and Yahya ibn Wathhab read (yakhtifu) with a kasra on the ta' (ṭāʾ). The fatha is more eloquent. From Ibn Mas'ud: (yakhtatifu). From al-Hasan: (yakhattifu) with a fatha on the ya' and the kha'. Its original form is (yakhtatifu), and the ta' was assimilated into the ṭāʾ. From ʿAsim, Qatadah, and also al-Hasan: (yakhiṭṭifu) with a fatha on the ya', a kasra on the kha', and a shadda on the ṭāʾ. Also from al-Hasan and al-A'mash: (yikhiṭṭifu) with a kasra on all three letters and a shadda. From Zayd: (yukhaṭṭifu) with a damma on the ya', a fatha on the kha', and a kasra on the shadda-ṭāʾ. This intensifies the meaning (for emphasis) and is not transitive. The kasra on the ṭāʾ in the past tense is the dialect of Quraysh, and it is the good dialect.

﴿كُلَّما أضاءَ لَهم مَشَوْا فِيهِ وإذا أظْلَمَ عَلَيْهِمْ قامُوا﴾ [Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it; and when it darkens over them, they stand still.] This is a third resumptive clause. It is as if, when it was said that they are afflicted by the continuous, repeated snatching of their sight, it was understood from this that they are busy doing what requires sight moment by moment; otherwise they would cover their eyes just as they stopped their ears. So it was asked, and it was said: "What do they do in the two states, when the lightning flashes and when it is absent?" It was answered: they are eager to walk; whenever it lights up for them, they seize the opportunity and walk; and when it darkens over them, they stop, watching.

(Kullama) in this verse and similar ones is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarfiyyah). Its governing element is (ma), which is in meaning the answer (jawab) of a conditional. (Ma) is either a masdariyyah particle or an indefinite noun meaning "time." Thus the clause after it is either a relative clause (silah) or a descriptive clause (sifah). It was made a conditional because of the meaning of conditionality it contains. It serves to render what follows it as an indefinite noun conveying general, distributive generality (umum badali). For this reason (kullama) conveys repetition, as the jurists of legal theory (usuliyyun) have explicitly stated, and some grammarians and philologists have held this view. The conveying of repetition by (idha) and the other conditional particles comes, according to the correct view, from external contextual indicators (qara'in kharijiyyah). An example of this is his statement:

"Whenever I find the heat of love in my liver,
I come toward the water-skin of the people to cool myself."

Abu Hayyan claimed that the repetition which the jurists and others mention in (kullama) comes from the generality of (kull) and not from its lexical meaning. This contradicts both transmitted and rational evidence. Here it has been used in its necessary implied meaning, either metonymically (kinayah) or figuratively (majaz), namely eagerness and love for what it is attached to. For this reason, with the illumination he said (kullama), and with the darkness he said (idha). Abu Hayyan's statement, that if repetition is understood from (kullama) here, then repetition necessarily follows in (idha), since the matter revolves between the lightning's illumination and darkness, and whenever the one exists the other is absent, so the recurrence of the existence of the one entails the recurrence of the absence of the other, is a heedlessness of what they intended by this metonymic and figurative meaning.

(Adā'a, "lit up") is either transitive, as in his statement:

"Look again, O servant of Qays, perhaps
the fire has lit up for you the donkey that is tied."

Here the object is omitted, meaning: whenever a place lit up for them, they walked in it and took it. Or it is intransitive, and then two words are to be understood: whenever it shone upon them, they walked in the place where its light fell. The supplying of this is necessary, since walking is not in the lightning itself but in its location and the place where its light falls. That (fi) is for causation, meaning "they walked because of the illumination in it," is doubted by anyone with a taste for Arabic. Confirming the intransitive usage is the reading of Ibn Abi 'Abla (da'a), in its triliteral form. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, instead of "they walked in it" there is "they passed through it" (madaw fihi).

Indicating their weakness of strength due to their extreme fear and bewilderment, God did not use anything that indicates speed. Since the object of (adā'a) was omitted, and the indefinite form is originally the basis, He indicated that because of their extreme confusion they were groping like the blind, walking in every direction.

The meaning of (adhlama 'alayhim) is "it became hidden from them." The well-known usage of (adhlama) is intransitive. Al-Azhari, and that is sufficient authority, mentioned in Al-Tahdhib that each of the verbs of darkness may be both intransitive and transitive. Given the possibility of transitivity here, this is confirmed by the reading of Zayd ibn Qutayb and al-Dahhak: (udhlima), in the passive form. The grammarians agree that the regular passive is formed from a verb transitive by itself, in which case the object is omitted. That is: "when the lightning became dark because of its hiding, so that they could not see the path, they stood," meaning they halted from walking. It is used figuratively for stagnation, as in "the market stood still" (qamat al-suq). Its opposite is said: "the state of affairs walked" (mashat al-hal).

﴿ولَوْ شاءَ اللَّهُ لَذَهَبَ بِسَمْعِهِمْ وأبْصارِهِمْ﴾ [And if God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight.] This is a conjunction (ʿatf) on the whole group of resumptive clauses. They did not make it conjoined to the nearest element. It is part of the same passage, since it has departed from the simile and is not fit to be the answer (of the conditional). Conjoining what is not an answer to the answer is not correct. Some scholars permitted it, saying there is no harm in adding to the answer what suits it, even if it has no bearing on it; indeed it may be considered good when the context calls for it, as in ﴿وما تِلْكَ بِيَمِينِكَ يا مُوسى﴾ [And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?]. As for its being a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "qamu" (they stood), with an assumed subject, or a conjunction on the first clause with intervening verbal and assumed separations, these are considered superfluous by those of discernment.

The view that it was brought to rebuke the hypocrites, because whoever is able to produce the crash of thunder and its flash, and to annihilate them both, is able to take away their hearing and sight, so why do they not turn back from their error, is a place of rebuke. But this is not valid, since the thing exemplified cannot be conjoined to the example.

The object of (shā'a) here is omitted, and its object is frequently omitted when it occurs within a conditional clause, and this is not strange. The meaning: if God willed to take away their hearing by the crash of thunder and their sight by the flash of lightning, He would have taken them away. Because the preceding words indicating restriction, namely "yaj'aluna" (they put) and "yakadu" (nearly), are present, the context's indication of this restriction is strong, and it removes the strangeness. You may choose not to restrict that omitted object and restrict only the answer, as al-Zamakhshari did, or you may not restrict at all. The meaning would then be: if God willed to remove those faculties, He would remove them without any cause, and therefore what they have done would not avail them.

According to the theologians, (mashi'ah) [will] and (irada) [volition] are the same. It has been said that the original meaning of (mashi'ah) is the bringing into existence of a thing and reaching it, even though in common usage it is employed in the sense of (irada). Ibn Abi 'Abla read: (la-adhhaba Allahu bi-asma'ihim) [God would have taken away their hearing], which is interpreted either as the insertion of the preposition (ba') to emphasize the transitivity, or as (adhhaba) being intransitive in the sense of (dhahaba) [go away], as was said of similar constructions in ﴿تَنْبُتُ بِالدُّهْنِ﴾ [it grows with oil] and ﴿ولا تُلْقُوا بِأيْدِيكُمْ﴾ [and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction], since combining two transitivizing particles is not permitted. Some scholars assume an object for it, i.e., (la-adhhabahum) [would have taken them away], which makes the matter easier.

The particle (law) is for making the occurrence of a past event, which is the consequent (jaza'), dependent upon the occurrence of a hypothetical event, which is the condition (shart), because of the connection between them, whether in reality or by claim. Of a hypothetically posed condition, its indication of the non-occurrence of that condition is certain, and whoever disputes this is obstinate. As for its indication of the non-occurrence of the consequent, it has been said and said again. The truth is this: if the connection between them is a concomitance on which the judgment is based, then it indicates it through its own meaning, because the absence of the cause necessitates the absence of the effect. In a universal concomitance, such as in the statement of the Exalted: ﴿ولَوْ شاءَ لَهَداكُمْ﴾ [And if He had willed, He would have guided you all], and your saying, "If you had come to me, I would have honored you," this is evident. Furthermore, the statement may be structured to give the reason for the absence of the consequent by the absence of the condition, as in the two examples above. This is the common usage of (law), and therefore it has been said that it is for the impossibility of the second because of the impossibility of the first. It may also be structured to infer the absence of the second from the absence of the first, since the second is evident or accepted, as in the statement of the Exalted: ﴿لَوْ كانَ فِيهِما آلِهَةٌ إلا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتا﴾ [If there were in them gods other than God, they would both have been ruined] and ﴿لَوْ كانَ خَيْرًا ما سَبَقُونا إلَيْهِ﴾ [If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it]. The connection in the first is real, and in the second it is claimed. The same applies to the absence of both correlates. This is not by way of external causation, but by way of rational inference, which returns to the causal relation of knowledge: knowledge of the absence of the second is the cause of knowledge of the absence of the first. Whoever does not notice this supposes that the absence of the first is the cause of the absence of the second.

As for the case of partial concomitance, as in your saying, "If the sun had risen, light would have existed," this is because the consequent dependent on the condition is not mere light in general, but the particular light arising from sunrise, and there is no doubt about its absence in the absence of the condition. This applies when the judgment is based on the consideration of concomitance. If it is based on its absence, then either another concomitant is considered for it or not. If another is considered, the indication follows the state of that concomitant. If there is an incompatibility between it and the first absence, the indication is determined, as when you say: "If the sun had not risen, light would have existed." The existence of light is in reality dependent on another cause, which is the concomitant, and the non-rising of the sun is placed in its position because it is an indicator of it. It is as if it were said: "If the sun had not risen, light would have existed by means of the moon, for example."

[p. 178]

There is no doubt that this consequent is negated when the condition is negated, because the lunar light is impossible at sunrise. And if there is no incompatibility between them, the absence of implication is established. Take the hadith: "(If my stepdaughter were not in my custody, she would not be lawful to me. She is indeed the daughter of my brother through fostering.)" The relevant ground within the condition, namely her being the daughter of the brother, is not incompatible with the negation of the condition, which is her being his stepdaughter. Rather, it is conjoined with it, and it necessarily entails the conjunction of their two effects, namely the prohibition arising from this and from that. Even if no other ground is established, and the ruling is instead built on the consideration of its absence, then the statement has no implication of that kind at all. The purpose of the speech in that case is to show that the consequent holds in every state, by attaching it to what contradicts it, so that its holding is known a fortiori when what does not contradict it occurs. This is as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Even if you possessed the treasures of the mercy of my Lord, you would then withhold them."﴾ Here the consequent is tied to what contradicts it, to indicate that in itself it is such that it must hold even on the supposition that its cause is absent or that the cause of its absence is realized. How much more so when it is not like this, in the manner of the conjunctive lau. As for the hadith: "(How excellent a servant Suhayb is! If he did not fear God, he would not disobey Him.)" If it is taken to mean that the non-disobedience is tied, within the absence of fear, to another ground, such as modesty, which is conjoined with fear, then it is of the kind of the hadith of the stepdaughter. If it is taken to indicate the impossibility of his disobedience as hyperbole, then it is of this kind as well. The noble verse is directed according to common usage, conveying the gravity of their condition and the terror that has overtaken them, and that the matter has reached the point where, if God's will were to attach to removing their powers, those powers would indeed be removed, because what requires it is realized with complete requirement. It has been said that the word lau in it, for linking its consequent to its condition, is free of indicating the negation of one of them for the negation of the other, and is like an (an). This is what the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, our master, has mentioned in full. I think he has hit the aim, but the words of our master al-Salikutti indicate a preference that lau is set only to tie the occurrence of one matter in the past to the occurrence of another matter in it, without any indication of the negation of the first or the second, or of the continuity of the consequent.

[p. 179]

Rather, all these matters lie outside its meaning and are derived through the aid of contextual indicators, so that one need not say it is homonymous or both literal and metaphorical without necessity. Some scholars have said so. As for what Ibn al-Hajib held, that it indicates the negation of the first because of the negation of the second is a necessary consequence of this concept, and that something being a necessary consequence does not entail its being intended in all contexts, since indication is not the same as intention. He mentioned that what they said, that it ties the occurrence of a matter in the past to the occurrence of another matter, supposed together with certainty of the latter's non-occurrence, so that its non-occurrence necessitates the non-occurrence of what was tied to it, thereby implying that the non-occurrence of the second in external reality is caused by the non-occurrence of the first in it, while depending on the non-occurrence of the first being taken within what follows it, and you have known that this entails contrary to the default. It is refuted by the point that what is derived from tying to a matter presupposed to occur is the showing of an impediment to the occurrence of the tied matter in the past, and that it has not moved from its original non-existence to the level of existence, and it remains in its state because its existence is linked to a non-existent matter. As for the claim that its negation is a cause of the negation of the first in external reality, that is not so. How can it be, when the grammatical condition may itself be a caused thing added to the consequent? Yes, this is the requirement of the technical condition. As for what Allama al-Taftazani adduced to establish that it indicates external causality, from the verse of al-Hamasi:

"Even if a one-hoofed creature had flown before it, it would have flown, but it did not fly."

Because the exception of the antecedent does not yield a conclusion. In reply: what follows from what has been mentioned is that it should not be used to infer the negation of the second from the negation of the first. It does not follow from this that it should not be used merely for tying, to indicate the showing of an impediment while the requirement remains present. How so? If its meaning were to indicate causality of negation, the exception would be emphasis and repetition. Unlike when its meaning is merely tying, in which case it is a statement and a founding. This is the essence of what they said, by way of rejection and acceptance, and the gist of what they stated in summary and in detail. Most of the muftis of the Arabic-speaking scholars have given legal opinions in accordance with what the Mufti of the Ottoman lands said. I do not oblige you to follow authority. The opinions are before you, so choose from them what you wish.

﴿Indeed God is over all things competent.﴾ This is as a rationale for the conditional clause and an affirmation of its content, which speaks of His exalted power to remove what was mentioned, because the one who is capable of all is capable of part. The word "thing" (shay') in lexical usage is what may be known and reported about, as Sibawayh explicitly stated. It includes the non-existent and the existent, the necessary and the contingent. Its applications vary, and what is meant by it is known through contextual indicators. It is sometimes used and means all its individuals, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God is knowing of all things﴾, by the indicator of the comprehensiveness of divine knowledge of the necessary, the contingent, the non-existent, the existent, and the impossible considered under some aspect. It is also used to mean the contingent absolutely, as in the noble verse, by the indicator of power, which relates only to the contingent. It is sometimes used to mean the external contingent that exists in the mind, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not say of anything, "Indeed I will do that tomorrow," ﴾ ﴿unless God wills﴾, by the indicator that it is conceived as an action that is willed for tomorrow. It is sometimes used to mean the contingent non-existent that is established in reality, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾, by the indicator of the will of bringing into being, which is specific to the non-existent. It is sometimes used to mean the external existent, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We created you before, while you were nothing﴾. That is, an existent in external reality, because it is impossible that it means negating that he was a thing in the broader lexical sense, which includes the non-existent established in reality. For every created thing is, from eternity, a thing, that is, a non-existent established in reality. The application of "thing" to it has been established. The default in application is literal meaning, and one does not turn from it except by a diverting indicator, and there is none. The frequency of its use for the existent does not serve as a diverting indicator in that case. It is rather because the concern in discourse is more with the states of existents, not because it is lexically specific to them. As for what our master al-Baydawi mentioned, that it is specific to the existent because originally it is a verbal noun of shaa' (to will), and it is applied in the meaning of "willed" at times, and in that case it includes the Creator, exalted is He, and in another meaning as "one who makes its existence willed," and so on. In that there is, along with what is in it, the implication that it necessarily entails in the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿And God is knowing of all things﴾, the use of the homonym in both its meanings. For if it means "willed," it does not include, in his view, things such as inanimate objects. And if it means "one who makes its existence willed," it does not include the Necessary Being, exalted is His state. There is disagreement about using a homonym in both its meanings, but there is no disagreement about inferring from the verse the comprehensiveness of God's exalted knowledge. As for what has been mentioned in the commentaries on al-Mawaqif and al-Maqasid, it is mere clamor, and I see no grinding. It is mere rattling, and I see no sharp weapon. Our master al-Kurani, may his secret be sanctified, has spared us the burden of lengthy refutation of it. The dispute over this, though verbal, and the investigation of it belong to the duties of the scholars of language. Yet it is based on the dispute over whether the possible non-existent is established in itself beforehand, and this is a question over which peoples have long been perplexed and over which feet have slipped.

[p. 180]

The truth that the knowers hold is the first view, because the possible non-existent, that is, what this concept applies to, can be conceived of, and some of it can be intended without the rest, and whatever is like this is distinct in itself without any supposition of the mind. And whatever is like this is established and fixed in the external sphere of our minds apart from external existence. So it is nothing but in reality. What is meant by it is the knowledge of the Real, exalted is He, considered in terms of its not being other than the Most Holy Essence. For the knowledge of the Real, exalted is He, has two considerations: one is that it is not other, and the second is that it is not identical. Under the first consideration, it cannot be said that knowledge follows the known, because following is a relation that requires two distinct things, even if only in consideration, and there is no distinction when there is no otherness. It is said under the second consideration, because of the relative distinction that makes following valid. The known that knowledge follows is the Essence of the Real, exalted is He, in all its modes, relations, and considerations. From this they said: His exalted knowledge of things from eternity is identical with His knowledge of Himself. For every thing is among the relations of His knowledge under the first consideration. So when He knows the Essence in all its relations, He knows every thing from the very identity of His knowledge of Himself. Since the partner is not among the relations of knowledge under the first consideration, as there is no establishment for it in itself without supposition, since what is established in this way is that He, exalted is He, has no partner, knowledge does not attach to it under the second consideration initially. And when the attachment of knowledge to things is eternal, they are not pure non-existents, since in that case they cannot be a term, because there is no distinction. So they have some subsistence in a certain respect, and they are eternal by the eternity of knowledge. Therefore, the quiddities are not made by their essences, because making follows will, which follows knowledge, which follows the established known. So subsistence precedes making by several degrees. Hence they are not, in terms of subsistence, an effect of making, otherwise it would be circular. They are made only in their existence, because the world is originated, and every originated thing is made. Existence is not an accident such that power would not attach to it, and it would follow that the Exalted Creator would not be the originator of possible things, nor capable of them, because it has been established that existence, in some sense, when joined to possible quiddities, makes their specific effects exist. First, because every concept other than existence exists only through a thing joined to it, which is existence. So it exists through its own essence, not through an additional thing, otherwise there would be an infinite regress. Its distinction from all else is that its existence is not added to its essence. Second, because if it were not existent, nothing would be made at all, since the possible quiddity before the joining of existence is characterized by external non-existence. So if existence were non-existent, it would be like it, needing what it needs. Then the quiddity would not acquire by joining the effects of quiddity, because if it were non-existent, after non-existence there would be nothing but need for existence. This is exactly what is realized in the quiddity before the joining, so by the joining it does not acquire a quality it did not have. So if this needy existence were to yield the effects, then the quiddity would be independent of existence while needing it, and the necessary consequence is false, because the joining of contradictories is impossible. So existence must exist through an existence that is itself, otherwise there would be an infinite regress or it would end at an existence that exists through its own essence. The first is false, and the second entails the desired conclusion. Yes, existence in the sense of existentness is a state, because it is a conventional attribute, neither an accident nor a privation. Nevertheless, making attaches to it, but not initially. Rather, by joining a portion of existent existence to the quiddity, so that the quiddity acquires existentness as a result. It is evident that the non-attachment of power to existence in the sense of existentness initially does not entail that it is not attached to it in some other way. And when it has become clear

The matter is that quiddities (*mahiyyat*, the "whatness" of things) are made in their existence. So the existence of every thing must be identical with its reality (*haqiqa*). This means that whatever external realities the reality of a thing applies to is the very same thing to which its existence applies. The two do not have distinct identities in external reality, as blackness and a body do. If existence subsisted in a quiddity that is non-existent, a contradiction would follow. If it subsisted in a quiddity that is existent, there would be two existences, leading to circularity (*dawr*) or infinite regress (*tasalsul*). The claim that existence is added to the quiddity as such, with no realization in it, is refuted. It has been established in its proper place that, before existence comes to it, the quiddity is described in reality as non-existent, with certainty, because it is impossible for it to be free of the two contradictories. The only point is that if we do not consider non-existence along with it, we cannot judge that it is non-existent. Our not considering non-existence along with it at the time existence comes to it does not make it separate from non-existence in reality. It makes it separate only by our consideration. The joining of existence to it happens to it in reality, not from the standpoint of our consideration. So its being free of non-existence by our consideration does not validate its being described by existence in itself, in reality, safe from the prohibited result. Therefore there are not two identities, one subsisting through the other. Rather, the individual's self in external reality is the very determination (*ta'ayyun*) of the quiddity in it, and it is also the very quiddity in it. Determination is not an existential matter distinct in essence from the individual, joined to the quiddity in external reality, distinguished from both within it, and composed of them and of the individual. Rather, there is no existence in external reality except for individuals, and these are the very determinations of the quiddity and the very quiddity in external reality, because the two are united there.

On this basis, there is no doubt about the possibility of being made (*maqduriyya*) for the contingent (*mumkin*). Its being made is by making its share of the absolute existence, which exists in external reality, conjoined with accidents and conditions required by the readiness of its share of the specific quiddity. Thus it becomes an individual. The bringing into existence of an individual of the quiddity in the aforementioned manner is the very bringing into existence of the quiddity, because the two are united in external reality in making and in existence, and distinguished only in the mind. This is the realization of their saying: "What is made is the particular existence." Nothing non-existent is ready to receive it unless it has a fixed reality (*thubut*) in reality. What has no reality, which is the negated, has no readiness at all to receive existence. Otherwise, the impossible would be possible, and the consequence is false. Therefore, the eternal fixity of the contingent's quiddity is what is termed the occurrence of possibility (*imkan*), which validates being made. It is not, as they imagined, an obstacle. This is the subject, the discussion is lengthy, and the matter is grand. We have fully treated this topic in *al-Ajwiba al-'Iraqiyya 'an al-As'ila al-Iraniyya*, in a manner in which we refuted the words of opposing objectors, when we followed our masters the Sufis, may God sanctify their secrets. This is a brief extract that will benefit you in the interpretation of the noble verse. Memorize it, for I do not think you will find it in any tafsir. Since "thing" (*shay'*) is general in language and in the terminology of the people of God, even though the Mu'tazila also hold this, in a matter like this one we must restrict it by the evidence of reason to the contingent.

According to the Ash'ariyya, power (*qudra*) is an essential attribute with a relation that requires the capacity to bring into existence, to annihilate, and to sustain. It is not the capacity itself, because that is a mental consideration. Nor is the negation of incapacity from Him, exalted is He, because that is among the negative attributes. Perhaps whoever chose this view did so to reduce the essential attributes or to negate them. The capable (*qadir*) is the one who, if He wills, acts, and if He does not will, does not act. Since will, according to us, is an attribute that determines one of the two sides of what is capable, and according to the philosophers it is eternal providence (*'inaya azaliyya*), it is permissible for us to define the capable by what has been mentioned, not as they do. Whoever imagined otherwise was mistaken. The Capable (*qadir*) is the Doer of what He wills in accordance with what wisdom requires. The term is rarely applied to anyone other than God, exalted is He. The term *muqtadir*, if used of God, means *qadir*. If used of a human, it means one who exerts himself and acquires power. The derivation of *qudra* (power) from *qadr* (measure), in the sense of determination and specification, is noted. In the verse there is evidence that the originated contingent is capable during its continuance, because it is a thing, and every thing is capable for Him, exalted is He. The meaning of its being capable is that the agent, if He wills, annihilates it, and if He wills, does not annihilate it. The contingent's need, during its continuance, for an effecting agent is something on which all agree who say that the cause of need is possibility, since possibility is necessarily attached to it during its continuance. As for those who say that the cause of need is occurrence alone, or occurrence together with possibility, they hold that it is independent, since at that time there is no occurrence. They rely on the continuance of a building after the annihilation of its builder. When some of them recognized the monstrousness of this, they said that substances are never free of accidents, and accidents do not persist for two times. Thus it is inconceivable to be independent of the Capable, glorified is He, in any state. This is what al-Ash'ari held.

Because this view contradicts the evident testimony of the senses, the people of the outward sense (*Ahl al-Zahir*) rejected it. Yes, the knowers among the people of witnessing (*Ahl al-Shuhud*) accept it, and that is enough of a testimony for them. They even went further and said that substances do not persist for two times either. People are in confusion about a new creation. I accept what they said and entrust my affair to God, who is not bound by any circumstance, who was and nothing was with Him, and who is now as He was.

Then, the purpose of this parable is to liken the condition of the hypocrites, in their severity and in the garment of their faith, which is lined with unbelief and embroidered with deception, out of fear of death, to the condition of those under a violent rainstorm containing what it contains. They put their fingers into their ears to avoid destruction, along with everything known of their attributes. The point of comparison is the finding of something whose outward appearance benefits while its inner reality contains a great calamity. It has been said that God, glorified is He, likened the hypocrites to the people of the rain cloud, and their faith, which is mixed with a rain cloud containing what was described, to a rain that in itself is beneficial, but when it has this character, its benefit becomes harm. Their hypocrisy, out of fear of injury, is like putting fingers in the ears from what startles them, out of fear of death, since death does not repel anything of destiny. It is also like their bewilderment because of the severity of what they face, and their ignorance of what they do or leave undone, since whenever they encounter a flash of lightning they seize the opportunity, fearing it might snatch their sight. So they walk a little. Then, when it vanishes, they remain standing still, unable to move. It has also been said that God made Islam, which is the cause of benefits in both abodes, like the rain cloud that is the cause of benefit, and what is in Islam of hardships and limits, like the darkness and thunder, and what it contains of spoils and benefits, like the lightning. Thus they put their fingers in their ears to avoid hearing its hardships. When the lightning of spoils gleams for them, they walk in it. When hardships darken for them, they stand bewildered. It has also been said other than this. What the eloquence of the revelation requires and the grandeur of its majestic affair demands is not hidden from you, when the flashes of care shine before you.

(From the inner meanings:) The comparison of those mentioned in the first comparison to the people of a rain cloud is intended. Then the words of the Exalted, ﴿Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it﴾ etc., are an indication that whenever they find sweetness in their obedience and immediate worldly gain, they walk in it. When the path of honors is closed to them, they abandon acts of obedience. Al-Husayn said: "When their aim from this world in religion lights up for them, they increase in attaining it. When it darkens for them, they stand bewildered."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 21 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾. When He, glorified be He, had explained the categories of those under obligation, dividing them into believers, disbelievers, and the wavering (mudhabdhabin), and had said regarding the first group, "those who believe," regarding the second, "it is the same for them," and regarding the third, "they deceive Allah," and had explained what their states lead to in this world and the Hereafter, He said, glorified be He, regarding the first, "They are upon guidance from their Lord, and they are the successful," and regarding the second, "Allah has sealed upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and for them is a great punishment," and regarding the third, "In their hearts is a disease, and for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie." He, exalted be His majesty, turned to them with direct address, by way of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), to rouse them to attentiveness and to direct their hearts toward receiving, and to soften what worship entails of hardship with the sweetness of direct address. The purpose (nukta) is sufficiently served by its presence in some (of the wording). The particle (ya) is a letter (harf), not a verb-noun (ism fi'l), according to the sound opinion. It was laid down for calling the distant, and it is said: for general calling, or it is shared among its categories. According to the first view, it is used to call the near, by treating him as if he were other than near, either because of the high rank of the caller or of the one called. Sometimes the heedlessness of the listener and his poor understanding are treated as his distance, and this may be for the sake of emphasizing the matter to which the one called is summoned and urging it, because calling the distant and requiring him to come is a matter that calls for emphasis and urging. So it is used for what necessarily follows from its meaning, and it is a majaz mursal (metonymy of a general kind), or a taba'iyya metaphor in the particle, or a makniyya and takhyiliyya (implicit and imaginative) metaphor. It, together with the vocative noun, in the accusative either verbally or by estimation, by way of substituting for a phrase like "nadaytu" (I called) which is an performative (insha'i), or with "nadaytu" which is necessarily elided, because its meaning is evident together with the intent of performing the speech act, forms a complete statement on which silence is good, as it is good in such cases as "la" (no) and "na'am" (yes). "Ayyu" has well-known meanings. The word used in the vocative is indefinite, set for a part of a whole, and then it becomes definite through the vocative; and by it is reached the calling of what has "al". (Ya) does not enter upon it except in the case of God, and then only as an anomaly, because combining two definite articles is impossible, for they are like two equals, and they do not come together except in what is anomalous, as in the verse:

"By Allah, no cure will be found for what is in me, nor for what is in them, ever."

Page 182

It is given the ruling of the vocative noun, and the intended object of the call is made its adjective, and it is obligatorily given this particular vowel called the damma, contrary to al-Mazini, who permitted its being in the accusative, and he has no precedent or successor in that, because it contradicts what is heard. He only required that out of an indication that it is the intended object of the call. This does not conflict with the adjective being a follower not intended in itself relative to its governing noun, because that is according to its original positing, where nothing has come upon it to make it intended in itself, such as its being an explainer of an ambiguous noun. Hence they did not stipulate derivation in this adjective, although the grammarians, except for a few such as Ibn al-Hajib, stipulated that for adjectives, as is explained in its proper place. The particle (ha) of alerting is an obligatory extra element for emphasis and for compensating for what the noun should take of an added-to noun, or what is in its ruling of tanwin, as in "ayyan ma tad'u" (whichever you call). Even if it is not used here as an annexed noun at all. The calling in the Glorious Book occurs much in this manner, because of the emphasis it contains, which the context often requires, through repetition of mention, clarification after ambiguity, emphasis with the particle of alerting, and the combination of the two definitions. This is what the majority held. Al-Akhfash rejected it, because of the weakness of his view, holding that "ayy" in the vocative is a relative pronoun whose first part of its relative clause is omitted obligatorily for the sake of suitability of lightening for the vocative. This was supported by its frequent occurrence in their speech as a relative pronoun, and the rarity of its occurrence as a qualifier. He excused its not being put in the accusative in that case, although it resembles an annexed noun, by saying that when the first part of its relative clause is omitted, the more likely status is building on the damma; so the particle of calling here enters upon a noun built on the damma and does not change it, even though it resembles an annexed noun. The first view is supported by the absence of need for deletion, the truth of the definiteness of the qualifier, and agreement with this, and that if it were a relative pronoun it would be permissible to connect it with a verbal or adverbial clause, and other things, by which the fair-minded person is certain of the superiority of the majority's view. Yes, a problem was raised against it, which some earlier Arabic grammarians found difficult, and said: there is no answer to it. It is that what they claimed to be a follower is in the nominative case, and every case-ending of i'rab occurs only through a governing factor, and there is no factor here requiring the nominative, because its governing noun is built verbally and is in the accusative place, so there is no basis for its nominative. I say: this is one of the discussions that took place between Abu Nizar and Ibn al-Shajari. A question arose about the damma of this follower. Abu Nizar wrote that it is the damma of building, not the damma of i'rab, because the damma of i'rab must have a governing factor that requires it, and there is no factor here requiring this damma. Shaykh Mansur Mawhub ibn Ahmad wrote that it is the damma of i'rab and cannot be the damma of building, and whoever said that has missed the right answer. That is because the thing upon which the calling falls, "ayy," is built on the damma, as it occupies the place of the particle; and the noun following it, although it is the intended object of the calling, is an adjective of "ayy," so it is impossible that it be built too, because it is raised in a sound nominative. For this reason al-Mazini permitted its accusative on the place, as it is permitted in "ya Zaydu al-zarif." The reason for the nominative is that when the damma persisted in every definite vocative noun, it resembled what the verb is attributed to, so its adjective was made to follow the wording, and so it was put in the nominative. Ibn al-Shajari answered with what the Shaykh answered, and wrote that it is the damma of i'rab, because the damma of the singular vocative has, by its regularity, a status between two statuses. It is not like the damma of "haythu," because that is not regular, for the cause that required it is not regular. Nor is it like the damma of "Zayd" in "kharaja Zaydun" (Zayd went out), because that arose from a verbal governing factor. And since the damma regularly occurs in "ya Zaydu, ya 'Amru," and likewise in "ya rajulu, ya ghulamu," and so on without being counted, regularity has taken the place of the abstract governing factor that is the inceptive of the subject, in that the nominative is regular in every noun begun without a verbal governing factor and given a predicate, such as "'Amrun munțaliq" and "Zaydun dhahib," and so on. When the damma of the vocative persisted in most nouns, just as the damma arising from the inceptive persisted in nominal nouns, the Arabs likened it to the damma of the subject, so they made the damma of i'rab follow it in the adjective of the vocative, as in "ya Zaydu al-Tawil." Both also share that regularity is a meaning, just as inception is likewise, and it is a habit of the Arabs to carry one thing over to another when there is even slight similarity between them, to the point that they have carried things over to their opposites. Do you not see that they made the case-vowel follow the building vowel in the reading of those who read "al-hamdu lillah" with a damma on the lam? Likewise they made the building vowel follow the case-vowel
Page 183
in the case of "ya Zayda ibn 'Amr," according to those who pronounced the dal of Zayd with a fatha. This is concluded in summary. Ibn al-Shajari mentioned this in his Amali, and he was extensive in criticizing Ibn Nizar, and he explained what took place between them face to face. Had it not been for the excess of length, I would have mentioned it in full, with its roughness and its smoothness. You know what weakness there is in all of that. For this reason some verifiers said: the truth is that it is a vowel of following and harmony with the damma of the vocative, like the kasra of the mim in "ghulami" (my boy). Then the difficulty is removed, as is not hidden from those of perfection.

What remains is the discussion about the lam that enters upon this adjective: is it for definiteness or not? What the majority holds, and what is well known, is that it is for definiteness, as the indication to it has already passed. When Abu Nizar was asked about this, he said: it is not for definiteness there, because definiteness occurs only between two in a third, and the lam in our case enters into the name of the addressee. Then he said: the correct view is that it entered in place of "ya" and "ayy"; and although it is a vocative, its vocative is verbal, and the one truly called is the one joined to "al." When they intended the emphasis of the alerting, and estimated the repetition of the vocative particle, they disliked the repetition, so they substituted for the vocative particle, a second "ha" and a third "al." Ibn al-Shajari criticized him, saying: this is a corrupt view. Rather, the lam there is for the definiteness of presence, like the definiteness in your saying "came this man," for example. But when it entered upon the name of the addressee, the ruling became that of address, since "ya ayyuha al-rajul" means "ya rajul." And since the man is the addressee in meaning, the ruling of address prevailed, so it sufficed with two, because names of address do not need a third present to define them. Do you not see that your saying "I went out, O this one," and "I set off" and "I honored you," has no need of a third? Not every way of definiteness requires that it be between two in a third. The pronoun of the speaker in "ana" and "kharajtu" is definite by consensus, and its definiteness does not depend on the presence of a third. Also, what was narrated of the story of substitution by its apparent sense requires that the origin of "ya ayyuha al-rajul" be, for example, "ya ayyu ya ya rajul," and that they substituted for the second "ya" the "ha," and for the third the "alif-lam." And you know that this, besides contradicting the view of the majority, is an absurd statement that the ear rejects and the nature disowns. So let it be understood.

"Al-nas" (the people) is a collective noun according to what a verifier established, and collectives and their like, when made definite by generality where there is no external reference, as indicated by the occurrence of the exception, and the basic principle in it is continuity, which requires inclusion with certainty, and it cannot be conceived except through generality. Such as "I struck Zayd except his head" and "I fasted Ramadan except its last ten days" are general in an interpretive sense. Likewise the emphasis with what indicates generality, for if there were no generality there, the emphasis would be a new establishment, and there is consensus against that. And the widespread use of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, of generality as proof, as in the hadith of the Saqifa, and they are the imams of guidance. Then this address in such as "ya ayyuha al-nas" is called by the usulis the oral address (al-khitab al-shafahi). They said: it is not general to those who come after those present at the time of revelation, or to those who come after those present at the places of revelation. The first is the more apt view, and its ruling applies to them only by another proof, from a text, analogy, or consensus; but by the mere form it does not. The Hanabila said: rather it is general to those after them until the Day of Resurrection. The first group argued: we know that one does not say "O mankind" to the non-existent. Al-Adud said: denying this is obstinacy.
