And: the address of a child and a madman is prohibited with such wording, and if we do not direct it toward them while they exist, because of their incapacity for address, then the non-existent is more deserving of being prevented, because its reaching them is more remote. The others argued: if the Messenger ﷺ were not addressing with it those after them, he would not have been sent to them, and the consequent is false. And: the scholars never ceased to argue against people of later ages after the Companions with the like of that, and that is a consensus on its generality for them.

It was answered: as for the first, the mission only requires conveyance in general, and that does not depend on oral address; rather it suffices that it reaches some orally and others through the establishment of signs and indications; and their ruling is the ruling of those he addressed orally. As for the second, it is not necessary that this be because it includes them; rather it may be because they knew that its ruling applies to them by another proof, as more than one said.

In the second commentary on al-Adudi's commentary by the Allama, it is said that the view that the oral address is general, although it is attributed to the Hanabila, is not far-fetched. And some said

Page 184

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 21 (part 2 of 3):

the eminent verifiers (ajillat al-muhaqqiqin). It is the well-known view, to the extent that they said: "The truth is that the generality (al-'umum) is known necessarily (bi'l-darurah) from the Muhammadan religion (al-din al-Muhammadi)," and this is the closer view. As for the statement of al-Adud (al-'Adud): "Denying it is obstinacy (mukabarah)," it is correct if the address was to the non-existent (al-ma'dumin) alone; but if it was to the existent and the non-existent by way of prevalence (al-taghlib), then it is not so. Its like is eloquent and common. Everything that was cited as evidence against it is weak, end of quote. Many of the Shafi'is also held the view of generality, that it is general according to the literal sense of its wording and its explicit meaning, without need for any other evidence. It has been said that it belongs to the category of general address that is applied to other than its apparent meaning, as in his saying:

"If you honour the noble, you possess him, and if you honour the base, he becomes defiant."

Moreover, in any case, what is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud and 'Alqamah, that every verse in which "O people" (ya ayyuha al-nas) occurs is Meccan, and every verse in which "O you who believe" (ya ayyuha alladhina amanu) occurs is Medinan, if it is sound and not interpreted, does not necessitate restricting this general address in any way to the disbelievers. Rather, they too are included in it, and they are commanded to perform worship, such as belief (al-i'tiqad). The command to a thing is a command to what the thing cannot be completed without. That faith is the foundation of the acts of worship, and that if it were obligatory by their obligation, the foundation would become secondary, is refuted by the fact that foundational status in terms of validity does not conflict with being secondary in terms of obligation. Furthermore, it is obligatory independently as well. It is astonishing how this was hidden from the shaykhs of Samarqand! This is the view held by the Iraqis and the Shafi'is, and the apparent sense of the verses supports it, such as His saying, exalted is He: "Woe to the polytheists, who do not give zakat" (Q. 41:6-7), and His saying, glorified is He: "What has brought you into Saqar? They will say: We were not among those who prayed, nor did we feed the poor" (Q. 74:42-44).

The Bukharis held that they are addressed (mukallafun) only regarding belief alone. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, did not explicitly state anything on the matter, but in the words of his second companion there is what indicates it. Perhaps this is from the Imam, because there is no fruit to the disagreement in this world, since there is agreement that as long as they are disbelievers, they are prevented from performing it and are not commanded to it, and when they become Muslims, making up its missed performance is not obligatory for them. Its fruit is only in the Hereafter: that they are punished for abandoning it, just as they are punished for abandoning faith according to the one who holds it obligatory upon them, and for abandoning faith alone according to the one who does not say so. This applies outside of punishments (al-'uqubat) and transactions (al-mu'amalat); as for those, there is agreement that they are addressed with them.

The command to worship here is addressed to the three groups, by considering that what is meant by it is that which includes the bringing into existence of its basis, its increase, and its persistence. "So worship" (fa'budu) indicates a demand in the present for a standalone act of worship. For the disbelievers it is initial worship, for some believers it is an increase, and for others it is steadfastness. Initiation, increase and steadfastness are not included in the meaning by convention, so there is no problem at all, contrary to the one who imagined it and laboured to dispel it. He, glorified is He, mentioned the Lord (al-Rabb) to indicate that the immediate cause of worship is the blessing of nurture (ni'mat al-tarbiyah), although the worship of those perfected is directed to His Essence, exalted is He, without any intermediary at all, except that He is He. Glorified is He as a God, how great He is, and as a Lord, how generous He is.

"Who created you and those before you" (alladhi khalaqakum wa'l-ladhina min qablikum). The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is a descriptive attribute praising the Lord, and in it there is also a reason for worship, or for lordship, as has been said. If the address in "your Lord" includes all three groups, then well and good. If it is restricted to the polytheists, and by "Lord" is meant what was customary among them regarding its application to other than Him, exalted is He, then it may be restrictive if the idafah is taken as generic, and explanatory if it is taken as referring to a specific known thing. It is not far from this that it be praising, because the unqualified term is understood as the Lord of lords; but making it restrictive and explanatory is more apparent, based on what they were in, and as an allusion to what they were upon, and because it is the basic meaning, so it is not abandoned except by evidence. Creation (al-khalq) is bringing into being without a pattern, and it can also mean determining. In the first sense, no one other than Him, glorified is He, can be described by it; in the second sense, others may be described by it. From this: "So blessed be Allah, the best of creators" (Q. 23:14), and "when you shape from clay" (Q. 5:110), and the saying of Zuhayr:

"Indeed you cut what you have shaped, while some of the people shape but do not cut."

It is astonishing that Abu 'Abd Allah al-Basri, the teacher of the judge 'Abd al-Jabbar, said: applying "Creator" (al-Khaliq) to Him, exalted is He, is impossible, because determination requires thought and calculation. This is a disputed question between him and Allah, exalted is He, who says: "He is the Creator, the Originator" (Q. 59:24). And I say with the saying of Allah, exalted is He.

The second relative pronoun is a conjunction (ataf) upon the object in "khalaqakum." "Qabl" is a noun of time frequently, and of place rarely, and it is used figuratively for precedence in nobility and rank. If the address includes both believers and others, then "those before them" means those who preceded them in existence, and those who exist and are higher in rank than them. In this there is a reminder of the perfection of the majesty of Allah, exalted is He, and His lordship, and in it is an emphasis on the matter of worship that is not hidden. He, glorified is He, placed first the alert to their creation, although it is later in time, because a person's knowledge of his own states is more evident, and because they are the ones addressed with the command to worship, so alerting them first to themselves is more emphatic and important. He used "creation" as the relative clause (silah), and relative clauses must be of known attribution to the addressee; this is why the relative pronoun is recognised by the addressee through what is in them of the known reference. The clause was required to be informative to indicate that none of the addressees denies that the Creator is Allah, exalted is He: "And if you asked them who created them" (Q. 43:87), or "who created the heavens and the earth, they will surely say: Allah" (Q. 31:25). The understanding of that from the description is based on what they said. The informative after knowledge is an attribute, and the attribute before knowledge is informative, as stated by some of the verifiers. If there is someone who does not know that Allah, exalted is He, is his Creator and the Creator of those before him, then it requires claiming prevalence (taghlib) or treating the non-knowing as the knowing, because the proofs are clear; so the sentence comes out in the manner of what is known, contrary to what the apparent sense requires.

Ibn al-Sumayqa read "wa khalaqa man qablakum," and Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read "wa'l-ladhina man qablakum" with a fatha on the mim. This raised a difficulty because two relative pronouns follow one another while the relative clause is single. It was explained by making "man" an emphatic (ta'kid) for "alladhina," so it needs no relative clause, as in the saying:

"Who are the company of men who, when they [the base] are feared..., they clank at the door-ring."

It was objected that a particle is not emphasised without repeating what it is attached to, so the relative pronoun is more deserving of this, since its emphasis would be almost like the emphasis of part of a noun. Then "man" is a relative pronoun or a descriptive, and it is the predicate of an implied subject, and what follows it is the relative clause or attribute, and together with the implied word it is the relative clause of the first relative pronoun; on one of the two possibilities it is like the saying: "I said and denied the faces, they are they."

The explanation of the verse according to this is similar. It has also been said that "man" is superfluous. Some grammarians permitted the superfluity of nouns, and al-Kisa'i permitted the superfluity of the relative "man," and he took as an example:

"And enough for us as favour over others than us is the love of the Prophet Muhammad for us."

Some have also raised a difficulty with the well-known reading, that "alladhina" is a noun of substance, and "min qablikum" is deficient, having no benefit in informing about them, so likewise connecting it is only through an interpretation. Its interpretation is that when a temporal adverb is described verbally or by implication with a clear indication, it is valid to inform about it and to connect through it: you say "we are in a good day," and what is here is in the sense of: "those who were from a time before your time." Abu al-Baqa' estimated: "those who created them before your creation," so the verb which is the relative clause is omitted, and its complement is put in its place. So reflect.

"So that you may be mindful" (la'allakum tattaqun). "La'alla" in the well-known usage is laid down for hope (al-tarajji), which is the longing for the attainment of a desirable matter that is possible to occur, and for apprehension (al-ishfaq), which is the expectation of a feared possible matter. The apparent sense is opposition, so it would be shared. Al-Radi mentioned that it is for hope, which is awaiting something whose occurrence is not certain, so it includes both longing and apprehension. What the heart inclines to is what some verifiers mentioned: that it is for creating the expectation of a matter that hovers between occurring and not occurring, with the first being more likely; if it is desirable it is called hope (raja'), and if it is disliked it is called apprehension (ishfaq). That expectation may be considered realised in fact, either from the side of the speaker, which is the most common, because the meanings of the performatives (inshaat) subsist in him; or from the side of the addressee, by treating him as the speaker in full engagement with the conversation taking place between them. From this: "Perhaps he will be mindful or fear" (Q. 20:44). It may also be considered realised potentially, by a kind of figurative usage, indicating that this matter in itself is a cause for expectation, qualified by a factor which validates it, without any expectation in fact being considered from an actual expecter at all. So in the noble verse, if you make the sentence a circumstantial clause (hal)...

The first of the three words of the verse, the particle *la'alla* (perhaps, so that), can be read as "so that" for the reason that... *(from the object of "created you")* and what is conjoined to it, through the device of giving precedence to the addressees over the absent ones, since they are the ones commanded to worship. The literal sense of *la'alla* cannot be taken, when it is related to the speaker, because hoping is impossible for the One who knows the unseen and the seen and who does whatever He wills. Nor can it be related to the addressees, because at the time of creation they did not yet exist as knowers, so how can hope be conceived from them? It also cannot be taken as a "presumed state" (*hal muqaddara*), because what is presumed at the time of creation is God-consciousness (*taqwa*), not the hope of it. So it must be taken in its figurative sense: the seeking of God-consciousness from them, after the gathering of its causes and motives, is likened to hoping, in that the one to whom each of the two is directed is free to act or not to act while the inclination lies toward acting. Thus the word *la'alla*, which is established for hope, is used in this figurative way, and this is a *metaphor in a secondary sense* (*isti'ara tab'iyya*). Alternatively, a constructed image drawn from the state of their Creator in relation to them is compared: after He enabled them to attain God-consciousness, yet they abandon it although its inclination is in them, He is in the state of one who hopes, in relation to the one from whom he hopes, who is able to bring about what he hopes for and to abandon it, although its existence is more likely. This is then a *metaphor in the form of a representation* (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*), except that it mentions from the comparison-element (*al-mushabbah bihi*) what is its essential part, namely the word *la'alla*. Or their persons are likened to those from whom God-consciousness is hoped for, and some of the necessary attributes of that are affirmed for them, namely hoping, so this is a *metaphor by implication* (*isti'ara bil-kinaya*). To make the comparison-element the will of God (*irada*) in the metaphor and in the representation is an Mu'tazilite slip, founded on the principle that what is willed may fail to occur despite God's will, exalted is His majesty.

Some have said that hoping is meant here, but not from the speaker nor from the addressee, rather from someone else, as in His saying, ﴿So perhaps you will leave out some of what is revealed to you﴾. For since every child is born upon the natural disposition (*fitra*), his reflection is one that a reflecting person may expect to make him God-conscious, and this is not far-fetched.

If it is taken as a presumed state of the agent of "created you", the literal sense is still impossible, and only some of the other aspects become determined. If it is taken as a state of the verb "worship" (*u'budu*), then it is permissible to keep hope in its literal sense, directed to the addressees, meaning "hoping for God-consciousness". Here God-consciousness means the ultimate of the stations of the wayfarers (*salikin*), namely casting off passion, rejecting all else, and attaining the Supreme Beloved. In that is the utmost of what is sought and the ascent beyond the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (*sidrat al-muntaha*). This is widely known among the highest and the lowest. By this the exhortation is valid, and what has been said is repelled: that the proper course for Qur'anic eloquence is to regard from the outset the ultimate purpose of their worship, which is what is a pleasure to them, namely the reward, not what is hard for them, namely God-consciousness, even though it leads to it. The manner of this repelling is evident. As for what the master al-Taftazani said, that restricting worship to hoping for God-consciousness has little meaning, and that what is fitting is to restrict it to God-consciousness, or to connect it with hope of its reward, this is repelled by the fact that in hoping there is an alert that the worshipper should not be separated in his worship, and should be one of fear and hope. Yes, they have said: the state (*hal*) is a qualifier of its governing element, and here the governing element is the command. If we say it is more general than obligation, there is no difficulty. If we say it is literally for obligation, it entails the obligation of the hope to which the worship commanded is restricted, and perhaps it is not obligatory. The saying that this entails the obligation of the qualifier without the qualified is a matter of the principles of jurisprudence that is not hidden from its specialists. As for what was raised, that on this aspect there follows an intermediate between the staff and its bark (an objection concerning the separation of the relative clause from its antecedent), since the one who made the earth for you (*alladhi ja'ala lakumu al-ard*) is connected to "your Lord" as an attribute of it, this is answered by saying that a break (*qat'*) makes the separation easier, even if there is a semantic connection. And if "the one who made" is taken as a subject whose predicate is "do not set up" (*la taj'alu*), the difficulty nearly disappears and the objection is removed. Yet despite this, there is no doubt that this aspect is less preferred, although the words of our master al-Baydawi seem to indicate its preferability.

Then it is not far-fetched to say that the meaning in the verse is causal (*ta'lil*), either because *la'alla* comes with the meaning of *kay* ("in order that"), as Ibn al-Anbari and others held, and they cited as evidence the verse:

*"So you said to us: 'Cease the wars, so that we may cease, and you pledged to us every covenant.'"*

Or because it is for expectations (*li-l-atmāʿ*), and it is then used figuratively, by the context, to indicate the realization of what follows it, in the manner of great men, and then it is extended from it to every realized thing, such as the realization of a cause, whether or not there are expectations along with it, as has been said.

*[Page 187]*

It is not objected that the causation of creation, which is His act, is something that most of the Ash'aris did not permit, since they forbade the causation of God's acts by purposes, lest it follow that He, exalted is His might, is completed by another, which is impossible. For we say: the truth from which there is no escape is that God's acts are caused by the benefits of His servants, while it is not obligatory upon Him to do what is best. Whoever denies the causation of some acts, especially the legal rulings such as the prescribed punishments (*hudud*), has nearly denied prophethood, as our master Sadr al-Shari'a said. To pause over this in every passage is not necessary. Moreover, some make the dispute in this question merely verbal, because if "cause" is interpreted as what depends upon something and by which the agent is completed, this is impossible for Him, glory be to Him. But if it is interpreted as the wisdom that necessitates the act, apparently, together with self-sufficiency, then there is no doubt in its occurrence, and none denies this except an ignorant person or an obstinate one.

As for why He, glory be to Him, did not say in the arrangement "you worship" (*ta'budun*) to correspond to "worship" (*u'budu*), or "be God-conscious" (*ittaqu*) to correspond to "you are God-conscious" (*tattaqun*), it is so that its two ends may respond to each other, along with its inclusion of a wondrous artifice of repeating the final part upon the first part (*radd al-ajuz ʿala al-sadr*), because God-consciousness is the utmost of the worshipper's aim. So the speech is more stirring toward worship and more binding. Thus it has been said, though there is something doubtful in it. The reason for omitting the object of "you are God-conscious" is not hidden.

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, estimates it as "shirk" (associating partners with God), and al-Dahhak estimates it as "Fire." I think you do not estimate anything.

When glory be to Him commanded the responsible persons to worship the Lord who gives them existence, and described Him with what He described Him with, and it is known that a description is an instrument for distinguishing the described from what is other than it, and that linking a ruling to a description indicates causation, the verse indicated that the way to know Him, and to know His oneness and that worship is due to Him, is to reflect upon His handiwork. And since the nurturing and creation to which worship is attached preceded its being requested, it is understood that the servant does not deserve a reward for having been favored, before worship, with countless blessings, whose thanks human capacity cannot fulfil, and whose tenth part of a tenth his worship cannot match. And whoever claims that the imposition of the impossible (*taklif bil-muhal*) occurs has taken the verse as evidence, since glory be to Him commanded to worship Him both him who believes and him who disbelieves, after informing about them that they do not believe and that they will not return from their misguidance. The discussion of this has already preceded, so return to it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 2, verse 22 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Who made the earth a bed for you and the sky a canopy﴾. The relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) may be in the accusative as an epithet (*na't*, adjective) of "your Lord," or as a substitute (*badal*) for it, or in the accusative by an implied "I specify" or "I praise." That it is the object of "so that you may be mindful" (*tattaqun*), as Abu al-Baqa said, is a weak (*ghath*) grammatical analysis from which the Qur'an is to be exonerated. That it is an epithet of the first noun is refuted by the fact that, according to the majority of grammarians, an epithet does not itself take an epithet except in cases like "O horseman, possessor of the forelock" (*ya ayyuha al-faris dhu al-jumma*). Moreover, this is also not unanimously agreed upon. It may also be in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, or as the subject whose predicate is a clause, "so do not set up" (*fa-la taj'alu*), and the *fa* (of consequence) may enter the predicate of a relative pronoun with a past-tense verb, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and women﴾ up to His saying: ﴿For them is the punishment of Hell﴾. The apparent noun serves as the connecting pronoun (*al-rabit*) according to al-Akhfash. A performative (*insha'*) utterance may also serve as a predicate according to the well-known interpretation. Nevertheless, despite all of this, it is preferable to abandon what requires it. Even more frigid (*abrad*), and more lacking in taste than anything, is the view of one who claimed that it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿provision for you﴾, with the implied meaning "He provides." "Made" (*ja'ala*) is taken to mean "rendered," and the two nouns in the accusative after it are its two objects. It was also said that "made" means "brought into being," and the accusative of the second noun is circumstantial (*al-haliyya*), meaning: bring the earth into being in a state where it is spread out as a bed for you, so that you do not need to strive to make it so. The meaning of rendering it a bed, that is, like a bed, in the soundness of sitting and sleeping upon it, is that He, glorified is He, made part of it stand out above the water, although its natural disposition is for the water to be above it because of its heaviness, and He made it intermediate between hardness and softness, so that settling upon it would be easy without further hardship. Thus "rendering" is understood in the sense that, since it was capable of other than that, it was as if it had been transferred from that state. Even if what is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is authentic, namely that the earth was created before the sky, not spread out, and was then spread out and extended after its creation, the matter of "rendering" is clear in that case. Nevertheless, not all people know this, and the attribute must be known to the addressee. Going to the flood, and considering "rendering" as relative to it, is from the turbulence of the waves of ignorance. Its sphericity does not contradict its being a bed, because when a sphere is very large, every piece of it is like a flat surface in its spreading out, as is not hidden. He, glorified is He, used the verb "made" here, and in what preceded He used "created" (*khalaqa*), due to the difference of context, or for variety of expression, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light﴾. The placing forward of the non-explicit object is for hastening the joy by showing that what follows it consists of benefits for the addressees, or for building suspense toward what comes after it, especially after an indication of its benefit, so that it settles most firmly when it arrives. Or it is because of a kind of length in the latter part and what is conjoined to it, so that if it were placed earlier, the correspondence of the extremes would be lost. He, glorified is He, chose the word "sky" (*sama'*) rather than "heavens" (*samawat*) to match the word "earth." There is no great benefit in explicitly mentioning its plurality here. Nevertheless, it is possible that what is meant by it is the totality of the heavens and each layer and direction of them. "Building" (*bina'*) is originally a verbal noun applied to what is built, whether a house, a dome, a tent, or a side. From it comes "he consummated the marriage with his wife" (*bana bi-ahlihi*) or "upon his family." This is contrary to al-Hariri, because when they married they would pitch a new tent for them to enter upon the bride in it. The meaning of the sky being a building is that it is like a pitched dome, or that it is like a roof for the earth. The roof of a house is also called a building (*bina'*). This was related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. He, glorified is He, placed the state of the earth first because their need for it and their benefit from it are greater and more evident. Or, because when He mentioned their creation, it was fitting to follow it with mention of the first thing they need after it, which is what is stable (*al-mustaqirr*). Or, so that ascent may occur from the lower to the higher. Or, because the creation of the earth precedes the creation of the sky, as the apparent meanings of many verses indicate. Or, because the earth, being the dwelling place of the prophets, and they having been created from it, is more excellent than the sky. There is a well-known disagreement on this. Yazid al-Shami read *bisatan* (carpet), and Talha read *mihadan* (cradle, bed), and these are equivalents. Abu Amr assimilated the *lam* of "made" (*ja'ala*) into the *lam* of "for you" (*lakum*). ﴿And He sent down water from the sky, and brought forth by it fruits as provision for you﴾ is conjoined to "made." The first "min" (from) denotes the starting point and is connected to "sent down," or to an implied word that occurs as a circumstantial state of the object. It was placed before the object for building suspense toward the first, together with the greater cohesion it has with what follows. Or, because the sky is its origin and source. And so that the circumstantial sense can be realized in the second case, for if the object were placed first and it is indefinite, the adverbial phrase would become a qualifier. It was mentioned in *al-Bahr al-Muhit* that on this reading "min" is partitive, meaning "from the waters of the sky." This, as you see, is [unsatisfactory]. What is meant by "sky" is the direction of height, or the clouds. Taking it to mean the specific celestial sphere (*falak*) based on the apparent meanings is not far-fetched, given the power of the King, the Mighty, may His majesty be exalted, and whose acts transcend the faculties of reason. Nevertheless, it is commonly held that when the sun passes over some seas and deserts, it raises from the seas a moist vapor and from the deserts a dry one. When the vapor rises to the third layer of the atmosphere, it condenses. If the cold is not strong, it gathers and drips down due to its weight from condensation; the gathered is cloud, and the dripping is rain. If the cold is strong, it becomes snow and hail. Sometimes it does not solidify, and this is called mist. ﴿And in everything He has a sign that indicates He is one﴾. On this basis, descent from the sky means its coming into being from celestial causes and ethereal influences, so the sky is a metaphorical origin for it. Furthermore, whoever has the cloud of ignorance removed from the eye of his insight sees that everything in this lower world descends from the throne of the will and the heaven of power, as wisdom requires, through an intermediary or without one, as His saying indicates, exalted is He: ﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasures, and We send it down only in a known measure﴾. Rather, whoever knows that Allah, glorified is He, is in the sky in the meaning He intended, and with the attribute befitting Him, together with the transcendence befitting the majesty of His essence, exalted is He, may say that whatever is in the worlds is from that sky. Attributing its descent to other than it at times is due to apparent considerations, and these ultimately return to Him in the Hereafter. Water is well known. Some have defined it as a fluid substance by which the existence of living beings is sustained. Its pattern is *fa'l*, its alif is converted from a *waw*, and its hamza is a substitute for a *ha'*, as indicated by *muwayh*, *miyah*, and *amwah*. Its tanwin indicates partiality. He, glorified is He, specified its descent from the sky in many verses, as a way of honoring its status because of the abundance of its benefit and the greatness of its blessing. The second "min" (from) may be partitive, since many fruits have not yet come out, so "provision" (*rizqan*) in that case is in the verbal-noun sense and is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) for "brought forth." "For you" (*lakum*) is an adverbial phrase of incidental complement and an indirect object. [Page 189]

(for provision), meaning: He brought forth some of the fruits, that is, some of them, for the sake of His providing you. It is also permitted that some of the fruits be the object of "brought forth," and "provision" in the sense of "provided" is a circumstantial state of the object, or both are in the accusative as a verbal noun for "brought forth." The second "min" may also be explanatory, in which case "provision" in the sense of "provided" is the object of "brought forth," "for you" is its qualifier, and "from the fruits" is also its qualifier. However, since it has been placed first, it becomes a circumstantial state according to the rule in such cases. Regarding placing the explanatory element before what it explains, there is a difference of opinion: al-Zamakhshari and many others permitted it, while the author of *al-Durr al-Masun* and others forbade it. The possibility of making "min" initial (for origin), with an implied "from the mention of," or interpreting "the fruits" as "the seed," is far-fetched and has no benefit. The definite article in "the fruits" is either generic or comprehensive, and [the author] took it as generic. The "min" is superfluous, which is not a sound view, because the superfluity of "min" occurs in affirmative contexts and before a definite noun, which no one maintains except al-Akhfash. It would also follow from this that all the fruits that were brought forth become provision for us, while many trees bear fruit that cannot be provision. He used the plural of paucity (*jam' qilla*) although the context calls for the plural of abundance. The appropriate form for this would have been "from the fruits," to indicate that what has appeared in the gardens of existence through the outpouring of the waters of generosity is like a little, indeed even less than a little in comparison with the fruits of Paradise and what is stored in the realms of the unseen. Or, to indicate that their kinds, since some are eaten entirely while others are eaten only in their outer part and others only in their inner part, point to what they point to, which is a few that do not reach the limit of abundance. As for what Imam al-Baydawi and others mentioned, that this plural was permissible here because he meant by "fruits" the plural of "fruit," used to express abundance, like "the fruits of such-and-such" in your saying, "the fruit of your garden has ripened," and the *ta'* is not for true singularity but for conventional singularity, this is supported by the reading of Ibn al-Sumayq, "from the fruit" (*min al-thamara*). Or, because plurals may substitute for one another, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How many gardens they left behind﴾ and ﴿three periods﴾. Or, because when it is prefixed with the definite article, it exits the sense of paucity. This purity is not free from turbidity, as the words of al-Shihab make clear. If it is said that the sound masculine and feminine plural is for abundance, or is shared and the context specifies it for abundance, the objection is dispelled and the argument ends. However, few people have held this view. The "ba'" in "by it" (*bihi*) is causal. It is well known among the Ash'aris that in such contexts it is customary causation, so water has no actual influence at all in bringing forth, nor in anything else. Rather, the only one who acts is Allah, exalted is He, at the occasions of causes, not through them, on the basis of the hadith about completion through another. They said: whoever believes that Allah, exalted is He, has deposited the power of satisfaction in water, for example, is a sinner, and there are two opinions about his disbelief. Whoever holds that it acts by its own essence is grouped with them in disbelief. So according to them, the responsible person must believe that satisfaction comes from the bountiful Source directly without intermediary, and that its arrival coincides with the drinking of water, without water having any role in that by any means other than formal correspondence. The humble one (the author) does not say this. Rather, I say: Allah, glorified is He, has linked causes with their effects, both legally and by decree, and made causes the locus of His wisdom in His religious legal command and His cosmic decreeing command, and the locus of His dominion and disposal. Thus denying causes and powers is a rejection of what is necessary, a defect in intellects and natures, an obstinate contradiction of the senses, and a rejection of the law and of retribution. Allah, exalted is His majesty, has made the interests of His servants in their livelihood and their return, reward and punishment, prescribed penalties, expiations, commands, prohibitions, lawfulness and unlawfulness, all of it linked to causes and established through them. Indeed, the servant himself, his attributes and his actions, are causes for what proceeds from him. The Qur'an is full of affirmations of causes; if we were to trace what indicates this from the Qur'an and the Sunnah, it would exceed ten thousand places, literally and not hyperbolically. And how marvelous it is, by Allah, exalted is He: if Allah is the creator of the cause and the effect, and He is the one who made this a cause of that, and causes and effects are subject to His will and power, obedient and compliant, then what defect would require [...]. [Page 190]

[Continuation of the commentary]

That is with regard to tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness). What association (shirk) could follow from it? We seek God's forgiveness for what they say. God, Mighty and Majestic, acts through the causes that wisdom requires, though He is free of need for them, just as it is sound that He acts at them, not through them. The argument of "completion" (istikmal) refutes this, because completion would only be necessary if the action truly depended on that cause, and the consequence is false, given His saying, ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ So causes are effective by powers that God has deposited in them, but by His permission. If He does not permit, and He prevents them from having effect, they do not have effect. This is indicated by His saying, ﴿They cannot harm anyone thereby except by God's permission.﴾ If these causes had no powers that the Mighty, the Wise, had deposited in them, He would not have said, ﴿O fire, be coolness and safety upon Abraham.﴾ For what would be the benefit of the command, if the fire had no power of burning? Burning comes from Him, Exalted, without intermediary. If the matter were as they claim, the fire could say, "My God, You have deposited nothing in me and granted me no power, and I am only like a paralyzed hand accompanied by a healthy hand that performs actions, acts and roams in the field of deeds." Would one say to the paralyzed hand, "Do not act," and "Do not descend into that field," while such a thing is not said to the active hand, which is more deserving of that statement? I do not think the Ash'aris (Ash'ariyya, followers of al-Ash'ari) can answer this, nor do I think they will offer a reply. What we have mentioned is what the pious predecessors (al-Salaf al-Salih) held, and what the people of God (Ahl Allah) accepted. Do not let the attribution of this view to the Mu'tazila (Mu'tazilites) cast doubt on it for you. For they also say, "There is no god but God." Would you doubt that statement because they said it? Far be it from God, from partisanship. Wisdom is the lost property of the believer, and the truth has more right to be followed. God says the truth, and He guides to the way.

﴿So do not set up rivals to God.﴾ This prohibition is conjoined to ﴿worship﴾ and follows from it, as if it were said: since it is obligatory upon you to worship your Lord, then do not set up a rival to God, and single Him out for worship, since there is no lord for you besides Him. Placing the noble Name in the position of a pronoun serves to identify the object of worship by His essence, after identifying Him by attributes, and to ground the ruling in the attribute of divinity (uluhiyya), on which the matter of oneness turns, and on the impossibility of partnership, and to signal that all other attributes follow from it. It has also been said: the word "Lord" (rabb) is used for the general concept, while "God" (Allah) is a proper name for the individual, real, necessarily existent Being, exalted be His majesty. So this is not a case of placing an apparent noun in the place of a pronoun. Then the difference becomes clear between this noble verse, where worship is linked to the attribute of lordship, so the appropriate particle is the fa', and between His saying, ﴿Worship God and do not associate anything with Him,﴾ where worship and not associating are linked to His essence, so the appropriate conjunction is the waw. Therefore it is not objected that the appropriate conjunction here is the waw, as in the second verse. Or the verb is a negated subjunctive governed by an implied "anna", as an answer to the imperative, as our master al-Baydawi (al-Baydawi) said. It was objected that this is inconsistent, because that applies when the first is a cause of the second, and there is no doubt that worship is not a cause of tawhid, which is its root and origin. It was answered that the foundation of His worship is tawhid and not associating anything with Him, whereas the foundation of worshipping the Lord is not the non-association with His essence, exalted be He, but rather one of its branches. The truth is that the verse includes worship of a Lord described by what makes Him as if witnessed by His creation: He created them and their forebears, He originated the great beings, and He bestowed great blessings graciously. These give an indication of Him that made them know Him. So its sense is: worship God, Exalted, whom you have known with a knowledge free of doubt. There is no doubt that worship and knowledge are a cause of not associating, for whoever knows God does not equate anything with Him. What led the objector astray is considering worship in isolation from knowledge. It may also be that the word "la'alla" ("perhaps") is connected to it, so the verb is in the subjunctive like "fa-attali'a" in the reading of Ja'far for ﴿Perhaps I may reach the ways﴾ and so on, according to one opinion that it is assimilated to the six particles, since they do not necessitate the attainment of what they contain, so they are like a condition in non-realization. The view that it is assimilated to "laytа" (if only), treating what is hoped for as what is wished for in non-occurrence, comes to this, if by non-occurrence is meant its non-occurrence at the time of the ruling, not its impossibility. The meaning is: He created you so that you might be pious and fear His punishment, so do not liken Him to His creation. Understand this. It is also possible that the fa' is superfluous, indicating causation, and the prohibitive clause, by interpretation as a saying, is a predicate of the one who is made the subject. It has also been said that the clause is connected to "who," and the fa' is the response of an implied conditional, and the meaning is: He is the one who made for you what was mentioned of abundant blessings; and if that is so, then do not set up etc. The "making" here means "rendering," which can be by a physical act, as in "I made the iron a sword," and it can also be by speech and contract, as in the earlier usage.

The "andad" (rivals) is the plural of nidd, like 'idl and a'dal, or of nadid, like yatim and aytam. A nidd is the like of a thing that opposes it, differs from it in its affairs, is repelled by it and stays far from it. It is not among the words with contrary meanings according to the more correct view. Its root is from nadda, nudud, meaning to flee. It has also been said: the nidd is that which shares only in substance, the shakl (counterpart) shares in magnitude and extent, the shabah (resemblance) shares only in quality, and the mithl (equal) in quantity only, while "mithl" in general covers all of these. Calling what the polytheists worship besides God "rivals," while they did not claim that these resemble Him in His essence and attributes, nor that they oppose Him in His actions, but they worshipped them only so that they would bring them near to Him, Exalted, in nearness, is a sign of a mocking metaphor, since "nazir" (equal) is used for one who is close and near, just as "bishara" (good news) is used for "indhar" (warning), and "asad" (lion) for a coward. If by "nidd" is meant "nazir" absolutely, there is no contradiction, and it is simply the metaphor of one of two similar things for the other, since the polytheists made the idols, in terms of their acts and states, similar to Him in worship. This is a shameful course and a foolish attribute, and mentioning it implies their folly and mockery. It is perhaps better to take the first meaning. The use of the plural is a further reproach, since they made rivals for One for whom it is impossible to have a single rival. By God, how well said is the monotheist of the interval (fatra), Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, may God be pleased with him, when he says about this:

Is it one Lord, or a thousand lords?
I serve when affairs are divided.
I have abandoned al-Lat and al-'Uzza together,
Thus does the discerning man act.

﴿While you know﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "do not set up," and the object is omitted, meaning: while your state is that you are among the people of knowledge, understanding, reflection, and sound judgment. So if you reflect even slightly, you will know the existence of a Creator who must be affirmed as one in His essence and attributes, and it is not fitting that anything other than Him be worshipped. Or it is an implied element fitting the context, and it fills the place of the two objects of "know," meaning: you know that He, glorified, has no like, or that they have no likeness to Him and cannot do what He does. The circumstantial clause, according to the first meaning, is for reproach or restriction, since knowledge is the basis of obligation, and there is no obligation when the capacity is lacking. According to the second meaning it is for reproach only, because the restriction of the ruling is the connection of knowledge to the object, whereas the basis of obligation is knowledge alone. The reproach is directed at some of those addressed by the prohibition, on the basis that the address is general, as was explained regarding the command. Therefore it does not require restricting the address to the unbelievers. Moreover, there is no harm in restricting it to them, in command and prohibition alike. Indeed, it has been said that this is preferable for avoiding strained interpretation and for the fitting arrangement of the passage, since in the apparent sense of the verse of challenge there is no escape from taking the address in its unrestricted sense, and restricting it to the unbelievers involves the risk of diminishing the standing of the believers and raising their rank above being included in the company of the base unbelievers, and it signals that they are constant in obedience and worship, needing no command or prohibition in this matter. So reflect.

These verses have included, from the wonders of craftsmanship, the subtleties of wisdom, and the clarity of proofs, what establishes that He, exalted be He, is the sole originator, the one deserving of worship to the exclusion of others, unlike the rivals who do not create, do not provide, and have neither benefit nor harm: "Surely creation and command belong to Him" (Q. 7:54).

* * *

From the sphere of allusion: God has symbolized the body by the earth, the soul by the sky, and the intellect by water, and what He bestows upon the receptive faculties of scientific and practical virtues, obtained through the use of intellect and the senses, and the pairing of the soul's and body's powers, with the fruits produced from the pairing of the active heavenly powers and the receptive earthly powers, by the permission of the free Agent. It may also be said: when God bestowed favor upon them by stating that He created them and those before them, He mentioned what guides them to know how they were created. He made the earth, which is a bed, like the mother upon whom the man lays his bed, and she too is called a bed. He compared the sky, which is raised above the earth, to the father who rises above the mother and covers her. He set the water descending from the sky as a parable for the sperm that descends from the father's loins, and He set what comes out of the earth of fruits as a parable for the child who comes out of the mother. All this is to make their minds comfortable, guide them to know the manner of creation, and inform them that He is the Creator of this child and the One who brings it out from its mother's womb, just as He is the Creator of the fruits and the One who brings them out from the bellies of their trees, and the One who brings their trees out from the belly of the earth. When this becomes clear to them, they single Him out for divinity, and devote worship to Him, and guidance is attained for them:

Reflect upon the meadows of the earth, and look at the traces of what the King has made.
Springs of silver standing upright, upon whose eyelids is refined gold.
Upon stems of emerald they bear witness that God has no partner.

When Allah, glorified is He, established the command of His Oneness in the best manner, He followed it with what indicates the truthfulness of His Messenger (ﷺ). Tawhid and tasdiq are twins, neither of which is separated from the other. Although the verse was brought to demonstrate the inimitability (i'jaz), its real purpose is to establish prophethood. The sequencing also contains an allusion refuting the Ta'limiyya (the Ismaili-type "instructionists"), who held that knowledge of Allah is derived from knowledge of the Messenger, and the Hashwiyya (the literalist extremists), who held that knowledge of Him, glorified is He, can be attained only from the Qur'an.

The statement (akhbar) and its conjunction (ʿatf) are either upon His saying, ﴿Worship your Lord﴾, or upon "(do not set up rivals)". The connection is explained as follows: since Allah, glorified and exalted is He, made worship obligatory and negated association (shirk) alongside those verses, and submission to them cannot occur without affirming that they are from Him, glorified is He, He guided them to what necessitates this knowledge. For this reason, the Majestic One did not say: "If you are in doubt concerning the mission of Our servant, it is not sound," since the rational proof would then become transmitted (sam'i). Had that been intended, "(worship)" and "(do not associate)" would have sufficed, without detailing the proofs from within the self (anfusi) and from the horizons (afaqi). The apparent reading is that the address here is to the disbelievers, which is the view transmitted from al-Hasan. It has also been said that it is addressed to the Jews, because the occasion of revelation, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, was that they said: "What Muhammad (ﷺ) brings us does not resemble revelation, and indeed we are in doubt about it." It has also been said that it is in the same manner as the address in "(worship)".

The word (in) (إنْ) is either for rebuke over doubting, depicting that it is something which should not be established except on the basis of supposition, because the context includes what removes it; or for giving precedence to those whose doubt is not certain over others; or because some of them were in doubt and some were not, so the whole was treated as though there was no certainty either of their doubt or of its absence. It has also been said that (in) carries the meaning of (idh) (إذْ), as claimed by some exegetes, contrary to the view of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun). The use of the word (kana) (كانَ) is to preserve the meaning of past time, since it is purely temporal and (in) does not transform it into the meaning of the future, as al-Mubarrad and those who agree with him held. The majority hold that it is like the other past verbs. Some supposed an implied element between it and (in), such as (if it be) or (if it becomes clear), but the heart does not incline to this.

The indefinite form of (rayb) (ريب) indicates that its due, if it is to exist, is to be weak and little, because of the clarity of what repels it and the strength of what removes it. Making it a container (zarf), by treating meanings as if they were physical bodies, with them settled within it and encompassing them, does not contradict considering its weakness and paucity, since what that requires is the continuity of their involvement with it, not its strength or abundance. (Min) (مِنِ) is the initial (ibtida'iyya) and modifies (rayb) (رَيْبٍ). It cannot be partitive (tab'id), and interpreting it as causal may suggest that the Sender is a locus of doubt, and far be that from Him. (Ma) (وما), whether relative (mawsula) or descriptive (mawsufa), refers to the Book. It has also been said that it refers to the common element between it and its parts. The meaning of their being in doubt concerning it is their doubt about it being revelation from Allah, exalted is His majesty. The doubling (tadh'if) in (nazzalna) (نَزَّلْنا) is for transference (naql), and it is synonymous with the hamza (of causation). This is supported by the reading of Zayd ibn Qutayb: (anzalna) (أنْزَلْنا). The doubling here does not indicate that it was revealed in installments (tanjim), so that choosing it over (inzal) would serve to remind of the source of their doubt. They said: ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ The building of the challenge upon it is a loosening of the reins (irkha' al-'inan), as held by many whose fingers are counted when they are mentioned, because that is a claim that the doubling indicates multiplicity (takthir). That is generally the case with verbs which were transitive before doubling, such as (fataḥtu) (فَتَحْتُ, I opened) and (qaṭa'tu) (قَطَعْتُ, I cut). (Nazzala) (نَزَّلَ) was not transitive before, and furthermore, doubling intended for multiplicity only indicates the frequency of the occurrence of the act, but not that it makes the intransitive transitive. The verb here was intransitive, so the fact that transitivity is derived from the doubling is evidence that it is for transference, not for multiplicity. Furthermore, if (nazzala) indicated gradual revelation, the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿Why was the Qur'an not sent down to him all at once?﴾ would need interpretation, because the second part (the rest of the verse) would contradict the first. The same applies to ﴿Why was a sign not sent down to him?﴾ and ﴿Had We sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾. It has been read in both ways in many places where installment and multiplicity are not possible. The multiplicity mentioned in grammar is different from this, namely the sense of gradualness, bringing something little by little, as they stated concerning (tasallalu) (تَسَلَّلُوا), where they interpreted it as "they slip away little by little". They said: its counterpart is (tadarraja) (تَدَرَّجَ, he proceeded step by step) and (tadakhkhala) (تَدَخَّلَ, he entered gradually), and similar to it is (rattabahu) (رَتَّبَهُ, he arranged it), meaning he brought it in rank by rank; and nothing other than this was found. In that case, the pattern (fa''ala) (فَعَّلَ), after being for transference, indicates this meaning either metaphorically or by homonymy (ishtirak). Therefore, its consistent application is not necessary, especially with the obscurity of the indicator.

The transitivity of (nazzala) with (ʿala) (عَلى, upon) indicates the superiority of the sender over the one upon whom it is sent down, his firm establishment over it, and that it becomes as one who is clothed with it. This contrasts with (ila) (إلى, to), which indicates no more than termination and arrival. Mentioning him (ﷺ) with the title of servanthood (ʿubudiyya), together with the attribution to the pronoun of majesty, alerts to the greatness of his station, his special relationship with Him, and his submission to His commands. In this is the utmost honour and exaltation of his station (ﷺ):

"Do not call me except by 'O His servant', for it is the most noble of my names."

It is read (ʿibadina) (عِبادِنا, Our servants) in the plural. It is possible that this refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his community, because the benefit of what is sent down and the guidance obtained through it are not exclusive, but both the followed and the follower share in them, so it is as though it was sent down upon them. It is also possible that what is meant is the prophets upon whom revelation was sent down, with the Messenger (ﷺ) being the first intended and the earliest entrant, because he is the one whose opponents demanded a challenge in his Book. In this is an announcement that doubt about it is doubt about what was sent down before it, since it confirms that and is a witness over it. Some have made the address in this to be to those who deny prophethood, whom Allah, exalted is He, described in His saying: ﴿They did not measure Allah with His true measure when they said: Allah did not send down anything upon a human being﴾.

In the verse there is a shift (iltifat) from the third-person absent to the first-person plural speaker. Otherwise He would have said: "from what He sent down upon His servant." However, He, glorified is He, turned to this in order to magnify either the sent-down thing or the one upon whom it was sent down, especially since He used (nā) (نا), which indicates complete exaltation and the magnification of the matter, in consideration of the elevated rank of his station, upon him be prayers and peace.

The (fa) (ف) of (fa'tu) (فَأْتُوا) is responsive (jawabiyya), and the causal aspect is evident. The command is one of challenge (ta'jiz), and the placing of the stone in the manner of His saying: ﴿So bring it from the west﴾. (Ityan) (الإتْيان) means coming with ease wherever it occurs, and it is said of good and evil, of physical bodies and accidents. Then it came to mean doing and undertaking, as in ﴿And they do not come to prayer except while they are lazy﴾. The original form of (fa'tu) is (fa'tiyu) (فَأْتِيُوا), which underwent the well-known elision (i'lal). Irregularly, the elision of the (fa) has also occurred, so it is said (ti) (تِ) and (tawwan) (تَوًّا).

The nunation (tanwin) in (surah) (سُورَةٍ) is for indefiniteness, meaning "bring a surah, any surah," namely a section of the Qur'an, the least of which is three verses. In this there is a rebuke and a humbling of them for their doubt, which is not hidden.

(Min mithlihi) (ومِن مِثْلِهِ) may be a stationary adverbial (zarf mustaqirr) modifying (surah), with the pronoun referring either to (ma), which denotes the sent-down thing, or to the servant. On the first reading, (min) may be partitive or explanatory (tabyin), and al-Akhfash permits its being extra (ziyada) with (mithl). The meaning is "with a surah similar to the Qur'an in eloquence and inimitable style." This is evident for the last two readings. As for the partitive reading, it is because no definite, specific counterpart of the Qur'an was intended, but rather something which would resemble it hypothetically, as is said: "Your like is not ignored." There is no doubt that partitiveness toward the hypothetical equal is necessary because of its similarity to the Qur'an. Therefore, the necessary (lazim) is mentioned, and the implied (malzum) is intended, by way of metonymy (kinaya), together with the sense of exaggeration in the partitive (min), which indicates paucity, a suitable exaggeration for the context of challenge. For this reason, some preferred partitiveness over explanation, although explanation makes explicit what was understood implicitly, since the similarity to the Qur'an is understood from the expression "surah." Yet this is supported by what follows. On the second reading, (min) must be initial, like its use in ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon﴾. Partitiveness, explanation, and extra use are ruled out, just as initiality is ruled out in the first reading.

It may also be that (min) is connected to (fa'tu) (فَأْتُوا). The common view is that in that case the pronoun must refer to the servant, because (min) cannot be explanatory, since there is no ambiguous element. Also, since it is always stationary, it does not relate to the command as a mere complement (laghw). Nor can it be partitive, for otherwise the act would fall directly upon it, as in "I took from the dirhams." There is no sense in "bringing a part," but rather the intended meaning is "bringing [something] from a part." There is no room for estimating a (ba') (بِ, with) when (min) is present. Moreover, it would result in the word "surah" being left without a clear reference. Therefore, it is necessarily initial, and in that case the pronoun must refer to the servant, not to the sent-down thing. Making the speaker the origin in custom for bringing speech from him is a meaningful and acceptable idea, unlike making the whole the origin for bringing a part of it, which no person of sound nature would accept. Also, the criterion for the origin of an act is either the agent origin, the material origin, the final origin, or a respect in which it is clothed. The whole, relative to the part, is none of these. Accordingly, the consideration of the similarity of what is brought to the Qur'an in eloquence is derived from the word "surah," and the context is understood with the help of the situation.

واعْتُرِضَ بِأنَّ مَعْنى (مِن) لا يَنْحَصِرُ فِيما ذُكِرَ، فَقَدْ تَجِيءُ لِلْبَدَلِ، نَحْوَ ﴿أرَضِيتُمْ بِالحَياةِ الدُّنْيا مِنَ الآخِرَةِ﴾ [التوبة: 38]، و"وجَعَلَنا مِنكم مَلائِكَةً" [الزخرف: 60]، وَلِلْمُجاوَزَةِ، كَقَوْلِكَ: عُذْتُ مِنهُ. فَعَلى هَذا، لَوْ عُلِّقَ (مِن مِثْلِهِ) بـِ(فَأْتُوا)، وحُمِلَ (مِن) عَلى البَدَلِ أوِ المُجاوَزَةِ، وَ(مِثْلُ) عَلى المُقْحَمِ [أي الزائد]، وَرَجَعَ الضَّمِيرُ إلى (ما أنْزَلَنا) عَلى مَعْنى: (فَأْتُوا) بَدَلَ ذَلِكَ الكِتابِ العَظِيمِ، شَأْنُهُ الواضِحُ، وبُرْهانُهُ الظّاهِرُ، أوْ (مُجاوِزِينَ) مِن هَذا الكِتابِ مَعَ فَخامَةِ أثَرِهِ وجَلالَةِ قَدْرِهِ، بِسُورَةٍ فَذَّةٍ، لَكانَ أبْلَغَ في التَّحَدِّي وأظْهَرَ في الإعْجازِ. عَلى أنَّ عَدَمَ صِحَّةِ شَيْءٍ مِمّا اعْتُبِرَ في المَبْدَإ مَمْنُوعٌ، فَإنَّ المُلابَسَةَ بَيْنَ الكُلِّ والبَعْضِ أقْوى مِنها بَيْنَ المَكانِ والمُتَمَكِّنِ، فَكَما يَجُوزُ جَعْلُ المَكانِ مَبْدَأ الفِعْلِ المُتَمَكِّنِ، يَجُوزُ أنْ يُجْعَلَ الكُلُّ مَبْدَأً لِلْإتْيانِ بِالبَعْضِ. وَلَعَلَّ مَن قالَ ذَلِكَ لَمْ يَطْرُقْ سَمْعَهُ قَوْلُ سِيبَوَيْهِ: "وبِمَنزِلَةِ المَكانِ ما لَيْسَ بِمَكانٍ، ولا زَمانٍ، نَحْوُ: قَرَأْتُ مِن أوَّلِ السُّورَةِ إلى آخِرِها، وأعْطَيْتُكَ مِن دِرْهَمٍ إلى دِينارٍ". وأيْضًا، فَالإتْيانُ بِبَعْضِ الشَّيْءِ تَفْرِيقُهُ مِنهُ، ولا يُسْتَرابُ أنَّ الكُلَّ مَبْدَأُ تَفْرِيقِ البَعْضِ مِنهُ.

وَيُمْكِنُ أنْ يُقالَ، وهو الَّذِي اخْتارَهُ مَوْلانا الشِّهابُ: إنَّ المُرادَ مِنَ الآيَةِ التَّحَدِّي، وتَعْجِيزُ بُلَغاءِ العَرَبِ المُرْتابِينَ فِيهِ عَنِ الإتْيانِ بِما يُضاهِيهِ، فَمُقْتَضى المَقامِ أنْ يُقالَ لَهم: مَعاشِرَ الفُصَحاءِ المُرْتابِينَ في أنَّ القُرْآنَ مِن عِنْدِ اللَّهِ، ائْتُوا بِمِقْدارِ أقْصَرِ سُورَةٍ مِن كَلامِ البَشَرِ، مُحَلّاةٍ بِطِرازِ الإعْجازِ ونَظْمِهِ. وما ذُكِرَ يَدُلُّ عَلى هَذا، إذا كانَ (مِن مِثْلِهِ) صِفَةَ سُورَةٍ، سَواءٌ كانَ الضَّمِيرُ لِـ(ما)، أوْ لِلْعَبْدِ، لِأنَّ مَعْناهُ: ائْتُوا بِمِقْدارِ سُورَةٍ تُماثِلُهُ في البَلاغَةِ، كائِنَةٍ مِن كَلامِ أحَدٍ مِثْلِ هَذا العَبْدِ في البَشَرِيَّةِ، فَهو مُعْجِزٌ لِلْبَشَرِ عَنِ الإتْيانِ بِمِثْلِهِ. أوْ: ائْتُوا بِمِقْدارِ سُورَةٍ مِن كَلامٍ هو مِثْلُ هَذا المُنَزَّلِ، ومِثْلُ الشَّيْءِ غَيْرُهُ، فَهو مِن كَلامِ البَشَرِ أيْضًا. فَإذا تَعَلَّقَ، ورَجَعَ الضَّمِيرُ لِلْعَبْدِ، فَمَعْناهُ أيْضًا: ائْتُوا مِن مِثْلِ هَذا العَبْدِ في البَشَرِيَّةِ بِمِقْدارِ سُورَةٍ تُماثِلُهُ، فَيُفِيدُ ما ذَكَرْنا. وَلَوْ رَجَعَ عَلى هَذا لَما كانَ مَعْناهُ: ائْتُوا مِن مِثْلِ هَذا المُنَزَّلِ بِسُورَةٍ. ولا شَكَّ أنَّ (مِن) لَيْسَتْ بَيانِيَّةً، لِأنَّها لا تَكُونُ لَغْوًا، ولا تَبْعِيضِيَّةً، لِأنَّ المَعْنى لَيْسَ عَلَيْهِ، فَهي ابْتِدائِيَّةٌ، والمَبْدَأُ لَيْسَ فاعِلِيًّا، بَلْ مادِّيًّا. فَحِينَئِذٍ، المَثَلُ الَّذِي السُّورَةُ بَعْضٌ مِنهُ لَمْ يُؤْمَرْ بِالإتْيانِ بِهِ، فَلا يَخْلُو مِن أنْ يُدَّعى وُجُودُهُ، وهو خِلافُ الواقِعِ، وابْتِناؤُهُ عَلى الزَّعْمِ أوِ الفَرْضِ تَعَسُّفٌ بِلا مُقْتَضٍ أوَّلًا، ولا يَلِيقُ بِالتَّنْزِيلِ. وكَيْفَ يَأْتُونَ بِبَعْضٍ مِن شَيْءٍ لا وُجُودَ لَهُ!

والحَقُّ عِنْدِي أنَّ رُجُوعَ الضَّمِيرِ إلى كُلٍّ مِنَ العَبْدِ، و(ما)، عَلى تَقْدِيرَيِ: اللَّغْوُ والِاسْتِقْرارُ،
[صفحة 195]
أمْرٌ مُمْكِنٌ، ودائِرَةُ التَّأْوِيلِ واسِعَةٌ، والِاسْتِحْسانُ مُفَوَّضٌ إلى الذَّوْقِ السَّلِيمِ، والَّذِي يُدْرِكُهُ ذَوْقِي، ولا أُزَكِّي نَفْسِي، أنَّهُ عَلى تَقْدِيرِ التَّعَلُّقِ يَكُونُ رُجُوعُ الضَّمِيرِ إلى العَبْدِ أحْلى. والبَحْثُ في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ مَشْهُورٌ، وقَدْ جَرى فِيهِ بَيْنَ العَضُدِ والجارَبَرْدِيِّ ما أدّى إلى تَأْلِيفِ الرَّسائِلِ في الِانْتِصارِ لِكُلٍّ، وقَدْ وُفِّقْتُ لِلْوُقُوفِ عَلى كَثِيرٍ مِنها، والحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، ونَقَلْتُ نُبْذَةً مِنها في الأجْوِبَةِ العِراقِيَّةِ.

ثُمَّ أوْلى الوُجُوهِ هُنا عَلى الإطْلاقِ جَعْلُ الظَّرْفِ صِفَةً لِلسُّورَةِ، والضَّمِيرِ لِلْمُنَزَّلِ، و(مِن) بَيانِيَّةً. أمّا أوَّلًا: فَلِأنَّهُ المُوافِقُ لِنَظائِرِهِ مِن آياتِ التَّحَدِّي، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿فَأْتُوا بِسُورَةٍ مِثْلِهِ﴾ [يونس: 38]، لِأنَّ المُماثَلَةَ فِيها صِفَةٌ لِلْمَأْتِيِّ بِهِ. وأمّا ثانِيًا: فَلِأنَّ الكَلامَ في المُنَزَّلِ لا المُنَزَّلِ عَلَيْهِ، وذِكْرُهُ إنَّما وقَعَ تَبَعًا، ولَوْ عادَ الضَّمِيرُ إلَيْهِ تُرِكَ التَّصْرِيحُ بِمُماثَلَةِ السُّورَةِ، وهو عُمْدَةُ التَّحَدِّي، وإنْ فُهِمَ. وأمّا ثالِثًا: فَلِأنَّ أمْرَ الجَمِّ الغَفِيرِ، لِأنْ يَأْتُوا مِن مِثْلِ ما أتى بِهِ واحِدٌ مِن جِنْسِهِمْ، أبْلَغُ مِن أمْرِهِمْ بِأنْ يَجِدُوا أحَدًا يَأْتِي بِمِثْلِ ما أتى بِهِ رَجُلٌ آخَرُ. وأمّا رابِعًا: فَلِأنَّهُ لَوْ رَجَعَ الضَّمِيرُ لِلْعَبْدِ لَأوْهَمَ أنَّ إعْجازَهُ لِكَوْنِهِ مِمَّنْ لَمْ يَدْرُسْ، ولَمْ يَكْتُبْ، لا أنَّهُ في نَفْسِهِ مُعْجِزٌ، مَعَ أنَّ الواقِعَ هَذا.

وَبَعْضُهم رَجَّحَ رَدَّ الضَّمِيرِ إلى العَبْدِ صَلّى اللَّهُ تَعالى عَلَيْهِ وسَلَّمَ (ﷺ)، بِاشْتِمالِهِ عَلى مَعْنى مُسْتَبْدَعٍ مُسْتَجَدٍّ، وبِأنَّ الكَلامَ مَسُوقٌ لِلْمُنَزَّلِ عَلَيْهِ، إذِ التَّوْحِيدُ والتَّصْدِيقُ بِالنُّبُوَّةِ تَوْأمانِ، فالمَقْصُودُ إثْباتُ النُّبُوَّةِ، والحُجَّةُ ذَرِيعَةٌ، فَلا يَلْزَمُ مِنَ الِافْتِتاحِ بِذِكْرِ (ما نَزَّلْنا) أنْ يَكُونَ الكَلامُ مَسُوقًا لَهُ. وبِأنَّ التَّحَدِّيَ عَلى ذَلِكَ أبْلَغُ، لِأنَّ المَعْنى: اجْتَمِعُوا كُلُّكم وانْظُرُوا هَلْ يَتَيَسَّرُ لَكُمُ الإتْيانُ بِسُورَةٍ مِمَّنْ لَمْ يُمارِسِ الكُتُبَ، ولَمْ يَدْرُسِ العُلُومَ؟! وضَمُّ بَناتِ أفْكارِ بَعْضِهِمْ إلى بَعْضٍ مُعارَضٌ بِهَذِهِ الحُجَّةِ، بَلْ هي أقْوى في الإفْحامِ، إذْ لا يَبْعُدُ أنْ يُعارِضُوهُ بِما يَصْدُرُ عَنْ بَعْضِ عُلَمائِهِمْ، مِمّا اشْتَمَلَ عَلى قِصَصِ الأُمَمِ الخالِيَةِ المَنقُولَةِ مِنَ الكُتُبِ الماضِيَةِ، وإنْ كانَ بَيْنَهُما بَوْنٌ، إذِ الغَرِيقُ يَتَشَبَّثُ بِالحَشِيشِ. وأمّا إذا تَحَدّى بِسُورَةٍ مِن أُمِّيٍّ كَذا وكَذا، لَمْ يَبْقَ لِلْعَوارِضِ مَجالٌ.

هَذا، ولا يَخْفى أنَّهُ صَرْحٌ مُمَرَّدٌ، ونُحاسٌ مُمَوَّهٌ، وظاهِرُ السِّياقِ يُؤَيِّدُ ما قُلْنا، ويُلائِمُهُ ظاهِرًا، كَما سَنُبَيِّنُهُ بِمَنِّهِ تَعالى.

وقَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿وادْعُوا شُهَداءَكم مِن دُونِ اللَّهِ إنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ﴾ [البقرة: 23]: الدُّعاءُ: النِّداءُ والِاسْتِعانَةُ، ولَعَلَّ الثّانِيَ مَجازٌ، أوْ كِنايَةٌ مَبْنِيَّةٌ عَلى النِّداءِ، لِأنَّ الشَّخْصَ إنَّما يُنادى لِيُسْتَعانَ بِهِ، ومِنهُ ﴿أغَيْرَ اللَّهِ تَدْعُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: 40]. والشُّهَداءُ جَمْعُ شَهِيدٍ أوْ شاهِدٍ، والشَّهِيدُ كَما قالَ الرّاغِبُ: كُلُّ مَن يُعْتَدُّ بِحُضُورِهِ مِمَّنْ لَهُ الحَلُّ والعَقْدُ، ولِذا سَمَّوْا غَيْرَهُ مُخَلَّفًا، وجاءَ بِمَعْنى الحاضِرِ، والقائِمِ بِالشَّهادَةِ، والنّاصِرِ، والإمامِ أيْضًا.

ودُونَ ظَرْفُ مَكانٍ، لا يَتَصَرَّفُ، ويُسْتَعْمَلُ بِـ(مِن) كَثِيرًا، وبِالباءِ قَلِيلًا، وخَصَّهُ في البَحْرِ بِـ(مِن) (دُونَها)، ورَفْعُهُ في قَوْلِهِ:
أَلَمْ تَرَيا أنِّي حَمَيْتُ حَقِيقَتِي ∗∗∗ وباشَرْتُ حَدَّ المَوْتِ والمَوْتُ دُونُها
نادِرٌ لا يُقاسُ عَلَيْهِ. ومَعْناها أقْرَبُ مَكانٍ مِنَ الشَّيْءِ، فَهو كَـ(عِنْدَ)، إلّا أنَّها تُنْبِئُ عَنْ دُنُوٍّ كَثِيرٍ، وانْحِطاطٍ يَسِيرٍ. ومِنهُ (دُونَكَ)، اسْمُ فِعْلٍ بِمَعْنى خُذْ، لا (تَدْوِينَ) الكُتُبِ، خِلافًا لِلْبَيْضاوِيِّ كَما قِيلَ، لِأنَّهُ مِنَ الدِّيوانِ، الدَّفْتَرِ ومَحَلِّهِ، وهي فارِسِيٌّ مُعَرَّبٌ مِن قَوْلِ كِسْرى، إذْ رَأى سُرْعَةَ الكُتّابِ في كِتابِهِمْ وحِسابِهِمْ: "دِيوانَهُ". وقَدْ يُقالُ: لا بُعْدَ فِيما ذَكَرَهُ البَيْضاوِيُّ، ودِيوانٌ مِمّا اشْتَرَكَتْ فِيهِ اللُّغَتانِ.

وقَدِ اسْتُعْمِلَ (دُونَ) في انْحِطاطٍ مَحْسُوسٍ، لا في ظَرْفٍ، كَـ(دُونَ زَيْدٍ) في القامَةِ، ثُمَّ اسْتُعِيرَ لِلتَّفاوُتِ في المَراتِبِ المَعْنَوِيَّةِ، تَشْبِيهًا بِالمَراتِبِ الحِسِّيَّةِ، كَـ(دُونَ عَمْرٍو) شَرَفًا. ولِشُيُوعِ ذَلِكَ اتُّسِعَ في هَذا المُسْتَعارِ، فاسْتُعْمِلَ في كُلِّ تَجاوُزِ حَدٍّ إلى حَدٍّ، ولَوْ مِن دُونِ تَفاوُتٍ وانْحِطاطٍ، وهو بِهَذا المَعْنى قَرِيبٌ مِن (غَيْرٍ)، فَكَأنَّهُ أداةُ اسْتِثْناءٍ. ومِنَ الشّائِعِ (دُونٌ) بِمَعْنى خَسِيسٍ، فَيَخْرُجُ عَنِ الظَّرْفِيَّةِ، ويُعَرَّفُ بِـ(أل)، ويُقْطَعُ عَنِ الإضافَةِ، كَما في قَوْلِهِ:
إذا ما عَلا المَرْءُ رامَ العُلا ∗∗∗ ويَقْنَعُ بِالدُّونِ مَن كانَ دُونا

وما في القامُوسِ مِن أنَّهُ يُقالُ: رَجُلٌ مِن دُونٍ، ولا يُقالُ: دُونٌ، مُخالِفٌ لِلدِّرايَةِ والرِّوايَةِ، ولَيْسَ عِنْدِي

وجْهٌ وجِيهٌ في تَوْجِيهِهِ، والمَشْهُورُ أنَّهُ لَيْسَ لِهَذا فُعِلَ، وقِيلَ: يُقالُ: دانَ يَدِينُ مِنهُ. واسْتِعْمالُهُ بِمَعْنى (فَضْلًا) وعَلَيْهِ حُمِلَ قَوْلُ أبِي تَمّامٍ:
الوُدُّ لِلْقُرْبى ولَكِنَّ عُرْفَهُ ∗∗∗ لِلْأبْعَدِ الأوْطانِ دُونَ الأقْرَبِ

Ruh al-Ma'ani: Commentary of al-Alusi on Surah 2, verse 23 (part 3 of 3)

The meticulous grammarians (*arbab al-tanqir*, literally "masters of close scrutiny") have not accepted this. Yes, some said that *wara'aka* means "in front of you," and also "above," and that it has an opposite meaning. *Min* is for the starting point of a limit (*li-ibtida' al-ghaya*) and is connected to *ud'u* ("call upon"). *Dūn* is used in the sense of "beyond" and is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). The meaning is: "Call upon for the counter-challenge whoever is present with you, or whoever will help you according to your claim, going beyond Allah, the Exalted, in the supplication by not calling upon Him." The command is for the purpose of showing your incapacity (*lil-ta'jiz*) and as guidance (*wa'l-irshad*). Or: "Call upon, apart from Allah, whoever can establish for you the testimony that what you have brought is similar to it, for they will not testify. And do not call upon Allah, the Exalted, as a witness, by saying, 'Allah, the Exalted, is a witness and knows that it is like Him,' for that is a sign of incapacity and of being cut off from establishing proof." In that case the command is for rebuke (*lil-tabkit*). The first *shuhada'* (witnesses) means "present," the second means "helpers," and the third means "those who establish testimony."

It was said: It is not permissible that it means "leaders" (*al-imam*), so that the intended witnesses are the false deities, because the command to call upon idols can only be mockery (*tahakkum*). If it were said, "Call upon the idols, and do not call upon Allah, the Exalted, and do not seek support from Him," the command would turn from mockery into a test (*imtihan*), since excluding Allah, the Exalted, from the calling has no place in mockery. In this there is the point that no mockery or ridicule is stronger than being told, "Seek help from the inanimate, and do not turn toward the Lord of the servants." In that case, *dūn* cannot be taken to mean "in front of," since there is no sense in saying, "Call upon them before Allah, the Exalted," that is, on the Day of Resurrection, for the purpose of seeking support from them in the counter-challenge that belongs to this world.

They also permitted *min* to be connected to *shuhada'akum*, and it is also for the starting point. *Dūn* is in the sense of "beyond" and in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier. What governs it is the meaning of the verb derived from the idafa of *shuhada'* (witnesses), namely *ittikhadh* (taking). The meaning is: "Call upon those whom you have taken as allies apart from Allah, the Exalted, and whom you claimed would testify for you on the Day of Resurrection." It is also possible that *dūn* means "in front of" literally, or metaphorically from its real meaning that fits it, namely the nearest place to a thing. It is then an adverbial complement (*zarf laghw*) governed by *shuhada'*, and the trace of the verb suffices for it, so there is no need to rely on something else, nor to supply an implied *li-yashhadu* ("so that they may testify").

*Min* is for partitive meaning (*lil-tab'id*), as they said in "from before him and from behind him" (*min bayni yadayhi wa min khalfihi*), because the act occurs in part of both directions. The apparent sense of the words of al-Damamini in his commentary on *al-Tashil* is that it is superfluous (*za'ida*), and this is the view of Ibn Malik. The majority hold that it is for the starting point. The meaning is: "Call upon those who will testify for you before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, according to your claim." The command is for mockery. In calling the idols "witnesses" there is a *tarshih* (a rhetorical reinforcement) of it, by recalling what they believed: that they have a standing with Allah, the Exalted, and that they will benefit them through their testimony. As if it were said: "These are your support and your refuge, so call upon them for this great calamity that has descended upon you." Thus there is no perfume after the bride, and there is nothing beyond Abadan (a village), that is, nothing further.

*Dūn* was not taken to mean "beyond" because they do not claim that He, the Exalted, shares with the idols in testimony, so there is no basis for exclusion.

It was also said that *min* may be for the starting point and the adverbial complement is a circumstantial qualifier, and a noun is omitted from the speech. The meaning is: "Call upon your witnesses from among the eloquent Arabs, who are the allies of the idols, going beyond in this the allies of Allah, so that they may testify for you that you have brought something like it." The purpose of the command in that case is to give free rein and lure (*irkha' al-'inan wa'l-istidraj*) to the extreme of rebuke, as if it were said: "We have left aside obligating you with the witnesses of truth, and turned to your witnesses known for defending you. For they too will not testify for you, out of fear of blame and disdain for testimony to what is utterly false. How could they, when the matter of inimitability (*i'jaz*) has reached such clarity that there is no way to deny it?"

The exclusion of Allah, the Exalted, in some respects is for emphasizing that the excepted term (*mustathna minhu*) covers everything other than it, not for showing His sole authority to do what they were charged with, lest it give the impression that if they called upon Him, He would answer them. In some respects, it is for explicitly stating from the outset their disavowal of Him, and that their being in the grip of opposition and hostility toward Him, they fall short in seeking support from anything other than Him.

The shift to the third person (*iltifat*) is either to instill awe and cultivate reverence, or to indicate the complete feebleness of their minds, since they preferred over the worship of the One who possesses comprehensive divinity the worship of one more lowly than whom there is none.

*Al-sidq* (truthfulness) is the correspondence of speech to reality, and the views on it are well known.

The response (*jawab*) to *in* is omitted, because the first clause indicates it, and it is not the response to both clauses. Likewise, the object of *al-sidq* (what one is truthful about) is omitted. That is: "If you are truthful in your claim that it is the speech of a human being, or that you are able to counter it, then bring it, and call upon your helpers, for the flood has reached the peaks (*qad balagha al-sayl al-zubba*)." This is like a repetition of the challenge and its reinforcement. For this reason the conjunction was omitted, and the object of the doubt was made what is anterior, because doubt is of the kind of conception in which neither truth nor falsehood applies, and what is not doubtful in its being delayed.

The claim that the intended meaning is "if you are truthful in the possibility that it is such-and-such" is not beneficial, despite its strain, because possibility is also doubt. And among the forced interpretations is the statement of al-Shihab: the intended meaning of the noble construction is progressive escalation in establishing the proof and clarifying the path. The meaning is: "If you are in doubt, then bring something like it so that your doubt may be removed and it becomes clear that you were right in what occurred to your minds. Then, if your claim that it is fabricated is true, bring it out, and do not fear."

This, and the appropriateness of the verse to what we have said about the preceding verse, is that He, glorified and exalted, commanded them to seek help, either literally or mockingly, with everything that aids them with supplies in producing something like it, or with testimony that what was brought is like it. There is no doubt that this fits only if they were commanded to bring something like it, unlike when the one commanded is one of them, for then they are inciting him to bring it. In that case, what fits is attributing the witnesses to him, since they are his witnesses. Though it is valid to attribute them to the ones who are commanded, by considering their participation with him in that claim through incitement and urging. The claim that they share with the one who produced it in the assertion of similarity is nothing, because it is testimony to similarity. Then, preferring that the pronoun refer to the revealed text (*al-munazzal*) requires preferring that the adverbial phrase also be a qualifier of the surah. Many lengthy matters have been raised here, with no benefit in them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 24 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So if you do not, and you will never do, then fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾. This is a summary (fadhlaka) of what preceded it, and therefore it is introduced with the particle fa'. That is, when you have exerted in the striving the utmost effort, and have transgressed every known limit, clinging to the skirts and riding the back of every difficult and easy thing, and you have been unable to produce anything like it, nor anything approaching it in its eloquence and excellence, it becomes clear that it is inimitable (mu'jiz), and belief in it is obligatory. So believe, and fear the Fire. He used the particle in (an), while the context called for idhā (when), to indicate the continuation of the inability. He, glory be to Him and exalted is He, is the Subtle, the All-Aware, mocking them, as one who is confident of victory says to his opponent: "If I defeat you, I will not spare you," and as a rebuke to them for their doubt regarding what is certain and very clear. Thus in the verse there is a mocking metaphor (isti'ara tahakkumiyya tab'iyya harfiyya), or it is a reality and an implicit meaning (haqiqa wa kinaya), like all that comes contrary to the apparent sense. It may be said that He expressed it this way in consideration of the state of the addressees, for the inability existed before reflection, like something doubtful to them because of their reliance on their eloquence. (Tafʿalū) is jussive by lam, and there is no contention (tanazu') between it and in (in), and in (in) is imagined (i.e., not truly). Ibn Hisham stated explicitly that there is no contention between particles, since they have no indication of an event (hadath) until they seek objects of governance; except that Ibn al-ʿIlj permitted it, citing this verse as evidence, and it was answered that in seeks an affirmative, while lam [seeks] a negative, and the condition for contention is unity of meaning.
