So in is here applied to the whole, governing its locus, as if he said: "If you abandon the act," and the sentence then conveys the continuation of the non-occurrence that was realized in the past, and with this their combination becomes permissible; otherwise, between their requirements, futurity and past, there is contradiction. Indeed, it has been said regarding this a difficulty whose solution has not yet been established in a way that heals the sick: namely, that if the locus is for the verb alone, there arises the convergence of two governors in such as: in lam yaqumna (if they do not stand); and if it is for the clause, it is answered that they did not count it among the things that have a locus; or for the locus together with the verb, then there is no parallel to it. Perhaps they pick out a verb from what follows them and jussify it with them, and this, as you see, is not [acceptable]. He, glory be to Him, expressed the specific act in a way other than the apparent: the apparent would be "If you do not bring a sūrah like it," but He used the general and absolute verb, for the sake of brevity of expression (ījāz al-qaṣr). In this is an indication that the intended aim of the obligation is the performance of the very act commanded, to manifest their inability to it, not the attainment of the object, given its impossibility. The pivot of the answer in the conditional, namely the command to guard oneself, is their inability to perform it, not the failure to achieve the intended aim. It has been said: the verb is used in general and what is meant is the bringing [of the sūrah] together with what is connected to it, by the method of mentioning the necessary concomitant and intending the necessitated, because of the mutual implication that justifies the transfer, with the help of contextual indications; or by the method of expressing the apparent nouns by pronouns referring back to them, to avoid repetition. The apparent view is that in what He expressed there is brevity, metonymy, and the suggestion of negating the bringing of the like, and what approaches it, and even beyond, though it is not the intended meaning. (Wa-lan) is, like lā, for negating the future, though it differs from it in being specific to the imperfect and in governing the accusative, except in what is anomalous, namely its jussifying in the verse:

"He who has hoped in you will not be disappointed now, nor will he who knocks at a door other than your gate."

It does not imply perpetual negation, though it conveys emphasis and intensification, nor does it imply that the duration is long or short, contrary to some of them. Its origin is not (lā an), as is reported from al-Khalil: the hamza was dropped for its frequency, the alif was dropped for the two sukūns, and the rule changed so that (lan) governs a complete sentence without (an) and its governed word. It has been said so on the basis of his saying:

"A man hopes for what he will not meet, and calamities intervene before he reaches the nearest of it."

The possibility that (an) is extra weakens the argument. And it is not (lā lā), as in al-Farra's view, for then its alif would have been changed to nūn, since there is no need for that, and it contradicts the original form. The sentence is a parenthetical insertion between the two parts of the conditional, apparently, establishing the content of its protasis and confirming the obligation of acting upon its consequent. This is a striking miracle, in that He reported the specific unseen matter, His knowledge of it, glory be to Him; and the matter came to pass just so. How could it not, since had they opposed it with something approaching it, the transmitters would have transmitted it, owing to the abundance of motives? What Musaylima the Liar brought, at which the bereaved woman would laugh, he did not intend as a counter-challenge, but claimed it as revelation. His saying, glory be to Him: "then guard yourselves," is the answer to the condition, on the basis that the Fire's being a metaphor for the manifestation of its inimitability, which requires belief and faith in it, or [a metaphor] for faith itself. By this, what is imagined is dispelled: that guarding against the Fire is necessary without depending on this condition, so what is the meaning of the conditionality? Also, the condition is a cause or a necessitant of the consequent, and not doing the act is neither a cause of guarding nor a necessitant of it, so how is it made a consequent of it? Some of them estimated an answer for this, and its requirement is a declarative clause, since the imperative is not used as a consequent just as it is not used as a predicate, except by interpretation; al-Zamakhshari does not require this in it, for there is no supposition requiring it. Al-Waqud with a fatha, as read by the majority, is what fire is kindled with; likewise every noun on the pattern fa'ūl is, in the familiar usage, a name for what is done with it, though it may be a verbal noun according to some, and they have reported wulū', qabūl, wuḍū', ṭahūr, wazū', and lughūb. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read (wiqūduhā), and ʿIsā ibn ʿAmr and others read (wuqūduhā) with a ḍamma. If it is a noun for what is kindled with it, like the fatha form, then that is so; and if it is a verbal noun, as is said of all that is on fa'ūl, then its being applied to the fire is for hyperbole, and for figurative usage in it, or in the comparison, or by supposing an omitted genitive first, as "possessor of its fuel," or second, as "burning," and that itself is outside, other than the concept; and that is the realization of the predication. It is related that some of the Arabs make the fatha form a verbal noun and the ḍamma form a noun, so the situation is reversed in what we are concerned with. Al-ḥijāra is like ḥijār, a plural of multitude of ḥajar; the plural of paucity is aḥjār; the plural of faʿal with two fathas on the pattern fiʿāl is anomalous, and Ibn Malik in al-Tashil says it is a collective noun because its pattern is dominant among singulars, and this is the apparent view. What is meant by them, according to what is sound from Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with them, and for such a thing the same ruling applies: stones of sulphur. In them are extreme heat, abundant blazing, swiftness of kindling, and greater adherence to bodies. The preparation of the people of the Fire is that they be fuel, together with foul smell, abundant smoke, and great density, which we seek refuge in Allah from. In this is a magnification of the matter of the Fire and a warning away from what leads to it by what is known in the witnessed world, and if the matter is beyond that, then the world beyond this world, and the vastness of the power of the Almighty, glory be to Him, in which this world is dwarfed. It has been said: what is meant by them are the idols they carved, and He joined them with those people in the Hereafter as an increase in their regret, since there appeared to them the opposite of what they had expected; and there they receive two kinds of punishment, spiritual and physical. This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: "Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell."
صفحة 199

Its interpretation as gold and silver, because both are called stone, as in the Qamus, is other than these two sayings; the more correct of the two, according to the scholars of hadith, is the first, and the second according to al-Zamakhshari, and the words of al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, point to it. The article (al) in it, in every case, is not for generality. Some people of knowledge held that it is for generality, and the meaning would be that the Fire promised to them is fit to burn what is cast into it of these two kinds. He expressed its fitness and readiness by a certain matter, and He mentioned people and stones to magnify the matter of Hell and to alert to the intensity of its fuel, so that this may strike the souls with the greatest effect, and that thereby there may arise from the warning what does not arise otherwise. The intended meaning is not literal, which is contrary to the apparent sense and to what is understood from the verses; it would border on an ill opinion about power. It is not to be supposed from restricting to these two kinds that there is nothing else in the Fire, by the evidence of what is mentioned in other places that jinn and devils are there also. Indeed, my master al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, said: they are its flame, and those are its embers. He, glory be to Him, began with people, because they are the ones who perceive pains, or because they are more kindled than inanimate things, for in them are skins, flesh, and fat; and because in that is greater warning. He made the Fire definite and made the clause a relative clause, and it must be that it is a known story, because the warning in the Surah of Tahrim was revealed first, so they heard it with its description; when this was revealed later, it came as something already known, so it was made definite and its description made a relative clause. That the description is thus, the matter here is light, since the addressees there are the believers, and it is evident that they heard that from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him; yet regarding whether the Surah of Tahrim was revealed first there is a discussion, so reflect. ﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾. This is the beginning of a sentence cut off from what precedes it, though the apparent requirement would be to join it to the preceding relative clause, in care for its matter by making it a principal matter for the purpose of the information, in exaggeration of the warning. Making it a clarifying resumption (isti'nāf bayānī), by estimating "For whom was it prepared?" or "Why was its fuel what it is?" and so on, is not supported by the coordination with "bashir" that follows, given the passive construction; for it is unsuitable as an answer, unless one says that what is conjoined to a resumption need not itself be a resumption, which taste rejects. As for the first, the context does not require it; as for the second, the aim of the relative clause is awe-inspiring terror, so the question "why was the state of the Fire thus?" has no meaning, and the answer does not fulfil it. Making it a circumstantial clause of the Fire, with "qad" implied, and the predicate being part of the relative clause belonging to the qualified noun, not of the pronoun of its fuel because of its being inert, or because of the intervention of a foreign predicate then, is nothing, for it is not good to restrict by this circumstance, unless one says that it is necessarily like the description, so it conveys the meaning that the relative clause conveys; therefore it is said: it is a relative clause after a relative clause, and the multiplicity of relative clauses is like that of descriptions and predicates, with or without a conjunction, as the Imam al-Marzuqi stated, though al-Sa'd did not find it. Or it is conjoined by omission of the particle, as Ibn Malik stated, and he made it a relative clause. (And its fuel is men): either it is an interposed parenthesis for emphasis, or a circumstantial clause of what should not be taken as the basis for interpreting the revelation. The meaning of "prepared" (u'iddat) is "made ready." Abdullah read (i'taddat), from al-ʿatād, in the sense of ʿuddah. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read (aʿaddaha Allah li-l-kafirin). The intended meaning is either their genus, with the addressees included in it by primary inclusion, or they specifically. The apparent noun is placed there in place of their pronoun, to censure them and to ground the ruling in their disbelief. That the preparation is for the disbelievers does not preclude the entry of others into it by way of incidental inclusion, so there is no need to say that the fire of the disobedient is other than the fire of the disbelievers. Then it is evident from the noble verse that the Fire is now created, and Allah the Exalted knows best its location in the vastness of His dominion. The future is used to express its certainty as a past event, as in "the Trumpet was blown," and the preparation is similar in "Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward," as the Mu'tazila say, contrary to the apparent sense. What the people of unveiling (ahl al-kashf) have gone to is that it is created, though it is not complete, and it is now among them a dwelling they have made ready, a burning air with no embers at all; and those in it of the angels of punishment are in mercy, blessed, glorifying Allah, exalted is He, without ceasing. Pains occur in it with the occurrence of the deeds of humans and jinn who enter it, and therefore the punishment of those who enter it alone differs after the reckoning is finished and their entry.
صفحة 200

the people of Paradise, Paradise... from the hollow of the sphere of the fixed stars down to the lowest of the lowest. For all this, it is increased beyond what it is now. This is why Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, used to say when he saw the sea: "O sea, when will you become fire?" He also disliked performing ablution with its water and would say: "Tayammum (dry ablution with earth) is more beloved to me than it." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when the seas are set ablaze﴾, meaning they are kindled. The disbelievers do not remain in it today; rather, they are presented to it, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿morning and evening﴾. There are two fires: a sensory fire, imposed upon the outer body, the sense perception, and the animal nature; and a spiritual fire, which penetrates the hearts, and by it is punished the spirit that governs the physical frame, which was commanded and disobeyed. Opposition, which is the very essence of ignorance, toward the One against whom one has been arrogant, is the greatest punishment. People have extended their discussion on this matter and brought wonderful and marvelous things, but the reality of the matter, in my view, none knows except Allah the Exalted. There is nothing better than submission to what the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, brought. The modality of what is in that otherworldly state cannot be known as it should be by one who has drowned in the seas of worldly attachments. And what harm is there for me if I believe in what has come, of the matters of revelation reported by the Truthful One, which are not impossible in light of what has come, and I entrust the matter to the Creator of the earth and the heavens. I ask Allah the Exalted to make our hearts firm upon His religion.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 25 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And give good news to those who believe and do righteous deeds.﴾ When, earlier, the Exalted mentioned the disbelievers and what their state would become in the Hereafter, and this contained the most forceful warning and admonition, He followed it with the believers. This is in keeping with the divine custom (al-sunnah al-ilahiyyah) of pairing encouragement with warning and promise with threat, because some people are not benefited by fear and are benefited by gentleness, while others are the opposite. So it is as if this verse and what follows are conjoined to the preceding passage as one story is joined to another. The connection between them lies in the fact that it is an explanation of the state of the two contrasting groups and an unveiling of the two opposing attributes. Is it conjoined to "And if you are in doubt" up to "prepared" (uʿiddat), or to "But if you do not do it" (fa-in lam tafʿalu) and what follows? There are two opinions. Al-Sayyid (al-Sharif al-Jurjani) chose the first, and some claimed that it is more fitting to the requirements of eloquence (balaghah) and more suitable to the coherence of the structure, because "O mankind, worship" is a general address that includes both groups, while "And if you are in doubt" and so on is specific to the opponent, and its content is warning, while "And give good news" and so on is specific to the one who agrees, and its content is good news. It is as if the Exalted revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ) that he should call people to worship Him, then he was commanded to warn those who opposed, and to give good news to those who affirmed. Al-Sa'd (al-Taftazani) chose the second, because the discourse is for explaining the state of the disbelievers and describing their punishment. It was also said that it is conjoined to "So fear" (fa-ittaqu), and the difference of the addressees does no harm, like "Joseph, turn away from this and seek forgiveness, [O wife]" (Yusuf aʿrid ʿan hadha wa-istaghfiri). Its being consequent upon the condition by virtue of the conjunction is because "fear" is a warning and admonition to the disbelievers, and "give good news" is good tidings to the believers. Each of them is consequent upon the absence of a challenge (muʿaraḍah) by the absence of a challenge (tahaddi), because the absence of a challenge entails the manifestation of its miraculous nature (iʿjaz), and that entails that its denier deserves punishment and its affirmer deserves reward, since the proof has been established and the call has been completed. Their deserving of these two entails the warning and the good news, so the consequence of the second clause upon the condition is like the consequence of the first upon it, and there is no difference. It may also be said that the answer of the condition, "then believe" (fa-amanu), is omitted, and what is mentioned stands in its place. The meaning is: if you do not do such, then believe, and give good news to those who believe, that is, let there be belief from them and good news from you. The apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun, and in this there is an incitement for them to believe, and this is perhaps less burdensome. The author of al-Idah (al-Khatib al-Qazwini) chose to conjoin it to "warn" (andhir), taken as implied after the clause "prepared." It was also said that it is conjoined to "say" (qul) before "But if you do not do it," and its estimate: before "O mankind" requires supplying "from what We have sent down upon Our servant" according to the manner of the speech of the great, or the estimate: "Allah said" after "say." "Bishārah" (good news), with a kasra or a damma, is a noun from "bashara, bashran wa-bushuran," and the bāʾ may be opened so that it means beauty (al-jamal). For the verb there are two forms: the doubled form (tashdid), which is the higher one, and the lightened form (takhfif), which is the dialect of the people of Tihamah. Both have been read in the imperfect in several places. The intensification in the doubled form is relative to the object, since the verb in it makes one thing do what was done by another. They explained it, in the well-known view, and it was deemed correct, as "news that delights, of which the informant has no knowledge." Some stipulated that it must be true. From Sibawayh it is: it is a report that affects the skin (bashrah) with sorrow or joy. Its use is frequent for good, and this was affirmed by al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit). "And give them news of a painful punishment" is evident for this, and it is of the category of irony (tahakkum) according to the first. The one commanded to give good news is the bearer of good news and the warner (ﷺ). It was also said: every one who is able to do that, as in his (ﷺ) saying: "Give good news to those who walk to the mosques in darkness..." (the hadith), wherein there is an allusion that the matter, because of its greatness, is worthy that every one who is able to do it should undertake giving good news of it. There would be a metaphor (majaz) if the pronoun were set for a particular by a universal setting, and otherwise the discussion of the literal and the metaphorical has its place. The believers were not addressed as the disbelievers were addressed, in order to magnify their status and as a complete announcement that they deserve to be given good news and congratulated for what has been prepared for them. It was also said: it is a change of style to imagine the complete contrast between the state of the two groups. In my view: when the Exalted clothed His Messenger (ﷺ) in the robe of His servanthood in His saying "from what We have sent down upon Our servant," it was fitting that He embroider it with the embroidery of obligation (taklif) with what increases the love of His beloved for Him, so that they increase in faith upon their faith. In that there is a kindness to him (ﷺ) and to them that is not hidden.

And Zayd ibn ʿAli read "wa-bushshira" (passive), and it is conjoined to "prepared," as is well known. It was also said that it is a report with the meaning of a command, so the two readings agree in meaning and conjunction. The linking of the good news to a relative clause (al-mawsul) indicates that it is caused by what is in the scope of the relative clause, namely faith and righteous deed, but not for their own sake; rather by the legislator's appointment and the requirement of His promise. He made the relative clause a verb indicating occurrence (huduth) after the mention of the disbelievers, in the form of the active participle, to urge the addressees, through the taking of heed, to bring about faith, and to warn them against persisting in disbelief. Then it is not hidden that the fact that the ground of the good news is the combination of the two matters does not require the absence of the good news when one of them is absent. So it does not follow from this that one who has bare faith will not enter Paradise, as is the view of the Mu'tazilah. Moreover, the implication by opposition (mafhum al-mukhalafah) is speculative and does not oppose the texts showing that Paradise is the reward of bare faith. The object of "believed" (amanu) is well known. Some estimated it here as: "that it is sent down from Allah, mighty and majestic." "Al-ṣāliḥāt" is the plural of "ṣāliḥah," which is in origin the feminine of "al-ṣāliḥ," the active participle from "ṣalaha, ṣulūḥan wa-ṣalāḥan," the opposite of "fasadat" (it became corrupt). Then it came to dominate over what the Law has sanctioned and made good. It is treated like the non-derived nouns in not taking agreement with the noun it modifies and otherwise. Its feminine form is according to the estimate of "the quality" (al-khallah), and because of the dominance of its use it was left in this form, and the tāʾ was not made a sign of transfer (naql), since it has not become a noun. The alif-lam in it is for the genus (al-jins), but not in regard to its realization in the individuals, since that is not within the capacity of the one under obligation. If distribution (al-tawzi') were intended, it would require that one deed suffice. Rather, the genuine meaning of the genus together with plurality, which is three or two, is intended, and what restricts it is the state of the believer. So what he is able to do of righteous deeds after the fulfilment of its conditions is what is meant. A believer who has done no deed at all, or has done only one deed, is not included in the verse. Knowing that he is a bearer of good news comes from other places. Some have made in it a trace of distribution, namely that he does every righteous deed that is obligatory, whether little or much, and one who embraced Islam and died before anything became obligatory upon him is included, or one for whom only one thing became obligatory. This is not distribution in the well-known sense, as in "the people rode their animals," since it may also be used for the matching of things with things, each taking what belongs to it: whether one with one, like the example, or a group with a group, as in "the men entered the mosques of their quarters," or the reverse, as in "the people wore their garments." From it is "and wash your faces and your hands." Al-Sayyid calls this a trace of distribution.

"That for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow" (anna lahum jannatin tajri min tahtiha al-anhar). The Exalted intended "that for them" and so on, because the good news is transitive with the bāʾ, so it was deleted, since the deletion of the preposition before "anna" is common, and "anna" without a substitute because of the length of the two by the relative clause. With other particles there is a well-known disagreement. As for the position after the deletion, there are two opinions: the accusative by removing the preposition, as is well known in such cases, and the genitive, because the preposition may leave its trace after deletion. The lām of the genitive indicates entitlement, and its manner is derived from outside, and there is no entitlement by essence. So it is by the requirement of the Legislator's promise, which He does not break, out of bounty and generosity, but on condition of dying in faith. "Jannah" in origin is the single noun from "jann" (with a fatha), the verbal noun of "janna-hu" when he covered it, and the root's basis is covering. Then it was named for the orchard whose trees cover its ground, or for every land in which there is trees and palms. If it is a vineyard, it is "firdaws." It is applied to the trees themselves, and it appears in the poetry of al-Aʿsha with the meaning of palm trees specifically. Then it was transferred and became a religious technical term (haqiqah shar'iyyah) for the abode of reward, since in it is of bliss what is hidden from us now. It is in the plural of paucity (jamʿ qillah) in the well-known view, because its number is few, like the paucity of the kinds of acts of worship. But in each of them there are various levels and differing degrees according to the differences of deeds and doers. What is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that they are seven, is not established by the transmitters of hadith. Its tanwin is either for classification (al-tanwin li-l-tanwiʿ) or for magnification (al-tanwin li-l-taʿzim). The fronting of the predicate is because of the nearness of the referent of the pronoun, and it is a secret for the hearer. The common practice is fronting when the subject is indefinite, as in "Indeed for us there is a reward" (inna lana la-ajran). "Taḥta" is an adverb of place, not used except with "min," as Abu al-Hasan (al-Akhfash) stated. The pronoun refers to the gardens. If the trees are meant, then that is with what is in it close in general. If the land is meant, it is said: "from beneath its trees," or it refers back to it by considering the trees, as a figure of speech (istikhdam) and the like. It was also said that "taḥta" means beside, like "my house is beneath the house of so-and-so." This was deemed weak, like the saying "from beneath the orders of its people." It was also said: "its dwellings." If the whole of the land and the trees is meant, then the consideration of being beneath is according to the apparent part that makes it correct to apply the name "Paradise" to the whole. What is transmitted in the sound report from Masruq is that the rivers of Paradise flow without a trench, and this is in a land whose pebbles are pearls and rubies, which is more eloquent in delight, more sweet in appearance, and more gladdening to the soul.

"The clear water spoke with the pebbles, so the breeze passed over it, hearing what passed."

"Al-anhar" is the plural of "nahr," with a fatha or a sukun on the hāʾ, and the fatha is more eloquent. Its root is splitting, and the root denotes spaciousness, even if spiritual, like the "nahr" of the questioner, on the basis that it is a powerful rebuke. It is applied to what is less than the sea and more than a stream. Is it the very channel of the water, or the water in the wide channel? Two opinions: the more famous is the first, and on it the meaning is its waters, or its water. The feminine of "tajri" is for the sake of the genitive noun that it is attached to, or for the form of the plural. In the speech there is a metaphor in the omission, or in the vessel (zarf). The attribution is metaphorical. The alif-lam is for the mental known (al-ʿahd al-dhihni). It was said: or for the external known, because the rivers were previously mentioned in His saying: "In them are rivers of water" and so on, for it is Meccan according to the soundest view, and some say it is Medinan, revealed after it. Al-Sayyid and al-Sa'd found this unlikely. It was also said: it is a substitute for the genitive noun, that is, its rivers. This is a Kufan view. Taking it as universal in meaning: all the rivers of Paradise flow beneath the trees, so it is a description of the abode of reward, that its trees are on the banks of the rivers, and its rivers beneath the shade of the trees are cooler than snow. The discussion of the paucity plural is not hidden.

**[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 25 (part 2 of 3)]**

﴿Whenever they are provided with fruit from it, they say, "This is what we were provided with before."﴾ This is a second attribute of *jannat* (gardens), placed after the first because the flowing of rivers beneath them describes the gardens in themselves, whereas this describes their inhabitants. Alternatively, it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are," and the indication of this omitted subject is its mention in the preceding and following clauses, and the fact that the speech is directed toward describing the condition of the believers. The purpose of omitting this subject is to achieve harmony among the three clauses, both in form, since they are all nominal sentences, and in meaning, since they are answers to a question, as if it were said: "What is their condition in those gardens?" and the answer was given: "For them therein are delicious, wondrous fruits, pure spouses, and they abide therein eternally." Estimating the subject as *huwa* (he) or *hiya* (she) as a pronoun referring to the matter or the account is not valid, on the basis that this pronoun cannot be omitted, and when it is not preceded by abrogating particles (*nawasikh*), its explanation must be a nominal sentence. Yes, it is permissible to estimate *hiya* as referring to the gardens, with the clause being a predicate, but harmony is more fitting. Or it is an independent resumptive clause (*jumla mustanafa'a*), as if, when describing the gardens with what was mentioned, it occurred to the mind that their fruits were like the fruits of the gardens of this world, so it clarified their condition. ﴿And for them therein are spouses﴾ is an addition to the answer. If the question were estimated as "Do they have in the gardens pleasures as in this abode? Or are they more complete and greater?", it would be more correct and clearer.

[Page 203]

Abu al-Baqa' permitted that this clause be a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of *alladhina* (those who), or of *jannat*, as a description of it. In that case it is a presumed circumstance (*hal muqaddara*), and the basic meaning of such a circumstance is accompaniment. The claim that it is a detached attribute (*sifa maqta'a*) is an assertion joined with ignorance, given the condition for detachment, which is that the listener knows that the described thing has that attribute; otherwise the attribute would be needed, and there is no detachment where there is need. (*Wa-kullama*) is put in the accusative as an adverb of time with *qalu* (they say). (*Rizqan*) is a second object of *ruziqu* (they were provided), as in *razaqahu malan* (he gave him wealth), meaning he gave him. It is not an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) emphasizing its verb, because *al-marzuq* (the thing provided) is more definite in meaning, and establishing a new meaning is better than emphasis, especially since the apparent sense of what follows requires it. Its indefiniteness is for classification (*tanwi'*) or for magnification, meaning a delicious kind different from what you know. (*Min*) in the first and second instances is for origin (*ibtida'*). What is intended by both is merely that the noun governed by them is a place from which the thing is separated. For this reason, it is not good to use *ila* (to) in opposition to them. Both are adverbial phrases that are stable and function as circumstances by interpenetration (*tadakhul*). The referent of the first is *rizqan*, and the referent of the second is its pronoun in the circumstance. The meaning is: at every time they are provided with a provision originating from the gardens, originating from its fruit. The more common view is that both are superfluous (*laghw*). The provision has originated from the gardens, and the provision from the gardens has originated from a fruit. This is treated as if you were to say: "So-and-so gave me," and it is asked: "From where?" and you say: "From his orchard," and it is asked: "From which fruit?" and you say: "From the pomegranates." Its precise explanation is that *ruziqu* was made absolute as originating from the gardens, then it was made restricted by origin from that, as originating from a fruit. On both opinions, there is no objection that they forbade the attachment of two prepositions of the same form and meaning to a single governing word, while the verse contradicts this. As for the first opinion, it is obvious. As for the second, that is because in that case they are both attached to it from one direction, originating without subordination, whereas what we are discussing is not like that, due to the distinction between absolute and restricted. According to this, the intended meaning of "fruit" is the kind, such as apples and pomegranates, not the individual, because the origin of the provision from the orchard from a single individual requires that the one provided be a piece of it, not all of it, and this is extremely weak. It is possible that the second is an explanation of the one provided, and the first adverbial phrase is superfluous, while the second is stable. This is contrary to those who erred in this matter. It occurred as a circumstance of the indefinite noun because it precedes it, and because of the implicit precedence of the latter, it is permissible to place the specified before the unspecified. *Thamara* (fruit) may be taken to mean a kind, or a single cluster. The verifiers did not turn to making the second *min* partitive in the position of the object. *Rizqan* is an emphatic infinitive, or in the position of a circumstance from *rizqan*, because it is far-fetched, even though the basic meaning is explanation and origin, and one does not deviate from them except for a reason. Moreover, the implication of the partitive *min* is that what precedes it or what follows it is a part of its governed noun, not a partial thing, so there would be weakness here. God, glory be to Him, combined *minha* (from it) and *min thamara* (from a fruit), and He did not say *min thamarihā* (from its fruit) instead, because the attachment of *minha* indicates that its inhabitants have no need of anything else, since in it is everything the souls desire. The attachment of *min thamara* indicates that the purpose is to explain the food in a manner that includes all fruits, apart from the rest of the pleasures known from the preceding and following context. This points to the kind of what they were provided with, and the perception of its individual instances suffices. This is like your saying, pointing to a flowing river: "This water does not cease," or pointing to a person himself. The reporting about it with *alladhi* (the one which), etc., is according to making it the thing itself, as an exaggeration, or estimating: "like the one we were provided with before," meaning in this world. The wisdom in the resemblance is that the soul inclines toward what is pleasant and seeks more of it.

*Ad'u dhikra Nu'manin lana, inna dhikrahu ∗∗∗ huwa al-miski ma karraratahu yatadaw'a*
"Repeat for us the mention of Nu'man, for his mention is musk, whenever you repeat it, it spreads its fragrance."

This varies according to circumstances and situations, or it is to clarify the doubt and the essence of the blessing in what they were provided with there, for had it been a kind not known, one would think it could not be other than this. Or it refers to the garden itself. The resemblance in appearance is either together with difference in taste, as is related from al-Hasan: "Indeed, one of them is brought a dish, and he eats from it, then another is brought to him and he sees it like the first, and says: 'This?' and the angel says: 'Eat.' The color is one, and the taste differs." Or resemblance in taste as well, as the saying of the Prophet, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, indicates: "By Him in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, indeed a man of the people of the Garden reaches for fruit to eat it, but before it reaches his mouth, God, exalted is He, replaces it with another like it." So perhaps when they see it in the first form, they say that. What prompts them to say this is their extreme astonishment and their boasting at the great difference they find.

[Page 204]

It is well known that the intended meaning of "before" is in this world, which is preferable to what is presented in the Hereafter, because *kullama* (whenever) indicates generality, and it is not conceivable that they would say that at the first time it was presented to them. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "before" is in the Hereafter, which is preferable, lest it follow that the fruits of the Garden are restricted to the kinds that exist in this world, while in it there is what you know and what you do not know. Moreover, this fulfills the meaning of the hadith on the resemblance of the fruits of the Garden, and its agreement with what resembles it. Furthermore, it is clearer in the provision of the Garden. Returning the pronoun to the provided thing in both abodes is a strain. You will hear it, by His favor, exalted is He. There is another interpretation of the verse that the heart inclines to: that what they were provided with before is the acts of obedience and the knowledge that people of natural disposition and sound intellects find delightful. This is a recompense resembling them in what has been mentioned of pleasure, like the recompense that is in its opposite in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Taste what you used to do﴾, meaning its recompense. Thus "what We provided" is a figurative metonymy (*majaz mursal*) for its recompense, by using the name of the effect for the cause. It does not harm this view that the Garden and what is in it of various honors is a recompense, as is not hidden. Or it is a metaphor (*isti'ara*), by likening the fruits and produce to acts of obedience and knowledge in what has been mentioned. It has also been said: The ground of the Garden is plains in which the deeds of this world appear, as some reports indicate. So the fruit of bliss is what they planted in this world. So reflect.

﴿And they are given it in resemblance﴾ is a concluding statement to the preceding speech, and an emphasis of it by what includes its meaning. It has no place in grammatical analysis. It may be an independent clause or a circumstantial clause by estimating *qad* (indeed), which is common. The agent is omitted because it is known, and it is apparently the servants and the youths, as indicated by the reading of Harun and al-Ataki: *wa-atu* (and they gave) with the agent expressed. In it there is an implied subject, indicated by the meaning. This has been made explicit in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there will circulate among them youths made eternal﴾ up to His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿and fruit of what they choose﴾. The pronoun in the genitive is either, by estimating that it is meant "from before in this world," referring to the single concept included by the two expressions. This is "what we were provided with before," which is the one provided in both abodes. That is, "they were given the one provided in both abodes, resembling one another in part." This method is called allusive metonymy (*kinaya ima'iyya*). If it referred to the spoken word, it would have said *bihima* (both of them). It expressed what is partly past and partly future in the past tense for the certainty of its occurrence. In *al-Kashshaf* (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari): what is intended by the provided thing in this world and the Hereafter is the kind suitable for consumption in each of them, not what is restricted to them. Or by estimating that it is meant "in the Garden," it refers to the provision, meaning: they were given the provided thing in the Garden, resembling in its individual instances. Abu Hayyan said: The apparent meaning is this, because their provided thing in the Hereafter is what is spoken about, and what is compared to "that which they were provided with before." Also, this sentence has come only to speak about the Garden and its conditions, and that the speaker reports about the provided thing in this world and the Hereafter that it is resembling is not part of the discourse about the Garden, except with strain. Against the claim of resemblance, what is in both abodes does not interfere, which al-Bayhaqi and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "There is nothing in the Garden of the foods of this world except the names." This is because it is not required that it be from all aspects. The resemblance exists in the form which is the basis of the name, even if it is not in quantity or taste. Its precise explanation is that applying the names to them, because they are by way of metaphor, requires sharing in what is their basis, which is the form. By this, the resemblance between them is realized. So what is excepted in the report is the names, and what is their basis is known by rational indication.

﴿And for them therein are purified spouses, and they abide therein eternally﴾ is a third attribute and a fourth attribute of the gardens. The first two were expressed by a verbal sentence to indicate renewal, and these two by a nominal sentence to indicate permanence. The conjunction was omitted in some and expressed in others. It has been said that this is to alert to the permissibility of both in attributes, and each has been specified with what is specific to it for a reason that is not hidden. Abu al-Baqa' went to the view that these two clauses are independent, and he permitted that the second be a circumstance of the plural pronoun in *lahum* (for them), with the governing element being the sense of stability. *Azwaj* (spouses) is the plural of paucity, and the plural of abundance is *zawjah*, like *awd* and *iwada*, and its use is not frequent in speech. It has been said: For this reason the plural of paucity was used instead, as an extension. Reports indicate the abundance of spouses in the Garden, of the *hur* and others. It is said: *zawj* is used for the male and the female, and it may refer to one of a pair or to both together. For the female it is said *zawjah* in the dialect of Tamim and many of Qays. What is intended here by *azwaj* is the women who belong exclusively to the man, with no one else sharing them. The concept does not include consideration of procreation, which is the basis of the continuation of

The Tafsir of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani), commentary on Surah 2, verse 25 (part 3 of 3):

...of the kind, so that the term "offspring" (nawʿ) cannot properly be applied to the spouses of Paradise, since they abide there forever and have no need of children. Yet some scholars have affirmed that procreation takes place in Paradise and have related reports to that effect, but in a manner befitting that station. Some also mentioned that the children (of Paradise) are spiritual beings. And God is capable of whatever He wills.

The meaning of their being "purified" (muṭahharah) is that God, glory be to Him, has exempted them from everything that would defile them. If they are of the *ḥūr* (the wide-eyed maidens of Paradise), as was related from ʿAbd Allah, then the meaning of being purified is that He created them in a state of purity, so that no inherent or external impurity clings to them. If they are of the daughters of Adam, as was related from al-Ḥasan: "They are among your old women, bleary-eyed and rheumy-eyed, who will become young women," then the intended meaning is the removal from them of every blemish, both inherent defects and others.

Purification (al-taṭhīr), as al-Rāghib (al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī) said, is applied to bodies, morals and actions alike. Thus it is general here by the indication of the context of praise, not absolute and restricted to the perfect sense. The perfection of purification is achieved only through both kinds, as has been said. For the customary usage of desiring perfection is the desire of its highest instances, not all of them.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī read *muṭahharāt* (purified, plural feminine) based on *ṭuhhirna* (they were purified), not *taharat* (she was purified), as in the first reading. Perhaps the former is more preferred in usage, although all of them are eloquent, because they said: the plural of non-rational things is either a plural of paucity (*jamʿ qillah*) or a plural of abundance (*jamʿ kathrah*). If it is a plural of abundance, then the pronoun coming in the manner of the feminine singular pronoun is preferable to its coming in the manner of the feminine plural pronoun. If it is a plural of paucity, then the reverse applies. Likewise, when the pronoun refers back to a plural of rational feminine beings, the form with *nūn* is preferred over the form with *tāʾ*, as in ﴿when they have reached their term﴾ and ﴿let mothers nurse their children﴾. They made no distinction in this between the plural of paucity and the plural of abundance.

The coming of this attribute in the passive form, and *ṭāhirah* not coming as a participle from *ṭahura* (with a fatḥah, the more eloquent form) or *ṭahura* (with a ḍammah), and of the first there is analogy, while of the second it is anomalous, is for magnification, because it conveys that she has one who purified her, and that is none other than God, Exalted is He. And how could describers describe one whom the Lord, glory be to Him, has purified!

Ubayd ibn ʿUmayr read *muṭṭahhirah* (the feminine singular), whose original form is *mutaṭahhirah*, and it was assimilated (idghām).

When God, glory be to Him and Exalted is He, mentioned the dwelling of the believers, their food, and their spouses, and these delights do not reach the degree of perfection while fear of their ending persists, for this reason it was said:

*The greatest grief for me amid joy*
*is when its possessor is certain of departing from it.*

Therefore He followed this with what removes whatever would spoil His bounty, namely the mention of abiding forever in the abode of honour. Abiding (*khulūd*), according to the Muʿtazila (the Muʿtazila), is lasting permanence that never ends. According to us, it is a long duration, whether it ends or does not end. Its use for lasting stay is because it is a long stay, not because of its specific meaning in the literal sense, and this is what is intended here. The verses and the sunnah bear witness to it. The Jahmiyya (Jahmiyya) claim that Paradise and its people will perish, and likewise the Fire and its inhabitants. What led them to this is that He, exalted is He, described Himself as "the First and the Last." Priority (*al-awwaliyyah*) is His precedence over all created things, and posteriority (*al-ākhiriyyah*) is His being after them. This cannot be except with the annihilation of all else. Were Paradise and its people to remain, that would involve likening Him to one who has no likeness, glory be to Him, and that is impossible. Also, if He did not know the breaths of the people of Paradise, He would be ignorant, exalted above that, and if He knew them, it would entail a termination, and termination is after all annihilation.

For us are the texts that indicate perpetuity, and reason agrees with them, because it is an abode of peace and holiness, without fear or sorrow. A person does not find pleasure in a life whose ending he fears. Indeed, it has been said: "Misery is better than a passing bliss." Disbelief is a pure transgression, so its recompense is a pure punishment that is not mixed with any deficiency.

The meaning of "the First and the Last" is not as it is in what is witnessed. Rather, it means that He has no beginning and no end in His essence, without depending on anything else. He is the Necessarily Existent, the Eternal, whose non-existence is impossible. Created beings are not like this, so where is the resemblance? Knowledge is not finite, so it relates to what is not finite. The breaths of the people of Paradise are nothing but like the orders of numbers! Shall it be said that God, glory be to Him, does not know them, or that they are finite? Woe to the Jahmiyya, how ignorant they are! And more ignorant than them is one who said that bodies are composed of contrary parts in their qualities, exposed to changes that lead to dissolution and disintegration, so how can perpetuity be possible? This is because the basis of this argument is the analogy of that mode of existence to this mode of existence. How far, how far! How can that perfect world be measured by the world of generation and corruption!

Furthermore, once it is established that He is capable and chooses, and that there is no agent in existence except Him, why should it not be permissible for Him to restore bodies in such a way that they do not dissolve, or if they dissolve, why should it not be permissible for Him to create, in place of what has dissolved, something that lasts forever? Glory be to the Capable, the Wise, whom nothing can overpower.

[Page 207]

Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, even of a gnat﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: It was revealed concerning the Jews, when Allah, exalted is He, cited examples in His Book using the spider, the fly, and other things that are regarded as insignificant. They said: Allah, exalted is He, is too mighty and too great to cite examples using such trivial things. So Allah, exalted is He, refuted them with this verse. The connection of this verse with what precedes it, on this view, is that it would have been more suitable for it to be placed in Surah al-'Ankabut (The Spider) as an example. It is a reply to a doubt raised against establishing the proof for the truth of the Qur'an, that it is inimitable. Hence it belongs to the kind of doubt that is on the verge of collapse, so mentioning it here is more fitting.

Mujahid and others said: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites, who said, when Allah, glorified is He, cited the parable of the one who kindles a fire and the parable of the rain-cloud: Allah, exalted is He, is too high and too great to cite examples using such things that have no worth. So Allah, exalted is He, refuted them. The connection on this view is clear, since this verse defends the preceding illustrations in the best and most eloquent manner.

It has also been said that it is connected to the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿So do not set up rivals to Allah﴾, meaning: ﴿He is not ashamed to present an example﴾ for these rivals.

It has also been said: This is an example cited for this world and its people, for the gnat lives as long as it is hungry, and when it is satisfied it dies. Likewise the people of this world: when they are sated with it, they perish. Or it is an example for the deeds of servants, and there is nothing to prevent Him from mentioning of them what is small or great, in order to reward or punish for it. On these two views there is no connection between the verse and what precedes it; rather it is the beginning of a new statement. Although this is permissible, I do not hold to it, since the appropriate approach for every verse is that it be connected to what precedes it.

In the verse there is an indication of the excellence of illustration: how could Allah, glorified is He, with His greatness and the perfection of His wisdom, leave it aside, or feel shame before it? The examples have never ceased to circulate among people.

Shame (al-haya'), as al-Raghib said, is the withdrawal of the soul from ugly things, and it is composed of cowardice and chastity. It is not embarrassment (al-khajal); rather, that is the bewilderment of the soul due to the intensity of shame. The two are distinct, though they are mutually implicative. Some have said: embarrassment occurs only after the occurrence of an additional matter that the one doing it did not intend, unlike shame, which may concern something that has not yet happened, so one abstains from it on its account. What is in the Qamus, that khajila means istahya (felt shame) and tasamaha (was lenient), is derived from life (hayah), because it affects the faculty specific to animals, namely the faculty of sensation and movement. The verse indicates the correctness of attributing shame to Him, exalted is He, because in ordinary usage shame is negated only from one who is characterized by it. Moreover, the negation enters upon a statement that contains a restriction, so the negation returns to the restriction, and thus it establishes the occurrence of the act itself, or its possibility, and no less than that. As for the hadiths, they explicitly state the attribution. People have two positions on this. Some hold to interpretation (ta'wil), since the withdrawal of the soul is something that does not hover around the precincts of His holiness, glorified is He. Thus what is meant by shame with regard to Him is the consequence that necessarily follows from withdrawal. It has also been permitted to make the particle (ma) here specifically an element of opposition to what was said by the disbelievers, based on what has been reported: that they said: "The Lord of Muhammad is not ashamed to present examples of the fly and the spider." And some, and I, praise be to Allah, am among them, do not hold to interpretation; rather, they let this and similar matters that have come from Him, glorified is He, in the verses and the hadiths, pass as they came, and after affirming His transcendence above what is found in the created world, they entrust their knowledge to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed.

The majority read (yastahyi) with two yas (ya'), and the past tense is (istahya). The form istaf'ala is used here to dispense with the bare triliteral, as in (ista'thara). Ibn Kathir, in one transmission, and some others read it with one ya', and this is the dialect of the Banu Tamim. There is a disagreement over whether the omitted letter is the lam, in which case the pattern is (yastaf'u), or the 'ayn, in which case the pattern is (yastafilu). The second is the more famous of the two views. This verb may be transitive by itself, or with a preposition, so one says (istahyaytuhu) and (istahyaytu minhu), and the verse admits of both.

Striking (ad-darb) is the placing of one thing upon another. The striking of an example is like the striking of coins, and it is the mention of something whose effect appears in something else. So the meaning of (yadrib) here is (yadhkuru), "mentions." It has been said: (yubayyin), "explains," and it has been said: (yada'), "sets forth," as in ﴿humiliation was stamped upon them﴾.

(Ma) is a noun meaning "a thing," and it is used as a qualifier for an indefinite noun to add greater vagueness and to block the ways of restriction. It may also indicate belittlement, as in "give him something or other," and magnification, as in "the matter is what it is; a short-nosed one has been cut," and variety, as in "strike him a certain kind of blow." It may also be considered like the sword of an orator. The Qur'an is too exalted for anything in it to be wasted.

(Ba'udah), either is a qualifier of (ma), or a substitute for it, or an explicative apposition, if it is said that this is permissible with indefinites. Or it is a substitute for (mathalan), or an explicative apposition for it, if it is said that (ma) is superfluous, or it is an object. And (mathalan) is a circumstantial accusative, and it is the intended element. Or it is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, meaning: "from a gnat and what is above it," as was transmitted from al-Farra'. The (fa) here means (ila), "up to." Or it is a second object, or a first object, based on the view that striking includes the meaning of making.

It is not an objection to the intended generality that the meaning of the example, according to the well-known view, is that Allah does not leave any example whatsoever, which implies that all examples are struck in His speech; so where are they? This is because the negated thing is not absolute abandonment, but abandonment for the sake of shame, so the meaning is: He does not leave any example out of shame, even if He leaves it for some other matter He intends.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah and a group read (ba'udatun) with the nominative. The common view is that it is the predicate, but they disagreed about what it is the predicate of. It was said: it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is a gnat" or "he is a gnat." The clause is then the relative clause of (ma), on the assumption that it is a relative pronoun. This is a Kufan analysis, by which the beginning of the relative clause is omitted without a long interval. It was also said: (ma) is an interrogative and is the subject. Abu Hayyan in al-Bahr preferred that (ma) be a relative clause or a qualifier, and that (wa-hiya ba'udatun) be a sentence, like an explanation of what the statement contains. It was also said: (ba'udatun) is the subject, (ma) is a negation particle, and the predicate is omitted, meaning "left," as indicated by ﴿He is not ashamed﴾.

The gnat is the singular of the gnats (ba'uud), and it is a well-known flying insect. In it there is such fine craftsmanship and wondrous originality that a human being is unable to encompass its description, and none denies this except Nimrud. Originally it is an adjective of the form (fa'ul), like (qatuu'), and for this reason it was called (khamush) in the dialect of Hudhayl, and then the name became fixed. Its derivation is from (al-ba'd), meaning "cutting."

﴿And what is above it﴾: the (fa) is a conjunction indicating sequence. (Ma) is coordinated with (ba'udah), or (ma) is the noun, if it is treated as a noun. The detail in it is not hidden. The "above" may mean either an increase in the size of the thing used as the example, and then it is an ascent from the small to the large, and Ibn 'Abbas held this view; or an increase in the quality in which the illustration occurs, which is smallness and insignificance, and then it is a descent from the insignificant to the more insignificant. These two views are given for the well-known reading. As for the reading with the nominative, they said: if (ma) is taken as a relative pronoun, both views apply; if it is taken as an interrogative, the first view is required, because the greatness is then the subject, beginning from the gnat.

It has also been said: He meant "what is above it and what is below it," and He was satisfied with one of the two items in place of the other, as in the verse ﴿garments that protect you from the heat﴾. Understand this.

[Page 208]

﴿As for those who believe, they know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾. This is a detailed explanation of what is indicated by the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed﴾, etc., namely that there is in it doubt, between verification and skepticism. Or it is in response to what results from striking the example, of ruling, after the verification that its issuance from Him, glorified is He, is true. The (fa) indicates that what follows it is a consequence of what its predecessor points to, and it is as though it were said: "As it has been said, so He strikes it." Then: ﴿As for those who believe﴾, etc. The mention of the state of the believers is placed first because of its nobility. As for "amma," according to the view of the verifiers, it is a particle that includes the meaning of a condition, and for this reason the (fa) is generally required after it. It also indicates, along with this, the emphasis of what it enters upon of the ruling, and it serves as a detailed explanation of a general statement that preceded it, either explicitly or by implication, or that did not precede it but is present in the mind, even if only by estimation. Since this is contrary to the apparent meaning in many of its uses, al-Radi and al-Murtada, among the verifiers, made it mostly a matter of general tendency. Sibawayh explained "amma zaydun fa-dhahibun" as: "Whatever may be the case, Zayd is going." This does not mean that it is a synonym of that noun and verb, since it has no equivalent. Rather, the meaning is that, since it conveys emphasis and the inevitability of occurrence in the future, the outcome of the meaning becomes that. Since it implies a condition, a condition is estimated that indicates the inevitability of occurrence, namely the existence of something in this world, since the world is never free of it. Thus what is attached to it is certain. Since the meaning is what Sibawayh stated, (mahma) is a subject, the nominal form is necessary for it, (yakun) is a conditional verb, and the (fa) is required and generally comes right after it. When (amma) occupies that position, the (fa) becomes necessary for it. The attaching of the noun is the placing of what is necessary in place of what it necessitates, and the preservation of its effect in the sentence. The original rule would have been that the (fa) enters upon the sentence in the cases mentioned, because it is the consequent. But they disliked placing it directly after the conditional particle, so they introduced the predicate and made the subject a substitute for the condition in form. It may also be placed before the (fa), as in al-Radi's list of parts of the consequent: the direct object, the adverbial phrase, the circumstantial phrase, and others, which they counted, though with some reservation.

In the beginning of both sentences with this particle there is praise and blame, which is not hidden. The relative pronoun refers to the known group of believers, just as the relative pronoun that follows refers to the group of the tyrannical disbelievers, not to those who believe in striking examples and those who disbelieve in it, since the meaning would be disrupted. The pronoun in (annahu) refers to the example, which is the nearest referent. [Or it refers to] striking, understood from (yadrib), which is "to strike." It has also been said: it refers to the abandonment of shame suggested by what has passed. It has also been said: it refers to the Qur'an. The truth is the opposite of falsehood. It is originally a verbal noun of (haqqa, yahiqqu), from the patterns (daraba) and (qatala), meaning "it became obligatory" or "it was established." Al-Raghib said: its origin is correspondence and conformity, and it can mean what is existent according to wisdom, what is existent in accordance with it, and a belief that corresponds to reality. It has also been said: it is the judgment that corresponds. It is applied to statements, beliefs, religions, and doctrines because they contain that quality. In the well-known usage, no distinction is made between it and truthfulness (sidq), except that correspondence became the term for a belief, and truthfulness for a statement in the same way. It may be distinguished in that correspondence is considered in truth from the side of reality, and in truthfulness from the side of the judgment.

Its definiteness here is either for the restrictive attribution (al-qasr al-idda'i), as one says "this is the truth," or for the claim of identity, and in that case the predicated subject is one whose attribution is accepted. (Min rabbihim): this is either a predicate after a predicate, or a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun of "the truth." (Min) here indicates the figurative starting point. The mention of the title of lordship is to indicate that they acknowledge the truth of the Qur'an, and of the blessings Allah has bestowed upon them, which are the reason for the revelation of this Book. This is suitable to His words: ﴿We sent down upon Our servant﴾. As for the disbelievers who deny His majesty and take others as lords, Allah, may His name be exalted, is the fitting one for their state. ﴿And Allah warns you of Himself﴾. It has also been said: the addition of the pronoun to Him here indicates honor and notifies that the striking of examples is an education for them and a guidance to what leads them to their perfection that befits them. The sentence occupies the place of the two objects of "they know" according to the majority, and the place of the first, with the second omitted, according to al-Akhfash, meaning: "they know its truth to be established."

﴿As for those who disbelieve, they say: What did Allah intend by this as an example?﴾ He, glorified is He, did not say: "As for those who disbelieve, they do not know," so as to match the preceding clause, because in this there is greater intensity in censuring them, and an alerting, in the best way, to the completeness of their ignorance, since the interrogative is either due to lack of knowledge or to denial, and each of these two indicates ignorance clearly.

And one who says to musk, "Where is the fragrance of the musk-plant?"
Its own fine scent refutes him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 26 (part 2 of 2):

It has been said: He, glorified be He, did not say there, "As for those who believe, they say, etc.," to indicate that the believers were satisfied with submission and obedience without any need for speech, whereas the disbelievers, because of their wickedness and obstinacy, cannot bear secrecy, for it is like hiding embers in dry reeds. It has also been said that *yaqulun* (they say) does not explicitly indicate knowledge, which is what is intended, and that among the disbelievers are the ignorant and the stubborn, so *fayaqulun etc.* (so they say) is more comprehensive and inclusive.

As for *(wa-madha)* (and what), it has six usages. The first is that *ma* is interrogative in the nominative position as the subject of the sentence, and *dha* is in the sense of *alladhi* (which), and its predicate follows. Here the definite is described by an indefinite as predicate, based on the position of Sibawayh (*Sibawayh*, the grammarian) on its permissibility with interrogative particles, whereas others make the indefinite a predicate of the relative pronoun. The second is that *madha* as a whole is an interrogative, an object of *arada* (intended). These two possibilities are eloquent, and all the exegetes and grammarians of the verse have considered them. The interrogative may carry the sense of astonishment, disapproval or mockery. ﴿Darknesses, one upon another﴾ (Q 24:40). The third is that *ma* is made interrogative and *dha* is made a relative link (*silah*), neither a demonstrative nor a relative pronoun. The fourth is that both are taken together as a relative pronoun, as in his saying: "Leave off what you know; I will guard against it." The fifth is that both are taken as an indefinite qualified noun. For the sixth, it has been permitted that *ma* is interrogative and *dha* is a demonstrative noun, serving as the predicate of *ma*.

*(And the will)*, as al-Raghib said, is derived from *rada yarudu*, meaning to strive in the pursuit of something. Originally it is a compound force made up of desire, impulse and hope. It has come to denote the inclination of the soul toward a thing together with a judgment that it should or should not be done. It is then used once for the starting point, which is the inclination of the soul toward a thing, and once for the endpoint, which is the judgment that it should be done, and so on. The meaning of the word, in the sense of mere intention, is another usage, and it is not our concern here. Between will and desire there is partial overlap, since will may relate to itself, unlike desire, which relates only to pleasures. A person may will a bitter medicine without desiring it, and desire a pleasant food without willing it when he knows it will destroy him, and sometimes he both desires and wills.

On the definition of will, the speculative theologians, both the people of truth and others, hold various positions. Al-Kalbi, al-Najjar and others hold that His, glorified be He, will for His acts means that He does them knowingly, aware of what they contain of benefit. As for the acts of others, His will means that He commanded them and sought them. On this view, sins are not by His will, glorified be He, and the saying "what Allah wills occurs, and what He does not will does not occur" is refuted by them. Al-Jahiz, some of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) and the philosophers hold that His will, exalted be His majesty, is His knowledge of all existents from eternity to eternity, and of how the order of existence should be so that it is in the most perfect form. It suffices that they proceed from Him so that what exists conforms to what is known, in the best order, without intention or yearning desire. They call this knowledge *'inayah* (providence). The Karramiyya, Abu 'Ali and Abu Hashim hold that it is an attribute additional to knowledge. According to the Karramiyya it is a newly created attribute subsisting in His essence, exalted be His majesty, while according to the two Abus it exists without a locus. The true position is that it is an essential, eternal, existential attribute, additional to knowledge and distinct from it and from power, which specifies one of the two possibilities of the object of power for occurrence. The claim that it is the very preponderance (*tarjih*), which is an attribute of acts, as al-Baydawi said, may he be pardoned, has not been held by anyone.

In the expression *hadha* (this) there is a belittling of the one pointed to, like its use in ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ (Q 25:41). It may also be used for exaltation according to the requirements of the context.

*(Mathalan)* (as a parable) is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyiz*) of the relation of astonishment and the like to the one pointed to. Al-Radi, and the responsibility is on him, mentioned that when the pronoun and the demonstrative are both indefinite, the specification comes after them, and the operator is them, since they are complete in themselves, the case in which their being made genitive is impossible. When they are definite, the specification is of the relation. It is also possible that it is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the name of Allah, the Exalted, or from *hadha*, meaning "illustrating," or "illustrated by it," or "by striking it."

﴿He leads many astray by it and guides many by it﴾. These are two clauses running in the place of explanation and elaboration for the two clauses introduced by *amma* (as for), since they include that both groups are described by multitude, and that knowing that it is true is among the guidance by which the believers gain light upon their light, while ignorance of its place in error is that by which the ignorant stumble further in their darkness. These two clauses increase the clarity of what they contain. Or they are an answer to dispel what they allege, namely that there is no benefit in striking parables with trivial things, by explaining that it contains a noble wisdom and a beautiful purpose, which is that it is a means to guiding those who are prepared for guidance and to misguiding those who are immersed in error. Some have stated that the two clauses answer *lima dha* (why). The two verbs are placed in the position of the verbal noun to indicate continuous renewal, and the present tense is used for this frequently. So the use of it here indicates that leading astray and guidance continue to renew themselves as time renews. It has been said that placing them in the position of the verb in the interrogative is an intensification in indicating their realization, for their being willed is not the same as their actually occurring. It also avoids joining the leading astray with guidance in the same category of will, lest it suggest that the two are equal in relation, which is not the case. The primary purpose of striking the parable is reminder and guidance, as His saying, exalted be He, indicates: ﴿And these parables We strike for people, that perhaps they will reflect﴾ (Q 59:21). As for leading astray, it is an incidental consequence following from wrong choice. In the arrangement, leading astray is placed before guidance, although mercy precedes wrath, and its precedence in rank and nobility is because their saying arises from error. Yet that the Qur'an is a cause of it requires more explanation, because its causing guidance is most evident, so attention to explaining it is more fitting. Each of the two groups is described as many with regard to themselves, for otherwise the guided are few in comparison with the people of error. It is far-fetched to interpret the multitude of the guided as a moral multitude, by making the multitude of subtle qualities equal to the multitude of noble persons, as it has been said:

"I have not seen men like one another differ
in the eyes of the diligent, until a thousand is counted as one."

Especially since the true multitude is mentioned alongside it. Moreover, some have permitted that His saying, exalted be He, ﴿He leads many astray by it﴾, etc., is in the position of a qualifier of *mathal* (parable), and so it is part of the speech of the disbelievers, and perhaps it is by way of accommodating the believers, since they do not acknowledge that this parable leads many astray by Allah and guides many by it. More strange than this is Ibn 'Atiyya's permission that ﴿He leads many astray by it﴾ is part of the speech of

[p. 210]

the disbelievers, while what follows it is the speech of Allah, exalted be He. This is confusion in the construction and deviation from the apparent sense without evidence. The attribution of leading astray to Him, exalted be He, is literal, and its aspect has been explained before, so no attention should be paid to what is in al-Kashshaf, because it is a Mu'tazili slip. The pronoun in *bihi* (by it) refers to the parable, or to its striking in both places. It has been said that in the first place it refers to the rejection, and in the second to the confirmation, and that the strength of the speech indicates this, though its weakness is not hidden.

Zayd ibn 'Ali read *yudallu* here and in what follows, and *yuhda* with the passive, while Ibn Abi 'Abla read all three with the active. They put the *fasiqin* (corrupt ones) in the nominative, "may Allah lower them." ﴿And He leads none astray by it except the corrupt﴾. This is an appendix (*tadhyil*) or a parenthetical statement at the end of the speech, according to the view of one who permitted it. It has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*). Al-Salikuti prohibited its being coordinated with what precedes it, saying: "It is not valid for it to be both an answer and an elaboration." Some permitted it as a completion of the answer and as an added specification of those whose leading astray is intended, by mentioning their ugly attributes which entail it, and as an indication that this is not an initial leading astray, but rather a confirmation in the various kinds of error they were upon, and an increase in it.

*(Al-fasiqin)* is the plural of *fasiq*, from *fisq*, which in the sacred law means the going out of rational beings from obedience. It thus includes disbelief and what is below it, both major and minor sins. By custom and usage it became specific to committing major sins, so it is applied to committing the other two only rarely, with a clear indication. It derives from the saying "*fasaqa al-rutab*" (the date fruit went out of its skin when it came out of its husk). Ibn al-A'rabi said: "The word *fisq* has not been heard as a description of a human being in the speech of the Arabs." Perhaps he meant the speech of the pre-Islamic period, as Ibn al-Anbari stated explicitly. Otherwise Ru'ba, who is an Islamic poet whose speech is used as evidence, said:

"They go in the highland and the lowland, wandering,
corrupt, turning aside from their intended course, deviating."

Yet it may be said that the word *fasiqat* in the verse did not depart from its original meaning, since its original meaning is the emergence of creatures and the appearance of bodies from non-rational beings, and in the verse what is meant is the emergence of camels, which do not reason. The *fasiqin* here are those who go out of the bounds of faith. Specifying the leading astray for them, consequent upon the attribute of corruption and the ugly things imposed upon them, indicates that this is what made them ready for leading astray and brought them to error. Their disbelief, their deviation from truth and their persistence in falsehood turned the faces of their gaze away from reflection and contemplation, until their ignorance became fixed and their error increased, so they denied and said what they said.

The *fasiqin* is in the accusative either as the object of *yudillu* (leads astray), or by way of exception, with the object omitted, meaning "anyone." It is not an exception from a non-stated (*tafrigh*) construction, as in his saying: "Salim escaped, though his soul was saved only with great difficulty, and only the sheath of a sword and a belt did not escape." Abu al-Baqa' prohibited this, and perhaps he is refuted by the verse,

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 27:**

﴿الَّذِينَ يَنْقُضُونَ عَهْدَ اللَّهِ مِن بَعْدِ مِيثاقِهِ﴾ "Those who break the covenant of God after its confirmation." This may be in the accusative or the nominative. The accusative is either by apposition (ittiba') or by separation (qat'), meaning "I condemn." The nominative is either as the second of the two possibilities for the first, or as the inceptive (ibtida'), with the predicate being the clause ﴿أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الخاسِرُونَ﴾ ("those are the losers"). On this reading the clause is as if it were an independent statement, with no connection to what precedes it except a distant one. Naqd (breaking) means undoing the structure of something. Its original use is for a rope, and its opposite is ibram (tightening). It is also used for a wall and the like, whose opposite is building. The use of naqd for annulling a covenant became common, as al-Zamakhshari said, since they called the covenant a rope, by way of metaphor, because of the strength of the bond between the two parties to the covenant. This is one of the secrets and subtleties of eloquence: one omits mention of the borrowed thing and then alludes to it by mentioning something from its associated attributes, so that by that allusion one is directed to its place. An example is your saying: "a scholar from whom people draw water" and "a brave man who devours his opponents."

The conclusion is that the verse contains an allusive metaphor (istiʿara bil-kināya, a metaphor by way of allusion), and naqd is an explicit, realised metaphor (istiʿara taḥqīqiyya taṣrīḥiyya), in which the annulment of the covenant is likened to the undoing of the composition of a body. The name of the thing compared to (al-mushabbah bihi) is then applied to the thing compared (al-mushabbah).
