However, this was only permissible and fitting after considering the comparison of the covenant to a rope. By this consideration, it becomes an indicator of the metaphor of the rope for the covenant. From this it becomes clear that an allusive metaphor may exist without an imaginative (takhyīliyya) element, and that its indicator may be a realised one. The full investigation of this should be sought in its proper place.

Al-ʿahd means a binding pact (al-mawthiq). One says ʿahida ilayhi fi kadhā when one enjoins someone to do something and entrusts him with it; wa-thaqqahu ʿalayhi; and istaʿhada minhu when one stipulates a condition upon him; and istawthaqa minhu (he obtained a firm assurance from him). The covenant intended here is either the covenant taken by reason, which is the proof established against God's servants, indicating His existence and unity, and the truthfulness of His messengers (ﷺ). Breaking it entails, as is clear, a great deal of blame, because they broke what God had confirmed by the proofs that He repeated to them in themselves and in the horizons, and by sending the prophets (peace be upon them) and sending down the books as confirmation of it. On this reading, those who break it are all the disbelievers.

Or it is the covenant taken through the messengers from the nations: that when a messenger was sent to them who confirmed his message with miracles, they should believe him, follow him, not conceal his matter, and that his mention is in the earlier books, and not oppose his judgement. On this reading, those who break it are the People of the Book and the hypocrites among them, since they cast all of that behind their backs and substituted (it). According to some, breaking the covenant on this reading is more heinous than on the first; others reversed this, and each has a viewpoint. It has also been said that the covenant is the trust (amāna) which man carried after the heavens and the earth refused to bear it. It has been said that it is what was taken from the Children of Israel: that they should not shed their own blood nor expel themselves from their homes, along with other sayings. These are based on differences concerning the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul). The apparent meaning is generality.

(Min) is for the beginning (of a point). That the word governed by it is a place from which a thing is separated and departs indicates that the breaking took place immediately after the covenant was firmly established, without any interval. This contains guidance that they did not care about the covenant: the effect of what God had firmly established upon them was that they broke it. It has been said that (min) is merely a connective particle (ṣila), but this is far-fetched.

Al-mīthāq is on the pattern mifʿāl. In adjectives this pattern is common, like minḥār (one who gives generously a great deal). It may also be a verbal noun (maṣdar), according to Abu al-Baqa' and al-Zamakhshari, like mīʿād (meaning a promise), in the sense of al-waʿd (promise). A group rejected this and said it is a noun in the place of the verbal noun, as in the poet's line:

"Would you disbelieve after death was turned back from me, and after your giving me the hundred grazing camels?"

It may also be an instrumental noun (ism ālah), like miḥrāth (plough). This did not become widespread, but it is not far-fetched. The intended meaning is what God confirmed His covenant with, of signs and books, or what they confirmed it with, of acceptance and commitment. The pronoun refers to the covenant, since that is what is being spoken of. It is also permissible for it to refer back to God (ﷺ... God Most High). Al-Salikuti did not permit this, because the meaning is not complete without considering the covenant, so it is more important than mentioning the agent, and because returning the pronoun to the genitive-annexed noun (al-muḍāf) is contrary to the norm.

Abu al-Baqa's statement implies that al-mīthāq here is a verbal noun meaning "the act of making firm," and in the pronoun there are the two possibilities. If it refers to the name of God Most High, the verbal noun is annexed to the agent; if it refers to the covenant, it is annexed to the object. The discussion of returning the pronoun to the annexed noun has been restricted by some scholars to non-verbal annexation. As for verbal annexation, it is common and regular, and what we are dealing with here is like that, because it is a verbal noun, or interpreted as a derivative. So it is like your saying: "The beating of Zayd pleased me while he was standing." The correct view is that it is intended as separated.

﴿ويَقْطَعُونَ ما أمَرَ اللَّهُ بِهِ أنْ يُوصَلَ﴾ "And they sever what God has commanded to be joined." The (mā) in "what is severed" is either a relative pronoun or, according to Abu al-Baqa', an indefinite noun described by a clause. There are several views concerning what is meant by it.

The first: the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They severed him by denial and disobedience. This is the view of al-Hasan. In this view, (mā) is used for one who understands, indeed for the lord of the intelligent, and rather for intellect itself.

The second: the word, for God commanded that it be joined by action, but they did not join it and did not act upon it. The apparent meaning of this is that the verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites.

The third: belief in the prophets. They were commanded to join it, but they severed it, by denying some and believing in some.

The fourth: kinship and blood relations (al-raḥim wal-qarāba). This is what Qatada said. The apparent meaning is that he intended the disbelievers of Quraysh and those like them.

The fifth: the general command that includes everything mentioned, the severing of which entails severing the connection between God Most High and the servant, which is the primary object of every connection and separation. Perhaps this is the most sound view, because it involves carrying the expression upon its generality, and there is no clear evidence for specification.

Some have preferred the view before it, on the grounds that the apparent meaning is that this is a description of the corrupt ones (al-fāsiqīn) as those who neglect the rights of creation after being described as neglecting the right of the Truth, glory be to Him, and the neglect of His right is by breaking His covenant, and the neglect of the right of His creation is by severing their kinship ties. But this is not strong.

(Al-amr) is a speech that demands an act. According to the Mu'tazila it carries the element of superiority (ʿulūw), and according to Abu al-Husayn it carries the element of dominance (istiʿlāʾ). Both are refuted by the apparent meaning of the words of the Most High, as related of Pharaoh: ﴿فَماذا تَأْمُرُونَ﴾ ("What do you advise?"). It is also used for speech expressed in the form (of a command), and for the form itself, and there is disagreement about what it entails. This is the demanding command (al-amr al-ṭalabī). It has been transferred to mean the matter that issues from a person, because it issues from a motive which resembles a command, so it is as if he is commanded by it; or because it is of the nature of a thing to be commanded, just as a grave matter and a great affair is called shaʾn (affair). It is originally a verbal noun meaning intention, and that is why it was given this name, because it is of the nature of a thing to be intended. The jurists hold that amr is a homonym (mushtarak) between speech and act, because it is used for it, as in the words: ﴿وما أمْرُ فِرْعَوْنَ بِرَشِيدٍ﴾ ("And the affair of Pharaoh was not rightly guided").

(And that it be joined) may be in the accusative or the genitive, as an apposition to (mā) or to its pronoun. The second is preferred because of proximity, and because severing what God commanded to be joined is more forceful than severing the joining of what God Himself commanded. The possibility of the nominative, by supposing "he is" (huwa), or the accusative by apposition with the position of the genitive-governed word, or by removing the preposition, or that it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi), meaning "because" or "out of dislike that," is not significant, as is not hidden.

﴿ويُفْسِدُونَ في الأرْضِ أُولَئِكَ هُمُ الخاسِرُونَ﴾ "And they cause corruption on the earth. Those are the losers." Their corruption is by inviting people to disbelief, encouraging it, and driving people toward it; or by terrifying travellers and cutting off the roads for those who wish to emigrate to God and His Messenger (ﷺ); or by their committing every sin whose harm extends and whose sparks fly out across the horizons. Perhaps this last is the best. Mention of "on the earth" indicates that the intended corruption is one that spreads beyond what is limited to themselves.

(Those) is an indication of the corrupt ones in view of the detailed mention of their ugly attributes. In it there is an allusion that they are in the most distant rank of blame. The restriction of the losers to them, in view of their perfection in loss, is because they neglected the intellect from reflection, did not seize the knowledge that brings eternal life and everlasting joy, and bought breaking for fidelity, corruption for righteousness, severance for connection, and reward for punishment. Thus both of their aims were lost, the capital and the profit, and they incurred a grievous harm. This is the great loss.

In the verse there is a supporting element (tarshīḥ, a supporting detail that sustains a metaphor) for the implied metaphor which the preceding verses contain. So understand.

[Page 212]

﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾ This is a shift from addressing the third person to addressing those people, after enumerating their ugly deeds, which call for an increase in God's wrath upon them, exalted is He. A denunciation directed at the addressee is more eloquent than one directed at a third party, and more effective in deterring him, since it may not reach him otherwise. (How, *kayfa*) is a noun, which is either an adverb of circumstance (*zarf*), attributed to Sibawayh, in which case its position is always accusative (*nasb*); or not an adverb, attributed to al-Akhfash, in which case its position is nominative (*raf'*) when it is followed by a subject (*mubtada'*) and accusative when it is followed by something else. Ibn Malik claimed that no one has held that it is an adverb, since it is neither a time nor a place. However, because it can be explained by your saying "in what state" (*'alā ayy ḥāl*), the name "adverb" was applied to it figuratively. Ibn Hisham approved of this. Its being preceded by a preposition (*jarr*) is anomalous. It is used most often as an interrogative. Its use as a conditional is rare, and its use as a jussive is not attested, though the Kufans and Qutrub permitted it by analogy. Its substitute (*badal*) or response (*jawāb*), when it occurs with a verb that is complete, is accusative, and when it occurs with something that is not complete, it is nominative if it is a subject and accusative if it is an abrogating (*nāsikh*) word. Ibn Mawhab claimed that it may occur as a conjunction, but this is worthless. Here it is an interrogative combined with denunciation and astonishment at their disbelief, by denying the state that is most specifically connected to it, namely knowledge of the Creator and ignorance of Him. Do you not see that disbelief is divided according to these two states, so that one says "an obstinate disbeliever" and "an ignorant disbeliever"? So the meaning is: "Do you disbelieve in a state of knowledge, or in a state of ignorance while you know this story?" And this implies knowledge of a Creator described by the attributes of perfection, free from deficiency, and this is a strong deterrent from disbelief. The occurrence of an act from one who is capable, in the presence of a strong deterrent, is a cause for astonishment and rebuke. It also indicates that their disbelief is out of obstinacy, which is more severe in censure. There is also in it, in terms of emphasis, what is not in "Do you disbelieve?" (*a-takfurūna*), because the denial, which is a negation, is directed at a state that cannot be separated from its possessor, and the negation of the state necessarily entails the negation of its possessor, by way of demonstration. If you wish, you may generalize the state. The denial that their disbelief has any state in which it exists, although every existent must exist in some state, entails denying the existence of disbelief in that way. And it is not an objection that interrogation is impossible for the Subtle, the All-Aware, exalted is His station, because: if it means seeking information, we do not accept that it is impossible, since it may serve to alert the addressee and rebuke him, and does not imply the ignorance of the questioner, and combining denial and astonishment with it does not require that. These two are among the figurative meanings of interrogation. Combining the literal and the figurative is permitted if the questioning is literal for the form, and combining two figurative meanings is permitted if it is figurative, because understanding by way of implication and necessary consequence is not from the core meaning. Or it is a figure on a figure, because the use of interrogation for the meaning of questioning is so well known that it is as if it were literal for it. And if it means interrogation, we say: there is no fault in its occurrence from one who knows what is asked about, because, as stated in *al-Itqān*, it is seeking understanding, and understanding on the part of the questioner, which is impossible for God, or the occurrence of understanding from one who does not understand, whoever he may be, is not impossible for Him, exalted is He. Likewise, there is no impossibility in the occurrence of astonishment from Him, exalted is He. Rather, they said: when astonishment is attributed to God, the great and exalted, no unacceptable consequence follows, because it is directed toward the addressee, or its ultimate purpose is meant, or it is referred back to the view of the early generations (*salaf*). He, glorified is He, used "you disbelieve" (*takfurūn*) and not the past tense, even though disbelief had already occurred from them, because what is denied is continuance, and the present tense is what indicates that. And so that the speech would not contain a rebuke to those among whom disbelief occurred and who believed, like most of the Companions, may God be pleased with them.

﴿And you were dead, and He gave you life; then He will cause you to die; then He will give you life; then to Him you will be returned.﴾ What comes before "then" (*thumma*) is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in "you disbelieve," with the implicit "qad" (indeed) unavoidably, contrary to someone who made a mistake about this. The meaning is: "How do you disbelieve, when He has created you?" He expressed creation by that, and because it is innately fixed in natures and created in minds that there is no creator except God, it is a state that requires that it not be combined with disbelief. The sentences after it are independent (*mustaʼnafa*), with no connection to the circumstance, and therefore they differ from what precedes them in particle and form. And you may make all the sentences fall under the circumstance, which in reality is knowledge of the story, as if it were said: "How do you disbelieve while you know this story and its beginning and its end?" So its containing past and future does not harm, since neither of them can be a circumstance. A group of verifying scholars preferred this. Life is a power that follows natural balance and from which all other powers emanate. It was said: the sensory faculty is life, and a paralyzed limb is alive, otherwise corruption would quickly reach it. The absence of actual sensation does not indicate the absence of the faculty, since the effect may be absent because of an impediment. It seems they meant the power of touch, because the distinctness of life from the other senses is evident: it is specific to one organ rather than another, it is absent in some kinds of animals, and it would entail multiple lives of one kind in one person if each of these were life, and their composition in reality if their totality were meant. It is also used figuratively for the vegetative power, because it is among its early stages and preliminaries, and for the virtues specific to the human being, such as intellect, knowledge, and faith, insofar as they are its perfection and goal. Death is its opposite in every rank, and all of this is in the Book of God, the Exalted. The life of God, glorified is He, is the validity of His being described by knowledge and power, or a meaning subsisting in His essence, exalted is He, which requires that. How far is dust from the Lord of lords! Then, there are various opinions among people about what is meant by what is in this noble verse. What is related from Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, and Mujahid, may God be pleased with them, is that the first death means the prior non-existence, the first life means creation, the second death means the death known in the worldly abode, and the second life means the resurrection for the Judgment. Some verifying scholars chose this and claimed that His saying, exalted is He, "and you were dead," and the attribution of the last causing to death to Him, exalted is He, strengthen it. Others chose that their being dead is from the time they settled as drops of semen in the wombs until the completion of the stages after them, that the first life is the breathing of the spirit after those stages, that the causing to die is the well-known death, and that the giving of life after it is the resurrection on the day the Trumpet is blown. Perhaps this is closer than the first. Applying the term "the dead" to those bodies is figurative if death is interpreted as the absence of life in the one who is described by it, and literal if it is interpreted as the absence of life from what is supposed to have it. This was said by al-Salikuti. Some of their statements imply that it means "like the dead" according to the second interpretation. If death is interpreted as the absence of life absolutely, it is literal, and this is the well-known view. And the view I find most remote is to take the first death as the well-known death after the term has ended, and the first life as what occurs in the questioning in the grave, so that the past tense is used for the future to indicate the certainty of its occurrence. Then there is no evidence in the verse for the view that chooses the denial of the punishment of the grave, since the most that it contains is the non-mention of the life that would validate it. We do not argue for it by that aspect, and we have, praise be to God, various proofs on that matter. Likewise, there is no evidence in "and to Him you will be returned" for the Mujassima, who say that God is in a place, because the intended meaning of returning to Him is gathering at the place of assembly, where no one else rules, and "the command on that day belongs to God." Beyond this is much discussion that is not hidden from the knowers. In His saying, exalted is He, "you are returned" (*turja'ūn*) in the passive form, instead of "He returns you" (*yurji'ukum*) which fits the context, there is consideration of the harmony of verse endings together with the existence of thematic harmony in the context. For this reason it was said that the reading of the majority is more eloquent than the reading of Ya'qub, Mujahid, and a group, who read "you return" (*tarji'ūn*) in the active form. There is no objection that if the verse is addressed to the disbelievers, and the meaning of knowledge is considered in it, then addressing them with what comes after "then," and "then" governing both verbs, would be impossible, because they do not know that. Their capacity for knowledge, due to the clarity of the proofs, both those in the horizons and those within themselves, and the radiance of their lights, rational and transmitted, is treated as knowledge in removing excuse. And with this, what was said is also refuted: that they are doubters regarding the attribution of what preceded to Him, exalted is He, so how could that address be made to them? It may also be, as was said, that the address in the verse is to both the believer and the disbeliever. When He, glorified is He, had explained the proofs of monotheism, from His saying, glorified is He, "O mankind" up to "so do not set up rivals to God" (*fa-lā tajʿalū*), and the proofs of prophethood, from "and if you are in doubt" up to "if you are truthful," and had threatened with "but if you do not, and you will never do it" up to the verse, and promised with "and give good tidings to those who believe" etc., He emphasized this by enumerating for them the general blessings, from His saying "and you were dead" up to "they will abide therein forever," and the particular blessings, from "O Children of Israel" up to "what We abrogate." He regarded the occurrence of disbelief despite those blessings from them as ugly, as a rebuke to the disbeliever and an affirmation to the believer. He counted causing death as a blessing, because it is a link to eternal life and to the reunion of the lover with the beloved. It may be said that what is counted against them in this manner is the meaning extracted from the entire story.

And from the allusive interpretation is the statement of Ibn 'Ata': "And you were dead" in the outward sense, "then He gave you life" through unveiling of secrets, "then He will cause you to die" from the attributes of servanthood, "then He will give you life" with the attributes of lordship. Fāris said: "And you were dead" through your own witnessing, "then He gave you life" through His witnessing, "then He will cause you to die" from your witnessing, "then He will give you life" by the subsistence of the Truth, "then to Him you will be returned" from everything you possess, so that you will belong to Him.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 29 (part 1 of 2):

﴿He it is who created for you whatever is on the earth, all of it﴾ is coordinated with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and you were﴾ [2:28]. The conjunction is omitted either because it is like the result of what precedes it, or to draw attention to its independence in conveying what it conveys. It is said that it is an explanation of another blessing that follows from the first. By its following, what is meant is that benefiting from it depends on the first, for a blessing is called a blessing only from the standpoint of benefit derived from it. (Huwa) is for other than the speaker and the addressee.
Page 215
It has dialectal variants: lightening the waw when vowelled with a fatha and omitting it in poetry; doubling it for the Hamdan tribe; and vowelling it with a sukun for the tribes of Asad and Qays. (Huwa) for the people of God, exalted is He, is one of His names, which indicates the essence of His specific reality, free of all aspects of multiplicity. It is a compound noun of two letters, the ha' and the waw; the ha' is the root, and the waw is an addition, as evidenced by its dropping out in the dual and plural. So in reality there is only one letter, indicating the one, the singular, besides whom nothing exists. "Everything perishes except His Face" [28:88]. Because of the abundance of secrets within it, the eminent ones have taken it as the basis of their remembrance and a lamp for their inner secret, and it runs with the breaths, while its referent is hidden from intuition and analogy. In making the pronoun the subject and the relative clause the predicate, there is an indication of its majesty that is not hidden. The fronting of the adverbial phrase before the direct object is to hasten delight. The lam indicates purpose and benefit: that is, He created for your sake all that is on the earth, so that you may benefit from it in your worldly affairs, directly or through intermediaries, and in your religious affairs through reasoning and reflection. Many of the Sunni scholars of the Hanafi and Shafi'i schools have used the verse as evidence for the permissibility of beneficial things before the arrival of the Shari'a, and most of the Mu'tazila hold this view, and Imam (al-Razi) in al-Mahsul and al-Baydawi in al-Minhaj adopted it.
It is objected that the lam comes for other than benefit, as in ﴿and if you do evil, then it is for it﴾ [17:7]. It is answered that this is figurative, since the leading linguists agree that it denotes ownership, and its meaning is exclusive beneficial relation; and also that what is meant is benefit through reasoning. It is answered that restriction goes against the apparent meaning, and moreover that this is achieved for every responsible person from himself, so it is to be understood as referring to others. Some held that the original status of things before prohibition is permissibility; others held suspension, since the evidences conflict in their view. The Ibahiyya used the verse for their claim, saying: it indicates that all that is on the earth was created for everyone, so no one has any exclusive right to anything at all. This is refuted by the fact that it indicates that all is for all, and this does not preclude the exclusive possession of some by some for a reason; so there is a kind of distribution, and specification is derived from a separate proof. It does not necessarily follow that each person has exclusive right to one thing, as al-Salikuti supposed. As for "whatever" covering all that is on the earth for itself, a thing is not a container of itself unless "lower direction" is meant, just as "heaven" is used for the direction of height; the encompassing throne suffices for the descent, or the direction is considered notional. Yes, it has been said that it covers every part of the parts of the earth, since among the necessities of its being is that the part exists in the whole, and the difference is notional. As for the view that the speech is under an implied conjunction, i.e., He created what is on the earth and the earth, not "I am pleased with it," and some did not burden themselves with any of that, and dispensed with it by the prior mention of the favour of the earth in His saying, ﴿and made the earth a bed for you﴾ [2:22]: (and "jami'an," "all of it") is a circumstantial qualifier emphasizing the word "ma" ("whatever"), and neither of them indicates, as some stated, simultaneity in time; this differs from "ma'an" (together). Making it a circumstantial of the pronoun in "lakum" (for you) is weakened by the context, because the verse enumerates blessings, not the one blessed; and since the position of favour calls for emphasis on the abundance of blessings, for the sake of this emphasis they did not make it a circumstantial of "the earth" either. ﴿Then He istawa towards the heaven﴾ means: He ascended to it and rose, without modality, likening, or delimitation, as said by al-Rabi'. Or it means He directed Himself to it with His will, in a straight intention, without a diverting obstacle or a turning hindrance, from the expression "istawa ilayhi" like an arrow loosed when one aims at it in a straight line without swerving toward anything; this was said by al-Farra'. It was also said: "istawla" (He seized) and took possession, as in the verse:
"When we rose and prevailed over them, we left them fallen to the vulture and the hawk."
This is contrary to the apparent meaning, since it requires "ila" to mean "ala"; also, seizing is subsequent to the existence of the one seized, so one would need to say that what is meant is that He seized control over the creation of the heaven, which does not entail precedence of existence, and what is wrong with this is not hidden. What is meant by "heaven" is the celestial bodies or the direction of height. "Thumma" (then) has been said to indicate temporal delay, and it has been said to indicate the difference between the two creations. The creation of the heaven was considered superior to the creation of the earth. People differ regarding the creation of the heavens and what is in them, and the earth and what is in it, in terms of priority and posteriority, due to the conflict of apparent indications on this. Some held that the creation of the heavens precedes, based on His saying, exalted is He:
Page 216
﴿Is it He who built the heaven? He raised its height and made it level. He darkened its night and brought out its forenoon. And after that He spread out the earth. He brought forth from it its water and its pasture. And the mountains He anchored﴾ [79:27–32]. Others held that the creation of the earth precedes, based on His saying: ﴿Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who created the earth in two days ... and He placed in it firm mountains above it, and blessed it, and measured in it its sustenance in four days, equal for the seekers. Then He istawa towards the heaven, and it was smoke, and He said to it and to the earth: come willingly or unwillingly. They said: we come willingly. So He completed them as seven heavens in two days, and inspired in each heaven its command﴾ [41:9–12]. Some combined them and said: "He brought forth from it its water" is a substitute or an explanatory apposition for "dahaha" (spread it out), i.e., its spreading out explains what is meant by it; so its posteriority is not a posteriority of its essence, but of the creation of what is in it, its completion and arrangement, indeed of the creation of enjoyment and benefit from it. For posteriority may be with respect to the thing itself, and also with respect to its last part and its mentioned qualifier, as if you said: "I sent you a messenger, then you had sent so-and-so to see what he would convey," where the second sending, though earlier, is for a purpose that comes later, so he made himself later. What al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated with a sound chain from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, in reconciling the two verses points to this. It is not contradicted by what Ibn Jarir and others narrated and authenticated from him as well: "The Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and asked him about the creation of the heavens and the earth. He said: God created the earth on Sunday and Monday, and created the mountains and what is in them of benefits on Tuesday, and created on Wednesday the trees, water, cities, habitation and ruin; these are four. Then He said: ﴿Do you indeed disbelieve...﴾ up to ﴿equal for the seekers﴾. And He created on Thursday the heaven, and on Friday He created the stars, the sun, the moon, and the angels." This may be taken to mean that He created the substance and roots of these things, since cities, habitation and ruin cannot be conceived before, so He joined them to it as a sign of this. The objection of Imam al-Razi, that the spreading out is delayed beyond the creation of the heaven, since the earth is a massive body and its creation cannot be separated from its spreading out, so if the spreading is later, its creation is also later, is based, as it has been said, on heedlessness, for whoever says that its spreading is later than its creation does not say that it was massive from the beginning; rather he says that at the first creation it was like a pebble, then it was spread out, so separation is realized and it is valid for its spreading to be later than its creation. As for the statement of the one whose secret is sanctified, that the creation of things in the earth is not possible unless it is already spread out, its refutation is not hidden, on the basis that what is meant is the creation of materials and roots, not the creation of things within it as is the case today. Some of the verifiers said: the exegetes differ on whether the creation of the heaven is prior or posterior to the creation of the earth; al-Wahidi reported the first view from Muqatil, and the verifiers adopted it, and they did not differ that all that is on the earth which you see is posterior to the creation of the seven heavens; rather they agreed on it. So in this case the creation in the noble verse is taken in the sense of decreeing, not bringing into being, or in its meaning, and the will is supposed, and the meaning is: He willed the creation of all that is on the earth for you, in the manner of ﴿when you stand up to prayer﴾ [5:6] and ﴿when you recite the Qur'an﴾ [16:98]; and this does not contradict it. ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾: what precedes the creation of the heaven is only the decree of the earth and all that is in it, or the will to bring it into being; and what is posterior to the creation of the heaven is the bringing into being of the earth and all that is in it; so there is no difficulty. As for His saying, exalted and high is He: ﴿He created the earth in two days﴾, it is on the basis of the will, and the meaning is: He willed the creation of the earth; likewise ﴿and placed in it firm mountains﴾ should be taken to mean He willed to place. This is supported by His saying: ﴿So He said to it and to the earth: come willingly or unwillingly, they said: we come willingly﴾, for the apparent meaning is that what is intended is: come into existence; and had the earth been existing previously, this would not be valid. It is as though He, glory be to Him, said: Do you indeed disbelieve in Him who willed the bringing into being of the earth and what is in it of firm mountains and sustenance in four days; then He turned to the heaven, so His will was connected to the bringing into being of the heaven and the earth, and they obeyed by the command of bringing into being; so He brought into being seven heavens in two days, and brought into being the earth and what is in it in four days.
There remains here an explanation of the point in the change of style, where He mentioned first here the creation of the earth and what is in it, and in (Ha Mim, the Prostration) [41:9–12]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 29 (part 2 of 2):

over the creation of the heavens. He used the reverse order in Surat al-Nazi'at. Perhaps the reason is that the context in the first two passages (the verses of 2:29 and 2:22) is one of bestowing favour (imtinan, the enumeration of blessings), so it requires mentioning first what is a blessing, with regard to those addressed. It is as if He, glorified and exalted, said: "He is the One who arranged your affair before the creation of the sky, then created the sky." The context in the third passage (Surat al-Nazi'at) is one of showing the perfection of power, so it requires mentioning first what is more indicative of its perfection.

Here, what is understood from some of the statements of the scholars, may God sanctify their secrets, is that the muhaddad (the outermost sphere, also called "sky") was created before the earth and what is in it, and that the earth itself was created afterwards. Then, after the creation of the earth, the seven heavens were created. Then, after the seven, there was created what is in the earth of minerals and plants. Then the world of animals appeared, then the world of humankind. Accordingly, the meaning of ﴿He created for you all that is on earth﴾ at that point is: He determined it, or He intended its existence, or He brought its materials into being. The meaning of ﴿and He placed firm mountains in it﴾ and so on, in the other verse, is similar to this. The creation of the earth in that verse is in its apparent sense, and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Then He said to it and to the earth: "Come, willingly or unwillingly"﴾ and so on, does not contradict this, because it may be taken to mean: "Come with what I have created in you both of influence and being influenced, and the bringing forth of what I have deposited in you of various conditions and diverse beings." Or the coming of the sky is its coming into existence, and the coming of the earth is that it becomes spread out (madhuwwah). Or: let each of you come to the other in the coming into being of what is intended to be generated from you both.

After all this, the discussion is not free from difficulty, and people have continued to find it difficult from the era of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, until now. For us, if God, exalted is He, wills, there is a return to it after a return, and we ask God, exalted is He, for success.

﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾: the pronoun refers to "the sky" if it is interpreted as the celestial bodies. It may also refer back to it on the basis that it is a plural noun, or that it is treated as such. Otherwise, it is an ambiguous pronoun (damir mubham) explained by what follows it, in the manner of the phrase niʿma rajulan ("what an excellent man"). In this there is a great deal of emphasis, arousal of interest, and firm establishment in the soul, which is not hidden.

Regarding the accusative of sabʿa ("seven"), there are five possibilities: it is a substitute (badal) for the ambiguous pronoun; or it is a substitute for the pronoun referring to the sky; or it is a direct object (maf'ul bihi), meaning He made them even from among them; or it is a circumstantial qualifier (hal muqaddarah); or it is a specification (tamyiz); or it is a second object of sawwa, on the basis that it has the meaning of ṣayyara ("made"), but this is not established. The substitution (al-badaliyyah) is preferred because of the absence of derivation (ishtiqaq). After it, the circumstantial qualifier is preferred, as in al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's al-Bahr al-Muhit).

By sawwahunna is meant: He perfected them, made them upright, and created them from the start, preserved from crookedness and flaws. It does not mean that He, glorified and exalted, made them even afterwards. If it is not like this, then it is in the manner of their saying: "Narrow the mouth of the well and widen the house."

In the juxtaposition of tasviyah (making even) and istiwa' (levelling/establishing) there is a beauty which is not hidden. It should not be said that the astronomers have established nine spheres, and are these anything but heavens? Because we say: they are still doubtful until now regarding their decrease and increase, since what they have found of movements can be accounted for by eight and seven, or even by one. Some of them have established between the sphere of the fixed stars and the atlas (al-atlas, the ninth sphere) a sphere to account for the total inclination. One of their verifiers has said: "It has not become clear to me until now whether the sphere of the fixed stars is one sphere or spheres enclosed within one another." Al-Imam al-Razi has extended discussion of this and done it well. Moreover, even if what has spread is correct, there is nothing in the verse indicating the negation of additional spheres, on the basis of what al-Imam has chosen: that the implication of number (mafhum al-'adad) is not a proof. The statement of al-Baydawi in his tafsir points to this, in contrast to what is in his Minhaj, which agrees with what al-Imam al-Shafi'i held, and al-Ghazali transmitted it from him in al-Mankhul. Al-Salikuti mentioned that the truth is that specifying a number in mention does not indicate the negation of the excess, and the disagreement on this is well known. And if we say that the Throne and the Chair are spherical, then no discussion remains.

﴿And He is, of everything, Knowing﴾: a concluding statement affirming what precedes it of the creation of the heavens and the earth and what is in them, in this wondrous pattern and strange method. ﴿You see no discrepancy in the creation of the Most Merciful. So look again: do you see any flaw? Then look again, twice; your sight will return to you humbled while it is weary﴾ (Qur'an 67:3–4).

In ʿalim ("Knowing") there is an intensification not found in ʿalim (the form of the active participle). This does not refer back to the attribute itself, because His knowledge, exalted is He, is one with no multiplicity in it. But since it relates to the universal and the particular, the existent and the non-existent, the finite and the infinite, He described Himself, glorified is He, with what indicates intensification. The word "thing" (shay') here is general, remaining upon its generality, with no specification in it in any respect, contrary to those who strayed from the right path.

The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa al-majrur) is connected to ʿalim, and it took bi (with) even though it comes from ʿalima, which is transitive by itself. The strengthening is by means of the lam (to), because the patterns of intensification (amthilat al-mubalaghah) (are like) what they have said: "khalafat af'aluha" (her deeds differed), because they resemble the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) in their indication of excess. So they were given its rule in transitivity, which is that if its verb is transitive, then if it conveys knowledge or ignorance it takes bi, as in a'lim bihi (more knowing of it), ajhil bihi (more ignorant of it), ʿalim bihi (knowing of it), jahul bihi (ignorant of it), and a'lam man yadill (the most knowing of who strays), according to one interpretation. Otherwise it takes lam, as in adrib li-Zayd (strike for Zayd), and "fa'"al limā yurīd" (Doer of what He wills) (Qur'an 85:16). Otherwise it takes that by which its verb is transitive, as in asbar 'ala al-nar (more patient toward the Fire) and sabur 'ala kadha (patient at such-and-such). Perhaps this is the majority usage, since one says raḥīm bihi (merciful to him). So understand.

[Page 218]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 30 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to place upon the earth a successive authority (khalifah)."﴾ When He (glory be to Him) had bestowed favour upon those who came before, by what came before, He followed that with a general blessing and complete honour. Kindness to the origin is kindness to the branch, and the child is the secret of his father. *Idh* (the adverb of time "when") is a temporal adverb referring to the past, and it is built (indeclinable) because it resembles a particle in form and in its need for what follows. What follows it is either a verbal or a nominal clause. Time is derived from it when its second component is a verb, or when its content is well known to have occurred at a specific time. When it precedes the present tense, it converts it to the past. It is always adverbial, except when a time expression is added to it. Whether it can function as a direct object, as a particle of causation or of surprise, as a place adverb, or as a superfluous particle is a matter of disagreement. Al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*) says that it cannot occur in these functions. If any of these meanings is derived from it, it is derived from the context. The grammarians (al-mu'ribun) disagreed about it here. It was said: it is superfluous, with the meaning of *qad* ("indeed"), and it is in the position of a nominative, meaning: the beginning of your creation was "when". It was also said: it is in the position of an accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning: "your creation began" or "He gave you life" when. It is considered a extended period of time, not the moment of the saying. It is also said that it is after *khalaqakum* (He created you), the earlier governed element, and the *waw* is superfluous, and the separation is by what nearly constitutes a surah. It is governed by *udhkur* ("remember"). For the adverbial sense to be valid, it is sufficient that the object is adverbial, as in "I shot the game in the sanctuary." These are several opinions, some of which are not correct and some of which are strained. The most fitting view is to make it accusative, governed by the later verb *qalu* ("they said"). There is a clear correspondence between them. The whole clause, with what it contains, is a connection to what precedes it, the connection of one narrative to another narrative, so it is said. But you know that the well-known view is the last one, and it is probably the better one, so reflect. The gentleness of the Lord is not hidden here, as He is added to His own pronoun in the form of address. Its variation and its movement from the general to the particular is a symbol that the one addressed directly receives the greatest share and the fullest portion of the content being announced. So he (ﷺ) is, in truth, the greatest successor among creation and the foremost leader on earth and in the high heavens. Were it not for him, Adam would not have been created. Rather, (no, no), and by God, how well my master Ibn al-Farid said, speaking in the voice of the Muhammadan reality:

"Although I am the son of Adam in form,
I have in him a meaning that witnesses to my fatherhood."

The *lam* prefixed is the *lam* of communication (*lam al-tabligh*). "Al-Malaikah" (the angels) is the plural of *malak*, on the pattern of *shama'il* and *sham'al*, and it is a metathesis of *ma'lak*, an adjective in the form of a qualitative attribute according to al-Kisa'i. It is the preferred view of the majority, from *al-alukah*, which means "message." So they are messengers to people, and like messengers to them. It was said: there is no metathesis. Ibn Kaysan holds that it is *fa'al* from *malak* with an added *hamza*, because he possesses (*malik*) what God has given to him, or because of his strength, since the root (m-l-k) revolves around strength and firmness. One says: "I kneaded the dough" meaning he firmly kneaded it. This is a distant derivation, and *fa'al* is rare. Abu Ubayda holds that it is *maf'al* from *lak*, meaning he sent, a noun of place or a masdar in the *mim* form with the meaning of the passive participle, or a place name in intensive form. This is also a distant derivation, and *lak* is not well known. The verb *kanna* (to make a sort of reference) is widely used in this sense, meaning "be for me a messenger." This form does not occur otherwise, so consider it as having a *hamza* as its middle radical, and that its origin is *alakani*. Some made it hollow from *lak*, *yaluk*. The *ta'* (in *malaika*) is for the feminine of the plural. It was also said that it is for intensification. It was not made for the feminine of the word, as in *zulmah*, because they treat the notional feminine in every plural, saying: "every plural is feminine in the sense of a group." It has occurred without a *ta'* in the saying: "Abu Khalid, the angels have prayed for you."

People have disagreed about their reality, although they agree that they exist, either through transmission or reason. Most Muslims hold that they are luminous bodies. It is also said that they are airy beings, able to take various forms and appear in different shapes by God's permission. The Christians said they are the rational souls, separated (from matter), and that the pure and good ones are angels, while the evil ones among them are devils. The idolaters said they are these stars: the auspicious ones among them are angels of mercy, and the inauspicious ones are angels of punishment. The philosophers say they are pure immaterial substances, differing in reality from the rational souls. Some of them explicitly stated that they are the ten intellects and the celestial souls that move the spheres. According to us, they are divided into two kinds. One kind's concern is total absorption in the knowledge of the Truth and freedom from being occupied with anything else. They glorify (God) night and day without slackening. They are the *'illiyyun* and the angels brought near. The other kind manages the affair from the heaven to the earth according to what was decreed in advance and what the pen has written. They do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded. They are "those who arrange the affair" (al-mudabbirat amran). Among them are heavenly ones, and among them are earthly ones. None knows their number but God. In a report: "The heaven has creaked, and it has the right to creak. There is not a space of a foot in it but there is an angel prostrating or bowing." They differ in forms and vary in size. None sees them as they really are except the people of holy souls, and they may appear in bodies that both the elite and the common people can see, yet they remain as they are. It is said that Gabriel (peace be upon him), when he appeared in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi before the Chosen One (ﷺ), did not leave the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha). Something similar happens to the perfected among the saints. This is beyond the level of reason, and I am among the believers in it. The people of God, may God sanctify their secrets, have mentioned that the first manifestation of the Truth (may His majesty be exalted) is the cloud (al-'ama). When it was colored by light, He opened within it the forms of the awe-struck angels, who are above the world of natural bodies, and there was no throne, nor any creation, before them. When He brought them into existence, He manifested to them through His beautiful name, so they were dazzled in the splendour of His beauty, and they do not come to their senses. When He willed to create the world of recording and inscribing, He chose one of these, and he was the first angel to emerge from the angels of that light. He named him the Intellect and the Pen. He manifested to him in the locus of the bestowed teaching, with what He wished to bring into existence of His creation, without an end. He accepted with his essence the knowledge of what will be, and of what the Truth possesses of the divine names that seek the emergence of this created world. From this Intellect he derived what he called the Tablet, and He commanded the Pen to descend to it and to deposit in it what will be until the Day of Resurrection, and nothing else. He gave this knowledge three hundred and sixty teeth (sinn) from its being a pen, and from its being an intellect, three hundred and sixty manifestations, or subtle layers. Each tooth or subtle layer differs from the other three hundred and sixty categories of general sciences in their separation within the Tablet. The first science that came into being in it was the science of nature (al-tabi'ah), and it was below the soul. All of this is in the world of pure light. Then God (glory be to Him) brought into existence pure darkness, which is opposite to this light, like absolute non-existence opposite to absolute existence. He poured light upon it by an essential outpouring, with the help of nature, so that light gathered its scattered parts, and the Throne appeared. The name of the Merciful settled upon it, through the manifest name. It is the first thing that appeared from the world of creation. From that mixed light He created the angels who surround (the Throne), and they have no occupation except being around the Throne, glorifying Him with His praise. Then He brought into existence the Footstool (al-Kursi) within the inside of this Throne, and He placed in it angels of the kind of its nature. Each sphere is a root for what is created in it of its inhabitants, like the elements for what He created in them of their inhabitants. In this Footstool He divided the Word into information and wisdom, and these are the two feet which hung down to it from the Throne, as is related in the report. Then He created in the inside of the Footstool the spheres: one sphere within another sphere, and in each sphere He created a world of them that inhabit it. He adorned them with the stars, and He revealed in each heaven its command, until He created the forms of generated beings. He manifested to each kind of them according to what it is, so from that the spirits of the forms came into being, and He commanded them to manage them. He made them not divisible, but one essence, and He distinguished some of them from others, so they were distinguished. Their distinction was according to their reception of the forms from that manifestation. These forms in reality are like the manifestations of those spirits. Then God (glory be to Him) brought into being the sensible, imaginal bodily forms by another manifestation, and He gave each of the spirits and forms a nourishment suitable to it. The Truth (glory be to Him) continues to create angels from the breaths of the world, as long as they breathe. Glory be to Him who says to a thing "Be," and it is.

When you know this, know that they differed about the angels to whom it was said. It was said: all of them, because of the generality of the wording and the absence of a specifier, so it includes the awe-struck and others. It was said: the angels of the earth, by the indication that the discourse concerns the successorship on earth. It was said: Iblis and those who were with him in fighting the jinn, who were settled on earth for a long time and then corrupted. God sent against them a host of angels, who were also called the jinn, and they were the guardians of Paradise, and the name was derived from it. They drove them out to the mountain ranges and the islands. What the Sufi masters, may God sanctify their secrets, hold is that those other than the two worlds (the world of the spirits and the world of the bodies) who had been entrusted with some of God's names and attributes, and that the two worlds are not included in the address, nor commanded to prostrate, because of their total absorption and their lack of awareness of anything but the Essence. The word of God the Exalted, "Have you become proud, or were you among the exalted?" points to that according to them. They counted among those the angel called the Spirit, the Supreme Pen, and the First Intellect, who is the mirror of His own Essence (exalted is He), so He does not manifest in His Essence except in this angel, and His manifestation in all created things is only through His attributes. He is the pole of the worldly and the otherworldly world, and the pole of the people of Paradise and Hell, and the people of the dune and the heights. There is nothing except that this angel has a face in it, and that creature revolves around his face, so he is its pole. He knew the creation of Adam and his rank, for he is the one who inscribed in the Tablet what was and what will be. The Tablet knew with the knowledge of taste what the Pen had inscribed in it. This angel has appeared in his perfection in the Muhammadan reality, as is indicated by the word of God the Exalted: "And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command." For this reason he (ﷺ) was the best of God's creation without any qualification, and indeed he is the true successor in the seven layers. This is not far-fetched, so understand.

(wa-jā‘ilun) is an active participle from al-ja‘l (making), in the sense of al-tasyir (rendering/making into), so it takes two objects. The first here is khalifah (vicegerent), and the second is fi al-ardi (on the earth). Or it may be in the sense of al-khalq (creating), in which case it takes one object, so fi al-ardi is attached to khalifah. It is placed first for suspense (li-l-tashwiq), and the adjectival form operates because it has the sense of the future, and it relies on a subject it refers to. Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr) preferred that it means al-khalq, because of what is in opposition to it. In the sense of al-tasyir, it requires mention of khalifah or its implied presence. By "the earth" is meant either all of it, which is the apparent meaning and what the majority hold, or the land of Makkah. This has been related as a marfu‘ report, but the apparent view is that it is not authentic, since otherwise one would not have turned away from it. Allah, glorified is He, singled out the earth because it belongs to the world of change and transformations, so the rule of all the Divine Names which the Truth sought to manifest through them becomes apparent in it through the rule of vicegerency, unlike the higher world. A khalifah is one who succeeds another and acts on his behalf. The ha’ is for emphasis (al-mubalaghah), which is why it is applied to the masculine. The well-known view is that what is meant by it is Adam, peace be upon him, which accords with the narration, with the singular wording, and with the context. The attribution of the shedding of blood and corruption to him at that time is by way of causation (bi-tariq al-tasabbub). Or what is meant by "one who will cause corruption" is one who possesses the capacity for that. The meaning of his being a khalifah is that he is the vicegerent of Allah, exalted is He, on His earth; and likewise every prophet whom He appointed as successors for the cultivation of the earth, the governance of people, the perfecting of their souls, and the execution of His command among them, not because He has any need, but because of the deficiency of the one appointed over it, since he is in extreme density and bodily darkness, while the Essence of Allah, exalted is He, is in extreme holiness. Affinity is a condition for accepting the overflow, according to the customary Divine practice, so there must be an intermediary possessing two aspects: detachment (tajarrud) and attachment (ta‘alluq), so that he receives from one side and emanates to another. It has been said: he and his offspring, peace be upon him. The apparent wording of the angels' statement supports this. Their being held to account at that time for displaying Adam's superiority over them is because he is the origin that the rest follow, just as mention of the father of a tribe suffices without mentioning them; except that mention of the father is by his proper name, whereas here it is by a descriptive attribute. The meaning of their being khulafa’ (successors) is that they succeed those before them among the jinn, the Banu al-Jann, or succeed Iblis and those with him among the angels who were sent to fight those, as the reports have stated; or that some of them succeed others. According to the people of Allah, exalted is He, what is meant by khalifah is Adam, peace be upon him, who is the vicegerent of Allah, exalted is He, the father of the successors, the one who manifests Him, glorified is He and exalted, and the one who combines the two attributes of His beauty and majesty. For this reason both hands were gathered for him, and both are right hands. There is no existent who encompasses the Truth other than him. From here the greatest vicegerent, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, said: "Allah, exalted is He, created Adam in His form, or in the form of the Most Merciful." By him opposites are combined, creation is perfected, and the Truth becomes manifest. That vicegerency remains in the Perfect Human until the Hour is established and at the moment of its establishment; indeed, whenever this human departs from the world, the world dies, for he is the spirit by which its existence is sustained. He is the spiritual pillar of the heavens, and the lower abode is a limb of the limbs of the body of the world whose spirit is the human. Since this comprehensive Name confronted the two presences with its essence, vicegerency and the governing of the world became valid for him, and Allah, glorified is He, is the Doer of what He wills, and there is no true doer besides Him. In this station there is narrowness, and the deniers are many, and there is no help except from Allah, mighty and majestic. The benefit of His saying, exalted is He, this to the angels is to teach consultation, since this dealing resembles it, or to magnify the status of the one appointed and to manifest his excellence. It is also possible that Allah, glorified is He, intended by this to make Adam, peace be upon him, known to them, so that they would recognize his worth, because he is hidden from the cosmic form by what he possesses of the Divine form, and what he knows by reason of his inwardness is from the higher assembly, except for the Preserved Tablet and the Pen. This statement, as mentioned by al-Shaykh al-Akbar, may his secret be sanctified, was in the state of the Spike (dawlat al-sunbulah), after seventeen thousand years had passed from the age of this world, and from the age of the Hereafter, which has no end in its permanence, eight thousand years, and from the age of the natural world, which is measured by time bounded by place, seventy-one thousand years of the known years, whose days come from the revolution of the First Sphere, which is one and a fifth days of the days of Dhu al-Ma‘arij. To Allah, exalted is He, belongs the command, before and after. Zayd ibn ‘Ali read (khalifatan)... 

[Note: the reading attributed to Zayd ibn ‘Ali is khaliqatan, with the qaf, and its meaning is clear: ﴿Said they: Wilt Thou place therein one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?﴾ This is a request for disclosure of the hidden wisdom and of what removes doubt, and it is not a question about the act of appointing and succession itself, since they already knew it beforehand. What is asked about is the appointing, but not in regard to its essence; rather in regard to its wisdom and to what removes its doubt. Or it is an expression of wonder that one who will cause corruption should be appointed to cultivate and reform the earth, or that one like them should be appointed in place of the people of corruption, or that the people of disobedience should be appointed in place of the people of obedience. It has been said that it is a pure interrogative from which the counterpart is omitted, meaning: "Wilt Thou place therein one who will corrupt, or wilt Thou place one who will not corrupt?" Some have taken it as a circumstantial clause: "Wilt Thou place therein such-and-such, while we glorify Thee with Thy praise, or do we change?" This was chosen by our shaykh 'Ala' al-Din al-Mawsili, may Allah refresh his spirit, but courtesy restrains me from speaking of it. In any case the hamzah is not for denial, as the Hashwiyyah claimed, citing the verse as evidence that the angels are not infallible because they objected to Allah, exalted is He, and disparaged the children of Adam. It is strange that Mawla al-Sha‘rani, who is among the great people of Sunnah and even among the shaykhs of the people of Allah, transmitted from his shaykh al-Khawwas that he restricted infallibility to the angels of the heavens, giving as reason that they are pure intellects without contention or desire, and said that the earthly angels are not infallible, which is why Iblis fell into what he fell into, since he was one of the angels of the earth dwelling on the mountain of ruby in the east at the line of the equator. Accordingly, objection is not far-fetched from one who was on the earth, and Allah is our refuge. It finds support in what is related in some reports, that those who spoke were ten thousand, and fire descended upon them and burned them; but in my view that is not sound. It has also been said that the speaker was Iblis, who at that time was counted among the angels, and the attribution of the speech to them is in the manner of "the Banu so-and-so killed so-and-so," where the killer is one of them. The correct view is what we have established. The repetition of the adverbial phrase (fiha) is to indicate excess in corruption; they did not repeat it afterward, being content with the first, together with what repetition carries that is not hidden. (Al-Safk) means pouring and shedding, and it is used only for blood, or for blood and tears. The conjunction is of the specific over the general, to indicate the gravity of this disobedience, for by it the bodily structures are dissolved. (Al-dima') is the plural of dam, whose final radical is either ya’ or waw; both its short and doubled forms are attested. Its original pattern is fa‘l or fa‘al. What is meant by it is the forbidden kind, by the indication of context. It has been said that it is general, encompassing all its kinds, lawful and unlawful, and the intent is that he does not distinguish among them. Ibn Abi ‘Ablah read (yasfuku) with a damma on the fa’; (yusfiku) is from asfaka; and with doubling it is from safaka. Ibn Hurmuz read with a fatha on the kaf, and this is explained as a fatha in answer to the interrogative. It was also read in the passive voice, and the returning pronoun to "man" then is the same whether it is taken as a relative pronoun or as a qualifying noun.

مَحْذُوفٌ، أي فِيهِمْ. وحُكْمُ المَلائِكَةِ بِالإفْسادِ والسَّفْكِ عَلى الإنْسانِ بِناءً عَلى بَعْضِ تِلْكَ الوُجُوهِ لَيْسَ مِنِ ادِّعاءِ عِلْمِ الغَيْبِ أوِ الحُكْمِ بِالظَّنِّ والتَّخْمِينِ، وإنَّما هو بِإخْبارٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ تَعالى. ولَمْ يَقُصَّ عَلَيْنا ذَلِكَ فِيما حَكاهُ عَنْهُمُ اكْتِفاءً بِدِلالَةِ الجَوابِ عَلَيْهِ لِلْإيجازِ، كَما هِيَ عادَةُ القُرْآنِ. ويُؤَيِّدُ ذَلِكَ ما رُوِيَ في بَعْضِ الآثارِ: أنَّهُ لَمّا قالَ اللَّهُ تَعالى ذَلِكَ قالُوا: وما يَكُونُ مِن ذَلِكَ الخَلِيفَةِ؟ قالَ: «تَكُونُ لَهُ ذُرِّيَّةٌ يُفْسِدُونَ في الأرْضِ، ويَقْتُلُ بَعْضُهم بَعْضًا»، فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ قالُوا: ﴿رَبَّنا أتَجْعَلُ فِيها مَن يُفْسِدُ فِيها ويَسْفِكُ الدِّماءَ﴾. وقِيلَ: عَرَفُوا ذَلِكَ مِنَ اللَّوْحِ، ويُبْعِدُهُ عَدَمُ عِلْمِهِمْ بِالجَوابِ، ويَحْتاجُ الجَوابُ إلى تَكَلُّفٍ. وقِيلَ: عَرَفُوهُ اسْتِنْباطًا مِمّا رَكَزَ في عُقُولِهِمْ مِن عَدَمِ عِصْمَةِ غَيْرِهِمْ، المُفْضِي إلى العِلْمِ بِصُدُورِ المَعْصِيَةِ عَمَّنْ عَداهُمْ، المُفْضِي إلى التَّنازُعِ والتَّشاجُرِ، إذْ مَن لا يَرْحَمُ نَفْسَهُ لا يَرْحَمُ غَيْرَهُ، وذَلِكَ يُفْضِي إلى الفَسادِ وسَفْكِ الدِّماءِ. وقِيلَ: قِياسًا لِأحَدِ الثَّقَلَيْنِ (الإنْسِ والجِنِّ) عَلى الآخَرِ، بِجامِعِ اشْتِراكِهِما في عَدَمِ العِصْمَةِ، ولا يَخْفى ما في القَوْلَيْنِ. ويُحْتَمَلُ أنَّهُمْ عَلِمُوا ذَلِكَ مِن تَسْمِيَتِهِ خَلِيفَةً، لِأنَّ الخِلافَةَ تَقْتَضِي الإصْلاحَ وقَهْرَ المُسْتَخْلَفِ عَلَيْهِ، وهُوَ يَسْتَلْزِمُ أنْ يَصْدُرَ مِنْهُ فَسادٌ، إمّا في ذاتِهِ بِمُقْتَضى الشَّهْوَةِ، أوْ في غَيْرِهِ مِنَ السَّفْكِ. أوْ لِأنَّها مَجْلى الجَلالِ كَما أنَّها مَجْلى الجَمالِ، ولِكُلٍّ آثارٌ، والإفْسادُ والسَّفْكُ مِن آثارِ الجَلالِ، وسَكَتُوا عَنْ آثارِ الجَمالِ إذْ لا غَرابَةَ فِيها. وهُمْ عَلى كُلِّ تَقْدِيرٍ ما قَدَرُوا اللَّهَ تَعالى حَقَّ قَدْرِهِ، ولا يُخِلُّ ذَلِكَ بِهِمْ، ﴿فَوْقَ كُلِّ ذِي عِلْمٍ عَلِيمٌ﴾.

﴿ونَحْنُ نُسَبِّحُ بِحَمْدِكَ ونُقَدِّسُ لَكَ﴾: "ونحن" حالٌ مِن ضَمِيرِ الفاعِلِ في ﴿أتَجْعَلُ﴾، وفِيها تَقْرِيرٌ لِجِهَةِ الإشْكالِ، والمَعْنى: تَسْتَخْلِفُ مَن ذُكِرَ ونَحْنُ المَعْصُومُونَ. ولَيْسَ المَقْصُودُ إلّا الِاسْتِفْسارَ عَنِ المُرَجِّحِ، لا العَجَبَ والتَّفاخُرَ، حَتّى يَضُرَّ بِعِصْمَتِهِمْ، كَما زَعَمَتِ الحَشْوِيَّةُ (طائفةٌ تُنْسَبُ إلى الحَرْفِيَّةِ والتَّشْبِيهِ في الصِّفاتِ). ولُزُومُ الضَّمِيرِ، وتَرْكُ الواوِ في الجُمْلَةِ الِاسْمِيَّةِ إذا وقَعَتْ حالًا مُؤَكِّدَةً، غَيْرُ مُسَلَّمٍ، كَما في شَرْحِ التَّسْهِيلِ. وصِيغَةُ المُضارِعِ لِلِاسْتِمْرارِ، وتَقْدِيمُ المُسْنَدِ إلَيْهِ عَلى المُسْنَدِ الفِعْلِيِّ لِلِاخْتِصاصِ. ومِنَ الغَرِيبِ جَعْلُ الجُمْلَةِ اسْتِفْهامِيَّةً حُذِفَ مِنها الأداةُ، وكَذا المُعادِلُ. والتَّسْبِيحُ في الأصْلِ مُطْلَقُ التَّبْعِيدِ، والمُرادُ بِهِ تَبْعِيدُ اللَّهِ تَعالى عَنِ السُّوءِ، وهُوَ مُتَعَدٍّ بِنَفْسِهِ، ويُعَدّى بِاللّامِ إشْعارًا بِأنَّ إيقاعَ الفِعْلِ لِأجْلِ اللَّهِ تَعالى، وخالِصًا لِوَجْهِهِ سُبْحانَهُ. فالمَفْعُولُ المُقَدَّرُ ها هُنا يُمْكِنُ أنْ يَكُونَ بِاللّامِ عَلى وفْقِ قَرِينَةٍ، وأنْ يَكُونَ بِدُونِهِ كَما هُوَ أصْلُهُ. (وبِحَمْدِكَ) في مَوْضِعِ الحالِ، والباءُ لِاسْتِدامَةِ الصُّحْبَةِ والمَعِيَّةِ. وإضافَةُ الحَمْدِ إمّا إلى الفاعِلِ، والمُرادُ لازِمُهُ مَجازًا مِنَ التَّوْفِيقِ والهِدايَةِ، أوْ إلى المَفْعُولِ، أيْ مُتَلَبِّسِينَ بِحَمْدِنا لَكَ عَلى ما وفَّقْتَنا لِتَسْبِيحِكَ. وفي ذَلِكَ نَفْيُ ما يُوهِمُهُ الإسْنادُ مِنَ العَجَبِ. وقِيلَ: المُرادُ بِهِ تَسْبِيحٌ خاصٌّ، وهُوَ: سُبْحانَ ذِي المُلْكِ والمَلَكُوتِ، سُبْحانَ ذِي العَظَمَةِ والجَبَرُوتِ، سُبْحانَ الحَيِّ الَّذِي لا يَمُوتُ، ويُعْرَفُ هَذا بِتَسْبِيحِ المَلائِكَةِ، أوْ: سُبْحانَ اللَّهِ وبِحَمْدِهِ.

وفي حَدِيثٍ عَنْ عُبادَةَ بْنِ الصّامِتِ عَنْ أبِي ذَرٍّ: «أنَّ النَّبِيَّ (ﷺ) سُئِلَ: أيُّ الكَلامِ أفْضَلُ؟ قالَ: (ما اصْطَفى اللَّهُ تَعالى لِمَلائِكَتِهِ، أوْ لِعِبادِهِ، سُبْحانَ اللَّهِ وبِحَمْدِهِ)»، أيْ: وبِحَمْدِهِ نُسَبِّحُ. والتَّقْدِيسُ في المَشْهُورِ كالتَّسْبِيحِ مَعْنًى، واحْتاجُوا لِدَفْعِ التَّكْرارِ إلى أنَّ أحَدَهُما بِاعْتِبارِ الطّاعاتِ، والآخَرَ بِاعْتِبارِ الِاعْتِقاداتِ. وقِيلَ: التَّسْبِيحُ تَنْزِيهُهُ تَعالى عَمّا لا يَلِيقُ بِهِ، والتَّقْدِيسُ تَنْزِيهُهُ في ذاتِهِ عَمّا لا يَراهُ لائِقًا بِنَفْسِهِ، فَهُوَ أبْلَغُ، ويَشْهَدُ لَهُ أنَّهُ حَيْثُ جُمِعَ بَيْنَهُما أُخِّرَ، نَحْوُ: سَبُّوحٍ قُدُّوسٍ. ويُحْتَمَلُ أنْ يَكُونَ بِمَعْنى التَّطْهِيرِ، والمُرادُ: نُسَبِّحُكَ ونُطَهِّرُ أنْفُسَنا مِنَ الأدْناسِ، أوْ أفْعالَنا مِنَ المَعاصِي، فَلا نَفْعَلُ فِعْلَهُمْ مِنَ الإفْسادِ والسَّفْكِ، أوْ نُطَهِّرُ قُلُوبَنا عَنِ الِالتِفاتِ إلى غَيْرِكَ. ولامُ (لَكَ) إمّا لِلْعِلَّةِ مُتَعَلِّقٌ بِـ(نُقَدِّسُ)، والحَمْلُ عَلى التَّنازُعِ مِمّا فِيهِ تَنازُعٌ، أوْ مُعَدِّيَةٌ لِلْفِعْلِ كَما في: سَجَدْتُ لِلَّهِ تَعالى، أوْ لِلْبَيانِ كَما في ﴿سَفَهًا لَكَ﴾، فَمُتَعَلِّقُها حِينَئِذٍ خَبَرُ مُبْتَدَإٍ مَحْذُوفٍ، أوْ زائِدَةٌ، والمَفْعُولُ هُوَ المَجْرُورُ.

ثُمَّ الظّاهِرُ أنَّ قائِلَ هَذِهِ الجُمْلَةِ هُوَ قائِلُ الجُمْلَةِ الأُولى. وأغْرَبَ الشَّيْخُ
[صفحة 223]
صَفِيُّ الدِّينِ الخَزْرَجِيُّ في كِتابِهِ (فَكُّ الأزْرارِ)، فَجَعَلَ القائِلَ مُخْتَلِفًا، وبَيَّنَ ذَلِكَ بِأنَّ المَلائِكَةَ كانُوا حِينَ وُرُودِ الخِطابِ عَلَيْهِمْ مُجْمَلِينَ، وكانَ إبْلِيسُ مُنْدَرِجًا في جُمْلَتِهِمْ، فَوَرَدَ الجَوابُ مِنْهُمْ مُجْمَلًا، فَلَمّا انْفَصَلَ إبْلِيسُ عَنْ جُمْلَتِهِمْ بِإبائِهِ، انْفَصَلَ الجَوابُ إلى نَوْعَيْنِ: فَنَوْعٌ الِاعْتِراضُ مِنْهُ، ونَوْعٌ التَّسْبِيحُ والتَّقْدِيسُ مِمَّنْ عَداهُ، فانْقَسَمَ الجَوابُ إلى قِسْمَيْنِ، كانْقِسامِ الجِنْسِ إلى جِنْسَيْنِ، وناسَبَ كُلُّ جَوابٍ مَن ظَهَرَ عَنْهُ. فالكَلامُ شَبِيهٌ بِقَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿وقالُوا كُونُوا هُودًا أوْ نَصارى تَهْتَدُوا﴾، وهُوَ تَأْوِيلٌ لا تَفْسِيرٌ.

﴿قالَ إنِّي أعْلَمُ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾: أيْ أعْلَمُ مِنَ الحِكَمِ في ذَلِكَ ما أنْتُمْ بِمَعْزِلٍ عَنْهُ. وقِيلَ: أرادَ بِذَلِكَ عِلْمَهُ بِمَعْصِيَةِ إبْلِيسَ، وطاعَةِ آدَمَ. وقِيلَ: بِأنَّهُ سَيَكُونُ مِن ذَلِكَ الخَلِيفَةِ أنْبِياءُ وصالِحُونَ. وقِيلَ: الأحْسَنُ أنْ يُفَسَّرَ هَذا المُبْهَمُ بِما أخْبَرَ بِهِ تَعالى عَنْهُ بِقَوْلِهِ سُبْحانَهُ: ﴿إنِّي أعْلَمُ غَيْبَ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾.

ويُفْهَمُ مِن كَلامِ القَوْمِ، قَدَّسَ اللَّهُ تَعالى أسْرارَهُمْ، أنَّ المُرادَ مِنَ الآيَةِ بَيانُ الحِكْمَةِ في الخِلافَةِ عَلى أدَقِّ وجْهٍ وأكْمَلِهِ، فَكَأنَّهُ قالَ جَلَّ شَأْنُهُ: أُرِيدُ الظُّهُورَ بِأسْمائِي وصِفاتِي، ولَمْ يَكْمُلْ ذَلِكَ بِخَلْقِكُمْ، فَإنِّي أعْلَمُ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَهُ، لِقُصُورِ اسْتِعْدادِكُمْ، ونُقْصانِ قابِلِيَّتِكُمْ، فَلا تَصْلُحُونَ لِظُهُورِ جَمِيعِ الأسْماءِ والصِّفاتِ فِيكُمْ، فَلا تَتِمُّ بِكُمْ مَعْرِفَتِي، ولا يَظْهَرُ عَلَيْكُمْ كَنْزِي، فَلا بُدَّ مِن إظْهارِ مَن تَمَّ اسْتِعْدادُهُ، وكَمُلَتْ قابِلِيَّتُهُ، لِيَكُونَ مَجْلًى لِي، ومِرْآةً لِأسْمائِي وصِفاتِي، ومَظْهَرًا لِلْمُتَقابِلاتِ فِيَّ، ومَظْهَرًا لِما خَفِيَ عِنْدِي، وبِي يَسْمَعُ، وبِي يُبْصِرُ، وبِي وبِي، وبَعْدَ ذاكَ يَرِقُّ الزُّجاجُ والخَمْرُ، وإلى اللَّهِ عَزَّ شَأْنُهُ يَرْجِعُ الأمْرُ.

(وأعْلَمُ) فِعْلٌ مُضارِعٌ، واحْتِمالُ أنَّهُ أفْعَلُ تَفْضِيلٍ مِمّا لا يَنْبَغِي أنْ يُخَرَّجَ عَلَيْهِ كِتابُ اللَّهِ سُبْحانَهُ، كَما لا يَخْفى.

This passage is a lengthy classical commentary with many citations and technical discussions. I'll translate it in full, following the rules you specified.

"And He taught Adam the names, all of them" (﴿وعَلَّمَ آدَمَ الأسْماءَ كُلَّها﴾) is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "He said" (qāla). It confirms the content of what came before. The apparent beginning with the narration of the teaching indicates that the preceding dialogue took place after Adam's creation, in his presence, such that it was said, immediately after the breathing of the spirit into him: "Indeed, I am placing him as a khalīfah (vicegerent)." Thus it is prior to what was said. It has also been said that it is conjoined to something omitted, meaning: "So He created and taught," or "So He created him, fashioned him, breathed into him the spirit, and taught," or "So He placed on earth a khalīfah and taught." The highlighting of Adam's name (peace be upon him) serves to specify him and to draw attention by mentioning him.

(Ādam) Al-Jawālīqī and many others stated explicitly that it is Arabic, and its pattern is afʿal, from al-udmah (with a ḍammah and then a sukūn), meaning brownness (al-sumrah). How beautiful is it in some [contexts]. Some explained it as whiteness. Or from al-adamah (with two fatḥahs), meaning model and exemplar. Or from adīm al-arḍ (the surface of the earth), meaning what appeared of it. Aḥmad and al-Tirmidhī narrated, and more than one scholar declared it sound, that God, exalted is He, took a handful from all of the earth, its plain and its rough, and created Adam from it. Therefore his descendants come in varied temperaments. Or it is from al-udm or al-udmah, meaning agreement and harmony. Its original form is ʾĀdam, with two hamzahs; the second was changed to an alif because it was quiescent after a fatḥah. It is not declined because of its being a proper noun and its resembling a verb's pattern. It has also been said that it is non-Arabic, and its pattern is fāʿal with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, and this is common in names, such as Shālikh and Āzar. What supports this is its plural on awādim with a waw, not āʾadim with a hamzah; likewise its diminutive is ʾUwaydim, not ʾUʾaydim. Al-Jawharī excused this by saying that the hamzah has no known root in word formation, so the waw was made the predominant letter in its place. They did not accept this from him. In that case, derivation (ishtiqāq) does not apply to it, because it is from that language, which we do not know, and from other languages it is not valid, and correspondence between languages is remote. If it is mentioned in this regard, that is to indicate that after arabization it has been attached to their speech. It is a presumed derivation (ishtiqāq taqdīrī) which they considered in order to know the pattern and the extra letter in it, from elsewhere. Whoever applied it to it in reality is like one who combined the ḍabb and the nūn. Perhaps this is closer to the correct view.

"The names" (al-asmāʾ) is the plural of ism, and by derivation it is that which is a sign for a thing and an indicator that raises it to the mind, from the words established in all languages, and attributes, and actions. By convention it is used for what is established for a meaning, whether singular or compound, as a subject or a predicate, or as a link between them. Both meanings are possible. Knowledge of single and compound words, whether in a declarative or imperative construction, entails knowledge of the conceptual and assentive meanings. Intending the technical meaning (al-maʿnā al-muṣṭalaḥ) is not suitable, since its occurrence would be after the Qur'an.

al-Imām (Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī) said: the intended meaning of "names" is the attributes of things, their descriptions and properties, because they are signs indicating their quiddities, so it is permissible to express them by "names." In this, as al-Shihāb said, there is scrutiny, since the use of "ism" for such is not known, to the point that the verse is interpreted by it. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the names of what was and what will be until the Day of Resurrection, and this is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It has been said: the languages. It has been said: the names of the angels. It has been said: the names of the stars. al-Ḥakīm al-Tirmidhī said: the names of Allah, exalted is He. It has been said, and it has been said, and it has been said. The truth in my view is what the People of Allah, exalted is He, hold, and it is what the rank of khilāfah that you know requires: that they are the names of things, heavenly and earthly, substantial or accidental. They are called, in their view, the names of Allah, exalted is He, by consideration of their indication of Him, and His manifestation in them is not restricted to them. For this reason they said: the names of Allah, exalted is He, are infinite, since there is nothing that emerges into existence from the treasures of generosity except that it is one of His names, exalted is He, and a mode of His modes, glorified is His majesty. He is the First, the Last, the Outward, and the Inward. Hence, may His secret be sanctified, said:

"Indeed existence, though it multiplies outwardly, and your life, there is nothing in it except you."

But for distinction there is a station, and for unity there is a station, and for every station there is a statement. Were it not for the degrees, the names and attributes would be void. Their teaching to him (peace be upon him), according to this, is the manifestation of the Truth, exalted and most high, in him, transcendent above incarnation, union, and resemblance, with all His names and His opposing attributes, according to his comprehensive receptivity, such that he knew the face of the Truth in those things, knew what they contained, and understood what they indicated, so that no hidden thing was concealed from him and no secret of theirs remained unknown. Wonderful! How this small body contained this abundant knowledge!

The formalist scholars differed among themselves regarding the manner of teaching, after it was explained as an act which normally results in knowledge, and after the attainment of what it depends upon on the part of the learner, such as his readiness to receive the overflow, and its reception from the teacher, without any failure. It was said: by Him creating in him (peace be upon him), according to his readiness, a necessary detailed knowledge of those names, their referents, their indication, and the mode of their indication. It was said: by His creating him from differing parts and diverse faculties, prepared to perceive kinds of perceptibles, and inspiring him with knowledge of the essences of things, their names, their properties, their realities, the foundations of knowledge, the rules of crafts, the details of their tools, and the modes of their use. In that case, the preceding dialogue would be before his creation (peace be upon him). As for the saying that the teaching was literal, and occurred through an angel who was not included in the general address with "Inform me" (anbiʾūnī), I do not accept it, unless a report about it is sound. Yet I say: the report has a meaning other than what is immediately apparent, which is not hidden from one who has taste. It has also been said: other than that.

Then this teaching does not require the prior existence of a conventional language, as Abū Hāshim claimed, and he argued for it with arguments that were refuted in the Great Commentary (al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr), since if it required that, it would lead to an infinite regress or circularity. Al-Imām al-Ashʿarī uses this verse to show that the one who originated all languages is Allah, exalted is He, initially, and it is permissible that some conventions arise from humans, as a man establishes the knowledge of his son. The Muʿtazilah say: the originator from humans is Adam or another, and this is called the doctrine of convention. It has been said: Allah, exalted is He, originated some of them, and humans originated the rest, and this is the doctrine of distribution, and al-Ustādh held this. The matter is detailed with its evidences, and what is for and against it, in the principles of jurisprudence.

Al-Yamānī read "wa-ʿullima" (passive). In al-Baḥr it is stated that the doubling is for transitivity, and it is by transmission (samāʿiyyah) with it; it has been said it is analogical (qiyāsiyyah). Al-Ḥarīrī in the commentary on his Lamḥah claims that ʿalima, transitive to two objects, may be transitive to three, and he erred in that.
