"Then He presented them to the angels" (thumma ʿaraḍahum ʿalā al-malāʾikah): that is, the named things understood from the speech. The masculine pronoun, according to some aspects, is for giving precedence to the rational beings included among them, and for honour by treating them as such in one opinion, and the others as the remainder. It has been said: the pronoun refers to the names, by way of metonymy in the manner of istikhdām. Whoever says "the name is the named" says: the names are the named, and the pronoun refers to them without strain, and this was the view of Makkī and al-Mahdawī. It is refuted by the fact that "Inform me of the names of these" indicates that the presentation is for asking about the names of the presented things, not about themselves; otherwise it would say "Inform me of these," so the presented must be other than what is asked about, and thus it is not the names themselves. The meaning of presenting the named things is making them present to the hearts of the angels, or displaying them to them like particles, or informing them of what He will bring into existence of rational and other beings, in summary, and asking them about what they need of knowledge and crafts by which the order of their livelihood and their return is established, also in summary. Otherwise, preference cannot be known except by the Subtle, the All-Aware. It is as if He, glorified is He, said: "I will create such and such; so inform Me what is for them and what is against them." As for the names of those kinds, it is like the saying "I presented my matter to so-and-so, and he said to me such-and-such." It is not objected that the named things, according to some, are entities and meanings, and how are meanings presented, such as joy, sadness, ignorance, and knowledge? In my view, presenting the named things to them may mean their being informed of the scientific forms and fixed entities, which some of Allah's solitary servants come to know in this life, or the manifestation of that to them in a world in which meanings are embodied. This is not impossible for Allah, exalted is He. Indeed, meanings are now formed in the world of malakūt, such that whoever sees them sees them, and one who has comprehensive knowledge of the world of imagination does not find that unlikely. It has also been said: they witnessed those named things in Adam (peace be upon him), and that is what is meant by presenting them.

"And you claim that you are a small body, / and within you the greater world is folded."

Ubayy read "thumma ʿaraḍahā" and ʿAbd Allāh read "ʿaraḍahunna." The meaning is: he presented their named things, or their named things (of those kinds). It has been said: there is no estimated object.

"He said: Inform Me of the names of these" (faqāla anbiʾūnī bi-asmāʾi hāʾulāʾ): a challenge to them. It is not a case of imposing what cannot be borne, as is wrongly supposed. In it is an indication that the matter of khilāfah, disposal, management, and establishing justice, without standing upon the degrees of readiness and the measures of rights, is something that can hardly be achieved. How then would one aspire to khilāfah who does not know that, or who does not know the very words? Far, far off is that, further than al-ʿAyyūq, and rarer than the eggs of the female crow. In my view, the intent is to show their incapacity and the deficiency of their readiness for the rank of khilāfah that comprises the outward and the inward, by commanding them to inform about those names in the manner that was intended. One incapable of informing itself is even more incapable of the required adornment in that noble office.

"How is the reaching of Suʿād, when beyond her / are the summits of mountains, and beyond them are deaths?
The foot is bare, and I have no mount, / and the hand is empty, and the road is fearful."

Informing (al-inbāʾ), in origin, is general information, and this is the apparent meaning here. It is also used for informing about something that has great benefit and produces knowledge or a predominant supposition. Some said: it is informing that includes making known, and for this reason it takes the place of each of the two. I prefer it here, as has been said, to indicate the elevation of the rank of the names and the greatness of their importance. This is based on the view that "naba'" is used only for a weighty report and a great matter. And in the use of "thumma" for what preceded, and "fa" here, is what is not hidden of the concern for Adam's rank (peace be upon him), and its absence in their case.

Al-Aʿmash read "anbiʾūnī" without a hamzah. "If you are truthful" (in kuntum ṣādiqīn): that is, in what has crossed your minds, that I will not create a creation except that you are more knowledgeable than it and more excellent. This is the transmitted explanation, for Ibn Jarīr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the angels said: "Allah will not create a creation more honoured by Him than us, nor more knowledgeable." And in the speech there is an indication of this, for their saying "and we glorify [You]..." indicates their superiority, and the glorification of Allah, exalted is He, or their glorifying themselves, also indicates perfection of knowledge. It has also been said: the meaning is: if you are truthful in your claim that you are more deserving of succession, or in your claim that their succession is not fitting, then establish it by demonstrating what you possess of the prior conditions. This is not at all disobedience, because it was a doubt that arose, and they asked about what would remove it, and it was not by their choice, and there is no objection to

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 31 (part 2 of 2):

That truthfulness and falsehood apply only to a statement (khabar), and they [the angels] were asked, not informed. For we say: both of them (truth and falsehood) extend to performative utterances (insha'at) secondarily (bi'l-qasd al-thani), by way of what their signification necessarily entails, even though they do not extend to them primarily (bi'l-qasd al-awwal), and by way of their explicit wording (manthuq).

The answer (jawab) of (in) in such a context is elided according to Sibawayh and the majority of the Basran grammarians; what indicates it is the preceding phrase, which here is (anbi'uni, "inform me"). According to the Kufans, and Abu Zayd and al-Mubarrad, the answer is the element that comes first. This is the correct transmission from those mentioned in the question, and some have erred and reversed the matter. As for one who claims that (in) here carries the meaning of the temporal (idha) and therefore needs no answer, he has erred. It seems that when he saw the infallibility of the angels, and supposed that the verse contained something that would undermine it, and found no interpretation for it while keeping (in) in its literal sense, he was compelled to this. Praise be to God, Most High, who has enriched us with His grace and did not make us in need of this, nor of the view that the purpose of the conditional is emphasis, to alert them to their deficiency and incapacity. The sense then becomes: "Inform me, and say nothing but the truth," as the Imam said.

﴿They said, "Glory be to You! We have no knowledge except what You have taught us."﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf, a sentence that answers an implied question) that stands in the place of a reply, as if it were said: "What did they say at that time? Did they fulfil the duty they were charged with, or not?" So it was said: "They said," and so on. Many scholars have mentioned that when clauses introduced by "said" are arranged in sequence in meaning, the more correct view is that no particle is used between them, since the meaning-based sequence is sufficient. Much of this occurs in Surat al-Shu'ara', and indeed the Qur'an is full of it.

(Subhana) has been said to be a verbal noun (masdar) whose verb is sabaha, in its lightened form, meaning "to declare far above (tanzih)." It is hardly ever used except in the genitive construction, either with the object or with the subject, and it is in the accusative by an obligatory implied verb. His statement:

"Glory be to Him, then glory, which we seek refuge in, and before us al-Judi and al-Jamad glorified."

is anomalous, like his statement: "Glory be to You, O Allah, Lord of Glory." Al-Kisa'i claimed that its occurrence as a vocative is valid, but he has no proof for this. A group of scholars held that it is a proper noun for the act of glorifying, meaning declaring God far above, and not the verbal noun of sabbaha meaning "to say," as in "Glory be to Allah," lest circularity arise, and because what is signified by that is a word, whereas what is signified by this is a meaning. This view is supported by his statement:

"When his boasting came to me I said: 'Glory be to Alqama al-Fakhir!'"

For if it were a proper noun, it would have to be unexpressed (not take nunation), since the alif and nun in non-adjectives prevent declension only together with being a proper noun. It is answered that in "subhana" there is an omitted genitive complement, that is, "Glory be to Allah," which is intended because it is known, and the governing noun is kept in its state out of regard for its most common condition, which is being free of nunation. It is also said that "min" is extra and the annexation to what follows is for mockery and ridicule. Among the strange views is that of someone who said that the meaning of "subhanaka" is "declaring You far above, after declaring You far above," just as they say in "labbayka" (here I am, answering You) meaning "answering again and again." Apparently this would imply that it is a dual form, whose singular is "subhan," that it is not in the accusative but in the nominative, that the nun was not dropped for annexation, and that only its fatha was kept, and "Glory be to Allah the Exalted" is said by whoever says it. The purpose of this response is to acknowledge incapacity regarding the matter of the vicegerency and deficiency in knowing the names in the most eloquent manner, as if they said: "We have no knowledge except what You have taught us," and You did not teach us the names, so how could we know them? It also indicates that their question was only an inquiry, since they have no knowledge except through teaching. Among that teaching is their knowledge of the wisdom of the vicegerency, which was mentioned earlier, so that too is by way of teaching. Thus the question that follows from it is the question of one seeking clarification, not of one objecting. It also contains praise of Him, the Exalted, for what He bestowed upon them, together with extreme humility, observance of good manners, and abandonment of claim. For all this, they did not say "We have no knowledge of the names," even though the apparent sense would have required that. Whoever claims that they lacked infallibility has taken this as repentance. The fair view is that it resembles repentance, but

[Page 227]

it is not for a sin that undermines infallibility; rather it is for a leaving that is better, relative to their high station and elevated rank, since what befits their condition in all circumstances is that they abandon inquiry and remain waiting attentively until the reality of the matter becomes clear.

(Ma) according to the majority is a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun is omitted, and it is either in the nominative position as a substitute (badal), or in the accusative position as an exception (istithna'). Ibn 'Atiyya related from al-Zahrawi that it is in the accusative position (governed by "'allamtana"). This requires elaborate justification: that the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), so "illa" means "but," and "ma" is conditional, with an omitted apodosis. It is as if they first negated all knowledge, then corrected themselves that in the future, whatever He taught them, they would know. This makes the disclaimer of claim even more emphatic, as is clear.

"Indeed You, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise." This is a concluding clause (tadhyil) that confirms the content of the preceding sentence. When they denied knowledge of themselves, they affirmed it for God, the Exalted, in its most perfect attributes, and followed it with the attribute of wisdom, since what had become clear to them was what had become clear. The root meaning of wisdom (hikma) is restraint; from it comes the bridle of an animal (hakama al-dabba), because it restrains the animal from deviating. It is also used for knowledge, because it restrains from committing falsehood, and for perfecting an action, because it prevents it from paths of corruption and objection. This latter is the intended meaning here, so that repetition is avoided. Thus the meaning of "al-Hakim" is one who possesses wisdom. It has also been said that it means one who makes his creations firm. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr: on the first view it is an attribute of essence, and on the second an attribute of act. The well-known view is that if it means the All-Knowing, it is among the attributes of essence, or if it means the Doer of what cannot be objected to, it is among the attributes of act. So understand this. He, glory be to Him, placed the attribute of knowledge before the attribute of wisdom because of the correspondence with what preceded, "Inform me" (anbi'uni) and "we have no knowledge," and because wisdom is not far from knowledge, and so that the last of their statement would be contrary to what might be imagined from its beginning.

"You" (anta) may be a separator (fasl) that has no grammatical position according to the well-known view, serving to emphasize the judgment and the restriction derived from defining the predicate. It has also been said that it is an emphasis, to affirm the subject, and that what is permissible for a follower is not permissible for the one followed. It has also been said that it is a subject whose predicate is what follows. "The All-Wise" is either a second predicate or an attribute of it. Their complements are omitted to indicate generality, though some have specified them, saying: "the All-Knowing of what You commanded and forbade, the All-Wise in what You decreed and measured," but generality is preferable.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 33:

﴿He said: "O Adam, inform them of their names."﴾ He, glorified is He, addressed Adam by his proper name, as is His custom, exalted is His majesty, with His prophets other than our Prophet (ﷺ), whom He addressed as "O Prophet" and "O Messenger," due to the elevation of his station and the loftiness of his rank, for he is the greatest Khalifa (vicegerent), and the secret in the creation of Adam. He did not say, "Inform me," as occurred in the command to the angels, although the purpose was also achieved in that case. The purpose was to show the virtue of Adam, to make clear the disparity between the two ranks, and to inform the angels that his knowledge (peace be upon him) is manifest and does not need what resembles a test, and that he is worthy of teaching others. Or it was so that the favour of teaching would be complete for him (peace be upon him), since he was placed in the position of the one who gives benefit, while they were placed in the position of those who benefit from him. Or it was so that awe would not overwhelm him, for the informing of a scholar is not like the informing of others. The meaning of "informing" here is notification, not merely reporting, as has been mentioned previously.

In this there is evidence for those who say that the knowledge and perfections of the angels are capable of increase. Some people denied this for the highest tier among them, and interpreted in its light ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾. The statement of some implied the prevention of the attainment of knowledge that would elevate them, so perhaps what is attained is knowledge. Another said: "No, it is a state." The difference is clear to whoever has taste.

Ibn 'Abbas read (أنْبِئْهِمْ) with a hamza and a kasra on the ha', and (أنْبِيهِمْ) with the hamza changed to a ya'. Al-Hasan read (أنْبِهِمْ) like (أعْطِهِمْ). The intended meaning of the "names" is what they were unable to know, and they acknowledged their deficiency in reaching its level. The pronoun refers to the things presented to them as previously mentioned.

﴿So when he informed them of their names﴾: this is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to an omitted sentence, the implied meaning being "so he informed them of them, and when he informed them," and so on. It was omitted because the meaning is understood. The explicit mention of "the names" in place of a pronoun serves to show full concern for their matter, together with an indication that he (peace be upon him) informed them of them in detail and not in summary, and taught them, by the indications that necessitate it, of his truthfulness. The matter is too evident to be hidden. It is not far-fetched that He, glorified is He, made them know the proof of this. The possibility that each category of them had a language or knowledge of a certain thing, and then all of them were present and each category recognised the correctness of his answer in that language or that thing, is far-fetched.

Page 228

﴿He said: "Did I not tell you that I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth, and I know what you reveal and what you were concealing?"﴾ This is the answer to (لما) (when), and an affirmation of the general answer that preceded it, and a recollection of it in a more expanded and explained form. The verse's conciseness is not hidden, for the apparent expression would have been: "I know the unseen of the heavens and the earth and their witnessed matters, and I know what you were revealing and what you were concealing, and what you will reveal and conceal." However, He, glorified is He, limited Himself to the unseen of the heavens and the earth, because knowing their unseen implies knowing their witnessed matters all the more. He limited the past to what was concealed, because knowing what was concealed implies knowing what was openly shown. And He limited the beginning of the future to what occurs first, because before it happens it is hidden, so there is no difference between it and His knowledge of the rest of the hidden matters. The change of style, where He did not say "and you conceal," perhaps serves to convey the continuity of concealment. So the meaning is: "I know what you reveal before you reveal it, and I know what you persist in concealing."

Al-Salikuti mentioned that the word (كان) is a connective particle that conveys nothing except pure emphasis suited to concealment. Then, the apparent meaning of the verse is generality. Yet, with that, (what you do not know) is broader in meaning, since it includes the unseen of the unseen, which encompasses the essence and attributes of God, exalted is He. Some restricted it. Among those who said: the unseen of the heavens is the eating of Adam and Eve from the tree, and the unseen of the earth is the killing of Abel by Cain. Among those who said: the first is what He decreed of the affairs of His creation, and the second is what they did in it after the decree. Among those who said: the first is what is hidden from those brought near of what God has reserved for Himself of the secrets of the supreme dominion, and the second is what is hidden from His chosen ones of the secrets of the lower kingdom, the affairs of the Hereafter and the present world. What they revealed before their saying, "Will You place in it...", and what they concealed is their saying, "God will never create one more honoured in His sight than us." It was said: what they revealed afterwards of obedience, and it was said: what Iblis concealed of pride. The attribution of concealment to all of them in this case is of the type of: "The sons of So-and-so killed So-and-so," when the killer is one of them. The meaning of concealment in every case is not making what is in the self apparent to anyone among those in the gathering. It is not intended that they concealed anything from God, exalted is He, by their own supposition, for that would not be possible even from Iblis. God, glorified is He, mentioned the agent in "what you reveal" etc. as a matter of concern to inform them of that which frightens them. The apparent reading is that it is conjoined to the first, so it is included with it under that statement. It is possible that it is conjoined to the sentence "Did I not tell you," in which case it is not included under it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 34 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam"﴾. The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is connected to an implied verb that the context indicates, such as "they submitted" or "they obeyed." The conjunction (al-'atf) is a conjunction of one narrative onto another. In each case there is an enumeration of the blessing, although the first (the grace of the Creator in favouring Adam) is a confirmation of the favour, and this (the command to prostrate) is an acknowledgment of it. It is not sound to conjoin one adverbial phrase to another, according to the suitable reading we have already mentioned, because the two times differ. It has also been permitted that the accusative of the former is governed by an implied verb. Prostration (al-sujud) originally means humbling oneself with lowering through bowing and other means. In the Sharia, it means placing the forehead on the ground with the intention of worship. Regarding the meaning of the command here, there is disagreement. It has been said: the Sharia meaning applies, and the one prostrated to in reality is Allah the Exalted, with Adam either being in front of them (as a direction, qibla) or being a cause (of the prostration). It is objected that if this were so, Iblis would not have refused. It is also objected that this does not indicate Adam's superiority over them. The words of the Exalted, ﴿Tell me, is this the one whom You have honoured above me?﴾, indicate it. Do you not see that the Ka'ba is not more honourable than the one who prostrates towards it? It is answered that the matter was confused for Iblis, and that honour makes him a direction for this worship, not them. The indication of the greatness of his rank in this is not hidden, just as the making of the Ka'ba the qibla among all other places. Some people permitted that the one prostrated to was in reality Adam, peace be upon him, claiming that prostration to a created being was only prohibited in our Sharia. It is replied that the Sharia prostration is worship, and worship of other than Him, glorified is He, is forbidden polytheism in all religions and all times, and I do not think it was permitted in any age of the ages. It has been said: the linguistic meaning is intended, and there was no placing of the foreheads in it, but merely humbling and submission. Then the *lam* (of *li-Adam*) either remains on its literal sense, or it means *ila* (to), like it in the words of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

*Was he not the first to pray towards your qibla,*
*and the most knowledgeable of people in the Qur'an and the Sunnas?*

Or it is causal (*sababiyya*), like it in the words of the Exalted, ﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun﴾. The wisdom in the command to prostrate is to show acknowledgment of his favour, peace be upon him, and an apology for what they had said about him, along with an indication that the right of the teacher over the one he taught is a great right. The Glorified changed the style, when He said first, ﴿And when your Lord said﴾, and here, ﴿And when We said﴾ with the pronoun of majesty. This is because in the first (verse) there was the creation of Adam and his appointment as successor, so it was fitting to mention lordship (*rububiyya*) attributed to the most beloved of His successors to Him. Here, the context is the presentation of a command that befits majesty. Also, in prostration there is exaltation, so when He commanded its performance for other than Him, He indicated His pride that is free from the need for exaltation. Abu Ja'far read the *ta'* of *al-malaika* with a *damma*, in conformity with the *damma* of the *jim*. This is the dialect of Azdishanu'a. It is a strange but genuine Arabic dialect and not a mistake, as al-Farisi thought. It is related that a woman saw her daughters with a man and said, "*Afi al-sawata tantunnahh*" ("Are you [rotten] in the shameful place?"), meaning *afi al-sawati antunnahh*.

﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis﴾. The *fa'* (so) is to convey the speed of their compliance and that they did not hesitate in it. "Iblis" (إبليس) is a non-Arabic proper noun, not declinable because of its definiteness as a proper name and its foreignness. Its form is *fi'lil*, as said by al-Zajjaj. Abu 'Ubayda and others said that it is Arabic, derived from *al-iblas*, which means distancing from good or despair of the mercy of Allah the Exalted. Its form on this view is *mif'il*, and its being undeclined then is because it has no counterpart among nouns. It is objected that this is not counted among the causes of non-declension, although it has counterparts, such as *ihlil* and *iklil*. This is open to scrutiny. It has also been said that it is because it resembles foreign names, since none of the Arabs has been named with it. This is not a valid argument. People differed about whether he was from the angels or from the jinn. A group went to the second view, citing the words of the Exalted, ﴿except Iblis, who was of the jinn﴾, and that angels do not act arrogantly while he acted arrogantly, and that angels, as Muslim related from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, were created from light, while the jinn were created from a smokeless fire, and he was created from what the jinn were created from. This is indicated by the words of the Exalted quoting him: ﴿I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay﴾. His refusal to prostrate is counted as recalcitrance and arrogance on this view, either because he was raised among the angels, submerged among thousands of them, so they overpowered him and the command reached him, but he did not comply; or because the jinn were also commanded along with the angels, but He dispensed with mentioning the jinn because of their greater nobility; or because he, may the curse be upon him, was commanded explicitly, not implicitly, as the apparent sense of the Exalted's words indicates: ﴿when I commanded you﴾. The pronoun in ﴿so they prostrated﴾ refers to those commanded to prostrate. The majority of scholars from the Companions and Successors went to the first view, citing the apparent sense of the exception. Its correction by what has been mentioned is forced, because although he was one of them, he was their chief and head, as the reports affirm, so he was not submerged among them. Also, returning the pronoun to all those commanded, although it is far-fetched, is not established, since it has not been transmitted that the jinn prostrated to Adam other than Iblis. As for his being explicitly commanded, the verse is not explicit about it, and establishing it is like pulling thorns from a *qatad* tree (i.e., an extremely difficult task). The implication of what has been mentioned from the verse that he was of the kind of jinn is disputed, since it is possible that what is meant is that he was of them in action. The words of the Exalted ﴿so he defied﴾ serve as an explanation of this. It is also possible that *kana* (was) means *sara* (became), as it is related that he was transformed because of this disobedience, so he became a jinn, just as the Jews were transformed and became apes and swine. Even if we concede this, there is no contradiction between his being a jinn and his being an angel, since *jinn* is applied to what is opposed to the angel, and it is also applied to a type of angel, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and they were the guardians of Paradise, or the goldsmiths of their ornaments. It has been said that there is a category of angels that the angels do not see as we do. Or it is said that angels are also called jinn, as Ibn Ishaq said, because they are hidden and concealed from people's eyes. With this some interpreted the words of the Exalted, ﴿and they made between Him and the jinn a kinship﴾. A similar usage occurs in Arabic speech, for al-A'sha said about our master Sulayman, peace be upon him:

*And he subjugated, from the jinn of the angels, nine,*
*standing before him, working without wage.*

That the angels do not act arrogantly, while he did, is not harmful, either because among the angels there are those who are not infallible, although the general rule is that they are infallible, in contrast to us. In the creed of Abu al-Mu'in al-Nasafi there is something that supports this. Or because Allah the Exalted stripped him of the angelic qualities and clothed him in the satanic qualities, so he disobeyed at that point, and an angel, as long as he is an angel, does not disobey.

*And who, O Mayy, does not change?*

That he was created from fire while they were created from light is also not harmful, nor does it damage his angelhood, because fire and light share the same substance in genus, and their difference is by accidents. Moreover, what is in the report of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, about the creation of angels from light proceeds as a general rule, and otherwise many apparent reports would contradict it, for in them it is stated that Allah the Exalted created angels from fire, angels from snow, and angels from this and that. It is also reported that under the Throne there is a river, and when Gabriel, peace be upon him, bathes in it and shakes himself, from every drop of it an angel is created. The words of some indicated that it is possible that a kind of angels does not differ from the devils in essence, but differs from them only in accidents and attributes, like the righteous and the wicked among humans and jinn, which include both. Iblis was of this category. So call him whatever you wish: angel, jinn, or devil. With this, the sayings are reconciled. And Allah the Exalted knows best the reality of the situation.

Then, the well-known view is that the exception is *continuous* (*muttasil*) if he was of the angels, and *disjunctive* (*munqati'*) if he was not of them. You have known their strain in making it continuous while holding the second view. It has become widespread among grammarians and jurists that the disjunctive exception is the exception from other than its genus, and the continuous exception is the exception from its own genus. Al-Qarafi said in *al-'Iqd al-Manzum*: this is an error on both counts. The words of the Exalted, ﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood, except that it be trade﴾, and ﴿They do not taste therein death, except the first death﴾, and ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾, the exception in them is disjunctive, although the excepted item is of the same genus as what precedes it. So both definitions collapse. The truth is that the continuous exception is that in which a judgment is made about the same genus as what you first judged, with the opposite of what you judged about it. Both of these conditions are necessary. Whenever one of them is absent, it is disjunctive, namely when it is of a different genus, whether a judgment is made about it with its opposite or not, as in: "I saw the people except a horse." So the disjunctive has two types and the continuous has one type. The disjunctive is like the contradictory of the continuous, for the contradictory of a compound is by the absence of its parts. So the words of the Exalted, ﴿They do not taste﴾ etc., are disjunctive, because the judgment is by other than the contradictory, since its contradictory would be "they tasted it therein," and this is not the case. Likewise ﴿except that it be trade﴾, because it is not consumed in falsehood but in truth. Likewise ﴿except by mistake﴾, because it is not permitted to him to kill absolutely, otherwise it would be permitted. The disjunctive then has three types: a judgment about the genus by other than the contradictory; a judgment about something other than it by the contradictory or by other than it; and the continuous, which is one type. This is the criterion. It has been said: what matters is connection and disconnection, which is entering into the judgment or not, not the reality of the wording or not. So reflect, and you will be guided.

The discourse of these people, may Allah benefit us through them, indicates that all created beings, higher and lower, the happy and the wretched, are created from the Muhammadan Reality, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, as indicated by the words of al-Nabulusi, may his secret be sanctified, refuting what is raised against the outward sense:

*Ta Ha the Prophet: from his light all creation came into being,*
*and even if the sparrow-hawk were left alone...*

And there are reports supporting this, except that the upper angels were created from him, peace and blessings be upon him, in terms of beauty, and Iblis in terms of majesty. This is ultimately interpreted to mean that Iblis is the manifestation of the majesty of Allah, glorified and exalted is He. For this reason, what came from him came to be, and he did not despair, did not repent, and did not seek forgiveness, because he knew that Allah the Exalted does what He wills, and that what He wills, glorified is He, is what the realities require, so there is no way to change or alter them. This was perceived from His calling him "Iblis," and that was not his name before, but his name was 'Azazil, or al-Harith, and his kunya was Abu Murra. Behind that is what cannot be disclosed. Allah the Exalted says the truth and He guides to the way. In the words of the Exalted, ﴿He refused and was arrogant, and he was among the disbelievers﴾, there is a kind of indication of some of what has been mentioned. The sentence is a resumptive answer to one who asks, "What did he do?" It has been said that the first two verbs are in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (*hal*), meaning "refusing and arrogant." "And he was among the disbelievers" is resumptive, or it is in the position of a circumstantial state. It has been said that the three sentences are a concluding statement after a concluding statement. *Ibaa* (refusal) is abstention together with aversion while being able to perform the action. For this reason, your saying "Zayd refused injustice" is more eloquent than "Zayd was not wronged." Because the verb conveys negation, the disjunctive exception may follow it, as in the words of the Exalted, ﴿and Allah refuses except that He perfect His light﴾, and in the words of the poet:

*Allah refused, except for His justice and His faithfulness,*
*so neither denial is recognised nor custom is lost.*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 34 (part 2 of 2):

The verb from it is *abā* with a fatha on the ba' (أبى). On this reading, *yaʾbā* (يَأْبى) is not regular (qiyasi). However, *abiya* (أبِيَ) with a kasra, on the pattern of *radiya*, has also been heard. In that case the present tense is regular. The object here is omitted, meaning "the prostration" (السُّجُودَ). *Al-istikbar* (الِاسْتِكْبارُ) means *al-takabbur* (arrogance). It is one of the forms where *istaf'ala* carries the meaning of *tafa''ala*. It has also been said that *takabbur* is for a person to see himself as greater than others, which is blameworthy even if he is in fact greater. *Al-istikbar* is seeking that status through feigned greatness. The refusal (*al-ibaʾ*) is mentioned before it, although *al-istikbar* comes later in rank, because refusal is an outward state, unlike *al-istikbar*, which is inward. Alternatively, the purpose is to report that his state opposed the state of the angels, so it was fitting to begin with the emphasis on what was judged against him in the exception, or with the creation of the report about his opposition. So it began with that in the most eloquent manner. The verb is "on its own pattern" (*wa-kāna ʿalā bābihā*), meaning it is a true past of its kind. The meaning is: he was, in the knowledge of Allah the Exalted, among the disbelievers, or he was one of the people who were disbelievers, those who were on earth before the creation of Adam. It has also been said that *kāna* means *ṣāra* (became). This is one of the usages that some grammarians affirmed. Ibn Furak said: "The principles of the discipline reject it." Also, because the apparent meaning at that point would have been, and so it would have been with *fa*. Furthermore, his disbelief was not due to abandoning an obligation, as the Khawarij (a sect) claimed, clinging to this verse. This is because abandoning an obligation does not entail disbelief in our religion, as the definitive proofs indicate. Making it obligatory before that is not definitively established. Rather, it is based on the repugnance of disobeying Allah's command to prostrate before one who believes he is better than and superior to him, as the refusal and arrogance indicate. Abu al-'Aliya said: the meaning of "among the disbelievers" is "among the disobedient." The apparent meaning is that his disbelief was out of ignorance, in that Allah the Glorified took back from him the knowledge that He had lent him, the knowledge with which he had been clothed when he was the peacock of the angels. The fingernails of destiny, when they scratch, draw blood, and the bows of decree, when they shoot, make deaf.

And the lamp of union had been shining brightly between us,
then a wind of separation blew upon it and it went out.

It has also been said that his disbelief was out of obstinacy, driven by love of leadership and admiration for the nobility he had been given. The wretched one did not realize that if he had obeyed, his rank would have risen, and his glory would have soared among the exalted assembly. But:

When there is no help from Allah for the young man,
the first thing his striving will bring upon him is harm.

How many eyelids this story has made sleepless, and how many eyes it has made to shed tears! Iblis remained for a period in the splendor of his obedience, strutting in the mantle of his companionship, and then he became what you see, and what the pen had written, has come to pass.

We were, with Layla, climbing the heights of love,
but when we met, I stayed firm and she slipped away.

From here the Shafi'iyya (followers of al-Shafi'i) and the Ash'ariyya (followers of al-Ash'ari, a school of kalam) said, and I say in this matter according to their saying: the consideration is for the faith with which the servant meets Allah, that he is characterized by at the end of his life and at the first stage of his Hereafter. This is why it is valid to say "I am a believer, if Allah the Exalted wills," with doubt. However, this is not about the present, actual faith but about the true faith that is considered at death and the sealing of deeds. It is authentically reported from Abu Hurayra, may Allah the Exalted be pleased with him, as al-Zurqani cited: "Among the completeness of the servant's faith is that he makes the exception (in saying 'if Allah wills'), for the outcomes of the believers are hidden from them. ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾."

[Page 232]

In the Sahih, from Jabir: the Prophet (ﷺ) used to frequently say: "O Turner of hearts, make our hearts firm upon Your religion." The report: "Whoever says, 'I am a believer, if Allah the Exalted wills,' then he has no share of Islam" is fabricated, by the consensus of the hadith scholars. And I am a believer with other than this (formulation), if Allah the Exalted wills. This is what I say. Know that what this noble verse requires, and likewise the verses in al-A'raf, Bani Isra'il, al-Kahf and Ta-Ha, is that the prostration of the angels was consequent upon the immediate command that came after his creation and the breathing of the spirit into him. This is what both transmission and reason attest. However, what is in al-Hijr, the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I am going to create a human being from clay of black mud altered"﴾ ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My spirit, then fall down to him in prostration﴾ ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them entirely﴾, and likewise what is in Sad, apparently requires that it follows from the conditional command in them, without anything intervening between them except the creation and its consequences. Some have said this. The commands in those verses are taken as the report of the conditional command after the condition's occurrence has been established in general. Then it has the status of an immediate command. The "then" (thumma) in the verse of al-A'raf indicates a gradual delay in rank, or a delay in reporting. Or it may be said that since the conditional command, before the condition's occurrence, was like non-existence in not making the commanded act obligatory, it was treated as if it came into being only after the condition's occurrence, so it is reported in the form of an immediate command. When some saw that this leads to the conclusion that what happened regarding the matter of the vicegerency, what they said, and what they heard, happened after the prostration, which was preceded by knowledge of his exalted status (peace be upon him), and after Iblis went out of the picture by being cursed, and after they witnessed all of that, this is a breach of the transmitted reality, indeed a breach of reason. So he was compelled to say that the prostration occurred twice. But far be it! "The perfumer cannot repair what time has spoiled." So the true truth is what those verses indicate. What the opponent cited as evidence does not stand as proof. For if the condition is a qualifier of the consequent, its meaning is, on the supposition: "He is right, if you have shaped him, then request building," and the condition is a qualifier of the request, as the Allama al-Taftazani explicitly stated: the meaning of our saying "If Zayd comes to you, then honor him" is, on the supposition "He is right, if Zayd comes to you, I request from you his honoring," and if the judgment is between the condition and the consequent, then the consequent in the form of a request must be interpreted as a report, meaning he deserves that it be said of him, "Honor him." In both suppositions, the meaning of ﴿so fall down to him in prostration﴾ is a request for the future, not for the present. So it does not follow that the command to prostrate happened before the shaping. Yes, if the condition were a qualifier of the required act, not of the request, the meaning would be a present request for prostration at the time of shaping, and that would indicate the command preceded the shaping. As for the statement of our master al-Razi, may his secret be sanctified: that the verse, just as it indicates the command to prostrate preceded the shaping, also indicates that the teaching and the informing took place after the prostration, because it indicates that Adam, peace be upon him, as soon as he became alive, became one to whom the angels prostrated, since the "fa" in (fa-qaʿū) indicates immediate sequence. What is in this is not hidden. This is because "fa" here indicates causation, not coordination, and causation does not require immediate sequence, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿When the call is made for prayer on the day of Friday, then hasten﴾ and the saying of the Glorified: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾. Some people interpreted the breathing of the spirit in the verse as teaching, because it is well known that knowledge is life and ignorance is death. But you are in no need of this. And Allah is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And We said: "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden"﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with "when We said" (idh qulna), either by supposing an "idh" or without it, or it is coordinated with "We said" (qulna). The time is broad and extended enough for both statements. The opening of the speech with the vocative is to alert the one commanded to what is about to be conveyed to him of the command, and to stir him toward what he is addressed with, since it is among the matters to which he should direct his attention. "Uskun" (dwell) is an imperative from al-sukna (dwelling), meaning to take a dwelling, not from al-sukun (stillness, the cessation of motion), since the latter apparently contradicts it. "Ḥaythu shi'tumā" (wherever you both wish) — its complement is mentioned without "fī" (in), and it is not an unspecified place. "Wa-anta" (and you) is an emphasis for the pronoun concealed in "uskun." Its primary purpose is the validity of the coordination, for without it there would be coordination upon a connected pronoun without separation, which is impermissible in eloquent usage according to the correct view. Conveying the affirmation of the one followed is also intended secondarily. The coordination is valid even though the coordinated element is not directly governed by the imperative verb, because it occurs as a follower (tabi'), and what is not excused in the principal element is excused in it. It has been said: there are two instances of prevalence (taghlib): the prevalence of the addressee over the absent, and of the masculine over the feminine. Because the prevalence is a metaphor, and the meaning of stillness and command exists in both literally, the matter became obscure. As for holding that prevalence may be a non-lexical metaphor, by the figure being in the attribution, or saying that it is lexical, because the form of the imperative here is for the addressee and has been used in the more general sense — to escape this, it has been said that it is coordinated with an implied "fa-li-yaskun" (so let him dwell). But in this, it would then be coordination of a clause upon a clause, so there is no point in the emphasis. The imperative may admit of being permissive, like "isṭādū" (hunt), and may admit of being obligatory, just as the prohibition that follows is for prohibition. Its preference over "uskunā" (dwell, dual) is to alert that he, peace be upon him, is the intended object of the ruling in all the commands, and they are subordinate to him, just as they are in creation likewise. For this reason some verifiers said: it is not valid to introduce "zawjuka" (your wife) without coordination, by making it accusative as an object with (maʿa). "Al-Janna" (the Garden), in the well-known usage, is the abode of reward for the believers on the Day of Resurrection, because it is what comes to mind upon unqualified mention, and because its mention preceded in the sūrah. The apparent reports also indicate this, and among them is what is in the Ṣaḥīḥ concerning the disputation between Adam and Moses, peace be upon them both. So it is then in the heaven, wherever God Most High wills from it. The Muʿtazilah, Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī, and others held that it is another garden which God Most High created as a trial for Adam, peace be upon him, and it was an orchard on earth between Fars and Kirman. It was said: in the land of Aden; and it was said: in Palestine, a district in Syria. It was not the well-known Garden. They interpreted the descent (hubūṭ) as moving from one place to another, as in "ihbiṭū miṣran" (go down to a city), or upon its apparent sense. It may be that it is in an elevated place. They said: because there is no dispute that God Most High created Adam on earth, and the story does not mention that He transported him to heaven; had He transported him there, it would have been more appropriate to mention. And because He, glory be to Him, said concerning that Garden and its people: "They hear therein no idle talk nor sin" [56:25], "except the saying: Peace, peace" [56:26], and "There is no idle talk therein nor sinning" [52:23], "and they will not be removed therefrom" [15:48]. Iblis did engage in idle talk therein and lied, and Adam and Eve were expelled from it, though they had entered it to dwell, unlike the entry of the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, on the night of the Ascension. And because the Garden of Eternity is an abode of bliss and rest, not an abode of obligation, and Adam was obligated not to eat of the tree. And because Iblis was among the disbelievers, and he entered it for the purpose of whispering, and had it been the Garden of Eternity he would not have entered it, nor would he have come close to it, for the eminent scholars explicitly stated that were a disbeliever brought to the gate of the Garden, he would be torn apart, and would not enter it, for he is darkness, and it is light; and his entering it concealed, with what is in it, does not benefit. And because it is a place of purification, so how is it fitting that disobedience and opposition occur therein, and that those not purified should dwell in it? And because the first pregnancy of Eve occurred in the Garden, according to some reports, and it is not related that this delicate food generates the sperm of this dense body. Committing to an answer to all of that is not free of artificiality and of committing to what is not required. What falls within the scope of the disputation can be taken to refer to this Garden. That taking it to mean what has been mentioned flows into the category of mocking religion and of defiance against the consensus of the Muslims is not accepted. It was said: it was in the heaven, and it is not the abode of reward but the Garden of Eternity. It was said: it was other than both. This is refuted by the fact that it is not established that in the heaven there are orchards other than the orchards of the well-known Garden; and the possibility that they were created at that time and then passed away is something no fair-minded person would embrace. It was said: all is possible, and God Most High is powerful over what He wills; the evidences are conflicting, so the safest and most secure course is to refrain from specifying it and from asserting it. To this inclined the author of al-Ta'wilat. What some of our Sufi masters, may God Most High sanctify their secrets, held is that it is on earth, near the Mountain of Ruby (Jabal al-Yaqut), beneath the line of equinox; they call it the Garden of the Barzakh, and it now exists, and that the knowers enter it today with their spirits, not their bodies. Were they to say that it is the Garden of Refuge (Jannat al-Ma'wa), it appeared wherever God Most High willed and however He willed, just as it appeared to our Prophet, as is reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ, along the width of the wall of the mosque, it would not be far-fetched according to their way. Were a speaker to say this, I would say it too; but for singularity in such matters there are dangers. And just as there is disagreement about this Garden, there is disagreement about the time of the creation of his wife, peace be upon him. Al-Suddi reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, and some Companions, may God Most High be pleased with them, that when God Most High expelled Iblis from the Garden and settled Adam in it, he remained in it alone, and there was no one with him to keep him company. So God Most High cast sleep upon him, then took a rib from his left side and put flesh in its place, and created Eve from it. When he awoke, he found her seated at his head, and he asked her: "Who are you?" She said: "A woman." He said: "And why were you created?" She said: "So that you may find rest in me." The angels then said, to test his knowledge: "Who is this?" He said: "A woman." They said: "Why was she named woman?" He said: "Because she was created from al-mir' (the human), (?)." They said: "What is her name?" He said: "Hawwa'." They said: "Why was she named Hawwa'?" He said: "Because she was created from a living thing (hayy)." Many said, and perhaps I say with their saying: she was created before the entry, and they both entered together, and the apparent meaning of the noble verse points to it, otherwise the command would be directed to a non-existent, though in God's knowledge she is existent. Also, in placing "zawjuka" (your wife) before "al-Janna" (the Garden) there is a kind of indication to it, and there is the proverb: "The companion before the road." Also, she is the dwelling of the heart, and the Garden is the dwelling of the body, and of wisdom is placing the first before the second. The report of al-Suddi, with what is in it that is not hidden from you, is opposed by what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God Most High be pleased with both of them, who said: God sent a host of angels who carried Adam and Eve on a golden throne, as kings are carried, and their garment was light, until they brought them into the Garden. This, as you see, indicates that she was created before entering the Garden.

﴿And eat from it in abundance, wherever you wish﴾ — the pronoun in the genitive refers to the Garden, by elision of a noun: that is, from its foods, of fruits and others. So He did not forbid them anything except what will come. The original of "kulā" is "u'kulā," with two hamzas, the first for connection and the second the root letter of the word; the second was elided because of the meeting of two like letters, as an anomalous elision, and the first was then dropped because the purpose was lost. It was said: both were elided together due to frequent use. "Raghad" with a fatḥa on the ghayn, and al-Nakha'i read it with a sukūn: the pleasant and effortless, or the wide. It is said: "raghuda ʿaysh al-qawm," and "raghida" with kasra and damma of the ghayn: they were in abundant wide provision; and "arghada al-qawm": they became fertile and were in ease of living. Its accusative is as an adjective of an elided verbal noun, that is: eating in abundance. Ibn Kaysan said it is a circumstantial accusative by interpretation as "rāghidīn" (living in ease and luxury). "Ḥaythu" is an adverb of unspecified place, necessarily adverbial; its i'rab is the dialect of the Banu Fa'as, and it is not an adverb of time, against al-Akhfash; it does not govern in the jussive except with "mā," against al-Farra'; it is not attached to a singular noun, against al-Kisa'i; and one does not say "Zayd ḥaythu ʿAmr," against the Kufans. The three vowels attach to its final letter with the yā', wāw and alif. It is said "ḥāythu," rarely. Here it is connected to "kulā," and what is meant by it is generality, by the context and by the absence of a preponderant restriction, that is: in whatever place of the Garden you both wish. He permitted them to eat thus to remove the excuse of taking from what was forbidden. It was not made connected to "uskun," because the generality of places is derived from making the Garden the object, together with the fact that the honouring is in eating from everything they desire from it, not in the non-specification of dwelling. And because His saying in another verse: "So eat from wherever you wish" [2:35 variant / 7:19] calls for what we have mentioned. Likewise His saying, glory be to Him: "And do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers." The apparent sense of this prohibition is forbiddance, and what is forbidden is eating from the tree; but He, glory be to Him, forbade approaching it for emphasis. For this reason He made the disobedience consequent upon eating consequent upon approach, and He turned away from "fa-tathmā" (and sin) to the expression by wrongdoing, which is applied to major sins. He did not suffice with saying "ẓālimīn" (wrongdoers), but said "min al-ẓālimīn" (among the wrongdoers), on the basis of what they mentioned: that your saying "Zayd is among the learned" is more emphatic than "Zayd is learned," because it makes him immersed in knowledge, as a father of a grandfather. And if we say that "takūnā" indicates permanence, the emphasis increases. Some people said: "lā taqrab" with fatḥa on the rā' is a prohibition from being involved in the thing; and with ḍamma it means do not draw near to it. Al-Jawhari said: "qaruba" with ḍamma, "yaqrubu" and "qurbānan"; and "qaribtuhu" with kasra, "qurbānan": I drew near to it. The tā' in "al-shajara" is for singular individuality, and this is most fitting to the station of removing the excuse, and it is permissible that the species is intended; in both cases the lām is for the genus, as in al-Kashshaf. There was disagreement about this tree: it was said: wheat; it was said: the date palm; it was said: the camphor tree, and it is attributed to ʿAlī, may God honour his face; it was said: the fig; it was said: the colocynth; it was said: the tree of love; it was said: the tree of nature and desire; it was said, and it was said, and the preferable course is not to assert or specify it, just as God Most High did not specify it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 35 (part 2 of 2):

by its name in the verse. I see no benefit in specifying which tree it was. It is also said of it: shijarah (شِجَرَة), with the shin kasra, and shayarah (شَيَرَة), with the jim replaced by a ya' and the shin either fatha or kasra. Some reciters have read it in each of these ways. It is reported from Abu 'Amr that he disliked shayarah, saying: "The Berbers and the Sudanese of Makkah recite it that way." The flaw in this is not hidden.

Ash-shajar (الشجر) is that which has a trunk, or everything that has branches and stalks, or it is more general than that, as shown by the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿a tree of gourd (shajarah min yaqtin)﴾. As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿fa-takuna (so that you would be)﴾, it is either jussive, with the nun dropped, conjoined to ﴿taqraba (you approach)﴾, in which case it is also forbidden and remains on the original meaning of its sense; or it is in the subjunctive, as an answer to the prohibition, like His words, glorified is He: ﴿and do not transgress therein, lest there descend upon you (fa-yahilla)﴾. The subjunctive is governed by an implied "an" according to the Basrans, by the fa' itself according to al-Jarmi, and by disagreement according to the Kufans. In that case, (kana) here carries the meaning of (sara), "became."

Whatever understanding of the causal link to what preceded is adopted, because they would be ﴿among the wrongdoers (zalimin)﴾, meaning those who wronged themselves by committing sin, or diminished their portions by engaging in what undermines honour and blessing, or transgressed the limits of Allah the Exalted. Perhaps the forbidden approach that becomes a cause of wrongdoing undermining infallibility is one not accompanied by an excuse, such as forgetfulness, for example, which is alluded to by His words, the Exalted: ﴿but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve (fa-nasiya wa-lam najid lahu 'azma)﴾. Thus, the prohibition does not require being read as prohibition in the strict sense of forbidden acts. The wrongdoing, which is said in an equivocal sense of committing a sin, does not indicate that Adam, peace be upon him, lacked infallibility by eating accompanied by forgetfulness, even though its consequences followed, considering that the good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of those brought near. The master may address his servant however he wishes. Yes, if that had not been accompanied by an excuse, its commission would then have been undermining, but establishing this is extremely difficult. Therefore, there is no proof in this story of the absence of infallibility. There is also no need to say that what occurred was before prophethood and not after it, as the Mu'tazilah claim, who hold that his manifestation with knowledge of the names was a miracle proving his prophethood at that time, and that the occurrence of sin before prophethood is permissible according to most of our companions. This is the view of Abu Hudhayl and Abu 'Ali among the Mu'tazilah. Nor is there need to read the prohibition as one of disapproval (tanzih), and the wrongdoing as diminishing one's portion, for example, which some have committed to.

It has been read as (tiqraba) with a kasra on the ta', and this is the dialect of the Hijazis. Ibn Muhaysin read (hadhi) with a ya'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 36:

﴿So Satan caused them to slip from it﴾, i.e., he moved them to the slip by means of it. Its verification is: he issued their slip from it. Similar to this, regarding "from it," is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Abraham's plea for forgiveness for his father was only from a promise he had made to him﴾. According to this, the pronoun refers to the tree. It has been said: "azallahuma" means "adhhabahuma" (he removed them), and the reading of Hamza, "fa-azalahuma," supports this. The two are close in meaning, except that azalla implies a stumbling together with removal, and in that case the pronoun refers to the Garden. Its return to the tree is by metaphor, or by supposing an omitted noun, i.e., its place, or to the obedience understood from the speech, is remote. His causing them to slip was by his lying to them and his swearing to them, as God Almighty related in His Book. Regarding the manner of his reaching that, there are opinions. It was said: he entered the Garden as a trial for Adam and Eve. It was said: he stood at the gate, called out to them, and corrupted their condition. It was said: he appeared in the form of an animal, entered, and the guardians did not recognize him. It was said: he sent some of his followers to them. It was said: while they were strolling in the Garden, a peacock appeared to them on the wall of the Garden, and Eve approached it, and Adam followed her, and he whispered to them from behind the wall. It was said: he reached them through a serpent that climbed into the Garden, and the story of the serpent is well known. These last two, the first of which is indicated by our masters the Sufis, point to his reaching them through desire outside the Garden, and the second to his reaching them through anger. The climbing over the Garden's wall, in their view, is an indication that anger is closer to the spiritual horizon and the heart's domain than desire. It was said: his reaching to what he reached at that time is like his reaching today to humiliating and misguiding whomever God Almighty wills. We know of this nothing but the stray thoughts and impulses that lead to what they lead to. Many do not affirm Satan's entry into the heart; rather, they do not conceive of it. For this reason they said: the report "Indeed Satan runs through the children of Adam as blood runs" is to be understood as a metaphor for the greatness of his authority over them and their submission to him, and I suppose you choose this view. Abu Mansur said: it is not for us to investigate the manner of that, nor do we pronounce a verdict without evidence, and this is a matter of great fairness. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read: (fa-waswasa lahuma ash-shaytanu 'anha) — and the pronoun in this reading refers to the tree alone, and its return to the Garden by including the meaning of removal or the like is remote. ﴿Then He brought them out from what they were in﴾, i.e., from the bliss and honor, or from the Garden. The first is consistent with the pronoun "anha" referring to the tree or the Garden, and the second is specified by the first supposition, lest the speech fall apart. It was said: He brought them out of the clothing they were in, for when they ate, it fell from them. In the speech there is a magnification that is not hidden. ﴿And We said: Go down, some of you to others an enemy﴾. Al-Hubut is descending, and the 'ayn of the present tense is vowelled with kasra or damma. Al-Mufaddal said: it means leaving a city and entering it, and it is among the antonyms, and it is also said of a lowering of rank. "Ba'd" is originally a verbal noun meaning cutting, and it is also used for a part; like "kull," it is necessarily linked to an addition, verbally or intentionally, and the article does not enter it. A pronoun referring back to it may be singular or plural when a group is intended. "'Aduww" derives from enmity, meaning transgressing the limit, or distance, or injustice; it is used for a single male and for others with one form, and it may be said "a'da'" and "'adawa." The address is to Adam and Eve, by His saying: ﴿He said: Go down from it, all of you﴾, and the story is one, and the pronoun is plural because they are treated as the whole of mankind. Since in the command to descend there is a lowering of the commanded one's rank, He did not open it with a call, as He opened the command to dwell. Al-Farra' chose that the addressees are they and their descendants, and this involves addressing one not yet existent. What is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and Mujahid and many of the early generations is that the address is to them and Iblis. This was objected to on the ground that he came out before them, and it was answered that reporting what he said to them separately does not preclude togetherness. It was said: they and the serpent; this was objected to on the ground that it is not obligated, and it was answered that the command is creational, and the nominal clause is in the accusative position as a presumed circumstantial clause, and the judgment is with regard to the descendants. When Iblis and the serpent are included, the command is more evident. It is not an objection that how can the command be restricted by enmity, which is forbidden; for we say that the nature of enmity is turned from the restriction, enmity being natural, and natural matters are not subject to obligation, and if it is obligated, it is with regard to its causes. When the command is made creational, the difficulty disappears, except that there is remoteness in it. Some make the clause a new sentence by supposing a question, to flee from this objection, together with the fact that in a nominal circumstantial clause the pronoun is used without the waw, which Al-Farra' considered anomalous; although the verified view is what some verifiers mentioned: that a circumstantial clause is either from the cause of its subject or foreign to it. If it is from its cause, it requires the returning pronoun and the waw, as in "Zayd came and his father was leaving," except what is anomalous, such as "kallamtuhu fuwah ila fi" (I spoke to him mouth to mouth). If it is foreign, it requires the waw standing in place of the returning pronoun, and both may be combined, as in "Bishr came and 'Amr was coming to him." It has also come with "la" and "la," as in his saying:

*Then we stood at the mountains of Sughd, facing the left, and on our right are the roads.*

It may also be an attribute of the subject of the circumstance, as in ﴿You turned away, except a few of you, while you were turning away﴾, and both possibilities are admissible here in a regular manner, and what we are discussing belongs to this category, so reflect.

The singular "'aduww" is either in view of the wording of "ba'd," or because its pattern is that of a verbal noun, like "qabul," and by it what precedes it is connected; the lam, as in the Bahr, strengthens it. Abu Haywa read "ihbutu" with a damma on the ba', and this is a dialect of it. By this command the preceding command and prohibition were abrogated. ﴿And for you on the earth is a settlement and enjoyment for a time﴾. By "the earth" he meant the place of descent, and what is intended is not his individual body, which for Adam, peace be upon him, is a place on the mountain of Sarandib, for Eve a place at Jeddah, for Iblis a place at al-Ubulla, and for his companion a place at Nusaybin, or Isfahan, or Sijistan. "Mustaqarr" is a place noun or a mimi verbal noun. It may remotely be a passive participle meaning that over which your dominion is established and your disposal of it; and more remote than this is the possibility that it is a noun of time

*(continued in the next page, p. 237)* — the subject, whose predicate is "for you," and "fihi" is connected to what it is connected to. "Mata'" is the provision sufficient for subsistence, derived from "mata'a al-nahar" when it rose; it is used for a benefit whose duration extends, and is not restricted to the base. "Hin" is a measure of time, short or long, and what is meant here is until the time of death, which is the minor resurrection; it was also said: until the Day of the Great Resurrection, and on this basis the dwelling in the grave is a form of enjoyment on the earth. Or the address may be taken as including Iblis, and the collective whole is intended. The prepositional phrase is connected to "mata'"; it was said: or to it, and to "mustaqarr," by way of dispute; or it is an attribute of "mata'," by measure. This sentence is like the preceding one, both as a new sentence and as a circumstantial clause.

﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾. The meaning of "receiving the words" (talaqqi al-kalimat) is accepting them, taking them in, believing in them and acting upon them. It is a metaphor borrowed from how people receive a beloved one who returns after a long absence: they leave no honour undone. The honouring of the words that come from the Presence (al-hadrah) is to take them, accept them and act by them. The use of the expression "receiving" (talaqqi) hints that Adam, peace be upon him, was at that time in a station of distance. "From his Lord" (min Rabbihi) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) of "words" (kalimat), placed before it. It has also been said that it is connected to "receive" (yatalaqqa), and that the verb is from talaqqahu minhu, meaning "to be taught by him." Were it not that this lacks the subtlety of the first reading, we would have accepted it. Ibn Kathir read "Adam" in the accusative and "words" in the nominative, with the meaning that the words received him, so that they were, as it were, honouring him, since they were the cause of his pardon. The word "receiving" may also be taken figuratively to mean "reaching," through the relation of causation. What is related in the well-known report from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that these words are ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾, and the verse goes on. From Ibn Mas'ud it is related that they are: "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You. Blessed is Your name and exalted is Your majesty. There is no god but You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for none forgives sins but You." It has also been said that he saw written on the leg of the Throne: "Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," so he sought intercession through him. And if the term "word" (kalimah) is applied to Jesus, peace be upon him, then the term "words" should be applied to the Supreme Spirit and the Most Noble Beloved, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. So Jesus is not [all of it], nor Moses, nor … nor …, and they are only a part of the manifestations of his lights and a blossom from the gardens of his lights. Other things have also been related.

﴿So He turned to him in forgiveness; indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful﴾. The root meaning of repentance (tawbah) is "return." When it is attributed to the servant, it is, as in the Ihya' ('Ulum al-Din), an expression for a combination of three things: knowledge, which is knowing the harm of sin and that it is a veil from every beloved thing; a state (hal) which this knowledge produces, namely the heart's pain at the loss of the beloved, which we call remorse (nadam); and action, which this state produces, namely abandoning sin, making amends, and resolving not to return to it. Often the term is applied to remorse alone, because it necessarily accompanies knowledge and necessarily entails action. In a hadith: "Remorse is repentance." The way to acquire it is to perfect faith in the affairs of the Hereafter and in the harm that sins bring there. When it is attributed to Him, glory be to Him, it is an expression for accepting repentance, pardoning the sin and the like, or enabling a person to repent and facilitating its causes, by showing the repentant some of His signs and making them aware of His warnings, until they feel fear and return to Him. In the Hereafter it comes to mean grace and kindness. For this reason it is construed with "upon" (ʿala). Glory be to Him uses the particle "fa" (then/so) because receiving the words is itself repentance or entails it, and there is no doubt that acceptance follows from it. So here the "fa" is merely for causation. It may be said that since repentance continued in him, sequence is valid when considering its last part, as there is then no interval. In any case, this does not contradict what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they both wept for two hundred years over what they had lost. And He, exalted be His majesty, did not say "so He turned to them both," because women are followers, and mention of the one followed suffices for them. For this reason their mention is omitted in many places in the Book and the Sunnah. In the nominal sentence there is something that strengthens the hope of sinners and mends the broken hearts of the erring: He began it with "indeed" (inna), used the pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), and made the predicate definite, and He used forms of intensification, indicating that He accepts repentance every time the servant repents. It is possible that this is due to the great number of those whom He pardons. He combined the two descriptions of being "Accepting of repentance" and "Most Merciful," indicating abundant grace. He put "the Accepting" first because of its clear relevance to what precedes it. It has been said that mentioning "the Most Merciful" after it indicates that the acceptance of repentance is not obligatory, as the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilites) claim, but rather by way of mercy and bounty; and that He is the One whose mercy precedes His wrath, so He shows mercy to His servant even in the midst of His wrath, just as He made Adam's descent a cause of his elevation, and after it a cause of his nearness. Glory be to Him, how generous is the Accepting, and how great is the Most Merciful. If "the Accepting" is interpreted as "the One who returns to forgiveness," then the sentence is a conclusion (tadhyil) to His saying ﴿so He turned to him﴾; or if it is interpreted as "the One who greatly aids in repentance," then it is a conclusion to His saying ﴿Then Adam received﴾, and so on. Nawfal read "anahu" (indeed He) with a fatha on the hamzah, under the assumption of "li-annahu" (because He).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 38:**

﴿We said: "Go down from it, all of you."﴾ It is repeated for emphasis (ta'kid). The lack of a conjunction (fasl) here is because the second clause is in complete connection (kamal al-ittisal) with the first. The fa' in (fa-talaqqa) is an interjection (i'tiraḍ), since it is not permissible for the conjoined element (ma'tuf) to precede the emphasis. Its benefit is to indicate the great importance of repentance (tawbah), that one must hasten to it and not delay, for delay is another sin. In addition, it shows Adam's desire for the improvement of his condition (peace be upon him) and the tranquillity of his mind, and removes whatever the angels (peace be upon them) might cling to, since he was preferred over them and they were commanded to prostrate to him. Alternatively, it is repeated so that a different meaning, other than the first, is attached to it. For the first mention of his descent was for hostility (ta'adi) and non-permanence (lack of eternal abode), and the command in it is cosmic (takwini). The second mention was so that whoever is guided is guided and whoever is led astray is led astray, and the command in it is legal (taklifi). This stylistic device is called tardid (alternation) in rhetoric (badi'). In that case, the fasl is for disconnection (infisal), due to the difference between the two purposes.

It has been said that the sending down of narratives (qasas) is for taking lessons (i'tibar) from the conditions of earlier people. Thus, the repetition of the command is a reminder that the fear arising from imagining the descent of Adam (peace be upon him), coupled with either of these two matters, hostility or legal obligation, is sufficient for one who has resolve and is free of any excuse that would prevent him from opposing the command of Allah, the Exalted. How then would one oppose the command arising from imagining a descent coupled with both of them? If the command were not repeated, then ﴿So when there comes to you﴾ would be conjoined to the first, and then only a descent that results in all these matters would be understood. It is also possible, though far-fetched, that the benefit of the repetition is to alert that He, the Exalted, is the One who willed this, and had He not willed it, it would not have occurred. For this reason He attributed the descent to Himself without any conditional cause, after attributing their expulsion to Satan. This is close to His saying, Exalted is His majesty: ﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾ (8:17).

Al-Jubba'i said: the first descent is from the Garden to the heaven, and the second from it to the earth. But this is weakened by the mention of ﴿And for you on earth is a dwelling place﴾ right after the first.

(Jami'an) is a circumstantial element (hal) from the subject of (ihbituu, "go down"), meaning "gathered together," whether at one time or not. Unity in time may be understood from the context of the speech, as was said regarding ﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾ (15:30). Ibn 'Atiyya was too far off when he made it an emphasis for a deleted verbal noun (masdar), meaning "a descending all together."

﴿So if there comes to you from Me guidance, then whoever follows My guidance, there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve﴾ (2:38). Those who are not legally responsible (ghayr al-mukallaf) are not included in the address, though many included Iblis, because he is addressed to believe. The fa' indicates that what follows is the result of the descent understood from the command. (Immā) is composed of the conditional particle (in) and the superfluous (zā'idah) (mā), used for emphasis. The verb after it is very often emphasized with the nun, though it is not obligatory, as Sibawayh's statement indicates: "If you wish, you do not insert the nun, just as if you wish, you do not bring the mā." This usage appears in his saying:

*O friend, do you not find me one of firm resolve? Abandoning friends is not my nature.*

And in his saying:

*Whether you stay or whether you depart, Allah guards what you leave and what you take.*

Those who held that it is obligatory interpreted it as poetic necessity (darurah), but there is no necessity for that. As for the claim that this would entail the superiority of the follower, the conditional particle, over the thing followed, the verb, this is refuted by the fact that the follower and its emphasis are both followers, so there is no superiority. Or, the mā is for emphasizing the verb at its beginning, just as the nun is for emphasizing it at its end. The particle of doubt is used because the occurrence is not certain. Allah, the Exalted, is not obligated to do anything; rather, if He wills He guides, and if He wwills He leaves.
