It has been said that it is with certainty, and the use of (inna) in its place is not without a subtle point, such as treating the one who knows as if he were other than one who knows, by his not acting in accordance with what his knowledge requires. This is made suitable by the preceding context, that this was the subject of what has been said, namely the occurrence from Adam.

It has also been said that the addition of mā and the emphasis with the heavy form (thaqilah) are no less effective in indicating certainty than (idha, "when"). Yes, the concern here is not with time, but rather with the fact that it is certain to occur while its time is unspecified. You know that what we have chosen is safer and further from artificiality than what has been mentioned, however great its proponent. So reflect.

(Minni, "from Me") is connected to what precedes it, and in it there is a semblance of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), as in al-Bahr (*Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit* by Abu Hayyan). The specific pronoun is used here as a symbol that what befits one who has been guided is pure monotheism (tawhid), and not paying attention to multiplicity. The word (huda, "guidance") is indefinite because the intended meaning is the absolute, and no prior reference preceded it that would require it to be definite. Regarding what is meant by it here, there are several views. It is said: the revealed books. It is said: the messengers. It is said: Muhammad (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him). Perhaps what is meant is his guidance, which his deputies (peace be upon them) brought.

The fa' in (fa-man) is for linking. (Ma) following a conditional sentence which served as the answer to the first condition is in the manner of: "If you come to me, then if you are able, I will do good to you." Al-Sajawandi said its answer is deleted, meaning "follow him." Abu Hayyan preferred that this (man) is a relative pronoun (mawsulah), because of the relative pronoun in the opposing clause, and the fa' entered its predicate because it includes the meaning of a condition. The apparent noun was put in place of the pronoun in (huda-ya, "My guidance") to indicate causation, because guidance, considered in itself, is obligatory to follow, and considered as being attributed to Him, the Exalted, with an attribution of honor, it is more deserving and more fitting to be followed. It has been said: He did not use a pronoun because it is more general than the first, since it includes what is attained by inference and reason. And he did not say "the guidance" so that the identity (ʿayniyyah) would not be understood as well, because an indefinite noun, when repeated in definite form, is generally the same as the first, together with the veneration of attributing it to Himself, the Exalted, which would not be there if it were stated with the definite article (al-).

Fear (khawf) is apprehension of what is future. Grief (huzn) is the opposite of joy, derived from (hazan), which is rough land, as if it were the roughness of worry. It occurs, according to the well-known view, only regarding a past matter. In that case, expressions like ﴿Indeed, it grieves me that you take him away﴾ (12:13) are interpreted as knowledge of that occurred reality. It has been said that both fear and grief refer to the future, but fear is the sense of the loss of something sought, and grief is the sense of distress at the loss of something beloved.

Here, the negation of fear is a metonymy (kinayah) for the negation of punishment, and the negation of grief is a metonymy for the negation of reward. These are more eloquent than explicit statements and more emphatic, because they are like claiming something with clear proof. The meaning is: there is no fear for them, let alone that something disliked should befall them, and they will not lose anything beloved so that they would grieve over it. So what is negated of the friends of Allah is the fear of the arrival of something disliked, and grief in the Hereafter. In this there is an indication that He will admit them into the Garden, which is the abode of joy and security, where there is no fear and no grief. In that case, the contrast between the two groups in the two verses becomes clear.

Some of the eminent scholars said: fear of something disliked is negated from them absolutely, while the fear of majesty (jalal) is at its utmost perfection, and the sincere ones are in great peril. It has been said: the meaning is there is no fear for them of misguidance in this world, and no grief over wretchedness in the next. The negation of fear is placed first because the negation of fear regarding what is coming is more than the negation of grief over what has passed. For this reason it begins with the indefinite noun, which is more inclusive in negation, and the pronoun is placed first to indicate that they are specifically free of grief, and that others grieve. The intended meaning is to express the continuity of the negation, not the negation of continuity, as might be imagined from the predicate in the second clause being in the present tense. This is because it has been established in its proper place that negation, even when applied to the present tense verb itself, indicates continuity and persistence according to context.

Some people mentioned that the shift from "there is no fear for them" or "with them" to "there is no fear upon them" indicates that their condition has reached a point where no one should fear for them. In al-Bahr it is said that He, glorified is He, used (ʿalayhim, "upon them") as a metaphor for domination and encompassing, indicating that fear is not entirely negated. Do you not see that the negation applies to the occurrence of fear upon them, and the negation of the domination of fear does not require its negation in every state? So there is no evidence in the verse for negating the terrors of the Resurrection and fear of it from the obedient. But you know that what we have indicated contains a sufficient metonymy that makes such a thing unnecessary. The same applies to what has been said: that the negation of domination is an allusion to the disbelievers and an indication that fear dominates them.

Furthermore, al-A'raj read (hudaya) with a sukun on the ya', and this involves the joining of two sakins, which results from treating the connected form as if it were the pausal form. Al-Jahdari and others read (hudayya) by converting the alif into ya' and merging it into the ya', according to the dialect of Hudhayl. Al-Zuhri and others read (fa-la khawfa, "there is no fear") with a fatha. Ibn Muhaysin, in a variant from him, read it with a damma without tanwin. It seems that the tanwin was omitted because of the intention of the idafah (annexation), or due to frequent usage, or in consideration of the lam in the noun, as in al-Bahr, so that there would be equivalence in that (la) governs the definite noun in both clauses. According to the reading of the majority, it is a subject (mubtada'), and (ʿalayhim) is its predicate. Or (la) acts like (laysa), as Ibn 'Atiyya said, but the first is better.

﴿Those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the companions of the Fire; therein they will abide forever.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿whoever follows﴾, and it is its counterpart (qasīm), as if He had said: "And whoever does not follow it." What was chosen instead, namely what is mentioned, serves to magnify the state of misguidance and to show the full extent of its ugliness. Or, since "whoever does not follow" includes those whom the call has not reached and who are not among the accountable, He turned away from that wording in order to exclude them. Also, it includes the wrongdoer (fāsiq), on the basis that the intended meaning of "following" is complete following, so that the absence of fear and grief would follow from it. Had He said that, it would have entailed that the wrongdoer abides in the Fire. When He said what He said, that did not follow, and the wrongdoer was excluded from both categories. It is understood by implication (faḥwā) that he has some fear and grief in proportion to his not following. If the words of the Exalted, ﴿and no fear shall be upon them﴾, were taken at that point to negate the continuance of fear and grief, and "following the guidance" were understood as faith in Him, the Exalted, then it would be included in ﴿whoever follows My guidance﴾. However, the friends of the Book of God do not accept or consent to that, and ﴿those, no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾. The relative pronoun is used in the plural form to indicate the multitude of the disbelievers. What is immediately understood by disbelief (kufr) is disbelief in God, the Exalted. It is possible that "disbelieved and denied" are both directed to the prepositional phrase, so that disbelief in the signs means denying them in the heart, and denial means denying them with the tongue. The word āya (sign) is originally a manifest sign in relation to the one who bears the sign, and from it comes the āya of the Qur'an, because it is a marker of the separation of the speech that follows it from the speech that precedes it, or because it is a sign of its meaning and its rulings. It has been said that it was called āya because āya is also applied to a group, as Abu ʿAmr said: "The people went out with their āya," meaning with their group. It is a group of the Qur'an and a portion of its letters. Some have mentioned that it was called that because it is a wonder at which one marvels for its inimitability, as one says: "So-and-so is one of the āyāt (marvels)." As for its root and its form (wazn), there are several opinions. The view of Sībawayh and al-Khalīl is that its root is *ayyah* with two fatḥas. The yā' was changed to alif because it was vowelized and the letter before it was open, contrary to analogy, as in ghāya and rāya, since the regular rule when two weak letters come together is to alter the latter, because it is the place of change. The view of al-Kisāʾī is that its root is *āyiyah* like *fāʿilah*, and by analogy it should have been assimilated, as in *dābbah*, but that was abandoned for lightness, so they deleted its middle radical. The view of al-Farrāʾ is that its form is *faʿlah* with a sukūn on the middle radical, from *ta'ayya al-qawm* (the people gathered), and they said in the plural *āyāʾ* on the pattern of *afʿāl*, so the yā' appeared and the final hamzah is a substitute for a yā', and the second alif is a substitute for a hamzah which is the first radical of the word. Had its middle radical been a wāw, they would have said *āwāʾ* in the plural. Then they changed the quiescent yā' into an alif contrary to analogy, because it was not vowelized and the letter before it was not open. The view of the Kufans is that its form is *ayyah* like *nabqah*, so it was altered, and in irregularity it is like the first view. It has been said that its form is *faʿulah* with a ḍammah on the middle radical. It has also been said that its root is *ayāh*, with the lām placed before and the ʿayn placed after, but this is weak. All the opinions on it are not free of irregularity, and there is nothing strange about it in the case of āya. The intended meaning of "the signs" here is the revealed books, or the prophets, or the Qur'an, or the indicators of Him, the Exalted, in His books and His creation. The intellectual matter is treated as if it were a spoken matter so that denial may be applicable to it. The Exalted used the plural of majesty (nūn al-ʿaẓamah) to cultivate awe and to instill dread, and the Exalted attributed the signs to Himself to show the full ugliness of denying them. He indicated ﴿those﴾ referring to the relative pronoun on the basis of its being characterized by what is in the sphere of the relative clause, to signal that those people are distinguished by that attribute in a way that justifies a sensory indication, together with an announcement of how far their rank is from it. It is the subject (mubtada'), its predicate is ﴿companions﴾, which is the plural of ṣāḥib. The plural of fāʿil on the pattern of afʿāl is irregular, as is stated in al-Baḥr. The meaning of ṣuḥbah is association with a thing, and in common usage it is most often applied to constant companionship. This whole sentence is the predicate of ﴿those who﴾. It is possible that the demonstrative is a substitute for it, or an explicative apposition, with ﴿companions﴾ as its predicate. The nominal sentence after it lies in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), because the explicit statement occurs in the words of the Exalted: ﴿those are the companions of the Fire, abiding therein forever﴾. It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause of ﴿the Fire﴾, because it contains a pronoun referring to it, and the governing element is the sense of the annexation, or the implied lām. Or it lies in the nominative position as another predicate for ﴿those﴾, according to the opinion of one who holds that view. Abu Ḥayyān said: "It is possible that it is explanatory of what was left vague in ‘companions of the Fire’, clarifying that this companionship is meant not as mere association but as eternal abiding. Therefore it has no place in i'rāb (grammatical case) in that case." Abiding here means permanence, in accordance with what the consensus (ijmāʿ) has settled upon. Among the rhetorical beauties (badīʿ) is what some have mentioned, that in the two verses there is a type of it called iḥtibāk (interlocking omission), and how excellent it is, were it not for the metonymy (kināyah) that suffices in place of what is there.

Page 241

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾: an address to a particular group of the disbelievers contemporary with the Prophet (ﷺ), after the general address and after the establishment of the proofs of Divine Unity (tawhid), prophethood (nubuwwah) and the Hereafter (ma'ad), and the reminder of the various kinds of blessings. He (glory be to Him) placed it after the story of Adam because these people, after they had come to clear explanation and manifest proof, and had been commanded, forbidden and urged to follow the unlettered Prophet whom they find written with them, showed the opposite of that. So they departed from the lofty Garden of faith and descended to the earth of nature, and the words (kalimat) came upon them, but they did not receive them with acceptance, so what was lost from them was lost. He turned to them with the call (nida') in order to stir them to hear what comes of commands and prohibitions.

"Banu" (بَنِي) is the plural of "ibn" (son), resembling the broken plural (jam' taksir) because its singular form changes. For this reason the feminine ta' is attached to its verb, as in "qalat Banu 'Amir" (the Banu 'Amir said). It is specific to male offspring, but when it is added to something, it commonly includes both males and females, and then it means "children" (awlad), which is what is intended here. Al-Salikuti mentioned that it is literally used for biological sons, as explained in the principles (usul), and its use for the general sense is metaphorical. Its lam is elided. There is a disagreement as to whether its underlying letter is a ya' or a waw. Ibn Duristawayh held the first view and considered it derived from "bina'" (construction), because the son is a branch of the father and is built upon him; for this reason the made thing is attributed to its maker, so a poem is called, for example, "the daughter of thought" (bint al-fikar). It was also used in the law of those before us for some created beings, "the sons of Allah," in this sense; but when ignorant fools imagined from this the meaning of begetting, that was forbidden until uttering it became disbelief. Al-Akhfash held the second view and supported it by their saying "al-bunuwwah" and by the fact that deletion of the waw is more common, since it is deleted in "ab" and "akh." Al-Jawhari also held this. Perhaps the first is more correct, and "al-bunuwwah" is not a proof, because they also said "al-futuwwah," and there is no dispute that it is from the ya' roots; and the matter of frequency is easy. On both views, as to the measure of "ibn," whether it is fi'l or fu'l, there is a disagreement.

"Isra'il" is a non-Arabic proper noun. They mentioned that it is composed of "i" (ي), meaning a name of His names (exalted be He), and "isra", which means "the servant," or "the chosen one," or "the human," or "the emigrant." It is the epithet (laqab) of our master Ya'qub (peace be upon him). The Arabs made various modifications to it: they said "Isra'il" with a hamza after the alif and a ya' after it, and this is how the majority recited; "Israyil" with two ya's after the alif, and this is how Abu Ja'far and others recited; "Isra'il" with a hamza and a lam, which is related from Warsh; "Isra'al" with an open or a kasra hamza after the ra' and a lam; "Isra'al" with an alif inclined (imalah) followed by a light lam, both with and without imalah, a narration from Nafi', and the recitation of al-Hasan and others; and "Isra'in" with a nun replacing the lam, as in his saying:

"The people of evil say, when we came: 'This, by the Lord of the House, is Isra'in.'"

He (glory be to Him) added these addressees to this epithet to emphasise stirring them to His obedience, for in "Isra'il" there is something that is not in his noble name Ya'qub. Your saying, "O son of the righteous, obey Allah the Exalted," is more urging to the one commanded than your saying, for example, "O son of Zayd, obey." For dispositions incline to follow the footsteps of fathers, even if they are not praiseworthy, so how much more when they are. Such a thing is used in the context of encouragement and warning, on the basis that a good deed is good in itself, and when it comes from the house of prophethood it is better; and an evil deed is evil in itself, and when it comes from the house of prophethood it is worse.

"Wadhkuru" (واذْكُرُوا) is an imperative from "dhikr" with a kasra or a damma on the dhal, both with one meaning, and both may be by the tongue and by the heart. Al-Kisa'i said: with the kasra it is for the tongue, and with the damma for the heart. The opposite of the first is silence, and the opposite of the second is forgetfulness. In general, it is either shared between them, or it is laid down for a general meaning that encompasses both. The apparent view is the first. The intended purpose of the command to this is thanks for the blessing and the discharge of its rights, not merely the recollection by the heart or the utterance by the tongue.

The attribution of the blessing (ni'mah) to His pronoun (exalted be He) is to honour it and to make obligatory the specification of its thanks to Him (glory be to Him). Some verifiers have said that it conveys comprehensiveness (istighraq), since there is no prior reference (ahd). Because of its appropriateness to the context of calling to faith, it includes both the general and the particular blessings for the addressees. The benefit of restricting it by "upon them" is that from this standpoint it is more conducive to thanks, for man is envious and jealous. Qatadah said: it means what He bestowed upon their fathers of what He related in His Book, and upon them of various kinds of blessing, the greatest of which is that they attained the time of the noblest of the prophets and made them part of the community of his call. The correction of the address in this case requires the consideration of predominance (taghlib), or treating the blessings of the fathers as their blessings, so there is no combining of the literal and the metaphorical, as was wrongly supposed.

It is permissible for the ya' in "ni'mati-ya" (نِعْمَتِيَ) to be sukun or fath, and the seven readers agree on fath. "Wa an'amtu" (وأنْعَمْتُ) is the relative clause (silah) of "allati" (which), and the returning pronoun is elided; the estimate is "an'amtuha" (I bestowed it).

It is recited "idda-kiru" (ادَّكِرُوا) with the unpointed dal and a shadda, on the pattern of "if-ta'ilu." 

﴿And fulfil My covenant, I will fulfil your covenant﴾: it is said "awfa" and "wafa," lightened and intensified, with one meaning. Ibn Qutaybah said: one says "awfaytu bil-'ahd" and "waffaytu bihi," and "awfaytu al-kayl" only. "Awfa" also came in the sense of "rose," as in his saying:

"Often I rose in knowledge, your garments lifted by the north winds."

The covenant ('ahd) is attributed to each of those who take charge of one of its two sides. The apparent view here is that the first is attributed to the agent and the second to the object, for He (exalted be He) commanded them to faith and action, and covenanted with them by what He set up of rational and transmitted proofs commanding that, and promised them good reward for their good deeds. The meaning is: fulfil My covenant by faith and obedience, I will fulfil your covenant by a good recompense. Because the command is in the middle, it is correct to demand fulfilment from them. What al-Taftazani said is refuted, though in it there is that there is no meaning in the fulfilment of a covenant by other than its agent. It has been said, and it is what is understood from the words of Qatadah and Mujahid, that both are attributed to the object: the meaning is, fulfil what you covenanted with Me of faith and commitment to obedience, I will fulfil what I covenanted with you of good recompense. The detail of the two covenants is His saying (exalted be He): ﴿Indeed We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ up to His saying (exalted be He): ﴿and We will surely admit you﴾, etc. This requires the consideration that the covenant of the fathers is the covenant of the sons, because of their affinity in religion; otherwise, those addressed by "fulfil" are those who were covenanted with the covenant mentioned in the verse. It has been said: if fulfilment is explained as completing the covenant, then the attribution is to the object in both places; and if it is explained as observing it, then the first attribution is to the agent and the second to the object. There is reflection in this.

It is not hidden that fulfilment has a wide scope. The first of the apparent stations from us is the uttering of the two words of testimony, and from Him (exalted be He) is the protection of blood and property. The last from us is annihilation even from annihilation, and from Him (exalted be He) is adornment with the lights of the attributes and names. As for what has been narrated of traditions, with various chains, sound and weak, in explaining the fulfilment of the two covenants, it refers to the intermediate stations, and by my life they are many. You may also say: the first of the stations from us is the unification of acts, its middle is the unification of attributes, and its last is the unification of the Essence. From Him is what He bestows upon the wayfarer at each station of what that station requires of knowledge and ethics.

Al-Zuhri recited "uwaffi'" (أُوَفِّ) with a shadda. If it agrees with the unintensified form, then that is so; and if by it is intended intensification (takthir) and this is inclined to, it is a sign of His great generosity and beneficence and His abundant bounty, in that He, who is the Truthful, informed that He gives much in exchange for little. He stated this in His saying (exalted be He): ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is ten times its like﴾. The jussive of the verb is because it occurs in the answer to the imperative, and the jussive is either by it, or by a conditional clause that is estimated; this is the choice of al-Farisi, and the text of Sibawayh.

﴿And of Me, fear Me﴾: "al-rahbah" is fear absolutely. It has been said: with caution (tahazzur), and by this it is differentiated from "al-ittiqa'," because the latter is with resolve. For this reason the first is for the common people and the second for the leaders. The more fitting to the contexts of usage is that "ittiqa'" is guarding oneself from what is feared, and making oneself in protection from it; and "rahbah" is the very fear. In the command to it there is a decisive threat, and it is not for intimidation and exaggeration, as in ﴿Do whatever you wish﴾, as was wrongly supposed, because this is required, and that is not required, as is not hidden.

"Iyya-ya" (وإيّايَ) is a detached pronoun in the accusative position, governed by an elided verb, which the stated one explains. In the view of some, the fa' is a conditional fa' that has been moved from the elided condition to its explanatory word, so that it may be evidence for the estimate of the condition. It may be that it explains the elided conditional fa' along with the elided condition. Whoever calls it a conditional fa' has been loose in speech. It cannot be a conjunctive fa', lest two conjunctions gather. The author of al-Miftah chose that it is for coordination with the elided verb. If temporal sequence is intended, it conveys requiring continuance of fear at all times without any interval; and if rank-order (ratabi) is intended, its significance is requiring ascent from one fear to a higher fear. Its gathering with the conjunctive waw, for example, does not harm this, because the latter is for coordinating the elided with what precedes it, and this fa' is for coordinating the stated with the elided. That "fahrabuni" explains the elided does not require that it be identical with it in every respect, nor that it convey no meaning beyond explanation, so as to make it correct to take it as conjunctive. Some later scholars found this good because it contains a wonderful meaning lacking in the conditional. Some others, as a middle view on the question, said: it is conjunctive by origin, and after the deletion it was moved and made conditional. On any estimate, the noble verse is more emphatic in conveying restriction than ﴿You alone do we worship﴾. Among the features of emphasis are: placing the detached pronoun first and the attached one later, and the fa' that makes its following clause a consequence; two items, one of them explicit and the other implicit, with its estimate: "Of Me, fear" (iyya-ya arhabu), then "fahrabuni." And there is in it the repetition of fear, and the meaning of a condition by the indication of the fa'. The meaning is: if you are characterised by fear, then single Me out for fear. The object of fear is elided for generality, i.e., fear Me in all that you do and leave undone. It has been said: "fahrabuni" concerning breaking the covenant. Perhaps the restriction to it is derived from mentioning the command to fear together with it. Then fear is of two kinds: fear of punishment, which is the portion of the people of the outward, and fear of reverence, which is the portion of the people of the hearts. What has been related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that the meaning is: fear Me lest I send down upon you what I sent down upon those before you of your fathers, of the vengeances of which you know, such as transformation and other things, is apparent in the category of the people of the outward, and it is appropriate to the state of these addressees who know the outward of the worldly life while they are heedless of the Hereafter.

The ya' of the pronoun is elided from "fahrabuni," because it is a fasila (a closing word of the verse). Ibn Abi Ishaq recited it with the ya', according to the original form.

[Page 244]

﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you﴾. It is coordinated with what precedes it (﴿Fulfil My covenant﴾). Its apparent meaning is that it is a command to the Children of Israel. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, the scholars and chiefs of the Jews, and so it is a command to them. God, exalted is He, singled out faith (al-iman) after it had already been included in ﴿fulfil My covenant﴾, by way of the whole command to it and the exhortation to it, which is understood from His words ﴿confirming what is with you﴾, to indicate that it is the intended matter, and that it is the foundation for fulfilling covenants. (Wa-ma) is a relative pronoun, (anzaltu) is its relative clause, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning anzaltuhu ("I sent it down"). (Musaddiqan) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), either from the relative pronoun or from its omitted pronoun. The lam in (lima) is emphatic. What is meant by "what I have sent down" is the Qur'an, and expressing it in this way is a glorification of its status. What is meant by "what is with you" is the Torah (al-Tawrah). Expressing it in this way serves to announce that they know it confirms the Qur'an, for being "with" someone implies repeatedly returning to it and examining its contents, which leads to knowing that the Qur'an confirms it. The meaning of the Qur'an's confirmation of the Torah is that it has come down in accordance with the description given of it in the Torah, or that it agrees with it in the fundamentals of religion and the creed, or in what has not been abrogated, such as the stories, the admonitions, and some prohibitions, such as lying, fornication, and usury, or in all of its contents. The disagreement in some particular rulings, which serve as remedies for spiritual diseases, like medicines for different bodily illnesses according to times and persons, is not in reality a disagreement; rather it is agreement with it, in that each of them is true in its own age and contains the wisdom around which the orbit of legislation revolves. The Torah contains nothing indicating the perpetuity of its rulings that were abrogated, such that what abrogates them would contradict them. Rather, its statement affirming the validity of the abrogating Qur'an is a statement of their abrogation and of the end of their time, for which they were legislated because of the benefit in it. This is not "al-bada'" (change of divine decision) in any way, as they imagine. Therefore, the disagreement regarding those abrogated rulings is only the difference of ages; even if the earlier revelation had been delayed, it would have come down in accordance with the earlier one, and if the later revelation had come first, it would have agreed with the earlier one. To this the report that Imam Ahmad and others transmitted from Jabir points: that he (ﷺ) said, when ʿUmar (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu) read some of the Torah in his presence: "If Musa were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me." In a narration of al-Darimi: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, if Musa appeared to you and you followed him and abandoned me, you would have strayed from the right path. And if he were alive and had reached my prophethood, he would have followed me." The restriction of the revealed book to being confirmatory of what is with them serves to emphasise the obligation of compliance, for their belief in what is with them requires belief in what confirms it, definitively. Some people have interpreted "what is sent down" as the Book and the Messenger (ﷺ), and "what is with them" as the Torah and the Gospel. There is nothing very far-fetched in this, except that it is somewhat distant to make (musaddiqan) a circumstantial accusative from the nominative pronoun, and more distant to make (ma) a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah) with (musaddiqan) a circumstantial accusative from the second (ma), and even more distant is making it a circumstantial accusative from an implied verbal noun.

﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾. That is, do not hasten to disbelieve in it, for your duty is to be the first to believe in it, since you know the reality of the matter and its truth. You used to say before: "We shall be the first to follow it." So do not place yourselves in a position other than what is expected of you, and what is required of you, and what is far from proceeding from you, and what is forbidden to you by being the first to disbelieve in it. (Awwal) in the well-known usage is an elative (af'al) form, as in their saying: "This is more first than you" (hadha awwalu minka), and it has no verb, because its first and middle radicals are waw, and induction has shown the absence of a verb for such a form; if one is found, it is rare. What is said in al-Shafiyah, that it derives from w-w-l, is an explanation of the implied verb. It has been said that its origin is awʾal, from wa'ala and wa'alan, meaning "to take refuge," and then it was lightened by replacing the hamzah with waw, and then assimilated; this lightening is not analogical. The derivational connection is that the true first, i.e., His essence, exalted is He, is the refuge of all. If we say it is from wa'ala meaning "to hasten," then the connection is that hastening is the cause of priority. It has been said that awʾal is from ʾala meaning "to return," and the derivational connection follows the pattern mentioned earlier. It was not made plural as awawil because they found it heavy to have two waws together with the plural alif between them. Al-Duraydi said that it is fawʿal, and the first waw was changed to hamzah and assimilated, the waw of fawʿal being in the middle radical position of the verb. This is refuted by its apparent prohibition of declension (منع الصرف), and it is a predicate about a plural pronoun. Here, according to the majority, there must be an interpretation of the comparative standard (al-mufaddal ʿalayhi): either by treating it as singular for a word that has a plural meaning, i.e., "the first group," for example, or by interpreting the compared element as meaning that not one of you individually is able to do so, and the intended sense is the generality of the negation, as in God's words ﴿Do not obey every oft-swearing one﴾. Some people do not require, in such a case, agreement between the indefinite noun to which the elative is attached and what it refers to; rather both options are permissible in their view, as in the verse:

"And when they eat, the basest of eaters; and when they go hungry, the worst of the hungry."

As for one who requires agreement in the first half of the verse, like the verse itself, their prohibition of being the first to disbelieve in it, despite the fact that the polytheists of the Arabs preceded them in disbelief, is because the intent is allusion, so the first of the disbelievers is other than them. Or [the meaning is], "do not be the first disbeliever" from among the People of the Book, and the address is to those present in his time (ﷺ), or rather to their scholars. It may be said that the pronoun refers to what is with you, and what is meant by "do not be the first disbeliever" is: do not be the first disbeliever among those who disbelieved in what was with him, and the Meccan polytheists, though they preceded them in disbelief in what the Qur'an confirms, preceded them in disbelief in it, and this entails that, but they are not among those who disbelieved in what was with him. The distinction between entailment of disbelief and undertaking it is not clear, except that this view is weakened by the fact that this is in contrast to ﴿and believe in what I have sent down﴾, which requires that the object of disbelief and belief be identical. It has been said: a similar expression is implied in the sentence. It has been said: "and the last of it" is implied, i.e., "do not be the first or last disbeliever in it." It has been said: awwal is a superfluous addition. All of these are far-fetched. By interpreting the allusion as a form of metonymy (kinayah), the reason for restricting the disbelief to being the first becomes clear. It has been said that it is a matching of phrases (mushakalah) to their saying: "We shall be the first to follow it." It may also be said that it means precedence and non-lagging behind, so understand.

﴿And do not trade My signs for a small price﴾. Trading (ishtira') is a metaphor for exchanging (istibdal), since it is specific to goods; either by using the restricted term in the general sense, like "nose-rope" (al-mirsan) for the nose, or by likening the mentioned exchange, in that it is desired, to actual buying. The sentence is elliptical, meaning: do not exchange faith in My signs and following them for the worldly portions, which are fleeting, few, and despicable in comparison with the portions of the Hereafter and what God has prepared for the believers of enduring great bliss. Expressing that by "price," although it is what is bought and not what is paid with, indicates that it is like a price in being cheap and degraded. Therefore there is strong rebuke and condemnation in this, since they reversed the matter and made the purpose a means and the means a purpose. There is also a subtle strangeness, in that what is bought is made a price by calling it a price, and then the price is made something bought by placing it as a substitute for what was made a price, through the particle "bi" (with). If it is asked: exchanging faith in the signs can only be valid if they were believers in them and then abandoned it for worldly portions, but they were far from faith. It is answered: the basis of this is that the faith in the Torah which they claim is faith in the signs, just as disbelief in the signs is disbelief in the Torah, so exchange is realized. Some people have taken "the signs" as a metonymy for the commands and prohibitions that they found in the Torah and the divine books concerning the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ), or for what they knew of his noble description and great character (peace be upon him). They used to take a known amount each year from the crops, livestock, and money of their followers. They feared that if they clarified this to them and they followed him (ﷺ), it would be lost to them, so they went astray and led others astray. It has been said that their kings would give them money so that they would conceal and distort. It has been said other than this. Some scholars have used this verse as evidence to prohibit taking payment for teaching the Book of God and knowledge. Some hadiths have also been related on this matter that are not authentic. It is authentically reported that they said: "O Messenger of God, do we take a wage for teaching?" He said: "The best of what you take a wage for is the Book of God, exalted is He." The statements of the scholars have consistently permitted this, though some are reported to have disliked it. There is no proof in the verse for what this proponent claimed, as is not hidden. The matter is explained in the books of jurisprudence (furu').

﴿And fear Me, so have taught fear of Me﴾. That is, by faith and following the truth, and turning away from trading the signs of God for a small price and a passing commodity. Since in the first verse "fear Me" (fa-rhabun) was mentioned, and here "fear Me, so be mindful of Me" (fa-ittaqun), it is because reverential awe (al-rahbah) is less than God-consciousness (al-taqwa). Wherever He addressed the masses, their scholars and their followers, and urged them to remember the blessing they share, He commanded them with the reverential awe that produces God-consciousness, in which they share. Hence it has been said: "Fear is the foundation of the whole matter." And wherever He intended by the address, in what follows, their scholars, and urged them to faith and to heeding the signs, He commanded them with God-consciousness, the first of which is abstaining from what is forbidden and the last of which is disassociating from everything other than the ultimate end of ends. And there is no village beyond ʿAbbadan.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 42:

﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾ This prohibition, together with what follows it, is conjunctively coordinated (ma'tuf) with the whole of the preceding verse, namely His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And believe﴾ etc. This is like what they said regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward﴾, that the combination of the last two attributes, after considering the conjunction, is coordinated with the combination of the first two in the same way. It is also permissible to coordinate it with one single sentence from the preceding sentences, but the relevance (munasabah) on the first view is stronger and the harmony (mula'amah) more complete. Al-labs, with a fatha on the lam, means mixing (al-khalt), and its verb is labasa, of the pattern daraba, and it can mean confusion (al-ishtibah), either by homonymy (al-ishtirak) or by literal and figurative usage (al-haqiqah wa al-majaz). The ba' is either for transitivity (lil-ta'diyah) or for instrumentality (lil-isti'anah). The lam in al-haqq and al-batil is for previous reference (lil-'ahd), meaning: do not mix the truth revealed in the Torah with the falsehood that you invented and wrote down; or: do not make that becoming confused, obscured, and unclear, such that people cannot perceive it, due to falsehood and its mention. The first is perhaps preferable because it is more apparent and more common, not because making the existence of falsehood a cause of the confusion of truth is any more proper than the reverse, since the blameworthy thing is the confusion of truth with falsehood, even though the reverse necessarily follows from it, and since this is secondary to that, it deserves the priority that was denied.

﴿and conceal the truth﴾ is in the jussive mood by coordination with ﴿mix﴾, so the prohibition applies to each of the two verbs. It has also been permitted that it be in the accusative mood by the implied "an". According to the Basrans this is coordination with an assumed verbal noun (masdar muttawahham). Al-Jarmi narrated that the accusative is by the waw itself, and in their view it has the meaning of ma'a (with). It is called waw al-jam' and waw al-sarf, because the verb is diverted by it from coordination. The meaning is: let there not be from you the confusing of the truth upon those who have heard it, and the concealing and hiding of the truth from those who have not heard it. The intent is to censure their evil conduct, which is the combination of two matters, each of which is independently ugly and requires cessation, and a wide path to misguidance and seduction. Since the confusing is in relation to those who have heard, and the concealing is in relation to those who have not heard, the objection is dispelled that the prohibition against combining two things is only valid if it is possible for them to be separated in some respect, and that the mixing of truth with falsehood together with concealing the truth is not like that, since mixing truth with falsehood is itself a concealing of it. The word "truth" is repeated either because the intended meaning of the latter is not the same as the former but is specifically the description of the Prophet ﷺ, or to increase the condemnation of what is forbidden, since in explicitly naming the truth there is what is not in its implication. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read (wa-taktumuna), and it has been explained that the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: while you are concealing, or as concealers. Regarding the permissibility of a circumstantial phrase introduced by the present tense being joined with waw, there are two opinions, and there is no proof on which the one who prohibits can rely. This circumstance, according to some verifiers, is obligatory, and the restriction serves to convey causation, as in: do not strike Zayd while he is your brother. Accordingly, the intended meaning of concealing the truth is what necessarily follows from mixing truth with falsehood, not hiding it from those who do not hear. It has also been permitted that it be coordinated with the clause of prohibition according to the view of one who permits that, namely Sibawayh and a group, and coordination of clauses does not require relevance.

﴿while you know﴾ is a circumstantial clause, and the object of ta'lamuna is omitted for brevity, meaning: while you are among those of knowledge. It is not fitting for one who has knowledge to be characterised by the state you are in. It is not far-fetched that the omission is for abbreviation, meaning: while you know that you are mixers and concealers, or you know its description, or the Resurrection and the Recompense. The purpose of restricting the prohibition by knowledge is to increase the condemnation of their state, since committing these ugly acts while knowing what has been mentioned is more heinous than committing them in ignorance, and one who knows is not like one who does not know. Ibn 'Atiyyah permitted that this clause be coordinated, even though it is affirmative, with what precedes it from the prohibition clauses, even if it is not suitable in informing. In his view it is a testimony against them of knowledge of a particular truth concerning the matter of the Prophet ﷺ, and it is not a testimony of knowledge in general, since they are far removed from it. It has been deduced from the verse that one who knows the truth is obliged to make it manifest, and it is forbidden for him to conceal it, under the conditions well known among the scholars.

And establish the prayer (ṣalāh) and give the zakāt (obligatory almsgiving). What is meant by these two, whether the definite article is for a specific reference or for the category, is the prayer and zakat of the Muslims, because whatever else the Qur'an has abrogated (naskh) is reduced to nothing. Zakāt originally means growth and purity, and it was transferred in the Sacred Law to a specific kind of payment. If it was transferred from the first meaning, then it is because it increases the blessing of wealth and gives the soul the virtue of generosity. Or it is because it occurs in wealth that grows. If it was transferred from the second meaning, then it is because it purifies wealth from impurity and the soul from stinginess. The verse is cited as evidence by one who says that disbelievers are addressed with the subsidiary rulings (furūʿ), since it was addressed to the Jews. The possibility that the command here is to accept the known prayer and zakat and to believe in them, or that it is a command to the Muslims as Shaykh Abū Manṣūr said, is contrary to the apparent meaning, and so it does not prevent using the apparent meaning as evidence. He placed the command to pray first because of the comprehensiveness of its obligation and because it contains sincerity and humble supplication before the Presence, and it is the best of the bodily acts of worship. He joined it with zakat because zakat is the best of the financial acts of worship. Then, one who says that it is not permissible to delay the explanation of what is general (mujmal) beyond the time of address said: this came only after the pillars and conditions of that were explained. One who says it is permissible said: it is permissible that the command be intended to get the listener to prepare himself, as a master says to his servant: "I want to command you to do something, so you must do it." "And bow with those who bow": that is, pray with those who pray. He expressed prayer by bowing (rukūʿ) to exclude the prayer of the Jews, for it has no bowing in it. He restricted this to being with those who bow only because the Jews used to pray alone, so they were commanded to pray in congregation because of its many benefits. Some used this verse as evidence that congregational prayer is obligatory. One who does not hold this interprets the command as recommended, or "with" as meaning agreement even if they are not with them. It was said: bowing means submission and compliance with what the Sacred Law requires of them. Al-Adbaṭ al-Saʿdī said:

Do not humiliate the poor, lest you one day bow down while Fate has raised him up.

It is possible that the command to bow here, after the command to give zakat, is because zakat is a cause of elevation (self-exaltation), so they were commanded to submit so that they would desist from that. However, the principle in the Lawgiver's usage is the legal meanings. Regarding who is meant by "those who bow," there are two views: it was said they are the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions; it was said they are the category in general, and this is the apparent meaning.

* * *

From the allusive (ishārī) interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: "And do not mix truth with falsehood," etc., meaning: do not cut off for yourselves the path to reaching the Truth by means of falsehood, which is the heart's attachment to other than Him. For the truest word a poet ever said is the word of Labīd:

Surely everything other than Allah is vain.

"And conceal not the truth" by turning your attention to other than Him, glory be to Him, while you know that other than Him has no real existence. Or: do not mix His established, true attributes, exalted is He, with falsehood, which is the attributes of your souls, and do not conceal them by the veil of the attributes of the self. You know from the knowledge of the unity of actions that the source of an act is the attribute, so just as you did not ascribe the act to other than Him, do not affirm its attribute for other than Him. "And establish the prayer" with vigilance of the hearts, "and give the zakāt," that is, strive in purifying the soul from blameworthy attributes, so that adornment may be attained after emptying. Or: pay the zakat of aspirations, for aspirations have a zakat just as wealth has a zakat. Indeed, everything has a zakat, as it was said:

Everything has a zakat that must be paid, and the zakat of beauty is mercy like mine.

"And bow" (ārkaʿū): that is, submit to what the Beloved does to you. Submission is the sign of contentment, which is the inheritance of the manifestation of the Supreme Attributes. Its essence is: be content with My decree when you contemplate My attributes, for I have beloveds, and the tongue of the state of each of them says:

Your torment is sweet to me, and your injustice toward me is justice, according to what your desire decrees.

[Page 248]

Then, when He, exalted is He, had commanded them to do good in gratitude for the blessings He had bestowed upon them, He urged them to it from another angle, by His saying, glory be to Him:

﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves?﴾ The hamza here is for affirmation (taqrir) combined with reproach (tawbikh) and wonder (ta'jib). Al-birr (righteousness) means breadth of goodness and benefit, and from it come al-barr (land) and al-bariyyah (the wilderness), because of their expanse. It encompasses every good. Forgetting (al-nisyan), as in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), is the lapse that occurs after knowledge. Here it is meant as abandonment, because no one truly forgets himself. Rather, he deprives himself and leaves himself behind, as one leaves a thing that has been forgotten, as an exaggeration of his disregard and heedlessness toward what he ought to do.

This verse was revealed, as it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, concerning the rabbis of Madinah. They used to secretly instruct those they advised to follow Muhammad (ﷺ), yet they themselves did not follow him. It was also said that they used to command charity while they themselves did not give charity. Thus, the meaning of al-birr here is either faith or kindness. Some scholars kept it on its apparent meaning, encompassing every good, according to what al-Suddi said: they used to command the people to obey Allah, the Exalted, and forbid them from disobeying Him, yet they themselves abandoned obedience and rushed into disobedience. The reproach is not directed at commanding people to righteousness itself, but at its being juxtaposed with the forgetting mentioned.

﴿while you recite the Book﴾, meaning the Torah. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "do you enjoin," and the purpose is rebuke (tabkit) and an increase in censure.

﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ The original form of this statement and similar ones, according to the majority, was with the conjunction placed before the hamza. But since the hamza has the right of initial position in the sentence, it was placed before the conjunction. Some scholars held that there is no advancing or postponing at all, and that between the hamza and the conjunction there is an implied element to which the conjunction can attach.

Reason ('aql) originally means restraint and holding back, and from it comes 'iqal al-ba'ir (the tether of a camel). The spiritual light by which souls perceive both necessary and theoretical knowledge is called 'aql, because it restrains one from engaging in what is ugly and guides one toward what is good. The verb may be used absolutely, treated as intransitive, or it may be transitive with an implied object. The meaning is: "Do you not have a reason that restrains you from what you know to be of evil outcome and grave consequence?" Or: "Will you not use your reason to recognize the ugliness of your conduct, legally, because it contradicts what you recite in the Torah, and rationally, because it combines two contradictory things?" The purpose of commanding righteousness is kindness, compliance, and restraint from disobedience. Their forgetting of themselves contradicts all these aims. There is no dispute that the ugliness of combining these rationally means that it is invalid. Accordingly, the Mu'tazilah have no proof in this verse for the rational ugliness (al-qubh al-'aqli) that they claim. Indeed, some verifying scholars have asserted that the verse is evidence against what they hold, because Allah, glory be to Him, attached the reproach to what they did after reciting the Book. Likewise, there is no proof in it for one who claims that a sinner may not command good or forbid evil, because the reproach concerns combining the two matters with regard to the second alone, not a prohibition of the sinner from admonition. Forbidding evil is obligatory even for the one who commits it, since abandoning the prohibition is a sin and committing the evil is another sin. Failing in one of them does not necessarily entail failing in the other.

Furthermore, although this reproach and rebuke are addressed to the Children of Israel, they are general in meaning for every preacher who commands but does not comply, who restrains but is not restrained, who calls people to hurry and hasten while content for himself to lag behind and perish, who invites creation to the truth yet shuns it, and who demands realities from the common folk while the scent of those realities is not detected from him. This is the one whose punishment will begin before the worshippers of idols, and whose suffering will be magnified because of the abundance of his failure, on a day when there is no judge but the King, the Judge.

It is related from Muhammad ibn Wasi', who said: "It has reached me that some people of Paradise looked down upon some people of the Fire, and said to them: 'You used to command us to do things, and we did them, and so we entered Paradise.' They replied: 'We used to command you to them, but we would oppose them and turn to other things.'"

Some people have held that this address is to the believers, and have taken "the Book" to mean the Qur'an. In that case, this would be a shift in the mode of address (talwin al-khitab), as in ﴿Joseph, turn away from this, and [you, wife], ask forgiveness﴾. However, the apparent meaning rules this out.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 45:

﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾. When He, glory be to Him, commanded them to abandon misguidance and misguiding others, and to adhere to the sacred laws, and this was hard for them because it involved the loss of what they loved and the failure of what they sought, He treated their sickness with this address. Patience (al-sabr) is restraining the self from what it dislikes. He placed it before prayer (al-salah) because prayer is not perfected without it, or because of its suitability to the condition of those addressed.

Or because its effect, as has been said, is in removing what is not fitting, while the effect of prayer is in attaining what is fitting, and the warding off of harms takes precedence over the securing of benefits. The lam in "al-sabr" is for the genus. It is also permissible that by "patience" is meant a kind of it, namely fasting, by the indication of its being mentioned alongside prayer. Seeking help through patience, on the first meaning, is because of what it entails of awaiting relief and success, relying upon Him who does not disappoint those who rely upon Him. For this reason it was said: "Patience is the key to relief." And seeking help through it, on the second meaning, is because of what it contains of breaking desire and purifying the self, which necessitate turning wholly to God, Exalted, and which necessitate the answering of supplication. As for seeking help through prayer, it is because of what it contains of kinds of worship that bring one near to God, Exalted, a nearness that calls for attaining what is sought and ascending to the Beloved. And enough is it of worship that is repeated in the day and night five times, in which the servant converses with the Knower of the unseen, and by which the sinner washes away the filth of faults. Hudhayfah narrated that "when a matter grieved him, the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, would pray," and Ahmad narrated that "when a matter grieved him, he would turn to prayer." Taking "prayer" in the verse, and likewise in the hadith, to mean supplication is not free from remoteness, and even more remote is that by "patience" is meant patience in prayer.

﴿And indeed it is a burden except for the humble﴾. The pronoun refers to prayer, as the apparent sense requires, and singling it out for the return of the pronoun is because of the greatness of its status and its combining of many kinds of patience. The meaning of its being a burden is its heaviness and difficulty for the one who performs it, in the manner of His saying, Exalted: ﴿Grievous to the polytheists is what you call them to﴾. The exception is an exception from the negative (mufarragh), meaning: a burden upon everyone except the humble. The humble (al-khashi'un) are those who are modest and submissive. The root of khushu' is ikhbat (lowliness), and from it comes "al-khashah," a flat, low-lying sand. They are not burdened by it because they know what results for them from it and anticipate what is stored up of its reward, so it becomes easy for them. For this reason it was said: whoever knows what he seeks, what he expends becomes easy for him, and whoever is certain of recompense is generous in giving. It is also permitted that the pronoun returns to seeking help, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Be just, that is nearer to piety﴾, and this is preferred for its comprehensiveness. As for what is said, that seeking help is not a burden, it is a claim with no substance beneath it, for seeking help through prayer is more specific than performing prayer, since it is performing it in the manner of seeking help through it for needs, or for the rest of the acts of obedience, by its drawing those in its train. It has also been said: it may be of the style of His saying: ﴿And God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, and His poet's saying:

"Indeed the bloom of youth and the black hair, as long as it is not disobedient, is madness."

The feminine is similar in His saying, Exalted, according to one opinion: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them﴾, or the meaning is each characteristic of them. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the mentioned matters commanded and forbidden, and their hardship for them is evident. This is closer than what al-Akhfash said, namely that it returns to the answering of the Messenger, may God bless him and grant him peace. And more remote, indeed the most remote, is its return to the Ka'bah, understood from the mention of prayer.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 46:**

﴿Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord, and that to Him they will return.﴾ Ẓann (supposition, assumption) originally means ḥusbān (reckoning or conjecture). Liqā' (meeting) is the arrival of one body at another such that it touches it. The meeting with the Lord, glorified is He, means either meeting His reward or seeing Him, according to those who permit the vision. Each of these is something supposed and anticipated, because although the humble person knows that there must be a reward for righteous deeds, and is certain that the believer will see his Lord on the Day of Return, yet from where does he know with what his deed will be concluded? So the description of those people with ẓann indicates their fear and their lack of security from the plotting (makr) of their Lord. Only the disbelieving folk feel secure from the plotting of God (cf. 7:99). The juxtaposition of the humble (khāshi'īn) with this is then a subtle point that is not hidden. However, the conjunction of ﴿and that to Him they will return﴾ with what precedes it prevents interpreting ẓann as described, because return to Him, the Most High, by resurrection or the arrival at recompense in general, is something for which ẓann and anticipation do not suffice; rather, certainty about it is required. Unless a verb is supposed for it, i.e., "and they know," or it is said that the ẓann relates to the whole taken as a whole, which is likewise not certain even if one of its two parts is certain. Or it is said that return to the Lord here means arrival at His specific recompense, namely the reward in the Abode of Peace (Dār al-Salām) and taking up residence in the vicinity of Him, exalted is His majesty. All of these are contrary to the apparent meaning. For this reason, the interpretation of ẓann as certainty (yaqīn) has been chosen as a metaphor, with the meaning of anticipation and waiting implicit within it. The meeting of God, the Most High, means being gathered (ḥashr) to Him, and return means being recompensed, whether with reward or punishment. So it is as if He, mighty is His majesty, said: "They know that they will be gathered to Him, and He will recompense them, while anticipating that." The point in using ẓann seems to be the exaggeration in suggesting that whoever supposes this does not find the aforementioned difficult, so how much less whoever is certain of it. The mention of the title of Lordship (rubūbiyya) is to indicate that Lordship and sovereignty are the cause of the ruling. The predicate of inna in both places has been made a noun to indicate the realization of the meeting and the return and their being established with Him. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read ﴿they know﴾ (ya'lamūn), and this supports this interpretation.

* * *

Among the allusive (ishāra) interpretations: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people﴾ (2:44), which is the beautiful action that brings about purity of heart and purification of the soul, ﴿while you forget yourselves﴾ (2:44), and do not do what would raise you from the station of the manifestation of actions (tajallī al-af'āl) to the manifestation of attributes (tajallī al-ṣifāt), ﴿while you recite the Book﴾ (2:44), the Book of your innate nature (fiṭra), which commands you with the religion that leads you along the path of unity (tawḥīd). ﴿Will you not then understand?﴾ (2:44), so that you restrain the unrestricted blameworthy attributes of yourselves with the fetter of what has been poured upon you of the ancient lights. Seek aid and help from the One who has true power, through patience with what is done to you, so that you may reach the station of contentment (riḍā) and prayer (ṣalāt), which is watchfulness (murāqaba) and presence of the heart to receive the manifestations (tajalliyāt) of the Lord. Indeed, watchfulness is arduous except for those whose hearts are broken and whose hearts are soft, for receiving the lights of subtle manifestations and for the dominion of their forceful, overpowering assaults. These are the ones who are certain that they are in the presence of their Lord, and that to Him they will return, through the annihilation (fanā') of their attributes and their effacement within His attributes. So they find in the abode nothing but the affairs of the Gentle King, the Subduer.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 47:

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you﴾. He repeated the reminder for emphasis, and to indicate how completely they had neglected to fulfil the rights of this blessing. It also links what follows, the severe promise, to it, so that the call is complete through both encouragement and warning. It is as if He, glorified is He, said: "If you will not obey Me out of gratitude for My earlier blessings, then obey Me out of fear of the consequences of My punishment." The reminder is also of the preference (al-tafdil), which is the greatest of the blessings. For this reason it deserves to be singled out for a particular reminder, while its greatness is also highlighted by repeating the blessing, of which it is one instance. ﴿And that I preferred you over the worlds﴾. This is a conjunction with "My favour," being the specific (al-khass) conjoined to the general (al-'amm). This is one of the usages in which the particle waw (و) is distinctive, as mentioned in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit). This type of conjunction is called tajrid (a rhetorical device of separating an item out from its general category), as though the conjoined item was stripped from the sentence and mentioned separately to give it special attention. The statement involves an omitted noun (hadhf mudaf), meaning "I preferred your forefathers," who were those before the alteration. Alternatively, the favour upon the forefathers is considered a favour upon them. Al-Zajjaj said: "The evidence for this is His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And when We delivered you﴾, etc." The addressees did not see Pharaoh or his people, but He, exalted is He, reminded them that He had always been bestowing favour upon them. By "the worlds" is meant all who existed at the time of the preference, and their preference is by the blessings He granted them, which are indicated by His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And when Moses said to his people: O my people, remember the favour of God upon you when He made among you prophets and made you kings﴾. Therefore the verse does not necessitate their preference over the Prophet (ﷺ), nor over his community, who are "the best community brought forth for mankind." Likewise, it is not valid to use it as evidence for the superiority of humans over angels in every respect. Even if that were valid, it would necessitate the preference of the common people among them over the elite of the angels, and no one holds that.

Among the subtleties: God, glorified and exalted is He, made the Children of Israel witness the superiority of themselves, saying: ﴿And that I preferred you﴾, etc., and He made the Muslims witness His own favour, saying: ﴿Say: By the grace of God and His mercy, so in that let them rejoice﴾. How vast is the difference between one whose witnessing is the favour of his Lord and one whose witnessing is the favour of himself. The former leads to annihilation (fana') in God, and the latter leads to self-admiration (i'jab). Praise be to God, who has distinguished us above many of those He created with distinction.

(Page 251)

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 48:**

﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything.﴾ *Al-yawm* (the day) means the time. Its accusative (*intisab*) is either as an adverbial accusative (*zarf*), with the object of guarding (*al-muttaqa*) omitted, meaning: "And guard yourselves against the punishment on a day." Or it is a direct object, and guarding against it means guarding against what is in it. This is either figurative, by making the container (*zarf*) an expression for what is contained (*mazruf*), or metonymic, because the day necessarily entails it. Guarding against the day itself is impossible, since it certainly comes, and both the people of Paradise and the people of Hell will all witness it. What is possible and within one's power is guarding against what is in it through righteous deeds. (*Taجzi*) is from *jaza* meaning "to settle/discharge," which is transitive by itself to its first object and by *'an* to the second. It may be treated as intransitive for emphasis. The meaning: on the Day of Resurrection, no soul will discharge on behalf of another soul anything of what was obligatory upon it, nor will it stand in for it, nor bear any of what has befallen it; or it will not settle any part of the recompense on its behalf. The accusative of *shay'an* is either as a direct object, or as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) standing in place of the verbal noun, meaning "any recompense." Abu al-Sammak read *wa-la tajzi'* (from *ajza'a 'anhu*, meaning "to suffice for"), which is intransitive, and *shay'an* is then only an absolute object. The meaning: no soul will suffice for another soul in any degree of sufficing, nor will it benefit it in any way. The indefiniteness of the nouns is for generalization regarding the intercessor, the one interceded for, and that which intercession concerns. It contains a great deal of terror and an announcement that hopes are cut off, as indicated by the words of God Most High: ﴿On the Day a man will flee from his brother, and his mother and his father, and his spouse and his children. For each of them on that Day will be a matter that occupies him.﴾ The clause is, according to the well-known view, a qualifier of *yawm* (day), and its connecting pronoun is omitted, meaning "will not settle in it." Al-Kisa'i (a Kufan grammarian) did not permit omitting the object of a preposition when it is not determined, so one does not say "I saw a man I desire," meaning "I desire him." His method in this is gradual: the preposition is first omitted, until the pronoun attaches to the verb and becomes accusative, so that its omission becomes valid, as in the verse:

*Fa-ma adri a-ghayyarahum tana'in wa-tuul al-'ahdi aw malun asabu*
I do not know whether distance and the long passage of time changed them, or wealth they acquired.

meaning *asabuhu* (they acquired it). According to the opinion of the Kufans, it is also possible that the clause is not a qualifier, but is attached to a noun, *yawm*, which is omitted because the preceding text indicates it, so no pronoun is needed; that omitted noun would be a substitute (*badal*) for the mentioned noun. Among examples of this is what al-Kisa'i reported: "Feed us tender meat, the sheep they slaughtered," with *shatin* in the genitive, on the assumption of "meat of a sheep." Al-Farra' also reported similar, and among it is the verse:

*Rahima Allahu a'zaman daffanuha bi-Sijistan Talhata al-Talahat*
May God have mercy on bones they buried in Sijistan, Talhah of the Talhahs.

according to the narration of those who read *Talhata* in the genitive. The Basrans (grammarians of Basra) do not permit omitting the *mudaf* (the first noun of an annexation) and leaving the *mudaf ilayhi* (second noun) in the genitive, and they say that what came of this is anomalous. Abu Sirar read *la tajzi nasamatun 'an nasamatin*, and *nasamah* means the same as *nafs*.

﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it.﴾ Intercession, as in *al-Bahr* (the Sea of Muhit), is joining another to one's means. It derives from *al-shaf'* (even number), the opposite of *al-watr* (odd number), because the intercessor joins the seeker in obtaining what he seeks, so the pair (*shaf'*) becomes two after having been one. *Al-'adl* (compensation) is the ransom (*fidyah*), as said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. It is also reported from him that it means a substitute, i.e., one man in place of another man. The root of *al-'adl*, with the letter 'ayn (ʿ) vowelled with a fatha, is what equals a thing in value and measure, even if it is not of its kind. With a kasra, it is what equals it in kind and bulk. Among the Arabs, some use the kasra on the 'ayn with the meaning of ransom. Al-Wahidi mentioned that *'adl* of a thing, with the fatha or the kasra, is the same, and he recited the verse of Ka'b ibn Malik:

*Sabarna la nara li-Llahi 'adlan 'ala ma nabana mutawakkilina*
We endured, seeing no compensation from God for what befell us, relying upon Him.

Tha'lab said: *al-'adl* means guarantor and bribe, but this does not affect the meaning of the verse. The two genitive pronouns with *min* (from) may refer to the second soul, because it is the nearest mentioned noun and because it agrees with God's words ﴿nor will they be helped﴾, and because it is what is immediately understood from His words ﴿nor will any compensation be taken from it﴾. The meaning of the non-acceptance of intercession in this case is that if an intercessor comes with an intercession, it will not be accepted from it. Or they may refer to the first soul, because it is the one spoken of, while the second is a secondary element. Also, what is immediately understood from the negation of the acceptance of intercession is that if it were to intercede, its intercession would not be accepted. In that case, the meaning of "no compensation taken from the first" is that if a compensation were given from the second, it would not be taken. It seems in the verse, according to this, there is a kind of ascending order (*taraqqi*) employed here, though it is not employed in another context, as if it were said: the first soul is unable to rescue its companion from fulfilling obligations and making amends for its debts, because it is preoccupied with its own affair. Then, if it is able to deny what was owed through intercession, that will not be accepted from it. And if it adds to that by offering ransom, that will not be taken from it. And if it tries to escape by force and dominance, how could that be possible for it? It will not be able to do so. Al-Kawashi chose to make the first pronoun refer to the first soul and the second to the second, by the device of *laff wa-nashr* (arrangement in which the two items are referred back in order), because this applies both sentences to their apparent meanings, and clarity makes the separation easy. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read *wa-la tuqbalu* with a *ta'* (feminine form), and Sufyan read *yaqbalu* with a fatha on the *ya'* and *shafa'atun* in the accusative, in the active voice. In this there is a shift (*iltifat*) from the first person pronoun in *ni'mati* (My blessing) etc. to the third person pronoun. Its passive form is more emphatic.

﴿Nor will they be helped.﴾ *Al-nasr* (help), in origin, is assistance, and from it comes the phrase *ard mansurah* (land given rain), meaning land watered by rain. What is meant here is what averts harm, meaning: nor will they be prevented from the punishment of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The pronoun refers either to what is indicated by the second, indefinite soul, which falls in the context of negation among many souls, so this is of the type of what was mentioned earlier in meaning by the indication of another word. Or it refers to the indefinite soul insofar as, being general by negation, it carries the sense of multiplicity, as it has been said regarding God's words ﴿There is none of you who could hold him back from it﴾. It is put in the masculine to account for the souls being interpreted as people and humans. In this there is a warning that those souls are servants, subdued and humbled under His dominion, Exalted is He, and that they are people like all other people in this matter. Its return to the two souls, on the basis that the dual is a plural, is not valid. Making the negation extend to the nominal sentence for emphasis, with *hum* (they) in the nominative as the subject, and the sentence after it as its predicate, or making it an object of the passive verb, with the verb after it as explanation, is possible. The harmony of the sentences is not something I agree with in his choice, though some eminent scholars took this view. The Mu'tazilah (a theological school) held to the generality of the verse for the negation of intercession for the people of major sins. That the address is to the disbelievers, and that the verse was revealed concerning them, does not remove the generality derived from the wording. It has been answered by specification in two ways. The first is by place and time, since the stations of the Resurrection and the length of its duration have breadth and extent. Perhaps this condition is at the beginning of its occurrence and its severity, and then intercession is permitted. Similar has been said regarding the reconciling between His words ﴿So there will be no kinship between them that Day, nor will they ask of one another﴾ and His words ﴿And some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾. That the station of threat refuses this is not accepted. The second is by individuals, since there must be specification for those other than the disobedient, for the sake of greater ranks. So the general term does not remain upon its generality according to them; otherwise it would necessitate the denial of the increase of benefits, and they do not hold that. We specify among the disobedient by the authentic hadiths which reach the level of *tawatur* (mass transmission). Since the door of specification has been opened, we also say: that negation is specified as applying before the permission, based on His words ﴿And intercession will not benefit with Him except for one whom He has permitted﴾. This is a specification which has evidence, and their specification (of the non-disobedient) has no evident proof. Furthermore, intercession for the increase of benefits almost ceases to be intercession at all. Otherwise we would be intercessors for the Messenger (ﷺ) at the time of prayer upon him, although the consensus has occurred among us and among them that he is the Intercessor. Also, in His words ﴿And seek forgiveness for your sin and for the believers﴾ there is something which indicates the intercession we claim, and urges the specification to which we go. May Allah grant us intercession, and gather us in the company of the People of the Sunnah and the Community (*Ahl al-Sunnah wa-l-Jama'ah*).

[Page 253]

When He, glory be to Him, had mentioned His blessings in general terms, He wished to detail them, so that the reminder would be more eloquent and the proof more forceful. So He said: ﴿And [remember] when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who inflicted on you the worst torment﴾. This is a coordination (ʿatf) on "My blessing" (niʿmatī) in the sense of "Remember" (udhkurū), in the sense that it is a coordination with what comes before. This avoids a separation (fasl) between the two coordinated elements by a foreign element, which is "Be mindful of" (ittaqū). What is useful for you here has already been mentioned before.

It has been read as "We delivered you" (anjaynākum) and "I delivered you" (anjaytukum). The first reading is attributed to al-Nakhaʿī. As for "the family" (āl), it is said that it means "the people" (ahl). It is said that its alif is a substitute for a hāʾ, and that its diminutive is uhayl. Some have held that its alif is a substitute for a silent hamza, and that this hamza is a substitute for a hāʾ. It is also said that it does not mean "people" (ahl), because ahl means kinship, whereas āl means one who returns to you through kinship, or opinion, or creed.
