Thus its alif is a substitute for a wāw, and for this reason Yunus said in its diminutive: uwayl. Al-Kisāʾī transmitted this explicitly from the Arabs. It is also reported from Abū ʿUmar, the student of Thaʿlab, that ahl means kinship, whether or not it has a follower, while āl means kinship together with its follower. Thus it is more specific than ahl. They also restricted it to being construed with people of importance, so it is not construed with non-rational beings or with those among them who have no importance. Thus one does not say "the family of Kufa" or "the family of cupping." Some added the condition that it must be masculine, so one does not say "the family of Fatimah." Perhaps all of this is a matter of majority usage; otherwise, it has occurred contrary to this, as in "āl Aʿwaj," the name of a horse, "āl al-Madīnah," "āl Nuʿm," "āl al-Ṣalīb," and "ālika." It is used unconstructed, as in "hum khayru āl" (they are the best of families). It is pluralized like ahl, so one says "ālūn."

Fir'awn is a title for whoever ruled the Amalekites, as Khosrow is for the king of the Persians, Caesar for the king of the Romans, Khaqan for the king of the Turks, Tubbaʿ for the king of Yemen, and al-Najashi for the king of Abyssinia. Al-Suhaylī said it is the name for everyone who ruled the Copts and Egypt. It is indeclinable because of its status as a proper noun and its foreignness. It has been derived from it, in consideration of what it entails, so it is said: "tafarʿana al-rajul" when a man became tyrannical and insolent.

The name of this Pharaoh was al-Walīd ibn Muṣʿab, as stated by Ibn Isḥāq and most of the exegetes. It is said that his father was Muṣʿab ibn Rayyān, as related by Ibn Jarīr. It is said that he was Qanṭūs, as related by Muqātil. Wahb ibn Munabbih mentioned that the People of the Two Scriptures said that his name was Qābūs and his kunya was Abū Murrah, and that he was from the Copts. It is said that he was from the Banū ʿAmlīq, or ʿImlāq ibn Lāwiz ibn Iram ibn Sām ibn Nūḥ, peace be upon him, and they are nations that dispersed in the lands. It was narrated that he was from the people of Iṣṭakhr, and came to Egypt where he became king. It is also said that he was a perfume seller in Isfahan, whom debts overwhelmed, so he entered Egypt, and his affair ended in what it ended in. The story of the melon is well known, and our master, the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, transmitted it in his tafsir.

The correct view is that he is not the Pharaoh of Joseph, peace be upon him. His name, according to the well-known view, was al-Rayyān ibn al-Walīd, and he believed in Joseph and died during his lifetime. He is one of the forefathers of the Pharaoh mentioned, according to one opinion. What supports that they are different is that the interval between Joseph's entry and Moses' entry, peace be upon them both, is more than four hundred years.

The intended meaning of "the family of Pharaoh" here is either the people of Egypt, or his household specifically, or his followers in his religion. And "We delivered you" means "We delivered your fathers," and similar expressions are likewise to be understood. Thus there is no proof in them for a transmigrationist (tanāsukhī). This usage is common in Arabic speech, like the saying of Ḥassān:

"We killed you at Badr, so your armies have become wandering among the dead."

"They afflict you" (yasūmūnakum) is from al-sawm, which originally means going forth in search of something. It is used for going alone at times, as in "al-sāʾimah" (the free-grazing animal). At other times it is used for seeking, as in "al-sawm" in trade. It is said: "sāmahu" means he burdened him with hard labor. "Al-sūʾ" is the verbal noun of sāʾa yasūʾu, and is intended as the bad thing. It is used for everything that is ugly, as in "aʿūdhu billāhi taʿālā min sūʾ al-khuluq" (I seek refuge in God, exalted be He, from bad character). "Sūʾ al-ʿadhāb" (the worst torment) is its most dreadful and severest kind in comparison to the rest. It is in the accusative as the object, either by dropping the preposition from "yasūmūnakum," or without dropping it. The clause may be an independent statement, describing a past state, and it may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "anjaynākum" or from "āl Fir'awn," and this is the closer view. The meaning is: they appoint you over, or assign to you, arduous tasks and dreadful affairs, or they send you to them and deploy you in them, or they seek for you the worst torment, explained by what follows.

It is related that Pharaoh made the Children of Israel servants and slaves, and divided them into occupations: one group builds, another group farms, and another group serves. Whoever was not engaged in work was assessed a poll tax that he had to pay every day. Whoever the sun set upon before he paid it had his hand shackled to his neck for a month. He also made the women spin and weave linen.

﴿They slaughter your sons﴾ is a circumstantial or resumptive clause, as if it were said: what did they impose on them? So he said: "yudhabbiḥūna" (they slaughter) and so on. It is permissible to take it as a substitution of verb for verb, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿he will meet a penalty﴾ ﴿the punishment will be doubled for him﴾. It was also said that it is by coordination, with its conjunction dropped, due to the verse of Ibrahim. The verifiers hold the distinction, and they interpreted "the worst torment" in that verse as the arduous obligations other than slaughter. It was coordinated for the difference, and that is considered there and not here, according to their view, because of the prior "And remind them of the days of God," which implies enumeration, and there is nothing here that implies it.

"Al-abnāʾ" (the sons) are the male children. It is said that they are the men, and they were called "sons" in consideration of what they had been before. It is reported in some accounts that he killed forty thousand boys. It is related that he would kill the men whom he feared might go out and assemble to corrupt his affair. The well-known view is to take "sons" in the first sense, and this is the appropriate and immediately understood sense. Regarding the cause of this there are various sayings and reports, and most of them indicate that Pharaoh feared the loss of his kingdom at the hand of a boy from the Children of Israel, so he did what he did. But the command of God is a decree decreed.

Al-Zuhrī and Ibn Muḥaysin read "yadhbaḥūna" with a light form, and ʿAbdullāh read "yuqattilūna" with an intensive form.

﴿And they spare your women﴾ is coordinated with "yudhabbiḥūna," meaning they let your daughters live and leave them alive.

It is also said: they examine their private parts to see whether they are pregnant. "Al-ḥayāʾ" here means the private parts, because one is shy to uncover them. "Al-nisāʾ" is the plural of "al-mar'ah" (woman). In al-Baḥr it is said that it is a broken plural of "niswah" on the pattern "fiʿlah," a paucal plural. Ibn al-Sarrāj claimed that it is a collective noun. On both views, it is not pronounced with a singular form from its own pattern. It originally refers to adult women, excluding young girls. So on the first view it is metaphorical with regard to the first meaning, to indicate that their sparing was so that they would become women to serve them. On the second view, it is the predominance of adult women over young girls. On the third view, it is literal.

He mentioned the slaughtering first because it is the most difficult of affairs and the most arduous among people, although that sparing is greater than killing for the zealous one.

﴿And in that is a great trial from your Lord﴾: this refers to the slaughtering and the sparing, or to the deliverance. The pronoun is plural, addressing the audience. It is permissible for "that" (dhālikum) to refer to the whole sentence. The original sense of "balāʾ" is testing. When it is attributed to Him, exalted be He, what is intended is what functions like it in relation to the servants, according to the well-known view. It sometimes occurs through pleasant things, so that they may give thanks, sometimes through harmful things, so that they may be patient, and sometimes through both, so that they may desire and fear. If the reference is taken in the first sense, then "trial" means affliction. If in the second sense, then it means blessing. If in the third sense, then it means the common element, like the general testing shared by both. The first is preferred by usage; the second because it occurs in the context of favor; the third because of the subtlety of combining encouragement and warning.

The meaning of "from your Lord" is from Him, exalted be He, either by giving them power over you, or by sending Moses, peace be upon him, and granting him success to deliver you, or by both together.

"Great" (ʿaẓīm) is an adjective of "trial." Indefiniteness of both is for magnification. The greatness is in relation to the addressees and the listeners, not in relation to Him, exalted be He, because He is the Great who does not consider anything great.

* * *

From the approach of allusion and esoteric interpretation: "And [remember] when We delivered you from the powers of Pharaoh," that is, the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammārah), veiled by its egotism and by regarding itself, exalted above destroying existence. "Egypt" is the city of the body, enslaved. It and its powers, which are imagination, fancy, anger, and desire, are the spiritual powers, the sons of God's elect Jacob, the spirit, and the natural bodily powers, namely the outward senses and the vegetative powers. Those (the commanding soul and its powers) impose on you the difficult hardships and arduous labors of gathering wealth, greed, arranging food and clothing, and other such things. They enslave you through reflecting on them and being preoccupied with them, so that you attain a pleasure which is in reality a torment and humiliation, because it prevents you from witnessing the lights and enjoying the abode of permanence.

"They slaughter your sons," which are the spiritual powers, from the theoretical powers, which are the right eye of the heart, and the practical powers, which are its left eye, and the understanding, which is its hearing, and the secret, which is its heart. "And they spare your women," your natural powers, so that they may use them, and prevent them from their fitting actions. In that deliverance is a great blessing from your Lord, who elevates you from station to station and from vision to vision, until you reach Him and lay down your saddles before Him. Or in the totality of that is a trial for you, and the manifestation of the effects of the various Names upon you. So give thanks and be patient, for all is from Him, and whatever the Beloved does is beloved.

[Page 256]

﴿And when We parted the sea for you﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with what precedes. *Al-farq* is separation between two things. Its transitive object "the sea" is construed through the implicit sense of *al-shaqq* (splitting), meaning: We split it, and We separated its parts from one another for your sake and because of your deliverance. The *bāʾ* here expresses causation (*al-sababiyya*), which is a motivating causation (*al-bāʾith*) equivalent to the *lām*, if we hold that God's acts are explained by purposes (*taʿlīl*). It also expresses a causation similar to this in that the act follows from it and is intended by it, if we do not hold that view. The Exalted said "for you" (*bikum*) rather than "for you" with *lakum* because the Arabs, as al-Dāmighānī relates, say: "I became angry *li-Zaydin*" when you are angry on his behalf while he is alive, and "I became angry *bi-Zaydin*" when you are angry on his behalf while he is dead. So there is an allusion in it that the parting was on account of the ancestors of those addressed. It is also possible that the *bāʾ* is for instrumentality (*istiʿāna*), meaning "by your conduct," and there is then a metaphor in a dependent form (*istiʿāra tabaʿiyya*), in which their conduct is likened to an instrument in being the means by which the parting came about from God the Exalted. The *bāʾ* may also be used for accompaniment. The statement of Imam al-Rāzī, may God sanctify his secret, that "they were walking, and the water parted at their walking, so it was as though it was parted by them," is refuted by the fact that the parting of the water preceded their walking, as the narrative indicates. Also, God's words ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it split, and each part became like a huge mountain﴾ show that. What is said, that the instrument was the staff, as the verse seems to indicate, is not granted. What is understood is that the staff was the instrument of the striking, not of the parting. Even if it were granted, it is permissible for the whole to be the instrument, with the instrumentality of the walking being in a figurative sense. It may also be said that the *bāʾ* is for association (*mulābasa*), and the prepositional phrase and its object form a fixed adverbial complement occupying the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) of the subject. God's association with them at the time of the parting is a rational association, namely that He is their helper and protector. This is what Moses, peace be upon him, pointed to with God's words ﴿By no means! Indeed my Lord is with me; He will guide me﴾. Some people made it a *ḥāl* of the sea, placed before it, but this is nothing, because the parting precedes their association with the sea, except in a loose usage (*tawassuʿ*). They differed about this sea. It was said to be the Qulzum, whose two shores were four farsakhs apart. It was said to be the Nile. The Arabs call salt water and sweet water *baḥr* when they are abundant, and from this comes ﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting together﴾. Its root meaning is breadth. It was also said that the root meaning is splitting. From the first meaning comes *al-baḥra*, a town, and from the second comes *al-baḥīra*, a she-camel whose ear has been split. There are two views about the manner of the splitting. The well-known view is that it was straight (*khaṭṭiyyan*). Some reports suggest that it was arched (*qawsiyyan*), since in them the exit was from the side by which they had entered, and the possibility of returning by the route of entry is almost impossible, because the enemies were on their trail. God willing, the verification of what relates to this discussion will come later.

﴿Then We delivered you and drowned the folk of Pharaoh﴾. There is an ellipsis in the speech, indicated by the meaning. The estimated sense is: "And when We parted the sea for you, and Pharaoh and his hosts followed you into its midst, then We delivered you," that is, from drowning, or from Pharaoh and his household catching up with you, or from what you disliked. The Exalted used the expression "the folk of Pharaoh" as a metonymy (*kināya*) for Pharaoh and his household, as one says "the Banū Hāshim," and as in His words ﴿We have honoured the children of Adam﴾, meaning this whole species, including Adam. Or He limited the mention to the household because, if they were punished by drowning, the beginning of obstinacy and the head of misguidance would be more deserving of it. The Exalted has mentioned the drowning of Pharaoh in other verses of His Book, such as His words ﴿So We drowned him and those with him, all of them﴾ and ﴿So We seized him and his hosts, and cast them into the sea﴾. Taking "household" (*āl*) to mean the person alone, although it is attested lexically as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, is weak and does not suit the context. What suits the context is generality. The deliverance of the people of Moses, by their being cast into the sea and coming out of it safe, corresponds to the deliverance of their prophet Moses, upon our Prophet and upon him be the best of prayers and peace, from slaughter, by being cast as an infant into the sea and coming out of it safe. Every nation has a share from its prophet. The destruction of Pharaoh and his people by drowning corresponds to the destruction of the Children of Israel at their hands by slaughter, because slaughter brings death quickly through the flow of blood, while drowning prolongs death, and no blood flows out. The thing through which life is had, which is water, as His words point to: ﴿And We made every living thing from water﴾, became the cause of their annihilation from existence. In this there is an indication of their despair and the reversal of their hopes, as it has been said:

"To water runs one who chokes on a morsel;
where does one run who chokes on water?"

Since drowning is among the most difficult deaths and the most severe in intensity, for this reason the drowned Muslim is a martyr. God the Exalted made it a deterrent for whoever claims lordship and says "I am your Lord Most High." The punishment is proportionate to the sin, and the claim to lordship and exaltation is fittingly met with the humbling of the claimant and his being buried in the depths of the water. You may also say: when Pharaoh took pride in the water, as His words relating his speech indicate: ﴿Is not the dominion of Egypt mine, and these rivers flowing beneath me?﴾, God the Exalted made his destruction through the water. The follower has a generous share of what he follows. That drowning, deliverance and drowning happened on the day of ʿĀshūrāʾ, and the discussion of this is well known.

﴿While you were looking on﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*jumla ḥāliyya*), and in it there is a figurative extension (*tajawwuz*), meaning: and your fathers were looking on. The object is omitted, meaning all that has passed. If the meaning is the rulings, then "looking" is in the sense of knowing, and this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him. If the meaning is the actions themselves, namely the parting, deliverance and drowning, then it means witnessing, and this is the view of the majority. The clause is then a circumstance of the subject, and it governs all the preceding verbs by the dispute over governance (*tanāzuʿ*). Its purpose is to establish the blessing upon them, as if it were said: "and you have no doubt about it." It is also permissible to estimate the object as specific, meaning: their drowning and the closing of the sea over them. Then the circumstance is linked to the nearest verb, which is "We drowned," and its purpose is to complete the blessing, since the destruction of the enemy is a blessing, and witnessing it is another blessing. In the stories of al-Kisāʾī it is reported that when the Children of Israel crossed the sea, they stood looking at the sea and at Pharaoh's hosts, reflecting on how they would act, or on the splitting of the sea. Then the circumstance is linked to the principal verb mentioned, which is "We parted," and its purpose is to bring the blessing before them so that they might marvel at its great significance and recognise its miraculous nature. Or it refers to the drowned household, so the circumstance, being from the object of "We drowned," is linked to it, and its purpose is to confirm and establish the drowning. It was also said: the meaning is that some of you look at others while you are travelling in the sea. It is reported that some of the people of Moses said to him: "Where are our companions?" He said: "Go on, for they are on a path like your path." They said: "We will not be satisfied until we see them." So God revealed: "Strike with your staff in this manner." He did so against the walls, and they became openings, so they saw one another and heard one another speaking. Then the circumstance is linked to "We parted," and its purpose is to complete the blessing, since their being at ease, each seeing the state of the other, is another blessing. Some people make the verb in this sense function as intransitive, and this is not far-fetched. Indeed, what is far-fetched is that "looking" here is made a metaphor for nearness, meaning: "while you were near them," that is, in a state where, if you had looked at them, you would have seen them, as people say: "You are in my sight and hearing," meaning you are near me such that I see you and hear you. Likewise it was made to mean consideration, meaning: "while you were taking warning from their fate and taking admonition from the places of the chastisement sent upon them." Moreover, they have related very lengthy accounts about the manner in which the Children of Israel came out and how they resisted while in the sea, and about the manner in which Pharaoh came out with his hosts, and about the size of the two groups. Neither the Qur'an nor the sound hadith indicates these, and God the Exalted knows best their reality.

The allusive (*ishāra*) meaning of the verse is that the sea is this world, and its water is its desires and pleasures. Moses is the heart, and his people are the qualities of the heart. Pharaoh is the commanding soul (*al-nafs al-ammāra*), and his people are the qualities of the soul, who are the enemies of Moses and his people, seeking them in order to kill them, while they are travelling toward God the Exalted. The enemy is behind them, and the sea of this world is in front of them. For them there is no escape in journeying to God the Exalted from crossing it. Were they to plunge into it without striking with the staff of "There is no god but God," in the hand of Moses, the heart, for he has a white hand in this matter, they would drown just as Pharaoh and his people drowned. And had this staff been in the hand of Pharaoh, the commanding soul, it would not have split. Just as the hand of Moses, the heart, is a condition for the splitting, so too the staff of remembrance is a condition for it. When both conditions are met, and Moses strikes with the staff of remembrance time after time, the sea of this world splits by negation, by God's leave, and the water of desires interlocks to right and left. God the Exalted sends the wind of providence and the sun of guidance onto the bed of that sea, so it becomes dry of the water of desires. Moses and his people then come out, by the providence of tawḥīd,

[Page 257]

to the shore of salvation. "And indeed to your Lord is the final end." And it is said to Pharaoh and his people, when they have drowned and been made to enter the fire: "Away with the wrongdoing folk!"

And [remember] when We appointed to Moses forty nights﴾. When the Children of Israel crossed the sea, they asked Moses, peace be upon him, to bring them a Book from Allah. So Allah, glorified is He, promised to give him the Torah, and Moses accepted that. He set for him an appointed time: the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten [days] of Dhu al-Hijjah, or the month of Dhu al-Hijjah and the first ten [days] of Muharram. The form *mufa'alah* (the verbal form expressing reciprocity) is therefore in its proper sense: it comes from one party's act and the other party's acceptance of it, like *'alajtu al-marid* (I treated the patient). To deny that this usage is permissible is not to be heeded, given that it occurs in the speech of the Arabs, the scholars explicitly state it, and they approve of it. It is also possible that *wa'adna* (We appointed) is from the sense of *muwafah* (meeting by appointment), and has nothing to do with promising, being derived from your saying: "Our meeting-place is on such a day, and at such a place." It may also carry the meaning of *wa'adna* (promising), and Abu 'Amr recited it that way. Or the meaning of meeting (*al-mula'ah*) may be supplied. Or the verb may be broken down into two verbs, with revelation supplied in one and coming in the other. There is no objection to any of this, as al-Damghani verified. Abu 'Ubaydah's statement that *al-muwa'adah* (mutual promising) occurs only among humans is not accepted. Abu Hatim's statement that it occurs most often among created beings of equal standing, even if granted, does us no harm.

*Arba'in* (forty) is the object, with a suppressed noun governing it through the slightest connection: that is, [the giving of] forty [nights], meaning at the completion of them, or in the last ten of them, or in all of them, or at their beginning, according to the differing reports. Alternatively, it is a stable adverbial phrase functioning as an attribute of a suppressed object of *wa'adna*, meaning: "We promised Moses a matter that would take place within forty [nights]." It has also been said that it is an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*), meaning: "We promised Moses a promise of forty nights."

Some people held that it is better not to supply an object, because the purpose is to explain who was promised, not what was promised. *Arba'in* is then in the accusative by being treated as the object in a loose extension of usage. In this there is exaggeration, by making the appointed time itself the thing promised, and by making forty [nights] an adverbial of *wa'adna*, in the manner of *ja'a Zayd yawma al-khamis* (Zayd came on Thursday). This is nothing, as is not hidden.

*Musa* (Moses) is a non-Arabic name, not declined, because of definiteness and foreignness. It is said that it is compounded of *mu*, which is water, and *sha*, which is tree, and it was altered to *sa* with the letter *sin*. It seems that whoever named him by it intended the water of the sea and the chest in which he was cast. Scholars have debated its morphological pattern. According to Sibawayh, its pattern is *maf'al*. It has also been said that it is *fu'la*, derived from *masa yamis* (to sway), with the *ya'* changed to *waw* because of the preceding *damma*, as they said *tuba* [for *tayba*]. But it is from the *ya'*-roots, since it derives from *taba yatib* (to be good). What weakens this is the consensus that it is declined when indefinite, whereas if it were *fu'la* it would not be declined, since the feminine *alif* alone prevents declension in both definite and indefinite forms. Moreover, the prefixing of *mim* is more common than the suffixing of *alif*.

Allah, glorified and exalted is He, referred to that time with "nights" rather than "days," because the beginning of the appointed time was at night. Nights are the starting points of the months of the Arabs, since these were set according to the course of the moon, and the crescent appears at night. Or [it is because] darkness precedes light, as evidenced by ﴿And a sign for them is the night; We strip from it the day﴾. Or it is an indication of continuous fasting by night and day. Had the reference been to days, one might have supposed that he broke his fast at night. When the nights were specified, it was understood from the force of the discourse that he fasted forty nights together with their days. The claim that mentioning "night" was to indicate that Moses's promise was in the observance of night-prayer is nothing, since what is related is that what was commanded was fasting, not standing [in prayer]. It may be said, by way of allusion, that mentioning the night indicates that this appointment took place after completing the journey to Allah, and after crossing the sea of obstacles and attachments. There the journey in Allah occurs, whose reality cannot be grasped and whose essence cannot be known, and in whose desert of majesty one sees nothing but bewilderment and perplexity. This journey varies according to persons and times, and I have with Allah, exalted is He, a time that points to this.

﴿Then you took the calf [for worship] after him, while you were wrongdoers﴾. *Al-ittikhadh* (taking) comes in the sense of beginning to make something, and it takes one object, as in *ittakhadhtu sayfan* (I took a sword), meaning: I made it. It also comes in the sense of taking a quality, in which case it functions like *al-ja'l* (making) and takes two objects, as in *ittakhadhtu Zaydan sadiqan* (I took Zayd as a friend). Both meanings are possible in the verse. On the second possibility the second object is suppressed because of its ugliness: meaning, you took the calf which al-Samiri made as a god. The reproach in this is clear, since they all worshipped it, except Harun together with twelve thousand [men], or except Harun and the seventy who were with Moses, peace be upon him. On the first possibility no second object is needed, and this is supported by the fact that it is not stated explicitly anywhere in the verses of this story. In that case the reproach is directed at the worship that resulted from the taking, or at the taking itself for that purpose. The Arabs blame or praise a tribe for what has issued from some of its members.

*Al-'ijl* (the calf) is the young of a cow. The Sufis took it as an allusion to the calf of the deficient self and its appetites. That what they took was a calf is evident in that it became flesh and blood, so it was a calf in reality, and attributing lowing to it in what follows is also literal. This is the view of al-Hasan. It has also been said that Allah, glorified is He, intended by the calf something resembling it in form and shape, and attributing lowing to it is figurative. This is the view of the majority, and we will address this, Allah willing, later.

It is strange that this [calf] was named a calf because they hastened (*'ajjalu*) to it before Moses's return. Or [it was so named] because of the brevity of its existence, since after Moses's return from the appointed time he burned it and scattered it into the sea, scattering it thoroughly. The pronoun in *ba'dihi* (after him) refers to Moses, meaning: after what you had seen from him of monotheism, declaring Allah free of all imperfection, adherence to it, and refraining from what contradicts it. The mention of the time-adverb serves to indicate the greater enormity of their act. It does not imply that Moses took a god, as has been wrongly imagined, since the meaning of the statement is that the taking occurred after Moses. From where would the taking by Moses be understood, especially in this context? It is also possible that something is omitted from the speech. The most likely omitted item is a verbal noun indicated by *wa'adna*, meaning: after his promise. It has also been said that the omitted item is the going, which is implied by the promise, since the promise requires it. The nominal clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase. The thing the wrongdoing relates to is associating partners with Allah, and placing worship in other than its proper place. It has also been said that it means refraining from objecting to what al-Samiri did and not denouncing him. The purpose of restricting by a circumstantial phrase is to indicate that the taking was wrongdoing in their own estimation too, had they returned to their reason with the slightest reflection. It has also been said that the clause is not a circumstantial phrase, but merely a report that their disposition is wrongdoing. The act of al-Samiri found acceptance among them only because of their extreme foolishness and the domination of Satan over them, as all their other conduct shows.

As for al-Samiri's taking for them the calf rather than any other animal, it is said that this was because they passed by a people devoted to idols of theirs in the form of cows. They said: ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾. It then occurred to al-Samiri that their temptation came from this direction, so he made this for them. It has also been said that he himself was from a people who worshipped cows, and he was a hypocrite, so he made a calf of the same kind as what he worshipped.

Then (thumma) indicates the disparity between their ugly deed and God's gentleness toward them, so it is not a repetition of "after that."

'Afa means "to efface, obliterate," and it is used both transitively and intransitively, as in "the abode was effaced" (ʿafat al-dar) and "the wind effaced it" (ʿafāhā al-rīh). The intended meaning of "pardon" (al-ʿafw) here is the erasure of the sin through repentance. "That" (dhālika) is placed in the position of "that" (dhālikum), and the demonstrative refers to the taking (of the calf as a god), as is apparent. Its use serves full attention to distinguishing it, as if He were making their wrongdoing visible before them. The form of the distant demonstrative, despite its nearness, serves to magnify it, so that through it one may approach the great rank of pardon.

By "hope" (al-tarajjī) is meant what you already know. The commonly held view here is that it is a metaphor for seeking gratitude for the pardon. As for those among the People of the Sunnah who assumed "will" (al-irāda) here, they meant absolute "demand" (al-ṭalab). This is not the doctrine of the Muʿtazilites (al-iʿtizāl), since there is no dispute that God may demand of His servants what does not occur.

Gratitude (al-shukr), according to al-Junayd, is the inability to give thanks. According to al-Shibli, it is humility beneath the sight of favor. Dhu al-Nun said: gratitude toward one above you is obedience, toward your equal is reciprocation, and toward one below you is kindness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 53:

﴿And [remember] when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion, that you might be guided.﴾ The Book is the Torah, by the consensus of the exegetes.

There are several views concerning "al-Furqan" (the Criterion). The first: it is also the Torah, and the conjunction is of the type of the conjunction of attributes, to indicate the independence of each of them, for the Torah has two attributes, which are said with gradation: that it is a Book comprehensive of what no other revealed scripture has gathered except the Qur'an, and that it is a Furqan, i.e., a proof that distinguishes between truth and falsehood. This was said by al-Zajjaj, and the words of the Exalted support this: ﴿And We certainly gave Moses and Aaron the Criterion and a light and a reminder﴾. The second: it is the law (shar') that distinguishes between the lawful and the unlawful, so the conjunction is like it in ﴿the descent of the angels and the Spirit﴾; this was said by Ibn Bahr. The third: it is the miracles that distinguish between truth and falsehood, such as the staff, the hand, and others; this was said by Mujahid. The fourth: it is the victory that distinguished between the enemy and the ally, and it was a sign for Moses, peace be upon him; and from this the Day of Badr was called the Day of the Furqan; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. It was also said: it is the Qur'an, and the meaning of its being given to Moses, peace be upon him, is the descent of its mention to him until he believed in it; this was related by Ibn al-Anbari, and it is far-fetched. Even further from this is what is reported from al-Farra' and Qutrub, that it is the Qur'an, and the sentence is elliptical of an object, i.e., "and Muhammad the Furqan." The mention of guidance following the mention of Moses being given the Book and the Furqan is appropriate, because guidance is consequent upon them for whoever gives ear while he is a witness.

﴿وإذْ قالَ مُوسى لِقَوْمِهِ يا قَوْمِ إنَّكم ظَلَمْتُمْ أنْفُسَكم بِاتِّخاذِكُمُ العِجْلَ﴾ [And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by your taking the calf (for worship)."] This is a blessing in the Hereafter for those among the Children of Israel who were killed, since they attained the rank of martyrs, just as the pardon is a blessing in this world for those who remained alive. He separated the two with His saying ﴿وإذْ آتَيْنا﴾ [And when We gave] and so on, because the purpose is to enumerate the blessings; had the two been joined, they would have become a single blessing. It has also been said that this verse and what follows are disconnected from what preceded of the reminder of blessings, but this is not correct. The lam in (لِقَوْمِهِ) [to his people] indicates conveyance. The benefit of mentioning it is to draw attention to the fact that Moses' address to his people was direct, not through an intermediary who relayed it from him, unlike the previously mentioned addresses to the Children of Israel. The word qawm (قوم) [people] is a collective noun (ism jam') with no singular derived from its own form; its singular is imru' (امرؤ) [man]. Analogically it should not be pluralized, but its plural aqawim (أقاويم) occurs as an anomaly. The well-known usage is that it is restricted to men, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿لا يَسْخَرْ قَوْمٌ مِن قَوْمٌ﴾ [Let not one people ridicule another people], together with His saying: ﴿ولا نِساءٌ مِن نِساءٌ﴾ [nor women (ridicule) other women]. Zuhayr said:

فَما أدْرِي وسَوْفَ أخالُ أدْرِي أقَوْمٌ آلُ حِصْنٍ أمْ نِساءُ
"I do not know, and I will suppose I know: are they a people, the family of Hisn, or women?"

It has been said that it is not restricted to men, but is also applied to women, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿إنّا أرْسَلْنا نُوحًا إلى قَوْمِهِ﴾ [Indeed, We sent Noah to his people]. The first view is more correct. The inclusion of women by way of following (istitba') and predominance (taghlib, the masculine being used to cover both) and by metaphorical usage (majaz) is better than the view that the word is a homonym (ishtirak). Men were called qawm because they stand (yaqumun) in matters in which women do not stand. In Moses' turning toward them with the vocative, and his address to them with (يا قوم) [O my people], there is an indication of tenderness toward them, and that he is one of them and they are of him. It also encourages them to accept the command to repent after rebuking them for having wronged themselves. The ba' in ﴿بِاتِّخاذِكُمُ﴾ [by your taking] is causal (sababiyyah). For the word ittikhadh (اتخاذ) [taking] here, the two possibilities mentioned earlier there apply.

﴿فَتُوبُوا إلى بارِئِكُمْ﴾ [so turn in repentance to your Creator]: the fa' is causal, because wronging oneself is the cause of repentance. It has conjoined what follows to ﴿إنَّكم ظَلَمْتُمْ﴾ [you have wronged]. Agreement between the informative (khabariyyah) and the imperative (insha'iyyah) form is required only in conjunction with the particle wa (و), while the expressions of some people suggest that the fa' is causal rather than conjunctive. The verification is that it is both together. Al-Bari' (البارئ) [the Creator] is the one who created creation free of disproportion, of disharmony of limbs and incompatibility of parts, such that one hand is extremely small and delicate while the other is not, and distinct from one another by attributes, forms, beauty and ugliness. Thus He is more specific than the Khaliq (الخالق) [the Creator in general]. The root meaning is the purity of a thing and its separation from other things, either as deliverance, as in the recovery (bur') of a sick person, or as origination, as in the saying "Allah bara'a Adam," meaning He created him at the outset distinct from the filth of clay. Mentioning Him in this context rebukes them for abandoning the worship of the All-Knowing, Wise One who created them with His subtle wisdom, to the point that they exposed themselves to the wrath of Allah the Exalted and to the descent of His command that He disassemble what He had composed of their creation and scatter what He had arranged of their forms and shapes, since they did not give thanks for this blessing, and they denied it by worshipping one who has power over none of it. This is a proverb for stupidity and dullness.

[p. 260]

Abu 'Amr read (بارئكم) [your Creator] with ikhtilas (a rapid, reduced vowel), and it is also reported from him with sukun (a silent pronunciation). This is the treatment of a connected form of two words as if it were a separated form within one word. People have various explanations for this, none of which is free from anomaly.

﴿فاقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ [then kill yourselves]: the fa' is for sequence (ta'qib). The obvious meaning of killing is the familiar killing that removes the soul, and a group of exegetes held this view. The verb is conjoined to what precedes it. If their repentance is killing, either specifically for them, or the repentance of an apostate in general in the law of Moses, peace be upon him, then the meaning of the Exalted's saying ﴿فَتُوبُوا﴾ [so turn in repentance] is "resolve to repent" so that the conjunction is valid. If repentance is regret, and killing is among its completions, like withdrawing from wrongs in our law, then it has its literal meaning and there is no difficulty. It may be said that repentance was made for these people identical with killing, and there is no need to interpret (تُوبُوا) [repent] as (اعزموا) [resolve], but rather the fa' is made explanatory (tafsir), just as the waw is made so. This has been said regarding the Exalted's saying: ﴿فانْتَقَمْنا مِنهم فَأغْرَقْناهم في اليَمِّ﴾ [So We took vengeance on them and drowned them in the sea]. The apparent sense of the command is that they were ordered that each one should carry out the killing of himself. In some reports they were ordered that some of them should kill others. Then the meaning of ﴿اقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ is that some of you should kill some others, as in the Exalted's saying: ﴿ولا تَقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ [And do not kill yourselves] and ﴿ولا تَلْمِزُوا أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ [And do not defame one another], and the believers are like a single soul. It has been reported that he commanded those who had not worshipped the calf to kill those who had worshipped it. The meaning based on this is: surrender yourselves to being killed. The surrender to being killed is called killing by way of metaphor. The killers are either unspecified, or those who had withdrawn with Harun, peace be upon him, and those who were with Moses, peace be upon him. There are reports about the manner of the killing which we will not lengthen by mentioning. The total number of the slain was seventy thousand, and when it was completed the repentance was revealed, and the blades fell from their hands. The Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar denied that Allah the Exalted commanded the Children of Israel to kill themselves, and said: "That is impermissible by reason, since a command is for the benefit of the one obligated, and after killing there is no state of obligation in which there could be benefit." This Qadi did not realize that for our souls there is a Creator, by whose command we keep them alive and by whose command we annihilate them; and that for them, after this life, which is play and diversion, there is an everlasting life and an eternal delight; and that the Last Abode is indeed the (true) life; and that killing them by His command brings them to a life better than it. Whoever knows that a human in this world is like a fighter stationed at a frontier post that he guards, or a governor in a land that he governs, and that however he is recalled, there is no difference between the king ordering him to leave by himself or ordering someone else to remove him, will find this clear, for one who has conceived the two states of this world and the Hereafter, and recognized the value of the two lives and the two deaths within them. Some people allowed this but considered its occurrence unlikely, and said: the meaning of ﴿اقْتُلُوا أنْفُسَكُمْ﴾ [kill yourselves] is "humble yourselves." From this is his saying:

إنَّ الَّتِي عاطَيْتَنِي فَرَدَدْتُها ∗∗∗ قُتِلَتْ قُتِلَتْ فَهاتِها لَمْ تُقْتَلِ
"Indeed, the one you handed me, I returned it; it was humbled, humbled; so bring it, it was not humbled."

Had the reports not contradicted that, I would have said it as an explanation. It is reported from Qatadah that he read (فأقيلوا أنفسكم) [then ask your souls to be retracted (cancel the sin)], and the meaning is that your souls have become entangled in the punishment of Allah the Exalted by this great deed which you committed, and they have perished; so retract them by repentance and commitment to obedience, and remove the traces of those sins by displaying acts of obedience.

﴿ذَلِكم خَيْرٌ لَكم عِنْدَ بارِئِكُمْ﴾ [That is better for you in the sight of your Creator] is a parenthetical clause (jumla mu'taridah) that urges repentance, or a clause giving the reason. The demonstrative refers to the verbal noun (masdar) understood from what precedes. Khayr (خير) is an elative (af'al tafdil) whose hamza has been dropped, and they pronounced it so in poetry. The rajiz said:

بِلالٌ خَيْرُ النّاسِ وابْنُ الأخْيَرِ
"Bilal is the best of people and the son of the best."

It also occurs without a comparative sense. The meaning is that that is better for you than disobedience and persistence in sin, or better than the fruit of disobedience, which is perpetual destruction. The expression is like the saying "honey is sweeter than vinegar." Or it means: better than any goods that exist for you. The concept of "with" (indiyyah) here is metaphorical. The word Creator is repeated with an explicit noun, out of concern to urge submission to Him in every state and to receive what comes from Him with acceptance and compliance, for just as He saw creating as preferable and so created, He saw annihilation as preferable and so commanded it. And He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.

﴿فَتابَ عَلَيْكُمْ﴾ [So He accepted your repentance] is the response to a deleted conditional clause, with the presumption of qad (قد) [indeed], if it is part of Moses' speech to them; its estimate is: "If you do what you were commanded, then He has accepted your repentance from you." It is conjoined to a deleted element if it is an address from Allah the Exalted to them, as if He said: "So you did what you were commanded, and your Creator accepted your repentance." There is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person) in it, since the reference to them in Moses' speech was earlier by the word "people," which is third person, and it is a shift from speech to the third person; or from first person to third person in (فتاب), since it does not say "so We accepted repentance." Conjunction was preferred for its soundness from deletion of the particle, the conditional, and the retention of the response; but the attestation of this from the Arabs is disputed. The apparent sense of the verse is that it is a report about those who were ordered to kill and carried out the command. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Allah the Exalted made killing a martyrdom for those who were killed, and accepted repentance from the rest and pardoned them. So the meaning of (عليكم) [upon you] in his view is "upon your remainder."

﴿إنَّهُ هو التَّوّابُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ [Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful] is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the saying of the Exalted "so turn in repentance," since repentance through killing, being hard on the soul, is made easier by Him, glory be to Him, who is the one who grants success for it, facilitates it, and is lavish in bestowing favor on whoever comes with it. Or it is a concluding statement to the saying of the Exalted "So He accepted your repentance," and repentance from Him, the Exalted, is then interpreted as acceptance of the repentance of those who sinned. The emphasis is for the sake of preceding anticipation (sabq al-mulawwih), or for the sake of attention to the content of the sentence. If the pronoun in the accusative (إنه) is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), then the pronoun in the nominative is a subject, which is the more suitable, since it indicates complete attention to the content of the sentence. If it refers back to the Creator, glory be to Him, then the nominative pronoun is either a separating pronoun (fasl) or a subject.

This is what I say: the share of the knower from this story is to know that his desire is in the position of the calf of the Children of Israel, so that he does not take it as a god: ﴿أفَرَأيْتَ مَنِ اتَّخَذَ إلَهَهُ هَواهُ﴾ [Have you seen one who takes his own desire as his god?]. And that Allah, glory be to Him, has created the self in its original nature ready to receive the overflow of Allah the Exalted and the upright religion, and prepared to follow the straight path and to ascend to the presence of holiness and the threshold of intimacy. This is the Book that Moses was given, the heart, and the criterion by which one is guided by its light in the nights of the journey to the presence of the Lord. So whenever the self inclines to the earth, follows its desire, and prefers its appetites over its Master, it is commanded to kill it by breaking its appetites and uprooting its desired things, so that it may be fit for survival after annihilation and sobriety after effacement. True repentance is nothing but the effacement of humanness by the affirmation of divinity. This is the greater struggle and the red death.

"He who dies and rests is not a dead man;
the dead man is the dead among the living."

This is difficult and is achieved only by the elect of the Truth and the men of sincerity, and to it refers the saying: "Die before you die." It has been said: the first step in servitude is the destruction and killing of the soul by abandoning appetites and cutting it off from pleasures. How then can one reach any station of the sincere and the ascending ranks of those brought near? Far, far! That is remote from us, and the Pleiades' perch is far from us.

"Come, let us hold a gathering of mourning for sorrows,
for the grieving one consoles the grieving one."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 55:

﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will never believe you"﴾ The speakers were the seventy whom Musa, peace be upon him, chose for the appointed time of the Torah (mīqāt al-Tawrāh). It is said: they said this after the return, after the killing of the worshippers of the calf and the burning of their calf. It is understood from some reports that the speakers were the people of the second appointed time, which Allah, exalted is He, set for the excuse concerning the worshippers of the calf, and they too were seventy. It is also said: the speakers were ten thousand of his people. It is also said: the pronoun refers to the rest of the Children of Israel, except those whom Allah, exalted is He, protected. What will benefit you here will come, if Allah wills, in al-A'raf. The lam in (laka) is either the lam of purpose (lam al-ajal), or it is for transitivity by implying the meaning of acknowledgment, that Musa acknowledges it for him,
(p. 262)
and the object of the acknowledgment is omitted, namely that Allah, exalted is He, gave him the Torah, or that Allah, exalted is He, spoke to him, so He commanded him and forbade him. These people had indeed believed in Musa, peace be upon him, before, but they denied this specific faith and this particular acknowledgment. It is also said: they meant the negation of perfection, i.e., our faith in you will not be complete, as it is said concerning his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "None of you believes until he loves for his believing brother what he loves for himself." As for the view that they were not believers at all, we have not seen it attributed to any of the imams of tafsir.

﴿until we see Allah openly﴾ "Until" (hattā) here is a particle of limit. Al-jahra (openly) is originally the verbal noun of jahartu bil-qira'a (I recited aloud), when you raise your voice with it. It was borrowed for direct observation (al-mu'aynah) on account of the complete manifestness. Al-Raghib said: al-jahr is said of the manifestness of a thing through the intensity of the sense of sight or the sense of hearing. As for sight, it is like: "I saw him openly (jihāran)." As for hearing, it is like: ﴿And if you speak aloud, then He knows the secret and what is more hidden﴾. Its accusative case is as a verbal noun emphasizing and removing the possibility that the seeing was a dream or knowledge by the heart. It is also said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), with the implied sense: "possessors of openness" (dhawī jahrah), or "openly declaring" (mujāhirīn). According to the first, jahrah is a description of the seeing; according to the second, it is a description of the seers. There is also a third view, that it refers back to the sense of the speech or the speakers, so the meaning is: "when you said such-and-such (a saying) openly, or openly declaring that saying, not caring nor minding." This is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Abu 'Ubayda. Sahl ibn Shu'ayb and others read (jahratan) with a fatha on the ha'; it is either a verbal noun like al-ghalabah, with the meaning of al-maskanah, and its i'rab is the same as its i'rab, or it is the plural of jahir like fasiq and fasaqah, and its accusative is as a circumstantial state.

﴿So the thunderbolt seized you﴾ That is, it overcame you and enveloped you. The original sense of akhdh is seizing with the hand. Al-sa'iqah here is either a fire from the sky that burned them, or a heavenly host whose sound they heard so that they died, or a heavenly cry before which they fell down stunned, dead for a day and a night. It has been disputed whether what befell them also befell Musa; the sound view is no, and that he was stunned but did not die, as is evident, then he recovered, regarding him, and then "Then We raised you up..." etc. regards them. Umar and Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read (al-sa'qah).

﴿while you were looking on﴾ This is a circumstantial clause. The object of the looking is what befell them of the thunderbolt, or its lasting trace on their bodies after the resurrection, or the revival of each of them, as occurred in the story of 'Uzayr; they said: he revived one limb after another. The meaning is: "while you knew that it was seizing you," or "while some of you faced others." In al-Bahr he said: If someone went to the view that the meaning is: "while you were looking on," meaning that they were witnessing the answer to their request for the sight to be granted to them, it would be a valid view from their usage: "I looked at the man," meaning "I waited for him," as the poet said:

"For if you two look at me for an hour of time, it will benefit me in the presence of Umm Jundub."

But this sense is not transmitted, so I do not dare to hold it, although the wording may bear it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 56:**

﴿Then We raised you up after your death﴾ because of the thunderbolt (al-sa'iqa). This happened through the supplication of Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam) and his entreaty to his Lord after he had recovered. It is related in some reports that when they died, Musa kept beseeching his Lord to bring them back to life and saying: "My Lord, the Children of Israel will say, 'You killed our best men,'" until Allah the Exalted brought them all back to life, one man after another, looking at one another, [wondering] how they had been revived. Here, "death" clearly means the soul's separation from the body. The raising (al-ba'th) is qualified by it because it may also be from sleep, as in the case of the People of the Cave, and it may also mean the sending of a person, which is common in the Qur'an. Some people said that this death was a fainting and a swooning, not true death, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And death comes to him from every place, yet he is not dead﴾. Others understood death figuratively as ignorance, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life…﴾. This usage is widespread in prose and in poetry, and from it is the saying of the poet:

*The man of knowledge lives forever after his death,*
*while his bones are crumbled beneath the dust.*

*The man of ignorance is dead, though he walks upon the earth,*
*he is thought to be among the living, yet he is nothing.*

According to this reading, the meaning of "raising" is teaching: that is, "Then We taught you after your ignorance," ﴿so that you may give thanks﴾, i.e., for Allah's blessing upon you in bringing you to life after death, or for His blessing after you had denied it, since you saw the might of Allah in being struck by the thunderbolt and tasting death.

The imposition of obligations upon those who were restored after death, which some scholars held, was so that no mature, sane person would be left without worship in this world after the sending of the messengers. Whoever takes the raising after death to mean figuratively teaching after ignorance makes the object of the thanks that [teaching]. In some reports it is said that when Allah brought them back to life, they asked Him to send them prophets, and He did so. The object of thanks then, as it has been said, is this raising, but this is remote. More remote still is the view that its object is the sending down of the Torah, in which is mentioned His acceptance of their repentance and the detailing of their laws, since they had no laws before that.

The Mu'tazila (a rationalist theological school) and some groups of innovators (mubtadi'a) have used this verse as evidence for the impossibility of seeing the Creator, the Exalted, since, they argue, if it were possible, the thunderbolt would not have seized them for asking for it. The answer is that the seizing by the thunderbolt was not for mere asking, but for what was joined to it of obstinacy and extreme stubbornness, as the context of the speech indicates, since they made their faith conditional upon it. It is also possible that this seizing was for their disbelief in Allah's giving the Torah to Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam) and His speaking to him, or his prophethood, and not for their asking. It may also be said that since they were not fit to see the Truth in this present state of existence, their asking for it was wrongdoing, so they were punished as they were punished. There is no proof in that for its absolute impossibility in this world and the Hereafter. The verification of this question, in a manner free from any objection, will come, Allah willing, later.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 57:**

﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to ﴿We raised you up﴾. It is also said that it is conjoined to ﴿you said﴾. The first is more apparent, because of proximity, because the subject of both verbs is shared, and because the two predicates are parallel in that each is a blessing. This is unlike ﴿you said﴾, which serves as a preface to them. Its implication is that the shading and the sending down came after the incident of their request to see God. On both readings, the omission of the word ﴿when﴾ (idh) here requires some rationale. Perhaps it is the sufficiency of the rational indication that each of the two is an independent blessing, together with avoiding its repetition in ﴿We shaded﴾ and ﴿We sent down﴾. Al-ghamām (the clouds) is a collective noun (ism jins), like ḥamāmah and ḥamām. It means the cloud. It is said that it means only its white part. Mujahid said: it is cooler and thinner than cloud. It was named ghamām because it covers (yaghummu) the face of the sky and conceals it, and from the same root come al-ghamm (distress) and al-ghamam (a veil of sorts). Was it truly a cloud, or something resembling one that was given its name? There are two opinions, and the well-known one is the first. It is the object of ﴿We shaded﴾, either with the preposition dropped, as you say "I shaded so-and-so with a cloak," or without dropping it. The meaning is: We made the clouds a shade over you. The apparent view is that the address is to all of them. It is related that when they were commanded to fight the giants (al-jabbarin) and refused, saying, "Go you and your Lord and fight," God tested them with wandering (al-tih) in the land between Syria and Egypt for forty years. They complained of the heat of the sun, so God, in His kindness, shaded them with the clouds and sent down manna and quails. It is also said that when they came out of the sea they arrived at a white, barren land with neither water nor shade, and they complained of the heat, so they were shielded from it. It is also said that those who were shaded by the clouds were only some of the Children of Israel. God had established a custom among them that whoever worshipped for thirty years without committing a sin would be shaded by a cloud. There were among them a group called the "people of clouds," so God bestowed His favour upon them, because among them were those who had this manifest honour and this dazzling blessing.

﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quails.﴾ Al-manna is a collective noun with no singular from its own form. The well-known view is that it is turanjabin, a substance resembling gum, sweet with some sourness. It used to descend upon them like dew from the break of dawn until sunrise every day, except on Saturday. Each person was commanded to take a measure of a ṣāʿ each day, or what would suffice him for a day and a night, and not to store any except on Friday, for storing the portion for Saturday was permitted. According to Wahb, it was thin flat bread (al-khubz al-ruqaq). It is also said that what is meant by it is everything God bestowed upon them in the wandering, which came to them effortlessly, without toil. This was the view of al-Zajjaj. It is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The mushroom is from the manna which God bestowed upon the Children of Israel." As for al-salwa, it is also a collective noun, its singular being salwāh, as al-Khalil said. The alif in it is not a feminine marker, for otherwise it would not have been feminized with the ta' marbuta in the verse:

*As the salawat shake off the wetness of the rain*

Al-Kisa'i said: salwa is singular, and its plural is salawa. According to al-Akhfash, the plural and singular share one form. It is also said: it is a plural with no singular from its own form, and it is a bird resembling the quail, or it is the quail itself. It would come to them from the sky in the morning and evening, or whenever they wished, and they would choose the fat ones and leave the lean ones. It is also said that the south wind would drive them to them, and they would choose what they needed and the rest would go away. In one report: "They would descend upon them cooked and roasted." Glory be to Him who says to a thing "Be," and it is.

Al-Sadusi mentioned that salwa is honey in the dialect of Kinana. This is supported by the verse of al-Hudhali:

*I swore to them openly by God that you are sweeter than salwa when its honey is taken*

Ibn ʿAṭiyya's statement that this is an error (ghalat) is itself an error. Its derivation is from al-salwa (consolation), because by its sweetness it consoles one for other foods. Its conjunction with some aspects of the manna is conjunction of the specific to the general (ʿaṭf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm), out of concern for its importance.

﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you.﴾ This is an imperative of permission, on the premise of an unstated saying: that is, "And We said," or "saying." The ṭayyibāt are the delectable things. Mentioning them is for the sake of showing favour to them. Or they are the lawful things, in which case the imperative is for forbidding storage. The min is partitive (lil-tab'īḍ). He who regarded it as generic (lil-jins) or as substitutive (lil-badal) is far off the mark. Similar is the view of him who claims there is an elided genitive (muḍāf), meaning "in exchange for good things," saying that God compensated them for all their former delicious foods with the manna and the quails, so these two became a substitute for the good things. (Ma) is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is elided, meaning "We provided you with it." Or it is a verbal noun (maṣdariyya), with the verbal noun carrying the sense of the passive participle. Some scholars derived from the verse that it is not sufficient for the owner to place food before a person for him to be permitted to eat it; rather, it is not lawful to make use of it except with the owner's permission. This is one of the opinions on the question.

﴿But they did not wrong Us﴾ is conjoined to an elided element, "so they disobeyed," and they did not respond to the blessings with gratitude. Or the meaning is "so they wronged, by disbelieving these blessings, and they did not wrong Us by that." It is also permissible, as in the previous passage (al-Bahr), to posit an elided element, since they committed from among them abominable acts, such as taking the calf as a god and asking to see God, which is wrongdoing. Then the statement ﴿But they did not wrong Us﴾ comes as a negated clause indicating that what they did of those abominations did not reach Us with any deficiency or harm. In this there is evidence that it is not a condition for negating something of something that its occurrence be possible, because the wronging of God by a human being is absolutely impossible to occur.

﴿But they were wronging themselves﴾ by ingratitude, or by what they did, since its harm does not go beyond them. The fronting of the object (taqdīm al-mafʿūl) indicates the restriction (qaṣr) required by the preceding negation, and in it is a kind of mockery of them. The combining of the past and the present forms indicates their persistence in wrongdoing and their continuation in it. And in mentioning "themselves" in the plural form of paucity (jamʿ al-qilla) there is belittlement and diminishment of them. The disobedient self is less than the least of every little thing.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 2, verse 58:**

﴿And when We said: "Enter this town"﴾ is in the accusative (manṣūb) as an adverb of place (ẓarfiyyah) according to Sibawayh, and as the object (mafʿūliyyah) according to al-Akhfash. The apparent meaning is that the command to enter was conveyed through Musa (peace be upon him), like the commands before and after it. The word al-qaryah (town), with a fatha or kasra on the qaf, is the dialect of the people of Yemen, meaning "the city," from qaryt, "I gathered," because it gathers people in the manner of dwelling together. It was said: if the population is small, it is called qaryah, and if it is large, it is called madīnah. Some scholars limited "smallness" to three. The plural is al-qurā, which is irregular; the regular pattern for such words is fiʿāl, as in ẓabyah and ẓibāʾ (gazelle, gazelles). There is considerable disagreement about what is meant here.

[p. 265]

The well-known view, reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Masʿud, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Rabiʿ and others, and held by the majority, is that it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). This command came after the wandering (al-tīh) and bewilderment (al-taḥayyur). It is a command of permission (amr ibāḥah), indicated by the conjunction of "then eat" (fa-kulū), etc. It is different from the command mentioned in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿O my people, enter the Holy Land which Allah has prescribed for you, and do not turn back on your heels, for you will turn around as losers﴾, because that came before this. That was a command of obligation (amr taklīf), as indicated by the conjunction of the prohibition. Some claimed that the two are one, and made this command also one of obligation, and took the "substitution of the command" to mean non-compliance with it, on the basis that they did not enter the Holy City during the lifetime of Musa (peace be upon him). Others claimed that the two are different, but they held that what is mentioned here was after the wandering, conveyed through Yusha` (Joshua), not through Musa, peace be upon them both, because he and his brother Harun died during the wandering, and Yusha` conquered the land of Syria with the Children of Israel three months after his (Musa's) death, peace be upon him. Others said: the command to enter during the wandering was after leaving it. There are problems with each of these views, so the most apparent is what we have mentioned. It has been narrated that Musa (peace be upon him), after leaving the wandering, travelled with those of the Children of Israel who remained to Ariha, which is in the land of al-Quds, and Yusha` ibn Nun was at its vanguard. He conquered it and remained there as long as Allah willed, then he was taken (died). It seems that after the conquest they were commanded to enter in the manner of settling and dwelling, as His words, "then eat," etc., indicate, and His words, the Exalted, in al-Aʿraf: ﴿Dwell in this town﴾. What supports that this was after the conquest is the use of the demonstrative for the near (al-ishārah bi-lafẓ al-qarīb). The view that it was placed in the position of the near in order to promote the matter is far-fetched. This does not contradict what has passed, that he died in the wandering, because what is meant by it is the desert (al-mafāzah), not the wandering. Tīh is the verbal noun of tāha yatīhu tīhan, with kasra or fatha, and taysharān, when one goes off bewildered. So let this be understood.

﴿So eat from it wherever you will, in abundance﴾: that is, widely and pleasantly. Its accusative is either as a verbal noun (maṣdar) or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the addressees. In the speech there is an indication of the permissibility of all its places for them, or permission to carry its produce to any place they wish, along with the implication of "in abundance" (raghadan) that they are licensed to eat from it freely and widely, and they are not obliged to be content with merely satisfying hunger. It is possible that it is a promise to them of abundant produce and absence of high prices. This accusative was delayed here, though it was placed earlier in the verse about Adam (peace be upon him), for the sake of the rhyme (al-fāṣilah) in His words, "and enter the gate prostrating." The disagreement over the accusative of "the gate" is like the disagreement over the accusative of ﴿this town﴾. What is meant by it, according to the well-known view, is one of the gates of Bayt al-Quds, which is now called the Gate of Ḥiṭṭah. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. It was also said: it is the eighth of its gates, which is now called the Gate of Repentance (tawbah), and Mujahid held this view. Some claimed that it is the gate of the dome which belonged to Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, where they worshipped, and which was made a qiblah for the Children of Israel during the wandering. Concerning its description there are wondrous matters in the stories which none knows except Allah, the Exalted.

(Prostrating) is a circumstantial state from the pronoun in (enter). What is meant is humbly, submissively, because it befits the state of a sinner who repents and an obedient one who complies that he be humble and meek. It is permissible to take "prostration" in its legal sense (al-maʿnā al-sharʿī), and the state may be concomitant (muqāranah) or anticipated (muqaddarah). The second is supported by what was narrated from Wahb concerning the meaning of the verse: "When you have entered it, prostrate in gratitude to Allah," that is, for what He has bestowed upon you, in that He brought you out of the wandering, granted you victory over those you feared, and returned you to what you love. As for al-Zamakhshari's statement, "They were commanded to prostrate upon reaching the gate, in gratitude to Allah, the Exalted, and in humility," we have not found anything in the Book or the Sunnah which indicates it. Ibn ʿAbbas interpreted prostration here as bowing (rukūʿ). Some interpreted it as lowering oneself and bending. They said: they were commanded to do this because the gate was small and narrow, so the one entering it needed to bend.

In the authentic (Ṣaḥīḥ) collection, from Abu Hurayrah, he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: It was said to the Children of Israel: "Enter the gate prostrating," but they entered crawling on their buttocks, and they said: "Ḥiṭṭah." That is: our request, or your affair, O our Lord, is that You remove our sins from us. It is a form (fiʿlah) from ḥaṭṭ (removal), like jilsah (a sitting). Aban mentioned that it means repentance, and he recited:

*He succeeded with the ḥiṭṭah by which Allah made the sin of His servant forgiven.*

[p. 266]

The truth is that interpreting it thus is an interpretation by necessary implication (tafsīr bi-l-lāzim). Far-fetched is the statement of Abu Muslim: the meaning is "our command is ḥiṭṭah," that is, that we remove ourselves (in the sense of settling) in this town and dwell in it, because there is no apparent connection of forgiveness with it, nor the consequence of the substitution upon it. Unless it is said: they were commanded to say this word upon removing themselves in the town merely as an act of worship (taʿabbud), and when they did not know the wisdom behind it, they substituted it. Ibn Abi ʿAblah read it in the accusative, meaning "remove our sins from us, a removal," or "we ask You for that." It is permissible that the accusative be the object of (say) (li-qūlū), that is, "say this very word," and this is what was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas. The object of "say" according to the lexicographers is singular when its wording is meant, and there is no weight to what is in al-Bahr of prohibition. However, this is weakened by the fact that this word is Arabic, and they did not speak it. Also, the apparent meaning is that they were commanded to say a statement indicating repentance and regret, so that even if they had said, "O Allah, we ask You forgiveness and turn to You," the intended purpose would have been achieved, and repentance does not depend on mentioning a specific word. For this reason it was said: the more suitable reading of it as the object of (say) is that what is intended is: say a word that removes your sins, namely seeking forgiveness, and in that case the dust is removed from this view. Furthermore, this word is in every case Arabic, with a known derivation, and its meaning is the apparent and heard one. Al-Asmaʿi said: it is from the words of the People of the Book; we do not know its meaning in Arabic. ʿIkrimah mentioned that its meaning is "there is no god but Allah," and this is extremely strange.

﴿We will forgive you your wrongs﴾ for your entering the gate prostrating and your saying ḥiṭṭah. The root of khaṭāyā (wrongs) is khaṭāyiʾ, with a yāʾ after an alif and then a hamzah. According to Sibawayh, the added yāʾ became a hamzah because it occurred after an alif, and two hamzahs came together, so the second was changed to a yāʾ, then to an alif, and the hamzah was between two alifs, so it was changed to a yāʾ. According to al-Khalil, the hamzah was placed before the yāʾ, and then what was mentioned was done to it. Nafiʿ read (yaghfir) with a yāʾ, and Ibn ʿAmir with a tāʾ, in the passive voice (li-l-majhūl), and the rest with a nūn and the active voice (li-l-maʿlūm), which is the one that follows the arrangement of what comes before and after it. None of the Seven read anything but "khaṭāyākum." al-Kisaʾi inclined it (imālah). al-Jahdari and Qatadah read (tughfar) with a ḍammah on the tāʾ and made "khaṭīʾah" singular. The majority read with the rāʾ of (yaghfir) clearly before the lām, and a group assimilated it, saying: it is weak.

﴿And We will increase the good-doers﴾ is conjoined to the clause "say ḥiṭṭah." It was mentioned that it is conjoined to the apodosis (jawāb), and was not put in the jussive because the sīn prevents the conditional from accepting the jussive. In presenting it in that form without hesitation there is evidence that the good-doer does this definitively. In the statement there is the attribute of the collective together with the distinct: "say ḥiṭṭah" is collective, and "We will forgive you and We will increase" is distinct. The object is omitted, that is, reward.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 59 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿So those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them﴾. That is, those who did wrong replaced the word that had been said to them with another word. *Fa-baddala* (replaced) takes two objects, one directly and the other with the preposition *bi*, and it may take the thing abandoned (the object being replaced); so the blame is directed at them. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *baddala* be construed according to its sense, meaning: "Then those who did wrong said a word other than..." And the view that *ghayr* is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, as if it were said: "They changed a word for another," is not an acceptable view of the word. God, exalted is He, explicitly stated the difference, although the substitution cannot be realised without it, to confirm their opposition and to affirm the difference in every respect. The apparent meaning of the verse indicates a division there into wrongdoers and non-wrongdoers, and that the wrongdoers are those who substituted, even though the one who substituted was all of them. The placing of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun here is to indicate the cause. There is disagreement about the word they substituted. In the two Sahihs it is reported that they said: "A grain in a barley seed." Al-Hakim related: "Hintah (wheat) instead of Hittah." In *al-Ma'alim* (al-Baghawi's tafsir): they said in their tongue: "Hitta samqatha," meaning "a red wheat," and they said this mockingly regarding what had been said to them. The reports on this are numerous. When they are authentic, the difference in wording is attributed to the difference of speakers. The view that there was no substitution on their part, and that the meaning of "they substituted" is that they did not do what they were commanded, rather than that they brought a replacement for it, is not accepted, even if Abu Muslim said it. The apparent meaning of the verse and the hadiths refutes it.

﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky because they were defiantly disobedient﴾. He placed the explicit noun in place of the pronoun to emphasise the abomination of their conduct, and to indicate that their wrongdoing and their harming of themselves was by abandoning what would have brought about their salvation. Or, their placing of what was not commanded in the place of what was commanded was the cause of sending down the *rijz*, which is the punishment. Its *ra'* may be kasra'd or damma'd, and the damma is the dialect of the Bani al-Su'udat, and Ibn Muhaysin recited with it. The meaning of it here, as reported from Ibn Abbas, is darkness and death. It is related that twenty-four thousand of them died in one hour. Wahb said: it was a plague, by which they were struck for forty nights, and then they died after that. Ibn Jubayr said: it was a hail, by which seventy thousand of them perished. If it is interpreted as hail, its being "from the sky" is apparent. If it is interpreted otherwise, then it is an indication of the direction from which the decree comes, or an emphasis on its exaltedness through dominance and power. Some of the scholars (muhaqqiqun) mentioned that the prepositional phrase is a stable adverbial complement (*zarf mustaqirr*) that functions as a qualifier of *rijzan*, and *bima kanu yafsuqun* (because they were defiantly disobedient) is connected to it, as a causal element by virtue of its substitution for the governing verb. The word *ma* is verbal-masdarial (*masdariyya*). The meaning is: We sent down upon those who did wrong, for their wrongdoing, a punishment determined by the reason that they were persistently in defiance in the past time. This is preferable to making the prepositional phrase a *zarf laghw* (a dependent adverb with no effect) connected to *anzalna*, because this is apparent in all the other views, and so that the causing of the sending down by defiance is not required, after the causation derived from the attachment to wrongdoing, to say that defiance is the very same as wrongdoing.
