It is repeated for emphasis. Or, wrongdoing is more general, and defiance must be among the major sins; so after describing them as wrongdoers, they are described as defiant, to signal that it is among the major sins. The first is the merchandise of the incapable, and the second does not remove the weakness of the causation. What has been said, that it is a causation of wrongdoing, so that the sending down of the punishment is caused by the wrongdoing which is caused by defiance, is nothing, since their wrongdoing mentioned earlier, which is the cause of the sending down, does not need a cause. Some people have argued by His saying, exalted is He, "So he substituted" etc., and the punishment being consequent upon the substitution, that whatever statements have been prescribed by revelation may not be altered or replaced by another wording. Others said: that is permissible if the second word performs the function of the first. On this the disagreement has proceeded, as in *al-Bahr* (al-Bahr al-Muhit, Abu Hayyan's tafsir), regarding the recitation of the Qur'an according to its meaning, and narrating a hadith according to its meaning, and it has proceeded regarding the opening takbir (*takbirat al-ihram*), and regarding permitting marriage with the wording of gift, sale, or conveyance of ownership. The discussion is detailed in its proper place.

Here, our master, the Imam al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, mentioned that this verse was mentioned in al-A'raf with differences in several respects, for reasons:
First: here He said: "And when We said" (*wa-idh qulna*), since He had mentioned the blessings first, it is necessary to mention the Bestower; and there, "And when it was said" (*wa-idh qila*), since there is no ambiguity after the explicit mention of Him.
Second: here He said: "Enter" (*udkhulu*), and there "Dwell" (*uskunu*), because entering is prior; and for this reason, that which is prior in nature is placed first in order.
Third: here He said: "your sins" (*khataya-kum*) with the plural of multitude (*jam' al-kathra*), since He attributed that saying to Himself, and what is fitting to His generosity is forgiveness of many sins; and there "your sins" (*khati'at-kum*) with the plural of paucity (*jam' al-qilla*), since He did not explicitly mention the agent.
Fourth: here He said: "plentifully" (*raghadan*), but not there, because the verb is attributed to Himself here, so it fits the mention of the greatest favour, and there is no attribution there.
Fifth: here He said: "Enter the gate prostrating and say: *Hittah*," and there the reverse, because the conjunction *wa* is for mere togetherness. Also, the addressees may be such that some of them are sinners and some are not sinners; the sinner must have his occupation with removing his sin prior to his occupation with worship, so it was necessary that the duty of these be to say "*Hittah*" and then enter. As for the one who is not a sinner, it is better for him to occupy himself first with worship and then mention repentance second, for humility and to remove self-admiration; so these must enter and then say. Since it was possible that those addressed were divided into these two categories, therefore the ruling of each of them was mentioned in another surah.
Sixth: here He said: "And We shall increase" (*wa-sanazidu*) with the *wa*, and there without it, since here He made forgiveness together with increase a single reward for the two actions combined; but there, forgiveness is the reward for saying "*Hittah*," and the increase is the reward for entering, so omitting the *wa* indicates the distribution of each of the two rewards over each of the two conditions.
Seventh: there He said: "those who did wrong among them" (*alladhina zalamu minhum*), and here He did not mention "among them," because the beginning of the story there is based on specification by *min*, where He said: "And among the people of Musa is a community that guides by the truth." So He specified at the end of the speech to match its beginning; and since in the verses before "So he substituted" He did not mention here any distinguishing and specifying, He did not mention that at the end of the story.
Eighth: here He said: "So We sent down" (*fa-anzalna*), and there "So We sent" (*fa-arsalna*), because sending down indicates its occurrence at the beginning of the matter, while sending indicates its being given power over them and their uprooting, and that happens at the end.
Ninth: here He said: "Then eat" (*fa-kulu*) with the *fa*, and there with the imperative in "*fa-kulu minha raghadan*" (so eat from it plentifully). The principle is that when a verb is followed by something coordinated to it, and the verb functions as a condition, that thing functions as the consequence, the second is connected to the first with *fa* and not *wa*. So when eating was linked to entering, it was said in the surah of al-Baqarah: "*fa-kulu*"; and when eating was not linked to dwelling in al-A'raf, it was said: "*wa-kulu*."
Tenth: here He said: "they are defiantly disobedient" (*yafsuqun*), and there "they do wrong" (*yazlimun*), because when He clarified here that defiance is wrongdoing, He sufficed with the word wrongdoing there. End.

And there is no hiding what is open to consideration in these answers. As for the first, second, eighth and tenth, they are valid only if the surah of al-Baqarah preceded the surah of al-A'raf in revelation, just as it precedes it in arrangement; but that is not the case. The whole of surah al-Baqarah is Madani, and the whole of surah al-A'raf is Makki, except eight verses from His saying, exalted is He, "And ask them about the town" up to His saying, exalted is He, "And when We uprooted the mountain." His saying, exalted is He, "Dwell in this town," falls within the Makki verses. Therefore the answers mentioned are not valid. As for what was mentioned in the ninth, it is refuted by disputing the claim that eating is not linked to dwelling, because when they dwell in the town, their dwelling causes them to eat from it, as Zamakhshari mentioned; so they combined in existence dwelling in it and eating from it. Therefore there is no difference between "*kulu*" and "*fa-kulu*," and the answer is not complete. As for the third, although He said in al-A'raf, "And when it was said," He said in both surahs, "We shall forgive you," and attributed the forgiveness to Himself; so by the rule of that fitness, it is fitting that He mention the plural of multitude in both surahs. Indeed, there is no doubt that observing "We shall forgive you" is preferable to observing "And when it was said to them," because forgiveness is linked to sins, as is not hidden from one who knows the excellences. As for the fourth, although He did not attribute the verb to Himself, exalted is He, it is attributed to Him in reality; so it is fitting that He mention the greatest favour in both surahs. As for the fifth, the story is one, and that some of them are sinners and some are not sinners is established; so according to what was mentioned, it should be that "And say: *Hittah*" is mentioned first in both surahs. As for the sixth, the story is one, and the *wa* is for mere togetherness; and His saying, "We shall forgive" (*naghfir*), corresponds to "say" (*qulu*), whether it is placed first or last; and His saying, "And We shall increase" (*wa-sanazidu*), corresponds to "And enter" (*wa-udkhulu*), whether the *wa* is mentioned or omitted. As for the seventh, He mentioned here, before "So he substituted," what indicates specification and distinction, where He, glorified is He, said: "And We shaded you with the cloud and sent down upon you the manna and the quails, eat of the good things with which We have provided you," etc., with the direct address and its form. So what is fitting then is that He mention the word "among them" also. The correct answer to all these questions and what resembles them is what Zamakhshari mentioned: that there is no harm in the difference of the two expressions, provided there is no contradiction. And there is no contradiction between His saying, exalted is He, "Dwell in this town" and His saying "And eat," because when they dwell in the town, their dwelling causes them to eat from it, so they combined in existence dwelling in it and eating from it. Whether they put *Hittah* before entering the gate or after it, they are combining the two in bringing them about. Omitting mention of *raghad* (plenty) does not contradict affirming it. His saying, exalted is He, "We shall forgive you your sins, and We shall increase the good-doers" is a promise of two things, forgiveness and increase; and dropping the *wa* does not harm, because it is a resumed sentence (*isti'naf*) arranged upon the assumption of someone asking: "What comes after forgiveness?" So it was said to him: "We shall increase the good-doers." Likewise, the addition of "among them" is an addition of clarification. "Sent" and "sent down," and "they do wrong" and "they are defiantly disobedient," all come from one source. End.

In sum, variation in expression has never ceased to be the habit of eloquent speakers, and it contains, as is not hidden, an indication of the elevated rank of the speaker. The noble Qur'an is full of this. Whoever seeks to explain a secret for each thing that occurs in it has sought what there is no path to except through sound unveiling and God-given knowledge. God gives His bounty to whom He wills, and glory be to Him who alone encompasses the secrets of His Book.

* * *

And from the allusive (ishara) meanings of the verses: "And when you said to Moses of the heart: 'We will not believe' in the true faith until we attain the station of direct witnessing (mushahada) and beholding ('iyan)," then the thunderbolt of death took you, which is annihilation (fana') in the self-manifestation (tajalli dhati), while you were watching or witnessing. Then We raised you up with true life and subsistence after annihilation, so that you might give thanks for the blessing of divine oneness (tawhid) and of arrival through spiritual wayfaring (suluk) in God, Mighty and Majestic. We shaded you with the cloud of the manifestation of the attributes (tajalli al-sifat), since these are veils over the scorching sun of the Essence, whose radiant glories (subuhat) reach as far as His sight extends. We sent down upon you, from the states (ahwal) and the stations (maqamat) of spiritual taste, what combines sweetness with the removal of the base qualities of the soul, such as trust in God (tawakkul) and contentment (rida), and the manna and quails of wisdom, the knowledge and the true sciences, which the wind of mercy and the divine breaths gather for you in the wilderness (tih) of the attributes as you travel through them. Thus you are consoled by that consolation, and you forget from the pleasures of this world everything that is desired. "Eat," that is, partake of and receive these good things that have been provided for you according to your capacity, and given to you by a promise made to you. "And they did not wrong Us," that is, they did not diminish Our rights and attributes by claiming the attributes of their own selves. Rather, "they were wronging their own selves" by depriving them of their rights and causing their loss. This is manifest loss.

"And when We said: Enter this town," that is, the sacred place which is the station of witnessing, "and enter the gate," which is acceptance of the decree (rida bi'l-qada'), for it is the greatest gate of God, Most High, "prostrating," bowing humbly and submitting to what comes upon you of the manifestations. "And say: 'Remove our burdens,'" that is, ask God Most High to lower from you the sins of your attributes, your characters and your deeds. "If you do that, We will forgive you your transgressions." [The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever draws near to Me a span, I draw near to him a cubit; whoever draws near to Me a cubit, I draw near to him a fathom; whoever comes to Me walking, I come to him running."] "And We will increase the good-doers," that is, the witnessers of what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived. And what is that but the complete unveiling of the Most Holy Essence? "But those who did wrong changed the word from what had been said to them," that is, they put themselves to waste and placed themselves in other than their fitting place, seeking fleeting portions and base desires. So "We sent down upon the wrongdoers," specifically, a punishment, darkness and constriction in the prison of nature, and confinement in the bonds of wishful thinking and the fetter of desire, deprivation and humiliation through love of lowly material things, and turning away from those sublime manifestations. This comes from the subjugation of the heaven of the spirit, and the withholding of subtle grace and spirit from them because of their corruption and their departure from obedience to the heart, which commands only guidance, as is related in the saying: "Consult your heart, even if the mufti issues you a fatwa," to obedience to the commanding self (nafs ammara bi'l-su').

This is the great trial and the mighty calamity.

Whoever desires safety, let him always seek refuge from the diseased eyes,
Do not be deceived by its slackness, for it is a gaze whose pleasure harms your heart;
Beware of the greed of wishful desire, for its mighty one is like its humbled one, and its wealthy one is its beggar.

[Page 270]

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 2, verse 60 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people﴾ is a reminder of a great blessing that they disbelieved in. This happened in the wilderness (al-tih) when they became thirsty. Some narrations report that they said during it: "Who will protect us from the heat of the sun?" So God cast the cloud over them. They said: "Who will provide us with food?" So God sent down to them the manna and the quails. They said: "Who will provide us with water?" So Moses was commanded to strike the rock. The order is changed in order to highlight each of the matters counted within the context of a separate command that must be remembered and recalled. Had the chronological order been observed, it would have been understood that all of them were one matter, a single matter to be mentioned. Istisqa' (seeking water) is asking for water when there is no water or when it is scarce. It has been said that the object of istasqa is omitted, meaning "his Lord" or "water." This verb in eloquent usage is transitive to the one from whom water is sought at times, and to the water sought at other times, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿when his people asked him﴾, and in the line of poetry:

"And a fair man, by whose face the clouds are sought for rain, the protector of orphans, the refuge of widows."

To transitivize it to both at once, as in saying "Zayd sought water from his Lord," is not found in any speech of the Arabs. The lam is connected to the verb and is causal, meaning "for the sake of his people." ﴿So We said: Strike the rock with your staff﴾, meaning: so We answered him, and We said, etc. The word 'asa (staff) is feminine, and its alif is converted from a waw, as evidenced by 'asawan, and 'asawtuhu means "I struck him with the staff." It is pluralized irregularly as afu'l, and regularly as fu'ul, so one says a'us and 'isiyy. The vowel of the 'ayn follows the vowel of the sad. The hajar (rock) is this known body, and its plurals are ahjar and hijar. They also said hijara, and derived from it they said istahjara al-tin (the mud became hard like stone). Derivation from concrete nouns is very rare. The staff referred to here is the one asked about in the words of God Most High: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾. It is commonly held that it is from the myrtle (asu) of Paradise, its length ten cubits, the height of Moses peace be upon him. It had two branches that would shine in darkness. It was inherited from elder to younger until it reached Shu'ayb, and from him to Moses, peace be upon them both. It has been said that an angel lifted it up for him on the road to Madyan.

As for what is meant by the rock, there is disagreement. Al-Hasan said: it was not a specific rock; rather, whatever rock he struck, water burst from it, and this is more eloquent in terms of miracle and clearer in terms of power. Wahb said: he would strike for them the nearest rock, and it would gush forth. According to this view, the lam in "al-hajar" is for the genus (lam al-jins). It has been said it is for the specific (lam al-'ahd), and it is a particular rock that he carried with him from Mount Sinai, a cube having four faces, from each face three springs gushing forth, one for each tribe, flowing in a stream to the tribe that they were commanded to water. They were six hundred thousand, besides their animals, and the breadth of the camp was twelve miles. It has been said: it was a rock that was with Adam, which reached Shu'ayb along with the staff, and was then given to Moses. It has been said: it is the rock that fled with his garment, and the story is well known. It has been said: it is a light rock taken from the bottom of the sea, resembling a human head, which he would place in his bag, and when he needed water he would strike it. The reports on this are numerous, and most of them apparently contradict each other. No religious ruling depends on identifying this rock, and the safest course is to entrust its knowledge to God Most High.

﴿So there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾ is an conjunction (atf) over an implied element, meaning: so he struck, and it split apart. The existence of the gushing forth indicates this omitted element, for if it were gushing forth without striking, the command would have no benefit. Some call this fa' the eloquent fa' (al-fa' al-fasiha), and posit a conditional, meaning: if you strike, then it has gushed forth. In meaning, this estimation requires the gushing to precede the striking, unless it is said that what is meant is: we have decreed that the gushing follows upon your striking. Some later scholars said: there is no omission; rather, the fa' is for conjunction, and an implied "an" (that) follows the fa', as is the rule after an imperative when the sense of causation is intended. The construction is of the type: "Visit me and I will honor you," meaning: strike with your staff the rock, so if it gushes forth, then let the striking be from you. The gushing forth ... and it is not hidden what is in each

[Page 271]

until the Mawla, the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, said about the first: it is not fitting for the sublime dignity of the noble composition, and the second is more grievous and bitter. Infijar (gushing forth) is the splitting of one thing from another, and from it come fajr (dawn) and fujur (corruption). Here the word used is infajarat, and in al-A'raf it is inbajasat. It has been said: the two are the same. It has been said: there is a difference between them, which is that inbijas is the first emergence of water, while infijar is its expansion and abundance. Or it has been said: inbijas is its coming forth from hard ground, and the other is its coming forth from soft ground. The apparent usage is that they carry one meaning, and even on the assumption of difference, there is no contradiction, since the circumstances differ.

Min (from) denotes the starting point (ibtida' al-ghaya), and the pronoun refers to the rock that was struck. Its reference to the striking is not to be entertained. Min is causal (sababiyya), in the sense of what should not be rushed into. The ta' in "ithnata" is for the feminine. It is also said "thinta," but the ta' in it, according to al-Bahr, is for assimilation (lil-ilhaq), and this is similar to anbata and nabata (both meaning "to grow"). Its final radical is elided, and it is a ya', because it derives from thaniytu. Mujahid and a group read 'ashirata (with a kasra on the shin), and it was transmitted by al-Sa'di from Abu 'Amr. This is the dialect of Banu Tamim. Al-Fadl al-Ansari read it with a fatha on the shin. Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is a weak dialect. Some grammarians stated its irregularity. It is understood from some later scholars that these dialects apply in the compound form and not in 'ashara alone, but the statements of the scholars do not support this. The 'ayn is the source of water, and it is pluralized irregularly as a'yun and regularly as 'uyun. They used the term a'yan for the nobles of people, and this occurs in the case of the eyes (al-basira) rarely, as in the words: "eyes for her and inner corners of the eyes." The word ('ayn, in singular) here is accusative as a specification (tamyiz), and its being singular in such a position is obligatory. Al-Farra' permitted that it be plural. This number was specifically chosen over others because they were twelve tribes, and there was enmity and rivalry among them. So God caused each tribe to have a spring for itself, which it would draw from, and no other tribe would share in it, to prevent the arousal of hatred. The wisdom of this division is alluded to in the words of God Most High: ﴿Each people knew their drinking place﴾. This is a resumptive clause (jumla mustaʼnafa) indicating that each tribe had a place of drinking it recognized, so it did not go beyond the drinking place of another. Unas (people) is a plural with no singular of its own form. What was mentioned about the irregularity of retaining its hamza applies only with the alif and lam; without them, it is common and correct. 'Alima (knew) here is transitive to one object, treated like 'arafa and wajada (in this sense), which is frequent. Al-mashrab (drinking place) is either a noun of place, meaning the site of drinking, or a mimi verbal noun meaning drinking. Some took it to mean what is drunk, namely water, but taking it to mean the place is preferred according to Abu Hayyan. The attribution of mashrab to them is because, once each drinking place became specific to those specified for it, it became as if it were their possession. The pronoun in "mashrabahum" refers to the meaning of "kull" (each), and it is not permissible for it to refer to its wording, because when kull is attached to an indefinite noun, the sense must be observed, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿the day We shall call every people with their leader﴾, and the line:

"And every people will surely enter among them a calamity from which the fingertips turn yellow."

The drinking place was specifically mentioned to draw attention to the great benefit, which is the cause of life. Although the natural flow of speech would require "Each people knew their spring," there is an omission in the sentence, meaning "from them," because ﴿knew﴾ is a description of "twelve springs," and so a connecting pronoun is necessary. He described them with it because it is another miracle, in that with the emergence of water there arise channels by which each tribe's drinking place is distinguished from another's. It is also possible that the sentence is circumstantial (hal) rather than a description of "twelve," so that a return pronoun need not be estimated, and to indicate the simultaneity of knowledge of the drinking places with the gushing forth. In that case, the drinking place is the spring itself.

﴿Eat and drink from the provision of God﴾, with the verb of saying implied. He began with eating because the body's sustenance depends on it, and the need for drinking follows from it. Min is for the starting point, and it is possible that it is partitive (lil-tab'id). Mentioning the provision as an attributed noun glorifies the favor and points to its having come to them without toil or effort. In this there is an iltifat (shift in grammatical person), since previously it was "So We said," and had it followed a single pattern, it would have said: "from Our provision." Had the implied speaker before "eat" been attributed to Moses, meaning "Moses said: eat and drink," this shift would not occur. Here "provision" means the thing provided, namely the food previously mentioned, the manna and the quails, and the drink is from the water.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 60 (part 2 of 2):

...the springs. It was also said that what is meant is water alone, because it is drunk and because food grows from it. This view is weakened by the fact that their food in the wilderness (tih) did not come from the crops of that water, as the Exalted's words indicate: "It brings forth from what the earth grows" (﴿It brings forth from what the earth grows﴾), and ﴿We will not endure one kind of food﴾. It also entails combining the literal and the metaphorical meanings, since it amounts to "Eat and drink from the water," where the attribution of drinking to the water is taken literally and the attribution of eating is taken to mean what is caused by it. Alternatively, one may say that the complement of one of the two verbs is omitted, meaning: "Eat from God's provision, and drink from God's provision." The view of some later scholars that "God's provision" refers to water is also possible. The verse contains another sign of its miraculous nature: this water, just as it quenches the thirsty, also satisfies the hungry, so it is food and drink at once, which is an extremely remote possibility. Closer to this is that "Eat and drink" is not part of what is reported from them through the implied verb "they said," but is an imperative placed after their mention of what happened at the time of the water-seeking, as a form of thanks and a reminder of God's power. Thus He commanded the addressees of this account to eat and drink from what God the Exalted provides them, and not to cause corruption by misleading creation and hoarding worldly goods. Its separation from what preceded it is then justified, because it explains the thanks that is commanded, or it is a result of what was mentioned.

The Mu'tazilah cited this verse as evidence that provision (rizq) means what is lawful (halal), because the least that this command can imply is permission (ibahah), so provision must be permitted. Thus if an unlawful provision existed, provision would be both permitted and forbidden, which is impossible. The answer is that provision here is not general, if what is meant is the manna and quails and the water gushing from the stone. The lawfulness of a particular kind does not entail the lawfulness of all kinds of provision. And even if we accept generality, it must be restricted to a part of it.

﴿And do not go about in the earth causing corruption﴾. When they were commanded to eat and drink from God the Exalted's provision, without being restricted in time, place, or quantity, this was a great blessing and favor toward them. This invited expansiveness in eating and drinking, so He forbade what might result from it, namely corruption, lest they meet those blessings with ingratitude. According to some verification scholars, al-'uthiyy (the root meaning of the word) is transgressing the limit in general, whether or not it is corruption, so it is like transgression (i'tida'). Then it came to be used predominantly for corruption. The phrase "causing corruption" (mufsidin) here is a circumstantial clause (haal) that is not emphatic (ghayr mu'akkidah), which is its basic function, as its definiteness indicates. Abu al-Baqa' mentioned that al-'uthiyy means corruption, and the circumstantial clause is emphatic. However, the objection is that bringing an emphatic circumstantial clause after a verbal sentence contradicts the view of the majority. Al-Zamakhshari held that its meaning is the most extreme corruption, and the sense is: "Do not persist in corruption while you are corrupting," and the aim is to forbid what they were engaged in, namely persistence in corruption. This is of the same style as ﴿Do not devour usury, doubled and redoubled﴾. Otherwise corruption is itself a reprehensible evil that is forbidden. The objection to this is that it is an unnecessary exaggeration, since what we have mentioned suffices.

According to the majority, the earth here means the land of the wilderness (tih). It is also permissible that it means that land and other lands they were able to reach, so that their corruption reaches them. It was also permitted that it means all the lands, with al (the definite article) denoting the whole genus. Their corruption in them would be because the abundance of disobedience, persistence in violations, and insolence invite the cutting off of rain, the drought of lands, and the removal of blessings. That is a retribution that encompasses the lands.

Furthermore, the apparent meaning of the Qur'an does not indicate that this water-seeking, striking, or gushing was repeated. So it is possible that it was repeated, and it is possible that it happened only once. The single occurrence is the established one. Accounts about this matter are numerous, and most of them have no soundness. Some natural philosophers (tabi'iyyun) denied this event, saying: "How is it conceivable that abundant great water would gush from a small stone?" This objector, although he conceives of God's power to change natures and transform substances, has abandoned reflection according to his own method. For it is established among them that the magnet attracts iron, the shaving stone shaves hair, and the stone that is hostile to vinegar repels it. All of this is among the secrets of nature. If such things are not considered strange among them, then there is nothing impossible in God creating in another stone the power to draw water from beneath the earth, and this power being created at the striking of the staff, or at the command of Moses, peace be upon him, according to what is reported, that afterward he would command it and it would gush forth. Its separation from the earth does not contradict this, as some have imagined. It is also possible that God, through a power He deposited in the stone, transforms the air into water by removing dryness from its parts and creating moisture within them. God is over all things capable.

The portion of the knower from this verse is to know the human soul (ruh insaniyyah) and its attributes in the world of the heart, in the position of Moses and his people, while he seeks his Lord to quench it with the water of wisdom and knowledge. He is commanded to strike with the staff of "there is no god but God" (la ilaha illa Allah). It has two branches of negation and affirmation, which blaze into light when the darkness of the self prevails. It was carried from the Presence of Might to the stone of the heart, which is like stones or even harder in hardness, so there gushed from it twelve springs of the waters of wisdom. This is because the phrase "there is no god but God" has twelve letters, and from each letter a spring gushed forth. Each tribe of the tribes of human attributes, which are twelve tribes of outer and inner senses, and two from the heart and the self, knows its own drinking place from a spring that flowed from one of the letters of the phrase. Each one knows its drinking place and the drinking place of each other, wherever its guide leads it and its leader directs it. So from one drinking place is sweet and pure, and from another is brackish and bitter. The souls approach the watering places of piety and acts of worship, and the spirits drink from the pure water of unveilings, witnessings, and secrets, and are quenched from the springs of realities, with the cup of the manifestation of the attributes, from the Cupbearer: ﴿And their Lord gave them a pure drink﴾, for dissolution into the reality of the Essence. ﴿Eat and drink from God's provision﴾, by His command and His pleasure. ﴿And do not go about causing corruption﴾ in this mold, by abandoning the command, choosing sin, selling religion for the world, preferring the first life over the hereafter, and placing them both ahead of the Master.
