**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 61 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will not endure one kind of food."﴾ Apparently this is included in the enumeration of the blessings and their details. It is the answer to their request, expressed by His words, exalted is He, ﴿Go down﴾ and so on, although they deserved the utmost wrath, because they were ungrateful for the blessing of sending down delicious food upon them while they were in the wilderness without toil or hardship. They asked (with "we will not endure"), and this indicates their dislike of it, since patience (sabr) is the restraining of the soul within a narrow state. For this reason He rebuked them with His words, exalted is He, ﴿Would you exchange...﴾ and so on. The verse in its style is like His words, exalted is He, ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will never believe you"﴾ and so on, where they persisted in obstinacy after hearing the speech and were destroyed, and then He bestowed upon them the blessing of life. Mawlana al-Salikuti said: From this it becomes clear how weak is what al-Imam al-Razi said: "If their request had been a sin, He would not have answered them, because answering toward sin is sinful, and that is impermissible for the prophets." And His words, exalted is He, ﴿Eat and drink﴾ are a command of permission, not of obligation, so their request for other than that food is not a sin. The description of the food as "one kind," although they were two kinds of food, al-Mann and al-Salwa, which they were provided with in the wilderness, is either because it was of one manner, as one says, "The food of the emir's table is one," even if it consists of various dishes, meaning that it does not change or vary according to the times; or because it was one type, since al-Mann and al-Salwa are foods of those who enjoy luxury and extravagance. It seems the people were farmers, so they wanted nothing but what they were accustomed to. It has been said that they used to cook the two together so that they became one food. The view that this statement was made before the descent of al-Salwa is a poor view, and less acceptable than it is the view that by "one food" they meant al-Salwa, because al-Mann was a drink or something they sweetened with, so they did not count it as another food. Otherwise, the view would be that He used "one" to refer to "two," just as He used "two" to refer to "one," as in His words, ﴿From both of them emerge the pearl and the coral﴾, although it emerges only from one of them, namely the salt, not the sweet water. ﴿So call upon your Lord for us﴾, that is, ask Him on our behalf by your supplication to Him that He bring forth for us such-and-such. The "fa'" (so) indicates the causal link: their lack of patience is the cause of their request for supplication. The dialect of the Banu 'Amir says (fad'i) with a kasra on the 'ayn, treating da'a, which is of the "ya" type, like ramā. They asked Moses to supplicate for them because the supplication of the prophets, peace be upon them, is closer to being answered than the supplication of others. Moreover, the supplication of another person on behalf of someone else in general is closer to being answered, so what do you think of the supplication of the prophets for their nations? For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Include us in your supplication." And it is reported in a narration: "Call upon Me with tongues in which you have not disobeyed Me." It has been interpreted as referring to the tongues of others. The mention of the title of Lordship (al-Rububiyyah) serves to pave the way for the beginnings of answering. They said "your Lord" and did not say "our Lord," because in that there is a particularity to Him that they did not share, namely His intimate conversation, His speaking to him, and His giving him the Torah. So it is as if they said: Supplicate for us to the One who has been good to you, with what He has not been good to us with. Just as He has been good to you before, we hope that He will be good to you in answering your supplication.

﴿He will bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions.﴾ The intended meaning of "bringing forth" is the figurative meaning which is necessarily connected to the literal meaning, namely manifesting by way of bringing into existence, not by way of removing concealment. Taking it in the literal sense would require a departure from it, and what is suitable for it here is the earth, and with that supposition the speech becomes absurd. ("Yukhrij," "He will bring forth") is in the jussive mood, because it is the response to the imperative (jawab al-amr). Jazming it by means of an elided lam of command (lam al-talab) is not permitted according to the Basran grammarians. ("Min," "from") in the first instance is partitive (tab'idiyyah), meaning: some of what is eaten of what it grows. al-Akhfash claimed that it is extra (ziyadah), but this is not correct. ("Ma," "what") is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is elided, meaning: which it grows. Making it a verbal-noun (masdariyyah) was not permitted by Abu al-Baqa', because what is estimated is a substance (jawhar). Attributing the growing to the earth is a figurative attribution by way of attributing to the recipient. Allah, exalted is He, has deposited in the clay stratum of the earth, or in it, a power receptive to this. That the receptive power is deposited in the grain and not in the soil may lead to the statement that the grain is eternal in its species. ("Min," "from") in the second instance is explicative (bayaniyyah), so the adverbial phrase is a stable complement standing in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: being of its herbs. Abu Hayyan said: it is partitive, standing in the position of an appositive to the word "ma," so the adverbial phrase is an unstressed complement related to ("yukhrij"). According to both estimations, as al-Salikuti said, it indicates that what is requested is the bringing forth of some of these. If it were taken as explicative, it would not give the meaning that the partitive "min" gives, as stated by Mawla 'Isam al-Din: the speech would be devoid of the stated benefit, and it would imply that what is requested is the bringing forth of all of these, due to the absence of a specific reference. "Al-Baql" (herbs) is a genus which includes green plants that people and livestock eat. Here it refers to the choicest herbs that people eat. "Al-Qitha'" is this well-known thing. al-Khalil said it is the cucumber (al-khiyar). Yahya ibn Wathhab and others read it with a damma on the qaf, and this is a dialect. "Al-Fum" is wheat, and most people hold this view, to the extent that al-Zajjaj said: there is no disagreement among the lexicographers that al-Fum is wheat, and all grains that are baked are also called al-Fum. al-Kisa'i and a group said it is garlic, and its tha' was changed to fa', as in jadath and jadaf. It goes with onion and lentil, and it is more fitting with them. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read it this way, and our shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, inclined toward it. The view that it is bread is far-fetched, since growing from the earth rules it out, and its mention alongside herbs and other things. What is in al-Ma'alim from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that al-Fum is bread, can be explained by saying that its meaning is that it is applied to it. The arrangement of the wording is such that first it mentions what combines heat, coldness, moistness, and dryness, namely herbs, for among them is what is cold and moist, like endive; among them is what is hot and dry, like celery and dill; and among them is what is hot and has moisture, like mint. Second, it mentions what is cold and moist, which is the cucumber. Third, what is hot and dry, which is garlic. Fourth, what is cold and dry, which is the lentil. Fifth, what is hot and moist, which is the onion. When it is cooked, according to some, it becomes cold and moist. Or it may be said that first it mentions what is eaten without the treatment of fire, and after it what is treated by fire together with what is appropriate for that and accepts it.

﴿He said, "Would you exchange that which is lower for that which is better?"﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (istinaf) that came as an answer to an estimated question, as if it were said: "What did he say to them?" So it was said: He said, ﴿Would you exchange﴾ and so on. The speaker is either Allah, exalted is He, through the tongue of Moses, peace be upon him, which is supported by the context being one of enumerating blessings; or Moses himself, which is more suitable to the context of the wording. The interrogative is for denunciation, and "istibdal" (exchanging) means taking in exchange.

Here the commentator raises an objection: If they were unable to endure one kind of food, this implies a request to add something to it, not to exchange it for something else. It is answered that their statement, ﴿we will not endure﴾, indicates their dislike of that food, and failure to give thanks for a blessing is a sign of its removal, so it is as if they sought its removal and the coming of something else. It has been said that they asked for that, and their address with this is an indication that when He gives them what they asked for, He withholds al-Mann and al-Salwa from them, so the two do not combine. It has been said that the exchange concerns the stomach, but as you see, this is not correct. Ubayy read ("Tubaddiluna," "Would you substitute"), and this is figurative, because the substitution is not theirs; rather it belongs to Allah, exalted is He. But since the substitution would occur through their request, they were treated as those who substitute, and the meaning would be: "Do you ask for the substitution of that which..." etc. "Alladhi" (that which) is the object of "tastabdilu," and it is the thing acquired. The one to which the preposition "ba'" is attached is the thing being left, and it is ("adna," "lower"), which is the relative clause of ("alladhi"). Here it must be affirmed according to the Basran grammarians, since there is no elongation (of the relative clause) here. ("Adna") is either from "dunuw" (nearness), or it is inverted from "dun" (lower). On the second it is clear, and on the first it is figurative: "dunuw" is used in the sense of physical nearness, in the meaning of lowliness, just as "bu'd" (distance) is used for nobility, so it is said: "far-reaching in place, far-reaching in aspiration." It may be that it is hamzated, from "dana'a" (baseness), and the hamza has been changed into an alif. This is supported by the reading of Zuhayr and al-Kisa'i, ("adna'," with a hamza). By "that which is better" is meant al-Mann and al-Salwa. The meaning of the superiority of this food over the other is the high price, the pleasant taste, the great benefit in eating it, the lack of hardship in obtaining it, and its freedom from any doubt about its lawfulness.

﴿Go down to a city﴾ is a sentence related by the verb of saying, like the first. The reason one of them was not conjoined to the other in the reported speech is that the first is a statement in meaning, while this one is not like that. And because it serves as an explanation for the first, since descending is the way to the exchange. This is when both sentences are taken as the speech of Allah, exalted is He, or of Moses. If one of them is from Moses and the other from Allah, exalted is He, then the reason for the separation is clear, and a pause on a complete statement is sufficient according to the first view, and a complete pause according to the second. Descent may be physical, in that the wilderness is higher than the city, or it may be by rank, and this is more suitable to the context. It was read ("ihbutu," with a damma on the hamza and the ba'). "Misr" is a great city, and its original sense is a limit and a barrier between two things. He said:

"And the maker of the sun a clear misr between the day and the night that has separated them."

Its application to a city is because it is bounded (mamsur), meaning limited. Deriving it from "masartu al-shah amsuruha," meaning when you milk all of the udder, is far-fetched. It is reported from Ashhab that he said: Malik said to me: "It is Misr, your village, the dwelling of Pharaoh." So it is then a proper name. Names of places may be considered from the standpoint of place and so are masculine, or considered from the standpoint of land and so are feminine. If it is taken as a proper name, then either by considering it as a city, in which case it is diptotic (unnunated) because of proper-name status and feminine gender with a sukun in the middle; or by considering it as a town (balad), in which case it is triptotic (regular), since a single derivative feature does not suffice to prohibit inflection. What Imam Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, said is supported by the fact that in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it is written ("Misra") without an alif after the ra'. What makes it less likely is that the apparent sense of the tanwin is indefiniteness, and that His words, exalted is He, ﴿Enter the holy land﴾, meaning Syria, which Allah has prescribed for you, indicate obligation, as the coordination of the prohibition shows; and that requires the prohibition of entering another land. Also, the command to descend may be restricted to the lands of the wilderness, which is what lies between Bayt al-Maqdis and Qinnasrin. Some people have said that "Misr" is an arabized form of "Misra'im," like "Isra'il," the name of one of the sons of Noah, peace be upon him, who was the first to lay out the city, so it was named after him. Triptoting it in this case is because the foreign origin is not considered, due to the presence of arabization and inflection in it. Understand this and reflect.

﴿For you will have what you asked for.﴾ This is the causal justification for the command to descend. In al-Bahr it is said that it is the response to the command (jawab al-amr). Just as a response may be given by a verb, it may also be given by a sentence. In this there are two elided elements: the pronoun that links the sentence to what precedes it, and the pronoun returning to "ma," and the estimate is: "For you therein will be what you asked for." The expression of the requested things as ("ma," "what") is for the sake of avoiding the mention of them as something shameful. al-Nakha'i and Yahya read ("sa'altum," with a kasra on the sin).

Page 277

﴿And humiliation and wretchedness were struck upon them﴾, meaning that this was made to encompass them as a dome encompasses what is set beneath it, or it was made to adhere to them as clay adheres to a wall when it is plastered on. In the speech there is an implicit metaphor (istiʿāra bi-l-kināya), in that this is likened to a dome or to clay. "Were struck" (ḍuribat) is a subsidiary, actualized metaphor (istiʿāra tabaʿiyya taḥqīqiyya) for the meaning of encompassing and comprehensiveness, or of clinging and adhering to them. On both readings, the statement is a metonymy (kināya) for their being abased and humbled. This is shown by the poll tax (jizya) imposed on them, which they pay "out of hand while humbled" (Qur'an 9:29); by the obligation laid on them to display a distinctive dress so that it is known that they are Jews and they are not confused with the Muslims; by the nature of their souls, which are marked by poverty of spirit and avarice, so that you will not find any community among the communities more greedy than they; by their habit of displaying bad circumstances for fear that the poll tax will be multiplied upon them; and by other matters that you see among the Jews today. This striking is a requital for them for their ingratitude for that blessing, and by this the verse is connected to what precedes it. The pronoun of the absent person is used to indicate that this applies to all Jews, and it encompasses those addressed by His words, exalted is He, "Indeed, for you is what you ask" (Qur'an 2:61 is the context of this clause), and those who come after them until the Day of Resurrection. So it is not a case of iltifāt (shift of grammatical person), contrary to what has been supposed. ﴿And they returned with anger from Allah﴾, meaning they alighted and settled in what befell them of affliction and punishments in this world, or in what was established for them of punishment in the Hereafter, or in what was written for them of hardships in both. Or they returned with wrath, meaning it became upon them, and for this reason there is no need to consider the one to whom they returned. Or they became deserving of it, or they earned the punishment by its cause, but this is far-fetched. The root of bawāʾ, with a fatḥa or a ḍamma, is equality of parts, and then it was used for any equality. It is said: "He is the bawāʾ of so-and-so," meaning his equal. From this comes "bu'" (a sacrifice/ atonement), for the thong of the sandal of Kulayb, and the ḥadīth: "Let him take his seat in the Fire" (fal-yatabawwaʾ maqʿadahu min al-nār). In describing the anger as being from Allah, exalted is He, there is magnification of His station after magnification, and exaltation after exaltation.

﴿That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right﴾. By "that" He points to what preceded: the striking of humiliation and wretchedness, and the returning with great anger. He used the distal demonstrative because some of it is distant, even though if it referred only to the returning it would not be in the form of the distal. Or it is to indicate that these matters overtook them although they were far from them, because they were People of the Book. Or it is to suggest how far they are in their enormity. The bāʾ is causal (sababiyya), and it governs the interpreted verbal noun (maṣdar muʾawwal), though it was not expressed as such. He expressed it as he did to draw attention to the recurrence of disbelief and killing from them time after time, and to their persistence in both in the past, or to bring to mind the ugliness of their conduct. "The signs" (āyāt) may be the miracles in general, or the nine (signs) that Moses, peace be upon him, brought, or what he brought of the nine and others, or the signs of the scriptures recited in general, or the Torah, or some of its signs such as the signs in which the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is found, or those in which stoning is found, or the Qur'an. In attributing the signs to His name there is an added condemnation of them. He, glory be to Him, began with their disbelief in His signs because it is the greatest of all great things, and He followed it with their killing of the prophets, because it is like its consequence. He used "al-nabiyyīn" (the prophets), which implies a small number, rather than "al-anbiyāʾ", which implies a large number, since the two plurals are distinguished when they are indefinite. But when the definite article (al-) enters on them, they are equal, as in al-Baḥr (al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ). So it is not objected that they killed three hundred prophets at the beginning of the day and set up their market at its end. He restricted the killing with "without right", although the killing of prophets is never anything but that, to indicate that this was without right in their view, since none of them believed the killing of any of them, peace be upon them, to be right. What drove them to it was love of this world, following of desire, excess in disobedience, and transgression. On this view the lām in al-ḥaqq is for the known (ʿahd). It has been said: the more evident view is that it is for the genus, and the intended meaning is "without any right at all", since the lām of the undetermined genus is like the indefinite noun. This is supported by what is in Āl ʿImrān ("without right"), so it indicates that it was not right by their own belief either. It is possible that the benefit of the restriction is to expose the faults of their conduct, for they killed a prophet, then a group of them, and then it was without right; and this is more in accordance with what is evident, namely that the prohibited thing is killing without right in reality,

Page 278

whether it was right in the eyes of the killer or not. However, restricting it to killing without right in their view is more fitting for an implicit rebuke concerning their situation, as has been said. As for the statement that one could say: had He not restricted it with "without right," it would indicate that among the special properties of prophethood is that if he killed anyone without right he would not be subjected to retaliation, so the benefit of the restriction is that the wording conveys the legal ruling, which is far-fetched, as is not hidden. Some later scholars said: all this applies when "ghayr" means negation, i.e., "without right". But if its meaning is "by means of a matter other than the right," i.e., falsehood (al-bāṭil), then the restriction is beneficial, because their killing of the prophets was by means of falsehood and its protection. Close to this is what al-Qaffāl said: that they used to say that the prophets were liars, that their miracles were deceptions, and they killed them on this ground, and because they wished to nullify what they themselves held to be the truth by their own claim. Probably this was the majority of their circumstances. Otherwise, Ishaya, Yahya and Zakariyya, peace be upon them, were not killed for that reason. Ishaya was killed because a king of the Children of Israel, when he died, the affair of the Children of Israel fell into disorder, they competed for kingship, and some of them killed others; he, peace be upon him, forbade them, so they rebelled against him and killed him. Yahya, peace be upon him, was killed on account of the story of that woman, may Allah curse her. Likewise Zakariyya, for when his son was killed he fled, and the king sent in pursuit of him in anger over what had happened to his wife concerning the killing of her son. He was found inside a tree, so they split the tree together with him lengthwise in two halves with a saw. Then, the apparent view is that the prepositional phrase is one of the items disputed between "disbelief" and "killing" (in the grammatical sense of tanāzuʿ, competition of two verbs for one complement). In al-Baḥr it is said that it is connected to what is before it. Some atheists claimed that between this verse, and what resembles it, and His saying, exalted is He, "Indeed We surely help Our messengers," there is a contradiction. It was answered that the ones killed among the prophets are different from the messengers promised victory. This was refuted by saying that His saying, exalted is He, "Is it that whenever a messenger came to you...," down to His saying, glory be to Him, "...a group you called liars and a group you kill" (Qur'an 2:87), shows that those killed were also messengers. Some answered that the meaning of victory is victory by overcoming with proof, or taking vengeance, as was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, that Allah decreed that for every prophet seventy thousand should be killed, and for every caliph thirty-five thousand. But what is in this is not hidden. So the best view is that the messengers meant are those commanded to fight, as one of the verifying scholars answered, because commanding them to fight and their not being protected from being killed is not befitting the wisdom of the Mighty, the Wise. ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, read "yuqattilūna" with the doubled letter, and al-Ḥasan in one narration read "wa-taqtulūna" with the tāʾ, and this is then an iltifāt. Nāfiʿ read with hamza "al-nabiyyīn", and likewise "al-nabī" and "al-nubuwwa". This has been questioned by what has been narrated: that a man said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Prophet of Allah" with the hamza, and he said: "I am not Nabiyy Allah" meaning with hamza, "but Nabiyy Allah," without the hamza, and he disapproved of that. For this reason some scholars forbade applying it to him, peace be upon him. Moreover, the plural of "nabī" as "nabiyyīn" has been questioned, since it is faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl, and they have explicitly stated that it is not made into the sound masculine plural. As for the first point, it was answered that Abū Zayd recorded "nabaʾtu min al-arḍ" (I emerged from the land) when you come out of it, so it was prohibited for fear that it might give the impression that its meaning is "O one expelled by Allah," and so he forbade it for that reason of misleading implication. It does not follow that since Allah, exalted is He, used it for His prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, whom He cleared of every deficiency, its use is permissible for human beings. It was said that the prohibition was specific to the early period of Islam, when the intrigues of the Jews were rife, and this is like the prohibition from saying "rāʿinā" in favour of "unẓurnā". As for the second point, it is not agreed upon, for it was said that it means fāʿil (active), and even if granted, it has departed from its original meaning and this was not taken into account in it, since those who use it of him do not know that. So its plural is valid in view of the predominant meaning of it. Reflect on this.

﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress﴾. It refers to the disbelief and killing, which were the causes of what has preceded. The demonstrative in the singular is permissible for a plurality on account of interpretation with what was mentioned, and similar singular-in-form but plural-in-meaning expressions; and such a thing may also occur with a pronoun, by analogy with it. The bāʾ is causal, and what follows it is a cause of a cause. The meaning is: what drove them to disbelief in the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and to killing the prophets is only the prior disobedience, transgression, and their exceeding the limits. Sin drags sin. He emphasized the first because it is the likely object of disbelief, unlike mere disobedience. It has been said: the bāʾ means "with" (maʿa). It has been said: the demonstrative refers to what was indicated by the first, and the conjunction is omitted to indicate that each of them is independently sufficient for deserving the striking, so how much more when both are combined. This view has been judged weak, because repetition is contrary to the original form, and a subtle meaning achieved by the first and its predecessor is lost, namely that the demonstrative then has no evident benefit, since the apparent wording would be "by what they disobeyed..." and that benefit would also be lost. The portion of the knowing person from these verses is to take a lesson from the state of those who did not accept the decree, did not give thanks for blessings, and did not endure tribulations. How He struck upon them the humiliation of rebellion before the existence of beings, and overpowered them with the slap of wretchedness in the wilderness of abandonment, and placed in their hearts the love of this world, and brought them down from the high station.

* * *

From the esoteric (ishāra) perspective: the single food is the spiritual nourishment of wisdom and knowledge; and what the earth brings forth is the vile desires, the base pleasures, and the cold delights arising from the earth of debased souls in the Egypt of the body. These cause humiliation to whoever tastes them, wretchedness to whoever chews them, and destruction to whoever swallows them. The cause of seeking that is veiling oneself from the signs of Allah, exalted is He, and His manifestations, and blackening the hearts with the filth of sins, and cutting off their vein by cutting off what flows to it. What leads to this is heedlessness of the Beloved, and the substitution of others for that sought object. We ask Allah, exalted is He, for well-being for us and for you.

[p. 279]

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾: When the discourse turned to the warning against the People of the Book, He, glory be to Him, followed it, as is His custom, with what contains the promise, combining encouragement (tarhib... no: targhib, encouragement) and warning (tarhib). By this the reason for placing this verse and the one before it between the enumeration of the blessings becomes clear. Regarding the intended meaning of "those who believe" here, there are several views. What is narrated from Sufyan al-Thawri (Sufyan al-Thawri) is that they are those who believe with their tongues, who are the hypocrites (munafiqun), as evidenced by their being grouped with the disbelievers. The expression of them by this description, rather than by the label of hypocrisy, is to make clear that this rank, even though it is described as faith, will not benefit them at all and will not rescue them from the peril of disbelief with certainty. From al-Suddi: they are the hanifs (hanifiyyun), those who did not reach the Messenger (ﷺ), such as Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, Qass ibn Sa'ida, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, and those who reached him, such as Abu Dhar and Bahira, and the delegation of the Negus who were awaiting the mission (al-ba'tha). From Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father): they are those who believed in Jesus before the Messenger (ﷺ) was sent. Al-Suddi narrated from his shaykhs that they are those who believed in Moses until Jesus came, peace be upon them both, and they then believed in him. It was also said: they are the companions of Salman, whose story he related to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to him: "They are in the Fire." The earth then grew dark for him, as Mujahid narrated from him, and at that moment the verse down to "they will grieve" was revealed. Salman said: "It was as if a mountain had been lifted from me." It was also said: they are those who adhere to the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) sincerely, or as hypocrites, and al-Qadi (al-Baydawi) preferred this. The cause of the difference is His saying afterwards: ﴿whoever believes﴾ etc., for that requires that what is meant by one of them be other than what is meant by the other. The least burdensome of the views is the first of them.

﴿Those who are Jews (alladhina hadu)﴾: that is, those who became Jews (tahawwadu). It is said: "hada" and "tahawwada" when one enters Judaism. "Yahud" is either Arabic, from "hada" meaning "to repent," and they were so named when they repented of worshipping the calf; the reason for the specification is that their repentance was the most arduous of deeds, as has passed. Or it is an arabicized form of Yahudha (Judah), with a dhal dotted and a short alif, as if they were named after the eldest son of Jacob, peace be upon him. It is read (hadu) with a fatha on the dal, meaning some of them inclined towards others. "Al-Nasara" is the plural of "nasran," with the meaning of "nasrani" (Christian), and this usage occurs in Arabic speech, though some deny it, such as the verse:

You see him, when the evening comes round, bowing like a hanif, and at the time of noon he is a Christian sun-scorched beside him.

It is said of the feminine: "nasran" like "nadman" and "nadmana," as Sibawayh said, and it was recited: "As a Christian woman prostrates without bowing (to the hanif)."

The yaa in "nasrani" according to him is for intensification (mubalagha), as one says of the red one "ahmari," indicating that he is deeply rooted in his description. It was said: it is for distinguishing the singular from the plural, like "zinj" and "zinji," and "rum" and "rumi." It was said: "al-Nasara" is the plural of "nasra," like "mahra" and "mahari," one of whose two yaas was deleted, and the kasra was changed to a fatha for lightness, so the yaa was changed to an alif. This is the view of al-Khalil. It is the name for the companions of Jesus, peace be upon him, and they were so named either because they helped him (nasarahu), or because some of them helped others. It was said: Jesus, peace be upon him, was born in Bethlehem near Jerusalem, then his mother took him to Egypt, and when he reached twelve years of age she brought him back to Syria and they settled in the village of Nazareth. It was said: "Nasraya," and it was said: "Nasra," and it was said: "Nasrana," and it was said: "Nasran," and al-Jawhari held this, so whoever was with him was named after it, or a name was derived for them from it.

﴿And the Sabians (al-Sabi'in)﴾: they are a people whose doctrines revolve around fanaticism for the spiritual beings (ruhaniyyin) and taking them as intermediaries. Since it was not possible for them to draw near to them in their very essences, nor to receive from them in their persons, a group of them resorted to their temples (hayakil). The Sabians of Rome resort to the planets (sayyarat), and the Sabians of India resort to the fixed stars (thawabit). A group descended from the temples to the individual figures that neither hear nor see, nor avail anyone anything. The first group are the worshippers of the stars, and the second are the worshippers of idols, and each of these two groups has various kinds, differing in beliefs and forms of worship. Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: they are not idol-worshippers, but they venerate the stars as the Ka'ba is venerated. It was also said: they are a monotheistic people who believe in the influence of the stars and acknowledge some prophets, such as Yahya, peace be upon him. It was said: they acknowledge Allah, the Exalted, read the Zabur, worship the angels, and pray towards the Ka'ba, and it was said: towards the south wind. They have taken something from every religion. Regarding the permissibility of marrying them and eating their slaughtered animals, there is discussion among the jurists, to be sought in its proper place. The word has been disputed: it was said it is not Arabic, and it was said it is Arabic from "sabi'a" with a hamza, meaning to go out, or from "saba" (defective), meaning to incline, because of their departure from the true religion and their inclination towards falsehood. Nafi' alone read it with a yaa, and that is either according to the original form, or substitution for lightness.

﴿Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds﴾: that is, whoever among these groups brings into being faith in Allah, the Exalted, His attributes and acts, the prophethoods, and the Second Creation in the fitting manner, and performs righteous deeds as faith in what has been mentioned requires. This is based on the first of the views. Those who hold the last of them, among them, interpret the verse as referring to whoever among those was characterized by pure faith in the origin and the return in general, whether this was by way of persistence and continuance in it, like the faith of the sincere ones, or by way of its coming into being and initiation, like the faith of the hypocrites and the rest of the groups. The benefit of the generality for the sincere ones is to increase the encouragement of the rest towards faith, by showing that their lateness in attaining it does not detract from their being an example for those earlier ones. Among them are those who interpret it as referring to whoever among them was in his religion before it was abrogated (nuskh), believing in his heart in the origin and the return, acting in accordance with the requirement of his law. Thus the ruling includes the sincere ones of the community of the Prophet (ﷺ), the hypocrites who repented, the Jews and Christians who died before distortion (tahrif) and abrogation, and the Sabians who died during the time their affair was upright, if it is said that they had a religion. Likewise it includes the Jews and Sabians who believed in Jesus, peace be upon him, and died in his time, and likewise whoever among these groups believed in Muhammad (ﷺ). The benefit of mentioning "those who believe" on this view, even though the preceding warning was about the Jews, is to calm the zeal of the Jews by equating the believers among them in that each one who was in his religion before abrogation earns reward, and after it brings deprivation. Just as the mention of the Sabians is to alert that they, despite being the most manifestly astray of those mentioned, may be turned to in repentance if faith and righteous deeds are sound from them, so others are by a fortiori reasoning. The understanding of "before abrogation" is derived from ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾, since there is no righteousness in deeds after it. This is the view most agreeable to the occasion of revelation, especially according to the narration that Salman, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ) the good state of the monks with whom he had kept company, and he said: "They died while they were in the Fire." So Allah revealed this verse, and the Prophet (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him, said: "Whoever died upon the religion of Jesus, peace be upon him, before he heard of me, he is upon good; and whoever heard and did not believe in me has perished."

What is suitable to the generality of the wording, and not restricting it to the specification of ﴿those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Christians﴾ to the disbelievers among them, [p. 280] and the specification of ﴿whoever believes﴾ etc. to entering into the religion of Islam, is that this entails that the Sabians have a religion, and many have stated that they have no religion whose observance is permissible at any time. In "al-Milal wa al-Nihal" it is stated that "sabwa" stands in opposition to "hanifiyya," and because of these people's deviation from the paths of truth and their swerving from the way of the prophets, they were called "Sabians." Even if it is granted that they had a heavenly religion, and then departed from it, those who passed away from the people of that religion before their departure from it are not among the Sabians. How, then, is it possible to refer the connecting pronoun between the subject of "inna" and its predicate back to them, according to the well-known view, or to undertake to refer it to the whole collectively, intending thereby to include the group mentioned among them, since whoever was among the People of the Book acting in accordance with his law before its abrogation is among the whole of those groups by virtue of including Jews and Christians, even if he is not among the Sabians, which is something the sanctity of revelation must be cleared of! Moreover, there is after this what is not hidden, so reflect.

"Man" (whoever) is a subject (mubtada'), and they have allowed that it be a relative (mawsula), with the predicate being the sentence of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿then for them is their reward with their Lord﴾, and the fa' has entered to imbue the subject with the meaning of a condition, as in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Indeed, those who afflicted﴾ etc. And that it be a conditional (shartiyya), and there is disagreement regarding its predicate: is it the condition, or the response, or both? And the sentence ﴿whoever believes﴾ etc. is the predicate of "inna"? If "man" is a relative, which is the most common here, it is necessary to posit a returning pronoun "minhum" (from among them). If it is conditional, there is no need to posit it, since the generality suffices for it, as if it were said: "These and others, if they believe, then for them etc.," as they said regarding His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, We do not waste the reward of one who does good in deed﴾. Some allowed that "man" be a substitute (badal) for the subject of "inna," and its predicate is ﴿then for them is their reward﴾. Abu Hayyan preferred that it be a substitute for the conjoined items that follow the subject of "inna," so the meaning is sound in that case, and as if it were said: "Indeed those who believe, from other than the three categories, and whoever among the three categories believes, then for them etc." The three pronouns have been construed according to the sense of the relative, just as the singular form of what is in the relative clause is according to its wording. In al-Bahr: these two constructions are not complete except by taking "man" as a subject; but as for its being a substitute, there is only construction according to the wording alone. So understand.

Then, what is meant by "reward" (ajr) is the recompense that they were promised for faith and righteous deeds. Its attribution to them and its being specific to them is merely by the promise, not by entitlement as al-Zamakhshari claimed out of regard for the Mu'tazila. Yet calling it "reward" (ajr) is due to its not failing. This is supported by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿with their Lord﴾, which indicates that it will not be lost, because He is with One who is Gentle and Watchful. It is connected to what is connected to "for them," and it may be a circumstantial phrase (hal) of "their reward."

﴿And no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾: it is conjoined to the sentence ﴿then for them is their reward﴾. The discussion of its like has already passed at the end of the story of Adam, peace be upon him, so it suffices here without repetition.

[p. 281]

﴿And when We took your covenant﴾: a reminder of another blessing, since He, glory be to Him, did that only for their benefit. The apparent meaning of *mithaq* (covenant) here is *'ahd* (pledge). He did not say *mawathiqakum* (covenants), because what was taken from each one of them was taken from the others as well, so it was one covenant. It was probably a covenant to submit to Musa, peace be upon him. Scholars differed about when it was made. It was said: before the lifting of the *Tur* (Mount), and then, when they broke it, it was raised above them, based on the apparent meaning of His, exalted be He, words: ﴿And We raised the Tur above them for their covenant﴾, and so on. It was also said: it was along with ﴿And We raised the Tur above you﴾, where the *wa* (and) is for coordination, and it was also said that it is for the circumstantial (*hal*). *Tur* was said to be a mountain among mountains, and it is Syriac, Arabicized (*mu'arrab*). It was also said: it refers to a specific mountain. Abu Hatim related from Ibn Abbas that when Musa, peace be upon him, brought them the Torah, and the heavy obligations it contained weighed upon them, they refused to accept it. So He commanded Jibril to uproot the Tur and it hovered over them until they accepted. It was the size of their army, a farsakh by a farsakh, and it was raised above them to the height of a man. This raises a difficulty: that this amounts to a kind of compulsion (*ilja'*) to faith, which contradicts legal obligation (*taklif*).
[p. 281 continues]
The Imam answered that there is no compulsion here, because the most that is involved is fear of it falling on them. When it remained in its place for a period, and they had seen the heavens raised without pillars, it was permissible for the fear to leave them, so the compulsion ceases and the obligation remains. The 'Allamah said: it seems that after this compulsion they reached a voluntary acceptance, or such faith was sufficient for the earlier nations. In this, as al-Salikuti said, the question is how obligation can be valid with ﴿Take﴾ and so on, together with coercion, when it has been established that its basis is choice. The truth is that it is coercion, because it is compelling another to do what he does not like and would not choose if left to himself. It thus eliminates contentment, not choice, since the act proceeds from his choice, as explained in the principles of jurisprudence. This is like fighting the unbelievers. As for His words ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, and His, glory be to Him, words ﴿Will you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾, these came before the command to fight, and then were abrogated (*nusikha*) by it.

﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾: this is with an elided verb (*idmar al-qawl*), meaning: We said, or saying, ﴿Take﴾. Some of the Kufans said it does not need an elided verb, because taking a covenant is itself a statement, and the meaning is: ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾ that you would take what We have given you. This is not correct.

The meaning of *quwwah* (strength) here is diligence and effort, as Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. It amounts to not being lax or negligent. Accordingly, the verse cannot serve as evidence for those who claim that capacity (*istita'ah*) precedes the act, since one does not say "take this with strength" unless the strength is already present in the one addressed. For strength in this sense, the precedence of its being prior to the act is not denied.

﴿And remember what is in it﴾: that is, study it and memorize it, and do not forget it, or contemplate its meaning, or act upon the rulings it contains. *Dhikr* (remembrance) may mean verbal remembrance, mental remembrance, the more general of the two, or what is necessarily connected with them, and the intended purpose of them, namely acting.

﴿So that you may be righteous﴾: the discussion of *la'alla* (so that, perhaps) in the speech of God, exalted be He, has already been treated. It has been mentioned here that the word *la'alla* relates to ﴿Take﴾ and ﴿remember﴾. It is either a metaphor, whose meaning after the figure of speech is interpreted as explaining the cause by its result, or a literal use expressing the hope of the addressee. The meaning is: take and remember, hoping that you will become righteous. The metaphorical meaning is favored because there is no sense in their hoping for what is hard for them, namely righteousness, except with the qualification that they had heard of the virtues and ranks of the righteous, and therefore they hoped to be enrolled among them.

The Mu'tazilites permitted that it relates to the implied *qulna* (We said), and interpreted the hope as intention: We said, remember, intending that you be righteous. This is built on their corrupt principle that God's intention regarding the acts of servants does not necessitate their occurrence, since it is merely an expression of knowledge of the benefit. The 'Allamah permitted that it relates to ﴿Take﴾ as well, if *tarajji* (hope) is interpreted as intention, as a qualifier of the command, not of the thing commanded. Shihab permitted that it relates to the statement, interpreting it as a demand, and the separation in this is permissible. But there is an objection: the statement mentioned, namely ﴿Take what We have given you﴾, itself is a demand for righteousness, so it cannot be said "take what We have given you, demanding from you righteousness" except with some kind of artificiality. Understand this.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 64:**

﴿Then you turned away after that⦆ i.e., you turned away from fulfilling the covenant after it had been taken, and you opposed it. The original sense of *tawalli* (turning away) is physical aversion; it was then used for figurative aversion, such as non-acceptance. The verse implies that they complied with the command and then abandoned it.

﴿Had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers﴾. The *fadl* (grace) is the success granted to repentance, and the *rahmah* (mercy) is its acceptance; or else the grace and mercy is the sending of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and your reaching his time. On the first interpretation, the address follows the pattern of earlier addresses figuratively, by reference to their forefathers; on the second, it is literal. *Khusran* (loss) is the loss of capital or its diminution, and the meaning is: you would have been defrauded and ruined through immersion in sins, or through stumbling into the abysses of misguidance during the interval (*fatrah*). The word *lawla* (had it not been) is either simple or compounded from *law* (the particle of counterfactual condition) and the negative particle. Its discussion has already been mentioned. The noun that follows it, according to Sibawayh, is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is obligatorily omitted because the context indicates it, and the answer (*jawab*) takes its place. The estimate is: "Had it not been that the grace of Allah and His mercy exist." The answer cannot be the predicate, because it is mostly devoid of a pronoun referring back to the subject. According to the Kufans, it is the agent (*fa'il*) of an omitted verb, i.e., "Had the grace of Allah ... been established," and *lakuntum* is the answer of *lawla*. The entry of the lam upon the answer is frequent when it is affirmative. It is said that it is obligatory except in poetic necessity, as in his saying:

"Had it not been for modesty and religion, I would have reproached you both for some of what is in you, since you reproached me for my faults."

It has also come in their speech after the lam the particle *qad*, as in his saying:

"Had it not been for the Amir and fear of his obedience, I would have drunk, and nothing is sweeter than honey."

The omission of the lam while retaining *qad* has also occurred, as in: *lawla Zaydun qad akramtuka* ("Had it not been for Zayd, I would have honored you"). It has not come in the Qur'an in affirmative form except with the lam, except that some claimed that His saying ﴿and she desired him﴾ is the answer of *lawla*, placed before it. This is it.

* * *

Among the mystical and allegorical (*ishara wa ta'wil*) readings of the verse: ﴿And when We took your covenant﴾, the covenant taken by the proofs of reason, through the unity of acts and attributes; ﴿and We raised over you the mount﴾, the mount of the brain, for the capacity to understand meanings and accept them. Or Glory be to Him indicated by the mount the Moses of the heart, and by its raising its exaltation and dominance in the atmosphere of guidance. ﴿And We said: Take﴾, i.e., accept, ﴿what We have given you﴾, the Book of the discerning intellect, with earnestness, and retain what it contains of wisdoms, knowledge, sciences and laws, ﴿that you may be mindful﴾ of polytheism, ignorance and wickedness. Then you turned away after that, with your attention directed toward the lower direction. ﴿Had it not been for the wisdom of Allah, the Exalted, in granting respite, and His judgment with bounty, the punishment would have hastened upon you, and the great calamity would have descended upon you.

To Allah is one invited by proofs who refuses; if he does not respond, the white swords will strike him down.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 65:**

﴿And you have certainly known those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath.﴾ The lam (اللّامُ, the emphatic lam) falls in the answer to a hidden oath (qasam muqaddar). Here ʿalima (عَلِمَ) has the sense of ʿarafa (عَرَفَ, "to know/recognize"), which is why it takes one object. The apparent meaning is that they knew the very persons who transgressed. Some scholars posited an omitted noun (muḍāf), meaning "the transgression of those who..." and others said "their rulings." ﴿among you﴾ (مِنكُمْ) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). As-sabt (السَّبْتُ) is the name of the well-known day. It is derived from as-sabt (السَّبْتُ), meaning "cutting off," because on it the creation of everything and its work were cut off. It was also said to derive from as-subut (السُّبُوتُ), meaning rest and tranquility, and the intended meaning here is the day itself. The statement is then elliptical, meaning "in the ruling of the Sabbath," because transgression did not occur on the day itself but in its ruling. This is based on what is related: Musa (عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ) wanted to make a day exclusively for worship, which was Friday, but they opposed him and said, "We will make it the Sabbath day, because Allah Most High created nothing in it." Allah Most High revealed to him, "Leave them with what they have chosen." Then He tested them with it: He commanded them to abstain from work and forbade them the hunting of fish on it. When the time of Dawud (عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ) came, they transgressed. They lived in a town on the coast called Ayla. On the Sabbath no fish would remain in the sea without being stopped there, and it would put forth its snout. When it passed, the fish dispersed. So they dug pools and ran channels to them, and fish would enter them on the Sabbath with the waves, but they could not leave because of the depth and the scarcity of water. They would then catch them on Sunday. It is related that they did this for a time and no punishment descended upon them, so they rejoiced and said, "Work on the Sabbath has now been made lawful for us." So they fished openly on it and sold in the markets. In accordance with this, it is valid to take the day as a time-frame (ẓarf) for the transgression, and no omitted noun is needed. It was also said that as-sabt here means the verbal noun of sabbatat al-Yahud (سَبَتَتِ اليَهُودُ), when the Jews magnified the Sabbath day. It does not mean the day itself, so there is no need for an omitted noun, since the meaning reverts to their transgressing in the magnification, violating the sanctity that was obligatory upon them. Some have mentioned that the Arabs' naming of the days by these well-known names came about after ʿIsa (عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ), and that their earlier names were other than these, as in the verse:

*"I hope that I will live, and that my day will be with the first, or with the easiest, or with Jubar,*
*or the following Dubar; if I miss it, then Munis,*
*or ʿArubah, or Shibar."*

It has been cited as evidence from this verse for prohibiting stratagems (ḥiyal, ḥiyal, "legal devices") in matters that were not legislated, such as riba (usury). Imam Malik went this way, so such stratagems are not permitted in his view under any circumstances. Al-Kawashi said: most scholars permitted them as long as they do not involve nullifying a right or validating falsehood. They answered the use of this verse as evidence by saying that it is not a stratagem but is the very thing prohibited, because they were forbidden only from taking it. The weakness of this answer is not hidden, and its verification is in the books of jurisprudence.

﴿So We said to them, "Be apes, despised."﴾ Qiradah (القِرَدَةُ) is the plural of qird (قِرْدٌ), which is well known. The noun may be pluralized on the pattern fiʿl (فِعْلٌ) by analogy with fuʿūl (فُعُولٌ), and rarely on the pattern fiʿalah (فِعَلَةٌ). Al-khusu' (الخُسُوُّ) means lowliness and abasement, and it may be transitive or intransitive. From it comes the saying said to a dog: akhsa' (أخْسَأْ, "begone"). It was also said that khusu' (خُسُوءٌ) and khasʾ (خَسْأٌ) are the verbal nouns of khasa'a al-kalb (خَسَأ الكَلْبُ), meaning the dog went far away. Some have mentioned expulsion (aṭ-ṭard) when explaining khusu', as in "distancing." It was said that this is for completing its meaning, not for explaining what is intended; otherwise khāsi' (خاسِئ) would mean "one who expels." The verified view is that it is considered part of the concept, but in the passive sense, and likewise distancing. So khāsi' (خاسِئ) means the abased, distanced, expelled one. The apparent sense of the Qur'an is that they were literally transformed into apes, and this is the view of the majority of exegetes and is the correct one. Many of them mentioned that after they were transformed they did not eat, did not drink, did not procreate, and did not live more than three days. Muqatil claimed that they lived seven days and died on the eighth day. Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi chose that they did live, and that the apes existing today are their offspring. This is refuted by what Muslim transmitted from Ibn Masʿud (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to one who asked him about apes and swine, "Are they from those who were transformed?" He said: "Allah Most High does not destroy a people, or punish a people, and then give them offspring; and apes and swine existed before that." Ibn Jarir related from Mujahid that their forms were not transformed, but their hearts were, so they accept no admonition and heed no reproof. In that case the intent of the verse is to liken them to apes, as in the verse:

*"If you have not loved, and do not know what passion is,*
*then be a stone, a hard, dry, smooth rock."*

As for ﴿Be﴾ (وكُونُوا) on the first interpretation, it is not a command in reality, because their turning into what was mentioned involves no acquisition (taksib) on their part, for they were not able to change their own essences. Rather, what is meant is the swiftness of the creating, and that they became such, just as He willed, without hesitation or delay.

On the second interpretation, the command is figurative for leaving (taklyah), abandoning (tark), and forsaking (khidhlan), as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do what you wish." The ʿAllamah has established this in his commentary on the verse: ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them and enjoy themselves﴾ (لِيَكْفُرُوا بِما آتَيْناهم ولِيَتَمَتَّعُوا). The two accusative words are predicates of the defective verb (al-fiʿl an-nāqis), and it is permissible that khāsiʾīn (خاسِئِينَ) be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the subject. It is also permissible that it be an adjective (ṣifah) of qiradah (قِرَدَةً). The intent is to describe them with abasement in the sight of Allah Most High, to forestall the supposition that their transformation and the hastening of their punishment in this world were for the expiation of their sins and the raising of their ranks.

It was objected that if it were an adjective of it, it would have to say khāsiʾah (خاسِئَةً), because the plural with the wāw and nūn is impossible for non-rational beings. It was answered that this is by treating them as rational beings, as in sājidīn (ساجِدِينَ), or by considering that they were rational before, or that the transformation was only a change of form, while their reality remained intact. This is in accordance with what is related: a man among them would be approached by a relative who had forbidden them, and he would say, "Did I not forbid you?" He would say, "Yes," and then tears would stream down his cheek. The verse does not mention that any of them were transformed into swine. It is related from Qatadah that the young among them became apes and the elders became swine, and that none were saved except those who had forbidden, while the rest perished. It was also read as qaridah (قَرِدَةً) with a fatḥah on the qāf and a kasrah on the rāʾ, and khāsīn (خاسِينَ) without a hamzah.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 66:**

﴿فَجَعَلْناها نَكالا﴾ means: We made it (*kaynūnatahum*, their being) and (*ṣayrūratahum*, their becoming) apes, or the transformation (*al-maskha*), or the punishment (*al-'uqūba*), or the sign (*al-āya*) indicated by His words, ﴿And you already knew﴾. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the town (*al-qarya*), and it was said that it refers to the fish (*al-ḥītān*). *Nakāl* is the singular of *ankāl*, which are shackles (*al-quyūd*). *Nakkala bihi* means he did to him what makes others take warning from it, so that they refrain from the like of it. ﴿For what was before it and what was after it﴾ means for their contemporaries and for those who came after them. This is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and others. It is also related from him (the reading) *li-mā* (for what) with *bi-ḥaḍratihā* (in its presence), meaning the towns near it, that is, their people, and what was far from it. Or (it means) for those who come later and those who have passed, and this is the preferred view of a group of scholars. Each of the two spatial adverbs is then used figuratively for time. The word *mā* was used in place of *man* (who), either to belittle them in a position of greatness and majesty, or because of consideration of the attribute, since *mā* is used for rational beings to exalt them when the attribute is intended, as in His saying: "Glory be to what subjected you." It is sound that it was a punishment (*nakāl*) for those who had passed, because it was mentioned in the scriptures of the ancients, and so they took warning from it. The particle *fa* (so) is also sound, because making that a punishment for both groups occurs only after the saying and the transformation. Or, because the *fa* only indicates the sequence of making the punishment a deterrent following the saying, and its being caused by it, whether it was upon themselves or upon the report of it. Thus it does not preclude the occurrence of taking warning before this event, through hearing this story. It was also said: the *lām* is the *lām* of purpose (*lām al-ajal*), *mā* is on its literal meaning, and *nakāl* means punishment, not lesson. What is meant by "what was before it" is all the other sins committed before catching the fish, and "what was after it" is what came after. The view that what is meant is: We made the transformation a punishment on account of their sins that preceded the transformation and those that followed it, requires that they remained responsible (*mukallafīn*) after the transformation. This does not hold except on the view of Mujahid. Interpreting the sins that came after the transformation as the lingering effects of evil deeds is not valid, as is clear. And the statement of Abu al-'Aliyah: that what is meant by "what was before it" is the sins that had passed, and "what was after it" is those who would come later, and the meaning is: We made it a punishment for the sins they had committed in the past and a lesson for those after them, is a very weak view, because of the great dislocation of the composition and the artificiality it involves. ﴿And an exhortation for the God-fearing﴾. *Al-mawʿiẓa* (exhortation) is what is mentioned that softens the heart, whether it is reward or punishment. What is meant by "the God-fearing" is everyone who is God-fearing from every nation. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It was also said: from the nation of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. And it was said: from among them. It is possible that they took heed from it and feared committing what they had been commanded against. It is also possible that some of them admonished one another with this event. The portion of the knower from this story is to know that Allah, glorified and exalted, created people for His worship, and made them such that if they were neglected, left, and let be according to their own natures, they would go to extremes and plunge into bodily pleasures and dark veils, because of their needs for them and their habituation to them from childhood.

*The soul is like a child: if you neglect it, it grows up loving the breast; and if you wean it, it will be weaned.*

So Allah, exalted, instituted acts of worship and made their repetition obligatory at specified times, so that through them the rust of nature accumulated during times of heedlessness would be removed, along with the darkness of the preoccupations that arise in times of committing desires. He also made one day of the week specifically for gathering for worship, removing the loneliness of division and repelling the darkness of preoccupation with worldly affairs. Thus He set Saturday for the Jews, because the sensory world to which the Jews call is the last of the worlds, and Saturday is the last of the week. Sunday is for the Christians, because the intellectual world to which they call is the first of the worlds, and Sunday is the first of the week. Friday is for the Muslims, because it is the day of gathering and sealing, so it is most suitable for them and best fitting to their condition. Whoever does not observe these arrangements and watchfulness at all, the light of his readiness vanishes, the lamp of his heart is extinguished, and he is transformed just as the people of the Sabbath were transformed. And whoever is overcome by an attribute of the animals and takes root in it, to the point that it removes his readiness and becomes firmly established in his nature, and becomes his essential form, is like water whose source is a sulphur mine, for example, which is named after that animal, until its nature becomes its nature and its soul becomes its soul. Therefore, let a person strive to preserve his humanity and manage his health with the drinks of the legal remedies and the wise electuaries, and let him urge his soul with the exhortations of promise and threat.

*It is the soul: if it is neglected, it clings to baseness; and if it is roused toward virtues, it longs for them.*

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 67:

﴿And when Moses said to his people: "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow"﴾. This is a statement of a kind of their bad conduct, without enumerating the blessings. The conjunction (ʿatf) is correct, because the mention of blessings earlier also included mention of their bad conduct, such as their opposition to the prophets, their denial of them, and other things. It may also be said that it follows the same pattern as what came before, because the slaughter was a worldly blessing, in that it ended the quarrel between the two parties, and an otherworldly blessing, in that it was a miracle for Moses, peace be upon him. Our master, the Imam al-Razi, seems to have overlooked this, and said: "When He, exalted is He, first enumerated the aspects of His favour upon them, He concluded that by explaining some of the hardships that were imposed upon them, and He made the second type what this verse points to." This is not far-fetched. The beginning of the story is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed about it﴾, and so on. The apparent wording would have been: Moses said, "When a slain man is found and there is dispute over his killer, Allah commands the slaughter of a cow of such and such description, and that some part of it be struck against that slain man, and he will inform of his killer, and so it will be such and such." However, some of it was separated and placed first, because it independently contains a kind of their bad conduct which He intended to censure them for, namely mockery of the command, excessive questioning, and abandoning argument in favour of compliance. Had it been arranged in the usual order, it would have been one single story, and the double rebuke would have been lost. In the arrangement there occurs a separation of construction and order similar to what occurs in some stories, and it is an acceptable inversion (maqlub), because it contains subtle points and benefits. It has been said that it is possible that the order in which these were revealed to Moses, peace be upon him, corresponds to their recitation: Allah commands them to slaughter the cow, then the killing occurs, and then they are commanded to strike some of it. But the well-known view is otherwise. The story is that some brothers from the Children of Israel plotted against a cousin of theirs, the son of their father's brother, and killed him in order to inherit his wealth, and they threw him at the gate of their quarter. Then they came seeking his blood. So Allah commanded the slaughter of a cow and that he be struck with some of it, so that he would come to life and inform of his killer. It has also been said that the killer was the brother of the slain man, and it has been said that he was his nephew, with no heir other than him; when his life was prolonged he killed him in order to inherit from him. It has also been said that he was married to a man called Ameel, a cousin who had no equal among the Children of Israel in beauty and loveliness, and a close relative of his killed him in order to marry her, and so what happened, happened. The majority read ﴿yaʾmurukum﴾ with a ḍammah on the rāʾ. From Abu ʿAmr, there is sukūn (silent vowelling), al-ikhtilās (a rapid, truncated vowel), and the replacing of the hamzah with an alif. ﴿An tadhbaḥū﴾ is in the position of the second object of ya'mur, and it is by the omission of the preposition, i.e., "to slaughter". ﴿They said: "Do you take us for a laughing-stock?"﴾ This is a resumptive statement (istiʾnaf) that came as an answer to what the discourse leads to, as if it were said: "What did they do? Did they hasten to comply or not?" So they were answered with this. The verb ittakhadha, like ṣayyara and ja'ala, takes two objects, whose original elements are the subject and predicate. ﴿Huzuwan﴾ is its second object. Because it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), it cannot be a second object, since it is in reality the predicate of the subject, and here it denotes a substance. So a noun is supposed to be understood, such as "place" or "people", or it is taken in the sense of "the one mocked", as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾, i.e., what is hunted. Or the substance is made the very meaning, for intensification, as in "a just man". They said this either after Moses, peace be upon him, commanded them to slaughter a cow without mentioning striking it to bring back the dead, or after he commanded them and mentioned to them the striking, considering what he said far-fetched and treating it lightly, as the interrogative indicates, since the meaning is: "Are you mocking us? For your answer does not match our question, and is not fitting. How is what we are in related to what you are commanding?" Their compliance does not contradict this, because after knowing that it was a firm and binding resolution. From here some said: their answer to their prophet, when he informed them of Allah's command that they slaughter a cow, with this response, is evidence of their bad opinion of their prophet and their denial of him, for had they known that this was a true report from Allah, exalted is He, they would not have asked this question, nor would they have answered in this way. Thus they disbelieved in Moses, peace be upon him. Some people have said: they were believers who affirmed him, but this happened in accordance with their coarseness of nature, harshness, and disobedience. The excuse for them is that when they asked Moses, peace be upon him, to specify the killer, he said what he said, and they saw what lay between the question and the answer, and they imagined that he, peace be upon him, was joking with them, or they thought that this was in the manner of mockery, so they answered as they answered. It has also been said that they asked by way of seeking guidance, not in a manner of denial and obstinacy. ʿĀṣim and Ibn Muḥaysin read ﴿yattakhidhunā﴾ with a yāʾ, on the basis that the pronoun refers to Allah, exalted is He. Ḥamzah and Ismaʿil, from Nafiʿ, read ﴿huzʾan﴾ with sukūn. Ḥafṣ, from ʿĀṣim, reads it with ḍammah, and changes the hamzah to a wāw. The rest read it with ḍammah and hamzah. All of these are dialectal forms of the word.

﴿He said: "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾ That is, from being counted among them. Ignorance, as al-Raghib said, has several meanings: the absence of knowledge; believing a thing to be other than what it is; and doing a thing contrary to what it should be done, whether one holds a correct or corrupt belief about it. This last is the meaning intended here. He, peace be upon him, negated it of himself, aiming to negate its necessary implication with which he was charged, namely mockery, by way of metonymy (kināya). This was expressed in the form of a metaphor (istiʿāra), to express its enormity, since mockery in a context of guidance nearly amounts to disbelief or something similar. Its occurrence in a context of contempt and ridicule, like His saying: ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾, is permissible and common, and there is a difference between the two contexts. Some have mentioned that seeking refuge in Allah from this is a matter of good manners and humility toward Him, exalted is He, as in His saying: ﴿And say: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the whisperings of the devils."﴾ For the prophets are protected from the like of this. But the first view is preferable, and it is the familiar practice in placing seeking refuge in the midst of speech. The difference between mockery and jesting is clear, so it does not preclude its occurrence from the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them, at times, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 68:

﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is."﴾ That is: ask your Lord on our behalf, the One who has accustomed you to what He has accustomed you to, that He may show us its condition and its description. In reality the question is about the attribute, because the quiddity (*mahiyyah*) and the referent of the name are both known, and there is no third thing between them, so that the question is about what is to be used with it. As for when a specific cow is intended, the matter is obvious, because it is a request for explanation (*istifsar*) to clarify what is general (*mujmal*). Otherwise, the question is due to astonishment, and it was supposed that such a cow could only be a specific one. The answer to the first is clarification (*bayan*), and to the second is abrogation (*naskh*) and tightening. The same applies to the questions and answers that follow.

The apparent meaning on the first view, that is, because the question is about what distinguishes the thing, whether by attribute or by essence, would require... And on the second view, how? Because the interrogative *kayfa* ("how") is designed to ask about the state. And *ma* ("what"), although it may be used to ask about the attribute, does so only rarely. This usage is either metaphorical (*majaz*) or homonymous (*ishtirak*), as stated explicitly in *al-Miftah* (of al-Sakkaki). The usual use of *ma* is to ask about the genus. If it is applied here according to the usual usage, then the unknown attribute is treated as the unknown reality, since its genus was not found in that form, namely the revival of the dead by striking part of it. So it becomes a question about the genus by figurative treatment (*tanzil*), and about the attribute in reality. If it is applied to the rare usage, then the said figurative treatment is not needed. As for the view that *ma hiya* ("what is it") can be read with an elided genitive (*mudaf*) understood, meaning "what is its condition," so that it is a question about a kind of state from which this distinctive property arises, even though this is far-fetched and lacks the refinement appropriate to the dignity of the Noble Book, and that *ma* is an interrogative which is the predicate preceding *hiya* (the subject), and the clause is in the place of the accusative after *yubayyin* ("He will make clear"), because it is suspended from it (*mu'allaq 'anha*). This was permitted because the verb resembles verbs of the heart. The meaning is: ﴿He will make clear to us﴾ the answer to this question.

﴿He said: "He says it is a cow, neither old nor virgin."﴾ *Al-fariḍ* is a name for the aged female whose bearing has ceased due to old age. The verb is *faradat*, with the *ra* vowelled either with fatha or with damma. It is said of anything that has grown old and whose matter has lengthened that it is *fariḍ*. From this is the saying of the poet:

"O many a one who bears a grudge against me, aged, for whom are menstrual cycles like the cycles of a menstruating woman."

It seems that the aged cow was called *fariḍ* because she has "fardha" her teeth, i.e., cut them and reached their end. *Al-bikr* is a name for the young one. Some have added: the one that has not given birth since youth. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is the one that has given birth to one offspring. *Al-bikr* among women is the one who has not been touched by men. It was also said: it is the one that has not conceived. *Al-bikr* among offspring is the first, and among needs the first ones. *Al-bakr* with a fatha on the *ba'* is the young camel, and its female is *bakrah*. Its origin is from precedence in time, and from it come *al-bakrah* and *al-bakurah*. The two words are adjectives of *baqarah* (cow), and the feminine ta' was not added because both are names for what has been mentioned. The particle *la* ("neither") is placed between the adjective and the qualified noun, and it is repeated because it must be repeated with the predicate, the qualifier and the circumstantial clause, except in cases of necessity, contrary to al-Mubarrad and Ibn Kaysan, as in the poet's saying:

"I have overcome my enemies, not by means of a band of supporters, but by various kinds of deceit and trickery."

As for one who made this a description by clauses, positing an implied subject, that is "neither she is old nor virgin," he has gone too far, since the original is description by a single word, and the original also is that nothing is elided. He mentioned *yaqulu* ("he says") to indicate that it is from God Most High and not from his own self.

﴿Between that: middle-aged﴾. That is, of middle age. It was also said: she is the one who has given birth to one or two litters, or it was said: once after another. It is pluralized on the pattern *fu'al*, as in the poet's saying:

"Tall, like the necks of the Hawadi (camels), delicate, between virgins and mature ones."

It is permitted to vowel the middle radical of the word with damma in poetry. The benefit of this, after "neither old nor virgin," is to negate that she should be a calf or a foetus. He intended by "that" the two attributes mentioned previously, and with this the singular is correct, as is the prepositional phrase *bayna* ("between") being attached to it, since *bayna* is not attached except to something plural. The sentence may have omitted a coordinated term, the meaning being indicated, and the sense being: "middle-aged between that and this," that is, between the old and the virgin. This would be like the poet's saying:

"Had Abu Hajar come back safe, he would not have been between the good and its doer except for a few nights." Here he meant "between the good and its doer," which is a strained reading that is unnecessary given what has been mentioned.

Al-Sajawandi preferred that what is meant is the middle of the period of suitability of the middle-aged cow and its moderation. You say: "I travelled to Rome and journeyed between that," so the indicated thing is *'awan*. Some verifiers (*muhaqqiqin*) endorsed this, claiming that it is more appropriate, lest the meaning of *bayna dhalika* be lost, because the people of the language said: "a cow that is middle-aged, neither old nor virgin." On the common view, the matter may perhaps need abstraction, as is not hidden.

Then, the return of the pronouns mentioned in the question and answer, and the application of those attributes to "a cow," indicates that what is meant by it is a specific one. This is because the first indicates that the discussion is about the cow commanded to be slaughtered, and the second indicates that the aim is to specify it and to remove its ambiguity through those attributes, as is the nature of the attribute, and not that they are different obligations. This is unlike the case where those attributes are mentioned without the application (of the pronouns). It was said: "neither old nor virgin" might intend the change of the previous ruling.
