The claim that when they were astonished at a dead cow with which a dead person would be struck so that he would live, they took it to be a specific one that is outside what the genus is upon, so they asked about its condition and description, and the pronouns came to refer to a specific one by their belief, so it was specified as a tightening upon them, even if what was meant by it at the beginning was not specific, is nothing, because in that case the pronouns would not have referred to what they were commanded to slaughter, but to what they believed. The apparent meaning is contrary to this, and the necessary consequence on this view is the delay of clarification beyond the time of address. This is not impossible; what is impossible is delaying it beyond the time of need, except according to those who permit the obligation of the impossible. And this is not necessary, since there is no proof that the command here is for immediacy, so that this could be imagined. Some people denied this and claimed that what is meant by it is a cow of the species of cows, without specification, and compliance would have been achieved if they had slaughtered any cow whatsoever, except that it became particularized by their question. This was the view of a group of exegetes, and they held to the apparent wording, since it is unrestricted, so it is left on its generality, along with what Ibn Jarir reported with a sound chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, as a statement of his own (*mawquf*): "If they had slaughtered any cow they wished, it would have sufficed them, but they tightened upon themselves, so Allah Most High tightened upon them." Sa'id ibn Mansur reported it in his *Sunan* from 'Ikrimah as a raised (*marfu'*) hadith, *mursal* (with a missing companion). And (the argument) that if it had been specific, He would not have rebuked them for persisting, nor forbidden them from returning to questioning. The necessary consequence then is abrogation before the act, based on the view of those who say that adding to the Book is abrogation, like the majority of the Hanafis, who hold that an unrestricted command implies choice (*takhyir*), and this is a legal ruling, and restriction removes it. This is permissible, indeed it has occurred, as in the hadith of the obligation of prayer on the night of the Ascension (*mi'raj*). Abrogation before the possibility of belief is impossible by consensus, because it would be a change of mind (*bada'*). Abrogation before the possibility of action is impossible according to the Mu'tazilah. It is not necessary, as has been said. Moreover, it has been said: it is possible to argue that this is not abrogation, because the unrestricted cow includes the specific cow, and slaughtering a specific cow is slaughtering a cow in general, so it is compliance with the first command, and therefore it is not abrogation.

It has been objected to the claim that choice is a legal ruling, etc., by denying it, on the basis that the unrestricted command only indicates the obligation of a quiddity as such without condition. However, when it is not realized except in a specific instance, choice comes by reason, without the text indicating it. The obligation of a thing does not entail the obligation of its rational prerequisite, since by obligation is meant the legal obligation. It is permissible that the responsible person be punished for leaving what a rational prerequisite includes, and not be punished for leaving the prerequisite. This objection is attributed to our master al-Qadi in his *Manhiyyat*, but there is room for reflection. Some verifiers mentioned that the realization of this matter is: if what is meant by the cow commanded to be slaughtered is the cow in general, whichever cow it was, then abrogation is permissible, because the condition of abrogation is the possibility of belief, and this is clearly present. If, however, it is a specific cow, then abrogation is not permissible, because the possibility of belief does not exist at that time, since it only came about after the questioning. So the disagreement of the scholars over the permissibility of abrogation and its absence in this matter is a verbal dispute. So reflect.

﴿So do what you are commanded﴾, that is, of slaughtering the cow, and do not repeat the question, and do not be obstinate. This sentence may be from God Most High's words to them, and it may be from the words of Musa, upon him be peace, urging them to comply with what they were commanded, out of compassion for them. *Ma* is a relative pronoun, and the returning pronoun is elided, that is, *ma tu'marunahu*, meaning *ma tu'marun bihi* ("what you are commanded with"). The elision of the preposition with this verb has become widespread, to the extent that it has joined the verbs that take two objects. Thus the elided element is initially the accusative. Some permitted that *ma* be a verbal-noun (*masdariyyah*), meaning: "do your command," and the verbal noun would then be in the sense of the object, as in His saying: ﴿Allah created you and what you do﴾, according to one of the two interpretations. This is far-fetched, because that occurs rarely in the sense of a product of the (verbal) construction, and it only became frequent in the form of the verbal noun.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 2, verse 69:

﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what its color is." He said, "Indeed, He says it is a yellow cow, bright in its yellowness, pleasing to the beholders."﴾ Attributing the clarification each time to God, Exalted and Majestic, shows the complete assistance in answering their request. The use of the present tense (*al-istiqbal*) is to bring the scene vividly before the mind. *Al-fuqu'* is the most intense and most forceful degree of yellowness, and describing the color with it serves as emphasis (*ta'kid*), as in *amsi al-dabir* ("yesterday, which has passed"). The same applies to their expressions *abyad nasi'* ("pure white"), *aswad halik* ("intensely black"), *ahmar qani* ("deep red"), and *akhdar nadir* ("lush green"). "Its color" (*lawnuha*) is in the nominative, governed by *faqi'* ("bright"). He did not settle for saying *safra'u faqi'a* ("yellow, bright"), because he intended to emphasize the attribution of yellowness. He first judged the cow to be yellow, then judged the color itself to be extremely yellow. He began by describing the cow as yellow, then confirmed this by describing its color as such, as if he had said: "It is yellow, and its color is intensely yellow." It is reported from al-Hasan that it means "intensely black" (*sawda'u shadidat al-sawad*). This is clearly contrary to the apparent meaning, because although the Arabs have used *al-safra'* (yellow) in this sense rarely, just as they applied *al-aswad* (black) to green, they used it only for camels, as is said regarding God's words ﴿yellow camels﴾ (77:33), since the blackness of camels is tinged with yellowness. Emphasizing it with *al-fuqu'* contradicts this, because in the well-known usage *al-fuqu'* is a description of yellowness. However, *al-Lumac* mentions that one says *asfar faqi'* ("bright yellow") and *ahmar faqi'* ("bright red"), and that for all colors one says *faqi'* and *nasi'* when they are pure. In light of this, what was mentioned does not refute the claim. Some people said that yellowness is here used metaphorically (*musta'ara*) for blackness, and likewise *faqi'* means "intensely black," which is a supporting metaphor (*tarshih*, a metaphorical element that sustains the main image), and its blackness is taken to refer to its shine and luster. But this is not correct. Some have permitted that *lawnuha* be the subject (*mubtada'*), with its predicate being either *faqi'* or the clause following it. The feminine form is then on one of two grounds: first, because it is attached to a feminine noun, as in the saying "some of his fingers went away." Second, because what is meant is the feminine, namely the yellowness, as if he said: "Its yellowness pleases the beholders." The distance of this is not hidden. Joy (*surur*) is originally a delight in the heart upon attaining a benefit, or anticipating it, or seeing a pleasing and attractive matter. As for its essence, it is an inner expansion of the heart. There is a close relation between *surur*, *hubur* and *farah*, but *surur* is the pure and concealed kind, named so with reference to secrecy (*al-israr*). *Hubur* is that whose trace (*habar*), meaning its effect, is seen on the surface of the skin. Both are used for praiseworthy things. As for *farah*, it is what arises from insolence and arrogance, and for this reason it is often censured, as God, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, God does not love the exultant﴾ (28:76). Here, according to some, what is meant is admiration (*al-i'jab*), used metaphorically because it usually accompanies it. The clause is a description of the cow, meaning that it pleases those who look at it. Most of the exegetes point out that yellow is among the colors that gladden. For this reason, 'Ali, may God ennoble his countenance, used to prefer yellow sandals and would say: "Whoever wears a yellow sandal, his worries become few." Ibn al-Zubayr and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir forbade wearing black sandals, because they cause sorrow. It is also read as *yasurru* with a *ya'* (the verb in the third person masculine), so *lawnuha* may be the subject, *yasurru* its predicate, and *faqi'* a description following *safra'* (yellow), in the manner of the poet's saying:

"Indeed I pour for the drinking company a yellow, bright (wine), as if fine musk is being crushed within it."

However, this is rare, to the extent that it is said its domain is poetry. It is also possible that *lawnuha* is the agent (*fa'il*) of *faqi'*, and *yasurru* is a new independent statement (*istie'naf*).

Page 289

﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what it is."﴾ This is a repetition of the question about its state and attributes, meant to reject the first answer as not matching, and to show that the question remains as it was. It seeks a further clarification beyond what was obtained, and shows that a complete explanation had not been achieved.

﴿Indeed, the cow has become confused to us.﴾ This is a reason given for His saying "call upon" (ud'u), as in His saying: ﴿And pray for them, for your prayer is a comfort for them﴾. It is an excuse for repeating the question, meaning: indeed the cow described with what was mentioned is numerous, so it has become confused to us. Similarity (tashabbuh) is well known regarding cows, and in a hadith: «Trials like the faces of cows», meaning some of them resemble one another.

Yahya, 'Ikrimah and al-Baqir read: (inna al-baqira). It is the name for a group of cows. Al-baqar is a collective noun of kind (ism jins jam'i), distinguished from its singular by the ta' marbuta. Like it, it may be treated as masculine or feminine (as in ﴿like hollow palm trunks﴾ and ﴿the palm trees, tall and towering﴾). Its plural is abaqir, and it is also said: buqur, with plural bawaqir. In al-Bahr it is said that this animal was named so because it "yabqur al-ard", that is, it splits the earth for ploughing.

Al-Hasan read (tashabaha) with a damma on the ha', making it an imperfect verb with the ta' omitted; its perfect is tashabaha, and in it is a pronoun referring to al-baqar, considering it feminine. Al-A'raj is similar, except that he doubled the shin, and the original is (tatashabahu), which was assimilated (udghima). It was also read (tashshabaha) with a doubled shin in the feminine form of the present tense, and (yashshabahu) with the ya' and doubling, also in the form of the present tense. Ibn Mas'ud read (yashshabahu) with the ya' and doubling, making it an imperfect from tafa'ala, but he assimilated the ta' into the shin. It was also read: (mushtabihun), (mutashabbihun), (yatashabahu). Al-A'mash read (mutashabihun) and (mutashabihatun). It was read (tashabahat) with light pronunciation, and in the Codex of Ubayy with doubling. It has been questioned that the ta' is only assimilated in the imperfect, and there is no perfect verb in the pattern of the verbs with doubled fa' of the form (tafaaala). It has been justified that its original form is:

[Page 290]

(inna al-baqarata tashabahat), so the first ta' is from al-baqara and the second from the verb. When two like letters came together, they were assimilated, as in: (al-shajaratu tamayalat). However, attributing similarity to a single cow (baqara) is weak, and the easier course is to say that this reading is not established, for to sound it out in a fitting way is like plucking thorns from the qatad plant. It is also problematic that (tashabaha) is without the feminine marker, since its sign should have been present, unless it is said that it is in the manner of his saying:

"Nor a land whose herbage sprouts as its sprouting"

Ibn Kaysan permits it as a matter of latitude.

﴿And indeed we, if God wills, shall surely be guided.﴾ That is, to the very cow commanded to be slaughtered, or to what was hidden of the matter of the killer, or to the wisdom for which we were commanded. Ibn Jarir has recorded from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) in a mu'dal form (a report with two or more consecutive omissions), and Sa'id from 'Ikrimah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) in a mursal form (a report omitting the companion), and Ibn Abi Hatim from Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) in a mawsul form (a connected report), that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «If they had not made the exception, they would never have been made clear to them until the end of time».

The verse has been used as evidence that events occur by the will of God, Exalted, since in what He related, He made the occurrence of guidance, which is among the events, dependent on the attaching of the will, which is the same as the will (irada). What God Exalted related in His Book without disapproval is a proof, as is known in its place. This is based on the view that will (mashi'a) and will (irada) are synonymous, and there is disagreement about it. Also, that what was mentioned is by will necessarily implies that all events occur by it, and in this there is room for consideration.

It has also been used as evidence that a command may be separate from will, and that it is not will, as the Mu'tazila say, since when He commanded them to slaughter, He willed their guidance in this event. Thus his saying "if God wills", which indicates doubt and the non-certainty of guidance, would have no benefit, unlike when we say that He, Exalted, may command what He does not will. As for saying that it is possible that those people believed contrary to what actually was, because of the separation, or that it is based on their hesitation about whether the command was from Him, Exalted, this is refuted by the affirmation. However, it is objected that the argument is complete only if the meaning of (lamuhtadun) is being guided to what is intended by the command. But if the meaning is "if God wills our guidance in some matter, we shall be guided," then no. Yet this is contrary to the apparent sense, like the claim that what is necessary is that the commanded thing, namely the slaughter, be willed, and guidance does not necessarily follow, since that will may have another wisdom. Rather, this is the most remote possibility.

The Mu'tazila and the Karramiyya use the verse as evidence that God's will is originated, based on the premise that will and volition (mashi'a) are the same, because the particle (in) indicates the fulfilment of a condition in the future, and guidance, which is originated, has been attached to it. It is answered that the attaching is with regard to the attachment, so what is necessary is the origination of the attachment, and it does not necessarily follow that the attribute itself is originated. The placing of the condition between the subject of (inna) and its predicate is so that the endings of the verses agree. The predicate of (inna) came as a noun because it indicates stability more clearly, and to show that guidance is obtained by them. And for the importance of this matter, the statement was emphasized.

[p. 291]

﴿He said: "Indeed, He says it is a cow neither broken to plough nor to water the field"﴾. (Lā dhalūl) is an attribute (ṣifah) of (baqarah). It is a descriptive with a single word (min al-waṣf bil-mufrad). Whoever says it is a descriptive with a clause (min al-waṣf bil-jumlah), and that the implied sense is "lā hiya dhalūl" (not she is broken), has strayed far from the correct view. (Lā) here does not mean "not" but "other than" (bi-ma'na ghayr). It is a noun, as al-Sakhāwī and others have stated explicitly. However, because it has the form of a particle, its case-ending (i'rāb) appears on the word that follows it. It is also possible that it is a particle, like (illā) in the sense of "other than", as in His saying ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾.

Al-dhalūl is the tamed animal whose difficulty has departed. One says: a dābbah dhalūl (a clearly tame beast), with the vowel of dh kasra (dhill), and a rajul dhalūl (a clearly submissive man), with dh ḍamma (dhull). ﴿It ploughs the earth and does not water the tilth﴾. (Lā) here is a necessary extra particle (ṣilah lāzimah), required for the repetition in this construction. It serves to make explicit the generality of the negation, since without it there would be the possibility that it negates only the combination (of the two acts). For this reason the act of stirring up and ploughing the earth for sowing is called (muthīrah) and (ithārah), from athartuhu when I aroused it. Al-ḥarth is land prepared for sowing, or the splitting of the earth so that seed may be cast into it. It is also applied to what has been ploughed and sown, and to the crop itself. The two verbs are attributes of (dhalūl). An attribute may itself be described, according to what some grammarians have preferred and al-Samīn explicitly stated. The first verb falls within the scope of the negation, and the intended meaning is the negation of her stirring up the earth, that is, "she does not stir up the earth", so that she is not made tame. This is of the kind of the line: "On a road that has no clear track, whose landmarks cannot be followed." So the negation applies both to the principal and to the subordinate, and the negation of the necessitated thing (malzūm) follows from the negation of the necessitating thing (lāzim).

Al-Ḥasan said: this cow was wild, and for this reason it was described as one that does not stir up the earth, etc. Some people held that (tuthīru) is affirmed both in form and in meaning, and that it affirms of the cow that she stirs up the earth and ploughs it, while negating of her the watering of the tilth. This was refuted on the grounds that one who ploughs cannot be denied being tame. Others said: what is meant is that she stirs up the earth without ploughing, out of wantonness and exuberance. It is a habit of cows, when they are exuberant, to strike with their horns and hooves, so they stir up the dust of the earth. Thus this would be part of the completion of his saying (lā dhalūl), since describing her as exuberant and wanton is evidence of that. This is not far-fetched in my view.

Some, as in al-Mawāshī, held that the clause (tuthīru) is in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: this is not permissible, because it comes from an indefinite noun (nakirah). This was objected to: if by the indefinite noun he means (baqarah), then it has been described, and a circumstantial clause from a described indefinite noun is permissible, quite acceptably. If he means by it (lā dhalūl), then the view of Sībawayh is that a circumstantial clause may come from an indefinite noun even when it is not described, and he stated this explicitly in several places in his book. The only way out is to say that he followed the majority in this, and they hold the prohibition. Making the clause a circumstantial clause from the pronoun concealed in (dhalūl), meaning "not tame while stirring up", is nothing.

Abū 'Abd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī recited (lā dhalūla) with a fatḥah, so that (fa-lā) is the particle of absolute negation (li-l-tabri'ah), and the predicate is omitted, meaning "there", and the intended meaning is a place in which she was found. The clause is an attribute of (dhalūl), and it is a negation of her being described as subdued. It is said: she is dhalūl by way of metonymy (kināyah), because if she were in the place of the cow she would be described by it, since an attribute necessarily belongs to the described; and since she was not in its place she was not described by it. This is like their saying: "the place of so-and-so is the seat of generosity and bounty." This is better than what has been said, that (tuthīru) is the predicate of (lā), and the clause is an interposition between the attribute and the described, because it is more eloquent, as is not hidden. Some explained the reading as indeclinable (binā'), with attention to the form of (lā), as in "kuntu bi-lā māl" with a fatḥah. This is not acceptable, because that is restricted to what has been heard, and it is not analogical, as the statement of al-Raḍī seems to indicate.

(Tusqī) is also read with a ḍammah on the initial letter of the imperfect, from asqā, with the meaning of saqā. Some distinguished between them: saqā is for oneself, and asqā is for another, as in "his livestock" and "his land."

﴿Entirely sound, with no mark on it﴾. That is, Allah Most High made it sound from defects, as Ibn 'Abbās said. Or its people left it free from all kinds of use, as al-Ḥasan said. Or it was pure from the unlawful, with no usurpation or theft in it, as 'Aṭā' said. Or its colour was unmixed with other colours, as Mujāhid said. The preferred view is that of Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, because the unqualified term is understood in its complete sense, and because it is an initial establishment (ta'sīs). According to the last of these views, ﴿with no mark on it﴾ means: no colour in it that differs from its colour, as an emphasis (ta'kīd). The doubling here is for transitivity and causation (naql wa-ta'diyah), and more than one person has erred in claiming that it is for intensification (mubālaghah).

Al-shiyah is the verbal noun of washaytu al-thawba, ashīhu washyan, when you decorate the garment with lines of differing colours. Its initial waw is dropped, as in 'idah and zinah. From it comes al-wāshī (the tale-bearer), said of the slanderer. It is said that one is not called wāshin until he alters his speech and embellishes it. One says: thawr ashyah (a bull with patches of colour), faras ablaq (a piebald horse), kabsh akhraj, taysun abraq, and ghurāb abqa', all with the meaning of spotted/piebald. In al-Baḥr it is stated that the ashyah in their saying thawr ashyah, meaning one with white patches, is not derived from al-shiyah, because the two roots differ. Shiyah is the noun of (lā), and fīhā is its predicate.

﴿They said: "Now you have brought the truth."﴾ That is, you have made manifest the reality of what we were commanded. Here (al-ḥaqq) means "the reality" (al-ḥaqīqah). It is also said: it means the decreed or binding matter, or the statement that corresponds to reality. They did not mean that what came before was not true; rather they meant that the truth had not been made manifest by it in full clarity, so he had not brought the truth, but had only pointed to it. On these views they did not disbelieve by this statement. Qatādah took it literally and understood it as implying that what they had brought before was false, and so he said: they disbelieved by this statement. The preferred view is not to declare them unbelievers.

(Al-ān) is a time-adverb that is necessarily indeclinable, with a fatḥah. It is not permissible to strip it of (al), and using it otherwise is a grammatical error (laḥn). It denotes the present moment, and it generally makes the imperfect verb following it refer to the present. It has sometimes come in places where it cannot denote the present, as in ﴿So now, have intercourse with them﴾, since the command is explicit about the future. Some claimed that it is inflected (muʿrab), citing the line: "As if the two were full, they have not changed," intending "from now", so that it is in the genitive. It may be built on kasra. The (al) in it is for presence according to some, and is an extra element according to others. It was built because it implies the meaning of demonstration, or because it implies the meaning of the definite article (al), like saḥara (the dawn). It is also read (ālān), with a long vowel, as an interrogative of confirmation, indicating impatience at their delay and their awaiting it.

Nāfi' read it with the hamzah omitted and its vowel placed on the lām, and two transmissions are reported from him: the omission of the waw in (qālū), and its retention.

﴿So they slaughtered her﴾. That is: they sought this cow, which combined the attributes mentioned previously, and obtained her, and then they slaughtered her. The fa is an eloquent conjunction (fā' faṣīḥah), coordinating with an omitted element, since slaughter does not follow from the mere command to slaughter and the explanation of her attributes. That element was omitted because the slaughter indicates it. Obtaining her was by purchase from the young man dutiful to his parents, as the opinions of most commentators agree, and the story is well known. It is said she was wild and they captured her. It is said she was not one of the cows of this world, but Allah sent her down from heaven, and this is a view that falls down to the depths of the earth. It is said that the wisdom in making a cow the means rather than another of the livestock is that they used to worship cows and calves, and this love had taken root in their hearts, as His saying Most High indicates: ﴿and the calf was made to sink into their hearts﴾. Then, after they repented, Allah Most High wished to test them by slaughtering that which had been made dear to them, so that it would be a real proof of their repentance. It is also said: perhaps it is more subtle and better that the wisdom in this command was to expose their reproach for worshipping the calf: "How could you worship what is in the form of a cow, when nature does not accept that Allah should create in it a property by which the dead is revived through a prophet's miracle?! And how did you accept the claim of the Sāmirī that it was your god, while you now accept the word of Allah, glory be to Him, that by striking a piece of it the dead is made to live? Glory be to Allah! What a monstrous absurdity!"

﴿And they almost did not do it﴾. He expressed the slaughter by the verb (fa'ala), meaning "and they were almost not slaughtering." The supposition that what is meant is "and they almost did not do what they were commanded after the slaughter, namely striking part of her on the dead" is remote. (Kāda) is designed to denote the imminence of the predicate's occurrence, and according to the well-known usage its predicate is never anything but an imperfect verb denoting the present, to emphasize proximity. Its meaning has been disputed. It is said: in the affirmative it is a negation, and in the negative it is an affirmation, so that the meaning of "kāda Zayd yakhruj" is "Zayd nearly went out," and yet he did not go out. This is corrupt, because its meaning is the approach of going out, while its non-occurrence is a rational matter outside the signified meaning; and if what he said were correct, then "qāraba" (approached) and similar would also be so, and no one has said that. It is also said: in the affirmative it is an affirmation, and in the past negative it is an affirmation, and in the future it follows the pattern of verbs. The one who holds this view relies on this verse, because if "wa-mā kādū" here meant a negation of the act from them, it would contradict His saying ﴿so they slaughtered her﴾, since that indicates the act's occurrence for them. The truth is that it is, in affirmation and negation, like the other verbs: its affirmative denotes the approach, and its negative denotes the negation of that approach. Affirmation and negation in the verse are to be taken as referring to different times or different considerations, so there is no contradiction, since a condition of contradiction is the unity of time and consideration. The meaning is: they did not approach slaughtering her until their excuses ran out, and then they slaughtered her as one compelled; or they slaughtered her under command, and they almost did not slaughter her out of fear of disgrace, or from reluctance because her price was so high, for it is reported that they bought her for her hide filled with gold, while the cow at that time was worth three dinars. The view of differing times faced an objection: the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "dhabaḥūhā", so the content of the clause must be contemporaneous with the content of the governing verb. The answer is that they stated that it may be restricted to the past: if it is affirmative, it is accompanied by (qad), because of its nearness to the present; and if it is negative, as here, it is not accompanied by it, because the basic sense of negation is continuity. Thus it conveys approach, which does not benefit, because the non-approach of an act cannot be conceived as being contemporaneous with it. For this reason some later scholars relied in their answer on the view that ﴿and they almost did not do it﴾ is a metonymy for the difficulty of the act and its heaviness upon them, and this remains constant. It has been explicitly stated in the commentary on al-Tashīl that a speaker may say "lam yakad Zayd yafʿal" (Zayd hardly did it), meaning that he did it with difficulty, not with ease; but this goes against the apparent meaning for which the word was coined, so understand.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 72:

﴿And when you killed a soul﴾: that is, a person, or one possessing a soul. The attribution of the killing to the addressees, although it was only one of them who did it, follows the Arab practice of attributing things to a tribe when some of its members have done something that is blameworthy or praiseworthy. The statement of some scholars that it is not proper to attribute an act or saying that came from some to all, unless it came from them with the support or consent of all, is not accepted. Yes, attributing it to all requires some purpose (nukta). Perhaps the purpose here is to indicate that all of them are such that it is not far-fetched that the killing came from them, because of their great greed, their abundant covetousness, and their great audacity:

*They are, by nature, like the fingers of the two palms,
and each of them is covetous and bold.*

It has also been said that the killer was a group, namely the heirs of the slain person. It has been narrated that they gathered together to kill him, and for this reason the killing was attributed to the group.

﴿So you disputed about it﴾: its original form is *tadāra'tum*, from *al-darʾ*, which means repelling. The *tāʾ* and the *dāl* came together, although their points of articulation are close, and since assimilation (*idghām*, merging of one letter into another) was intended, the *tāʾ* was changed into a *dāl* and made quiescent for the sake of assimilation. Thus the hamzat al-wasl (the connecting hamza, a hamza pronounced only to allow the beginning of the word with a vowel) was brought in to enable pronunciation at the start. This applies consistently to every verb of the form *tafāʿala* or *tafaʿʿala* whose first radical is *tāʾ*, *ṭāʾ*, *ẓāʾ*, *ṣād* or *ḍād*. The *tadāruʾ* here is either a metaphor (*majāz*, figurative usage) for disagreement and contention, or a metonymy (*kināya*, an indirect expression) for it, since each of two disputants repels the other. Or it is used in its literal sense, namely mutual repelling, in that each of them cast the killing of her off himself onto his companion. Thus each of them, insofar as it is cast upon him, repels the other, insofar as he is the one casting. It has also been said that casting the killing onto oneself is itself repelling the companion, and each of the two casters is a repeller, so their casting upon one another is a mutual repelling. It has also been said that each of them repels the other from innocence to accusation: when one of them says, "I am innocent and you are accused," the other says, "Rather you are the accused, and I am the innocent." It is not hidden that what has been mentioned, despite its shortcomings, is more fitting as a metaphor, and for this reason Abu Hayyan counted it as metaphor.

The pronoun in *fīhā* (concerning it) refers back to the soul (*nafs*). It has also been said that it refers to the killers understood from the verb, and it has been said that it refers to the accusation indicated by the meaning of the speech.

Abu Haywa read *fa-tadārāʾtum* according to the original form. It has also been said that he and Abu al-Suwar read *fa-iddarʾtum* without an alif before the *rāʾ*, and that another group read *fa-tadārāʾtum*.

﴿And God will bring forth what you were concealing﴾: that is, He will certainly make manifest what you were hiding concerning the matter of the slain person and the killer, as the construction of the nominal sentence indicates, and the construction of the active participle upon the subject (*mubtadaʾ*), which conveys the emphasis and strengthening of the judgment. This is by way of grace (*tafaḍḍul*) according to us, and by way of obligation according to the Mu'tazilah. Specifying the restricted object of the verb as the majority of scholars do is what has been adopted. It has been said that it is permissible for it to be general, covering the slain person and other things, with the slain person being among its instances. But there is a problem with this, since not everything they concealed from people has God, exalted is He, made manifest. The participle *mukhrij* (bringing forth) is made to govern because it is future relative to the judgment preceding it, namely the disputing, and its being past now does no harm. The combining of the two forms, the past and the future, indicates continuity. In al-Bahr: if it is to indicate the precedence of the concealing,

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 73:**

﴿So We said: "Strike him with part of it."﴾ This is conjoined (*'atf*) to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and you disputed about it﴾. What lies between them is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD*) that indicates that concealing the killer will not benefit him. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: while you know this. The pronoun in (*idribuhu*, "strike him") refers to the soul (*nafs*), on the basis of treating it as masculine, since it is feminine in form. This is the most well-known view. Treating it as masculine may also be taken as referring to the person, or to the slain man, or the sentence may contain an elided modifier, meaning "one with a soul," and after the elision the modified noun was placed in its position. It has also been said: the more apparent view is that the masculine form is used because the meaning is masculine. When the wording is masculine and the meaning feminine, or the reverse, there are two possibilities. This pronoun is made masculine despite the earlier feminine reference for variety of style (*tafannun*), or to distinguish this pronoun from the one that follows it, for clarity. The apparent meaning is that "part" (*al-ba'D*) refers to any part whatsoever, since there is no benefit in specifying it, and no sound transmission (*naql*) has come concerning it.

[p. 294]

It is disputed with what they struck him. It has been said: with its tongue, or with its two smaller parts, or with its right thigh, or with its tail, or with the cartilage, or with the bone adjacent to it, or with the piece of flesh between the two shoulders, or with the *'ajb* (the coccyx, the base of the spine), or with a bone of its bones. It is also reported that the striking was on the neck of the slain man, and that this was before his burial. As for the one who said that they remained searching for her for forty years, or that they were commanded to seek her when she was neither in a loin nor a womb, he said that the striking was upon the grave after burial. The more apparent view is that the one who directly struck was the one who struck, not the grave. In some reports, he rose up while his jugular veins were gushing blood and said: "My nephew (*ibn akhi*) has killed me." In another version: "So-and-so and so-and-so," naming his two cousins (*ibn 'ammihi*). Then he fell dead. They were seized and killed, and no killer inherited from him after that. In some narratives, the killer swore by God, exalted is He, that he had not killed him, and so he denied the truth after witnessing it. Al-Mawardi said: the striking was with a dead thing that had no life in it, so that it would not be confused in the mind of one with doubts that life had passed into him from what he was struck with. Thus, to remove the doubt and to confirm the proof, this was done.

﴿Thus God brings the dead to life﴾ is a parenthetical clause that indicates the certainty of the thing compared, and the assurance of it, by likening the promised to the witnessed. The similarity lies in the general notion of bringing to life. In the speech there is an elision indicated by the clause, meaning: so they struck him, and he came to life. The speech from God, exalted is He, is addressed to those present at the time of the life-giving. The particle of address (*kaf*) is addressed to everyone who is able to be addressed and to hear this speech, because the matter of bringing to life is great, and its importance requires that everyone who is capable of hearing be addressed with it. Thus those [present] enter into it first and foremost. This is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He shows you﴾, etc. On this view, it is necessary to supply a verb of saying, meaning: "We said," or "And We said to them, thus," so that the speech is connected to what precedes it. It has also been said that the particle of address is directed at them, and the expected form would have been *kadhalikum* ("thus, you") in agreement with what follows it, but it was used in the singular for the purpose of addressing each one individually, or by treating them as a group (*fari*q), and the like, for the sake of lightness. It is also possible that the speech is with those present at the revelation of the verse. On this view, no supplied element is needed, since the sentence is coherent without it. Indeed, supplying it may disrupt the coherence. Al-Mawardi went further and made it an address from Musa himself, peace be upon him.

﴿And He shows you His signs﴾ is either a new sentence or conjoined to what precedes it. The apparent meaning is that *ayat* ("signs") is plural in both form and meaning. By it are meant the evidences that indicate that God, exalted is He, is powerful over everything. It is also possible that what is meant is this act of bringing to life, and the plural is used for it because it contains wondrous matters: the sequence of life following the striking with a dead limb, the dead man's report of his killer, and what accompanies it of matters that break customary patterns. In *al-Muntakhab* it is said that the expression of a single sign as "signs" is because it indicates the existence of the Creator, capable of all things that can be done, knowing of all things that can be known, choosing in origination and innovation, and indicates the truthfulness of Musa, peace be upon him, the innocence of one who was not a killer, and the specific identity of the accusation against the one who committed the killing.

﴿So that you may understand﴾, that is, so that you may comprehend life after death, resurrection and gathering. For whoever is able to bring one soul to life is able to bring all souls to life, since there is no restriction in that. ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only as [that of] a single soul﴾. Or [it means]: so that your reason may be perfected, or so that you may refrain from disobeying Him and act according to what your reasons require. The exegetes have mentioned legal rulings (*ahkam fiqhiyya*) which they derived and for which they argued from the story of this slain man, but these do not appear from the verse. I see no benefit in mentioning them, apart from making the discussion lengthy. This is all.

And by way of allusion (*ishara*): the cow is the animal soul when the wantonness of youth has departed from it, and the weakness of old age has not yet reached it. It is fascinating and pleasing to look upon, and does not stir the earth of readiness (*isti'dad*) with righteous deeds, nor water the field of the knowledge and wisdoms that lie within it potentially with the waters of turning toward the presence of holiness and journeying to the gardens of intimacy. It has been left free to graze upon the flowers of desires, and has not been bound with the fetters of good conduct and acts of obedience. Thus no school of thought or belief has taken firm root in it, and what was deposited in it of the lights of readiness has not appeared upon it. Its slaughter is the suppression of its passion and the preventing of it from its particular actions, with the blade of the knife of spiritual discipline (*riyada*). Whoever wishes that his heart may live a good life, and be adorned with divine knowledge and true sciences, and that the state of the dominion (*mulk*) and the kingdom (*malakut*) may be unveiled to him, and that the secrets of divinity (*lahut*) and sovereignty (*jabarut*) may be manifested to him, and that the dispute and contention between his intellect and his imagination, arising from habituation to sensible things, may be removed, then let him slaughter it, and let its effect reach his dead heart. There the hidden thing emerges, and the seas of knowledge overflow. This slaughter is the greatest struggle (*jihad*) and the red death, and its outcome is the true life and everlasting happiness.

Whoever does not die in His love does not live through it, and without the gathering of the bee, what the bee gathers is not [obtained].

By the old man, the old woman, the child, and the young man who was slain, in some reports concerning this story, are indicated the spirit (*ruh*), the bodily nature (*tabi'a*), the intellect (*'aql*), and the heart (*qalb*). The application of the rest of what is in the story after this is up to you. And may the peace of God, exalted is He, be upon you.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 2, verse 74 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾. Al-qaswah (hardness) originally means dryness and firmness. Here the state of their hearts is compared, in their being unresponsive to admonition, to the state of stones' hardness, in that the work of gentleness does not take effect in them. So in (qasat, "hardened") there is a *isti'arah tabi'iyyah* (derivative metaphor), or a *tamthiliyyah* (allegorical metaphor). (Thumma, "then") is for expressing the improbability of hardness after witnessing what removes it. It has been said that it denotes temporal sequence, because their hearts hardened after a period of time, when they said that the dead man had lied about them. Or it is an expression for the hardening of their descendants. The pronoun in (qulubukum, "your hearts") refers, according to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, to the heirs of the slain man, and according to Abu al-'Aliyah and others, to the Children of Israel.

﴿after that﴾, that is, after the reviving of the dead man. It has been said: after his speech. It has been said: after the signs that preceded, which they knew, such as their transformation into apes and swine, the lifting of the mountain, the gushing of water, and the reviving. Al-Zajjaj went to this view. On this reading, ﴿then hardened﴾ and so on is a conjunction over the content of all the preceding stories and the mentioned signs. On the previous reading, it is a conjunction over the story of ﴿And when you killed﴾.

﴿so they are like stones﴾, that is, in hardness and non-responsiveness. The plural is used for the plural of hearts, and to indicate that they vary in hardness, just as stones vary in firmness. (Ka, "like") is for comparison. According to Sibawayh and the majority of grammarians it is a particle; al-Akhfash claims it is a noun. Here it is connected to an omitted element, meaning "being like stones", contrary to Ibn 'Usfur, who claimed that the comparative *ka* is not connected to anything.

﴿or harder in hardness﴾, that is, than stones. So they are like iron, for example, or like something that is not affected at all, even in imagination. (Aw, "or") is for giving the option of one who exaggerates, and it occurs in comparison as it occurs after an imperative. Or it is for classification, meaning some are like stones and some are harder. Or it is for indecision, in the sense of permitting both matters without regard to anything else, as has been said. Or it means *bal* ("rather"), which requires positing a subject if we accept that this usage is restricted to sentences. Or it means *waw* ("and"). Or it is for doubt, which, since doubt is impossible for Allah, is redirected to others. Al-'Allamah (al-Alusi's source, al-Zamakhshari) does not accept this, because it leads to permitting that the meanings of particles be determined relative to the listener, and it removes words from their established usages, since they were only established so that the speaker may express what is in his mind. The truth is that it is permissible to consider the listener in the meanings of words when their operation according to their original sense is impossible with regard to the speaker. So there is no harm in treating *aw* in the sense of doubt in the manner of *la'alla* ("perhaps") in the expression of hope occurring in the speech of Allah, Exalted. That is a well-trodden path of the People of the Sunnah, and the indication of this has passed, so reflect.

(Wa-ashaddu, "or harder") is conjoined to (ka-l-hijarah, "like stones") by conjoining a single word to a single word, just as you say: "Zayd is traveling or resident." Some have estimated: "or they are harder", which makes it conjunction of sentences. Some people posit an omitted genitive construction, meaning "like what is harder", and make it conjoined to the *ka* if it is a noun, or to the whole prepositional phrase if it is a particle. Then, when the genitive construction is omitted, the genitive complement is placed in its position and takes its case. It is not hidden that considering the comparison in the conjoined element without conjoining it to the element governed by *ka* is very improbable.

Al-A'mash read (aw ashadda) in the genitive with a *fathah*, because it is not declined, due to its being descriptive and its form matching a verb pattern. Here it is conjoined to *al-hijarah* ("stones"), and the consideration of comparison is then evident.

[Page 296]

He, glorified and exalted, did not say *aqsa* ("harder"), although the verb of hardness is among those from which the elative form (af'al) is derived, and it is more concise and occurs in eloquent usage, as in the saying of the poet:

*Every slender one is more delicate than wine,*
*with a heart harder than the boulder.*

This is because *ashadd* contains greater emphasis, since it indicates increase both in its substance and in its form, unlike *aqsa*, whose indication is only by form. In it there is an indication of the intensification of both hardnesses. Had it been *aqsa*, it would indicate that hearts and stones share hardness, with hearts containing an increase of hardness, but not in intensity of hardness. This is not like your saying "Zayd is more generous than 'Amr" (*zaydun ashaddu ikraman min 'amrin*), where they mentioned that its meaning is nothing but that they both share generosity, and Zayd's generosity exceeds 'Amr's, not that they both share intensity of generosity, with Zayd's intensity exceeding 'Amr's intensity. This is due to the difference between what is constructed for achieving a purpose and what is constructed for something else. What we are dealing with here is the second, even though the first is more common. The objection that *ashadd* is taken as referring to the hearts rather than to the hardness is not valid, because it is taken as referring to them in meaning, since it is a *tamyiz* (specification) transferred from the subject, or transferred from the predicate, as in *al-Bahr* (the commentary of Abu Hayyan). It is possible to say that Allah, Exalted, presented hardness in the framework of visible defects, to draw attention to the fact that it is among the defects, indeed the entire defect is what turns away from the unseen world: *For indeed it is not the eyes that are blinded, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blinded* (Q. 22:46).

﴿And indeed among stones is that from which rivers gush forth, and indeed among them is that which splits and water comes out of it, and indeed among them is that which falls down from fear of Allah﴾ (Q. 2:74).

This is a *tadhyil* (concluding appendix) to explain the superiority of their hearts over stones, or a *i'tiraḍ* (parenthetical insertion) between His saying ﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾ and the state (*hal*) regarding them, which is ﴿And Allah is not unaware﴾, to explain the reason for that. For, because it is strange, it needs an explanation of its cause, as in the saying of the poet:

*So there is no emigration to be revealed, and in despair there is rest,*
*nor is its description clear to us, so that we may honor it.*

Making it a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*) that indicates causation is rejected by taste, since there is no sense in restriction. Its being an explanation and clarification in meaning of what preceded, while in wording it is conjoined to the sentence ﴿so they are like stones or harder﴾, as stated by al-'Allamah, is something whose basis is not apparent. For if it is an explanation in meaning, how is it correct to conjoin it, and leave aside making it an explanation?

The meaning is: stones are affected and responsive, while the hearts of these people are not affected or responsive to the command of Allah, Exalted, at all. He, glorified, has ascended in explaining the superiority, as if He first explained the superiority of their hearts in hardness over stones, which are affected by an impact that results in a great benefit from the gushing of rivers. Then over stones which are affected by a weak impact that results in a small benefit from the flow of water. Then over stones which are affected without any benefit. So it is as if He, glorified, said: The hearts of these people are harder than stones, because they are not affected in a way that results in great benefit, nor even small benefit, but are not affected at all.

By what has been mentioned, the point of mentioning the gushing of rivers and the flowing of water, and leaving out the benefit of falling, becomes clear. Many have mentioned that the verse is in the manner of *tatmim* (completion) rather than progression (*tarqi*), like (al-Rahman al-Rahim, "the Compassionate, the Merciful"). For if progression were intended, it would say: "And indeed among them is that which splits and water comes out of it, and indeed among them is that which gushes forth rivers." Its benefit is comprehensiveness of all the affections that go against the nature of this substance, and this is more eloquent than progression. The final ﴿and indeed among them﴾ serves as a completion of the completion. It is not hidden that this is refuted by denying that it conveys comprehensiveness of all the affections, and it lacks the subtlety of what we have mentioned.

(Al-Fajr, "gushing") means opening up with breadth and abundance, as the root of the word indicates and as the *tafa'ul* form (the form used here) shows. By "rivers" is meant the abundant water that flows in rivers. The expression is either by omitting the genitive (rivers' water) or by mentioning the locus while intending what is in it, or the attribution is metaphorical. Some researchers said: Taking it in its literal meaning is an error, since opening up cannot be attributed to rivers, except by including the meaning of coming into being, such that it is said: it gushes and rivers come forth from it. Moreover, a stone being gushed out such that it becomes a river is unusual, let alone that they are rivers.

(Al-Tashaqqu, "splitting") means cracking lengthwise or widthwise. (Al-Khashyah, "fear") means dread. It has been disputed what is meant by it. Some people, and this is what is reported from Mujahid and others, held that it is here literal. It is attributed to the noble Name through the attribution of the verbal noun to its object, meaning "fear of Allah by the stones." It is possible that Allah, Exalted, creates reason and life in the stone, and the balance of temperament and structure are not conditions for that, contrary to the Mu'tazilah. The apparent sense of the verses speaks to this. In the authentic hadith: "Indeed I know a stone that used to greet me before I was sent (as a prophet)." And that after his mission, the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, did not pass by any stone or clod of earth without greeting him. It is reported regarding the Black Stone that it testifies for whoever touches it. And the hadith of the pebbles glorifying Allah in his blessed hand, peace be upon him, is well-known.

It has also been said: it is literal, and the attribution is the attribution (as before), except that the agent is omitted, namely, the servants. The meaning is: among stones is that which some of it descends from others at an earthquake, out of the fear of the servants of Allah, Exalted, of Him. Its realization is that since the intended purpose of them is fear of Allah, Exalted, that fear became like an effective cause for that descent. So the meaning is interpreted as: it descends so that the servants may come to fear Allah, Exalted.

Abu Muslim went to the view that the fear is literal, and that the pronoun in ﴿among them is that which falls﴾ refers to the hearts. The meaning is: among hearts are hearts that become tranquil, settle, and return to Allah, Exalted, and these are the hearts of the sincere. So He expressed this by "falling." It has also been said: it is literal, except that its attribution is the attribution of the verbal noun to its agent. The stone is hail, and its being feared by Allah, Exalted, means His frightening His servants by sending it down. This view is colder than hail, and the one before it is denser than a stone, and what comes before both is in between.

Some people said: fear is a metaphor for submission to the command of Allah, Exalted, by naming the necessary concomitant with its consequence. It should not be understood in its literal sense. As for the view that the balance of temperament and structure is a condition, and what has come that suggests the opposite is understood to mean that Allah, Exalted, joined His angels with these inanimate things, and among them are those acts, and similar is the hadith: "This is a mountain that loves us and we love it," by omitting a genitive, meaning: its people love us, and we love its people. This is evident.

As for the view that it is not a condition: the falling and the fear, on the supposition of the creation of reason and life, cannot validly be an explanation for the stones being in themselves less hard, and that is what suits the context. The objection that their hearts only refuse to submit to the command of obligation by way of intention and choice, and they do not refuse what is intended for them by way of compulsion and force, as is the case with stones, and on this the claim does not hold, so the preferable course is to take it literally. This has been answered: the meaning is that their hearts are harder than stones, because stones accept the impact that suits them and for which they were created, whereas their hearts turn away from the impact that suits them and for which they were created. The answer that the signs they saw are of the kind that compels the heart and forces it, and since their hearts were not affected by many compelling things while a stone is affected by one compelling thing, their hearts are harder, is not free from scrutiny. For if what is meant is exaggeration in indicating sincerity, it does not help. If what is meant is the reality of compulsion, that is disputed, since otherwise its effect would not fail to follow, and whoever believed after seeing them would not deserve reward, because his faith would be compelled, and no one holds that. Then, on this view, the apparent reading is that the fear of Allah is connected to the three preceding acts.

It has been read (wa-in, "and indeed") as the lightened form of the heavy (*in* with *inna*'s function), and then the distinguishing *lam* must accompany it, separating it from the negative particle. Al-Farra' says it is the negative particle and the *lam* means *illa* ("except"). Al-Kisa'i claimed that *inna* is the lightened form if a noun follows it, and the negative particle if a verb follows it. Qutrub said: if a verb follows it, it has the meaning of *qad* ("indeed"). Malik ibn Dinar read (yanfajir), the imperfect of *infajara*, and al-A'mash read (yatashaqqaq), and (yahbut) with a *dammah*.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 74 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ This is a warning concerning what has been mentioned, as if it were said: Indeed Allah, exalted is He, is on the watch (lil-mirsad) for these whose hearts are hard, guarding their deeds and reckoning them, so He will requite them for them in this world and the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir read (ya'malun) with the yā' (third person, "they do"), joining it to what follows in His, glorified is He, saying: "that they should believe, while a group of them used to hear" (an yu'minu wa-yasma'una) and a group of them. The rest read with the tā' (second person, "you do"), in keeping with (wa-idh qataltum) and (idaraʼtum) and (taktumun), etc. It was also said: it is joined to His, exalted is He, saying: (afatat'maʽuna) so that the address in it is to the believers, a promise to them. But this is far-fetched, since there is no basis for mentioning the promise to the believers as a concluding remark (dhayl) explaining the ugly conduct of the Jews.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 75:

﴿Do you then hope﴾ The interrogative is for expressing improbability (istib'ad), or for rebuke-laden denial (inkar tawbikhi). The sentence is said to be conjunctive (ma'tufa) upon His saying, exalted is He, ﴿then their hearts hardened﴾, or upon an assumed element between the hamza and the fa' according to other than Sibawayh, meaning: "Do you think that your hearts are fit for faith, so that you hope [for it]?" Tamaʻ (hope/desire) is the soul's strong attachment to attaining a sought object, and it is stronger than raja' (expectation). It arises only from a strong desire and intense will. The address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, or to the believers alone, as said by Abu al-'Aliyah and Qatadah, or to the Ansar, as said by al-Naqqash. What is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil is that it is addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) alone, and the plural is for glorification (ta'zim). ﴿That they would believe for you﴾, i.e., that they would affirm, responding to you. So "faith" is in its linguistic meaning, and the transitivity by the lam is by way of implication (tadmin), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So Lut believed in him﴾, meaning "for the sake of your summons to them." Thus the verb is treated as intransitive, and the intended meaning of faith is its legal (shar'i) meaning. The lam is the lam of cause (lam al-ajal). On both readings, "that they would believe" is the object of "you hope," with the preposition dropped; it is in the accusative position according to Sibawayh, and in the genitive position according to al-Khalil and al-Kisa'i. The pronoun of the third person refers to the Jews contemporary with him, since they are the ones whose faith is hoped for. It is said that the intended meaning is the Jews as a class, so that a group of them can be made the object of hoped-for faith and another group the distorters; there is in this what is not hidden.

﴿And there was a group among them﴾, i.e., a party of their predecessors, namely the rabbis, ﴿who heard the words of Allah then distorted them﴾, i.e., they heard the Torah and interpreted it with corrupt interpretation according to their aims. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, went to this view. The majority hold that its distortion was by substituting words of their own invention, as they did regarding his description (ﷺ), for it is related that among his attributes in it was that he was white, of medium height, and they changed it to dark, tall. And they changed the verse of stoning to blackening (taskhim) and blackening of the face, as in al-Bukhari. It is also said that what is meant by the words of Allah is what they heard at Mount Sinai, so the group is a party from those seventy. Al-Kalbi related that they asked Musa, peace be upon him, to let them hear His speech, and he said to them: "Perform ghusl and wear clean clothes," and they did so; then Allah made them hear His speech, and then they said: "We have heard," and at its end it is said: "If you are able to do these things, do them, and if you wish, do not do them." Distortion in this sense is the addition.

Then it is not hidden that in what they invented there is evidence of its corruption, in that they tied the command to ability and the prohibition to will, and these two are not opposites. It seems they intended by the command a non-obligatory sense, meaning "do if you wish, and if you wish, do not do." Thus the Allamah stated, and his purpose is to explain the source of their corrupt distortion, so it does not conflict with the lack of opposition being evidence of its corruption. What this narration implies is that these people heard His speech without intermediary, as Musa, peace be upon him, heard it. The sound view is that they did not hear without an intermediary, and that this was specific to him, peace be upon him. It is also said that what is meant is the revelation sent down upon our Prophet (ﷺ): a group of the Jews used to hear it and distort it, intending to introduce into the religion what is not from it and to produce contradiction in its rulings. ﴿And Allah refuses except to perfect His light﴾. Al-A'mash read (kalima Allah).

﴿After they had understood it﴾, i.e., they had retained it and comprehended it, and its soundness was not unclear to them. (Ma) is verbal-masdariyya, i.e., after their understanding of it. The pronoun in ﴿they understood it﴾ refers to the words of Allah. It is also said that (ma) is relative (mawsula), and the pronoun refers back to it, but this is far-fetched.

﴿And they know﴾: the object of knowledge is omitted, i.e., that they are falsifiers and liars, or the punishment that is in their distortion. In this is the completeness of their blame. By this explanation the supposed repetition of what was mentioned after "after they had understood it" is dispelled. The summary of the verse is the improbability of hoping that faith would come from these base people, when their rabbis and leaders were in this shameful state, and there is no doubt that these are worse in character and less discerning than their predecessors. Or it is an improbability of hope for the faith of these disbelieving distorters and their predecessors who were in the time of their Prophet and did that, for they have a precedent in it. By this is dispelled what might occur to the mind: how does it follow that the undertaking of some of them to distort leads to despair of the faith of the rest of them?

When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe." This is a resumed sentence (jumlah musta'nafah), not one following directly from the explanation of what their predecessors did, but rather to explain what they themselves did, namely the disgraceful acts that undermined their faith: the hypocrisy of some of them and the rebuke others directed at them. It is possible that it is conjoined (ma'tufah) to "And there was a group of them..." and so on. It was also said that it is conjoined to (they hear) and it was said: it is conjoined to His saying, exalted is He: "And when you killed a soul..." (the narrative conjoined to a narrative). The pronoun in (they met) refers to the Jews, in accordance with "that they should believe you," and the pronoun in (they said) refers to those who met them. However, not all of them actually take up the speech itself, but rather it is done by their hypocrites, while the rest remain silent; so this is the attribution of what belongs to some to all. Its like is more than can be counted. This is more fitting, as our master, the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, said in condemning the state of those who first remained silent and then rebuked, because it indicates their hypocrisy, the variation of their states, and the contradiction of their opinions, by attributing the speech to the direct actors only, with an elided genitive, i.e., their hypocrites said, as some of them did. It was also said: the first pronoun refers to the hypocrites of the Jews, as the second does, so that the subject of the condition and the consequent is unified, out of regard for the requirements of the composition. This is supported by what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah in explaining "and when they meet": that is, the hypocrites of the Jews meet the sincere believers and say... However, the sequence and the continuation, as you have seen and will see, make this distant.

Ibn al-Sumayqa read (laqaw) as (laqawa).

"And when some of them are alone with others": that is, when some of those mentioned, namely the silent ones among them, withdraw after finishing with the business of the believers, heading off and joining with another group of them, who are the hypocrites. This is almost an explicit statement that the silent ones share in meeting the believers, since being alone occurs only after engagement, and because their rebuke is attached to the mere being alone; and were they not present during the exchange, their hearing would have to be made part of the condition. Also, because it adds further censure on them for their silence and then their rebuke. "They say": that is, that group who were alone, rebuking their hypocrites for what they did in their presence.

"Do you speak to them of what Allah has opened up to you?" That is: do you inform the believers of what Allah has made clear to you alone regarding the description of His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), or of the covenants taken from your prophets to confirm him (ﷺ) and to support him. The expression "opening" is used for it to signal that it is a hidden secret and a locked door. In the verse there is an indication that they did not suffice with saying "we believe," but gave a reason for it, namely what has been mentioned; and it did not state this explicitly, relying on the testimony of the rebuke. Some people have permitted that this rebuke came from the hypocrites to their successors and remnants who had not become hypocrites; in that case the group that is the subject of "were alone" would refer to the hypocrites. Here the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to increase the meaning. The interrogative is a denial and a prohibition against speaking about it in the future. This is not worth anything, however exalted its speaker, unless there is a sound narration in it; and anything beyond that is like scraping at thorns.

"That they may argue with you before your Lord": this is connected to "speak" and not to "opened," contrary to those who strained to connect it to "opened." The purpose is to emphasise the denial and to intensify the rebuke, for speaking, though reprehensible in itself, is for this purpose something that scarcely proceeds from a sensible person. The reciprocal form (mufa'alah) here is not intended; the meaning is that they may argue against you with it, but the form was used for emphasis. Ibn Tamjid mentioned that if someone were to take the form to mean mutual participation between the one arguing and the one argued against, with arguing on one side and hearing on the other, it would have a basis, as in "I pledged allegiance to Zayd." What benefits you here has already been mentioned, so reflect on it. This lam is the lam of purpose (lam kay), and the verb is put in the subjunctive by an implied "an" after it, or by "an" itself; it expresses causation. Perhaps this is metaphorical here, because those who speak did not aim at that purpose, but since their speaking inevitably results in it, they are treated as if they were doing it for that purpose, to demonstrate the utter foolishness of their minds and the weakness of their opinions. The pronoun in (with it) refers to "what Allah has opened," as the outward sense requires. "Before your Lord": that is, in His Book and His judgment. "Before a group of your Lord" is a substitute (badal) for "with it," and its being a substitute means that its governing element, which stands in place of it, is a substitute for it: either a substitute of the whole if the form is taken as an active participle, or a substitute of inclusion if it is taken as a verbal noun. Its benefit is to specify the aspect of arguing by what Allah has opened, since arguing by it can be conceived in many ways. It is as if it were said: that they may argue with you by it through its being in His Book, i.e., they would say: it is mentioned in His Book in which you believed. By this the unity of His saying "with it" (i.e., by what Allah has opened to you) with His saying "before your Lord" becomes clear. The objection that it cannot be a substitute, because a substitute and what it replaces must agree in case, is answered: here they do not agree, since the second is an adverbial phrase of place and the first is an object with a preposition. It was also said that the meaning is: "with what is before your Lord," so the adverbial phrase is a circumstantial element (hal) from the pronoun in "with it," its purpose being to make explicit that the argument is with a matter established before Him, exalted is He, even though this is understood from "what Allah has opened." It was also said: "before the mention of your Lord," so the speech is elliptical, the intended "mention" being the Book, and the arguing by what Allah has opened is taken as arguing before Him in a figurative sense. All these views are based on the argument being in this world, which is clear, since this world is the abode of argument. The interpretation of "before your Lord" in these views is figurative. It was also said that "before your Lord" is literal, and the argument takes place on the Day of Resurrection. It was objected that concealment does not prevent this argument, for concealment is either so that the believers do not learn what they would argue with, which they already have through revelation, or so that the one being argued against has a way to deny; and in that case it would not be possible before Him on the Day of Resurrection. It cannot be supposed of the People of the Book that they believed that concealing what is in the Book in this world would prevent the argument by its being in it in the Hereafter, for that would be a belief that Allah does not know what He sent down in His Book, and they are innocent of that. The view that the meaning is "that they may argue with you on the Day of Resurrection, and in the presence of the questioning," so that it adds to the exposure of your disgrace and rebuke before the assembled witnesses on the great standing, is one that the people held: they believed that the manifestation of that in this world would increase it in the Hereafter, distinguishing between one who confessed and concealed and one who persisted in denial. Or it was said that arguing by "you were delivered and you opposed" is prevented by concealment; this is answered by the fact that concealment in that case prevents only argument by their confession, not by what Allah has opened to them; and moreover, what is prevented in the first aspect is increased rebuke and exposure, not the argument itself. It was also said: "before your Lord" is with the implied "from before your Lord," and it is governed by His saying "by what Allah has opened to you"; this is something that should not be committed in eloquent speech. Al-Damghani permitted that "before" means "for nearness," i.e., that they may argue with you by it, drawing near to Allah, exalted is He; this too is distant, like the saying of some later scholars that arguing by it before the Lord can be taken as a metaphor for mutual invocation (mubahalah) in establishing what they narrate, and on that basis the arguing is in accordance with the reciprocal form. In my view, the pronoun in "with it" returns to "what Allah has opened" insofar as it is what is narrated, and the qualifier is made the main point; or it returns to the narrating understood from "do you speak to them." Taking "before your Lord" as the Day of Resurrection, and holding that concealment prevents this argument, is not far-fetched, though no one has explicitly stated it; and perhaps it is preferable to some of the views. Reflect on this.

"Do you not then reason?" It is conjoined either to "do you speak to them," and the "fa" indicates that their lack of reason follows from their speaking; or to an implied clause, i.e., "do you not then reflect and so not reason?" This sentence reinforces the denial of speaking and is part of the speech of the rebukers. Its object is either what was mentioned first, or there is no object, which is more eloquent. It was also said that it is an address from Allah, exalted is He, to the believers, connected to His saying "do you then hope," and the meaning is: "Do you not reason the state of these Jews, and that there is no hope in their believing, while they have these reprehensible attributes and ugly characters?" This is made distant by His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Do they not know?﴾ This is a rebuke from Him, the Exalted, concerning what He related about them. Therefore, inserting the address to the believers in the midst of it is like placing a separation between the tree and its bark. Moreover, there is a certain strain in restricting the address to the believers, and generalizing it to the Prophet (ﷺ) is, as is well known, a breach of etiquette. The interrogation here is for denial together with reproach, because the People of the Book knew of the all-encompassing knowledge of Allah, the Exalted. The intended purpose is to show the grave wickedness of their act, namely that they do what has been mentioned while knowing.

﴿That Allah knows what they conceal and what they reveal.﴾ In this there is an indication that one who commits disobedience while knowing that it is disobedience bears a greater burden. The waw is for coordination with an implied element that the mind is led to. The pronoun refers to those who were reproached, meaning: Do they blame them for the aforementioned speech, out of fear of being challenged, while not knowing what has been mentioned? It has been said that the pronoun refers to the hypocrites only, or to them and to those reproached, or to their forefathers who distorted (the Scripture). The apparent reading is to take "what" in both places as general, and it includes the disbelief they concealed and the faith they displayed. Some exegetes restricted it to these two. It has also been said that it refers to enmity and friendship, and it has been said that it refers to the description of him (ﷺ) in the revealed Torah, and the description they displayed as a fabrication against Allah, the Exalted. He, glory be to Him, placed concealment before display either because the rank of the secret precedes the rank of the open, since nothing is made public except that it, or its beginnings, was previously hidden in the heart, to which concealment usually attaches; so the connection of His knowledge to its first state precedes its connection to its second state. Or it is to announce their exposure and the befalling of what they feared from the very beginning. Or it is for emphasis in showing the comprehensiveness of His all-encompassing knowledge of all things, such that His knowledge of what they conceal is more ancient than His knowledge of what they make public, although in reality both are on an equal footing. For His knowledge, exalted be He, is not by way of the acquisition of a form; rather, the existence of each thing in itself is knowledge in relation to Him, the Exalted. In this sense the situation does not differ between things that are manifest and things that are hidden. The matter is reversed in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾, because the principle regarding what accountability attaches to is the manifest matters, not the hidden ones.

Ibn Muhaysin read (﴿أوَ لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾), with the ta', so it is possible that this is an address to the believers, or an address to them. Then He, the Exalted, turned away from addressing them and returned the pronoun to the third person, neglecting them, and this would be a case of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 78:**

﴿And among them are unlettered people who do not know the Book﴾ is a resumptive clause (musta'nafah), brought to explain the ugly traits of the ignorant among the Jews, following the explanation of the abominable deeds of the earlier groups. It has been said that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with ﴿And there was a group among them﴾, and on that basis the plural is used. It has also been said that it is coordinated with ﴿And when they meet﴾. Some later scholars chose that the clause which it is coordinated with is an interjection (i'tirad) that occurred in between, to explain the categories of Jews by way of digression (istitrad) to those distorters.

*Ummiyyun* is the plural of *ummi*, which, as in *al-Mughrib*, means one who neither writes nor reads. It is attributed to the Arab nation (ummat al-'Arab), who used not to write or read. It is also said to be attributed to *al-umm* (mother), in the sense that he is as his mother bore him, or to *Umm al-Qura*, because its people generally did not write. The intended meaning is that they are ignorant. "The Book" is the Torah, as the context and the flow of the wording require. The definite article in it is either for prior reference (al-'ahd), or it is one of the dominant proper designations. Taking it as a verbal noun of *kataba kitaban*, with the article for genus, is remote.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read *ummiyyun* with the letter *ya* lightened. ﴿Except wishful fancies﴾: *amaniyy* is the plural of *umniyyah*, whose original form is *umnuwnah* (on the pattern *uf'ulah*).
