Originally it is what a person conjectures within himself of wishes when he conjectures. For this reason it is applied to falsehood, to what one wishes for, and to what is recited. What is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with them, is that *al-amani* here means lies, namely falsehoods they took on the authority of their distorting devils. It has also been said: it means the wishful beliefs they hold, that Allah the Exalted will pardon them, have mercy on them, and not hold them accountable for their sins, and that their forefathers, the prophets, will intercede for them. It has been said: it means mere promises they heard from their rabbis, such as that no one enters Paradise except one who is a Jew (hud), and that the Fire will not touch them except for a number of days. Abu Muslim chose this view, and on it the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), because what they hold of falsehoods, or what they heard of lies, is not part of the Book. It has also been said: it means only what they recite as ordinary recitation without knowing its meaning and reflecting upon it, so the exception is then connected (muttasil) on the apparent reading. It has also been said that it is disjunctive too, since what is recited is not of the same kind as knowledge of the Book. This view has been objected to on the grounds that it does not fit the explanation that follows with what is in *al-Mughrib*. It was answered that its meaning is that he does not read from the Book and does not know the script. Or it is by way of taking from others, for they often recite without knowledge of the meanings or the shapes of the letters. This is strained, since one does not call a blind memorizer unlettered. Yes, if *ummi* is explained as one who does not do well in writing and reading, as a group of scholars held, then it does not preclude that he writes and reads to some degree.

It is argued for this by what al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), on the day of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, took the document while he did not do well at writing, and wrote: "This is what Muhammad, son of 'Abd Allah, agreed to," and so on. Whoever explains *ummi* by what preceded at the beginning of the hadith, that he "wrote" in the sense of commanded writing, has been answered. Some commentators on the hadith extended the discussion on this point, but this is not its place.

Abu Ja'far, al-A'raj, and Ibn Jammaz, from Nafi', and Harun, from Abu 'Amr, read *amaniyya* with the letter *ya* lightened. ﴿But they only suppose﴾: the exception here is an exception with an omitted subject (istithna mufarragh), and the excepted noun has been omitted, its attribute being placed in its stead. That is, they are only people whose utmost matter is conjecture, without attaining the level of knowledge. So how can faith founded on the foundations of certainty be expected from them? The term *zann* (supposition) is sometimes applied to what is opposed to certain knowledge based on a decisive proof, whether it is held without any proof, or with an unsound proof, or is not held firmly. Thus ascribing supposition to them does not conflict, if they hold it with conviction.

[Page 302]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 79:

﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands.﴾ *Al-waylu* (woe, ruin) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) that has no verb derived from its own root. What is reported from some speakers, *wala* (as a made-up form), appears in *al-Bahr* (al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan). Similar words are *waykh*, *waybun*, *waysun*, *wayhun*, and *awlun*. It has no dual and no plural. It is also said *waylah*, whose plural is *waylat*. When it is followed by a genitive (*idafah*), the best reading is with the accusative (*nasb*), and according to some scholars nothing else is permitted. When it stands alone, the nominative (*raf'*) is preferred. Its meaning is disgrace and regret. Al-Khalil said it means the intensity of evil. Ibn al-Mufaddal said it means grief. Others said it means destruction. Al-Asma'i said it is an expression of lamentation, and it may also be an expression of pity. From this is the saying: "Woe to his mother, the one who kindles war (*mis'ar harb*)."

It has been transmitted through several chains, which the hadith scholars (*huffaz*) have authenticated, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "*Al-waylu* is a valley in Hell, into which the disbeliever is cast and falls for forty autumns before he reaches its bottom." In some narrations: "It is a mountain in it." Applying the word to this is either a technical Islamic usage (*haqiqah shar'iyyah*) or a linguistic metaphor (*majaz lughawi*), by using the name of the one who resides for the place where he resides. It cannot be a literal linguistic usage (*haqiqah lughawiyyah*), because the Arabs used it in their poetry and prose before the Qur'an came, and they did not apply it to that.

In any case, here it is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is "*li-alladhina*" (for those who). If it is a definite proper noun, then the matter is clear. Otherwise, what permitted its use as a subject is that it is a supplication (*du'a'*). It has been changed from the accusative verbal noun to indicate permanence and continuance. Such a construction is permissible for it, because it is not a predicated subject. It is also said that the indefiniteness of the word is specified by the one who calls down the curse, as *salam* is specified in "*salamun 'alayka*" (peace be upon you) by the one who greets, since the meaning is "my greeting upon you." Similarly, the meaning here is: my supplication against them for destruction is established for them.

Writing is well known. Mentioning the hands is for emphasis, to remove the suspicion of metaphor. It is said: the first to write with a pen was Idris, and it is also said Adam, peace be upon them both. The intended "Book" is the altered one. It is related that they wrote in the Torah what indicates the opposite of the description of the Prophet (ﷺ), spread it among their fools and among the Arabs, and hid the copies that they had without alteration. When they were asked about the Prophet (ﷺ), they said: "This is not the one described in our Torah." They would bring out the altered Torah, read it, and say: "This is the Torah that was sent down from Allah."

It is possible that the intended meaning is what they wrote of false interpretations (*ta'wilat za'ighah*), and they circulated these among the common people. Some scholars have said: No divinely revealed book has been free of containing a mention of the Prophet (ﷺ), but by an allusion that only the learned know. If it had been clear to the common people, their scholars would not have been rebuked for concealing it. Then this became even more obscure through its transmission from one language to another. Words have been found in the Torah which, when considered, show the authenticity of his prophethood, peace be upon him, by an implication that is clear to the firmly grounded (*rasikhun*) in knowledge and obscure to the common people. So some Jewish rabbis (*ahbar*) deliberately interpreted it and wrote their distorted interpretations with their own hands. Then they would say: "This is from Allah," to magnify its status and to establish it in the hearts of their unlettered followers.

The "*thumma*" (then) is for remote sequence in rank (*lil-tarakhi al-rutbi*), since explicitly attributing the distortion and the false interpretation to Allah, glorified is He, is more shameful than the distortion and interpretation itself. The demonstrative (*al-ishara*) refers either to all of it or to a particular part.

﴿in order to exchange it for a small price.﴾ That is, in order to obtain, by what they indicated, an aim from the base aims of this world. Even if it is great, it is the smallest of small things compared with what they deserved of the everlasting punishment and what they were deprived of from the enduring reward. This clause is the cause (*'illah*) of the saying, as in *al-Bahr*. I do not see in the verse any proof for prohibiting taking a wage for writing copies of the Qur'an, nor for disliking selling them. Al-A'mash interpreted the verse and used it as evidence for disapproval, but the fair-minded eye is blind to that. Yes, a group of scholars held disapproval, among them Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and some imams said so. But I do not think they use this verse as evidence, and the full discussion belongs in its proper place.

﴿So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.﴾ The "fa" (so) is for detailing what was summarized in His words, exalted is He: "So woe to those who write," and so on. It indicates that the woe is established for those described by what was mentioned, because of their being characterized by it, on the basis of attaching the judgment to the attribute, without indicating that it is established because of the whole of what was mentioned first, but rather because of each one. So He explained that by saying "woe to them," and so on, together with what it contains of explicitly stating the cause. The exaggeration in warning, reprimand, and terror contained in this summary and detail is not hidden.

"*Min*" (for, because of) is causal (*ta'lili*), attached to "woe" or to the stability (*al-istiqrar*) in the predicate. "*Ma*" is said to be a relative noun (*mawsulah ismiyyah*), with its returning pronoun omitted, meaning "what their hands wrote." It is also said to be a verbal-masdar (*masdariyyah*). The first is more effective in restraining from engaging in distortion, and the second in restraining from distortion itself. The second "*ma*" is similar to the first. Some scholars preferred the verbal-masdar in both places, both in wording and in meaning, because the returning pronoun is not then to be supplied. Also, what a servant truly earns is his own act for which he is punished or rewarded. Some researchers (*muhaqqiqun*) mentioned that the verified view is that the servant is punished for the act itself, and also for its effect, because it leads to another prohibited act. Here, it leads to misguiding others and to eating what is forbidden. He distinguished between the two verses: in the first He showed that they deserve punishment for the act itself, and in the second that they deserve it for its effect. For this reason the "fa" came. It is not hidden that this is a statement devoid of verification, as is not hidden to the people of close scrutiny. From what we have mentioned, the benefit of mentioning "woe" three times becomes clear.

It is also said that its benefit is that the Jews committed three crimes: changing the description of the Prophet (ﷺ), slandering Allah, Exalted, and taking bribes. So each crime was threatened with "woe." It seems that the author took the benefit to lie in His words, "So woe to those who," up to the end of the conjoined clause, as in the report "A man should not lead people in prayer and single out himself with supplication." Although this is far-fetched, it does not clearly show the reason for introducing "fa" in the second.

Furthermore, the apparent reading is that the object of the earning is specific, namely what the context of the verse indicates. It is also said that what they earn means all evil deeds, so as to include speech. But its remoteness is not hidden. He did not mention speech because it is among the beginnings of promoting "what their hands have written." The verse was revealed about the Jewish rabbis who feared that their leadership would be lost if the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) remained as it was, so they changed it. It is also said that their kings feared for their kingship if the people believed, so they bribed them, and they distorted [the text].

[Page 304]

As for the view that it was revealed about those who did not believe in any prophet and did not follow any book, but wrote a book with their own hands, made lawful in it what they chose, made unlawful what they chose, and said, "This is from Allah," it is unacceptable. Likewise the view that it was revealed about 'Abd Allah ibn Sarh, the scribe of the Prophet (ﷺ), who used to alter the Qur'an and then apostatized, is unacceptable.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 80:**

﴿And they said: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few days."﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah ḥāliyyah*), conjoined (*ma'ṭūfah*) to His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And a group of them had already...﴾ According to some scholars, it is conjoined to the group's statement, and according to others to ﴿And when you killed...﴾, as a narrative conjoined to a narrative. Some of the verifiers (*al-muḥaqqiqūn*) chose that it is a parenthetical insertion (*i'tirāḍ*) to refute what they said when they were threatened, upon what preceded, with ﴿woe﴾. Indeed, according to him, all the clauses from His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Do you then hope...﴾ up to His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And when We took the covenant...﴾ and so on, are mentioned as a digression (*istiṭrād*) between the two conjoined narratives. Thus the pronoun in (*qālū*) refers to "those who write the Book." The *mass* (*massa*) is the contact of one of two things with another in the manner of sensation and striking. Al-Raghib mentioned that it is like *lams* (touching), but *lams* may be used for seeking a thing even if it is not found, as in the verse of poetry:

*"I seek him, but I do not find him."*

By "the Fire" is meant the Fire of the Hereafter. By "the counted" is meant the limited, the few. He expressed "the counted" as a metonym for "the few," because the Arabs, due to their lack of knowledge of calculation and its rules, pictured the few as easily counted and the many as hard to count. So they said: "a thing that is counted" meaning few, and "not counted" meaning many. The view that fewness is derived from the fact that when time is long it is not counted in days but in months, years and centuries, is problematic in light of His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Fasting has been prescribed for you... for a certain number of days﴾ and His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿And We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾. It is also narrated from them that they would be punished for forty days, the number of their worship of the calf, then it would be proclaimed: "Bring out every circumcised one from the Children of Israel." In another narration: they would be punished for seven days, one day for every thousand years of the days of this world, which totals seven thousand years. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they claimed they found written in the Torah: "The distance between the two edges of Hell is a journey of forty years, until one reaches the tree of Zaqqum, and they will cross in each day a journey of a year, and so they will complete it." They said this when the Prophet (ﷺ) entered Medina, and the Muslims heard it, so this verse was revealed.

﴿Say: "Have you taken a covenant with Allah?"﴾ This is a rebuke and reproach to them. "Covenant" (*'ahd*) is a metaphor for His information (*khabar*) or His promise of the Fire not touching them except for the counted days. That was called a covenant because it is more emphatic than covenants reinforced by oath or vow. Qatadah interpreted it here as "promise," citing His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah...﴾ up to His, glorified is He, saying: ﴿because they broke with Allah what they had promised Him﴾.

It has been objected that there is no basis for restricting it, since ﴿Will not touch us...﴾ and so on is a consequence of promise and threat, because the touching of the Fire is a threat. It was answered that the verse did not address the threat because the intended matter of the interrogation is the promise, not the threat, since the threat is established against them. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the meaning of the verse is: "Have you said: 'There is no god but Allah,' and believed and obeyed, so that you may rely on that and know your exit from the Fire?" It returns to: "Have you sent ahead with Allah deeds that necessitate what you claim?" The first meaning is more apparent. Ibn Kathir and Hafs read with clear pronunciation of the *dhāl* (*idhhār*), and the rest with its assimilation (*idghām*). The *hamzat al-wasl* was dropped from (*ittakhadhtum*) because it falls in running speech (*al-darj*).

﴿Then Allah will not break His covenant.﴾ This is the answer (*jawāb*) to an implied condition (*shart muqaddar*), meaning: "If you have taken a covenant with Allah, then it will not be broken." Al-'Allamah estimated it as: "If you have indeed taken [a covenant]," since the meaning is not about the future, and this is based on the principle that the particle of condition does not change the meaning of the past tense, a matter on which there is a well-known disagreement. If you say: it is not valid to make ﴿then Allah will not break...﴾ a consequence (*jaza'*) because the causal relation is impossible, and the sequence is impossible since (*lan*) is purely for the future; I say: that is not necessary in the eloquent *fa* (*al-fā' al-faṣīḥah*), as in the verse:

*"They said: 'Khurasan is the farthest that we are aimed at; then the return, for we have come to Khurasan.'"*

Even if it be granted, the judgment of not breaking the covenant regarding the future time only has been ordered upon taking the covenant, as in His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿Whatever blessing you have is from Allah﴾. So al-'Allamah stated. The first answer is based on the view that the eloquent *fa* does not contradict the estimation of a condition, and that it indicates that what follows it is the cause of the omitted matter, whether it is consequent upon it or delayed, because it depends on another matter. The evidence is that the statement "then we have come to Khurasan" is known to them in the eloquent *fa* together with its being under the estimation of a condition without consequence, as in the commentary on *al-Miftah al-Sharifi*. The basis of the second answer is that what is meant is their judgment, not His judgment at the time of revelation. Because of the obscurity of that, al-Mawla 'Isam said: "The more apparent is that it is the evidence of the consequent placed in its position, i.e., if you have taken a covenant with Allah, then you have been saved, because Allah will not break His covenant. So understand."

Some people do not estimate an omitted matter and make the *fa* causal, so that the taking of the covenant is consequent upon the non-breaking of the covenant by Allah, and the indefinite noun is then the whole. So reflect.

This clause, as Ibn 'Atiyyah said, is parenthetical between (*ittakhadhtum*) and its counterpart (*mu'ādil*), so it has no place in grammatical analysis (*i'rāb*). The manifest mention of the Glorious Name is to indicate the cause of the judgment, since non-breaking is a requirement of divinity. The covenant is attached to His pronoun, exalted is He, for the same reason, or because what is meant is all His covenants due to its generality by annexation, so the specific covenant is included, while avoiding explicit affirmation of the realization of the content of their statement, even though it is conditional upon taking the conditional bound to the ropes of non-existence. Whoever holds that there is no breaking in promise and threat has used the verse, by taking the covenant to mean information that includes both. Some claimed that the covenant is apparent in the promise, indeed a customary (*ḥaqīqah 'urfiyyah*) real meaning in it, so there is no evidence in it for negating breaking in the threat.

﴿Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾ "Or" (*am*) may be connected (*muttaṣilah*) for equalization between two things, meaning: "Which of these two has occurred: your taking of a covenant, or your saying about Allah what you do not know?" That was brought out as an expression of one hesitant in determining it, in the manner of confirmation (*taqrīr*) for those addressed, because the questioner, who is the Prophet (ﷺ), knows that one of them has occurred, namely their statement, with regard to what they do not know, definitely. So the interrogation is not in its literal sense. From this it is known that what comes after connected *am* may be a sentence, because equalization may be between two judgments, and Ibn al-Hajib expressly stated this in *al-Idah*. It is possible that it is disconnected (*munqaṭi'ah*) in the sense of *bal* (rather), and the estimate is: "Rather, do you say...?" The meaning of *bal* here is turning away and moving from rebuke for taking to what its *hamzah* conveys of rebuke for saying. The apparent words of the author of *al-Miftah* stipulate disconnection, since he made the sign of the disconnected as that what follows it is a sentence. The rebuke was linked to their attributing to Him, glorified and exalted is He, what they do not know to have occurred, although what they attributed to Him is of the kind of what they know not to have occurred, for the sake of emphasis in rebuke, since rebuke for the lesser entails rebuke for the greater, by way of priority. Their statement as reported, although it is not explicit in fabricating against Him, may He be exalted, it necessarily implies it, because that certainty can only be by attributing its cause to Him, exalted is He.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 81:**

﴿Yes! Whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ This is a response to their stated claim, and a refutation of it in a more general form that includes them and all the disbelievers. It is as if He said: "Rather, you and others will be touched (by the Fire) for a long time and an extended period, not as you claim." The affirmation of the universal principle serves as a proof for refuting that claim, by making it the major premise (*kubra*) of an easily accepted minor premise (*sughra*). So *bala* (بَلى) is attached to what comes after it. The concision of abbreviation (*ijaz al-ikhtisar*) is more eloquent than the concision of omission (*ijaz al-hadhf*). Some claimed that *bala* is attached to an omitted element, and that the meaning is "(you will be touched) for a few counted days." This is not correct. *Bala* is a particle of response, like *jayr* and *na'am*, except that it is only used as a response to a preceding negation, whether or not that negation contains an interrogative. It affirms what the negation denied. It is a simple (non-compound) particle. It was also said that its origin is *bal* (بَلْ) to which an *alif* was added. *Kasb* (earning) means acquiring a benefit. *Sayyi'ah* (evil deed) means a grave offense that makes the Fire obligatory. This is the view of al-Suddi, and the interpretation of those who explained it as "major sin" (*kabirah*) is based on it, because it is what makes the Fire obligatory, meaning that its doer deserves the Fire unless he is forgiven.

[p. 306]

Many of the early Muslim generations (*al-salaf*) held that here it means disbelief (*kufr*). Attaching *kasb* to *sayyi'ah* is in the manner of mockery (*tahakkum*). It was also said that by committing the evil deed they acquired a small, transient benefit, and on this basis *kasb* was applied to it. By *ihatah* (encompassing) is meant domination, comprehensiveness, and the covering of the outward and inward. *Khati'ah* means evil deed, and it is predominantly used for what is intended incidentally (*bil-'arad*), meaning it is not intended in itself. Rather, the intention is directed to something else, but that act resulted from it. Like someone who shoots at game and hits a person, or who drinks an intoxicant and thereby commits a crime. Some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*) said: "For this reason, He attributed the encompassing to it (*khati'ah*), indicating that evil deeds, in terms of the quality of encompassing, fall under what is intended incidentally, because it results from forgetting repentance. And because it is firmly established in him and fixed at the time of encompassing, He attributed it to him. This is unlike the state of earning, for that is directly the object of intention and is not present in him, let alone firmly established. Therefore, He attributed the earning to an *sayyi'ah* and made it indefinite." The attribution of "companions" (*ashab*) to "the Fire" means constant attachment, because companionship, although it includes little and much, is in common usage specifically restricted to frequency and constancy. For this reason, they said: "If someone who meets Zayd swears that he has not accompanied him, he does not break his oath." By *khulud* (abiding) is meant lasting. There is no proof in the verse for the eternal abiding of the one who commits a major sin, because encompassing is only valid regarding the disbeliever. As for others, if they have nothing except the affirmation of their heart and the verbal confession of their tongue, then their sin has not encompassed them, because their heart and tongue are free from sin. This does not depend on the affirmation and confession being good deeds, but only on their not being evil deeds. Therefore, the objection does not arise that the opponent makes action a condition for them to be good deeds, just as he makes belief a condition for actions to be good deeds. So, according to him, it is not established that encompassing is only valid regarding the disbeliever. And there is no need for the answer that the intention is that there is no proof for him in the verse. This is complete merely by the fact that encompassing is prohibited in the case of non-disbelievers. So if it were established that action falls within faith, the verse would become a proof, and without establishing it, it is "scratching thorns" (an impossible task). Furthermore, the negation of the proof through interpreting encompassing as stated is only needed if *sayyi'ah* and *khati'ah* have one meaning, which is general grave offense. But if *sayyi'ah* is interpreted as disbelief, or *khati'ah* as disbelief, as narrated by Ibn Abi Hatim from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, and Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ibn Jarir from Abu Wa'il, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ata', and al-Rabi', then the negation of the proof is more evident than fire on a mountain (i.e., it is self-evident).

Some people negated it by interpreting *khulud* according to its original lexical meaning, which is a long stay. This is not correct, because it entails diminishing the gravity in a context of intimidation, and it is also not compatible with interpreting *khulud* in Paradise as permanence. Likewise, there is no proof in His saying: ﴿And they said: The Fire will not touch us except for a few days﴾ etc., based on what al-Jubba'i claimed, when he said: "The verse indicates that He did not promise Moses, nor any of the prophets after him, that the people of major sins and disobedience would be removed from the Fire after being punished. Otherwise, He would not have denounced the Jews with His saying: ﴿Say: Have you taken a covenant with Allah?﴾ etc. It is established that He threatened the sinners with punishment to deter them from disobedience. So it is established that their punishment would be permanent. And when that is established for the other nations, it must be established for this nation, since threat cannot differ among nations when the degree of disobedience is the same. Because what Allah denounced them for was their certainty that the punishment would be light since it would end completely. Moreover, that applies to disbelievers, not sinners, as is not hidden."

(*Man*) may be conditional, or it may be relative (*mawsulah*). The factors permitting the entry of the *fa'* (فَ) into the predicate when the subject is a relative pronoun are present. What makes the relative reading preferable is that the relative pronoun appears in its counterpart. And the demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*) indicates the presence in the mind of the one being pointed to with all his attributes, to signal that these attributes are the cause of their being companions of the Fire. And the element of distance in it indicates how far they are in disbelief and sins. They were pointed to with the plural form, taking into account the meaning of the word *man* after taking into account its form in the three pronouns, because that is what is appropriate to what was attributed to them in those two states. For earning an evil deed and the encompassing of sin around him in the state of singularity, and being companions of the Fire in the state of plurality. So said some of the verifiers, and it is not without merit.

Nafi' read *khati'atuhu* (خَطِيئَآتُهُ), and some read *khatiyyahu* (خَطِيّاهُ), *khatiyyatuhu* (خَطِيَّتُهُ), and *khatiyyatuhu* (خَطِيّاتُهُ), with metathesis (*qalb*) and assimilation (*idgham*). They regarded the plural reading as better, because encompassing does not apply to a single thing. The singular reading was justified by saying that although *khati'ah* is singular, because it is attached to a plural pronoun it is plural in meaning. Also, a single thing may encompass, like a ring. So do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 2, verse 82:

﴿Those who believe and do righteous deeds—they are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide forever.﴾ When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the people of the Fire and the destruction prepared for them, He followed that with mention of the people of faith and the everlasting life prepared for them in the Gardens. It is His customary practice, exalted is His majesty, to couple His promise with His threat, in accordance with what wisdom requires in guiding the servants, by encouragement at one time and warning at another. It has been said that combining them serves to reinforce the threat by mentioning the reward its people have missed, and to reinforce the promise by mentioning the punishment its people have escaped. The conjunction of "deeds" with "faith" indicates that deeds are outside its definition (*musamma*), since a part is not conjoined with the whole. It does not, however, indicate that faith is not conditioned by deeds, so as to show that the perpetrator of a grave sin is not outside faith. The verse may serve as proof against the Wa'idiyya (the group who hold that the divine threat must be fulfilled), as al-Mawla 'Isam said. If one objects that the opponent may say the conjunction is for honour, because deeds are harder and more arduous than assent, and the most excellent deeds are the most arduous, the reply is that faith is nobler than deeds, because it is the foundation of all good deeds, since deeds fall from the level of consideration when it is absent. It occurs to the mind that mentioning righteous deeds here alongside faith may have a subtle purpose: faith corresponds to the evil deed explained by some as disbelief, and righteous deeds correspond to the sin explained as everything other than that. By "those who believe" is meant the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the believers of the nations before them. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and others, and it is the apparent meaning. Ibn Zayd said that it refers specifically to the Prophet (ﷺ) and his community.

As for the presence of the *fa'* (ﻓ, "so") in what preceded and its absence here: either because a threat from the Generous One is more liable to be broken than a promise, so the first was fit for emphasis and the second was not; or to indicate the precedence of mercy. The grammarians said: "Whoever enters my house, *fa-akrimhu* (so honour him)" implies honouring every entrant, but with the risk that he may not be honoured; without the *fa'*, "Whoever enters my house, akrimhu" implies honouring him absolutely. Or the absence indicates that their abiding in the Fire is because of their evil deeds and disobedience, while their abiding in Paradise is by the sheer grace and generosity of Allah, exalted is He; for otherwise faith and righteous deeds would not suffice to thank Allah for the immediate blessings the servant has received. Some scholars held each of these views. The claim that the omission of the *fa'* here is for the sake of greater eagerness in mentioning what they will receive is not worth anything.

[p. 308 begins at the next paragraph, after the marker "صفحة 308"]

﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ This begins a further enumeration of the vile deeds of the forefathers of the Jews, which call for doubt about the faith of their descendants. It has been said that this is another kind of the favours which Allah the Exalted bestowed upon them. This is because being charged with these duties leads to the greatest of favours, which is Paradise, and that which leads to a favour is itself a favour. This covenant was taken from them through Moses and others of their prophets, peace be upon them, or it was a covenant taken from them in the Torah. As for the statement of Makki, that it was a covenant Allah took from them while they were in their fathers' loins like particles of dust, its meaning does not appear to be relevant here.

﴿Serve none but Allah﴾ This is in the sense of "saying" (that is, "We said," or "saying"), so that it is connected to what precedes it. It is an informative statement with the meaning of a prohibition, like His saying: ﴿nor let any scribe or witness be harmed﴾, and like your saying: "You go to so-and-so and say to him such-and-such." This is the view of al-Farra', and what supports it is that it is more emphatic than an explicit prohibition, because it gives the impression that the one being prohibited has hastened to do it, so that it has already occurred from him, to the point that it is reported about him in the present or past tense; that is, it ought to be so. Thus there is no objection that the state of the one reported about contradicts this. Ibn Mas'ud recited it as "Do not serve" (لا تعبدوا) in the prohibitive form, and "say" (قولوا) is then conjoined to it, so that a semantic coherence arises between them in being imperatives, although it is permissible to conjoin an imperative to an informative statement where the latter has a place in i'rab (grammatical inflection). It has also been said that its underlying form is "that you do not serve." When the particle governing the verb is elided, the verb becomes marked by the nominative. The nominative is not obligatory after elision in such a construction, contrary to some grammarians. This is the view of al-Akhfash. A parallel from Arab prose is: "Tell him to dig it," and from Arab verse:

*"Unhappy one who rebukes me, attend the battle, and if I witness pleasures, will you make me immortal?"*

This is supported by the reading "that you do not serve" (أن لا تعبدوا). It is weakened, however, by the fact that "that" (أن) is not elided by analogy in positions where this does not apply, so the verse should not be explained on this basis. On this explanation, the phrase is a verbal noun in the form of a clause (مصدر مؤول), in apposition to "the covenant," or an object with the preposition elided, meaning "with [the condition] that not," or "on [the condition] that not." It has also been said that it is the answer to an oath implied by the context, meaning "We made them swear: you shall not serve," or that it is the answer to the covenant itself, since the covenant has the status of an oath. On this view the discourse is free of what was mentioned as the reason for preferring the first view. Nafi', Ibn Amir, Abu Amr, Asim and Ya'qub read it with the second person "you" (تعبدون), as a quotation of what they were addressed with. The rest read it with the third person "they" (يعبدون), because they are absent. In that case there are two shifts in the verse: in the name of Allah (the Divine name), and in "they serve" (يعبدون).

﴿And to parents, kindness﴾ This is connected to an implied verb whose estimated form is "and you will show kindness" or "show kindness," and the clause is conjoined to "serve." It is also permissible for it to be connected to "kindness" (إحسانا), which takes the preposition bi- ("to") and ila ("to"), as in ﴿He was good to me when He brought me out of the prison﴾ and ﴿and be good as Allah has been good to you﴾. To forbid the fronting of a complement of the verbal noun absolutely is itself forbidden. Some grammarians estimated the verb as "enjoin," so that "to the parents" (فبالوالدين) is connected to it, and "kindness" (إحسانا) is its object. Others estimated "We charged them," so that "kindness" is an object of purpose (مفعول لأجله). "Parents" (الوالدان) is the dual of "walid" (parent), since this word applies to both father and mother. Alternatively it is a dual by the principle of predominance (تغليب), on the basis that it is applied only to the father, as al-Halabi held. The verse indicates an exhortation to honour one's parents and to respect them. The verses and hadiths on this are numerous, and it suffices to show their importance that Allah, glorified is His name, joined this to His own worship.

﴿and to kinsfolk, orphans and the needy﴾ This is conjoined to "the parents." "Qurba" (kinship) is a verbal noun like "ruj'a" (return), and its alif is the feminine marker. It refers to kinship of blood and lineage. "Yatama" (orphans) is of the pattern fa'ala, and its alif is the feminine marker. It is the plural of "yatim" (orphan), like "nadim" and "nadama" (companion, companions). This plural pattern is not regular. It is also pluralized as "aytam." The root of "yutm" fundamentally means being alone, and from it comes the "lone pearl" (الدرة اليتيمة). Tha'lab said it means heedlessness, and the orphan is called "yatim" because he is neglected in terms of kindness. Abu Amr said it means delay, due to the delay of kindness towards him. In humans it derives from the fathers' side, and there is no orphanhood after puberty. In animals it derives from the mothers' side, and in birds from both. Al-Mawardi reported that it is also said of a human whose mother is lost, but the first usage is the well-known one. "Masakin" (the needy) is the plural of "miskin" on the pattern mif'il, derived from stillness (sukun), as if need had made him still. The mim is an added letter, like "mahdar" from "huduur" (presence). It has been reported that someone "tamaskana" (became needy), but the more correct form is "tasakkana," meaning he became needy. The difference between him and the poor (faqir) is well known, and it will come, Allah willing. This order has been adopted to give priority to the more emphatic. It began with the parents, since their precedence over everyone else in kindness towards them is clear. Then it moved to kinsfolk, because maintaining ties of kinship is emphasized, and because the parents share in kinship and are its source. It has been transmitted in a report that Allah the Exalted addressed the womb (rahim), saying: "(You are the womb, and I am the Merciful. I join with whoever joins you, and I sever from whoever severs you)." Then it moved to orphans, because they do not have full ability to earn. It has been related: "(I and the one who sponsors an orphan will be in Paradise like these two)," and he (ﷺ) indicated the index and middle fingers. The rank of the needy is placed later, because the needy man can look after himself by working and can manage his livelihood as far as possible, unlike the orphan, who being young cannot benefit himself and needs someone to benefit him. He used the singular "kinsman" (ذي القربى), as is mentioned in al-Bahr, because the generic is intended by it, and because its being added to the verbal noun includes every kinsman in it. There is also an indication that the kinsfolk, though many, are like one thing; one should not grow weary of showing kindness to them.

﴿and speak to people kindly﴾ That is, "a good word" (قولا حسنا). It was called "husn" for emphasis. It has also been said that it is a dialectal form of "husn," like "bukhl" and "bakhal," "rushd" and "rashad," and "'urb" and "'arab." The meaning is: say to them the good word, and answer them with the best that they love. This is the statement of Abu al-Aliyah. Sufyan al-Thawri said: enjoin upon them what is right and forbid them what is wrong. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: say to them, "There is no god but Allah," and command them with it. Ibn Jurayj said: inform them of what is in your Book about the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Abu al-Aliyah's statement is on the lofty level. The apparent view is that this command is part of the covenant taken from the Children of Israel. As for one who says that those addressed are the community (of Muhammad), and that it is a muhkam (firm, unabrogated) verse, or one abrogated by the verse of the sword, or that "people" is restricted to righteous believers, since good speech is not owed to unbelievers and sinners, because we have been commanded to curse them, censure them and fight them, then he has gone too far. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read "hasanan" with two fathas, while Ata' and Isa read it with two dammas, which is the dialect of the Hijaz. Abu Talhah ibn Musarrif read "husna" on the pattern fu'la. There is disagreement about its form. It has been said that it is a verbal noun like "ruj'a," but Abu Hayyan objected that it is not analogical and is not attested. It has been said that it is an adjective like "hubla," meaning "a word or statement that is good." There are two views on describing with it. The first is that it remains in its comparative sense, and its use without "al-" and without being annexed to a definite noun is rare, though it occurs in poetry, as in the line:

*"If you call to glory and nobility on a day when the noble chiefs of men are present, then call us."*

The second is that it is stripped of the comparative sense and means "good," as they said in "Joseph is the best of his brothers." Al-Jahdari read "ihsanan" as the verbal noun of "ahsana," whose hamza indicates becoming, as you say: "The land became green" (a'shabat al-ardu i'shaban), meaning it became full of herbage. It is then an adjective of an elided verbal noun, meaning "a speech characterized by goodness."

﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾ By these two He meant what was prescribed for them in their own religion, because this is a report of what occurred in the time of Moses, peace be upon him. Their zakat of wealth, as is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, was an offering: a fire would descend and consume it, and this was a sign of acceptance. What the fire did not consume in this way was not accepted. The view that these two refer to this prayer and this zakat prescribed upon us, and that the address is only to the sons of the Jews present in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that the command to them is a metaphor for the command to Islam, or to indicate that unbelievers are also addressed with the branches of the law, is not valid, as is not hidden.

﴿Then you turned away﴾ That is, you turned away from the covenant and abandoned it. "Thumma" (then) is for expressing improbability, or for the actual sense of delay, so that it is a rebuke to them for apostasy after obedience over a lengthy period, and this is more heinous than the disobedience from the first. Some scholars mentioned that if the governing verb of the adverbial phrase is taken to be an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers, then this is a shift to addressing all the Children of Israel, with their descendants given precedence over their ancestors, since all of them are mentioned at that point in the third-person manner. The earlier addresses to the ancestors are reported with the implied verb "We said" before "you serve not," as though they had been summoned at the mention of their crimes, and their faults were enumerated against them. If it is taken as an address to the contemporary Jews, then this is a generalization of the address by placing the ancestors in the position of the descendants, just as it is also a generalization of the turning away by placing the descendants in the position of the ancestors, for the sake of intensifying the rebuke. It has also been said that the shift occurs only on the reading "they do not serve" (لا يعبدون) in the third person, and that on the reading with the second person there is no shift. Some people took this address to be specific to those present in the time of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and what preceded it to be specific to those who came before. They took the shift to occur on both readings, but in a sense other than the technical one, since a shift between two addresses because of their difference has not been affirmed by the rhetoricians. Yet something like this occurs in the speech of some men of letters. What we have mentioned about predominance is better and more fitting, contrary to those who turned away from it.

﴿except a few of you﴾ These are, among the ancestors, those who maintained Judaism in its proper form before abrogation (naskh, the replacement of a ruling by a later one). Among the descendants, they are those who embraced Islam, such as Abdullah ibn Salam and his like. So the paucity is in the number of persons. The statement of Ibn Atiyyah, that it may be in faith, meaning that when they disobeyed and their last generation disbelieved in Muhammad (ﷺ), there remained only a little faith, since it would not benefit them, and only a few who were not given understanding of Arabic words would embrace it, is what he said. It is reported from Abu Amr and others that "qalilun" is read in the nominative. The more famous reading in such cases is the accusative, because what precedes it is affirmative. They differed on the analysis of the nominative. It has been said that the nominative noun is an emphasis of the pronoun, or in apposition to it, and this is permissible because "you turned away" has the sense of negation, that is, they did not fulfil. Several have cited in support the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), in what is authentically reported by the sound authorities: "(The learned are destroyed except those who act on their knowledge, those who act are destroyed except the sincere, and the sincere are in peril)," and the line of the poet:

*"In the stony ground among them is a dwelling, worn, effaced, changed, except the rain-marks and the stake."*

Abu Hayyan's statement that it is not valid, since every affirmative can be interpreted as negative, which would make permissible "The people stood up, except Zayd" with the nominative by interpretation and substitution, which the grammarians did not allow, is not valid, as is not hidden. It has also been said that "illa" (except) is an adjective meaning "other than," and that its i'rab appears in what follows it. Sibawayh devoted a chapter to this in his book, saying: "This is the chapter on what in which 'illa' and what follows it function as an adjective like 'ghayr' (other than)." He gave examples from this chapter, such as: "If there were with us a man except Zayd, we would have prevailed," and "Had there been in them gods except Allah, they would have been corrupted." And his saying:

*"They made their camels kneel and settled in a town above a town, in which the voices are few except its lowing."*

[End of part 1]

The rest of the list of all the preceding views has been derived from this. However, this is not consistent with what we are discussing except according to the school of Ibn 'Usfur (Ibn Usfur), who held that a descriptive modifier with ﴿إلا﴾ (illa, "except") differs from modifiers with other particles in that it can describe an indefinite noun and a definite noun, and an apparent noun and a pronoun. As for the view of others, namely Ibn Shahin (in relation to him), that it is not used as a modifier except when the modified noun is indefinite or definite with the definite article of genus, then it is not applicable here. Al-Mubarrad (al-Mubarrad) stipulates for its use as a modifier that it be suitable to stand as a badal (substitute, or apposition) in its place. It has also been said that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning "they did not say." Nothing from what has preceded refutes this, except that there is a discussion about it that we will mention, God willing, at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Except Iblis, who was not among those who prostrated﴾ (2:34).

﴿And you are turning away﴾ is a parenthetical clause, meaning: "and you are a people whose habit is turning away and turning one's back on the covenants." That it is their habit is understood from the nominal form, which indicates permanence. It has also been said that it is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal), and that turning away (tawalli) and aversion (i'rad) are one and the same thing. It is permissible for the emphatic circumstantial clause to be separated by a waw according to the verifiers (muhaqqiqun). Some have distinguished between tawalli and i'rad, saying that the former may occur due to a need that calls for departing while the covenant remains in force, whereas i'rad is departing from a thing in the heart. It has also been said that tawalli is when one's return turns back to its starting point, and i'rad is when one abandons the path and takes to the side of the road. The one who does tawalli is closer to the matter than the one who does i'rad, because whenever he resolves, it is easy for him to return to following the path, whereas the one who does i'rad, having abandoned the path and taken to the side of the road, needs to seek his path, so returning to it becomes difficult for him.

Some people have permitted that ﴿you are turning away﴾ be understood in its literal sense, and the clause be a restrictive circumstantial clause (hal muqayyadah), meaning: the few did not turn away, while ﴿you are turning away﴾ from them, angry with them. In this there is additional rebuke for them and praise for the few. But this is far-fetched, like the view that the clause is restrictive. The object of tawalli and i'rad differs: that is, you turned away by persisting in the covenant, and you turned away from following this Prophet (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 84:

﴿And when We took your covenant: You shall not shed your blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes.﴾ This is in the same manner as what preceded in ﴿You shall not worship [anyone but Allah]﴾. The meaning is that none of you should attack another by killing or expelling. Killing a man's fellow [believer] is treated as killing himself, because of their close bond by lineage or religion, or because it necessitates retaliation (qisas). Thus the verse contains a figurative usage (majaz), either in the pronoun (kum), where it refers to those who are connected to one another, or in (tasfikun), where what is meant is the cause of shedding. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not commit what would make the shedding of your blood, and your expulsion from your homes, permissible; or do not do what would destroy you and divert you from the pleasures of the eternal life, for that is truly killing. Do not commit what would bar you from the Garden, which is your abode. In reality, the banishment is not the expulsion from homelands but the distance from the gardens of Paradise. Perhaps what the noble structure of the verse supports is the first meaning.

Ad-dima' (blood) is the plural of dam (blood), a well-known word, and its missing radical (lam) is a ya' according to some, as in the line of poetry:

"The two bloods flowed with the certain news."

It is a waw according to others, based on their saying damawan. Its form is fa'ul or fa'il. It has also been heard as maqsur (short), and likewise as mushaddad (with doubled consonant). Talhah and Shu'ayb read (tasfukun) with a damma on the fa'. Abu Nahik read it with a damma on the ta', a fatha on the sin, and a kasra on the doubled fa'. Ibn Abi Ishaq did the same, except that he made the sin sukun and lightened the fa'.

﴿Then you acknowledged﴾, i.e., to the covenant, and you confessed its obligation, one generation after another. Al-iqrar (acknowledgment, affirmation) is the opposite of denial (jahd), and it takes the preposition bi. It has been said that it may mean leaving a thing in its state without acknowledging it, but this is not correct, since it does not fit the context in that case.

﴿And you were witnesses﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal), removing the possibility that acknowledgment refers to mentioning another matter; yet it necessarily entails it. Coordinating it by conjunction is not permitted due to its complete connection, nor is it an interjected parenthetical, since the meaning is not "and you were, as a habit, witnesses"; rather, the meaning is restrictive. It has been said: "And you, who are present, are witnesses to it, to the acknowledgment of your forefathers." In that case, attributing the acknowledgment to them is figurative. This was deemed weak, because then the abhorrence of killing and expulsion would be directed at them, even though the taking of the covenant and the acknowledgment came from their forefathers, given their connection to them by lineage and religion. This differs from the case where the attribution of acknowledgment to them is taken literally, for then it is by reason of their own acknowledgment and testimony, which is more eloquent in demonstrating the ugliness of their conduct. Some have claimed that the more apparent meaning is: you acknowledged while being witnesses to your own acknowledgment, in the way that each person witnesses the acknowledgment of another, as is the manner of testimony. The weakness of the emphasis in that case is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 85 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then you are these who kill your own selves﴾. It was revealed, as is mentioned in al-Bahr, concerning the Jewish tribes of Banu Qaynuqa', Banu Qurayza and Banu al-Nadir. Banu Qaynuqa' were enemies of Banu Qurayza, and al-Aws were allies of Banu Qaynuqa', while al-Khazraj were allies of Banu Qurayza. Al-Nadir, al-Aws and al-Khazraj were brothers, and Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir were brothers. Then they split apart, so Banu al-Nadir became allies of al-Khazraj, and Banu Qurayza became allies of al-Aws. They used to fight one another, and there occurred from them what God Most High has related, so God Most High reproached them for that. "Thumma" (then) here indicates remoteness in the occurrence [of the act], not temporal sequence, because it is what actually occurred, as has been said. "Antum" (you) is the subject (mubtada'), and "haw'ula'" (these) is its predicate (khabar), meaning: you, after that mentioned covenant, affirmation and testimony, are these violators, like your saying: "You are that man who did such-and-such." The apparent expectation would have been: "Then you, after that affirmation in the covenant, broke the pledge, so you kill your selves, etc.," meaning: your present state is not the state you were in before. But "haw'ula'" is inserted and made the predicate in order to convey that what changed is the very essence itself, as a rebuke to them for the severity of their breach of the covenant and their laxity regarding it. The change of essence is understood from placing the demonstrative, which is designed for the essence, in the position of the attribute, not from making a single referent both addressed and absent within one address; otherwise it would be understood likewise from something like ﴿Nay, you are a people who are ignorant﴾ also. The predication is valid with the consideration of change, since it is claimed figuratively, while in reality the referent is one. They are counted as present and witnessing with regard to the knowledge attached to the actions mentioned previously that were attributed to them, and as absent with regard to the non-attachment of knowledge to them concerning the actions that will be related of them later. This is not because sins necessitate absence from what is not present; otherwise the appropriate form would be the third person in "taqtulun" (you kill) and "tukhrijun" (you expel), as said by al-Salikuti. "Taqtulun" is either a circumstantial clause (hal), and its governing element is the meaning of the demonstrative, or it is an explanation (bayan), as if, when it was said: "Then you are these," they said: "How are we?" So "taqtulun" was brought as an explanation of it. It is also possible that it be made explanatory of it without presupposing a question. Ibn Kaysan and others held that "antum" is the subject, "taqtulun" is the predicate, and "haw'ula'" is a specification of the addressees, once they were alerted to the state they were persisting in, so it would then be in the accusative governed by "a'ni" (I mean). In this there is the objection that the grammarians stated that specification does not occur with demonstratives or with indefinite nouns, while the established usage of the Arabs is that it occurs with "ayyuha" (O you), as in "Allahumma ighfir lana ayyatuha al-'isaba" (O God, forgive us, O you group), and with the definite article, as in "nahnu al-'arab aqra al-nas lil-dayf" (we Arabs are the most generous of people to the guest), or with an annexation, as in "nahnu ma'ashira al-anbiya' la nurathu" (we, the company of prophets, are not inherited from). It may also occur with a proper name, as in "bina Tamiman nakshif al-dabab" (we, Tamim, uncover the dust-storm). It most often comes after a first-person pronoun, and it may also come after a second-person pronoun, as in "biki Allah narju al-fadl" (by you, O God, we hope for grace). It was also said: "haw'ula'" is a linguistic emphasis of "antum," so it is either a substitute (badal) for it or an explanatory apposition (atf bayan) upon it. Making it an emphasis by synonymous verbal repetition is a mistaken notion, and the discourse according to this view is free of that subtle point. It was also said: "haw'ula'" means "alladhina" (those who), and the clause is its relative clause, and the whole is the predicate. This is based on the school of the Kufans, who permitted all demonstratives to be relative pronouns, whether they come after "ma" or not, while the Basrans restrict this to when they come after the interrogative "ma." This is the sound view on which the discourse then becomes of the type of the poet's saying:

"I am the one whom my mother named Haydara"

And this is weak, as al-Shihab said. Al-Hasan read "tuqattilun" with intensive form (to indicate frequency), and in the tafsir of al-Mahdawi it is said that this is the reading of Abu Nahik. "Wa tukhrijuna fariqan minkum min diyarihim" (and you expel a group of you from their homes) is coordinated with what precedes it, and the pronoun in "diyarihim" refers to the group. The choice of the third person, even though the second person "diyarikum" would be permissible as in the first instance, is to guard against the supposition that the intended meaning is expelling them from the homes of the addressees, in that their homes are the homes of the addressees, and not the homes of those expelled. ﴿Supporting one another against them in sin and transgression﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "tukhrijuna" or from its object. It was said: or from both of them together, because it contains a pronoun referring to both, which specifies their condition. The meaning on the first view is: you expel while supporting one another against them; on the second: you expel a group who are supported against by you; and on the third: you expel while the support against them is being carried out by them. "Tazahur" means mutual assistance, and its root is from "zahr" (back), as if each of the two who assist one another leans his back upon the other. "Ithm" (sin) is the act for which its doer deserves blame and reproach. It was said: it is what the soul recoils from and the heart does not find peace in. And in a hadith: "Sin is what troubles your breast." It is connected to "tazahur" as a circumstantial clause from its subject, meaning: wearing sin, and its being a figurative usage here for what sin necessitates is the employment of the effect for its cause, as wine was called sin in the saying:

"I drank sin until my reason was lost; so sin takes away the intellects,"

because of what a caller calls to. "'Udwan" (transgression) is going beyond the limit in wrongdoing. 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "tazahurun" with the letter "zha'" lightened, and its original form was with two "ta'"s, of which the second was elided according to Abu Hayyan, and the first according to Hashim. The rest of the seven read it with doubling, by assimilating the "ta'" into the "zha'." Abu Haywa read "tuzahiruna" with a damma on the "ta'" and a kasra on the "ha'." Mujahid and Qatada, with variation from them, read "tazzahharun" with the "ta'," "zha'," and "ha'" all vowelled with fatha and doubled, without an alif, and it was also transmitted from Abu 'Amr. Some read "tatazahharun" in its original form.

﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾, i.e., you bring them out of captivity by giving ransom. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and Ibn 'Amir read "tafdu-hum" (you ransom them), and upon this is based part of the reading of the others, since there is no mutual action (mufa'ala) in it. Some scholars distinguished between "fada" and "fadda": the first means exchanging one captive for another captive, and the second means collecting ransom. This is contradicted by the saying of al-'Abbas, may God be pleased with him: "I ransomed myself, and I ransomed 'Aqil," since it is known that he did not exchange a captive for a captive. It was also said: "tufadu-hum" means with force, and "tafdu-hum" means with reconciliation. It was also said: "tufadu-hum" means you demand the ransom from the captive who is in your hands from your enemies, and from it is his saying:

"Stop, O one who ransoms your captive, for my people and your people, I do not see them having any festivity."

Abu 'Ali said: its lexical meaning is that you release them after you have taken something from them, and I think that here it is, like the preceding, in the utmost remoteness. The view that the meaning of the verse is: and if they come to you as captives in the hands of the devils, you strive to rescue them by guidance and admonition, while you waste yourselves to the bellies, is closer, as is not hidden. "Al-usara'" (captives) is said to be the plural of "asir" in the sense of "ma'sur" (one who is captured). It seems they treated "asir" as analogous to "kaslan" (lazy), so they formed its plural in the same way as they treated "kaslan," saying "kasla," as Sibawayh said. The point of resemblance is that captivity restrains one from much of his freedom of action, and the lazy person is restrained from that by his habit. It was also said: it is a plural from the beginning without analogy, as they said "qudama" as plural of "qadim." It was heard with the hamza vowelled with fatha, and this is not the most eminent form, contrary to some who claimed that fatha is the original and damma was adopted to increase its strength. It was also said: it is the plural of "usra," and with it Hamzah read, and it is the plural of "asir" like "jarih" and "jarha," so "usara" is a plural of a plural. This is said by al-Mufaddal. Abu 'Amr said: "al-asra" are those in the hand, and "al-usara'" are those in bonds. I do not see a distinction; rather, those taken by way of compulsion and domination, without qualification, are "asra" and "usara'."

﴿And its expulsion is forbidden to you﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "you expel a group of you," or from its object after considering the restriction by the preceding circumstantial clause. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if they come to you﴾ is a parenthetical interjection between them, not a coordinated element upon "tazahurun," because the coming was not concurrent with the expulsion. The expulsion was restricted by this circumstance to indicate that it was not from entitlement or from disobedience that necessitated it. Its specification by restriction, without killing, is for the sake of concern for its matter, since it is more severe than that. ﴿And sedition is worse than killing﴾. It was also said: no, rather it is because it is of lesser danger in comparison to killing, so it was a likely place for laxity. And because the discourse's thrust is to censure them and rebuke them for their crimes and the contradiction of their actions, and that is specific to the case of expulsion, since it was not reported from them that they made amends for the slain with any blood-money or retaliation. This is the secret in specifying the mutual support in what preceded. It was also said: the point in repeating the prohibition of expulsion, which had been conveyed by ﴿And you do not expel your selves﴾ in the most eloquent manner, and in specifying the prohibition of expulsion by repetition and not killing, is that they obeyed a ruling in the matter of the expelled, namely ransom, and contradicted a ruling, namely expulsion. So the prohibition of expulsion was joined with the ransom, so that it would be connected to it. ﴿Then do you believe﴾ etc., most closely connected, and their disbelief becomes clear through some and their belief through some with the fullest clarity, since it occurred concerning one single person. The pronoun is for the matter (dhamir al-sha'n), and the sentence after it is its predicate. It was said: its predicate is "muharram" (forbidden), and "ikhrajuhum" (their expulsion) is a substitute-subject (na'ib fa'il). This is the view of the Kufans, and al-Mahdawi followed them. They resorted to it because a predicate that contains a raised pronoun cannot be placed before the subject; therefore they do not permit "qa'imun Zayd" (standing is Zayd) with "qa'im" as a fronted predicate. The Basrans permit that, and they permit this view as well, because the pronoun of the matter is not predicated of, in their opinion, except by a sentence whose two parts are explicitly stated. It was also said: it is a pronoun of ambiguous reference, also a subject (mubtada'), and "muharram" is its predicate, and "ikhrajuhum" is a substitute for it that explains it. This is based on the permissibility of substituting a noun for a pronoun that has no antecedent preceding it, and some prohibited this; al-Kisa'i permitted it. It was also said: it refers back to the expulsion understood from "tukhrijuna," and "ikhrajuhum" is an explanatory apposition for it, or a substitute for it, or from the pronoun of "muharram." This was judged weak, because after its reference back to the expulsion there is no basis for making it a substitute for it. Among the strange things reported from the Kufans is that it may be possible that it is a pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl), and this was already mentioned along with the predicate. The estimated meaning is: "and their expulsion, it is forbidden to you," so when the predicate of the subject was fronted, it was fronted with it. The Basrans do not permit this, because the occurrence of a separator between a definite and an indefinite is not permitted according to them, since the definite is close to the indefinite. Its placement between the subject and predicate, or between what they are originally, is also a condition according to them. Ibn 'Atiyya had a discourse concerning this pronoun which must be elided. ﴿Do you believe in some of the Book and disbelieve in some?﴾ is coordinated upon "taqtulun" or upon an elided element, meaning: do you do what has been mentioned and then believe, etc.? The interrogative is for threat and rebuke concerning the division between God's rulings, since the covenant was with three things: abandoning killing, abandoning expulsion, and ransoming the captives. They killed and expelled contrary to the covenant, and they ransomed in accordance with its requirement. It was also said: the covenants were four, and abandoning support was added. Ibn Jarir reported from Abu al-'Aliya that 'Abdullah ibn Salam passed by the head of

...al-Jalut in Kufa, and he would ransom the women whom the Arabs had not taken captive, but would not ransom those whom the Arabs had taken. Abdullah ibn Salam said to him: "Indeed, it is written in your Book that you must ransom all of them." Muhyi al-Sunnah related from al-Suddi that Allah, exalted is He, took a covenant from the Children of Israel in the Torah that none of them should kill another, nor expel one another from their homes, and that whichever slave or female slave you find from the Children of Israel, you should buy them with the price that is due for them and free them. Perhaps their disbelief in what they committed was because they believed the prohibition had no force, despite the clear indication of the Torah on it. However, what is in al-Kashshaf, that it was said to them: "How do you fight them and then ransom them?" and they said: "We were commanded to ransom, and fighting was forbidden to us, but we would be ashamed before our allies," indicates that they did not deny the prohibition of fighting. Then the application of the word "disbelief" (kufr) at that point to the act of what was prohibited is either because it was disbelief in their law, or it is for emphasis, as it is applied to abandoning the prayer and the like in our law. The view that the meaning is "Do you employ some and abandon others?", so that the statement is taken figuratively in this respect, is not to be considered, just as is the view that by "some" is meant the part believed in, the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him), and "the other part" is the prophethood of our Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿Then what is the recompense for those who do that among you except disgrace in the worldly life﴾. The demonstrative refers to disbelief in part of the Book and belief in part, or to what they did of killing and expulsion together with ransoming the captives. "Recompense" (jaza') means reward, and it is used for both good and evil. "Disgrace" (khizy) means humiliation. The past tense is "khaziya" with a kasrah. Ibn al-Sikkit said: the meaning of khaziya is that he fell into a calamity, and khazia al-rajul khazayah means he felt shame, so he is khazyan, and people are khazaya. Here it means disgrace and punishment, or the imposition of the jizyah (poll tax) for all time, or the victory of the enemy, or the killing of Qurayzah and the expulsion of al-Nadir from their dwellings to Ariha and Adhri'at.

It has been related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "The custom of the Banu Qurayzah was killing, and the custom of the Banu al-Nadir was expulsion. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prevailed, he expelled the Banu al-Nadir, killed the men of Qurayzah, and took their women and children captive." The indefiniteness of "disgrace" (khizy) is to signal the monstrousness of its matter, and that it reached a degree whose reality cannot be grasped. For this reason some did not restrict it to a particular aspect, and claimed that this is the more apparent view, and they made the demonstrative refer to disbelief in part of the Book and belief in part, meaning any part at all, and for this reason it is singular. In that case it includes the disbelievers in the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and its parallel is "whoever does all of that." "Dunya" (the worldly life) is derived from dana yadnu, and its ya' is converted from a waw. The alif and lam are not omitted from it except rarely, and Abu Hayyan restricted that to poetry. "Ma" is a negation particle. "Man" (who), if it is taken as a relative pronoun, then "li-yafal" has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis); if it is taken as a qualifying word, then its place is in the genitive, as it is its attribute. "Minkum" is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the subject of "yaf'al." "Illa khizy" is an exceptive phrase in which the exception is incomplete (istithna' mufarragh), and it occupies the position of the predicate of the subject. Putting it in the accusative is not permitted in such a construction according to the well-known view. It is reported from Yunus that he permitted its being accusative in the predicate after "illa," whatever it may be. Some said: if what follows "illa" is the first in meaning, or is treated as occupying its position, then only the nominative is permitted in it according to the majority. The Kufans permitted the accusative where the second term is treated as occupying the position of the first, and if it is a descriptive word, al-Farra' permitted the accusative in it, but the Basrans prohibited it. It is related from them that they do not permit the accusative except in verbal nouns (masadir), unless the meaning is known, in which case a governing verb is then implied. Its full treatment is in its proper place.

﴿And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment﴾. That is, they will arrive at it, so it does not necessitate that they were in the most severe punishment before that. The "return" may also mean returning to what they were in, as in His saying: ﴿So We returned him to his mother﴾. It is as if they were in the most severe punishment in this world or in the graves as well, and so they were returned to it. What is meant is abiding in the Fire, and its being "most severe" is in terms of its having no end, or what is meant is the most severe of all kinds of punishment, but in comparison with the punishment of one who did not commit this disobedience, because their disobedience is greater than the disobedience of these people. "And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it." What supports what we have established is His saying: ﴿who does that among you﴾. So it does not refute what Imam al-Razi raised: how could the punishment of the Jews be more severe than that of the materialists (al-dahriyyah) who deny the Creator? It does not avail what has been said, because they disbelieved after recognizing that it is the Book of Allah, exalted is He, and after acknowledging and testifying to it. For how can it be said that a disbeliever who affirms the oneness of God is more severely punished than a polytheist or one who denies the Creator? Even if his disbelief is with knowledge and recognition. The pronoun in "yuraddun" refers to "man." The plural form was chosen in view of its meaning, after the singular was chosen in view of its wording, because returning happens through gathering, and non-compound construction, since he did not say, for example, "and the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection." This is to signal the complete contrast between the recompenses of the two states of existence. And placing "the Day" before mention of what occurs in it is to magnify the gravity of the matter and to make the state appalling from the very beginning. Al-Hasan and Ibn Hurmuz, with variation between them, and Asim in the transmission of al-Mufaddal, read "turaddun" in the second person (addressing). The majority read it in the third person. The reasoning for this is that "yuraddun" refers to "man yafal." So whoever reads with the third person looks to the form of "man," and whoever reads with the second person looks to its inclusion in "minkum," not that the pronoun in that case refers to "kum," as has been wrongly supposed. ﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾. This is a parenthetical interjection and a concluding clause to affirm the threat derived from what precedes it, meaning: He is ever watchful and does not neglect what you do of abominations, of which this evil is one. The one addressed by it is whoever was addressed by the verse before it. It is related from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The Children of Israel have passed away, and you are the ones meant by this, O community of Muhammad," and what is similar to it. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, and Abu Bakr read "ya'malun" with the ya' (third person), taking the pronoun as referring to "man," while the rest read it with the ta' from above (second person).

[Page 315]

**[Page 316]** No. Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life at the price of the Hereafter: that is, they preferred the worldly life, substituted it for the Hereafter, and turned away from the Hereafter even though they were able to attain it. ﴿So the punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, those who are threatened with it on the Day of Resurrection, or the punishment in general, whether worldly or otherwise. ﴿Nor will they be helped﴾ by averting disgrace until the end of the world, or by averting the jizya (poll tax, here understood as humiliation) in this world and punishment in the next. On the first interpretation, the negation of averting punishment is inferred from the negation of its lightening in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. Some have preferred the second interpretation, arguing that the context in that case requires placing the negation of averting before the negation of lightening, and placing the subject first for the sake of the fasilah (the rhyming end of the verse). The restriction (al-qasr) is not intended, since the context does not call for it. For this reason it did not say "so the punishment will not be lightened from them." The sentence is conjoined to the relative clause (al-silah). It is permissible for the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) to be connected to two relative clauses differing in tense. It has also been permitted that ﴿those﴾ (ulaika) is the subject (mubtada'), ﴿who﴾ (alladhina) is its predicate (khabar), and this sentence is a second predicate after the first. The fa' (so) is used because when the relative pronoun's relative clause is a verb, it carries the meaning of a conditional (shart). However, the meaning of the conditional does not extend to the subject that is a predicate of it. It has also been permitted that ﴿ulaika﴾ is the subject, ﴿alladhina﴾ is a second subject, this sentence is the predicate of the second, and the whole is the predicate of the first. In this case no linking pronoun (rabit) is needed, because ﴿alladhina﴾ is ﴿ulaika﴾. The difficulty in this is not hidden. This concludes the discussion.
