And from the mode of allusory (ishari) interpretation in these verses: ﴿And when We took your covenant: You shall not shed your blood﴾ by your inclination toward the desires and dispositions of the self, and your abandoning of your true life for the sake of obtaining your base pleasures and worldly aims; and ﴿you shall not expel yourselves from your spiritual abodes and your holy disciplines﴾. ﴿Then you affirmed﴾ by your acceptance of that, ﴿while you were witnessing﴾ to it through your primordial capacities and your innate intellects. ﴿Then you are these ones﴾, those who have fallen away from the primordial nature and are veiled from the light of capacity, ﴿who kill yourselves﴾ and destroy them through your misguidance and your following of desire. ﴿And expel a group of you﴾ from their former homelands by their seduction, their misleading, and your incitement of them to commit sins, while you cooperate against them in committing abominations so that they will see you and follow you in them, and by your imposing upon them the vices of the bestial and the predatory faculties and your inciting them to them. ﴿And if they come to you as captives﴾ in the bonds of what they committed and the chains of the disgrace of what they did, when remorse has seized them, and their intellects and the intellects of their kind reproach them for the shame and infamy that has befallen them, you ransom them with words of wisdom and admonition indicating that the elevated pleasures are the intellectual and spiritual ones, and that following the self is blameworthy and base, so that they may take heed by that and be freed from those fetters in a brief moment. ﴿Do you believe in part of the Book of the intellect and the Sharia by word and affirmation, and disbelieve in part by deed and action, so that you do not desist from what He has forbidden you?﴾ ﴿So what is the recompense of those among you who do that﴾ except humiliation and disgrace in the worldly life. And on the day of the separation of the spirit from the body you will be returned to the most severe punishment, which is their being tormented by the dark states firmly rooted in their souls, and their burning in its fires. ﴿And Allah is not unaware﴾ of your deeds; He has counted them, preserved them in your souls, and recorded them against you.

[p. 317]

﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book.﴾ This begins the explanation of another of their crimes. Introducing it with the oath-clause (al-jumla al-qasamiyya) shows how much importance is given to it. *Al-itha'* means giving. *Al-Kitab* is the Torah according to the majority of scholars, and it is the second object of *atayna* (We gave). According to al-Suhayli, it is the first object. Its being "given" to him means its being sent down to him. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the Torah was sent down all at once. Allah ordered Moses, peace be upon him, to carry it, but he could not bear it. So Allah sent an angel with each letter of it, but they could not bear to carry it either. Then Allah lightened it for Moses, peace be upon him, and he carried it. It has also been said that *atayna* may mean: We made him understand what it contained of limits, rulings, reports, stories, and other matters. In that case the speech contains an omitted modifier, meaning *the knowledge of the Book* or *its understanding*. But this is not the apparent meaning.

﴿And We followed him up with the Messengers.﴾ One says *qafaahu* when one follows him, and *qaffahu bihi* when one makes another follow him, from *al-qafa* (the back of the neck or the back). The original letter of this *ya'* is a *waw*, because whenever it occurs in fourth position it is changed, as when you say *ʿaraytu min al-ʿarw* (I have been stripped of the ʿarw). The meaning is: We sent them one after another, as in His saying ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾. From their time to the time of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, there were four thousand of them, and it has also been said seventy thousand. All of them followed his law, peace be upon him. Among them were Yusha ʿ, Shamwil, Sham ʿun, Dawud, Sulayman, Ishaya, Irmiya, ʿUzayr, Hizqil, Ilyas, al-Yasaʿ, Yunus, Zakariyya, Yahya, and others, peace and blessings be upon them. Al-Hasan and Yahya ibn Yaʿmar read *bi-l-rusli* with the *sin* unvocalized (*bi-l-rusl*). This is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, while vocalizing it is the dialect of Tamim.

﴿And We gave ʿIsa son of Maryam the clear proofs.﴾ That is, the clear evidences that indicate his prophethood. This covers every miracle he was given, peace be upon him, and this is the apparent meaning. It has also been said that it means the Gospel (al-Injil). The name ʿIsa in Hebrew is originally *Eshua* (Īshūʿ), with a hamza pronounced between the two positions or with a kasra, and its meaning is "the lord" (al-sayyid). It has also been said that it means "the blessed," and it was then Arabized. The relative adjective is *ʿIsi* and *ʿIsawi*, and its plural is *ʿIsawn* with a fatha on the *sin*, though it may also take a damma. He is mentioned singly apart from the Messengers, peace be upon him, to distinguish him from them, because he is one of the *Ulu al-ʿAzm* (the Messengers of steadfast resolve) and the possessor of a Book. It has also been said that this is because he did not follow the law of Musa, peace be upon him, since he abrogated much of his law. He attributed him to his mother in refutation of the Jews, who claimed that he had a father. *Maryam* in Hebrew means "the servant." Jesus's mother was named after it, because her mother had dedicated her to serving the Temple of Jerusalem. It has also been said that it means "the worshipper." In Arabic, a woman called *maryam* is one who loves to converse with men, just as a *zir* is a man who loves to converse with women. It has been said that it is not suitable for Maryam to be an Arabic name, because she was free from any love for conversing with men. Only if one says she was named this by way of tasmiya (naming by contrast), as a black man is called *kafur* (camphor). Some researchers said there is no objection to naming her this, on the basis that the custom of women who serve in such a role is this. In the Qamus (the dictionary of al-Firuzabadi) it says: she is the one who loves conversing with men but does not commit fornication, and on this basis there is no harm in the naming, as the author of Mawla ʿIsam mentioned. My own preference is that the naming took place in Hebrew, not Arabic, and indeed this almost has to be the case, as is clear to the fair-minded. From al-Azhari: *al-maryam* is the woman who does not love sitting with men, and it seems she was given this name by way of likening her to Maryam the virgin. Its weight in Arabic is *mafʿal*, not *faʿīl*,
[p. 318]
because according to the well-known view this pattern is not established in the morphological forms. Al-Saghani, however, established it in al-Dhayl, and said that it is among the words that escaped Sibawayh. Among such words are *ʿathyar* (dust), and *Dahyad* with the unmarked and marked letters (for the backbone, and also a place name), and *Madyan* on the view that its *mim* is original, and *Dahya* with a short vowel, which is a woman who does not menstruate, or who has no breasts, from *al-muḍāhāh* (resemblance), as if she were so named because she resembles a man. Ibn Jinni says that *Dahyad* and *ʿAthyar* are artificial words, so there is no proof in them for the establishment of the pattern *faʿīl*. Al-Salikuti mentioned that *ʿIthyar* with the *ʿayn* vowelled with a kasra means dust. If it is a *mafʿal*, this is also contrary to analogy, since analogical formation would have required the *ya'* to be transferred to the *ra'* and changed to an *alif*, as in *mubāʿ*. But this is an anomaly, just as *Madyan* and *Mazid* are anomalies. If it is from *rāma yarīmu*, meaning to part and depart, then analogy requires that its *ya'* also be vowelled with a kasra.

﴿And We strengthened him with the Holy Spirit.﴾ That is, We strengthened him with Jibril, peace be upon him. The designation of Jibril as the Holy Spirit (Ruh al-Qudus) is common. Allah, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Say: the Holy Spirit has brought it down﴾. The Prophet ﷺ said to Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him: "Satirize them, and the Holy Spirit is with you," and on another occasion he said to him: "And Jibril is with you." Hassan said:

*Jibril and the Holy Spirit are among us, and the Holy Spirit has no equal.*

*Al-Quds* means purity and blessing, or sanctification (al-taqdis), and its meaning is purification. The construction is an *idafa* (genitive construction) of the qualified to its qualifier, for intensifying the sense of exclusivity. It is a non-verbal *idafa*, in the sense of *al-lam* (the particle "of" for ownership). When the proper name is so construed, it is to be interpreted as referring to one of the two named by it. Mujahid and al-Rabi said: *al-Quds* is among the names of Allah, like *al-Quddus*. Some claimed that applying the term *ruh* (spirit) to Jibril is metaphorical, because the spirit is the wind that moves within the human passages, and it is known that Jibril is not like this. But it was applied to him by way of comparison, in that the spirit is the cause of physical life, while Jibril is the cause of spiritual life through knowledge. It seems this claim arose from the coarseness of the claimant's own spirit and its lack of nourishment from any knowledge. ʿIsa, peace be upon him, was specifically singled out for mention of the support of the Holy Spirit, because Allah singled him out with it from his childhood to his old age, as He said: ﴿When I supported you with the Holy Spirit, you spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾. Also because He protected him so that Satan could not approach him. And also because twelve thousand Jews tried to kill him, so ʿIsa entered a house and God raised him, peace be upon him, to a lofty place. It has also been said that *al-Ruh* here is the greatest name of Allah, by which He used to give life to the dead. This was narrated, like the first view, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. Ibn Zayd said: it is the Gospel, just as in the case of the Qur'an His saying: ﴿And thus We revealed to you a spirit from Our command﴾. This is because it is the cause of eternal life, the adornment with knowledge and insights which is the life of hearts, and the ordering of livelihood which is the cause of worldly life. It has also been said: the spirit of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, is himself, and He described it as such for its purity from contact with Satan, or for its honor with Him, and for this reason He attributed it to Himself. Or because it was not contained in the loins or the wombs of menstruating women, but came about from the breath of Jibril, peace be upon him, into the shirt of his mother, so the breath entered her inside. Ibn Kathir read *al-Qudsi* with the *dal* unvocalized wherever it occurs, and Abu Haywa read *al-Quddus* with a *waw*.

﴿So whenever a Messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, did you wax arrogant?﴾ This is a consequence of His saying ﴿And We certainly gave﴾, in such a way that the previous speech is not complete without it, like a condition without its answer. The interrogative *hamza* has been placed between the cause and the effect, to rebuke them for following that with this, and to express wonder at their conduct. The meaning is: We gave Musa the Book, and We bestowed upon you such-and-such blessings, so that you would thank Us by receiving it with acceptance, but you reversed this by denying. It is also possible that this is the beginning of a new speech, and the *fa'* (then) is a conjunction on an implied element, as if it were said: Did you do what you did, and then whenever a messenger came to you? Then the implied element may be an expression of what came after the *fa'*, so the conjunction would be explanatory. Or it may be something else, such as: Did you deny the blessing and follow your desires? In that case the sequence is literal. This second possibility has been weakened by what al-Radi mentioned,
[p. 318 continued]
that if it were so, it would be permissible for the interrogative *hamza* to occur in speech before the element it was conjoined to, whereas it only comes after a preceding speech. As for whether the interrogative *hamza* that enters upon a clause conjoined by *waw*, *fa'*, or *thumma* stands in its original position, or is moved forward from a later place, since its position after the conjunction is a well-known disputed point among the grammarians, some researchers take it in some cases to be of one type and in others of the other type, according to the requirements of the context and the course of the speech. The inclination of the heart is toward this view. It has been said that the primacy of the interrogative *hamza* is not invalidated, since nothing has preceded it in the speech on which it entered, and its meaning is connected to its content. The only point is that it is placed between two utterances to express denial of the second's combination with the first, or because the second occurs after the first with a gap, or without a gap. This is the intended meaning of those who said it is an inserted, superfluous element to establish the sense of denial or affirmation. That is, it is inserted into the conjoined element, and superfluous after considering its conjunction. It was not said that it is a relative clause. *Tahwa* (desires) is from *hawiya*, with a kasra, when one loves. Its verbal noun is *hawan*, with a short vowel. As for *hawa* with a fatha, it means to fall, and its verbal noun is *huwiyy* with a damma, whose original form is *fa'ul*, which was then altered. Al-Marzuqi said: *hawa* means to plunge down like a star or a bird. Al-Asmaʿi said: the eagle *hawat* when it plunged down for other than hunting, and *ahwat* when it plunged for hunting. Some reported that one says *hawa yahwi hawiyyan* with a fatha on the *ha'* when the direction is from high to low, and *hawa yahwi huwiyyan* with a damma when it is from low to high. What we mentioned first is the well-known usage. *Al-hawa* (desire) occurs both with regard to truth and otherwise. When it is attached to *al-nafs* (the soul), what is meant is usually the second sense, and this verse is of that kind. He expressed it as love, because the basis of their acceptance and rejection is opposition to their souls' desires and agreement with them, and nothing else. The object of *istakbartum* (you became arrogant) is omitted, meaning, for example, arrogant about believing in what he brought. Here *istaf ʿala* is used in the sense of *tafaʿʿala*.

﴿So some you denied, and some you kill.﴾ The apparent meaning is that it is a conjunction upon *istakbartum*, and the *fa'* indicates causation if the denial and the killing are consequences of the arrogance, and indicates division if they are two kinds of it. Al-Raghib permitted that it be a conjunction upon *wa-ayyadnahu*, with *Afa-kullama* and what follows it being a parenthetical element between them, by way of denial. He placed *fariqan* first in both places, for emphasis and to arouse the listener's interest in what they did to them, not for restriction. There is an omitted element here: meaning *a group of them*. He began with denial, because it is the first evil they commit, and because it is the common element between the one denied and the one killed. The killing is attributed to them even though their fathers were the killers, because they were pleased with it, and the blame for it falls upon them. He expressed it in the present tense to narrate a past situation and to bring its image before the mind, because of its horror and grandeur. Or for the sake of consistency with the present-tense verbs in the verse-endings before it. Or to indicate that you are now engaged in it, for you are around the killing of Muhammad ﷺ. Were it not that I protect him, you would have killed him. For this reason you bewitched him and poisoned a sheep for him. So the present tense indicates the present. This is not contradicted by the killing of some of them. What is meant by killing is engaging in the causes that bring about the cessation of life, whether or not it results in that. It has been said: there is no need for generalization, because he, ﷺ, was actually killed by the poison they gave him, as occurs in the authentic report with the words: "This is the time when I have found the severing of my aorta because of that poison." But it is objected that the killing had not actually been carried out by them at the time the verse was revealed, rather only the causes had been engaged, so generalization is necessary.

﴿وقالُوا قُلُوبُنا غُلْفٌ﴾ [And they said, "Our hearts are uncovered"] is a coordination (*ʿaṭf*) on ﴿اسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ﴾ [you were arrogant] or on ﴿كَذَّبْتُمْ﴾ [you denied], in which case it is an explanation (*tafsir*) of the arrogance. On both readings there is an *iltifat* (shift of address) from the second person to the third, turning away from addressing them and distancing them from the honour of being present. Those who spoke were those living in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ). *Ghulf* is the plural of *aghlaf*, like *ahmar* and *humr*, and means one who does not understand. It is said that its root is *dhu al-ghulfah*, one who has not been circumcised. Or it is the plural of *ghilaf* (covering), and it may also be pluralised as *ghulf* with two *ḍammah*s, and Ibn ʿAbbas and others read it this way. On the first reading, they meant: our hearts are covered with natural coverings that prevent what you have brought from penetrating them. This is like their saying: ﴿قُلُوبُنا في أكِنَّةٍ مِمّا تَدْعُونا إلَيْهِ﴾ [Our hearts are in coverings against that to which you call us]. By this they intended to despair the Prophet (ﷺ) of a response and to cut off his hope of them entirely. It is also said: they are covered with knowledge from the Torah, which protects them from anything you bring reaching them; or they are covered with soundness of natural disposition (*fitrah*) in this manner. On the second reading, they meant that hearts are receptacles of knowledge, so if what you say were true and right, they would have retained it. This is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi. Or [they meant] that hearts are filled with knowledge, so they have no room left for anything further, and therefore we are self-sufficient with what we have, not needing anything else. This too is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. It was also said: they meant that hearts are receptacles of knowledge, so how is it lawful for us to follow the Unlettered (ﷺ)? Its remoteness is not hidden.

﴿بَلْ لَعَنَهُمُ اللَّهُ بِكُفْرِهِمْ﴾ [Rather, God has cursed them for their disbelief] is a refutation of what they said and a denial of what they claimed. The meaning is that hearts were created with the disposition to be able to reflect correctly, which leads to the truth; but God distanced them and nullified their natural readiness for correct reflection, because of their corrupt beliefs and false ignorance that are firmly rooted in their hearts. Or, their hearts did not refuse to accept what you say because it is not true and right; rather, because He, glorified is He, expelled and forsook them for their disbelief, so He made them deaf and blinded their sight. Or, God has removed them far from His mercy, so how can they claim knowledge, which is its most exalted effect? From these aspects it is known how to answer what was said earlier among the other aspects.

﴿فَقَلِيلا ما يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾ [So little is it that they believe]: the *fa*' indicates that the curse is the cause, because of their lack of faith. *Qalilan* is in the accusative because it is a qualifier (*naʿt*) of an omitted verbal noun (*masdar*), meaning "a little faith," namely their belief in some of the Book. The *ma* is superfluous (*mazidah*), to emphasise the meaning of paucity, not a negation, because what follows *ma* in its scope does not precede it. Also, although it means "they do not believe a little, let alone much," it may perhaps be misunderstood, especially with the fronting, to mean that they do not believe a little but do believe much. The *ma* is not a verbal-noun particle (*masdariyyah*), because that would require *qalil* to be in the nominative as a predicate, with the definite verbal noun as subject, the sense being "so their faith is little." Some permitted it to be a negation, on the basis of the Kufans' view that what is in the scope of *ma* may precede it, and disregarded the misunderstanding. Others permitted it to be a verbal-noun particle, with the verbal noun as the subject of *qalilan*, and *kanu* (they were) being implied in the structure of the sentence, so it would be of the type of ﴿كانُوا قَلِيلا مِنَ اللَّيْلِ ما يَهْجَعُونَ﴾ [They used to sleep little of the night]. Its artificiality is not hidden. It is also permitted for *qalilan* to be in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), either of the pronoun of faith or of the subject of *yu'minun*, the sense being: "they believe it," that is, the faith, in a state of its paucity; this is reported from Sibawayh. Or: "they believe in a state in which they are a small group," that is, few of them are believers; this is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Talhah and Qatadah. For this reason it is also permitted for it to be a qualifier of time, meaning "a short time," namely the time of the opening (of the revelation), or the time when the soul reaches the collarbones (at death), or what they said: ﴿آمِنُوا بِالَّذِي أُنْزِلَ عَلى الَّذِينَ آمِنُوا وجْهَ النَّهارِ واكْفُرُوا آخِرَهُ﴾ [Believe in what was revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end] (3:72). The first of these aspects is the best. The apparent meaning is that *iman* (faith) is intended in its lexical sense, and *qillah* (paucity) is the opposite of *kathrah* (abundance). Al-Zamakhshari said: it may be that it means non-existence, apparently taking this from al-Waqidi's words, "neither little nor much." Abu Hayyan objected to this in *al-Bahr* that paucity in the sense of negation, even if it is attested, occurs in other constructions, because *qalilan* here is governed by the affirmative verb, so it becomes like *qumtu qalilan* (I stood a little), meaning "a little standing." No one would suppose that if you use an affirmative verb and make *qalilan* a qualifier of its verbal noun, the affirmative action performed in a certain attribute or manner means the total negation of that action and its complete non-occurrence. What the grammarians have transmitted is only that paucity may be intended as pure negation, as in their saying *aqallu rajulin yaqulu dhalika* (few a man says that) and *qallama yaqumu Zayd* (Zayd rarely stands). Therefore, interpreting it here in that sense is not correct. I wish I knew what meaning there is in our saying "they believe a non-existent faith." As for what al-Kisa'i reported from the Arabs, that they say *marrana bi-ardin qalilan ma tunbitu* (we passed by a land that produces little), meaning it produces nothing, this is because *qalilan* is a circumstantial qualifier of the land, although it is indefinite, and *ma* is a verbal-noun particle, the sense being "its production being little." There is therefore no obstacle in it to interpreting paucity as non-existence. But where does that stand relative to what we are discussing? Except on some of the less preferred readings, though al-Zamakhshari does not hold that. It may be said that this is by way of metonymy (*kinayah*), since the paucity of a thing entails its non-existence at most times, not that the word "paucity" is used with the meaning of non-existence. But here that is a very cold statement, even if al-Waqidi had kindled it for a thousand years.

[Page 319]

[Page 320]

﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah﴾, meaning the Qur'an. Its being indefinite (*kitab*) is for glorification, and describing it (as from Allah) is for honour and to indicate that it deserves to be accepted and followed in what it contains, because it comes from their Creator and their God, who watches over their welfare. The clause is conjoined (*'atf*) to "They said: our hearts are uncovered" (*qalubuna ghalaf*), meaning: and they denied it when there came to them, and so on.

﴿confirming what is with them﴾, that is, their Book. This means it was revealed in accordance with what was described (of it), or it agrees with it. "Confirming" (*musaddiq*) is a second attribute of *kitab*, and the first attribute was placed before it because describing it as coming from Allah, the Exalted, is more emphatic, and describing it as confirming arises from that. Describing it as confirming *their* Book, rather than as confirmed by it, indicates that it is in the position of the reality and actual fact (*nafs al-amr*) regarding their Book, because it contains information about it, depends for its truthfulness on it, and because, by its miraculous nature, it is independent of the confirmation of others.

In the Mushaf of Ubayy the word is *musaddiqan* in the accusative, and Ibn Abi Abla read it that way. In that case it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun resting in the adverbial phrase, or from "a Book," because it has been specified by a descriptive phrase that brings it close to definiteness. The possibility that the adverbial phrase in the language is connected to "came" (*ja'a*) is remote, but this does no harm, since Sibawayh permitted a circumstantial clause to come from an indefinite noun without a condition.

﴿And previously they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved﴾. It was revealed concerning the Banu Qurayzah and the Banu al-Nadir, who used to seek victory over the Aws and the Khazraj through the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before his mission. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and by Qatadah. The meaning is that they asked Allah, the Exalted, to grant them victory over the polytheists through him. This is as al-Suddi narrated: when the fighting between them and the polytheists grew fierce, they would bring out the Torah and place their hands on the place where the Prophet (ﷺ) was mentioned, and they would say: "O Allah, we ask You by the right of Your Prophet whom You promised us You would send at the end of time, that You grant us victory today over our enemy." Then they would be given victory. So the *sin* (in *yastaftihuna*) is for requesting, and "to conquer" (*al-fath*) means victory through the particle "over" (*'ala*).

Alternatively, they would inform (*yaftahuna*) them about him, from the expression "*fataha 'alayhi*" when he taught him and informed him, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do you inform them of what Allah has disclosed to you?﴾ That is, they would make the polytheists aware that a prophet would be sent from among them, and that his time was near. Then the *sin* is additional for emphasis, as if they had conquered (the enemy) after asking it of themselves, and a thing after it has been requested is more eloquent. This is of the category of *tajrid* (rhetorical abstraction: speaking as if one addresses another), in which they abstracted from themselves persons and asked them for the conquest, like their saying "*ista'jala*" (he hastened), as if he sought haste from himself. The meaning ultimately returns to: "O self, inform the polytheists that a prophet will be sent from among them."

It has also been said that *yastaftihuna* means they would ask for information about him (ﷺ): whether a child had been born with such-and-such attributes. This was reported by al-Raghib and others. As for what has been said, that it is not transitive with "over" (*'ala*), it is not heard by mere whim.

﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾. He referred to the earlier Book by "what they recognised," because knowing the one to whom it was revealed is knowing it, and seeking victory through it is seeking victory through him. The mention of the relative pronoun (*ma*) rather than simply using a pronoun is to show the full extent of their obstinacy. It may be that by it is meant the Prophet (ﷺ), since *ma* is sometimes used for the attributes of one who has reason. Some interpreters explained it as "the truth," indicating the reason for expressing him (ﷺ) with *ma*: that what is meant is the truth, not the specific identity of his pure person. Their recognition of that came through the evidence of the miracles and his conformity with what was described in their Book, for that is as clear as day to those firmly grounded in knowledge. So there is no objection that if the description of the Messenger in the Torah was explicitly mentioned, how could they deny him, since it is mentioned by continuous transmission (*tawatur*)? And if not, there is no recognition because of confusion. Moreover, the objection is extremely weak, because the verse is framed in the manner of His words: ﴿They denied them while their souls were convinced of them﴾, meaning they denied it while knowing it. This is more eloquent in blaming them.

"They disbelieved" (*kafaru*) is the answer to the first *lamma*, and the second *lamma* is a repetition of it because of the length of time, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done, and love to be praised for what they have not done, will escape the punishment﴾. Al-Mubarrad went to this view. Al-Farra' said: the second *lamma* together with its answer is the answer to the first, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿If guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance...﴾ and so on. On both views, His words, glorified is He, "And previously they used to..." are a circumstantial clause, with the implied "*qad*" (indeed) as a confirming particle.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Akhfash chose that the answer to the first (*lamma*) is omitted, meaning "they denied it," for example. In that case, "And previously they used to..." together with what is conjoined to it, from His words "So when there came to them," forms with the condition and its answer a sentence conjoined to "when there came to them" after it is complete. The first indicates their treatment of the confirming Book, and the second their treatment of the Messenger through whom victory was sought. Some researchers preferred this, because the first view entails the necessity of emphasis, whereas establishing (a new meaning) is better than it. Also, the use of *fa'* (so) indicates a sequence of rank, since the rank of the emphasising element comes after the rank of what is emphasised. And in the second there is the entry of *fa'* into the answer of *lamma* although it is a past tense, which is very rare, to the extent that the Basrans did not permit it. Even if it were permitted for it to occur as an extraneous element, "*fa lamma*" (so when) would not be answered by a similar one. One does not say: "When Zayd came, when 'Amr sat, I honoured you." Rather, as you see, it is a construction established in their speech, with the two aspects having no great benefit, which is the statement of the badness of their treatment of the Messenger. Their both entailing that "*wa kanu*" (and they were) is a circumstantial clause.

Abu al-Baqa' chose that "they disbelieved" is the answer to both the first and the second *lamma*, with no omission, because their import is one. This is not right, just as making His words "Then the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers" the answer to the first is not right, with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion. The definite article in "the disbelievers" (*al-kafirin*) is for a known reference, meaning upon them. Placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun indicates that the descent of the curse upon them is due to their disbelief, just as the *fa'* indicates its consequence from it. It is permitted for it to be for the genus, and they enter into it as a primary entry. This was objected to on the ground that the implication of a general term is equal, so there is nothing in it that is first or prior to anything else. The answer is that what is meant is entry by intention, because the speech was directed primarily at them. This is of the allusive metonymy (*kinayah ima'iyyah*), which is resorted to when the one described is extreme in that quality and immersed in it, so that when it is mentioned, that quality comes to mind, as when people say to one who acquires a vice and persists in it: "Whenever I look at you, your abuse comes to my mind, and the abuse of everyone of your kind." So the Jews, since they had exceeded in disbelief, obstinacy, and concealing the matter of the Messenger (ﷺ), and Allah, the Exalted, had censured them for that, disbelief became as if it were an attribute never separated from their mention. This statement became necessarily linked with their mention and its companion. And they are the most entitled of people to enter into it, because they were the cause of bringing this statement upon others.

Al-Sakkaki counted among this category the poet's words:

*When Allah gives drink only to the generous, He gives drink to the faces of the Banu Hanbal.*

As you see, in conveying the generosity of the Banu Hanbal, there is no obscurity in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 90:

﴿Evil is that for which they have sold their souls: that they should disbelieve in what God has sent down.﴾ That is, they sold. So "souls" stands in the position of the thing priced (al-muthamman), and "disbelief" stands in the position of the price (al-thaman), because their wicked souls are not bought but sold. This is used figuratively: they chose disbelief over faith and gave up their souls for it. It has also been said that it is in its well-known sense, because the accountable person, when he fears punishment for himself, performs deeds that he thinks will save him, so it is as if he bought himself with them. The Jews, when they believed that what they did would save them from punishment, thought that they had bought their souls and freed them, so God censured them for this. It is objected: how can it be claimed that they thought this, given His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾? If they knew that it contradicted the truth, how could they think their deliverance lay in what they did? Also, taking the intended punishment to be worldly, such as losing leadership, is not correct, because souls are not bought with that. The answer may be given that the meaning is that they thought, according to their outward condition, of their rigid adherence to Judaism, their fear regarding what they did and did not do, and their claim that they were right in it. So this does not contradict the fact that they did not in reality think this, as the verse indicates. What is meant by ﴿what God has sent down﴾ is the confirming Book. The change from "coming" to "sending down", which implies that it is from the higher world, together with its attribution to Him, the Exalted, signals the exaltedness of its status and its greatness, which necessitates belief in it. It has been said that it may mean the Torah and the Gospel, and it may mean all of them, and disbelief in some of them is disbelief in all of them. Scholars have differed concerning the ﻣﺎ (ma) that follows ﺑﺌﺲ (bi'sa, "evil is"): does it have a place in the grammatical structure (i'rab) or not? Al-Farra' held that it has no place, and that it is one thing with bi'sa, like ḥabbadhā (how excellent). The majority held that it has a place, and they differed as to whether that place is accusative or nominative. Al-Akhfash held the first view, that it is accusative, on the basis that it is a specification (tamyiz), and the sentence after it is in the place of an accusative as a description. The agent of bi'sa is a pronoun explained by it, and the estimate is: "Evil is it, a thing they sold for it." And "that they should disbelieve" is the one specified with the dispraise. The expression in the imperfect form indicates the continuance upon disbelief, for it is what necessitates the humiliating punishment. It is possible on this view that the specified element is omitted, with "they sold" as a description of it, and the estimate is: "Evil is a thing they sold for it." Then "that they should disbelieve" is either a substitute for the omitted element, or the predicate of an omitted subject. Al-Kisa'i also held the accusative as a specification, except that he estimated after it a relative ﻣﺎ (ma), which is the one specified with dispraise, and "they sold" is its relative clause. The estimate is: "Evil is a thing, the one they sold." Sibawayh held the second view, that it is the agent of bi'sa, and that it is a complete definite noun, and the specified element is omitted, meaning "a thing they sold." This was also attributed to al-Kisa'i. It has been said that it is a relative pronoun, which is one of the two opinions of al-Farisi. Ibn Atiyyah attributed it to Sibawayh, but this is an error. Al-Mahdawi reported from al-Kisa'i that ﻣﺎ is a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyya), and the thing obtained is the agent of bi'sa. It is objected that bi'sa does not enter upon a specific noun defined by annexation to a pronoun. You may, on this estimate, not make that the agent, but make it the specified element, with the agent a hidden pronoun, and the specification omitted for the sake of understanding the meaning. The estimate is: "Evil is a purchase, their purchase." Then the objection does not apply. Yes, there arises the return of the pronoun in ﺑﻪ (bihi, "with it") to ﻣﺎ (ma), and the verbal-noun ﻣﺎ cannot have a pronoun return to it, because according to other than al-Akhfash it is a particle. So understand this.

﴿Out of outrage that God should send down﴾: ﺑﻐﻲ (baghy) originally means injustice and corruption, from their saying: "The wound baghā," meaning it became corrupt; this was said by al-Asma'i. It has also been said that its origin is seeking. Its kinds differ: in seeking the removal of a blessing there is envy, transgressing against others is injustice, and fornication is debauchery. What is meant here, by the help of the context, is seeking what is not theirs, which leads to envy. This is the view of Qatada, Abu al-Aliyah and al-Suddi. It has also been said that it means injustice. Its accusative case is as an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and it indicates that their disbelief was for mere obstinacy, which is the result of envy, and not from ignorance. This is more emphatic in dispraise, because the ignorant may be excused. Al-Zamakhshari held that it is the cause of "they sold". This was rejected on the ground that it entails a separation by a foreign element, namely the specified element of dispraise. Although it is not foreign in relation to the verb of dispraise and its agent, it is clearly foreign in relation to the verb that is described by the specifying of the agent. The saying that the meaning is dispraise of what they sold their souls for, namely disbelief, out of envy, and not dispraise of what they sold their souls for, namely disbelief, out of envy, is arbitrary. Yes, it may be said that the separation by a foreign element arises only when the specified element is a subject whose predicate is "evil is", but if it is the predicate of an omitted subject, which is the preferred view, then no. For then the sentence is an answer to the question about the agent of bi'sa, so the separation falls between the caused and its cause by what is an explanation of the caused, and there is no barrier to this. Some of them made it the cause of an omitted "they sold" to avoid the separation. Others parsed it as a circumstantial accusative (ḥal) and as an absolute object (maf'ul muṭlaq) for an omitted verb, meaning "they transgressed a transgression." ﴿That God should send down﴾ is either an object of purpose for the outrage, meaning envy for the sake of God's sending down, or, by removing the preposition attached to the outrage, meaning envy at His sending down. The view that it is in the genitive place as an inclusive substitute (badal al-ishtimal) for ﻣﺎ in His saying: ﴿with what God has sent down﴾ is very distant. Something close to it is what has been said: that it is in the place of the second object, and that the outrage here means seeking what is not one's own. It transitively takes its object sometimes directly, and sometimes with the lam. The first object here, namely Muhammad, upon him be blessings and peace, is omitted because it is determined, and to indicate that envy is blameworthy in itself, whatever the one envied. As is not hidden. Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr and Ya'qub read ﴿yunazzila﴾ with the lightened form.

﴿From His bounty﴾: by it is meant revelation. ﻣﻦ (min) here denotes the starting point and is an adjective of an omitted noun, meaning "a thing being from His bounty." Abu al-Baqa' permitted that it be extra, according to the view of al-Akhfash.

﴿upon whomever He wills of His servants﴾: that is, upon whomever He chooses for a messengership. In al-Bahr it is said that what is meant is Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, because they envied him when it had not been among them, and he was from the Arabs and from the descendants of Isma'il, and no prophet came from his descendants other than him, upon him be blessings and peace. The annexation of the servants to His pronoun is for honour. ﻣﻦ (man, "whom") is either a relative pronoun or a qualifying one.

﴿So they returned bearing wrath upon wrath﴾: this is a consequence of what has preceded, meaning they came back clothed in wrath, which is upon wrath, deserving it according to what they committed of disbelief and envy. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the first wrath was for the worship of the calf, and the second for their disbelief in him, upon him be blessings. Qatada said: the first is their disbelief in the Gospel, and the second their disbelief in the Qur'an. It has been said: they are disbelief in Jesus and Muhammad, upon both of them be blessings and peace; or their saying: ﴿Uzayr is the son of God﴾ and ﴿God's hand is chained﴾, and other kinds of their disbelief. Their last disbelief was in the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. It is not hidden that the conjunctive ﻓﺎء (fa') requires that they became deserving of the successive wrath because of what preceded. Their saying ﴿Uzayr is the son of God﴾, for example, was not mentioned in what preceded. It may be that by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿with wrath upon wrath﴾ is meant succession and multiplicity, not two wraths only. This indicates the intensifying of the state against them greatly, as in the verse of the poet:

Had it been a single spear, I would have guarded against it,
but it is a spear, and a second, and a third.

Among people is one who claimed that the fa' is an eloquent (faṣīḥa) fa', meaning: "So when they disbelieved and envied upon what was mentioned, they returned," etc. This is not worth anything.

﴿And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾: the definite article in "the disbelievers" is for a known reference (li-l-'ahd), and the explicit noun in place of a pronoun is to indicate that their disbelief is the cause of what befell them. It may also be that the article is generic, so that the known ones enter into it in the same manner as what has passed. "Humiliating" means degrading, and its origin is muhwin, which was altered. Attributing it to the punishment is metaphorical, from attributing to the cause. The description with it is for restriction and specification, which is conveyed by placing the predicate before the subject. Thus, if others than the disbelievers are punished, they are punished for purification and not for humiliation and degradation. For this reason the punishment of others is not described with it in the Qur'an. So the Kharijites have no proof from the claim that it restricted the punishment to the disbelievers, so that the sinner would be a disbeliever because he is punished; nor do the Murji'ah have proof either.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 91:

﴿And when it is said to them﴾ is an adverbial clause (zarf) dependent on "qalu" (they said), and the clause is coordinated (ʿatf) with "qalu qulubuna ghulf" (they said, "Our hearts are wrapped"). There is no purpose connected to the speaker, so for this reason the verb is put in the passive form (lam yusamma fa'iluh, the agent is not named). The apparent reading is that it comes from the side of the believers.

﴿Believe in what Allah has sent down﴾. The majority (al-Jumhur) hold that this refers to the Qur'an. It has also been said that it refers to all the divine books that were sent down, taking the wording in its general sense. Nevertheless, the main purpose is the command to believe in the Qur'an, but the verse adopts a general manner of expression in order to indicate that obedience is obligatory, because the Qur'an shares with what they already believed in (that which is within the relative clause) and agrees with it in content, and to draw attention to the fact that belief in anything other than it, without belief in it, is not belief in what Allah has sent down. ﴿They said, "We believe in what was sent down to us"﴾, meaning: we continue to believe in the Torah and what is similar to it of what was sent down to confirm its rulings. The agent is omitted because it is known: it is evident that books are sent down only by Him, glory be to Him, and because His mention has preceded in the discourse. As for the pronoun of the speaker ("us"), their intended meaning is either the prophets of the Children of Israel, which is the apparent reading, and in this there is an allusion that their not believing in the Qur'an was out of envy and jealousy at its being sent down to one who was not of them; or themselves, and the meaning of "sent down upon them" is that they were charged with what was in the revealed rulings. They were blamed for this statement because of what it contains of disparagement regarding the Qur'an, and the intrigues of the Jews are well known. Or [they are blamed] because they interpreted the absolute, general command and restricted it to a specific matter, namely belief in what was sent down to them, as is their habit in interpreting the small book (al-kitab al-saghir) whose intended meaning they take from it.

﴿And they disbelieve in what is beyond it﴾ is coordinated with "qalu." The use of the present tense is to narrate the state, expressing astonishment at disbelief in a thing after knowledge of its truth, or to draw attention to the fact that their disbelief continues up to the time of the report. It has also been said that it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), and Ibn al-Anbari held this view. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal), either according to the view of one who permits the affirmative present to occur as a circumstantial clause with a waw, or by supposing an implied subject, i.e., "and they"
صفحة 324
are disbelieving. The restriction by the circumstantial clause in that case serves to explain the enormity of their condition, that they are contradictory in their belief, because their disbelief in what is beyond it while believing in the Torah entails not believing in it. This is more effective in refuting their statement, and for this reason some scholars chose this view.

"Wara'" (beyond/behind) originally is a noun from which the verb "muwara" (concealment) and "tawarri" (hiding) are derived. The derived form is a branch of the basic form, except that its basic verb was never used at all. Then it was made into a noun of place, and it may be annexed to the agent, so that it means the patient, or annexed to the patient, so that it means the agent, namely "the one that follows." Because it applies to the two opposites, "khalf" (behind) and "amam" (in front), it is counted among the words with contrary meanings (al-adadd), though it is not coined for both. In al-Muwazana by al-Amawi there is an explicit statement that it is not among them, but rather it derives from concealment and hiding: whatever is hidden from you is "wara'," whether behind or in front, when you do not see it; but when you see it, it is not "wara'" for you. The meaning here of "what is beyond it" is what follows it, as Qatada said, or what is other than it. It has been interpreted in this sense in ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that﴾, and what is meant there is the Qur'an, as the majority hold. Al-Wahidi said that it includes the Gospel too. There is also the possibility that "what is beyond it" means the inner meanings of what was sent down to them, which lie beyond their verbal expressions. This implies that their belief in the apparent wording is worth nothing, unless by that inner meaning is meant the Qur'an, but this is far-fetched.

﴿And it is the truth﴾. The pronoun refers to "what is beyond it" and is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it. It has been said that it refers to the subject of "yakfurun" (they disbelieve). A circumstantial clause introduced by waw does not necessarily require a pronoun returning from it to the person in the state, as in "Zayd came while the sun was rising." Even if it is required, the existence of the pronoun in what is part of its completion is treated as its existence within it. The meaning is: they are coincident with its truth, i.e., they know it. This is more eloquent in censure than their disbelief in what is true in itself. The first view is preferable because it is more apparent, and that eloquence is not lost in it either, since the definite article in "al-haqq" indicates that the one judged upon is accepted as possessing the attribute, which is known, as in "your father is the slave." This indicates that their disbelief in it was merely out of obstinacy. It has also been said that the definite article is for increased rebuke and ignorance, meaning that it is specifically the truth that accompanies confirmation of their book. Were it not for the circumstantial clause, namely "confirming," the restriction would not hold, because it is in opposition to their book, which is also true. This is problematic, because even if the circumstantial clause is taken into account, on the basis that the pronoun-bearing item is restricted to the Qur'an, the Gospel is also a truth confirming the Torah. Yes, if "al-haqq" were meant as "the established," opposed to "the abrogated," the restriction would hold absolutely, but this is far-fetched.

﴿Confirming what is with them﴾ is a emphasizing circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkida), because the books of Allah the Exalted confirm one another, so confirmation is a necessary attribute that does not pass to others. It has established the content of the report, since it serves as evidence for it. For this reason it contains a refutation of their statement, "We believe in what was sent down to us," since whoever does not confirm what agrees with the Torah does not confirm the Torah either. It is possible that what is "with them" means the Torah and the Gospel, as in al-Bahr, since both were sent down to the Children of Israel, and both do not contradict the Qur'an. But this contradicts what the taste (dhawq) of the context and sequence requires.

﴿Say: "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before?"﴾ This is a command to the Prophet ﷺ to say this as a rebuke to them, since they killed the prophets while claiming to believe in the Torah, which does not permit it. It is also possible that it is a command to whoever wants to argue with them, whoever he may be. The "fa" is the answer to an implied condition, i.e., "if you are believers, then why..." "Ma" is interrogative; its alif was dropped because of the preposition lam. Al-Bazzi pauses on such forms with a ha', while others pause without it. The use of the present tense with an adverb that denotes past time indicates their continued killing in past times. It has also been said that it narrates that state. "Killing" is meant in its literal sense. Attributing it to the later generations contemporary with him, ﷺ, while its actual occurrence was by the earlier ancestors, is metaphorical, due to the connection between the real agent and what is attributed to him. This is like saying to the people of a tribe, "You killed Zayd," when the killers were their forefathers. It has also been said that killing is a metaphor for approval or resolve to do it. It is not hidden that the objection on the first view is stronger in rebuke than on the other views, so reflect. The annexation of "prophets" to the noble Name is a great honour, and an announcement that whoever comes from Allah the Exalted should have been honoured and supported, not killed.

﴿If you are believers﴾
صفحة 325
is a repetition of the objection, to emphasize the obligation and intensify the dread: meaning, if you are believers, then why do you kill them? From each of the two conditional clauses, what is omitted has been omitted in reliance on what is stated in the other, by way of ihtibak (mutual omission). It has also been said that what was mentioned before is the answer to this condition, on the basis that it may be placed first, which is the view of the Kufans and Abu Zayd, and al-Bahr chose it. Al-Zajjaj said that "in" here is negating, but this is far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 92:

﴿And Moses did come to you with clear proofs﴾ falls under the (preceding) command, so it is part of the full rebuke and reproach. Likewise, what comes after it is a repetition of what was related earlier. By "the clear proofs" (al-bayyinat) is meant the evidences that indicate his truthfulness, peace be upon him, in his call, and the miracles that confirm his prophethood, such as the staff, the hand, and the splitting of the sea, for example. It has been said: the more apparent view is that they refer to the evidences of God's oneness (tawhid), since that is more suited to the reproach that follows. In my view, however, taking the term in its general sense, so that it also includes these, is preferable and more apparent.

﴿Then you took the calf﴾, that is, the one which al-Samiri made for you from your ornaments, as a god after him, meaning after Moses, peace be upon him, had come with them. Whoever counts the Torah and the gushing of water from the rock among the proofs does not intend all of them but only the category, because these occurred after the story of the calf. The word "then" (thumma), on this reading, is for distancing (al-istib'ad), so that the qualifier does not become meaningless. It may also be said that the pronoun refers to something mentioned earlier in meaning, namely the going up to Mount Sinai (al-Tur), so that "then" retains its literal sense, and counting what we have mentioned as clear proofs is then evident. This conjunction also indicates that they did this after a delay following their consideration of the signs, and that is greater in sin and more abominable for their state. Some have insisted that the pronoun refers to the clear proofs, with an omitted modifier, meaning "after reflecting on the signs," so that this would become apparent. Others have taken the pronoun to refer to the calf, and the meaning is "after its existence," that is, you worshipped the newly created thing that came into being in your presence, so that there is great reproach in it. What is in this of great remoteness is not hidden, and it is unnecessary given what we have pointed out.

﴿And you are wrongdoers﴾, that is, placing a thing in other than its fitting place, or violating the signs of God, exalted is He. The clause is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥal) that emphasizes the reproach and the threat. It serves as an indication (qarinah) that worship is intended by the "taking." It also implies that they diverted worship from its original place to something other than its proper object. The impression of exaggeration arises from the fact that the unqualified term "wrongdoing" suggests that worship of the calf is the utmost wrongdoing, and that whoever commits it leaves no form of wrongdoing undone. Some have preferred to make this clause a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ), to emphasize the whole sentence without specifying the state that a circumstantial qualifier would require, meaning: "And you are a people whose custom is wrongdoing, and the worship of the calf persisted among you and by you." What led to this view is the claim that, under the circumstantial reading, the clause would be a pure repetition, since worship of the calf can only be wrongdoing, whereas on this reading it would be an explanation of a vice in them that calls for such conduct. This, however, overlooks what we have mentioned. When "taking" is understood literally, as in "I took a ring," the circumstantial reading is undoubtedly preferable, because "taking" is not necessarily wrongdoing unless it is qualified by worship of it, as is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 93:

﴿And when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you: "Take what We have given you with determination."﴾ That is, We said to them: "Take what I have commanded you in the Torah with earnestness and without slackness, and listen," that is, listen with acceptance and obedience. For there is no benefit in an unrestricted command following the command to take with determination, unlike the case where it is restricted, since the unrestricted command emphasizes and affirms it, because it entails their complete refusal to accept what He gave them. This is why the mountain was raised over them. The word "listening" often means "acceptance," and from this is "God hears whoever praises Him" (sami' Allah liman hamidah), and the saying of the poet:

*I called upon God until I feared that God did not hear what I say.*

﴿They said: "We hear and we disobey."﴾ That is, they heard your words, "Take" and "Listen," and "We disobey your command, so we will not take, and we will not listen with the listening of obedience." This is not a response to "listen," considering that it contains two commands, because "take" would then remain without a response. Many have taken this view, and they raised here a question and an answer. The gist of the first is that if "listening" in the command is taken in its apparent meaning, then their saying "We hear" is obedience, and "we disobey" contradicts it [page 326]. If it means acceptance, then if the answer is likewise, it is a lie and a contradiction; otherwise it has no connection to the question. The essence of the answer is that the listening there is restricted, and the command comprises two things: hearing His word and accepting it through action. They said: "We comply with one of them without the other," and this returns to the position of "responding in accordance with the implication" (al-qawl bil-mujib). A parallel is ﴿And they say, "He is an ear." Say, "An ear of good for you."﴾ It is also said: the meaning is that they said with the tongue of speech "We hear," and with the tongue of state "We disobey," or "We heard the rulings before, and we disobeyed, so we fear we will disobey after hearing this word of yours." It is also said: "We hear" is the response to "listen," and "we disobey" is the response to "take." Abu Mansur said: their saying "we disobey" did not come right after their saying "we hear," but after a time, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you turned away﴾. So there is no need to repel the objection by what was mentioned. You know that there is no need for all of that after what you have heard, as is not hidden.

﴿And they were made to drink in their hearts the calf﴾: it is coordinated with "they said," or it is a new sentence, or it is a circumstantial clause with the implied "qad" (indeed), or without it. The governing element is "they said." Al-ishrab (imbibing) means the mixing of a liquid with a solid, and it was extended in usage until it applied to colors, and from it comes "whiteness mixed with redness." The expression is elliptical, meaning "the love of the calf." It is permitted that "the calf" be a metaphor for its image, so no ellipsis is needed. Mentioning the hearts indicates the place of the imbibing, and mentioning a specific location gives greater emphasis to the affirmation. The meaning: the love of the calf entered them and its image became firmly fixed in their hearts due to their extreme infatuation with it, just as dye penetrates cloth. They recited:

*When the heart is made to drink the love of something, do not hope for it to turn away from it.*

It is also said: "ushribu" derives from "ushribat al-ba'ir," when one tightens a rope around the camel's neck, as if the calf was tied into their hearts due to their infatuation with it. It is also said: it derives from "al-sharab" (drink). Their custom, when they expressed the penetration of love or hatred, was to borrow the name of drink for it, since it is the most easily absorbed substance in the body. This is why physicians said: water is the vehicle of foods and medicines, and its vessel by which they travel to the regions of the body. The poet said:

*It seeped in where drink did not reach, nor grief, nor joy did reach.*

It is also said: it is from drinking in the literal sense. This is because al-Suddi reported that Musa, peace be upon him, filed the calf with a file, threw it into water, and said to them: "Drink," and they all drank, so whoever loved the calf had its dust come out on his lips. The statement "in their hearts" greatly weakens this view. Moreover, what God, exalted is He, has related to us in His Book about what Musa, peace be upon him, did to the calf also weakens the apparent sense of this report. The passive form "ushribu" indicates that this was done to them, and there is no agent other than Him, exalted is He. The Mu'tazilah said: it is in the manner of someone saying "you forgot such-and-such," without meaning that someone else did that to him; rather, the meaning is "you forgot," and the agent is the one who adorned it for them and invited them to it, like the Samiri. ﴿Because of their disbelief﴾: that is, on account of their disbelief, because they were anthropomorphists who permitted that some body among bodies could be a god, or incarnationists who permitted its indwelling in it, exalted is He far above that, and they had not seen a body more wondrous than it. So what was adorned for them took firm root in their hearts. The serpent of the staff did not last for a long time, and it is not far-fetched that such people would believe a calf they had fashioned in the form of a beast to be a god, even if they had witnessed what they witnessed from Musa, peace be upon him, as you see from the worshippers of idols, most of whom were more intelligent than many of the Children of Israel. It is also said: the "ba'" means "ma'" (with), that is, accompanied by their disbelief, so that would be disbelief upon disbelief.

﴿Say: "Evil is what your faith commands you"﴾: that is, with what was sent down to you of the Torah, as you claim. The attribution of the command to faith, and its addition to their pronoun, is for mockery, as in His saying: ﴿Does your prayer command you?﴾ The object of the dispraise is omitted, that is, the killing of the prophets and so on. It is permitted that the object be specified by their saying "we disobey your command," but I consider this far-fetched.

﴿If you are believers﴾: this is a disparagement of their claim to faith in the Torah and a nullification of it. The answer to the condition is what is understood from His saying [page 327]: ﴿Why then do you kill﴾, through to the end of the verses mentioned in refutation of their claim to faith. Or the answer is the earlier declarative sentence, either with an interpretation or without one. The explanation of that: "If you are believers," your faith did not permit you the vile acts you committed; rather, it forbade them, so you contradicted yourselves in your claim to it, and it is therefore false. Or: if you believe in it, then evil is what your faith commands you with respect to it; or your faith has commanded you with falsehood, but faith in it does not command that, so you are not believers. The connection between the condition and the consequent in the first case is considered with respect to the matter itself, and the nullification of the claim is by the necessity of contradiction. In the second case the connection is considered with respect to their condition of engaging in vile acts while claiming faith, and a believer by nature does not engage except in what his faith permits; the nullification of the consequent is considered with respect to the matter itself. Some scholars have favored, in this and similar cases, that the consequent is the knowledge of the antecedent, that is: "If you are believers, you know that it is an evil thing that is commanded." It is said: "in" is negative. It is said: it is for doubt, and the words of al-Kashshaf point to this. In it is that the intent is to nullify their claim by presenting their certain faith as if it were not certain to be absent, for rebuke and obligation, not for doubt. Moreover, the use of "in" to cast doubt upon the hearer is not known, as stated by some verifiers.

And al-Hasan and Muslim ibn Jundub read (bi-hu iman-ukum) with a damma on the ha', connected with a waw.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 94:

﴿Say: If the Abode of the Hereafter with Allah is exclusively yours⦆ is a refutation of another claim they made after the refutation of their claim to faith in what was revealed to them. Because the purposes differ, he did not conjoin one of the two to the other, even though the connection that would justify the conjunction is evident. The verse was revealed concerning what Ibn al-Jawzi related, when the Jews said: "Allah, exalted is He, did not create Paradise except for Israel and his sons." Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Rabi' said: its occasion of revelation was their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise﴾ etc., and ﴿We are the children of Allah﴾ etc., and ﴿The Fire will not touch us﴾ etc. The same was related from Qatadah. The pronoun in (Say), refers either to the Prophet (ﷺ) or to whoever seeks to establish the proof against them. By "the Abode of the Hereafter" is meant Paradise, which is the common interpretation. In al-Bahr, the supposition of an omitted modifier was deemed good, i.e., the bliss of the Abode of the Hereafter.

﴿with Allah⦆ means in His judgment. It was said that by "with" (indiyyah) is meant rank and nobility. Interpreting it as spatial nearness, as was said as a possibility, is far-fetched. ﴿exclusively, to the exclusion of other people⦆ means specifically for you, as you claim. Khalis (exclusive) is that which is not mixed with anything, or that from which any admixture has been removed. The accusative of (exclusively) is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "the Abode," which is the subject of kana (was/is). (For you) is its predicate, placed first for emphasis or to convey restriction. What follows is for emphasis. This is the case if it is permitted for a circumstantial qualifier to come from the subject of kana, which is the more correct view. Whoever does not permit it, on the basis that it is not an agent, makes it a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun concealed in the predicate. It was also said that (exclusively) is the predicate, and (for you) is an adverbial phrase of incomplete sense (zarf laghw) attached either to kana or to khalisah. Its remoteness is not hidden, for it restricts the judgment before it has been stated, and there is no justification for placing the complement of the predicate before the subject while the adverbial phrase must come between the subject and predicate. Al-Mahdawi and Ibn 'Atiyyah also held this view to be remote, and they made (exclusively) a circumstantial qualifier, with (with Allah) as the predicate, although the sentence cannot stand on that alone. (Apart from) here indicates exclusivity and severing of partnership. It is said: "This is mine apart from you," meaning you have no right in it with me, nor any share. It is connected to (exclusively). By "people" is meant the category, which is the apparent meaning. It was said that by them is meant the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims. It was said that it refers to the Prophet (ﷺ) alone, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. They said: "people" may be used to mean a single man, though this is probably only a metaphor, treating the one as though he were the group.

﴿then wish for death, if you are truthful⦆ in your claim that Paradise is exclusively yours. For whoever is certain that he is among the people of Paradise chooses to move to the abode of permanence, and loves to be freed from dwelling in the house of troubles. Thus it is related from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he used to walk between the two rows (in battle) wearing a light shirt (ghulalah). Al-Hasan said to him: "What is this? It is the dress of those who fight." He replied: "O my son, your father does not mind whether he falls upon death or death falls upon him." 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah, while fighting the Romans, used to recite:

O how wonderful is Paradise and its nearness,
Pleasant and cool is its drink,
And the Romans are Romans, whose punishment has drawn near.

'Ammar said at Siffin:

Tomorrow we shall meet the beloved,
Muhammad and his companions.

It is related from Hudhayfah that he used to wish for death, and when he was dying he said: "A beloved has come upon poverty." It is also related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when news reached him of those killed at Bi'r Ma'unah, he said: "Would that I had been left with them, in the folds of the mountain." From this it is known that wishing for death out of longing for the abode of bliss and the meeting with the Generous is not forbidden. What is forbidden is wishing for it because of a harm that has befallen one, for that is a result of impatience and of not being content with the decree. In a report: "Let none of you wish for death because of a harm that has come upon him. If he must, let him say: O Allah, keep me alive as long as life is better for me, and cause me to die when death is better for me." By "wishing" is meant a person's saying: "Would that it were so," and "would that" is one of the acts of the heart, or the desire of the heart together with the wish to attain it along with speech. So the meaning of the verse is: ask for death with the tongue, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, or desire it with your hearts and ask for it with your tongues, as said by a group. On both interpretations, the command to wish is literal. There is also the possibility that the meaning is: put yourselves in the way of death and do not guard against it, like one who wishes for it. So fight whoever opposes you, and do not be among the people of the poll-tax and humiliation. Or be in a state in which those who wish for death and desire Paradise, because of good deeds, are not hindered by what the reports do not support. Ibn Abi Hatim related with a sound chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, as a statement of his own (mawquf): "If they had wished for death, each of them would have choked on his saliva." Al-Bayhaqi related from him as a saying traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) (marfu'): "No man among them will say it without choking on his saliva." Al-Bukhari also related from him, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If the Jews had wished for death, they would have died."

Ibn Abi Ishaq read (fatamannaw al-mawt) with a kasrah on the waw. Al-Hasan ibn Ibrahim related from Abu 'Amr that it is read with a fathah. It is also related from him that the damma was swiftly elided.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 95:**

﴿And they will never wish for it, ever.﴾ The apparent reading is that this is a resumed, interposed sentence, not included under the command. It was brought from Him, exalted is He, to explain what they would do by way of holding back, which shows that their claim is false. The meaning is that they will never wish for it as long as they live. This applies specifically to those who were contemporaries of the Prophet (ﷺ), according to what is reported from Nafi', may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A Jew disputed with us and said: 'In your Book there is ﴿So wish for death﴾, etc. So I wish for death. Why then do I not die?' Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, heard this and became angry, entered his house, drew his sword and came out. When the Jew saw him he fled from him. Ibn Umar said: 'By Allah, if I had caught him I would have struck off his neck. This accursed, ignorant dog imagined that this applies to every Jew, or to the Jews at every time. No, it is only for those who were obstinate and denied the prophethood of the Prophet (ﷺ) after they had recognized it. Their argument with him was by tongue, not by sword.'"

This is supported by what Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Abbas, as a statement of his own (mawquf): "If they had wished for it on the day he said that to them, not a single Jew left on the face of the earth would have survived but would have died."

This sentence is a prediction of the unseen and a miracle for the Prophet (ﷺ). It also contains evidence that they acknowledged his prophethood, for if they had not been certain of that, they would not have refrained from wishing. It has been said: there is no evidence in it, rather the refraining was by the divine turning away (sarfah), as was said regarding the inability to produce a rival to the Qur'an. As for the objection that how could this be a miracle when it is impossible to know that no one wished, and wishing is an inner matter not perceived by others: the answer is that we do not accept that the wishing meant here is an inner matter; rather it is to say "Would that it were so," and the like, as has passed just above. Even if it is granted that it is an inner matter, it is mentioned here by way of argument and manifesting the miracle, so it is refuted only by outward expression and utterance. This is like when a man says to his wife: "You are divorced, if you wish or desire," where the matter is tied to the outward statement, not to the hidden intention. Since it is established that they did not utter it outwardly, and also that had it occurred it would have been transmitted and become widely known, because the motives to transmit it would have been strong (since it is a great matter on which a great affair of prophethood turns: if it did not happen, his truthfulness becomes evident, and if it happened, the claim of his prophethood would be void), it is established that it is a miracle by which his Lord supported him.

As for one who takes wishing in its figurative sense, this question does not arise for him and he does not need this answer. You have learned what is wrong with it.

The majority of exegetes held that the ruling of this verse applies to all Jews in all ages. I am not among those who say this, even though a great multitude has approved it, and they said: it is the well-known view that accords with the apparent sense of the noble wording. Yet unless this refers to all the Jews who believe in his prophethood (ﷺ) and deny it at all times, and not to the Jews absolutely at all times, I still have reservations about it.

﴿Because of what their hands have sent forward﴾, i.e., because of what they did of sins that necessitate the Fire, such as disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and the Qur'an, and killing the prophets. (What) is a relative pronoun, and its returning pronoun is omitted; or it is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), and then there is no omission. The hand is a metaphor for the person himself, and it is also used as a metaphor for power, because it is among the limbs of a human being the basis of most of his crafts and the locus of most of his benefits. The attribution need not be made figurative: the hand may be taken in its literal sense, so the meaning becomes: "what they sent forward with their hands," such as the altering of the Torah, so that it includes what they sent forward by all the other limbs as well, and this is more forceful in censure.

﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) to the threat, and to alert that they are wrongdoers in claiming what is not theirs and in denying it to others. The knowledge may be taken in its apparent sense, or it may be a figurative expression for requital. The article (al-) is either for a specific reference (ahd), and the choice of the explicit noun instead of a pronoun is for censure; or it is for the category (jins), and then those specifically referred to enter it in the same manner as what has preceded.

[Page 329]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 96:

﴿And you will surely find them the most avid of people for life﴾. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ). The verb "tajidu" (تَجِدُ), when it means "to know" (ʿalima) through the intellect, is transitive to two objects: the pronoun is the first object, and "aḥraṣa" (أَحْرَصَ) is the second object. There is also the possibility that it is from "wajada" meaning "to meet" or "to befall," in which case it takes one object, and "aḥraṣa" would be a circumstantial state (ḥāl). This does not work according to the view of those who say that the genitive construction of "afʿal" (ʾafʿal, the elative) is definite (maḥḍa), as will come later. The pronoun refers to the Jews, about whom it was stated that they do not wish for death. It was also said that it refers to all of them, and it was said that it refers to the scholars of the Children of Israel. The "al-" in "an-nās" (النّاسِ) is for the genus, which is the apparent meaning. It was also said that it is for a specific group (ʿahd), and the intended ones are a group known for their excessive greed. The indefiniteness of "ḥayāh" (حَياةٍ) is because a generic individual is intended by it, namely the long life, so the tanwīn is for magnification (taʿẓīm). It may also be for belittlement (taḥqīr), since the true life is the Hereafter, and "the Abode of the Hereafter is indeed the true life" (al-ḥayawān). The indefiniteness may also be for vagueness (ʾibhām); indeed it was said that this is the more correct view, meaning "for a life whose amount is unspecified." From this one knows their greed for long life a fortiori. Abū Ḥayyān permitted that the speech contains an omitted modifier (ḥadhf muḍāf) or a qualifier, meaning "the length of life" or "a long life," but you know that there is no need for this. The sentence is either a circumstantial clause from the subject of "qul" (قُلْ), as the view of al-Zajjāj, or a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) to confirm that they do not wish for death. Ubayy recited "ʿalā al-ḥayāh" (عَلى الحَياةِ) with the definite article.

﴿And of those who associated partners﴾: they are the Magians (al-Majūs). They were described as associators because they hold to light and darkness, and their greeting when someone sneezed was "live a thousand years." It was also said they are the idolaters of the Arabs who worshipped idols.
