This is from interpretation by meaning (al-ḥaml ʿalā al-maʿnā), as if he had said: "more avid than the people, and than those who..." etc., based on the view of Ibn al-Sarrāj, ʿAbd al-Qāhir, al-Jazūlī, and Abū ʿAlī, that the genitive of an elative, when the intended meaning is excess over what it is attached to, is verbal (lafẓiyyah), because the meaning is upon affirming "min" (مِنَ) of origin, and the prepositional phrase is in the position of an object. Sībawayh makes it semantic (maʿnawiyyah) by estimating a "lām" (لام). The intended meaning of "an-nās" according to this estimate is: other than the Jews, since it is established that the object of "min" is surpassed by all its parts, or the more general. There is no necessity that a thing is preferred over itself, because the elative has two aspects: the establishment of the root meaning, and the excess. So its being among them is by the first aspect and not the second. "Min" was used in the second because a condition of the elative intended as excess over what it is attached to is that it be attached to what is part of it, since it is placed to be a part of a specific whole that comes after it and is gathered from it and its like. There is no doubt that the Jews are not included among those who associated partners, since in the Qur'an the two are commonly mentioned in contrast. It may be that this is by ellipsis, meaning "and more avid than those who," and this is the view of Muqātil. The meaning of the verse according to Sībawayh's view, and under both estimates, is that mentioning the associators is a specification after generalization, in the apparent way with the "lām," to add emphasis to their greed. The addition is a rebuke and reproach, in that they, despite being People of the Book who hope for reward and fear punishment, are more avid than one who does not hope for that, does not believe in resurrection, and knows only the immediate life. Their greed was more intense because they knew they were heading to punishment, and whoever anticipates evil is most averse to it and most eager for the means of distancing from it.

Some people permitted that "min alladhīna" (مِنَ الَّذِينَ) is a qualifier of an omitted word coordinated with the pronoun in the accusative in "latajidannahum" (لَتَجِدَنَّهُمْ), and the speech is by inversion (taqdīm wa-taʾkhīr), meaning: "you will surely find them and a group of those who associated partners as the most avid of people." I do not think anyone with even a little taste would take this in the Book of God, because although it is a sound meaning in itself, the construction rejects it, eloquence refuses it, and there is no necessity calling for it, especially according to those who restrict inversion to necessity. Yes, it may be that there is an omitted item which is a subject, with what is mentioned being its qualifier, or what is mentioned is the predicate of an omitted subject whose qualifier is...

﴿Each one of them wishes﴾: omitting the modified noun of the clause, when it is a part of its preceding antecedent governed by "min" or "fī," is permitted in ordinary usage, and otherwise is restricted to necessity, as in the line: "I am the son of Jalā and the climber of the heights." In that case, "those who associated partners" means the Jews, since they said "ʿUzayr is the son of God," and placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun is a rebuke for them for associating. Some permitted that by this is meant the category, and by "whom each one of them wishes" the Jews, with the meaning each individual of them, but this is far-fetched. The clause "yawaddu" (يَوَدُّ) and what follows, according to the first two views, is resumptive (mustaʾnafah), as if it was said: "What is the intensity of their greed?" It was also said it is a circumstantial state from "alladhīna," or from the pronoun in "ashrakū," or from the accusative pronoun in "latajidannahum."

﴿If he were given a life of a thousand years﴾: the answer of "law" (لَوْ) is omitted, meaning "he would be delighted by that," and likewise the object of "yawaddu," meaning the lengthening of life, is omitted, because "law yuʿammar" indicates it, just as the answer is omitted because "yawaddu" indicates it. This is what follows the rules of the Basrans in such a place. Some Kufans went in such cases to the view that "law" is verbal (maṣdariyyah) in the sense of "an" (أَنْ), so it has no answer, and from it a verbal noun is formed which is the object of "yawaddu," as if he said: "each of them wishes the lengthening of a thousand years." It was also said that "law" means "layta" (لَيْتَ, would that), and it needs no answer, and the clause is quoted after "yawaddu" in the position of the object. Although it is not a speech nor in its meaning, it is a mental verb from which statements proceed, so it is treated as such. Its original form was "law ʾuʿmira" (لَوْ أُعْمِرَ), but it was expressed with the third person to match "yawaddu," since he is absent, as one says: "He swore: he will surely do it" (layafʿalanna), in place of "I will surely do it" (la-afʿalanna). This differs from when one uses the direct speech, which is not permitted: "he said: he will surely do it" (la-yafʿalanna) is not permitted. If we say that "law" which expresses wishing is verbal, there is no need to consider quotation. Ibn Mālik, may God be pleased with him, says that "law" in such cases is purely verbal, but it resembles "layta" in poetry in expressing wish, and it is not a particle set for it, like "layta." Similar is "law taʾtīnī fa-tuḥaddithanī" with the subjunctive, its origin being "waddadtu law taʾtiyanī," so the verb of wishing was omitted because "law" indicates it. It was also said it is the conditional "law" which has taken on the meaning of wishing. The meaning of "a thousand years" is multiplicity, so as to include whoever wishes never to die at all. It may also be intended literally as a thousand years, and "the thousand" is a known number derived from "ulfah" (companionship), since it is composed of kinds of numbers according to common usage, although the correct view is that a number is composed of the units beneath it, not of numbers. The root of "sanah" (سَنَةٍ) is "sanawah," given the plural "sanawāt." It was also said "sanhah," like "jabhah," given their saying "sānahtuhu" and "tasannahat al-nakhlah" when the years passed over it. It was also heard in the plural "sanahāt."

﴿And it is not one who will remove him from the punishment by being given long life﴾: "mā" is either Ḥijāzi or Tamīmi. "Huwa" (هُوَ) is a pronoun referring to "aḥadahum," its subject, or a subject, and "bi-muzaḥzihihi" is its predicate, or the predicate of it, with the "bāʾ" being superfluous, and "an yuʿammar" (أَنْ يُعَمَّرَ) is the agent of "muzaḥzih," and the meaning is: none of them is removed from the punishment by his being given long life. This contains an indication that there is one whom long life would remove, namely whoever believed and did righteous deeds. According to the scholars of verification (al-muḥaqqiqīn), the raised pronoun cannot be a pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), because its explanatory element would be a clause, and "bi-" does not enter the predicate of "mā" except when it is singular, according to other than al-Farrāʾ. Abū ʿAlī permitted that, and this is an inclination on his part toward the view of the Kufans, that the explanation of the pronoun of the matter may be other than a clause when it forms a semantic predication, as in: "mā huwa bi-qāʾimin Zayd" (it is not that Zayd is standing). Yes, they permitted that it refers to what is indicated by "yuʿammar" and "an yuʿammar" is a substitute (badal) from it, meaning "his being given long life is not what removes him from the punishment." It was objected that there is weakness in it because of the separation between the substitute and what it replaces, and because of substitution without need. One of the verifiers answered that since the word "taʿmīr" (lengthening) is not mentioned but its pronoun is, substitution is good; and had "taʿmīr" been mentioned by its own word, the second would have been an emphasis rather than a substitute. Because it is in reality a repetition, serving the purpose of establishing the subject of the judgment, to pay attention to the importance of the judgment on the basis of the intensity of his greed for lengthening and his affection for it, the separation between it and what it replaces by the predicate is permitted, as in emphasis in His saying: ﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾. It was also said: it is an ambiguous pronoun explained by the substitute, so it refers to that and not to something previously mentioned that is understood from the verb, and explanation after ambiguity is for it to be more effective in the hearer's soul and for it to settle in his mind that he is the one judged by that judgment. The separation by an adverb between it and its explainer is permitted, as what al-Radī's discussion on the verbs of praise and blame implies. The possibility that "huwa" is a pronoun of separation (ḍamīr faṣl) brought forward with the predicate is remote. "Al-zaḥzaḥah" (الزَّحْزَحَةُ) is removal to a distance, and it is a reduplicated form of "zaḥḥa, yazuḥḥu, zaḥḥan," like "kabkaba" from "kabba." There is emphasis in it, but it is directed to the negation, in the manner of His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾. Thus it comes to mean that lengthening has no effect at all in removing the punishment, and this is correct even though lengthening does bring the lifting of punishment for the duration of life, because respite is by time, and although it occurs, they, by committing sins during the lengthening, increased in severity against themselves, so it had no effect at all in removing it, and rather added to it, since in exchange for "a number of days" they deserved the punishment of eternity.

﴿And God is Seeing of what they do﴾: that is, knowing of their hidden deeds, so He will surely recompense them. Interpreting "seeing" as "knowing" here, though it means sight, is also an attribute of God, because some deeds cannot be seen, according to what some verifiers held. In this sentence there is the threat and warning that is evident. "Mā" is either relative or verbal. The present tense was used for the harmony of the verse-endings (tawākhī al-fawāṣil). Al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, al-Aʿraj, and Yaʿqūb read "taʿmalūn" with the "t," by way of iltifāt (shift of person).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 97:

﴿Say: whoever is an enemy to Jibril...﴾ Ibn Abi Shayba in his Musnad, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Sha'bi that: "'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, entered the schools of the Jews one day and asked them about Jibril. They said: 'He is our enemy. He discloses Muhammad's secrets to him, and he is the one in charge of every cataclysm and punishment. Mika'il is the one in charge of fertility and peace.' He said: 'What is their rank with Allah, the Exalted?' They said: 'Jibril is on His right and Mika'il is on His left, and between them there is enmity.' He said: 'If they are as you say, then they are not enemies. And you are more disbelieving than donkeys. Whoever is an enemy to one of them is an enemy to Allah.' Then 'Umar returned and found that Jibril had preceded him with the revelation. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Your Lord has agreed with you, O 'Umar.' 'Umar said: 'After that, I saw myself to be harder than a rock.'" It has also been said that it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Suriya, who was a Jew and one of the rabbis of Fadak. He asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about who descends upon him, and he said: "Jibril." He said: "That one is our enemy. He has been hostile to us repeatedly, and the worst of it is that he revealed to our Prophet that Bayt al-Maqdis would be destroyed by Bukhtnassar (Nebuchadnezzar). So we sent someone to kill him, and he saw him in Babil, but Jibril repelled him and said: 'If your Lord has ordered you to destroy yourselves, then He will not give you power over him. Otherwise, why would you kill him?' The man who had been sent believed him and returned to us. Bukhtnassar grew in strength and became powerful, invaded us, and destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis." Some of the memorizers of hadith narrated this. Al-'Iraqi said: "I have not found a chain of narration for it, so the first report is perhaps stronger than it, even if the practice of some of them suggests the reverse."

Jibril is the name of an angel who used to descend upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with the Qur'an. It is a non-Arabic name, not declined (mamnu' min al-sarf) because of being a proper noun ('alamiyya) and foreign origin ('ujma). Whoever held that it is derived from the jabarut (sovereignty) of Allah, and considered it a blended compound (tarkib mazj) of a mudaf (governing noun) and a mudaf ilayhi (governed noun), so that it is not declined because of being a proper noun and being compounded, is far from the truth and has nothing to it. This is because whatever is compounded in this way is permitted to take the forms of indeclinability (bina'), idafa (construct) and non-declension. The fact that no idafa or bina' has been heard with it is evidence that it is not a blended compound. The Arabs have modified it according to their custom in changing non-Arabic names, to the extent that it has reached thirteen forms. The most eloquent and most well-known of them is Jibril, like qindil, and this is the recitation of Abu 'Amr, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Hafs from 'Asim. It is the dialect of the Hijaz. Waraqa ibn Nawfal said:

"And Jibril comes to him, and Mika'il with them,
from Allah a revelation that expands the breast, sent down."

The second is the same, except with a fatha on the jim. This is the recitation of Ibn Kathir, al-Hasan and Ibn Muhaysin. Al-Farra' said: "I do not like it, because there is no fa'lil form in speech." This is not correct, because when they Arabized the foreign word they sometimes attached it to their patterns, as in lijam, and sometimes did not, as in ibrisam (silk). Jibril belongs to this category, even though samawal (for a bird) has been heard. The third is Jabra'il like salsabil, and this is how Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hammad from Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited it. It is the dialect of Qays, Tamim and many of the people of Najd. Al-Farra' transmitted it, and al-Zajjaj preferred it and said: "It is the best of the dialects." Hassan said:

"We witnessed, and no army meets us
for all time except Jabra'il in front of it."

The fourth is the same, except without a ya' after the hamza. This is the transmission of Yahya ibn Adam from Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and it is also reported from Yahya ibn Ya'mar. The fifth is the same, except that the lam is shaddah (doubled). This is the recitation of Aban from 'Asim, and also of Yahya ibn Ya'mar. The sixth is Jabra'il, with an alif and a hamza followed by a kasra, without a ya'. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and 'Ikrima recited with it. The seventh is like it with an added ya' after the hamza. The eighth is Jabra'iyil with two ya's after the alif. al-A'mash and Ibn Ya'mar recited with it, and al-Kisa'i transmitted it from 'Asim. The ninth is Jabra'al. The tenth is Jibril with a ya' and the qasr (short vowel form), which is the recitation of Talha ibn Musarrif. The eleventh is Jibrin, with a fatha on the jim and the nun. The twelfth is the same except with a kasra on the jim, and this is the dialect of Asad. The thirteenth is Jabrayin. Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: "Jibril has been made plural in the broken form (jam' taksir) as jaba'in, according to the high-register dialect." It is well known that its meaning is "servant of Allah," on the basis that jabr is Allah, the Exalted, and il is the servant. It has also been said that it is the reverse. Some of them rejected this, saying: "The known practice in foreign speech is to place the governed noun before the governing noun." This requires consideration.

﴿For indeed, it has brought it down upon your heart﴾: this is the answer to the conditional, either by proxy (niyaba) or in actuality (haqiqa). The meaning is: whoever among them shows enmity to him has cast off the bond of fairness, or has disbelieved in what is with him of the Book by being hostile to him, because he descended to you with the revelation, since it has brought down a Book confirming the earlier scriptures. Or, the cause of their enmity is that he descended upon you, and the subject of this last view is not omitted, and "it has brought it down" is its predicate, so that the objection does not arise that the position is for the fa' (the particle of the conditional/consequence). Rather, the fa' enters upon the cause, and it has come as a response in terms of informing and reporting its causality for what precedes it. So the meaning returns to: whoever is hostile to him, then I inform you that the cause of his enmity is such-and-such. It is like your saying: "If so-and-so is hostile to you, then you have harmed him", meaning: he informed you that the cause of your enmity is that you harmed him. It has also been said that the response is omitted in such a way that what is mentioned does not replace it, and it is estimated as following it, and that the mention is an explanation and clarification of the cause of the enmity. The meaning is: whoever is hostile to him because he brought it down upon your heart, then let him die of rage, or: he is my enemy and I am his enemy. The indication for omitting the second is the parenthetical clause mentioned after it in their threat. It is also possible that "whoever is an enemy" and so on is an interrogative for disapproval or threat, and "for indeed" is the cause of the enmity and a restriction of it, or the cause of the command to say something that should not be committed in the Great Qur'an. The first pronoun is for Jibril, and the second is for the Qur'an, as the circumstances indicate, because they are all attributes of the Qur'an apparently. It has also been said that the first is for Allah, the Exalted, and the second is for Jibril, meaning: indeed Allah sent down Jibril with the Qur'an upon your heart. In each of the two views there is an implied pronoun referring to what the context indicates, and in that there is a grandeur of rank that is not hidden. He, glorified is He, did not say "upon you," as in His saying: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched﴾, but rather said: ﴿upon your heart﴾, because it is the first receiver of revelation if by it is meant the spirit, and the locus of understanding and memorization if by it is meant the organ, based on the denial of the inner senses. It has also been said that "heart" is a metonym for the whole human being, as a part of something is used to refer to its whole. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿He brought it down upon your heart﴾ is: He made your heart characterized by the character traits of the Qur'an and disciplined by its etiquettes, as in the hadith of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her: "His character was the Qur'an; he was pleased with what pleases it, and angered by what angers it." It would have been more apparent to say "upon my heart," since the speaker is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), but he related what Allah said to him, and made the speaker as though it were Allah, the Exalted, because he is a pure messenger by the permission of Allah, that is, by His command, or by His knowledge and His enabling him to attain this rank, or by His choice, or by His facilitation and ease. The original meaning of permission regarding a thing is the notification of its authorization and the granting of leave for it. So all the meanings mentioned are figurative, and the relation is evident. According to al-Muntakhab, as in the Muntakhab, the first meaning is preferred. The Mu'tazila, since they did not hold to inner speech (kalam nafsi), and attributing permission to Him, the Exalted, in terms of verbal speech requires strained interpretation, restricted themselves to the last view. Al-Zamakhshari said: "If permission means command, and if by the descent is meant its apparent meaning, and by it is meant facilitation, if by it is meant preservation and comprehension, it has no basis."

﴿confirming what is before it﴾: of the divine books, the greatest of which is the Torah. The accusative of "confirming" (musaddiqan) is a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "brought it down" if it refers to the Qur'an. If it refers to Jibril, then it has two possibilities. The first is that it is a circumstantial state from the omitted element, to understand the meaning, as we have indicated. The second is that it is a state from Jibril, and the pronoun is either for the Qur'an or for Jibril, for he too confirms what is before him of the messengers and books. ﴿And a guidance and good news for the believers﴾ are coordinated with "confirming," so they are states like it, and the interpretation is not obscure. The believers are specifically mentioned because for others it is blindness. The verse indicates the exaltation of Jibril and the highlighting of his rank, in that He made him the intermediary between Himself and the noblest of His creation, and the one who brought down the Book that combines the attributes mentioned. It also indicates the censure of the Jews, in that they hated the one who held this great and exalted station with Allah, the Exalted. It is said: The Batiniyya (esoteric sect) have clung to this verse and said: "The Qur'an is inspiration, and the letters are the expression of the Messenger (ﷺ)." It was refuted by saying: it is an outward and inward miracle, Allah, the Exalted, named it Qur'an, Book and Arabic, Jibril descended with it, and the one who is inspired does not need it.

[p. 334]

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 2, verse 98:

﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His angels, His messengers, Jibril and Mika'il, then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers.﴾ *Al-'aduww* (enemy) for a person is the opposite of *al-sadiq* (friend). It applies equally to the masculine, the feminine, the dual and the plural, though it may also be made feminine, dual and plural. It denotes one who wishes to inflict harm upon another. This meaning is valid only with respect to created beings, not with respect to Allah, the Exalted. Therefore the enmity of Allah here is figurative (*majaz*), either referring to His opposition and to the failure to obey Him, since that is necessarily entailed by enmity, or referring to enmity toward His allies. As for the enmity of the disbelievers toward Jibril and the messengers, peace be upon them, it is genuine, since harm is directed at them. The only point is that their enmity has no effect, because they are incapable of the things that would have an effect upon them. The statement follows the last possibility by mentioning them in order to magnify the status of those allies, since He made their enmity His own enmity, the Exalted. The two angels were singled out for mention in honour and distinction of them

[p. 335]

and as if they were of another kind, treating the difference in attribute as though it were a difference in essence, as in his saying:

*"Though you surpass mankind, and you are of them, indeed musk is but a part of the blood of the gazelle."*

It is also said: this is because the Jews mentioned them, and the verse was revealed on account of them. It is also said: this is to draw attention to the fact that opposing one or all of them is equal in disbelief, and that enmity toward them invites enmity from Allah, the Exalted; and that whoever is hostile to one of them is as though he is hostile to all, because the true cause of their love and enmity is one, even though it differs according to conjecture and belief. For this reason the Jews loved Mika'il and hated Jibril. Some have argued from the mention of Jibril before Mika'il that he is more excellent than him, and this is the well-known view. They also argued that Jibril descends with revelation and knowledge, which is the substance of spirits, while Mika'il is responsible for fertility and rain, which is the substance of bodies, and nourishment of spirits is more excellent than nourishment of bodies. It has been objected that precedence in mention does not indicate superiority, since it may be for ascending order or for another reason, just as the angels were mentioned before the messengers, and they are not more excellent than them according to us. Likewise, his descent with revelation is not definitive proof of superiority, since what is in the less excellent may be found that is not in the more excellent. Thus superiority requires a clear and explicit text. I say, however, that they are superior, and I have no stronger proof for this than his unique companionship with the Beloved of the Truth, by consensus, and the Master of Creation without qualification (ﷺ), and his great support for him and his love for him and his community. I see nothing that equals this. Allah, the Exalted, has praised him (peace be upon him) with what He did not praise Mika'il with, nor Israfil and 'Izra'il and all the other angels. Al-Tabarani narrated, though through a weak chain, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "(Shall I not inform you of the best of the angels? Jibra'il.)" Abu al-Shaykh narrated from Musa ibn 'A'isha who said: "(It reached me that Jibril is the imam of the people of the heavens.)"

(*Man*) is a conditional particle. Its response is said to be omitted, and its implied meaning is: then he is a disbeliever, deserving the most severe punishment. It is also said that the response is: then indeed Allah... and so on, in the manner you have understood. He mentioned the name Allah explicitly and did not say "then indeed He is an enemy," in order to prevent a misunderstanding of what is not intended, or for the sake of glorification and magnification. When the Arabs wish to magnify something, they repeat it by the noun that preceded it. From this is: (Allah will surely support him, indeed Allah...), and the saying: "I do not see death overtaking death, anything..."

The definite article in *al-kafirin* (the disbelievers) is for a known reference. Choosing the nominal sentence indicates confirmation and firmness. Placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun signals that the enmity of the ones mentioned is disbelief, that this is evident and does not need to be stated, and that the basis of Allah's enmity toward them and His wrath, which necessitates the severest punishment and torment, is their aforementioned disbelief. It is said: it is possible that He, the Exalted, turned away from the pronoun because He knew that some of them would believe, and so it would not be proper to describe them with Allah's enmity in terms of their eventual outcome. This is a possibility more remote than al-'Ayyuq. It is also possible that *al* is for the genus, as has preceded. Some people narrate that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, spoke this verse in response to some Jews who said, "That is our enemy," meaning Jibril, and so the verse was revealed on the tongue of 'Umar. This report is weak, as Ibn 'Atiyya explicitly stated. The discussion regarding the non-declension of Mika'il is like the discussion regarding Jibril. It is well known that its meaning is "servant of Allah" (*'Ubayd Allah*), and it is said that it means "slave of Allah" (*'Abd Allah*). It has several readings: The first is *Mikal*, on the pattern of *Mif'al*, and this is how Abu 'Amr and Hafs read it, and it is the dialect of the Hijaz. The second is the same, except that after the alif there is a hamza, and Nafi' read it so, and Ibn Shanbudh, according to Qunbul. The third is the same, except that after the hamza there is a ya', and this is how Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr, and others besides Ibn Shanbudh according to Qunbul, and al-Bazzi read it. The fourth is *Mika'il*, like *Mikafil*, and Ibn Muhaysin read it so. The fifth is the same, except that there is no ya' after the hamza, and it has been read so. The sixth is *Mikayil*, with two ya's after the alif, the first of which is kasra, and al-A'mash read it so.

Regarding these two angels, and even regarding their brothers Israfil and 'Izra'il, peace be upon them, our masters among the Sufis, may Allah sanctify their secrets, have an extensive discourse. The well-known view is that Jibril is the Active Intellect (*al-'aql al-fa''al*), that Mika'il is the spirit of the sixth sphere and its intellect, which emanates the universal vegetative soul entrusted with the provisions of creatures, and that Israfil is the spirit of the fourth sphere and its intellect, which emanates the universal animal soul entrusted with animals, and that 'Izra'il is the spirit of the seventh sphere, entrusted with all human spirits, some of them through its agents who are its helpers, and some of them by itself. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best the reality of the matter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 99:

﴿And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs, and none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient.﴾ It was revealed concerning Ibn Suriya, as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, when he said to the Messenger of Allah: "You have brought us nothing that we recognise, and no signs have been sent down to you that we would follow you by." It is connected (ʿatf) to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy…﴾ and so on, as a coordination of one narrative with another narrative. "And none disbelieve" is coordinated (ʿatf) with the answer to the oath (qasam), for just as it is introduced with the lam, it is also introduced with the particle of negation. The "signs" are the Qur'an, the miracles, the reports of what was hidden and concealed in the earlier scriptures, or the laws and obligations, or all of what has preceded together. The apparent meaning is the unrestricted one. "The defiantly disobedient" are those who are rebellious in disbelief and who go beyond the limits, for whoever does not possess those qualities among the disbelievers does not dare to disbelieve in such clear signs. Al-Hasan said: When the word fisq (disobedience) is used for a type of sin, it falls upon the most extreme instances of that type, whether of disbelief or of something else. So when it is said: "He is a fasiq in drinking," its meaning is that he is the most frequent in committing it; and when it is said: "He is a fasiq in fornication," its meaning is that he is the most intense in committing it. Its root is from "fasaqat al-ruṭaba," meaning when the date came out of its skin. The lam is either for a specific reference (ʿahd), since the context of the verses indicates that this refers to the Jews, or it is for the category (jins), and they are included in it, as has been mentioned more than once.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 100:

﴿Whenever they make a covenant, [will] a party of them cast it aside?﴾ It was revealed concerning Malik ibn al-Sayf, who said: "By God, no covenant was taken from us in our Book that we should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ), nor any pledge." It was also said that it concerns the Jews: they made a covenant that if he (ﷺ) emerged, they would believe in him and would certainly be with him against the polytheists of the Arabs. But when he was sent, they disbelieved in him. ʿAṭāʾ said: it concerns the Jews, who made covenants with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and then broke them, as the Qurayẓa and the Naḍīr did.

The hamzah (interrogative particle, the "alif of denial") here carries the sense of "it was not fitting that...". In it there is the magnification of what they undertake of repeated covenants and their breaking of them, until this became their disposition and habit. In this there is consolation for him, and an indication that he should not be concerned with their affair, and that their opposition should not grieve him. The waw is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon an omitted element, meaning: "disbelieve in the signs, and whenever they make a covenant..." This is a conjunction of a verbal clause upon a verbal clause, because kullamā (whenever) is an adverb of time (ẓarf). The clause "nabadhahu" (cast it aside) follows. The indication of that omitted element is His words, exalted is He: ﴿And none disbelieve in them except the defiantly disobedient﴾, etc.

Some scholars estimate that the conjoined element is taken from the preceding speech, and they hold that the hamzah is placed between the conjoined and that upon which it is conjoined, for a purpose related specifically to the conjoined element. Their estimate is: "They broke this covenant and that covenant; [and] ﴿whenever they make a covenant﴾." With this, along with committing what there is no necessity for, is that the sentences mentioned near it do not include any mention of breaking a covenant.

Al-Akhfash said: the hamzah is superfluous. Al-Kisāʾī said: it is the (ʾaw) [or] which is quiescent, its waw was vocalised with a fatḥah, and it means bal (rather). The weakness of the two opinions is not hidden. Yes, Ibn al-Sammāk al-ʿAdawī and others read (ʾaw) with sukūn, and in that case there is no harm in saying that it is for transition (idrāb), according to the view of the Kufan grammarians (al-Kufiyyun). They recited:

They appeared like the disc of the sun in the brightness of forenoon, and their form, or you are, in the eye, more graceful.

The conjunction upon this view is upon the relative clause (ṣilah) of the relative pronoun, which is the lām in (al-fāsiqūn) [the defiantly disobedient], inclining towards the side of the meaning. Although in it there is a transformation (maskh) of the relative lām, it is as if it were said: "except those who transgressed, rather whenever they make a covenant." The indication of that is: "rather most of them..." etc. In this there is a progression to the more severe and then the most severe.

You may also not incline with the meaning, but conjoin upon the relative clause. The alif-lām (al-) enters upon the verb by way of following, extensively, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed the male givers of charity and the female givers of charity, and those who lend to God﴾, because they tolerate in the secondary elements what is not tolerated in the primary ones.

Among people there is one who permits this conjunction with a possibility upon the first reading as well, and he did not need that omitted element. Al-Ḥasan and Abū Rajāʾ read (ʿūhidū) [they were made to covenant]. The accusative of (ʿahdan) [a covenant] is as a verbal noun not from its own root, i.e. (muʿāhadatan) [a mutual covenanting]. This is supported by its being read as (ʿahidū). Or it is an object, with (ʿāhadū) implying the sense of (aʿṭaw) [they gave]. ﴿a party of them cast it aside﴾, i.e. broke it and abandoned acting upon it. The original sense of nabdh is throwing away what is not regarded as of value, like a worn-out sandal, but it became predominant for that which by its nature is forgotten, since it is not regarded. Attributing nabdh to a covenant is a metaphor (majāz). Nabdh in its literal sense is only with corporeal things, as in His words: ﴿So We seized him and his soldiers and cast them into the sea﴾. The word firīq (party) is a collective noun (ism jins) with no singular, applying to the few and the many. He said "a party" only because among them are those who did not cast it aside. Ibn Masʿūd (ʿAbd Allāh) read (naqaḍahu) [broke it]. Abū Ḥayyān said in al-Baḥr: this is a reading that contradicts the consonantal text of the Mushaf, so it is better to take it as an explanation (tafsīr), but this is not strong, since an explanation does not appear without mention of the one explaining. Within the reading there is a possibility.

﴿Rather, most of them do not believe﴾. It is possible that by "most" is meant those who cast it aside, and it is possible that what is meant is those other than them. On the first, that is a rejection of what might be imagined, that the party are the minority, based on the understanding that the apparent sense of the term is the few. On the second, it is a rejection of what might be imagined, that whoever did not openly cast it aside believes in it in secret. The conjunction on both interpretations is a conjunction of sentences. It is possible that it is a conjunction of single words, with "most of them" conjoined upon "a party", and the clause "do not believe" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "most of them", and the governing element in it is "cast it aside".

(Page 336)

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 101:**

﴿And when there came to them a messenger﴾: the adverbial clause (*zarf*) modifies (*linabadha*, "they cast away"), and the clause is a coordinated clause (*ʿatf*) following what precedes it, falling under the reproach. The pronoun refers to the Children of Israel, not only to their scholars. The messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ), and the plural is for magnification. It is also said that he is ʿIsa (peace be upon him). Taking the word as a verbal noun meaning "the message," as in his saying:

*Certainly the slanderers lied: I did not disclose to them what was between me and Layla, nor did I send them as a messenger.*

is contrary to the apparent meaning. ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to (*jaʾa*, "came"), or to an omitted element functioning as an attribute of the messenger, to convey greater exaltation of him, since the rank of the messenger is according to the rank of the one who sent him. ﴿confirming what is with them﴾: that is, of the Torah, insofar as he (ﷺ) came in accordance with the description mentioned in it; or he informed that it is the speech of Allah sent down to His prophet Musa (peace be upon him); or he confirmed what is in it of the foundations of monotheism, the principles of religion, the reports of past nations, and the admonitions and wisdoms; or he made clear what they asked him about of its obscure matters. Some scholars took *ma* (what) in its general sense, to include all the divine books that were revealed before. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read *muṣaddiqan* (confirming) in the accusative, as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*) of the indefinite qualified noun.

﴿a party of those who were given the Book cast away﴾: that is, the Torah. They are the Jews who were in his time (ﷺ), not those who were in the time of Sulayman (peace be upon him), as some have imagined by way of attachment, because casting it away at the coming of the Prophet (ﷺ) is not conceivable from them. The singling out of this casting away by mention, though it is included in His saying ﴿Is it not that whenever they made a covenant...﴾ and so on, is because it is the greatest of their crimes and because it is a preparation for what comes after. The meaning of "given" is either the giving of its knowledge, so the relative clause refers to their scholars, or merely its being sent down to them, so it refers to all of them. He did not say "a party of them" to indicate the complete incompatibility between what was established for them within the relative clause and what issued from them of casting away.

﴿the Book of Allah﴾ is the object of (*nabadha*). It refers to the Torah, based on what is narrated from al-Suddi, who said: When Muhammad (ﷺ) came to them, they confronted him with the Torah, and the Torah and the Furqan (criterion) agreed. They then cast aside the Torah and took up the book of Asif and the sorcery of Harut and Marut, and it did not agree with the Qur'an. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿And when there came to them a messenger﴾ and so on. This is supported by the fact that casting away implies a prior taking up in general, which is realized with respect to it, and by the principle that when a definite noun is repeated as definite, the second is the same as the first. Also, their blame for casting away the Book that was given to them, while acknowledging its truth, is greater, for it indicates that it was mere obstinacy and enmity. The meaning of their casting it away is abandoning its rulings, or what is in it of the description of the Prophet (ﷺ). It is also said that the Book means the Qur'an, and Abu Hayyan supported this by saying that the speech is with the Messenger, so the meaning becomes that he confirms what is in their hands of the Torah, while they, on the contrary, deny what he brought of the Qur'an and reject it, even though they are obliged to receive it with acceptance.

Page 337

It is also said that it means the Gospel, but this is nothing. He attributed the Book to the Noble Name to glorify it and to emphasize the magnitude of their audacity in disbelieving in Him.

﴿behind their backs﴾: *ẓuhūr* is the plural of *ẓahr* (back), a known word, and it is also plural as *ẓihrān*. Their leaving the Book of Allah and turning away from it is compared to the state of something thrown behind the back, the common element being disregard and lack of concern. Then the expression used there, which is casting behind the back, is used here. The Arabs very often use it in this sense, and from it is his saying:

*Tamim ibn Murr, let not my need be behind (my) back, and let not its answer be difficult for you.*

They also say: "He made this matter the back of his ear," meaning what has been mentioned.

﴿as if they did not know﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*): that is, they cast it away, likened to one who does not know that it is the Book of Allah, or who does not know it at all, or who does not know it with mastery, and do not recognize what it contains of the proofs of his prophethood (ﷺ). This is on the assumption that the rabbis are meant, and in it is an indication that their knowledge of it is firm, but they feign ignorance. In the first two interpretations there is additional emphasis on their turning away from what is in the Torah of the proofs of prophethood. As for the one who interprets the Book of Allah as the Qur'an, the object of knowledge becomes that it is the Book of Allah, meaning: as if they do not know that the Qur'an is the Book of Allah, although that is established among them and confirmed for them. This includes an indication that they cast it away not out of doubt, but out of envy and rebelliousness. Making the object of knowledge that he is a truthful prophet is far-fetched.

The two verses, His saying ﴿Is it not that whenever they made a covenant...﴾ and His saying ﴿And when there came to them...﴾, indicate, on the basis of the possibility that most of them were not casters-away, that the Jews are four groups: one group believed in the Torah and fulfilled its obligations, like the believers among the People of the Book, and they are the few referred to by ﴿but most of them do not believe﴾; a group openly cast away the covenants and transgressed the limits, and they are those meant by His saying "a party of them cast away"; a group did not openly do so but cast away out of ignorance, and they are the majority; and a group held to it outwardly but cast it away secretly, and they are the feigning ignorant.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 102 (part 1 of 5):

﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾ is conjoined to (nabadha, "threw away"), and the pronoun refers to a group of those who were given the Book, according to what preceded from al-Suddi. It has also been said: it is conjoined to the whole of what precedes it, a narrative conjoined to a narrative, and the pronoun refers to those among the Jews who came before, or those who were in the time of Sulayman (peace be upon him), or those who were in the time of our Prophet (ﷺ), or to what encompasses all of them, because the former is not apparent, since it requires entering within the scope of "ma" (what), and their followers. This does not follow from the coming of the Messenger (ﷺ). In this there is that which you know from the saying of al-Suddi, which opens the door to what is apparent, except that the basis is other than it. It has also been said: it is conjoined to (ushribu, "were made to drink"), and this is extremely remote; rather, no one who has swallowed a single draught of fairness would advance it. The meaning of "following" (ittiba') is penetrating deeply into and devoting oneself wholly to a thing. It has also been said: it means imitation. "Ma" is a relative pronoun, and "tatlu" (recites) is its relative clause, and its meaning is: follows, or recites. This is a narration of a past state, and the original form is "talat." The statement of the Kufans, that the meaning is "what they used to recite," is to be understood in this sense, not that there is an implied "kana" there. The most immediate sense of "the devils" is the rebellious jinn, and this is the view of most. It has also been said that they are the devils of mankind, and this is the view of the Mu'tazilite theologians. al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read "al-shayatun" (with the nominative ending), following what al-Asma'i narrated from the Arabs: "The garden of so-and-so has gardens (bisatun) around it." This is an extremely anomalous form, to the point that it has been said it is a grammatical error.

﴿over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾ is related to "tatlu," and there is an omitted genitive construction in the speech, i.e., "the reign of his kingdom" and "his time," or "kingdom" is a metaphor for "reign." In both interpretations, "ʿala" is in the sense of "fi" (in), just as "fi" is in the sense of "ʿala" in His saying: ﴿and I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees﴾. It has been explicitly stated in al-Tashil that it comes for the sense of place, and he cited this verse as an example, because kingship and reign cannot be the thing over which one recites. Some of the scholars of our school denied that "ʿala" comes in the sense of "fi," and considered this to be an instance of the verb "tatlu" being construed with the meaning of "tataqawwalu" (to fabricate), or that "mulk" is an expression for the throne, since it was one of the instruments of his kingship; so the speech is like: "I read upon the pulpit." What is meant by what they recite is magic. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, Ibn Jarir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The devils used to eavesdrop on the heavens; whenever one of them heard a word, he would lie about it a thousand lies, and the hearts of the people were made to drink it, and they took it as registers. Allah Most High informed Sulayman ibn Dawud of this, so he seized them and cast them beneath the throne. When Sulayman died, a devil stood on the road and said: "Shall I direct you to the treasure of Sulayman, for which there is no treasure like his, the guarded one?" They said: "Yes," so they brought it out, and behold, it was magic. The nations then copied it, so Allah Most High sent down the exoneration of Sulayman regarding what they said of magic. It has also been said: it was narrated that Sulayman had buried much of the knowledge with which Allah had singled him out beneath the seat of his kingdom, fearing that when its apparent part perished, that buried part would remain. When a period passed over that, a group of hypocrites managed to write among those matters some items of magic that resemble those things in some respects. Then, after his death, when the people came upon those books, they led them to believe that they were from the knowledge of Sulayman. The weakness of this report is not hidden. Sulayman, as in al-Bahr, is a non-Arabic name, and it is diptote (not declined) because of being a proper name and non-Arabic. Its parallel among non-Arabic names, in that its ending is alif and nun, is Haman, Mahan and Shaman. Its being diptote is not because of being a proper name and the addition of alif and nun, like 'Uthman, because the addition of these two depends on derivation and inflection, and they enter non-Arabic names; and many people today hold the opposite.

﴿And Sulayman did not disbelieve﴾ is a parenthetical clause to absolve Sulayman (peace be upon him) of what they attributed to him. Ibn Jarir narrated from Shahr ibn Hawshab, who said: The Jews said: "Look at Muhammad, mixing truth with falsehood; he mentions Sulayman with the prophets, while he was only a magician who rides the wind." He, glorified be He, expressed magic by disbelief by way of metonymy, observing the relation of the adversative "but" in His saying: ﴿But the devils disbelieved, teaching people magic﴾. For "disbelieved" with it is used in its literal meaning. The clause "teaching" is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun. It has been said it is from "the devils," and this was refuted on the ground that "but" does not govern a circumstantial clause; it was answered that it carries a trace of the verb. It has also been said it is a substitute for "disbelieved." It has been said it is a resumptive sentence, and the pronoun refers to the devils, or to those who followed. Magic, originally, is the verbal noun of "sahara, yasharu" with the vowel of the eye in both, meaning to reveal what is subtle and hidden, and it is one of the rare verbal nouns. It is used for whatever is delicate and whose cause is hidden. What is meant by it is a strange matter resembling a marvel, and it is not of the kind to which learning applies in this sense. Its acquisition is aided by drawing near to the devil through committing vile acts, in speech such as incantations that contain words of association, and praise and subjection of the devil; and in deed, such as worshipping the stars and persisting in sin and all manner of wickedness; and in belief, such as deeming good what brings one nearer to him and his love for him. This is not established except with one who is akin to him in wickedness and evil disposition, for kinship is the condition of mutual support and cooperation. Just as the angels only assist the good among people who resemble them in constancy in worship and drawing near to God Most High by word and deed, so the devils only assist the wicked who resemble them in treachery and impurity in speech, deed and belief. By this the magician is distinguished from the prophet and the saint. Thus there is no rebuttal of what the Mu'tazilites said: that if it were possible for a person, through the devil, to manifest marvels and report unseen things, the path of prophethood would be confused with the path of magic. As for what is marvelled at, as done by practitioners of tricks, by the aid of machines assembled according to geometric proportion at times, and by making an empty space full at other times, and by the aid of medicines like the citron preparations, or what a master of sleight of hand shows, calling it magic by way of figurative usage, this too is blameworthy in the view of some, and al-Nawawi in al-Rawdah explicitly stated its prohibition.

The majority defined it as: a supernatural matter that appears from a wicked soul through performing specific acts. The majority hold that it has a real existence, and that the magician may reach the point where he flies in the air, walks upon water, kills a soul, and turns a man into a donkey; but the true agent in all of that is God Most High. His custom has not been to enable the magician to split the sea, revive the dead, make the dumb speak, or other signs of the messengers, peace be upon them. The Mu'tazilites and Abu Ja'far al-Istarabadhi from among our companions hold that it has no reality, and that it is only imagination. The Mu'tazilites declared disbelief for whoever said that a magician can reach the point of what we have mentioned, on the claim that this would close the path of prophethood; but it is not as they claimed, as is not hidden. Some of the verifiers distinguished between magic and miracle by the miracle being accompanied by a challenge, unlike magic, for it cannot manifest at the hand of a false claimant to prophethood, as God Most High's continuous custom has run, preserving this noble station from being scaled by liars. It is widely known that practicing it is disbelief, to the point that the scholar al-Taftazani said: "No difference of opinion is reported on that." Counting it as a kind of major sin distinct from polytheism does not contradict that, since disbelief is more general and polytheism is one kind of it. There is, however, a discussion here. First: Shaykh Abu Mansur held that the claim that magic is disbelief absolutely is an error; rather, its reality must be investigated. If it involves denying something that is a condition of faith, then it is disbelief; otherwise it is not. Perhaps the scholar's view is based on the earlier interpretation, for on that interpretation the disbelief of its practitioner is hardly in doubt. Second: the intended meaning of polytheism in what is other than the major sins is absolute disbelief, otherwise the kinds of disbelief would be excluded from it. Then, magic that is disbelief is punished by death for males but not for females; and what is not disbelief but involves destruction of a soul carries the ruling of highway robbers, and males and females are equal in it, and its repentance is accepted if one repents. Whoever says it is not accepted has erred, for the repentance of Moses's sorcerers was accepted; so it is in the Madarik, and perhaps this is closer to the principles. The well-known position of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, is that the magician is killed absolutely, once it is known that he is a magician, and his statement "I will abandon magic and repent of it" is not accepted. If he confesses, "I used to practise magic for a period, and I have given it up since some time ago," his statement is accepted and he is not killed. He cited the report that a slave-girl of Hafsah, the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with her, practised magic on her; they seized her, and she confessed to that; so she ordered 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, and he killed her. 'Uthman's denial was only because she was killed without his permission. He also cited what is reported from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Kill every magician, male and female," and they killed three sorceresses. The Shafi'is examined this argument and objected to the view of absolute killing, on the ground that the Prophet (ﷺ) did not kill the Jew who had bewitched him; so a believer is like him, based on his saying (peace be upon him): "They have what the Muslims have, and they have what is upon the Muslims." Its verification is in the books of jurisprudence. Scholars differed regarding teaching and learning it. It was said: it is disbelief, on the basis of this verse, since in it the ruling is attached to a suitable attribute, which indicates causation. It was answered: we do not concede that the verse has this, because the meaning is that they disbelieved, and yet they teach people magic. It was also said: both are forbidden, and the majority adhered to this. It was said: both are disliked, and some scholars held this. It was said: both are permissible; and the teaching addressed here for censure is to be understood as teaching for misguidance and leading astray. Imam al-Razi inclined to this, saying: "The scholars agree that knowledge of magic is neither vile nor prohibited, for knowledge in itself is noble, by the generality of His saying: ﴿Are those who know equal to those who do not know?﴾ And if magic were not known, it would not be possible to distinguish it from a miracle, and knowledge that the one who performs a miracle is performing one is obligatory, and what an obligation depends upon is itself obligatory; so this requires that acquiring knowledge of magic be obligatory, and how can what is obligatory be forbidden or vile?" Some have reported that learning it is obligatory for the mufti, until he knows what kills by it and what does not kill by it, so that he may give a ruling regarding the obligation of retaliation, end of quote. My own view is that it is prohibited, following the majority, unless there is a lawful reason. There is something to consider in what he said, may Allah have mercy on him. First: we do not claim that it is vile in itself; rather its vileness is by reference to what follows from it, so its prohibition

Ibn al-Qayyim... no. This is al-Alusi's commentary, continued from the preceding part. The passage follows.

It is from the category of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i', the principle of prohibiting what leads to harm), and many things have been prohibited on this basis. In a hadith: "Whoever grazes his animals around the sanctuary will soon fall into it."

Second: the distinction between sorcery and a miracle does not depend on knowing sorcery. Consider that most scholars, or all of them except a rare few, knew the difference between them without knowing the science of sorcery. The distinction mentioned earlier is sufficient to separate them. Had learning it been obligatory for this purpose, you would find the best-informed people about it to be the first generation, yet nothing of that kind is reported from them. Do you think they neglected this obligation while this speaker fulfilled it, or that he neglected it as they did?

Third: what is reported from some of them is not sound, because a jurist's ruling on whether retaliation (qawad) is required or not does not entail that he knows sorcery. The form of his ruling, as mentioned by the scholar Ibn Hajar, is: if two just witnesses testify that they knew sorcery and that the accused repented from it, then the sorcerer is usually put to death; otherwise, not.

Furthermore, some scholars have applied the term "sorcery" to walking among people carrying tale-bearing (namimah), because it turns a friend into an enemy and an enemy into a friend. It has also been applied to the fine use of eloquent, pleasing speech, because of the attraction it creates, and it is called "permissible sorcery." From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, there is sorcery in eloquence." The claim that this was said in the sense of disparaging eloquence and rhetoric is far-fetched, even though 'Amir al-Sha'bi, the transmitter of the hadith, held that view.

The apparent meaning of the phrase "they teach" (yu'allimuna) and what follows is that they cause people to understand it through reading and instruction. It has been said that they direct people to those books, so the indication is called teaching, by naming the cause for its effect. It has also been said that the meaning is that they fix in people's hearts that it is true, that it harms and benefits, and that Solomon (peace be upon him) achieved what he achieved through it. The application of the term to him is the same application. It has been said that yu'allimuna means yu'limuna from i'lam (informing), that is, they inform people of what they learn it by, or who they learn it from, or the sorcery itself.

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the word "lakinna" with shaddah (tashdid), while Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it without shaddah (takhfif). The noun following it is in the nominative, as a subject and predicate. There is disagreement over whether it may still govern its following noun when it is made light (lakin being the light form). The majority hold that it may not, and this is the correct view. Yunus and al-Akhfash held that it may. The correct view is that it is a simple particle. Some claim that it is compound, made of the negative la, the second-person kaf, and the emphatic an whose hamzah has been dropped for ease of pronunciation. But this view is closer to corruption.

"And what was sent down to the two angels" (wa ma unzila 'ala al-malakayn): the intended sense is the genus. It is coordinated with "sorcery" (al-sihr), and the two are one thing, except that the difference in concept has been treated as a difference in essence, as in the poet's line: "To the lordly king and son of the valiant..." [the verse continues]. The purpose of the coordination is to make explicit that they teach what combines being sorcery and being sent down to the two angels as a trial. This conveys their blame for committing the prohibited act in two respects. The relative pronoun may also refer to a specific known thing, which is another, stronger kind of sorcery; then it is coordination of the specific upon the general, to indicate its completeness. Mujahid said: it is less than sorcery, namely what is used to separate a man from his wife, and nothing more. The well-known view is the first.

It is permissible that the coordination be upon what is recited (ma tatlu), so that it is as if it were said: they followed the sorcery recorded in books and elsewhere. These two angels were sent down to teach sorcery as a trial from Allah Most High for mankind. Whoever learns it and acts upon it disbelieves, and whoever learns it and guards himself against acting upon it remains firm in faith. Allah Most High may test His servants with whatever He wills, as He tested the people of Talut with the river. It also serves to distinguish it from a miracle, since sorcery had spread greatly in that era, and the sorcerers displayed strange things by which doubt arose about prophethood. So Allah Most High sent the two angels to teach the gates of sorcery, so that they might remove doubts and clear harm from the path. It was said that this occurred in the time of Idris (peace be upon him).

As for what is related, that the angels marvelled at the children of Adam for disobeying what Allah Most High had commanded, and said to Him: "If we were in their place we would not disobey You." He said: "Choose two angels from among you," and they chose them. The two descended to earth and took human form, and Allah Most High placed desire upon them, and they judged among people. They were tempted by a woman called Zuhra, who refused them unless they worshipped an idol, or drank wine, or killed a soul. They did so. Then she learned from them the means by which she ascended to heaven, so she ascended and was transformed into this star. The two then wanted to ascend, but could not. They were given the choice between the punishment of this world and that of the Hereafter, and they chose the punishment of this world, so they are now being punished in it. This is among many reports whose chains reach some twenty. Yet al-Qadi 'Iyad and a group denied it. He mentioned that what the reporters and the commentators cited in the story of Harut and Marut has nothing from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), neither weak nor sound, and that it is not something to be known by analogy. In al-Bahr it is mentioned that none of it is sound. It is also not established that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed Zuhra, and Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) is contrary to the one who related that.

Imam al-Razi, after citing the report on this, said: this report is corrupt, rejected, and unacceptable. Al-Shihab al-'Iraqi stated that whoever believes that Harut and Marut are two angels punished for their sin with Zuhra is a disbeliever in Allah the Mighty, for the angels are protected from sin: "They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded." "They do not disdain His worship, nor do they grow weary." "They glorify Him night and day, never tiring." Zuhra existed on the day Allah Most High created the heavens and the earth. The claim that she appeared to them and that what happened happened, and that she was returned to her place, is neither reasonable nor acceptable.

Imam al-Suyuti, objecting to those who denied the story, said that Imam Ahmad, Ibn Hibban, al-Bayhaqi and others narrated it both as attributed to the Prophet (ﷺ) and as halted at 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar and Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with them), through many sound chains, such that one who examines them is nearly certain of their soundness because of their number and the strength of their compilers. Some researchers held that what was narrated is related as a recounting of what the Jews said, and that its falsity in itself does not contradict the soundness of the narration. This does not refute what Imam al-Suyuti said against it; it refutes only those who reject the story entirely.

Perhaps this is in the category of symbols and allusions. By the two angels is meant the theoretical intellect and the practical intellect, which are from the world of holiness. By the woman called Zuhra is meant the rational soul. Their approach to her means their teaching her what makes her happy. Her inciting them to sin means her urging them, by the nature of temperament, toward inclining to lowly worldly things that defile their two essences. Her ascent to heaven by what she learned from them means her ascent to the exalted assembly and her association with the holy ones through her receiving their counsel. Their remaining punished means their remaining occupied with managing the body, and their deprivation of ascent to the heaven of the presence, because the bird of the intellect does not circle around its sanctuary.

Among the great scholars, one said in resolving this symbol: the spirit and the intellect, which are from the world of pure immaterial beings, descended from the heaven of detachment to the earth of attachment, and they fell in love with the body, which is like Zuhra in the utmost beauty and loveliness, since their perfection depends upon it. Through its mediation they acquired sins, polytheism, and the attainment of base sensual pleasures. Then she ascended to heaven, in that through their good management she reached the perfection fitting for her. Then she was transformed, in that attachment ended and the elements separated. The two remained punished with the punishment of deprivation from union with the world of holiness, suffering spiritual pains, their state inverted, since attachment dominated detachment and nearness was reversed into distance.

It has also been said: the purpose of this is to indicate that whoever is an angel, if he follows desire, falls from the rank of the angels to the rank of the beast; and whoever is a woman with desire, if she breaks her desire and overcomes it, ascends to the rank of an angel and reaches the heaven of stations and degrees. One of them wrote to resolve it:

"I have grown weary, by Allah, my soul, my soul,
and the length of my life's confinement has grown long.
I wake in my bed, and I am the same at evening,
my day is like my yesterday, and my yesterday like my day.
How good is the day of my descent into my grave,
the beginning of my fortune and the end of my misfortune.
Every kind clings to its kind,
a substance (jawhar) which ascends to the abode of intimacy,
and an accident (arad) which remains in the abode of the senses."

[Page 342]

[Page 343]

That said, whoever holds that this story is authentic in reality and takes it at face value has indeed committed excess, spoken an error, and opened a door of sorcery that makes the dead laugh, makes the living weep, lowers the banner of Islam, and raises the heads of the vile disbelievers. This is not hidden from the fair-minded scholars who investigate the truth.

Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu al-Aswad, and al-Dahhak read (al-malakayni) with a kasra on the lam. Some have made the reading with a fatha conform to this, saying: "They are two men, but they were called two angels because of their righteousness." What supports this is what has been said: they are Dawud and Sulayman. But al-Hasan's statement refutes it: "They are two uncouth men who were in Babil of Iraq." Others say: "They are two angels who appeared in the form of kings." In this view, the kasra is taken to mean the fatha, in the reverse of what was previously mentioned. The "descent" (al-inzal) is either on its literal sense, or it means being cast into their hearts.

(Bi-Babil) — the ba' here means fi (in). It is connected either to (unzila), or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the two angels, or of the pronoun in (unzila). Babil, as Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with them both) said, is a town in the outskirts of Kufa. It has also been said: it is Babil of Iraq. Qatada said: it extends from Nusaybin to Ras al-'Ayn. It has also been said: it is the Mount of Damawand, and it has been said: it is a land in the West. The well-known view today is the second, while for some the first is the one held. It is said that it was called Babil because of the confusion of tongues (tabalbul al-alsina) there when the palace of Nimrod fell. Al-Dinawari in al-Mujalasa and Ibn Asakir narrated through the chain of Nu'aym ibn Salim, who is accused (of fabrication), from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "When Allah the Exalted gathered the creatures to Babil, He sent to them an eastern wind, a western wind, a southern wind and a northern wind, and they gathered them to Babil. They assembled that day, looking at what they had been gathered for, when a caller called out: 'Whoever makes the West on his right and the East on his left, and heads straight to the Sacred House with his face, will have the speech of the people of heaven.' So Ya'rub ibn Qahtan stood up, and it was said to him: 'O Ya'rub ibn Qahtan ibn Hud, it is you!' He was the first to speak Arabic. The caller kept calling: 'Whoever does such and such, for him is such and such,' until they dispersed into seventy-two tongues. The voice ceased, the tongues were confused, and it was called Babil. The language at that time was Babylonian." I have doubts about both views, indeed I do not accept them. What I incline to is that Babil is a non-Arabic name, as Abu Hayyan explicitly stated, not an Arabic one, as the words of al-Akhfash indicate. Originally it was the name of a great river in some ancient non-Arabic languages, and it was applied to that land because the Euphrates is near it. Perhaps this is of the same kind as the naming of Baghdad as Dar al-Salam, on the basis that al-Salam is a name for the Tigris. I have seen a detailed discussion of this, which I cannot recall today in which book, and I think it is close to what I have mentioned, so let this be retained.

Some have forbidden prayer in the land of Babil, citing what Abu Dawud, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated: "From Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that my beloved (ﷺ) forbade me to pray in the land of Babil, for it is cursed." Al-Khattabi said: "There is criticism in the chain of this hadith. I do not know of any scholar who prohibited prayer there. If the hadith is established, it resembles that he forbade him from taking it as a homeland and residence. When one settles there, his prayer is there (i.e., it is included in that prohibition). This is of the type of restriction (al-ta'liq) in the science of eloquence (ilm al-bayan). Or perhaps the prohibition was specific to him. Do you not see that he said, 'He forbade me,' and a similar hadith: '(He) forbade me from reciting while prostrating or bowing,' and he did not say, 'He forbade you.' This was a warning from him about the trial he would encounter in that region."

(Harut wa Marut) — an appositive (atf bayan) to the two angels. Both are non-Arabic names for them, and they are not inflected (ghayr munsarif) due to definiteness and foreignness. It has been said they are Arabic, from al-hart and al-mart, meaning breaking. Their earlier names were 'Aza and 'Azaya. When they committed the sin they were named thus. It is problematic for this view that they are not inflected, for there is only definiteness. Some have strained to answer this, saying: it may be said that they are formed by deviation (ma'dulan) from al-Harit and al-Marit, and the restriction of deviation to the preserved patterns is not granted, and this is, as you see, (weak). Al-Hasan and al-Zuhri read them in the nominative, on the basis that the estimate is: they are Harut and Marut. Among the matters that give rise to wonder is what Imam al-Qurtubi said: that Harut and Marut are a substitute (badal) for the devils (al-shayatin) according to the reading with tashdid, and that (ma) in (wa ma unzila) is negative, and what is meant by the two angels is Jibril and Mika'il, because the Jews claimed that Allah the Exalted sent down the two with sorcery. In the statement there is inversion and reordering, and the estimate is: "And Sulayman did not disbelieve, and what was sent down upon the two angels was not (sorcery), but the devils, Harut and Marut, disbelieved, teaching people sorcery at Babil." On this basis the substitution is either a substitution of part for whole, and they were mentioned specifically because of their rebellion and because they were the heads in teaching; or a substitution of whole for whole, either on the basis that the plural is used for two, or on the basis that they are expressions for two tribes of devils, none of whom had this attribute other than them. More wondrous than this statement is his saying: "This is the most fitting of the interpretations to which the verse may be applied and the most correct of what has been said about it, and do not turn to anything else." It is not hidden from any fair-minded person that it is not befitting for a believer to bear the words of Allah the Exalted, which are at the highest levels of eloquence and fluency, upon something lower than that. This is nothing but a distortion of the Book of Allah the Exalted, may His majesty be glorified, and a lowering of it from its lofty station, and the corruptions of scant understanding are beyond counting. It has also been said that they are a substitution for mankind, meaning: they teach people, specifically Harut and Marut, and the negation is the negation (as stated).

﴿And they do not teach anyone until they say: We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve﴾. That is: the two angels do not teach anyone until they advise him and say to him: "We are only a test from Allah the Mighty and Majestic. Whoever learns from us and acts upon it disbelieves, and whoever learns and refrains remains steadfast in faith." (So do not disbelieve) by believing in it and permitting acting upon it. It has also been said: "So do not learn while believing it to be true, lest you disbelieve." This is based on the view of the Mu'tazila that sorcery is mere deception and imagination, and whoever believes it to be real disbelieves. (Min) is added in the object for emphasizing the comprehensiveness of the negation. The singular "trial" is used although the subject is plural, because it is a verbal noun (masdar), and the predication is by identity for the sake of exaggeration. The restriction (qasr) is to clarify that they have no concern in what they undertake other than this, so that people turn away from learning it. (Hatta) is for the limit (ghayah). It has also been said it means "illa" (except). The clause is in the position of a circumstantial accusative (nasb ala al-hal) from the pronoun in (yu'allimun). The apparent view is that the saying occurs once; the claim that it occurs three, seven, or nine times has no basis.

The manner of receiving this knowledge from them has been disputed. Mujahid said: "No one from among the people reaches them, but two devils visit them once each year, and they learn from them." It has also been said, and this is the apparent view: "They used to directly undertake the teaching themselves at some time, and the closer view is that at that time they were not in angelic form." As for what Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "A woman from the people of Dumat al-Jandal came to me seeking the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after his death, asking him about something she had entered into of the matter of sorcery and had not acted upon. She said: 'I had a husband who had been away from me, so I went to an old woman and complained to her. She said: If you do what I command you, I will make him come to you. When night came, she brought me two black dogs. She rode one and I rode the other, and it was not like anything, until we stopped at Babil. Suddenly I saw two men hanging by their feet. They said: What brought you? I said: I want to learn sorcery. They said: We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve, and return. I refused and said: No. They said: Then go to that oven and urinate in it. ...' until she said: 'I went and urinated in it, and I saw a horseman, veiled in iron, come out of me, rise to the sky, and vanish from me until I could no longer see him. I came to them and told them, and they said: You have spoken the truth. That was your faith that departed from you. Go, for you will not desire anything except that it will happen.'" — the whole report at length — then this, and its like among the stories the exegetes have mentioned on this subject, are not relied upon by people of intellect. Hastening to deny the likes of this Dumat woman is more fitting than suspecting reason in accepting this account, for nothing authentic has been transmitted about it from the Messenger of the Lord of creation (ﷺ). Would that the books of Islam had not included these fables which no sane person believes, even if they were confused dreams.

Those who permit learning sorcery have used this verse as evidence. Its basis is that it indicates that teaching occurred from angels despite their infallibility, and learning is the verbal correlate of teaching. Indeed, the two are identical in essence and differ only in relation, like the act of giving and receiving.

[Page 344]

and the obligation. It is not hidden that there is no proof in it for permissibility absolutely, because that teaching was for the sake of trial and distinction, as we have mentioned before. Those who hold the prohibition have said: if the learning of magic is undertaken when it has spread in a region, and the aim is to make its corruption clear to them so that they may return to the truth, it is not forbidden, just as the learning of philosophy is not forbidden for one appointed to defend the religion by refuting doubts, although its most common state is prohibition. This contradicts unqualified speech about it. And whoever said that Harut and Marut were of the devils said: the meaning of the verse is "they do not teach anyone magic until they advise him and say: indeed we are a trial, so do not be like us in that by believing it permissible and acting upon it, lest you disbelieve." In that case there is no inference at all. What we have mentioned, that the saying is by way of advice in this aspect, is the apparent meaning. Al-Mahdawi related that it is by way of mockery, not advice, and this is more fitting to the state of the devils. Talhah ibn Musarrif read (yu'limani) with the light form, from i'lam (informing), and some interpreted the doubled reading accordingly. Ubayy read with the agent expressed. ﴿and they learn from both of them﴾ is coordinated with the negated clause, because it has the force of an affirmative clause, as if he said: they teach them after that saying, so they learn. It is not coordinated with the negated clause without this consideration, as Abu 'Ali supposed from the words of al-Zajjaj. Some coordinated it with a deleted "(they) teach," and some with "(they) come" in the same way. The raised pronoun refers to what is implied by "anyone," which is people, or to "anyone," taking it according to meaning, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So none of you could hold back from Him﴾.
