Al-Mahdawi related the permissibility of coordinating it with ﴿they teach people﴾, in which case the reference of the pronoun is clear. It was also said: there is a deleted subject in the sentence, i.e. "so they learn," making it an independent nominal clause coordinated with what precedes it, from coordinating a nominal clause with a verbal one. This is attributed to Sibawayh, but it is not the best. The pronoun in (minhuma) refers to the two angels. Some of the people made it refer to magic and disbelief, or to trial and magic. They coordinated (yataʿallamun) with (yuʿallimun) and took (ma yuʿallimani) as negation, with (hatta yaqula) as its emphasis: that is, they do not teach anyone magic but forbid him until they say, and so on. It is like your saying: "I did not order him to do such-and-such until I said to him: if you do it, such-and-such will befall you." Also (ma unzila) was made a negation coordinated with (ma kafara), and this, as you see, is weak. ﴿with which they cause division between a man and his wife﴾: that is, "that which," or "something with which they cause division," namely magic that removes, by way of causation, the affection and love between the spouses, producing hatred and enmity which necessitate their separation. It was also said: what is meant is that which divides because it is disbelief, for when he learns it he disbelieves, so his wife is separated from him; or when he learns and practices it, people see it and believe it to be true, and so they disbelieve, and their wives are separated from them. (Al-mar') means the man, and the most eloquent form is with a fatha on the mim in all cases. A damma on it in all cases is also reported, and following the vowel of case is reported. Its feminine is (al-mar'ah), and its plural has come with the waw and nun, so they said (al-mar'un). (Al-zawj) is a man's wife. It was also said that what is meant here is a relative or a suitable brother, and from this is His saying: ﴿of every fine pair﴾ and ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their pairs﴾. Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and Qatadah read (al-mari) without a hamza, lightened; Ibn Abi Ishaq read (al-mur'i) with a damma on the mim and the hamza; al-Ashhab read it with a kasra and hamza, and it is reported from al-Hasan; al-Zuhri also read (al-marri) with a fatha, dropping the hamza and doubling the ra. ﴿and they do not harm anyone thereby except by permission of God﴾: the pronoun refers to the magicians, to whom the pronoun of (fa-yatallamun) returns; it was also said it refers to the Jews, to whom the pronoun of (wa-ittaba'u) returns; and it was said it refers to the devils. The pronoun in (bihi) refers to (ma), and (min) is extra, for the generality of the negation, as if it were said: they harm no one thereby. Al-A'mash read (bi-darri) with the nun deleted, and it is explained as deleted for lightness, although the active participle is not a relative clause of "al-", and Ibn Malik stated that this condition is not required, by his saying:
"And we, when you come to Salma, are not claimants against you, except that we ask to be at peace, and we keep peace."
And the saying of them: "qatatha, your eggs are two hundred and mine are a hundred." It was also said that it was deleted for annexation to a deleted noun understood in form, in the manner of his saying: "O Taym of Taym 'Adi," in one of the views. It was also said that it was deleted for annexation to "ahad" with the preposition made part of it, and the separation by the adverb is
صفحة 345
attested, as in his saying:
"They are two brothers in war, whom I do not consider... and if he fears a stumble one day, he calls both of them."
Al-Zamakhshari chose this. But in it: making the preposition part of the genitive is nothing, because it governs it, and a part of a thing does not govern it; and also the separation between the two terms of an annexation by an adverb, though heard in poetic necessity, as Abu Hayyan stated. Ibn Jinni said, because of a doubt that this was the only way out: this reading is the most remote of the anomalous readings. ﴿except by permission of God﴾: an exceptive clause from the circumstantial accusatives; the preposition is attached to a deleted word that stands as a circumstance of the subject of (darrin) or of its object relying on the negation, or of the pronoun deleted in (bihi), or of the verbal noun understood from the description. The permission here is meant as leaving the bewitched person to the harm of the magic; said by al-Hasan. In it is evidence that there is an inherent harm in it: when God wills, He prevents it between him and it, and when He wills, He leaves it, and what He placed in it. This is the position of the early scholars regarding all causes and their effects. It was also said: permission means command, and it is used figuratively for creation, by the relation of the existence following each of the two in general, and the indicator is that evil things are not commanded; in it is negation that causes act by themselves, but rather by His making them causes, either customary or real. It was also said that here it means knowledge, and it contains no indication of negating causal influence in itself, as in the first two views.

﴿And they learn what harms them﴾: because they intend to act upon it with firm resolve, and intending disobedience is likewise disobedience; or because knowledge calls to action and draws toward it, especially the action of evil which is the desire of the soul. So the present tense indicates the present on the first view and the future on the second. (And it does not benefit them) is coordinated with what precedes it, to announce that it is pure evil and unmixed harm, not like some harmful things mixed with benefit and harm, because they do not intend by it escape from being deceived by the lies of magicians, nor the removal of harm from the road, so that there would be some benefit in it. The use of (la) indicates that it is not beneficial in either abode, since it has no connection to the ordering of livelihood or of the hereafter. In the ruling that it is harmful and not beneficial lies a strong warning to whoever gives ear while he is a witness, against engaging in it, and an incitement to guard against it. Some permitted that (la yanfa'uhum) be with a pronoun "huwa" understood, so that it is in the place of a nominative, and the waw is for the circumstantial; its weakness is not hidden.

﴿And they had certainly known﴾ is connected to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when there came to them﴾ etc., and the story of magic is a digression in between. So the pronoun refers to those Jews. It was also said the pronoun refers to the Jews who were in the time of Solomon, peace be upon him. It was also said it refers to the two angels, because they used to say: "so do not disbelieve"; and he used the plural pronoun according to the view of one who holds that. ﴿that whoever bought it﴾: that is, exchanged what the devils recite for the Book of God. The lam is the lam of initiation; it enters upon the subject and upon the imperfect verb; its entry upon the perfect with "qad" is common, and without it is impermissible; and it enters upon the predicate of the subject when that is placed before it, and upon the object of the predicate when it occupies the place of the subject. The Kufans make it in all of these the response of an implied oath. There is, in their view, no lam of initiation in existence, as the words of al-Radi indicate. Here (knew) has been suspended from operating, whether it is transitive to one object or two. So (man) is a relative pronoun, subject; (ishtaraha) is its relative clause; and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿he has no portion in the hereafter﴾ is an independent nominal clause as its predicate; (min) is extra in the subject; (fi al-akhirah) is connected to what the predicate is connected to, or is a circumstance of the pronoun in it, or of its referent. (Khalaq) means portion, said by Mujahid; or sustenance, said by Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both; or measure, said by Qatadah. From it is his saying:
"So you have no house by the lofty ones, and you have no portion among Ghalib."
Al-Zajjaj said: it is used mostly for good, and for evil rarely. Abu al-Baqa', following al-Farra', went to the view that the lam is a preface to an oath, (man) is a conditional noun as subject, (ishtaraha) is its predicate, and (ma lahu) etc. is the answer of the oath; the answer of the condition is deleted, indicated by that, because when an oath and a condition are combined, the earlier of the two is generally answered. In this there is what there is, for it is reported from al-Zajjaj that he rejected whoever said that (man) here is conditional, on the ground that it is not a place of condition. Abu Hayyan explained it by saying that the verb is past in form and in meaning, because the buying has already taken place, so making it a condition is not valid, since a conditional verb that is past in form must be future in meaning. Al-Radi mentioned in "la-Zaydun qa'imun" that it is preferable that the lam there be the lam of initiation, giving emphasis, and that the oath is not to be assumed as the Kufans did, because the original is non-assumption, and the emphasis sought from the oath is obtained from the lam. The claim that the lam is an emphasis of the first or is extra is hardly correct: as for the first, because a word built on a single letter is not repeated alone, but only with its support, except in poetic necessity, as al-Radi preferred; and as for the second, because the known usage is the extra lam of the genitive, which is kasra in the apparent noun.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 102 (part 5 of 5):

﴿And surely wretched is that for which they sold their souls﴾. The lam here is also the lam of initiation (*lam al-ibtida'*, the emphatic lam that opens a sentence). The well-known view is that it is the response to the oath (*jawab al-qasam*), and the clause is conjoined to the earlier oath-clause. (*Ma*) is an indefinite noun (*nakira*) specifying the vague pronoun in *bi'sa*, and the object of dispraise is omitted. (*Sharaw*) may bear both meanings, and the apparent meaning is the apparent meaning: that is, by God, wretched is the thing for which they sold the shares of their souls, meaning they sold them, or in their own supposition they bought that purchase. In *al-Bahr* (Abu Hayyan's *al-Bahr al-Muhit*): "Wretched is what they sold their souls for: sorcery or disbelief."

﴿If only they knew﴾, that is, if they had known the blameworthiness of the aforementioned purchase, they would have refrained from it. There is no contradiction between affirming knowledge for them at first and negating it for them afterward, either because what is affirmed for them is innate reason (*al-'aql al-gharizi*), while what is negated is acquired knowledge (*al-kasb*), which is part of moral obligation (*al-taklif*); or because the first is general knowledge and the second is detailed knowledge. A person may know, for example, the ugliness of a thing without knowing that his own act is ugly. Thus it is as if they knew that buying one's soul with sorcery was blameworthy, but did not reflect that what they were doing was part of that ugliness. Or because they knew the punishment but did not know its reality and its severity. Or because the speech is framed by treating one who knows a matter as if he were ignorant of it, and the existence of a thing as if it were its non-existence, due to the absence of its fruit, since they did not act upon their knowledge. Or by treating one who knows the benefit of a statement and its implication as if he were ignorant, on the basis that God's words ﴿if only they knew﴾ mean: if they had knowledge of that purchase they would have refrained from it, i.e., they have no knowledge, so they do not refrain. This is the statement addressed to them.

The objection of the *'Allama* (al-Zamakhshari, or the author of the glosses, as cited) is that even if this statement were addressed to them, there would be no sense in saying they know its content, since ﴿And they certainly knew﴾ establishes its opposite, that they have knowledge of it. After all this, there is no sense in treating them as ignorant by saying they have no knowledge that whoever buys it has no share in the Hereafter. Rather, if this is so, they must be treated as ignorant of their having knowledge of that. The answer to this is: first, the address is explicitly to the Messenger (ﷺ) and implicitly to them, and for this reason it was emphasized. Second, what is established by ﴿And they certainly knew﴾ is the real existence of knowledge for them, while what is conveyed by the statement addressed to them is the negation of knowledge for them in the sense of treating them as such (*tanzil*). There is no contradiction between the two. Third, when one who knows acts contrary to his knowledge, he knows that he is in the position of one who is ignorant, in that the fruit of his knowledge does not follow. The requirement of this knowledge is that he refrain from that act. In our case they knew, regarding it, that they had no knowledge, and that they were in the position of the ignorant in that purchase. The requirement of this knowledge is that they refrain from it. When they did not refrain, they were in the position of the ignorant in not acting upon this knowledge. So the statement was addressed to them that they have no knowledge, while they know it. Thus it is said, but its great artificiality is not hidden.

Some have answered the apparent contradiction by saying that the object of ﴿they know﴾ is what is indicated by ﴿wretched is what they sold﴾, etc., namely the blameworthiness of the purchase, while the object of ﴿they knew﴾ is that they have no share (in the Hereafter). Knowing that they have no share in the Hereafter does not contradict the negation of knowledge of the blameworthiness of the purchase, in that they might believe it permissible. Thus there is no need then for all that has preceded. But this is objected to: knowing that the aforementioned purchase entails deprivation in the Hereafter, without knowing that it is blameworthy in the extreme, is something hardly conceivable to people of intellect. The view that the object of ﴿they knew﴾ is omitted, meaning ﴿they certainly knew that it harms them and does not benefit them﴾, is also weak.

﴿And whoever bought it﴾ is connected to the beginning of the story. The pronoun in ﴿wretched is what they sold﴾ referring to ﴿whoever bought it﴾ is extremely weak, and what is sold is not wretched. The answer that the statement affirmed first the knowledge of the evil of what they sold with the Book in terms of the Hereafter, and then condemned it as evil absolutely in religion and in this world, since *bi'sa* is for general dispraise, so what is negated is knowledge of absolute evil, meaning: if they had known its harm in religion and in this world, they would have refrained. What deceived them was the illusion of immediate benefit. Or the answer that what was affirmed first is knowledge that what they bought has no share for them in the Hereafter, not that they sold their souls for it and removed them from their hands entirely, but rather they thought their forefathers, the prophets, would intercede for them in the Hereafter. The knowledge that is negated is this knowledge. But what is in this is not hidden. First, because the generality of dispraise in *bi'sa*, even if it is held, applies to the singular agent in itself, without reference to times or places, and maintaining that requires some difficulty. Second, because restricting the share (*nasib*) to "from it," while it is indefinite and conjoined with *min*, in the context of negation brought for emphasis of magnitude, is something only narrowness of mind would require. The answer of returning the pronoun of ﴿they knew﴾ to the people, or the devils, and ﴿they bought﴾ to the Jews, is a resort to disjunction without any necessity requiring it and without any clear indication pointing to it.

After all this reckoning, my own preference in the answer is that the speech is framed according to the *tanzil* (treating one as in a different state), and there is no doubt about the great frequency of this in the Glorious Book. The answers mentioned earlier, though the discussion in them proceeds according to the apparent meaning, are not free of something in the inner meaning, so reflect.

[p. 347]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 103:**

﴿And if only they had believed﴾, that is, in the Messenger, or in what was sent down to him of the signs, or in the Torah, ﴿and had been mindful of God﴾, that is, had refrained from the acts of disobedience reported of them, ﴿a reward from God would be better﴾. This is the answer (jawab) to the conditional particle law ("if only"). Its underlying form is: "they would have been rewarded with a reward from God that is better than what they sold their souls for." The verb was omitted and the construction was altered to the form you see, so that, with the help of the context, it might indicate the permanence of the reward and the permanence of the attribution of superiority to it, together with the certainty of its being a statement of fact. For when a sentence conveys the permanence of the reward, the ruling takes the place of a qualification by a derived noun (ism mushtaq), as if it were said: "a lasting reward is better, because of its permanence and endurance." The comparative object was omitted out of reverence for the one being preferred, lest it be attributed to Him in any comparison. He did not say "the reward of God," although that is shorter, so that the indefiniteness (tankir) would suggest paucity, and thus the meaning would be that a small portion of God's reward in the eternal Hereafter is better than a great deal of reward in the transient world. How much more so when God's reward is abundant and everlasting. In it there is encouragement and warning appropriate to the situation, which is evident. By explaining the underlying form, two difficulties are resolved. The first is verbal: the answer to law is normally a past verbal sentence. The second is conceptual: the superiority of the reward is fixed and has no connection with whether they believe or not. Because of these two difficulties, al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat) said, and a group adopted his view, that the answer is a nominal sentence for its freedom from appearing in the outward form as the answer to law, which is not customary in the Arabic language. As in al-Bahr (of Abu Hayyan), the lam is the answer to an elided oath, and the estimate is: "And if only they had believed and been mindful of God, it would indeed be better for them; and a reward with God is better." Some insisted that the sentence expresses a wish (tamanni), but this is from the side of the servants, not from the side of God, Exalted is He. This differs from those who withdrew from this, in order to repel both difficulties, since there is then no answer to it, and the statement would be a new (independent) sentence, as if, when He expressed a wish for them in this regard, it was said: "What is this regret and wishing?" It was answered that these vile people sold what, of a small part of it, is better than the world and what is in it. In this there is exhortation and urging toward faith. Abu Hayyan held that "better" (khayr) here is used for comparison, not for mere superiority, in the manner of the verse of the poet:

*"So the better of you two is a ransom for the worse of you two."*

The word al-mathuba is a form of mafa'ala with a damma on its 'ayn, derived from al-thawab (reward). The damma was moved to the letter before it, so it is a noun of place-like form in the verbal noun category (masdar mimi). It was also said that it is of the form maf'ula, its original being mathuwba, the damma of the waw was moved to the preceding letter, and the waw was elided because of the meeting of two quiescent letters. Thus it is among the verbal nouns that came in the form maf'ula, like masduqa, as al-Wahidi transmitted. It is also said mathwaba with the thā' quiescent and the waw open. The original rule was that it should be given a weak-letter alteration (i'lal) and be said mathaba, like muqama, but they kept it sound, as they kept makuza in proper names. It was recited thus by Qatada and Abu al-Sammak. What is meant by it is recompense and wage, and it was so named because the doer of good returns (yathubu) to it. The view that what is meant by it is a return to Him, Exalted is He, is remote. ﴿If only they knew﴾. The object is elided by the indication of what precedes, that is, that God's reward is better. The word law is either conditional, with the answer elided (that is, "they would have believed"), or it expresses a wish, in which case there is no elision. The negation of knowledge on both readings is by negating its fruit, which is action, or it is because they neglected reflection. This is what was said.

* * *

Among the allusive (ishari) interpretations of the verses: ﴿and they followed﴾, that is, the Jews, and these are the spiritual faculties (al-quwa al-ruhaniyya). ﴿What the devils recited﴾ are, from among mankind, the rebellious wicked, and from among the jinn, the illusions and imaginings veiled from the light of the spirit (ruh), rebellious against the obedience of the heart, disobedient to the command of the intellect and the Sharia, and the earthly, dark souls (nufus), strong in the era of Solomon's kingdom, who is the spirit, the vicegerent of God in His earth. Solomon did not disbelieve, by observing other than God, following desire, and ascribing influence to what is other than God. But the devils disbelieved and concealed the effectiveness of God, Exalted is He, and His manifestation, which erased the darkness of nonexistence.

﴿They taught people magic﴾, and the doubts that turn them away from the journey and the spiritual path to the King of kings. ﴿And what was sent down to the two angels﴾, and these are the theoretical intellect ('aql nazari) and the practical intellect ('aql 'amali), descending from the heaven of holiness (quds) to the earth of nature, and inverted in its well, because they turned toward it, through the soul's drawing them to it, in Babylon of the breast, tormented by the narrowness of the place, between the vapours of love of status, the materials of anger, and the smoke of the fires of desires, tested with kinds of imaginings and false fancies, of tricks, sorcery, talismans, and magical practices. ﴿And they do not teach anyone until they say﴾ to him: "We are only a trial and a test from God, Exalted is He," ﴿so do not disbelieve﴾. This is because of the strength of their light (nuriyya) and the remnant of the angelic realm (malakutiyya) within them, for the intellect always alerts its possessor when he wakes from his intoxication and rises from his sleep, away from disbelief and veiling. ﴿So they learn from the two what they use to separate between﴾ the heart and the soul, or between the spirit and the soul, by darkening the heart. ﴿And they learn what harms them﴾ by increasing veiling and the dominance of the desire of the soul, and what does not benefit them, like the rest of the sciences, in lifting the veil, emptying the soul and purifying it. ﴿And they certainly knew that whoever bought it would have no share﴾ in the station of annihilation (fana') and return to the Truth, glory be to Him, because of his turning toward the lower world and his distance from the higher world, through the darkening of the essence of his heart, and his absorption in seeing others. ﴿And if only they had believed﴾ by seeing actions as from God, Exalted is He, ﴿and been mindful of association﴾ by affirming other than Him, ﴿they would have been rewarded with a reward from God, Exalted is He, lasting,﴾ ﴿and they would have returned to Him﴾. ﴿That would be better for them, if only they were of those possessing knowledge, gnosis, insight, and certainty.﴾

(p. 348)

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 104:

﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Ra'ina"﴾. Ra'y (watching over, guarding) is the preservation of another's welfare, whether that other is rational or not. The occasion of revelation of the verse is what Abu Nu'aym related in al-Dala'il from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Jews used to say this secretly to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and it was an ugly insult in their language. When they heard his Companions, upon them be blessing and peace, saying it, they said it openly and laughed among themselves. So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse. It is also narrated that Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah, may Allah be pleased with him, heard it from them and said: "O enemies of Allah, upon you be the curse of Allah! By Him in whose hand is my soul, if I hear any one of you say it to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, I will surely strike his neck." They said: "Do you not say it yourselves?" So the verse was revealed. The believers were forbidden, as a means of closing the door, cutting off tongues, and keeping away from resemblance. 'Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and al-Nahhas related from 'Ata', who said: "Ra'ina was the language of the Ansar in the Jahiliyyah, so Allah the Exalted forbade them from it in Islam." Perhaps the meaning is that they used it frequently in their speech.
Page 349
The Jews used it as an insult, so they were forbidden from it. As for the claim that it is a word peculiar to them, it is not evident, because it is preserved in the language of all the Arabs since they existed. It has also been said: the meaning of this word for the Jews, may Allah curse them, was "Listen, may you not hear." It has also been said: they intended to attribute him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and far be it from him, to the word "ra'an" (foolishness), and made it derived from "ru'unah," which is ignorance and stupidity. When they wanted to call someone a fool, they would say "Ra'ina," meaning "O fool." In that case the alif is for lengthening the voice, and the vocative particle is omitted. Al-Farra' mentioned that the original of "ya Zayd" was "ya Zaydā," with the alif, so that the one addressed would be between two sounds; then "ya" was suffice and the alif was intended. It is also possible that they meant it as a verbal noun, i.e., "you acted foolishly with foolishness," or they meant "you became one of us (ra'ina)." Dropping the tanwin is according to the view of pausing. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Layla, Abu Haywah and Ibn Muhaysin read it with tanwin, and the majority took it as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e., the word "Ra'ina," and the form fa'il in that case is for attribution, like laabin and tamir, and the word was described with it for emphasis, as one says "a foolish word" (kalimah hamqa'). 'Abd Allah and Ubayy read (ra'awna), attributing the verb to the plural pronoun for reverence, as al-Farisi confirmed. It is also mentioned that in the codex of 'Abd Allah it is (ir'awna). Some scholars held that the reason for the prohibition is that the form of mufa'alah generally implies mutuality, so the meaning would be that from you there is watching over us and from us there is watching over you, and this is detrimental to honouring him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Its remoteness from the occasion of revelation is, however, far indeed. ﴿And say, "Unzurna"﴾, i.e., "Intazirna" (wait for us) and be patient with us, or "unzur ilayna" (look upon us), so that this is stronger in conveying and clarifying. The original was that the verb be transitive with "ila," but it was used with latitude and so was transitive by itself, following the line of poetry:

Manifest in beauty and goodliness, they look as the gazelles look at the arak trees.

It has also been said that it is from the sight of insight, and what is meant is reflection and contemplation regarding what sets right the condition of the one looked upon in his affair; the meaning is: reflect upon our matter, and the best of affairs in my view is the middle one. However, the sight of the eye should be restricted to what is joined with arranging the condition, so that this word stands in place of the first, free of deception. He began with the prohibition because it belongs to the category of abandonments, and so it is easier; then he followed it with the command, which is harder, since familiarity is first achieved through the prohibition. Ubayy and al-A'mash read (anzirna) with a hamzah at the beginning and a kasrah on the zay, from inzar (granting respite), meaning: give us respite until we receive from you and memorize what we hear from you. This reading supports the first meaning in the reading of the majority, though it is irregular, and it does not contradict what we have chosen. ﴿And listen﴾, i.e., to what I have commanded you and forbidden you, with earnestness, so that you do not return to what I have forbidden you and do not abandon what I have commanded you. Or it is a command to listen well, by bringing the heart present and emptying it of distractions, so that one does not need to ask explicitly for consideration. In it is an alert to shortcoming in listening, to the point that they committed what caused the forbidden matter. What is meant is listening of acceptance and obedience, so it is an allusion to the Jews, who said: "We heard and we disobeyed." If what is meant is hearing this command and prohibition, then it is an emphasis of what preceded.

﴿And for the disbelievers there is a painful punishment﴾. The lam is for prior reference, so what is meant by "the disbelievers" is the Jews who said what they said, showing contempt for the Messenger ﷺ, which is known from what preceded by the context. The explicit noun was placed in the place of the pronoun to signal that contempt for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is disbelief that necessitates painful punishment, and in it is what there is of emphasis on the prohibition. Taking it as generic, so that the Jews enter it as Abu Hayyan chose, is not evident according to what has been said, because the discourse is with the believers, so this cannot serve as a concluding statement.

﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would not wish﴾. *Al-wudd* is love for a thing and wishing for its existence. Each of the two words is used both to mean its own sense directly and, in other places, as a secondary sense. The distinction lies in the object that follows: when the verb means wishing, its object is a clause, and when it means loving, its object is a single noun. So one says, for the first, *waddidtu law tafʿalu kadha* ("I wished you would do such-and-such"), and for the second, *waddadtu al-rajul* ("I loved the man"). Negating it is a metaphor for hatred. The word *bi-ma* ("with what") is used to indicate that those people are characterized by it. The word *min* ("from") is for specification (*tabyin*). It was also said that it is for partition (*tab'id*). Placing *kufr* (disbelief) as a relative-clause complement to the relative pronoun, and explaining it with what is explained, and using the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, indicates that their Book calls them to follow the truth, but their disbelief prevents them. Disbelief is wholly evil, because it is what produces envy and moves its bearer to hate good and not love it. Likewise, faith is wholly good, because it moves its bearer to entrust all affairs to God, exalted is He. The word *wa-la* ("nor") is an additional particle used to emphasize the negation. It is used here and not in His saying ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not⦆ because the basis of the negation is envy, and the Jews are most famous for this disease, especially since what precedes already indicates that they were tested with it. Therefore, from the negation of their wishing this, it does not follow that the polytheists do not wish it, and that is not present in *lam yakun*.

The occasion of revelation of the verse was that the Muslims said to their Jewish allies, "Believe in Muhammad." They said, "We would wish that he were something better than what we are upon, so that we might follow him." So God refuted them with this. It was also said that it was revealed as a rebuttal of a group of Jews who showed affection for the believers and claimed that they wished them well. The verse is separated from what precedes it, although both share in describing the abominable qualities of the Jews, with the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, because the two aims differ: the former is to discipline the believers, and this one is to refute those disbelievers. Because of this difference, the earlier verse is separated from its predecessor. From what we have mentioned, the connection of the verse with what precedes it becomes known. As for the view that this is because the forbidden speech often occurred at the time of the descent of the revelation, which is expressed by "good" in it, so it was as if it were indicated that the cause of their distortion of it is what is reported of them, since it occurred amid the arrival of what they dislike of the descent of good, being directed by way of hoping. I think it is closer to wishing.

It was read *wa-la al-mushrikūna* ("nor the polytheists") with the nominative, as a conjunction with *alladhina kafaru* ("those who disbelieved"). *An yunazzala ʿalaykum* ("that there be sent down upon you") is in the accusative position, as the object of *yawaddu* ("would wish"). The verb is in the passive voice because the agent is certain from its specification, and in order to state it explicitly afterward. The word *tanzil* ("sending down") is mentioned rather than *inzal*, observing the fitting correspondence with the actual occurrence of the sending down of goods in succession and their renewal. This is especially so if by *khayr* ("good") in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿min khayr﴾ ("of good"), the revelation is intended, and it stands in place of the subject. The word *min* here is a supplementary particle, and *khayr* is an added word. The first negation extends over it, and for this reason its addition was permitted according to the majority. There is no need for what was said, that the estimate is "would wish that no good be sent down." Some people went to the view that it is for partition, and according to this, *ʿalaykum* ("upon you") stands in that position. The meaning of "good" is either the revelation, or the Qur'an, or the victory, or what the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was singled out with of excellences, or it is general to all kinds of good, because those mentioned do not wish the sending down of all of that upon the believers, out of enmity and envy and fear of losing the study, and the loss of leadership. The most apparent of the views, as in *al-Bahr*, is the last one, and what comes later does not contradict it, because of what comes later.

﴿from your Lord﴾. It is in the position of a qualifier of *khayr* ("good"). The word *min* here is for origin (*ibtida'iyya*). The mention of the title of lordship is to indicate that the sending down is caused by it. The attribution to the pronoun of the addressees is to honor them. ﴿And God singles out with His mercy whom He wills﴾. This is an independent sentence brought to affirm what preceded of the sending down of good, to alert to its wisdom, and to humble those who hate it. By mercy is intended that good, except that it was expressed by it out of care for it and magnification of its status. The meaning of specification in the first view is clear, and that is why whoever chose it chose it. On the last view, the meaning is the singling out of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers with the whole of it, and the non-participation of those haters in it, and their being empty of its effects. It was also said that the purpose of the verse is to repel the objection that envy alludes to: that whoever has the right to specify is not challenged when he generalizes. Placing the word *Allah* in place of the pronoun of "your Lord" is a warning that the specification of some people with good over others suits divinity, just as the sending down of good in general suits lordship. The letter *ba'* ("with") enters upon the restricted object, meaning He gives His mercy. The word *man* ("whom") is the object. It was also said that the verb is intransitive and *man* is the subject. In both estimates, the returning pronoun is omitted. ﴿And God is possessor of mighty bounty﴾. This is a concluding statement for what preceded, [Page 351] and in it is a reminder to the haters and envious of what ought to restrain them, because the meaning is that He, glorified is He, is the one who bestows all kinds of bounties upon all His servants. So no one should envy another or wish that good not reach him, and all are drowning in the seas of His vast and abundant bounty. Thus it is said. When bounty is taken as general, and it was said that prophethood enters into it as a primary entrance, because the discussion of prophethood in it, according to one of the views, indicates that prophethood is among bounty, not as the wise men say, that it is by purifying the inner self, and that the deprivation of some of His servants is not because of the narrowness of His bounty but because of His will, and what He knows in it of His wisdom. The opening of this sentence with the noble Name is for the suitability of "the Mighty."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 106 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾ was revealed when the polytheists, or the Jews, said: "Do you not see Muhammad (ﷺ) commanding his companions to do something and then forbidding them from it, ordering them to do its opposite, saying one thing today and retracting it tomorrow? This Qur'an is nothing but the speech of Muhammad (peace be upon him), which he says of his own accord, and it is speech that contradicts itself." Naskh (abrogation) in the linguistic sense means removing the form of a thing, or what is in its ruling, and establishing the like of it in something else, whether in accidents or in substances. Among its uses in the collective sense is tanasukh (transference, i.e. copying). Each of these two has been used for the other as a metaphor, and this is preferable to it being a homonym, which is why al-Raghib favoured it. From the first sense comes "the wind abrogated the trace," meaning it removed it; from the second comes "I abrogated the book" when it established what is in it in another place. The abrogation of a verse, according to what some of the legal theorists (usuliyyun) have chosen, is the declaration that the obligation of reciting it has ended, like the verse: "The elderly man and the elderly woman, if they commit adultery, then stone them as a punishment from God, and God is Mighty and Wise." Or it is the ending of the ruling derived from it, like the verse: "And those of you who die and leave wives, a bequest for their wives, provision for a year without expulsion." Or it is both together, like the verse: "Ten known sucklings make [marriage] unlawful." In this definition there is the lifting of the permanence derived from its unrestricted wording. For this reason some defined it as the lifting of a legislated ruling. It is thus a declaration with respect to the Lawgiver and a lifting with respect to us. The term "obligation" (taʿabbud) excludes the limit (ghayah), for a limit is a declaration of the end of the duration of the ruling itself, not of the obligation to it. The definition is restricted to rulings, since there is no obligation in the reports themselves. Their forgetting (insa') is their removal from the hearts, such that they do not remain in memory, and this has indeed occurred. For some of the Companions wanted to recite some of what he had memorised, but did not find it in his breast, so he asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "It was abrogated last night from the breasts." Muslim narrated from Abu Musa: "We used to recite a sura which we likened in length and severity to Bara'a (al-Tawba), but it was made to be forgotten by us, except that I memorised from it: 'If the son of Adam had two valleys of wealth, he would seek a third valley, and nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust.' And we used to recite a sura which we likened to one of the Musabbihat, but it was made to be forgotten by us, except that I memorised from it: 'O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do? Testimony is written on your necks, and you will be questioned about it on the Day of Resurrection.'" Would that be the case for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) just as it was for others, or not? There is a difference of opinion. Those who hold the first view argued with the words of God, the Exalted: "We shall make you recite, and you will not forget, except what God wills." This is the view of al-Hasan. Those who hold the second view argued with the words of God, the Exalted: "And if We willed, We would surely take away what We have revealed to you," for this indicates that He does not will to take away what was revealed to him (ﷺ). This is the view of al-Zajjaj, but it is not strong, because the word "what" (alladhi) may be taken to refer to kinds of revelation to which such [forgetting] cannot apply. Abu Ali said: the meaning is "We did not take away all of it," and on either reading it does not conflict with the exception. "Glory be to Him who does not forget." Some have explained abrogation as the removal of the ruling, whether or not the wording remains, and forgetting as the removal of the wording, whether or not its ruling remains. Others explained the first as removal in exchange for a replacement of the previous ruling, and the second as removal without replacement. Both explanations have been objected to: restricting abrogation to this meaning contradicts both the lexical usage and the technical usage, and forgetting is literally the removal from the hearts, so taking it as a metaphor without the literal meaning being impossible is an artificial stretch. Perhaps what is cited in support of the soundness of these two explanations, from some of the great authorities, is not established. "Ma" is a conditional and jussive particle, governing "nansakh" in the accusative as its object. There is no contradiction between its being both governing and governed, since the aspect differs: by containing the condition it is governing, and by being a noun it is governed. And a jussive is assumed for it on its own, otherwise two governing particles would apply to a single governed term. It indicates that what follows it is permissible, since its basic use is with matters that are possible. The people of the revealed religions agree that abrogation is permissible and has occurred, but the Jews, other than the Isawiyya, disagreed about its permissibility and said it is impossible by reason. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani disagreed about its occurrence and said: although it is possible by reason, it has not occurred. The detailed discussion of this belongs in the foundations of jurisprudence. "Min ayah" is in the accusative position as a specifier (tamyiz, a grammatical term for a noun clarifying the sense of a word). The specified term is "ma," meaning "whatever." "Nansakh min ayah": the possibility that "min" is extra and that "ayah" is a circumstantial accusative is nothing, as is the possibility that "ma" is a verbal noun and conditional, and "ayah" the direct object, meaning "whatever abrogation We abrogate a sign." Rather, this possibility is more awkward and more bitter, as is not hidden. The pronoun in the accusative refers back to "ayah," in the manner of "I have a dirham and its half," because the abrogated is other than the forgotten. The specification of "ayah" by mention is in view of the general case, but the ruling is not restricted to it, rather it applies to what is less than it too, according to what has been said. A group, and Ibn Amir among the Seven, read "nunsikh," in the causative form (af'al), and the hamza, as Abu Ali said, indicates "finding in a state," like "I found him praised," meaning "I found him praised." So the meaning is: "whatever We find abrogated," and We do not find it thus except by abrogating it. Thus the two readings agree in meaning though they differ in wording. Ibn Atiyya allowed that the hamza indicates transitivity, so the verb is then transitive to two objects, and the sense is: "whatever We cause you to abrogate," meaning "whatever We permit you to abrogate." As if, when God abrogated it, He permitted His Prophet (ﷺ) to leave it by that abrogation, and so called that permission "causing abrogation." Some made causing abrogation an expression for commanding abrogation, and the one commanded is the Prophet (ﷺ) or Gabriel (peace be upon him). It is possible that it is from the abrogation of the Book, meaning "whatever We write and send down from the Preserved Tablet, or what We delay in it and leave, so We do not send it down." The two pronouns that come after are referring back to what the pronoun in "nunsiha" refers to. This arises from neglect of the rule that a conditional noun must have a pronoun in its response that refers back to it. Umar, Ibn Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Abu Amr, Ibn Kathir and Kathir read "nunsa'ha," with the vowel of the present-tense nun and the sin open and the hamza silent. Some others read likewise, except that they used an alif without a hamza. They did not drop it for the jussive, because its original form is the hamza from "nasa'a" meaning "delayed." The meaning according to the well-known interpretation: "We delay it in the Preserved Tablet, so We do not send it down," or "We remove it from the mind such that its meaning and wording are not remembered," and this is the meaning of "nunsiha," so the two readings coincide. It has also been said, and perhaps this is more subtle: the meaning is "We delay its sending down," and this concerns the abrogating (nasikha) verse, in that He delayed it for the duration of the abrogated verse's remaining. So the one that comes later is then an expression for the abrogated verse, just as at the time of abrogation it is an expression for the abrogating verse. So the meaning of the verse on this reading is that lifting the abrogated verse through sending down the abrogating verse, and delaying the abrogating verse through sending down the abrogated verse, each of them contains a benefit at its time. Al-Dahhak and Abu al-Raja' read "nunsiha" in the form of the active verb with the first person plural, which includes others, in the dual form, and the first object is omitted. One says: "God caused me to forget it," and "He caused me to forget it" in the sense of the same, meaning "We cause someone to forget it." Al-Hasan and Ibn Ya'mar read "tansaha," with a fatha on the ta, from forgetting. "You forgot" is attributed to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and a group likewise except that they used a hamza. Abu Haywa likewise except that he put a damma on the ta, as being from causing to forget. Ma'bad read like that without a hamza. Ubayy read "nunsika," with a damma on the first nun and a kasra on the sin without a hamza, and with the kaf of address. In the codex of Salim, mawla of Abu Hudhayfa, it is "nunsikaha," with both objects made explicit. Al-A'mash read: "Whatever sign We cause you to forget or cause to be abrogated, We will bring one better than it or like it." The connection of the verse with what precedes it is that it includes what is of the kind of abrogation, since the Companions, may God be pleased with them, were allowed for a period to say "ra'ina," and his (ﷺ) permitting something is treated as commanding it and permitting it. Then they were forbidden from that, so it was a likely occasion for what resembles what was related concerning the occasion of revelation. Or, because God, when He mentioned that He is the Lord of great bounty, the riffraff almost raised their heads and said: "Indeed, among bounty is the absence of abrogation," because when souls persist in something it becomes easy for them. So He, glorified be He, brought what turns their heads down and breaks their pride, and indicates that abrogation is among the parts of His great bounty and His generous liberality. Or, because He, when He pointed to the truth of the revelation and rejected the speech of those who hate it outright, followed that with what explains the secret of abrogation, which is one instance of the sending down of revelation, and the refutation of the claim of those who attack it. So let it be pondered.

﴿Bring a better one than it or its like﴾: that is, with something that is better for the servants than it, ﴿or its like﴾ in ruling, whether that ruling exists or not, or in written revelation (wahy matluww, recited revelation), or otherwise. The "betterness" (khayriyyah) is more general than being only in benefit, or only in reward, or in both. The "likeness" (mithliyyah) is specific to reward, according to what some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) indicated. One of them explained this: when the abrogating text (nasikh) abrogates a ruling (hukm), whether or not it also abrogates the recitation (tilawah), it must include a benefit (maslahah) that the earlier ruling lacked, because rulings vary only according to benefits, and their change is contingent on their change according to times. Therefore the abrogating text is better than the abrogated one in benefit, whether it is better in reward, or equal to it in reward, or carries no reward at all, as when the abrogating text involves permissibility (ibahah) or the absence of a ruling. When it abrogates only the recitation, betterness in benefit cannot be conceived, since the earlier ruling and its benefit have not changed; so it is either better in reward or equal in reward. The same applies to causing to be forgotten (insa'), for when the forgotten text included a ruling, the text brought in its place is better in benefit, whether the benefit is because it is free of any ruling altogether, or because it is free of that particular ruling while including a ruling that contains a benefit the forgotten ruling lacked, with the possibility that it is better in reward and equal to it in the time when the forgotten ruling was absent. When the forgotten text did not include a ruling, what is brought after it is either better in reward or equal to it. The conclusion is that equality in benefit cannot be conceived, because if the ruling changes, the benefit changes, and so it is better than it; and if the ruling does not change, the first benefit remains in its state. End of quotation. Then, it should not be overlooked that the generalization mentioned above is based on the permissibility of abrogation without a replacement (naskh bila badal), and on the permissibility of abrogating the Book by the Sunnah, which is the preferred position (al-madhhab al-mansur). Some people prohibited this, and also prohibited abrogation with a heavier replacement (badal athqal), and they argued from the apparent meaning of the verse. As for the first, it is because it cannot be conceived that what is brought is better or equal except in a replacement. As for the second, it is because the abrogating text is what is brought as a replacement, and it is better or equal, and the one who brings it is God Most High; but the Sunnah is neither better than nor equal to the Qur'an, nor is it something God, glorified and exalted, brought. As for the third, it is because the heavier is not better than the lighter, nor equal to it. This was refuted: as for the first and third, we do not accept that what is brought being better or equal can only be conceived in a replacement, nor that the heavier cannot be better than the lighter, since rulings were legislated and verses were revealed for the benefits of the servants and the perfecting of their souls, as a grace and mercy from Him, and this varies with the differences of eras and persons, like the medicine by which illnesses are treated: what benefits in one era may harm in another, and what removes one person's ailment may not remove another's. Thus the absence of a ruling, or a heavier one, may be more suitable for the regulation of livelihood and more orderly for the reform of the hereafter, and God Most High is Subtle and Wise. It is not objected that what is apparent from ﴿bring a better one than it﴾ is a verse better than it, and that the absence of a ruling is not something brought, because the disagreement about the permissibility of abrogation without replacement is not about bringing a wording in place of the first verse, but about the ruling, as is not hidden from one who consults the foundations of jurisprudence (usul). As for the second, we do not accept restricting the abrogating text to what was mentioned, since it is possible that abrogation be known through something other than what is brought; for the content of the verse is only that abrogating a verse entails bringing what is better than it or equal to it, and it does not follow that this is the abrogating text itself. So it is possible that it is a different matter that occurs after the abrogation has taken place. If that is possible, then the abrogating text may be a Sunnah, while what is brought, which is better or equal, is another verse. Also, the Sunnah is among what God, glorified be He, brought, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor does he speak from desire. It is not but revelation revealed﴾ [al-Najm 53:3–4]. The intended meaning of betterness and equality is not in wording, so that the Sunnah would not be like that; rather it is in benefit and reward, so it is possible that what the Sunnah contains is better in that respect. The Mu'tazilah argued from the verse for the createdness (huduth) of the Qur'an, since the change derived from abrogation, and the difference derived from being better at one time rather than another, are among the attendants and consequences of createdness, and so cannot be realized without it. It was answered that change and difference are accidents of what the eternal inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsi al-qadim) relates to, namely actions in commands and prohibitions, and propositional relations in information; and that requires them in its objects, not in its essence. Imam al-Razi answered that what is described by these is the verbal speech (al-kalam al-lafzi), while the eternal in our view is the inner speech. It was objected that this contradicts what the Ash'ari scholars agreed upon: that the ruling is eternal, and abrogation applies only to rulings. Abu 'Amr read (natati) with the hamzah converted into an alif.

﴿Do you not know that God is over all things Powerful?﴾ The interrogative has been said to be for affirmation (taqrir), and it has been said to be for denial (inkar). The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), and by way of metonymy (kinayah) he and his community, the Muslims, are intended. He addressed him singularly because he (ﷺ) is the most knowledgeable of them and the source of their knowledge, and to convey emphasis together with brevity. It has also been said that it is for every one who looks upon it, in the sense of the hadith: "Give glad tidings to those who walk to the mosques in darkness." It has also been said that it is for those who deny abrogation. The purpose is to take as evidence the addressee's knowledge of what has been mentioned for God's power over abrogation, and over bringing what is better or equal, because that is among the things subdued under His power, glorified be He. So from knowledge of the comprehensiveness of His power, Mighty and Majestic, over all things, follows knowledge of His power over that with certainty. The shift (iltifat) by placing the Glorious Name in the position of the pronoun is to cultivate awe, and because it is the proper name that encompasses all the attributes, so within it is the attribute of power; thus it is more eloquent in attributing power to Him than the pronoun of the speaker who magnifies. The same applies to His saying, Mighty is His majesty:

[Page 354]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 107:

﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ That is: you have already known, O addressed one, that Allah, exalted is He, possesses the overpowering authority and the dominating control, which entail complete power over the total disposal of affairs, by bringing into existence, by annihilating, by commanding and by forbidding, according as His will requires, with none opposing His command and none repelling His judgment. For one whose state is this, how could anything among things escape His power! So the statement, on this reading, serves as a proof for what precedes it in providing clarification. It is therefore placed in the position of an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān) to its governing clause in providing elucidation; for this reason the conjunction is omitted. It is also permitted that it be a repetition of the first clause and a re-presentation of evidence for what was mentioned. The reason that (anna), together with what falls within its scope, is not conjoined to the like of it that preceded is, by way of intentional omission, to add emphasis and to indicate that knowledge of each of the two is independent, and sufficient for arriving at the intended meaning. He specified the heavens and the earth for dominion because they are among the greatest visible created things, and because every created thing cannot be free of being in one of these two directions; thus control over the two of them contains an indication of control over what they encompass. Glorified is He, He began with the affirmation of the attribute of power, because it is the originator of the attribute of control and authority. He, exalted is His majesty, did not say "Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion," etc., intending to strengthen the judgment by repeating the predication.

﴿And you have not, besides Allah, any guardian or any helper.﴾ It is a conjunction upon the clause that falls as the predicate of (anna), entering with it where it enters. In it is an indication that the address before this also encompasses the community. The second (min) is a particle of connection, so it is not attached to anything. The first (min) denotes the starting point of the limit, and it is attached to an elided element that occurs as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the object of the second (min); originally it was an attribute of it, and when it was fronted, it became accusative in the circumstantial sense. In al-Bahr it is said that it is attached to what (lakum) is attached to, and that occupies the position of the predicate. It is permissible that (mā) be Tamimi (non-operative), and that it be Hijazi (operative) according to the view of one who permits fronting its predicate when it is an adverbial or prepositional phrase. The walī is the owner, and the naṣīr is the helper. The difference between them is that the owner may not be able to give help, or may be able and yet not act, whereas the helper may be an owner, and may not be one but rather a stranger. The purpose of the verse is to cite evidence for the connection of His, exalted is He, will with what was mentioned of bringing what is better than the abrogated, or its like; for mere His, exalted is He, power over that does not at all necessitate its occurrence. What requires it is His, exalted is He, being, together with that, a guardian and helper for them. So whoever knows that He, exalted is He, is his guardian and helper, and that there is no guardian and no helper for him other than Him, knows with certainty that He does to him only what is good for him, and so he entrusts his affair to Him, exalted is He, and no doubt about the matter of abrogation or otherwise occurs to his mind at all.

[Page 355]

﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before?﴾ The (*am*) here may be taken as connected (*muttasila*) or disconnected (*munqati'a*). If one supposes "Do you not know" (*a-lam ta'lam*) before "Do you wish" (*turidun*), based on the indication of the preceding context (*al-sibaq*) and the wider context (*al-siyaq*), which is the making of demands (*al-iqtirah*), since this occurs only out of obstinacy, and knowledge is contrary to it, then it is connected, as if it were said: "Which of the two matters is it: lack of knowledge of what has preceded, or knowledge together with making demands?" The interrogative is then for disapproval (*li'l-inkar*), meaning that neither of them should be the case. If it is not supposed, then it is disconnected, for a transition (*li'l-idrab*) away from their lack of knowledge of what came before, to a question about their demands, like the demands of the Jews, as a rebuke to them that this too should not happen. Some have decided firmly on one of the two, based on whether the Messenger (ﷺ) is included in the address or not. His not being included here is because he is the one to whom demands are made, not the one making them, and this would undermine the connection. It has been answered that it does not undermine it, since the connection is achieved in relation to the purpose. The intention of the Messenger (ﷺ) in the first case was merely for depiction and transition, since, as we have stated, it is by way of allusion (*kinaya*). The meaning under both suppositions is his instruction to the Muslims to place their trust in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and to abandon making demands after the rejection of the polytheists' or the Jews' objection regarding abrogation (*naskh*). So it is as if it were said: "Do not be, regarding what has been sent down to you of the Qur'an, like the Jews in abandoning trust in the clear signs and demanding other than them, lest you go astray and disbelieve after faith." In this instruction there is the utmost emphasis and eloquence, to the point that it is as though they were about to intend it, so they were forbidden from it, let alone from asking. That is, it is incumbent upon a sensible person not to take steps toward such an intention. He (glorified is He) did not say "as the people of Moses, peace be upon him, asked," or "as the Jews asked," in order to indicate that whoever asks this deserves that the tongue be guarded from mentioning it, and it does not imply that making the demand had previously occurred among them. The meaning of the verse does not depend on it, since an instruction does not require that the thing have occurred previously, especially since it is disbelief, as what follows indicates, and it hardly occurs from a believer. From what we have mentioned, the reason for mentioning this verse after His saying ﴿what We abrogate﴾ becomes clear, for the purpose of each of them is to make them firm in the signs and to instruct them to trust in them. As for the explanation that perhaps they were asking him (peace be upon him) to explain the detailed wisdoms that call for abrogation, and that is why the verse of abrogation was followed by this, I consider it closer to wishing (*al-tamanni*). Some exegetes have mentioned: "They proposed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during the Battle of Khaybar that he make for them a *Dhat Anwat* (a tree of worship) as the polytheists had. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Glory be to Allah! This is just as the people of Moses said: ﴿Make for us a god just as they have gods﴾. By He in whose hand is my soul, you will surely follow the ways of those before you, step by step, and stride by stride, to the extent that if there was among them one who went in to his mother, there would be among you one who does the same. I do not know, will you worship the calf or not?'" And this, with the need for it, requires that the addressees in the verses are the believers, and the context (*al-sibaq*), the wider context (*al-siyaq*), and the concluding statement (*al-tadhyil*) all bear witness to this. In light of this, connection is preferred, based on what is reported from al-Radi: that when two verbal clauses share the same subject, such as *aqamta am qa'adta* ("Did you stand or did you sit?"), then (*fa-am*) is connected. Some people claimed that the addressees are the Jews, and that the verse was revealed about them when they asked that a book be sent down to them from heaven all at once, as the Torah was sent down to Moses (peace be upon him). He addressed them with this after rejecting their objection, as a threat to them. In that case, the present-tense verb that follows has the meaning of the past tense, but it was expressed in this form to bring the shameful image into view. This was the view chosen by the Imam al-Razi, who said: "It is the more correct, because this is a surah from the beginning of His saying ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing﴾, recounting the Jews and disputing with them, and because their mention has been ongoing and the mention of others has not. And because a believer in the Messenger hardly asks for something by which disbelief would replace faith." What is in this is not hidden. It seems that he (may Allah have mercy on him) forgot His saying ﴿O you who have believed, do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna"﴾. It was also said that the addressees are the people of Mecca, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). It has been narrated from him that the verse was revealed concerning 'Abdullah ibn Umayya and a group of Quraysh who said: "O Muhammad, make Safa gold for us, widen the land of Mecca for us, and make rivers gush forth through it for us, a gushing; then we will believe in you." Other accounts of the cause of revelation have been related besides this, and there is no barrier, as in the case of the sea, to making all of them causes. On the difference regarding the addressees, the discussion of ﴿your Messenger﴾ proceeds as follows: if they are the believers, then the idafa (possessive construction) is according to what is in reality, and what they acknowledged of his messengership (ﷺ). If they are others, then it is according to what is in reality, not according to their acknowledgment. (*Ma*) is verbal-source (*masdariyya*). The most famous view is that the genitive phrase is an adjective (*na't*) for an omitted verbal noun, meaning a question (*su'alan*) "as" (*kama*). Sibawayh held that it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial state (*hal*), and the implied meaning according to him is: "that you ask him," i.e., the question "as." Al-Hawfi permitted that (*ma*) be a relative pronoun (*mawsula*) in the position of the direct object of *tas'alu*, meaning "like the things Moses asked before," and this is the most suitable, because the disapproval directed at them is only for the corruption of the proposals and their being a calamity upon them in the end. There is a consideration in this, because the thing compared (*al-mushabbah*) is "that you ask," which is a verbal noun, so the apparent meaning is that the thing compared to is likewise. The ugliness of the question is only due to the ugliness of what is asked about. Rather, the question itself may be ugly in some circumstances. Moreover, the verbal-source (*masdariyya*) does not need an implied linking element (*rabit*), so it is preferable. (*Min qablu*) is related to *su'ila*, and it was brought for emphasis (*li'l-ta'kid*). Al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammal read *sila* with a kasra on the sin and a *ya'*. Abu Ja'far and al-Zuhri read it with *ishmam* (partial rounding) of the *shin* toward damma, and a *ya'*. Some read it with the hamza softened between itself and the vowel, and a damma on the sin.

﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the right way.﴾ This is an independent sentence containing a universal ruling, delivered in the form of a proverb (*makhraj al-mathal*). It was brought to emphasize the prohibition on making demands, which is understood from His saying "Or do you wish..." etc. It is conjoined to it, so it is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) for it, in view of the fact that those who make demands and doubt are among those who have strayed from the straight path, and who exchange it. (*Sawa'*) means either "middle" or "equal." The idafa here is of the type of the attribute to the thing described, for the purpose of exaggerating the depiction of the strength of the attribute, as if he were the very essence of evenness (*nafs al-sawa'*), according to the pattern of the image appearing in the image that has appeared. The *fa'* is a linking particle, and what follows it cannot be the response (*jaza'*) of the conditional, because the going astray from the straight path precedes the substitution, and apostasy is not consequent upon it. Also, when the response is in the past tense with *qad*, it remains in its past tense, because *qad* signifies confirmation, and what has been firmly established and settled does not reverse, and the past does not follow from the future. Also, the conditional being in the present and the response in the past is a weak form, which does not occur in the Noble Book, as stated by al-Radi and others. Therefore, an implied element is necessary, so that it is said: "And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith, then the cause of that is that he has abandoned it," and the meaning returns to this: that the going astray from the straight path, which is manifest disbelief in the verses, is a cause for the exchange and apostasy. Some have explained the aforementioned exchange as abandoning trust in the verses, on the ground that it is a necessary consequence of it, so it is an allusion to it. The sum of the verse then is: "And whoever abandons trust in the clear verses, sent down according to the interests, among which are the abrogating verses that are pure good and sheer truth, and proposes other than them, has then deviated and wronged, without knowing, from the straight path that leads to the landmarks of truth and guidance, and has wandered in the bewilderment of desire, and fallen into the pits of destruction." The noble composition has chosen, at the outset of the matter, in the most eloquent manner, to announce that this is disbelief and apostasy. Perhaps what we have pointed to is better, as will not be hidden from one who reflects. It is read (*wa-man yubdil*) from *abdala*. The assimilation of the *dal* into the *dad* and the clear pronunciation are two well-known readings.

[Page 357]

﴿Many of the People of the Book wish﴾: they are a group of the rabbis of the Jews, who said to the Muslims after the Battle of Uhud: "Have you not seen what has befallen you? Had you been upon the truth, you would not have been defeated. So return to our religion, for it is better for you." This was narrated by al-Wahidi from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him. It is also narrated that Finhas ibn ʿAzura, Zayd ibn Qays, and a number of Jews said this to Hudhayfah, may God be pleased with him, in a long hadith. Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar mentioned that it is not found in any of the books of hadith.

﴿if they could turn you back﴾: this is a report of their wish. The discussion of this "law" (law, *law*) has already preceded, so there is no need to repeat it. ﴿after your belief, into disbelievers﴾, that is, apostates. This is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the addressees. It indicates the conjunction of disbelief with the turning back, and so it signifies that disbelief occurs merely by apostasy, regardless of what one is turned back to. For this reason He did not say "turn you back to disbelief." It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the subject of *wadda* (wished). Some have chosen that it is a second object of *yaruddūnakum* (turn you back), with *al-radd* (turning back) construed to mean *al-taṣyīr* (making into), since some of them had not disbelieved, so that they would be turned back to it. This would then require *al-taghlīb* (the predominance of one term over another), as in ﴿you will surely return to our religion﴾. Moreover, in that case the disbelief is imposed by way of compulsion, which is more heinous. As for the phrase ﴿min baʿdi﴾ (after) in place of the apparent ʿan (from): this is because *al-radd* is used with it, and it expresses an affirmation that faith had indeed taken place for them. It was also said that it was placed in the middle to show the complete abhorrence of what they intended, and the utmost remoteness of its occurrence. This is either to increase its ugliness, which deters the sensible person from committing it, or because faith resists it, as if it were said: "after your firm faith." In this there is much strengthening of the believers, which is not hidden.

﴿out of envy﴾: this is the cause of *wadda* (wished), not of *yaruddūnakum* (turn you back), because they wished for their apostasy absolutely, not for an apostasy caused by envy. They also permitted that it be a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the accusative, functioning as a circumstantial clause, meaning "envious." It was not made plural because it is a verbal noun. But this is weak, because making a verbal noun into a circumstantial clause, as Abu Hayyan said, is not analogous (not a general rule). It was also said that it may be accusative as an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq), with its governing verb omitted and indicated by the meaning, that is: "they envied you with envy." This, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿from their own selves﴾: this is related to a omitted element and functions as a qualifier. It may qualify *ḥasadan* (envy), meaning envy arising from the very essence of their selves, so that it is as if it were intrinsic to them. In this there is an indication that it has reached an extreme, unbounded degree. This strengthens the matter of the *tanwīn* (nunation) if it is taken to express multiplicity or magnitude. Or it may qualify *al-wudād* (wishing) understood from *wadda*, meaning a wishing arising from their own selves and their desires, not from reflection or inclination toward the truth. To make it a loose adverbial (ẓarf laghw) governed by *wadda* or by *ḥasadan*, as was transmitted from Makki, is remote, because the two are not used with the particle *min* (from), as Ibn al-Shajari said.

﴿after the truth has become clear to them﴾: through the attributes mentioned in the Torah and the miracles. This is like an evidence for specifying the "many" as the rabbis, because the becoming clear through these things was only for them, not for the ignorant. Perhaps the one who said that the wishing was also from their common folk did so lest their religion, which they inherited, be nullified, and the leadership of their rabbis, whom they believed in and took as leaders, be undermined. Therefore, by "the many" is meant all of them, both their disbelievers and their hypocrites. Its mention serves to exclude those among them who believed secretly and openly. It is claimed that the clarity (of truth) also occurred for all of them, but its causes differ and vary. This is what prevails in opinion. For whoever witnessed those dazzling miracles and radiant signs, it is remote for him, in any case, not to have the truth made clear to him and not to recognize the signs of truthfulness. However, the self's desires, the base appetites, and the satanic embellishments veiled whoever was veiled from faith, and shackled whoever was shackled in the fetter of abandonment.

﴿So pardon and overlook﴾: *al-ʿafw* (pardon) is leaving off the punishment of the wrongdoer. *Al-ṣafḥ* (overlooking) is leaving off reproach and blame. It is more eloquent than *al-ʿafw*, since a person may pardon without overlooking. Perhaps it is derived from turning the face of the page away in aversion, or from *taṣaffaḥtu al-waraqa* (I scanned the page), when you pass over what is in it. He preferred *al-ʿafw* over patience with their harm, as a notice of the believers' empowerment, intended to frighten the disbelievers.

﴿until God brings His command﴾: *amr* here is one of the commands (awāmir). What is meant is the command to fight, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Fight those who do not believe in God nor in the Last Day ... while they are humbled﴾. Or it is the command to kill Qurayẓah and to expel Banu al-Nadir. It was also said that it is one of the matters (umūr), and what is meant is the Resurrection, or the requital on its day, or the strength of the Message and the multiplication of the community. Some people interpreted *al-ṣafḥ* as turning away from them and abandoning mixing with them, and they made the limit of pardon the coming of the verse of fighting, and the limit of aversion God's bringing His command. He interpreted it as the Islam of those among them who embraced Islam, as al-Kalbi said, but this is nothing, because it requires that *amr* be understood as both one of the commands and one of the matters, and this, according to the verifiers, is combining the literal and the metaphorical meanings. It was transmitted from Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them all, that the verse is abrogated (mansūkha) by the verse of the sword. This was challenged, because *naskh* (abrogation, meaning the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation) is, with respect to the Lawgiver, an explanation of the period of termination, and, with respect to us, a removal of the apparent indication of perpetuity arising from absolute wording. This requires that the abrogated ruling be free of any time limit or perpetuity, for if it were time-limited, the abrogating text would be an explanation of it with respect to us too, and if it were perpetual, it would be an initiation rather than an explanation with respect to the Lawgiver. The command here is time-limited by a limit, and the limit not being known requires that the verse of fighting be an explanation of its generality. By this it becomes clear how weak is the answer given by Imam al-Razi, which many followed, that when the limit that the command is attached to is known only through revelation, the text does not cease to be abrogating, and it takes the place of ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾ until I abrogate it for you. Thus this is not like His saying: ﴿Then complete the fast until night﴾. As for al-Tibi's support for it by the ruling of the Torah and the Gospel, because he mentioned in them the end of the period of the ruling with them through the sending of the Unlettered Prophet, in the sense of His saying: ﴿those who follow the Messenger, the Unlettered Prophet, whom they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel﴾, and the manifestation of his (ﷺ) was an abrogation, then this is refuted by what is in *al-Talwīḥ*: that what occurs in them is the good tidings of the Law of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the obligation to return to him. That does not require the time-limiting of rulings, because it is possible that the return to him is in the sense of his being an interpreter, or a confirmer, or a changer of some rulings but not others. So from where does the time-limiting follow? Rather, they are unrestricted, from which perpetuity is understood, so changing them would be abrogation. It was answered regarding the challenge that it is not far to say that those who hold abrogation meant by it explanation, metaphorically, or it is said: by their knowledge they interpreted the limit as their death or the establishment of the Hour. Perpetuity only contradicts the unrestrictedness of the ruling when it is a limit of the obligation. But when it is a limit of the obligatory act, then it does not.
