In this case abrogation applies according to the majority, as Mawlana al-Salkoti said. Yet the apparent sense does not support this, so reflect.

﴿Indeed God is over all things Competent﴾: a concluding statement (*tadhyīl*) confirming what was understood from what preceded. In it there is an indication of vengeance upon the disbelievers, and a promise to the believers of victory and empowerment. It may also, though remotely, be a mention of the reason for accepting His command to pardon and overlook, and a threat to whoever opposes His command.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 110:

﴿Establish the prayer and give the zakat.﴾ This is coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical conjunction) with ﴿pardon and overlook﴾, as if He, glory be to Him, had commanded them to oppose [their enemies] and to seek refuge in Him through bodily and financial worship, because these [acts] ward off from them what they dislike. The statement of al-Tabari, that they were commanded here to pray and give zakat in order to nullify what had preceded of their inclination toward the Jews' saying (*ra'ina*), is inferior to the level of consideration.

﴿Whatever good you send forward for yourselves﴾: that is, whatever good it may be. In this there is an emphasis on the command to pardon and overlook, and on the prayer and zakat, and an encouragement toward them. The lam is for benefit (*nafʿiyya*). Restricting the good to prayer and charity goes against the apparent meaning. It has been read as (*taqdamū*), from *qadima* (to arrive) from a journey, and *aqdamahu* (to cause to arrive) by another, meaning he made him an arriver. It is close to the first reading, not from *iqdām* (boldness), the opposite of *ihjām* (holding back).

﴿You will find it with Allah﴾: that is, you will find its reward with Him, glory be to Him. The speech is then elliptical, with an omitted modifier (*mudaf*). It was also said: the apparent meaning is that what is intended is that you will find it in the knowledge of Allah, the Exalted, and Allah the Exalted has knowledge of it. However, He is extravagant in the perfection of His knowledge, so He made its being established in His knowledge equivalent to its being established with Him in His own essence. This exaggeration is reinforced by His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, in that He made everything they do visible to Him, the Exalted. Thus He expressed His knowledge, the Exalted, by sight, even though only a few of what they do are visible things. Perhaps for this reason al-Zamakhshari interpreted *basir* (seeing) as *'alim* (knowing). As for the statement of the Allamah, that it is an indication of the negation of attributes, and that the meaning of hearing and sight in relation to Him, the Exalted, is nothing other than the connection of His essence to the known things, there is in it the point that the interpretation does not convey anything except that what is meant by *basir* here is *'alim*, and there is no indication that this is the essence, or in addition to it, nor that the meaning of hearing and sight in relation to Him, the Exalted, is nothing but the mentioned connection. It has been read as (*ya'malūna*) with the ya', and the pronoun then is a metonymy for many, or for the People of the Book. Thus it becomes an appended conclusion (*tadhyil*) to His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾, and so on, emphasizing the content of the goal. The fitting interpretation is that it is a warning to those [people], so that it serves as consolation and as settling the believers in pardon and overlooking, and as removing their impatience at the arrival of the command. It was also permitted that it be a metonymy for the believers addressed by the preceding address, and the statement is a warning to the believers. What is derived from the *iltifat* (shift of address, a rhetorical turn of speech from second person to third person), which occurs in turning the speech from direct address to the third person, is the particular point specific to this *iltifat*. It is not hidden that this is a statement to which one should not give attention.

Page 359

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 111:

﴿And they say: None shall enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "wadda" (they wish), and what lies between them, namely ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾, is either a parenthetical clause introduced by the fa' (iʿtirāḍ bi-l-fāʾ), or is also coordinated with "wadda". The coordination of a performative (inshāʾ) statement with an informative (ikhbār) statement, where the clause has no place in i'rab, is permissible with other particles besides the waw. The pronoun refers to the People of the Book, not to many of them, as would be understood from the coordination, and by them is meant the Jews and the Christians together. It seems that the original wording was: The Jews said, "None shall enter Paradise except those who are Jews," and the Christians said, "None shall enter Paradise except those who are Christians." So the two statements were wrapped together and made into one statement, for brevity and trusting the listener's understanding that the intent is not that each of the two groups says this disjunctive statement, nor is it because each one knows the other misleads him. Rather the intent is to divide the aforementioned statement with respect to them. Thus the word "aw" (or), as in Mughni al-Labib, is for specification and division (al-tafsil wa-l-taqsim), not for doubt (al-tardid), so there is no difficulty.

"Hud" is the plural of ha'id, like ʿawdh the plural of ʿa'idh. It has been said that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in which the singular and the plural are alike. It has also been said that it is a shortened form of "yahud" with the yaʾ removed, but this is weak. On the view that it is a plural, the subject of "kana" is singular, referring back to "man" according to its wording, and the predicate is plural according to its meaning; this is common in speech, contrary to those who prohibited it, and from it is his saying: "And he who awakened those among you who were sleeping."

Ubayy read "Yahudiyyan aw Nasraniyyan", so the predicate and the subject were both taken according to the wording.

﴿Those are their wishful fancies﴾. "Amani" is the plural of "umniyya", which is what is wished for, like "udhuka" (a laughing-stock) and "uʿjuba" (a marvel). The sentence is a parenthetical insertion between their saying that and the demand for proof of the soundness of their claim. "Tilka" (those) is a demonstrative referring to ﴿none shall enter Paradise﴾ and so on. The predicate is plural although what is pointed to is one wish, in order to indicate that the wish recurred and repeated in their souls. It has been said, to indicate that it reached every extent, since the plural conveys an increase in individual units, so it is used for mere increase; this is among the wondrous figures of speech and the precious features of eloquence. It has been said: there is no need for all this; rather the plural is used because "tilka" contains the assurance that only the Jews will enter Paradise, and the assurance that only the Christians will enter it, and the deprivation of the Muslims from it. Also, its speaker is multiple, and it is a wish with respect to each speaker, and with respect to all of them it is many assurances. Some people have made it a reference to: that no good from their Lord should descend upon the believers, that they should return them to disbelief, and that no one else should enter Paradise; in this case "amanihim" is used figuratively (taghlib), because the first two are wishes in the literal sense, and the third is a false claim. It is also permitted that it refers to what is in the verse by omitting a modifier, i.e., "the likes of that wish are their wishful fancies." If "amani" is taken to mean falsehoods, then calling their claim a "wish" is in the literal sense; if it is taken to mean things wished for, then it is by metaphor, likening it to what is wished for in its impossibility. What is in both views of remoteness is not hidden, especially the first, because every sentence in which their desire for something is mentioned has been separated, completed, and become independent in its revelation, so it is very remote that it should be pointed to.

﴿Say: Bring your proof﴾, that is, for what you claim concerning your exclusive entry into Paradise. It is thus connected in meaning with the Exalted's saying: ﴿And they say, None shall enter﴾ and so on, as a response to it and nothing more. ("Hatu") means "bring forth" (ihdaru). The "ha'" is original, not a substitute for the hamza of "atu", nor for alerting (li-l-tanbih). It is an imperative verb, contrary to those who claimed it is a verb-name (ism fiʿl) or a sound like "ha". On the occurrence of the past, present and verbal noun from this root there is disagreement, but Abu Hayyan affirmed "hatá yuhati muhatah". "Burhan" (proof) is the evidence for the soundness of a claim. It has been said that it is derived from "baraha", meaning to cut, so the nun is extra; and it has been said that it is from "barhana", meaning to make clear, so the nun is original, since the pattern fa'lan is absent and fa'lal is present. On this derivation is based the disagreement over whether "Burhan" is diptote when used as a proper name. ﴿If you are truthful﴾: the answer to the conditional is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. The object of "truthful" is their earlier claim, not faith, nor the wishful fancies, as has been said. The conditional implies that the truthful person must have proof to establish his claim, and it has been explained that every statement without evidence is not established for the opponent and so is not counted, and for this reason it was said: whoever claims something without a witness, his claim must be void. There is no evidence in the verse for prohibiting imitation (taqlid), since the evidence of the one who imitates is the evidence of the one he imitates, as is not hidden. And interpreting "truthful" here as "righteous" is something that only corruption of mind would call for.

"Yes, [indeed]" (bala) is a rejection of their claim that they assert, and an affirmation of what it implies of the negation of others' entry into Paradise. And it is said that it is a rejection of what He alluded to in "Say: Produce your proof" (qul hatu burhanakum), from the negation that they have any proof, which has no basis and no evidence for it. "Whoever submits his face to Allah" (man aslama wajhahu lillah): that is, submits himself to what Allah the Exalted has decreed and ordained, or sincerely devotes himself to Him, or intends Him, not associating anyone else with Him the Exalted, or does not intend anything other than Him. Thus "face" (wajh) is either a metaphor for the essence (dhat), and its specific mention is because it is the most noble of the limbs and the seat of the senses; or it is a metaphor for intention, because one who intends something faces it.

"And he is a doer of good" (wa huwa muhsin) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (aslama), meaning: while he is in fact a doer of good in all his deeds. If what was mentioned earlier is intended as shirk, the meaning reverts to "believes and does righteous deeds." The Prophet (ﷺ) explained ihsan (excellence) with his saying: "(That you worship Allah as if you see Him; and if you do not see Him, then indeed He sees you)."

"Then for him is his reward" (fa-lahu ajruhu): that is, the reward that was promised to him for that, not what he deserves, as al-Zamakhshari said, in keeping with the Mu'tazili school. The expression of what He promised as "reward" indicates the strength of its connection to the deed.

"With his Lord" ('inda rabbihi) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from (ajruhu), and its governing element is the meaning of settledness (istiqrar). The "with" (indiyya) is for honor, and the intended meaning is that it will not be lost or diminished. He used "Lord" (Rabb) in construct with the pronoun of (man aslama), to show extra kindness toward him and to affirm the content of the sentence.

The sentence is the answer to (man) if it is conditional, and its predicate if it is relative; and the fa' in it is because it includes the meaning of a condition. In both cases, the rejection is by "bala" alone, and what follows is a new independent statement, as if it were said: "If what they claimed is void, what then is the truth in this matter?"

It is also permitted that (man) be a relative pronoun, the subject of a deleted verb (yadkhula) and (bala) together with what follows it is a rejection of their claim; and "then for him is his reward" would be conjoined to that deleted element, conjoining a nominal clause to a verbal clause, because the first is intended to indicate renewal and the second permanence. Al-Sakkaki has stated explicitly that when two clauses differ in renewal and permanence, the aspect of meaning is observed, and so they are conjoined.

"Nor fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve" (wa la khawfun 'alayhim wa la hum yahzanun): the like of this has preceded. The plural in the three pronouns is in consideration of the meaning of (man), just as the singular in the first pronouns is in consideration of the wording. The reverse is permissible in such a case, but the more eloquent practice is to begin with agreement with the wording, then with agreement with the meaning, because the wording precedes it in comprehension.

[Page 361]

﴿The Jews say, "The Christians have nothing [of substance]," and the Christians say, "The Jews have nothing [of substance]."﴾ The intended Jews are the Jews of Madinah, and the delegation of the Christians of Najran disputed in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and insulted one another. The Jews denied the Injil and the prophethood of Isa (peace be upon him), and the Christians denied the Tawrat and the prophethood of Musa (peace be upon him). The definite article (*alif-lam*) in both places is then for specific reference (*al-'ahd*). It has also been said that the intended meaning is the Jews in general and the Christians in general, and this is a report about past nations. It contains a rebuke to those present with the Prophet (ﷺ) and a consolation for him (peace be upon him), since they denied the messengers and scriptures before him. In this view the definite article in both places is for the category (*al-jins*). The first view is the one related in the reports on the occasions of revelation (*asbab al-nuzul*), and according to it the speaker may be understood as each individual from both groups, which is the apparent meaning. It is also possible that the intended meaning is two men: a man from the Jews called Nafi' ibn Harmalah, and a man from the Christians of Najran. The attribution of the statement to all of them, since it came from some of them, is a well-known method in Arabic in both verse and prose. This is a statement of the misguidance of each party's specific companion, following the statement of their general misguidance of everyone else. (*'Ala shay'*, "of anything") is the predicate of *laysa* ("is not"). According to some, it is an instance of an omitted qualifier, meaning "anything that is considered valid in religion," since it is known that each of them is "of something." The better view is not to assume an omission. In this there is great emphasis, because *shay'* ("thing"), as Sibawayh's words indicate, is what can be known and spoken about. When it is negated absolutely, this is an intensified denial of any value in what they hold, and it becomes like their saying: "less than nothing." ﴿While they recite the Book﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to both groups, by making them the subject of a single verb, so that two governing words do not govern a single object. The meaning is that they said this while knowing what their explicit books contain, contrary to what they claim. In this there is a reproach to them and guidance to the believers that whoever has knowledge of the Qur'an should not say what contradicts its contents. The word "the Book" here is generic, so it applies to the Tawrat and the Injil. It has also been said that it refers specifically to the Tawrat, because the Christians also follow it.

﴿Thus said those who have no knowledge﴾: they are, according to the majority, the polytheist Arabs. It has been said they are the polytheists of Quraysh, and it has been said they are nations that existed before the Jews and Christians. As for the view that they are the Jews, and that their statement is repeated as the statement of the Christians, and that knowledge is denied of them because they did not benefit from it, the apparent meaning is that it is the statement of "those who have no knowledge." The *kaf* in (*kadhalika*, "thus") is in the accusative position, as an adjective of an omitted, accusative verbal noun governed by (*qala*, "said") which precedes it. That is: "a statement like the statement of the Jews and Christians." ﴿Those who have no knowledge said﴾ and in this case ﴿like their statement﴾ is accusative, governed by (*ya'lamun*, "know"). "Statement" here means belief, or it may be read as the direct object, or as an apposition to the position of the *kaf*. It has also been said that (*kadhalika*) is the direct object, and (*mithla*, "like") is an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*). The intended meaning is to liken the thing said to the thing said in its outcome and result, and to liken the statement to the statement in that both proceed from mere whim, desire and partisanship. They also allowed that the *kaf* could be in the nominative position as the subject of a sentence, with the following clause as its predicate, and with an omitted returning pronoun, meaning "he said it." (*Mithla*) would be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, or the direct object of (*ya'lamun*). It is not permissible for it to be the object of (*qala*), because that verb has already had its object filled. This was objected to on the grounds that omitting the returning pronoun in a subject that, if the verb were without a pronoun, would be in the accusative, is among the things that many scholars restrict to necessity (*darurah*), and they cited as an example the verse:

*"And Khalid praises our masters with truth; they are not praised with falsehood."*

It has also been said that, on this view and on what precedes it, the use of *kaf* as a noun (rather than a particle) is problematic. Although al-Akhfash permitted it, a group of scholars restricted it to poetic necessity. Moreover, what is reported of it in that usage may be interpreted otherwise. The difficulty of the two comparisons is not hidden: they involve artificiality and departure from the apparent meaning, merely to avoid the suspicion of redundancy. Perhaps the better view is that (*mithla qawlihim*, "like their statement") is a repetition of the divine phrase (*kadhalika*, "thus") for emphasis and affirmation, as in the verse: ﴿The penalty is that he in whose bag it is found, he himself is the penalty﴾. This is the view of some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*). It may also be said that (*kadhalika*) here is not for comparison, but to indicate that this matter is great and established. Wazir Asim ibn Ayyub transmitted, in his commentary on the verse of Zuhayr:

*"Thus is their tent, and for every people, when hardship touches them, there is a tent."*

from the Imam al-Jurjani: "Indeed *kadhalika* comes for confirmation, either for a preceding predicate or for a following predicate, and it is the opposite of *kalla* ('no'), because *kalla* negates while *kadhalika* affirms." A similar usage is in: ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾. In the commentary on *al-Miftah* by al-Sharif: the purpose of comparisons is not only their literal meanings, since the comparisons of eloquent speakers rarely lack figurative and metonymic senses. So we say: "We have seen them using such and such," sometimes for continuity, as in: "Zayd has been just in the case of so-and-so, and so on," meaning any ongoing justice. And al-Hamasi said:

*"Thus time goes, and knowledge perishes in it, and traces are effaced."*

This is stated by al-Tabrizi in his commentary on the *Hamasa*, and it has many examples. And in the commentary on the verse of Abu Tammam:

*"Thus let the matter be grave, and let the affair be weighty."*

he said it is for magnification and emphasis, and in the beginning of that poem nothing preceded it that it is compared to. There will be a continuation of this, God willing. The statement of those people was made the thing compared because it is more reprehensible, since falsehood from a scholar is more reprehensible than from an ignorant person. Some make the comparison on the pattern of: ﴿Trade is only like usury﴾, and in this there is an emphasis and a rebuke for resembling the ignorant that is not hidden. They were rebuked although they spoke the truth in one respect, since after abrogation (*naskh*, the replacement of a ruling by a later one) neither religion is anything. This is because they did not intend that. Rather, each party intended to nullify the other's religion from its root, and to disbelieve in its prophet and its book. Moreover, it is not valid to rule that both religions after abrogation are nothing of value, because what is apparent from it is that they are not so in themselves. Whatever part of them has not been abrogated is a truth that must be accepted and acted upon, so it is something of value in itself, even if it is nothing in relation to them, because there is no benefit from what has not been abrogated while disbelieving in the abrogating law.

﴿So Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾: that is, between the Jews and the Christians, not among the three groups, because the context of the discourse is to explain the state of those two groups. The mention of the saying of others is to show the complete falsehood of their statement. Judgment means decision and adjudication, and it requires two parties. One says: "The judge ruled in this case with such and such." Here one of the two has been omitted for brevity and to magnify its affair, by distributing to each group what befits it of punishment. What is most apparent from judgment between two parties is that it is decided in favor of one of them over the other, so its use in the sense mentioned is figurative. Al-Hasan said that the intended meaning of judgment between these two groups is their condemnation and their entry into the Fire, and in this there is a sharing in a single judgment. This is far from the real meaning of judgment. (*Yawma*, "on the day") is connected to (*yahkumu*, "will judge"), and so is what follows it. The difference in meaning is no problem. (*Fihi*, "in it") is connected to (*yakhtalifun*, "they differ"), not to (*kanu*, "they were"). It was placed before it to preserve the rhyme endings of the verses.

* * *

From the allusive (*ishari*) interpretation of the verses: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate﴾: that is, whatever We remove of your attributes from the register of your heart, or We conceal it by the shining of Our lights upon it, except that We inscribe in it of Our attributes what you do not suppose you are capable of, which share its name, and what you suppose to be present in you without its sharing. ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion﴾ of the world of spirits and the earth of bodies, and He is the one who disposes of both by the hand of His power. Rather, the worlds, in their diversity, are the apparent manifestations of the affairs of His essence and the locus of manifestation of His names and attributes, so there remains nothing other than Him to help you or to protect you. ﴿Or do you wish to ask your Messenger﴾, the intellect, about the base pleasures and worldly desires, as Musa was asked by the heart before. Whoever exchanges darkness for light has indeed strayed from the straight path. The Jews said, "None will enter Paradise" meaning the Paradise known to them, which is the Paradise of the outward and the world of dominion, the Paradise of actions and of the self, "except one who is a Jew." The Christians said, "None will enter Paradise" meaning the Paradise known to them, which is the Paradise of the inward and the world of the kingdom of heaven (*malakut*), the Paradise of attributes and of the heart, "except one who is a Christian." For this reason Isa (peace be upon him) said: "None will enter the kingdom of the heavens unless he is born twice." ﴿These are their wishful thinkings﴾, that is, the ultimate of their aims, at whose limit they stopped and by which they veiled themselves from what is above it. ﴿Say: Produce your proof, if you should be truthful﴾, the proof that indicates the exclusion of others from entering, if you are truthful in your claim. Rather, the proof indicates the contrary of your claim, for whoever submits his face and purifies his essence from all its necessary and accidental qualities for Allah, the Exalted, through essential unity (*tawhid dhati*) at the complete effacement (*mahw kulli*), and who is upright in his states through subsistence after annihilation, witnessing his Lord in his actions, returning from the essential witnessing to the station of excellence in attributes (*ihsan sifati*), which is the contemplation of the real existence (*wujud haqqani*): ﴿For him is his reward with his Lord﴾, that is, what you have mentioned of Paradise, and more, because he is singled out for the station of nearness (*'indiyyah*) from which you are veiled. ﴿And there is for them an addition beyond that﴾, which is that they do not fear the veiling of the essence, and do not grieve over what has escaped them of the Paradise of actions and attributes, in which you are veiled by standing still at them. ﴿The Jews said, "The Christians have nothing [of substance]"﴾, because of their veiling by the inward from the outward. ﴿The Christians said, "The Jews have nothing [of substance]"﴾, because of their veiling from the inward by the outward. ﴿While they recite the Book﴾, and in it is what guides them to lifting the veil and seeing the truth of every doctrine in its rank. ﴿Thus said those who have no knowledge of the ranks, a statement like theirs﴾, so each group among them declared the other group in error. They did not distinguish between the cosmic will (*al-iradah al-kawniyyah*) and the legislative will (*al-iradah al-shar'iyyah*), and they did not know the face of truth in every rank of the levels of existence. So Allah, the Exalted, who combines all attributes in their diverse ranks and varied degrees, will judge between them in truth regarding their disputes on the Day of the Great Resurrection, and at the manifestation of essential unity, and the manifestation of the Lord in the forms of beliefs, until they deny Him. Then none will prostrate to Him except one whom He, glory be to Him, has not restricted even by the restriction of absoluteness,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 114:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah﴾. It was revealed concerning Titus ibn Isyanus al-Rumi (Titus, son of Vespasian) and his companions. They raided the Children of Israel, killed their fighters, took their offspring captive, burned the Torah, ruined Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), threw carrion into it, and slaughtered swine in it. It remained in ruins until the Muslims rebuilt it in the days of Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him. But ʿAta' narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning the polytheist Arabs, who prevented the Muslims from remembering Allah in al-Masjid al-Haram. According to the first view, the verse is joined by conjunction to His words, ﴿and the Christians said﴾, a conjunction of one narrative to another, to expose their abominations. According to the second view, it is a parenthetical statement placed between the conjoined and the conjoining, containing more than one sentence: the conjoined part, namely "they said: He has taken [a son]", and the conjoining part, namely "the Jews said", are separated in order to explain the condition of the polytheists who have been mentioned, as a demonstration of the full extent of the vileness of the People of the Book. For the polytheists who resemble them, if they are the most unjust of the disbelievers, [this is evident]. The apparent meaning of the verse is general, covering every one who prevents and every mosque, and the specific occasion of revelation does not restrict it.

(Wa-aẓlamu) is an elative form (af'al al-tafdil) serving as the predicate of "man" (who). The interrogative is not intended in its literal sense; it carries the sense of negation, and so it returns to a declarative statement, meaning: no one is more unjust than that. It has been objected that this construction is established in the Qur'an in such phrases as: ﴿Who is more unjust than one who was reminded of the verses of his Lord, then turned away from them?﴾ ﴿So who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ ﴿So who is more unjust than one who denies the signs of Allah?﴾ and so on. If the meaning were as stated, this would lead to contradiction. It has been answered by specification, either by what is understood from the relative clauses themselves, or by reference to those who came after that category, and its meaning reverts to precedence in preventing, or in fabricating, for example. It has been objected that this is far from the indication of the speech and its Arabic usage, and a kind of foreignness in the tongue that is followed by obscurity of meaning. The better answer is that this does not indicate the denial of equality in being most unjust. What is understood from the verses at most is that those mentioned in them are more unjust than others, just as when you say: "No one is more knowledgeable than Zayd, ʿAmr and Khalid," this indicates no more than the negation that anyone is more knowledgeable than them. It does not indicate that one of them is more knowledgeable than another. It is not objected that one who prevents the mosques of Allah, for example, and did not fabricate a lie against Allah, is less unjust than one who combined both; therefore he is not equal in being most unjust. This is because these verses concern the disbelievers, and they are equal in it, since disbelief is one thing, and no increase is possible in it with regard to the individuals who are characterized by it. Increase is possible only with regard to them in relation to the sinful believers, by the common ground of what they share of opposition. This is what Abu Hayyan said, though its flaw is not hidden. Many have said: your saying, "Who is more unjust than one who did such and such?" is a denial that anyone could be more unjust than him or equal to him. Even though the composition of the phrase does not explicitly address the denial or affirmation of equality, the widespread custom and consistent usage testify to it. When it is said, "Who is more generous than so-and-so?" or "No one is more excellent than so-and-so," what is meant with certainty is that he is more generous than every generous person and more excellent than every excellent person. Therefore, it is perhaps better to revert to one of the two answers while observing the aspect (of the statement). If you take that statement as expressed in the form of hyperbole in threatening and rebuke, setting aside the negation of equality or superiority in reality, as has been said, relying also on custom, the difficulty disappears, the dispute ends, and the talk is settled. So reflect.

﴿that his name be mentioned therein﴾ is a second object of "prevented" (manaʿa), or an object of purpose, meaning: he prevented them out of disliking that His name be mentioned; or it is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "mosques." The second object is then implied, meaning: their upkeep, or worship therein, or something similar; or [it means] "people, the mosques of Allah Most High"; or there is no implied object, and the verb is transitive to one object. The mention of the name of Allah Most High is used as a metonymy for what takes place in the mosques of prayers and acts of drawing near to Allah Most High through inner and outer acts that are permitted to be performed in them.

﴿and strove for their ruin﴾, that is, for their demolition and their being left unused. Al-Wahidi said that it is a conjunction of explanation, because their upkeep is through worship in them. ﴿Those﴾ are the unjust, the preventers, the strivers for their ruin.

﴿It was not for them to enter them except in fear﴾. The lam in (lahum) is either for exclusivity in the manner of fitness, as in the saddle cloth for the horse, and "fear" here means fear of Allah Most High; or for entitlement, as in Paradise for the believer, and "fear" here means fear of the believers; or merely for connection with occurrence, meaning: it was not for them, in the knowledge and decree of Allah Most High, that they would enter them in what is to come except in fear. According to the first view, the sentence is a new independent statement, an answer to a question arising from His words, ﴿and strove for their ruin﴾, as if it were said: "What is fitting for them?" and "injustice" here means putting a thing in other than its place. According to the second view, it is an answer to a question arising from His words, glorified is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents﴾, as if it were said: "What was their due?" and "injustice" here means dealing with the right of another. According to the third view, it is a parenthetical statement between two statements connected in meaning. It contains a promise to the believers of victory and the purification of the mosques from the disbelievers. For the sake of emphasis on this, it was placed in the middle. Allah Most High has fulfilled His promise, and praise be to Allah. It is narrated that no Christian enters Bayt al-Maqdis except disguised and secretly. Qatadah said: No Christian is found in Bayt al-Maqdis except that he is beaten and subjected to the severest punishment. There is no contradiction with the conquest of al-Aqra' and the remaining of Bayt al-Maqdis in the hands of the Christians for more than a hundred years, until the king Salah al-Din recovered it, because the fulfilment of a promise requires its realization at some time, and it does not indicate repetition. It has been said: the negation has the sense of a prohibition, and its meaning, by way of metonymy, is a prohibition against allowing them and enabling them to enter the mosques. This necessarily entails that they enter them only in fear of the believers. The necessary consequence is mentioned while the necessitated meaning is intended. It is not hidden that the prohibition against allowing and enabling mentioned here, at a time when the disbelievers were strong and preventing the mosques, has no benefit except to give notice of the promise to the believers of victory and of recovering them from the disbelievers. So interpreting it this way from the beginning is better.

The scholars differed about the entry of disbelievers into the mosque. Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, permitted it absolutely, on the basis of the verse, since it indicates that they enter with awe and humility. Also, the delegation of Thaqif came to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and he lodged them in the mosque. He also said, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe, and whoever enters the Kaʿbah is safe." The prohibition is understood as reprehensible (tanzih), or as referring to entering the sacred precinct (haram) with the intention of pilgrimage. Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, prohibited it absolutely, based on the words of Allah Most High: ﴿The polytheists are only unclean﴾, and mosques must be purified from impurities; for this reason the one in a state of major impurity is prevented from entering. He permitted it for a need. Imam al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, distinguished between al-Masjid al-Haram and other mosques, and said: the hadith is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse. ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read: ﴿except in fear (khifan)﴾, which is like ṣīm (a plural form of ṣā'im). ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾, that is, a great one, by the killing of their champions and their chiefs, the breaking of their idols, the foolishness of their minds, and their expulsion from the Arabian Peninsula, which is their dwelling place and the place where they were born. Or it is by the imposition of the jizyah (poll tax) on those of them who are protected dhimmis. ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾, which is the punishment of the Fire, because its cause, which is what was recounted of their injustice, is also of such magnitude. The placing of the adverbial phrase at the front in both places is for creating suspense for what is mentioned after it.

[Page 365]

Among the allusive (ishari) interpretations of the verse: And who is more deprived of portion and more diminished of right than one who prevents the places of prostration to Allah Most High, which are the hearts, in which He is known, and so prostration is made to Him through essential annihilation (fana' dhati), that His special name be mentioned therein, which is the Greatest Name, since He is manifested through this name only in the heart, and it is the manifestation through the Essence together with all the attributes; or through His name specific to each one of them, that is, the perfection fitting to its readiness that necessitates it. And [who] strives for their ruin by corrupting them with partisanships and the dominance of desire, and by preventing their people by stirring up the trials that necessarily result from the tugging of the faculties of the soul and the call of Satan and of illusion. Those, it was not for them to enter them and pray toward them, except in fear, humbled, because of the manifest self-disclosure of the Truth in them. For them in this world is disgrace and exposure, and humiliation through the manifestation of the falsehood of what they are upon. For them in the Hereafter is a great punishment, which is their being veiled from the Truth, glorified is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 115:

﴿To God belong the East and the West.﴾ That is, the two known regions adjoining a point from which the sun rises and sets. He used their ownership as a metaphor (kinayah) for the ownership of the whole earth. Some said: if the earth is spherical, then every east is a west relative to something else, and the whole earth is like that, so there is no need to adhere to the metaphor. But this is far-fetched. ﴿Wherever you turn, there is the Face of God.⦆ That is, in whatever place you turn toward the qiblah. Al-Hasan read (tawallaw) in the third person (ghaybah). ﴿Then there is the Face of God.﴾ That is, there is His direction, glorified is He, which you were commanded to face. Thus the place of turning is not restricted to one mosque over another, nor one place over another. (Fa-ayna) is an adverb (zarf) that is necessarily adverbial and includes the meaning of a condition (shart). It is not an object of (tuwallu), and (tawliyah) in the sense of turning away is treated as intransitive. (Thamma) is a demonstrative for a distant place only, indeclinable on fatha, and is not used except with (min). Whoever parsed it as an object in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And when you see there, you see bliss⦆ has erred; it is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and what follows it is a postponed subject (mubtada' muakhkhar), and the clause is the response of the condition. The word (wajh) means direction, like (wazn) and (zinah). The specification of the idafah is by consideration of it being something commanded, in which is His good pleasure, glorified is He. To this view went al-Hasan, Mujahid, Muqatil and Qatadah. It was also said: (wajh) means the essence (dhat), like His words, ﴿Everything perishes except His Face⦆, except that here it is taken as a metaphor for His knowledge and awareness of what is done there. Abu Mansur said: it means status (jah), which returns to majesty and greatness. On this reading the clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) to console the hearts of the believers that remembrance and prayer are permitted throughout the whole earth, not only in mosques. In the sound hadith: "The earth has been made for me a mosque and a means of purification." Perhaps it was not permitted for others before him, peace be upon him, to pray except in churches and synagogues, and the prayer of Jesus, peace be upon him, during his journeys elsewhere was out of necessity; so there is no need to say that the collective is specific. It is also permitted that (fa-ayna) be the object of (tuwallu) in the sense of direction, for it is common in usage: "wherever they turn" meaning "whatever direction they turn." This is based on what is narrated from Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with them both, that the verse was revealed concerning the prayer of the traveller and voluntary prayer on the mount; and on what is narrated from Jabir that it was revealed concerning a people for whom the qiblah became obscure during a campaign in which I was with them; they prayed toward the south and the north, and when they woke, their error became clear. It is possible on these two narrations that (fa-ayna), as in the first view too, is taken to mean: in whatever place you do whatever turning. This is because omitting the object gives generality. Some restricted it to this, claiming that what preceded was said by none of the people of Arabic grammar. Among people some said: the verse is a preparation for the abrogation of the qiblah and a declaration of God's transcendence above being in a direction, for otherwise it would have had more right to be faced. It is to be understood in its generality, not restricted to the state of travel or the state of seeking the qiblah. By (wherever) is meant whatever direction, and by (face) is meant the essence. The connection then is that, since the mention of mosques preceded, it brings in, as an interjection, a near ruling on the qiblah. Some claimed this is the most sound of the opinions, but there is room for reflection. ﴿Indeed God is All-Encompassing⦆, that is, encompassing things in ownership or mercy; therefore He made the qiblah wide for you and did not constrict it upon you. ﴿All-Knowing⦆ of the interests of His servants and their deeds
Page 366
in places. The clause, on the first reading, is a conclusion (tadhyil) to the whole of ﴿To God belong the East and the West⦆ etc.; on the second, it is a conclusion to His words ﴿Wherever you turn⦆ etc. It is strange to make this a threat to those who prevent God's mosques, and to make the earlier address also directed at them; so the meaning becomes that there is no escape from God for whoever transgresses, and no refuge for whoever rebels, for His dominion encompasses the directions and His knowledge encompasses the revolving spheres.

Where is the escape? There is no fleeing for a fugitive, and to Him belong the two expanses, the dust and the water.

From the way of allusion (ishara): the East is an expression for the world of light and manifestation, which is the paradise of the Christians and their qiblah in reality, its inner aspect; and the West is the world of secrets and concealment, which is the paradise of the Jews and their qiblah in reality, its inner aspect. Or, the East is an expression for His glorified illumination upon the hearts through the manifestation of His lights in them and His self-disclosure to them with the attribute of His beauty in the state of witnessing; and the West is an expression for His setting by veiling Himself, concealing Himself and hiding through the attribute of His majesty in the state of subsistence after annihilation. All of this belongs to God, the Exalted. Whatever direction a person turns to, outwardly or inwardly, there is the Face of God, adorned with all attributes, manifest in whatever He wills, transcending directions. The poet of the people has said:

The face is one, yet it is not the same: when you count the mirrors, it multiplies.

﴿Indeed God is All-Encompassing⦆: nothing escapes His encompassing. ﴿All-Knowing⦆: nothing is hidden from Him of the conditions of His creation and the manifestations of His attributes.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 116:

﴿وقالُوا اتَّخَذَ اللَّهُ ولَدًا﴾ [They say: "God has taken a son."] It was revealed concerning the Jews, when they said, "'Uzayr is the son of God," and concerning the Christians of Najran, when they said, "The Messiah is the son of God," and concerning the polytheists of the Arabs, when they said, "The angels are the daughters of God." The pronoun (in qalu) refers to those previously mentioned among the Christians, the Jews, and the polytheists who do not know. It is coordinated (ʿataf) with "The Jews said." Abu al-Baqa' said: it is coordinated with "And they say: None shall enter Paradise." It is also permitted that it be a coordination with (manaʿa, "prevented"), or with the implied meaning of "who is more unjust" without its wording, because of the difference between the imperative (inshaʾiyya) and the declarative (khabariyya) forms. The implied sense is: "They wronged with a severe wronging by preventing, and they said." If it is taken as the coordination of one narrative upon another narrative, no interpretation is needed, and the resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) is then explanatory (bayani), as if it were said, after enumerating their ugly deeds: "Has the thread of their verbosity in fabricating against God, exalted is He, been cut off, or has it extended?" It is answered: "Rather it has extended, for they said what is more shameful and more monstrous." The verb (ittakhadha, "take") is either in the sense of making or doing, in which case it transitively takes only one object, or in the sense of making into, in which case the first object is omitted, meaning: He made some of His creatures a son. Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿAmir, and others read (qalu, "they said") without the waw, either as a resumption, or with the sense of coordination kept in view, and the pronoun and the connection through it suffice instead of the waw, as in al-Bahr. ﴿سُبْحانَهُ﴾ [Glorified is He] is a declaration of transcendence and absolving Him, exalted is He, from what they say, in the most emphatic form. The complement of (subhan) is omitted, as you see, because the speech points to it.

﴿بَلْ لَهُ ما في السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ [Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth.] This is a refutation of what they claimed, and a turning away from what their false saying implies: the comparison with created things in procreation and begetting, and the need for a son to carry out what a father needs, and swift perishing, since that is a necessary consequence of the composition that necessitates need, and everything composed is near and swift to perish. Also, the wisdom in begetting is that the species be preserved through successive similar beings, where there is no way for the individual itself to remain for the duration of time. All of this is impossible for God, exalted is He, for He is the Everlasting, the Eternal, and the Absolutely Self-Sufficient, transcendent above resemblance to created things. The preposition (lam) in (lahu, "to Him") is said to denote ownership, and it is said that it is like the one in your saying "for Zayd is a blow," indicating the attribution of an effect to its agent. It is also said that it denotes exclusivity in whatever manner, and this is the more apparent. The meaning is: the matter is not as they fabricate. Rather, He is the Creator of all existing things, of which what they claimed to be a son is one, and the Creator of every existing thing has no need of a son, since He brings into being what He wills, transcendent above need for begetting.

﴿كُلٌّ لَهُ قانِتُونَ﴾ [All are obedient to Him.] That is, everything in them, of whatever kind, all together are submissive to Him, none of them refuses His will and His bringing into being, whether bringing into existence, annihilation, or change from one state to another. This necessitates origination and contingency, which contradict essential necessity (wujub dhati). Therefore whoever is characterized by this attribute cannot be a father, because it is required of a son that he share his father's nature, being a part of him, even if he does not resemble him. The apparent wording would have been (min, "of") with (qanitun), so as to avoid applying the principle of predominance (taghlib) to it, and to conform to the flow of speech, since the discussion concerns ʿUzayr, the Messiah, and the angels, who are rational beings. However, it came with (ma), which is specific to non-rational beings, as one of the scholars said, citing the story of al-Zib'ara, in disagreement with what al-Radi holds, that it is mostly used for what is not known, and with what most scholars hold, that it is general, as in al-Talwih. Predominance is taken into account in (qanitun) as an indication that those whom they made a son of God, exalted and glorified is He, are beside His greatness lifeless things, equal in feet with them in lacking the capacity to take a son. It was also said: (ma) was used in the first place because it indicates the station of divinity, in which rational beings are like lifeless things, and rational beings are gathered in the second place because it indicates the station of servanthood, in which lifeless things are like rational beings.

It is also possible that the genitive complement be understood as: all that they made a son, supplied by what the saying implies, not as a general term supplied by what refutes it. Submission (qunut) is then taken as obedience to the command of obligation, just as in general it is submission to the command of creation. In that case there is no predominance in (qanitun), and the sentence is a binding argument that what they claimed as a son is obedient to God, exalted is He, and acknowledges His servanthood, after the proof has been established against them by what preceded. The conjunction was omitted to draw attention to the independence of each of the two in indicating corruption, and to their difference, in that one of them is a proof and the other a binding argument. On the first view, the latter serves to confirm what came before it. Al-Jassas mentioned that this verse indicates that a person's ownership does not remain over his child, because it negated the son by affirming ownership, on the basis that (lam) denotes possession. So whenever one owns his son, he is freed from him. The Prophet (ﷺ) has ruled similarly concerning a father whom his son owns. It is not hidden that this is far from what the verse intends, especially since the more apparent meaning is exclusivity, as you have known.

[p. 368]

﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning their Originator (*mubdi'uhuma*). It is a *fa'il* (an intensive pattern) derived from *af'ala*. Al-Asma'i used to deny that *fa'il* can mean *maf'il*. Ibn Barri said: "It has come often, such as *musakhkhin* and *sakhin*, *muq'id* and *qa'id*, *muwsi* and *wasiyy*, *muhkim* and *hakim*, *mubrim* and *barim*, *muwniq* and *anik*, along with its other counterparts. Among this is *al-sami'* in the line of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib al-Sabi'." The citation of these examples is based on the apparent and immediate sense, which is most suitable to the topics of Arabic grammar. Therefore, what has been said about the line does not refute it, since that [claim] goes against it, as is not hidden from the fair-minded.

It has also been said that it is an annexation of the adjectival noun (*sifa mushabbaha*) to its agent, for lightness, meaning "Originator of His heavens." You know that it has been established that when an adjective is annexed to its agent, there is a pronoun in it referring back to the described thing. So the annexation is valid only if the described thing can validly be characterized by it, as in *husn al-wajh* ("handsome of face"), where it is valid for a man to be described as handsome because his face is handsome, unlike *husn al-jariya* ("handsome of the girl"). And "Zayd *kathir al-ikhwan*" ("Zayd, of many brothers") is valid because he is characterized as being supported by them. In our case, although the described thing cannot be characterized by the stated attribute, it can be characterized by what the attribute indicates, namely his being the Originator of them. This implies that it is preferable to keep *al-mubdi'* on its apparent meaning, which is the view of the leading authorities of the lexicographers.

*Ibda'* (origination) is bringing a thing into existence neither from a material nor in a time. It is used of God's bringing the first entities into being, as al-Raghib said. It is other than *sun'* (fashioning), for *sun'* is the composition of a form with an element. It is used for bringing bodies into existence, and for what is other than *takwin* (bringing into being), since *takwin* generally occurs through change and in time.

If by "the heavens and the earth" is meant everything other than Him, namely originated things, made things, and brought-into-being things, since they include the realm of dominion (*mulk*) and the realm of the unseen (*malakut*), then after accounting for the figure of speech by which the part stands for the whole (*taghlib*), it is valid to use each of the three terms. However, the word *ibda'* is more fitting, because it indicates the perfection of His power.

The claim that *ibda'* must be understood as *takwin* from a material or from parts, because the creation of the heavens was from something, as indicated by His words:

﴿Then He turned to the heaven while it was smoke﴾

is a view arising from heedlessness of what we have mentioned. The verse is another proof against that hideous doctrine. Its explanation: He is the Originator of everything other than Himself, the Doer in the absolute sense. Nothing of the begetter [is like this], since the begetter is necessarily affected by the separation of the child's material from him. So God is not a begetter.

Al-Mansur read *Badi'* with a *fatha* as an expression of praise. It was also read with a *kasra* as a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun in *lahu* ("to Him"), according to the view of those who permit that.

﴿And when He decrees a matter﴾, meaning He wills a thing, as indicated by His words: ﴿His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ *Qada'* (decree) comes in several senses, all of which return to the completion of a thing, whether by word or by deed. Using it for *irada* (will) is a metaphorical usage (*majaz*), in which the word denoting the effect is used for the cause, since the bringing into being, which is the completion of a thing, is an effect of the will's connection to it, because the will necessitates it. Ibn al-Sayyid equated *qada'* with *qadar* (destiny). The prevalent view distinguishes them: *qadar* is the measuring out of matters before they occur, while *qada'* is the execution of that *qadar* and its emergence from non-existence to the state of actuality. The majority of scholars affirmed this distinction, because it has come in a hadith that "the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a leaning wall about to collapse, so he hastened his step until he had passed it. He was asked: 'Do you flee from God's decree?' He said: 'I flee from His decree to His destiny.'" Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) distinguished between *qada'* and *qadar*.

﴿then He only says to it, "Be," and it is.﴾ The apparent view is that both verbs are from *kana* in its complete (*tamma*) usage, since no predicate is mentioned, although the complete usage is the original one: "He creates, and it comes to be." It indicates the meaning of the incomplete (*naqisa*) usage, because absolute existence is more general than existence in itself or in another. The command is understood in its literal sense, as the realization scholars among our Hanafi masters held. God has established His custom in bringing things into being that He creates them by this word, although creating them by other than it is not impossible. The intended meaning is the eternal speech (*kalam azali*), because it is impossible for a sequenced word to subsist in the Essence of God, and because it is originated and would then require another address, which leads to an infinite regress. Its delay after the will and its precedence over the existence of the being are in terms of its connection. Since the address of creation does not involve understanding, yet includes the greatest benefits, it may be connected to the non-existent.

The Mu'tazila and many of the People of the Sunna held that the command does not refer to a real command and obedience, but is an allegory for the realization of what the will has connected to, without delay, through the immediate obedience of the obedient subordinate, without hesitation. Therefore there is an allegorical metaphor (*isti'ara tamthiliyya*), in which the state of the attainment of the desired thing after the will's connection, without delay, and with the subordinate's immediate obedience to the command of the one obeyed without hesitation or refusal, is likened to the depiction of the absent by the image of the present. Then the sentence, which was originally for the thing likened, was used for the thing used as the likeness, without considering a metaphor in its individual words. The original sentence was: "When He decrees a matter, it is attained immediately upon it, as if He says to it, 'Be,' and it is." Then the likened part was omitted, and the likeness was put in its place. Some scholars hold that the expression contains a realized explicit metaphor (*isti'ara tahqiqiyya tasrihiyya*), based on the likeness of one state to another.

Perhaps what led these scholars away from the apparent meaning is their claim that it is impossible, for several reasons mentioned by some of their leading figures.

First: God's words *kun* ("Be") are either eternal or originated. They cannot be eternal, because the *nun* comes after the *kaf*, and what is preceded is necessarily originated, and likewise what precedes it by a determined time. Also, *idha* ("when") denotes the future, so the decree is originated, and *kun* is subsequent to it by the particle of sequence *fa'*, and what follows the originated is originated. Nor can it be originated, for then it would either be circular or lead to an infinite regress.

Second: either the created thing is addressed with "Be" before entering existence, and addressing the non-existent is folly, or it is addressed after entering existence, and there is no benefit in that.

Third: the created thing may be inanimate, and imposing obligation on it is not befitting wisdom.

Fourth: if we suppose the capable and willing agent separated from his saying "Be," then if he is able to bring the thing into being, there is no need for it; and if he is not able, then the capable agent is not capable of the act except at the moment of his uttering "Be," and thus he would be incapable in terms of his own essence.

Fifth: we know by necessity that this word has no effect when we utter it, so likewise when another utters it.

Sixth: the effective cause is either the combination of the *kaf* and the *nun*, but the two do not exist together, or one of them, which contradicts the supposition.

When you reflect on what we have mentioned, it becomes clear to you that all these arguments are refuted. How strange is it for one who holds the inner speech (*kalam nafsi*) and makes this a sign of it! How can these clatterings alarm him, or how can these bubbles deceive him! Yes, if someone were to adopt this view, because it establishes a greater magnificence for God than the first view does, that is not because the first view is invalid in itself. Indeed, it would be worthy of acceptance, and perhaps I myself hold it.

The verse is presented to explain the mode of origination, and it is joined to His words ﴿the Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾, containing an affirmation of the meaning of origination. In it there is an allusion to another proof against that nonsense: the taking of a child from a begetter occurs only after intending it, through stages and a delay, since that is impossible except after the separation of its material from him and its becoming a living being. But God's act occurs after His will, or the connection of His word is free of delay. So taking a child is not an act of God.

The cause of this error appears to be that in earlier scriptures God was called "Father" in the sense of being the first cause. This usage was frequent in the Gospel of John (*Yuhanna*). Then the ignorant assumed that it meant begetting, so they believed that out of imitation, and they disbelieved. The scholars of today do not permit applying that term to God even metaphorically, to cut off the source of corruption.

Ibn 'Amir read *fa-yakuna* ("so that it may be") with a *fatha*. This reading has troubled the grammarians, to the point that Ahmad ibn Musa dared to judge it erroneous. That is bad manners, and indeed one of the worst errors. Its justification is that it is the answer to the imperative (*jawab al-amr*), modeled on the form of the wording, even though its meaning is a statement, since the meaning does not involve making the consequent of the particle *fa'* (the event after it) dependent on the meaning of the imperative form, which requires the causal relation of what precedes the *fa'* to what follows it, as is required in the answer to an imperative with *fa'*. For there is no sense in our saying "Let there be a being from you, so a being [results]." It has also been said: the reason for interpreting it by the wording is that the imperative is not real, so its answer is not put in the subjunctive. And a condition for that is that a conditional and a consequent be formed from the two, as in "Come to me, and I will honor you," for its implied meaning is "If you come to me, I will honor you." Here it is valid to say "let it be" (*yakun*), or else it would follow that a thing is the cause of itself. It was answered that the intended meaning is: if it is in the knowledge and will of God that it be, then it will be in the external world. This is like the hadith: "Whoever's migration was to God and His Messenger, his migration is to God and His Messenger." And it is also answered that the claim that a non-real imperative is put in the subjunctive in its answer is not granted. If it is with a word, then it is clear, but it is a metaphor for the speed of bringing into being. If it is not regarded as a word, then it is a metaphor for the will of its speed, so it reverts to the meaning that the speed of the existence of a thing that exists immediately is intended. There is no objection then to the apparent difference. This is not hidden from scrutiny.

The nominative reading (*raf'*) is by way of a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*), meaning "so it is." This is the view of Sibawayh. Al-Zajjaj held that it is conjoined to *yaqulu* ("He says"). In either case, what is said does not include *yakunu* ("it is") itself. As a completion of this, the shift from address to third person has been explained as an *iltifat* (shift in the grammatical person), in order to belittle the matter's affair by its ease of coming into being. Many have explained it this way, on the assumption of its inclusion.

﴿And those who do not know say﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "God has taken a son."﴾ The connection is that the first statement was a disparagement of tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), and this one is a disparagement of nubuwwa (prophethood). What is meant by the relative clause is the ignorant among the polytheists. This has been narrated from Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Hasan, and a group of others, and most of the exegetes (mufassirun) hold this view. It is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾, and they said: "Why does God not speak to us, or a sign come to us?" and they said: "Why was not an angel sent down to us, or do we see our Lord?"

It was also said that what is meant are the Jews who were in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The evidence for this is what has been narrated "from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, that Rafiʿ ibn Khuzaymah, from among the Jews, said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ): 'If you are a messenger from God, then ask God to speak to us so that we may hear His speech.' So God revealed this verse." And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The People of the Book ask you to bring down to them a book from heaven. They had asked Moses for greater than that﴾. Mujahid said: what is meant are the Christians. al-Tabari preferred this view, on the ground that they are the ones mentioned in the verse, but as you see, it is weak.

The negation of knowledge (nafy al-ʿilm) regarding them, according to the first view, is literal, because they had no scripture and were not followers of any prophethood.

Page 370

According to the last two views, it is due to their ignorance (tajahul), or because they did not know its requirement. ﴿Why does God not speak to us﴾, that is: why does He not speak to us to say that you are His messenger, either directly, as He speaks to the angels, or by sending down revelation to us? This is arrogance on their part, by counting their own corrupt selves as equal to the angels and the sanctified prophets, upon them be prayer and peace. ﴿Or a sign come to us﴾, that is, a proof of your truthfulness. This is obstinacy on their part. May God destroy them, given the clear signs and the dazzling proofs He had given them, before which the solid mountains would crumble. It was also said that what is meant is the coming of a specific sign that they proposed (muqtarahah). In this there is the point that specifying an indefinite noun (takhsis al-nakirah) goes against the apparent meaning.

﴿Thus said those before them﴾ is a reply to their doubt. The meaning is that they ask out of obstinacy and arrogance, like the earlier nations, and one who asks out of obstinacy does not deserve to have his request answered. ﴿The like of their saying﴾, this foul falsehood, ﴿so they said: "Show us God openly"﴾, ﴿"Can your Lord send down to us a table spread with food?"﴾, ﴿"Make for us a god"﴾. These two comparisons have already been discussed. Some have added here, beyond what has passed, the possibility that ﴿thus﴾ (kadhalika) is connected to ﴿come to us﴾ (taʾtina), in which case the pause would fall on it and not on "a sign." Or ﴿the like of their saying﴾ is connected to ﴿have become similar﴾ (tashabahat), in which case the pause would fall on ﴿before them﴾. You know that the noble speech of God should not be interpreted according to such cold possibilities.

﴿Their hearts have become similar﴾, that is, the hearts of these people and of those before them in blindness and obstinacy. It was also said: in obstinacy and in demanding (iqtirah). The sentence explains what precedes it. Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi Ishaq read the shin with tashdid (doubling). Abu ʿAmr al-Dani said: this is not permissible, because it is a past tense verb, and the two added letters (al-taʾanin al-mazidatan) occur only in the present tense, where they are assimilated (fa-yudgham). As for the past tense, this does not apply. In Gharaʾib al-Tafsir it is stated that they agreed that it is an error. al-Raghib justified it by saying that he treated the past tense as if it were the present, so that what is added to the present was added to it. But it is not hidden that this degree of justification does not remove the difficulty. Ibn Sahmi said in his work on the irregular readings (al-shawadhdh) that the Arabs sometimes add a taʾ to the beginning of the past tense of tafaʿʿala, saying tatafaʿʿala, and he cited the line: "The means have been cut off from me beyond you." But this is an unacceptable and unaccepted view. The correct position is that this reading cannot be validly attributed to these two imams. We have already pointed to something similar earlier.

﴿We have made the signs clear﴾, that is, we revealed them clear by making them so in themselves. This is like the saying: "Glory be to Him who made the gnat small and the elephant large." ﴿For a people who have certainty﴾, that is, who know the realities with a knowledge of firmness that is not affected by doubt or obstinacy. These people are not like that, which is why they were obstinate, arrogant, and said what they said. On this reading the sentence gives the reason for His saying: ﴿Thus said those before them﴾, as some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) have stated. It is also possible that what is meant by "coming" is the seeking of truth and certainty, and that the verse is a response to their request for a sign. The mention of the signs in definite form and plural, and the use of "made clear" in place of the "coming" they asked for, carries an eloquence that is not hidden. The meaning is that they proposed a singular sign, while we have made clear the great signs for a people who seek truth and certainty. The reason He, glory be to Him, did not address their saying ﴿Why does God not speak to us﴾ is to indicate that it is most like the speech of a fool, and the response to a fool is silence.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 119:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth﴾: meaning, accompanied by it and supported with it. Here the adverbial phrase is a *zarf mustaqarr* (a complement of stable location, i.e. it has a stable, understood predicate). It has also been said that it is a *laghw* (a superfluous complement) attached either to *arsalna* (We sent) or to what follows it. The truth has been interpreted as the Qur'an, or as Islam, and it is better to keep it general. ﴿as a bringer of good news and a warner﴾ are two circumstantial accusatives (*hal*) of the *kaf* (the "you" in *arsalnaka*). It has also been said that they are circumstantial of "the truth." The verse is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD*) intended to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because he used to be deeply concerned, and his chest would tighten because of their persistence in disbelief. The meaning is: We sent you so that you would give good news to those who obey and warn those who disobey, not to compel them to believe. So there is no blame on you if they persist or defiantly refuse. The emphasis (*ta'kid*) is to treat the one who is not denying as if he were the denier, given the signs of denial that were apparent in him. The restriction (*qaSr*) is of the individual type (*qaSr ifrad*).

﴿And you will not be asked about the companions of the Hellfire﴾: this is a concluding clause (*tadhyil*) conjoined to what precedes it, or a parenthetical clause, or a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: We sent you without being held accountable for the companions of the Hellfire, as to why they did not believe after you had conveyed what you were sent with and established the proof against them!
