Ubayy read *wa-ma* (and not) instead of *wa-la* (and not). Ibn Mas'ud read *wa-lan* (and never) instead of *dhalika* (that). Nafi' and Ya'qub read *la tas'al* (do not ask) in the form of a prohibition, to announce the complete severity of the punishment of the disbelievers and to magnify it, just as you say, "How is so-and-so doing?" when he has fallen into something disliked, and it is said to you, "Do not ask about him," meaning that because of the extreme awfulness of what has befallen him, the informant cannot bring it out with his tongue, or the listener cannot bear to hear it. On this reading the clause is a parenthetical clause, or a conjunction with an implied element, meaning "so convey," and the prohibition is figurative (*majaz*). Some have taken it literally (*haqiqa*), and the primary purpose of it is the prohibition against asking about the condition of his two parents, based on what is narrated: that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked Jibril about their graves, and he showed them to him. So he went and supplicated for them, and wished to know their condition in the Hereafter, and said, "Would that I knew what became of my parents!" Then the verse was revealed. The weakness of this report is not hidden, because the Prophet (ﷺ), as is in *al-Muntakhab*, knows what their affair came to. The Shaykh Wali al-Din al-Iraqi mentioned that he did not come across it. Imam al-Suyuti said: nothing has come concerning this except a *mu'dal* report (one with two or more consecutive missing narrators) of weak chain, so it is not to be relied upon. What is definitively known is that the verse concerns the disbelievers among the People of the Book, like the verses preceding it and following it, not the parents of the Prophet (ﷺ). Because the narrations on this subject conflict and are weak, al-Sakhawi said: "What we hold ourselves accountable to before Allah is to refrain from them and from delving into their conditions. What I hold myself accountable to before Allah is that they both died as monotheists during the time of disbelief." On this view the statement of Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, is to be understood, if it is authentic. Indeed, I nearly say: they are more excellent than Ali al-Qari and his like.

*Al-Jahim* is the fire itself when its blaze is ignited. It is said: "The fire blazed (*jahamat*), blazing (*tajhamu*) with a blaze (*jahman*)," when it became agitated.

﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their creed﴾. This is a statement of the utmost severity of the stubbornness of these two groups, following the statement of what encompasses them and the polytheists, as mentioned earlier. The negation is not placed between the two conjoined nouns (lā bayna al-ma'tūfayn) in order to emphasise the negation, and to indicate that the pleasure of each of them is opposed to the pleasure of the other. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ). It contains such an exaggeration in despairing him (ﷺ) of their conversion that there is no beyond it. For since they are not pleased with him (ﷺ), even if he left them to do what they do, but rather they hoped for what can hardly enter the sphere of possibility, namely that he follow their creed which he came to abrogate, how could it be imagined that they would follow his creed (ﷺ)? This exaggeration was needed because of his (ﷺ) excessive eagerness for their faith, according to what has been related, that he would conciliate each group, hoping that they would embrace Islam, whereupon this was revealed.

The word milla (creed) is, in origin, a noun derived from amlaltu al-kitāb, meaning "I dictated the book," as al-Rāghib (al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī) said. From it comes ṭarīq malūl, meaning a well-trodden known path, as al-Azharī (al-Azharī) transmitted. Then it was transferred to the fundamentals of the sharī'as (religious laws), on the basis that the Prophet (ﷺ) dictates them, and the prophets (peace be upon them) do not differ regarding them. It may also be applied to falsehood, as in "Unbelief is one creed." It is not attributed to Him, glory be to Him, so one does not say "the creed of God," nor to individuals of the community. Dīn (religion) is synonymous with it in truth, but it is considered in terms of the acceptance of those who are commanded, since in origin it is obedience and submission. And because what confirms both of them is one, He, exalted is He, said ﴿an upright religion, the creed of Abraham﴾. Dīn may also be applied to the subsidiary matters figuratively, and it is attributed to God, exalted is He, to individuals, and to specific groups, considering the root. Moreover, the difference of consideration is sufficient for the validity of the attribution. It may also be applied to falsehood. As for sharī'a (the sacred law), it is in origin the watering place, and it has been made a term for the particular rulings relating to this life and the hereafter, whether they are explicitly stated by the Lawgiver or not, but they return to Him. Abrogation and alteration occur within them. It may also be applied figuratively to the universal fundamentals. This was said by some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn).

The word milla is in the singular, although they have two creeds, for brevity, or because the two are gathered under unbelief, which is one creed.

Then, this is not the beginning of a statement from Him, exalted is He, about their not being pleased, but rather it is a report of the meaning of a statement that they uttered in the form of speech, so that His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of God is the guidance﴾ corresponds to it. For it is in the manner of a reply to their saying. Perhaps they did not say that except because they claimed that their religion is the truth and other than it is falsehood. So they were answered with the qaṣr qalbī (contrastive restriction by reversal), that is: the religion of God, exalted is He, is the truth and your religion is falsehood, and the guidance of God, exalted is He, which is Islam, is the guidance, and what they call to is not guidance, but rather desire, in the most eloquent manner. This is through the attribution of guidance to Him, exalted is He, its emphasis with inna (indeed), the repetition of "guidance" in the predicate according to the pattern of "my poetry is my poetry," making it the very verbal noun of guidance, the insertion of the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl), and the definiteness of the predicate.

It is possible that they said that among themselves, and the command to them to say this statement does not need to be a response to that exact expression, but rather a response to what entails its content, or what it necessitates from the call to Judaism or Christianity, and that guidance lies in them both.

It has also been said that it may be for despairing them of what they wish for and hope for, and that it is not a response. ﴿And if you follow their desires﴾, that is, their deviant opinions, deviating from the truth, issuing from them by following the desires of their souls, and these are what He expressed earlier by "creed." It would have been expected to say "if you follow it," but He changed the arrangement and placed the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, using different wording, as an indication that they had altered what God, glory be to Him, had legislated, with an alteration by which they took it out of its proper place. And in the use of the plural there is an indication of the great number of disagreements among them, and that some of them declare others to be unbelievers.

﴿After the knowledge that has come to you﴾, that is, the known (al-ma'lūm), which is the revelation, or the religion, because it is what is described as "coming," not knowledge itself. You may also interpret "coming" as "attaining," so that knowledge remains on its apparent meaning. ﴿you would have no protector from God, nor any helper﴾ is the answer to the oath indicated by the preparatory lām (lām al-muwaṭṭi'a). If the conditional were answered by it here, the fā' (then) would be required. It has been said that it is the answer to the conditional, and it needs the supposition of an oath placed after the conditional, and the interpretation of the nominal clause as a future verbal clause, that is: "what will be for you." This is far-fetched, since none of the grammarians has said that the oath is postponed with the preparatory lām, and interpreting the nominal clause as a verbal clause has no evidence. It has also been said that it is the answer to both: the oath indicated by the lām, and the conditional in, one of them by its wording and the other by its meaning. This, as you see, is [unsound].

The address is also to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). Restricting the condition by what it is restricted by serves to indicate that following their desires is impossible, because it is contrary to what is known to be true. So if its occurrence were assumed, as the impossible is assumed, he would have no protector, nor any helper to repel punishment from him. In this there is also an exaggeration in despairing [him] that is not hidden.

It has been said: the address there and here, although it is apparent to the Prophet (ﷺ), its real intent is his community. But you know, from what we have mentioned, that this does not need to be assumed,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 121:

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) to describe the condition of the believers among the People of the Book, after mention of the condition of their disbelievers. It was not joined by a conjunction (lam yu'taf), as a signal of the complete contrast between the two groups. The verse was revealed concerning them, and they are the ones intended by it, whether the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is understood as the category (al-jins) or as a specific group (al-ahd), according to what has been said: that they were the forty who came from Abyssinia with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, thirty-two of them from Yemen and eight scholars from the Levant (al-Sham). ﴿who recite it with its due recitation﴾: that is, they read it with its true reading. This is a recitation that takes hold of the whole heart, so that attention is paid to correct pronunciation of the words (dabt al-lafz), reflection upon the meaning (ta'ammul fi al-ma'na), and the rights of its commands and prohibitions (haqq al-amr wa al-nahy). The clause is a conditional circumstantial clause (hal muqaddarah), meaning: We gave them the Book with their recitation of it intended (muqaddaran tilawatuhum), because they were not reciting at the time of its giving. This circumstance is restrictive (mukhassasah), because not everyone who is given it recites it. (Haqqa) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), since it is annexed to a verbal noun. It is also permitted that it be an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, and that it be a circumstantial term, meaning "those who are truly sincere." The predicate is the words of the Exalted: ﴿those believe in it﴾. It is also possible that (yatlunahu) is a predicate rather than a circumstantial clause, and (ulaika) and what follows is a predicate after a predicate, or an independent sentence. On the first of the two possibilities, the relative pronoun is for the category, and on the second it is for a specific group, meaning the believers among the People of the Book. The placing of the subject before the verbal predicate indicates restriction (lil-hasr) and allusion (lil-ta'rid). The pronoun refers to the Book, meaning: ﴿they believe in their Book﴾, as opposed to the distorters, for they do not believe in it. From here the benefit of the statement in the last interpretation becomes clear. You may also say: the focal point of the benefit is what belief in it necessarily entails of gain, by the indication of what follows.

Among people there are those who took the relative pronoun to refer to the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this view was taken by Ikrimah and Qatadah; in that case the Book means the Qur'an. Others took it to refer to the prophets and messengers (peace be upon them), and this view was taken by Ibn Kaysan; in that case the Book means the category, so as to include the scattered scriptures. Others said what we have said, except that they permitted the pronoun in "bihi" to refer to guidance (al-huda), or to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to Allah the Exalted. On both of these estimations there is a shift in the speech (iltifat) from address to the third person, or from the first person plural to it. What is in some of these views of remoteness is not hidden.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in it﴾: that is, in the Book, by means of distortion and disbelief in what confirms it. The possibilities regarding the similar pronoun here are also stated concerning it.

﴿Those are the losers﴾: in the sense that they exchanged disbelief for belief. It was said: by their trade, which they used to practice by taking bribes for distortion.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verses 122–123:**

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything, nor will any ransom be accepted from it, nor will intercession benefit it, nor will they be helped.﴾

This is a repetition to remind the Children of Israel, and a restatement of the warning to them, for the sake of emphasis in giving counsel, and to signal that this is the *fadhlaka* (a concluding summary of a narrative, gathering its main point) of the story and its purpose. He has varied the expression: intercession is mentioned first with the word "acceptance," placed before "ransom," and here with the word "benefit," placed after it. Perhaps, as has been said, this indicates the negation of the essence of the thing and the negation of what follows from it. The first item, which comes first in existence, is also mentioned first, and the item that comes later in existence is also mentioned later.

It has also been said that the earlier verse was for the command to fulfil the rights of the earlier blessings, while this verse is a reminder of a blessing by which He preferred them over the worlds, namely the blessing of faith in the prophet of their time and their submission to his rulings, so that they might seize it, believe, and become among the excellent rather than the lesser. And so that they might, by following him, guard themselves against the terrors of the Resurrection and its fear, just as they guarded themselves by following Musa, peace be upon him,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 124 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with words﴾. Regarding what the clause introduced by (idh, "when") is connected to, there are possibilities whose indication was already given in the parallel verse. Abu Hayyan chose for it to be connected to the later "qala" (He said), and some connect it to a deleted verb placed afterward, meaning "such-and-such was the case." The well-known view is that it is connected to a deleted verb placed beforehand, whose estimate is: "Remember," or "Remember the time when such-and-such." In that case the sentence is coordinated with what precedes it, as the coordination of one narrative with another, and the common element is the unity of purpose. The purpose of reminding them and warning them is to urge them to accept his religion (ﷺ), to follow the truth, and to abandon partisanship and love of leadership. Likewise, the purpose of the story of Abraham (peace be upon him) and the explanation of his circumstances is calling to the religion of Islam and abandoning partisanship in religion. This is because, when they know that he attained the imamate by submitting to the judgment of the Most High, and that his supplication concerning the wrongdoers was not answered, and that the Ka'bah was in his time a place of circumambulation and a place of worship, and that he was commanded to purify it, and that he used to make pilgrimage to the House calling out and supplicating as is the case in the religion of the Prophet (ﷺ), and that our Prophet (peace be upon him) is from his supplication, and that he supplicated for himself and his offspring for the religion of Islam, it becomes obligatory upon whoever acknowledges his virtue, and that he is from his descendants, and claims to follow his religion, and boasts that he is among the residents of his sanctuary and the guardians of his House, that his own condition should be like that.

Imam Izz al-Millah wa'l-Din (ʿIṣām al-Millah wa'l-Dīn) went to the permissibility of coordinating with "ni'mati" (My blessing), meaning: remember the time of Abraham's testing, for in it is what benefits you and refutes your corrupt belief that your fathers will be your intercessors on the Day of Resurrection, because He did not accept Abraham's supplication concerning the wrongdoers. And it removes from you love of leadership, which prevents following the Messenger (ﷺ), for it is known from it that leadership is not attained by wrongdoers. It was objected that this is a departure from the path of eloquence, along with the necessity of restricting the address to the People of the Book, and that "ittaqu" (fear) intervenes between the two coordinated items. Testing (ibtila') in its original sense is examination, as we have mentioned before. The intended meaning here is obligation (taklif), or treatment in the manner of testing, metaphorically, since the true sense of testing is impossible for Him, the Most High, as He is the Knower of the secret and the hidden things. "Ibrahim" is a non-Arabic proper name; it is said that its meaning before arabization is "a compassionate father." It is a fronted object, since its agent is idafa to its pronoun. Mention of the title of Lordship is an honouring of him (peace be upon him), and an indication that this testing is an upbringing for him and a preparation for a momentous matter. "Al-kalimat" (the words) is the plural of "kalimah," whose original meaning is the single word, and it is used for meaningful sentences and applied to the meanings of those, because of the very close connection between word and meaning. It has been disputed. Tawus related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are the ten of the natural disposition (fitrah): rinsing the mouth, sniffing water into the nose, trimming the moustache, letting the beard grow, parting the hair, plucking the armpit hair, paring the nails, shaving the pubic area, cleansing after excretion, and circumcision. ʿIkrimah, in another narration from him, said: No one was tested with this religion and fulfilled all of it except Abraham; Allah tested him with thirty characteristics of Islam: ten of them are in Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), beginning "the penitent" (al-tā'ibūn), etc.; ten in al-Ahzab: "Indeed the Muslim men and the Muslim women" etc.; and ten in al-Mu'minun, beginning "And one who asked" down to "and those who are steadfast in their prayers." In a narration of al-Hakim in his Mustadrak, they are thirty; he counted the first three surahs and did not count the last surah. So what is in Bara'ah: repentance, worship, praise, wandering, bowing, prostration, enjoining good, forbidding evil, guarding the limits of Allah, and faith derived from "And give good tidings to the believers" or from "Indeed Allah has purchased from the believers." In al-Ahzab: Islam, faith, devotion, truthfulness, patience, humility, charity, fasting, guarding the private parts, and remembrance. And what is in al-Mu'minun: faith, humility, turning away from vain talk, zakah, guarding the private parts except with spouses or slave-women (counted as three), safeguarding trusts and covenants (counted as two), and observance of prayer. This is based on the premise that the necessary recurrence of some characteristics after gathering the mentioned tens, such as faith and guarding the private parts, does not contradict their being thirty in number; it contradicts only their being distinct in essence. From here the basmalah is counted as one hundred and thirteen verses according to the Shafi'is, by considering its recurrence at the beginning of every surah. What is in ʿIkrimah's narration is based on considering distinctness in essence and dropping repeated items; he counts as the tenth the good tidings to the believers in Bara'ah, and considers constancy in prayer and observance of it as one item. "And those in whose wealth there is a known right" (70:24) "for the beggar and the deprived" (70:25), not those who give zakah, because it includes voluntary charity and maintaining kinship. What is reported, that they are forty, and their explanation by what is in the four surahs, is also based on the first consideration, so there is no difficulty. It is said: Allah tested him with seven things: the stars, the two moons, circumcision in old age, the fire, the slaughter of the son, the emigration from Kuthā to Syria. This is reported from al-Hasan. It is also said: they are what the subsequent verses contain of imamate, purifying the House, raising its foundations, and Islam. And it is said, and it is said, up to thirteen opinions.

Ibn ʿAmir, Ibn al-Zubayr and others read "Ibrahama," and Abu Bakrah read "Ibrahima," with a kasra on the ha' and the ya' deleted. Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu al-Sha'tha' and Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with them, read "Ibrahimu" with a damma (as subject) and "rabbahu" with a fatha (as object). Then "ibtila'" in the sense of testing is literal, because it is valid from the servant, and the meaning is that he supplicated his Lord with words such as "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead" and "Make this city secure," to see whether He answers him. There is no need to interpret it metaphorically. As for what is said, that although it is valid from the servant, it is not valid, or not proper, to attribute it to the Lord, its reasoning is not evident apart from the mention of the word ibtila'. It may be that this occurred in a station of intimacy and the station of friendship, without being hidden.

"Fa-atammahunna" (and he fulfilled them): the pronoun in the accusative refers to the words only, and the hidden nominative pronoun may refer to Abraham or to his Lord, according to both readings, raf' and nasb. So there are four possibilities. The first: it refers to "Ibrahim" in the accusative, and the meaning then is that he carried them out in the most complete way and performed them as is fitting. The second: it refers to "rabbahu" in the nominative, and the meaning then is: He facilitated for him the practice of them and strengthened him to complete them, or He completed for him their rewards, or He made them a lasting practice in him and in his posterity until the Day of Religion. The third: it refers to "Ibrahim" in the nominative, and the meaning according to it: Abraham completed the words he supplicated with, by observing the conditions of their answering, and did not after them do anything that would waste them. The fourth: it refers to "rabbahu" in the accusative, and the meaning according to it: He, glorified be He, gave Abraham everything he asked. The most apparent possibilities are the first and fourth, since praise is not evident in the second, along with the deletion of the annexed noun on one of its possibilities, and the usual usage is not followed in the third, because the verb in opposition to testing must have the tester's verb as a passive participle.

﴿He said: Indeed I am making you an imam for the people﴾. This is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), since it is as if it were said: "What then came after that?" and it was answered with that. Or it is an explanation of "ibtila'," based on the view of those who make "the words" an expression for what was mentioned as its effect. Some make this an explanation of the universal by one of its particulars. If "idh" is made to govern "qala," as Abu Hayyan went to, the whole becomes a sentence coordinated with what precedes it in the manner whose detail has passed. It is said: it is an digression (mustatrida) or an interposition (mu'tarida), so that His statement "Or were you witnesses" (2:133) falls in its place, if it is taken as addressed to the Jews, and fits His statement "And they say: Be Jews or Christians" (2:135). The second item is "jā'il" taken from "ja'ala" in the sense of "sayyara" (made), which is transitive to two objects. The second is either a complement attached to "jā'il," meaning "for their sake," or in the position of a circumstantial clause, since it is an indefinite qualifier preceded by its noun, meaning "an imam existing for them." "Imam" is a noun for the model that is followed, and from it it is said of the foundation line of a building: imam. It is a singular on the pattern fi'āl. Some made it a noun of instrument, since fi'āl is one of its patterns, like "izār" (waist-wrapper). It was objected that "imam" is what is followed and "izār" is what is wrapped with, so they are objects, and the object of a verb is not an instrument, because an instrument is the intermediary between agent and object in the arrival of its effect to it; and if the object were an instrument, the agent would be likewise, and it is not so. It may be the plural of "āmm," the active participle of "amma yaummu," like "jā'i'" and "jiyā'," and "qā'im" and "qiyām." This is according to the concept, and although it includes the prophet, the caliph, and the prayer leader, indeed everyone who is followed in anything, even if falsely, as His statement indicates: "And We made them imams calling to the Fire" (28:41). However, what is meant here is the prophet who is followed, for whoever else is, being the follower of the Prophet, his imamate is not like his imamate. This imamate is either perpetual, as the definition of "the people" and the form of the active participle indicating continuity require, and the coming of prophets after him does no harm, since no prophet was sent except that he was from his descendants, and was commanded to follow him in general, not in all rulings, because the subsequent laws do not agree with it in everything; so his imamate remains through the imamate of his offspring, which are parts of him, in alternation. Or it is limited, based on the view that what has been abrogated, even partly, is not called perpetual; otherwise the imamate of every prophet would be perpetual, and that has not spread. Then "the people" here means his nation who followed him. You may also maintain the view that the imamate of every prophet is perpetual, but in the foundations of monotheism, which were not abrogated; rather they are never abrogated, as His statement indicates: "Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance" (6:90). The lack of spread is not conceded, and even if conceded, it does no harm. The bestowal upon Abraham (peace be upon him) of this, and not upon others, is for a particularity that required it, which is not hard to see, so ponder.

Then it should not be hidden that the apparent sense of the verse indicates that the testing occurred before prophethood, because He, the Most High, made the performance of those words a cause for making him imam. It was said that it occurred after them, because it requires the precedence of revelation. It was answered that mere revelation does not entail mission to creation. You know that if the slaughter of the son, the emigration and the fire are among the words, the matter becomes problematic, because these were after prophethood, without doubt; and likewise circumcision also, based on what is reported, that when he circumcised himself he was one hundred and twenty years old. Then it becomes necessary that the completion of the words be the cause of the imamate in terms of its generality for the people, and the answering of his supplication concerning some of his descendants. Al-Razi related from al-Qadi that on this view the meaning of His statement "fa-atammahunna" is that He, glorified and exalted be He, knew from his condition that he would complete them and carry them out after prophethood; therefore He bestowed upon him the robe of imamate and prophethood. It is not hidden that the particle "fa" refuses to be taken in this sense.

(He said) is a resumptive clause explaining what came before (*istinaf bayani*). The pronoun refers to Ibrahim, upon him be peace. (And of my offspring) is conjoined (*'atf*) to the *kaf* (the "you" of "I will make you"). It is said: "I will honour you," and you reply, "and Zayd," meaning "and Zayd as well." Taking it to mean "what will become of my offspring?" is far-fetched. Abu Hayyan held that it is connected to an implied verb, "will You make of my offspring an imam?", because Ibrahim, upon him be peace, understood from "I am making you" that the appointment was specific to him. Some scholars preferred this view. Objections were raised to the first view: first, that a prepositional phrase cannot serve as a genitive complement and so cannot be conjoined to it; second, how conjunction to a pronoun can be valid without repeating the preposition; and third, how the conjoined element can be the quoted speech of another speaker. The first two objections are answered by saying that the genitive construction is, in effect, a separated one, and that "and of my offspring" means "some of my offspring." So it is as if he said: "and making some of my offspring [an imam]." This is sound, though conjunction to a pronoun governed by a preposition without repeating the preposition is rejected by most grammarians. Nevertheless, the verifying scholars of the Arabic language and the imams of the religion permit it. The author of *al-'Ubab* even said that it occurs in the seven widely transmitted recitations (*qira'at*). Whoever rejects this has rejected the Prophet (ﷺ). The third objection is answered by saying that this is a case of *'atf al-talqin* (conjunction of prompting), where the clause is a statement in the sense of a command. Its underlying form is: "and make some of my offspring [imams]," as the objector suggested. But it was changed to the form revealed because of its rhetorical excellence, in that it makes the phrase part of the speaker's own words, as if the conjoined element deserves the same status as the element it is conjoined to, and makes himself as if a substitute for the speaker. The shift from the imperative form serves to emphasise certainty and to observe courtesy by avoiding the appearance of a command. It also contains a brevity suited to its place that pleases every beholder. A parallel to this conjunction is what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "O Allah, have mercy on those who shave their heads." They said: "And those who trim, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "O Allah, have mercy on those who shave their heads." They said: "And those who trim, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "And those who trim."

The scholars of legal theory (*usuliyyun*) have mentioned that *talqin* occurs with the conjunction *wa* ("and") and with other particles, and that it occurs in exception, as in the hadith: "Indeed Allah has forbidden the tree of the Sacred Precinct." They said: "Except the *idhkhir*, O Messenger of Allah." Another objection is also raised: that conjunction requires that the imamate of his offspring be general for all people, as the imamate of Ibrahim, upon him be peace, is said to be general. This is not the case. It is answered that sharing in the basic meaning is sufficient for conjunction. It is also said that it is sufficient that it be accepted with respect to our Prophet, upon him be the best of blessings and peace.

*Dhurriyyah* means a man's progeny. Its original meaning is young children, and then it came to include both adults and children, singular and plural. It is also said that it includes the fathers, based on Allah's words: ﴿Indeed We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾, meaning Nuh and his sons. The correct view is the opposite. The word has three vowelisations: with a *dammah* on the *dhal*, with a *fathah*, and with a *kasrah*, and all three have been recited. It is either of the form *fu'ulah* from *dharawtu* or *dharaytu*. The original is *dharuwah* or *dharuwiyah*. In the first case, two *waw*s came together, one additional and one original. The original was changed into a *ya'*, making it like the second, so a *ya'* and a *waw* came together. One of them was preceded by a sukun, so the *waw* was changed into a *ya'* and the *ya'* was assimilated into the *ya'*, becoming *dhurriyyah*. Or it is of the form *fi'liyyah* from the same root, and the original of the first is *dhariwiyah*, so the *waw* was changed into a *ya'* for the reason already given, becoming *dhariyiyah* like the second, and then the *ya'* was assimilated into its like, becoming *dhurriyyah*. Or it is *fu'liyyah* from *dhar*, meaning creation, and the original is *dhar'iyyah*, so the *hamzah* was changed into a *ya'* and assimilated. Or it is *fi'liyyah* from *dhar*, meaning dispersal, and the original is *dhariyrah*, so the last *ra'* was changed into a *ya'* to avoid the heaviness of repetition, as they said *tazannantu* becoming *tazanniytu*, and *taqaddadtu* becoming *taqaddaytu*. Or it is *fu'ulah* from it, with the original *dharurah*, so the last *ra'* was changed into a *ya'*, and assimilation followed. Or it is *fi'liyyah* from it in the form of the relative adjective (*nisbah*). They said: this is the most apparent, because this pattern is common, as in *hurriyyah* and *durriyyah*, and because it does not need the changes of *i'lal*. The *dhal* was given a *dammah* because forms are changed in the relative adjective specifically, as they said of the relative adjective of *al-dahr* (time): *dahri*.

(He said) is also a resumptive explanatory clause, and the pronoun refers to Allah, may His name be exalted. ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers.﴾ This is a reply to his having shown courtesy in asking that some of his offspring be made prophets, just as it was granted with the specification of the kind of "some" that was left vague in his supplication, upon him be peace, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. It denies the ruling from one of two opposites while pointing to the evidence for its negation, so that this serves as evidence for the affirmation of the other. What comes first to mind from "covenant" is the imamate, and here it means nothing but prophethood. He expressed it with this term to indicate that it is a trust of Allah, the Exalted, and His covenant, which only those of His servants whom Allah wills can uphold. He chose "reaching" (*nayl*) rather than "making" (*ja'l*) as a hint that the imamate of the prophets among his offspring, upon them be peace, is not an independent appointment, but is included within his own imamate, reaching each of them at the time appointed for him. No deficiency results from this in the rank of the prophethood of our Prophet (ﷺ), because it works by way of *taghlib* (the dominant term standing for the group). Moreover, if such a thing diminished its rank, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have been addressed with Allah's words: ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Ibrahim﴾.

What comes first to mind from "wrongdoing" is disbelief, because it is the complete instance among its kinds. This is supported by Allah's words: ﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers﴾. Therefore the verse contains no proof of the infallibility of the prophets, upon them be peace, from major sins before their mission, nor that a wicked person is unfit for the caliphate. Yes, it does contain the cutting off of hopes of the disbelievers who used to wish for prophethood, and the closing of the doors of their vain aspirations to attain it. Some of the Shi'a have used it as evidence for denying the imamate of al-Siddiq and his two companions, may Allah be pleased with them, since they lived for a long period in polytheism, and ﴿Indeed, polytheism is a great wrong﴾, and by the explicit text of the verse, a wrongdoer does not attain the imamate. It has been answered that the most that follows is that a wrongdoer, while in the state of wrongdoing, does not attain it. The imamate was attained by them, may Allah be pleased with them, at the time of the perfection of their faith and the utmost of their uprightness. It has been objected that "of" (*min*) is partitive. So Ibrahim's request for the imamate is either for the upright part of his offspring during their lifetime, or for the wrongdoer during the period of the imamate, whether or not he is upright for the rest of his life, or for the one who is upright in some part and wrongdoing in another part, or for the more general category. On the first, the answer would not match the question. On the second, the Friend (Ibrahim) would be ignorant, and he is far above that. On the third, what is sought is achieved, and how fine that is. On the fourth, either what is sought is achieved, or there is corruption. You know that the basis of the argument is to read "covenant" as the more general category including the prophethood and the imamate they claim. Without establishing this, one is trying to pull up a thorn bush by its roots. The explicit statement of some scholars, such as al-Jassas, does not justify imposing it on all. And even on the supposition of conceding the point, it may be answered that we choose the view that the request for the imamate in its more general sense, for some indefinite part, does not require that the person be described as upright, and that wrongdoing at the time of the request is not relevant. The verse is a reply to his supplication with an addition beyond what we have pointed to. The same applies if the first alternative is chosen, and indeed the addition is itself an addition. It is also possible to answer by choosing the third alternative as well: we say that it is of two kinds. One is the person who was a wrongdoer before the imamate and who, at the time of the imamate, is upright in an absolute sense, having repented of his earlier injustices. At the time of the imamate he is described by absolute uprightness. The second is the person who was a wrongdoer before the imamate and who refrains from wrongdoing during it, but is not described by absolute uprightness because he has not repented. It is permissible that the request includes this second kind, and there is no harm in that, since the corruption that is the object of the request is brought about by this kind among the subjects. So the answer is the negation of the attainment of the imamate for this second kind. The two Shaykhs (Abu Bakr and 'Umar) and 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with them, are not of this kind. Rather they are at the highest ranks of the first kind, being described by sincere repentance, absolute uprightness and firm faith. The imam must necessarily be like this at the time of his imamate. Whoever disbelieved or wronged and then repented and reformed cannot properly be called a disbeliever or a wrongdoer in language, custom or law. For it has been established in the principles of jurisprudence that a derived term (*mushtaqq*) applied to what the root meaning currently subsists in is a literal use, and applied to what is other than that is a metaphorical use. Nor is the metaphorical use general, but it is used where it is customary; otherwise it would be permissible to call a child "old man" and a sleeper "awake," a rich man "poor," a hungry man "full," a living man "dead," and vice versa. Also, if it were general, it would follow that someone who swears not to greet a disbeliever, then greets a believing man at present, who had been a disbeliever many years before, would break his oath, and no one holds that. Moreover, some of our companions have taken the verse as evidence for the infallibility of the prophets from major sins before the mission, and that a wicked person is not fit for the caliphate. This is based on reading "covenant" as the imamate and making it general to include prophethood and the caliphate, and reading "wrongdoer" as one who has committed a sin that removes uprightness, on the basis that wrongdoing is the opposite of justice. The reasoning then is that the verse shows that attaining the imamate is incompatible with previous wrongdoing. So when attainment is realised, as with the prophets, it is known that they were not described by previous wrongdoing at the time of attainment. This is either because nothing that would require it proceeded from them, or because it was removed after occurring by repentance. No one holds the second, since the disagreement concerns whether committing a major sin is permissible before the mission. So the second is ruled out, and what is left is infallibility. Or the intended meaning here is the non-occurrence of sin, not the inherent quality. Likewise, when the description of wrongdoing is realised, as with the wicked person, it is known that the imamate is not attained for as long as he remains described by it. The derivation of the unfitness of a wicked person for the imamate, according to what we have established from the explicit text of the verse, is either as a matter of implication by equal weight, or by analogy requiring the claim of equality, and there is no less, or it is a comprehensive implication. These two are the basis of the 'Ayyuq (a star), and the only thing that calls for them is reading the imamate as prophethood. You already know that the foundation is reading it in the more general sense.

It was apparent that wrongdoing that arises later and wickedness that comes upon a person prevent the imamate in continuance, just as they prevent it from the beginning, since the incompatibility between the two qualities is established at every moment. This was the view of some of the early scholars (*salaf*). However, the majority hold otherwise, arguing that incompatibility at the beginning does not entail incompatibility in continuance, because removal is easier than lifting. They support this with the example that if a man says to a woman of unknown lineage, of the kind who is born to his kind, "This is my daughter," it is not lawful for him to marry her. But if he says this to his wife, who is described by it, the marriage is not thereby annulled; however, if he persists in it, the judge separates the two. What they have said is accepted only when the wrongdoing has not reached the level of disbelief. When it reaches that, it certainly contradicts the imamate in continuance too, without doubt, and the caliph is definitely deposed by it. Some people have used the verse as evidence that if a wrongdoer is made a covenant, fulfilling the covenant is not binding. This was supported by what is related from al-Hasan that he said: "Allah has not made a covenant for the wrongdoer." This is as you see. Abu al-Raja', Qatadah and al-A'mash read *al-zalimun* ("the wrongdoers") with a *raf'* (nominative), taking *'ahdi* ("my covenant") as a fronted object before the subject, for emphasis and out of regard for the verse-endings (*fawasil*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 125 (part 1 of 2):

﴿And when We made the House﴾ is coordinated with ﴿And when Abraham was tried﴾. "The House" (al-Bayt) is one of the names that have become dominant for the Ka'bah, like "the Star" (al-Najm) for the Pleiades (al-Thurayya). ﴿A place of return (mathabah) for the people﴾ means a gathering place for them. This was said by al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) and Qatadah. Or it means a refuge and a sanctuary (ma'adh wa-malja'), which was said by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Or it means a place to which the visitors return, or their counterparts, which was said by Mujahid and Jubayr. Or it means a place that deserves to be returned to and sought as a refuge, which was said by some of the scholars (muhaqqiqin). Or it means a place of reward, where they are rewarded for their Hajj and 'Umrah, which was said by 'Ata' and transmitted by al-Mawardi from some of the people of the language. The letter ta' (in mathabah) and its omission are two dialectal forms, as in maqam and maqamah. The ta' indicates the feminine of "the spot" (al-buq'ah). This is the view of al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Al-Akhfash said that the ta' in it is for emphasis (al-mubalaghah), as in nassabah ("genealogist") and 'allamah ("very learned"). Its original form is mathubah, on the pattern maf'alah, a mimi noun of action, or a noun of place. The lam in "the people" (al-nas) is for the genus, and this is the apparent meaning. It is also permissible to take it as referring to a known group or as the customary universal (al-istighraq al-'urfi). Al-A'mash and Talhah read mathabat in the plural, because it is a place of return for each one of the people, and none of them is exclusive to it.

﴿Equal for the one who stays there and the one who comes from outside﴾. Although it is singular in essence, it is plural in terms of its relations (al-idafat). It was also said that the plural is due to treating the multiplicity of the returns as the multiplicity of the place, or on the basis that each part of it is a mathabah. Some scholars preferred this, thinking that the first view implies that it would be correct to describe a group's slave as "the slaves," which is not known. In response: this is an analogy with a difference, because the slave has an attribution of slavery to all of them collectively, not to each one of them individually.

﴿And a sanctuary (amnan)﴾ is coordinated with ﴿a place of return﴾. It is a verbal noun (masdar) described with it for emphasis. The intended meaning is a place of security, either for its inhabitants from being snatched away, or for its visitors from punishment, since Hajj removes and erases what came before it, except the rights of people and financial rights, such as expiation (kaffarah), according to the sound view. Or it means a place of security for the offender who takes refuge in it from being killed. This is the view of Imam Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, since according to him retaliatory punishment for life (qisas al-nafs) is not carried out in the Haram, but the offender is restricted, not spoken to, not fed, not dealt with, until he leaves and is then killed. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, whoever is liable to the prescribed punishment (hadd) and takes refuge in it, the ruler orders that he be restricted in a way that leads to his leaving. When he leaves, the prescribed punishment is carried out on him outside the Haram. If he does not leave, it is permitted to kill him inside it. According to Imam Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him, no retaliation is carried out against one who takes refuge in it, in any case, even retaliation for injuries to limbs, until he leaves.

Some people took amnan as a second object of an omitted verb in the sense of a command, meaning "and make it a sanctuary," just as We made it a place of return. This is far from the apparent sense of the wording. The word "people" is not mentioned here as it was mentioned before, either because it has already been mentioned, or to indicate generality, meaning that it is a sanctuary for everything, whatever it may be, even birds and wild animals, except the five harmful creatures (al-khamsah al-fawasiq), which were excluded from this by the word of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The security of people is included in it as a primary inclusion.

﴿And take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer (musalla)﴾ is coordinated with ﴿We made﴾, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from its agent (fa'il), with the intention of speech, meaning "and We said," or "saying to them: take." The one commanded is the people, as is apparent, or it is Abraham, peace be upon him, and his descendants, as has been said. Or it is coordinated with the omitted "remember" that is the governing verb of idh. Or it is coordinated with a hidden element whose estimated form is: "return to it, and take." This is parenthetical in terms of its substitution for that, between ﴿We made﴾ and ﴿We covenanted﴾. The parenthetical was not considered without coordination, although it is not needed, so that the connection with the preceding sentence would be clearer. On these two interpretations, the address is to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and he (ﷺ) is the head of those addressed.

The word "from" (min) is either partitive, or in the sense of "in," or extra according to the view of al-Akhfash. The more apparent is the first. Al-Qaffal said: it is like "I took from so-and-so a friend," and "Allah gave me from so-and-so a righteous brother." It introduces the explanation and distinction of what was taken as a gift.

Maqam is a noun of place from qiyam (standing), and it is intended as the place where he stood. It is the stone on which Abraham, peace be upon him, stood when he became weak from lifting the stones that his son Ishmael handed him while building the House. In it are the marks of his two feet. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Jabir, Qatadah and others. Al-Bukhari transmitted it, and it is the view of the majority of the exegetes (jumhur al-mufassirin). It was transmitted from al-Hasan that it is the stone that the wife of Ishmael, peace be upon him, placed under one of his feet while he was riding. She washed one side of his head, then lifted it from beneath, and it had sunk into the stone. She placed it under his other foot, and washed his other side, and his other foot also sank into it. Or it is the place where the stone was when he stood on it, called the people to Hajj, and raised the building of the House, and that is its place today. So maqam, in one of the two meanings, is a literal linguistic meaning, and in the other it is a conventional metaphor. It is permissible to apply the word to either of them, so they said.

However, specifying the place as the spot where it is today has been questioned, because of what is in Fath al-Bari, that the maqam, that is the stone, was from the time of Abraham, peace be upon him, adjacent to the House until 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, moved it to the place where it is now. 'Abd al-Razzaq transmitted this with a strong chain. Ibn Mardawayh transmitted with a weak chain, from Mujahid, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the one who moved it. This indicates that the two places are different, whether the one who moved it was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. Also, how is it possible to raise the building while standing on it, when it is in its place today? It is twenty-seven cubits far from the Black Stone.

Also, it is well known that the call of the people to Hajj was from above Abu Qubays, since he climbed it after finishing the construction of the House and called out: "O people, make Hajj to the House of your Lord." If the stone was not with him at that time, it is problematic to say that he stood on it and called. If it was with him, and standing on it was above the mountain, as the words of Rawdat al-Ahbab indicate, and by this the harmonization is achieved, the identification with what is there today becomes problematic. The best way to reconcile this is to say: there is no doubt that he, peace be upon him, used to move the stone during the building from one place to another and stand on it, so it did not have a fixed place. Likewise, at the time of the call, it was not beside the House, but above Abu Qubays. So the statements must be interpreted away from their apparent meaning, by saying: the place where that stone was during the time he stood on it and was occupied with the call, or with raising the building, not at the time of standing on it.

It has been stated in some books that this maqam, in which the stone is now, was the house of Abraham, peace be upon him, and that he used to move this stone to it after finishing the work. The stone after Abraham was placed inside the Ka'bah. Perhaps this is the reason for specifying this place for the moving. What occurs in Fath al-Bari, that the maqam was from the time of Abraham adjacent to the House, means after the completion of the construction. So it does not contradict that during its construction it was in the place where it is today. This was mentioned by some of the scholars (muhaqqiqin), so let it be understood.

The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) is what Abu Nu'aym transmitted from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, that the Prophet (ﷺ) took the hand of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "O 'Umar, this is the station of Abraham." 'Umar said: "Shall we not take it as a place of prayer?" He said: "I have not been commanded with that." Before the sun had set, this verse was revealed.

The command in it is for recommendation (istihbab), since the immediate understanding of musalla is a place of prayer in general. It was said: what is meant by it is the command to perform the two rak'ahs of tawaf, because Muslim transmitted from Jabir that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished his tawaf, he went to the station of Abraham and prayed two rak'ahs behind it, and recited this verse. Thus the command is for obligation according to some views. But its weakness is not hidden, because it restricts it to a particular prayer without evidence. His recitation of the verse, peace and blessings be upon him, while performing the two rak'ahs does not require restricting it to them.

Al-Nakha'i and Mujahid held that what is meant by the station of Abraham is the whole Haram. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ata' held that it is all the stations of Hajj. Al-Sha'bi held that it is 'Arafah, Muzdalifah and the stoning places (al-jimar). The meaning of taking it as a place of prayer is that one supplicates in it and draws near to Allah Most High at it. What the majority hold, which is what we presented first, is the one that agrees with the apparent meaning of the wording, with the custom of people today, and the apparent sense of the reports supports it.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿and they took﴾ (wa-ittakhadhu) with a fatha on the kha', as a past tense verb. In that case it is coordinated with "We made." That is, "and the people took from the place of Abraham, by which he became known, and where he settled his offspring, which is the Ka'bah, as a qiblah toward which they pray." The station is then a metaphor for that place, and likewise the musalla in the sense of qiblah is a metaphor for the place one faces in prayer, by the relation of nearness and adjacency.

﴿And We covenanted with Abraham and Ishmael﴾, meaning: We charged, or commanded, or revealed, or said. What the verifiers (muhaqqiqun) hold is that when 'ahida is followed by ila, it means "to charge," and it is used figuratively for "to command." Ishmael is a non-Arabic proper name. It was said that its meaning in Arabic is "obedient to Allah." It is related that Abraham, peace be upon him, used to pray that Allah would grant him a child and say: "Ism'a Il," meaning "answer my supplication, O Allah." When Allah granted him that, he named him with that phrase. I consider this far-fetched. The Arabs have two forms of it, with lam and with nun.

﴿That purify My House﴾, meaning: by purifying, with "that" being a verbal (masdariyyah) particle. It is joined to the imperative verb as an explanation of the thing commanded. Sibawayh and Abu 'Ali permitted the complement of the verbal particles to be a command or prohibition. The majority forbade this, arguing that when a verbal noun is formed from it, the meaning of the command is lost, and that the complement of the relative pronoun must be declarative, and the particle-relative is like it. Here they estimated "We said," so that what follows the verbal particle would be a predicate. This is objected to first: that its being with the verb in the sense of a verbal noun does not require that their meanings be identical, since a verbal noun does not indicate time while the verb does. Second: the requirement that the complement of a nominal relative be declarative is only so that descriptive phrases can be attached to definites by sentences, and these can only be attached if they are declarative. As for the particle-relative, it is not like this. Third: estimating "We said" leads to the command being speech, and that is not the case. It was also permitted for this "that" to be explanatory, because a phrase containing the meaning of speech without its letters has preceded it, namely the covenant. In that case it is necessary to estimate the object, since with the preceding element mentioned it is required that what follows the explanatory particle explain an estimated or spoken object, meaning: "We said to them something, which is: purify." The purification intended is cleansing from everything that is not suitable, so it includes idols, impurities, all filth, and what is forbidden by the law, such as a menstruating woman. Mujahid, Ibn 'Ata', Muqatil and Ibn Jubayr restricted purification to the removal of idols. They mentioned that the House was inhabited in the time of Noah, peace be upon him, and that there were idols in it in the forms of its righteous people, and that it lasted...

Page 381

The command was directed at them because the House had been worshipped besides Allah, so Allah commanded that it be purified of that. It has also been said that the meaning is: purify it, clean it, and make it [free of] filth, and remove from it the dung and blood that used to be thrown into it. It has also been said that the meaning is: make it sincere for those mentioned, such that no one other than them approaches it. Thus "purification" is an expression for its necessary implication. It is related from al-Suddi that the meaning is building and establishing it upon purity and monotheism, but this is far-fetched. Directing the command here to Abraham and Isma'il does not conflict with what is in Surat al-Hajj regarding its being specific to Abraham (peace be upon him), for that occurred before the building of the House, as indicated by the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿And [remember] when We settled Abraham at the site of the House﴾. At that time Isma'il was far from being addressed, and it is evident that this [command] came after he reached the stage of commanding and forbidding and after the building was completed through his own direct involvement, as indicated by its mention right after the account of Our making it a place of return. The attribution of "House" to the Divine Name is for honour, like "the she-camel of Allah," and not that it is a place for Him, exalted is He far above that with great exaltation. ﴿For those who circumambulate﴾, meaning for their sake, so the lam is causal (ta'liliyyah). If purification is interpreted by its implication, then it is connected to it (as a complement). The tha'if is an active participle from tafa bihi, meaning he circled around it. The apparent meaning is that it refers to everyone who circumambulates, whether a resident or a nomad, and this is the view of 'Ata' and others. Ibn Jubayr said: it refers to the strangers who come to Makkah as pilgrims and visitors.
﴿And those who remain in devotion﴾, and they are the people of the Sacred Land who reside there, according to Ibn Jubayr. 'Ata' said: they are those who sit without circumambulating, whether local or foreign. Mujahid said: they are the foreigners who stay near it as neighbours. It has also been said: they are those who perform i'tikaf (retreat for worship) in it. ﴿And those who bow and prostrate﴾, and they are those who pray, the plural of rakic (one who bows) and sajid (one who prostrates). Bowing and prostration were singled out for mention from among all the states of the worshipper, because they are the closest states of his to Allah, Exalted, and they are the two greatest pillars [of prayer]. The prayer is often referred to by them, and for this reason the conjunction between them was omitted. He did not say "the worshippers" even though that is more concise, to indicate that what is considered is prayer possessing bowing and prostration, not the prayer of the Jews. He placed bowing first because it precedes in time. Both were given in the broken plural (jam' taksir) because the form of the singular changes, and in contrast to the preceding sound plurals (jam' salamah), and in that there is a variety in eloquence. He varied the patterns of their broken plurals for variety, along with the difference in forms. The last of them is in the pattern fu'ul, for the sake of its being a fasilah (verse-ending rhyme). The verse-endings before and after its last letter have a letter preceded by a letter of prolongation (madd) and softness (layn).

[p. 382]

**"And when Abraham said, 'My Lord, make this a secure city'"** (2:126). The reference of "this" is the valley mentioned in His saying: **"Our Lord, I have settled some of my offspring in a valley without cultivation, by Your Sacred House"** (14:37). The meaning is: make this barren place a city, and so on. So what is requested is urbanity (*baladiyyah*) together with security. This differs from what appears in Surah Ibrahim: **"My Lord, make this city secure"** (14:35). Perhaps the request was repeated, and what occurs in that surah came later. The security requested there is either the first (the same security), and he repeated his request without the urbanity, desiring its continuance because it is the primary aim, or because it is customary for urbanity to continue once it has been achieved, unlike the other. Or the request there is something other than this: the security first requested was merely the security that makes settlement valid, and the second was the security already known. You may also take "this city" in that surah as a reference to something conceived in the mind, as indicated by **"Our Lord, I have settled..."** and so on. Then the two supplications correspond. If, however, the reference here is taken to be the city, the supplication comes after it has become a city, and what is sought is that it be secure in accordance with what is stated in the surah, without strain. Yet this conveys emphasis, meaning: a city complete in security, as if it were said: make it a city known for being secure and famous for it, like your saying: "This day was a hot day."

The description "secure" (*āmin*) is either in the sense of a relative adjective (*nisbah*), meaning possessing security, following the manner said of **"a pleasing life"** (69:21), or it is by extension (*ittisā'*) and metaphorical attribution (*isnād majāzī*). The original would be "its people secure," so what belongs to the state is attributed to the place, because security and fear are attributes of beings possessed of perception.

Is the supplication that He make it secure from tyrants and domineering rulers, or that its sanctuary not become lawful (to violate), or that it not be emptied of its people, or from being swallowed or struck (by disasters), or from drought and barrenness, or from the entry of the Dajjal (Antichrist), or from the entry of the People of the Elephant? There are opinions, and the actual event refutes some of them, for tyrants did enter it and shed blood in it, such as Amr ibn Luhayy al-Jurhumi, al-Hajjaj al-Thaqafi, the Qaramita, and others. That some did not enter it for destruction, but had some other purpose, yields no benefit, as with the saying that no tyrant harmed its people except that God Most High crushed him. Hence the proverb:

*"If I die thirsty, may no rain fall."*

The address with the word "Lord" (*Rabb*) was joined (to the request) because of the gentleness it contains in the petition, and because of the description that indicates the acceptance of the petitioner and the answering of his entreaty. We have already pointed out earlier what benefits you here, so reflect upon it.

**"And provide its people with fruits"** (2:126). That is, with varieties of them, either by making villages near it where such things are produced, or by bringing them to it from distant regions. Both have occurred, so that fruits of the spring, summer and autumn gather in it on a single day. It is related that when Abraham made this supplication, God, glorified be He, commanded Jibril (Gabriel) who uprooted a piece of land from Palestine, and it is said from the Jordan, and circumambulated it seven times around the House, then placed it where he placed it as provision for the Sanctuary. This is the land known today as al-Ta'if, and it was named after that circumambulation. This, if its authenticity is granted, is not far from the power of the Sovereign, the Powerful, may His majesty be exalted. And if you refuse to keep it on its apparent meaning, the door of interpretation is wide. The plural of paucity (*jam' al-qillah*) is used to show contentment, and we have pointed out that it often stands in place of the plural of abundance. The particle "min" (some of) is partitive, and it is said it is explanatory of kind (*li-bayān al-jins*).

**"Whoever of them believes in God and the Last Day"** is a partitive substitute (*badal al-ba'd*) for "its people." It specifies what the substituted term indicates. Regarding the object of belief, only the origin (God) and the return (the Last Day) are mentioned, because belief in these two includes belief in everything that must be believed. He (God) said: that is, God, Most High, said: **"And whoever disbelieves"** is conjoined to "whoever believes," meaning: and provide also for whoever disbelieves. So the imperative here has the sense of a declarative, in reverse. **"Some of my offspring"**. The purpose of this transition is to teach the generality of the supplication for provision, and that one should not restrict oneself in asking for kindness. Abraham, peace be upon him, had analogized provision to the imamate (leadership), so God, glorified be He, alerted him that provision is a worldly mercy not restricted to the believer, unlike the imamate. Alternatively, when he, peace be upon him, heard **"My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers"** (2:124) and so on, he refrained from supplicating for one not pleasing to God, Most High, so He directed him to His all-encompassing generosity. By what we have mentioned, the objection raised in *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*, the Ocean, by Abu Hayyan) is answered: that this conjunction is not valid because it requires sharing the governing element, so that it would become "Abraham said: provide in it what follows." You may also take the conjunction as being upon an elided element, meaning: provide for whoever believes and whoever disbelieves, in the form of a declarative. Whoever does not hold to the conjunction of instruction (*'atf al-talqīn*, the conjunction by which an unexpressed word is supplied for the listener) requires this. It is permissible that "man" (whoever) be a conditional subject (*mubtada' shartiyyah*) or a relative (*mawsūlah*). **"Then I will grant him enjoyment for a little"** (2:126): on the first (conditional) reading, it is conjoined to "disbelieves." On the second (relative) reading, it is the predicate of the subject. The particle "fa" (then) is used because the subject contains the sense of a condition. There is no need to supply "I" (*anā*), because Ibn al-Hajib stated that the present tense in the apodosis may be connected with "fa," unless it is an exception to the rule (*istiḥsān*). Al-Mubarrad held the view that no supply is needed, while Sibawayh's position is that supply is obligatory. It is supported by the argument that the present tense is by itself apt for the apodosis, so had it not been the predicate of a subject, "fa" would not have entered upon it. Moreover, although disbelief is not the cause of enjoyment in the absolute sense, it is apt to be the cause of its diminution, and its being joined with the torment of the Fire. "A little" (*qalīlan*) is a qualifier of an elided noun, meaning: a little enjoyment, or a little time.

Ibn Amir read *fa-umtiʿuhu* (with the causative form), in the declarative and lightened; and likewise Yahya ibn Wathhab, except that he read the hamza with a kasra. Ubayy read *fa-numattiʿuhu* with a nun. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid read *fa-amtiʿhu* in the imperative form. On this reading, it is necessary that the pronoun in "said" (*qāla*) refer to Abraham. The repetition of "said" is made good by the length of the speech, and by his transition from supplicating for one group to supplicating against others, as if he had begun another speech. That its pronoun refers to God, Most High, meaning God said: "Then grant him enjoyment, O Powerful, O Provider," addressing Himself by way of abstraction (*tajrīd*), is very far-fetched and should not be given attention.

**"Then I will compel him to the torment of the Fire"** (2:126). *Iḍṭirār* (compulsion) is the opposite of *ikhtiyār* (choice). It is literally the state in which an act proceeds from a person without his will being attached to it, as when someone is thrown from a roof, for example. It is metaphorically the state in which the act is by his choice, but in such a way that he cannot refrain from it, because an external factor coerces him into his choice, as when someone eats carrion in a state of famine. Some have held both meanings. The first is supported by God's saying: **"On the Day they will be pushed into the Fire of Hell with a violent pushing"** (52:13), **"They will be dragged through the Fire upon their faces"** (54:48), and **"They will be seized by their forelocks and feet"** (55:41). The second is supported by God's saying: **"Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups, until, when they reach it, its gates will be opened"** (39:71), **"There is not one of you who will not pass over it"** (19:71), and **"Indeed you and what you worship besides God are the fuel of Hell; you will come to it"** (21:98). The verification is that the states of the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, at their entry into the Fire, are varied, and by this the verses are reconciled. The compulsion is a metaphor for the torment being inflicted upon him in a definite manner, so that it seems to be bound to him. It has been said that this compulsion is in this world, and it too is metaphorical, as if the state of the disbeliever to whom God granted a bounty by which He gave him a little respite, and then led him toward what destroys him, is likened to one who cannot refrain from what he is compelled to. So the same term is used for the likened as for the likeness. This is a fine statement, except that it requires taking "then" (*thumma*) as indicating a sequence of rank rather than of time, which is contrary to the apparent sense.

Ibn Amir read *iḍṭurruhu* with a kasra on the hamza. Yazid ibn Abi Habib read *aḍṭurruhu* with a damma on the ṭā'. Ubayy read *naḍṭurruhu* with a nun. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid read it in the imperative form. Ibn Muhaysin read *aṭṭurruhu*, with the ḍād assimilated into the ṭā', in the declarative. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is a despised dialect, because the letters of the mnemonic *ḍamma shafar* (the letters ḍ, sh, f, r, which are assimilated into what neighbours them, but not the reverse) are assimilated into what adjoins them, and not vice versa. In reply: these letters have been assimilated into others. Abu Amr assimilated the rā' into the lām in **"We will forgive you"** (71:4), the ḍād into the shīn in **"for some of their affairs"** (24:62), and the shīn into the sīn in **"a way to the Throne"** (17:42). Al-Kisa'i assimilated the fā' into the bā' in **"We will cause the earth to swallow them"** (34:9). Sibawayh related from the Arabs that they said *muḍṭajiʿun* and *muṭṭajiʿun* (reclining). However, non-assimilation is more common. The original root of *iḍṭarra*, according to what is said, is *iḍtarra*, then the tā' was changed into ṭā' and assimilation occurred.

**"And wretched is the destination"** (2:126). The element particularized by the dispraise is elided, being understood from the meaning: and wretched is the destination, the Fire, if *maṣīr* is a noun of place. If it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), according to those who permit that, the meaning is: and wretched is the becoming, its becoming to the torment.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 127:**

﴿And when Abraham was raising﴾ is conjoined to ﴿and when Abraham said﴾. The particle *idh* here refers to the past. He used the present tense (*mudari'*) although the story is in the past, in order to bring this matter vividly before the mind, so that people may follow his example in performing arduous acts of worship while earnestly beseeching God for their acceptance, and so that they may know the greatness of the House that was built and thus honour it. ﴿The foundations of the House﴾: *al-qawa'id* is the plural of *qa'idah*, which means foundation (*asas*), as Abu 'Ubayda stated. It is an adjective that by long usage became like a rigid noun, such that no modified noun is mentioned with it and none is assumed. It derives from *al-qu'ud* in the sense of steadfastness, and perhaps it is a figurative usage (*majaz*) from its opposite, *al-qiyam* (standing). From this comes the supplication *qa''adaka Allah ta'ala*, meaning "may God Most High keep you enduring and steadfast." On this meaning, the raising of the foundations is a figurative expression for building upon them, since the apparent sense of raising a thing is making it high and elevated, whereas a foundation does not rise but remains in its own state. However, its state before building upon it was one of lowness, and when it was built upon it moved to a state of elevation, in the sense that together with what is built upon it, that state came to it, so that building upon it became a cause of the attainment of that state, like raising. Thus the word "raising" was used for building upon it, and from this was derived *yarfa'u* in the sense of "builds upon them." It was also said: the *qawa'id* are the supports of the building, and every support is a foundation for what is above it; so the meaning of raising them on this view is the building of the supports themselves, and the reason for the plural in this case is clear. On the first view, the plural is because the House is quadrangular and every wall has a foundation. This view has been judged weak because it diverts the word *qawa'id* from its evident meaning, whereas the diversion of *raising* in the first view is not of this kind. It was also said: *raising* means elevation and nobility, and *qawa'id* carries its original literal meaning; on this view it is a metaphorical analogy (*isti'arah tamthiliyyah*), but this is remote, since on it there would be no evident benefit in mentioning the foundations. ﴿From the House﴾ (*min*) is an initial particle (indicating origin) and is connected to *yarfa'u*, or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) describing *al-qawa'id*. He did not say "the foundations of the House" because of the attention conveyed by vagueness followed by specification, which indicates exaltation, as is not hidden.

﴿And Isma'il﴾ is conjoined to Abraham. The placing of his name after the object, which is posterior to it in rank, indicates that his role in raising the building and in the work was not equal to that of Abraham, peace be upon him. It is related that he used to hand him the stones. It was also said that they built at two ends, or alternately. Some have gone further astray and claimed that Isma'il is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is omitted, meaning: he says, "Our Lord." This is an inclination toward the view that Abraham, peace be upon him, alone undertook the building, with no role for Isma'il in it at all, based on what is reported from 'Ali, may God ennoble his face, that he was then a small child. The correct view is that this report is not authentic. Here the people of reports have mentioned matters concerning the essence of this House, its antiquity and its origination, from what it was made, what its two doors were, how many times Adam performed pilgrimage to it, from what material Abraham built it, who assisted him in building it, and from where he brought the Black Stone. These are matters that neither the Mighty Qur'an nor the sound Hadith includes, and some of them contradict others. This is in accordance with their habit of transmitting whatever circulates and spreads. Among the well-known reports is that the Ka'bah was sent down from heaven in the time of Adam, and it had two doors, one to the east and one to the west. Adam performed pilgrimage from the land of India, and the angels met him forty farsakhs away; he circumambulated the House and entered it. Then it was raised up in the time of Noah's flood to heaven, and then it was sent down again in the time of Abraham, who visited it, raised its foundations, and made its two doors into one door. Then Mount Abu Qubays split open and the Black Stone emerged from it; it had been a white ruby from the jewels of Paradise, which Gabriel had brought down, and it had been hidden during the time of the flood until the time of Abraham, who placed it in its position. Then it turned black through the touching of menstruating women. If this report and similar ones are sound, then for those among the people of God Most High they are indications and symbols for one who gives ear while he is a witness. Thus its descent in the time of Adam, peace be upon him, is an indication of the manifestation of the world of origin and return, and of knowledge of the world of light and the world of darkness in his time, apart from the world of unity. His intention to visit it from the land of India is an indication of his turning, through generation and moderation, from the dark corporeal natural world to the station of the heart. The angels' meeting him is an indication of the attachment of the vegetative and animal faculties to the body, and the appearance of their effects in it before the effects of the heart, during the forty days in which his structure was formed and his clay was leavened. Or it indicates his turning, by travel and spiritual journey (*suluk*), from the shadowy world of the soul to the station of the heart, and the angels' meeting him indicates the reception by the psychic and bodily faculties of him, by accepting good manners, noble character, virtuous dispositions, and by training and progressing through the stations before his arrival at the station of the heart. His circumambulation of the House is an indication of his arrival at the station of the heart and his conduct within it with variation of states (*talwin*). His entering it is an indication of his establishment and steadfastness in it. His being raised to heaven in the time of the flood is an indication of people being veiled from the station of the heart by the dominance of desire and the flood of ignorance in the time of Noah. Its remaining in heaven until the Frequented House, which is the heart of the world, and its descent again in the time of Abraham is an indication of people being guided in his time to the station of the heart through his guidance. Abraham's raising of its foundations and making it one with one door is an indication of the heart's ascent to the station of unity, for he was the first to manifest essential unity, which is referred to in God Most High's words, quoted from him: ﴿I have turned my face toward Him who originated the heavens and the earth, as a monotheist, and I am not of those who associate others with God﴾.
