The Black Stone is an indication of the Spirit, which is the command of God, exalted be His majesty, and His right hand, and the locus of His secret. The splitting of Mount Abu Qubays and its emergence from it is an indication of its manifestation through spiritual discipline and the movement of the bodily faculties in using them for reflection and worship in seeking its manifestation. For this reason it was said: it was hidden, i.e., veiled by the body. Its blackening through the touching of menstruating women is an indication of its being clouded by the dominance of the psychic faculties over the heart, and their gaining control over it and blackening the luminous face that is adjacent to the Spirit from it.

And if the sandgrouse were left at night, it would sleep.

﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾, i.e., they both say, "Our Lord." Ubayy also read it this way. The clause is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of the subject of *yarfa'u*. It was also said: it is conjoined to what precedes it, by making the saying dependent on *idh*. Acceptance (*taqabbul*) is a figurative usage (*majaz*) for reward and good pleasure, because every deed that God Most High accepts is one for which He rewards its doer and is pleased with him for it. In asking for reward for the deed there is evidence that its being rewarded is not obligatory, for otherwise it would not be requested. In choosing the form *tafa''ul* there is an acknowledgment of deficiency, because it carries the implication of effort in acceptance, although acceptance and receiving are equal in relation to Him, for it is not possible to conceive of effort with respect to Him, exalted be His majesty. It is possible that by acceptance is meant only good pleasure, not reward, because the utmost that sincere servants aim for is that their actions be placed in a position of acceptance and good pleasure before their master, and reward does not occur to their minds. Perhaps this is the most fitting for the state of the Friend (Abraham) and his son Isma'il, peace be upon them both. ﴿Indeed You, You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is a justification for the request for acceptance. What is meant is: the All-Hearing of our supplication and the All-Knowing of our intentions. With this, the restriction derived from the definition of the two predicates is valid, and it implies negation of ostentation and show in the supplication and the deed, which is a condition of acceptance. The emphasis of the sentence is to show the perfection of the strength of their certainty regarding its content. The placing first of the attribute of hearing, although the request for acceptance comes after the deed, is for the sake of proximity, and because hearing is not like knowledge in comprehensiveness.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 128:

﴿Our Lord, and make us two submitting to You﴾. That is, two who are compliant and who uphold the laws of Islam, or two who are sincere and who affirm Your oneness. The word "muslimayn" (two who submit) is derived either from "istaslama" (to submit, to comply) when one complies, or from "aslama wajhahu" (to devote oneself) when one makes one's self or one's intention sincere. Each of the two meanings has broad scope. So what is intended is a request for an increase in both, or for steadfastness in both. The first is preferable in view of their rank, although the second is preferable in view of its being more complete in displaying attachment to Him, may His majesty be exalted. Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, read "Muslimin" (in the plural form), meaning that what is intended is themselves and those who existed of their family, like Hajar. This is preferable to taking the plural form to mean the dual, although that has been said here. ﴿And of our offspring﴾ is coordinated with the pronoun in the verb "make us" (ij'alna), which is in the position of the first object. ﴿A community submitting to You﴾ is in the position of the second object, coordinated with ﴿two submitting to You﴾. If the omission of the verb "make" (ij'al) is considered, then it must be understood in the sense of "making" (taslil, rendering something into a state), not "creating" (ijad, bringing into existence), because although the latter is valid in terms of meaning, the former does not indicate it. They singled out the offspring for the supplication because they have a greater claim to compassion, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾. And because they are the children of prophets, and with their righteousness comes the righteousness of all people, so concern for their righteousness was greater. They singled out a part because of what they knew from His words, glorified be He: ﴿And of their offspring is one who does good and one who wrongs himself﴾, or from His words, mighty is His majesty: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾. By the context, it is understood that among their offspring are wrongdoers. And the divine wisdom requires diversity, for without it the spheres of the names would not revolve, nor would what exists among the angels of heaven have come to be. "Ummah" (community) means a group, or a generation. Some restricted it to the community of Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the indefiniteness (of the word) was taken to be for specification. This was supported by His words, "And send forth" (wab'ath), etc. It is not hidden that this is diverting the word from its apparent meaning and using as evidence something that does not indicate it. Abu al-Baqa permitted that "ummah" be the first object, with ﴿of our offspring﴾ as a circumstantial phrase (hal), because it is a modifier of an indefinite noun placed before it, and ﴿submitting﴾ (muslimah) be the second object. The original would be: "and make a community from our offspring submitting to You." So the conjunction (waw) enters originally before "ummah," and it has been separated from it by the prepositional phrase. According to some of them, "min" ("of") in this case is explanatory, in the manner of ﴿Allah has promised those of you who believe﴾. Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying that Abu Ali and others forbade separating the conjunction particle from the conjoined word by an adverbial phrase, and separation by a circumstantial phrase is even more remote than separation by an adverbial phrase. They considered what has been transmitted of that to be a poetic necessity. Also, that "min" being explanatory is something the scholars reject, and they interpret what seems to be indicated by its apparent meaning. It is not hidden that the matter is disputed, and what he mentioned is the view of some, which does not constitute proof against the others. ﴿And show us our rites﴾. Qatadah said: the landmarks of the pilgrimage. Ata' and Jurayj said: the places of sacrifice. It has been said: our actions which we perform when we make the pilgrimage. So "manasik" with a fatha on the sin is the place or the act, and with a kasra is anomalous. It is either a verbal noun or a place noun. The root "nusuk," with two dammas, means the utmost degree of worship, and it became common for the pilgrimage, because of the hardship it generally involves and its departure from habit. "Arina" (show us) is from "ra'a" in the sense of seeing with the eye, and because of the causative prefix of the verb it takes two objects. Or it is from "ra'a" in the sense of the heart, meaning "to know" (arafa), not "to know" (alima), for otherwise it would take three objects. Ibn al-Hajib denied, and Abu Hayyan followed him, the existence of "ra'a" in the sense of "arafa." Al-Zamakhshari mentioned it in al-Mufassal, and al-Raghib in his Mufradat (Vocabulary of the Qur'an). Page 386 They are both among the trustworthy scholars, so their denial carries no weight. Ibn Mas'ud read "wa-arihim manasikahum" (and show them their rites), by returning the pronoun to the offspring. Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read "wa-arna" (and show us) with a sukun on the letter "ra'". The separate pronoun has been treated like the attached pronoun, so it was given the same treatment as "fakhudh" (so take), in its being made quiescent for lightness. The Arabs have used it in this way, and from it is his saying:

"Show us the water-skin of Abd Allah, we shall fill it from the water of Zamzam, for indeed the people have become thirsty."

As for al-Zamakhshari's statement that this reading has been regarded as inferior, because the kasra is transferred from the dropped hamzah that indicates it, so dropping it is excessive in a way that is not fitting, because the reading is among the mutawatir (the widely transmitted readings), and similar things are also found in the speech of the pure Arabs. ﴿And accept our repentance﴾. That is: grant us success in repentance (tawbah, turning back to Allah), or accept it from us. Repentance differs according to the differences of those who repent. The repentance of ordinary Muslims is remorse, the resolve not to return to sin, the restoration of wrongful gains where possible, and the intention to restore them where not possible. The repentance of the elite is turning away from disliked things, from evil thoughts, from slackness in deeds, and from performing worship without perfection. The repentance of the elite of the elite is for the raising of ranks and advancement in stations. If Ibrahim and Isma'il, peace be upon them both, sought repentance for themselves alone, then what is intended by it is what belongs to the last category. If the pronoun included both of them and their offspring, the supplication for it applies to those among them who may commit a sin that undermines the rank of prophethood. If it is said that the request is for the offspring only, and the figure of speech is employed in the attribution by treating the child as the self, through the relation of part to whole, so as to be closer to being answered, or in the term by naming the branch with the name of the root, or it is said that a noun has been omitted, meaning "our disobedient ones," the problem is resolved. As when we say that this concerns minor sins that slipped from them through forgetfulness. The view that they did not truly intend the request, but mentioned it to legislate and to teach people that those places are places of disclaiming and seeking repentance from sins, is very far-fetched. Making the request a matter of confirmation, which I do not think is beneficial here, does not help, as is not hidden. Abdullah read "wa-tub alayhim" (and accept their repentance), also with the third-person plural pronoun. ﴿Indeed You are the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾. This is a reason for the supplication and an added urging for it to be answered. The repentance is mentioned first for its proximity to the preceding matter, and the mercy is delayed for its generality, and because it fits better with the rhyme endings.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 129:

﴿Our Lord, and raise up among them﴾ i.e., send within the Muslim community. It has also been said: among their offspring (dhurriyyah). The return of the pronoun to the people of Makkah is remote. ﴿a messenger from among them﴾, i.e., from among themselves. Describing him thus is so that he would be more compassionate toward them, that they would be more honored and exalted through him, and closer to being answered, because they know his origin, his truthfulness, and his trustworthiness. None was raised from the offspring of both of them except Muhammad (ﷺ). All the prophets of the Children of Israel are from the offspring of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), not from the offspring of both of them. Thus he is the one through whom their supplication was answered, as Imam Ahmad and Sharh al-Sunnah narrated from al-Irbad, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: «(I will inform you of the beginning of my affair: I am the supplication of Ibrahim, the glad tidings of Isa, and the vision of my mother, which she saw when she gave birth to me).» By this, the Prophet (ﷺ) meant the effect of his supplication, or the one supplicated for, or the very essence of his supplication, as an exaggeration. Since Isma'il (peace be upon him) was a partner in the supplication, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was also the supplication of Isma'il, except that he specified Ibrahim for his nobility and because he was the origin of the supplication. Whoever said that the limitation in the hadith to Ibrahim indicates that what was answered of the two supplications was the supplication of Ibrahim alone, excluding Isma'il (peace be upon them both), was mistaken. Ubayy recited (and raise up among them, in their last, a messenger), and this supports that what is meant is our Prophet. It is reported in a narration that when Ibrahim supplicated, it was said to him: "It has been answered for you," and that is at the end of time.

﴿who recites to them Your verses﴾, i.e., reads to them what You reveal to him of the signs indicating Tawhid, prophethood, and other things.
Page 387
It has also been said: it is the report of those who passed and those who will come until the Day of Resurrection. The clause is a description of (a messenger), and it has been said that it is in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal) from him.

﴿and teaches them the Book﴾, by making them understand its wording, explaining to them the manner of its recitation, and making them comprehend its realities and secrets.

It is apparent that their intent from this supplication is that the Messenger should be a bearer of a Book that brings them out of the darkness of ignorance into the light of knowledge. And Allah, glorified is He, answered this supplication with the Qur'an. That the Qur'an specifically was what was supplicated for is not clear, nor is it explicit.

﴿and wisdom﴾, i.e., the placing of things in their proper places, or that which removes from hearts the blaze of love of this world, or understanding of the religion, or the Sunnah which explains the Book, or the Book itself. It is repeated for emphasis, showing concern for its matter. It may also be said that what is meant by it is the realities of the Book, its subtleties, and all that is deposited in it. Teaching the Book is then an expression for making its words understood and explaining the manner of its recitation, and teaching wisdom is making them aware of what is deposited in it. Some have explained it as that by which souls are perfected with knowledge and rulings, so it includes theoretical and practical wisdom. They said: between it and what is in the Book there is a partial overlap (umum min wajh), because the Qur'an includes stories and promises; and that some matters which perfect the soul in knowledge and action are not mentioned in the Book. You know that this statement, after hearing His saying: ﴿We have neglected nothing in the Book﴾ and His saying, glorified is He: ﴿an exposition of all things﴾, is something one should not venture into. Unless this relation is between what is in the Book that is in the supplication, apart from what it was answered with, and wisdom, so reflect.

﴿and purify them﴾, i.e., cleanse them from the filth of polytheism, the impurities of doubt, and the defilements of sins. This is an indication of takhliyah (emptying), just as teaching is an indication of tahliyah (adorning). Perhaps the mention of the second before the first is because of its nobility. The view that it means he takes zakah from them, which is a cause of their purity, or that he bears witness to their purification and uprightness, is remote.

﴿Indeed, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾, i.e., the Overpowering, the Perfecter of what He wills. So You may specify one of them with the all-comprehensive messengership possessing these attributes, by His will without any specifier. Taking "al-Aziz" here to mean the one without equal, as Ibn Abbas said, or the avenger, as al-Kalbi said, and "al-Hakim" to mean the knowing, as has been said, is not free from remoteness.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 130:**

﴿And who would turn away from the creed of Abraham﴾ is a denial and a rejection of the idea that any of the sensible would turn away from his creed, which is the truth in its utmost clarity. That is, no one turns away from it, ﴿except one who makes a fool of himself﴾, that is, one who makes himself humiliated and abased. The root of *safah* (foolishness) is lightness, and from it comes *zimam safih*, meaning a light (loose) bridle. *Safiha* with a kasra, as al-Mubarrad and Tha'lab said, is transitive by itself, and *nafsahu* ("himself") is its direct object. As for *safuha* with a damma, it is intransitive. What supports this is the hadith: "Arrogance is to belittle the truth and to despise people." It was also said that it is intransitive too, and that it became transitive because it implies the meaning of a verb that takes an object, that is, he ignored himself due to the lightness of his intellect and his failure to reflect. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Or it means he destroyed himself, which is the view of Abu 'Ubayda. It was also said that the accusative is by removal of the preposition, that is, "in himself," so it does not contradict intransitivity. This is the view of some of the Basran grammarians. It was also said that it is a specification (*tamyiz*), as in the verse of al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani:

*"And after him we take the tail of a life whose back is hump-less, having no hump."*

It was also said that it is by analogy to the direct object. Abu Hayyan objected to all of these views, saying: the implication (*tadmin*) and the removal of the preposition are not analogical; the analogy to the direct object is, according to the majority, restricted to the adjective, as was said regarding the line of poetry; and the Basran grammarians prohibited the specification from being definite. Therefore, the view that should not be departed from is the view of transitivity.

*Man* (who) is either a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun, in the place of nominative case according to the preferred view, as a substitute for the pronoun in *yarghabu* (turns away), because it is an exception from a negative (non-affirmative) context.

The cause of the revelation of the verse is what is narrated: that ʿAbdullah ibn Salam invited his two nephews, Salama and Muhajir, to Islam, and said to them: "You both know that God Most High said in the Torah: 'Indeed, I will raise up from the offspring of Ishmael a prophet whose name is Ahmad. Whoever believes in him has been guided and has become rightly guided, and whoever does not believe in him is cursed.'" So Salama embraced Islam, and Muhajir refused, and this verse was revealed.

﴿And We certainly chose him in this world﴾, that is, We selected him for the prophethood through that creed, and We elected him from among all creation. Its root is taking the choicest part of a thing, that is, its purest essence.

﴿And indeed he, in the Hereafter, is among the righteous﴾, that is, among those who are testified to be steadfast in uprightness, goodness and righteousness. This clause is conjoined to what precedes it, and in terms of meaning it is a clear proof that the one who turns away from the creed of Abraham is a fool, since chosenness and honor in this world are the ultimate goals of worldly pursuits, while righteousness encompasses the perfections of the Hereafter, and no non-foolish person has any aim except the good of both abodes.

As for the wording, it is possible that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) confirming the aspect of the denial, with the *lam* being the *lam* of initiation (*lam al-ibtida'*), meaning: "Would he turn away from his creed?" Accompanying it is what necessitates the opposite of that, and this is the apparent wording, since there is no need to estimate an oath. Al-Radi preferred this view. It is also possible that it is a conjunction to what precedes it, or a parenthetical insertion between the two conjoined clauses, with the *lam* being the answer to an implied oath. This is the apparent meaning, because the basic principle of sentences is independence, and it serves to add the emphasis required in this context and to signal that the claim does not need explanation, while the intended purpose is to praise him, peace be upon him. The first clause is expressed in the past tense because it has elapsed from the time of the report, and the second is a nominal sentence because it is not restricted by time, since his inclusion among the righteous of the people of the Hereafter is a continuous matter in both abodes, not something that happens in the Hereafter. The emphasis with *inna* and the *lam* is because the matters of the Hereafter are hidden from the addressees, so their need for emphasis is greater than for matters whose effects we witness.

The word *fi* ("in") is related to *al-salihin* (the righteous), with *al* in it being the definite article, not a relative pronoun, so that it would not require placing part of the relative clause before it. Moreover, a temporal adverb may be permitted what is not permitted otherwise. It may also be related to a deleted element, meaning *salih* (righteous), or "I mean." Relating it to *aṣṭafaynāhu* ("We chose him") is also possible, but there is a transposition in the verse. Relating it to a deleted element that is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the adjective is far-fetched.

﴿Idh qala lahu rabbuhu aslim qala aslamtu li-rabbi al-alamin﴾ ("When his Lord said to him, 'Submit,' he said, 'I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds'"). It is a *zarf* (temporal adverbial complement, "when") governing (*li-isṭafaynāhu*, "We chose him"). The intervening *ma'tūf* (conjoined element) is not foreign to the sentence, because the thing it refers to is a confirmation of what is attached to it, since his being chosen in this world was only for the prophetic mission, and what relates to the good of the Hereafter does not need to be treated as a parenthetical clause (*i'tirāḍ*), or a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) understood to be implied, as has been said, or as a causal clause (*ta'līl*) for it, or as an object of (*idhkur*, "remember"), as if it were said: "Remember that time, so that you may understand that he was the chosen righteous one, and that he attained what he attained only through his eagerness and submission to what he was commanded, and the sincerity of his inner self when his Lord called him." It has also been permitted to make it a temporal adverbial of (*qala*, "he said"). The command and what follows it in the reply are not to be taken in their literal sense; rather, it is a figurative expression, and the meaning is: the proofs that lead to knowledge occurred to his mind, he reasoned by them, submitted to what they indicated. However, Allah, glorified and exalted, expressed this by the two statements, to depict the swiftness of the transition through the swiftness of the response. Thus it is an allusion to his (peace be upon him) reasoning through the star, the sun and the moon, and his awareness of the signs of created existence, as the words of al-Hasan and Ibn 'Abbas indicate, that this was before prophethood and before puberty. Whoever holds that it was after prophethood says: the intended meaning is the command to obedience, submission to the particular rulings, steadfastness, and firmness upon monotheism, in the manner of: ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah﴾. It is not possible to read it in its literal sense, I mean the initiation of Islam and faith, because the prophets are protected from disbelief both before prophethood and after it, and because revelation and prophetic commissioning cannot be conceived before Islam. Yes, if Islam is understood as action by the limbs and not in the sense of faith, then the literal reading becomes possible, as has been said. In the shift (of address) together with the mention of the title of Lordship and its attribution to him (peace be upon him), there is a display of greater kindness toward him and of care for his upbringing. And the attribution of "Lord" in the reply to "the worlds" indicates the perfection of the strength of his submission, in that he, upon reflection, perfectly grasped the comprehensiveness of the Lordship of the Exalted over all the worlds without exception, not only over himself, as is what is ostensibly commanded.

[p. 389]

﴿And Abraham enjoined it upon his sons﴾. This praises him, peace be upon him, for perfecting others after praising his own perfection in himself. It also affirms that there is a desire for his religion (millah). A *tawsiyah* (enjoining or bequest) is advancing to another person with an act that contains goodness and nearness to God. This applies whether it occurs at the time of death (*ihtidar*) or earlier, and whether the advance is by speech or by indication. Although the common usage of the word is for a specific utterance at the time of death, its root meaning is connection, from the saying "a *ard wasiyah*," meaning land whose vegetation is connected. It is also said, "wassahu" when one connects something, and "fassahu" when one separates it, as if the one who enjoins connects his act with the act of the one enjoined. The pronoun in *bihā* ("by it") may refer either to the religion (*millah*), or, by interpreting the word or the sentence, to his saying "I have submitted." The first is preferred because the referent is explicitly mentioned, and because the pronoun is not shifted to a noun that is more explicit. Also, the conjunction of *Ya'qub* with it indicates that this is the beginning of another statement, explaining that the prophets enjoined one another to hold fast to the true religion, which comprises all the rulings of the fundamentals and the branches, so that they would inherit the upright religion and the straight law generation after generation. Ya'qub mentioned the religion (*dīn*) in his enjoining to his sons, and the religion and the *millah* are two synonyms. If the pronoun referred to the second [i.e., Ya'qub's statement], the word would be *al-Islam* instead of it. The second reading is supported by the fact that the object of enjoining matches "aslamtu" in wording, and the conjoined element is brought close to it, because then it would be conjoined to "qala aslamtu," meaning he did not suffice with compliance but added the enjoining of his sons to submission. This differs from the first assumption, in which it is conjoined to "man yarghab" (who would turn away), because, as we have indicated, it has the sense of negation. He specified the sons because he was most compassionate toward them, they were most worthy of accepting his enjoining, and the benefit through them is greater. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read *awsā* (with a short vowel and no intensification), and there is no indication in it of multiplicity, unlike the first, which indicates it by the form *tafʿīl* (*wassā*, intensive form).

﴿And Ya'qub﴾ is conjoined to Ibrahim. It is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence (*mubtada'*), and the predicate is omitted, meaning "Ya'qub [did] likewise." The sentence is conjoined to the verbal sentence. To make him the subject of an implied *wassā* is remote. It has also been read in the accusative, in which case it is conjoined to *banīhi* ("his sons"). The sons here are the biological sons. He, peace be upon him, was a grandson (*nāfilah*). He was named Ya'qub because he and 'Is were twins; 'Is came out first, and Ya'qub came out following him, holding onto his heel (*'aqib*). This is what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, but I do not think it is authentic. [Then] ﴿O my sons﴾. This is governed by an implied verb of speech, according to the Basrans, which is understood in the singular if Ya'qub is in the accusative (meaning "he said" or "saying"), and in the dual if he is in the nominative. For a sentence to follow a verb of speech is conditional upon the purpose being merely to report the speech. The reported statement is shared between Ibrahim and Ya'qub, even though the addressees in the two situations differ. The Kufans held that there is no implied verb, because the enjoining, by including the meaning of speech, is itself a specific utterance, so it has the same ruling as speech, and therefore a sentence may occur in the position of its object. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read *an yā banīy*. According to the Basrans, there is then no need to posit an implied verb of speech; rather, according to them, it is not permissible, as the statement of some researchers indicates. The sons of Ibrahim, according to *al-Itqan*, are twelve: Isma'il, Is'haq, Madyan, Zimran, Sarh, Naqsh, Naqshan, Umaym, Kaysan, Sawraj, Lutan, and Nafis. The sons of Ya'qub are likewise twelve: Yusuf, Ruwbil, Sham'un, Lawi, Yahudha, Dan, Tafthani, Kad, Asbar, Iyasajir, Raykun, and Binyamin.

﴿Indeed Allah has chosen for you the religion﴾. That is, He has made the religion, which is the choicest of religions, for you, by legislating it for you and enabling you to adhere to it. The intended meaning is the religion of Islam, through which one is sincere to Allah, and submits to Him. The meaning is not what might appear, that Allah made it the choicest of religions for you, because this religion is choice in itself, not specific to anyone, and there is nothing else with Allah. From here it is known that Islam may be applied to religions other than ours, but usage has restricted it to ours. Some claim that it is not applied this way, and one of them composed a treatise on this, straining himself to the utmost in doing so.

﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾. This is a prohibition against being characterized by a state contrary to submission at the time of death. The apparent implication of the verse is a prohibition against dying in a state other than that, which is not the intended meaning, because it is not within one's power; what is within one's power is its condition, so the prohibition returns to that, as you have heard. This is because refraining from being characterized by that state entails refraining from dying in that state. Either it may be said that the word originally for the first is used for the second, and thus it is a metaphor (*majāz*), or it may be said that the word is used for its meaning in order to move from it to what necessarily accompanies it, and thus it is a metonymy (*kināyah*). The learned Yamani said that this is a metonymy by negating the essence in order to negate the state, the reverse of what is said about the verse ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah?﴾, namely that it is a metonymy by negating the state in order to negate the essence. But in this there is the point that negating the essence becomes a metonymy for negating all attributes, not a specific attribute; so understand. The intended matter indicated by this prohibition is steadfastness upon Islam, because that is what necessarily accompanies it, and that is the purpose of the enjoining; and because the root of Islam was already present in them. The negative particle was placed before the verb, even though it is not a prohibition on that, to indicate that their dying not upon Islam is a death with no good in it, that it ought not to befall them, and that they must guard against it with the utmost caution. Some have mentioned that the Islam commanded here is that which is in the heart, not the practice of the limbs, because that is almost impossible at the time of death. For this reason it is reported in a hadith: "O Allah, whoever of us You cause to live, cause him to live upon Islam, and whoever of us You cause to die, cause him to die upon faith (*īmān*)." The problems in this are not hidden.

﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub?﴾ The address is either to the Jewish people as a category, or to those who were present in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, as the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) indicates. Al-Wahidi reports that the verse was revealed concerning the Jews when they said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Do you not know that when Ya'qub died he enjoined his sons to follow Judaism?" The particle (أم) may be disjunctive (munqati'a), meaning "rather" (بل), together with the interrogative hamza of denial. The meaning of (بل) here is retraction (idrab, a turning away from the previous statement), namely the statement about the enjoining, toward rebuking the Jews for their claim that Ya'qub and his sons were Jews. Its benefit is the transition from one sentence to another that is more important. That is: you were not present at his death, peace be upon him, nor at his asking his sons about the religion, so why do you make the claims you make? You may also take the interrogative as a affirmation (taqrir), meaning: your forefathers were present when he, peace be upon him, enjoined his sons to Islam and monotheism, and you know this, so why do you claim against him the opposite of what you know? In this case, their knowledge through the testimony of their forefathers is treated as if it were testimony, so they were addressed as they were addressed. Or the particle may be conjunctive (muttasila), with an ellipsis in the speech, the estimated sense being: "Were you absent, or were you witnesses?" On this reading the interrogative is not literal, since it is not seeking knowledge of the first being realized and the second being negated. Rather it is for compulsion and rebuke. That is: whichever of the two matters was the case, your claim is false. As for the first, it is conjecture about the unseen (rajm bil-ghayb). As for the second, it contradicts what is well known. Abu Hayyan objected to this view: we do not know of anyone who permitted the omission of the clause coordinated with (أم) in the conjunctive (أم المتصلة), and the omission has only been heard with (أم) together with the coordinated element, because the later elements can bear what the earlier ones cannot. It has also been said that the address is to the believers, and the meaning of (بل) is retraction from the previous speech and turning to what is more important, namely urging them to follow him ﷺ by establishing some of his miracles, which is informing about the states of the earlier prophets without having heard it from anyone or read it from a book. It is as if Allah, after mentioning what preceded, turned to the believers of the community: "Did you witness what took place, or did you know it through revelation and the report of the Messenger ﷺ? Then follow him." However, He only mentioned the dialogue of Ya'qub and his sons, so that it would be known that they were not present at the time of Ibrahim's enjoining, peace be upon him, by way of a fortiori argument. It is not hidden that this speaker did not take the occasion of revelation into account, perhaps because of its weakness, to the point that the Imam al-Suyuti said: "I have not found it."

(The witnesses, al-shuhada'), the plural of shahid or shahid, in the sense of present (hadir). (حضر) is of the pattern of (قعد). It was also read as (حَضِرَ) with kasra, and its present tense is also (يَحْضُرُ) with damma, which is an anomalous dialect. It has been said that it is by interchange (tadakhul) of the two forms.

﴿When he said to his sons﴾: (إذ قال لبنيه) is a substitute for (إذ حضر) as a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). Both are intended, as is established in the substitution of sentences, except that the substitute carries an added explanation not present in the substituted element. If (إذ) were linked here to (قالوا), the speech would not be coherent.

﴿"What will you worship after me?"﴾ That is: what thing will you worship after my death? (ما) is in the nominative position, and the returning pronoun (العائد) is omitted. Its being in the accusative position as the object would lose the sense of comprehensiveness that suits the context, since (ما) is used to ask about any thing. When it is about definition, (من) is used for rational beings when one asks about their identity, and one replies with what conveys it. When one asks about their attribute, one says: "What is Zayd, a writer or a poet?" In asking about their condition after his death there is evidence that the purpose is to urge them to what they had been upon during his lifetime of monotheism and Islam, and to take a covenant from them to it. Thus the interrogation is not genuine. This was after he, peace be upon him, had entered Egypt and seen there those who worshipped fire, and he feared for his son, so he urged them to what he urged them to.

﴿They said: "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq."﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) that came as an answer to a question arising from the narration of the question. In attributing "God" (الإله) to the plural (the fathers), there is an indication of agreement on His existence and His divinity. Isma'il was mentioned before Ishaq because he was older than him. He was counted among the fathers of Ya'qub though he was his paternal uncle, by giving precedence to the majority over the minority, or because the uncle was likened to the father for their being bound in a single chain, which is brotherhood, so the father's name was applied to him. This is supported by what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) reported: "The paternal uncle of a man is the twin of his father." In that case, what is meant by "your fathers" is what the word applies to, so that the combination of the literal and the metaphorical is avoided. The verse is in the manner of what Ibn Abi Shaybah and others reported from his saying, peace be upon him: "Protect me in regard to al-Abbas, for he is the remainder of my fathers." Al-Hasan read (أبيك) (your father, singular). It is then either singular, with Isma'il and Ishaq coordinated to it by conjunction, and Ibrahim alone as an explicative apposition (badal/ 'atf bayan); or it is plural, with its nun dropped because of the construction (idafa), as in the verse of the poet:

"When our voices became distinct to them, they wept, and we ransomed them with the most noble of our fathers."

﴿One God﴾ (إلهًا واحدًا) is a substitute for "the God of your fathers." An indefinite noun may be substituted for a definite one on condition that it is qualified, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By the forelock, a lying, sinful forelock﴾ (ناصية كاذبة). The Basran grammarians do not stipulate this condition. The benefit of the substitution is to remove the suspicion of plurality arising from mentioning "God" twice. Or it is in the accusative on the basis of praise (al-madh), or as a circumstantial preparatory state (al-hal al-muwatti'a), as in al-Bahr (of Abu Hayyan).

﴿And we are to Him submitting﴾ (مسلمون): that is, humbly submissive, acknowledging servitude. It has also been said: subservient, compliant, submitting to His prohibition and command, in speech and conviction. It has also been said: entering into Islam and remaining steadfast upon it. The sentence is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject, or from the object, or from both, because both their pronouns are present. Or it is a parenthetical sentence (i'tiradiyya) confirming the content of what preceded at the end of the speech without a statement. Abu Hayyan said: the more eloquent is that it be coordinated to (نعبد), so that they answered with two things. This is from the category of the answer that is trained (al-jawab al-murabba) from the question.

This is Ruh al-Ma'ani, commentary of al-Alusi, on surah 2, verse 134:

﴿That is a community that has passed away.﴾ The reference (al-ishara) is to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) and his descendants. The word ummah (community) has several meanings. Here it means a group, derived from amma, meaning "intended" (qasada). Every group bound together by some common matter, whether a single religion, a single era, or a single place, is called an ummah, because its members aim at one another and intend it. Khala (passed away) means to have gone by; its root meaning is isolation (infirad).

﴿For them is what they earned, and for you is what you have earned.﴾ This is either a resumptive statement (isti'naf), or an apposition (badal) to the phrase "has passed away," because it means "you do not share with them." It is like an incomplete sentence (ghayr al-wafiya), whereas this one is complete in conveying the full meaning. Alternatively, the first phrase may be another description (sifa) of "community," or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "has passed away." The second phrase is an independent sentence (jumla mubtada'a), since it has no connecting link (rabit) and there is no simultaneity in time. In the speech there is an omitted modifier (mudaf mahdhuf), known from the context, meaning: for each one is the reward of his deed. The fronting of the predicate (taqdim al-musnad) restricts the predicate to the subject (qasr al-musnad ilayhi 'ala al-musnad). The meaning is that your affiliation to them does not necessitate your benefiting from their deeds; you benefit only by agreeing with them and following them, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O assembly of Quraysh, the people most entitled to the Prophet are the righteous. So be on a path of that, and beware lest people come to me bearing deeds while you come to me with the world, and I turn my face away from you." It is also possible to take the first sentence to mean: "for them is what they themselves earned, and it does not go beyond them to others," and the second to mean: "and for you is what you yourselves earned, not what others earned." Thus the two restrictions differ, as the context requires that.

﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾ If the question is taken in its literal sense, the sentence confirms the content of what precedes it. If what is meant is its cause, namely the reward, then it is a concluding statement (tadhyil) completing what precedes it. The sentence is either resumptive or parenthetical (mu'tarida). The purpose is to disappoint the addressees and cut off their hopes of benefiting from the good deeds of those who passed before them. The deed is stated without qualification in order to establish the ruling through demonstrative method (al-tariq al-burhani) within a universal proposition. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted the verse to mean: "you will not be held accountable for their evil deeds, just as you will not be rewarded for their good deeds." This was objected to on the grounds that it is not fitting for the status of revelation, for how could it be otherwise, since they are free of committing evil deeds? How, then, could the burden of them be imagined to fall on others, so that it would be necessary to explain their absence? You know that if the intended purpose is to present this through a universal demonstrative method, the aforementioned misunderstanding does not arise.

Furthermore, it is strange to take the demonstrative reference as applying to each of Ibrahim, Isma'il and Ishaq, and to hold that the meaning is: each one of them is a community, that is, in the same rank of nobility and splendor. "Has passed away" means: has gone by. You are not commanded to follow them. "For them is what they earned" refers to what Allah the Exalted commanded them. "And for you is what you earned" refers to what He, glory be to Him, commands you. Their acquisition does not benefit you, because it is not accepted from you, since it is not in your right. What benefits you is only what it is obligatory upon you to acquire. "And you will not be asked about what they used to do" means: were you practicing it? You are only asked about what your Prophet, whom you are commanded to follow, used to do, for his deeds are what your acquisition is asked about. So leave aside the claim that this is what Ibrahim or someone else commanded, and hold fast to what your Prophet commanded, and take note that the deed is attributed to him, not to them. It is not hidden that if these verses were the words of this commentator, it would have been possible to interpret them in this way, which has neither branch nor root. But they are the speech of the Lord of the worlds, who is too exalted to be interpreted in such a manner.

* * *

Among the mode of allusion (ishara) and interpretation (ta'wil) in the preceding verses up to here: ﴿And when his Lord tried Ibrahim with words﴾, that is, with the levels of spiritual realities (al-ruhaniyyat), such as the heart (qalb), the secret (sirr), the spirit (ruh), the hidden (khafa'), and solitude (wahda), and the states (ahwal) and stations (maqamat) through which one passes over those levels, such as submission (taslim), reliance (tawakkul), contentment (rida), and their sciences. ﴿He fulfilled them﴾ by journeying toward Allah the Exalted, and in Allah the Exalted, until annihilation in Him (fana'). ﴿He said: I am making you an imam for the people﴾ by remaining after annihilation and returning to creation from the Truth, leading them and guiding them along the path of My way, and they follow you and are guided. ﴿He said: And of my offspring? He said: My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾; so they will not be my successors despite their wrongdoing, and their darkness through seeing other than Allah and transgressing the limits. ﴿And when We made﴾ the house of the heart a place of return for people, and a place of security and safety for them when they reach it and dwell in it, from the evil of the consequences of the attributes of the soul, the destruction of the battle of the natural powers and their corruption, and the imaginings of the satans of illusion and imagination and their seduction. ﴿And take from the station of Ibrahim﴾, which is the station of the spirit and intimate friendship (khulla), a place of prayer for the true prayer, which is witnessing and intimate tasting of friendship. ﴿And We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾, commanding them to purify the house of the heart from the filth of the soul's discourses, the impurities of satanic whisperings, the defilements of the impulses of desire, and the stains of the attributes of the powers, for the seekers who are longing, who circle around the heart in their journey and reach its station through reliance, which is the unification of actions, and for the humble who have attained the station of the manifestation of the attributes and the perfection of the rank of contentment, who are absent in unity and annihilated therein. ﴿And when Ibrahim said: My Lord, make this﴾, the breast, which is the sanctuary (hanm) of the heart, ﴿a secure land﴾, safe from the domination of the attributes of the soul, from the assassination of the accursed enemy, and from the seizing of the jinn of the bodily powers. ﴿And provide its people with﴾ fruits of the knowledge of the spirit, for whoever among them affirmed Allah the Exalted and knew the return to Him. He said: and also whoever veils himself among those who dwell in the breast and do not pass its limit by ascending to the station of the eye (ayn), because of their reliance on knowledge whose vessel is the breast. ﴿Then I will let him enjoy briefly﴾ of the rational meanings and universal knowledge descending to them from the world of the spirit according to their capacity, ﴿then I will drive him to the punishment﴾ of the fire of deprivation and veiling, ﴿and evil is the destination﴾, their destination, for their punishment through their deficiency and their failure to perfect their creation. ﴿And when Ibrahim raised the foundations of the House﴾ in the manner we mentioned earlier, and Isma'il likewise, saying: ﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾ our striving and our efforts in journeying to You, through the supply of success. ﴿Indeed You are the All-Hearing﴾ of the whisperings of our thoughts about You, ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ of our intentions and our secrets. ﴿Our Lord, and make us submitting to You﴾; do not leave us to ourselves. ﴿And from our offspring﴾, those affiliated to us, ﴿a community submitting to You; and show us﴾ the ways of reaching the negation of all other than You, ﴿and turn to us﴾ so that we may pass away in You from ourselves and our annihilation. ﴿Indeed You are the Ever-Returning﴾, who grants success in returning to You, ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ to whoever relies upon You alone. ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from among them﴾, who is the Muhammadan reality (al-haqiqa al-Muhammadiyya), ﴿who recites to them Your verses﴾ which indicate You, ﴿and teaches them﴾ the Book of the intellect, which comprises Your attributes, ﴿and the wisdom﴾ which indicates the negation of other than You, ﴿and purifies them﴾ and cleanses them from the stain of polytheism. ﴿Indeed You are the Mighty﴾, the Dominant, so how could other than You appear, the Firm in what You have manifested in it, so that none is seen except You. ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Ibrahim﴾, which is pure monotheism, except one who has completely veiled himself from the light of the intellect and remains in the darkness of his soul. ﴿And indeed We chose him﴾, so he was among the beloved ones, those intended by the eternal preordainment in the world of dominion, and in the world of the realm of dominion he is among the people of uprightness, fit to govern the order and perfect the species. ﴿When his Lord said to him: Submit!﴾, that is, affirm the oneness of God and submit your very self to Allah the Exalted. ﴿He said: I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾, and I have been annihilated in Him. Ibrahim enjoined the word of monotheism upon his sons, those travelers who journeyed by his hand, and likewise Ya'qub: ﴿O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you﴾ His religion, of which there is no other religion in His sight. ﴿So do not die﴾ with natural death or the death of ignorance, but be dead to yourselves and alive in Allah forever, so that the death of the body overtakes you in this state. ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾; so do not be bound by mere blind imitation of them, for no one has anything except what he has earned of knowledge and action, belief and conduct. So be upon insight in your affair, and seek what they sought so that you may attain what they attained. ﴿And those who strive for Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾. Whoever knocks persistently at the door of the Generous One and presses on, enters.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 2, verse 135:

﴿They say: "Be Jews or Christians, and you will be guided."﴾ The pronoun (*damir*, pronoun) "they" refers to the People of the Book, and the sentence is conjoined (*'atf*, coordination) to what precedes it as a narrative coordinated with a narrative. Its purpose is to reject their call to their false religion, following the rejection of their claim that Ya'qub (peace be upon him) was a Jew. "*Aw*" (or) is for variety of speech (*tanwi' al-maqal*), not for choice (*takhyir*), as evidenced by the fact that each of the two groups declares the other to be unbelievers. That is, the Jews said to the believers, "Be Jews," and the Christians said to them, "Be Christians." "*Wa-tahtadu*" (and you will be guided) is the answer to the imperative, meaning: if you are like that, you will be guided.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it was revealed concerning the leaders of the Jews of Madinah: Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Malik ibn al-Sayf, Wahb ibn Yahudha, and Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab; and concerning the Christians of Najran. That is because they disputed with the Muslims about religion, each group claiming that it had more right to the religion of Allah than the others. The Jews said: "Our prophet Musa is the best of the prophets, our book the Torah is the best of books, and our religion is the best of religions," and they disbelieved in 'Isa, the Injil, Muhammad, and the Qur'an. The Christians said: "Our prophet 'Isa is the best of the prophets, our book the Injil is the best of books, and our religion is the best of religions," and they disbelieved in Muhammad and the Qur'an. Each of the two groups said to the believers: "Be upon our religion, for there is no religion but this."

In the narration of Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, and others, from him, 'Abdullah ibn Suriya al-A'war said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Guidance is nothing but what we are upon, so follow us, O Muhammad, and you will be guided." The Christians said the same, and Allah revealed the verse concerning them.

"*Qul*" (say) is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: say to those who spoke thus, by way of refutation of them, and by making clear to them what is the truth according to them, and guiding them to it.

﴿Rather, the religion of Ibrahim﴾. That is: we will not be as you say, but we will be the religion of Ibrahim, i.e., the people of his religion; or, rather, we follow the religion of Ibrahim. The first reading (requiring the omission of a *mudaf*, governed noun) is required by respect for the wording of what came before, even though it needs an elided *mudaf*; the second is required by the inclination toward the meaning, since the first would reduce to "follow the religion of the Jews or the Christians," without the need for any supposition. It is also permissible that the meaning be: "rather, you yourselves follow his religion, or become the people of his religion." It has been said: "The more evident is: rather, we bring the religion of Ibrahim," but its wording has not become clear to me. It was also read as "*bal millatu*" (with the *dammah*), meaning: rather, our religion is his religion, or our affair is his religion, or we are his religion, i.e., its people. It has been said: "Rather, guidance, or the religion of Ibrahim guides," and this, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿Hanifan﴾ means upright, or inclining away from falsehood toward truth. It is used to describe the one who adheres to a religion, and also the religion itself. It is a circumstantial state (*haal*, circumstantial accusative), either from the *mudaf* ("religion") by interpreting it as "the religion," or by treating it as analogous to *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul*, as in His saying, ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah is near to the good-doers﴾ (7:56). This is evident on the reading with the accusative and the supposition "we follow." As for the supposition "you will be upon it," it is because "millah" is the agent of the verb implied by the genitive construction, meaning: it will be a religion established for Ibrahim. On the reading with the nominative, the state is emphatic, because it comes after nominal sentences whose two parts are fixed definite nouns, confirming their content, since his religion is well known for this, peace be upon him. So the construction is like: "I am Hatim, generous," or it is from the *mudaf ilayhi* (the genitive complement), according to what they accepted: that a state may come from it in three cases: when the *mudaf* is a derived active participle, or a part, or in the position of a part in permissibility of its omission, as here, since it is correct to say: "follow Ibrahim," meaning: follow his religion. It has been said that what permits a state to come from the *mudaf ilayhi* is that it is an object of the verbal sense implied by the genitive construction or by the *lam*. Abu al-Baqa' alludes to this, and it is perhaps preferable because it is consistently applicable in the first supposition. It has also been said that it is in the accusative by the supposition "I mean."

﴿Nor was he of the polytheists﴾ is coordinated with ﴿hanifan﴾ according to the pattern of ﴿upright toward Allah, not associating partners with Him﴾ (22:31). So it is a state from the *mudaf ilayhi*, not from the *mudaf*, unless one supposes "and the religion of the polytheists was not...," which is a strained reading. The intended purpose is an allusion (*ta'ridh*) to the People of the Book and to the Arabs, who claim to follow him and adhere to specific laws attributed to him, such as the pilgrimage to the House and circumcision, and others. For in each of these communities there are associates of Allah. The Jews said: "'Uzayr is the son of Allah"; the Christians: "The Messiah is the son of Allah"; and the Arabs worshipped idols and said: "The angels are the daughters of Allah."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 136:

﴿Say: "We believe in Allah"﴾ This is addressed to the believers, not to the disbelievers, as has been said, because of the difficulty and artificiality that would be involved otherwise. It explains the following of what is commanded. It therefore stands in the position of a partial substitution (badal al-ba'd, a substitution of a part for the whole) for His words, glorified is He: ﴿but rather the religion of Abraham﴾, because following (ittiba') includes belief (i'tiqad) and action, and this clause explains the belief. Or it is a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), because it contains a detail that is absent from the first. It has also been said that it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), as if they had asked, "How is the following?", and were answered with this. The command was first given in the singular form and then in the plural form, to indicate that the Messenger's statement on behalf of all the believers suffices as the answer, unlike following, which requires the statement of each individual, because it is a condition of faith, or a part of it. This was said by some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqun). The claim that it stands in the position of an explanation (bayan) and an emphasis of the first statement, and that for this reason the conjunction was omitted, is not free from objection. Belief in Allah, glorified is He, is given precedence because it is the first of the obligations, and because by first knowing Him, knowledge of the prophethoods and the legal matters becomes sound.

﴿and what was sent down to us﴾ That is, the Qur'an. Although in order of revelation it came later than other things, in the order of faith it precedes them, because it is the cause of belief in the others, by virtue of its confirming them. For this reason it was mentioned first.

﴿and what was sent down to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes﴾ This means the scrolls (suhuf). Although they were sent down to Abraham, upon him be prayers and peace, since those mentioned after him were under obligation to follow their details and were subject to their rulings, it is correct to attribute their descent to them also, just as our being under obligation to follow the details of the Qur'an and our being subject to its rulings makes it correct to attribute its descent to us. The tribes (al-asbat) are the plural of sibt, like ahmal and himl. They are the sons of Israel. It has been said that they are among the descendants of Isaac in the way that the clans (qaba'il) are among the descendants of Ishmael. The word is derived from sibt, which is a tree with many branches, so it is as if they were named thus because of their multiplicity. It has also been said that it is derived from subutah, which means flowing freely, or that it is an inversion of bast (spreading). It has also been said that the two grandsons of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) are called sibtan because of the spread of their offspring. Then every son of a daughter came to be called sibt, and likewise he is called hafid (grandson) too. People have differed concerning the tribes, the sons of Jacob, as to whether they were all prophets or not. What is sound in my view is the second opinion, which is related from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and to which Imam al-Suyuti went, and on which he wrote a work. This is because what occurred from them with Joseph, upon him be prayers and peace, definitely contradicts prophethood. That they were before puberty is not accepted, because it involved actions that only adults are capable of. Even if it is granted, it would be of no benefit according to the correct view concerning the status of the prophets, and that act involved many grave sins. The Qur'an contains nothing indicating their prophethood. You have known what we have mentioned concerning the verse, so keep this in mind, may you be guided.

﴿and what was given to Moses and Jesus﴾ That is, the Torah and the Gospel. Because the People of the Book had added to and subtracted from them and altered them, and claimed that they had been revealed in that form, while the believers deny this, it gave importance to their matter, mentioned them separately, and explained the way of believing in them. It did not include them in the earlier relative clause. Also, their case in relation to Moses and Jesus is that they were literally sent down upon them, not merely in terms of being under obligation to follow them, as is the case with what was sent down to Isaac, Jacob and the tribes. It did not repeat the relative pronoun for Jesus, because his law did not differ from the law of Moses except in minor matters. Because of this importance, it used the verb "given" (utiya) rather than "sent down" (unzila), because it is more eloquent, since giving is the intended meaning, and because it indicates bestowing, which carries a sense of transferring ownership and entrusting. For this reason one says, "I lowered the bucket into the well," but one does not say, "I gave it to it." You may also say that what is meant by the relative clause here is more general than the Torah and the Gospel, including all the manifest miracles carried by these two noble prophets, as detailed in the glorious revelation. The choice of the verb "given" for it indicates generality. The two prophets are specified by mention because the discourse is with the Jews and the Christians.

﴿and what was given to the prophets﴾ These are the books granted to those among them to whom they were granted, or what includes that along with the miracles. This is a generalization after a specification, so that no prophet is excluded from belief. ﴿from their Lord﴾ This is connected to "was given" before it. The pronoun refers to the prophets specifically. It has been said that it refers also to Moses and Jesus, and that "what was given" is a repetition of the first, with the prepositional phrase connected to it. In both cases it is an adverbial phrase of incidental relation (zarf laghw). It is permitted that it be in the place of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the omitted returning pronoun. The possibility that "what" (ma) is a subject (mubtada') and the prepositional phrase its predicate is remote. ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾ That is, unlike the People of the Book, who distinguished so that they believed in some and disbelieved in others, rather we believe in all of them together. The non-distinction was regarded between them, although the discourse concerns what they were given, because making no distinction between them entails making no distinction in what was given to them. ("Ahad," "any one," originally is wahad, meaning "one.") Whenever it occurs in a context of negation, it becomes general, and the singular and plural are equal in it, and it is correct to intend either of them. Here it is intended to mean a group. For this reason it is permissible for "bayn" (between) to be prefixed to it, and it conveys the generality of groups. This is what some of the verifiers said, but it contradicts what is well known among the masters of Arabic grammar, that the term used in general negation, or used in affirmation together with kull, has an original hamza, unlike what is used in affirmation without kull, whose hamza is changed from a waw. For this reason the scholar al-Taftazani said that ahad in the sense of a group is by lexical convention, because it is a noun for one who can be addressed, in which the masculine, the feminine, the singular, the dual and the plural are equal. It is required that its use be with the word kull or with negation. Abu 'Ali and other imams of Arabic have stated this. This is other than the ahad that is the first of the numbers in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Say: He is Allah, One (ahad)﴾. Its meaning of a group does not derive from its being an indefinite noun in a context of negation, as was previously mentioned, which has led many into error. Do you not see that "We make no distinction between any messenger of the messengers" is not sound except by supposing the conjunction "any messenger and messenger"? And "You are not like any one (ahad) of the women" does not mean "like a woman among them," concluding his words. After reflection you will know that what the scholar mentioned does not refute that position, but only refutes it regarding the question of whether it is original or not. Perhaps this matter is easy. Moreover, the claim that this sound usage is only possible with that supposition is not agreed upon. It has been mentioned in al-Intisaf that an indefinite noun in a context of negation indicates generality verbally, an inclusive generality, so that the singular in it is treated as the plural in encompassing the individuals directly, not as some of the usuliyyun (scholars of legal theory) claimed, that its signification by direct correspondence (mutabaqa) in negation is like its signification in affirmation. This plurality and generality have been made the lexical basis that justifies the entry of "bayn" upon it here. Some people permitted that "ahad" in the verse means "one," and its generality is alternative (badali), and the correctness of prefixing "bayn" to it is considered in relation to a conjoined term that is omitted because it is evident between "one of them" and other than it. In this there is an indication of the realization of the distinction between each single individual of them and anyone else other than him, whoever he may be, which is not present in saying, "We make no distinction between them." There is no concealment of what is in it. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "we believe" (amanna). ﴿and to Him we are submitting (muslimun)﴾ That is, we are humbly obedient to Allah, exalted is He, acknowledging servitude. It has been said: yielding to His command and prohibition. Whoever makes the genitive pronoun refer to what was previously mentioned, the prophets, has gone far astray. The clause is another circumstantial clause, or it is conjoined to "we believe."

**[Commentary of al-Alusi, *Ruh al-Ma'ani*, on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 137]**

﴿So if they believe in the like of that in which you believe, then they are guided.﴾ This is connected either to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say: "We believe in Allah..."﴾ etc., or to His saying, Mighty is His affair, ﴿Rather, [follow] the religion of Abraham...﴾ etc. Its "if" (in) may be for the sake of mere supposition. The speech is of the kind of *al-istidraj* (gradually drawing the opponent on) and *irkha' al-'inan ma'a al-khasm* (giving free rein to the adversary), where the aim is to silence him. This is among the matters in which the horses of debaters gallop, so there is no harm in interpreting the words of Allah, Exalted is He, in this way. The meaning is: "We do not say that we are upon the truth and you are upon falsehood. Rather, if you attain something equal to what we hold of matters that must be believed in or practised as religion, then you have been guided. Our aim is your guidance, however it comes about." If the opponent looks at this speech with an eye of fairness and reflects upon it, he will know that the truth is only what the Muslims hold, since there is no equal to what they believe in, namely the Essence of Allah, Exalted is He, and His Books sent down to His prophets, and there is no religion like their religion.

(*Fa-amanu*) is transitive with the particle *bi*, and *mithl* is taken in its apparent sense. It has also been said that *amanu* is used in the manner of an intransitive verb, and the *ba'* is either for seeking help and instrumentality. The meaning is: "If they enter into faith by means of a testimony like your testimony, in word and in belief, then they are guided." Or: "If they seek faith by a path that leads to the truth, like your path, then the unity of the goal does not preclude a plurality of paths, as it has been said: 'The paths to Allah, Exalted is He, are as numerous as the breaths of creatures.'" The context is one of specifying the true religion, not one of specifying the particular person who conveys the path to it, so that this interpretation would fit.

The *ba'* may also be superfluous for emphasis, and *ma* is a verbal-noun (*masdariyyah*). The pronoun in (*bihi*) refers to Allah, or to His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿We believe in Allah...﴾ etc., with the sense of "that which has been mentioned," or to the Qur'an, or to Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is: "If they believe in what has been mentioned, like your belief in it."

The *ba'* may also be for accompaniment, meaning: "They believe while accompanied by the like of what you believe, while you are accompanied by it," or "If they believe with a faith accompanied by the like of what you believe with a faith accompanied by it, in submission and sincerity and in not making distinction between the prophets, peace be upon them."

It has been said that *mithl* is inserted (*muqhamun*), as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾, meaning "to it." This is supported by the reading of Ubayy, (*bi-alladhi amantum bihi*) ["in that which you believed in"], and the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, (*bi-ma amantum bihi*) ["in what you believed in"]. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, used to say: "Recite it thus, for Allah has no like." It is likely that this is to be understood as an explanation (of meaning) and not as his denial of a mutawatir reading, nor as his being unaware of its meaning.

Some people have said that all of this can be dispensed with by saying: "If the Jews believe in the like of what you believe, as their believers did before the distortion, then they have believed in the like of what the believers believed, for what was given to the prophets in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ) includes what was sent down to him, and that was not so before him." However, this interpretation requires keeping the past form of the verb in its meaning, as in their saying: "If she honours me, then I have honoured you." So reflect. The end of his speech.

You know that the object of belief cannot be conceived as plural, and that keeping the speech on its apparent sense and dispensing with all that has been mentioned would require the existence of that impossible plurality. So what benefit is there in this, other than multiplying talk and dispute and widening the circle of contention and argument? So reflect.

﴿And if they turn away﴾, that is, they turn aside from the faith that was commanded, or from your statement in reply to their statement.

﴿then they are only in opposition﴾, that is, in opposition to Allah, Exalted is He, as said by Ibn 'Abbas; or in dispute and warfare, as said by Ibn Zayd; or in enmity, as said by al-Hasan. It has been disputed regarding the derivation of *shiqaq*. It has been said that it comes from *shiqq*, meaning "side." It has been said that it comes from *shuqqah* (distance). It has been said that it is derived from their saying *shaqqa al-'asa* ("he split the staff"), meaning he openly displayed enmity. The tanwin is for magnification. The clause is the answer to the conditional, either on the basis that the intended meaning is their opposition arising after their turning away from faith, and the nominal sentence is chosen to indicate their steadfastness and firm establishment in that state; or by interpretation as if it were "then know."

﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾. This is a consolation to him (ﷺ) and a gladdening of the believers with a promise of victory and triumph, and a guarantee of support and honour, in the most emphatic manner, through the *sin* that indicates the absolute certainty of occurrence. Or it is for the following concluding phrase, since the *sin* in the well-known usage indicates no more than deferment after the mention of what leads to dispute and fighting. The meaning is: "He will suffice you against their plotting and their opposition," for sufficiency relates not to entities but to actions. The shift of address to him (ﷺ) alone, although Allah, Glorified is He, fulfilled His noble promise by what amounts to sufficiency for all, namely the killing and capture of the Banu Qurayzah and the expulsion of the Banu al-Nadir, is because he (ﷺ) is the foundation and the pillar in that matter, and he is the one who unites the hearts of the believers and the target of the plots of the disbelievers. It also signals that undertaking the affairs of war, bearing its hardships, and enduring its trials in confronting enemies are among the duties of leaders, so the blessing of Allah, Exalted is He, in sufficiency and victory for him is more complete and perfect.

﴿And He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾. This is a concluding phrase to the preceding promise, and an affirmation of it. That is: He is the All-Hearing of what you call upon Him with, the All-Knowing of what is in your intention of making His religion manifest, so He will respond to you and bring you to your aim. Or it is a warning to the disbelievers, in the sense that He hears what they utter and knows what they conceal of what is not good, and He will punish them for it. It also contains an affirmation of the earlier promise, for the warning to the disbelievers is a promise to the believers.

[p. 397]

**﴿The baptism of God﴾.** *Al-ṣibgha* (the dye, or colouring), with a kasra, is a noun of the form *fi'la*, derived from *ṣabagha*, like *al-jilsa* from *jalasa*. It denotes the state in which the dyeing takes place. He used it as a figure for purification through faith, with what was mentioned, in the manner that was detailed, because its effect appeared on them just as dye appears on what is dyed, and it penetrated their hearts as it penetrates the dyed object, and it became their adornment. Thus there is a *istiʿāra taḥqīqiyya taṣrīḥiyya* (an explicit, actual metaphor), the indicator being the genitive construction, and the common element being what was mentioned. It has also been said that it is for *al-mushākala al-taqdīriyya* (an implied correspondence of wording), since the Christians used to dye their children with a yellow water which they called *al-maʿmūdiyya* (baptism). They claimed that it was the water in which ʿIsā, upon him be peace, was born, and they believed that it was a purification for the newborn, like circumcision for others. It has also been said that it is water that is sanctified by the recitation of the Gospel, and then pregnant women are washed with it. On this view, it is objected that the statement is general to the Jews as well and is not specific to the Christians, unless it is considered that this practice exists among them in general.

Its accusative case is because it is an emphatic *maṣdar* (verbal noun) for His saying, exalted is He, *(āmannā)* (we believed). It is one of the emphatic verbal nouns that emphasise themselves, so its being for the category (of action) does not contradict this. The governing verb for it is *ṣabaghanā* (He dyed us), as if it were said: "God dyed us with His dye." The verbal noun was considered to be in an annexed construction with the agent, in order to fulfil the condition for obligatory deletion of its governing verb, namely that it emphasises the content of the whole sentence. For if it were taken as indefinite, it would emphasise the content of only one of its two components, namely the verb alone, as in *ḍarabtu ḍarban* (I struck a striking).

It has also been said that it is in the accusative by the verb of incitement, meaning: "Hold fast to the dye of God," not "upon you," since otherwise its mention would be obligatory, as has been said. This is the view of al-Wāḥidī. In that case there is no need to posit an implied governing verb, because the incitement construction is specific to the forms of repetition or conjunction, as in *al-ʿahd al-ʿahd* (the covenant, the covenant), and *al-ahl wa-l-walad* (the family and the child). Al-Akhfash, al-Zajjāj, al-Kisāʾī and others held that it is an apposition to *millat Ibrāhīm* (the creed of Abraham).

**﴿And who is better than God in dye?﴾** This is a subject and predicate, and the interrogative is for denial. His saying, exalted is He, *(ṣibgha)* (in dye) is a *tamyīz* (specification) transferred from the subject, as in *Zayd aḥsanu min ʿAmr wajhan* (Zayd is better than ʿAmr in face). The underlying sense is: "Who has a dye better than the dye of God, exalted is He?", just as one would say: "The face of Zayd is better than the face of ʿAmr." The comparison applies between the two dyes, not between their agents. That is, there is no dye better than His dye, exalted is He, in the sense that it is better than every dye. Since the basis of the comparison is the generalisation of beauty to the real and the presumed, which is built on the claim of the unbelievers, it does not follow that there is some beauty in the dye of anyone other than Him, exalted is He.

The sentence is parenthetical, confirming what there is in the dye of God, exalted is He, of exultation and rejoicing. Or it runs in the manner of a reason for the incitement.

**﴿And we are to Him worshippers﴾**, i.e., monotheists, or obedient ones following the creed of Abraham, or humble ones submitting in following that creed. Placing the prepositional phrase first serves to convey the restriction of worship to Him, exalted is He. Placing the subject first serves to convey that this restriction is limited to them and does not extend to the People of the Book, so it is an allusion to their polytheism, or to their failure to submit to Him, exalted is He, by following the creed of Abraham. The sentence is conjoined to *(āmannā)* (we believed). This requires that **﴿the dye of God﴾** be included within the object of *qūlū* (say), so that there is no intervening foreign element between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined.

The choice of the nominal sentence indicates continuity. For the one who put *(ṣibgha)* in the accusative as an incitement or apposition, it is permissible to posit *qūlū* (say) before this sentence, conjoined to *ilzamū* (hold fast), on the assumption of incitement. Positing an implied verb of saying is lawful and common, and the indicator is the context, since what precedes it is the speech of the believers. It is also possible to posit *ittabiʿū* (follow) in **﴿Rather, the creed of Abraham﴾**, meaning: "We will not follow," and **﴿Say: We believe﴾** would then be an apposition of partial type to *ittabiʿū* (follow), because belief is included in following the creed of Abraham. Thus there is no intervening foreign element between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, nor between the apposition and that to which it is apposed.

As for what has been said, that an intervening element arises through the apposition of the verb between the object and that to which it is apposed, the reply is that *qūlū* (say) is not an apposition of the verb alone; rather the whole sentence is an apposition of the whole sentence, so there is no objection.

As for the claim that this sentence may be made a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the word "God" in His saying, exalted is He, **﴿And who is better than God in dye?﴾**, meaning: "His dye, by the purification of the heart, or guidance, or the preservation of the innate nature, is the best of dyes when worship is sincerely directed to Him," then it is nothing, as is not hidden.

[p. 399]
