﴿Say: Do you dispute with us﴾ The address is turned away from the audience and directed to the Prophet (ﷺ), since what he is commanded to do is among the duties specific to him, peace be upon him. The interrogative hamzah (alif of interrogation) expresses denial. Zayd, al-Hasan and others read it with the assimilation of the nun (idgham), that is, *tujadilunana* (you argue with us). ﴿concerning God﴾ means concerning His religion, and you claim that His true religion is Judaism and Christianity, and you base your entry into Paradise and guidance upon them. It has also been said that the meaning is concerning the affair of God, and His choosing a prophet from among the Arabs rather than from among you. This is based on the view that the address is to the People of the Book. The structure of the discourse requires that the disputation be interpreted in terms that pertain specifically to them, whereas disputation about religion in general is not of that kind. The indication for this restriction is His saying before it, ﴿and what was sent down to us﴾, and after it, ﴿And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony﴾, since it is an allusion to the People of the Book concealing God's testimony concerning the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). As for what is related regarding the occasion of revelation, namely that the People of the Book said: "All the prophets are from us; so if you were a prophet you would be from us," and so this was revealed, you should be aware that disputation concerning religion, in the sense we have mentioned, is specific to them. Moreover, the apparent structure requires their censure for what had become their habit and their established character, so much so that they were known for it. The Arab polytheists, although they also disputed about religion, did not reach the level of the People of the Book in this, because they were unlettered (*ummiyyun*), ignorant of all other sciences, and entirely unaware of the methods of inquiry, considering those who stood at the forefront of the debate. The preceding and following indications for the restriction are extremely obscure. And what is related regarding the occasion of revelation is not mentioned in any of the books of hadith or the authoritative exegeses, as al-Imam al-Suyuti explicitly stated, and his statement is sufficient proof in this matter.

﴿And He is our Lord and your Lord﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), meaning: Do you dispute with us while the situation is that there is no basis at all for disputation, because He, the Exalted, is the Owner of our affair and your affair. ﴿And to us are our deeds and to you are your deeds﴾ This is coordinated (*'atf*) with what precedes it, meaning: for us is the reward of our good deeds, which accord with His command, and for you is the reward of your evil deeds, which oppose His judgment. ﴿And we are sincerely devoted to Him﴾ in those deeds; we seek by them nothing but His countenance. Then how can you dispute, and claim the truth of what you hold, and assert with certainty entry into Paradise by means of it, and call people to it? This clause is circumstantial, like the preceding one. Some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*) held that this clause is like the two clauses ﴿and we are to Him Muslims﴾ and ﴿and we are to Him worshippers﴾, and is an interjection (*i'tiraD*) and a concluding remark (*tadhyil*) to the speech that is followed by it, being said by the tongues of the servants through God's instruction, not a coordination. Its explanation is that ﴿and we are to Him Muslims﴾ corresponds to (*li-amanna*), that is, we believe in God and in what He sent down upon the prophets, may the blessings and peace of God be upon them, and we submit to Him, and we yield to His commands and prohibitions. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿and we are to Him worshippers﴾ is in harmony with His saying, ﴿the dye of God﴾, because it means the religion of God, so the verb is like a summary (*fadhlakah*) of what has preceded. This verse is consistent with what comes before it, and perhaps sound taste does not reject it. As for the claim that the meaning of ﴿And He is our Lord﴾ and so on is that He has no particular relation to one people over another, and so He bestows His mercy on whom He wills; therefore it is not far-fetched that He should honour us for our deeds as He honoured you for yours, it is as if He obliged them, on every position they adopt, to be silenced and rebuked. For the honour of prophethood is either a bounty from God, the Exalted, in which case all are equal in it, or it is the outpouring of a right upon those who deserve it through persistence in obedience and adornment with sincerity. Thus, just as you have deeds which God, the Exalted, may take into account in bestowing it, so we also have deeds, and we are sincerely devoted to Him in them, not you. Yet, together with its being built upon what you know to be feeble, it is not in harmony with the context and flow of the noble arrangement, indeed it is not even correct in itself, as the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, our master, ruled, because what is meant by deeds from both sides is what has been pointed out as righteous and evil deeds, and there is no doubt that the matter of righteousness and evil revolves around conformity to the religion founded on the mission (*ba'tha*) and opposition to it. So how can it be imagined that those deeds be taken into account for the entitlement to prophethood and the preparedness for it, which precedes the mission, by such grades as these! People have differed concerning sincerity (*ikhlas*). It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I asked Gabriel about sincerity, what is it? He said: I asked the Lord of Might about it, and He said: It is one of My secrets, which I have deposited in the heart of whomever I love among My servants." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Sincerity is that you do not associate anyone with His religion, and you do not show off to anyone in your deed. Al-Fudayl said: Abandoning deeds for the sake of people is ostentation (*riya'*), and doing deeds for the sake of people is associating partners (*shirk*), and sincerity is that God protects you from both of them. Hudhayfah al-Mar'ashi said: It is that the servant's deeds be equal in the inward and the outward. Abu Ya'qub said: The one who conceals is the servant who hides his good deeds as he hides his evil deeds. Sahl said: It is destitution (*iflas*), and its meaning is the belittling of deeds, and this is the meaning of Ruwaym's saying: It is the elevation of your deed above seeing it. It has been said: The opposite of sincerity is ostentation. Sulayman al-Darani mentioned three signs of it: laziness in worship when alone, eagerness when in company, and love of praise for the deed.

[Page 400]

**"Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians?"** (*Am*) may be a *muttasilah mu'adilah* (connected, equalizing) particle, corresponding to the hamzah in **"Do you dispute with us about God?"** (*a-tuhājjūnanā*), and falling within the scope of the command. The question is meant to deny both claims together, meaning: each of the two matters is rejected, and it is required that proof be established and the evidence made clear for the truth of what you hold, when the situation is as described, and that you cling to the tail of blind imitation and to slander against the prophets, peace be upon them. The benefit of this style, although knowledge of the establishment of both matters is already present, is to point out that either one of them is sufficient for blame, so how much more so when both are combined. This is like saying to someone who has erred in both action and speech: "Is it your management or your planning?" By this, the objection of Abū Ḥayyān is answered. He argued that connection requires that one of the two sentences occur and that the question be about identifying one of them, but this is not the case, since both occurred together. (*Am*) may also be a *munqati'ah muqaddarah* (disconnected, implied), equivalent to *bal* (rather), with the hamzah indicating a turning away and a shift from rebuke for disputation to rebuke for slander against the prophets, peace be upon them.

Ghayr Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ read **"Or do they say"** with the *yā'* (third person). In this case (*am*) must be *munqati'ah*, because of the turning away it contains, from address (second person) to absence (third person). In a *muttasilah* construction, the address does not shift from one addressee to another, as it may in a *munqati'ah*. The statement becomes a new beginning (*isti'nāf*), not included under the command, but a direct address from Him, exalted is He, as rebuke for them and denial against them. Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭabarī related from some grammarians the permissibility of connection, because when you say: "Are you standing, O Zayd, or is ʿAmr standing?" connection is valid. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah objected to this, saying that the example is not good, because the speaker in it is one and the addressee is one, whereas the speech in the verse comes from two and the addressees are two. Even if the equalization of (*am*) with the hamzah were to be accepted in terms of the meaningful judgment, the sense would be: "Say: Do you dispute with us, or do they say..., O Muḥammad?" It is not hidden that if the claim of disconnection is not determined, it is at least preferable.

**"Say: Are you more knowing or is God?"** That is, you are not more knowing of the state of Abraham, peace be upon him, in matters of religion; rather God, exalted is He, is more knowing of that. He, glorified is He, has informed of the denial of Judaism and Christianity from him, and argued for their negation from him with His words: **"The Torah and the Gospel were not sent down except after him."** These are the ones who are linked to him, his followers in religion by consensus, so their state is his state. Why do you claim for him and for them what God has negated? This is nothing but excessive ignorance and pure obstinacy. **"And who is more unjust"** is a denial that anyone could be more unjust **"than one who conceals a testimony"** that is established with him and reaches him **"from God."** This testimony is the testimony of Him, exalted is He, to Abraham, peace be upon him, that he was a *ḥanīf* and free of Judaism and Christianity, as was recited just before. The two descriptions were brought to explain the denial and to strengthen it, for the establishment of the testimony with him, and its being from the side of the Most High, exalted in rank, is among the strongest motives for upholding it and the most powerful deterrent against concealing it. The first is mentioned first, although it is later in existence, to observe the path of ascent (*taraqqī*). The meaning is: there is no one more unjust than the People of the Book, since they concealed this testimony and affirmed its opposite by the slander mentioned. The clause is a *tadhyīl* (concluding statement) that establishes what was denied against them regarding their claim of Judaism and Christianity. The attribution of injustice to the mere act of concealment indicates that the rank of one who rejects it and testifies to the contrary is outside the scope of explanation. Alternatively, the meaning is: there is no one more unjust than us if we concealed this testimony and did not uphold it in the context of disputation. In that case, the clause is a *tadhyīl* that confirms what was implied in the words of the Exalted: **"Are you more knowing or is God?"** that they are witnesses to what God testified to, affirming it by what He made them know. On this reading, it is part of the completion of **"Say: We believe"** (verse 136), because it has the sense of making the testimony manifest. On the first reading, it is part of the completion of **"Say: Do you dispute with us?"** because it has the sense of concealing it, which is clearly far-fetched. It is not hidden that the verse contains an allusion to the extreme injustice of the People of the Book in the manner indicated. Using the word "testimony" without restriction, though the intended meaning is the specific testimony mentioned before, is an allusion to their concealment of God's testimony to His Prophet Muḥammad (ﷺ) in the Torah and the Gospel. In *Rayy al-Ẓamʾān*, it is said that (*man*) is the complement of (*aẓlam*), and the statement is in inverted order, as if it were said: "Who is more unjust than God, [namely] one who concealed a testimony that was present with him?" Like your saying: "Who is more unjust than Zayd, from among those who conceal testimony?" The meaning: if Abraham and his sons were Jews or Christians, and then God concealed this testimony, there would be no one among those who conceal testimony more unjust than Him. But since that is impossible given His justice and His transcendence above what is unseemly, we know that the matter is not so. It has also been said that (*man*) is the complement of (*katama*), and the statement involves an omitted *muḍāf* (genitive noun), meaning: he concealed from the servants of God a testimony in his possession. Its meaning is that He, exalted is He, censured them for preventing the conveyance of the testimony of truth to the servants of God and for not delivering it to them. There is no hiding the excessive artificiality and forced interpretation in these two views, and the diminishment of meaning, so let the great Book of God be exalted above them. Moreover, if you look with an eye of fairness, you will see that the second of the first two views is not free from remoteness, because the verse was preceded only by a denial concerning what was attributed to Abraham, peace be upon him, and those mentioned with him. What fits is that the speech is addressed to the People of the Book, not to the Messenger (ﷺ) and his followers, because they affirm what God, exalted is He, has informed of, and know it, so it is not supposed that they conceal it. Also, the concluding statement claimed to be the case is contrary to the apparent meaning.

**"And God is not unaware of what you do."** This is a warning and a threat. It means that God, exalted is He, does not leave your affairs neglected; rather He records your deeds and encompasses everything you do and leave undone, and He will punish you with the severest punishment for it. Included in this is their concealment of His testimony and their slander against His prophets, peace be upon them. It was also read as **"what they do"** in the third person, in which case the pronoun refers either to those who concealed (*katama*), according to meaning, or to the People of the Book.

﴿That was a community that has passed away. They will have what they earned, and you will have what you have earned, and you will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾ This is a repetition of what came before, for the sake of emphasis in warning against what has become firmly rooted in human nature: boasting of one's forefathers and relying on them. It is like saying, "Fear God, fear God." Alternatively, it is a confirmation and establishment of the threat, meaning that God will recompense you for your deeds, your forefathers will not benefit you, and on the Day of Resurrection you will not be questioned about their deeds, but about the deeds of your own selves.

It has also been said that the address in what preceded is to the People of the Book, and that this verse is a warning to us against imitating them. It has also been said that the word "community" (ummah) in the first instance refers to the prophets, and in the second instance to the ancestors of the Jews, because when the people said about Abraham and his descendants that "they were what they were," it was as if they had said, "They were upon the same path as our ancestors." Thus their ancestors came to be in the category of those mentioned, and so it was permissible for the verse to refer to them. The apparent artificiality in this is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 142:

Page 2
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾

That is, the light-minded (al-khifaf al-ahlam), or those who make them foolish by pure imitation (taqlid) and turning away from reflection (tadabbur). What is apparent from them is that it includes all the deniers of the change of the qibla: the hypocrites, the Jews, and the polytheists. It is narrated from al-Suddi that it is limited to the first group, from Ibn 'Abbas that it is limited to the second, and from al-Hasan that it is limited to the third. Perhaps the purpose is to identify a group for whom this verse was revealed, not to restrict the verse to them, because the plural here is preceded by the definite article (al-) and that indicates generality, so it includes all; restricting it to some requires a reason. The announcement of the saying before its occurrence is for preparing the soul for it, since being surprised by what is disliked is more painful, and knowing of it before it occurs is further from agitation; and because in it is the preparation of a reply, and a reply prepared before the need for it is more decisive against the opponent. And in the proverb: "Before the shot, the arrow is feathered." And so that the occurrence after the announcement would be a miracle for him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him. It was also said that the reason for the preposing is instruction and alerting that this saying is a product of foolishness, so one should not care about it nor be pained by it; and it is objected that the instruction and alerting mentioned are achieved by merely mentioning this question and answer even after the occurrence. Al-Qaffal said: the verse was revealed after the change of the qibla, and the word "sayaqulu" (will say) is meant to refer to the past. This is like when a man does a deed and some of his enemies criticize it, and he says: "I know that they will criticize me," as if he means that when it is mentioned once, they will mention it many more times. This is supported by what al-Bukhari narrated from al-Bara' (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Madinah, he prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved to face the Ka'bah, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿We see the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾ up to the end of the verse, and the foolish among the people, who were the Jews, said: ﴿What has turned them from their qiblah which they used to face?﴾ up to the end of the verse." In the narration of Abu Ishaq, 'Ubayd ibn Humayd and Abu Hatim from him, there is an addition: "Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾ etc." The connection of the verse with what precedes it is that the former is a criticism of the fundamentals (usul), while this concerns a matter related to the branches (furu'), and it was not joined by a conjunction to indicate the independence of each of them in its grievousness.

﴿among the people﴾

It is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal). The intended meaning of "people" is the species, and the benefit of mentioning it is to draw attention to the perfection of their foolishness in comparison to the species. It was also said: it means the disbelievers, and the benefit of this is to clarify that this saying reported was not uttered by every single individual of those groups, but rather by their wretched ones who habitually immerse themselves in foul corruption. The first is preferable, as is not hidden.

﴿What has turned them﴾

That is, what thing has turned them away. Its root is from al-wali (proximity), which is the occurrence of the second directly after the first without interval. The interrogation is for denial.

﴿from their qiblah﴾

That is, Bayt al-Maqdis. It is of the pattern fi'lah from al-muqabalah (facing), like al-wijhah from al-wajihah. Its original meaning is the state in which the one facing was, except that in common usage it is a noun for the place faced and turned toward for prayer.

Page 3
﴿which they used to face﴾

That is, while facing it. The relative clause is an attribute of the qiblah. Describing it thus after its attribution to the pronoun of the Muslims is an emphasis of the denial. The basis of this denial with regard to the Jews is their claim of the impossibility of abrogation (naskh), and their dislike of the Prophet's (ﷺ) opposing them in the qiblah, to the extent that they said to him: "Return to our qiblah and we will follow you and believe in you." Perhaps they intended by that nothing but to tempt him, peace be upon him. With regard to the polytheists of the Arabs, the aim was to attack the religion and to show that both facing it and turning away from it were without any reason; to the extent that they used to say: "He turned away from the qiblah of his forefathers, then returned to it, and he will surely return to their religion too." With regard to the hypocrites, it varies according to their origins, since among them are Jews and others. People differed about the duration of his facing Bayt al-Maqdis: in the narration of al-Bukhari it is what you have known; in the narration of Malik ibn Anas it is nine or ten months; from Mu'adh, thirteen months; from al-Sadiq, seven months. Did he face anything else before in Makkah or not? There are two opinions, the more famous of which is the second, and it is also narrated from al-Sadiq (may Allah be pleased with him).

﴿Say: To Allah belong the east and the west﴾

That is, all places and directions are owned by Him, the Exalted, and are equal in relation to Him, glorified is His state; no single one of them is specifically His. Rather, the matter is compliance with His command; so He may obligate His servants to face any place and any direction He wills.

﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾

That is, a level road, which is what wisdom requires of turning toward Bayt al-Maqdis at one time and toward the Ka'bah at another. The sentence is a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for what came before it. The former is an indication of the justification for the turning, and this is an indication of its preference, as if it were said: for the aforementioned turning there is a guidance which Allah the Exalted singles out for whom He wills and chooses from His servants, and He has singled us out with it, so to Him be praise.

﴿And thus We made you a justly balanced community﴾

This is an interjection between two connected statements, which were addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) in passing (istitrad), to praise the believers in another respect. Or it is an emphatic confirmation in response to the denial, namely that this community, and the people of this religion, are witnesses over you on the Day of Recompense, and their testimony is accepted by you. So you are more entitled to follow them and take them as models, and there is no basis for your denial of them. "Thus" (dhalika) refers to the making (al-ja'l) implied by "We made you." It is phrased with something that indicates distance, for the sake of magnification. The kaf (ka) is inserted (muqhamah) for emphasis, and this kind of insertion is common. Its original position is the accusative, as an attribute of a deleted verbal noun (masdar). The original construction is: "We made you a justly balanced community with a making like that making." It was placed before the verb to convey restriction (qasr), and the kaf was inserted, so that it became the verbal noun itself, emphasizing it, not an attribute of it. That is: that wondrous making is what We made you, not another making that is inferior to it. So they said. We have previously mentioned that "thus" (kadhalika) is often used to establish what follows, because the point of resemblance is often in the category and the genus, as when you say: "This garment is like that garment in being silk or cotton." This comparison requires the existence of its like and its establishment within the species. So by way of metonymy (kinayah) it is intended to convey merely the establishment of what follows it. Since the sentence indicates establishment, its meaning exists without it, and it emphasizes it, so it is like a superfluous word. This is the meaning of their saying that the kaf is inserted, not that it is superfluous, as their statement may seem to imply. As for deriving that what follows it is wondrous, this is only because what is not like that does not need explanation. So when it is given importance by establishing it in eloquent speech, it is known that it is a strange matter. Or the distance understood from this is taken as distance in rank. Some people have made "thus" a comparison with "made" understood from the preceding speech, meaning: just as We made you guided, or made your qibla the best of qiblas, [so] We made you a justly balanced community. It is objected to this that the thing compared to is not specific to this community, because the believers of earlier nations were also guided to the straight path, and the qibla of some of them was also the best of qiblas. And the making that is compared is specific to them, so the comparison is not good. Moreover, nothing is understood from the preceding except that turning to each of the two qiblas in its time is the straight path, and the command to it at that time is guidance, and it is not understood from it that their qibla is the best of qiblas. The abrogating (nasikh) does not necessarily have to be better than the abrogated (mansukh). Unless the intention of the speaker is: "As We made your qibla the Ka'bah, which is in fact the best of qiblas, We made..." But even with this, it does not settle the objection, as is evident.

And the meaning of "justly balanced" (wasatan) is excellent or upright. In origin it is a noun for what the sides are equally distant from, like the center. Then it was borrowed for praiseworthy human qualities, because they are the middle points between the blameworthy qualities that flank them from the two extremes of excess and deficiency, such as generosity between extravagance and stinginess, courage between cowardice and recklessness, wisdom between cleverness and dullness. Then it was applied to the one characterized by them, as an attribute is applied to its locus, and it is used equally for the singular and others, because in origin it is a noun that does not require agreement. Sometimes agreement is observed in it. This application is not consistent, as is thought from their saying: "The best of matters is the middle." For it is contradicted by their saying in dispraise: "Heavier than a singer is the middling one," because, as al-Jahiz said, he seals the heart and takes the breath, and he is not good enough to delight, nor bad enough to make one laugh. And their saying: "The brother of the base is the middling one." Rather, it is a term of praise in two respects: in lineage, because the middle of a tribe is its most noble and pure; and in testimony, as here, because it is justice (adalah), which is the perfection of the rational, appetitive and irascible faculties, I mean using them in what is fitting, in the fitting way. And since the knowledge of servants is only given by what is apparent, the jurists established avoidance of major sins and non-persistence in minor sins in its place, and called it justice in the preservation of rights. So let this be remembered. It is widely reported from Abu Mansur that he cited the verse as evidence that consensus (ijma') is authoritative (hujjah). For if what the community agreed upon were false, their justice would be broken by it. And this argument, together with its basis on interpreting "justly balanced" as "just," has the opponent's counter that it may be interpreted as "excellent," so it is not complete. For their being excellent requires their excellence in all matters, and so it contradicts their agreement upon error. It is not free of something:

First: justice does not contradict error in ijtihad, since there is no sin in it. How, when the mujtahid who errs is rewarded?

Second: because the intention is that they are balanced relative to the rest of the nations.

Third: because there is no meaning in the justice of the whole after the certainty of the injustice of each one.

Fourth: because it does not follow that they must be just at all times, but at the time of giving testimony, which is the Day of Resurrection.

Fifth: because what it indicates, after all the arguments, is the authority of the consensus of the whole community, or of all the people of binding and loosing (ahl al-hall wa-l-'aqd) among them, and this is impossible; and it does not indicate the authority of the consensus of the mujtahids of every age, while the one arguing is concerned with that.

It was answered regarding the first and second that justice in the intended sense requires infallibility in belief, speech and action; otherwise the middle would not be achieved between excess and deficiency. And [it was answered] that it is an expression for a similar state arising from the mixing of the middle portions of the faculties we mentioned, so it is not a relative matter.

Regarding the third, [it was answered] that the intention is that among them there are those who are found with this quality. So when we do not know them by their individual identities, we need their gathering, so that those who have this quality are not excluded. But those considered enter into their gathering, and once they enter and error occurs, the justice of the whole is broken.

Regarding the fourth, [it was answered] that "We made" requires the realization of justice in fact, and the use of the past tense with the meaning of the present is contrary to the apparent sense.

Regarding the fifth, [it was answered] that the address is to those present, namely the Companions, as is its original sense, so it indicates the authority of consensus in general.

You know that this last answer does not heal the sick nor quench the thirst, because it is far from the aim of the one arguing. Whoever looks with an eye of fairness will see in the verse nothing more than its indication of the superiority of this community over the rest of the nations, and that does not indicate the authority or non-authority of consensus. Yes, some of the Shi'ah went to the view that the verse is specific to the Twelve Imams, and they narrated from al-Baqir that he said: "We are the justly balanced community, and we are the witnesses of God over His creation, and His proof on His earth." And from 'Ali, may God honor his face: "We are those of whom God the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We made you a justly balanced community﴾." And they said: the saying of each one of those is a proof, let alone their consensus. And that the earth is never empty of one of them until God the Exalted inherits the earth and whoever is upon it. And it is not hidden that without establishing what they have said, it is like trying to pluck thorns with bare hands.

﴿So that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾, that is, over the rest of the nations on the Day of Resurrection, that God the Exalted made clear the ways and sent the messengers, and they conveyed and advised. And this is the goal of the making mentioned, consequent upon it. Imam Ahmad and others narrated from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "A prophet will come on the Day of Resurrection with one man with him, and a prophet with two men with him, and more than that. His people will be called and it will be said to them: Did this one convey [the message] to you? They will say: No. Then it will be said to him: Did you convey to your people? He will say: Yes. Then it will be said to him: Who testifies for you? He will say: Muhammad and his community. Then Muhammad and his community will be called, and it will be said to them: Did this one convey to his people? They will say: Yes. It will be said: And how do you know? They will say: Our Prophet (ﷺ) came to us and informed us that the messengers had conveyed. That is His saying: ﴿And thus We made you a justly balanced community﴾." And in another narration: "Then Muhammad (ﷺ) will be brought and asked about the state of his community, and he will vouch for them and testify to their justice." That is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾.

The preposition "over" (ʿalā) is used because the witness has the meaning of a watcher. Or it is for conformity with what precedes it. The object of the testimony was placed first in the first instance and placed last in the second, because the intention in the first is to establish their testimony over the nations, and in the second the exclusivity of the Messenger being a witness over them. It was also said: "So that you may be witnesses over mankind" in this world, in matters that cannot be sound except by the testimony of just and good people; "and the Messenger will be a witness over you," and will vouch for you and know of your justice. But the reports do not support that in the sense intended.

﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you were upon﴾, and it is the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, according to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that the qiblah of the Prophet (ﷺ) in Makkah was Bayt al-Maqdis, but he did not turn his back to the Ka'bah; rather he made it between himself and it. "Which" (allati) is the second object of "made," not an attribute of "qiblah." The second object is deleted, meaning: a qiblah, as has been said. Abu Hayyan said: making is the transformation of a thing from one state to another, so what is clothed in the second state is the second object, as in: "I made the clay into pottery." So the first object should be the relative pronoun, and the second should be "qiblah," which is what comes to mind upon a beautiful consideration. But careful reflection guides to what we have mentioned, because "qiblah" is an expression for the direction faced for prayer, which is a universal, and the direction you were upon is a particular of its particulars. So the making mentioned is of the kind of making the universal into a particular. There is no doubt that the universal becomes a particular, like the animal becoming a human, but not the reverse. The meaning is that the origin of your affair was that you face the Ka'bah as it is now. "And We did not make" your qiblah Bayt al-Maqdis for any reason "except that We might know" that is, at that time, "who follows the Messenger," that is, follows you in praying toward it. The shift to the third person, together with mentioning him (ﷺ) by the title of messengership, is to indicate the reason for following.

﴿From those who turn back on their heels﴾, that is, who apostatize from the religion of Islam and so do not follow you in it, out of attachment to the qiblah of their fathers. The "from" here is for distinction, like the one in His saying: ﴿And God knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾. The statement is a metaphorical allegory (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), with the common element that one who turns back leaves what is in his hand and withdraws from it in the worst state of return. Likewise the apostate returns from Islam and leaves the proofs in his hand in the worst condition. "We know" is a narration of a past state. "Follows" and "turns back" with the meaning of occurrence, and "making" is a metaphor in view of the fact that the origin was facing the Ka'bah. Or the meaning is: We did not make your qiblah Bayt al-Maqdis except that We might now know, after the change to the Ka'bah, who follows you at that time from among those who do not follow you, like some of the People of the Book who apostatized when the qiblah changed, so that We know the true state of affairs. The summary is that what We did was for an incidental matter, namely testing the people.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 143 (part 2 of 2):

Either at the time of the appointing (al-ja'l) or at the time of the changing (al-tahwil), and it was due to a temporary cause that ends when that cause ends. It has also been said that the intended meaning of "the qiblah" is the Ka'bah, on the basis that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray towards it in Makkah. The meaning would then be: We did not make you turn "except that We might know" the one who is steadfast, whom no doubt misleads and no unrest affects, from the one who turns back in confusion and agitation because of the change, [reasoning] that if the first was true there is no reason to change from it, and if the second is true there is no sense in the command to follow the first. On this view, "making" (al-ja'l) is literal, and "follows" (yattabi'u) indicates continuity, by the indication of its opposite. This view is weakened by the fact that it implies the claim of abrogating the qiblah twice. The verse has been challenged on the ground that it implies the occurrence of knowledge in the future, whereas He, exalted is He, has always been knowing. It has been answered in several ways:

The first: this is by way of illustration (tamthil), i.e., Our doing that is like the doing of one who wishes to know.

The second: the intended meaning is actual knowledge (al-'ilm al-hali), upon which the reward revolves, i.e., so that Our knowledge may relate to it as existing in fact. Thus the knowledge is restricted to the occurring event, and the occurrence returns to the restriction.

The third: the intended meaning is that the Messenger and the believers may know. It is permissible to attribute the act of one of the special prerogatives of sovereignty to him, as a sign of the honour of closeness and distinction. This is like the words of a king: "We conquered the city," when in fact his army conquered it.

The fourth: He has embedded in "knowing" the meaning of "distinguishing" (al-tamyiz), or it is intended to mean distinguishing in external reality, and the name of the cause is used for the effect (ithlaq ism al-sabab 'ala al-musabbab). It is supported by its being followed by "min" (from), as with "distinguishing," and Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) interpreted it thus. It is confirmed by the reading "liya'lama" (in the passive voice), since the intended meaning is: that everyone who comes from him (the knowledge) may know. It is evident that He made His distinguishing and separating between them in external reality so that it is not hidden from anyone.

The fifth: the intended meaning is the reward, i.e., so that We may reward the obedient and the disobedient. Threat in the Qur'an often occurs through the mention of knowledge.

The sixth: "We know" (na'lama) is used for the speaker together with others, so the intended meaning is that knowledge be shared between Me and the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers. It is objected to this view that his opposition is together with Our making, "the one who turns back," and also that associating Allah, exalted is He, with another in a single pronoun is not appropriate. Furthermore, if knowledge is used metaphorically for distinguishing, then "man" and "mimman" are its two objects, direct and indirect. If it is literal, then either it is from perception (idrak) which transitively takes one object, in which case "man" is a relative pronoun in the accusative position as its object, and "mimman" is a circumstantial clause (hal), i.e., distinguished from those who [...]; or it is from knowledge which transitively takes two objects, in which case "man" is an interrogative in the position of the subject (mubtada'), "yattabi'u" is in the position of the predicate (khabar), and the clause is in the position of the two objects.

﴿mimman yanqalibu﴾ (from those who turn back) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "yattabi'u." By this, the objection of Abu al-Baqa' is refuted: that it is not permissible for "man" to be interrogative, because then the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿mimman yanqalibu﴾ would have no complement, since what precedes the interrogative does not govern what follows it; and there is no sense in its being connected to "yattabi'u," while the context indicates this estimation. So it is not meant that there is no indication for it. Then the clause "wa-ma ja'alna" (and We did not make) etc. is coordinated like the two following clauses to the whole question, and the answer is an explanation of the wisdom of the change. It has also been said that it is coordinated to ﴿lillahi al-mashriqu wa-al-maghrib﴾ (to Allah belong the east and the west). This requires saying that he is then commanded to convey the content of this statement in its own words, since the first-person pronoun cannot be applied to his speech, upon him be blessings and peace. But this is far-fetched, as is not hidden.

﴿wa-in kanat la-kabirah﴾ (and indeed it was a great [matter]) means: heavy and burdensome. The pronoun refers to what is indicated by the words "wa-ma ja'alna" etc., of the making, or the turning, or the return, or the change, or the transformation, or the following, or the qiblah. The benefit of taking the feminine into account on some of these readings is to indicate that this turning and change happened once, and that it was specific to the Prophet (ﷺ). It was heavy for them because they had not known it before. As for the claim that the feminine of "kabirah" makes it a new attribute, and that the feminine of the pronoun is due to the feminine of the predicate, so that it returns to the making, or the turning, or the change, without strain, it is a strained claim devoid of benefit. "In" here is the light form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), which serves to emphasise the ruling, and it is nullified from governing what follows it by the intervention of "kana." The "lam" is the separator between the light "in" and the negative. The Kufans claimed that "in" is the negative and the "lam" means "illa" (except). The Basrans said: if it were so, it would be permissible to say "jā'a al-qawmu la-Zaydan," meaning "except Zayd," and this is not permissible.

It was also read as "la-kabirat(un)" in the nominative, so in "kana" the pronoun is that of the matter (damir al-qissah), "kabirah" is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "lahiya kabirah" (it is indeed great), and the clause is the predicate of "kana." It has been said that "in kanat" is superfluous, as in the verse: "wa-ikhwanun lana kanu kirām" (and brothers of ours, they were noble).

It was objected that if it is meant that "kana" with its subject is superfluous, then "kabirah" would stand without a subject, and the light "in" without a clause, and this is outside analogy. If it is meant that "kana" alone is so, and the pronoun remains in the nominative by virtue of being the subject (mubtada'), then there is no basis for its being attached and concealed. It was answered that since it came after "kana," and "kana" in terms of meaning occupies the position of the subject of "kana," it was made concealed, by analogy with the noun, even though it is actually a subject (mubtada') in reality. It is not hidden that this is the utmost of strain and the extreme of far-fetchedness.

﴿illa 'ala alladhina hada Allah﴾ (except for those whom Allah guided) means: to the secret of the legal rulings founded upon wisdoms and benefits, in general or in detail. The intended people are those who follow the Messenger, from among those firm in faith, not wavering, and not turning back on their heels.

﴿wa-ma kana Allahu li-yudi'a imanakum﴾ (and Allah would not let your faith be lost) means: your prayers towards the abrogated qiblah (al-qiblah al-mansukhah). In the authentic report it is narrated that "when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was turned towards the qiblah, they said: O Messenger of Allah, what about those who died while they were praying towards Bayt al-Maqdis? Then this was revealed." So "iman" (faith) is a metaphor through the use of the necessary for the thing necessitating it, and the context is the indication, which is the explanation transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) and other imams of the religion. There is no sense in weakening it, as the practice of some of them indicates. It has been said: the intended meaning is your steadfastness upon faith, or your faith in the abrogated qiblah. The "lam" in ﴿li-yudi'a﴾ is connected to the omitted predicate of "kana," as is the view of the Basrans, and the verb after it is in the accusative by an implied "an" (that), i.e., "he was not intending that he should lose." In directing the negation to the intention of the act there is an emphasis not present in directing it to the act itself. The Kufans said: the "lam" is superfluous and is the governing particle for the verb, and "yudi'u" is the predicate. Its superfluity does not harm its governing, just as the superfluity of prepositions does not harm their governing. By this, the objection of Abu al-Baqa' is refuted, who found it unlikely that "yudi'a" is a predicate on the grounds that the "lam" is the preposition "li," and "an" after it is intended, so the sense would be "Allah was not [the cause of] the loss of your faith," which requires interpretation. Yet you know that what the Kufans held is distant from another aspect, which is not hidden.

﴿inna Allaha bi-al-nasi la-ra'ufun rahim﴾ (indeed Allah is, toward mankind, most kind, most merciful) is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for all that preceded. For His being characterized by these two attributes necessarily requires that Allah does not waste their rewards, and does not leave what is good for them. The "ba'" (with/toward) is connected to "ra'uf." "Ra'uf" is placed before "rahim" because ra'fah (tenderness) is an intensification of a special mercy, namely the removal of what is disliked and the averting of harm, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa-la ta'khudhkum bihima ra'fatun fi dini Allah﴾ (and let not pity for them seize you in the religion of Allah), meaning: do not show pity to them so that you lift the flogging from them. Mercy is more general than that and than bestowal of favour, and averting harm is more important than bringing benefit. As for the statement of al-Qadi, may Allah whiten the face of his conditions (bayyada Allahu ghurrata ahwalih): "Perhaps placing al-Ra'uf first, though it is more eloquent, is for the sake of preserving the rhyme (fawasil)," this is nothing; for the rhyme-endings of the Qur'an are not governed by the last letter as in rhymed prose (saj'), so the consideration is achieved in every case. Also, wherever mercy occurs in the Qur'an it is placed first, even outside the rhyme-endings, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ra'fatan wa-rahmatan wa-rahbaniyyatan ibtada'uha﴾ (tenderness and mercy and monasticism which they invented), in the middle of the verse. The words of al-Jawhari on this point are rubbish and not to be relied upon. And the words of 'Isam: "It is not far-fetched to say: al-Ra'uf is an indication of the intensity of His mercy toward His elite servants, and al-Rahim an indication of mercy toward those below them, so they are ordered according to their rank, and al-Ra'uf is placed first because its object is first in honour and rank," there is no honour and no rank in this, nor even any 'Isam for him, since it is a particularization for which neither the Book, nor the Sunnah, nor usage provides evidence.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read "la-ra'ufun" with a long vowel (madd), and the rest read it without a long vowel, like "nadsin."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 144 (part 1 of 2):

Page 8

﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the sky﴾. That is: We often see the turning back and forth of your face and the shifting of your gaze toward the direction of the sky, awaiting revelation. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would have this thought arise in his heart and would anticipate from his Lord that He would turn him toward the Ka'bah, because the Jews used to say: "Muhammad opposes us and follows our qiblah," and because it was the qiblah of his father Ibrahim (peace be upon him), the earliest of the two qiblahs, and more likely to draw the Arabs to faith. Apparently the Prophet (ﷺ) did not ask his Lord for this, but merely waited; for had he asked, it would have been more apt to mention it. In this is an indication of the perfection of his (ﷺ) courtesy. Qatadah, al-Suddi and others said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would turn his face while supplicating to Allah that He turn him toward the Ka'bah. According to this, the request was indeed made by him (peace be upon him) though it is not mentioned, because the turning of the face toward the sky, which is the direction of supplication, points to it in general. Perhaps this was after he had received permission to supplicate, because the Prophets do not ask Allah for anything without being given permission to do so, since it may be that there is no benefit in it, so it would not be granted, and it would become a trial for their people. This is supported by what is in some reports, that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked Jibril to supplicate to Allah, and he informed him that Allah had given him permission to supplicate. This is how their words are understood. But what I hold is that there is no obstacle to his (ﷺ) supplication, and his request for the turning was for a benefit he was inspired with and a religious advantage he was granted understanding of; this does not depend on seeking permission nor on explicit permission. For whoever has attained nearness through supererogatory acts is independent of that, so how much more so one who has attained the station of nearness through obligatory acts, until he became the chief of his people. Whoever knows the rank of the Beloved counts all that proceeds from him as being in the utmost perfection, together with observing the utmost courtesy. As for his (ﷺ) being rebuked for some of what occurred, it is not due to any deficiency in him nor to a breach of courtesy in his act—far be it—but for hidden secrets and divine wisdoms, known to those who know them and unknown to those who do not. Remaining: Did the Prophet (ﷺ) supplicate explicitly in this incident or not? The apparent view is the second, based on what is established for us from the apparent reports, since in them there is nothing but love for the turning. Al-Bukhari and Muslim in their Sahihs narrated from al-Bara', who said: "We prayed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after his arrival in Madinah for sixteen months facing Bayt al-Maqdis. Then Allah, exalted is He, knew the desire of His Prophet (peace be upon him), and ﴿We have certainly seen﴾ the verse was revealed." There is nothing in the verse that explicitly indicates either of the two matters, and as for allusion, it may suit this, as is not hidden. Furthermore, some people have made qad here to mean diminution, supposing that the occurrence of the turning being little is more indicative of the perfection of the courtesy of the Prophet (ﷺ). It has been objected that one who raises his gaze to the sky once is not said to have "turned his gaze to the sky"; rather it is said "he turned" only when it is continued. Thus multiplicity is necessarily understood from the verse, because the turning (tagallub), which is the intransitive form of taqlib (turning), indicates it. Is the multiplicity a figurative meaning of (qad) or a literal one? There are two opinions, the second of which is attributed to Sibawayh. This multiplicity or paucity here is directed to the turning. Some grammarians mentioned that qad may turn the present tense into the past, and this includes what is here, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah certainly knows what you are upon﴾ and ﴿And We certainly know that your breast is constricted﴾, and beyond that.

﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah﴾. That is: We will surely enable you to face it, from your saying "I appointed him (wallaytuhu) as such" when you make him a governor over it; or: We will surely make you take charge of its direction rather than the direction of Bayt al-Maqdis, from waliya him, meaning he drew near to him, and wallaytuhu, I brought him near. The fa' is for the causality of what precedes it for what follows, and it is in reality attached to an omitted oath indicated by the lam. This promise came in the form of an implied oath for emphasis of its occurrence, because it confirms the content of the sentence sworn to. It came before the command for the joy of the soul at the answer, and then at the fulfilment of the promise, so joy comes twice. Nuwalli is transitive to two objects: the kaf is the first and qiblatan the second. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that you are pleased with﴾, that is: you love it and incline toward it, for the sound purposes you conceal, and which agree with the will and wisdom of Allah, Exalted, in the place of an accusative as an attribute of qiblah. He made it indefinite because nothing preceding it required that it be known, so it would be defined by the article; and there is nothing in the wording indicating that the Prophet (ﷺ) was seeking a specific qiblah.

Page 9

﴿So turn your face﴾. The fa' is for the consequence of the command upon the promise. The specifying of turning with the face is because it is the locus and criterion of facing. It was said: what is meant is the whole body, and it was expressed by it because it is the most noble of the limbs, and by it some people are distinguished from others; or out of regard for what came before. When the verb "turning" is transitive by itself to both objects, it is used in one of the two meanings previously mentioned; when it is transitive to one object, its meaning is turning away from something or toward something, according to the difference of the particle that follows the second object. Here it has this meaning, so (wajjahaka) is the first object. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿toward the Sacred Mosque﴾, that is: toward it, as narrated from Ibn Abbas; or in its direction, as narrated from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face; or in its presence, as narrated from Qatadah. It is an indefinite place-noun, like its explainer, in the accusative of place, and it has the sense of (nahwa, "toward") or (qibala, "in the direction of") or (tilqa', "in front of") the mosque. The meaning of "turn your face" is: toward the mosque. The command was not made a verb transitive to two objects, with shatr being its second object, as has been said, because its placement after the fa' and its being the fulfilment of the promise—that Allah makes the one facing the qiblah, or near its direction, by being commanded to pray toward it—fits with his being commanded to turn his face toward it, not with his making himself face it or be near its direction. For the fitting phrasing of this would be: "So We will command you to turn (fa-lanaamurannaka bi-an tuwalli)". Also, it would then necessarily follow that the obligation is observing the side of the direction, since the Sacred Mosque is the direction of the qiblah; so when the Prophet (ﷺ) is commanded to make himself face the direction of the mosque or near it, he is commanded to face the direction of the direction, or near the direction of the direction. This differs from when turning is taken in the sense of turning away and shatr is taken as an adverb; then the meaning becomes: turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque and in its presence, which is the direction of the qiblah, so he is commanded to be aligned with and to hit the direction. This was said by some of the verifiers. It was also said: shatr originally means what is separated from a thing, then it was used for its side, even if not separated, so it means part of a thing; and in that case it is necessary to take it as the second object. In this there is the point that although it does not then necessitate the obligation of observing the direction of the direction, the lack of its fitness with the fulfilment of the promise remains. The saying that shatr here means "half" is hardly valid. Al-haram means the forbidden, that is, a place in which fighting is forbidden, or one protected from the oppressors' attack. In mentioning the Sacred Mosque, which encloses the Ka'bah, rather than the Ka'bah itself, though it is the qiblah indicated by the sound hadiths, there is an indication that for one who is far away it suffices to face the direction of the qiblah even if he does not hit its exact point. This benefit is not obtained from the word shatr, as a group said, because if it were said "turn your face toward the Ka'bah," the meaning would be: make the turning of the face in a place that is aligned and facing the Ka'bah. This is the position of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ahmad, and the view of most of the Khurasanian Shafi'is, and Hujjat al-Islam preferred it in al-Ihya'. Except that they said: the intention of one turning toward the direction must be the very point in that direction, so that the qiblah is the very Ka'bah. The Iraqis and al-Qaffal among them said: hitting the exact point is obligatory. Imam Malik said: the Ka'bah is the qiblah of the people of the mosque, the mosque is the qiblah of Makkah, Makkah is the qiblah of the Haram, and the Haram is the qiblah of the world. The marfu' hadith of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, contains something indicating this. This disagreement concerns those other than the witness; as for the one who is a witness, it is obligatory for him to hit the exact point by consensus. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, did not restrict the turning to the prayer, because what was sought was nothing other than that, so the mention was dispensed with. It was also said: because the verse was revealed while he, (ﷺ), was in prayer, so his engagement in it dispensed with mentioning it. The one who holds this view relied on what al-Qadi cited following others: "He (ﷺ) came to Madinah and prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen months, then he was turned toward the Ka'bah in Rajab after midday, two months before the battle of Badr, and he had prayed with his companions in the mosque of Bani Salamah two rak'ahs of Zuhr, then he turned during the prayer and faced the spout, and men and women exchanged their rows, so the mosque was named the Mosque of the Two Qiblahs."

Page 10

This, as Imam al-Suyuti said, is a distortion of the hadith, for in the story of Bani Salamah the Prophet (ﷺ) was not the imam, nor was he the one who turned during the prayer. Al-Nasa'i narrated from Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla, who said: "We used to set out to the mosque, and one day we passed while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was sitting on the pulpit. I said: Something has happened, so I sat down. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the sky﴾, the verse. I said to my companion: Come, let us pray two rak'ahs before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) descends, so that we will be the first to pray. We prayed them, then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) descended and led the people in the Zuhr prayer that day." Abu Dawud narrated from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions used to pray toward Bayt al-Maqdis. When this verse was revealed, a man passed by Bani Salamah and called out to them while they were bowing in the Fajr prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis: 'Behold, the qiblah has been changed to the Ka'bah.' So they turned as they were, bowing, toward the Ka'bah." What was mentioned contradicts the sound narrations established among the people of this field, so it is not to be relied upon. Ubayy recited: (tilqa'a al-Masjid al-Haram), and this supports the first view regarding shatr, as is not hidden.

And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it (﴿وحَيْثُ ما كُنْتُمْ فَوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكم شَطْرَهُ﴾) is coordinated (ʿatf) with ﴿So turn your face﴾ and is part of the completion of the fulfillment of the promise. The *fa'* (فاء) is the response of the conditional (jawab al-shart, the answer clause of a conditional sentence), because when *ḥaythu* (حيث) is followed by the restrictive *mā* (ما الكافة, the particle that detaches it from annexation to a following noun), it becomes one of the conditional words (kalim al-mujazah), whereas al-Farrāʾ does not stipulate this for it. *Kāna* (كان) is complete (tāmmah), meaning: in whatever place you are found. The origin of *wallū* (ولّوا) is *waliyū* (ولِيوا). The *ḍammah* was felt to be heavy on the *yāʾ*, so it was deleted; two unvocalized letters then met, so the first of them was deleted and the letter before the *yāʾ* was given a *ḍammah* for harmony. Its pattern is therefore *faʿʿū* (فَعّوا). This is an explicit statement of the generality of the ruling derived from the preceding verse, given out of concern for it, since an address concerning the Prophet ﷺ has a general ruling as long as no indication of its being specific to him appears, peace be upon him. The benefit of generalizing the places, according to what some have held, is to remove the illusion that this qibla is specific to the people of Madinah. It was said: since the turning away from the Kaʿbah was to win over the hearts of the Jews, and it was likely that one would not face it while they were present, he indicated the generalization of the turning to all places. Or it may be said: he stated that turning toward the Kaʿbah is obligatory even with the presence of Bayt al-Maqdis and its people as well, lest it be thought that the presence of Bayt al-Maqdis prevents turning toward the direction of the Kaʿbah when it is absent; so let this be understood. ʿAbd Allah read: "فَوَلُّوا وُجُوهَكم قِبَلَهُ."

﴿Indeed, those who were given the Book﴾, i.e., of the Jews and the Christians, ﴿certainly know that it﴾, i.e., the change, or the turning implied by the word "turning", ﴿is the truth from their Lord﴾, and not other than that, due to their knowledge that Muhammad ﷺ does not command falsehood, for he is the Prophet announced in their books; and their certainty that he does not move each law (sharīʿah) from its qibla to the qibla of another law. As for the Prophet's and Abraham's (peace be upon him) sharing this qibla, it is because they share in the sharīʿah, as indicated by His saying: ﴿Rather, the religion of Abraham, a ḥanīf (ḥanīf: one who turns away from falsehood to pure monotheism)﴾; and their awareness of what their books contained, that he would pray toward both qiblas. This sentence is coordinated with ﴿We have seen﴾ on the basis that the preceding one is meant to explain the origin of the change, while this one explains its truth. It was said: or it is parenthetical (iʿtirāḍiyyah, a clause inserted between sentences) to emphasize the matter of the qibla.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what they do﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the two statements, brought for the promise and the threat to the two groups of the People of the Book who fall under the preceding generality indicated by them, which will come soon, God willing: those who concealed and those who did not conceal. Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read *taʿmalūna* (تَعْمَلُونَ) with a *tāʾ*, so it is a promise to the believers. It was said: on the reading of address, it is a turning (ʿadl) from the third person to the second. On the reading with the *yāʾ* (third person), it is a threat to the People of the Book in general. It was also said: the pronoun in both readings refers to all people, so it is a promise and a threat to two groups: the believers and the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 145:

﴿And if you were to bring to those who were given the Book every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with ﴿And indeed those who﴾ (in the preceding verse), with the common point that each of them confirms the matter of the qibla and clarifies its truth. The intended meaning of the relative (al-mawsul) is the disbelievers from among "those" (ulā'ika), as is shown by the answer (al-jawab). For this reason the explicit noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun. As for one who restricted what preceded to the disbelievers, he made this placement serve to indicate the complete badness of their state in obstinacy, while the Book, which proclaims the truth of what they were arrogant in accepting, is established as contrary to it. ﴿with every sign﴾ and a conclusive proof indicating that your turning toward the Ka'bah is the truth. The lam is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwatti'ah) for an omitted oath. ﴿they would not follow your qibla﴾ is the answer of the oath, standing in place of the answer of the conditional, not the answer of the conditional itself, because it is established that when the oath precedes the conditional, the answer belongs to the oath and not to the condition, if there is no impediment. How much more so when, as here, the fa' is omitted, since it is obligatory in a negated past verb when it occurs as a response (jaza').

This is a consolation (tasliyah) for the Prophet ﹘ may God's blessings and peace be upon him ﹘ regarding their refusal to accept the truth. The meaning is that they did not abandon ﴿your qibla﴾ because of a doubt that you could dispel with an argument; rather they opposed you only out of pure obstinacy and sheer stubbornness. The purpose of the conditional is not to inform that they will not follow you in the most emphatic and forceful manner, such that the meaning would be that they will never follow you at all even if you brought every proof. Thus the objection is dismissed: how could he judge that they will not follow, when a group of them has believed? And one need not say that this applies to particular people, or that the judgment applies to all and not to parts, for that is an unnecessary strain. The attribution of the qibla to his pronoun (may God's blessings and peace be upon him) is because God made him worship by facing it.

﴿And you will not be a follower of their qibla﴾: that is, this will not happen from you, and it is impossible that it would. The sentence is declarative in form and meaning, brought to emphasize the truth of the matter of the qibla with the utmost emphasis, and to cut off the hopes of the People of the Book, for they said: "O Muhammad, return to our qibla and we will believe in you and follow you," as deception from them, may God curse them. It also contains an indication that this qibla will never be abrogated. It has also been said that it is declarative in form but imperative in meaning, and its meaning is a prohibition: that is, do not follow their qibla, i.e., persist in not following it. The qibla is stated in the singular although there are two, for the Jews have a qibla and the Christians have a qibla, because the two share in being false, so the two become one in terms of falsehood; and the antithesis (muqabalah) made this acceptable, because before it is ﴿they did not follow your qibla﴾. It may also be said that the singular is based on the view that the true qibla of both groups was originally Bayt al-Maqdis, and ʿIsa (peace be upon him) did not face the east until he was raised; his qibla was the qibla of the Children of Israel of today. Then after his raising, the elders of the Christians legislated facing east for them, and they justified it by saying that the Messiah (peace be upon him) delegated to them the authority to make lawful and unlawful and to legislate rulings, and that what they made lawful and unlawful, he too had made lawful and unlawful in heaven. They also told them that the east has secrets not found elsewhere, and for this reason the birth of the Messiah was in the east, as His saying the Exalted indicates: ﴿when she withdrew from her family to a place in the east﴾. And the Messiah, when he was crucified, according to their claim, faced the east. It has also been said that one of their monks told them: "I met ʿIsa (peace be upon him), and he said to me: 'For the sun there is a star that I love, which conveys my greeting every day, so command my people to face it in their prayers.' They believed him and did so." This is supported by the fact that facing the east is not found in the Gospel. Ibn al-Qayyim held that the present qibla of both groups was not a qibla by revelation and divine instruction from God, the Exalted, but by their own counsel and ijtihad. As for the Christians, they exercised ijtihad and made the east the qibla; ʿIsa, before being raised, used to pray toward the rock. As for the Jews, they used to pray toward the Ark that was with them: when they went out and when they came to Bayt al-Maqdis, they set it up facing the rock and prayed toward it. When he was raised, they exercised ijtihad, and their ijtihad led them to pray toward its place, which is the rock. There is no command for this in the Torah. Among them, the Samaritans pray toward their mount in al-Sham near the town of Nablus. These two views, if they are sound, are problematic for the claim that it is His, the Exalted, custom to assign each law a qibla. So reflect.

Furthermore, this sentence is more emphatic in negation than the first sentence in several respects: it is nominal in form, the noun is repeated twice within it, and its negation is emphasized with the bāʾ (ب). This was done out of concern for what came before.

﴿And some of them are not followers of the qibla of others﴾: that is, the Jews do not follow the qibla of the Christians, nor do the Christians follow the qibla of the Jews, so long as they remain upon Judaism and Christianity. In this is an explanation of their rigidity in desire and their obstinacy, that this opposition and obstinacy is not specific to you; rather their situation among themselves is likewise. The sentence is coordinated with what precedes, confirming the matter of the qibla by explaining that their denial of it arises from excessive obstinacy, and it is a consolation for the Messenger (may God's blessings and peace be upon him).

﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾: that is, on the assumption of supposition, for otherwise there is no sense in using ʾin (إن), which is set for possible meanings, after the negation has been established in what preceded. The purpose of this supposition is to mention an example of following desire and to mention its ugliness, without regard to the particularity of the one who follows or the one who is followed.

﴿After the knowledge that has come to you﴾: that is, the known that was revealed to you, as shown by the attribution of coming to it; and what is meant is after the truth has become manifest to you. ﴿Indeed, you would then be among the wrongdoers﴾: that is, those who commit gross wrongdoing. This sentence is also a confirmation of the matter of the (qibla), and it contains several aspects of emphasis and exaggeration: the oath, the preparatory lam for it, the conditional ʾin (for supposition), the emphatic ʾinna (إن) with the lam in its scope, the definition of "the wrongdoers," the nominal sentence, and the conditional ʾidhan (إذًا). The choice of "among the wrongdoers" over "a wrongdoer" or "the wrongdoer" is because it indicates that he is established and confirmed, and that he is counted in their company, firmly among them. The application of following to what he called "desire," that is, what no proof supports and no clear revelation was sent down concerning, and the generalization and specification, and making the one who came the very knowledge, and counting this also among these, counting him as one of the wrongdoers, submerged among them and not singled out as he is singled out among the Muslims, for in this is a great exaggeration, indicating a transition from the rank of justice to wrongdoing, and from the rank of distinction and absolute lordship to baseness and obscurity. Had kuntа in "kunta ʿalayha" been taken in the sense of "became" (ṣirta), it would have been higher in value in conveying meaning. You know that the construction requires exaggeration in usage, not obscurity; and even if it required it in this case, the counting would have been counted among those accepted. In these exaggerations there is glorification of the matter of the truth, incitement to follow it, warning against following desire, and magnification of the occurrence of sin from the Prophets. The one of lofty rank needs the renewal of warning against it more, to preserve his rank and safeguard his station, so there is no need to say that the address is to the Prophet while the one meant is someone else.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 146:

﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recognize it﴾ is a subject (mubtada') and predicate (khabar). The intended referents are the scholars, because recognition (al-'irfan) is genuinely theirs. For this reason the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun. Also, the verb (utu) is used of those who have no receptiveness, whereas (atayna) is most often used of those who do have it. It is also permitted that the relative clause be a substitute (badal) for the first relative clause, or for (from among the wrongdoers), in which case the sentence is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the Book" or from the relative pronoun. It is also permissible that it be in the accusative (nasb) governed by (a'ni, "I mean"), or in the nominative (raf') according to the estimate "they". The pronoun in (yaʿrifunahu, "they recognize it") refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), even though his mention has not preceded, because of the words of Allah, ﴿as they recognize their sons﴾, which indicate it. For the comparison of their recognition of him with the recognition of (the sons) is evidence that he is the intended referent. It was also said: the referent is mentioned explicitly in what precedes, by way of direct address, so there is no need to consider a semantic anticipation (al-taqdim al-ma'nawi). The most that can be said is that there is here a shift to the third person (iltifat ila al-ghaybah), to signal that what is intended is not their recognition of him, peace be upon him, in terms of his person and his luminous lineage, but in terms of his being written about in the Book and described in it with the attributes that would confound them, among which is that he would pray towards both qiblahs. It is as if He said: "Those to whom We have given the Book recognize the one We have described in it." It has been answered that although he (ﷺ) was addressed many times in the discourse concerning the (direction of) the qiblah, he is not suited to having the pronoun refer back to him, because this sentence is a parenthetical digression (i'tiradiyyah mustatradah) after the mention of the matter of the qiblah, and its being manifest to the People of the Book is by the common quality of clear knowledge together with the reproach. For this reason it was not joined by a conjunction. So if the pronoun referred to what was mentioned, it would give the impression of a kind of connection, and that would not be fitting. The evidence for the digression is (wa-li-kullin wijhah, "and for each there is a direction"). Yes, if it is said merely as a permissibility, there is no harm in it, since it is a possibility, and it is perhaps the apparent meaning on careful consideration. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the knowledge mentioned in the words of Allah, ﴿after the knowledge that has come to you﴾, or to the Qur'an, on the claim that it is present in minds, or it is for the (Torah) on account of the implication of the preceding discourse. Against this is that the comparison refuses it, because the appropriate thing is to compare a thing with what is of its own kind. So in the view of eloquence (balaghah), it would have been required, in that case, to say "as they recognize the Torah" or "the rock." Also, the restriction to (the People of the Book) requires that this recognition be derived from (the Book), and He, glory be to Him, has informed of the mention of his description, peace be upon him, in the Torah and the Gospel, unlike the other things, for these are not mentioned in them. (The kaf, "as," ) is in the accusative position, being an attribute of an omitted verbal noun (masdar); that is: they recognize him (yaʿrifunahu) by the descriptions mentioned in (the Book), that he is the promised Prophet, in such a way that there is no confusion for them in recognition like (their recognition of their sons), in such a way that their persons are not confused with others. This is a comparison of rational knowledge that arises from reading the heavenly Books with sensory knowledge, in that each of them makes confusion impossible. By (the sons) is meant the males, because they are more constantly in contact with and in company with their fathers, and more attached and more firmly fixed in their hearts than daughters, so the suspicion of confusion of their persons is more remote. The comparison with the recognition of sons is more emphatic than comparison with oneself, because a person may pass through a period of time in which he does not know himself, such as the time of childhood, (unlike sons), for no time passes over him without his knowing his son. As for what is related from Abdullah ibn Salam, that he said about him (ﷺ): "I know him better than I know my son," and Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said to him: "Why?" He said: "Because I have no doubt about Muhammad that he is a Prophet, but as for my son, perhaps his mother betrayed (him)," and Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, kissed his head. Its meaning: I have no doubt in any way about his prophethood, peace be upon him, but as for my son, I doubt his sonship, though I do not doubt his person; and this is the thing compared in the verse. So it should not be imagined from it that (the recognition of sons) does not deserve to be compared with it, because it is inferior to the thing compared, owing to the possibility (of doubt). Nor does one need to say that it suffices for the basis of comparison that it be more well known in the thing compared to, even if it is not stronger, and (the recognition of sons) is more well known than other things; nor to an artificial claim that the thing compared to in the verse is the attribution of "sons" to them in general, whether it is rightful or not. What Ibn Salam mentioned is that he (the son) is in reality his son. ﴿And indeed a party of them﴾, and they are those who did not embrace Islam.

﴿Surely they conceal the truth﴾, which they recognize ﴿while they know﴾ (146). It is a circumstantial clause (jumlah haliyyah). (Ya'lamun, "they know") is either treated as intransitive, in which case it indicates the utmost abomination of concealing the truth and that it does not befit people of knowledge; or the object is omitted, that is (yu'allimunahu, "they teach it"), in which case it is an emphatic circumstantial clause, because the phrase (yaktumuna al-haqq, "they conceal the truth") itself indicates their knowledge of it, since concealment (al-katm) is hiding what one knows. Or (yaʿlamun) means they know the punishment for concealment. Or they conceal it, in which case it is explanatory (mubayyinah). This sentence is a conjunction upon what precedes, being the conjunction of the specific upon the general, and its benefit is to single out the one who opposed and concealed for blame, and to make an exception for (the one who believed) and manifested his knowledge from the ruling on concealment.

[p. 13]

[Page 14]

﴿The truth is from your Lord.﴾ This is a resumed statement, intended to refute those who conceal (the truth) and to confirm the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).
