That is why it is separated (from what precedes it, without a conjunction). The word "the truth" (al-haqq) may be a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is the prepositional phrase. The definite article (al-lam) may then be for previous reference (al-'ahd, the article pointing back to something already known), indicating what the Prophet (ﷺ) brought, which is why it is mentioned with a noun in the apparent form (al-mazhar) rather than a pronoun. Or it may refer to "the truth that these people concealed," and the apparent noun is placed where a pronoun would normally go, to establish its truthfulness and affirm it. Or the article may be for the genus (al-jins), which conveys restriction (qasr) of the genus of "the truth" to what has been established from Allah. That is, "the truth" is like what you (ﷺ) follow, and not anything else, such as what the People of the Book follow. Or the word may be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "it is the truth" or "this is the truth." In that case "from your Lord" is a second predicate or a emphasising circumstantial phrase (hal mu'akkida), and the article is then for the genus, as in ﴿This is the Book﴾. The meaning is that what they conceal is the truth, not what they claim and assert. In this reading there is no sense in the article being for previous reference, since that would lead to repetition, which requires strained interpretation.

Imam Ali (may Allah honour his face) read "al-haqq" in the accusative, as the object of "they know" (ya'lamuna) or as an apposition (badal). "From your Lord" is then a circumstantial phrase (hal) describing it. This achieves a distinction from the first occurrence, even though the wording is the same. He also permitted the accusative with an implied verb, such as "keep to" (alzam). The mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya) together with the possessive pronoun shows a clear kindness toward him (ﷺ), which is obvious.

﴿So do not be among the doubters.﴾ That is, among those who doubt or waver regarding their concealment of the truth while knowing it, or regarding whether it is ﴿from your Lord﴾. The intention is not to forbid the Messenger (ﷺ) from this, because a prohibition concerning something implies that it might occur or be expected from the one prohibited, and that is not to be expected from the sacred presence of the prophetic mission (ﷺ). So there is no benefit in forbidding him. Also, what is legally required (al-mukallaf bihi, the obligation) must be within one's choice, and doubt and wavering are not things that arise by intention and choice. Rather, the intention is either to affirm the matter, so that it is such that no one, whoever he may be, would doubt it, or it is a command to the community to acquire the knowledge that removes what is forbidden, so the prohibition is read figuratively as that command. There is an obvious exaggeration in making the doubting of the community equal to his doubting (ﷺ). You may also say that doubt and the like, though not something one can directly produce, are nonetheless something one can do to remove lingering doubt, and perhaps the prohibition is with this consideration in mind. This is why Allah said ﴿do not be among the doubters﴾ rather than "do not doubt." Whoever thinks that the source of the difficulty is the fact that existence cannot be commanded, because it is not within one's power, and so one is not forbidden from it but only from doubt and wavering, has not come up with anything.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 148:

﴿And for each there is a direction (wijhah) toward which it turns.﴾ That is: for each community of the religion or group among the Muslims, Jews and Christians; or for each people among the Muslims there is a direction and side of the Ka'bah toward which they pray, whether southward, northward, eastward or westward. The tanwin on (kull) is a substitute for the genitive noun that follows it, and (wijhah) comes in its original form; the analogical form would be (jihah), like (iddah) and (zinah). It is a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of the thing toward which one turns, like (al-khalq) in the sense of (al-makhluq). Its extra letters have been dropped, because the verb is (tawajjaha) or (ittajaha), and the verbal noun is (al-tawajjuh) or (al-ittijah); and no form of (wijhah) is used like (wa'd). It has also been said that it is a noun for the place toward which one turns, so the retention of the waw is not anomalous. Ubayy recited (wa-li-kull qiblah).

﴿He is one who turns it﴾ The pronoun (huwa) refers to (kull) in view of its wording. The second object of the participle is omitted; that is, (wajhahu) or (nafsahu), i.e. (musta'qiluha, facing it). It is possible that the pronoun refers to God Most High; that is, God is the one who turns them to it. Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he recited (wa-li-kulli wijhatin) with the genitive construction. Its explanation has been very difficult, to the point that some dared to reject it, and that is a grave error. Some explained it as follows: (kull) was originally in the accusative as the direct object of an omitted verb whose sense is explained by (muwalliha), and the pronoun (huwa) refers to God, Most High, with certainty. Then the lam was added to the explicit direct object because the implied verb is weak in two respects: it is an active participle, and the object precedes it. The other object is omitted; that is, (li-kulli wijhati Allahi mawlan muwalliha, for each direction of God there is a master who turns it). It was rebutted that the lam of emphasis is not added to one of the two objects of a verb that takes two objects; for either it is added to the other, for which there is no parallel, or it is not, in which case preference without a preferring factor follows. Even if it is answered that the grammarians' general statement permits it, the preference without a preferring factor is answered here by the fact that it is preferred through its being placed first. It has also been said that the genitive noun is an object of the mentioned participle, taken as a direct object with the lam being extra; or that the sentence belongs to the category of (ishtighal) with a pronoun. It should not be hidden that these two explanations require, in the first case, referring the genitive pronoun attached to the participle back to the turning, and making it an absolute object, as in the verse: "This is Suraqah reciting the Qur'an" (so that it is not said: how does the participle operate while occupied with a pronoun?). In the second case, it requires saying that the genitive may come under (ishtighal) according to the reading of one who recited (wal-zalimina a'adda lahum). The view that the lam is original, with the preposition related to an omitted (sallu) or to (istabiqu), and the fa' being extra, is far-fetched; indeed I can hardly permit it. Ibn 'Amir recited, and it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: (mawlaha), in the form of the passive participle; that is, he has made that direction turn. Then the pronoun in that case refers to (kull) without any doubt, and it is not permissible for it to refer to God Most High, because the meaning would be corrupted. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Dawud in the Masahif reported from Mansur, who said: "We recite (wa-li-kullin ja'alna qiblatan yardawnaha)."

﴿So race to the good works﴾ (khayrat) is the plural of (khiyrah) with a light pronunciation, and it means the best of everything; the feminine is in view of the quality. The (lam) is for totality, so the definite noun covers the matter of the qiblah and other things. The address is to the believers. (Istibaq) is transitive, as in the Taj; and it has been said to be intransitive, with (ila) after it implied. That is: since it is so, hasten, O believers, to what brings happiness in both abodes, from facing the qiblah and other things, and do not dispute with those who oppose you, since there is no way to unite upon one qiblah, because it is the custom for each people to turn to a qiblah they face. In the command to the believers to seek to outdo one another, there is an indication of seeking to outdo others by way of priority, as al-Sa'd said. It has been said: limiting it to outdoing some of them is an indication that others are not on the path of good, so that a command to race to good would not be conceivable for them. It is also permissible that the (lam) is for previous reference; then the meaning of the good things is the excellent directions that align with the Ka'bah, and in this there is an indication that praying toward the very Ka'bah is more rewarding than praying toward its direction. It has been said that it may be intended as the excellent prayers, and that (istibaq) means haste in them and performing them at the beginning of their times; but this is far-fetched, and more far-fetched is what has been said: the meaning is "race to your qiblah," and it was expressed by "the good things" to indicate that it includes every good.

The Shafi'is used this verse to establish that praying at the beginning of the time, once it has begun, is more excellent; this is a matter already settled in the books of jurisprudence. Some of the gnostics have another reading of the verse: God Most High placed people in varying states in their affairs of this world and the hereafter, so that some are helpers of others: one plants, another grinds, another bakes. Likewise in matters of religion: one collects hadith, another acquires jurisprudence, another seeks the principles. They are apparently free, but inwardly subjected. To this points the saying of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: "Each is made easy for what he was created for." For this reason one of the righteous, when asked about the variation among people in their deeds, said: "All of that is paths to God Most High; He wished to populate them with His servants. Whoever seeks the face of God Most High in every path he takes arrives at Him; but it is fitting to seek the best of those paths, since the ranks differ, the states vary, and the manifestations of the Names are diverse." It has also been said that what is meant is that each person has a qiblah: the qiblah of the nearest ones is the Throne, of the spiritual beings the Kursi, and of the cherubim the Bayt al-Ma'mur; the prophets before you had Bayt al-Maqdis, and your qiblah is the Ka'bah, which is the qiblah of your body; as for the qiblah of your spirit, it is I, and my qiblah is you, as is indicated by: "I am with those whose hearts are broken for My sake."

﴿Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together﴾ ("wherever," ayna) is a noun of place that contains the meaning of a condition, and (ma) is extra, and (ya'ti) is its response. The meaning: in whatever place you are, from places agreeable to your nature like the earth, or opposed like the sky, or places whose parts are gathered like a rock, or scattered places in which what is in them mixes, like sand, God Most High will gather you to Him for the recompense of your deeds: if good, then good; if evil, then evil. The clause gives the reason for what precedes it, and it contains an urging toward racing by means of encouragement and warning. It is in the manner of His saying: "O my son, indeed it, if it be the weight of a mustard seed and it be within a rock or in the heavens or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth" (31:16). Or: wherever you are, from the depths of the earth or the peaks of mountains, God Most High will take your souls to Himself; this is in the manner of His saying: "Wherever you are, death will overtake you, even if you were in towers built up" (4:78); so in it is an urging to racing by seizing the opportunity, for death is not specific to one place over another. Or: "wherever you are" from the opposite directions, right and left, east and west, God Most High will make your prayers, despite the difference of their directions, as if they were toward the very Ka'bah or in the Masjid al-Haram; here "He will bring you together" is a metaphor for making the prayer single in direction, and the benefit of the clause explained in this way is to state the ruling of the command to race. Some said: the address in "istabaqu" is either general to believers and disbelievers, or specific to believers. On the first, the generality is intended here; that is, wherever you are, from places agreeing with the truth or opposing it. On the second, it is specific; that is, wherever you are in prayer, O believers, from the opposite directions, north, south, east and west, after you turn toward the direction of the Ka'bah, God Most High will make your prayers as if they were toward a single direction, because of your unity in the direction you were commanded to face. This is not a thing, as is not hidden.

﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾ (148). Among that is your dying and your living and your gathering. The clause is a conclusion and an emphasis of what came before.

**Translation**

﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with ﴿so race to good deeds﴾. *Ḥaythu* (حيث) is an adverb of place (*ẓarf*) that almost always requires a sentence after it as its complement. The word that governs it is the one that stands in the position of the apodosis (*jawāb*, the main clause of a conditional), not the protasis (*sharṭ*, the conditional clause). Accordingly, here it is connected to *wallī* (ولِّ, "turn"). The *fa'* (فاء) is extra (*ṣila*), serving to draw attention to the fact that what follows it is necessarily linked to what precedes it, just as the apodosis is necessarily linked to the protasis. This is because *ḥaythu*, although it is not a conditional particle, resembles conditional words in indicating generality, so it carries a trace of the conditional. It is not permissible for it to be connected to *kharajta* (خرجت) verbally, even though it is in meaning an adverb of it, lest the requirement of its being followed by a sentence be violated. The meaning is: from whatever place you went out from, turn your face from that place toward, and so on. The *min* (من) is inceptive (*ibtidā'iyya*), because going out is the origin of an extended action, namely walking, and likewise turning is the origin of facing the qibla at the time of prayer, which is itself an extended period.

It has been said that *ḥaythu* is connected to *wallī*, and that the *fa'* is not extra, and that what follows it governs what precedes it, as explained in its proper place. However, there is no justification for combining the *fa'* and the *wāw* (واو). Therefore the better view is that the implied sense is: do what you have been commanded, ﴿from wherever you went out, then turn﴾, so that *fawalli* is coordinated with the implied element. It is also permissible to take ﴿from wherever you went out﴾ to mean "wherever you are and whichever direction you face," in which case *fawalli* is the apodosis of it, on the basis that it is a conditional whose governing element is the condition. (The difficulty of this is not hidden.) The derivation according to a weak opinion, which only al-Farrā' (الفراء) adopted, is that *ḥaythu* is a conditional word even without *mā* (ما), to the point that some said it has not been attested in the speech of the Arabs.

Then, the command to turn is restricted to standing up for prayer, by consensus (*ijmā'*) that facing the qibla is not obligatory at other times.

﴿And indeed it is the truth from your Lord﴾: the pronoun in *innahu* (إنَّهُ), that is, the facing or the redirection or the turning, is masculine according to one of these explanations: because it is a matter among matters; or to make the report masculine; or because the feminine form of the verbal noun is not taken into account; or because of the word with the *tā'* (ة) which has no meaning when stripped of it, whether it is a verbal noun or otherwise. Referring the pronoun back to the preceding command, the singular of "commands," is far-fetched, even though it is near.

﴿The truth from your Lord﴾: that is, the established, which agrees with wisdom.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ (149): so He will reward you for that with the best reward. This is therefore a warning (*wa'īd*) to the believers. It has been recited (*quri'a*, a reading) as *ya'malūn* (يَعْمَلُونَ) in the third-person form, in which case it is a warning to the disbelievers. The sentence is coordinated with what precedes it, and both are parenthetical insertions (*i'tirāḍ*) for emphasis.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 150:

﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it.﴾ This is conjoined (ma'tuf) either to the whole of His saying, ﴿To each there is a direction﴾, etc., or to His saying, ﴿We see your face turning about﴾, etc., as a conjoining of one narrative to another narrative. It is not conjoined to His saying, ﴿And from wherever you set out﴾, which falls under the causal particle fa' (fa' al-sababiyya), indicating that it is consequent upon His saying, ﴿To each there is a direction﴾. That is because it is motivated (mu'allal) by His saying, ﴿So that people will have no argument against you﴾. Although this is a cause of "turn" (wallu), not of an elided element, meaning: We have made known to you the correct direction of your qibla, and the argument in this matter is, as has been said, the following. Yet it is understood from it that it is a cause of "turn" (walli), because when the cutting off of argument through the turning is achieved for the community, its achievement for the Messenger (ﷺ) is by way of priority. If the address is made general to the Messenger (ﷺ) and the community, without restricting it to the community according to the manner of the verse's addresses, then it is a cause for both. He repeated this ruling only because its causes are multiple. The restriction derived from ﴿except that We may know﴾, etc., is relative (idafi) or claimed (idda'i). He, exalted is He, mentioned three causes for the change of direction: first, the magnification of the Messenger (ﷺ) by seeking his pleasure; second, the divine custom that every people of a religion be given a direction; and third, the repelling of the arguments of opponents. The turning toward the Ka'bah repels the Jews' argument that the one described in the Torah has the Ka'bah as his qibla, not the Rock, and that this prophet prays toward the Rock, so he cannot be the awaited prophet; and it repels their claim that he (ﷺ) is a bearer of a sharia and follows our qibla, and between these two there is contradiction. For God's custom, exalted and glorified is He, is to assign each bearer of a sharia a qibla. It also repels the argument of the polytheists that he (upon him be blessings and peace) claims the religion of Abraham yet opposes his qibla. He, glorified is He, left out generalization after specification in the ranking. The third: sufficiency with the generality derived from the cause. He added ﴿from wherever you set out﴾ to prevent the supposition that the state of travel differs from the state of residence, such that the state of travel remains as it was, as in prayer, where two rak'as are added in residence; or that one is free to choose between the two directions, as in fasting.

It may be said: the benefit of this repetition is to give attention to the matter of the ruling, because it is a place of attack, and many oppose it because they do not distinguish between abrogation (naskh) and change of mind (bada'). It has also been said: there is no repetition, for the states are three: being in the Mosque; being in the city outside the Mosque; and being outside the city. The first is carried to the first, the second to the second, and the third to the third. It is not hidden that this is mere whim, for which no proof stands.

﴿Except those of them who have done wrong﴾: an exclusion from "people." It is a substitute (badal) according to the preferred view. The meaning according to those who say that an exception from a negation is an affirmation: so that people have no argument against you, ﴿except those who have done wrong﴾ by obstinacy, for they do have an argument against you. The Jews among them say: he turned to the Ka'bah only out of inclination to the religion of his people and love for his land. The polytheists among them say: it became clear to him, so he returned to the qibla of his fathers, and he is about to return to their religion. Calling this false doubt an argument, though it is an expression for a proof that establishes the intended matter, is because it resembles it, in that they drive it in its course. It is objected that if the beginning of the statement included this, it would require combining the literal and the figurative, and otherwise the exception would not be valid, because argument is specific to the literal. There is no escape except that by argument is meant what is held to, whether true or false. It is answered that he did not exclude their doubt from argument, but rather their persons from people; however, it required calling their doubt an argument by way of the concept of contrary implication (mafhum al-mukhalafa), so there is no need for the beginning to include it. You know that the objector's meaning is: the exception, though it is from people, still establishes for the excepted what was negated of the excepted-from, by the premise that an exception from a negation is an affirmation. If the beginning includes what is affirmed for the excepted, the combination is required; otherwise the exception is not realized according to its requirement, since what is affirmed for the excepted-from is one thing and what is affirmed for the excepted is another. There is no escape from this except that by argument is meant what is held to, or what is in general called argument, so the exception is then realized according to its requirement, because doubt is an argument in this sense, like proof. And the combination of literal and figurative is not required. You may also take argument to mean disputation and contention, as in His saying: ﴿There is no argument between us and you﴾. Then the matter of the exception is clear, though the phrasing is remote from usage when this meaning is intended. It has also been said: the exception is disjunct (munqati'), and it is from affirming a thing by its opposite and establishing it by its negation. The meaning: if they have an argument, it is wrongdoing, and wrongdoing cannot be an argument, so their argument is impossible altogether. This is an affirmation by way of proof, in the manner of His poet's saying:

"There is no fault in them, except that their guest is blamed for forgetting the beloved and the homeland."

Zayd ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, read ﴿ألا﴾ (alā) with a fatha and light emphasis. It is a particle by which speech is opened to alert the hearer to attend. ﴿Those who﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), whose predicate is His saying, ﴿so do not fear them﴾, and the fa' is extra for emphasis. It has also been said that it is for the subject's containing the meaning of a condition. It is permitted that the relative pronoun be in the accusative under the rule of exegetical specification. The well-known view is that "fear" (khashya) is synonymous with "fear" (khawf): meaning, do not fear the wrongdoers, for they have no power to benefit or harm. It is also permitted that the pronoun return to "people," but that is remote.

﴿And fear Me﴾, meaning: fear Me, so do not oppose My command, for I am capable of everything. Some of the people of the Sunna have used the verse as evidence for the prohibition of taqiyya (dissimulation), which the Imamiyya hold, and God willing, its verification will come in its proper place.

﴿And that I may complete My favor upon you, and that you may be guided﴾ (150). Literally, the apparent reading is that it is conjoined to His saying, ﴿so that﴾, as if it were said: turn your faces toward it so that people will have no argument, and so that I complete, etc. Thus it is a cause for what was mentioned, meaning: I commanded you this so that I might gather for you the good of both abodes: in this world, through the manifestation of your authority over opponents; and in the hereafter, through granting you the complete reward. The separation by the exception and what follows does not present a problem, because it is, as it were, not a separation, since it belongs to the scope of the first cause. Indeed, it has been objected that the relation is distant, and that the intention of guidance, which implies hope, is fit to be a cause only for the command to turn, not for the act of the one commanded, as is apparent in the conjoined element. So the apparent meaning is to make it a cause of an elided element, meaning: I commanded you to turn and to fear for the completion of My favor upon you and My will for your guidance. The causal clause is conjoined to the previous causal clause, or conjoined to an assumed cause like ﴿and fear Me﴾, meaning: so that I may protect you, and so that I may complete, etc. Some have preferred this view on the basis of what al-Bukhari recorded in al-Adab al-Mufrad and al-Tirmidhi from the hadith of Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "The completion of the favor is entry into Paradise." It is not hidden that on the first view the statement may be interpreted as meaning: worship, and pray facing the Sacred Mosque, so that I may admit you into Paradise. The hadith does not forbid this; rather it corresponds to it exactly, feather to feather. So its being a preponderating factor for this is far from verification. If it is said that He sent down, near the approach of the death of the Messenger (ﷺ), ﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion and completed upon you My favor﴾, thereby showing that the completion of the favor happened that day, how then did He say years earlier in this verse: ﴿and that I may complete My favor upon you﴾? It is answered that the completion of the favor is at every time in what is fitting to it, so reflect.

صفحة 17

صفحة 18

﴿Just as We sent among you a messenger from among yourselves﴾ is connected to what precedes it. The *kaf* (الكاف) here is for comparison (*tashbih*), and it is in the accusative position as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun. The implied meaning is: "so that I may complete My favour upon you regarding the matter of the qibla, or in the Hereafter, with a completion like the sending of the Messenger." Mentioning the sending while intending the completion is the substitution of the cause for the effect (*iqamat al-sabab maqam al-musabbab*). The phrase *fikum* (فيكم) is connected to *arsalna* and is placed before the direct object to hasten the delight it brings, and because of the greatness of his qualities. It has also been said that it is connected to what follows, meaning: "Remember Me with a remembrance like My remembrance of you through the sending," or "Remember Me in exchange for Our sending among you a Messenger." In that case the *kaf* is for correspondence (*al-muqabalah*), and it is connected to *udhkurūnī* (اذكروني). From this comparison is derived, because two corresponding things are similar and mutually exchanged. The use of the form of the first person plural after the singular is an elegant turn of speech (*iftinan*) and follows the customs of majesty, and it is an indication of the greatness of the favour of this sending and of this Messenger (ﷺ). ﴿Reciting to you Our verses﴾ is an attribute of (*rasulan*) "a messenger." In it there is an indication of the way to establish his prophethood (peace and blessings be upon him), because the recitation by an unlettered man of verses beyond human capacity, in terms of their eloquence and their inclusion of reports of unseen things and of the interests by which the affairs of the Hereafter and of this life are organised, is the strongest proof of his prophethood.

﴿And purifies you﴾, that is, cleanses you from polytheism. This is another attribute of the Messenger. It was mentioned immediately after the recitation, because purification from that arises from the manifestation of the miracle to whomever God, exalted is He, wills to grant success.

﴿And teaches you the Book and wisdom﴾ is an attribute following an attribute. It was placed later, because teaching the Book and making understood what it contains of divine wisdom and godly secrets occurs only after being freed from the filth of polytheism and the impurity of doubt through following. Before that, disbelief is a veil. In this verse purification was placed before teaching, and in the supplication of Abraham it was placed after teaching, because the intended meaning differs in the two places, and every context has its own speech.

It has also been said: purification is an expression for the perfecting of the soul according to the practical faculty, and its refinement, which branches from its perfecting according to the theoretical faculty, which is achieved through teaching that follows recitation. Yet it was placed between the recitation and the teaching that follows it, to signal that each of the consequential matters is a great favour on its own, deserving of gratitude. Had the order of existence been observed, as in the supplication of Abraham (peace be upon him), it would have come to the mind that all of them are one single favour.

It has also been said: purification was placed first at one time and later at another, because it is the final cause for the teaching of (*al-kitab wa-l-hikmah*) "the Book and wisdom." It is prior in intention and conception, but posterior in existence and action. So it was placed first and later, in regard to each of the two aspects. It has been objected that the ultimate aim of teaching is that they become pure from ignorance, not the Messenger's purifying them (peace and blessings be upon him), which is explained as guiding them to that by which they become pure. For that is either by his teaching them or by ordering them to act upon it. So it is either the teaching itself or a matter unrelated to it. The most that can be said is this: teaching, insofar as it results in the removal of doubt and of the other vices, is his purifying them. So it is, in one respect, an end, and in another respect, something ended by it, like "shooting" and "killing" in their saying: "He shot him and killed him." Understand this.

﴿And teaches you what you did not know﴾ (151), of that which there is no way to know except through revelation. The apparent form would have been *wa-ma lam takūnū* (وما لم تكونوا) so that it would be a coordination of a singular with a singular. But God, exalted is He, repeated the verb to indicate that it is a different kind, not sharing with what precedes it at all. So it is a specification after a generalisation, clarifying that his sending (ﷺ) is a great favour. Had it not been for him, creation would have been bewildered regarding the matter of their religion, not knowing what to do.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 152:

﴿So remember Me﴾ through obedience, with the heart and with the body, so that remembrance encompasses the tongue, the heart and the limbs. The first, as in al-Muntakhab, is praise (al-hamd), glorification (al-tasbih), extolling (al-tahmid) and the recitation of the Book of God, Exalted is He. The second is reflection (al-fikr) upon the proofs that indicate the obligations, the promise and the threat, and upon the divine attributes and the lordly secrets.

The third is the total engagement of the limbs in the acts commanded, free of the acts forbidden. Because prayer (al-salah) comprises these three, God, Exalted is He, named it "remembrance" in His saying: ﴿So hasten to the remembrance of God﴾. The people of haqiqa (inner realities, mystical truth) said: the reality of the remembrance of God, Exalted is He, is that everything other than Him is forgotten.

﴿I will remember you﴾, i.e., I will reward you with recompense. He expressed this by "remembrance" for the sake of mushakala (correspondence of expression), and because it is its result and its source. In the two Sahihs (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim) it is reported: "Whoever remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself; and whoever remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than his assembly."

﴿And give thanks to Me﴾ for what I have bestowed upon you. And it is: ﴿wa-ushkuruni﴾ with the same meaning, and "li" (to Me) is more eloquent with "thanks" (al-shukr). He placed remembrance before thanks because remembrance is occupation with His Essence, Exalted is He, whereas thanks is occupation with His blessing, and occupation with His Essence, Exalted is He, is more excellent than occupation with His blessing.

﴿And do not disbelieve (ungratefully)﴾ by denying My blessing and disobeying My command. He followed the command with this prohibition to convey the generality of times. The deletion of the first-person ya' (of "Me") is for lightness, to suit the rhyme of the verse endings (al-fawasil), and the nun of the indicative (nun al-rafi') was dropped due to the jussive (li-l-jazim).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 153:

﴿O you who have believed, seek help through patience﴾ in remembrance (dhikr) and gratitude (shukr) and the rest of the acts of obedience, such as fasting and jihad, and in disregarding the taunts of the stubborn opponents regarding the matter of the qibla (direction of prayer).

﴿And prayer﴾, which is the foundation and that which brings about the perfection of drawing near to Him, exalted is He.

﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾ (153). This is a special companionship of aid and support. He did not say "with those who pray," because if He is with the patient, He is with those who pray all the more, since prayer includes patience.

[Page 20]

**"And do not say"** (﴿ولا تَقُولُوا﴾): this is conjoined to **"and seek help"** (﴿واسْتَعِينُوا﴾), etc., and is introduced to clarify that there is no harm in what the believers are commanded to do, and that martyrdom, to which patience may sometimes lead, is an everlasting life.

**"Concerning those who are killed in the way of God"** (﴿لِمَن يُقْتَلُ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾): that is, in His obedience and in raising His word, and they are the martyrs (*shuhada*). The *lam* here indicates cause (*ta'lil*), not reporting (*tabligh*), because they did not report the martyrs' saying: **"They are dead"** (﴿أمْواتٌ﴾), that is, they are dead.

**"Rather, they are alive"** (﴿بَلْ أحْياءٌ﴾): that is, rather, they are alive. The clause is conjoined to "do not say" as a rejection (*idrab*) of it. It is not a conjunction of a singular to a singular, which would place it within the scope of the verb "say," so that the meaning would be "Rather, say: 'alive'." This is because the intended purpose is to affirm life for them, not to command them to say that they are alive, although that too is correct.

**"But you do not perceive"** (﴿ولَكِنْ لا تَشْعُرُونَ﴾): that is, you do not sense or comprehend by the senses what their condition is, because it is among the states of the *barzakh* (intermediate state) which are not disclosed, and there is no way to know them except through revelation. The nature of this life has been disputed. Many of the early scholars (*salaf*) held that it is real, with the soul and the body, but we do not perceive it in this world. They based this on the context of the saying of Exalted God: **"With their Lord they are provided for"** (﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ يُرْزَقُونَ﴾), and on the fact that a spiritual life which is not of the body is not peculiar to them, so they would have no distinction thereby over others. Some held that it is spiritual, and that their being provided for does not contradict this. It is narrated from al-Hasan that the martyrs are alive with God, Exalted is He, their provisions being presented to their souls, so that refreshment and joy reach them, just as the Fire is presented to the souls of Pharaoh's family morning and evening, so that pain reaches them. Thus the arrival of this spirit at the spirit is the provision and the distinction; it is not merely life, but along with what is joined to it of their being specially near to God, Exalted is His majesty, and of greater delight and honor. Al-Balkhi held the negation of actual life for them absolutely, and he removed the nominal sentence, which indicates continuity encompassing all times from the time of killing to what has no end, from its apparent meaning. He said: the meaning of **"but they are alive"** is that they will be alive on the Day of Resurrection, and they will be rewarded with the best reward. So the verse is like **"Indeed the righteous are in bliss"** and **"Indeed the wicked are in Hellfire."** The benefit of informing of this is the refutation of the polytheists, who said: the companions of Muhammad kill themselves and leave the world without benefit, and waste their lives. So it is as if it were said: the matter is not as you claim; rather, they live and they depart. Some held that the affirmation of life for them is life by judgment (*hukmiyya*), through what they gained of good remembrance and lofty praise, as is narrated from Ali, may God honor his face: "The keepers of wealth perish, while the scholars remain as long as time remains; their persons are absent, but their traces are present in hearts." It is related from al-Asamm that the intended meaning of death and life is misguidance and guidance; that is: do not say they are dead in religion, astray from the straight path, but rather they are alive through obedience, bearing its burdens. It is not hidden that these views, other than the first two, are extremely weak, indeed utterly false. The well-known preference is for the first view. It is attributed to Ibn Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, al-Hasan, Amr ibn Ubayd, Wasil ibn Ata, al-Jubba'i, al-Rummani and a group of exegetes (*mufassirun*). However, they differ regarding what is meant by the body. It is said: it is this body whose structure was destroyed by killing, and God, Exalted is He, is not incapable of giving it a life which becomes the cause of sensation and perception, although we see it as a decayed remnant cast upon the earth, which does not act, and in which no sign of the living appears. For there came in a hadith: "Indeed the believer has his sight extended, and it is said to him: sleep the sleep of the bride," though we do not witness that, since the *barzakh* is another *barzakh*, far removed from our minds and the perception of our faculties. It is also said: it is another body in the form of a bird, in which the soul is attached. They cite what Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Abdullah ibn Ka'b ibn Malik, who said: the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "Indeed the souls of the martyrs are in the forms of green birds, hanging in lamps of Paradise until God returns them on the Day of Resurrection." This is not contradicted by what Malik, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from Ka'b ibn Malik that the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, said: "Indeed the souls of the martyrs are in the bellies of green birds which eat from the fruit of Paradise, or the trees of Paradise." Nor by what Muslim narrated in his Sahih from Ibn Mas'ud, traced to the Prophet: "Indeed the souls of the martyrs are with God in the crops of green birds which graze in the rivers of Paradise wherever they wish, then they return to lamps beneath the Throne." For their being in the bellies or in the crops is compatible with their being in those forms, since the beholder sees nothing but them. It is also said: it is another body in the forms of their bodies in this world, such that if a beholder saw one of them he would say: "I saw so-and-so." This view was held by some of the Imamiyya, and they cited what Abu Ja'far narrated with a chain going back to Yunus ibn Zabyan, who said: I was sitting with Abu Abdullah, and he said: "What do people say about the souls of the believers?" I said: "They say: in the crops of green birds, in lamps beneath the Throne." Abu Abdullah said: "Glory be to God! The believer is too honored by God, Exalted is He, for his soul to be placed in the crop of a green bird. The believer is delighted when God takes him; He makes his soul into a form like his form in this world, so they eat and drink, and when the newcomer arrives among them, they recognize him in that form which he had in this world." The argument from this, if by "believers" is meant the martyrs, is evident; and if what is meant is all who believed, then the condition of the martyrs is known from it, and that their souls are not in crops by a fortiori reasoning. In my view, life in the *barzakh* is established for everyone who dies, whether martyr or other, and that souls, though they are substances subsisting in themselves and distinct from what the body perceives, there is no obstacle to their being attached to a *barzakhi* body distinct from this dense body. This is not transmigration (*tanasukh*) which the people of misguidance held. Transmigration would only occur if it did not return to the body of its own self, in which it was, and return is attained in the Paradisal existence. Indeed, even if we say it does not return to it and we hold the return to a body similar to what was in this world, whether or not it contains the original constituent parts, this does not necessarily entail transmigration either; for they said it in a manner by which they denied the gathering and the return, and affirmed in it the eternity of the world of generation and corruption. And the souls of the martyrs have this attachment established for them in a manner by which they are distinguished from others, either in the very fact of attachment, or in the very life, based on the view that it is of the ambiguous (*mushakkik*) and not of the univocal (*mutawatii*) type, or in the very thing to which it is attached, together with what is joined to that of joy, gladness and bliss befitting them. What the heart inclines to is that those other bodies have a complete formal resemblance to these bodies, while their matter is different and their parts diverse, for there is a difference between the two worlds, and how far apart are the two *barzakhs*. The hadiths about birds can be understood as likening these tender, fresh bodies, in the swiftness of their movement and their going wherever they wish, to green birds, and the "form" can be taken as "attribute," just as it is taken so in the hadith: "Adam was created in the form of the Merciful." The objection of Abu Abdullah, may God be pleased with him, to what preceded is to be understood as what the common people grasp from the apparent wording; and for the sake of clarification suitable to the common people of his time, he turned from it to an expression in which no trace of objection appears, as appears in the apparent wording of the hadith. So much so that some scholars, for this reason, read *fi* (in) in it as *ala* (upon). This is either ignorance or feigned ignorance, of the fact that the smallness or narrowness of the container, if it existed in what we are discussing, would not harm the soul in any way, nor would it negate its bliss. Or they assumed that this form has a soul other than the soul of the martyr, so two souls cannot be attached to it; but the matter is contrary to what they suppose. If you wish, you may say that the soul itself takes the form of an image, for souls are of extreme subtlety, and they have the power of embodiment, as indicated by the appearance of the Trustworthy Spirit (Gabriel), peace be upon him, in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi, may God be pleased with him. As for the view that this decayed body lives while its structure is destroyed, its parts scattered and its shape gone, although that is not far from the power of He who originates creation and then restores it, nevertheless there is not great need for it, nor great grace in it, nor great favor, nor a great blessing. Rather, there is in it nothing but causing the weak of the believers to fall into doubts and illusions, and imposing upon them, without need, belief in what they consider the saying of one of foolish dreams. As for what is related of the witnessing of some martyrs who were killed hundreds of years ago, and that to this day their wounds bleed when the bandage is removed from them, this is among what Hayyan ibn Bayyan narrated. It is nothing but a tale of superstition, a speech which testifies against those who believe it to the presence of folly.

Then, the prohibition to the believers from saying about the martyrs "they are dead" is either to repel the impression that they are equal to others in that *barzakh*, while that is a particularity for them even if they share in the bliss; indeed, some of God's near servants excel them, and it may be said of them such a thing. Or it is to protect them from uttering a word which the enemies of the religion and the hypocrites said about those noble ones, intending thereby that they were deprived of bliss and never experienced it. The verse does not contain a prohibition against attributing death to them absolutely, such that they never tasted it at all, not even for a blink of an eye. Otherwise He, Exalted, would have said: "Do not say of those who are killed in the way of God: they died." Since He turned from that to what you see, it is known that they were distinguished, after they were killed, by a life befitting them, which prevents it from being said of them that they are dead. God, Glorified is He, turned from "were killed" (*qutilu*), expressed in Al-'Imran, to "is killed" (*yuqtalu*) for the sake of emphasis in the prohibition; and the emphasis of the verb in that surah serves the same purpose as this turn here, as one of our learned contemporary friends established. The verse was revealed, as Ibn Mandah narrated from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him, concerning the martyrs of Badr, who were, as to their number, eight from the Ansar and six from the Muhajirun, may God be pleased with them all.

[p. 23]

﴿And We will surely test you﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf, grammatical conjunction) with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and seek help﴾ etc., as a coordination of one content over another content. The common element is that the content of the first is a call to patience, and the content of the second is an explanation of its occasions. The meaning is: We will surely treat you in the manner of one who is tested and examined. Thus there is an allegorical metaphor (istiʿāra tamthīliyya), because testing (ibtilāʾ) in its literal sense is for the acquisition of knowledge, and that is impossible for the All-Subtle, the All-Aware. The address is general to all the believers. It was said that it is for the Companions alone, and it was said that it is for the people of Makkah alone.

﴿with something of fear and hunger﴾ means: with a small amount of that. The smallness is relative to what He protected them from, of what did not befall them. He, glory be to Him, informed them of it before it occurred, so that they might prepare their souls for it, since the surprise of what is disliked is harder. Their certainty increases when they witness it, in accordance with what He informed them of, and so that they know it is a slight matter with a praiseworthy outcome.

﴿and loss of wealth, lives and fruits﴾ is coordinated either with (something) (shayʾ), and this is supported by the agreement in indefiniteness and by the clarification coming after each item; or with (fear) (al-khawf), and this is supported by the closeness of the coordinated item to what it is coordinated with and its inclusion under (something). By (fear) is meant fear of the enemy, and by (hunger) is meant drought, by mentioning the cause in place of the effect, as Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said. By the loss of (wealth) is meant the destruction of livestock; by the loss of (lives) is meant the departure of loved ones through killing and death; and by the loss of (fruits) is meant their ruin through calamities. It specified them explicitly even though they are among (wealth), because they may not be owned property.

Al-Imam al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, said: (fear) is fear of Allah, the Exalted, (hunger) is the fasting of Ramadan, the loss of (wealth) is the zakat and charities, the loss of (lives) is illnesses, and the loss of (fruits) is the death of children. The use of (fruit) for a child is a well-known metaphor, because a fruit is everything that is gained and obtained, as it is said: the fruit of knowledge is action.

Al-Tirmidhi transmitted, and graded as good (ḥasan), from the hadith of Abu Musa, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "When the child of a servant dies, Allah, the Exalted, says to the angels: Have you taken the child of My servant? They say: Yes. He says: Have you taken the fruit of his heart? They say: Yes. Allah, the Exalted, says: What did My servant say? They say: He praised You and said 'Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi rajiʿun.' Allah, the Exalted, says: Build for My servant a house in Paradise, and name it the House of Praise."

I object to what the Imam said, after accepting that the verse was revealed before the obligation of fasting and zakat, on the ground that the fear of Allah, the Exalted, has always filled the hearts of the believers before the revelation of the verse, and likewise illnesses and the death of children existed before. So there is no sense in the promise of testing with these things. Likewise there is no sense in describing zakat, which is growth and increase, as a loss.

It is answered that the hearts of the believers being filled with fear beforehand does not preclude their being tested in the future with another fear, since fear increases with the descent of verses. Likewise illnesses and the death of children are recurring matters through which testing can occur in later times. The description of zakat as a loss is because it appears as a loss in form, though it is an increase in meaning. So at the time of testing it is called a loss, and at the time of the command to pay it, it is called zakat, making its payment easy.

﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ (155). It is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone from whom good tidings can come. The sentence is coordinated with what precedes it, as a coordination of content over content, without regard to the difference between declarative and imperative form. The common element is evident. It is as if it were said: the testing is established for you, and likewise the good tidings, but only for whoever among you is patient. It was also said that it depends on an omitted element, meaning: warn those who are distressed, and give good tidings.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verses 156–157:

In the description of the patient (al-sabirun) by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who, when a calamity strikes them, say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return."﴾ 156, there is an indication that the reward belongs to the one who is patient at the moment of the calamity's striking, as in the report: "Patience is only at the first shock." Calamity (musibah) covers whatever harm befalls a person in his self, his wealth or his family, whether the harm is small or great, even the prick of a thorn, the sting of a gnat, the snapping of a sandal strap, or the extinguishing of a lamp. The Prophet (ﷺ) himself said the words of return (istirja') over such things, and said: "Everything that harms the believer is a calamity for him and a reward." Patience is not merely saying the words of return with the tongue; rather, patience is with the tongue and with the heart, by bringing to mind what he was created for: knowledge of Allah, Exalted is He, and perfecting his soul, and that he is returning to his Lord and going back to Him for everlasting survival, and departing from this perishing world and leaving it in its imperfect state. He remembers the blessings of Allah, Exalted is He, upon him, so that he sees that what He gave him is many times what was taken from him, and thus he eases his soul and submits to Him. Patience is among the special qualities of the human being, because in it reason and desire contend; and the words of return are among the special qualities of this community. Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "My community has been given something that no other nation has been given: that they say at the time of calamity: 'Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return.'" And in another narration: "This community has been given at the time of calamity something that the prophets before them were not given. 'Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return.' Had the prophets before them been given it, Jacob would have been given it when he said: 'Alas for Joseph!'" It is recommended that after the words of return one says: "O Allah, reward me in my calamity and give me something better than it," for Muslim reported from Umm Salamah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "No servant who is struck by a calamity says: 'Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return. O Allah, reward me in my calamity... etc.,' except that Allah, Exalted is He, rewards him in his calamity and gives him something better than it." She said: When Abu Salamah died, I said as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had commanded me, and Allah, Exalted is He, gave me in his place something better than him: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The object of (bashshir) is omitted; that is, "with a great mercy and abundant kindness," as is shown by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord, and mercy.﴾ Salah (blessing) originally, according to what most lexicographers hold, is supplication (du'a'), and when it comes from Allah it is mercy. It is also said to be praise, or glorification, or forgiveness. Imam al-Ghazali said: it is care for a matter. The meaning that fits what is intended here, whether literal or figurative, is praise and forgiveness, because intending mercy would entail repetition, and it would contradict what is reported: "How excellent are the two gifts for the patient: the salah and the mercy." Taking it to mean glorification and care for the matter is rejected by the plural form. Then, if we allow the intention of both meanings by permitting the general use of the homonym, or by combining literal and figurative senses, or by combining two figurative senses, both of the mentioned meanings can be intended; otherwise one of them is intended.
Page 24
Mercy has already had its meaning explained. The use of (upon, ʿalā) indicates that they are immersed in this, and it has overtaken and enveloped them, so it is more emphatic than (li). The plural ﴿blessings﴾ indicates that it includes many kinds, according to the differing attributes by which praise is given and the sins with which forgiveness is connected. It is also said that it indicates that the intended meaning is blessing after blessing, in the manner of the dual in (labbayka wa-sa'dayka). It is objected that the use of the plural merely for repetition has no parallel. The nunation in it, and likewise in what is conjoined to it, is for magnification. Mentioning the title of Lordship together with the attachment to their pronoun serves to show exceptional care for them. (Min, from) is for origin, and it is also said to be partitive; there is an omitted noun: "from the blessings of their Lord." The sentence is nominal to indicate that the descent of this upon them occurs both in this world and in the Hereafter. Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, as a marfu' report: "Whoever says the words of return at the time of calamity, Allah repairs his calamity, makes his final outcome good, and gives him a righteous successor whom He is pleased with."

﴿And those⟩ is an indication, like the preceding, to the patient described with the qualities mentioned; the repetition is to show complete care for them. It may also be an indication to them in respect of their possessing the blessings and mercy mentioned, which are consequent upon what preceded. According to the first view, the guidance in His words, Glorified is His affair: ﴿They are the guided ones⟩ is guidance to truth and right in general. The sentence confirms what came before, as if it were said: "And those are the ones specially guided to every truth and right, and for this reason they said the words of return and submitted to the decree of Allah, Exalted is He." According to the second view, it is guidance and attainment of aims, and the meaning is "those are the successful ones" in their religious and worldly aims, for whoever attains the purification and mercy of Allah, Exalted is He, misses no aim.

* * *

From the path of allusion and esoteric interpretation: ﴿O you who believe⟩ — the direct faith (al-iman al-'iyani) — ﴿seek help⟩ through patience with Me at the onslaughts of the manifestations of My greatness and My majesty, and the prayer, that is, true witnessing.

﴿Indeed Allah is with the patient⟩ who are able to bear the manifestations of My lights. ﴿And do not say of those⟩ who are made annihilated, slain in the path of tawhid, ﴿they are dead⟩, that is, helpless wretches, ﴿rather they are alive with their Lord⟩ in the true, everlasting life, witnesses for Allah, Exalted is He, enabled by Him. ﴿But you do not perceive⟩ because of the blindness of your insight and your deprivation of the light by which hearts see the realities of the world of holiness and the truths of spirits. ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear⟩, that is, My fear, which necessitates the breaking and defeat of the self, ﴿and hunger⟩, which necessitates the wearing down of the body, weakness of powers, lifting of the veil of desire, and narrowing of the channels by which Satan reaches the heart; ﴿and loss of wealth⟩, which is the material of desires that strengthen the self in its increasing rebellion; ﴿and lives⟩, which dominate the heart by their qualities, or the lives of loved ones to whom you turn so that you are cut off toward Me; ﴿and fruits⟩, that is, the sensual delights, so that you may take pleasure in the unveilings, the heart-knowledges and the spiritual witnessings when your inner states are purified and the gold of your hearts is refined by the fire of discipline. ﴿And give good news to the patient⟩ who are with Me, or who are detached from their cherished things, with the sweetness of My love, ﴿who, when a calamity strikes them⟩ from My disposings of them, they witness the traces of My power, indeed the lights of the manifestations of My attribute, and they submit and are certain that they are My possession, which I dispose of by My manifestations, and they are annihilated in Me and witness their perishing by Me, and so they say: "Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return." ﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord⟩, by the existence bestowed upon them after annihilation, upon which My attributes pour down and upon which My lights shine; ﴿and mercy⟩, that is, guidance by which they guide My creatures and whoever wishes to turn toward Me. ﴿And they are the guided ones⟩ by Me, who arrive at Me after being freed from their existence, which is the greatest sin in My sight.
