﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾. When He, glorified is He, alluded earlier to jihad, He followed that with an explanation of the landmarks of Hajj. It is as if He combined Hajj and warfare, since both involve hardship to the self and the loss of wealth. It was also said: when He mentioned patience, He followed it with a discussion of Hajj, because of the matters in it that people need.

Al-Safa (the smooth rock), originally, is a smooth stone, derived from safa, yasfu, meaning "to be pure" or "to be clear." Its singular is safah, like hasa and hasah, and nawa and nawah. It was also said that al-Safa is a collective noun. Al-Mubarrad said: it is any rock not mixed with anything else, such as clay or dust. Its root is from the letter waw, because one says in its dual form safwan, and it is not permissible to incline it (imalah). Al-Marwah, originally, is a white, soft stone. Al-marw is a dialectal form of it. It was also said that it is a plural, like tamrah and tamr. Then, by custom, the two became proper names for two known places in Makkah, by predominance of usage, and the definite article is obligatory in both.

It was also said that al-Safa was so named because Adam, the chosen one of Allah, the Exalted, sat on it, and al-Marwah was so named because his wife Hawwa' sat on it. The word shaʿa'ir (symbols) is the plural of shaʿirah or shiʿarah, meaning a sign. What is meant by them is either the markers of acts of worship or the rites of Hajj. It was also said: the meaning is that circumambulating between these two mountains is one of the signs of the religion of Allah, the Exalted, or that they are among the places where His religion is established, or among its signs, by which worship is performed through running between them, and not among the signs of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic ignorance).

﴿So whoever makes Hajj to the House or performs ʿUmrah﴾. Hajj, linguistically, means intending something in general or intending something great. Some scholars restricted it to being performed repeatedly. ʿUmrah means visitation, derived from ʿimarah (populating), as if the visitor populates the place by visiting it. Both were specifically applied in the Shariʿah to the intention directed at the House and visiting it in the two specific forms. The House (al-Bayt) is outside the concept, and the relation is taken into it, so it must be mentioned. Therefore it is not objected that the House is taken into the meaning of both, so it would suffice to say "whoever makes Hajj or performs ʿUmrah." There is no need to strain by saying that it is taken into the meaning of the two nouns but outside the meaning of the two verbs. On the assumption that it is taken into the meaning of both, the abstraction is considered so that the honor of the House may appear.

﴿there is no sin upon him for going around them﴾. That is: there is no sin upon him in circumambulating. The root of junah (sin) is inclination, and from it comes ﴿and if they incline toward peace﴾. The term was named this because it is an inclination from truth toward falsehood. The original form yattawwafa is yatatawwafa, and the taʾ was assimilated into the ṭaʾ. The occasion of revelation is what is authentically related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that on al-Safa there was an idol in the form of a man called Isaf, and on al-Marwah there was an idol in the form of a woman called Nailah. The People of the Book claimed that the two had committed adultery in the Kaʿbah, so Allah, the Exalted, transformed them into two stones, and they were placed on al-Safa and al-Marwah as a lesson. When the period lengthened, they were worshipped besides Allah, the Exalted. So when the people of the Jahiliyyah circumambulated between them, they would touch the two idols. When Islam came and the idols were broken, the Muslims disliked circumambulating between them because of the two idols, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse. From this is known the answer to what seems to be an objection: that there is no point in negating sin after establishing that both are among the symbols. Indeed, they may not even be mutually entailing, since the lowest level of the first is recommendation (nadb), and the highest level of the second is permissibility (ibahah). The consensus (ijmaʿ) has been reached on the legislation of circumambulating between them in Hajj and ʿUmrah, due to the definitive indication of the negation of sin concerning it. However, they differed regarding whether it is obligatory. It is related from Ahmad that it is a Sunnah, and this was the view of Anas, Ibn ʿAbbas, and Ibn al-Zubayr, because the negation of sin indicates permissibility, and what is understood from it is the absence of obligation, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿there is no sin upon the two of them if they return to one another﴾. That is not permissible by consensus. And due to the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿from the symbols of Allah﴾, so it is recommended. This was refuted by saying that the negation of sin, although it indicates permissibility, from which the absence of obligation is understood, nevertheless is compatible with obligation, so it neither removes it nor negates it, and that is the point. Perhaps there is here a proof that indicates obligation, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿there is no sin upon you if you shorten the prayer﴾. Perhaps this is like your saying to one who has the obligation of the noon prayer, for example, and thinks it is not permissible to perform it at sunset, and he asks about that: "There is no sin upon you if you pray it at this time." This is a correct answer, and it does not imply the negation of the obligation of the noon prayer.

From al-Shafiʿi and Malik: it is a pillar (rukn), and this is also a narration from Imam Ahmad. They argued with what al-Tabarani related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked, and he said: 'Indeed Allah, the Exalted, has prescribed for you the running (saʿy), so run.'" The position of our Imam Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) is that it is obligatory (wajib), and it is compensated by a sacrifice (damm), because the verse indicates only the negation of sin, which entails permissibility, and being a pillar is not established except by a definitive proof, and none exists. The hadith only indicates the establishment of the ruling as a cause and as something fixed in the mind, and it does not indicate that it reaches the level of obligation to the extent that permissibility is lost if it is missed, because the pillar status is established. Its authenticity is speculative (zanni al-sanad), and even if its indication is taken to be definitive (qatʿi al-dalalah), it does not indicate obligation (fardiyyah). As for what Muslim related from ʿAisha, that she said: "By my life, Allah has not completed the Hajj of one who does not run between al-Safa and al-Marwah, nor his ʿUmrah," there is no proof in it for obligation either. Even if we grant it, it is her own view, and the matter is one of ijtihad, so it does not bind others. Moreover, it is opposed by what al-Shaʿbi related from ʿUrwah ibn Mudarris al-Taʾi, that he said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) at Muzdalifah, and I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I came from the mountain of Tayy. I did not leave a mountain without standing upon it. So is there Hajj for me?' He said: 'Whoever prays this prayer with us, and stands with us at this standing, and had reached ʿArafah before that, by night or by day, his Hajj is complete, and he has fulfilled his obligations (tafath).'" So he informed of the completion of his Hajj, and there is no mention in it of running between them. Had it been one of its obligations, he would have explained it to the questioner, since he knew of his ignorance.

Ibn Masʿud and Ubayy recited: (an la yatawwafa), but this cannot serve as support for the first view, because it is an irregular reading (shadhdh) on which no practice is based, along with what opposes it, and because the "la" may be superfluous, as the context suggests.

﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾. That is: whoever submits to obedience with goodness, or with good, or bringing good, whether obligatory or voluntary. It is coordinated with ﴿whoever makes Hajj﴾, etc., emphasizing the matter of Hajj, ʿUmrah, and circumambulation, as emphasis of a universal ruling for a particular case. Or it means: whoever volunteers in good, or with good, or bringing good, from Hajj or ʿUmrah or circumambulation, based on the context. In this case the sentence is intended to indicate the legitimacy of voluntary acts with the three matters. The benefit of "good" on both interpretations, although voluntary acts are not except as such, is the explicit statement of the generality of the ruling: that whoever does good, whatever good it is, will be rewarded for it. Or: whoever volunteers in good, or with good, or bringing good, of running only, based on the view that it is a Sunnah. The sentence in that case completes the removal of what might be feared from the negation of sin as permissibility. The benefit of the restriction is the explicit statement of the goodness of circumambulation, to remove hardship from the Muslims. Ibn Masʿud recited: (wa man tatawwaʿa bi-khayrin). Hamzah, al-Kisaʾi, and Yaʿqub recited: (yattawwaʿ), in the jussive form of the present tense, since "man" implies the meaning of a condition. Its original form is yatatawwaʿu, and it was assimilated.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Appreciative﴾. That is: He repays obedience with reward. In expressing it this way there is an intensification of kindness to His servants.

﴿All-Knowing﴾. The verse 158: (He is) intensive in knowledge of things, so He knows the measures of their deeds and their manners, and He does not diminish their rewards in the least. With this the wisdom of placing this attribute after the preceding one becomes clear. As for one who said: the two attributes are mentioned here because volunteering good includes the act and the intention, so it is fitting to mention gratitude in regard to the act, and mention knowledge in regard to the intention, and the attribute of knowledge is delayed although it precedes gratitude, just as intention precedes the act, in order to harmonize with the ends of verses, he has said nothing of value.

This sentence is a cause (ʿillah) for the omitted answer of the conditional, standing in its place, as if it were said: "And whoever volunteers good, Allah will recompense him, or reward him, for indeed Allah is Appreciative, All-Knowing."

﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾. A group related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: Muʿadh ibn Jabal, Saʿd ibn Muʿadh, and Kharijah ibn Zayd asked a group of Jewish rabbis about some of what was in the Torah, and they concealed it from them and refused to inform them, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse concerning them. It is related from Qatadah that it was revealed concerning those Jews and Christians who concealed. It was also said: it was revealed concerning everyone who conceals anything of the rulings of religion, because of the generality of the ruling for all. Al-Bukhari, Ibn Majah, and others related from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: "Were it not for a verse in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, I would never have narrated anything to anyone," and then he recited this verse. Abu Yaʿla and al-Tabarani related with a sound chain from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it will come on the Day of Resurrection bridled with a bridle of fire." The closer view is that it was revealed concerning the Jews, and the ruling is general, as the reports indicate. That it was revealed concerning the Jews does not require restriction, for the lesson is drawn from the generality of the wording, not from the specificity of the cause. So the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is for totality, and it includes those mentioned by initial inclusion. Concealment (al-katm and al-kitman) is leaving off the manifestation of a thing intentionally, while the need for it is pressing and the motive to manifest it is established. This may be by merely covering and hiding it, or by removing it and putting something else in its place. The Jews, may Allah fight them, committed both.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 159:**

﴿What We sent down﴾ upon the prophets ﴿of the clear proofs﴾, that is, the manifest verses that point to the truth. Among these is what We sent down to Musa and Isa, upon them be peace, concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿And the guidance﴾ is conjoined to "the clear proofs." Its meaning is that which leads to right conduct in general, and among it is that which guides to the obligation of following him (ﷺ) and believing in him. These are the verses that bear witness to his truthfulness, upon him be peace. The conjunction is based on a difference in concept, like the saying "the eater has come, then the drinker" (*ja'ani al-akil fa al-sharib*). It has also been said that it is conjoined to "what We sent down," etc. In that case, the first term refers to the transmitted proofs (*al-adillah al-naqliyyah*), and the second to what includes the rational proofs (*al-adillah al-'aqliyyah*). Or, the first refers to the revelation (*al-tanzil*), and the second to the benefits it entails. It is not hidden that this is a forced interpretation, which the closeness of the conjoined term refuses. The clarifying term that indicates complete clarity appears in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿after We made it clear to the people﴾, that is, We explained it and made it manifest to them. The adverbial phrase is connected to (*yaktumuna*, "they conceal"). The *lam* in (*al-nas*, "the people") is either a complement of (*bayyana*, "We made clear") or the *lam* of purpose (*lam al-ajal*). By "the people" is meant either the genus or the totality (*al-istighraq*). In restricting the concealment with the adverbial phrase there is an indication of the abominable nature of their state, namely that they conceal what has been made clear to the people, and an indication of the magnitude of the sin, namely that they conceal what carries general benefit. ﴿in the Book﴾ is connected to (*bayyanahu*, "We made it clear"). The attachment of two prepositional phrases to one verb, when the meanings differ, is not doubted as permissible. Or it is connected to an implied element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from its object. By "the Book" is meant the genus. It has been said: the Torah. It has been said: the Torah and the Gospel. It has been said: the Qur'an. By "the people" is meant the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). Some have taken "the clear proofs" to mean what is in the Qur'an, and have connected (*min ba'di*, "after") to (*anzalna*, "We sent down"). They have interpreted "the Book" as the Torah, and "concealment" as non-acknowledgment of its truth. Yet what we have pursued is perhaps better than all of that.

﴿Those—Allah curses them﴾, that is, He removes them far from His mercy and makes them taste the painful consequence of His vengeance. The shift to the third person by mentioning the proper name of the Essence is to cultivate awe, and to indicate that the source of the curse is the attribute of majesty, which differs from the source of sending down and clarification, which is the attribute of beauty. The particle *fa'* is not used in this clause, which is the predicate of the relative pronoun, as it is used later in His words, glory be to Him: ﴿so to them I turn in forgiveness﴾, although the relative construction contains the sense of a conditional and the intention of causality in both places. For this reason the demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*) was used, since attaching the judgment to it is like attaching it to a derived noun. It has been said: this is so that it is not supposed that their being cursed is only because of this cause, on the basis that the *fa'* of causation (*fa' al-sababiyyah*) is, originally, the *fa'* of sequence (*fa' al-ta'qib*), which indicates that the occurrence of the effect follows the cause without delay. It may be intended in that sense by the help of the context, as in the verse that follows. But it is not so; rather, it has many causes. From this it is known that the demonstrative does not replace the *fa'*, because it indicates causality but does not indicate sequence, which would imply restriction, on the basis that two causes cannot coincide.

﴿And the cursers curse them﴾ (159). That is, whoever is able to curse them from among the angels and the two species (humans and jinn). So "the cursers" is meant in its literal sense, and it is not like the saying of the famous case "whoever kills a slain man." The totality here is conventional (*'urfi*), that is, every individual within what the word encompasses according to what is commonly understood. It is not strictly total, so that it might be objected that not every curser in this world curses them, which would require specification. The verb is repeated because the cursing of those who curse means invoking on them removal far from the mercy of God, exalted is He. Al-Bayhaqi, in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, transmitted from Mujahid the interpretation of "the cursers" as the beasts of the earth, even scorpions and beetles. Perhaps the plural then is in the manner of His words, exalted is He: ﴿and the sun and the moon and the stars, I saw them prostrating to me﴾. From this verse it has been used as evidence for the obligation to make the knowledge of the Shari'ah manifest and the prohibition of concealing it. However, they stipulated for this that the scholar not fear for his own self, and that the matter be specifically incumbent upon him. Otherwise, concealment is not forbidden for him, unless he is asked, in which case the answer becomes obligatory for him, so long as its sin is not greater than its benefit.
Page 28
They said: In it is also evidence for the obligation of accepting the report of a single narrator (*khabar al-wahid*), because it is not obligatory upon him to make things clear unless the acceptance of his words has also become obligatory. It may also be used as evidence that this obligation does not apply to women, on the basis that they are not included in the address directed to men.

﴿Except those who repent﴾: that is, they turned back from concealment, or from it and from all else that must be repented of, on the basis that the omission of the object (of the verb) implies generality. This also indicates that repentance from concealment alone does not remove the curse from them unless they repent of everything, for their cursing has many causes.

﴿And amend﴾ what they had corrupted, by making amends in matters concerning the rights of God and of creation. Among this is that they reform their people by guiding them to Islam after misguiding them, and that they remove the altered speech and write in its place what they had removed at the time of distortion.

﴿And make clear﴾: that is, they made manifest what God, may He be exalted, had made clear to people in plain sight. These two matters complete repentance. It has also been said: they made manifest the repentance they had undertaken, so as to erase the mark of disbelief from themselves, and so that their likes might follow them, for the manifestation of repentance by one who is followed is a condition of it, as some reports indicate. But it is objected that the correct view is that the manifestation of repentance is only to remove the sin of misguiding others, and is not a condition of repentance from the sin itself. Thus it falls under His words, may He be exalted: ﴿and amend﴾.

﴿Those, I shall turn to them﴾ in acceptance, and pour forth forgiveness and mercy.

﴿And I am the Ever-Returning, the Most Merciful﴾ (160): this is a conjunction with what precedes it, serving as a concluding affirmation of it. The shift to the first person is for the sake of variety and eloquence, along with the allusion it contains to a difference in origin, so the one before and the one after are upon it.

﴿Indeed those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers﴾: the relative pronoun is for a specific reference, as is the basic usage, and what is meant by it are those who concealed. He expressed concealment as disbelief in order to censure them for it. The clause is parallel to what is in it. The phrase "except" is not conjoined with it, to indicate the complete contrast between the two groups. The verse combines and separates: it gathers the concealers under a single ruling, namely that they are cursed, then it separates, saying: as for those who repented, God, may He be exalted, has turned to them and removed from them the punishment of the curse; and as for those who died in concealment and did not repent of it, the curse has become firmly established upon them and has not ceased from them. He placed the word of exception in the first clause, although it is not for excluding from the preceding ruling; rather, it means "but," to indicate that repentance has become an expiation for the curse upon them, so that it is as if they had not been touched by it nor entered beneath it. This was said by some of the verifiers, but it involves departing from the apparent sense of the exception. For this reason some said: what is meant by the clause from which the exception is made is the explanation of the perpetuity and continuance of the curse. On this view the exception is a connected one (istithna' muttasil). The clause "indeed those who disbelieved" and so on is a resumptive clause, brought to establish the continuance of the curse for those beyond the exception, and to affirm its perpetuity and continuance upon those who do not repent. Restricting mention to disbelief in the relative clause, without addressing the absence of repentance and amendment, and the explanation, is based on the premise that the existence of disbelief entails the absence of all of them, just as the existence of repentance entails faith, which necessitates the absence of disbelief. Therefore faith was not stated explicitly among the attributes of those who repent. The difference between the two perpetuities is that the first is renewing (tajaddudi) and the second is established (thubuti). It is not hidden that this accords better with the apparent wording, whereas what some verifiers stated is more magnificent in meaning, higher in standing, and more subtle in insight. It has also been said that the relative pronoun is general, covering those who concealed and others, as the apparent sense of the relative clause requires, and the verse is by way of a concluding affirmation, so the concealers who died in concealment enter it primarily. It is objected that restricting the threat to the absence of lightening is the clearest evidence that the verse concerns the concealers who died in that state, for they are the most extreme and wicked of the disbelievers, since the threat concerning disbelievers is absolute eternity in the Fire. You know that this is open to dispute; indeed there is no disbelieving inhabitant of Hell whose condition on the Day of Resurrection is not identical to what is mentioned in the verse, and I do not think you have any doubt about that after hearing His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed the guilty will be in the punishment of Hell, abiding eternally﴾ ﴿it will not be lightened for them, and they will be in it despairing﴾. So it is not far-fetched to hold the goodness of this view, and the Imam (al-Razi) went to it, and the words of al-Tibi point to its goodness and excellence. So reflect.

[Page 29]

﴿Upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.﴾ What is meant is the continuation and permanence of that (curse). This ruling is therefore different from what preceded it, since what is meant by it is that the curse comes into being and befalls them. The mention of the angels and mankind is not intended as a specification that would contradict the earlier generality, nor as a generality that would require excluding those who have no awareness of their own selves (the *muhayminun*, the insensate), or the many pious people who curse no one. Rather, what is meant is that these transgressors are cursed by them (the angels and mankind) after him (the curse of Allah). *Ajma'in* (all together) is an emphatic (*ta'kid*) with respect to the whole, not only to *al-nas* (mankind). By "mankind" is meant the believers, because they are the transgressors among them, while the disbelievers are like the cattle; this is because (this interpretation) does not resolve the difficulty entirely. It was also said that the verse remains upon its generality, and that the disbelievers curse one another on the Day of Resurrection. Or the sentence is brought for the purpose of informing that those people deserve the curse from the whole, not that it has actually occurred. He did not repeat the word "curse" here as he repeated the verb before it, being content with the earlier mention, and for the sake of the elegance of the noble composition, and to suit what the emphasis implies.

Al-Hasan recited *wal-malā'ikatu wal-nāsu ajma'ūna* (with the nominative case) in the raised form. It has been interpreted in several ways. It was said that it is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon *la'natun* (a curse) with the implied sense "the curse of Allah and the curse of the angels," so the governing noun was omitted from the second part and the governed noun was put in its place. It was also said that it is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is omitted, meaning "the angels and mankind curse them." Or that it is the agent (*fa'il*) of an omitted verb, meaning "they curse them." It was also said that *la'natun* is a verbal noun (*masdar*) annexed to its agent, and the noun in the nominative is a conjunction upon its position (*mahall*), since the Arabs have made the agent of the verbal noun follow its position in the nominative, as in the verse: "*mashā al-hal­ūku 'alayhā al-khay'alu* (al-fadilu)" with *al-fadlu* in the nominative, and it is a qualifier (*na't*) of *al-halūk* according to its position. When this is established in the qualifier, it is permissible in the conjunction, since there is no difference between them. Abu Hayyan claimed that it is not permissible, because the condition for conjunction upon the position is that there be a governing element and a fixed, unchanging position, and also, *la'natun*, even if its being a verbal noun is granted, only acts when it is dissolved into *an* and the verb, whereas here the intended meaning is established fact, so it is not valid to dissolve it into both. Others granted this to him, and they said that it is the view of Sibawayh.

﴿خالِدِينَ فِيها﴾ means: remaining (abiding) in the curse. This emphasizes what the nominal sentence (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah, a sentence beginning with a noun) conveys of permanence. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the Fire. Mentioning it before any prior reference (al-idmar qabla al-dhikr) indicates that it is present in the mind, which implies care and leads to magnification and awe. It was also said that the cursing itself indicates the Fire, since the continuance of being expelled from mercy necessarily entails eternal abiding in the Fire, both in reality and in the mind. Dying in disbelief, although it necessarily entails that in reality, does not necessarily entail it in the mind, so the curse does not indicate it. And ﴿خالِدِينَ﴾, under both interpretations of the referent, is a circumstantial clause (hal) accompanying the continuance of the curse, not, as some have said, a "hal muqaddarah" (a circumstance that is anticipated) under the second interpretation.

﴿لا يُخَفَّفُ عَنْهُمُ العَذابُ﴾: this is either a resumptive new sentence (isti'naf) explaining the severity of their punishment in terms of its quality, following the explanation of its quantity, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ as well, or from the pronoun in (خالِدِينَ).

﴿ولا هم يُنْظَرُونَ 162﴾: this is coordinated (ataf) with what precedes it, and what applied there applies here. The choice of the nominal sentence serves to convey the continuity and persistence of the negation. The verb may derive from al-inzar, meaning delay, i.e., they will not be granted respite from the punishment, nor will they be postponed from it for an hour. Or it may derive from al-nazar, meaning waiting, i.e., they will not be awaited so that they may make excuses. Or it may derive from al-nazar meaning seeing, i.e., Allah, exalted is He, will not look upon them with a look of mercy. The verb in this sense is also transitive by itself, as in al-Asas, so a passive form may be derived from it.

[p. 30]

﴿And your God is one God﴾: It was revealed, as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, when the disbelievers of Quraysh said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Describe your Lord to us." The address is general to everyone who can be addressed, as is the apparent meaning, and it is not restricted to the occasion of revelation (shaʾn al-nuzul, the circumstances of the revelation). The sentence is conjoined to ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾, conjoining one narrative to another. What unites them is that the first is directed toward establishing his prophethood (ﷺ), and this one toward establishing His oneness, may He be exalted. It has also been said that the address is to those who conceal. In that case there is a shift from rebuking them for how they treat their Messenger to rebuking them for how they treat their Lord, in that they conceal His oneness and say: "ʿUzayr and ʿIsa are the sons of Allah, Mighty and Majestic." However, against this view: although the arrangement is then fine, it removes the occasion of revelation from the verse, and that is false. The attribution of "God" (ilah) to the pronoun of the addressees is on the basis of entitlement (al-istihqaq), not on the basis of actual occurrence, since the gods that are not deserving of worship are many. The repetition of the word "God" (ilah) and describing it with "one" serves to convey that what is considered is oneness in divinity and the entitlement to worship. Had it not been for this, ﴿And your God is one﴾ would have sufficed. It is like their describing a man as "one lord" and "one scholar."

Abu al-Baqaʾ said: "ilah" is the predicate of the subject (khabar al-mubtadaʾ), and "wahid" (one) is an adjective of it. The purpose here is the adjective, since if he had said "And your God is one," that would have been the intended meaning, but mentioning it adds emphasis. This resembles the preparatory circumstantial (al-hal al-muwattiʾa, a qualifier that prepares the ground for a following word), as in your saying: "I passed by Zayd, a righteous man," and as in your saying of the predicate: "Zayd is a righteous person." Perhaps the first is more refined. Most people hold that "one" here means that there is no equal to Him, no likeness to Him in His essence, nor in His attributes, nor in His actions. It has been said that what is meant by it is that which has no parts, is not subject to division, and does not admit of partition at all. The meaning here is not the starting point of counting. The most correct view according to those of sound intellect is that He is the one who has no equal and no likeness in entitlement to worship, and this entails every perfection, free of any flaw or deficiency.

﴿There is no god but Him﴾: It is a second predicate of the subject, or another adjective of the predicate, or a parenthetical clause (jumla iʿtiraḍiyya) with no place in terms of grammatical case (iʿrab, the grammatical analysis of word endings). Under any of these readings, it affirms the oneness and removes, as has been said, what might be imagined: that there exists in reality a god who does not deserve worship. The pronoun "Him," according to the correct view, is an appositive (badal) of the implicit pronoun within the omitted predicate; thus it is a nominative appositive of a nominative pronoun. There has been disagreement about what is negated: is it the god worshipped in truth, or the god worshipped falsely? Muhammad al-Shishini said: the negation applies only to the gods worshipped falsely, treating them as if they were non-existent. ʿAbd Allah al-Habati said: it applies only to the gods worshipped in truth. Each has been supported by some. Al-Mallawi mentioned that the truth lies with the second view, because the falsely worshipped god has existence in external reality, and existence in the mind of the believer under the description of being false, and existence in the mind of the disbeliever under the description of being true. Thus, from the standpoint of its existence in external reality, in itself it is not negated, because the essence is not negated. Likewise, from the standpoint of its being worshipped falsely, it is not negated either, since its being worshipped falsely is a true matter that cannot be negated, or else it would be a lie. It is negated only from the standpoint of its existence in the mind of the disbeliever, insofar as it exists in his mind under the description of being worshipped in truth. So the falsely worshipped deities were negated only insofar as they are worshipped in truth. Therefore, in this statement, only the one worshipped in truth other than Him, may He be exalted, is negated. Understand this. The verification of what is in this good statement will come in its proper place, God willing, may He be exalted.

﴿the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾ 163: These are two further predicates after a predicate or two predicates of the phrase "your God" (ilahakum), or of an omitted subject, and the sentence is parenthetical; or they are two appositives according to one opinion. They were brought to distinguish the essence described by oneness from anything else, and so that the answer corresponds to what they asked. In this there is an indication of the proof of oneness: since He is the master of all blessings, both roots and branches, worldly and otherworldly, and everything else is either pure goodness or predominant goodness, and that is either a blessing or one who is blessed, no one deserves worship except Him, because all are equal in their need of Him, may He be exalted, for existence and for what follows from it of perfections.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 164 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾: al-Bayhaqi related from Abu al-Duha, as a mu'dal (a report with two or more consecutive omitted narrators): "The polytheists had three hundred and sixty idols around the Ka'bah. When they heard this verse, they were amazed and said: 'If you are truthful, bring a sign by which we may know your truthfulness.' So it was revealed." Because of the extreme extent of their ignorance, the general proof indicated by the two descriptions did not suffice them. The plural (al-samawat, "the heavens") and the singular (al-ard, "the earth") are used because the first is benefited in all its parts, in terms of the light of its stars and other things in it, whereas the second is not, since only one of its units is benefited from, namely that which we witness of it. Abu Hayyan said: "al-Ard" is not made plural, because its plural is heavy and contrary to analogy. Many a singular word does not occur in the Qur'an in plural form due to its heaviness, and light singular forms, and plurals whose singular does not occur, such as al-albab, and something similar is found in al-Mathal al-Sa'ir. Some of the researchers said: "al-Samawat" is made plural because they are distinct layers, each one distinct from the others in its own individual essence, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So He completed them as seven heavens﴾, whether they are contiguous, as is the view of the philosophers, or not, as came in the reports that between every two heavens is a distance of five hundred years, being of different reality, since the difference in the effects referred to by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He inspired in each heaven its command﴾ indicates this. "Al-Ard" is not made plural, because its layers do not possess all of that. Whether they are separate in their essences, as is reported in the hadiths that: "Between every two earths is as between every two heavens," or they are not separate, as is the view of the philosophers, they are not different in reality, by agreement.

﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾: that is, their succession and each one being a replacement for the other; or the difference of each of them in itself, in increase and decrease, or in darkness and light. The night is mentioned first either because it preceded in creation or because of its nobility.

﴿and the ship that runs in the sea﴾: it is coordinated with "the creation of the heavens", not with "the heavens", or it is coordinated with "the night and the day". Al-Fulk (ship) is one of the words used both as singular and plural, and a notional difference is assumed between them. If its vowel is considered original, as in the vowel of "qufl" (lock), it is singular; if it is considered incidental, as in the vowel of "usd" (lions), it is plural. The first usage is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in the laden ship﴾, and the second is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When you are in the ships and they sail with them﴾. It is said that it is the plural of "falk", with a fatha on the fa and sukun on the lam; it is said that it is a collective noun; and some claimed that it was read as "fulk" with two dammas, which some regard as singular only. Al-Kawashi said: "al-Falak" and "al-Fulk" (with two dammas) are two dialectal forms, the singular and plural being the same in pronunciation, and this is distinguished by the agreement of the verb's pronoun in plurality or singularity.

﴿with what benefits mankind﴾: "ma" is either a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, meaning "with their benefit", or a relative pronoun, meaning "with that which benefits them". On the first reading, the pronoun of the subject refers either to al-fulk, since it is masculine in wording but feminine in meaning, as has been said; or to the sailing; or to the sea. The possibility that it is a descriptive (mawsufah) is not suited to the context of argument.

﴿and what Allah sends down from the sky of water﴾: it is coordinated with "al-fulk". It has been said that its being placed after mention of the ship, although it is more general in benefit, is for the sake of added distinction. It has also been said that the intended purpose of the first is to argue by means of "the sea" and its conditions, not by the ship running in it, because argument by that is either through its construction in a manner that runs on water, or knowledge of how it is made to run, or through the subjugation of the wind and sea for that, or its conveyance to ﴿what benefits mankind﴾; and none of these is a condition of it in itself. Also, argument by the ship running in the sea is argument by one of the conditions of the sea, unlike if one argued by "the sea" and all its conditions, which is more comprehensive and more fitting to the context. Yet He specified the ship for mention, although the requirement of the context at that point would be to say: "and the wonders that are in the sea", because it is the means of becoming acquainted with its conditions and wonders; so mentioning it is mentioning all its conditions and a path to knowing the aspects of its indication. For this reason it was placed before the mention of rain and clouds, because their origin is the sea in most cases. Otherwise, after mention of the alternation of night and day, which is among the heavenly signs, the appropriate thing would be to mention "rain and clouds", which are among the phenomena of the atmosphere; and the ship is not placed between them because it is among the earthly signs. In my view this is very contrary to the apparent meaning, and most of those who say it are so; for the meaning would be interpreted as: "and the sea in which the ships run, with what benefits mankind", which is an inversion of the noble arrangement without any reason requiring it and without any evidence to rely upon. And what prevents argument by the variation of the ships and their going, once this way and once that, according to what the divine decrees move them, or by the ships running in the sea insofar as they run in it, heavy, advancing and retreating, held by the cords of the air despite its subtlety, and by their density they do not sink to the bottom of the sea despite the clashing of its waves and the agitation of its depths; and that some of that is not a condition of them in themselves is not accepted. The order, in my view, is that He, glory be to Him, first mentioned the creation of two matters, one heavenly and one earthly, and the alternation of two things through the involvement of two matters, heavenly and earthly; second: since the succession of night and day, or their difference in increase and decrease, or in darkness and light, is only through the involvement of the course of the ship and the interposition of the body of the earth in two specific manners; then he followed that with what resembles the two signs of night and day: the ship swimming, each one, in the deep of the sea of its orbit, revolving, subjugated to running in it, going and returning, ﴿with what benefits mankind﴾ in the affairs of their livelihood and the ordering of their conditions. This is the ships which run upon the back of the sea by that, and their running differs eastward and westward according to the divine decrees' routing them through those paths. So the verse in this sense is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a sign for them is the night: We strip from it the day, and behold, they are in darkness﴾, ﴿And the sun runs toward its resting place; that is the decree of the Mighty, the Knowing﴾, ﴿And the moon, We have measured for it stations, until it returns like the old withered palm stalk﴾, ﴿It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day, and each in an orbit they swim﴾, ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾. Except that the difference between the two verses is that in the second, the two verses are mentioned explicitly as intermediaries between the narrative of the ship and the matter of night and day; while in the first, something indicating them and pointing to them precedes. Then He followed that with what the heavenly and earthly worlds share, and which has a relation to the mention of the sea, indeed to the mention of the ship running in it, with what benefits mankind: that is the sending down of water from the sky and the bringing forth, by life, of what was hidden in the earth; and in that is complete benefit and general bounty.

"Min" in the first instance is initial (ibtida'iyyah) and the second is explanatory (bayaniyyah). It is permitted that it be partitive (tab'idiyyah), and that it be a substitute for the first. The intended meaning of "the sky" is the direction of height, and this has been verified previously.

﴿Then He gave life thereby to the earth﴾: by stirring its growing powers and bringing forth what He placed within it of kinds of plants, flowers and trees, ﴿after its death﴾, and the absence of that appearing in it due to the dominance of dryness over it, as its nature requires. ﴿And He spread throughout it every kind of moving creature﴾: this is coordinated either with "sent down", the common factor being that each of them is an independent sign of His oneness, exalted is He, which is the purpose the speech is directed toward, with the agent being shared; and "gave life" is part of the first, so argument is by the sending down which causes the giving of life, and thus separation by it is not a barrier to the conjunction. Or it is coordinated with "gave life", and so it falls under the fa' of causation; and the causation of sending down water for the spreading is in terms of water being the cause of the life of livestock and beasts, and spreading is a branch of life. It does not need a pronoun to be supplied for linkage, since the fa' of causation suffices for it according to the well-known view. It has been said that it needs the supplying of "bihi" (by it, i.e., by the water), to indicate its independent connection with "anzala" like "ahya"; the fa' of causation is not sufficient for this, since the cause may be the combination of both. And since the genitive is only omitted if the relative is governed by a similar particle, this is a majority rule, not a universal one. "Min" is explanatory according to the first supposition, in the sound view. The intended meaning of ﴿every kind of moving creature﴾ is every species of moving creature. The meaning of "spreading" them is multiplying them through breeding and generation. So the argument is by the multiplication of every species of what crawls upon the earth, and its not being confined to some. It has been said that it is partitive, because God did not spread except some of the individuals in relation to what is within His power. Moreover, al-Zamakhshari affirmed that there are also creatures in the heaven, in the surah of Ha Mim, 'Ayn Sin Qaf. But it may be objected that the spreading of every species of what crawls upon the earth does not contradict some of its individuals being predetermined, nor their existence in the heaven. Moreover, the implication of partitiveness is that a thing is a part of what follows it, not one individual of it. And it is explanatory according to the second supposition, since there is no preceding referent, and partitive sense is not valid; and this is an addition in affirmative speech which none permitted except al-Akhfash.

﴿and the turning of the winds﴾: that is, God, exalted is He, turning them: south, north, east and west; hot and cold; violent and gentle; barren and fertilizing; and at times with mercy, and at other times with punishment. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "al-rih" in the singular, and by it is intended the genus. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "'al-Riyah' (plural) is for mercy, and 'al-Rih' (singular) is for punishment." It is also related that the Prophet (ﷺ), whenever a wind blew, would say: "O Allah, make it winds (of mercy) and do not make it a wind (of punishment)." Perhaps he intended by the first and second His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good tidings﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And in 'Ad, when We sent upon them the barren wind﴾.

Then He followed the giving of life to the earth with rain, and the spreading of every creature in it with the turning of the winds, because in that is the nurture of plants and the continuation of life for animals that crawl upon the face of the earth; and if Allah, exalted is He, withheld the wind for an hour, what is between the heaven and the earth would become foul, as some reports have stated.

﴿and the clouds﴾: coordinated with what precedes it. It is a collective noun whose singular is "sahabah", named so either for its being drawn along (insihab) in the atmosphere, or because the winds drag it.

"Al-Musakhkhari bayna as-sama'i wal-ard" (the one subjected between heaven and earth) is an adjective (sifa) describing "as-sahab" (the clouds) according to its wording, though its meaning may also be taken into account, so it is described in the plural as in ﴿sahaban thiqala﴾ (heavy clouds). "Bayna" (between) is an adverbial phrase of incomplete sense (zarf laghw) related to "al-musakhkhar." The meaning of its subjugation is that it neither descends nor moves away, even though its nature requires its rising if it is light and its descending if it is dense. It has also been said: the adverbial phrase is a complete (mustaqirr) phrase that occurs as a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in "al-musakhkhar," and its complement is omitted; that is, subjugated to the winds, as they turn it around in the atmosphere by the will of Allah, the Exalted. The mention of the clouds after the turning of the winds is because the clouds are, as it were, an effect of the winds, as indicated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is the One who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾. Also, placing it last among the conjoined items corresponds in a general way to what the verse began with, since it is both earthly and heavenly, so the beginning and end of the speech are linked. By what we have mentioned, the reason for the order in the verse is known. Some scholars said: perhaps the delay of mentioning the turning of the winds and the subjugation of the clouds, after the running of the ship and the sending down of water, while the external order is reversed, is to indicate that each of the matters enumerated is independently a sign. Had the external order been observed, it might have been imagined that the whole ordered group, some following others, was one single sign. It is not hidden that the apparent meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿for signs﴾ removes this imagining. The noun of "inna" is preceded by the lam (la-) because it is delayed past its predicate, and the indefiniteness is for magnification in quantity and quality, meaning: great and numerous signs indicating the overpowering power, the dazzling wisdom, and the vast mercy, which require that divinity belong exclusively to Him, glory be to Him. ﴿For a people who understand 164﴾, that is, who reflect. "Reason" is thus a metaphor for reflection, which is its fruit. Ibn Abi al-Dunya and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that "when the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse he said: 'Woe to whoever recites it and does not reflect upon it.'" In it there is an allusion to the polytheists who proposed to the Prophet (ﷺ) a sign that would confirm him, and a recording against them of the weakness of their minds. Otherwise, whoever contemplates those signs finds that each of them contains many aspects of indication to the existence of Allah, the Exalted, His oneness, and His other perfect attributes, which necessitate devoting worship to Him alone, the Exalted, and dispensing with all others. The summary of the matter is that each of these enumerated things has come into being in a particular way among the possible ways, rather than others, bearing specific effects and particular rulings, without its essence requiring its existence, let alone its existence in that particular pattern. Therefore it must have a originator, since a possible thing cannot exist without an capable originator who, if He wills, acts, and if He does not will, does not act, wise, knowing the realities of things and the corruptions and benefits in them, bringing it into being according to what His knowledge of the benefit in it requires and what His will demands, exalted above being opposed by others. For if there were with Him a necessary existent able to do what the Truth, the Exalted, is able to do, then if the wills of each of them agreed on bringing it into being in a particular way, which the other also willed, then if the influence belonged to each of them, it would follow that two agents would converge on one effect, which entails the convergence of two complete causes. And if the act belonged to one of them, it would follow that the agent is preferred without a preferrer, since both are equal in willing its independent existence, while the other is incapable because the first has blocked him from bringing about what he willed. If the two wills differed, such that one wished its existence in one manner and the other wished its existence in another manner, then mutual obstruction and mutual exclusion would follow, for lack of a preferrer, and so both would be incapable, and incapacity is manifestly incompatible with divinity. In the verse there is an affirmation of reasoning by rational proofs, and an alert to the nobility of the science of kalam and the merit of its people. It may also point to the nobility of the science of cosmology (al-hay'a).

[p. 34]

**"Among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals (andad) [who] they love as they love Allah."** This is an explanation of the state of the polytheists after the proofs indicating His unity, exalted is He, were set forth. The phrase **"besides Allah"** is a circumstantial clause (hal) related to the pronoun in **"takes"**. **Al-andad** means equals, and what is intended by them is the idols, as is common usage in the Qur'an. This is related from Qatadah, Mujahid, and most of the exegetes. It has also been said that they are the leaders whom people obey with the obedience owed to lords among men. It is related from al-Suddi, and attributed to al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him. It has also been said that what is intended is more general than both, namely anything that distracts one from Allah, exalted is He. The meaning is: **"Among the people are those who take"**, going beyond the one God whose sublime attributes have been mentioned, equals, so they do not restrict obedience to Him, glory be to Him, but associate others with Him in it. The choice of the noble Name (Allah) here serves to specify Him, exalted is He, by His essence, after He was specified by His attributes.

**"They love them as they love Allah."** This is either a new independent sentence, or an attribute of **al-andad**, or an attribute of **"those [who]"** if you take it as an indefinite noun with a qualifying clause, used to explain the manner of the taking. **Al-mahabbah** (love) is the inclination of the heart, from **al-habb**, meaning the grain (seed). It is used figuratively for the core of the heart and its center, and from it the word **al-hubb** (love) is derived, because it affects the innermost part of the heart and becomes firmly rooted in it. The love of servants for Allah, exalted is He, according to the majority of the **mutakallimun** (theologians of kalam), is a kind of volition (irada), whether we say it is the very inclination that follows belief in benefit, as is the view of the **Mu'tazilah** (a rationalist theological school), or a distinct preponderant attribute, as is the doctrine of **Ahl al-Sunnah** (the Sunni tradition). It is therefore only connected with what is permissible, and it is not possible for it to be connected with His essence, exalted is He. Thus the servant's love for Him, glory be to Him, is the intention to obey Him and to attain His good pleasure. This is based on the premise that what is sought in itself is limited to pleasure and the removal of pain. But the knowers of Allah, glory be to Him (the **'arifun**, mystics), have said that perfection is also loved for its own sake, so the servant loves Allah, exalted is He, for His own essence, because He is the absolutely Perfect, whose perfection nothing approaches. As for the love of His service and His reward, that is a lower rank. The love of Allah, exalted is He, for His servants is an attribute of His, mighty is His glory; it has no modality (is not qualified by how), and the bird of thought does not hover around its protected domain. It has also been said that it means His honoring them, employing them in obedience, and preserving them from sins. The love here means reverence and obedience; that is, they equate between Allah, exalted is He, and the equals they have taken, so they revere and obey them as they revere Allah and incline to obey Him. The plural pronoun in the accusative refers to the equals. If what is meant by them is the leaders, then it is clear. Otherwise, the reference to them by the pronoun for rational beings is in accordance with that false supposition that they are equals of Allah, exalted is He. The verbal noun (al-masdar) that is attached (in the phrase "their love"), being derived from the active form, has as its agent the pronoun **"them"**, by the indication of prior mention. And the polytheists acknowledge Him, exalted is He, and turn to Him in times of hardship: **"And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, 'Allah.'"** **"So when they board a ship, they call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion."**

It has also been said, and this is the apparent disagreement, that there is a departure from what would be required by the clause **"they love them"** being an explanation of the manner of taking, namely that it is the verbal noun of the passive form, and the one who loves is omitted because he is not ambiguous. The meaning, according to the likening of the lovability of the equals from the side of the polytheists to His lovability, exalted is He, from the side of the believers, is not contradicted by His saying, exalted is He: **"But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah."** This is because the comparison occurs only between the two objects of love, and that requires that the lovability of the idols be similar to His lovability, exalted is He. The preference between the two loves is in terms of the firmness of one of them rather than the other. For the intensity of the believers' love means its intensity in its locus, which is its firm establishment in them and its never leaving them under any circumstance. It is not like the love of the polytheists for their gods, since they turn away from them to Allah, exalted is He, in times of hardship, and disavow them at the sight of terrors, and worship the idol for a time and then abandon it for another. Sometimes they even eat it, as it is related that the tribe of Bahilah had idols made of dates and clarified butter, and they became hungry in a famine that struck them, so they ate them. By Allah, their father (i.e., the one who coined the saying), no polytheist ever benefited from his gods as these benefited from theirs, for they tasted the sweetness of disbelief. The intended meaning of intensity of love is not its intensity and strength in itself, so as to be refuted by saying that we see the disbelievers performing arduous acts of worship that most believers do not perform, so how can it be said that their love is more intense than the believers' love? From this the reason for choosing **"stronger in love"** (ashadd hubban) over **"loves more"** (ahabb) becomes apparent. For what is meant is not an increase in the act itself, but firmness and steadfastness, and that is the essence of the matter. This is why the verse was revealed: **"So remain steadfast as you have been commanded."** And the most beloved of deeds to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, was the most constant of them. The **'Allamah** (al-Alusi's teacher or a major scholar, as cited) said: He departed from **ahabba** to **ashadda** because lovability became widely associated with the superlative, so he avoided it to guard against ambiguity. It has also been said that **ahabba** is more frequent than **habba**, so if the form **af'ala** were derived from it, it might be mistakenly thought to be from the augmented form.

[p. 35]

**"If only those who did wrong could see..."** That is: if only those who did wrong, by taking [equals] as described, knew. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to show that this taking is a great wrong, and that the attribution of this to those who take [equals] is a known and widely recognized matter, since it is described by the general term "wrong." The relative pronoun and its clause serve to allude to the cause of **"their seeing the punishment,"** understood from His saying, glory be to Him: **"when they see the punishment."** That is: they witness and see the punishment prepared for them on the Day of Resurrection. The future form is used after **law** (if only) and **idha** (when), which are specific to the past, to affirm the certainty of its meaning. Thus it is past in its interpretation and future in its certainty, so both aspects are observed.

**"That power belongs entirely to Allah."** This fills the place of the two objects of **"see"**. The answer to **law** (if) is omitted, to indicate that it has gone beyond the scope of explanation. That is: they would fall into regret and remorse in ways that can hardly be described. It has also been said that this clause is the complement of the answer, and the two objects are omitted, and the estimate is: **"If only those who did wrong could see"** their equals are of no benefit, **"they would know that power belongs entirely to Allah."** None benefits or harms except Him.

Ibn 'Amir, Nafi', and Ya'qub read **"tara"** (you see), with the address to him, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, or to everyone fit to be addressed. The answer then is: **"you would see a matter beyond description in its terror and horror."** Ibn 'Amir reads **"yuraw"** (they are shown) in the passive. Ya'qub reads **"inna"** (that) with a kasra, and likewise **"and that Allah is severe in punishment,"** either as a new sentence or by implying "saying" (qa'ilin), that is, saying that. The purpose of this clause is to exaggerate the magnitude of the matter and the horror of the situation, for the exclusivity of **"power"** to Him, exalted is He, does not necessitate severity of **"punishment,"** since He may forgo punishment by pardon even though He is able to inflict it.

﴿إذْ تَبَرَّأ الَّذِينَ اتُّبِعُوا﴾ ("when those who were followed disown those who followed") is a *badal* (substitute, in grammar an apposition-type replacement) for ﴿إذْ يَرَوْنَ﴾ ("when they see") without qualification. The separation between the *badal* and the word it replaces (*mubdal minhu*) by the response and its complement is permissible because the *badal* is long. It is also permitted that ﴿إذْ تَبَرَّأ﴾ be an adverbial of time (*zarf*) modifying ﴿شَدِيدِ العَذابِ﴾ ("severe punishment"), or an object of ﴿اذْكُرُوا﴾ ("remember"). Some have claimed that it is a *badal* of the object of ﴿تَرى﴾ ("you see") according to the reading with the second-person form, just as ﴿إذْ يَرَوْنَ﴾ is also a *badal* of it. And ﴿أنَّ القُوَّةَ﴾ ("that the power") is in the position of a *badal al-ishtimal* (inclusive apposition, where the substitute includes part of or is connected to the original) with respect to ﴿العَذابِ﴾.

It should be noted that this view implies that a single word may have more than one *badal*, and this is not found in any of the books of grammar. Furthermore, it is objected that in *badal al-ishtimal* the substituted word must require the substitute and indicate it in general terms, and the substitute must contain a pronoun referring back to the substituted word; both of these conditions are absent here. The meaning is: when the leaders who were followed disown the followers, i.e. the subordinates, by their saying: ﴿تَبَرَّأْنا إلَيْكَ ما كانُوا إيّانا يَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("We disown to You; it was not us that they worshipped").

Mujahid read the first verb (*al-awwal*) in the active form and the second (*al-thani*) in the passive form, meaning: the followers disowned and separated themselves from those they had followed, and regretted their worship of them. ﴿ورَأوُا العَذابَ﴾ ("and they see the punishment") is a *hal* (circumstantial clause) relating to both the followers and the leaders, as in "I met him riding" (*laqītuhu rākibīn*), meaning: seeing it. The *waw* is the *waw* of circumstance, and *qad* ("indeed") is implied. It has also been said that it is conjoined (*ʿaṭf*) to ﴿تَبَرَّأ﴾, but this leads to the substitution of ﴿إذْ رَأوُا العَذابَ﴾ ("when they saw the punishment") for ﴿إذْ يَرَوْنَ العَذابَ﴾ ("when they see the punishment"), and there is little benefit in it. Although the agents of the two verbs are different, the terror of the time is conveyed by what occurs in it, namely the sight of the punishment; and what truly deserves astonishment is their disowning at the moment of seeing the punishment, not the seeing itself. It has been answered that the substitute is the time attached to both matters, while the substituted time is the time attached only to one, namely the seeing. But it is objected that this also does not free the construction from awkwardness, since once the time has been made terrifying by attaching it to ﴿رُؤْيَةِ العَذابِ﴾ ("the sight of the punishment"), there is no need to combine it with the disowning. This is unlike the case where it is made a *hal*, for then the substitute is the disowning that occurs in the state of seeing the punishment.

[p. 36]

﴿وتَقَطَّعَتْ بِهِمُ الأسْبابُ﴾ ("and their means are cut off from them") is either conjoined (*ʿaṭf*) to ﴿تَبَرَّأ﴾ or to ﴿رَأوْا﴾, or is a circumstantial clause. The first is preferred, because the original function of the *waw* is conjunction, and because a clause is independent in itself, and because it conveys the multiplicity of causes of terror and horror, while avoiding the need to supply ﴿قَدْ﴾ ("indeed") and to treat the *bāʾ* in ﴿بِهِمْ﴾ ("with them") as a *bāʾ* of cause. The meaning is: their means, by which they hoped to be saved, were cut off because of their disbelief. It has been said that the *bāʾ* expresses association: the means were cut off while connected to them, as when you say "Zayd went out with his clothes." It has also been said that it means "from" (*ʿan*). And it has been said that it expresses transitivity, meaning: the means cut them off, as you say "the roads scattered them," and from this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿فَتَفَرَّقَ بِكم عَنْ سَبِيلِهِ﴾ ("so that He scatters you away from His way").

The root meaning of *sabab* ("means, cause") is a rope in general, or the rope by which one reaches water, or a rope one end of which is fastened to the ceiling, or the rope by which one climbs a palm tree. What is meant by *al-asbab* here is the ties that existed between the followers and the leaders in the world: kinship, affection, agreement upon the religion, and the relationship of following and being followed. The verb ﴿تَقَطَّعَتْ﴾ has also been read in the passive form, and ﴿تَقَطَّعَ﴾ has come both intransitive and transitive.

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 167:]

﴿And those who followed said: "If only we had a return"﴾ That is: if only a return and a coming back to the world were established for us.

﴿Then we would disavow them﴾ That is, the ones who were followed, ﴿as they have disavowed us﴾. They wish to return to the world so that they may obey God, Exalted is He, and thereby disavow their leaders in the Hereafter when they are all gathered, in the same way that the leaders disavowed them. This is a requital for them in kind. That is: just as they were made to suffer, enraged and bewildered, by the leaders' disavowal, we will likewise make the leaders suffer, enraged and bewildered, by our disavowal over what has befallen us through abandoning our following of them. For this reason they did not disavow them before wishing for a return, because this enrages the leaders: they disavowed the followers or not. From here the reading in the active voice (al-bina' lil-fa'il) becomes clear, because the followers' disavowal of the leaders in the Hereafter comes through separating from them after it has become evident to them that the leaders are of no benefit. This does not enrage the leaders, since each of them is occupied with what he is suffering. Therefore they wish to return to the world so that they may disavow them with a disavowal that enrages them. As for His saying, glorified is He, ﴿as they have disavowed﴾, it requires only that the disavowal by the leaders occurred, which is stated in another verse, and it does not require that it be mentioned in what precedes. It has been said: after the followers disavowed the leaders on the Day of Resurrection, they wished for a return to the world together with their leaders so that they might disavow them there and forsake them, and thus they would combine the humiliation of this world and the Hereafter. This interpretation requires taking "for us" (lana) as including the leaders by way of predominance (ta'ghib), that is, "for us and for them," since disavowal in this world can only be conceived if both groups return.

﴿Thus﴾ is in the position of an absolute object (mafʿul muṭlaq, a verbal object of the same root) for what follows it. The thing indicated is the seeing implied by ﴿when they see﴾. That is: like the seeing of the punishment, accompanied by the manifestation of ﴿that power belongs to God﴾, and the disavowal, and the severing of the means, and the wish for a return.

﴿God will show them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾ It has been permitted that the thing indicated be the verbal noun (maṣdar) implied by what follows, and the particle "ka" is inserted to emphasize the grandeur indicated by the demonstrative noun. Its place is in the accusative as well, by way of a verbal noun. That is: that dreadful seeing will show them, in the same manner as has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to emphasize the threat and to explain the state of the polytheists in the Hereafter and the eternity of their punishment. It is also permissible that it be a new sentence (isti'naf), as if, when their threat and the horror of their punishment were emphasized, it was fitting that the listener should wonder and ask: "Do they have other punishment besides this, or is it complete?" So he is answered with what you see. "Ḥasarāt" means regrets. It is the third object of "yara" (to see) if the seeing is mental, and a state (ḥal) qualifying "their deeds" if it is visual. The meaning of these polytheists' seeing their evil deeds on the Day of Resurrection as regrets is their seeing them recorded in a Book that leaves nothing small or great unaccounted for, and their certainty of the recompense for them. At that point they regret what they neglected regarding the right of God, Exalted is He. "Upon them" is a qualifier of "regrets." It has been permitted that it be connected to it, with an elided modifier, that is: their neglect (tafrīṭuhum), because "ḥasara" takes "ʿalā" (upon). The verse was cited by those who hold that unbelievers are addressed with the branches of the law (al-furuʿ) as an argument.

﴿And they will not emerge from the Fire﴾. What is apparent in similar constructions is that the negation is restricted to the predicate's subject, as in ﴿And I am not one to drive away those who believed﴾ and ﴿And you are not against us mighty﴾. In this there is an indication that the disobedient believers, who are included in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for God﴾, will not remain eternally in the Fire. If by "those who wronged" is meant unbelievers in general and not only polytheists, the restriction is real, and its purpose is to intensify the threat: that no one else shares with them in eternity, since sharing lessens punishments. It has been said that the intended meaning is the negation of the act itself, since that is what befits the context of threat, and not a restriction of the negation, since the context is not one of doubt and dispute about whether the ones who come out are they or others, whether in partnership or alone. Although this is correct with regard to the disobedient, the wording has been changed to what you see in order to convey intensification regarding eternity and despair of deliverance and of returning to the world. The addition of the particle "bi" (in "bikhārijīn") and the removal of their essence from the category of those who come out serve to emphasize the negation. You know that if the restriction does not take into account the state of the addressee, nothing remains to be said, except that the apparent meanings of some verses require that the restriction not be intended. Among these is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not emerge from it﴾. So the claim that the restriction is not explicit is not, as was imagined, an explicit doctrine of the Mu'tazila (i'tizāl).

* * *

Among the allusive interpretations (min bab al-ishara) of the verses is His saying: ﴿Indeed, as-Safa﴾, that is, the soul purified of the grime of transgressions, ﴿and al-Marwah﴾, that is, the self standing in service to its Master, through the making known of the religion of God and its rites, both inward and outward. Whoever attains the station of essential unity (waḥdah dhātiyyah) and enters the house of the Divine Presence (ḥaḍrah ilāhiyyah) through annihilation (fanāʾ, the passing away of all but God) from otherness, or visits the Presence through the unity of the attributes, and is clothed with the lights of majesty and beauty, then there is no fault upon him at that time ﴿in going around between them﴾, and returning to their station through the existence bestowed after the sought-after establishment. Whoever volunteers good through teaching and advice and guiding those who seek guidance, God will thank his deed and know its recompense. ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾ what We have poured upon them of the lights of knowledge and the guidance of states ﴿after what We have made clear to the people in﴾ the Book of their illuminated intellects, illumined with the light of following: those, God, Exalted is He, will distance and veil from Him. ﴿And the cursers will curse them﴾ from the Higher Assembly, so they will not extend help to them; and from among the prepared, so they will not accompany them. ﴿Except those who﴾ return to God, Exalted is He, and know that what they are in is a trial from Him, Mighty and Majestic, and who rectify their states through discipline, and manifest what was veiled from them through sincerity in conduct: ﴿those I accept their repentance﴾, ﴿and I am the Relenting, the Merciful﴾.

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾ and veiled themselves from the Truth, and remained in their veiling until their readiness vanished and the light of their natural disposition (fiṭrah) was extinguished: those deserve expulsion and distance from the Truth and the world of dominion (malakūt), remaining in that forever. ﴿Their punishment will not be lightened for them﴾, because the causes requiring it are firmly fixed in them. ﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾, because those dark states are bound to them. ﴿And your God is one God﴾, one in essence, and nothing in existence other than Him exists. So how is other than Him worshipped, when it is pure nonexistence? Indeed, in the creation of the heavens of spirits and the earth of souls, and the alternation of light and darkness between them, and the ship of the body that sails in the sea of readiness with what benefits people in acquiring their perfections and completing their formation, and in what God sends down from the heaven of spirits, water of knowledge, by which He revives the earth of souls after its death through ignorance, and scatters in it the animal faculties, and disperses in its orbits the planets of the world of dominion, and in the turning of the winds of breaths that stir the branches of the trees of longing in the gardens of hearts, and the cloud of manifestations (tajalliyāt) subjected between the heaven of the spirit and the earth of the soul, so that it may rain drops of address upon the fires of minds, so that they may rest for a moment from burning by the blaze of the fire of ecstasy: are signs and proofs ﴿for a people who reason﴾ with the intellect illumined by the holy lights, free of the impurities of illusion.

﴿And among the people are those who﴾ worship, besides God, things that have kept them from serving their Lord and turning toward Him, ﴿who love them﴾ and incline toward them as they love God, and equate them with Him, glorified is He, because they have not tasted the sweetness of His love, nor seen the light of His witnessing and the realities of His union and nearness. ﴿But those who believe﴾ with complete faith ﴿are stronger in love for God﴾, because they are absorbed in witnessing Him, bewildered by the delight of His address, from the covenant of ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾, not turning to other than Him for the blink of an eye. So far be it that their love should cease, or that their intellect should incline to other things. They loved Him with His love, and their hearts became the throne of His manifestations and nearness.

﴿And if those who wronged﴾ and associated partners with God, taking as God what in reality is nothing, not alive and not able, saw at the time of their seeing the punishment of being veiled from the Lord of lords, and that power belongs to God entirely, and that their gods who diverted them from Him have no share of it, they would regret and be grieved, because they did not seek the Face of God, Exalted is He, nor pursue Him. At that point the followers will disavow the leaders, having seen the punishment of deprivation, and the bonds that were between them in the world will be severed, and they will wish for what is impossible in any way, and they will remain in grief and punishment. Likewise is the state of the spiritual faculties, pure, relative to the soul's faculties that follow them in attaining their pleasures. Blessed are those who love each other for God, Exalted is His majesty.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 168:

﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good﴾. It was revealed concerning the polytheists who forbade for themselves the baḥīrah, the sā'ibah, the waṣīlah and the ḥām, as Ibn Jarīr and Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with them both) reported. It is also said: it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Salām and his like, since they forbade for themselves the flesh of camels when it was unlawful in the religion of the Jews. And it is said: it was revealed concerning a people of Thaqīf, Banū 'Āmir ibn Ṣa'ṣa'ah, Khuzā'ah and Banū Mudlij, since they forbade dates and aqiṭ (dried curd) for themselves. As for ﴿ḥalālan﴾ (lawful), it is either the object of ﴿kulū﴾ (eat), or a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of the relative pronoun, meaning: eat it while it is lawful; or an attribute of an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar), meaning: eating that is lawful. On the last two interpretations, min (from) is partitive (tab'īḍ), so that it is the object of ﴿kulū﴾. On the first interpretation, it may be a min of origin (ibtidā'iyyah) connected to ﴿kulū﴾, or a circumstantial qualifier of ﴿ḥalālan﴾, and it was placed before it because it is indefinite; and it may be a min of origin, indeed it is definite, as in al-Kashshāf, according to the view of those who hold that the original status of things is permissibility. It may also be partitive, based on what al-Radī preferred, that the partitive min is originally a min of origin; however, there must be a thing, apparent or implied, which is part of what follows min, and it is not required that the word "part" be able to stand in its place. Al-'Allāmah al-Taftazānī rejected its being partitive on this interpretation, because it then occupies the position of the direct object, and the verb does not govern two objects, and it is built (mabnī), according to what is in al-Tas-hīl and elsewhere, that tab'īḍ is a literal meaning of min, and its sign is that the word "part" can stand in its place. The imperative is for obligation when eating is for sustaining the body, for recommendation when it is for entertaining a guest, and for permissibility in other cases.
