(The connection of the verse to what precedes it): when He, glory be to Him, explained tawḥīd, its proofs, and what is for those who repent and those who disobey, He followed that with mention of His favour and the comprehensiveness of His mercy, to show that disbelief does not prevent the cutting off of His favour. His saying ﴿ṭayyiban﴾ (good) is an attribute of ﴿ḥalālan﴾; its meaning, as Imam Mālik said, is what the palate of the Sharia finds delicious, which it does not reject or dislike, or what the eye sees as pure from the stain of doubt. The benefit of describing the lawful with it is to generalize the ruling, as in His saying ﴿and there is no creature on the earth﴾, so that there is a refutation of whoever forbade some lawful things, for an indefinite noun described by a general attribute encompasses all, unlike an undescribed one. Imam al-Shāfi'ī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: what is meant by it is what upright appetite, arising from sound temperament, finds good. It was objected that what appetite does not find good is either lawful without any doubt, so there is no prohibition, or else it falls outside the condition of lawfulness. It was answered that what is meant by the lawful is what the Lawgiver stated to be permitted, and by this is meant what has no explicit text but which the natural disposition finds pleasant and desires, and there is nothing in the Sharia indicating its prohibition, such as intoxicants and harm. The better view, given the context, is that the restriction is not meant to exclude what corrupt appetite finds good, but because it is included in its meaning; for "good" and "pleasant" are said only of what upright appetite finds pleasant, and the benefit of the description then is the explicit permission of what they had forbidden. The claim that in the verse, on this interpretation, there is an allusion to the prohibition of eating to fill the stomach and of false appetite, because that is not found good, since pleasant food eaten in that way is something appetite finds good, except that it is not eaten by upright appetite, and there is a vast distance between the two meanings, as some scholars of verification have said. Some scholars inferred from the verse that whoever forbids a food, for example, is void and it is not made unlawful for him, and there is an obscurity in this that is not hidden.

﴿and do not follow the steps of Satan﴾, i.e. his traces, as was reported from al-Khalīl, or his deeds, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbās (may Allah be pleased with him), or his sins, as was transmitted from Mujāhid. The sum of the meaning: do not believe in him and follow his way, so that you forbid the lawful and make lawful the forbidden. And it is related from al-Ṣādiq: "Among the steps of Satan are swearing by divorce, vows in disobedience, and every oath by other than Allah, the Exalted." Nāfi', Abū 'Amr and Ḥamzah read ﴿khuṭuwāt﴾ with a sukūn on the ṭā', and both are dialectal forms of the plural of ﴿khuṭwah﴾ (step), which is the distance between the feet of a walker. 'Alī (may Allah ennoble his face) read it with two ḍammahs and a hamzah, and there are two explanations of this reading. The first: what is said, that the hamzah is original, from ﴿al-khaṭa'﴾ (error) in the sense of ﴿al-khaṭī'ah﴾ (sin). The second: the waw was changed into a hamzah, because a waw that is ḍammah is changed into it, as in ﴿ujūh﴾; and this one, since it neighboured the ḍammah, was treated as if it were on it. Al-Zajjāj said: this is permissible in Arabic. And from Abū al-Simāl, that he read it with two fatḥahs, as the plural of ﴿khuṭwah﴾, which is the single instance of the verb khaṭā (to step).

﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ [168]. This is a reason for the prohibition. ﴿Mubīn﴾ (clear) is from abāna, meaning bāna and ẓahara (became evident); i.e. manifest in enmity to those of insight, even if he shows friendship to whom he misleads; and for this reason he is called a ﴿walī﴾ (protector) in His saying ﴿their protectors are the Ṭāghūt﴾. It may be that this is from the usage of "their greeting is the sword". It is also said: abāna means aẓhara, i.e. one who makes enmity manifest; and the first is more fitting to the context of the reason.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 169:**

﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality.﴾ This is a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence that continues the argument) explaining the manner of his enmity. It is also a detailed account of the kinds of his harm and corruption, and of the fact that his dealings with them are confined to this. Alternatively, it is a cause of the previous cause (taken together with it). Whoever is of this character is a clear enemy. Or it is a cause of the original ruling (taken together with it): whoever is of this character should not be followed. So the ruling is grounded in two causes: the enmity, and the commanding of what has been mentioned. The command is not meant literally, however, because His saying, ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾, contradicts that. This is so because it rests on the view that what matters in commanding is superiority, as is the position of the Mu'tazilah. Otherwise, mere superiority does not preclude his having authority. It also rests on the reading that "My servants" is general, as the exception shows, and on the reading that the address in "He commands you" is to all people, not only to those who follow him. Nor is there any contradiction in this. Rather, we find within ourselves that he does not demand the act from us, but only adorns it and urges us toward it. Hence this is a metaphor of the dependent kind (isti'arah tab'iyyah) on that basis. It is followed by an allusion to the fact that the addressees are in the position of those commanded who submit to him. This contains a rebuke of their judgment and a belittling of their standing. It is not objected that if "commanding" means "adorning," it should be said "commands for you," and if it means "urging," it should be said "commands you to evil" or "for evil," since the word used is the verb "commands." One must observe the usage of the verb. The word "evil" (al-su') is originally a verbal noun of sa'ahu, yasu'uhu, su'an or musa'ah, meaning to grieve him. Then it was applied to all sins, whether they are speech, deeds, or beliefs, because all of them share the trait of grieving their doer. ﴿And immorality﴾ is the worst of its kinds and the greatest in grieving. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that "evil" is that for which there is no prescribed punishment (hadd), and "immorality" is that for which there is one. It is also said that the two are the same in meaning: it is what reason denies, judges to have no benefit or good outcome, and what the Sharia finds ugly. The conjunction in that case serves to treat the difference of the two descriptions as if it were a difference of two realities, since that is evil because it distresses the rational person, and immorality because he finds it repugnant. Perhaps what led to this view is that He, glory be to Him, named all sins and abominations "bad deeds" in His saying: ﴿Whoever earns a bad deed﴾, ﴿Indeed, good deeds remove bad deeds﴾, and ﴿The recompense for a bad deed is a bad deed like it﴾. He also named all sins "abominations," saying: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden abominations, what is apparent of them and what is hidden﴾. It may be said: Granted, but "bad deed" and "abomination," when they are combined, are distinct, and when they are distinct, they are combined, so the argument is not complete. ﴿And that you say about Allah what you do not know﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it. That is: and the Devil commands you to fabricate lies against Allah, claiming that He has forbidden this and permitted that, or that He has commanded the taking of rivals and approved of your corruption. Page 40. The explicit mention of the command to speak about Allah, although it falls under what precedes, is for the sake of emphasis on its importance. The object of knowing is omitted: that is, what you do not know. The permission in this matter comes from Him, exalted be He. The warning against this entails a warning against fabricating about Him, glory be to Him, with what they know to be unpermitted, as is the case of many of the polytheists, by an apparent implication. The apparent meaning of the verse is a prohibition of following conjecture (zann) altogether, since conjecture is the opposite of knowledge both linguistically and in common usage. An objection arises: the mujtahid acts according to his conjecture, which he has derived from the texts, so how can it be permitted for the muqallid (one who follows another's ruling) to follow it? It is answered that the conjectured ruling of the mujtahid must be acted upon, and the decisive proof for this is the consensus (ijma'). Every ruling that must be acted upon with certainty is known with certainty to be a ruling of Allah, Exalted; otherwise it would not be obligatory to act on it with certainty. And everything known with certainty to be a ruling of Allah, Exalted, is known with certainty. Therefore the conjectured ruling of the mujtahid is known with certainty. The gist is that conjecture suffices as the means of attaining it, and then, through the consensus on the obligation to act, the conjectured becomes known, and conjecture is transformed into knowledge. Thus the muqallid's following of the mujtahid is not at all the following of conjecture. The claim that it is the following of conjecture is a misunderstanding of the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 170:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has revealed,"﴾ The pronoun refers to the people, and the shift from direct address to the third person (ghaybah) serves to alert that, due to the extremity of their ignorance and their lack of worth, they are not fit to be addressed directly; rather, one should turn away from them to whoever has understanding. In this there is a call to every intelligent person, despite their misguidance, that is absent when they are addressed directly with it. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Jews, even though they are not mentioned, based on what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that the verse was revealed concerning them when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) invited them to Islam. It has also been said that it refers to whoever takes (a path), or to what is understood from "those who conceal" (alladhina yaktumun), and the sentence is independent (mustaʾnafah), based on what is narrated that it was revealed concerning the polytheists. You know that the revelation being concerning the Jews or the polytheists does not necessitate restricting the pronoun to them, and it is well known that the generality of the referent does not necessitate the generality of the pronoun, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the divorced women await (by themselves) for three periods﴾ and His saying: ﴿and their husbands have more right to take them back﴾. Moreover, the structure of the Noble Qur'an rejects this saying. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is either general to all the true rulings sent down from Allah, Exalted is He, or specific to what the context requires. ﴿They say, "Rather we will follow what we found our fathers upon."﴾ That is, "what we found them upon." The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is either a circumstantial accusative (hal) from "ābāʾinā," and "alfaynā" is transitive to one object; or it is a second object of it, placed before the first.

﴿Even though their fathers had no understanding at all, nor were they guided?﴾ 170 The answer to the conditional is omitted; that is: "Even if their fathers were ignorant, not reflecting upon the matter of religion, and not guided to the truth, they would still follow them." The waw is either for the circumstantial (hal) or for coordination (ʿatf), and the conditional clause is either a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in (qalū) or coordinated to it. The hamza is for denying the content of that clause, namely their commitment to following, under a supposition that contradicts it, which is that they are not intelligent nor guided, which entails their commitment to following regardless of their condition, without distinction and without knowledge of whether they are right or wrong; and this is blameworthy imitation (taqlid). From this denial there arises the sense of wonder (ta'jib). It is also permitted that the sentence be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of an omitted sentence; that is: "Would they follow them while supposing them to be unintelligent and unguided?" and that it be coordinated to an assumed conditional; that is: "Would they follow them if they were not unintelligent, and even if they were unintelligent?" The first view was taken by al-Zamakhshari and the second by al-Jurmi. It is not hidden that, on the assumption of omitting the preceding sentence, there is no need to say the apodosis is omitted. Perhaps what was mentioned first is more preferable, because it avoids excessive omission and keeps "law" (law) in its well-known meaning, and the interrogative hamza in its original function, which is to place the item about which the question is asked; and the claim that the meaning revolves around coordination with something omitted in such cases in all languages is not accepted. Al-Radi chose that the waw entering on the conditional particle in such a case is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), and by a parenthetical clause is meant that which falls between parts of speech, or comes at the end while being semantically connected to it, and is syntactically independent. It has been said: in the verse there is evidence for prohibiting taqlid for one who is able to reflect; as for following others in religion after knowing by some proof that they are right, this is in reality following what Allah, Exalted is He, has revealed, and it is not in any way the blameworthy taqlid. And He, glory be to Him, has said: ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know.﴾

The likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to what hears nothing but calls and cries. ﴿ومَثَلُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي يَنْعِقُ بِما لا يَسْمَعُ إلا دُعاءً ونِداءً﴾ This is an independent sentence (jumlah ibtida'iyyah), coming either to confirm what precedes it or as a sentence conjoined to it. The point of connection is that the former sentence describes the state of the disbelievers, and this one is an analogy (tamthil) for it. In it there is an omitted element (mudaf mahdhuf), either on the side of the likened (al-mushabbah) or the likened-to (al-mushabbah bihi). That is: "The likeness of the caller of those who disbelieve is like that of the one who shouts," or "The likeness of those who disbelieve is like the likeness of the cattle of the one who shouts." The apparent noun, which is the relative pronoun, has been placed in the position of the pronoun, which is "the cattle" (al-bahaʾim), so that the attribute that is the point of resemblance can be applied to it. The sense on both readings is that the disbelievers, because of their immersion in blind imitation (taqlid) and their inclination toward the misguidance they are upon, do not direct their minds to what is recited to them, and do not reflect on what is set before them. In this they are like the cattle that are shouted at, which hear nothing but the jingle of the tone and the echo of the voice. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the likening of them, in following their fathers on the surface of their condition while ignorant of its reality, to cattle that hear a sound but do not understand what is beneath it. Or it is the likening of their calling upon idols to the caller in his shouting. This would dispense with the omission, but the words of the Exalted, ﴿إلا دُعاءً ونِداءً﴾, do not support it, because idols have no part in that. So the exception has no bearing on the comparison, unless it is taken as a compound comparison (tashbih murakkab), and one holds that the whole of ﴿لا يَسْمَعُ إلا دُعاءً ونِداءً﴾ is a metaphor (kinayah) for lack of understanding and response. The naʿiq is continuous vocalizing to cattle in order to drive them. It is said: "naʿaqa al-ghurab nuʿaqan wa naʿiqan," when the crow calls out without stretching and moving its neck. Naghaqa with a ghayn has the same meaning. When it stretches and moves its neck and then cries out, it is said to be "naʿaba" with a yaʾ. Duʿaʾ and nidaʾ have the same meaning. It has been said that duʿaʾ is what is heard, while nidaʾ may or may not be heard. It has also been said that duʿaʾ is for the near and nidaʾ is for the distant.

﴿صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ﴾ Deaf, dumb, blind. It is in the nominative on the basis of dham (censure), since it carries the sense of a description together with a verbal impediment to describing them with it. ﴿فَهم لا يَعْقِلُونَ 171﴾ That is: they do not perceive anything, because the three senses are lacking. It has been said: whoever loses a sense has lost a form of knowledge. The intended meaning is not the negation of innate reason ('aql gharizi) on the ground that its fruit is absent, as some have said, because its being connected by "fa" (so) to what precedes it does not allow that.

O you who have believed, eat of the good things with which We have provided you. That is, of its delicious things, or of its lawful things. The verse may be either a command to the believers to pursue what befits their station, namely seeking out good things and not being extravagant in consuming what they have been provided of what is lawful, and this is not derived from the preceding command; or it may be a command to them in the same sense as what came before, except that the benefit of singling them out after the general address is to honour them with direct address and to pave the way for the call to thanksgiving. The word "eat" (*kulu*) covers all the ways of benefiting from something, both by its implication (*dalalah*) and by its direct expression (*ʿibarah*). ﴿And give thanks to God﴾ for what He has bestowed upon you. The shift to the third person (*iltifat*, a shift in grammatical person) serves to cultivate reverence. ﴿If it is indeed Him that you worship﴾ (172). This stands in the position of a reason for the call to thanksgiving, as if it were said: "And give thanks to Him, because you single Him out for worship; and your singling Him out for worship indicates that you intend a complete worship befitting His majesty, and this cannot be complete without thanksgiving, for it is among the most excellent of acts of worship, which is why it was made half of faith." It has been narrated in a hadith from Abu al-Darda, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), that God the Exalted says: "Indeed, I and humankind and the jinn are in a great matter: I create, and others are worshipped; I provide sustenance, and others are thanked." The view that the meaning is "if you know Him" or "if you intend to worship Him" is an inferior statement.

[p. 42]

﴿He has only forbidden you carrion﴾: that is, eating it and benefiting from it. He attributed the prohibition to the thing itself, even though prohibition is one of the legal rulings (aḥkām shar'iyya), which are attributes of the act of the responsible person (mukallaf) and do not pertain to physical objects. This indicates the prohibition of any disposal of carrion (al-maytah), meaning an animal that died without a valid legal slaughter (dhakāh shar'iyya) in every respect, by the shortest and most emphatic route. By making the thing itself not admissible to any act of the responsible person, he forbade all such acts, except what the evidence has specified, such as the use of a tanned hide (al-madbūgh). He also attached to "carrion" what is cut off from a living animal, on the basis of the hadith that Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī narrated and graded as ḥasan, from Abū Wāqid al-Laythī, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "What is cut from a beast while it is alive is carrion." Fish and locusts are excluded from this, on the basis of the hadith that Ibn Mājah and al-Ḥākim narrated from Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both), marfūʿ: "Two kinds of carrion and two kinds of blood have been made lawful for us: fish and locusts, and liver and spleen." Also, by custom: when someone says, "So-and-so ate carrion," the mind does not go to these two. Yes, some of them (the Mālikīs) forbade the carrion of fish that float and of locusts that die without a cause, and most Mālikīs hold this view. The generality of the verse was cited as evidence for prohibiting embryos (al-ajinna) and for prohibiting what has no flowing blood, in contrast to those Mālikīs who permitted them. Abū Jaʿfar recited (al-maytatu) with a shadda (the doubled consonant). ﴿And blood﴾ is restricted in Sūrat al-Anʿām to "poured out" (masfūḥ), as will come. Its generality was cited as evidence for the impurity (najāsa) of the blood of fish and of what has no flowing blood.

﴿And the flesh of swine﴾: the flesh was singled out for mention, although the rest of its parts are also forbidden, contrary to the al-Ẓāhiriyya (literalist school). This is because flesh is the main part of an animal that is eaten, and the rest of its parts follow it. It was also said that the flesh was singled out to indicate the prohibition of the swine itself, whether it was slaughtered or not. There is in this what is not hidden. Perhaps the secret in inserting the word "flesh" here is to show the prohibition of what they found pleasant and preferred over other meats, and they considered the prohibition of it to be a great matter. Our companions (the Ḥanafīs) cited the generality of "swine" as evidence for the prohibition of sea swine. Al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: there is no harm in it. It is narrated from Imam Mālik that a man said to him: "What do you say about sea swine?" He said: "It is forbidden." Then another came and said: "What do you say about an animal in the sea that is in the form of a swine?" He said: "It is lawful." He was asked about this, and he said: "Allah the Exalted forbade the swine, and did not forbid what is in its form." The question differs between the two forms.

﴿And that over which the name of other than Allah has been invoked﴾: that is, what is bound up with it, namely, the cry (al-ṣawt) for other than Allah, Exalted is He, at its slaughter. The original meaning of ihlāl, according to many lexicographers, is the sighting of the crescent moon (hilāl). But since it became the custom to raise the voice with takbīr when it was sighted, the term was applied to that, and then it was said for the raising of the voice even when it was for something else. By "other than Allah, Exalted is He," what is meant is an idol (ṣanam) and other things, as is the apparent meaning. ʿAṭāʾ, Makḥūl, al-Shaʿbī, al-Ḥasan, and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib held that "other than" is restricted to the former, and they permitted the slaughter of a Christian when he invoked the name of the Messiah over it. This is contrary to what the Imams have agreed upon regarding its prohibition. It was placed first here because it is more directly related to the act, and it was postponed in other places in view of the purpose there, which is the mention of what is abhorred, namely slaughter for other than Allah, Mighty is His majesty.

﴿But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing﴾: "neither desiring" means by concealing oneself from another person in compulsion, by being the only one to consume it, so that the other perishes. "Nor transgressing" means exceeding what keeps the soul alive and removes hunger. This is apparent in the prohibition of satiation, and it is the position of the majority. From Imam Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī (may Allah be pleased with them both) it is related: "The compelled person should eat from the carrion only the amount that keeps his soul from perishing, because the permission is due to necessity, and it has been removed by that." ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥasan al-ʿIbrī said: he eats from it the amount that satisfies his hunger. Imam Mālik differed on this and said: he eats from it until he is satisfied and takes provision; if he finds independence from it, he discards it. It is reported from al-Shāfiʿī that the meaning of "neither desiring nor transgressing" is not rebelling against the ruler (wālī) nor committing highway robbery (qaṭʿ al-ṭarīq). He included in this a journey undertaken in disobedience, so that the disobedient traveller is not permitted to eat these prohibited things. This is also what is related from Imam Aḥmad, and it is contrary to our school. The ruling of the concession (ruhṣa) on this view requires a qualification: that it not exceed the measure of necessity from outside. The generality of the verse was cited as evidence for permitting the compelled person to eat the carrion of swine and of a human being, contrary to those who prohibited this. The people of the Ḥijāz and Syria, and al-Kisāʾī, recited (famani ḍṭurra) with a ḍamma on the nūn; Abū Jaʿfar among them recited (mani iḍṭirra) with a kasra on the ṭāʾ.

﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾: that is, in consuming it. Indeed, he may even incur sin by abandoning consumption.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (2:173): therefore He removed the prohibition from consuming it and granted the concession. It was also said: the prohibition remains, except that the sin is removed from the compelled person and he is forgiven for his compulsion. This is apparent from restricting the sin to "upon him." The first view was supported by His saying: ﴿except what you are compelled to﴾ (6:119), where an exception is made from the prohibition.

[p. 43]

Know further that the verse does not mean the restriction (qaṣr) of prohibition to what was mentioned, absolutely, as is apparent, such that the objection of denying restriction on account of the prohibition of things not mentioned would arise. Rather, it is restricted to what they believed to be lawful, by the indication that they used to consider lawful what was mentioned. It is as if it were said: "He has only forbidden you what was mentioned, in respect of what you considered lawful for other things." The purpose of restricting prohibition to what they mentioned is their belief in its permissibility, in the most emphatic and forceful manner. Thus it is a restriction of reversal (qaṣr qalb), except that the second part is not to refute belief in prohibition, since they did not believe in the prohibition of anything they had made lawful. Rather, it emphasizes the first part. The address is to people in general, with regard to the inclusion of the polytheists among them. Thus the purpose of the verse is a rebuke against making the forbidden lawful, just as ﴿O people, eat﴾ (2:168) is a rebuke against prohibiting what is lawful. Or the meaning is a restriction of prohibition of what was mentioned to the state of choice, as if it were said: "He has only forbidden you these things so long as you are not compelled to them." The more fitting reading then is that the address is to the believers, so that the focus of benefit is the qualification, since they were believers in the prohibition of these things. The benefit of the ruling is the concession after restriction upon them by requiring what is lawful and good, or the honouring of them by bestowing favour through this concession after bestowing favour upon them by permitting pleasant things.

Some of them chose that the restriction is intended as a refutation of the polytheists in their prohibition of what Allah the Exalted had permitted, such as the baḥīra, the waṣīla, the ḥām, and the like, in order to eat these prohibited things mentioned in the verse. So it is as if they said: "Those were prohibited to us, but these have been made lawful for us." It was said: "Nothing has been prohibited except these." So it is then a relative restriction (qaṣr iḍāfī). Others held that it is a restriction of singling out (qaṣr ifrād) in relation to what the believers prohibited along with the mentioned pleasant things. In this there is the objection that the believers did not believe in the prohibition of pleasant things, but rather prohibited them upon themselves because of what they heard of the severe reckoning and questioning about blessings. This was said by one of the verifying scholars (al-muḥaqqiqīn), so let it be pondered.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 174:**

﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has sent down of the Book﴾, which includes the various rulings of the law, among which are the rulings on what is lawful and what is unlawful. The verse was revealed, as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, concerning the scholars of the Jews who used to receive gifts from their inferiors. They hoped that the Prophet who would be sent would be from among them. When he was sent from among others, they concealed and altered his description, ﷺ, so that he would not be followed, and thus their leadership would end and their gifts would cease.

﴿And they exchange it﴾, that is, they take in its place, in reality, and the pronoun refers to the Book, or to what was sent down, or to the concealment. ﴿For a small price﴾, that is, a contemptible return.

﴿They consume nothing into their bellies except the Fire﴾. This is either in the present, as is the primary sense of the imperfect verb, because they consumed what is connected with the Fire, which is the bribe (al-rishā), since it is the cause of the Fire. In this case there is an allegorical metaphor (istiʿārah tamthīliyyah, a metaphor drawn from a whole scene), in which the state resulting from their consuming what is connected with the Fire is likened to the state derived from their consuming the Fire itself, in that the consequence of the consumption of each of them is the tearing of the intestines and pain, just as the consequence of the other. The expression of the thing likened-to is therefore used for the thing likened. Or it refers to the outcome, that is, they will not consume anything on the Day of Resurrection except the Fire. In both possibilities the word "fire" is used in its literal meaning. It has been said that it is a metaphor for the bribe when the present is meant, with the relation being causal and effectual, and it is literal when the outcome is meant. It is not hidden that the first is the more fitting for the context of threat. The prepositional phrase is a presumed circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddarah); that is, they consume nothing that is present in their bellies except the Fire, since presence in the belly is not simultaneous with eating. By this estimation, the weakness of placing the circumstantial clause before the exception is avoided, and there is no need to say that it is connected to "they consume", and that it means "in the path of their bellies," as Abu al-Baqa' chose. The restriction by "bellies" serves to convey fullness, not emphasis, as has been said. The use of "in" (fī) as a container, although it does not require that the container encompass the whole of what it contains, has nonetheless become common in using the belly as a container with the sense of encompassing, just as the containment of a part of it in the sense of not encompassing has become common, as in his saying:

*Eat in part of your bellies, you may be spared,
For your time is a time of hunger.*

﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾, that is, speech of mercy, as al-Hasan said, so this does not contradict His questioning them, may He be glorified. It has been said: ﴿He will not speak to them﴾ at all, because of the increase of His anger, may His majesty be exalted, against them; the questioning is through the angels.

﴿Nor will He purify them﴾, that is, He will not cleanse them from the defilement of sins, or He will not praise them.

﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ (174), that is, painful. These statements have come arranged according to meaning, because when He, may He be glorified, mentioned their purchasing with that small price, which was a metaphor for their wicked and transient greed, He began first in the report with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They consume nothing into their bellies except the Fire﴾. Then He matched their concealment of the truth and their not speaking it with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾. And upon their concealment and their purchasing with what Allah has sent down a small price, He based that they are false witnesses and evil scholars who, by this false testimony, harmed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and caused him pain. So they were answered with His saying, may He be glorified: ﴿Nor will He purify them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾ He began first with what corresponds to each individually, and secondly with what corresponds to the whole.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 175:

﴿Those are the ones who have bought﴾ by means of their concealing the truth in pursuit of base greeds and worldly aims, ﴿the misguidance in exchange for guidance﴾ in this world, ﴿and the punishment in exchange for forgiveness﴾ in the Hereafter. The sentence may be a new (independent) statement, since when the threat against those who conceal (the truth) was so grave, it was apt that one would ask about the cause of the greatness of their threat, so it was said: because of concealment they have lost both this world and the Hereafter. Or it may be a predicate following another predicate of inna, the first sentence explaining the severity of their threat and this one explaining the monstrousness of their concealment.

﴿So how patient they are over the Fire!﴾ That is, how intense is their endurance! It is an expression of wonder for the believers at their committing what brings it about without any concern. Otherwise, what patience do they have? As for (ma) in this kind of construction, it is said to be an indefinite complete (nakirah tammah) noun, which is the view of the majority; it is said to be an interrogative (istifhamiyyah) that has taken on the meaning of wonder, which is the view of al-Farra'; it is said to be a relative (mawsulah), which is the view of al-Akhfash; and it is related from him also that it is an indefinite qualifying (nakirah mawsufah). On these views it is in the place of nominative (raf') as a subject (mubtada'), with the sentence as its predicate, or its predicate is omitted if it is a qualifier or a relative clause. The full discussion is in the books of grammar.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 176:

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ means: the totality of what has been mentioned, namely the consuming of fire, the absence of speech (from Allah) and of purification, and the punishment that is consequent upon concealment.

﴿بِأنَّ اللَّهَ نَزَّلَ الكِتابَ بِالحَقِّ﴾ means: because of the fact that Allah, exalted is He, sent down the Book (al-Kitab) — the Qur'an or the Torah — bearing the truth, with no trace of falsehood whatsoever; and they rejected it, by denial or by concealment.

﴿وإنَّ الَّذِينَ اخْتَلَفُوا في الكِتابِ﴾ means: concerning its kind, by believing in some of the Books of Allah, exalted is He, and disbelieving in others; or concerning the Torah, where "they differed" (ikhtalafu) means they deviated from following the path of truth regarding it, or they made what they altered a substitute for what it contained; or concerning the Qur'an, and their disagreement about it is the saying of some of them that it is sorcery, of others that it is poetry, and of others that it is the fables of the ancients.

﴿لَفِي شِقاقٍ﴾ means: in opposition (khilaf).

﴿بَعِيدٍ﴾ means: far from the truth, entailing the most severe punishment. This sentence is a tadhyil (concluding appendix) to what preceded it, connected to it by a conjunction. Some people made the "wa" (waw) for the state (hal), and the causal relation mentioned earlier refers back to it, and the tadhyil has been placed within the blame, as is not hidden.

[Page 45]

﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west.﴾ (al-birr) is a comprehensive term for all kinds of good and acts of obedience that bring one closer to Allah the Exalted. The address is to the People of the Two Books. What is meant by ﴿toward the east or the west﴾ is the two specific directions: the Jews prayed facing the west, toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), from the horizon of Makkah, and the Christians prayed facing the east. The verse was revealed in response to them, since they had engaged extensively in disputing the matter of the qibla. Each group claimed that righteousness was confined to its own qibla, in refutation of the other. So Allah the Exalted refuted them all together by negating the whole category of righteousness from their qiblas, because those qiblas had been abrogated. Thus the definite article in al-birr is for the category (jins), to indicate the generality of the negation, not for restriction (qasr), since the intended meaning is not the negation of restriction nor the restriction of negation. It is possible that the address is general, to them and to the Muslims, in which case it is a return to the starting point (awd ala bad'), since the discourse concerning the qibla and their criticism of the Prophet (ﷺ) for it was the basis of the discussion up to this point. So it was made a comprehensive conclusion that summarizes what had been detailed. The mention of east and west is meant as generalization, not as specifying the two directions. The definite article in al-birr in this case is either for the category, which implies restriction, the intended meaning being the negation of righteousness being specifically tied to the matter of the qibla in an absolute sense, in accordance with what the situation demands of excessive preoccupation with it and neglect of everything else; or it is for a specific known thing, meaning: ﴿It is not the righteousness﴾ — the great righteousness — about which you have excessively disputed and neglected everything else. ‘East’ is placed before ‘west’ even though the Christian religion came later, out of regard for the order between them that follows the order of sunrise and sunset. Hamza and Hafs read al-birr in the accusative (naṣb), and the rest read it in the nominative (raf'). The reasoning for the first reading is that it is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), as in the verse of poetry:

"Ask, if people are ignorant of us and of him, so the knower and the ignorant are not equal."

What makes this acceptable is that the interpreted infinitive (al-maṣdar al-mu'awwal) is more definite than the noun with the definite article, since it resembles a pronoun in that it is neither described nor used as a description, and the more definite deserves to be the subject. Also, a noun is lengthy, so if the customary order were observed, the harmony of the parts of the noble structure would be lost. The reasoning for the second reading is that each group claims that righteousness is this, so the refutation must agree with their claim, and that is only so if al-birr is the subject (ism), as is made clear by making it the one spoken of in the following adversative clause. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, read ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ with the accusative and with ﴿that you turn﴾ using the particle bi, and ﴿But righteousness is that one believes in Allah...﴾ is a establishment of the truth after explaining the falsehood of the falsehood. The definite article in al-birr is either for the category, in which case the restriction is claimed (qasr idda'i) for the perfection of that category in this individual; or it is for a specific known thing, meaning: what should be cared about, given attention to, and striven for in attaining. The statement is by omitting a modifying word, i.e. (the righteousness of one who believes), since one does not report a physical body about an abstract meaning. It is permissible not to resort to the omission and to make the verbal noun (maṣdar) carry the meaning of the active participle (ism al-fa'il), or to say that al-birr is used of the one who is righteous as an intensification. The first is more suited to His saying ﴿It is not righteousness﴾ and better in itself, since it is like removing the leather sock upon reaching water. And because the purpose of making the possessor of righteousness the one who believes is to convey that his belief is righteousness, it reverts to the first. What is meant by this belief is a belief free of any taint of associating partners, unlike the belief of the Jews and Christians who say: Uzayr is the son of Allah, and the Messiah is the son of Allah. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿but﴾ (wa-lakin) with the lightened form, and some read al-barr with the form of the active participle.

﴿and the Last Day﴾: i.e., the resurrection (al-ma'ad), which the Muslims affirm, and what follows it according to them. ﴿and the angels﴾: i.e., and one believes in them and affirms that they are honored servants, who are not described as male or female, and among them are those who mediate between Him, the Exalted, and His prophets, peace be upon them, by conveying revelation and sending down books. ﴿and the Book﴾: i.e., its kind, so it includes all the divine books, because righteousness is belief in all of them. This is the apparent meaning, which agrees with its companion (the preceding item), and with what occurred in the hadith: "That you believe in Allah, His angels, His books, and His messengers." Or it refers to the Qur'an, because it is the one intended by the call and the complete one deserving of being called a Book, and belief in it is belief in all the books, since it confirms what is before it. It was also said that it refers to the Torah, but this is weakened by the absence of any clear indication specifying it, and by the fact that belief in it does not necessarily entail belief in all of them, except through its implying belief in the Qur'an. Belief in the books is to believe that they are the speech of the Lord, glorified is His majesty, uncreated, sent down to their possessors and clear to them, according to what wisdom required in languages. ﴿and the prophets﴾: i.e., all of them, without distinguishing between any one of them as the People of the Two Books did. Belief in them is to affirm that they are infallible and purified, that they are the noblest of people in lineage and descent, that there is no blemish or repulsive defect in them, and that it is believed that their master and seal is Muhammad (ﷺ), and that his law abrogates all the laws, and adherence to it is obligatory for all those under obligation until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿and gives wealth in spite of love for it﴾: a circumstantial qualifier (hal) from the pronoun of āta (gave) and the pronoun attached to the wealth; i.e., he gives wealth while loving wealth. The restriction is to explain the best kind of charity. Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best charity is that you give while you are healthy, hoping to live and fearing poverty, and do not delay until when the throat has reached [the collarbone], then you say: 'To so-and-so such-and-such, to so-and-so such-and-such,' and indeed it already belonged to so-and-so." In this is an indication that the degrees of reward vary according to the varying levels of love (for wealth), so that the charity of the poor and the miser may be more excellent than the charity of the rich and the generous, unless they love wealth more than them. This is supported by his saying (ﷺ): "The best deeds are the most difficult ones." It is also permitted that the pronoun returns to Allah the Exalted, or to the verbal noun understood from the verb, and the restriction then serves completion, and explains the consideration of sincerity or good disposition in charity, and removes the notion that giving wealth in any form is righteousness. The first is what is transmitted from the righteous predecessors, and it is probably what is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿to the near of kin﴾: the first object of āta (gave), whose second object was fronted for emphasis; or because there is, together with mā, a coordination after it that would be lengthy if the order were observed, and the order would lose the harmony of the parts. This is also what required the fronting of the circumstantial qualifier. It was also said that it is the second object. The meaning of ﴿near of kin﴾ is the relatives of the giver, but only the needy among them, not in general, as indicated by the context of the discourse. The mention of the categories of zakat is an indication that the meaning is goodness and charity, and that giving to the rich is a gift, not charity. This category is mentioned first because giving to them is more important. It is authentically reported from Umm Kulthum bint 'Uqbah, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The best charity is that given to a close relative who is hostile." Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and others related from Salman ibn 'Amir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Charity given to the poor is one charity, but to a close relative it is two: charity and maintaining kinship."

﴿and orphans﴾: coordinated with ﴿near of kin﴾. It was also said that it is coordinated with "the near of kin," since it is not valid to deliver wealth to one who does not understand, so the giver in that case is their guardian on their behalf, and there is in this what is not hidden.

﴿and the needy﴾: plural of miskin (needy), which is one who is constantly still, because need has stilled him to the point of having no movement, or one who is constantly still and dependent on people. Restricting it to one who has nothing, or to one who does not own what would fill his need, goes beyond its meaning.

﴿and the wayfarer﴾ (ibn al-sabil): i.e., the traveler, as Mujahid said. He was named so because he sticks to the road while traveling, or because the road brings him out, as if it had given birth to him. The reason for calling him by the singular is his isolation from his loved ones, homeland and companions, so he is always longing for gathering and yearning for home, and the noble person longs for his homeland as the she-camel longs for her resting place. Or it is because, since there is usually no acquaintance between the wayfarers and the giver, it lessens the matter of giving and encourages it toward their individuals, to lessen the matter of giving to them; and to indicate that although they are a group, they should be regarded as one soul, so he does not grow weary of giving to them because of not knowing them and their distant benefit; so let this be understood. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and Ibn Jubayr that it is the guest who alights among the Muslims, and the askers, i.e., those seeking food, whether they are rich but what they have does not suffice for their need, or poor, as the apparent meaning of what Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud and Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, indicates. He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The asker has a right, even if he comes on a horse," for the one who comes on a horse is usually rich. It was also said that he meant the needy who ask, so their condition is known by their asking. ﴿And the needy﴾, the one mentioned earlier, are those who do not ask and whose need is known from their condition, even if their outward appearance is wealth. In that case, the restriction in the hadith serves to emphasize the care for the right of the asker and to establish that asking is a cause of entitlement, even if it is supposed that he is wealthy, like the relative and the orphan.

[p. 48]

﴿And for the slaves﴾: this is dependent on *ātā* (gave), meaning he gave wealth toward freeing necks and ransoming them, by helping those in a contract of manumission (*mukātabīn*), or ransoming captives, or buying slaves in order to free them. "Neck" (*raqaba*) is a metaphor (*majāz*) for the person. The use of the word "in" (*fī*) indicates that what is given to these people is spent on freeing them, and they do not own it, unlike the other categories of expenditure. ﴿And established prayer﴾ is coordinated (*ʿaṭf*) with the relative clause of "whoever" (*man*). By "prayer" is meant the obligatory prayer, as with ﴿and gave zakat﴾, on the basis that what was mentioned earlier, giving wealth, refers to voluntary charities. It was placed before the obligatory charity for emphasis in encouraging it. Alternatively, it refers to rights in wealth that were not fixed apart from zakat. Al-Tirmidhī, al-Dāraqutnī and a group related from Fāṭima bint Qays, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is a right in wealth other than zakat," and then he recited the verse. Al-Bukhārī in his *Tārīkh* related something similar from Abū Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him). It has been disputed whether this right remains or not. A group held that it does not, and they cited what is related from ʿAlī (may Allah honor his face), traced to the Prophet (*marfūʿan*): "The Sacrifice abrogated every slaughter, Ramadan abrogated every fast, the ritual bath of impurity abrogated every bath, and zakat abrogated every charity." Another group held the first view, citing His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾, and the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "He does not believe in Allah and the Last Day who sleeps satisfied while his neighbor beside him is hungry," and by consensus (*ijmāʿ*) that when need reaches the point of necessity, people must give an amount sufficient to remove the necessity, even if zakat is not obligatory on them; and if they refuse to pay, it is permissible to take from them. They answered regarding the hadith that it is *gharīb* (a narration with a single or unusual transmission) and contested, and in its chain is al-Musayyab ibn Sharīk, who is not considered strong by them, and that what is meant is that zakat abrogated every fixed charity. It is also permitted that what was mentioned earlier refers also to obligatory zakat, with no repetition, because the purpose of what preceded is to explain its recipients, and from this comes the explanation of its payment and encouragement to it. Some categories of recipients were omitted, because the aim here is to indicate the avenues of good in general, not to limit them. The explanation of the recipient was given precedence to show concern for its matter, for charity is only considered valid when it is in its proper recipient and place, as indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents and relatives﴾. On this basis, it is necessary that "the beggars" means the poor. ﴿And those who fulfill their covenant when they make one﴾ is coordinated with "whoever believes" (*man āmana*). It did not say "and fulfilled" (*awfā*) as in the preceding case, indicating the necessity of the stability of fulfilling. It was said: as a signal that it is an intended matter in itself. It was also said: as an indication that it differs from what preceded, for it is among the rights of Allah, Exalted is He, whereas the preceding is among the rights of people. On this basis, "covenant" means what does not make lawful what is unlawful or make unlawful what is lawful, from the agreements existing among people. The apparent meaning is to take "covenant" as including both the rights of Allah and the rights of creatures, and the omission of the object indicates this. The restriction by the adverbial phrase (*ẓarf*) is to indicate that their fulfillment of the covenant does not come after the time of making it. It was also said: it is to indicate that the covenant is not among the necessities of religion, and it is not for emphasis, as some have said.

﴿And the patient in misfortune and adversity﴾ is in the accusative as a praise (*madḥ*), with the implied "I specify" or "I praise." Its construction was changed from what precedes it, as an alert to the excellence and distinction of patience over all other deeds, so that it is as if it is not of the same kind as the first. The use of a shift in case (*qaṭʿ*) in coordination is among what the leading imams have established, and it occurs in the Book (the Qur'an) as well, and the eminent scholars approved it and considered it more eloquent than continuity of case (*ittibāʿ*). It also comes with an indefinite noun, as in the saying of al-Hudhalī:
And he takes refuge with women unadorned, ***
and disheveled ones who nurse, like the ghouls.
*[p. 48]* "Al-Basāʾ" means misery and poverty, and "al-Ḍarrāʾ" means sickness and pain. Both are verbal nouns (*maṣdar*) formed on the pattern *faʿlāʾ*, and they have no *afʿal* form, because *afʿal* and *faʿlāʾ* are used for adjectives and descriptions, and they did not come in nouns that are not descriptions. It was also read as "and the patient ones" (*al-ṣābirūn*), just as it was read as "and those who fulfill" (*al-mūfūn*).

﴿And at the time of battle﴾: that is, the time of fighting and striving against the enemy. This is from the manner of ascending in patience from the severe to the more severe, because patience over sickness is greater than patience over poverty, and patience in fighting is greater than patience over sickness. Patience over the first two was governed by "in" (*fī*), because a person is counted among the praised when he is patient in any of those, except when poverty and sickness become like an environment for him. As for when they afflict him for a time and he is patient, there is no great praise in it, since most people are like that. The word "time" (*ḥīna*) was used for the last, because fighting is a state that does not usually last for most of the time.

﴿Those are the ones who are truthful﴾ in their faith or in seeking righteousness.

﴿And those are the God-fearing﴾: who guard against the punishment of Allah, Exalted is He, by avoiding His disobedience and carrying out His commands. The predicate of the first "those" was expressed as a relative clause with a past-tense verb, to indicate the actual realization of their attribute, and that this has occurred from them and become established. The predicate of the second was varied to indicate that this is not renewed, but has become like a disposition for them. Also, had it been expressed in the same form as the preceding, it would not have been fitting for it to occur as a closing rhyme (*fāṣila*). This verse, as you see, includes fifteen characteristics, and they return to three categories. The first five of them relate to human perfections that are of the kind of soundness of belief, and the last of them is His saying: ﴿and the prophets﴾. It began with belief in Allah and the Last Day, because these two indicate the origin and the return, which are in reality the east and the west, so it harmonizes perfectly with what was negated at the beginning. The six that follow relate to the perfections of the soul, which are of the kind of good companionship with the servants; the first of them is ﴿and gave wealth﴾ and the last ﴿and in the captives﴾. The last four relate to human perfections of the kind of refining the soul; the first of them is ﴿and established prayer﴾ and the last ﴿and at the time of battle﴾. By my life, whoever acts according to this verse has perfected faith and attained the highest levels of certainty.

By way of esoteric interpretation (*ta'wīl*): ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward﴾ the east of the world of spirits or the west of the world of bodies, for that is restriction and veiling, ﴿but righteousness is﴾ the righteousness of the monotheist who believes in Allah and the return in the station of unification (*jamʿ*), and who witnesses unification within the details of multiplicity, and is not veiled by unification from the detail, which is the inner aspect of the world of angels and the outer aspect of the world of prophets. The Book combines the outer and the inner. [He] gave (*ātā*) knowledge, which is the wealth of the heart, while it is beloved, to ﴿the near of kin﴾, the spiritual faculties close to Him; ﴿orphans﴾, the soulful faculties cut off from the true Father, which is the light of the spirit; ﴿the needy﴾, the natural faculties which have never ceased to be constantly at rest in the dust of the body; ﴿the wayfarer﴾, those traveling toward the stations of the Truth; ﴿the beggars﴾, those seeking through the tongue of their readiness what will be nourishment for their spirits; and in ﴿freeing the necks﴾ of the worshipers of this world and the captives of desires, through admonition and guidance. ﴿And established the prayer﴾ of presence; ﴿and gave﴾ what purifies his soul by negating thoughts and effacing attributes; ﴿those who fulfill﴾ the covenant of pre-eternity by abandoning opposition in servanthood and turning away from all but the Truth in the station of knowing; ﴿the patient﴾ in the misfortune of constant need of Allah, Exalted is He, and in the adversity of breaking the self; and ﴿at the time of the battle﴾ against the greatest enemy. ﴿Those are the ones who are truthful﴾ toward Allah, Exalted is He, in journeying toward Him and giving up existence. ﴿And those are the God-fearing﴾ who guard against polytheism, free from all other vices.

[Page 49]

﴿O you who believe﴾: this begins the explanation of some of the legal rulings (ahkam shar'iyyah), as a remedy for what was neglected by those who fell short, following the foundational principles of the religion (qawa'id al-din) on which the affairs of this life and the Hereafter rest. ﴿Prescribed for you﴾ means: obligated and required, upon the demand of the rightful claimant (sahib al-haqq). The power of the guardian (wali) to pardon does not diminish this, for the obligation is considered only in relation to the authorities (hukkam) or the killers. The original meaning of kitabah (writing) is inscription, and it was then used as a metaphor for obligation. The word ʿala ("upon") is explicit in this sense.

﴿Retaliation (al-qisas) for the slain﴾ means: on account of them, in the manner of the hadith, "A woman entered the Fire because of a cat that she tied up." It has also been said that the verb qassa is construed with fi ("in") because it implies the meaning of equality (al-musawah), since its sense is that a person should have done to him the same as he did. From this root comes the word miqass (scissors), so named because its two blades are equal, and qissah (story) is so called because the narration equals what is narrated, and qassas (storyteller) is so called because he recounts the like of people's reports. The word al-qatla is the plural of qatil, like jarih and jarha (wounded). It is also read as kataba (with the verb in the active form), and al-qisas (in the accusative). There is no pronoun referring forward to something not yet mentioned in this reading, since the determined object is established before its mention.

﴿The free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾: this sentence explains what precedes it, meaning that a free person is subject to retaliation for a free person. It has also been said that it means he is held accountable for it. It is narrated that in the pre-Islamic period, between two tribes of the Arabs, there were blood feuds, and one of them had superiority over the other. They swore that they would kill the free man among them for a slave of the other, and the male for the female. When Islam came, they brought the matter to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed, and he commanded them to reach settlement (yatabawa'u). Thus, the verse indicates that a slave is not to be killed for a free person, nor a female for a male. This is because the implicit contrast reasoning (mafhum al-mukhalafah) is considered only when its negation is not known through implicit agreement reasoning (mafhum al-muwafaqah). It is known from the killing of a slave for a slave, and a female for a female, that a slave is to be killed for a free person, and a female for a male, by way of priority (al-awla). Thus the verse does not indicate that a free person is not to be killed for a slave, nor a male for a female. This is because implicit contrast reasoning, just as it is conditioned upon that condition, is also conditioned on there being no other benefit to the specification. The ruling here lies between two benefits: prohibiting transgression, and establishing equality between free and free and slave and slave.

Al-Shafi'i and Malik prohibited killing a free person for a slave, whether it was his own slave or the slave of another. Their evidence is not from this verse, but from the Sunnah, consensus (ijma') and analogy (qiyas). As for the first, Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that "a man killed his slave, and the Messenger (ﷺ) flogged him and exiled him for a year, and did not impose retaliation upon him for it." He also reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "It is part of the Sunnah that a Muslim is not to be killed for one under covenant, nor a free man for a slave." As for the second, it is reported that Abu Bakr and Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) did not kill a free man for a slave, in the presence of the Companions, and none of them objected to this. They were those whom the blame of any blamer did not deter in the cause of Allah. As for the third, there is no retaliation for injuries (al-atraf) between a free person and a slave by agreement, so killing is analogized to it.

According to our great Imam (may Allah be pleased with him), a free man is killed for a slave, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "The blood of the Muslims is equal." Also, retaliation depends on equality in inviolability (al-'ismah), which is by religion or by abode, and both are equal in these. Distinction in persons is not considered, as evidenced by the fact that if a group kills one person, they are all killed for him. Also, the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That the life for the life﴾. The law of those before us, when it is related to us without any indication of its abrogation, is binding upon us as a law for us.

Some people said that the verse indicates what the opponent holds, because ﴿the free for the free﴾ is an explanation and clarification of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you for the slain﴾. Thus it indicates that observing equality in "freedom and servitude" is required, and imposing retaliation on the free for killing a slave is neglect of observing equality in that respect. The consequence of this is that a slave should not be killed except for a slave, and a female should not be killed except for a female. However, the opponent did not hold this, and went against the apparent meaning for the sake of analogy and consensus. Whoever among us accepts this claims that the verse was abrogated by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That the life for the life﴾, because its generality abrogates the requirement of equality in freedom and maleness derived from it. This is what is related from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, and al-Thawri.

[Page 50]

It has been objected that the verse is a recounting of what is in the Torah, and the authority (hujjiyyah) of the recounting of the law of those before us is conditioned on the non-appearance of its abrogator, as they have stated explicitly. This depends on there not being found in the Qur'an anything that contradicts what is recounted, for if that were found, it would be its abrogator, since it comes later. Then the recounting would be a recounting of the abrogated, and would not be authoritative, let alone be an abrogator. Even after granting the indication, an abrogator exists, as is not hidden.

Our masters of the Hanafi and Maliki schools, and a group, held that the guardian has only retaliation (qisas), and does not take blood money (diyah) except with the consent of the killer. This is because Allah, the Exalted, mentioned blood money for accidental killing, so it is established that retaliation is for what is the opposite of accidental, which is intentional. Since it is established for intentional killing, one turns away from it, so as not to incur adding to the text by opinion. It was objected that the explicit meaning of the text is the obligation of observing equality in retaliation, which does not require the obligation of retaliation itself. It was answered that retaliation, which is qawd (lex talionis) by way of equality, requires both of them.

﴿So whoever is pardoned something by his brother﴾ means: whatever is called "something" of pardon and forgiveness, even the least amount. The indefinite noun (al-masdar al-mubham) is in the position of a qualified noun, so it is permissible for it to substitute for the subject (na'ib 'an al-fa'il), and it has a direct object. The phrase "from his brother" may be connected to the verb, or it may be a circumstantial clause (hal) of "something." Placing "something" in the position of the subject indicates that some pardon is possible, such as pardoning part of the blood, or some of the heirs pardoning, just as a complete pardon removes retaliation, since it is not divisible. The word "brother" refers to the guardian of the blood, and he was called a brother to appeal to his feelings by reminding him of the brotherhood of humanity and religion. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the slain, and the phrase is elliptical, meaning "from the blood of his brother." He was called the brother of the killer to indicate that the brotherhood of Islam between them is not severed by killing.

The verb "afa" transitively takes the perpetrator directly and the offense with "'an," as one says, "I pardoned Zaid" and "I pardoned him for his sin." When it is construed with the offense as the intended object, whether it is mentioned or not, as in the verse, it is construed with the perpetrator with "li" (for), since pardoning the first and benefit to the second. So the intention here is pardoning the offense, but it omitted mentioning it because concern is for the perpetrator. Some have assumed that this "'an" is inserted before "something," but when it is omitted, it takes the nominative because it occupies the position of the subject. This is a case of deletion and conveyance restricted to what is heard. Some people interpreted "afiya" as "tarak" (to leave), so it is then transitive, and its direct object is put in the position of its subject. It was objected that "afa al-shay'" in the sense of "taraka" is not established, and what is established is "a'fahu." It was answered that it has occurred, and was transmitted by the lexicographers on whom reliance is placed in this matter. Although it is not well known, the attribution of the passive verb to its direct object, which is the original, favors its consideration and makes it preferable to the well-known usage, because in that there is attribution of the passive to the verbal noun, which is contrary to the original. The statement that "shay'" is in the nominative by the deletion of a verb implied by "'ufiya" is not valid, since after taking the meaning of pardon into account there is no need for the meaning of leaving. Rather, it is weak, as is not hidden.

﴿Then pursuing with fairness and paying it with good conduct﴾ means: let there be pursuit, or the matter is pursuit. The intended meaning is the instruction of the pardoner not to press hard in demanding the blood money from the one pardoned, and to give him time if he is in difficulty, and not to demand more than it. And for the one pardoned, not to delay the pardoner in it, nor to diminish any of it, and to pay it when possible. Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Mujahid held this view. It has also been said that the intended meaning is that the one pardoned has the obligation of pursuit and payment. The sentence is the predicate of "man" if it is taken as a relative pronoun, and the answer to the conditional if it is taken as a conditional. It may be cited as evidence from the verse that the requirement of intentional killing is retaliation alone, since the command to pay blood money is ordered after the pardon, which is ordered after the obligation of retaliation. Some have used it as evidence that blood money is one of the requirements of intentional killing, otherwise the command to pay blood money would not be ordered upon any pardon, comprehensive of pardon for all of the blood or part of it. Rather, the consent of the killer and restriction to part would be required. It was objected that this is only valid if the tanwin on "shay'" is for generality, meaning "some pardon, whatever it is, whether like all of it or part of it." But if it is for diminution, then no, since the command to pay would then be ordered upon part of the pardon, and there is no doubt that when it is realized concerning the blood, the remainder becomes property, even if the killer does not consent.

[Page 51]

Also, the verse was revealed concerning reconciliation (sulh), which agrees with the usage, for when "afa" is used with it, its meaning is substitution (badal). That is, whoever is given something of the property from his slain brother's side by way of reconciliation, then the one who gave it, who is the guardian, has the right to demand the substitute out of courtesy and good dealing. Unless it is said that it was revealed concerning pardon, as is the apparent wording, and this is what most of the exegetes said.

﴿That﴾ means the ruling mentioned within the explanation of pardon and blood money. ﴿Is a lightening from your Lord and mercy﴾, because in the legislation of pardon there is ease for the killer, and in the legislation of blood money there is benefit for the heirs of the slain. It is related from Muqatil that he prescribed retaliation alone upon the Jews, pardon absolutely upon the Christians, and gave this community the choice among the three, as ease for them and placing the ruling according to their stations. According to this, ﴿Then whoever gives charity﴾ is an explanation of the ruling of this law after recounting a ruling that was in the Torah, and it is not included within the recounting.

﴿And whoever transgresses after that﴾ means: exceeds what was legislated, by killing someone other than the killer after the revelation of this ruling, or killing the killer after pardon and taking blood money. ﴿For him is a painful punishment﴾ means: a kind of punishment that is painful. The more obvious meaning is that it is in the Hereafter. It is related from al-Hasan and Ibn Jubayr that it is in this world, by his being killed without fail, and no blood money being accepted from him, based on what Abu Dawud reported from the hadith of Samurah, raised to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I do not pardon anyone who kills after taking blood money."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 179:

﴿And for you in retribution (qisas) there is life﴾ is conjoined to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Retribution is prescribed for you﴾. The purpose of it is to settle the soul to submit to the ruling of retribution, because it is hard on the soul. This is a statement of the utmost eloquence. The most concise statement they had on this meaning was: "Killing prevents killing" (al-qatl anfa al-qatl). This statement is preferred over it for several reasons. The first: fewness of letters, for the words spoken here are ten letters, if the tanwin is not counted as a separate letter, whereas there are fourteen letters there. The second: consistency, for in every act of retribution there is life, but not every killing prevents killing, for killing unjustly is more likely to provoke further killing. The third: what is in the tanwin of "hayat" (life) of the sense of kind or of magnification.

The fourth: the figure of antithesis (tibaq) between "qisas" (retribution) and "hayat" (life), for "qisas" is the removal of life, so it is its opposite.

The fifth: the explicit mention of what is sought in itself, namely life, for the prohibition of killing is only sought for its sake and not for its own sake.

The sixth: strangeness in that a thing is made to be present in its opposite, and in that the contained thing, when the container holds it, protects it from scattering, so "qisas" in our context protects life from calamities. The seventh: freedom from repetition together with closeness, for it is not free from ugliness, and reversing the second half upon the first is not counted as an embellishment. The eighth: the sweetness and smoothness of the wording, in that it does not contain what their saying contains of successive light syllables, for in their saying there are two consecutive moving letters only in one place, and there is no doubt that this detracts from the smoothness of the wording and its flowing on the tongue. Also, moving from the fa' to the lam is more balanced than moving from the lam to the hamza, because the hamza is far from the lam, and likewise moving from the sad to the ha' is more balanced than moving from the alif to the lam. The ninth: not needing the phrase "from the aspect of" (al-haythiyya), and their saying "it needs it."

The tenth: defining "qisas" with the definite article of the genus, which indicates the reality of this ruling, encompassing "striking, wounding, killing" and other things, whereas their saying does not encompass it. The eleventh: its freedom from "af'al" (the comparative form), which suggests that in abstaining there is also a negation of killing.

The twelfth: its containing what is suitable for fighting, namely life, unlike their saying, which contains a negation flanked by two killings, and that is something befitting them. The thirteenth: its freedom from what the apparent sense of their saying suggests, that a thing is the cause of the negation of itself, which is impossible, and other things. Glory be to Him whose word is exalted and whose sign is dazzling.

Then, the meaning of "life" is either the worldly life, which is the apparent meaning, because in legislating retribution and knowing it, the killer is deterred from killing, so it becomes the cause of the "life" of two souls in this world, and because they used to kill other than the killer, and a group for one person, so strife would erupt among them, and the war of al-Basus would arise in full force; when retribution is taken from the killer, the rest are safe, and that becomes a cause of their life. On the first view this requires an implied element, and on the second it requires restriction. As for the otherworldly life, on the basis that if retribution is taken from the killer in this world, he is not held to account for the rights of the one killed in the Hereafter; on this view the address is specific to the killers, whereas the apparent sense is that it is general. The two adverbial phrases are either both predicates of "life", or one is a predicate and the other a complement to it, or a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun within it.

Abu al-Jawza' read: ﴿fi al-qasas﴾ (in retribution), and it is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, and what is meant by "maqsus" is this ruling in particular, or the Qur'an in general; in that case "life" is meant as the life of hearts and not the life of bodies. It is also permitted that "qasas" be a verbal noun in the sense of "qisas", and then "life" remains as it is.

﴿O people of understanding﴾: O possessors of intellects pure of the taint of desire. He singled them out for the address, although the preceding address is general, because they are the people who reflect on the wisdom of retribution, namely preserving lives and safeguarding souls. It has been said: this is to indicate that the ruling is specific to the adult and not to children. ﴿That you may be God-fearing 179﴾: [that you may be mindful of] your Lord by avoiding His acts of disobedience that lead to punishment or killing, through fear of retribution. This is what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Zayd, may Allah be pleased with them. The clause is connected to the beginning of the discourse.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 180 (part 1 of 2):

﴿It has been prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves behind wealth, that he make a bequest to parents and relatives, in a fair manner; a duty upon the God-fearing.﴾ This is the explanation of another ruling among the rulings mentioned. Its separation from what preceded it serves to indicate that it is an independent ruling, just as the following ruling is separated from it. He did not introduce it with "O you who have believed," because the time since the previous alert is recent, and because it is connected to the preceding verse in that each of them concerns the dead. Or, because it was not burdensome, he did not introduce it as he introduced the burdensome matter, to encourage its performance. What is meant by "the approach of death" is the approach of its causes and the appearance of its signs, namely the frightening illnesses and diseases; or its own presence and imminence. The fronting of the object (ahadakum, "one of you") serves to convey the complete dominance of the agent (death) over the soul at the moment it reaches it.

﴿If he leaves behind wealth﴾ means: property, as Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) and Mujahid said. Some scholars restricted it to being abundant, since in common usage the word for wealth (khayr) is not applied to property unless it is abundant, just as one does not say "so-and-so has wealth" unless he has a great deal of it. This is supported by what al-Bayhaqi and a group related from 'Urwa, that 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) entered upon a freedman of his who was dying, and who had seven hundred or six hundred dirhams. He said: "Shall I not make a bequest?" He said: "No. Allah the Exalted only said: ﴿If he leaves behind wealth﴾, and you do not have much wealth; so leave your property to your heirs." And what Ibn Abi Shayba related from 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her): a man said to her: "I wish to make a bequest." She said: "How much is your wealth?" He said: "Three thousand." She said: "How many dependents do you have?" He said: "Four." She said: "Allah the Exalted said: ﴿If he leaves behind wealth﴾, and this is a small amount; so leave it to your dependents, for that is better." The apparent meaning of this is that abundance is not fixed by a specific measure, but varies according to the condition of the man; for with a certain amount of wealth a man is described as rich, and another is not described as such because of the number of his dependents. And from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) its quantity is specified: 'Abd ibn Humayd related from him: "Whoever does not leave sixty dinars has not left wealth." The view of al-Zuhri is that the bequest is legislated whether the amount is small or large, so "wealth" (khayr) in his view means property in general, which is one of its usages. Perhaps his choice indicates that the bequeathed property should be lawful and good, not unlawful; for unlawful wealth must be returned to its owners, and one incurs sin by bequeathing it.

﴿The bequest to parents and relatives﴾: it is in the nominative, governed by "prescribed" (kutiba).
