In al-Radi's view, when the apparent subject is not feminine in its true sense and is separated, omitting the marker is better, to show the superiority of the true feminine over others; for this reason the verb is masculine here. "Wasiyya" (bequest) is a noun from awsa, yusi; in al-Qamus: awsahu and wassahu, tawsiya, meaning he committed to him; the noun is "wisaya," and "wasiyya" is also the thing bequeathed. The prepositional phrase is connected to it, so it must be interpreted either as "an" with the verb according to the majority, or as a verbal noun, based on al-Radi's verification that the verbal noun's governance does not depend on its interpretation, which is the preferred view; therefore he mentioned the preferred view in its substitution. It is also permitted that "upon you" (alaykum) is the deputy subject and "the bequest" is the predicate of an omitted subject, as if it were said: "What is written?" and it was answered: "It is the bequest." The conditional's response is omitted, indicated by "It has been prescribed for you." It was also said: it is a subject whose predicate is "to parents," and the sentence is the response of the condition with the particle fa' omitted, since a nominal sentence serving as a response must contain it; and the conditional sentence is governed by "prescribed," or by "upon you" alone, and the sentence is resumptive. This was rejected: omitting the fa' is not sound and one would not venture it except in poetic necessity, as al-Khalil said. The governing element of "idha" (when) is the meaning of "prescribed," and the time phrase is restricted to the obligation in terms of occurrence and happening. The meaning is that God's address is directed at you, and the consequence of its writing when death approaches and is brought near is what you see, so that it is combined with the meaning that it is written in eternity. It is also permitted that the governing element is "the bequest," and although it is a noun, it is interpreted as a verbal noun or as "an" with the verb, and the time phrase is of a kind that the scent of the verb suffices for, because it has a status not found in others, by treating it as part of the thing, since it occurs within it and is inseparable from it; for this reason time phrases are permitted more latitude than others. Not every interpreted element has the ruling of what it is interpreted as. The fronting of the complement of the verbal noun before it is common in speech, and the estimation is contrived. Against both estimations it is not objected that the bequest is obligatory upon the one whom death approaches, not upon all believers when one of them faces death; for "one of you" (ahadakum) conveys generality by way of alternation, so the meaning of "when one of you is brought near" is when one after another is brought near. The word "one" (ahad) was added only to make explicit that it is an individual obligation and not a collective one, as in ﴿Retaliation is prescribed for you regarding the slain﴾. The claim that the bequest was not imposed on the one whom death approaches alone, but on him to make a bequest, and on others to preserve it and not alter it, for this reason he said "upon you" and said "one of you," because death approaches one of those addressed, is nothing; for the preservation of a bequest is imposed on some only after the bequest, not at the time of dying. How then can it be said: "It is prescribed upon you to preserve the bequest when one of you is approached by death"? Also, the intention of bequeathing and its preservation as part of the bequest is an evident artifice. Some verifiers chose that "idha" is conditional and the response of each of the two conditions is omitted; the sense being: "When one of you is approached by death, let him bequeath if he leaves wealth, let him bequeath." The response of the first condition is omitted for the indication of context, and the response of the second condition is omitted for the indication of the first condition and its response. The second condition, according to the author of al-Tashil, restricts the first, as if it were said: ﴿When death approaches one of you﴾ leaving wealth, let him bequeath. The two conditions together are inserted between "prescribed" and its subject to explain how the bequest is to be made. It is not hidden that this view, together with its freedom from the artifice of validating the adverbial sense and adding the word "one," is more fitting to Qur'anic eloquence; for the ruling came first in general, then in detail, and the parenthetical insertion occurred between the verb and its subject to emphasize explaining the manner of the obligatory bequest. End. You know what is in that of the abundance of omission which lessens what preceded it. Then this ruling was at the beginning of Islam, and then it was abrogated by the verse of inheritance, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Qatada, Shurayh, Mujahid and others. Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah related from 'Amr ibn Kharija (may Allah be pleased with them): "The Prophet (ﷺ) addressed them while on his mount, saying: 'Allah has apportioned to every person his share of inheritance, so no bequest is permitted to an heir.'" Ahmad and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related from Abu Umama al-Bahili: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during the Farewell Pilgrimage in his sermon say: 'Allah has given every rightful person his right, so there is no bequest to an heir.'" 'Abd ibn Humayd related from al-Hasan something similar. These hadiths, since the Ummah received them with acceptance, are counted among the mutawatir in the validity of abrogation by them according to our imams, may Allah sanctify their secrets. Indeed some said: they are among the mutawatir, and that tawatur may come through the transmission of those whose collusion in lying is inconceivable, and it may come through their practice, by their having acted upon it without denial from them. Furthermore, the abrogation in reality is by the verse of inheritance, and the hadiths clarify the aspect of its abrogation. Fakhr al-Islam explained this in two ways. First: it was revealed after the verse of bequest by agreement, and God said: ﴿After a bequest he makes or a debt﴾, so inheritance was ordered upon "a bequest" in indefinite form, while "the bequest" earlier was known; had that known bequest remained, the inheritance would have to be ordered upon the known one; since it was not, and was ordered upon the unrestricted, this indicates the abrogation of the restricted bequest, because unrestriction after restriction is abrogation, just as restriction after unrestriction is, since the two meanings differ. Second: abrogation is of two kinds: one is an absolute beginning after a complete end, and the other is by way of transfer from one locus to another, as in the abrogation of the qibla; and this is of the second kind, because God obligated the bequest for the nearest relatives of servants, on condition that they observe the limits and specify each relative's right according to his kinship; and to this His words point: ﴿in a fair manner﴾, i.e., justly. Then since the testator may not be skilled at estimating what he bequeaths to each of them, and may intend harm, He Himself undertook to specify that right in a way by which it is certain to be correct, and that it contains perfect wisdom, and restricted it to fixed shares: a sixth, a third, a half, an eighth, which cannot change. So it passed from the bequest to inheritance, saying: ﴿Allah enjoins you concerning your children﴾, i.e., He to whom you delegated it has Himself undertaken its matter, since you were unable to determine its quantities because of your ignorance. Since He Himself specified that right exactly, the ruling of that bequest ended, because the aim was achieved in the strongest way, like one who was ordered by another to free his slave and then freed him himself; by this the ruling of agency ends. The hadiths point to this, since the particle fa' indicates the causality of what precedes for what follows. As for the claim that the verse of inheritance does not oppose this ruling but confirms it, inasmuch as it indicates the priority of bequest in general, and the hadiths are from the solitary reports, and the Ummah's acceptance of them does not raise them to the mutawatir: perhaps he who interpreted the bequest as what God bequeathed through the inheritance of parents and relatives, by His saying "Allah enjoins you," avoided abrogation; or [he interpreted it as] the dying person's bequest to them to fulfill what God enjoined upon them, which is far from verification. Likewise, what was said: the bequest to an heir was obligatory by this verse without specifying their shares; when the verse of inheritance came as an explanation of the shares, using the wording of bequest, it was understood through the Prophet's (ﷺ) alert that what was meant by it was this bequest which had been obligatory, as if it were said: God Himself bequeathed that bequest and did not delegate it to you; so inheritance took the place of bequest, and this is what abrogation means, not that it contains an indication of lifting that ruling; because that the verse of inheritance lifts that ruling and clarifies its termination is not something that should be confused for anyone. Then those who hold abrogation differed. Some said: its obligation became abrogated for relatives who inherit, and it remained for those who do not inherit among parents and relatives, such as when they are unbelievers; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him). It is related from 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face): whoever does not make a bequest at his death to his relatives who do not inherit has ended his deeds with disobedience. Others said: the obligation became abrogated for all, and it is recommended for those who do not inherit; this is the view of most. Muhammad ibn al-Hasan used the verse as evidence that the unrestricted "relatives" does not include parents, because it is conjoined to them by coordination.

﴿A duty upon the God-fearing﴾ (108): it is a verbal noun emphasizing the event implied by "prescribed," whose governing element is either "prescribed" or a suppressed "was made obligatory" (huqqa); that is, "that was made obligatory as an obligation," so it is of the pattern of "I sat, a sitting." It may also be a verbal noun emphasizing the content of the sentence "prescribed upon you," if it is considered as a performative utterance, so it is of the pattern of the customary "he owes me a thousand." And he made it an adjective

for a verbal noun that is omitted, i.e., "a bequest" (īṣāʾan), truly ("ḥaqqan"), not "laysa bi-shayʾ" ... 

Let me restate faithfully:

It is for an omitted verbal noun, meaning a bequest (ījāʾan), a truth (ḥaqqan). Upon both estimations, ﴿upon the God-fearing﴾ is either a qualifier of it, or it is related to the omitted verb according to the preferred view. It is also permissible for it to be related to the verbal noun, because the absolute object (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq) functions as a substitute for the verb. By "al-muttaqīn" (the God-conscious, those who guard against wrongdoing) is meant the believers. The explicit noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that observing the bequest and carrying it out is among the rites of the God-conscious who fear Allah, exalted is He.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 181:**

﴿Then whoever alters it﴾: that is, alters the bequest, whether of the witness or of the executor (waṣī). The alteration of either of them may be by denying the bequest altogether, or by diminishing it, or by changing its description, or otherwise. The Shafi'is (al-Shāfi'iyyah, the followers of al-Shafi'i) counted among alteration the general scope of a bequest made to someone for a specific matter. So, according to them, one who is appointed executor for a particular thing is not an executor for anything else. According to us (the Hanafis), he is. This is not alteration at all. ﴿After he has heard it﴾: that is, after he has known it and it has been established for him. He expressed knowledge by hearing, because hearing is the means by which knowledge is acquired. ﴿Its sin is only upon those who alter it﴾: that is, the sin of the altered bequest or of the alteration is nothing else. The first reading takes account of the wording, and the second takes account of the meaning. The sin falls only on those who alter it, not on the testator, because they are the ones who opposed the law and betrayed trust. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun to show that alteration is the cause of the sin. The use of the plural form takes account of the meaning of (man, "whoever"), and it implies that the sin extends to all individuals.

﴿Indeed Allah is Hearing, Knowing﴾: He hears the words of those who alter and of those who bequeath, and He knows their intentions, and He repays them according to them. In this there is a warning to those who alter and a promise to those who bequeath. The verse has been cited as evidence that the obligation falls from the testator by the bequest itself, and that he is not harmed if the executor does not act upon it. It has also been cited as evidence that whoever owes a debt and bequeaths its settlement is saved from its consequences in the Hereafter, even if the executor or heir leaves its settlement undone. Al-Kiya (Ilkiya al-Harrasi) adopted this view. But what the heart inclines to is that the debtor bears no consequence after death in any absolute sense, and he is not confined in his grave, as people say. As for the case where he left nothing and died insolvent, the matter is clear. For if he were still alive, nothing would be due from him once his insolvency was established, apart from waiting until a time of ease. So to call him to account and confine him in his grave after he has gone to the All-Subtle, the All-Aware, is something that can hardly be conceived. As for the case where he left something and the heir knew of the debt, or knew of a pledge given for it, then the heir is the one required to pay it and bound to discharge it. If he does not pay and does not discharge it, then he himself is held to account, not the one who died and left behind what could cover his debt, wholly or partly. For to hold to account one who says, "My Lord, I left what would suffice, but he did not discharge it after me, the one You obligated to discharge it; and if You had granted me respite, I would have paid," is something that contradicts wisdom and is not required by mercy. Yes, accountability is conceivable for one who borrowed for something forbidden and spent the money in what does not please the King, the All-Knowing. What has been reported in the hadiths is to be understood in this sense or something similar to it. To take it as absolute is something that sound reason and a straight mind do not accept.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 182:**

﴿Then whoever fears deviation (janaf) or sin on the part of a testator﴾. Janaf is a verbal noun of janifa (like fariha), meaning deviation and injustice in general. Here it means deviation in the bequest without intent. The context supports this, since it is contrasted with sin (ithm), which only occurs by intent. The word khafa (fear) here means to anticipate and to know. An example of this usage is the verse: "When I die, bury me beside a vine whose roots water my bones after my death, and do not bury me in the wasteland, for I fear that when I die I will not taste it." The reality of this is that fear is a state that arises upon apprehension of an anticipated evil. Because of this association, it is used for anticipation, which may be assumed to occur or may be known to occur. It is therefore used for both at a secondary level. Because the first meaning is more common, its use in that sense is more apparent. Its original use is for suspicion and knowledge of what is to be avoided, and it may be extended to the general sense. It is understood metaphorically here because there is no meaning to fearing deviation or sin after the bequest has been made.

The People of Kufa, except Hafs and Ya'qub, read ﴿muwassin﴾ with a shadda, while the rest read it without one.

﴿Then he brings about reconciliation among them﴾, that is, among the beneficiaries from among the parents and relatives, by causing them to follow the way of the Sharia. It was also said that the meaning is doing what is good between the testator and the beneficiary, by ordering justice and a return from the excess, and making it for the rich. According to this view, the reconciliation that follows discord is not intended, since no discord had occurred between the testator and the beneficiary.

﴿Then there is no sin upon him﴾ for that alteration, because it is an alteration from falsehood to truth, unlike the earlier one. The verse has been used as evidence that if someone bequeaths more than a third, the whole bequest is not void, contrary to the one who claims otherwise. Only the excess beyond a third is void, because God, exalted is He, did not nullify the bequest entirely because of injustice in it, but instead provided in it the most beneficial course.

﴿Indeed, God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (182). This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) brought for the promise of reward to the one who reconciles, for his reconciliation. Mention of forgiveness, although reconciliation is among the acts of obedience, is appropriate here because the preceding mention of sin, to which forgiveness relates, makes it fitting. For this reason its mention is good. Its benefit is to draw attention to the higher by means of the lower, meaning that God, exalted is He, forgives sins, so it is all the more certain that He is merciful to whoever obeys Him. It may also be that its mention is a promise to the reconciler of forgiveness for whatever slips from him in the reconciliation, since he may need to make false statements and perform acts that are better left undone. It was also said that the meaning is: Forgiving of the deviation and sin that occurred from the testator through the reconciliation of the executor and his bequest, or forgiving of the testator for what he entertained in his soul of error and action, when he returned to the truth, or forgiving of the reconciler through his reconciliation, such that the reconciliation expiates his evil deeds. All of these are far-fetched.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 183:

﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ is an explanation of another of the legal rulings (al-ahkam al-shar'iyyah). The repetition of the address (al-nida') serves to show special concern, given the length of time since the previous address. *Al-siyam* is, like *al-sawm*, the verbal noun of *sama*. Linguistically it means abstention (al-imsak), and from this root the silence of a person is called *sawm*, because it is an abstention from speech. Ibn Duraid said: "Everything whose movement remains still has fasted (sama)." From this is the saying of al-Nabighah:

Horses that are fasting, and other horses that are not fasting, under the dust-cloud,
And others that chew the bit, so the wind fasted (became still), it stood still.

*Sama al-shams* means the sun stood still when it reached the middle of the day. In the sacred law (shar'an), fasting is abstention from specific things, in a specific manner, during a specific time, by those who possess specific qualifications.

﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾, that is, the prophets and the nations from the time of Adam, upon him be peace, until our day, as the apparent general sense of the relative pronoun indicates. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab). It is related from al-Hasan, al-Suddi and al-Sha'bi that they are the Christians.

In this there is an affirmation of the ruling, an encouragement toward it, and a consolation to the hearts of those addressed, for difficult matters become easier when they are shared by everyone. The intended likeness (al-mumathalah) is either the likeness in the basic obligation (asl al-wujub), which is the view of Abu Muslim and al-Jubba'i, or the likeness in the time and the quantity. The latter is based on the view that the People of the Book were obligated to fast Ramadan, but the Jews abandoned it for the fasting of one day in the year, which they claimed was the day on which Pharaoh was drowned. The Christians added a day before it and a day after it as a precaution, until they reached fifty days. It then became hard for them in the heat, so they moved it to the season when the sun enters the sign of Aries (burj al-hamal).

Ibn Hanzalah, al-Nahhas and al-Tabarani narrated from Mughaffal ibn Hanzalah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Fasting Ramadan was obligatory on the Christians. Their king became ill, so they said: 'If Allah restores him to health, we will add ten days.' Then another (king) came and ate meat, and his mouth was injured, so they said: 'If Allah restores him to health, we will add seven.' Then there was another king over them, who said: 'We will not leave anything of these three days; we will complete them and make our fasting in spring.' He did so, and it became fifty days."

There are five possibilities regarding *ka-ma* (as):

First: its position is in the accusative (nasb) as an adjective (na't) of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: it was prescribed as a prescribing, like what was prescribed.

Second: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the definite verbal noun, meaning: fasting was prescribed for you, the prescribing being made similar to what was prescribed. In both of these cases, *ma* is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah).

Third: it is an adjective of a verbal noun derived from the word *siyam*, meaning: a fasting similar to the fasting prescribed for those before you.

Fourth: it is a circumstantial qualifier of *siyam*, meaning: in the state of its being similar to what was prescribed. In both of these cases, *ma* is a relative pronoun (mawsulah).

Fifth: it is in the nominative (raf') position as an attribute of *siyam*, based on the view that the word defined by the generic *al* (al-jinsiyyah) is close to an indefinite noun.

﴿so that you may be God-conscious (la'allakum tattaqun)﴾, that is, so that you may guard against acts of disobedience (al-ma'asi). Fasting weakens (yu'qimu) the desire (al-shahwah), which is its mother, or breaks it. Al-Bukhari and Muslim both related in their Sahihs from 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to us: "O assembly of young men, whoever among you is able to marry (al-ba'ah), let him marry, for it lowers the gaze and guards the private parts. And whoever is not able, then let him fast, for fasting is a shield (wija')."

It is possible that the object is understood as the neglect of its performance (al-ikhlal bi-ada'ihi). On the first reading, the sentence is connected to the verb *kutiba* without regard to the comparison; on the second, it is connected with regard to the comparison. That is: the likeness of what was prescribed for the earlier people has been prescribed for you, so that you may be God-conscious by avoiding neglect of its performance, after knowing its origin and antiquity. There is no need to posit an omitted element, meaning: "I have informed you of the ruling mentioned for this purpose," as some have said. It is also permitted that the verb be treated as intransitive, meaning: so that through this you may attain the rank of taqwa.

[p. 58]

﴿Days numbered﴾: that is, specified by counting, or few in number. For what is few is easy to count and so is counted, whereas what is many is taken in estimation. Muqatil said: every "ma'dudat" (numbered) in the Qur'an, or "ma'dudah" (numbered), is under forty, and it is not said of anything more than that. The meaning of these days is either Ramadan, and this was chosen by Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu Muslim, may Allah be pleased with him, and most of the researchers, and it is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Then Allah, glorified and exalted, will have first informed that He prescribed fasting for us, then clarified it by His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿numbered days﴾, so some of the ambiguity was removed, and then He clarified it by His saying, may He be exalted, the Speaker: ﴿the month of Ramadan﴾ (﴿شَهْرُ رَمَضانَ﴾), to accustom the soul to it. It was objected that if this were the meaning, then mentioning the sick and the traveller would be a repetition. It was answered that at the beginning, fasting Ramadan was obligatory with a choice between it and the ransom (fidyah), so when the choice was abrogated (naskh, meaning the cancellation of a ruling by a later one), and it became obligatory in a definite way, there was a likelihood that one would suppose this ruling applies to everyone, even the sick and the traveller being like the resident and the healthy. So their ruling was restated, as an alert that their concession remains as it was and has not changed, as the ruling on the resident and the healthy has changed. As for what was obligatory to fast before its obligation, which is three days of every month, the "white days" (ayyam al-bid), as related from Ata', and attributed to Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him; or three days of every month, and the Day of Ashura, as related from Qatada. The people of this view agreed that this obligation has been abrogated by the fasting of Ramadan. It was questioned: its obligatoriness was established only by what is in this verse, so if that ruling was acted upon for a long period, as has been said, how can the abrogating ruling be contiguous? And if it was not acted upon, then abrogation is not valid, since there is no abrogation before action. It was answered: as for the first choice, contiguity in recitation does not indicate contiguity in revelation; and as for the second choice, the more correct view is that abrogation before action is permissible. So reflect.

The accusative of (أيّامًا) (ayyaman, "days") is not governed by al-siyam (the fasting), as has been said, because a foreign element intervenes between them. Rather it is governed by an implied verb, which it indicates, namely "fast" (صُومُوا), either as an adverb of time or as an object, by extension. It was also said: it is governed by a verb derived from the comparative particle (kaf of al-tashbih, "like"), and in this is an explanation of the aspect of similarity, as if it were said: fasting has been prescribed for you, resembling the fasting of those before you in being ﴿numbered days﴾; that is, the similarity exists between the two fastings from this aspect, which is that each of them is tied to a period not long-drawn-out. So the statement is like "Zayd is like 'Amr in jurisprudence." It was also said: it is governed as a second object of (kutiba, "was prescribed"), by extension. Al-Bahr (the Ocean, i.e. Abu Hayyan's commentary) rejected this, saying that the extension is based on the permissibility of its occurring as an adverb of (kutiba), and this is not valid, because the adverb is the place of the action, and the writing (of the prescription) did not occur in the days; rather what occurs in them is its object, which is the fasting. It was answered that for it to be an adverb it suffices that the object is an adverb, as in ﴿He knows what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ (﴿يَعْلَمُ ما في السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾), and that the meaning of (kutiba) is "was made obligatory," and the obligatoriness of fasting occurs in the days.

﴿So whoever among you is sick﴾: a sickness in which fasting is difficult for him, as is indicated by His saying, exalted, after this: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾ (﴿يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ بِكُمُ اليُسْرَ ولا يُرِيدُ بِكُمُ العُسْرَ﴾). Most jurists hold this. Ibn Sirin, Ata', and al-Bukhari held that the concession applies to any sickness at all, acting on the absoluteness of the wording. It is related that they entered upon Ibn Sirin during Ramadan while he was eating, and he excused himself by the pain in his finger. This is also an opinion of the Shafi'is.

﴿or upon a journey﴾: or one riding a journey, mounted upon it and able to undertake it, by having occupied himself with it before dawn. In this there is a hint that whoever travels in the course of the day does not break his fast. For this meaning, the wording (ʿala safar) was preferred over (musafiran, "traveller"). It was argued from the unrestricted use of "journey" that a short journey and a journey of disobedience also permit breaking the fast. Most scholars restrict it to a permissible journey and one that usually entails hardship, namely a journey to the distance fixed in the Sharia.

﴿then a number of other days﴾: that is, then upon him is the fasting of the number of days of sickness and journey, from other days, if he broke the fast. The condition and the two annexed nouns are omitted, because they are known. As for the condition, the sick and the traveller are included in the general address, so it indicates the obligation of fasting upon them both. If the ruling were not restricted to this here, it would follow that sickness and travel, which are by Sharia and reason causes of ease, would become causes of hardship. As for the first annexed noun, the discussion is about fasting and its obligation. As for the second, because when it was said: "whoever is sick or travelling, then upon him is a number," meaning numbered days, described as being from other days, it is understood that the intended meaning is numbered by the number of days of sickness and travel, and the annexation is dispensed with. This breaking of the fast is prescribed as a concession. So the sick and the traveller, if they wish, fast, and if they wish, break their fast, as most jurists hold. However, Abu Hanifa and Malik said: fasting is more preferable; al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and al-Awza'i said: breaking the fast is more preferable. The view of the Zahiriyya (Literalists) is that breaking the fast is obligatory, and that if they fast, their fast is not valid, because it is before the time indicated by the apparent meaning of the verse. This is attributed to Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar, Abu Hurayra, and a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, and the Imamiyya (Imami Shi'a) said the same, and they extended the argument for this with what they related from the Ahl al-Bayt (the People of the House). It was argued from the verse that making up the days may be consecutive or separate, and that it is not required immediately, against Dawud (al-Zahiri). It was also argued that whoever broke the fast for the whole of Ramadan makes up ﴿a number of days﴾; so if the month were complete, a deficient month would not suffice for him, and if it were deficient, a complete month would not be obligatory for him. This is against those who disagreed in the two cases. It was also used as evidence by those who said there is no ransom together with making up the fast, and likewise by those who said that if the traveller becomes resident, or the sick person recovers during the day, neither of them is obliged to abstain for the rest of it; because Allah, exalted, only obligated "a number of other days," and they have both broken the fast, so the ruling of breaking the fast remains for them. And among its ruling is that no more than one day is obligatory; if we commanded him to abstain and then make up, we would be obligating for the day more than that, and what is in this is not hidden.

It was read (fa-ʿiddatan) in the accusative, as an object of an implied verb, meaning: then let him fast a number; and whoever supposed the condition there supposes it here. ﴿And upon those who are able to fast it﴾ (﴿وعَلى الَّذِينَ يُطِيقُونَهُ﴾): that is, upon those capable of fasting, if they break their fast, ﴿a ransom﴾ (﴿فِدْيَةٌ﴾): that is, giving it.

﴿Feeding a poor person﴾ (﴿طَعامُ مِسْكِينٍ﴾): this is the amount he eats each day. It is half a sa' of wheat or one sa' of other grain according to the people of Iraq, and one mudd according to the people of the Hijaz, for each day. This was at the beginning of Islam, because fasting had been made obligatory upon them, and they were not accustomed to it, so it was hard upon them, and so they were granted a concession to break the fast with the ransom. Al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, al-Tabarani, and others reported from Salama ibn al-Akwa', may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And upon those who are able to fast it﴾, whoever among us wished fasted, and whoever wished broke his fast and paid a ransom, until the verse after it came and abrogated it: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ (﴿فَمَن شَهِدَ مِنكُمُ الشَّهْرَ فَلْيَصُمْهُ﴾)."

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab recited (yuṭayyiqūnahu) with a damma on the first ya' and a shadda on the second ya'. Mujahid and Ikrima recited (yuṭṭayyiqūnahu) with a shadda on the ta' and on the second ya'. Both recitations are in the active form, on the basis that their original forms are (yuṭayyiqūnahu) and (yataṭayyaqūnahu), from the patterns fayʿala and tafayʿala, not from faʿala and tafaʿʿala; otherwise it would have been with a waw and not a ya', since it is from ṭawwaqa, which is waw-based. The waw has been made into a ya' in both, and then the ya' was assimilated into the ya'. Their meaning is "they burden themselves with it" (yatakallafūnahu). Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, recited (yuṭawwiqūnahu) in the passive form of the intensive pattern (tafʿīl); that is, they are charged with it, or they are made to wear it as a necklace (ṭawq), meaning capacity (ṭāqa) or necklace (qilāda). All three readings are also related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and from him (yataṭawwaqūnahu), meaning "they burden themselves with it" or "they wear it as a necklace," and (yuṭawwiqūnahu) with assimilation of the ta' into the ta'. He held that it is not abrogated, as al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and others related, and said: the verse was revealed concerning the very old elderly man and the very old elderly woman. Some people also did not hold abrogation on the basis of the mutawatir (widely transmitted) reading, and interpreted it as "they fast with their utmost effort and capacity." This is based on the view that (al-wus', "capacity") is a term for power to do a thing with ease, and (al-ṭāqa, "endurance") is a term for power together with severity and hardship. So the meaning becomes: ﴿upon those who﴾ fast it with severity and hardship, so it includes the pregnant woman and the nursing woman as well. It is also based on the view that it derives from (aṭāqa al-fiʿl), meaning he reached the utmost of his capacity, or his capacity was exhausted in it. It is also possible that the hamza is for negation, as if he negated his capacity by burdening himself with the effort, so his capacity was negated upon its completion, and this would be an exaggeration in exerting the utmost effort, since he is nearing the end of that, as in al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari). The truth is that each of the readings can be taken as bearing either what admits abrogation or what does not admit it, and each has its advocates. It is related from Hafsa that she recited: ﴿And upon those who are not able to fast it﴾ (﴿وعَلى الَّذِينَ لا يُطِيقُونَهُ﴾). Nafi' and Ibn Amir recited "ransom" (fidyah) as annexed to "food" (ṭaʿām), and "poor person" (miskin) in the plural. The annexation in that case is of the thing to its genus, like "a ring of silver," because the food of the poor person may be a ransom or other than it. The plural of "poor person" is because it is plural in ﴿And upon those who are able to fast it﴾, so the plural corresponds to the plural. "Ransom" was not made plural because it is a verbal noun, and the (ta') in it is for feminine marking, not for the single instance; and because when it was annexed to an annexed noun that is plural, the plural was understood from it.

﴿Whoever volunteers good﴾: by exceeding the stated amount in the ransom. Mujahid said: or by exceeding the number of those whom he is obliged to feed, so he feeds two poor persons or more, as Ibn Abbas said; or by combining feeding and fasting, as Ibn Shihab said.

﴿it is better for him﴾: that is, the volunteering, or the good which he volunteered. Some scholars made the first "good" (khayr) a verbal noun from (kharta, ya rajul, wa anta khā'ir), meaning "good," and made the second "good" an elative (ism tafḍīl, "more"), which without doubt also yields the sense of carrying (the ruling), and returning the pronoun to "whoever" (man), meaning: the one who volunteers is better than others on account of the volunteering, is not hidden as far-fetched.

﴿And that you fast﴾: that is, you who are capable, resident, healthy; or those burdened among the elderly men and women; or those who are granted the concession to break the fast from both groups, the sick and the travellers. In this there is a shift (iltifat) from the third person to the second person, to compensate for the burden of fasting with the pleasure of direct address. Ubayy recited: (wa-al-siyām, "and the fasting").

﴿is better for you﴾: than the ransom, or than volunteering good, according to the first two views; or than both of them and than delaying for making up, according to the last view. ﴿If you knew﴾ (﴿إنْ كُنْتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾): what excellence there is in fasting, and the answer of (in, "if") is omitted, relying on its being evident; that is, you chose it. It was also said: the meaning is, if you are among the people of knowledge, you knew that fasting is better for you than that. On this view the clause is an emphasis on the superiority of fasting; on the first view it is an establishment (of a new point).

[p. 60]

**"Shahru Ramadan"** (the month of Ramadan) may be a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate (*khabar*) is the relative clause (*al-mawsul*) that follows it. In that case, mentioning the sentence serves as an introduction to the obligation of fasting by mentioning its excellence. Or it may be taken with **"fa-man shahida"** (so whoever witnesses), with the *fa'* (so) because the phrase contains the sense of a conditional (*shart*), since it is described by the relative clause. Or it may be the predicate of an omitted subject, whose estimate is: "That is the time in which fasting was prescribed for you," or "What was prescribed is the month of Ramadan." Or it may be a substitute (*badal*) for "al-Siyam" (the fasting), a *badal kull* (substitute of the whole), with an omitted noun in the estimate, meaning: "Fasting was prescribed for you, the fasting of the month of Ramadan." The intervening material between them is connected to *kutiba* (was prescribed), either verbally or in meaning, so it is not entirely foreign. If you regard it as a *badal ishtimal* (substitute of inclusion), you need no estimate. However, the fact that the prior ruling, namely the obligation of fasting, is intended in itself, and that mentioning the substituted element does not create an expectation for the substitute, makes this less likely.

It has also been read as **"shahra"** (in the accusative), as the object of an omitted *sumu* (fast). It has been said that it is the object of **"wa an tasumu"** (and that you fast), but this entails separating the parts of the verbal noun (*masdariyya*) from its predicate. It is also permissible for it to be the object of **"ta'lamun"** (you know), with an omitted noun in the estimate, meaning: "the excellence of the month of Ramadan and the like." It has been said that no estimate is needed, and that the intended meaning of **"in kuntum ta'lamun"** (if you know) is the month itself, without doubting it. In this there is an indication that fasting is not appropriate when there is doubt. This is not valid, as is clear.

The *shahr* (month) is a specified period whose beginning is the sighting of the crescent moon. Its plural in the small number is *ashhur*, and in the large number *shuhur*. Its root is from *shahara al-shay'* (he made the thing manifest). Because it serves as a fixed time for acts of worship and transactions, it became well known among people. **"Ramadan"** is a verbal noun (*masdar*) of *ramida* (with the vowel of the 'ain as kasra), meaning "to be burnt." In *Shams al-'Ulum* (a dictionary), it is mentioned among the verbal nouns shared by verbs of the pattern *fa'alan* (with fatha on the *fa'* and the *'ain*). Most of these come with the meaning of coming, going, and agitation, such as *khafaqan*, *'asalan*, and *lamha'an*. It has also come with other meanings than coming and going, as in *shana'tuhu sha'nan* (I hated him), when I disliked him. What is in *al-Bahr* (the Ocean, i.e., *al-Bahr al-Muhit*) about its being a verbal noun needing transmission (*naql*) is not correct, for *fa'alan* is not the verbal noun of an intransitive verb. If something of it comes, it is anomalous (*shadhdh*). The better view is that it is original (*murtajal*) and not transmitted, and that claim arises from little acquaintance with the sources. Al-Khalil says it is from *al-ramd* (with the *mim* sukun), which is a rain that comes before autumn and cleanses the face of the earth from dust. The combination of the *mudaf* (genitive construction) and its *mudaf ilayh* (the second term) has become a proper name (*'alam*) for the known month. Were it not so, the attribution of *shahr* to it would not be good, just as "*insan Zayd*" (the human of Zayd) is not good. The attribution of a general term to a specific one is only valid when it is well known that the specific one is among its members. For this reason, "Shahr Rajab" and "Shahr Sha'ban" have not been heard. In general, they agreed that the proper name in three months is the combined *mudaf* and *mudaf ilayh*: Shahr Ramadan, Shahr Rabi' al-Awwal, and Shahr Rabi' al-Thani. In the rest, *shahr* is not attributed to them. Some have versified this:

"Do not attribute a month to the name of a month,
except what begins with *al-ra'*; understand this.
Exclude from them Rajab, so it is prohibited,
for it, in what they transmitted, has not been heard."

In attribution, the cause of preventing declension (*man' al-sarf*) and the prohibition of *al-lam* (the definite article) and its necessity are considered when the *mudaf ilayh* is in the state [of being in the genitive]. So in an example like "*shahru Ramadan*," declension is prevented and the definite article is not added. Ibn Dayah is prevented from declension and takes the definite article. In an example like "*shahr Rabi' al-Awwal*" and "*Ibn 'Abbas*," it is declined. In an example like "*Imru' al-Qays*," the definite article is required, because it occurred as a component when it was made definite by the article. It is permissible in an example like "*Ibn 'Abbas*": adding the article is for considering the original, and omitting it is because it is free in its origin. On this basis, the phrase "*man sama Ramadan*" (whoever fasted Ramadan) is an omission of part of the proper name, because there is no confusion. So it has been said, but there is an objection to this. First, the attribution of a general term to a specific one is referred to taste (*dhawq*). For this reason it is sometimes good, as in "*shajar al-Arak*" (the tree of the Arak), and sometimes ugly, as in "*insan Zayd*." Its ugliness in "*shahr Ramadan*" is not recognized except by one whose taste has changed through the effect of fasting. Second, their saying that "Shahr Rajab has not been heard," etc., is among what was heard among the later scholars, and has no basis. In *Sharh al-Tashil* (the Commentary on *al-Tashil*), the attribution of *shahr* to all the names of the months is permitted, and this is the view of most grammarians. So claiming consensus is not a consensus. The source of the error of the later scholars is what is in *Adab al-Katib* (the Literary Manual of the Scribe), that it is a convention of scribes. He said: when they set the dating system in the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and made the beginning of the year Muharram, they did not write a month in their dates except with Ramadan and the two Rabi's. So it is a conventional matter, not an original linguistic one. Its reason for Ramadan is agreement with the Qur'an, and for Rabi' is the separation of one from another. For this reason Sibawayh validated the permissibility of attributing *shahr* to all the names of the months, and he distinguished between mentioning it and not mentioning it: when it is mentioned, it does not indicate generality, and when it is omitted, it does. On this basis, the difference between "*insan Zayd*" and "*shahr Ramadan*" becomes clear, and the crescent of that is not obscured. Third, their saying "then in the attribution" etc. contradicts what the grammarians explicitly stated. Ibn Dayah was heard both with prevention of declension and with declension, as in his saying:

"When I saw the eagle, Ibn Dayah was mighty,
and nested in its two nests, my chest was agitated for him."

They said: each has its reason. As for the non-declension, it is because the two words, by composition, became one word by naming, so it was like *Talhah* as a single word, which is not declined. As for declension, it is because the *mudaf ilayh* in its origin is a common noun, and the *mudaf* is similar; each of them by itself is not a proper name, but the proper name is their combination, so definiteness does not affect it, and preventing declension has no role. Overall, the reliable view is that "Ramadan" alone is a proper name, and it is a *'alam jins* (generic proper name) for what you know. Some prohibited saying "Ramadan" without "shahr," because of what Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn 'Adi, al-Bayhaqi, and al-Daylami transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, both as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) and as a mawquf (ending with a companion): "Do not say 'Ramadan,' for Ramadan is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, but say 'the month of Ramadan.'" Mujahid went to this view. The correct view is permissibility, for this has been transmitted in the Sahih, and caution is not hidden. The month was named after it because sins are burnt in it. Ibn 'Umar said this, and Anas and 'Aisha transmitted this as a marfu' to the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace. It has also been said that it is because it coincided with the days of intense heat (*ramad al-harr*). They took the names of the months from the ancient language, and its name was previously *Natiq*. Perhaps what was transmitted from him, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, clarifies what should be the reason for the naming among Muslims. Otherwise, this name existed long before the obligation of fasting, according to what is apparent.

**"Alladhi unzila fihi al-Qur'an"** (the one in which the Qur'an was sent down): that is, its sending down began in it. This was the Night of Power (*Laylat al-Qadr*), as Ibn Ishaq said. It was transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Hasan, that it was sent down in its entirety to the lowest heaven, then it was sent down in installments (*munajjaman*) to the earth over twenty-three years. It has been said: the Qur'an was sent down concerning it, namely the Exalted's saying: "The fasting has been prescribed for you" (*kutiba 'alaykum al-siyam*). Imam Ahmad and al-Tabarani recorded from the narration of Wathilah ibn al-Asqa', from the Prophet, may Allah exalt him and grant him peace, that he said: "The scrolls of Ibrahim were sent down on the first night of Ramadan, the Torah was sent down after six nights had passed, the Gospel on the thirteenth, and the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth." Since there is a great correspondence between fasting and the sending down of the divine books, this month, specific to their sending down, is specific to fasting, which is a great kind of signs of servanthood and a strong cause for removing the human attachments that prevent the illumination of the eternal lights.

**"Hudan lil-nas wa bayyinatin min al-huda wa al-furqan"** (a guidance for the people and clear proofs of guidance and the criterion): these are two necessary states (*hal lazim*) from the Qur'an, and the governing element in them is "anzala" (He sent down). That is: He sent it down, and it is guidance for the people through its unique inimitability (*i'jaz*), as the indefiniteness (*tankir*) indicates. And clear signs, from among the divine books that guide to the truth, and that distinguish between truth and falsehood through containing divine knowledge and practical rulings, as his making them clear signs from among them indicates. So it is a guide through two matters: one specific and one not specific. Therefore "al-huda" is not repeated. It has been said that it is repeated, to honour and magnify its matter and to emphasise the meaning of guidance in it, as you say "a learned, expert scholar."

**"Fa-man shahida minkum al-shahra fal-yasumhu"** (So whoever among you witnesses the month, let him fast it): "man" is either conditional (*shartiyya*) or relative (*mawsula*). The *fa'* is either the answer of the condition, or superfluous in the predicate. "Minkum" is in the accusative position (*mahall nasb*) as a state (*hal*) from the pronoun in *shahida*. The restriction by it is to exclude the child and the insane. *Shahida* is from *shuhud*, and the root indicates presence, either in essence or in knowledge. It has been said that both are meant here. "Al-shahr," according to the first, is an adverbial object (*maf'ul fih*), and the direct object is omitted because the purpose does not depend on it. Thus the estimate of "*al-balad*" (the land) or "*al-misr*" (the city) is not valid. According to the second, it is a direct object with the omission of a *mudaf*, meaning "the crescent of the month." The definite article in it, according to both estimates, is for prior reference (*al-'ahd*). The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun for honour, and the attached pronoun in "*fal-yasumhu*" was put in the accusative by extension (*ittisa'*), because *sama* (to fast) is intransitive. The meaning is: whoever is present during the month and is not a traveller, let him fast in it; or whoever knows the crescent of the month and is certain of it, let him fast. On this basis, the import of the verse is that fasting is not obligatory on the one who doubts the crescent. The *mudaf* was estimated because witnessing the whole month occurs only after it ends, and there is no sense in the obligation of fasting in it being consequent upon its completion. On this basis, the Exalted's saying: "But whoever is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days" (*fa-'iddatun min ayyamin ukhar*) is a specifier (*mukhassas*) with respect to both the ill and the traveller. On the first, it specifies only the first and not the second, and its repetition in that case is for this specification, or so that its abrogation is not assumed, just as its companion was abrogated. The first, as it has been said, is according to the opinion of those who stipulate that a specifier must be subsequent and connected (*mu'akhkhiran mawsulan*). The second is according to the opinion of those who allow it to be prior. This is by making the specifier the preceding verse. "*Ma*" here is only to dispel an assumption. The first of the two meanings was preferred for two reasons: it does not need an estimate, and because the *fa'* in "*fa-man shahida*" is in its place detailing what was summarised in the Exalted's saying "the month of Ramadan," concerning the obligation of honouring it, derived from what is in its effect upon everyone who reaches it. Whoever reaches it is either present or travelling. So whoever is present, his ruling is such-and-such, and so on. It is not appropriate to say "whoever knows the crescent, let him fast." "But whoever is ill or on a journey, then let him make up" is the second category entering the first, and the detailing conjunction requires a difference between them, so it has been said. However, mentioning the ill person strengthens that he is a specifier, because he is included in "whoever witnesses" on both views. For this reason most grammarians held that "*al-shahr*" is the direct object, so the *fa'* is for causation or sequence, not for detailing.

**"Yuridu Allahu bikumu al-yusra wa la yuridu bikumu al-'usra"** (Allah desires for you ease and does not desire for you hardship): with this concession (*tarkhis*), out of the utmost of His mercy and the vastness of His compassion. The Mu'tazila used the verse to show that something may occur from the servant that Allah, the Exalted, does not desire. This is because if the ill person and the traveller fast until fasting exhausts them, they have done the opposite of what Allah, the Exalted, willed, since He willed ease and His will was not fulfilled. It was answered that Allah, the Exalted, willed ease and the absence of hardship concerning them by permitting breaking the fast, and this was achieved merely by the command in His saying, Mighty is His affair: "then a number of other days," without any failure. In *al-Bahr*, the will is explained here as demand (*talab*). In this there is an obligation to the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, that His will concerning the acts of servants is an expression for command, and that He, the Exalted, did not demand ease from us, but rather prescribed it for us. Explaining "*al-yusr*" as "what is made easy" is far-fetched. Abu Ja'far read "*al-yusra*" and "*al-'usra*" with two dammas.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 185 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And that you complete the period, and that you glorify Allah for having guided you, and perhaps you will be thankful.﴾ This is a reason (ʿillah) for a deleted verb that is indicated by ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month﴾, and so on. That is, He prescribed for you the whole of what was mentioned about the obligation on the one who witnesses the month to fast it, which is derived from His statement, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾; and He commanded the one granted a concession to make up the fasts however they may be, whether consecutively or separately, and to observe the number of the days he broke without any shortfall in it. These two are derived from His statement, glorified is He: ﴿so [make up] a number of other days﴾. And [it is derived] from the concession derived from His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾, or from His statement, exalted is He: "a number, etc.," [as a reason] for "that you complete, etc."

The first (reading) is the reason for the command to observe the number of the month's days, by performing the fasts while the month is witnessed and by making them up when one breaks the fast due to an excuse. Thus it is a reason for two things being caused; that is, We commanded you with these two commands so that you complete the number of the month's days by performance and by making up, and so you obtain its good things, and nothing of its blessings escapes you, whether its days are fewer or complete.

﴿And that you glorify Allah﴾ is the reason for the command to make up the fasts and for explaining how it is to be done. ﴿And perhaps you will be thankful﴾ is the reason for the concession and the facilitation. The change of style to indicate this sought-after matter is like what is hoped for, because of the strength of the interlinked causes that lead to its attainment, namely the manifestation that the concession is a blessing. The addressee is certain of His complete kindness and generosity, along with the fact that the blessings of the month are not lost. This is a kind of subtle wrapping of expression, rarely reached, because the apparent requirement would be to omit the conjunction "wa" (and), since these are reasons for what preceded. For this reason, [some] said, [whoever] has not reached the level of perfection [may say]: that the "wa" is either superfluous or conjunctive, coordinating with a presumed reason. The reason for choosing this is: as for the first (view), it is obvious; and as for the second, it is because of the greater attention it gives to the earlier rulings while avoiding artificiality. This is because the presumed verb, since it includes what preceded in summary, makes what preceded serve as an indicator of it, while the reason remains in its state; and because it differs from it in summary and detail, it is correct to coordinate it with it. In mentioning the rulings first in detail, then in summary a second time, and in giving their reasons without specifying a reliable (reason) for the listener's understanding, by considering them once after another and returning each reason to what befits it, there is no hidden consideration.

It was also permitted that these be reasons for presumed verbs, each verb with a reason. The presumption is: ﴿And that you complete the period﴾ — He obligated for you a number of other days; ﴿and that you glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ — He taught you the manner of making up; ﴿and perhaps you will be thankful﴾ — He granted you permission to break the fast. If you wish, you may make it coordinated with a presumed reason, that is: so that it may be easy for you, or so that you may know what you do, ﴿and that you complete﴾, etc. The whole has been made a reason for the earlier rulings, either with regard to themselves or with regard to informing about them. Thus His saying: "so that it may be easy" or "so that you may know" is a reason for what preceded with respect to informing, and what follows it is a reason for the rulings mentioned, as has passed. You may also not presume anything at all, and make the coordination with "ease": that is, "and He intends for you, that you complete, etc." The lam is superfluous, and a presumed "an" follows it, after which it is inserted, as it has been said: after the verb of intention, as emphasis for it, because of the meaning of intention in your saying "I came to you for your honour." It has also been said that it means "an," as in al-Radi, except that on this view it would follow that ﴿and perhaps you will be thankful﴾ is coordinated with "intends" (yurid), since there is no meaning in our saying "He intends perhaps you will be thankful." In that case the coordinated elements would become disjointed, which is remote. Because this view entails that, and because of the many deletions in some of the previous views and the obscurity of some of them, some scholars departed from all of them, and made the speech an instance of "al-mayl maʿa al-maʿna" (inclining with the meaning), since what precedes it is a reason for the concession. It is as if it were said: He granted you permission in that because He intends ease for you, not "that you complete, etc." The most fitting for the dignity of the Mighty Book is not hidden from you.

What is meant by "takbir" is praise and commendation, metaphorically, because it is a single instance of it. For this reason it is construed with ʿala (upon), and with the consideration of tadmin (implicit extension of meaning). That is, "that you glorify [Allah], praising Him," is not a valid consideration, because praise is itself the glorification. Since on this view it is a verbal act of worship, it fits that the command to make up the fasts, which is also a verbal blessing, be explained by it.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam that what is meant by it is the takbir on the day of ʿEid. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that it is the takbir at the sighting (of the new moon). Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: "It is a duty upon the Muslims, when they look at the crescent of Shawwal, to say takbir to Allah, exalted is He, until they finish their ʿEid, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿and that you complete the period, and that you glorify Allah﴾."

On these two views, it does not fit the explanation of the earlier rulings. The "ma" may be either verbal (maṣdariyyah) or relative (mawṣūlah): that is, "the One who guided you to it" or "for having guided you to it." What is meant by gratitude is what is more general than praise. For this reason it is fitting that its requirement be made a reason for the concession, which is a practical blessing.

Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read: ﴿wa-litukammilū﴾ with the doubled letter (shaddah).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 186:**

﴿When My servants ask you﴾. The shift in address, together with directing it to the master of those endowed with understanding (peace be upon him), carries an honour and an elevation of rank that are obvious. ﴿concerning Me﴾, that is, concerning My nearness and My distance, since the question is not about His essence, exalted is He. ﴿Then indeed I am near﴾, that is, say to them so, by informing them of nearness in whatever manner it is. A supplied element is necessary here, for without it the conditional does not follow. It was not stated explicitly, as is done in similar cases, to indicate that He, exalted is He, undertook to answer them Himself and did not leave them to His Messenger, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, as a sign of the perfection of His gentleness. Nearness in its literal sense is spatial nearness, which is far removed from Him, exalted is He. It is therefore a metaphor for His knowledge of the deeds and words of the servants and His awareness of all their circumstances. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna and 'Abdullah ibn Ahmad narrated from Ubayy, who said: "The Muslims said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is our Lord near that we may whisper to Him, or far that we must call out to Him?' So Allah revealed the verse: ﴿I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me.﴾" This is evidence for nearness and confirmation of it, so the categorical form (the omission of a conjunction) denotes perfect closeness of connection. It also contains a promise to the one who calls that his supplication will be answered in general, as the word ( إذا ) indicates, not universally. Hence there is no need to restrict it by the condition of His will, which is implied by His words in another verse: ﴿He removes that for which you call upon Him, if He wills﴾. Nor is there need to say that answering the call is other than granting the need, because His words, glorified and exalted is He, "Here I am, O My servant," are a promise that exists for every believer who calls. Nor is there need to restrict the call to what contains no sin or severing of kinship, or to the call of one who is obedient and humble. Yet it is true that being so is more hopeful for an answer, especially at specified times, in known places, and in well-known manners. Despite this, the answer may sometimes fail altogether, and sometimes it may be replaced by something else. In the Sahih it is narrated from Abu Sa'id, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, said: "No Muslim calls upon Allah with a supplication that contains no sin or severing of kinship, except that Allah, blessed and exalted is He, gives him one of three things: either He hastens his supplication for him, or He stores it for him, or He averts from him an evil equal to it." The detailed verification of this will come, if Allah wills.

﴿So let them answer Me﴾, that is, let them seek My answer to them when they call upon Me; or, let them respond to Me when I call them to faith and obedience, just as I answer them when they call upon Me for their needs. "Istajaba" and "ajaba" are one in meaning. Its meaning is the cutting off of a request by fulfilling what is desired from it, taking "al-jawb" in the sense of cutting off. This is the view of most of the exegetes. This does not dispense with ﴿and let them believe in Me﴾, because it is a command to persist and continue in faith. ﴿So that they may be rightly guided﴾ (186), that is, that they may be guided to the interests of their religion and their worldly life. The root of the word means attaining good. It is recited with a fatha and a kasra on the shin. When He, exalted is He, commanded them to fast the month and observe the prescribed number of days, and urged them to perform the duties of magnifying and giving thanks, He followed it with this verse, which indicates that He is aware of their deeds and hears their words and will recompense them for their actions, as confirmation of this and encouragement toward it. Or, when He abrogated the rulings concerning fasting (naskh, abrogation), He mentioned this verse, which indicates His perfect knowledge of the state of the servants, His perfect power over them, and the utmost of His gentleness toward them in the midst of the abrogation of rulings, to establish them in faith and to confirm them in responding. For the situation of abrogation is one of the places of doubt and wavering. So the sentence, on both interpretations, is a parenthetical clause placed between two statements that are connected in meaning, the first of which is what preceded it.

(Page 64)

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 1 of 3):**

The second [matter] is His, glorified and exalted be He, saying: ﴿It has been made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in to your wives﴾. Ahmad and a group [of narrators] related from Ka'b ibn Malik, who said: "In Ramadan, when a man fasted and then slept, food, drink and women became forbidden to him until he broke his fast the next day. One night 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, returned from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, after conversing with him in the evening, and found his wife had fallen asleep. He woke her and wanted her, but she said, 'I have already slept.' He said, 'You have not slept.' Then he had intercourse with her. Ka'b ibn Malik did the same. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, went in the morning to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and informed him, and [the verse] was revealed." In the narration of Ibn Jarir, [it is related] from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "While he was asleep, his self tempted him, so he went to his wife. Then he came to the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, I apologise to Allah and to you for this sinful self of mine. It adorned [the act] for me, so I had relations with my wife. Is there any concession for me?' He said, '[No], you were not deserving of that, O 'Umar.'" When he reached his house, [the Prophet] sent for him and informed him of his excuse in a verse of the Qur'an, and Allah, exalted be He, commanded His Messenger to place it in the middle hundred [verses] of Surat al-Baqarah. So He said: ﴿It has been made lawful for you﴾, and so on.

﴿Night of the fast﴾: this is the night after which one begins the fast in the morning. The idafah (annexation construction) is for the slightest connection, and what is intended by it is the category [of nights]. Its governing element is ﴿al-rafath﴾ (the sexual speech/intercourse) mentioned, or a deleted element indicated by it, on the basis that a verbal noun (maṣdar) does not govern when it precedes [its complement]. It is also permitted for it to be a adverbial of time governed by ''uḥilla'' (it has been made lawful), because the lawfulness of intercourse on the night of the fast and the lawfulness of intercourse occurring during it are mutually implicated.

''Al-rafath'' derives from ''rafatha fī kalāmihi'' and ''arfatha'' and ''tarfuthu'': he was most obscene and most explicit in speech about what is normally euphemised. What is meant here is intercourse, because it hardly avoids being explicit. As for what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he recited, while in the state of ihram (pilgrim's consecration):

*And they walk with us in a whisper; if the bird tells the truth, we shall have intercourse.*

It was said to him, "Did you commit rafath?" He said, "Rafath is only what occurs in the presence of women."

The word ''rafath'' here may be verbal or physical. Its original construction is to be transitive with the particle ''bi-'', but it was made transitive with ''ilā'' because it contains the sense of ''ifḍā'' (reaching/going in to). It was not made a euphemism from the outset, because the intended meaning is intercourse, so the distance [of the expression] is shortened. Its choice here, over what is euphemised by in the whole Qur'an, such as ''taghshiyah'' (covering), ''mubāsharah'' (touching), ''lams'' (touching), ''dukhūl'' (entering) and the like, is to express disapproval of what they had done before the permission, and for this reason later [the Qur'an] called it ''ikhtiyān'' (betrayal).

''Al-nisā'''' is the plural of ''niswah'', so it is a plural of a plural, or the plural of ''imra'ah'' (woman) in a form that departs from the singular. Its annexation to the pronoun of the addressees is for specification, since intercourse is lawful only for one who has exclusive right to the one he has intercourse with, either by marriage or by ownership. ''Abdullah [ibn Mas'ud] read: ''al-rufūth''.

﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾: that is, they are a dwelling/comfort for you and you are a dwelling/comfort for them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas when Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him. When Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, was asked whether the Arabs knew this, he recited the verse of al-Dhubyani:

*When the bedfellow turns his side, she turns around him and becomes a garment.*

Since the man and the woman embrace, and each envelops the other, each one is likened in regard to the other to a garment; or because each one covers the other and prevents him from immorality. It has been stated in a report: "Whoever marries has secured two-thirds of his religion."

The two clauses are an independent resumptive clause (''isti'nāf naḥwī'', a grammatical resumption that is a new sentence), and the rhetorical elaboration (''bayānī'') is rejected by good taste. Their meaning explains the cause of the preceding ruling, which is the scarcity of patience regarding them, as is understood from the first, and the difficulty of abstaining from them, as the second indicates. Because the man's need for them is evident and his patience is scarce, the first was put first. In a report: "There is no good in women, nor patience with them. They overcome the generous one and the base one overcomes them. I would love to be a generous one who is overcome, and I would not love to be a base one who overcomes."

﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾: this is a parenthetical clause (''jumlah mu'tarigah'') between His saying ''uḥilla'' (it has been made lawful) and what is connected to it, namely ﴿So now﴾ and so on, to explain their condition with respect to what had preceded from them before the permission. The meaning of ''knew'' is that His knowledge was related. ''Al-ikhtiyān'' is the stirring of a person's desire to seek betrayal, or it is intense betrayal. So the meaning is: you diminish yourselves completely by exposing them to punishment and diminishing their share of reward. It returns to the meaning: you wrong yourselves thereby. What is intended is the continuation of this in the past before they informed [the Prophet] of the situation, as the two forms, the past and the present, indicate. This is the object of the knowledge. What the first form conveys, namely that their being in betrayal preceded the knowledge, rejects interpreting it as eternal, which is the view some have taken.

﴿So He accepted your repentance﴾ is coordinated with ''ʿilm'' (knowledge). The ''fa'' is for mere sequence. What is meant is before your repentance, when you repented from the forbidden act which you had committed. ﴿And pardoned you﴾: that is, He erased its trace from you and removed its prohibition. It was said: the first is the removal of the prohibition, and this is forgiveness of the sin.

﴿So now﴾ is connected to His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿It has been made lawful for you﴾, with regard to what is the aim of the permission, which is the removal of the prohibition. That is: when He abrogated (''naskh'', the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one) for you the prohibition of intimacy, which is the night of fasting, as the final limit indicates, for it is a limit to the four commands whose time-frame this is. The presence understood from it refers to the act of abrogating the prohibition, and it is not present with respect to the address in His saying ﴿Associate with them﴾. It was said that although it is literally in the present time, it may be used for the near future, treating it as if it were the present, and that is what is meant here. Or it is used in its literal sense, and the implied meaning is: We have now permitted you to associate with them. The original sense of ''mubāsharah'' is the joining of skin to skin, and it was applied to intercourse because it necessarily involves that.

﴿And seek what Allah has prescribed for you﴾: that is, seek what Allah, exalted be He, has decreed for you on the Preserved Tablet, namely offspring. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, and others, may Allah be pleased with them. What is meant is supplication to ask for it, by saying: "O Allah, grant us what You have written for us." This does not depend on each one knowing that a child has been decreed for him. It was also said: what is meant is what He has decreed for your species, and the expression ''mā'' (what) is used with regard to the attribute, as in His saying: ﴿By the heaven and what built it﴾.

The verse indicates that the one who has intercourse should, in marriage, aim at preserving the offspring, not merely the satisfaction of desire. For He, glorified and exalted be He, made for us the desire for intercourse so that our species may endure until a fixed term, just as He made for us the desire for food so that our individual persons may endure until a fixed term. Mere satisfaction of desire should be only for beasts. Some have made this seeking a metaphor for the prohibition of coitus interruptus (''ʿazl'', withdrawal) or of anal intercourse. Others explained ''what was written'' from the outset as what has been legislated and prescribed of pouring water in its proper place, meaning: seek that, apart from withdrawal and the aforementioned anal intercourse, and the well-known view is that both are forbidden. As for the first, what is stated in the books is that a man should not practise withdrawal with a free woman without her consent, nor with a female slave he has married without her consent or the consent of her master, according to the disagreement between Imam [Abu Hanifah] and his two companions. There is no harm in withdrawal with his own slave-girl without her consent, since she has no right in this. As for the second, its full discussion will come later, if Allah, exalted be He, wills.

It is related from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, that this [phrase] is to be interpreted as the Night of Power (''laylat al-qadr''), and it is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him. From Qatadah it is related that what is intended by ''seek'' is the concession ﴿which Allah has prescribed﴾ for you, for Allah, exalted be He, loves that His concessions be taken, just as He loves that His firm commands (''ʿazāʾim'', strict obligations) be observed. On this reading, the clause serves as an emphasis of what precedes it. It is also related from 'Ata' that he was asked of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, how this verse is to be read: ''ibtaghū'' (seek) or ''ittabiʿū'' (follow)? He said: "Whichever you wish, but adhere to the first reading."

﴿And eat and drink﴾ all night long, ﴿until the white thread becomes distinct to you﴾, that is, becomes manifest.

﴿From the black thread﴾: the white thread is the first thing that appears of the true dawn (''fajr ṣādiq'', the true dawn) which spreads across the horizon before it disperses. To take it as the false dawn (''fajr kādhib'', the false dawn), which extends lengthwise like a wolf's tail, is an error. ﴿The black thread﴾ is the darkness of the end of the night which extends alongside the whiteness of the dawn.

﴿Of the dawn﴾: an explanation of the first of the two threads, and from it the second becomes distinct. He singled out the first for explanation because it is the object [of concern]. It was also said that it is an explanation of both, on the basis that ''al-fajr'' (the dawn) is an expression for the combination of the two, as in the saying of the poet al-Ta'i:

*The dawn's blue-grey appears before its white.*

So it is in the pattern of your saying: "until the scholar becomes distinct from the ignorant among the people." By this explanation the two threads passed from metaphor (''istiʿārah'') to simile (''tashbīh''), because the condition of metaphor according to them is that the comparison be entirely forgotten, and the claim that the likened thing is the likened-to thing without a clue, whereas the explanation shows that what is meant is like this thread and like this thread, since they do not need it. It was also permitted that ''min'' be partitive, because what appears is a part of the dawn, just as it is the dawn, on the basis that it is a name for the common quality shared by the whole and the part. As for the first ''min'', it was said to be for the beginning of the limit. But in this there is an objection: the verb transitive with it must be extended, or be the origin of something extended, and its mark is that it is good to put ''ilā'' (until) opposite it or what conveys its meaning; but what is here is not like that. So the apparent view is that it is connected to ''yatabayyan'' (becomes distinct) by including the sense of distinguishing, and the meaning is: until the dawn becomes clear to you, distinguished from the dimness of the night. Thus the limit is the permission of what came before.

﴿Until it becomes distinct﴾: one of them from the other, and they are distinguished from each other. This is the reason why [the Qur'an] did not suffice with ''until it becomes distinct to you the dawn'', or ''until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread from the dawn'', because the distinction of the dawn has many levels, so the ruling would become general and in need of explanation. And what al-Bukhari, Muslim and others related from Sahl ibn Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "﴿And eat and drink﴾ and so on was revealed, but ﴿of the dawn﴾ had not yet been revealed. So when men wanted to fast, one of them would tie a white thread and a black thread to his feet, and he would continue to eat and drink until he could see them distinctly. Then Allah, exalted be He, revealed ﴿of the dawn﴾ afterwards, and they understood that it meant night and day." There is in this no text that the preceding verse needed explanation to the extent that its intended meaning could not be understood without it. Also, delaying the explanation beyond the time of need is permissible, since the two threads could have been well known in their meaning, but He explicitly gave the explanation because it had become confusing to some.
