This is supported by the fact that [the Prophet], peace and blessings be upon him, described as dull-witted the one who did not understand the meaning of the verse before the explanation was stated. Had the matter depended on the explanation, the intelligent and the dull would have been equal in it.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah, Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and a group [of transmitters] related from 'Adi ibn Hatim, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When this verse was revealed..."

[Page 67]

﴿And eat and drink﴾ etc. "I took two threads, one black and the other white, and put them under my pillow, and I kept looking at them, but the white did not become distinct to me from the black. When I woke up, I went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and told him what I had done. He said: 'Your pillow must be wide indeed. That is only the whiteness of day from the blackness of night.' In another narration: 'You must have a broad nape.'"

It was said that the revelation of the verse occurred before Ramadan began, and that it is ambiguous (mubham), and clarification (bayan) is necessary, except that it was delayed beyond the time of address but not beyond the time of need, and that does not harm. What is in this is not hidden. Abu Hayyan said: this is from the category of abrogation (naskh). Do you not see that the Companions acted upon the apparent meaning of the wording, and then it became figurative (majaz) through clarification? This is refuted by what is in it, because naskh occurs through an independent statement, and such naskh is not known. In these commands there is evidence for the permissibility of abrogating the Sunnah by the Book, indeed for its actual occurrence, based on the view that the abrogated ruling, the prohibition of intercourse, eating and drinking, was established by the Sunnah, while there is nothing in the Qur'an indicating it. The word ﴿uhilla﴾ ("it is made lawful") also indicates this, except that it is abrogation without a replacement, which is a disputed matter.

The verse was also cited as evidence for the validity of the fast of one who is in a state of major ritual impurity (janabah). This is because permission of intimacy until the dawn becomes clear implies permission of it in the last part of the night connected to the morning. If it occurs in this way, the person becomes junub in the morning. If his fast were not valid, given that intimacy was permitted, then since impurity is necessarily attached to it, and negating the necessary negates the necessitating, the fast would be invalid. There is no objection from the emission of semen after dawn resulting from intercourse that occurred before it, because the fast becomes invalid only because it completes the intercourse, so it is intercourse occurring at dawn, and it is not necessarily attached to intercourse as impurity is. Some scholars disagreed with this and denied the validity of the fast, claiming that the limit (ghayah) is connected to what precedes it, and they argued with reports which the scholars of hadith have found to be authentically contrary.

It was also cited as evidence for the permissibility of eating for one who doubts the emergence of dawn, because He permitted what He permitted, limited by its clarification (tabayyun), and there is no clarity in the case of doubt. This is contrary to Malik. Mujahid used it as evidence that no makeup fast (qada') is required in this situation if it becomes clear that he ate after dawn, because he ate at a time when he was permitted to do so. The same is narrated from Sa'id ibn Mansur, and he is not "al-Mansur." The four imams, may Allah be pleased with them, hold that the legal day begins at dawn, so no prohibited acts may be done after it. Al-A'mash disagreed, and none follows him except the blind. He claimed that the beginning of the day is sunrise, like the customary day, and permitted prohibited acts after dawn. The Imamiyya also hold this view. He interpreted ﴿min al-fajr﴾ ("from the dawn") as partitive, meaning its last part. What led him to this is the report: "The prayer of the day is mute (ʿajmāʾ)," and the dawn prayer is not silent, so it belongs to the night. Some supported him, arguing that just as the mixing of darkness with light did not prevent it from being night after sunset, it should not prevent it before sunrise, and the two extremes are equal, which is something admired in wisdom, and "to the beginning is the return." In reply: even granting the soundness of this report, the word "day" in it may be understood in its customary sense. Had He intended this ruling, He would have said: "Eat and drink until the day, then complete the fast until night," which is shorter and more appropriate than what He actually said. Since He did not, it is understood that the command is tied to dawn and not to sunrise, whether or not that is counted as day. What is mentioned about admiring the equality of two extremes, while it neither fattens nor satisfies hunger, can be countered in this matter: making the beginning of the day like the beginning of the night, when they are opposites, indicates the greatness of the power of the Wise Creator. ﴿Ila al-layl﴾ ("until the night") means up to the completion as its limit. It may be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of the fasting, and so it is connected to an omitted element. It cannot be the limit of the obligation because the obligation does not extend. On both interpretations, the verse indicates the negation of night being a place of fasting, and that the two days are one fasting. The Prophet (ﷺ) derived from it the prohibition of continuous fasting (wiṣāl), as it is said. Aḥmad related through Layla, the wife of Bashir ibn al-Khasasiyya, that she said: "I wanted to fast two days continuously, but Bashir prevented me and said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade it, and said: The Christians do that, but fast as Allah, may He be exalted, has commanded you.'" And ﴿Complete the fast until the night﴾; "so when the night comes, break your fast." The verse does not indicate that fasting is not permitted until a break intervenes, contrary to his claim.

Yes, it was cited as evidence for the validity of the intention (niyyah) for Ramadan during the day. The reasoning is that His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Then complete﴾ etc., is conjoined to ﴿associate with them﴾ up to His saying ﴿until it becomes clear﴾. The word ﴿thumma﴾ ("then") indicates delay and sequence with an interval. The lam in ﴿al-ṣiyām﴾ ("the fast") is for the known (ʿahd), as is the basic meaning. So the meaning of ﴿Then complete﴾ etc. is a command to complete the known fast, which is the abstention indicated by the limit. This may be understood as bringing it in complete form, or as making it so after the mentioned matters that end with the dawn, in order to achieve the meaning of "then." Thus the intention for the fast comes after a part of the dawn has passed, because the obligation to intend an act binds us at the time the address is directed to us. The address to complete the fast is directed after the dawn, since it comes after the part which is the limit of the end of the night, for the sense of delay. The night does not end except connected to a part of the dawn, so the intention occurs after the passing of the part of the dawn by which the night ended and in which the abstention indicated by the limit took place. If it is asked: if this were so, the intention would be obligatory after this passing. It is answered: its abandonment is by consensus, and applying both evidences, even in some way, is better than neglecting one of them. So if we said that the intention must be like this, in accordance with the verse, the hadith "There is no fast for one who does not intend to fast from the night" would be void. If we said that the intention is a condition before it, in accordance with the report, the verse would be void. So we say it is permissible, acting upon both. If it is asked: the implication of the verse, as stated, is obligation, and a single-transmission report (khabar al-wāḥid) cannot oppose it. It is answered: its apparent meaning has been abandoned by consensus, so it is no longer decisive, and therefore the report may be a clarification of it. Some of the companions have another way of establishing the argument, and perhaps what we have mentioned is less burdensome, so reflect.

Some of the Shafi'is claimed that the verse indicates the obligation of intending at night (tabyīt), because the meaning of ﴿thumma atimmū﴾ is "make it complete after the bursting of dawn," and this requires beginning it before that, and this is only through intention, since abstention before dawn is not obligatory. What is in this is not hidden.

﴿And do not have intercourse with them while you are devoted (ʿākifūna) in the mosques﴾, that is, while you are secluding yourselves (muʿtakifūna) in them. Linguistically, iʿtikāf means confinement and staying in place in general. From it is his saying:

"The daughters of night stayed around me, devoted, a devotion like weeping women around whom a stricken one..."

Legally, it is a specific period of staying. The prohibition is connected to the first commands, and the ﴿mubāshara﴾ ("intimacy") in it is the same as the ﴿mubāshara﴾ mentioned earlier. It was previously mentioned that its meaning is intercourse. However, the permission of intercourse entails the permission of touching, kissing and other things, unlike the prohibition, which does not entail the prohibition of these. So they are either permitted by agreement if done without desire, or forbidden if done with desire. "The iʿtikāf is void unless he ejaculates." Most of al-Shafi'i's companions held that it is void. It was said that ﴿mubāshara﴾ means the meeting of two skins, so the verse prohibits any kind of intimacy. This is not correct, for ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, used to comb the hair of the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in iʿtikāf.

The restriction of iʿtikāf to "mosques" indicates that it is valid only in a mosque. For if it were legally valid elsewhere, it would be valid in a house, and that is void by consensus. According to al-Zuhri, it is restricted to the congregational mosque (al-masjid al-jāmiʿ). It is narrated from Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, that it is restricted to a mosque which has a regular imam and muezzin. Ḥudhayfa, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is restricted to the three mosques. From ʿAlī, may Allah honour his face, it is not permitted except in the Masjid al-Ḥarām. From Ibn al-Musayyab: it is not permitted except there or in the Prophet's Mosque. The view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is that it is valid in all mosques absolutely, based on the generality of the wording, and not considering that the absolute is understood as the complete. He cited the verse as evidence for the validity of a woman's iʿtikāf outside the mosque, on the basis that she is not included in the address to men. He also cited it for the condition of fasting in iʿtikāf, because the verse restricted the address to those who are fasting. If fasting were not a condition, this restriction would have no meaning. This view is narrated from Nāfiʿ, the freedman of Ibn ʿUmar, and from ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with them. He also cited it as evidence that a period less than a day is not sufficient for it, just as fasting is not valid for less than a day. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him,

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 187 (part 3 of 3):

...(may Allah be exalted of him) does not stipulate a day or a fast, based on what al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no fasting upon the one in seclusion (i'tikaf), unless he makes it binding upon himself." A similar report comes from Ibn Mas'ud, and from 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) there are two narrations recorded by Ibn Abi Shaybah through two chains: one requires the condition, and the second does not.

Also, if the one in seclusion leaves the mosque and engages in intimacy outside, it is permitted, because the prohibition of intimacy is restricted to the state of his being within it. It is answered that the meaning is: "Do not have intimacy with them" while you are in the state of being told, "You are those who are secluding themselves (ʿākifūna) in the mosques." Whoever leaves the mosque to relieve a need, his seclusion remains intact. This is supported by what is related from Qatadah: "A man would seclude himself, then go out to his wife, have intimacy with her, and then return; so they were forbidden from that."

It is also used as evidence that sexual intercourse invalidates seclusion, because the prohibition indicates prohibition (tahrim), and in acts of worship prohibition necessitates invalidity (fasad). But in this there is the point that the thing prohibited here is intimacy during seclusion, and it is not one of the acts of worship. It may not be said that when a prohibited matter occurs within an act of worship, such as intercourse during seclusion, that act of worship becomes prohibited by virtue of containing the prohibited matter and being accompanied by it; for it is said: there is a difference between a thing being prohibited by virtue of what accompanies it, and the accompanying thing being prohibited within that thing. The discussion concerns the former, and what we are dealing with belongs to the latter category.

﴿Those﴾, i.e., the six rulings mentioned, which include obligation, prohibition and permission, are ﴿the limits of Allah﴾, i.e., barriers between the truth and falsehood. ﴿So do not approach them﴾, lest falsehood draw near. The prohibition of approaching those limits, which are the rulings, is a metaphorical expression (kinayah) for the prohibition of approaching falsehood, because the first necessarily entails the second. It is more eloquent than "do not transgress them," because it forbids approaching falsehood by way of kinayah, which is more eloquent than the explicit, and that is a prohibition against falling into falsehood by way of the explicit. On this basis, "do not approach them" does not present a difficulty regarding those rulings, given what they contain as you have heard, and there is no contradiction with ﴿so do not transgress them﴾ in another verse, since the combination has been achieved and "do not approach them" is valid for all of them. It has also been said that it is permissible to mean by "the limits of Allah" His prohibitions and what He forbids; either because the preceding commands necessarily imply prohibitions, since they are qualified by a limit, or because what is referred to is His saying, ﴿and do not have intimacy with them﴾ and similar. Abu Muslim said: the meaning of "do not approach them" is do not interfere with them by altering them, like His saying: ﴿and do not approach the property of the orphan﴾. This encompasses all the rulings. The difficulties in both views are not hidden. The statement that "those" refers to the rulings, and that "the limit" is either in the sense of prohibition or in the sense of a barrier between two things: on the first, the meaning is that those rulings are things forbidden by Allah, exalted is He, to others; it is not for anyone else to rule on anything, ﴿so do not approach them﴾, i.e., do not rule on yourselves or on His servants from your own opinions on anything, for judgment belongs to Allah, exalted is His majesty. On the second, it means that those rulings are limits serving as barriers between divinity and servitude: the Deity rules and the servants submit, so do not approach the rulings, lest you become associators with Allah, exalted is He. This is scarcely presented to a person of understanding who would approve it, and it is far removed from the intended meaning, as is not hidden.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., like that clarification which occurred in the rulings of fasting, ﴿Allah makes clear His signs﴾, either in general or the signs indicating the rest of the rulings He has legislated, ﴿for the people, that they may be God-conscious﴾ 187, by avoiding the violation of His commands and prohibitions. The sentence is a parenthetical insertion between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, serving to confirm the preceding rulings and to encourage compliance with them, in that they were legislated for the sake of your God-consciousness (taqwa).

(Page 70)

When He, glory be to Him, mentioned fasting and what it involves, He followed it with a prohibition against consuming unlawful wealth, which leads to one's worship, including fasting and i'tikaf, not being accepted. He said: ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly﴾. The "consuming" here means what includes taking and seizing, and it is expressed by it because eating is the most important of needs, and the destruction of wealth usually occurs through it. The meaning is: "Let none of you consume another's wealth." This is like ﴿And do not defame one another﴾. It is not a case of distributing a plural over a plural, as in "they mounted their animals," so that the meaning would be "Let none of you consume his own wealth." The evidence is His saying, glory be to Him, "between you" (baynakum), for "between" (bayn) means an intermediary, and this requires that what is attributed to it be divided into two parties, with the act of eating and the wealth being intermediate between them. This is evident according to the meaning mentioned.

The adverbial phrase is related to "do not consume" (ta'kulu), like the prepositional phrase after it, or it is related to an omitted circumstantial clause describing "the wealth" (al-amwal). The bāʾ (ba) is causal (sababiyya). By "unjustly" (al-batil) is meant the unlawful, such as theft and usurpation, and everything for which the Sharia has not permitted taking.

﴿And do not send it forth to the rulers (al-hukkam)﴾ is coordinated with "do not consume," so it is prohibited in the same way and is put in the jussive mood like what precedes it. Its being in the subjunctive, with an implied "an," is also permitted. Although this construction is for prohibiting the combination of the two, it does not preclude that each of the two matters is prohibited. Idla' (sending forth) originally means lowering a rope into a well, and then it was used figuratively for reaching a thing or throwing it. The bāʾ is the complement of the verb "idla'." It is also permitted that it be causal, with the pronoun (attached to the verb, referring) to "the wealth"; that is: "do not reach through it," or "do not throw its judgement, and the dispute concerning it, before the rulers." It was also said: "Do not throw part of it before corrupt rulers by way of bribery." Ubayy read: "wa-la tudullu ... li-ta'kulu" (and do not send it forth ... in order that you may consume) by litigating and bringing the matter before them.

﴿A portion﴾, a piece and a part, ﴿of the wealth of people with sin﴾, that is, by means of what entails sin, such as false testimony and a wicked oath. It is possible that the bāʾ is for accompaniment, meaning "while committing sin." In the first case the prepositional phrase is related to "consume" (ta'kulu), and in the second it is a circumstantial clause of its subject. Likewise ﴿while you know﴾ (188), and the object of knowledge is omitted, meaning "while you know that you are wrongdoers." This indicates that whoever does not know he is a wrongdoer, and a judge rules in his favour to take property, is permitted to take it. Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, as a mursal report (a report in which the Companion is omitted from the chain): "That Abdan ibn Ashwa' al-Hadrami and Imru' al-Qays ibn Abis disputed over land, and there was no evidence. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ruled that Imru' al-Qays should take an oath. He intended to do so, whereupon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾ and he refrained from the oath and handed over the land, and this verse was revealed."

It has been used as evidence that a judge's ruling does not take effect inwardly, so taking the property is not permitted in reality. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad held this view. It is supported by what al-Bukhari and Muslim transmitted from Umm Salama, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I am only a human being, and you bring your disputes to me. Perhaps one of you is more eloquent in his argument than another, so I rule for him according to what I hear from him. Whoever I rule for him from the right of his brother, let him not take it, for I am only cutting for him a piece of the Fire."

Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, held that if a judge rules on the basis of evidence regarding a contract, or the annulment of a contract, of a kind that can be initiated, it is binding outwardly and inwardly, and it is as if the two parties had concluded the contract between them, even if the witnesses were false. This is as it is related that a man proposed to a woman who was beneath him, and she refused. He claimed before Ali, may Allah honour his face, that he had married her, and he produced two witnesses. The woman said, "I did not marry him," and she asked for the marriage contract. Ali, may Allah honour his face, said, "The two witnesses have married you." Regarding one who claims a right in the possession of a man and produces evidence indicating that it belongs to him, and the judge rules accordingly, he held that it is not permitted for him to take it, and that the judge's ruling does not make permissible for him what was previously forbidden to him. The hadith is interpreted in this way. The verse is not explicit evidence for the claim of its opponents, for if they mean that it is evidence for non-enforcement absolutely, that is denied, and if they mean that it is evidence for non-enforcement in general, that is granted, and there is no dispute about it, since the Great Imam, may Allah be pleased with him, also says this. But that is in what I have heard. The question is well known in the branches and the foundations of jurisprudence, and it has a detailed treatment in the etiquette of the judge, so refer to it.

[p. 71]

﴿They ask you about the crescent moons﴾. Ibn 'Asakir reported with a weak chain of narration that Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'labah ibn Ghanm said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the matter with the crescent? It appears and rises thin like a thread, then it grows until it becomes large, full and round, and then it keeps diminishing and thinning until it returns as it was. It is never in one state." Then the verse was revealed. In another narration: "Mu'adh said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the Jews ask us a great deal about the crescents,' so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse." According to the first narration, the plural is taken to mean more than one questioner, or the bystanders waiting for the answer are treated as the questioner. Its apparent and immediate meaning according to the second narration is based on the idea that the Jews' question to some of his companions is like a question put to him, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, since they were the means of their knowledge and the source of their overflow of understanding.

"Al-ahilla" is the plural of "hilal" (crescent). Its derivation is from "istahalla al-sabiyy" (the child cried out and shouted when born). From the same root is "ahalla al-qawm bil-hajj" (the people raised their voices in the talbiyah when pilgrimaging). The moon is called "hilal" on the second or third night of the month, or until it becomes circular (yahjur), and "tahjir" means that it becomes encircled by a thin line; this is the view of al-Asma'i. Or it is called hilal until its light overpowers the darkness of the night. Some have set this period at seven nights. It is so named because when people see it they raise their voices in remembrance (of Allah) or in takbir. For this reason one says "ahalla al-hilal" and "istuhilla," but not "halla."

The question may concern the end purpose and wisdom, or it may concern the cause and reason. The verse contains no explicit text deciding between them. The answer relates to one of the two. As for what is spoken in the verse, it is clear. As for what is omitted, one may supply either the cause of its varying phases or its wisdom. Although the question is outwardly about its multiplicity, in reality it implicitly includes a question about the variation of its luminous forms, since multiplicity follows from their variation: if the crescent had one form, no multiplicity would arise, as is evident. As for the report, the word "ma" in it is used to ask about the genus and its reality. So the question is then about the true nature and condition of the crescent during the variation of its luminous forms, and its return to its former state. That matter, whose reality is asked about, undoubtedly admits both of these aspects.

On the first aspect, the answer given by His saying: ﴿Say: they are times marked out for people and for the hajj﴾ corresponds to the question and clarifies the apparent wisdom that suits the universal call to the truth. It serves to remind of Allah's blessing and His abundant mercy, namely that it is a sign for people by which they fix their worldly affairs, know the times of their crops and trade, and know the times of periodic acts of worship, such as fasting and breaking the fast, and especially the hajj, since time is essential to it both in performance and in making up for it. If the crescent were round like the sun, or remained in one state, it would scarcely be possible to fix times by it. He, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, did not mention the hidden wisdom of this, such as the fact that the variation of its forms is a customary or appointed cause for the variation of the states of the elemental births, as explained in its proper place. This is because it is among the matters that not everyone can grasp.

On the second aspect, the answer comes in the wise style, called "al-qawl bil-muwjab" (answering according to what the question implies). It means that the questioner is met with something other than what he sought, by treating his question as if it were another, to alert him that this is more appropriate for his situation. al-Sakkaki and a group of scholars chose this. Thus, in this answer there is an indication that, given that the question was asked, it would have been better for them to ask about the wisdom rather than the cause, since the welfare of their livelihood and their hereafter does not depend on the cause, and the Prophet was sent to explain what does depend on it. This is not because the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, are not among those who grasp the fine details of the science of astronomy (ʿilm al-hayʾa), which rests on observation and philosophical proofs, as some have wrongly supposed. For that, even if granted in their case, belongs to those who walked in the service of prophethood, who were trained in the portico of chivalry, who attained the illumination of lights, and who perceived the subtle secrets through the observatories of their hearts. Although this would not diminish their rank, it does indicate that the cause of the variation is what is explained in astronomy: the moon's distance from the sun and its nearness to it. This is false according to the people of the Shariah, since it is built on premises none of which has been firmly established. The best that can be said is that the early philosophers imagined these to agree with what the Wise Absolute has originated, as the words of our master, al-Shaykh al-Akbar (Ibn 'Arabi), may his secret be sanctified, in his Futuhat indicate. What proves that what they held is mere imagination is that

[p. 72]

wisdom does not reject it, and it does not correspond to reality: the later figures who were counted among the philosophers, such as Herschel the sage and his followers, the people of the observations and the New Zij (astronomical tables), imagined something different from what the earlier ones held about the structure of the heavens. They said that the sun is the center, and that the earth and likewise the stars revolve around it. They built their rulings on eclipses and the like upon this, proved it, and refuted those who opposed it. None of their rulings in this field failed, but events occur just as they occur according to what the earlier ones said, based on their own assumptions. Since the rulings agree despite the difference of the two foundations and the opposition of the two schools, and each of the two claims refutes the other, trust in both doctrines is lost. It becomes necessary to return to the knowledge drawn from the niche of the Message and kindled from the lights of the sun of nobility and valor, and to rely on what the Greatest Lawgiver, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said, after deep reflection upon it and interpreting it in its best meanings. When it is possible to reconcile what the philosophers say, however they say it, with what is accepted by reason, and with what the lord of the wise and the light of the people of earth and heaven says, there is no harm in it. Indeed, it is then the most fitting and most proper means of removing the doubts that often beset the weak among the believers. If this is not possible, then hold fast to what the orbits of the Shariah turn upon and what the angels of the Truth descended with.

"If Hadham says something, believe her, for what is said is what Hadham said." More of this discussion will come, Allah willing.

"Mawaqit" is the plural of "miqat," which is a form denoting an instrument, i.e., that by which the time is known. The distinction between it and "muddah" (duration) and "zaman" (time), as understood from the words of al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani), is that absolute duration is the extension of the motion of the celestial sphere, outwardly, from its beginning to its end. Time (zaman) is a duration divided into years, months, days and hours. And "waqt" (a set time) is the determined and specified time.

It was recited with the assimilation of the nun of "ʿan" into the "l" of "al-ahilla" after transferring the vowel and omitting the hamza. The verse has been cited as evidence for the permissibility of entering the state of ihram for the hajj at any time of the year. But this is far-fetched. Indeed, it may even be cited as evidence for the opposite, since if that were valid, the crescent would not be needed for the hajj. It is needed only because the hajj is restricted to specific known months, and these must be distinguished from others by means of it. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him.

The connection of the verse to what precedes it is clear, since that passage concerns the ruling on fasting. The mention of the month of Ramadan and the discussion of the crescents suits this, because fasting is tied to the sighting of the crescent, and so is breaking the fast. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, said: "Fast when you see it, and break your fast when you see it." This is the end of it.

* * *

From the allusive (ishari) dimension of the verses: He, glorified is He, mentioned sublime laws from the laws of justice. Among them is retaliation (qisas), which was prescribed to remove the aggression of predatory force. It is a shadow of His justice. When He deals with His servant by annihilating and slaying him with the sword of His love, He compensates him for the free spirit with a spirit, for the servant of the heart with a heart, and for the female of the self with a self. For just as He prescribed retribution for your slain, ﴿He prescribed upon Himself mercy﴾ for His slain. In some traditions of the people of the path it is reported that He, glorified is He, says: "Whoever loves Me, I slay him, and whoever I slay, I am his blood-money." For you, in Allah's retribution upon you by what has been mentioned, there is great life after which there is no death, O people of pure intellects, free from the husk of illusions and the veils of individuation and sins, ﴿so that you may have taqwa﴾, that is, so that you may guard against abandoning Him or associating partners with the existence of you.

Among them is the bequest (wasiyyah), which is another law prescribed to remove the deficiency of the angelic power and its shortfall from what wisdom requires of conduct. The bequest of the people of Allah, sanctified be their secrets, is to safeguard the covenant of eternity by leaving aside everything other than the Truth.

Among them is fasting, which is a law prescribed to remove the domination of the bestial powers. In the view of the people of reality, it is abstention from every word, deed and movement that is not for the sake of the Truth through the Truth. ﴿The numbered days﴾ are the days of this world, which will soon pass away. So make all of them your days of fasting, and make your breaking of the fast the festival of meeting Allah, the Exalted. The month of Ramadan is the time of the burning of the self and its dissolution by the lights of the manifestations of nearness, in which the Qur'an was sent down. It is the general knowledge that gathers guidance for people toward unity in terms of collectedness, and detailed proofs from collectedness. As for the distinction: whoever among you is present at that time

[p. 73]

and reaches the station of witnessing, let him abstain from everything except for Him, by Him, in Him, from Him and toward Him. And whoever is afflicted with diseases of the heart and with the carnal veils that prevent witnessing, ﴿or is on a journey﴾, and sets his face toward that station, has other stages to traverse until he reaches it. ﴿Allah intends ease for you﴾, which is the arrival at the station of Oneness and empowerment by His power. ﴿And He does not intend hardship for you﴾, which is the forcing of actions upon the weak self. ﴿And that you complete the count﴾ of the stages, and ﴿that you glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ to the station of collectedness. ﴿And perhaps you will be grateful﴾ through steadfastness.

﴿And when My servants ask you﴾, those specially devoted to Me, who have cut themselves off toward Me, about knowing Me, ﴿then indeed I am near﴾ to them without where, without between, without union and without separation. ﴿I answer﴾ whoever calls upon Me with the tongue of state, by giving him what his state and his readiness require. ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾ by purifying their readiness, and let them witness Me at the time of purification, when I manifest in the mirrors of their hearts, so that they may remain upright in the station of tranquility and the realities of establishment.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 189 (part 2 of 2):

Since a person has varying states according to the differences in the divine names, at times, by the rule of the dominance of the spiritual attributes (al-sifat al-ruhaniyya), during the day of the divine visitations (al-waridat al-rabbaniyya), he fasts from human appetites (al-huzuz al-insaniyya). At other times, by the rule of the human motives and needs, and as wisdom requires, he is returned to the darkness of the animal attributes (al-sifat al-hayawaniyya). This is the time of heedlessness (al-ghafla) that intervenes in that abstinence. He (God) permitted him, at certain times, to descend to the coupling of souls, which is approaching women (al-rafath ila al-nisa'), and He gave the reason in His words, glorified is He: ﴿They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them﴾, meaning: you have no patience with them by the demand of nature, because they clothe you and you clothe them through necessary attachment. ﴿God knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾, and diminishing for yourselves their remaining portions by stealing those perishable portions during the times of spiritual travel (al-suluk) and discipline (al-riyada). So He turned to you and pardoned you. ﴿Now﴾, meaning at the time of steadfastness (al-istiqama) and establishment (al-tamkin), in the state of subsistence after annihilation (al-baqa' ba'd al-fana'), ﴿have relations with them﴾ to the extent of necessary need. ﴿And seek﴾ through the strength of this contact ﴿what God has prescribed for you﴾ of piety and the ability to fulfill the rights of steadfastness and to reach the rational stations (al-maqamat al-'aqliyya). ﴿And eat and drink﴾ in the nights of clarity, until there appear to you the first signs of presence (bawadir al-hudur) and its flashes, and its traces and lights overcome the blackness of heedlessness and its darkness. Then be in true abstinence through presence with the Truth, until the time of the other heedlessness comes, for every present one has a share of it. Were it not so, the interests of livelihood would be disrupted. To this points the report: "I have a time with God in which neither a near angel nor a sent prophet can contain me, and I have a time with Hafsa and Zaynab." And do not approach them during your seclusion and your presence in the stations of nearness and intimacy and the mosques of the hearts. ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves in falsehood﴾, the falsehood of the desires of the soul, and do not send it to the rulers of the commanding souls (al-nufus al-ammara bi'l-su') so that they may consume a portion of the wealth of the spiritual powers unjustly, by your spending it on the pleasures of the carnal powers. ﴿And you know﴾ that this is sin and placing a thing in other than its place. ﴿They ask you about the crescents﴾, which are the inner risings of the heart (al-tawali' al-qalbiyya) when the light of the spirit shines upon them. ﴿Say: they are timings﴾ for the wayfarers (al-salikin), by which are known the times of the obligation of dealing on the path of God, the resolve of the spiritual journey, the circumambulation of the House of the heart, the standing at 'Arafat of gnosis ('irfan), and the running between the purity of Safa and the manliness of Marwa. It has been said: "the crescents" are for the ascetics (al-zahidin) timings of their litanies (awrad), and for the truthful ones (al-siddiqin) timings of their vigilance (muraqabat). The first group is predominantly concerned with the outward aspects of the Sharia, and the latter with the rulings of the Reality (al-haqiqa). If He manifests Himself to them through the attribute of majesty (al-jalal), they are overwhelmed; and if He manifests Himself to them through the attribute of beauty (al-jamal), they live. So they are between majesty and beauty, submission and coquetry. May God, exalted is He, benefit us through them and pour upon us from their blessings. ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs﴾. Ibn Jarir and al-Bukhari transmitted from al-Bara', who said: "When they were in the state of ihram in the Jahiliyya, they would come to the House from its back. Then God revealed ﴿It is not righteousness...﴾ the verse." It seems they were scrupulous about entering through the door because the roof of the door would stand between them and the sky, as al-Zuhri stated explicitly in the narration of Ibn Jarir
[Page 74]
concerning it, and they considered their doing so to be righteousness. So He explained to them that it is not righteousness. ﴿But righteousness is in one who fears God﴾, meaning: the righteousness of one who avoids the forbidden things and the desires. Or: "but the one of righteousness, or the righteous one, is he who fears God." The apparent point is that the negative clause is coordinated with what is said in ( Say ), so there must be a common link between them. Either it is said: they asked about both matters in whatever order it happened, and He combined them in the answer, based on the accidental coincidence in the question, and the second matter is implied, but He omitted mentioning it for brevity and because the answer indicates it, and to announce that this matter is one that should not occur, so that one would not need to ask about it. Or it is said: the question was only about "the crescents," and this is used either literally, mentioned as a digression, since He mentioned the timings of the Hajj, and what is mentioned of their actions in it is also limited to the five; or to alert that what befits their state is to ask about such matters, and not to occupy themselves with what does not concern them rather than the matter of the crescents. Or it is used as an allegorical metaphor (al-isti'ara al-tamthiliyya): their condition in asking about what does not concern them, and leaving what is important, is likened to the condition of leaving the door and coming from another way, to alert to their reversing the matter in this question. So the meaning is: ﴿It is not righteousness that﴾ you reverse your questions, ﴿but righteousness is in one who fears God﴾ in that, and does not force himself into the like of it. It is also permissible that the coordination is with His saying, glorified is He: (They ask you), and the common link between them is that the first is a statement that should not be made, and the second is an action that should not be done by the Ansar, as some reports relate.
﴿And enter the houses through their doors﴾, since there is no righteousness in deviating. Deal with matters in their proper ways. The clause is coordinated with ﴿It is not righteousness﴾, either because it is in the sense of (and do not enter the houses from their backs), or because it is part of the speech being reported. Coordinating an imperative with a declarative is permissible where it has a place in grammatical parsing (i'rab), especially after "say." Ibn Kathir and Kathir read the "ba'" of "al-buyut" with kasra wherever it occurs. ﴿And fear God﴾ in changing His rulings, such as entering houses other than through their doors, and asking about what does not concern you, and among the wisdoms and benefits deposited in His creations, exalted is He, after knowledge that He perfected everything, or in all your affairs.
﴿So that you may prosper﴾, meaning: so that you may succeed in attaining what is sought of guidance and righteousness, for whoever fears God, exalted is He, the springs of wisdom gush from his heart, and the subtleties of secrets are revealed to him according to his piety.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 190:

﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ That is: strive to exalt the religion of Allah, the Exalted, and to raise high His word. Thus "the way" (al-sabil) is used metaphorically for the religion of Allah, the Exalted, and His word, because the believer reaches His good pleasure through it. The "fi" of location that is indicated here serves as a supporting element (tarshih) for the metaphor. ﴿Those who fight you﴾ That is: those of the disbelievers who engage you in actual fighting. This was, according to what is narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah, before they were commanded to fight all the polytheists, both those who fight and those who withhold from fighting. Then that becomes a generalization after the specification derived from this command, confirming its explicit meaning and abrogating its implicit meaning; that is, "do not fight those who withhold." Likewise the explicit meaning of the prohibition that follows, for on this view it also includes the prohibition of fighting them. It is also said that its meaning is: those who set themselves against you in fighting, and from whom such conduct is expected, excluding others such as the elderly, children, women and monks. Then the verse specifies the general command, excluding those from whom such conduct is not expected. It is also said that what is meant is what encompasses all disbelievers, since they are poised to fight the Muslims and intend it, so they are in the ruling of combatants, whether they have fought or not. The first view is supported by what Abu Salih transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "the polytheists barred the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, from the House in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and they made a treaty with him that he would return in the following year, and they would vacate Makkah for him for three days, so that he could circumambulate the House and do what he wished. When the following year came, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and his Companions prepared for the 'Umrat al-Qada'. They feared that Quraysh would not keep their word in this, and that they would bar them from the Sacred Mosque and fight them. His Companions disliked fighting them in the sacred month within the Sacred Precinct, so Allah the Exalted revealed the verse." A fourth view, which takes what is understood from the report as the intended meaning of the relative pronoun, namely those among the polytheists who confront the fighting within the Sacred Precinct and in the sacred month as some of them did, is distant, because it is a specification without evidence, and the specificity of the occasion does not necessitate the specificity of the ruling. ﴿But do not transgress﴾ That is: do not kill women, children, the aged old man, nor one who offers you peace and withholds his hand. If you do so, you have transgressed. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas. (Or) "do not transgress" in any of the ways, such as initiating the fighting, fighting a covenanted person, surprising him with it without a call, or killing one whom you have been forbidden to kill. This was said by some of them, and it is supported by the point that the negated verb conveys generality.

﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors﴾ 190 That is, those who exceed what has been prescribed for them. This is in the manner of a reason for what precedes it. In the well-known view, Allah's love for His servants is an expression for willing good and reward for them. There is no intermediate state between love and hatred with regard to Him, the Mighty in Majesty; this is unlike human love and hatred, for between them there is an intermediate state, which is the absence of both.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 2, Verse 191:**

﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾. That is, "find them," as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said when Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him about it, and he recited against him the verse of Hassan, may Allah be pleased with him:

*"If Judhayma should overtake the sons of Lu'ayy, indeed their killing is a cure."*

The root of *thaqf* (overtaking, gaining mastery) is skill in reaching a thing, whether in action or in knowledge, and it is often used for reaching in general. Its verb is *thaqifa*, patterned like *karuma* and *fariha*.

﴿And expel them from where they expelled you﴾. That is, from Makkah, and this was done to them in the year of the Conquest. This command is coordinated with the one before it, and the meaning is: do whatever is easy for you of these two matters against the polytheists. This dismisses what was said, namely that the command to expel does not go together with the command to kill, since killing and expelling do not coincide. There is no need for what has been strained into the claim that the intended meaning is expelling those who entered under safe-conduct or whom they found under safe-conduct, as is not hidden.

﴿And disorder is worse than killing﴾. That is, their polytheism in the Sacred Precinct is more gravely ugly, so do not hesitate to fight them there, for it is the committing of an ugly act to repel an uglier one. Thus it is permitted for you, and it will be expiated for you. Or, *al-fitnah* means the trial by which a person is put to test, such as being expelled from the homeland, which is beloved to sound natures, and it is harder than killing, because its hardship lasts and the soul is pained by it. From here it was said: "Death by the edge of a sword is easier in its effect upon the soul than death by the edge of separation." The sentence, on the first reading, belongs to the category of *takammul* (completion) and *ihtiras* (precaution), against the assumption, implied by His saying "and fight them," that fighting within the Sacred Precinct is ugly, so how could one be commanded to do it. On the second reading, it is a *tadhyil* (concluding appendage) to His saying "and expel them," explaining the state of expulsion and encouraging it. The original meaning of *fitnah* is placing gold over fire to extract it from its impurities, then it came to be used for testing, punishment, barring from the religion of Allah, and associating partners with Him. Abu al-'Aliyah explained it in the verse with the last of these meanings.

﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque until they fight you there﴾. This is a prohibition to the believers that they should not initiate fighting in that noble place until they themselves are the ones who initiate it. The prohibition against *muqatalah* (fighting), which is an act of two parties, is considered in terms of forbidding them to initiate it, which is the cause of its occurrence. Likewise, its being a limit (*ghayah*) is considered in terms of *mufatahah* (initiating hostilities), so that it does not entail a thing being a limit to itself.

﴿But if they fight you, then kill them﴾. This is the removal of blame for fighting within the Sacred Precinct, which the Muslims feared and disliked. That is: if they fight you there, do not mind fighting them, because they are the ones who violated the sanctity, and you, in fighting them, are repelling killing from yourselves. The expected form would have been the reciprocal form (*mufa'alah*), but it turned away from that to the form of a single act (*fi'l*), as good news to the believers of victory over them; that is, they are so abandoned and unaided that you are commanded to kill them. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: *"And do not kill them until they kill you; but if they kill you, then kill them."* Al-A'mash objected to Hamzah regarding this reading, saying to him: "What about your reading when a man becomes one who is killed? After that, how does he become a killer of others?" Hamzah said: "When one of them is killed, the Arabs say, 'We have killed,' and when one of them strikes, they say, 'We have struck.'" The summary is that the sentence is based on omitting the noun annexed to the object, which is the word *ba'd* (some), so it does not follow that the one killed is a killer. As for attributing the verb to the pronoun, it is based on the principle that an act done by some of them with the consent of the others is attributed to all, through figurative attribution, so there is no need for an estimation in it. For this reason al-A'mash, in his question, was content with the side of the object. Likewise, His saying "do not kill them" is correct literally without interpretation, because the meaning is total negation: no one of you kills one of them until some of them kill some of you. Then this interpretation is specific to this reading, and there is no need for it in *"do not fight them"*, because the meaning there is "do not initiate hostilities against them," and initiating hostilities is only by one party beginning to fight the other. This was said by some of the scholars who verified, and it was hidden from some of the observers, so reflect.

﴿Such is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾ (191). This is a *tadhyil* to what precedes it; that is, they will be done to what they did. The word *al-kafirin* (the disbelievers) is either the placing of the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun, to censure them for disbelief, or it means the category, and those mentioned are included in it by primary inclusion. The prepositional phrase, according to the well-known view, is a fronted predicate and what follows it is a delayed subject. Abu al-Baqa' preferred that *al-kaf* (the particle *ka*, "like") means *mithl* (like) as the subject, and *jaza'* (recompense) is its predicate, since there is no reason for the fronting.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 192:

﴿Then if they desist﴾ from disbelief by repenting of it, as has been related from Mujahid and others; or from it and from fighting, as has been said, due to the indication of the mention of both matters.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ (192). So He forgives them what has already passed. It has been cited from al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, the "Ocean" of Abu Hayyan) as evidence for the acceptance of the repentance of one who has committed deliberate murder, since disbelief is a greater sin than killing, and He, glory be to Him, has informed that He accepts repentance from it.

(Page 77)

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 193:

﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) with "﴿fight those who fight you﴾" (2:190). The first is directed at the obligation of fighting itself, while this one states its limit (ghayah). By "fitnah" is meant shirk (polytheism), as is transmitted (al-ma'thur) from Qatadah, al-Suddi and others. This is supported by the fact that for the Arab polytheists there was nothing but Islam or the sword, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿you fight them or they submit﴾. ﴿And religion be for Allah﴾ means: sincerely for Him, as the lam indicates. The word "kullihi" (all of it) is not used here, as it is in the verse of al-Anfal, because what is here concerns the Arab polytheists, while what is there concerns the disbelievers in general. So generality suits there and its omission suits here. ﴿But if they cease﴾ is an explicit statement of the implied meaning of the limit (mafhum al-ghayah), so the object of cessation is shirk. The fa' indicates sequence (ta'qib). ﴿Then there is to be no aggression except against the wrongdoers (193)﴾ is a reason (ʿillah) for an omitted apodosis (jaza'), which it has taken the place of. The estimated sense is: "But if they cease and submit, then do not transgress against them, because aggression is only against the wrongdoers, and those who cease are not wrongdoers." The intended meaning is the negation of goodness and permissibility, not the negation of occurrence, because aggression does occur against non-wrongdoers. By "aggression" is meant punishment by killing. Killing is called aggression because it is a punishment (ʿuqubah) for aggression (ʿudwan), which is injustice, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in like manner﴾ and ﴿the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾. This is justified by the pairing (izdiwaj) of the speech, and the pairing here is semantic. It may also be said that the recompense for injustice is called injustice, because although it is just from the one who requites, it is an injustice against the wrongdoer by his own doing, since it is an injustice by cause, in that this recompense is imposed upon him. It has also been said: there is no omission, and what is mentioned is the apodosis, in the sense "do not transgress against those who cease." This is either by making ﴿there is no aggression except against the wrongdoers﴾ mean "there is no aggression against anyone other than the wrongdoers," with this being a kinayah (metonymy) for those who cease; or by making the restriction of aggression to the wrongdoers a kinayah for the impermissibility of aggression against others, namely those who cease. It has been objected that on the first estimate the affirmative ruling derived from the restriction (qasr) becomes superfluous, and on the second the thing referred to by the kinayah becomes the same as the thing used to refer to it. It is also permitted that what is mentioned is the apodosis.

Page 77 (continued)

The meaning of "the wrongdoers" is those who exceed the limit of the ruling on fighting, as if it were said: ﴿But if they cease﴾ from shirk, ﴿then there is no aggression except against﴾ those who exceed what Allah, exalted is He, has set as the limit for fighting. These are the ones who attack those who have ceased. The meaning returns to this: if you attack the God-fearing, you become wrongdoers, and the situation is reversed upon you. In this there is an extreme emphasis in forbidding fighting those who cease, which is clear. Some have held that this meaning requires omitting the apodosis and making what is mentioned the reason for it, in the sense: "But if they cease, do not attack them, lest you become wrongdoers, and Allah would then empower over you those who would transgress against you, because aggression only occurs ﴿against the wrongdoers﴾." Or: "If they cease, Allah would empower over you those who transgress against you, on the supposition that you attack them, since you would thereby become wrongdoers." In this there is a remoteness that is clear, so reflect.

﴿The sacred month is for the sacred month﴾. The polytheists fought them in the year of Hudaybiyyah, in Dhu al-Qa'dah, with a light fighting by shooting arrows and throwing stones. Then it happened that they went out in it for the 'Umrat al-Qada' (the make-up 'umrah), so they disliked fighting them because of its sanctity. It was said: this sacred month is in exchange for that one, and violating it is in exchange for its violation, so do not be concerned about it. ﴿And sacred things are subject to retaliation (qisas)﴾. That is, the matters that must be preserved are things that have (qisas), or mutual retaliation (muqassah). This implies establishing the proof for the previous ruling, as if it were said: do not be concerned about your entering it by force, and the violation of the sanctity of this month at the outset by superiority, for the sacred things are subject to qisas. So the obstruction (of the pilgrims) is answered by force. ﴿So if they fight you, then kill them﴾ and ﴿whoever transgresses against you, then transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾. This is a summary (fadhlakah) of what preceded it, and it is more specific in its indication than that, because the first includes what happens if one violates the sanctity of the state of ihram, hunting, or grass, for example, unlike this. In it is an emphasis on His statement, exalted is He: ﴿The sacred month is for the sacred month﴾. This summary being connected by ﴿fa'﴾ does not contradict that, and the command is for permission, since pardon is permissible. The word "man" (whoever) may be conditional or relative, and on the second view the ﴿fa'﴾ is an element connecting the predicate, and the ﴿ba'﴾ (with) necessarily allows both the addition and its absence. Al-Shafi'i used the verse as evidence that the killer is killed in the same manner as he killed, with a sharp instrument, strangulation, burning, starvation, or drowning; so that if he threw him into fresh water, he is not thrown into salt water. It has also been used as evidence that whoever seizes something and destroys it must return its equivalent. Then, the equivalent may be in form, as with things that have equivalents (dhawat al-amthal), and it may be in meaning, as with values (qiyam) for what has no equivalent. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in avenging yourselves and in refraining from transgression by what He has not permitted you. ﴿And know that Allah is with the righteous﴾ 194 with victory and help. ﴿And spend in the way of Allah﴾: it is coordinated (ʿataf) with ﴿they fought﴾, meaning: let there be among you spending for His cause. ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ by abandoning the raid and spending in it. So it is connected to the whole of what is coordinated and what it is coordinated with, as a prohibition of their opposites, to emphasize both of them. This is supported by what many have related from Abu 'Imran, who said: "We were in Constantinople, when a great line of the Romans came out, and a man from the Muslims charged until he entered among them. The people said: he has thrown himself with his own hands into destruction. Then Abu Ayyub al-Ansari stood up and said: O people, you interpret this verse with this interpretation, but it was only revealed about us, the company of the Ansar. When Allah, exalted is He, honored His religion and its supporters multiplied, some of us said to others secretly, without the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Indeed our wealth has been lost, and Allah, exalted is He, has honored Islam and its supporters have multiplied, so if we stay with our wealth and repair what has been lost of it, then Allah, exalted is He, revealed to His Prophet (ﷺ) what answers what we said."

[Page 78]

﴿And spend﴾ and so on. So "destruction" (al-tahlukah) means remaining at home with one's wealth, looking after it, and abandoning the military campaign. Al-Jubba'i said: "Al-tahlukah" means extravagance in spending. The meaning of the verse, then, is a prohibition of it after the command to spend, in pursuit of the middle course between excess and neglect in spending. Al-Bayhaqi narrated in al-Shu'ab, from al-Hasan, that it means stinginess, since it leads to everlasting destruction, so the prohibition would be emphasising the earlier command. Al-Balkhi preferred that it means rushing into war without caution and casting oneself into danger and ruin, so the statement would relate to "fight" (qatilu), a prohibition of excess and neglect in courage. Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna and a group narrated from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib that he was asked about ﴿And do not cast yourselves by your own hands into destruction﴾, and whether it refers to a man who meets the enemy and fights until he is killed. He said: "No, rather it is the man who commits a sin and then throws up his hands and says: 'Allah the Exalted will never forgive me.'" The same was narrated from 'Ubayda al-Salmani. On this reading, it relates to His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, but this is very far-fetched. I have not seen anyone authenticate the report from al-Bara' (may Allah be pleased with him) except al-Hakim, and his authentication is reliable. The apparent meaning of the wording is general. "Ilqa'" (casting) means causing a thing to go downward, and "ilqa' 'alayhi mas'alah" (he cast a question upon him) is a metaphor. It is said of anyone who sets about a task that he "cast his hands" to it and into it. From this is the saying of Labid about the sun:

"Until, when it cast a hand into the unbeliever, and covered the nakedness of the frontiers with its darkness."

"Ilqa'" is transitive with "ila" (to) because it includes the meaning of "ifda'" (leading to) or "inha'" (reaching). The "ba'" (with) in the object is superfluous, for emphasis of the sense of prohibition, because "alqa" is transitive by itself, as in ﴿So Musa threw down his staff﴾. Its addition to the object is not a regular pattern. The word "al-aydi" (hands) is used metaphorically to mean the selves, and it is used to express them because most of their actions occur through them. It is also said: it may be that the "ba'" is superfluous and "al-aydi" has the same meaning, so the sense is: do not make destruction a thing that takes hold of your hands and seizes them. Or the "ba'" is not superfluous, and "al-aydi" retains its literal meaning, and the object is omitted, meaning: do not cast your selves by your hands into ﴿destruction﴾. In that case the benefit of mentioning "al-aydi" is to make explicit the prohibition of casting oneself into it deliberately and by choice. "Al-tahlukah" is a verbal noun like "al-halak" and "al-halak." In the language of the Arabs there is no verbal noun of the form taf'ulah with a damma on the 'ayn, except this one in the well-known usage. Sibawayh narrated from the Arabs "tadurrah" and "tasurrah" as well, meaning harm and joy. It is permitted that its original form was "tahlikah" with a kasra on the lam, a verbal noun of the doubled verb halaka, like "al-tajribah" and "al-tabsirah," and then the kasra was changed to a damma. But in this there is an objection: the form taf'ilah with a kasra from a doubled, sound, non-hamzated verb is anomalous, and the analogical form is tif'il. Changing the kasra to a damma without any cause is extremely anomalous. Its illustration by "al-juwar" with a damma on the jim in place of "jiwar" with a kasra is not valid, because that is not a clear example of substitution, since the verbal noun there may be built on the pattern fu'al with a damma on the first radical, as an anomaly. This is supported by what is in al-Sihah: "jawartuhu mujawarah wa jiwaran wa juwaran," and the kasra is more eloquent. Some distinguished between "al-tahlukah" and "al-halak": the first is what can be guarded against, and the second is what cannot. It was also said: "al-halak" is a verbal noun, and "al-tahlukah" is the very thing that causes destruction. Both of these views go against what is well known. The verse has been cited as evidence for the prohibition of undertaking what may lead to the loss of one's life, and for the permissibility of making peace with unbelievers and rebels when the leader fears for himself or for the Muslims.

﴿And do good﴾, that is, by returning to the needy, as 'Ikrimah said. It was also said: do good in your opinion of Allah the Exalted, and do good in your deeds by carrying out acts of obedience. Perhaps this is the better view.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves the doers of good﴾ 195, and rewards them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 196 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for God.﴾ That is: make them complete when you undertake to perform them for the sake of God, exalted is He. So there is no indication in the verse of more than the obligation of completing them once one has begun them, and this is agreed upon between the Hanafis (the Hanafi school) and the Shafiʿis (the Shafiʿi school), may God be pleased with them. For the invalidation (ifsad) of Hajj and ʿUmrah, in any case, requires continuing with the remaining acts and making up (qadaʾ) the rite, and does not indicate the obligation of the original act. The claim that the indication exists, based on the premise that the command to complete is unrestricted and therefore entails a command to perform, [Page 79] is untenable, because it is established that what is necessary for an unrestricted obligation to be fulfilled is itself obligatory. Rather, the command to complete presupposes prior commencement, so the command to complete is restricted to commencement. The claim that the meaning is "perform them while they are complete, fulfilling all the conditions and pillars," and that this indicates their obligation, because the command is apparent in it, is likewise not sound. The reading "And establish the Hajj and the ʿUmrah" supports this claim, but it is not correct, for two reasons. First, because it contradicts the apparent meaning. Second, even if it were accepted in the context of argument, the obligation derived from the command in it could be directed at the qualifier, namely "complete," and not at the very act of performing it, as in his (ﷺ) saying: "Sell like for like." Second, the command in the reading is taken to mean the figurative meaning common to obligation and recommendation, namely requesting the act. The indication of this is the hadiths that show the recommendation of ʿUmrah. Al-Shafiʿi in al-Umm, ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Majah reported that he (ﷺ) said: "Hajj is struggle (jihad) and ʿUmrah is voluntary." At-Tirmidhi reported and authenticated from Jabir that "a man asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about ʿUmrah: Is it obligatory? He said: 'No, but to perform it is better for you.'" This is supported by the fact that Ibn Masʿud, the companion associated with this reading, said, as reported from him by Ibn Abi Shaybah and ʿAbd ibn Humayd: "Hajj is an obligation and ʿUmrah is voluntary." Ibn Abi Dawud also reported in al-Masahif, from him as well, that he used to recite it that way and then say: "By God, were it not for my scruple that I did not hear anything about it from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), I would say that ʿUmrah is obligatory like Hajj." This indicates that he, may God be pleased with him, did not take the command regarding it as implying obligation, since he had not heard anything about it, and perhaps he had heard what contradicts it. For this reason he, in the first report from him, asserted the obligation of Hajj and the recommendation of ʿUmrah. It is probably for this reason that he understood the command in his reading to mean only the common element we have mentioned, on the basis of the impossibility of using a homonym (mushtarak) in both its meanings, and the impermissibility of combining the literal and the figurative sense, and the inclination against positing an act conforming to what is mentioned that is meant to be recommended. Yes, what has been mentioned is not considered a qualifying factor (sarif) unless it is established that it preceded the verse. But if it is established that it came after it, then it is not, because that would entail abrogation (naskh) of the Book by a single report (khabar al-wahid), since the command is apparent in obligation and is not ambiguous (mujmal) in its meanings according to the sound view, so that the report could be understood as delayed explanation (taʾkhir al-bayan), as has been wrongly supposed. And the claim that the hadiths of recommendation came earlier and do not divert the command from its apparent meaning, but that this would be abrogating them, is an obvious error, because the hadiths are explicit (nass) in recommendation, while the Qur'an is apparent in obligation. How could the apparent be abrogating the explicit, when the explicit takes precedence over the apparent in case of conflict?

Furthermore, this which we have mentioned, although it does not invalidate the basis of the support, does greatly weaken it. Some have claimed that the hadiths indicating the recommendation of ʿUmrah are opposed by those among them that indicate its obligation. Al-Hakim reported from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Hajj and ʿUmrah are two obligations; it does not harm you which of them you begin with." Abu Dawud and an-Nasa'i reported that "a man said to ʿUmar: I found Hajj and ʿUmrah written upon me, so I entered into the state of consecration (ihlal) for both of them together. He said: You have been guided to the sunnah of your Prophet." This indicates that entering into consecration for both is the practice of the Prophet (ﷺ), because deriving evidence from what a companion relates of his sunnah (peace be upon him) is deriving evidence from the practical hadith that the companion transmitted. The claim that "I entered into consecration for both" is an explanatory clause for "I found," so that the obligation could be due to entering into consecration for both, and therefore the hadith does not indicate obligation in the first place, is worthless, because the clause is independent (mustaʾnafah), as though it were said: "What did you do?" He said: "I entered into consecration." This indicates that finding was the cause of entering into consecration and not the reverse, because the questioner's intent was to ask about the validity of his entering into consecration for both. How could he say "I found them written" because "I entered into consecration for them"? It would only be valid on the assumption that he knew the validity of his entering into consecration for both. ʿUmar's answer, may God be pleased with him, is entirely unrelated to the obligation of completion, because the fact that commencing something makes its completion obligatory is not described as the practice of the Prophet (ﷺ), but rather is said of the performance of the rites and acts of worship. This is supported by what occurs in some reports: "so I entered into consecration" with the particle fa, which indicates sequence. What is mentioned from Ibn Masʿud, may God be pleased with him, is opposed by what is reported from him regarding the view of obligation. ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, also said this, and he used to recite "And establish" as well, as Ibn Jarir and others reported from him. Likewise Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them. End of quotation. Fairness requires accepting that the reports conflict, and each of the imams has followed what was authentic to him. The matter is one of the derivative rulings (furuʿ), and disagreement regarding such matters is a mercy. The truth is that the verse cannot serve as proof for the Shafiʿis and those who agree with them, such as the Imamis, against us. On close examination, it contains nothing more than the statement of the obligation to complete their acts when undertaking to perform them, and guiding people to remedy whatever obstacles may befall them that spoil this completion, such as being prevented (ihsar) and the like, without addressing whether they are obligatory or not. The obligation of Hajj is derived from His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And due to God from the people is the pilgrimage to the House, for whoever is able to find a way to it.﴾ As for whoever among the opponents claims that this is evidence for them, he has overstepped and spoken error, as is not hidden from one who listens attentively while being a witness. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Bayhaqi and a group reported from ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, that completing Hajj and ʿUmrah for God means that you enter into consecration for them from the dwelling of your household. The same is reported from Abu Hurayrah, traced back (marfuʿ) to the Messenger of God (ﷺ). ʿAbd al-Razzaq and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿUmar, may God be pleased with them both, that completing them means that each one is performed separately from the other, and that ʿUmrah is performed outside the months of Hajj. It was also said that completing them means that the expenses are lawful. It was said that it means initiating a separate journey for each. It was said that it means setting out intending them alone and not for trade or the like. It has been recited: "to the House" and "for the House." The first is reported from Ibn Masʿud, and the second from ʿAli, may God ennoble his face.

﴿But if you are prevented (uhsirtum)﴾ is contrasted with an omitted clause, meaning: this applies if you are able to complete them. Ihsar and hasr both, in the original linguistic usage, mean restraint in general, and hasr is not restricted to what comes from an enemy, nor is ihsar restricted to what comes from illness or fear, as al-Zajjaj supposed, due to their frequent usage in that sense. For a word that is originally applied to a general meaning may come to be widely used for one of its particular instances. The evidence for this is that one says: "The enemy confined him (hasarahu al-ʿaduww) and prevented him (ahsarahu)," like "he hindered him (saddahu) and prevented him (asadda)." If attribution to the enemy were included in the concept of hasr, then explicitly attributing it to the enemy would be redundant. And if attribution to illness and the like were included in the concept of ihsar, then attributing it to the enemy would be figurative, and both are contrary to the basic principle. The meaning of ihsar here, according to Malik and al-Shafiʿi, may God have mercy on them both, is the confinement by an enemy, because of His saying: ﴿But when you are secure (amintum)﴾, since security (amn) in language is the opposite of fear, and because of its revelation in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah, and because of the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both: "There is no confinement except the confinement by an enemy," thereby restricting the unrestricted (taqyid) wording of the verse, and he knows best the occasions of revelation. Abu Hanifah held that it refers to whatever includes every prevention from an enemy, illness or other things. Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi, who graded it as good (hasan), an-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and al-Hakim reported from the hadith of al-Hajjaj ibn ʿAmr: "Whoever is broken or lamed, upon him is Hajj in the following year." At-Tahawi reported from the hadith of ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd, who said: a man named ʿUmar ibn Saʿid entered into consecration for an ʿUmrah, then he was stung, and while he lay prostrate on the road, a caravan passed by, among whom was Ibn Masʿud. They asked him, and he said: "Send the offering (hadi), and set a time between you and him for a sign. When that time comes, let him exit the state of consecration." Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from ʿAta': "There is no ihsar except from illness, an enemy, or a restraining matter." al-Bukhari reported something similar from him. ʿUrwah said: Everything that restrains the one in consecration is ihsar. What the opponent used as evidence is answered as follows. As for the first, you will learn what is in it. As for the second, the particular occasion of revelation carries no weight, and the claim that the particle lam is for emphasis, its mention with the lam as an independent item makes that unlikely. The claim that "you are prevented" is not general, because an affirmative verb has no generality, so it is not intended except for what was reported concerning it, namely the restraint by an enemy, by agreement, is not a valid argument, because although it is not general, it is unrestricted (mutlaq), so it is applied in its unrestricted sense. As for the third, after accepting the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas's statement [Page 81] (may God be pleased with him) regarding such matters, it is opposed by what Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him in explaining the verse, that he said: he says: "Whoever enters into consecration for Hajj or ʿUmrah and is then held back from the House by illness that exhausts him or by an enemy that restrains him, upon him is the slaughter of whatever offering is feasible." Just as he restricted in the first report, he generalized in this one, and he knows best the occasions of revelation. The claim that the hadith of al-Hajjaj is weak is itself weak, since it has various chains in the collections of hadith. Abu Dawud reported that ʿIkrimah asked al-ʿAbbas and Abu Hurayrah, may God be pleased with them both, about this, and they said: "He spoke the truth." The Hanafis interpreted it as applying when the one in consecration stipulates, at the time of intention, release (ihlal) upon the occurrence of the impediment of illness, based on his (ﷺ) saying to Dubaʿah: "Perform Hajj and stipulate, and say: O God, my place of release is where You restrain me." This does not fit with what is established in the principles of the Hanafis, that an unrestricted statement is applied in its unrestricted sense, except where the incident and the ruling are the same and the unrestriction and restriction apply to the ruling. For what we are discussing is not like that, as is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 196 (part 2 of 3):**

﴿فَما اسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ الهَدْيِ﴾ That is: ﴿then (it is incumbent) upon you﴾, or ﴿then what is obligatory is﴾, or ﴿then offer what is easy (istaysara)﴾; that is, what is made easy (tayassara). It is like ṣaʿuba and istuṣʿiba (was difficult). The sīn here is not for seeking (istidhāʾ). The word al-hady (the sacrificial offering, hady) is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, that is, al-mahdiyy (the thing offered). For this reason it is applied to the singular and the plural, or it is the plural of hadiyyah (as jadyin is the plural of jadiyyah).
