It was also read as hadiyy with shaddah, the plural of hadiyyah (as maṭiyy is the plural of maṭiyyah). It stands in the position of a ḥāl (circumstantial clause) relative to the concealed pronoun. The meaning is that the muḥrim (one in the state of iḥrām) who is prevented (uḥṣira) and wishes to exit the state (taḥallul) exits it by slaughtering an offering that is easy for him, of a camel, a cow, or a sheep. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Whatever is greater is more excellent." It is related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he restricted the offering to a cow or a camel. It was said to him: "Is a sheep not sufficient for him?" He said: "No." According to the majority, he slaughters it at the place where he was prevented, because the Prophet (ﷺ) slaughtered there in the year of al-Ḥudaybiyah (Hudaybiyah), and that place is within the ḥill (the area outside the sacred precinct). Among us (the Ḥanafīs), the one who is prevented sends the offering and assigns for the one sent with it a designated day as a sign (amārah). When the day arrives and it becomes his strong opinion (ghalaba ʿalā ẓannihi) that it has been slaughtered, he exits the state, based on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And do not shave your heads until the offering reaches its place of sacrifice﴾. The shaving of the head is a metaphor for the exit from the state, which is achieved by shortening (taqṣīr) in the case of women. The address is to those who are prevented, because that is the nearest thing mentioned. The second hady is the same as the first, as is apparent. That is: do not exit until you know that the offering sent to the sacred precinct (al-Ḥaram) has reached the place where it must be slaughtered, which is the sacred precinct, based on the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then its place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House﴾.

﴿هَدْيًا بالِغَ الكَعْبَةِ﴾ ﴿An offering reaching the Kaʿbah﴾. As for what is reported of the Prophet (ﷺ) slaughtering at al-Ḥudaybiyah, the fact of it is accepted, but his having slaughtered in the ḥill is not accepted. The Ḥanafiyyah (Ḥanafī scholars) say: the place where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was prevented was on the road of al-Ḥudaybiyah, below Makkah, and al-Ḥudaybiyah is adjacent to the sacred precinct. The slaughter took place in the adjoining part where the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stopped. By this, what Mālik said is reconciled with what al-Zuhrī narrated: "that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sacrificed in the sacred precinct." As for the report from him not being authentic, that is within the scope of prohibition (i.e., it is not an established proof). The earlier scholars understood the arrival of the offering at its place (of sacrifice) to mean its slaughter at the place where its slaughter is permitted, whether that is the ḥill or the sacred precinct. This is contrary to the apparent meaning, but it does not require the supposition of the word "knowing" as in the preceding case. It was used as evidence that, since restricting oneself to the offering in a context of explanation indicates that the making up of the pilgrimage (qaḍāʾ) is not obligatory. But among us, making up is obligatory, because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions made up the ʿUmrah of al-Ḥudaybiyah in which they were prevented, and it was called the ʿUmrat al-Qaḍāʾ (the ʿUmrah of making up). The context is the context of explaining how the one who is prevented exits the state of iḥrām, not the context of explaining everything that is obligatory for him. The ruling for one who is not prevented was not known explicitly from the verse, just as the ruling for the one who is prevented was known from the impermissibility of exit before the offering reaches (its place). This is derived by indication of the text (dalālat al-naṣṣ). The address was made general to the one prevented and others, on the basis that the conjunction of ﴿and do not shave﴾ is to the words of His, glorified be He: ﴿and complete﴾, not to ﴿then what is easy﴾, since that would require cutting off the composition, because ﴿then when you are secure﴾ is a conjunction to ﴿if you are prevented﴾, as is not hidden. The word al-maḥall, with a kasrah, from the pattern ḍaraba, is used for a place, as is apparent in the verse, and for a time, as one says: "maḥall al-dīn" (the due time of a debt) for the time of its falling due and the end of its term.

﴿فَمَن كانَ مِنكم مَرِيضًا﴾ ﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾ who needs to shave. This is a specification (takhṣīṣ) of the words of Allah, glorified be He: ﴿and do not shave﴾, which is a branch of it.

Page 82

﴿أوْ بِهِ أذًى مِن رَأْسِهِ﴾ ﴿or has an injury from his head﴾, from a wound, lice, or headache. ﴿فَفِدْيَةٌ﴾ ﴿then there is a ransom﴾, that is: upon him is a ransom if he shaves.

﴿مِن صِيامٍ أوْ صَدَقَةٍ أوْ نُسُكٍ﴾ ﴿of fasting, or charity, or sacrifice﴾ is an explanation of the kind of ransom. As for its quantity, al-Baghawī (the author of al-Maṣābīḥ) reported: "from Kaʿb ibn ʿUjrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by him while he was at al-Ḥudaybiyah before he entered Makkah, while he was in the state of iḥrām, and he was lighting a fire under a cooking pot while the lice were falling onto his face. He (ﷺ) said: 'Do your parasites harm you?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then shave your head, and feed a farq (measure) among six poor people, the farq being three ṣāʿs, or fast three days, or offer a nusuk (sacrifice).'" In the narration of al-Bukhārī, Muslim, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Mājah, and al-Tirmidhī: "that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'I did not think that the hardship had reached you to this extent. Do you not find a sheep?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Fast three days, or feed six poor people, for each poor person half a ṣāʿ of food, and shave your head.'" In this narration he explained what is to be fed to each poor person, but he did not specify the place of the ransom. The apparent meaning is generality in all the places, as Ibn al-Faras said, and this is the school of Imām Mālik.

﴿فَإذا أمِنتُمْ﴾ ﴿Then when you are secure﴾: from amn (security), the opposite of fear, or al-amanah (the ceasing) of it. According to the first, the meaning is: when you are in security and ease and are not afraid. According to the second: when the fear of being prevented has ceased from you. From this is understood the ruling for one who was initially secure by way of indication (dalālah). The fāʾ here is a conjunction to ﴿if you are prevented﴾, indicating sequence (taʿqīb), whether what is meant is the prevention by an enemy or any prohibition in general. It is said of a sick person when his illness ceases and he recovers: "amina" (he became secure), as is related from Ibn Masʿūd and Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, by the chain of Ibrāhīm (al-Nakhaʿī). Therefore, the argument of al-Shāfiʿī and Mālik from the verse, for what they held, is weakened.

﴿فَمَن تَمَتَّعَ بِالعُمْرَةِ إلى الحَجِّ﴾ ﴿Then whoever enjoys (tamattaʿa) the ʿUmrah until the Ḥajj﴾. The fāʾ falls in the response to (idhā). The bāʾ and ilā are connected to the tamattuʿ. The meaning: whoever benefits and gains by drawing near to Allah, the Exalted, through the ʿUmrah until the time of the Ḥajj; that is, before benefiting from the Ḥajj in its months. It was said: the bāʾ is causal (sababiyyah) and the object of tamattuʿ is omitted; that is, by means of some one of the prohibitions of iḥrām. He did not specify it because the purpose is not tied to specifying it. The meaning: whoever enjoys, by reason of the time of the ʿUmrah and exiting from it by making permissible the prohibitions of iḥrām, until he enters the state of iḥrām for the Ḥajj. In this there is a shifting of tamattuʿ from its legal sense to its linguistic sense. The second meaning is benefiting absolutely. The first is that one enters the state of iḥrām for the ʿUmrah in the months of Ḥajj, performs its rites, then enters the state of iḥrām for the Ḥajj from within Makkah, and performs its acts. Its opposite is qirān (combining), which is to enter the state for both together and perform the rites of the Ḥajj, incorporating the rites of the ʿUmrah into it, and ifrād (single Ḥajj), which is to enter the state for the Ḥajj and, after finishing it, for the ʿUmrah.

﴿فَما اسْتَيْسَرَ مِنَ الهَدْيِ﴾ ﴿Then what is easy of the offering﴾. The fāʾ falls in the response to (man). That is: upon him is a sacrifice made easy for him because of the tamattuʿ. It is therefore a sacrifice of compensation (dam jubrān), because what is obligatory for him is to enter the state of iḥrām for the Ḥajj from the miqāt (the prescribed boundary point). When he entered it not from the miqāt, this produced a defect in it, so this sacrifice compensates for it. For this reason it is not obligatory for a Makkan or one in his position. He slaughters it when he enters the state for the Ḥajj, and it is not permissible before entering the state. It is not fixed for him on the Day of Sacrifice, rather it is recommended (to slaughter it then), and he does not eat from it. This is the school of al-Shāfiʿī. Abū Ḥanīfah held that it is a sacrifice of rite (dam nusuk), like the sacrifice of the one performing qirān, because it became obligatory upon him as thanks for combining the two rites, so it is like the udhiyyah (festival sacrifice), and it is slaughtered on the Day of Sacrifice. ﴿فَمَن لَمْ يَجِدْ﴾ ﴿Then whoever does not find﴾, that is, the offering. This is a conjunction to (fa-idhā amintum) (then when you are secure).

﴿فَصِيامُ ثَلاثَةِ أيّامٍ في الحَجِّ﴾ ﴿Then a fast of three days during the Ḥajj﴾, that is: upon him is a fast. It was also read as fa-ṣiyāma (in the accusative), that is: let him fast. The time-frame (ẓarf) of the fast is omitted, since it is impossible for any of the acts of the Ḥajj to be its time-frame. Abū Ḥanīfah said: what is meant is the time of the Ḥajj absolutely, but between the two states, the state of the Ḥajj and the state of the ʿUmrah, and this is a metaphor for not exiting from both of them. It thus includes what happens before entering the state for the Ḥajj, whether or not he has exited from the ʿUmrah, and what happens after it, as evidenced by the fact that if he becomes able to obtain an offering after fasting the three days but before exiting, the slaughter becomes obligatory upon him, and if he becomes able after exiting, it is not obligatory upon him, because the purpose is achieved by the fast, which is exiting. Al-Shāfiʿī said: what is meant is the time of performing the Ḥajj, which is the days of occupation with it after entering the state and before exiting. Fasting is not permissible according to him before entering the state for the Ḥajj. The preferred practice is to fast on the seventh, eighth, and ninth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, because that is the furthest delay possible, given the possibility of ability to obtain the original (obligation), which is the offering. It is not permissible on the Day of Sacrifice or the days of tashrīq (the days of drying meat, 11th–13th of Dhū al-Ḥijjah), because fasting is forbidden on them. Some permitted fasting the last three days, relying on what Ibn Jarīr, al-Dāraquṭnī, and al-Bayhaqī reported from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) gave a concession to the tamattuʿ-performer who does not find an offering and has not fasted until the ten days have passed, that he may fast the days of tashrīq in their place." Mālik reported from al-Zuhrī, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent ʿAbd Allāh ibn Ḥudhāfah, and he proclaimed during the days of tashrīq: 'These are days of eating, drinking, and remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, except for one who has an obligation of fasting due to an offering.'" al-Dāraquṭnī reported the like of it by the chain of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab. al-Bukhārī and a group reported from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not grant a concession for fasting during the days of tashrīq except to one performing tamattuʿ who does not find an offering." Imām Mālik adopted this. Perhaps our masters of the Ḥanafiyyah relied on the hadiths of prohibition, and they said: if he misses the fast until the Day of Sacrifice arrives, only the offering suffices for him, and he does not make it up after the days of tashrīq, as the Shāfiʿiyyah held, because it is a substitute (badal), and substitution is not established except by legislation, and the text restricted it to the time of the Ḥajj. The permissibility of the offering is based on the original rule. And from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, it is reported that in a similar case he ordered the slaughter of a sheep.

﴿وسَبْعَةٍ إذا رَجَعْتُمْ﴾ ﴿And seven when you return﴾, that is: when you have finished and departed from its rites. The return is mentioned and its cause is intended. Or the meaning: when you return from Mina. Al-Shāfiʿī, may Allah be pleased with him, according to what is most sound among the majority of his companions, said: when you return to your households. This is supported by what al-Bukhārī reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him: "When you return to your cities." And the word "return" is more apparent in this meaning. The ruling for one who intends to reside in Makkah permanently is the ruling of one returning to his homeland, because the Law placed the place of residence in the position of the homeland. (In al-Baḥr) the intended meaning of "return to one's household" is the beginning of it according to some, and completion by arrival at them according to others. In the speech there is a shift (iltifāt) of person, and it is interpreted according to the meaning after the interpretation according to its wording in singularity and absence. It was also read as sabʿatan (in the accusative), as a conjunction to the place (maḥall) of "three days," because it is an object in an expanded sense (ittisāʿan). Whoever does not permit this supposes the verb "and fast" (wa-ṣūmū) as implied, and Abū Ḥayyān held this.

[p. 84]

﴿That is ten complete.﴾ The reference is to "the three and the seven." The counted noun, *ayyām* (days), is omitted. Keeping the *tā'* in the number while omitting the counted noun is the better of the two usages. The benefit of the *fadhlaka* (a summing-up or recapitulation that states the total) is that it prevents the supposition that the *wa* ("and") carries the meaning of the optional *aw* ("or"). Al-Sirafi, in his commentary on *al-Kitab* (Sibawayh's grammar), explicitly stated that it comes with that meaning. It is not a condition that an explicit command precede it; a statement that has the sense of a command is likewise (acceptable). The remote supposition that we pointed to in the introduction on the inimitability of the Qur'an is dispelled, and the number is known as a whole, just as it was known in detail, so that it is encompassed from two aspects and knowledge is confirmed. Among their proverbs: "Two kinds of knowledge are better than one." Especially since most Arabs do not do arithmetic well, the fitting approach for a general address, by which both the elite and the common people, who are of natural disposition and not trained in learning, understand, is repetition of the speech and increase of clarity. It also announces that by "seven" the number is meant, not abundance, since the word is used in both senses.

If you ask: what is the wisdom in its being so, that it needs to be separated, which requires what has been mentioned? The answer: since these (days) were a substitute for the *hady* (sacrificial animal), and a substitute generally occupies the place of what it replaces, the three were made a substitute for it during the time of the Hajj, and the seven were added to them as a supplement so that they would equal it without any reduction in reward, because the *fidyah* (compensation) is based on ease. And the seven were not made fasting during the Hajj because of the hardship of fasting in the Hajj. To indicate this equivalence, the ten were described as "complete," as if it were said: ﴿That is ten complete﴾ in their taking the place of the sacrifice. It has also been said that it is an emphatic descriptive term that conveys increased recommendation to fast them, and that they should not be neglected or reduced in number, as if it were said: "That is ten complete, so observe their completeness and do not diminish them." It has also been said that it is a descriptive term clarifying the completeness of the ten, for it is a number in which the special properties of numbers are complete. The one is the beginning of number, the two is the first number, the three is the first odd number, the four is the first squared number, the five is the first circular number, the six is the first perfect number, the seven is a prime number, the eight is the first number of even-times-even, the nine is the first triangular number, and the ten itself is the end to which number arrives, for every number after it is composed of it and of what precedes it. This was said by some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqin*).

Al-Imam (al-Razi) mentioned for this summation together with the description ten aspects, but they are ten incomplete aspects. Were it not for the excess of length, I would have mentioned them with what is in their favor and against them.

﴿That﴾ refers to the *tamattu'* (combining Hajj and Umrah) understood from His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Whoever enjoys (tamattu')﴾. According to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, there is no *mut'ah* (tamattu') and no *qiran* (combining) for the residents of the Sacred Mosque, because the legislation of both is for ease through dropping one of the two journeys. This applies to the one coming from afar (*afaqi*), not to the people of Makkah and those in their position. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it refers to the nearest thing, which is the ruling mentioned, namely the obligation of the sacrifice or its substitute upon the *mutamatti'*. This obligation applies only if the *mutamatti'* is an *afaqi*, because it is obligatory to enter the state of ihram for Hajj from the *miqat* (boundary point). When he entered ihram from the miqat for Umrah and then entered ihram for Hajj not from the miqat, a defect occurred, so it was made to be compensated by a sacrifice. The Makkan is not required to enter ihram from the miqat, so his undertaking tamattu' does not cause a defect in his Hajj, and therefore he is not obliged to a sacrifice or its substitute. This is refuted by the fact that if the reference were to the sacrifice and fasting, He would have used *'ala* rather than the *lam* in His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿for him whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾, because the sacrifice and its substitute are obligatory upon the *mutamatti'*, and the obligatory is construed with *'ala*, not with *li*. That the *lam* is used in place of *'ala*, as has been said in "stipulate for them the wala'" (a hadith), is contrary to the apparent meaning. The relative clause refers to one who is from the Haram at the distance of shortening the prayer according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him; to one whose dwelling is beyond the miqat according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him; to the people of the Hill (*ahl al-Hill*) according to Tawus; and to non-people of Makkah according to Malik, may Allah be pleased with him. "Present" (*hadir*) in the first sense is the opposite of traveler, and in the other senses means witness, as opposed to absent. The meaning of the presence of the family is the presence of the one in ihram, and it is expressed thus because, as has been said, the usual condition of a man is that he resides where his family resides. The Sacred Mosque has two applications: one is the mosque itself, and the second is the entire Haram. From the latter is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque﴾, based on the view that he, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, was taken on the night journey from the Haram and not from the mosque. The majority of the imams of the religion hold that the last meaning is intended in this verse.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ in everything He commands you and forbids you, as is derived from the omission of the object. It includes Hajj by primary inclusion, and by it the arrangement is completed.

﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ (196) for whoever does not fear Him. That is: keep this in mind so that you refrain from disobedience. The placing of the majestic Name in the place of the pronoun is to cultivate awe and introduce dread. The phrase *shadid* (severe) is in an annexation of the attributive adjective (*sifah mushabbahah*) to its raised noun.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 197:**

﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾: that is, its time is those months, and by this the predication is made sound. It has also been said: "There is an omitted word, meaning 'the time of Hajj is months' or 'the actions of Hajj are in months'." And it has been said: "No omission is needed, and the Hajj, which is an act among acts, is made to be the time itself, for emphasis." It is not hidden that the purpose is to state the time of Hajj, as what follows indicates, so explicitly specifying it is more appropriate. The meaning of His words, glorified and exalted be He, ﴿well-known﴾ is: known among the people. These months are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah according to us (the Hanafis). This is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ibn 'Umar and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them all. It is supported by the fact that the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr) is the time for a pillar of Hajj, which is the Tawaf al-Ziyarah (the circumambulation of visitation), and by the fact that it (the verse) explained "the Day of the Greatest Hajj" as the Day of Sacrifice.

According to Malik, the first two months and the whole of Dhu al-Hijjah are (the months), acting upon the apparent wording of "months." Also, some of the acts of Hajj are performed during the days of sacrifice: the Tawaf al-Ziyarah, shaving the head, and throwing the pebbles at the Jamarat. A woman who menstruates postpones the obligatory circumambulation until after the ten days are over. Also, it is permissible, as has been said, to delay the Tawaf al-Ziyarah until the end of the month, according to what is related from 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr. And also because the apparent meanings of the reports speak to this. Al-Tabarani, al-Khatib and others have related by various chains that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) counted the three months as Hajj." Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir related the like of this from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him: the first two months and the nine days of Dhu al-Hijjah together with the night of sacrifice, because Hajj is lost by the break of dawn on the Day of Sacrifice, and an act of worship is not lost while its time remains. This is what al-Razi said. In it (this argument) there is the point that Hajj is lost by the loss of its greatest pillar, which is standing at 'Arafat, and not by the loss of its time absolutely. The root of the disagreement is whether the intended meaning of "its time" is the time of its rites and acts without disapproval, and the rites that are not proper at other times absolutely, or the time of its entering into ihram (the state of sacred consecration). Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, holds the latter view. Ihram is not valid after the break of dawn on the Day of Sacrifice because performance is no longer possible, even though some of the acts of Hajj may be performed during the days of sacrifice. Malik holds the second view, for it is said that he disliked performing 'Umrah during the rest of Dhu al-Hijjah, because it is related that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, used to frighten the people with the whip and forbid them from it during those days. It is also related that his son, may Allah be pleased with him, said to a man: "If you obey me, wait until the new moon of the sacred month appears, then go out to Dhat 'Irq and pronounce the talbiyah from there for 'Umrah."

Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, holds the first view, because the tenth day is a time for performing the stoning, shaving and other acts, while the rest of the days of sacrifice, although they are also a time for that, were specified for the ten days only, in accordance with what is related in reports mentioning the ten days. Perhaps the reason is that the intended meaning is the time in which the responsible person can be free from his rites, such that everything becomes lawful for him, and this is the tenth day, and what is other than it of the remaining days of sacrifice. This is for facilitating the performance of the circumambulation and completing the stoning.

"Months" is used in its literal sense, except that it was used figuratively for some of its instances, for the least number of a plural is three units according to the majority. So he made some who were singular into singular units and then gathered them into a plural. It has also been said: it is metaphorical for more than one, by the relation of association. It is not a plural in the literal sense according to the established doctrine on this matter, for its application is valid only for two, or three, not for two plus part of a third. And the statement that the intended meaning is two, with the third being in the status of non-existence, [is in the status of non-existence]. It has also been said: the intended meaning is three, and it is not used figuratively for some of the instances, because nouns of time (adverbs) are applied to some of their parts literally, since they carry the meaning of "in" (fi). So one says: "I saw him in such-and-such a year, or such-and-such a month, or such-and-such a day," and you have seen him in an hour of that. (This view) is perhaps closer to the truth.

The plural form of the masculine for non-rational beings comes with alif and ta' (the feminine plural ending). ﴿Then whoever undertakes﴾, that is, obliges himself, ﴿therein to Hajj﴾ by entering ihram. He becomes a muhrim (one in the state of ihram) merely by intention according to al-Shafi'i, because ihram is the commitment to refrain from prohibited things, so he begins to be in it merely by that, like fasting. According to us, it is not so; rather, the accompaniment of the talbiyah is necessary, because (ihram) is contracted for performance, so a mention is necessary, as in the opening takbir of prayer. Since the chapter of Hajj is wider than the chapter of prayer, a mention intended for glorification suffices in place of the talbiyah, whether it is in Persian or Arabic. Likewise is the action of driving the offering animal (al-hady) or garlanding it.

The verse was used as evidence that it is not permissible to enter ihram for Hajj except in those months, as Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said, and 'Ata' and others. For if it were permissible at other times, as the Hanafis hold, then His words, glorified be He, "therein" would have no benefit. It is answered that the benefit of mentioning "therein" is that these are the times for its acts without disapproval, so it is not understood from it that entering ihram before them is impermissible. Thus, if ihram were entered earlier, it would be valid as Hajj, with disapproval. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, (one who enters ihram early) becomes a muhrim for 'Umrah. The root of the disagreement is that it (ihram) is a pillar according to him and a condition according to us. So it resembles purification (tahara) in the permissibility of advancing it before its time. The disapproval came because of doubt. It is related from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is not fitting for anyone to enter ihram for Hajj except in the months of Hajj."

﴿So there shall be no obscenity﴾, that is, no intercourse, or no indecent speech. ﴿Nor wickedness﴾, nor going beyond the bounds of the Shari'ah by committing prohibited things. It has also been said: by abuse and mutual insulting with nicknames. ﴿Nor quarrelling﴾, nor disputing with servants and companions on the journey.

﴿During the Hajj﴾, that is, during its days. The explicit mention in the place where a pronoun would be expected is to show full concern for its matter and to indicate the reason for the ruling, for visiting the honoured House and drawing near to Allah by it, Exalted be He, requires leaving aside the mentioned defiling matters for the one who intends to journey and travel to the King of kings. The use of negation is for emphasis in forbidding, and to indicate that these matters by their nature deserve not to exist. Whatever is reprehensible and abhorrent in itself and forbidden absolutely is more abominable and more hideous for the one in ihram, who is engaged in the most noble and most arduous worship. This is like wearing silk in prayer, or beautifying the voice to the extent that the letters of the Qur'an come out of their proper forms.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "al-awwalin" (the first ones) with a nominative ending (raf') (i.e., "rafathun wa-la fusuqun"), taking the first two as having the sense of a prohibition, meaning: "Let there not be obscenity or wickedness." The third, "wa-la jidala" is with the fatha ending (naṣb), according to the sense of a statement that there is no dispute in the Hajj. That is because the Quraysh used to stand at al-Mash'ar al-Haram (Muzdalifah), while the rest of the Arabs stood at 'Arafat. After everyone was commanded to stand at 'Arafat, the disagreement was removed, so it was reported. It was also read with the nominative in "fihinna" (therein, with the nominative), and its explanation is not hidden.

﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾. By interpreting it as a command, it is conjoined with ﴿So there shall be no obscenity﴾, meaning: do not commit obscenity, and do good deeds. In this there is an iltifat (shift of grammatical person). And it is an exhortation to good following the prohibition of evil, so that it may be replaced by it. For this reason He specified the object of knowledge, although He, Exalted be He, knows all that they do of good or evil. The meaning of "knowledge" is either its apparent meaning, so that He will reward them for it, or the figurative sense of recompense. ﴿And take provision, for the best provision is taqwa (God-consciousness)﴾. Al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Hibban and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The people of Yemen used to perform Hajj without taking provision, and they would say: 'We are reliant upon Allah (mutawakkilun).' Then they would arrive and ask the people (for food), so this verse was revealed." So "taking provision" (tazawwud) in its real meaning is the preparation of food for the journey, and "taqwa" in its linguistic meaning is guarding oneself from asking (begging).

It has been said: the meaning of the verse is, "Take taqwa as your provision for your return (ma'ad), for it is the best provision." So the object of "tazawwadu" is omitted, by the indication of the predicate of "inna" (indeed), which is taqwa in its Shari'ah meaning. The apparent arrangement would have been to take "the best provision" as taqwa, for the subject and predicate, if both are definite, make that which is to be affirmed the predicate, and what is sought to be affirmed here is the affirmation of "best provision" for taqwa, because it is evidence of taking it as provision. However, the speech was brought out contrary to the apparent arrangement for emphasis, for then the meaning becomes: "The thing which has reached you as being the best provision, and for which you seek a description, is taqwa." So this conveys the identity of "the best provision" with it. ﴿And be mindful of Me, O people of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾, that is, make your taqwa sincerely for Me, for the requirement of pure intellect free of impurities is that. There is no repetition with what precedes it on this view, because it is an exhortation to sincerity after the exhortation to taqwa.

﴿There is no blame upon you﴾, i.e., no sin, ﴿in seeking﴾, i.e., seeking, ﴿bounty from your Lord﴾, i.e., provision from Him, exalted is He, through profit from trade during the seasons of the Hajj (the pilgrimage). Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "'Ukaz, Majannah and Dhu al-Majaz were markets in the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period). They regarded it as sinful to trade during the season, so they asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)

[p. 87]

about that, and this was revealed." It has been used as evidence for the permissibility of trade, hiring and all other kinds of earning during the Hajj, and that this does not nullify the reward or diminish the recompense. The connection is that when He, exalted is He, forbade disputing during the Hajj, this was a likely occasion for forbidding trade in it as well, because trade usually leads to disputes over the price, whether it is low or high. So He followed that with a ruling on it. Abu Muslim went to the view that trade is prohibited during the Hajj, and he took the verse to refer to the period after the Hajj, saying the meaning is: "Be mindful of Me in all the acts of the Hajj; then, after that, there is no blame upon you..." etc., like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek of Allah's bounty﴾. He rejected this by saying that it is better to take the verse to refer to the area of doubt, and the area of doubt is trade during the time of the Hajj. As for after its completion, the lifting of blame is known. Analogizing the Hajj to the prayer is invalid, because the actions of the prayer are continuous, so it is not permitted to occupy oneself with other things during it, whereas the actions of the Hajj are separated and can allow for trade in between them. Also, the reports do not support what he said, for you have heard what al-Bukhari narrated. Ahmad and others also narrated from Abu Umamah al-Taymi, who said: "I asked Ibn 'Umar, saying: 'We are a people who hire out animals on this route, and some people claim that there is no Hajj for us.' He said: 'Do you not say the talbiyah (the call 'Here I am, O Allah')? Do you not circumambulate between al-Safa and al-Marwah? Do you not, do you not?' I said: 'Yes.' He said: 'A man asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about what you asked about, and he did not know how to answer him until this was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon you﴾, the verse. So he called him, recited it to him as it had been revealed, and said: "You are the pilgrims."'" Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) used to recite, as al-Bukhari, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and others narrated from him: "There is no blame upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord during the seasons of the Hajj," and this was also narrated from Ibn Mas'ud. Also, the particle fa (then/so) in His saying, ﴿So when you pour forth from 'Arafat﴾, clearly indicates that this pouring forth occurred immediately after seeking bounty, and this indicates that the intended meaning is the occurrence of trade during the time of the Hajj. Yes, some scholars said: if the motive for setting out to the Hajj is trade, or if it is part of the cause, this harms the Hajj, because it contradicts sincerity to Allah, exalted is He, in it, and this is not the case for the servant...

﴿Afadtum﴾ (you poured forth) is from ifada, from fada al-ma' (the water flowed) when it flows pouring down, and afadtuhu means I caused it to flow. The hamza in it is for transitivity, and its object is omitted, as it is obligatory to omit it because it is known. Its original form was afyadtum, and the vowel of the ya' was moved to the fa' before it, so the ya' became mobile in the original and the letter before it is now open, so the ya' was changed to alif (in the form), then it was deleted. The meaning here is: when you push yourselves forth in large numbers from 'Arafat. Min (from) indicates the starting point. 'Arafat is a place near Mina. It is a noun in the plural form, so it is not pluralized. Al-Farra' said: "It has no correct singular." The people's saying "we alighted at 'Arafah" is similar to a later coinage and is not purely Arabic. This was objected to with the hadith: "The Hajj is 'Arafah," and it was answered that 'Arafah in that hadith is a name for the ninth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, as al-Raghib, al-Baghawi and al-Kirmani explicitly stated. What is rejected is its use for a place, so the objection arises from failing to understand the intended meaning. From here it was said that it is the plural of 'Arafah, and Shams al-'Ulum held this view. The plurality in this case is by consideration of naming each part of that place 'Arafah, like the saying of people: "he cut off his male organs" (plural). So what al-Allamah (the scholar) said does not refute this: that even if it is granted that 'Arafah is purely Arabic, then 'Arafah and 'Arafat refer to the same thing, and there are no multiple places each of which is 'Arafah such that it is pluralized into 'Arafat. It is nunated and kasra-ed (given tanwin and the kasra ending) even though it has both the status of proper noun and feminine gender, because the tanwin of the feminine plural corresponds to the nun of the masculine plural. The nun in the masculine plural stands in place of the tanwin that is in the singular, in the general sense that encompasses the types of tanwin, which is that it is merely a sign of the completion of the noun. The nun has nothing of the meanings of the types of tanwin. Likewise, the tanwin in the feminine plural is merely a sign of the completion of the noun, and there is also nothing of those meanings in it except correspondence. What is prohibited in the diptotes (ghayr munsarif) is not this tanwin, but the tanwin of tamkin (nominal tanwin), because it is what indicates that the noun is not resembling a verb. The removal of the kasra according to the preferred view follows the removal of tanwin without compensation, due to the lack of inflection (sarf). Here this is not the case, as the majority said. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It was nunated and kasra-ed only because it is inflected (munsarif), since the two considered factors that would make it diptote are absent. The feminine status that is considered together with proper-nounhood as a bar to inflection must either be by the tā' mentioned, but that is not a feminine tā' but a sign of the plural, or by a presumed tā' as in Zaynab. The specificity of this tā' to the feminine plural refuses to assume a tā' for it, since that would amount to two feminine markers together. So this tā' is like the tā' in bint (daughter); it is not for feminine marking, but a substitute for the omitted waw, and it is specific to the feminine, so it prevents presuming a tā'. Accordingly, if one names something Muslimat (Muslim women) or Bint (daughter), which is feminine, it is inflected (munsarif)." Ibn al-Hajib's statement that this implies that when it is named with that it is prohibited from inflection is not valid, because the implication is not accepted. Similarly, what 'Isam al-Din said, that feminine status for prohibiting inflection does not require strength, is also not valid. Do you not see that Talhah's feminine status is considered for prohibiting inflection, but is not considered for the feminine pronoun referring back to it? Because the basis of the argument is not on considering strength and weakness, but on the non-establishment of femininity. Yes, what al-Radi raised is refuted: that if there were no femininity in it, he would not have obligated the feminine pronoun referring to it. It is answered that the specificity of this pattern to the feminine is sufficient for the pronoun to refer back, and it does not require the presence of the tā' either verbally or presumptively. This specific place was named with a term that indicates recognition, because it is a description of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), so it made it known. This was narrated from 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) and Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them). Or because Jibril used to go around with him in the holy sites, and when he saw it he said: "I have recognized (qad 'arafta)." It was narrated from 'Ata'. Or because Adam and Hawwa' gathered there and recognized one another (ta'arafa). It was narrated from al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. Or because Jibril (peace be upon him) said to Adam there: "Acknowledge your sin and recognize your rites," said by some. It was also said it was named so for its height and elevation, and from it comes 'urf al-dik (the rooster's comb). The plural was chosen for the naming as an intensification of what was mentioned of its aspects, as if it were multiple 'Arafat. It is among the names that are coined (murtajalah) with certainty according to the verifiers. 'Arafah may be from them, and it may be derived from the plural of 'arif (knower), but there is no certainty of derivation, since there is no evidence for making it the plural of 'arif, and the default is non-derivation.

﴿Then remember Allah﴾, by the talbiyah, the tahlil (saying La ilaha illa Allah) and supplication. It was also said: by the prayer of the two evening prayers (Maghrib and 'Isha'), because the apparent command indicates obligation, and there is no obligatory remembrance ﴿at the sacred monument﴾ except the prayer. It is well known that the sacred monument (al-mash'ar al-haram) is all of Muzdalifah. Waki', Sufyan, Ibn Jarir, al-Bayhaqi and a group narrated from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that he was asked about the sacred monument, and he remained silent until the mounts' hooves had come down in Muzdalifah, and he said: "This is the sacred monument." It is strengthened by the fa' (then) indicating that the remembrance at the monument occurs immediately after the pouring forth from 'Arafat, and that is only by staying overnight in Muzdalifah. Many scholars held that it is a mountain on which the imam stands in Muzdalifah, called Quzah. Allah, exalted is He, specified the remembrance at it, although it is commanded throughout all of Muzdalifah, because all of it is a place of standing except the valley of Muhassar, as the authentic reports indicate, for its added virtue and nobility. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "What lies between the two mountains of Muzdalifah is the sacred monument," and similarly from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them). It was called "mash'ar" because it is a landmark of worship, and it was described as "sacred" because of its sanctity. The adverbial phrase (zarf) is connected either to "udhkuru" (remember) or to an omitted circumstantial clause (hal) that is the subject of the verb.

﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾, i.e., as He taught you the rites. The comparison is for clarifying the state and conveying restriction; that is: remember Him in that manner and do not deviate from it. It is possible that the meaning is absolute guidance, and the implication of the comparison is equality in goodness and perfection; that is: remember Him with a good remembrance, as He guided you with good guidance to the rites and other things.

The particle "ma" (as/what), according to both meanings, may be a verbal-masdar particle (ma masdariyyah, forming a verbal noun), so the position of ﴿as He has guided you﴾ is accusative as a verbal noun, with the qualified noun omitted; that is: a remembrance similar to your guidance. It may also be a kafrah (a particle that cancels the governing force of the kaf), in which case it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). The purpose of the kaf is merely to liken the content of the clause to the clause. For this reason, it does not require a governing word whose meaning would lead to what follows it. Some scholars held that the kaf is for causation, and that it is connected to what is next to it, and "ma" is only a verbal-masdar particle; that is: "remember Him" and magnify Him because of His previous guidance to you.

﴿And indeed you were﴾, i.e., "and indeed you were," so "in" was lightened, its noun was omitted, it was disconnected from governing, and the lam was retained in what follows it. It was also said that "in" is a negation particle, and the lam means "except."

﴿before it﴾, i.e., before the guidance. The prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted word that is indicated by ﴿among those astray﴾ (198). They did not connect it to that, because what follows the relative particle (al-mawsul) does not govern what precedes it, and there is consideration in this. The intended meaning of straying is ignorance of faith and the customs of acts of obedience. The clause is a concluding remark (tadhyil) to what precedes it, as if it were said: "remember Him now," since your previous remembrance that contradicted what He guided you to is not counted, because it is from straying. Taking it as a circumstantial clause is a distant assumption far from the intended meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 199:

﴿Then depart from where the people depart.﴾ That is: from ʿArafat, not from Muzdalifah. The address is general, and the intended purpose is to nullify what the Hums (al-Ḥums, the Quraysh and those who followed their religion) used to do regarding standing at Jamʿ (Muzdalifah). Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from ʿAʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Quraysh and those who followed their religion used to stand at Muzdalifah, and they were called the Hums. The rest of the Arabs used to stand at ʿArafat. When Islam came, Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, to go to ʿArafat, stand there, and then depart from it. That is the meaning of His words, glorified is He: ﴿Then depart﴾ — the verse."

Its meaning: ﴿Then depart﴾, O pilgrims, from the place from which the people in general have departed, past and present, and that is ʿArafat, not Muzdalifah. Making the pronoun refer to the Hums would necessitate disrupting the structure of the discourse, since the preceding and following pronouns are all general. The sentence is coordinated with His words: ﴿So when you have departed﴾. Since the purpose of this allusion is [a warning], it carries the force of: "Then do not depart from Muzdalifah." He used ﴿thumma﴾ (then) to indicate the difference in rank between the two departures, namely that one is correct and the other is an error. It does not undermine this that the difference is only considered between coordinated items and not between the coordinated item and what precedes it with a negative particle, because the restriction is not intended; likewise, it does no harm that the difference is understood from one being commanded and the other forbidden, however the coordination is taken, because what is meant is that the word ﴿thumma﴾ indicates this regardless of the connection of command and prohibition. It is also permitted that the coordination be with ﴿fadhkurū﴾ (remember), with the difference between the two departures considered as well, as in the preceding case, without any difference. Some have made it coordinated with an elided element, that is: "Depart to Mina, then depart..." and so on, but this is nothing. Likewise the view that there is inversion and reordering in the verse, the intended sense being: ﴿There is no blame upon you if you seek bounty from your Lord; then depart from where the people depart; and when you have departed from ʿArafat, remember Allah at the sacred landmark, and seek forgiveness﴾. If the one departed from is taken to be Muzdalifah and the one departed to is Mina, as al-Jubba'i said, then ﴿thumma﴾ remains in its literal sense, because departing to Mina is far from departing from ʿArafat; for when the pilgrims depart from it at sunset on the Day of ʿArafat, they come to Muzdalifah on the night of sacrifice and spend the night there. When dawn breaks and they have prayed in the dark, they go to Quzah, and climb upon it or stand near it, then they go to the valley of Muhassir, and from there to Mina. The address on this view is undoubtedly general, and the intended "people" is the category, as is evident; that is, from where all people, past and present, have departed. It has been said that the intended "people" are Abraham, peace be upon him, and he was called "people" because he was an imam to the people. It has also been said that the intended are he and his sons. It was read as ﴿an-nāsi﴾ with a kasra, meaning "the forgetful," and the intended one is Adam, peace be upon him, due to His words, exalted is He, concerning him: ﴿but he forgot (fa-nasiya)﴾. The word ﴿thumma﴾ in this reading indicates the distance between departing from ʿArafat and deviating from it, on the basis that the meaning of ﴿thumma adīḍū﴾ is: "Depart from it, then do not deviate from it, because it is an ancient legislated practice." Thus it has been said, so let it be pondered.

﴿And seek forgiveness of Allah﴾ for your ignorance in altering the rites and the like. ﴿Indeed Allah is Forgiving﴾ toward those who seek forgiveness, ﴿Merciful 199﴾ toward them, bestowing favor upon them.

[Page 90]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 200:

﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾ means: when you have performed your pilgrimage acts of worship and finished with them. ﴿then remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾ means: as you used to mention your fathers with boasting at the end of your pilgrimage. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: The people of the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) would sit after the pilgrimage and mention the days of their fathers and the lineages they counted, the whole day long. So Allah the Exalted revealed this. ﴿Or with even greater remembrance﴾: the phrase is either in the genitive, coordinated with "remembrance" (al-dhikr), by treating "remembrance" as if it were the one who remembers, in a metaphorical sense. The meaning is: remember Allah with a remembrance like your remembrance of your fathers, or with a remembrance more intense and more eloquent than that. Or it is coordinated with what is annexed to it (the pronoun of "kadhikrikum"), according to the view of the Kufans (the grammarians of Kufa), who permit coordinating on a genitive pronoun without repeating the preposition, by ease of usage, with the meaning: "or like the remembrance of a people more intense in remembrance than you." Or it is in the accusative, coordinated with "your fathers," and "dhikran" is taken from the verb in the passive form, with the meaning: "or as your being mentioned is more intense than your fathers' being mentioned." Or it is governed by a hidden term indicated by the meaning; that is: let your remembrance of Allah the Exalted be more intense than your remembrance of your fathers, or be more intense in remembering Allah the Exalted than you are in remembering your fathers. This is what has been said. Abu Hayyan, in al-Bahr (Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit), chose that "ashadda" (more intense) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "dhikran," the object of "udhkuru" (remember). For if it came after it, it would be a descriptive qualifier (sifa) of it. It is good that "dhikran" is placed later, because it acts as a separating element and to remove the awkwardness of repetition. For if it were placed earlier, the structure would be: "fa-udhkurū Allāha kadhikrikum ābā'akum" or "udhkurū dhikran ashadda." In this view, it is objectionable that the apparent form would be "aw ashaddu" without "dhikran," with it being coordinated with "kadhikrikum" as a qualifier of the implied remembrance. The required thing is remembrance described as more intense, not the seeking of it while in a state of greater intensity.

﴿Among the people is he who says﴾: this is a parenthetical sentence placed between the two coordinated commands, to urge and increase the remembrance of Allah the Exalted and the seeking of what is with Him. Within it is a distinction of those who remember, in general, whether pilgrims or others, as is the apparent meaning: between one of little means who, by remembering Allah the Exalted, seeks only this world, and one of abundant means who seeks the good of both abodes. What has been transmitted from some of the Sufis, that their worship of His Essence is free of purposes and accidental ends, is great ignorance, which may lead to disbelief, as Hujjat al-Islam (the Proof of Islam, al-Ghazali), may his secret be sanctified, said. This is because the absence of causation in actions is particular to His Essence, the Exalted. Moreover, some hold that His actions, glorified is He, are also caused by what wisdom requires. Yes, His worship, the Exalted, may be for seeking His good pleasure, not for fear of something disliked or for attaining something loved; but this, for the sake of the other good things, is sought by His sincere servants. The Exalted said: ﴿And the pleasure of Allah is greater﴾. He, glorified is He, joined remembrance with supplication to indicate that what is considered of remembrance is that which comes from a present heart and an inward turning, as is the state of one supplicating when seeking a need, not merely uttering and pronouncing it with the tongue. Al-Imam (al-Razi) and Abu Hayyan held that the distinction is for those who supplicate, who are commanded to remember after finishing the rites. He, glorified and exalted is He, began with remembrance because it is the key to answering. Then He explained, majestic is His state, that in seeking from Allah the Exalted they divide into those whose love of this world dominates them, so that they supplicate only for it, and those who supplicate for the rectification of their state in this world and the Hereafter. In the verse there is a shift (iltifat) from direct address to the third person, to lower the seeker of this world from the court of the honor of presence. It is not hidden that the first (division) is the more suitable for keeping "the people" in its generality, and it matches what will come in His, glorified is He, words: ﴿And among the people is he whose speech pleases you﴾ etc. ﴿And among the people is he who sells himself﴾. Yes, the cause of revelation, as related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: a group of Bedouins came to the place of standing (at Arafat) and sought this world, while a group of believers came to it and sought this world and the Hereafter. This does not require restriction (of the verse to them).

﴿Our Lord, give us in this world﴾: that is, make all our giving and bestowal be in it. So the second object is omitted, and the verb, by analogy, is treated as if it were intransitive, going toward the generality of the verb, to indicate that his aspiration is confined to the goals of this world.

﴿And he has no share in the Hereafter, of any portion﴾: this is a report from Him, the Exalted, explaining the state of this category in the Hereafter; that is, he has no portion or share in it. "Khalaq" (portion) is from "khalaqa bihi" when it suits him, or from "khalq" (creation), as if it were the matter for which he was created and decreed. It has been said: the sentence is an explanation of his state in this world, so it is an explicit statement of what was known implicitly from what precedes it, as confirmation and emphasis. That is: he has no seeking in this world of a portion in the Hereafter. It is not meant that he has no seeking in the Hereafter for the portion, so as to say that this is the ruling for everyone, since there is no seeking in the Hereafter, and there is only fortune and deprivation in it. This is answered by denying that there is no seeking, since believers seek an increase in ranks and disbelievers seek escape from severe punishment. "Min" here is extra (silah), and "lahu" has a preposed predicate, and the prepositional phrase after it is related to what it is related to, or is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of what follows it.

[Page 91]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 201:

﴿And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good"﴾. It means: well-being and sufficiency, said by Qatadah. Or: a righteous wife, said by Ali (may Allah ennoble his face). Or: knowledge and worship, said by al-Hasan. Or: righteous wealth, said by al-Suddi. Or: righteous children. Or: the good opinion of people, said by Ibn Umar. Or: health, sufficiency, victory over enemies, and understanding of the Book of Allah, the Exalted. Or: the companionship of the righteous, said by Ja'far. Apparently, although "good" (hasanah) is indefinite in an affirmative context and does not signify generality, it is unrestricted, so it refers to the complete form. The complete good in this world is that which includes all its goods, which is the granting of success in goodness. Specifying it with a particular thing is not a determination of the intended meaning, since an unrestricted term has no indication of a restricted one at all. Rather, it is by way of example. The same applies to His words, the Exalted: ﴿and in the Hereafter good﴾. It has been said that it is Paradise. It has been said that it is safety from the terror of the Standing and from a bad reckoning. It has been said that it is the wide-eyed houris, and this is related from Ali (may Allah ennoble his face). It has been said that it is the delight of seeing (Allah). And it has been said, and it has been said... The apparent meaning is the unrestricted sense, intending the complete form, which is mercy and beneficence. ﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire [102]﴾, that is: guard us from it by pardon and forgiveness, and make us among those who enter Paradise without punishment. Al-Hasan said: guard us from desires and sins that lead to the punishment of the Fire. Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) said: the punishment of the Fire is an evil wife, may Allah the Exalted protect us from her. This is in the same manner as what has preceded. The Prophet (ﷺ) used to make this supplication very often, as related by al-Bukhari and Muslim from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him). They both also related from him that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called upon a man from among the Muslims who had become like a plucked chick, and he said to him: 'Were you supplicating Allah, the Exalted, for anything?' He said: 'Yes, I used to say: O Allah, whatever You would punish me with in the Hereafter, hasten it for me in this world.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Glory be to Allah! Then you cannot bear it and you cannot endure it. Why did you not say: Our Lord, give us in this world good, and in the Hereafter good, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire?' And he supplicated for him, so Allah healed him, the Exalted."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 202:**

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the second group, and the sentence stands in contrast to (﴿and they have no share in the Hereafter﴾). The use of the demonstrative signifies that their being characterized by what preceded is the reason for the stated ruling. For this reason the conjunction is omitted here, since the sentence is like a result of what came before it. It has been said that the sense of distance contained in the demonstrative indicates the elevation of their rank and the remoteness of their station in virtue. It is also permissible that the demonstrative refers to both of the two preceding groups. On the first view, the tanwin in His words, ﴿For them there is a share of what they have earned﴾, is for magnification; on the second view, it is for classification, meaning that each of them has a share of the kind of what they earned, or on account of it, or of what they asked for: We will give them from it what We have decreed. The particle ﴿min﴾ (from) may be partitive or indicate origin. If it indicates origin, it is understood as causal, in the sense of "because of." In the verse, on the third possibility, the apparent noun has been placed in the position of the pronoun without using the word of the previous clause, because what is understood from ﴿Our Lord, give us﴾ is supplication, not earning. However, it is called earning because it is among the deeds. It was also read: ﴿of what they have acquired﴾.

﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning﴾ (202). He reckons with the servants, despite their multitude, in the space of half a day of the days of this world. It is narrated: in the time between two milkings of a she-camel. It is narrated: in the blink of an eye. Or: He is about to establish the Resurrection and reckon with people, so hasten to acts of obedience and to acquiring good deeds. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to His words, ﴿So remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾, and so on. As for reckoning, it is either in its literal sense, as is the view of the People of Truth, that the texts are to be taken in their apparent meaning unless some diverting indication turns them away from it; or it is a metaphor for creating in them a necessary knowledge of their deeds and their recompense, in quantity and quality; or it is the requiting of them for these. This is the end.

* * *

Among the allusive (ishari) readings of the verses is His words: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter houses from their backs﴾, meaning: entering the houses of your hearts from the direction of your senses and your bodily perceptions that are taken from the faculties of perception, for these are the outer surfaces of the hearts that adjoin the body. ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah﴾: [one who is preoccupied] with the distractions of the senses, the imaginings of the faculty of imagination, and the whisperings of the commanding soul. ﴿And enter houses through their doors﴾, which adjoin the spirit, and through which the Truth enters. ﴿And fear Allah﴾, [by not seeing] your piety, so that you may be successful through Him. ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾, from the powers of your souls and the impulses of your human nature, for that is the greater jihad. ﴿But do not transgress﴾ by neglecting them and by standing with their portions, or by going beyond limits in the fighting, to the point that you weaken the body from performing the rites of obedience and the duties of servanthood. (For many a hunger is worse than surfeit.)

﴿Indeed, Allah does not love transgressors﴾, those who stand with their souls, or those who exceed the shade of unity, which is justice. ﴿And kill them﴾ wherever you find them; that is, restrain those powers from tasting the delights of desires and passions wherever they may be. ﴿And expel them﴾ from Mecca of the breast, as they expelled you from it, and lured you down to the plain of the soul, and stood between you and the abode of the heart. Their temptation, which is the worship of passion and prostration to the idols of pleasures, is more severe than complete death; or your tribulation, when the soul gains dominion, is more severe upon you than killing, which is the erasure of readiness and the obliteration of innate dispositions, because of what follows from that of the pain of separation from the presence of holiness, which has no end. ﴿And do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque﴾, which is the station (maqam) of the heart, when they agree with you in your orientation, until they dispute with you over your aims and drag you away from the religion of truth, and call you to the worship of the calf of looking at others. If they dispute with you, then fight them with the sword of sincerity and cut off the source of those impulses. ﴿Such is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾, who conceal the truth. ﴿But if they desist﴾ from their dispute, ﴿then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. And fight them to maintain constant vigilance and sincerity in servanthood ﴿until there is no more fitnah﴾, and no turning toward anything other [than Him] occurs ﴿and religion is entirely for Allah﴾, by the gathering of the whole [being] toward the most holy Presence and the most sacred Essence. ﴿But if they desist, then there is no aggression﴾ except against those who exceed the limits.

﴿The sacred month﴾, in which the soul stands for its rights, [is retaliated for by] ﴿the sacred month﴾, which is the time of your presence and watchfulness. ﴿And for violations, there is retribution﴾, so do not be concerned about violating their sanctity. ﴿And spend in the way of Allah﴾ from the knowledge you possess, by acting upon it and by guiding others. ﴿And do not throw yourselves by your own hands into﴾ the destruction of negligence. ﴿And do good﴾ by being witnesses of your Lord in all your deeds: ﴿indeed, Allah loves those who witness Him﴾.

﴿And complete﴾ the pilgrimage of the unity of the Essence and the lesser pilgrimage of the unity of the Attributes, for Allah, by completing all the stations and states. ﴿But if you are prevented﴾ by the obstruction of the enemies of the souls or by the illness of lethargy, then strive in Allah by driving the sacrificial animal of the soul and slaughtering it by annihilation at the Kaaba of the heart. Because souls differ in their readiness, He said: ﴿Then what is feasible﴾. ﴿And do not shave your heads﴾, that is, do not remove the traces of nature, and do not choose the emptiness of the mind, until the sacrifice of the soul reaches its place. Then you will be safe from disturbance and the turbidity of purity. ﴿So whoever among you is ill﴾, weak in readiness, ﴿or has an ailment of the head﴾, that is, is afflicted with attachments and has not been able to travel the path as he should, then he must make a ransom, by refraining from some of his pleasures and distractions, or by performing an act of righteousness or discipline that subdues some of the powers. ﴿And when you are secure﴾ from the obstructing hindrance, then whoever enjoys the taste of the manifestation of the Attributes, using it as a means to the pilgrimage of the manifestation of the Essence, must offer what sacrifice he can according to his condition. ﴿But whoever does not find﴾, because of the weakness of his soul and its subjugation, ﴿then a fast of three days during the pilgrimage﴾; that is, he must refrain from the actions of the powers that are the strong roots at the time of manifestation, of absorption in the collective, and of annihilation, namely the intellect, the estimative faculty, and the imaginative faculty. ﴿And seven when you return﴾ to the station of detail and multiplicity, namely the five outward senses, anger, and desire, so that in uprightness toward things, they are through Allah, Mighty and Majestic. ﴿These are ten complete﴾, bringing about wondrous effects that contain strange secrets. ﴿That is for one whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque﴾, among the perfected ones present at the station of unity, for those are not addressed and not reproached; and whoever has arrived has found rest.

﴿The pilgrimage is in well-known months﴾, which is either the duration of the transient life, or from the time of reaching puberty until forty, as He said in al-Baqarah: ﴿Neither old nor virgin, but between that﴾ (2:68). From here it has been said: "The Sufi after forty is cold." Yes, a weak eye is better than blindness, and little is better than deprivation. ﴿So whoever has made obligatory upon himself the pilgrimage in them﴾ by firm resolve, ﴿then there is no sexual misconduct﴾, that is, he should not incline toward this world and its adornments; ﴿nor wickedness﴾, nor should he take the irascible faculty out of obedience to the heart, but rather he should not leave the appointed time and should not enter into what brings about hatred; ﴿nor disputation during the pilgrimage﴾, that is, he should not dispute with anyone in the station of orientation toward Him, Exalted is He, since everything is from Him and returns to Him. Whoever disputes with him over something should surrender it to Him and greet Him with peace. ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾. Whatever virtue you do in leaving any of these matters, Allah knows it and will reward you for it. Provision yourselves with the virtues, which necessarily entail avoidance of vices. ﴿Indeed, the best provision is piety﴾, and its completion is the negation of all other than Him. ﴿And fear Me, O people of understanding﴾, for the requirement of pure intellect, free from the admixture of illusion and the husk of matter, is to fear Allah, Exalted is He. There is no blame upon you, when you return to multiplicity, for seeking ease for your souls according to what the greatest manifestation (ﷺ) has set as its limit. So when you push your souls away from the Arafat of knowledge, ﴿then remember Allah at the Sacred Monument﴾; that is, witness His beauty, glorified is He, at the spiritual secret called the hidden (al-khafi). It is called a monument (mash'ar) because it is the place of perception of beauty, and it is described as sacred because it is forbidden for others to reach it. ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾ to remembering Him in the stations, ﴿although before that you were among those astray﴾, before reaching the Arafat of knowledge and standing there, ﴿from these remembrances in the pursuit of this world. Then depart﴾ toward the outward forms of worship, ﴿from where the people depart﴾ toward them; and be like one of them, for the end is a return to the beginning. Or: depart from where the prophets (peace be upon them) departed, for the sake of fulfilling rights and out of compassion for the servants of Allah, Exalted is He, through guidance and teaching. ﴿And seek forgiveness from Allah﴾, for the Greatest Lawgiver (ﷺ) used to be covered over on his heart and would seek forgiveness from Allah, Exalted is He, seventy times a day. And who are you, O poor wretch, after him? ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾ and finished the pilgrimage, ﴿then remember Allah as you remember your fathers﴾ before the journey, ﴿or with a more intense remembrance﴾, for the true origin is: be occupied with Him as His Essence, glorified is He, requires. Some people seek only this world and worship only for its sake, and they have no share in the station of annihilation, because of the weakness of their resolve and their acquisition of darkness, which is contrary to light. Among them is one who seeks the good of both abodes and guards against being veiled by the thirst and tormented by the fires of nature. ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾: of the portions of the Hereafter, the dazzling lights, the enduring delights, and the lofty stations. ﴿And Allah is swift in reckoning.﴾

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 203:

﴿وَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ﴾ That is: glorify Him (say "Allahu akbar") after the prayers, at the slaughtering of the sacrificial animals, at the stoning of the pillars (ramy al-jimar), and at other times.

﴿فِي أَيَّامٍ مَعْدُودَاتٍ﴾ These are the three Days of Tashriq (the days after the Day of Sacrifice, on which the pilgrims remain in Mina). This is the well-known view related from Umar, Ali and Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that they are four days, by adding the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) to them. Some who hold the restricted reading argue that this clause is joined by "fa" (then) to the words of His, glorified is He: ﴿فَاذْكُرُوا اللَّهَ﴾ etc. It is as if it were said: "When you have completed your rites, then remember Allah during the appointed days." The "fa" denotes sequence, and so this excludes the Day of Sacrifice from the days. Whoever takes the conjunction and the sequence into account, and regards part of a day as a day, derives from the verse the beginning of the takbir after the prayer from the noon prayer of the Day of Sacrifice. And whoever takes its general wording as evidence says that one should say the takbir after supererogatory prayers too.

The description of "days" as "appointed (ma'dudat)" has been questioned, since ayyam is the plural of yawm, which is masculine, while ma'dudat is the plural of ma'dudah, which is feminine. How then can it be an attribute of it? The apparent form would be ma'dud. The attribution of the feminine singular adjective to the plural of a non-rational noun is permissible. It has been answered that ma'dudat is the plural of ma'dud, not of ma'dudah, and the masculine is often pluralised like the feminine, as in hammamat and sijillat. It has also been said that he considered "day" as feminine in view of its hours. It has been said too that the meaning is that they are appointed each year, and in the years they are "appointed" (plural), so ma'dudat is strictly the plural of ma'dudah. What this entails is not hidden.

﴿فَمَنْ تَعَجَّلَ﴾ That is: hastened in leaving (al-nafr), or sought to hasten departure from Mina. Many have mentioned that ta'ajjala and isti'jala come as intransitive forms (mutawi'ayn) meaning "hastened", as one says: ta'ajjala fi al-amr and isti'jala; and as transitive: one says ta'ajjala al-dhahaba (he hastened the going). The intransitive sense is, according to al-Zamakhshari, more fitting to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿وَمَنْ تَأَخَّرَ﴾, as it is also in the words of the poet:

*Qad yudriku al-mutana'ii ba'da hajatihi*
*Wa qad yakunu min al-musta'jili al-zalalu*

("The deliberate man may attain some of his need, and error may come from the one who hastens.")

Some masters of verification preferred the transitive sense, because the intention is to explain the matters of haste, not hastening in general. It has also been said: the intransitive form requires the supposition of (fi), and then two prepositions would govern "two days", one of them being the supposed (fi) and the second (fi yawmayn) being governed by the verb; and this is not permissible. The two days are the Day of Rest (yawm al-qarr), the Day of Heads (yawm al-ru'us), and the day after it. The meaning is: whoever leaves on the second of the Days of Tashriq before sunset, and after stoning the pillars, according to the Shafi'is; and before dawn of the third day, once he has finished stoning the pillars, according to us (the Hanafis). Leaving on the first day of them is not permitted. So the adverbial use of "the two days" for it is by extension, on account of the preparation for it on the first day. The view that the supposition is "on one of the two days" but it is ambiguous and is explained by the second day, or "at the end of the two days", departs from the sense of the discourse.

﴿فَلَا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ for hastening. ﴿وَمَنْ تَأَخَّرَ﴾ in leaving, until he stones the pillars on the third day, before or after noon according to us, and according to al-Shafi'i only after noon. ﴿فَلَا إِثْمَ عَلَيْهِ﴾ for what he did in delaying. The intention is the choice between hastening and delaying, and the superiority of the second does not undermine this, contrary to the author of al-Insaf. The negation of sin is stated explicitly to refute the people of the Jahiliyyah, who disagreed about it: some deemed the one who hastened sinful, and some deemed the one who delayed sinful.

﴿لِمَنِ اتَّقَى﴾ is a predicate for an omitted subject. The lam is either for causation (ta'lil) or for particularisation (ikhtisas). That is: this choice mentioned is for the sake of the one who has taqwa (God-consciousness), by the indication of proximity, so that he is not harmed by abandoning what he intends of hastening or delaying, because he is cautious and guards against what troubles him. Or the aforesaid is among the rulings of the Hajj in general, in view of the absence of a definitive specifier. And although it is general for all believers, it is specific to the one who has taqwa, because he is the true pilgrim and the one who benefits from it. The meaning of taqwa under both views is avoiding what makes one sinful, whether by action or omission. It is not permissible to interpret it as avoiding shirk, because the address in everything preceding is to the believers. Some have used the verse as evidence that if the pilgrim has taqwa in performing the limits and obligations of the Hajj, all his sins are forgiven. This is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, and Ibn Jarir related from him that he interpreted the verse in this way, then said: "People interpret it other than its true interpretation," and this is quite strange.

﴿وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ﴾ in all your affairs in which resolve is involved, so that you may be included among those who profit by the rulings mentioned; or beware of neglecting what has been mentioned of the matters of Hajj. ﴿وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّكُمْ إِلَيْهِ تُحْشَرُونَ﴾ for recompense for your deeds after revival and resurrection. The root of "hashr" is gathering and bringing together what is scattered. This is an emphasis of the command to taqwa and a motive for complying with it, for whoever knows of the gathering, the reckoning and the recompense, this will be among the strongest incentives for him to persist in taqwa. He placed "ilayhi" first for the sake of concern with the one to whom the gathering is, and for the harmony of the verse endings (fawasil).

[p. 94]

[Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 204]

﴿And among the people is one whose speech impresses you﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to His saying, Exalted is He: (And among the people is one who says). The common link is that when He, glorified is He, extended the explanation of the rulings of the Hajj to an explanation of how people divide in remembrance and supplication during those rites into disbelievers and believers, He completed this with an explanation of two other categories: the hypocrite and the sincere believer. The origin of *taʿajjub* (being impressed or amazed) is a bewilderment that comes over a person due to his ignorance of the cause of what amazes him. Here it is used figuratively (*majāz*) for what it entails of being pleasing and striking, since a strange and unknown matter pleases the nature and its impact is great upon the hearts. It is not used in its literal sense (*ḥaqīqa*), because the cause is not unknown, namely eloquence and sweetness. So the meaning is: among them is one who pleases you and whose speech looms large in your soul.

﴿in the life of this world﴾ means: in the affairs of this world and the means of livelihood, whether or not these return to him. Thus "life" refers to that by which life and subsistence are sustained. Or it means "this world" (*al-dunyā*) itself, since it is intended by his claim of love and display of faith. In that case "the life of this world" retains its own meaning, and making it a time-frame (*ẓarf*) for the speech is like the expression used in the headings of scholarly discussions: "the first chapter is on such-and-such, and the discussion is on such-and-such," meaning that this is what is intended by it. Neither of the two interpretations involves any omission, contrary to what has been supposed. In that case the *ẓarfiyya* (time-frame sense) is merely notional (*taqdīriyya*), as in his saying, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "For a believing soul, one hundred camels [are due]," meaning: for killing it. The cause, which is the killing, implicitly contains the blood-money in the way a container contains what is in it.
