This is what is called the causal sense, as stated by al-Radi, and it was mentioned by some of the verifiers. It is also permitted that the prepositional phrase be connected to the verb preceding it. That is: his speech impresses you in this world due to its eloquence and the freshness of its words, but it does not impress you in the Hereafter, either because of the bewilderment and stammering that overtake him there, or because he will not be permitted to speak, so he does not speak until it impresses you.

The verse, as al-Suddi said, was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shuraiq al-Thaqafi, an ally of Banu Zuhra. He came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in Madina and displayed Islam to him. This pleased the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and [al-Akhnas] said: "I have only come wanting Islam, and Allah, exalted is He, knows that I am truthful." Then he left the presence of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and passed by a field of the Muslims and some donkeys, and he burned the crop and hamstrung the donkeys. It was also said that it refers to the hypocrites in general.

﴿and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ means: according to his claim, since he says, "Allah knows that my heart agrees with what is on my tongue." It is conjoined to ﴿impresses you﴾. In the codex of Ubayy it reads *wa-yastashhidu Allāha* ("and he seeks Allah as a witness"). It was also read *wa-yashhadu Allāhu* with the nominative (*raf*ʿ), meaning "and Allah bears witness." In that case "what is in his heart" means what is actually in it. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "and Allah bears witness to what is in his heart," where the preposition *ʿalā* indicates that what is witnessed is detrimental to him. The clause in that case is parenthetical (*iʿtirāḍiyya*).

﴿and he is the most contentious of opponents﴾ means: the most vehement in disputing falsehood, as Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said, and he cited as evidence the verse of Muhalhil:

Indeed beneath the stones are a hidden crime, an injustice,
and a contentious adversary, the most quarrelsome, of cutting disputes.

*Aladdu* is an adjective like *aḥmar*, as shown by its plural *luddun* and its feminine *laddāʾ*, not an elative (*afʿal al-tafḍīl*). The annexation is an annexation of an adjective to its agent, like *ḥusn al-wajh* ("beauty of face"), on the basis of metaphorical attribution. Some have made it mean "in" (*bi-maʿnā fī*) in the notional sense of the time-frame: that is, vehement in contention. Abu Hayyan transmitted from al-Khalil that *aladdu* is an elative, so it is necessary to supply: "and his contention is the most contentious contention," or "the most contentious of those who contend," or it is taken to refer to the contention understood from the context, though from a distance. Or it is said that *khiṣām* is the plural of *khaṣm*, like *baḥr* and *biḥār*, and *ṣaʿb* and *ṣiʿāb*, so the meaning is: the most contentious of contenders in contention. The annexation in that case is for specification, as in "the best of people in face."

In the verse there is an indication that great vehemence in contention is blameworthy. Al-Bukhari and Muslim transmitted from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "The most hateful of men to Allah, exalted is He, is the most contentious opponent." Ahmad transmitted from Abu al-Darda': "It is enough sin for you that you never cease to be disputatious; and it is enough wrongdoing for you that you never cease to be contentious; and it is enough lying for you that you never cease to speak, except about the matters of the essence of Allah, mighty and majestic." Intense contentiousness is one of the attributes of the hypocrites, because they love this world, so they multiply disputes over it.

[Page 95]

﴿Wa-idha tawalla﴾ means: he turned his back and turned away, as said by al-Hasan. Or it means: when he prevailed and became a ruler, as said by al-Dahhak.

﴿Sa'a﴾ means: he hastened in walking, or he worked ﴿fi al-ard li-yufsida fiha﴾ (on the earth, to cause corruption therein) to the extent he was able.

﴿Wa-yuhlika al-harth wa-al-nasl﴾ (and to destroy the crops and the offspring), as al-Akhnas did, or as the rulers of evil do through killing and destruction, or through the injustice by which Allah, exalted is He, withholds rain because of its wickedness. Al-harth is the crops, and al-nasl is every living creature. It is said: yanslu nusulan, when it comes out and falls. From this comes nasl al-ba'ir (the wool of the camel) or rish al-ta'ir (the feathers of the bird). The descendants among offspring are called nasl because they come out from their father's back and their mother's womb. Al-Azhari mentioned

[p. 96]

that al-harth here means the women and al-nasl means the children. It is reported from al-Sadiq that al-harth in this place means the religion, and al-nasl means the people. It was also read: (wa-yahlaku al-harthu wa-al-naslu), with the verb referring to al-harth and al-nasl, and the nominative case (raf') is by conjunction with sa'a. Al-Hasan read it with a fatha on the lam, which is the dialect of (aba ya'ba) (he refused, he refuses). It is also reported from him: (wa-yuhlaka), in the passive form.

﴿Wa-Allahu la yuhibbu al-fasad﴾ (And Allah does not love corruption) means: He does not approve of it, so beware of His wrath because of it. The sentence is an interjected clause (i'tiraḍ, a parenthetical clause) of warning. He was content with (al-fasad) because it includes the second term, being a case of the general conjoined to the particular (min 'atf al-'amm 'ala al-khass). It is not objected that Allah, exalted is He, is the one who corrupts things before corruption occurs, so how does He judge that He does not love corruption? This is because it is said: corruption, as has been said in its reality, is removing a thing from a praiseworthy state without a valid purpose, and this does not exist in His action, exalted is He, nor is He one who commands it. What we see of His action, glorified and exalted is He, as corruption is in relation to us. But regarding Him, exalted is He, all of it is goodness. As for His command to destroy animals, for example, for their consumption, it is for the improvement of man, who is the essence of this world. As for His causing death, it is one of the causes of his eternal life and his return to his original homeland. What may be needed here has already been discussed.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 206:**

﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah"﴾ in your conduct, ﴿pride takes hold of him﴾. That is, it encompasses him and surrounds him, and he becomes as one seized by it. Originally, *al-izzah* (pride, might) is the opposite of *dhull* (humiliation), and it is used here figuratively to mean arrogance and zealous self-regard. ﴿with sin﴾, that is, accompanied by it or accompanying it, or because of his earlier sin. It is also permissible for *akhadha* to derive from *al-akhdh* in the sense of *al-asr* (capture), and from this comes *al-akhidh* for "the captive." That is, *al-izzah* (pride) and the zealotry of the Days of Ignorance (*jahiliyyah*) make him a captive, bound by the fetter of sin from which he cannot free himself. ﴿Sufficient for him is Jahannam﴾: this is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate), meaning that Jahannam is sufficient for him as punishment. It has also been said that *Jahannam* is the fa'il (agent) of *hasbahu*, which fills the place of its predicate, and that this is a masdar (verbal noun) in the sense of the active participle. It is strengthened by its reliance on the *fa'* (the conjunction "so") that links the sentence to what precedes it. It has also been said that *hasb* is a verb-like noun (*ism fi'l*) in the past tense meaning *kafa* ("it suffices"), but this is open to question. *Jahannam* is a proper name for the abode of punishment or for one of its levels, and it is diptote (*mamnu'ah min al-sarf*) because of its being a proper noun and feminine. It is among the words assimilated to the quinqueliteral pattern by the addition of the third radical, and its form is *fa'nal*. In *al-Bahr* it is said that it is derived from their saying *rakiyyatun jihnam*, when a well is very deep. Both derive from *al-jahm*, which means dislike and harshness, and its form is *fa'nal*. One should not heed those who say its form is *fa'nalal*, like *arandas*, and that *fa'nal* is nonexistent because *fa'nal* exists in words such as *dunaka*, *khifnaka*, and others. It has also been said that it is Persian, its original form being *kihnam*, which was Arabized by replacing the *kaf* with a *jim* and dropping the *alif*. In that case, its diptotic status is due to being a proper noun and to its foreignness (*ujmah*). ﴿And wretched is the resting place﴾: this is the response to an implied oath (*jawab qasam*). The thing praised or blamed is omitted because it is evident and determined. *Al-mihad* means bedding, and it has been said it is that which is prepared for the side to lie upon. The use of this term is sarcastic. The verse also condemns the one who becomes angry when told, "Fear Allah." For this reason the scholars said: if an opponent says to the judge, "Be just" or something similar, the judge may discipline him, but if he says to him, "Fear Allah," he may not discipline him. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Among the greatest of sins is that a man says to his brother, 'Fear Allah,' and he replies, 'Look to yourself! Look to yourself!'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 207:

﴿And among mankind is one who sells himself﴾, i.e., sells himself by expending it in jihad (struggle in the way of God), according to what is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak, may God be pleased with them both, that the verse was revealed concerning the expedition of al-Raji (sariyyat al-Raji). Or it was revealed concerning enjoining good and forbidding evil, according to what Ibn Jarir reported from Abu al-Khalil, who said: ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, heard a man reciting this verse and said "to God we belong and to Him we return," and said: "A man stood up enjoining good and forbidding evil, and was killed."

﴿seeking the pleasure of God﴾, i.e., seeking His approval. So ibtigha' (seeking) is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and marda't (pleasure) is a verbal noun built with a ta' (ta' marbuta), like mad'ah, whereas the analogical form would be without it. It is written with a ta' in the Mushaf, and it is pausally pronounced with a ta' or a ha'. As mentioned in al-Bahr, most reports state that the verse was revealed concerning Suhayb al-Rumi, may God be pleased with him. A group has reported that "Suhayb came as an emigrant toward the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, and a group of the polytheists pursued him. He dismounted from his mount, scattered what was in his quiver, took his bow, and then said: 'O assembly of Quraysh, you know that I am among the most skilled archers of you, a man. By God, you shall not reach me until I have shot all that is in my quiver, then I shall strike with my sword as long as anything remains in my hand; then do whatever you wish.' They said: 'Show us your house and your property in Mecca and we will leave you alone.' They covenanted with him that if he showed them, they would let him go, and he did. When he came to the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, he said: 'Abu Yahya, the sale has profited, the sale has profited,' and recited the verse to him." According to this, the word shira' (purchase) stays on its apparent meaning, in the sense of ishtira' (purchasing).

In al-Kawashi it is mentioned that it was revealed concerning al-Zubayr ibn al-ʿAwwam and his companion al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, when "the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, said: 'Whoever brings down Khubayb from his cross, for him is Paradise,' and they said: 'I and my companion al-Miqdad,' and Khubayb had been crucified by the people of Mecca." The Imamiyya and some of us said: it was revealed concerning ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, when the Prophet, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, appointed him to his bed in Mecca when he left for the cave. According to this, the word shira' is used in the same way as was done at first.

﴿And God is Kind to the servants﴾ (207), i.e., the believers, in that He guided them to what contains His pleasure, made lasting bliss the reward for transient deeds, and rewarded the exchange of His property with His property.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 208:

﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace completely﴾ Several narrators related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Salam and his companions. That was because when they believed in the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and believed in his laws and the laws of Musa, peace be upon him, they glorified the Sabbath and disliked the flesh of camels and their milk after they had embraced Islam. The Muslims denounced them for this, and they said: "We are able to do this and that." And they said to the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: "The Torah is the Book of Allah, the Exalted, so leave us and let us act by it." So Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse. Thus the address is to the believers among the People of the Book. Al-Silm (peace) means Islam. Kaffah (completely) is originally an adjective derived from kaffa, meaning "to restrain," and it is used in the sense of "the whole" by way of the relation that it restrains the parts from scattering. The ta' in it is either for the feminine, or for transferring it from being an adjective to being a noun, like ʿamma (general), khassa (special) and qatiba (all), or for emphasis. Al-Tibi preferred the first view, claiming that saying the last two is a departure from the original without necessity. The comprehensiveness derived from it is the comprehensiveness of the whole over its parts, not the universal over its particulars, nor the more general of the two. It is not restricted to those who reason, nor to it being a circumstantial qualifier (hal) or an indefinite (nakira), contrary to Ibn Hisham, though he has no proof for that. Here it is a circumstantial qualifier from the pronoun in (udkhulu, "enter"), and the meaning is: enter into Islam with your whole selves, and leave nothing of your outward and inward aspects except that Islam encompasses it, such that no place remains for anything else of the law of Musa, peace be upon him. It is said: the address is to the hypocrites, and al-silm means submission and obedience, as is its original sense, and kaffah is also a circumstantial qualifier from the pronoun; i.e., submit to Allah, the Exalted, and obey Him entirely, abandon hypocrisy, and believe outwardly and inwardly. It is said: the address is to the disbelievers among the People of the Book who claimed belief in their own law, and what is meant by al-silm is all the laws, by mentioning the particular while intending the general, based on the view that Islam is the law of our Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him. The definite article (al-) is taken to denote totality, and kaffah is a circumstantial qualifier from al-silm. The meaning is: enter, O believers, into one law among all the laws, and do not separate them. It is said: the address is to the sincere Muslims, and what is meant by al-silm is the branches of Islam, and kaffah is a circumstantial qualifier of it. The meaning is: enter, O Muslims who believe in Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, into all the branches of faith, and do not neglect any of its rulings. Al-Zajjaj said regarding this view: what is meant by "al-silm" is Islam, and the intent is commanding the believers to remain steadfast in it. In this there is: that expressing steadfastness in Islam by entering into it is extremely distant. This is what some verifiers have chosen, from sixteen possibilities in the verse resulting from multiplying the two possibilities of al-silm by the two possibilities of kaffah, and multiplying the total by the possibilities of the address. The basis of this rests on two matters: first, that kaffah is for encompassing the parts; second, that the locus of benefit in speech lies in the restriction, as is established among the eloquent, and al-Shaykh stated this in Dala'il al-I'jaz. If the circumstantial status is considered for both the pronoun and the apparent noun together, as in his saying: "I went out with her, walking, dragging behind us upon our traces the hem of a striped, patterned cloak," the possibilities reach twenty-four, and what is most suitable among them in light of the occasion of revelation is not hidden. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read (al-salm) with a fatha on the sin, while the rest read it with a kasra, and both are well-known dialects for it. Al-A'mash read it with a fatha on both the sin and the lam.

﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ by opposing what you have been commanded, or by scattering among yourselves, or by dividing into laws or branches. ﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ 208 — manifest in enmity, or a manifestation of it. This is a reason for the prohibition and the cessation.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 209:**

﴿Then if you slip﴾, i.e., you turn away from entering ﴿into peace﴾ and withdraw. Its original meaning is "to fall," and it is here used figuratively for what has been mentioned.

﴿after the clear proofs have come to you﴾, i.e., the evident arguments that it is the truth, or the verses of the Book explicitly stating this, which necessitate entering (into peace). ﴿Then know that Allah is Mighty﴾, dominant over His affair, nothing can frustrate Him from taking vengeance upon you.

﴿Wise 209﴾, He does not abandon what wisdom requires of seizing the criminals.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 210:

﴿Are they waiting﴾ is an interrogative used in the sense of negation. The pronoun refers to the preceding relative (al-mawsul), if by it is meant the hypocrites or the People of the Book, or to the one who "pleases you" (man yu'jibuk), if by it is meant the believers among the People of the Book or the Muslims.

﴿Unless Allah comes to them﴾ in the meaning that befits Him, exalted is His majesty, transcendent above resemblance to created things and above being bound by the attributes of contingent beings.

﴿In canopies﴾ is the plural of ẓullah (canopy), like qullah and qulal, and it is that which shades you. It has also been read ẓilāl, like qilāl.

﴿Of clouds﴾ i.e., of cloud, or of the white part of it.

﴿And the angels﴾ come. It has also been read "wa'l-malā'ikati" with the genitive, as a conjunction with ẓulal or al-ghamām; the meaning is "together with the angels."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah, may He be exalted, will gather the first and the last for the appointed time of a known day, standing, their eyes fixed on the sky, looking at the decisive judgment. Allah, may He be exalted, will descend in canopies of clouds from the Throne to the Kursi." Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Abdullah ibn Umar concerning this verse that he said: "He descends when He descends, and between Him and His creation are seventy thousand veils, among them light, darkness and water; the water will then produce in that majesty a sound by which hearts are dislodged." And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that there are canopies of clouds in which Allah, may He be exalted, comes, surrounded by angels. Ubayy read: "Unless Allah and the angels come to them in canopies." Some people, regarding such ambiguous (mutashabihat) expressions, posited an omitted element and said: the attribution in the verse is metaphorical, and what is meant is that the command of Allah and His punishment come to them; or it is literal, and the object is omitted, meaning Allah comes to them with His might, the thing brought being omitted because it is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾, for might and wisdom indicate retribution in truth, which is the might and the punishment. The angels are mentioned because they are the intermediaries in bringing His command, or because they are the ones who literally come; and the mention of Allah, may He be exalted, in that case serves as a preface to mentioning them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They deceive Allah and those who believe﴾, according to one interpretation. The cloud is singled out as the locus of punishment because it is the place of expected mercy; so when punishment comes from it, it is more dreadful, for evil that comes from an unexpected direction is harder, how much more when it comes from the direction from which good is expected. And it is not hidden that whoever knows that Allah, may He be exalted, manifests by whatever He wills, however He wills and whenever He wills, and that in His manifestation He remains upon His absoluteness, even beyond the bond of absoluteness, transcendent above restriction and free from multiplicity, as the early generations of the Ummah and the masters of hearts among our Sufi shaykhs, may Allah sanctify their secrets, held, did not need these burdensome explanations and did not circle around these interpretations.
Page 99
﴿And the matter is decided﴾ i.e., the affair of the servants and their reckoning is completed, so the obedient is rewarded and the disobedient is punished, and the matter of their destruction is accomplished and concluded. It is coordinated with ("Are they waiting"), since it is meaningfully a report; and the past tense is placed in the position of the future to express the nearness and certainty of its occurrence. Mu'adh ibn Jabal read: "wa-qaḍā'u'l-amr," as a conjunction with the angels.

﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾ 120 is a concluding affirmation for emphasis, as if it were said: and to Allah return the matters of which the reckoning and the destruction are part. On the reading of Mu'adh it is a conjunction with ("Are they waiting"), i.e., they are waiting only for the coming, and the matter of that is up to Allah, may He be exalted. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Asim read "turja'u" in the passive, deriving it from ar-raj'; the rest read it in the active with feminine form, except Ya'qub, deriving it from ar-ruju'; it has also been read with masculine form and the passive.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 211:

﴿Ask the Children of Israel⦆ is a command to the Messenger (ﷺ), as is the usual principle in address; or it is addressed to each one of those who are capable of asking. The purpose of this question is to rebuke and reproach them for their transgression and their denial of the truth after the signs had become clear, not that they should answer, so that their answer would make known [the matter], as when one of us wishes to reproach someone and says to those present: "Ask him how many favours I have bestowed upon him." As for connecting the verse with what precedes it, according to what has been said: if the pronoun in (Do they wait) refers to the People of the Book, then this [verse] serves as evidence for it; and if it refers to those who please you, then it is an explanation of the state of the obstinate People of the Book after the explanation of the state of the hypocrites among the People of Polytheism.

﴿How many clear signs did We give them?⦆ That is: manifest proofs, namely the miracles that indicate the truthfulness of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as said by al-Hasan and Mujahid. The specification of giving miracles to the People of the Book, despite its generality for all, is because they know more than others about miracles and how they indicate truthfulness, owing to their knowledge of the miracles of earlier prophets. The word "ayah" may also be taken in its common meaning, which is a portion of the Qur'an or other [things], and "bayyinah" is from "bana" (to be evident), intransitive. So the question concerns the giving of the signs that include the description of the Messenger (ﷺ), the confirmation of his prophethood, and belief in what he brought.

(Kam) is either khabariyyah (affirmative, "how many"), in which case the thing asked about is omitted, and the sentence is independent with no place in i'rab, being built upon their deserving reproach, as if it were said: "Ask the Children of Israel about their transgression and their denial of the truth after its clarity, for We gave them many clear signs." It was claimed that the sentence must be cut off from what precedes under this assessment, but they are, as you see, [mistaken]. Or it is istifhamiyyah (interrogative, "how many"), and the sentence is in the position of the second object of (ask). It was said it is in the position of a verbal noun, i.e., "Ask them this question"; and it was said it is in the position of a circumstantial clause, i.e., "Ask them, saying: how many did We give them." The interrogation is for taqrir (eliciting affirmation), meaning leading the addressee to acknowledge; and it was said it means tahqiq (verification) and ta'kid (confirmation). It was objected that the meaning of reproach is disapproval and remoteness, which does not combine with verification; and it was answered that the reproach is indeed upon their denial of the truth and their rejection of it, which is compatible with the giving of signs, not upon the giving itself so that it would be separated from it. Its place is in the accusative, as a second object of (We gave), and it is not of the category of ishtighal (the object being governed by a verb on its pronoun) as was wrongly thought; or in the nominative by beginning, with the returning pronoun omitted, the estimate being: (We gave them them) or (We gave them it). This is weak according to Sibawayh. (Ayah) is a tamyiz (specification), and (man) is a silah (particle) brought for separation between "ayah" being an object of (We gave) and its being a specification of (kam); and it must be brought in such a position. Al-Radi said: "When the separation between khabariyyah kam and its specification is by a transitive verb, man must be brought, lest the specified noun be confused with the object of that transitive verb, as in: ﴿How many gardens did they leave?⦆ and ﴿How many a town did We destroy?⦆ The state of interrogative kam with a genitive specification, with separation, is like the state of khabariyyah kam in all that we have mentioned, end." It is related from him that he denied the addition of "min" in the specification of the interrogative; this is to be understood as applying to addition without separation, not absolutely, so there is no contradiction between his two statements.

﴿And whoever substitutes the favour of Allah⦆ That is: His signs, for they are the cause of guidance, which is the greatest of favours. In this, the apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, with a word other than the previous one, to magnify the signs. Substituting them is distorting and misinterpreting them in a deviant way, or making them a cause of misguidance and increase of abomination. On both assessments there is no ellipsis in the verse. Abu Hayyan said: the preposition has been omitted from "ni'mah" and the second object of (yubaddil) has been omitted, the estimate being: "whoever substitutes for the favour of Allah disbelief," and what indicates this is the arrangement of the answer of the condition upon it. There is in this what is not hidden. It was also read as (yubdil) with light pronunciation.

﴿after what has come to him⦆ That is: after it reached him and he became able to know it. The benefit of this addition, although substituting the signs in general is blameworthy, is an allusion that they substituted them after they had understood them; and in this is great censure of them and condemnation of the ugliness of their state, and evidence for their deserving a severe punishment, since they substituted after knowledge. By this, the apparent objection is dispelled, that substitution occurs only after coming; so what is the benefit of mentioning it?

﴿Indeed Allah is severe in punishment⦆ (211) This is an explanation of the answer, placed in its stead; the estimate being: whoever substitutes the favour of Allah, He will punish him with the most severe punishment, because He is severe in punishment. It may also be that this is itself the answer, with the pronoun omitted; that is, "severe in punishment to him." The mention of the noble Name is to instil awe and bring about dread.

The Qur'an's words "Adorned for those who disbelieve is the life of this world" (﴿زُيِّنَ لِلَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا الحَياةُ الدُّنْيا﴾) mean: it was made to exist as something fair, and it was made beloved in their hearts. So they rushed toward it as moths rush toward a fire, and they turned away from everything else. For this reason the People of the Book turned away from the (divine) signs and altered them. The one who adorns in this sense, in its literal meaning, is Allah, exalted is He. If the adornment is interpreted as making something seem good through speech and similar whispering (waswasa), as in His words, "I will certainly adorn for them (evil) on earth and will surely mislead them all" (﴿لأُزَيِّنَنَّ لَهم في الأرْضِ ولأُغْوِيَنَّهُمْ﴾), then the one doing it is Satan. The verse admits of both meanings, and the adornment is literal in both, as the apparent sense of al-Raghib's words requires.

"And they mock those who believe" (﴿ويَسْخَرُونَ مِنَ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾). The relative pronoun (al-ladhina) is definite by prior reference (li-l-ʿahd), and what is meant is the poor believers, such as Suhayb, Bilal and ʿAmmar. That is, they mock them for their renunciation of this world and their devotion to the next. The particle min is for transitivity (li-l-taʿdiya) and conveys the sense of starting point (al-ibtida'), as though they made their poverty and shabby condition the source of their mockery. The verb sakhara may also take the preposition bi-, but that usage is considered a poor dialect. The conjunction "and" (al-ʿatf) is upon "was adorned" (zuyyina), and the choice of the present tense expresses continuity. It has also been allowed that the waw is for circumstance (li-l-hal), with "they mock" (wa-yusakhkhirun) being the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "while they are mocking." The verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl and his like among the chiefs of Quraysh, to whom the world had been spread wide, and who used to mock the poor believers, saying: "If Muhammad (ﷺ) were a prophet, our nobles would have followed him." This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him. It has also been said that it was revealed concerning Ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and it has been said that it was revealed concerning the chiefs of the Jews from the Banu Qurayza, al-Nadir and Qaynuqa, who mocked the poor emigrants. And from ʿAta': there is no obstacle to its being revealed concerning all of them.

"And those who have taramount piety" (﴿والَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا﴾) are precisely those who believe. Its wording was chosen to praise them for their piety and to indicate the reason for the ruling. It is also permissible that the general sense is intended, and these (believers) enter into it in the first instance.

"Above them on the Day of Resurrection" (﴿فَوْقَهم يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾): in place, because the believers are in ʿIlliyyin (the highest of the high), while those others are in the lowest of the low. Or in rank, because the believers are at the peak of honour, while those others are in the depths of humiliation and disgrace. Or because the believers will exalt themselves over them in the Hereafter, and so they will mock them as they mocked them in this world. The clause is coordinated with what precedes it, and the choice of the nominal form expresses the permanence of its meaning. In this there is consolation for the believers that is not hidden.

"And Allah provides" (﴿واللَّهُ يَرْزُقُ﴾) in the Hereafter "whom He wills without account" (﴿مَن يَشاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسابٍ 212﴾), meaning without limit to what He gives. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: this provision is in this world. In this there is an allusion to the believers, who had been mocked, coming to possess the wealth of the Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir. It is also permissible that both abodes are intended, in which case it serves as a concluding statement (tadhyil) for both rulings.

[Page 101]

﴿Mankind was one community﴾ agreeing upon monotheism and acknowledging servitude, when Allah, exalted is He, took the covenant from them. This is narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Or (it was) between Adam and Idris, peace be upon them both, based on what is in *Rawdat al-Ahbab* (the Garden of the Beloved), that the people in the time of Adam were monotheists adhering to his religion, to the extent that they shook hands with the angels, except for a few from Qabil (Cain) and his followers, until the time of Idris's elevation. Or (it was) between Adam and Nuh (Noah), peace be upon them both, as al-Bazzar and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that there were ten generations between them upon a law of truth. Or (it was) after the Flood, for after him there remained only eighty men and women, and then they died, except Nuh and his sons Ham, Sam, and Yafith, and their wives. All of them were upon the religion of Nuh, peace be upon him. So the generality (istighraq) at the first and the last (periods) is literal (haqiqi), and at the second and third it is figurative (idda'i), by treating the few as if they were nonexistent. It has also been said: they were agreed upon ignorance and disbelief, based on what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they were disbelievers, from the time of Idris's elevation until Nuh was sent, or from the death of Nuh, peace be upon him, until Hud, peace be upon him, was sent.

﴿So Allah sent the prophets﴾ meaning: they differed, so He sent... etc. This is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him. The verb was omitted because reliance is placed on what is mentioned after it.

﴿as bearers of good tidings﴾ to those who believed, with reward.

﴿and as warners﴾ to those who disbelieved, with punishment; and they are many. Ahmad and Ibn Hibban transmitted: "From Abu Dharr, that he asked the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him: 'How many are the prophets?' He said: 'One hundred and twenty-four thousand.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, how many are the messengers?' He said: 'Three hundred and thirteen, a great number.'" This is not contradicted by His saying: ﴿And messengers We have already related to you﴾, and so on, as will come, Allah willing. The two plural words (mubashshirin and mundhirin) are in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (hal) of "the prophets." The apparent view is that it is a future circumstance (haal muqaddarah, a circumstance that is anticipated), and the view that it is a contemporaneous circumstance (haal muqarinah) contradicts the apparent meaning.

﴿and sent down with them the Book﴾. The alif-lam in "al-Kitab" is for the genus. The phrase ma'ahum (with them) is a future circumstance (haal muqaddarah) relating to "al-Kitab," so it is connected to an omitted element, and it is not an accusative object of "anzal" (sent down). The meaning is: He sent down the genus of the Book, anticipating its accompaniment and association with the prophets, since each of them took rulings either from a book specific to him or from a book before him. The revealed books are said, according to the well-known view, to be one hundred and four: ten scrolls were sent down to Adam, fifty to Idris, thirty to Shith, and ten to Musa before the Torah; then the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Furqan. It is also permitted that the alif-lam is for a specific reference (ahd), and that the pronoun in "ma'ahum" refers to the prophets in terms of some of them; that is, He sent down with each of some of the prophets his Book. The weakness in this is not hidden.

﴿with the truth﴾ is connected to "anzal," or is a circumstance of "al-Kitab," meaning: accompanied by, bearing witness to it. ﴿that he might judge between the people﴾ is the reason for the sending down mentioned at its beginning and for the sending of the prophets. This sending that is given as the reason is the one that came after the disagreement, so the earlier sending of Adam, Shith, and Idris, peace be upon them, does not conflict with this, according to some of the earlier aspects. "Hukm" (judgment) here means separation (fasl), by the indication that "bayn" (between) is connected to it. If it meant "qada'" (judgment/decree), it would have taken "'ala" (upon). The hidden pronoun refers to Allah, glorified is He. This is supported by the reading of al-Jahdari, as transmitted from him by Makki, "li-nahkuma" (that We may judge), with the plural of majesty. Or it refers to the Prophet, and the verb is singular because each of the prophets is a judge. It is also permitted that it refers to "al-Kitab," and the attribution then is figurative, in terms of its containing that by which separation is made. Some claimed that this is the more apparent view, since returning it to Allah, exalted is He, requires some strained meaning (yazhar hukmuhu, i.e., "that its ruling becomes manifest"), and returning it to the Prophet requires strained wording, since it did not say "li-yahkumu" (that they may judge). From what we have mentioned, the weakness in this is known. The people intended are those mentioned. The use of the noun in place of the pronoun is for added specification.

﴿concerning that about which they differed﴾ meaning: concerning the truth about which they differed, based on the principle that the unity of the community is by agreement upon the truth. If unity is interpreted as agreement upon ignorance and disbelief, then "ikhtilaf" (difference) becomes figurative for confusion and ambiguity that is necessarily associated with it, and the meaning is: concerning that which was obscure to them. ﴿And none differed concerning it﴾ meaning: concerning the truth, by denying it and being obstinate against it, or concerning the revealed Book, bearing it, by distorting it and interpreting it through deviant interpretations. The waw is circumstantial (waw haliyyah).

﴿except those who were given it﴾ meaning: the Book revealed to remove disagreement and dispel discord. That is, they reversed the matter, since they made what was sent down, which was meant to remove disagreement, a cause for its being firmly established and entrenched. By this, the objection is dispelled: since disagreement was only from those who were given it, disagreement could not be prior to the sending (of prophets). Its summary is that the intended meaning here is the entrenchment and intensification of the disagreement. "Giving" (ita') is used in place of "sending down" (inzal) to alert from the outset to their complete ability to recognize the truth in it, since "sending down" does not convey that. It was also said: it was expressed this way so that the relative clause would be restricted to the people of knowledge and study among those disagreeing, and singled out for mention to add to the enormity of their act, and because others follow them.

﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾ meaning: the manifest arguments indicating the truth had become firmly established in their minds. The phrase "min" (after) is connected to "ikhtalafu" (differed), with an omitted verb. The restriction (hasr), if it is intended, is understood from the context or from the omission of the verb, and the placement of the adverbial phrase after the particle of exception verbally, or from positing the omitted element as coming later. In Ad-Durr al-Masun, it is permitted that it be connected to what differed before it. Nothing prevents this except as Abu al-Baqa' said. Grammarians have a discussion on this point, the summary of which is that the exception of two things with one particle without conjunction is impermissible absolutely according to most (grammarians), whether as substitution (badal) or otherwise. It is permissible according to a group absolutely. The distinction of some (grammarians) is: if the item excepted from is mentioned together with each of the two exceptions, and both are substitutions, it is permissible; otherwise, it is not. Those who permit it absolutely cite the verse: ﴿And we do not see that anyone followed you except those who are the lowest of us in judgment at first sight﴾. Here no excepted-from item is mentioned at all, and the sense is: "We do not see that anyone followed you in any state except our lowest at first sight." Those who do not permit it answer that the accusative is by a hidden verb, meaning "they followed," and that the adverbial phrase is sufficient for the trace of the verb, so it allows what is not allowed elsewhere; this is said by al-Radi, and it is the basis of the disagreement concerning the verse.

﴿out of envious rivalry among themselves﴾. The phrase "bayn-ahum" is connected to what "min" is connected to. "Al-baghy" (envious transgression) means injustice or envy. "Baynahum" is connected to an omitted attribute of "baghyan," and in this there is an indication, in my view, that this envious transgression has laid eggs and hatched among them. It hovers over them and circulates among them, having no hope in others and no refuge other than them. In this there is a notice of their firm establishment in it and their reaching its utmost extent. This is the purpose of describing it with the adverbial phrase. It was also said: by this He pointed out that transgression is a shared matter among them, and that all of them are base. Its source is their excessive greed for this world and their pursuit of it.

﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed, by His permission﴾ meaning: by His command, or by His granting success and facilitation. "Min" (of) is explanatory for "lima" (concerning that), and the intended meaning is the truth about which people differed. The pronoun is general, including the earlier and later differing parties. It does not refer to "those who were given it" as the earlier pronouns do. The indication of this is the generality of guidance to the believers who preceded the difference of the People of the Book and those who came after their difference. It was also said: the intended "those who believed" is the community of Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, and the pronoun in "ikhtalafu" refers to "those who were given it," that is, the Book. This is supported by what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "They differed about Friday, so the Jews took Saturday and the Christians Sunday, and Allah guided the community of Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to Friday. They differed about the qiblah: the Christians faced the east and the Jews faced Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and Allah guided the community of Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to the qiblah. They differed about prayer: some of them bowed but did not prostrate, some prostrated but did not bow, some prayed while speaking, and some prayed while walking; Allah guided the community of Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to the truth in that. They differed about fasting: some fasted day and night, and some fasted from some food; Allah guided the community of Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to the truth in that. They differed about Abraham, peace be upon him: the Jews said he was a Jew, and the Christians said he was a Christian; Allah made him a upright monotheist, a Muslim, and Allah guided the community of Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to the truth in that. They differed about Jesus, peace be upon him: the Jews denied him and said a great calumny against his mother, and the Christians made him a god and a son, while Allah made him His Spirit and His Word; Allah guided the community of Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, to the truth in that." The reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b is: ﴿So Allah guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed, by His permission, that they might be witnesses over the people﴾.

﴿And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [123], which is the path of truth, whose traveler does not go astray. The sentence confirms the content of what precedes it.

[Page 102]

[Page 103]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 214 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Or do you think that you will enter Paradise﴾ It was revealed concerning the Battle of the Trench (Ghazwat al-Khandaq) when the Muslims suffered what they suffered of hardship, hardship, fear, cold, bad living conditions and various kinds of harm, until "the hearts reached the throats." It was also said that it was revealed concerning the Battle of Uhud. ʿAṭāʾ said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions entered Medina, the harm weighed heavily upon them, because they had left without wealth, had left their homes and their property in the hands of the polytheists, and had preferred the pleasure of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ). The Jews openly displayed enmity towards the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a group of the wealthy concealed hypocrisy. So Allah revealed this verse to comfort their hearts." The address is either to the believers specifically, or to the Prophet (ﷺ) and those with him. The attribution of "thinking" (al-ḥusbān) to him (peace be upon him) is either because, when his noble chest was constricted by the severities of the polytheists, he was placed in the position of one who supposes that he will enter Paradise without bearing hardships, or it is by way of predominance (al-taghlīb), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or you will return to our religion﴾. The ʾam here is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿa), and the implied hamza is for the denial of that supposition and that it should not be the case. It was also said that it is conjunctive (muttaṣila) with an implied counterpart (muʿādil), and it was also said that it is disjunctive without any implied counterpart. In the statement there is an iltifāt (shift of grammatical person), though it is not a clear shift from the third person to the second, because His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾ is a statement comprising mention of the earlier nations, the past generations, mention of the prophets who were sent to them and what they suffered from them of severities, and the display of miracles, as encouragement for the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers to steadfastness and patience upon the harm of the polytheists. Or it is for the believers specifically, and thus they were, from this aspect, intended as absent (ghāʾibīn). What supports this is ﴿So Allah guided those who believed﴾ etc. So when it is said that after ﴿or do you think﴾ it is a transfer from the third person to the second, or because the first statement is an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to the believers for not being steadfast and patient upon the harm of the polytheists, it is as if it was placed in the position of: "It was incumbent upon the believers to be encouraged and patient, following the example of those before them." This is indicated by what al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasaʾi and Imam Ahmad transmitted: "From Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, who said: We complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about what we were suffering from the polytheists, and we said: Will you not seek victory for us, will you not supplicate Allah for us? He said: 'Indeed, whoever was before you, one of them would have a saw placed upon the middle of his head, and it would split him to his feet, and that would not turn him from his religion. And they would be combed with iron combs between his flesh and bone, and that would not turn him from his religion.' Then he said: 'By Allah, this matter will certainly be completed, until a rider travels from Sanaa to Hadramawt, fearing none but Allah the Exalted and the wolf for his sheep, but you are hastening.'" This is what is negated by "rather" (bal) which is contained in ʾam, meaning: leave that aside, ﴿did they suppose that they would enter Paradise﴾. He turned from this to the address, and the iltifāt occurred in meaning. From what has been mentioned, the connection of the verse with what precedes it is known. It was also said that the connection is that when He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾, and the intended "path" (al-ṣirāt) was the truth whose following leads to entering Paradise, but that is not completed except by bearing hardships and obligations.

﴿And has not yet come to you﴾ The wāw is for the state (ḥāl), and the sentence after it is in the accusative as a state; i.e., not yet coming to you. Lamma is a jussive particle like (lam), and grammarians in their books distinguish between them. The well-known view is that it is simple (basīṭa). It was also said that it is compound (murakkaba) from (lam) and the negative (mā), and it is analogous to (qad) in that the verb mentioned after it is awaited to occur.

﴿The example of those who passed away before you﴾ i.e., the likeness of their example and their wondrous state. So the statement is elliptical (ḥadhf muḍāf), and "those who" (alladhīna) is an attribute of an elided noun; i.e., the believers. And "before you" (min qablikum) is connected to "passed away" and is like an emphasis for what is understood from it.

﴿Misfortune and adversity touched them﴾ is an explanation of the example by way of resumption (istiʾnāf), whether or not it is determined how that example is. Abu al-Baqaʾ permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (ḥāliyya) with the implied qad.

﴿And they were shaken﴾ i.e., they were disturbed with a severe disturbance by various kinds of trial.

﴿Until the Messenger and those who believed with him said﴾ i.e., their affair from trial reached the point where they were compelled to say: ﴿the Messenger says﴾ and he is the most knowledgeable of people about what befits Him, Exalted is He, and what His wisdom requires; and the believers who follow his traces, guided by his lights, ﴿When will come﴾ the help of Allah, seeking and wishing for it, and lengthening the period of hardship, not out of doubt or suspicion. The intended "messenger" is the category, not one specific individual. It was also said he is Yasaʿ; it was said he is Shaʿyaʾ; and it was said he is Ashʿiyaʾ. And according to the specific identification, the intended "those who passed away" are a people specifically, who are the followers of these messengers. Nafiʿ recited "yaqūlu" (says) with the nominative case, as a report of a past circumstance. And "maʿahu" may be in the accusative governed by "yaqūla," i.e., they accompanied him in this saying, and it may be in the accusative governed by "āmanū," i.e., they agreed with him in faith.

﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near﴾ is a grammatical resumption (istiʾnāf naḥwī) on the presumption of a saying; i.e., it was then said to them at that time, to comfort their souls by granting them their desire. The choice of a nominal sentence over a verbal one, which suits what precedes it, and beginning it with the particle of alerting and emphasis, indicates the affirmation of its content and its confirmation to a degree that is not hidden. The choice of reporting the promise of victory, since it is in the ruling of a promise made to the Messenger, and restricting the report to it rather than reporting the victory itself, though it is realized, is to indicate that there is no need for that because the breaking of the promise is impossible. It was also said: since the question with "when" (matā) indicates seeking knowledge of nearness, the answer included nearness, and it was sufficed with it so that the answer would correspond to the question. It was also permitted that this be a remark from Him, Exalted is He, at the time of reporting, in the manner of an interjection (iʿtirāḍ), not a remark at the time the reported event occurred. The claim that this sentence is the Messenger's saying and "When is the help of Allah" is the saying of those with him, by way of the non-ordered "lafʿ wa-nashr" (wrapping and unfolding) is nothing. Verbally, because it is not good for the speakers to be coordinated without the sayings being coordinated. And in meaning, because it is not good to mention the Messenger's saying "Unquestionably, the help of Allah is near" in the context whose purpose is to demonstrate the extremity of the affair in severity. And the claim that leaving out the conjunction is to alert that each is the saying of one of the two of them, and to guard against the supposition that the whole is one saying, and to alert that the Messenger said it to them in reply to them, and that the station of prophethood requires the Messenger's exemption from being shaken, should not be heeded. Because if the conjunction is left out, it is not coordinated upon the first saying, so how is there alerting that each is a saying of one of the two? And we are not safe from denying that the station of prophethood requires that exemption, and shaking and disturbance are not greater than fear, and the messengers, peace and blessings of Allah be upon them, were consoled, as many verses explicitly state. And in the verse there is an allusion that reaching the most holy presence is attained only by abandoning pleasures and enduring hardships, as indicated by the report: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and Hellfire is surrounded by desires." And al-Hakim transmitted and authenticated from Abu Malik, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah the Exalted tests one of you with trial, while He is most knowing of it, just as one of you tests his gold with fire. Among them is one who comes out like pure refined gold; that is the one whom Allah the Exalted has saved from evil deeds. And among them is one who comes out like black gold; that is the one who has been afflicted with trial."

* * *

From the way of allusion (ishāra) in the verses: ﴿And of the people is one whose speech about the worldly life pleases you﴾ He claims love and speaks of the subtleties of secrets, and displays the characteristics of states, while he is in the station of the commanding soul (al-nafs al-ammāra).

﴿And he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾ of knowledge and sincerity according to his own claim. ﴿And he is the most contentious of opponents﴾ severely hostile to the people of Allah the Exalted in reality. ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein﴾ by casting doubts upon weak novices. ﴿And destroys the crops﴾ and reaps, with the sickle of his deceptions, the crop of faith growing in the gardens of the hearts of the seekers, and cuts off the offspring of the guides. ﴿And Allah does not like corruption﴾ so how does this liar claim the love of Allah the Exalted while committing what He does not love? ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah,"﴾ the fanaticism of the soul, the fanaticism of ignorance, drives him to sin out of obstinacy, out of love for displaying himself, and out of the claim that he knows Allah, Exalted is He, better than his advisor. ﴿Hell is sufficient for him﴾ i.e., it suffices him that he is confined in the prison (sijjīn) of nature and its darknesses. This is the description of most of the people of outward forms (arbāb al-rusūm) who have been veiled from perceiving the realities by the knowledge they possess. ﴿And of the people is one who﴾ spends himself in treading the path of Allah seeking His pleasure, does not turn to idle talk and rumor, and whose pursuit of his Lord is not lax, sublime.

﴿O you who believe, enter into submission﴾ and the surrender of existence to Allah the Exalted and submission under the courses of power, for you and against you, entirely. So if you slip from the station of surrender and contentment with the decree, after there have come to you the clear proofs of the manifestations of the acts and attributes, know that Allah the Exalted is Mighty, Dominant, who subdues you; Wise, who does not subdue except according to the requirement of wisdom. ﴿Do they await﴾ except that Allah, Exalted is He, manifests Himself ﴿in shadows﴾ of subduing attributes, from among the manifestations of the attributes and the forms of the angels of the heavenly powers. ﴿And the matter is decided﴾ by each one's arrival at what was predestined for him in eternity.

﴿And to Allah are all matters returned﴾ by annihilation (fanāʾ).

﴿Mankind was one community﴾ upon the natural disposition and the religion of truth in the world of totality (ʿālam al-ijmāl). Then they differed in their upbringing according to the difference of their natures, the dominance of the attributes of their souls, and each one's being veiled by the substance of his body. ﴿So Allah sent the prophets﴾ to call them from disagreement to harmony, from multiplicity to unity, and from enmity to love. ﴿They differed﴾ and formed factions against them and became distinct. The lowly ones increased in disagreement and obstinacy, while the exalted ones, whom Allah the Exalted guided to the truth, followed the straight path.

﴿Or do you think that you will enter﴾ the Paradise of witnessing and the assemblies of intimacy by the light of unveiling ﴿and there has not yet come to you﴾ the state of those who traveled before you ﴿misfortune and adversity touched them﴾ of the hardship of poverty, the adversity of striving, and the breaking of the soul through worship, until they grew weary from the long duration of the veil, their patience with witnessing beauty was overcome, and they sought the help of Allah the Exalted through manifestation. They were answered: when the torrent reaches the hills. And it was said to them: ﴿Unquestionably, the help of Allah﴾ by the lifting of the veil and the appearance of the traces of beauty ﴿is near﴾ to the one who gave up his soul and turned his beauty away from other than his Master, bore hardships, and slaughtered desires with the sword of longings. He who has not died in His love has not lived by it.

Without the bee's gathering, what the bee gathers is not [honey].

﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said in the narration of Abu Salih: "ʿAmr ibn al-Jamuh was an old man with much wealth, and he said: O Messenger of Allah, with what should we give charity, and upon whom should we spend? So it was revealed." And in the narration of ʿAṭāʾ from him: No, rather it was revealed concerning "a man who came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'I have a dinar.' He said: 'Spend it on yourself.' He said: 'I have two dinars.' He said: 'Spend them on your family.' He said: 'I have three.' He said: 'Spend them on your servant.' He said: 'I have four.' He said: 'Spend them on your parents.' He said: 'I have five.' He said: 'Spend them on your relatives.' He said: 'I have six.' He said: 'Spend them in the way of Allah the Exalted.'"

And from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "The believers asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) where they should place their wealth, and so this was revealed."

[Page 106]

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the Prophet was asked about what is to be spent, but he answered by explaining the recipients explicitly, because that matters more. The reckoning of the expenditure depends on them. He alluded briefly to explaining what is spent, since ﴿*min khayrin*﴾ ("of good") implies that it is lawful, for anything else is not called good. He mentioned this only incidentally, as the question did not call for it, because a question asked in order to learn is not asked for disputation. The duty of the teacher in such a case is to be like a gentle physician, who seeks out what brings healing whether or not the patient asked for it. Since their need for someone to spend on is as great as their need for what is spent, he explained both matters. This is like a man suffering from bile who asked a physician for permission to eat honey, and the physician said: "Eat it with vinegar." The speech is therefore from the style of the wise (*uslub al-hakim*). It is possible that the speech also mentioned the recipients, as the first narration about the occasion of revelation indicates, but he did not state it in the verse, for brevity of composition, relying on the answer. Thus the verse is an answer to two matters, one of which was asked about. Limiting the explanation of what is spent to a general statement, without elaboration, is like explaining the recipients, to indicate that the second is more important. Whether the verse, by this, falls outside being from the style of the wise is disputed. There are two opinions, the more well-known of which is the second, since what was asked about was answered explicitly and what was not asked about was answered implicitly. Most scholars hold that the verse concerns voluntary charity (*tatawwu'*). It was said that it concerns obligatory zakat. Whoever permits giving zakat to parents has cited it as evidence. But there is an objection: the generality of ﴿khayr﴾ conflicts with its being about zakat, because the obligation in zakat is a specified amount by consensus (*ijma'*). He, glorified is He, did not address the questioners. As for ﴿al-riqab﴾ ("the captives" or "those in bondage"), it is either because it was sufficient to mention it in the other passages, or because they are included under the generality of His words, exalted is He: ﴿wa ma taf'alu min khayrin﴾ ("and whatever good you do"), for it encompasses every good that occurs in any recipient whatsoever. ﴿Ma﴾ here is conditional and is the object of ﴿taf'alu﴾, and the verb is more general than spending. He used a term that encompasses in order to emphasize the specific that occurs in the answer.

﴿*Fa-inna Allaha bihi 'alim*﴾ ("Indeed Allah is knowing of it") — He knows its reality, as the form ﴿*fa'il*﴾ together with the emphasized nominal sentence indicates. The sentence is the answer to the condition in terms of its figurative meaning (*kinaya*), since what is intended by it is the full payment of reward. It was said that it is an indication of the answer, but it is not that. The connection of this verse to what precedes it is that patience in spending and the giving of wealth is among the greatest qualities with which the believer adorns himself, and it is among the strongest means that lead to Paradise, to the extent that it has been reported: "Charity extinguishes the anger of the Lord."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 216:**

﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾, meaning: fighting the disbelievers. It is a *fard 'ayn* (individual obligation, binding on every person) if they enter our lands, and a *fard kifaya* (collective obligation, binding on the community as a whole, which is discharged when enough people undertake it) if they are in their own lands. It is also read with the verb in the active voice, where the subject is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and with *al-qital* (الْقِتَالَ) in the accusative. It is also read: ﴿Killing has been prescribed for you﴾, meaning: killing the disbelievers.

﴿And it is hateful to you﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with *kutiba* (كُتِبَ). Coordinating a nominal clause (*ismiyya*) with a verbal clause (*fi'liyya*) is permissible, as has been explicitly stated. It was also said that the *waw* is for the circumstantial (*hal*), and the clause is a circumstantial clause. It was objected that an emphasizing circumstantial clause (*al-hal al-mu'akkida*) does not take the *waw*, and that a transitional circumstantial clause (*al-hal al-muntaqila*) has no benefit in this position. *Al-kurh* (الْكُرْهُ) with a *damma* and *al-kark* (الْكَرْهُ) with a *fatha* are both acceptable, and both have been read as *al-karaha* (الْكَرَاهَةُ). It was said that the *fatha* form denotes the hardship that befalls a person from outside, and the *damma* form denotes what befalls him from within himself. It was also said that the *fatha* form is a noun meaning compulsion (*al-ikrah*), and the *damma* form means aversion (*al-karaha*). In any case, if it is a verbal noun (*masdar*), it is either interpreted (*mu'awwal*), or taken as an intensive expression (*mahmul 'ala al-mubalagha*), or it is an adjective, as in *khubzun makhbuz* (bread that has been baked). If it means compulsion, and it is understood to mean aversion as a result of that compulsion, then it is an intensive metaphor (*al-tashbih al-baligh*), as if they were compelled to it because of its severity and the greatness of its hardship. That killing is hateful does not contradict faith, because that aversion is natural, given what it involves: killing, capture, the destruction of the body, and the loss of property. Such aversion does not contradict acceptance of what one is charged with, like a sick person who drinks a bitter medicine, hating it because of its bitterness, yet accepting it for another reason.

﴿And it may be that you dislike a thing and it is good for you﴾, meaning all that they were charged with, since the natural disposition dislikes it, although it is the basis of their well-being. Among these things is fighting, for in it are victory, booty, and martyrdom, which is the greatest means of attaining the highest honour.

﴿And it may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you﴾, meaning all that they were forbidden, since the soul loves it and desires it, although it leads the soul to ruin. Among this is abandoning the fight against the enemies, for in it are humiliation, weakness of affairs, the taking of women and children captive, the plundering of wealth, the loss of cities, and the deprivation of the greater share of everlasting bliss. The two nominal clauses are circumstantial clauses (*hal*) from an indefinite noun (*nakira*), which is rare. Sibawayh explicitly stated that this is permissible, as in *al-Bahr*. Abu al-Baqa' permitted that they be adjectives of the noun. The *waw* is acceptable here because the form of the clause here is like its form when it is a circumstantial clause.

The first *'asa* (عَسَى) denotes apprehension (*al-ishfaq*), and the second denotes hope (*al-tarajji*), according to some scholars. The reason the expression *'asa*, which indicates the absence of certainty, is used is that when the soul is disciplined and purified, what happened to it before is reversed upon it, so that what it loved becomes hateful and what it hated becomes beloved. Since the soul is capable, through discipline, of such a reversal, it is not certain that it will dislike what is good for it or love what is bad for it. Therefore there is no need to say that *'asa* is used here in the sense of certainty, as it is elsewhere in the Qur'an, except in the verse ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him better wives﴾.

﴿And Allah knows﴾ what is good for you and what is bad for you. The object is omitted for brevity.

﴿And you do not know﴾ this. So hasten to what He commands you, for He commands you only in what He knows to be good for you. And refrain from what He forbids you, for He forbids you only what is bad for you. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is clear, because it contains *jihad*, which is the giving of one's self, and that is greater than the giving of wealth.
