Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 217 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Bayhaqi related, through the route of Zayd ibn Ruman from Urwah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Abdullah ibn Jahsh, who was the son of the paternal aunt of the Prophet (ﷺ), to Nakhlah, and said: 'Stay there until you bring us news of the Quraysh.' He did not order him to fight, and that was in the sacred month. He wrote him a letter before telling him where to go, and said: 'Set out with your companions, and when you have travelled two days, open your letter and look into it. Whatever I have ordered you, carry it out, and do not compel any of your companions to go with you.' When he had travelled two days he opened the letter, and in it was: 'Go on until you reach Nakhlah, and bring us news of the Quraysh of what has reached you of them.' He said to his companions, who were eight in number, when he had read the letter: 'Hearing and obeying. Whoever among you has a desire for martyrdom, let him go with me, for I am proceeding in obedience to the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Whoever among you dislikes that, let him return, for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has forbidden me to compel any of you.' The party went on with him until, when they were at Bakhran, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and Utbah ibn Ghazwan lost a camel of theirs which they had been riding in turns, so they stayed behind to search for it, while the rest went on until they reached Nakhlah. There passed by them Amr ibn al-Hadrami, al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, Uthman ibn Abdullah ibn al-Mughirah and Nawfal ibn Abdullah, with them a trade caravan which they had brought from al-Ta'if, consisting of leather and raisins. When the party saw them, Waqid ibn Abdullah, who had shaved his head, looked out at them, and when they saw him shaved they said: 'They are pilgrims (umar); you have no cause to fear them from them.' The companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took counsel about them, and it was the last day of Jumada. They said: 'If you kill them, you will be killing them in the sacred month, and if you leave them, they will enter the Sacred Mosque of Makkah this very night, and will protect themselves from you.' So the party resolved to kill them. Waqid ibn Abdullah al-Sahmi shot Amr ibn al-Hadrami with an arrow and killed him, and they took Uthman ibn Abdullah and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan captive, while Nawfal escaped and outran them, and they seized the caravan and brought it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He said to them: 'By Allah, I did not order you to fight in the sacred month.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) detained the two captives and the caravan and took nothing from it. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them what he said, they were struck with dismay, and thought they had perished, and their brethren among the Muslims rebuked them. The Quraysh said, when news of these men reached them: 'Muhammad has shed sacred blood, taken property, taken men captive, and made lawful the sacred month.' Then this was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took the caravan and ransomed the two captives." In the Sirah of Ibn Sayyid al-Nas it is stated that this took place in Rajab, and that they met those men on the last day of it. In the narration of al-Zuhri from Urwah: "When that deed reached the disbelievers of Quraysh, a delegation of them rode until they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Is fighting permitted in the sacred month?' Then Allah revealed the verse." From here it was said that the questioners were the polytheists, and this is strengthened by the fact that what follows of mention of hindering (from the path), disbelief and expulsion is the greatest witness to the truth of that, so that it would be a rebuke to them corresponding to their rebuke of the believers. But most of the exegetes chose that the questioners were the Muslims. They said: "Most of the narrations require this, and the evidence is not explicit regarding the intended meaning." The sacred month is meant to be Rajab or Jumada, so the (al-) in it is for specific reference (al-'ahd). The more common and more apparent view is that it is for the genus (al-jins), so that the sacred months are intended, namely Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram and Rajab, and they were called "sacred" (ḥurum) because fighting is forbidden in them. The meaning is: they ask you — that is, the Muslims or the disbelievers — about fighting in the sacred month, with "fighting in it" being a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from "the month", since the first does not fully convey the intended meaning, which makes one eager for the second, which is connected to it without the relation of whole and part. And since the indefinite noun is qualified or governing, it is valid to substitute it for a definite noun; the requirement of qualification applies only to a substitute of the whole, as Radi has stated explicitly. Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) read: "concerning fighting" (ʿan qitāl), which is also a substitute of inclusion, but with the governing verb repeated. Ikrimah read: "killing in it" (qatlin fīhi). Likewise in ﴿Say: fighting in it is great﴾, meaning great in burden of sin. In this there is confirmation of the prohibition of fighting in the sacred month, and that what was believed concerning his (ﷺ) making it lawful to fight in it is false, and what occurred from his companions (peace be upon him) was an error of ijtihad, for which he is pardoned — indeed, whoever strives and errs has one reward, as in the hadith. Most scholars hold that this ruling was abrogated (mansukh) by His saying — glorified is He —: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾. For the sacred months here are specific months in which the polytheists were permitted to travel freely, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾. It is not meant by them the sacred months of every year. Thus restricting by them indicates that killing them after their passing is commanded in all places and times, and this is the abrogation of the specific by the general. Our masters of the Hanafi school say this. As for the Shafi'is, they say that the specific, whether it precedes the general or follows it, specifies it, because the general is in their view probable (zanni), and the probable does not oppose the certain (qat'i). Al-Imam (al-Razi) said: "What I hold is that the verse does not indicate the prohibition of fighting absolutely in the sacred month, because fighting in it is an indefinite noun within an affirmative context, so it does not generalise; therefore there is no need then to say abrogation." It was objected that it is general, because it is qualified by a general attribute or by the context. Even if this is granted, fighting the polytheists is certainly intended, because fighting the Muslims is forbidden absolutely without restriction to the sacred months. In reply: we do not grant that it is qualified, since the prepositional phrase may be an adverbial complement (zarf laghw); and even if the generality of the attribute is granted, it is rather specified by fighting occurring in the specific sacred month. The attribute which indicates generality is the attribute whose generality equals the generality of the genus, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is no creature on the earth nor a bird that flies with its wings﴾, and the poet's saying: "And you do not see the lizard creeping in it." That the original principle is correspondence of the answer to the question is an indication of specificity. And that the intended meaning is fighting the polytheists in its generality is not granted; for the discussion concerns specific fighting. Even if its generality in the question is granted, we do not grant its generality in the answer, based on what al-Raghib mentioned: that an indefinite noun mentioned, when mentioned again, is repeated as definite, as in: "You asked me about a man, and the man is such and such." So its indefiniteness here is an indication that it is not every fighting that has this ruling, for the fighting of the Prophet (ﷺ) against the people of Makkah did not have this ruling. He (peace be upon him) said: "A part of a day was made lawful for me." As for the prohibition of fighting Muslims absolutely, what is wrong with it is not hidden, for fighting the rebels (ahl al-baghy) is lawful though they are Muslims. So the fair view is that saying abrogation is not necessary. Yes, it is possible, and Ibn Abbas, the interpreter of the Qur'an, said so, as al-Dahhak related from him. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Sufyan al-Thawri that he was asked about this verse and said: "This is something abrogated, and there is no harm in fighting in the sacred month." He differed from Ata' in this, for it is related from him that he was asked about fighting in the sacred month, and he swore by Allah, exalted is He, that it is not lawful for people to raid in the Haram or in the sacred month, unless they are fought in it, and he made that a continuing ruling until the Day of Resurrection; yet the Ummah today differs from it in all the lands.

﴿And hindering﴾, that is, prevention and turning away, ﴿from the way of Allah﴾, which is (Islam), as said by Muqatil; or (the Hajj), as said by Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi; or (the Hijrah), as has been said; or (all that brings the servant to Allah, exalted is He, of acts of obedience). The genitive is either for specific reference or for the genus. ﴿And disbelief in Him﴾, that is, in Allah or in His way. ﴿And the Sacred Mosque﴾: Abu Hayyan chose to conjoin it to the pronoun in the genitive although the preposition is not repeated; the Kufans, Yunus, al-Akhfash and Abu Ali permitted this, and it is common in the Arabic language in verse and prose. It was objected that there is no sense in disbelief in the Sacred Mosque, which follows from the conjunction; but there is discussion here, since disbelief may be attributed to objects by reason of the ruling connected with them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever disbelieves in the Taghut﴾. The qadi chose to supply a conjoined genitive governed by hindering, meaning: "and hindering from the Sacred Mosque those who circumambulate it, those who dwell in it, and those who bow and prostrate." It was objected that omitting the genitive and leaving the genitive-complement in its case is restricted to what is heard; it was answered by denying the absoluteness: in al-Tashil it is stated that when the genitive-complement follows a conjunction connected to it, or separated from it without preceding a genitive like the omitted one in form and meaning, it is permitted to omit the genitive and leave the complement in the genitive by analogy, as in: "The like of Zayd and his father say that", meaning "the like of his father", and: "Not every black thing is a date, nor every white thing fat." When one of the conditions is absent, it is restricted to what is heard; and in what we are discussing, a genitive like what was omitted has preceded. Al-Zamakhshari chose to conjoin it to "the way of Allah, exalted is He", and it was objected that conjoining ﴿and disbelief in Him﴾ to "and hindering" prevents that, since the conjunction is not placed before the relative clause in a conjunction to the relative clause. Two reasons were given for the validity of this: the first, that ﴿and disbelief in Him﴾ has the sense of hindering from the way of Allah, so the conjunction is by way of explanation, as if it were said: "and hindering from the way of Allah, I mean disbelief in Him and in the Sacred Mosque", and the intervening element is not foreign. The second, that the place of ﴿and disbelief in Him﴾ was after "and the Sacred Mosque", but it was placed first for the sake of great concern, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and there was none comparable to Him, any one﴾, where the proper order of speech would have been: "and there was no one comparable to Him." It is not hidden that the first reason is preferable, for placing it first does not remove the danger of separation and adds another danger. Al-Sajawandi chose conjunction to "the sacred month", and this was judged weak because the people did not ask about the Sacred Mosque. Abu al-Baqa' chose that it is connected to a verb omitted, indicated by hindering: that is, "and they hinder from the Sacred Mosque", as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and hindered you from the Sacred Mosque﴾. This was judged weak because omitting the preposition and leaving its governance is nearly found only in poetry. It was also said that the waw is for oath, placed in the midst of speech, and "as you see" that is far-fetched.

﴿And the expulsion of its people from it﴾, and they are the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers. They were its people because they are the ones who uphold its rights. It was also said that this is by way of their becoming its people in the future, after the conquest of Makkah.

﴿Is greater in the sight of Allah﴾: it is the predicate of the things enumerated from the major sins of the Quraysh. The form (af'al) is one in which the singular, plural and feminine are alike, and the comparative object is omitted; that is, greater than what the expedition did in error of ijtihad. The existence of the root of the act in that act is based on supposition.

[Page 110]

﴿And persecution is greater than killing﴾ is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) following what came before, for emphasis. It is conjoined to it as a universal rule is conjoined to a particular one. That is, what the Muslims are tempted and tormented by, so that they disbelieve, ﴿is greater in the sight of Allah﴾ than killing. What was mentioned earlier falls under this by primary inclusion. It has also been said that the intended meaning of *fitna* is disbelief, and the statement is a major premise (*kubra*) whose minor premise (*sughra*) is omitted. It is brought as a justification for the preceding ruling.

﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion﴾ is conjoined to *yas'alunaka* (they ask you), by the unity of the subject, if the questioners were the polytheists. Or it is a parenthetical clause (*mu'tarida*) if the questioners were others. The purpose is to inform of the continuing enmity of the disbelievers, by way of metonymy (*kinaya*), as a warning to the believers against them, and as an awakening for them to not care about agreeing with them in some matters. *Hatta* here expresses causation, and the meaning is: they continue to oppose you in order that they may turn you back from your religion. The words of the Exalted, ﴿if they are able﴾, are connected to what is in their possession. The expression with *in* (if) serves to make their ability seem remote, and that it is permissible only on the basis of supposition, as the impossible is supposed. The benefit of restricting it with a condition is to alert to the feebleness of their minds, and that the continuation of their enmity is an aimless act that does not lead to its purpose. It is not connected to *la yazaluna yuqatilunakum* (they will not cease fighting you), since there is no meaning in their persistence in enmity if they were able to do it, but it is unlikely.

Ibn 'Atiyya held that *hatta* indicates a limit (*ghaya*), and the restriction by a condition in that case serves to indicate that the limit is unlikely to occur. Restricting by a limit whose occurrence is impossible is common, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾. However, it may be said that the stating of the unlikelihood of the limit's occurrence is something that entails the non-cessation of enmity, and this is already conveyed by the opening of the statement. Saying that it is for emphasis is not a convincing position. Yes, it is possible to take it as a limit if *al-muqatala* (fighting) is understood in its literal sense, and the condition is connected to *la yazaluna* (they will not cease). Then the restriction indicates that their abandoning fighting at some times is due to their inability. However, the meaning in that case becomes trite, as is not hidden.

﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion﴾, by their misguidance and seduction of them, or from fear of their enmity, ﴿and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾, by not returning to Islam, ﴿those﴾ is a reference to the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) in view of its being characterized by what is in the clause of the relative, namely apostasy and dying upon disbelief, and the remoteness of that is implied, to indicate the remoteness of the rank of one who does that in evil and corruption. The plural and singular are used in view of the wording and the meaning. ﴿Their deeds have become void﴾, meaning their good deeds which they did in the state of Islam have become corrupt, like what was never done. It was said: the root of *habaṭ* is corruption that afflicts livestock from eating *ḥubāṭ*, which is a kind of harmful pasture. In *al-Nihaya* (Ibn al-Athir): Allah the Exalted nullified (*ahbata*) his deed, meaning He annulled it. It is said: his deed became void (*habita*) and was nullified (*uhbita*), and another nullified it. It derives from their saying: the beast became bloated (*habitat al-dabba habaṭan*), by the vowel of *fatḥa*, when it finds good pasture and overeats until it swells and dies. It is also read as *ḥabaṭat* with a *fatḥa*, and this is a dialectal form of it.

﴿In this world and the Hereafter﴾: because what they imagined is null and void, and the benefits of Islam are lost in the first, and the reward is forfeited in the second.

﴿And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever﴾ (2:217), like the rest of the disbelievers. Their earlier faith prior to apostasy will not avail them anything. Al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) used the verse as evidence that apostasy does not nullify deeds unless one dies upon it. This is based on the premise that if it nullified deeds unconditionally, the restriction by the words ﴿and dies while he is a disbeliever﴾ would have no benefit. The claim that its benefit is that the nullification of *all* deeds, so that he has no deed at all, depends on dying upon disbelief; so that even if he dies as a believer, his faith is not nullified, nor any deed accompanying it. That does not contradict the nullification of deeds prior to apostasy by mere apostasy, since what is meant by deeds in the verse is the deeds prior to apostasy, for there is no sense in the nullification of what was not done. Therefore this claim does not hold, as is not hidden. It has also been said that it is based on his making dying upon it a condition for nullification, and when the condition is absent, the conditioned thing is absent. This was objected to on the grounds that the grammatical and conditional *shart* does not have this meaning; rather at most it indicates causation and implication, and the absence of a cause or of what is implied does not necessitate the absence of the effect or what is entailed, since multiple causes are possible. And if it were a condition in this sense, there would be no conceivable disagreement regarding the implication (*mafhum*) of the condition.

Our Imam Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) held that mere apostasy necessitates nullification, based on the words of the Exalted: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in faith, his deed has become void﴾ (5:5). What al-Shafi'i used as evidence is not explicit in the intended meaning, because it is complete only if the clause ﴿and those...﴾ etc. is a concluding statement conjoined to the conditional clause. But if it were conjoined to the *jaza'* (apodosis), and the combination of nullification and eternal abiding in the Fire were consequent upon dying in apostasy, then we do not grant its completeness. Whoever holds this objects to Imam Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) that the necessary consequence for him is to apply the unrestricted (*mutlaq*) to the restricted (*muqayyad*), in acting upon both texts. It is answered that applying the unrestricted to the restricted is conditioned, according to him, upon the unrestricted and restricted being in the same ruling and the same event being unified, whereas here the difference is in the cause, so applying one to the other is not permitted, since the unrestricted may be a cause just like the restricted. The fruit of the disagreement, as is said, appears in one who prayed, then apostatized, then embraced Islam while the time is still present: according to Imam Abu Hanifa, it is obligatory for him to make up the prayer, contrary to al-Shafi'i. Likewise for the Hajj.

The Shafi'is differed regarding one who returned to Islam after apostasy: does his deed return to him with its reward or not? Some held the first view, except for companionship (*suhba*), for it returns stripped of reward. Most held the second, that his deeds return without reward, and there is no difference between companionship and other deeds. Perhaps this is the relied-upon position in the school, so understand.

﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾. Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani, in *al-Kabir*, related from the hadith of Jundub ibn Abd Allah that it was revealed concerning the expedition (*sariyya*, a small military detachment sent out without the Prophet himself), because it was feared that they, if they were safe from sin, would have no reward.

﴿And those who emigrated﴾, that is, they left their homelands. Its root is from *al-hajr* (abandonment), the opposite of *al-wasl* (union).

﴿and strove in the way of Allah﴾ to raise high His religion. The relative pronoun was repeated, although both refer to the same group, in order to magnify the status of emigration and jihad. Although both are in reality conditional upon faith, they are independent in the realization of hope, as if they were two separate matters. Emigration was placed before jihad because it precedes it in occurrence, just as faith precedes both.

﴿Those﴾, described with these sublime attributes, ﴿hope for the mercy of Allah﴾, that is, they hope that His mercy, glorified is He, will attach itself to them, or [hope for] His reward for their deeds. Among these deeds is that raid in the sacred month. Some scholars restricted it to this, based on what al-Zuhri related: "When Allah, exalted is He, relieved the people of that expedition of the distress they were in, they desired what was with Allah, exalted is He, of His reward. They said: 'O Prophet of Allah, do we hope that this raid will be one for which we are given the reward of the emigrants in the way of Allah, exalted is He?' Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse."

It is not hidden that the general meaning is more far-reaching in benefit. He affirmed for them hope rather than the attainment of what is hoped for, to indicate that deeds are not obligatory [upon Allah], since there is no entitlement through them, and they do not indicate with certainty the realization of reward, since there is no rational connection between them. Rather, it is a bounty from Him, exalted is He. Especially since what counts is the final outcome, so perhaps after that there may occur what causes the nullification [of deeds]. This indeed happened, and Allah, exalted is He, forbid, many times. Therefore one should not rely upon deeds.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful 228﴾. It is a concluding statement for what preceded and an emphasis upon it. He did not mention forgiveness in what preceded because hope for mercy indicates it. He placed the attribute of forgiveness first because averting harms takes precedence over attaining benefits.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 219 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They ask you about wine and gambling.﴾ Al-Wahidi said: "It was revealed concerning ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, Muʿadh ibn Jabal, and a group of the Ansar who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Give us a ruling about wine and gambling, for they take away the intellect and strip away wealth.' So Allah revealed this verse." In some narrations: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to Madinah while they were drinking wine and consuming gambling (maysir), so they asked him about that, and Allah revealed this verse." Some people said: "They have not been forbidden to us," so they continued drinking wine until ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf prepared a meal, invited some of the Companions, and brought them wine. They drank, became intoxicated, and when the time of the Maghrib prayer came, they put ʿAli (may Allah ennoble his face) forward to lead the prayer. He recited: "Say: O you disbelievers," and so on, with the "not" (la) omitted. Then Allah revealed: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾, and after that few would drink it. Then ʿUtban ibn Malik prepared a feast and invited men from among the Muslims, among them Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas. He had roasted for them the head of a camel, so they ate from it and drank wine until it overcame them. Then they boasted at that point
[p. 112]
and recited poetry to one another. Saʿd recited poetry containing satire of the Ansar and boasting of his own people. A man from the Ansar took the jawbone of the camel and struck Saʿd on the head with it, wounding him with a severe wound. Saʿd went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and complained to him about the Ansar. He said: "O Allah, make Your opinion on wine clear to us with a healing clarity." So Allah revealed: ﴿Indeed, wine and gambling...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ and that was a few days after the Battle of the Confederates. ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "We have desisted, O Lord."

And from ʿAli (may Allah ennoble his face): "If a single drop of it fell into a well, and a minaret were built on its spot, I would not call the adhan from it. And if it fell into a sea and then it dried up and grass grew in it, I would not let my animal graze on it." And from Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both): "If I put my finger into it, it would not follow me," and this is true faith and piety.

According to Imam Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him), khamr is that which is made from the juice of grapes when it boils, becomes intense, and froths up. It is called khamr because it veils the intellect (yukhammir al-ʿaql), that is, it covers it. From this comes khimar (a woman's head covering), because it covers her face, and al-khamir, who is one who conceals testimony. It was also said: it is called that because it is left covered until it becomes strong. From this comes the saying: "Cover your vessels" (khammiru aniyatakum), that is, cover them. It was also said: because it mixes with the intellect, and "disease mixed with him" (khamarahu dāʾ) means a disease that mingled with him. It was also said: because it is left until it ripens, from which comes "the dough fermented" (ikhtamara al-ʿajin), that is, it reached its ripeness. These statements are close in meaning. Based on them, khamr is a verbal noun used to mean the active or passive participle, and it is permissible for it to remain a verbal noun for emphasis.

The two Imams (Abu Yusuf and Muhammad) held that frothing is not a condition, and that intensification suffices, because the forbidden meaning is attained by it. Abu Hanifa's argument is that boiling is the beginning of intensity and its completion is by the frothing and settling of it, since by it the clear is distinguished from the turbid. Legal rulings are definitive, so they are attached to the final state, like the hadd punishment, declaring unbelief of one who deems it lawful, and the prohibition of sale. Some scholars followed the view of the two Imams regarding the prohibition of drinking, as a precaution. Moreover, applying the term khamr to other than what has been mentioned is metaphorical according to us, and this is what is known among the lexicographers. Some people said: it is literal for every intoxicant, based on what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, and al-Nasa'i recorded: "Every intoxicant is khamr."

Abu Dawud recorded: "The prohibition of khamr was revealed on the day it was revealed, and it is from five things: from grapes, dates, wheat, barley, and millet." And "khamr" is that which veils the intellect. Muslim recorded from Abu Hurayrah: "Khamr is from these two trees," and he pointed to the grapevine and the palm tree. al-Bukhari recorded from Anas: "Khamr was made unlawful when it was made unlawful, and very little of what is made from grape khamr existed, and most of our khamr was al-busr (unripe dates) and tamr (ripe dates)." It may be answered that the purpose of all of this is to explain the ruling and to teach that whatever intoxicates is forbidden like khamr, and this is what the station of guidance requires, not teaching the Arabic languages, especially since the addressees were at the utmost level of knowledge of them. As for what is said, that it is derived from the veiling of the intellect, which exists in every intoxicant, this does not require generality, and it does not contradict the term being specific in the earlier case, for al-najm (the star) is derived from "appearance," yet it is a specific name for the known star, not for everything that appears. This is very common. Some scholars took a middle position and said: khamr is literal in the Arabic language for that which comes from the juice of grapes when it becomes intoxicating, and when it is used for other than that, it is metaphorical. However, the Lawgiver made it literal for every intoxicant that resembles its linguistic referent, so in this it is a legal (shar'i) literal meaning, like prayer (salah), fasting (sawm), and zakat in their known legal senses. The disagreement is strong. Because of its strength, and because there is consensus on calling what is made from grapes khamr and not other intoxicants, they declared the one who deems the former lawful to be a disbeliever, but did not declare the one who deems the latter lawful to be a disbeliever. Rather, they said: the substance of the former is forbidden, not dependent on intoxication nor contingent on it. Whoever denies the prohibition of the substance and says that its intoxication alone is forbidden, because by it corruption occurs, has disbelieved by rejecting the Book, since it called it rijs (impurity) in it, and rijs is something whose substance is forbidden, so its large amount is forbidden even if it does not intoxicate, and likewise its small amount, even a single drop. The drinker is punished with the hadd regardless of amount. In the report: "Khamr was made unlawful for its substance," and in another narration: "by its substance; its little and its much are equal," and intoxication comes from every drink.

They said: cooking does not affect it, because cooking is for preventing the establishment of the prohibition, not for removing it after it has been established. However, one is not punished with the hadd for it unless one becomes intoxicated from it, based on the principle that the hadd
[p. 113]
applies only to the raw small amount, and this has been cooked. As for other than this: grape juice that is cooked until less than two-thirds of it evaporates, and this is the lightly cooked form, called al-baadhiq, and al-munassaf, which is what has lost half its volume by cooking, is forbidden according to us when it boils, becomes intense, and froths up, or when it becomes intense, according to the difference of opinion. al-Awza'i and most of the Mu'tazila (a theological school) said: it is permissible, because it is a good drink and is not khamr. Our argument is that it is thin, intoxicating, and exhilarating, and for this reason the sinners gather around it, so drinking it is prohibited to remove the corruption associated with it. As for naqi' al-tamr, which is the intoxicating (sukar), namely the raw liquid from dates' water, it is forbidden and reprehensible. Shurayk said it is permissible, because of the favor (imtinan) mentioned in the verse, and that it is not an impermissible thing. This is refuted by the consensus of the Companions, and the verse is to be understood as referring to the beginning, as the exegetes have agreed. It was also said: the verse is intended as a reproach, that is: do you take from it "intoxicant" (sakaran) and call it "good provision" (rizqan hasanan)? As for naqi' al-zabib, which is the raw liquid from raisin water, it is forbidden when it becomes intense and boils, and there is al-Awza'i's disagreement about it. Nabidh of raisins and dates, when each of them is cooked to the lightest cooking, is permissible, even if it becomes intense, provided that what is drunk from it is what one's opinion is inclined to consider as not intoxicating, without amusement or exhilaration, according to Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf. According to Muhammad and al-Shafi'i, it is forbidden. The nabidh of honey, figs, wheat, millet, barley, and grape juice when cooked until two-thirds of it evaporates is permissible according to the first two Imams (Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf). According to Muhammad and al-Shafi'i, it is also forbidden. The later scholars issued legal opinions according to Muhammad's view concerning all other drinks. Ibn Wahban mentioned that it is transmitted from all of them, and he versified that, saying:

"In our time it was chosen as a hadd, and they imposed divorce on whoever among those who drink an intoxicant made from grain becomes intoxicated.
It is transmitted from all of them, and Muhammad issued a legal opinion on the prohibition of what is little, and it is the one that is decided."

In my view, the truth from which one should not deviate is that the drink made from anything other than grapes, however it is made and whatever name it is given, when it intoxicates one who is not accustomed to it, is forbidden. Its little is like its much. Its drinker is punished with the hadd, divorce takes effect by it, and its impurity is severe.

In the two Sahih collections: "He (ﷺ) was asked about al-naqi', which is honey nabidh, and he said: 'Every drink that intoxicates is forbidden.'" Abu Dawud related: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade every intoxicant and every stupefier." It is authentic: "What its large amount intoxicates, its small amount is forbidden." In another hadith: "What the faraq (a measure) of it intoxicates, a handful of it is forbidden." The hadiths are mutually reinforcing in this. By my life, the gathering of sinners in our time upon drinking intoxicants other than khamr, and their desire for them, is far greater than their gathering upon drinking khamr and their desire for it by a great deal. They have given these drinks names such as "al-Anbariyya" and "al-Iksir" and similar ones, thinking that these names remove them from prohibition and make their drinking permissible for the community. But far, far is that, the matter is beyond what they suppose. Indeed we belong to Allah and to Him we return. Yes, the prohibition of these drinks is less than the prohibition of khamr, so that one who deems them lawful is not declared a disbeliever, as we mentioned earlier, because they are matters of independent reasoning (ijtihadiyya). If someone were to hold the view of declaring disbelief, there would remain in his hand today only a few people.

As for maysir: it is a mimi (with a mim prefix) verbal noun from "yasara," like al-mawʿid and al-marji'. It is said: "yasarta-hu" when you won against him in a game of chance (qamara). Its derivation is either from al-yusr (ease), because one takes the wealth with ease and facility, or from al-yasar (wealth/affluence), because it is taken from him. It was also said: from "yassaru al-shay'" when they divided it. The gambler is called yasir, because by means of that act he provides meat from the slaughtered camel. al-Wahidi said: from "yusr al-shay'" when it became obligatory, and the yasir is one who is obligated by means of the arrow. Its description is that they had ten arrows, which were al-azlam and al-aqlam: al-fadhdh, al-tawam, al-raqib, al-hils, al-nafis, al-musbil, al-mu'alla, al-manih, al-safih, and al-wagh. Each of them had a known share of a slaughtered camel, which they slaughtered and divided into twenty-eight parts, except the three, which are al-manih, al-safih, and al-wagh. The fadh had one share, the tawam had two shares, the raqib had three, the hils had four, the nafis had five, the musbil had six, and the mu'alla had seven. They placed them in a rababa (a bag/pouch) and put them in the hands of a trustworthy person, then
[p. 114]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 219 (part 2 of 2):

He would shake them up, and he would put his hand in and bring out, under the name of each man, an arrow from them. Whoever had drawn an arrow from the ones bearing shares (dhawat al-ansiba') took the share marked on that arrow. Whoever drew an arrow from those that have no share received nothing and had to pay the price of the whole camel (al-jazur) in addition to being deprived. They used to give those shares to the poor and did not eat from them, and they took pride in this and blamed whoever did not take part in it, calling him al-barim (the stingy one).

Al-Azhari (al-Azhari) transmitted another method for this, and he did not mention al-wagh among the names but mentioned others. What al-Zamakhshari and many others relied upon is what we have mentioned. Some people have put these names into verse, saying:

"All the arrows of the gamblers are ten,
so place them in inscribed pages.
They have shares (furud), and they have portions:
al-Fadhdh, al-Tawam, al-Raqib, al-Hils,
then al-Nafis follows them, then
after him al-Musbil, the sixth,
then al-Mu'alla, as its name indicates,
its owner is among the top gamblers.
Al-Wagh, al-Safih, and al-Manih are blanks,
and in what is seen there is no gain (raba)."

The ruling on this includes all kinds of gambling (qimar), such as backgammon (nard), chess (shatranj) and others, to the point that they included in it the games of children with walnuts, knucklebones (al-ka'ab), and drawing lots outside of division, and every kind of wagering and betting. From Ibn Sirin: "Everything in which there is risk (khatar) is from maysir (gambling)."

The meaning of the verse is: they ask you about what is in engaging in these two matters. It indicated the omitted word by His saying ﴿Say: In both of them﴾, since what is meant is, without doubt, in engaging in them. ﴿there is great sin﴾, in that engaging in them leads to what necessitates sin, which is abandoning what is commanded and doing what is forbidden. ﴿and benefits for people﴾, namely pleasure, joy, digestion of food, clearing of complexion, strengthening of virility, encouraging the coward, loosening the miser, and aiding the weak. These benefits remain both before and after the prohibition. Their removal after the prohibition is not something that reason accepts or that any evidence indicates. As for the report: "Allah, exalted is He, did not place the cure of my community in what has been forbidden to them," there is no proof in it upon close examination, as is not hidden.

﴿But their sin is greater than their benefit﴾, that is: the corruptions that arise from them are greater than the benefits expected from them. Among the corruptions of wine is the removal of the intellect ('aql), which is the most noble of human attributes. Since it is opposed to the most noble, it must be the basest of matters, for intellect is only called 'aql because it restrains (ya'qilu), that is, it prevents its possessor from the vices toward which he is naturally inclined. So when one drinks, that restraining intellect departs from vices, and habituation to them (ilf, which is the natural disposition) takes hold, so he commits them and increases in them. Perhaps he becomes a laughingstock for children until his intellect returns to him. Ibn Abi al-Dunya mentioned that he passed by a drunkard who was urinating with his hand and washing his face with it in the manner of one performing ablution, saying: "Praise be to Allah who made Islam a light and water a purifier." From al-Abbas ibn Mirdas: it was said to him in the Jahiliyyah: "Will you not drink wine? For it increases your warmth." He said: "I am not one who takes my ignorance in my hand and puts it into my belly, nor am I pleased that I should become the chief of a people and in the evening be their fool."

Among its corruptions is that it turns one away from the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, and from prayer, and that it generally causes enmity and hatred. Killing sometimes occurs among drinkers in a drinking gathering. Among its corruptions also is that when a person becomes accustomed to it, his inclination toward it grows strong, and parting from it and leaving it becomes almost impossible for him. It may also cause diseases that become the cause of his destruction. The physicians have mentioned many bodily harms from it, as is not hidden to whoever consults the books of medicine. In sum, even if there were nothing in it but the removal of the intellect and departure from the path of uprightness, that would be enough, for when the intellect is impaired all evil comes together. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Avoid wine, for it is the mother of all evils." It is not established that the prophets, peace be upon them, drank it at any time at all. From the corruptions of gambling (maysir) is that in it is the consuming of wealth by falsehood, and that it calls many gamblers to theft, the destruction of life, the neglect of dependents, the commission of ugly deeds and shameful vices, and hidden and open enmity. This is a matter that is observed, which none denies except one whom Allah, exalted is He, has blinded and deafened.

Because the verse indicates the greatness of the corruptions, some scholars held that it is what forbids wine, for when the corruption outweighs the benefit it requires the prohibition of the act. Some added to that that the verse informs that in them is "great sin," and sin (ithm) is either punishment or its cause, and neither of these is described except for what is forbidden. But the truth is that the verse is not explicit in prohibition, as Qatadah said, since one may say: "sin" means corruption, and the outweighing of corruption does not require the prohibition of the act but only its outweighing. From here the senior Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, drank it after its revelation, saying: "We only drink what benefits us," and they did not refrain until the verse of al-Ma'idah was revealed. It is the one that forbids it in several respects, as will come, Allah willing.

It was read as ﴿kathir﴾ ("much") with the letter thaa (ithm kathir). In placing "sin" first and describing it as great or much, and delaying the mention of benefits while restricting them to people, there is an indication of the predominance of the first, which is not hidden.

Ubayy read: ﴿and their sin is nearer than their benefit﴾.

﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾. Ibn Ishaq reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "That some Companions were commanded to spend in the way of Allah, exalted is He, and they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'We do not know what this spending is which we have been commanded to do with our wealth, so what should we spend from it?' Then it was revealed." Before that, a man would spend his wealth until he had nothing left to give in charity, nor anything to eat until someone gave him charity.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported through the route of Aban from Yahya that it reached him: "Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'labah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we have slaves and dependents, so what should we spend from our wealth?' Then Allah revealed this verse." It is connected to what they asked before it, a narrative joined to a narrative. It was also said that it was revealed concerning Amr ibn al-Jamuh, similarly. It seems that he was first asked about what is spent and the recipient, then he was asked about the manner of spending, by the context of the answer. So the meaning is: they ask you about the attribute of what they spend. ﴿Say: the surplus (al-'afw)﴾, that is, its attribute is that it be surplus. Thus the word ma is used to ask about the attribute, as one says: "What is Zayd?" and it is answered: "Generous," though this usage is rare. The root of 'afw is the opposite of effort (juhd), and for this reason easy, smooth ground that is easy to walk on is called 'afw. What is meant by it is what is not noticeable in wealth. In a report from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: the excess over the dependents. From al-Hasan: what does not cause hardship.

Al-Shaykhan, Abu Dawud, and al-Nasa'i reported from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best charity is that which is given out of richness, and begin with those you support." Ibn Khuzaymah also reported from him: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The best charity is that which leaves wealth behind (ma abqat ghina), and the upper hand is better than the lower hand, and begin with those you support. A wife says: 'Spend on me or divorce me,' and your slave says: 'Spend on me or sell me,' and your child says: 'To whom will you leave me?'"

Ibn Sa'd reported from Jabir, who said: "Abu Husayn al-Sulami came with an amount of gold the size of a dove's egg and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I found this in a mine, so take it, it is a charity, and I have no other than it.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned away from him. Then he came to him from his right side and said the same to him, and he turned away from him. Then he came to him from his left side, and he turned away from him. Then he came to him from behind, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took it and threw it at him, and if it had hit him it would have hurt him or wounded him. Then he said: 'One of you brings what he owns and says: "This is a charity," then sits begging from people. The best charity is that which is given out of richness, and begin with those you support.'"

Abu Amr read with ra' (al-raf') by supposing a subject, so that ﴿what they should spend﴾ is a subject and predicate. The rest read with the accusative (al-nasb) by supposing a verb, and ﴿what﴾ is the object of ﴿they spend﴾, so that the answer matches the question.

﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾, that is, in the same manner as He made clear that surplus is better than effort, because it is more lasting for the heart and more beneficial in the Hereafter. So the indicated matter is what is understood from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Say: the surplus﴾. The use of the far demonstrative form despite its nearness is because it is something mentioned earlier in meaning. It is also possible that what is indicated is everything mentioned from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿They ask you what they should spend﴾, since there is no specifying factor and generality is more beneficial. Nearness only gives preference to the nearer over others. Making the indicated matter His saying, mighty is His majesty: ﴿But their sin is greater than their benefit﴾ is, as is not hidden, far-fetched. The kaf is in the accusative position as an attribute of an omitted word. The lam in ﴿the verses﴾ is generic; that is: Allah makes clear to you the verses containing the rulings with a clarification like this clarification, either by sending them down clear in indication, or by removing their generality through another verse, or by an explanation from the Messenger (ﷺ).

The apparent expectation would be to say ﴿kadhalikum﴾ to match ﴿lakum﴾, but it was made singular, considering a tribe or a group, or a collective word singular in form but plural in meaning, for lightness, because the sign of address is very often attached to the demonstrative. It was also said that the singular is to indicate that what is meant is everyone who receives the speech, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We pardoned you after that﴾. But it is objected that this would require multiple addresses in one speech without conjunction, and that is not permitted, as al-Radi stated. ﴿So that you may reflect (la'allakum tatafakkarun)﴾, that is: upon the verses, so that you may derive the rulings from them and understand the interests and benefits attached to them. With this estimation, it is good that hoping for reflection is a purpose for making the verses clear.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 220:**

﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾ That is, in their affairs, so that you take what is best for you in both, and avoid what harms you and does not benefit you, or what harms you more than it benefits you. The prepositional phrase, after supplying the omitted noun (*mudaf*), is connected to *tatafakkarun* ("you may reflect"), after it has been restricted by the first meaning. It was also said that it may be connected to *yubayyinu* ("He makes clear"), meaning: He makes the signs clear to you concerning matters related to the affairs of this world and the Hereafter. ﴿So that you may reflect﴾ The reflection is placed first for emphasis. There is a problem with this: it contradicts the apparent structure of the sentence, and the hope for the very occurrence of reflection is not the purpose of the general clarification. Therefore, there must be a general reflection, and the meaning becomes "so that you may reflect upon the affairs of this world and the Hereafter." Repetition in this reading is weak. It was also said that the phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of the signs, meaning: He clarifies them for you as existing in these two (worlds), that is, clarifying your conditions related to them. The weakness of this is not hidden. Some people did not take *li-yatafakkarun* as a connected element, and instead connected the mentioned phrase to *bayyana* ("He made clear"), meaning: Allah made the signs clear to you so that you would reflect on this world and its passing, and on the Hereafter and its permanence, and so that you would know the superiority of the Hereafter over this world. This is what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), Qatadah and al-Hasan.

﴿And they ask you about orphans﴾ This is coordinated with what precedes it, having the same structure. Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir and a group reported from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "When Allah revealed ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾ and ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans...﴾ (4:10), those who had an orphan in their care went off, separated their food from his food and his drink from theirs. They began to set aside some of his food for him, and it would be kept for him until he ate it or it spoiled, and then they would throw it away. This became difficult for them, so they mentioned it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then this verse was revealed." The meaning is: they ask you about taking charge of the affairs of orphans, or about managing their property, or about their affairs and how they should deal with them. ﴿Say: Setting things right for them is good﴾ That is, mixing with them in a manner that results in their betterment, or the betterment of their property through growing and preserving it, is better than keeping away from them. In the first possibility there is the placing of the goal of a thing in the position of the thing itself.

﴿And if you mix with them, they are your brothers﴾ This is coordinated with the preceding statement. The intended purpose is to encourage mixing, provided it is conditioned on setting things right in general. That is: if you mix with them in food, drink, housing and intermarriage, you will render what is fitting for you, because they are your brothers, that is, brothers in religion. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) read it this way. 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from him: "Mixing is that he drinks from your milk and you drink from his milk, he eats from your bowl and you eat from his bowl, and he eats from your dates and you eat from his dates." Abu Muslim al-Isfahani preferred that the intended meaning of mixing is intermarriage. This is supported by what al-Zajjaj transmitted, that they used to wrong orphans by marrying ten of them and consuming their property. Therefore, Allah made the matter of orphans so strict upon them that they feared marrying them. [Page 117] Then this verse was revealed, and He (glory be to Him) informed them that setting things right for them is the best of things, and that mixing with them through marriage, while being careful to set things right, is permissible. It is also argued that, in this manner, there is *ta'sis* (establishing a new ruling, ta'sis: introducing a new meaning rather than merely repeating a known one), since mixing in the sense of partnership was already understood from what came before. It is also argued that intermarriage is a form of mixing with the orphan himself, unlike the other forms. It is further argued that the connection with His saying ﴿they are your brothers﴾ is then clearly evident, because this is conditioned upon Islam: if the orphan is a polytheist, it is obligatory to be careful to set things right in mixing with him except regarding intermarriage. It is also argued that on this basis the forthcoming prohibition is connected to what precedes it, as if it were said: the recommended mixing is only with orphans who are your brothers; if the orphan is one of the polytheists, then do not do this. It is not hidden that what al-Zajjaj transmitted is weaker than glass (*zujaj*, the same root as the name al-Zajjaj); for this is not established in the reports on the occasions of revelation in any book that may be relied upon, and al-Zajjaj and his like are not among the masters of this discipline. It is also argued that *ta'sis* does not contradict the encouragement of mixing, since the people had avoided it entirely, and that the general sense of "mixing" is more apparent than restricting it to mixing one's own self, and that the connection and coherence are achieved by including intermarriage within the general sense of mixing.

﴿And Allah knows the corrupter﴾ in their affairs through mixing ﴿from the one who sets things right﴾ through it. Then He will reward each according to his deed or intention. Thus, in the verse there is a warning, and it also contains a promise. He placed the corrupter first to emphasize the fear that it would instil in him. The definite article (*al-*) in both places is for previous reference (*'ahd*, a definite article referring to something already known), and it was also said that it is for totality (*istighraq*, the all-inclusive use of the definite article). The known (referent) enters at first instance. The word *min* ("from") indicates distinction, and the verb *ya'lamu* ("knows") implicitly carries the meaning of *yumayyizu* ("distinguishes"), which is why it governs *min*.

﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have put you in distress﴾ That is, He would have constricted you and would not have permitted you to mix with them. Or He would have made what you took from the property of orphans a destructive ruin (*mubiqan*). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him). The root meaning of *i'nat* is imposing upon someone a hardship that does not relieve a burden. It is said: "*'anita al-'azmu 'anatan*" when a bone suffers weakness or a fracture after having been set. The object of the will (*mashi'ah*) is omitted because the answer (*jawab*) indicates it. In this there is an indication of the perfection of His kindness and mercy (glory be to Him), in that He did not condition His will upon what would be difficult for us even in its wording. And within the sentence there is a reminder of His favour toward the guardians of orphans.

﴿Indeed Allah is Mighty﴾ overpowering in His command, such that no matter, among those matters of which putting you in distress is one, can overcome Him ﴿Wise﴾ acting in His actions according to what wisdom requires and what capacity, which is the basis of obligation, can bear. This clause is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) and a confirmation of what has preceded concerning the ruling of negation and affirmation. That is: if He had willed, He would have put you in distress, because He is Mighty, but He did not will it, because He is Wise. As al-Kiya said, in the verse there is evidence for those who permitted combining the property of the guardian with the property of the orphan, and disposing of it through buying and selling, and entrusting it on the basis of *mudarabah* (a profit-sharing partnership), when this accords with setting things right. There is also evidence in it for the permissibility of *ijtihad* (independent legal reasoning) in the rulings of new events, since the setting-right contained in the verse is only known through *ijtihad* and the predominance of probable opinion. And there is evidence in it that there is no harm in disciplining an orphan and striking him gently in order to set him right. The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when He (glory be to Him) mentioned the question about wine and gambling, and abstaining from them was a means of preserving and growing wealth, this fittingly corresponded to considering the condition of the orphan. The common element between the two verses is that abstaining from wine and gambling sets right the condition of the people themselves, and considering the affairs of orphans sets right others who are unable to set themselves right. Whoever abandons the former and does the latter has combined benefit for himself and benefit for others.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 221 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe.﴾ Al-Wahidi and others narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a man from the Ghani tribe, called Murthad ibn Abi Murthad, an ally of the Banu Hashim, to Makkah to bring out some Muslims held there as captives. When he arrived there, a woman called 'Anaq heard of him. She had been his mistress in the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance). When he became Muslim, he turned away from her. She came to him and said: 'Woe to you, O Murthad, will you not come together with me?' He said to her: 'Islam has come between me and you and has forbidden it to us. But if you wish, I will marry you.' She said: 'Yes.' He said: 'When I return to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I will ask his permission about that, and then I will marry you.' She said to him: 'Are you not going to be a tyrant?' Then she sought help against him, and they beat him severely, then they let him go. When he had finished his need in Makkah, he returned to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and informed him of what had happened to him and of 'Anaq, and what he had suffered because of her. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, is it lawful for me to marry her?' – and in another narration: 'She pleases me' – so this verse was revealed.'" Al-Suyuti refuted this by saying that this is not the cause of the revelation of this verse, but it is rather the cause of the revelation of the verse of Surat al-Nur: ﴿The fornicator does not marry except a fornicatress or a polytheist.﴾

Al-Suddi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that this verse was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah, who had a black female slave. He became angry with her and slapped her. Then he regretted it and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of her story. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "What is she, O 'Abd Allah?" He said: "She, O Messenger of Allah, fasts, prays, performs wudu' well, and testifies that there is no god but Allah and that you are His Messenger." He said: "O 'Abd Allah, she is a believer." 'Abd Allah said: "By the One who sent you with the truth as a prophet, I will certainly free her and marry her." He did so. Some Muslims criticised him, saying: "He married a slave woman?" They wished to marry into the polytheists and to have them marry into their own families out of desire for their lineages. So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And do not marry…﴾ the verse.'"

It is read with a fatha and with a damma on the letter ta' (i.e., *tankihu* and *tunkihu*), and this is narrated from al-A'mash. That is: do not marry them (yourselves), or do not give them in marriage to Muslims. Many scholars took (*al-mushrikat*, "polytheistic women") to refer to all except the People of the Book (*kitabiyyat*). According to them, marrying the women of the People of the Book is permissible, based on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not...﴾ and ﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would like...﴾. The conjunction (*'atf*) requires difference. Ibn Humayd narrated from Qatadah: the intended meaning of "polytheistic women" is the polytheistic women of the Arabs who have no scripture. And from Hammad, who said: I asked Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i) about marrying a Jewish or Christian woman, and he said: "There is no harm in it." I said: "Does Allah not say: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women﴾?" He said: "That refers only to the Magian women and the women who worship idols."

Others held that it includes the women of the People of the Book. It was said: because whoever denies the prophethood of our Prophet (peace be upon him) has denied his miracle and attributed it to someone other than Allah the Exalted, and this is exactly shirk (associating partners with Allah). Also because shirk is set in opposition to faith later on. Also because Allah the Exalted has applied the term shirk to the People of the Book, saying: ﴿The Jews say, "Ezra is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah"…﴾ until His words, glorified is He: ﴿from what they associate.﴾

Al-Bukhari and al-Nahhas in his *Nasikh* narrated from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that when he was asked about a man marrying a Christian or Jewish woman, he said: "Allah the Exalted has forbidden polytheistic women to the Muslims, and I know of no shirk greater than that a woman says: 'Her lord is Jesus,' or 'he is one of the servants of Allah the Exalted.'" This is the view of the Imamiyyah and some of the Zaydiyyah. They considered the verse of al-Ma'idah: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture﴾ abrogated by this verse, by the abrogation of the specific by the general (*naskh al-khass bi'l-'amm*). Although that verse came later in recitation, it came earlier in revelation. There is a consensus that nothing from Surat al-Ma'idah has been abrogated, which is forbidden. In *al-Itqan*: From al-Ma'idah is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Nor the sacred month﴾, which is abrogated by the permission of fighting in it. And the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾, which is abrogated by His words, glorified is He: ﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾. And His words, the Exalted: ﴿or two others from among you﴾, which is abrogated by His words, mighty is His majesty: ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you.﴾

The well-known view on which practice rests is that this verse has been abrogated by what is in al-Ma'idah, according to what the apparent meaning requires. Abu Dawud in his *Nasikh* narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said concerning ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women﴾: "It abrogated from this the marriage of the women of the People of the Book. He made them lawful to the Muslims, and forbade Muslim women to their men." The same was narrated from al-Hasan and Mujahid. This is the view taken by the Hanafis and the Shafi'is, who say it is specification (*takhsis*) not abrogation (*naskh*). The root of the disagreement is that restricting a general statement by an independent statement is specification according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, but abrogation according to us.

﴿And a believing slave woman is better than a polytheist, even if she pleases you.﴾ This is a justification (*ta'lil*) for the prohibition, and an encouragement to connect with believing women. It begins with the *lam* of initiation, which resembles the *lam* of oath in conveying emphasis, as an exaggeration in urging restraint. The original form of *amah* is (*amwa*); its final letter was deleted without analogy, and the feminine *ha'* was substituted for it. That its final letter is a *waw* is shown by its return in the plural, as in the words of the poet:

*"As for the female slaves, they will not call me a son,*
*when the sons of the Amwan claim descent with shame."*

And its appearance in the verbal noun: one says, "She is a slave woman clearly in slavehood (*umuwwah*)," and "She acknowledged him in slavehood (*umuwwah*)." Is its pattern *fu'lah* with a sukun on the 'ayn, or *fa'alah* with a fatha on it? There are two views; most scholars chose the second. It is pluralised as (*amm*), and in use this is preferred to *ima'*. Its origin is (*a'mu*) with two hamzas: the first is fatha-vowelled and additional, the second is sukun and is the first radical of the word. The *waw* came to stand as a final letter after a damma in a declinable noun, and there is no parallel for this, so it was changed into a *ya'*, and the damma before it became a kasra so that the *ya'* could be sound. So the noun came to be of the type of (*ghazin* and *qadin*). Then the second hamza was changed into an *alif* because it was sukun after another fatha-vowelled hamza, so they became (*amm*). Its declension is like *qadin*.

The apparent meaning is that by *amah* is meant what is the opposite of a free woman (*hurrah*). The occasion of revelation supports this, because the reproach was directed at one who married a slave woman, and the encouragement was to marry a free polytheist woman. So in the verse there is a preference of a believing slave woman over a polytheist woman absolutely, even if she is free. From this one knows the preference of a free woman over her, by the stronger reasoning (*bi'l-tariq al-ula*). Furthermore, preference requires that there be good in the association, so either "good" means worldly benefit, which is shared between them, or it is in the sense of: ﴿The companions of the Garden on that day are better in their resting place.﴾

It was also said that by *amah* is meant a woman, whether free or owned, for all people are the servants and bondwomen of Allah the Exalted. It should not be taken as referring to the female slave, because it is necessary to supply the qualified noun for "polytheist". If one supplies (*amah*) by the context, it does not convey the superiority of a believing slave woman over a free polytheist woman. If one supplies (*hurrah*, free woman) or (*imra'ah*, woman), it is contrary to the apparent meaning. What is mentioned in the occasion of revelation is marriage to a slave woman after her manumission. A slave woman after manumission is a free woman, and one does not call her "slave woman" by way of metaphor of what she was. The truth is that *amah* in the sense of female slave is what is understood immediately, and that the supplied qualified noun for "polytheist" is general, and that its being contrary to the apparent meaning is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Even if one grants this, it bears a shared obligation of argument (*mushtarak al-ilzam*). Perhaps committing this at the end is easier than committing it at the first moment, for it is like removing a boot before reaching water. What is in the occasion of revelation is supported, not proven. It has been said about it: 'Abd Allah married a slave woman, whether this is true or false. So the meaning is: ﴿And a believing slave woman﴾, with her lowliness of servitude and her lack of worth, ﴿is better﴾ than one who is characterised by polytheism, together with her nobility of freedom and elevation of rank, ﴿even if she pleases you﴾, by her beauty, her wealth, and all else that causes desire for her. Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Majah narrated from Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Do not marry women for their beauty, for their beauty may ruin them; and do not marry them for their wealth, for their wealth may make them rebellious; but marry them for their religion, for a black slave woman, slit-eared, who is religious, is better." Al-Shaykhan narrated from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "A woman is married for four things: for her wealth, for her lineage, for her beauty, and for her religion. So win the one with religion; may your hands be rubbed with dust."

The *waw* is for the state (*hal*), even if merely for the sake of supposition, free of the meaning of a condition (*shart*). For this reason it does not need an apodosis (*jaza'*), and the supposition is that her being pleasing is in beauty and the like. Al-Jirmi said: the *waw* is for conjunction to an implied element, meaning: "[even if] she did not please you, and [even if] she pleased you." The apodosis of the condition is omitted, indicated by the preceding clause. Al-Radi said: it is parenthetical (*i'tiradiyyah*), occurring in the middle and end of speech. In all these views, the ruling is affirmed in the opposite of the condition by the stronger reasoning, so that it is established in all suppositions.

Some scholars used the verse as evidence for the permissibility of marrying a believing slave woman while one has the means to marry a free woman (*tawl al-hurrah*). Al-Kiya objected that the verse does not concern marrying slave women; rather it is a deterrent from marrying a free polytheist woman, because the Arabs by their nature were averse to marrying slave women, so it was said to them: "If you are averse to the slave woman, then the polytheist is more deserving of aversion." This is open to question. In *al-Bahr*: the implication of the qualifier requires that it is not permissible to marry a disbelieving slave woman, whether a People of the Book or otherwise. As for intercourse with her by right of ownership (*milk al-yamin*), it is permissible absolutely.

﴿And do not give polytheistic men [in marriage] until they believe.﴾ That is: do not give Muslim women in marriage to disbelievers, whether the disbeliever is one of the People of the Book or otherwise, and whether the believing woman is a slave or a free woman. So *tunkihu* with a damma on the ta' only, and fatha is not possible, otherwise it would have to be: "and let them not marry polytheists." It has been used as evidence for the requirement of a guardian (*wali*) in marriage absolutely, which is contrary to our school. In the indication of the verse for this there is obscurity, because the intended meaning is the prohibition of performing this act and enabling it, and all Muslims are guardians in this matter.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 2, verse 221 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And a believing slave[^1] — despite the humiliation of being owned — ﴾ is ﴿better than a polytheist﴾ despite the honour attributed to being an owner, ﴿even though you admire them﴾ for what they have of the causes of desire. ﴿Those﴾, namely the aforementioned polytheist men and women, ﴿invite to the Fire﴾, meaning to disbelief, which leads to it, either by speech or by affection and close association. Therefore, marrying them is not fitting. If it is said: just as the disbelievers invite the believers to the Fire, so the believers invite them to Paradise by one of two means. The answer is that the purpose of the verse is that the believer must be cautious of what harms him in the Hereafter, must not hover around the boundaries of that, and must avoid what is doubtful, while the self (*nafs*) and Satan assist one another toward what leads to the Fire. Human natures had become accustomed to this in the pre-Islamic period. This was said by some of the verifiers (*muhaqqiqun*). The clause "and..." (*wa al-jumlah*) and so on is a causal clause explaining the superiority of the believing men and believing women over the polytheist men and polytheist women. ﴿And God invites﴾ through the believers those close to them ﴿to Paradise and forgiveness﴾, that is, to the true belief and the righteous deed that lead to them both. The mention of Paradise before forgiveness, along with their saying, "clearing away (*takhliyah*)[^2] takes precedence over adorning (*tahliyah*)", is for the sake of matching the Fire, which is mentioned first. ﴿By His leave﴾ is connected to "invites": that is, He invites to that while accompanied by His success, which includes guiding believers to goodness for those close to them. Thus, they deserve to be joined in marriage.

﴿And He makes His signs clear to the people, that they may remember﴾, so that they may take heed, or recall what they already know, on the basis that the knowledge of God, exalted is He, is embedded in minds. The clause is a concluding remark (*tadhyil*) to the advice and guidance. The "and" is either parenthetical (*i'tiradiyyah*) or conjunctive. The previous verse ended with "they reflect" (*yatafakkarun*), because it was explaining rulings, interests, benefits, and the desire for them, which are the domain of the intellect's operation and clarification for believers, so reflection was appropriate. This verse ends with "they remember" (*yatadhakkarun*), because it is a concluding remark to the report of the invitation to Paradise and the Fire, which cannot be known except through transmission (*naql*), and the clarification is for all people, so remembrance was appropriate.

Some have assumed an elided word in the verse, meaning "the party of God" (*fariq Allah*) or "His friends" (*awliya'uh*), who are the believers. The qualifying noun was omitted and the noun in the genitive was put in its place, to honour them. It was objected that the pronoun in the clause conjoined to the predicate refers to God, exalted is He, so this entails a shift of reference without any reason for it. The answer is that the reason for it is that this clause makes the earlier superiority explained, and the explanation does not appear without the elided word. Likewise, the fitting connection with His words, "by His leave," does not appear without that elision, since restricting His invitation with "by His leave" would have little benefit under any interpretation of "leave." As for the shift of reference, it is easy, since after the genitive has been put in place of the qualified noun for honour, the verb of the first is made, in form, the verb of the second, so the pronouns are harmonious, as in *al-Kashshaf*, though its flaw is not hidden. In any case, this is preferable to what has been said: that what is meant by "God invites" is that He invites to that through the tongue of His Messenger, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, so that accepting his call would require marrying his close relatives. For although this reading yields the unity of reference in the two conjoined clauses, which are predicates, it loses the causal explanation, the fine contrast between it and "Those invite to the Fire," and likewise the subtlety of the restriction, as is not hidden.
