Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 222 (part 1 of 2):

﴿They ask you concerning menstruation.﴾ Imam Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others related from Anas, may Allah be pleased with them, that: "The Jews, when a woman among them menstruated, would expel her from the house, would not eat with her, would not drink with her, and would not have intercourse with her in the houses. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about that, and Allah revealed this verse. The Prophet (ﷺ) then said: 'Have intercourse with them in the houses, and do everything except marriage (al-nikah).'" And from al-Suddi: the one who asked about that was Thabit ibn al-Dahdah, may Allah be pleased with him. The sentence is conjoined (ma'tufah) to what preceded it of its kind, and the manner of its connection to what came before is that when He forbade marrying polytheists and encouraged marrying the people of faith, He explained a great ruling among the rulings of marriage, namely the ruling on marriage during menstruation. Perhaps the narration of these three questions with conjunction (bil-'atf) is because all of them occurred at one time, a customary (urfi) matter, namely the time of the question about wine and gambling. So it is as if it were said: "They gather for you between asking about these two and asking about such-and-such." The narration of the others without conjunction is because they occurred at different times, so each was an independent question, and the combining of them was not intended; rather the report concerns each one separately. For this reason He did not bring the waw between them. The author of al-Intisaf, in explaining conjunction and its omission, said: the first of the conjoined items specified the first of the unconjoined ones, but its answer came first with the mention of the disbursement (al-masrif), because it is more important, although the thing asked about was actually the spending itself and not the manner of its disbursement. Then, since the first answer did not explicitly state the thing asked about, the question was repeated so that they would answer explicitly about what was asked, namely the surplus (al-'afw). So it was necessary, when conjoining it, that it be linked to the first. As for the second question of the paired group, it concerned the conditions of orphans and whether it is permitted to mix with them in maintenance and lodging, so it had a connection with the spending, in that if they mixed with them they would spend on them; therefore it was conjoined to the question about spending. As for the third question, since it included withdrawing from menstruating women, it was apt to conjoin it to what preceded it, because it contained a statement of what they used to do of withdrawing from orphans. If the unconjoined questions are considered, you will find no proximity or connection between them at all, since the first of them is about spending, the second about fighting in the sacred month, and the third about wine and gambling, and the disparity and discontinuity between them is obvious. So they were mentioned thus, unconnected, disjoined, not linked to one another. This is one of the wonders of eloquence that you will not find except in the Mighty Book.

I do not find the heart at rest with this, as is not hidden from one who has thoroughly grasped what we have mentioned, so reflect. And al-mahid, as al-Zajjaj said, and most agree: it is the verbal noun (masdar) of "hadat al-mar'ah tahidu haydan wa mahadan," so it is like al-maji' and al-mabit. Its root meaning is flowing; it is said: "the torrent flowed and overflowed (haada al-sayl wa fada)." Al-Azhari said: from this comes "hawd" (basin) for the pond, because the water flows (yahidu) into it, i.e. it flows. The Arabs insert a waw in place of a ya', because they are of one kind. It was also said that here it is a noun of place, and this is attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Al-Wahidi related from Ibn al-Sikkit that when the verb is of the three-letter root, such as kala yakilu and hada yahidu, the noun of place from it is with kasra, and the verbal noun from it is with fatha. Others related from others the option (takhyir) in such a case; indeed it was said that both kasra and fatha are permitted in the noun of time, the noun of place and the verbal noun. And what is attributed to al-Turjuman, and what al-Imam chose, requires an ellipsis in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Say: it is an injury (adha)﴾, i.e. a place of injury; and likewise it requires considering time in His saying, glorified be He: ﴿So keep away from women during menstruation (al-mahid)﴾, because of the awkwardness of our saying "keep away in the place of menstruation." Although al-Imam chose it and said the meaning is: keep away from the places of menstruation. Adha is the verbal noun of "adhahu yu'dhihi, idhan and idha'an," and it is not said in the well-known usage "i'dha'." Its application to menstruation is by way of intensification (mubalaghah), and the meaning intended by it is what is loathsome (al-mustaqdhar), and Qatadah interpreted it so, and it was used in that sense by way of metonymy (kinayah). The intended meaning of keeping away from women is abstaining from intercourse with them, as the end of the verse indicates. The verb was ascribed to the essence (al-dhat) for intensification, as in His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun for complete care for its matter, such that nothing else could be imagined at all. It may be said: there is no such placement; and the matter of repetition (haditha al-i'adah) is largely a matter of likelihood. Rather, what we have pointed to as requiring consideration is to be considered, in what we have pointed to as not requiring it, because the relation is weak and the motive for estimating (al-taqdir) is strong, and not estimating is preferable. It was described as an injury and the ruling was connected to it with the fa' (so), and the answer was not confined to the command, in order to indicate that it is the cause ('illah), and a ruling given with its cause is more effective on the soul.

﴿And do not approach them until they become clean (yathurna).﴾ This is an affirmation of the preceding ruling, because the command to keep away entails a prohibition of approaching, and vice versa; so each of them is affirmed, even if they differ in meaning. Therefore one of them is conjoined to the other. It also contains a statement of its limit, for restricting the withdrawal by His saying, exalted be He: ﴿in the menstruation﴾, and its being consequent upon its being an injury, indicates restricting the prohibition to that time, and the cessation of it after that is understood by reason, though the wording does not explicitly indicate it, unlike ﴿until they become clean﴾. The limit is the cessation of the blood according to Imam Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him. If the cessation occurs at the completion of the maximum period of menstruation, approach becomes lawful merely by the cessation; if it is for less than that, it is not lawful except by ghusl or what is in its ruling, namely the passing of the time of a prayer. According to the Shafi'is, the limit is ghusl after the cessation. They say that this is explicitly indicated by the reading of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in the transmission of Ibn 'Ayyash: (yattahharna), with shaddah, i.e. (yatatahharna), and what is meant is that they perform ghusl. Not because ghusl is the literal meaning of tathhir, as some of their expressions seem to imply, since its use for other than ghusl is common in the glorious speech and the hadiths, as is not hidden from the careful researcher; but because the intensive form (sighat al-mubalaghah) conveys complete purity, and complete purity of women from menstruation is ghusl. So when the intensive reading indicated that the limit of the prohibition of approach is ghusl, and the principle in readings is harmony, the reading with lightness was interpreted in its light. Indeed it may be claimed that tuhr also indicates ghusl by linguistic usage: in the Qamus: "the woman became pure (tahurat al-mar'ah): her blood ceased and she performed ghusl from menstruation, like tatahharat." Also His saying: ﴿So when they have purified themselves, come to them﴾ indicates by implication that the limit is ghusl, since it requires that the permissibility of coming be delayed until after ghusl. So it strengthens that the meaning of the light reading is ghusl, not cessation. Perhaps it is a qarinah (indicator) of metaphorical use of tuhr by interpreting it as ghusl, if the preceding is not granted. And on the assumption that neither this nor that is granted, and one returns to the view that the light reading is from tuhr, which is literal for the cessation of blood only, with no metaphor and no indicator, and the intensive reading is from tatahhur, from which ghusl is derived: it is said also, regarding the way of reconciliation as in al-Kashf, that the intensive reading is to express the complete limit and the light reading to express the incomplete one. And "hatta" in verbs is akin to "ila" in that it does not entail the inclusion of what follows it, so it is the complete limit absolutely. Its explanation: the complete limit is that which is a limit in all its parts, and it is what lies outside what it limits; and the incomplete limit is that which is a limit with respect to its last part. The "hatta" that governs nouns entails the inclusion of what follows it were it not for the limit; and the "hatta" governing verbs, like "ila," does not entail that what follows is a part of what precedes it. So the cessation of blood is a limit of the prohibition with respect to its last part, so the time of cessation is included in it, and ghusl is a limit of it with respect to its first part. So there is no contradiction between the two readings. Perhaps the benefit of stating the two limits is to state the degrees of the prohibition of approach, for it is stronger before cessation than after it. When our masters, the Hanafis, saw that here there are two readings, the light and the intensive, and that the implication of the first is the ending of the prohibition that was imposed upon what was permitted, by the cessation of blood absolutely, so when the imposed prohibition ends, it becomes permitted by necessity; and that the implication of the second is that it does not end according to him except after ghusl; and they saw that tuhr, when attributed to a woman, does not indicate ghusl linguistically, but its meaning concerning her is the cessation of blood, as is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid; and in Taj al-Bayhaqi: "tahurat," contrary to "tamathat"; and in Shams al-'Ulum: "imra'ah tahir" without the ha', meaning her blood has ceased; and in al-Asas: "imra'ah tahir and nisa' tawahir, they became pure from menstruation." This is not contradicted by what is in the Qamus, since it may be an explanation of usage, even if metaphorical, according to its method in many words; and that reading it as ghusl by metaphor without a specific indicator is not valid; and that taking ﴿So when they have purified themselves, come to them﴾ as an indicator, according to what they mention, is nothing.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 222 (part 2 of 2):

The indication from the implication (iqtida', the meaning that a text must imply to make sense) in it is open to discussion, because the fa' (the particle of consequence) that enters upon a clause which cannot serve as a condition, such as an imperative clause, is merely for connection. Ibn Hisham stated this in al-Mughni and gave as an example His saying, ﴿Say: If you love Allah, then follow me﴾. And even if it were granted, what is necessarily implied is that the permissibility of approaching (ityan) is delayed until after washing in the (second) clause, not absolutely. This would then serve as evidence that the intended meaning of the lightened reading (qira'at al-takhfif) is also washing. The claim that one of the two limits (ghayatan) is included in the ruling while the other is excluded contradicts what is immediately understood. Therefore, they needed to reconcile the two by making each one a separate verse. They interpreted the first as referring to the cessation of bleeding after the maximum period, and the second as referring to the completion of the waiting period ('idda), which is not more than the maximum period of menstruation (hayd). In the same way, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i interpreted the readings of nasb and jarr in (arjulikum) as referring to the two states of lightening and not lightening, and this is the appropriate view. This is because making intercourse depend on washing when bleeding stops after the maximum period would mean that she has, in effect, been made to menstruate while in a state of impurity, which contradicts the ruling of the Shari'ah, since prayer is obligatory for her, and that obligation entails that she is pure in ruling. This is unlike the completion of the 'idda, for the Shari'ah does not establish her purity with certainty there, but allows menstruation to recur after it. Accordingly, if she bled beyond that and did not exceed ten days, the whole period is considered menstruation by consensus. It remains that what the second reading requires is the continuation of the prohibition before washing. Thus, lifting the prohibition before washing, by the passing of the earliest time of prayer, namely its minimum, which falls at the end, and treating washing as a legal (hukman) fulfilment, as they claim, is a case of setting the explicit text against an inferred meaning (mu'aradat al-nass bi-al-ma'na). The answer is that the second reading was particularized (khussa) in the case of bleeding that stops after ten days by the lightened reading, so it is permissible for it to be particularized secondly by the meaning, as some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) have said. What the Imam's school contains of ease and caution is not hidden. It is related from al-Awza'i that the permissibility of intercourse depends on purification (tatahhur), and he interpreted this as washing the place of menstruation. It may be said that cleaning the place is also called purification (tathir). Al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Nasa'i reported from A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that: "A woman asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about washing herself after menstruation, so he instructed her before she washed, saying: 'Take a piece of musk-scented cloth and purify yourself with it.' She said: 'How do I purify myself with it?' He said: 'Purify yourself with it.' She said: 'How?' He said: 'Subhan Allah! Purify yourself with it.' So I drew her close and said to her: 'Follow the trace of the blood with it.'" Tawus and Mujahid, in one narration from him, held that washing the place together with wudu' is sufficient for the permissibility of intercourse, and the Imamiyya (Imamis) also held this view. It is not hidden that none of these is complete purification for women. It is only complete purification of their limbs, and this contradicts what is immediately understood from the verse. What is immediately understood is the first view, together with what is in the hadith. Although the hadith is a command to that woman to purify herself, what is meant by it is emphasis on purifying the place. However, for some reason, the Prophet (ﷺ) did not state this explicitly. We do not deny the use of the word purification for cleaning the place, but we do deny the use of (yathurna) for those who cleaned the places of their menstruation, and we do not affirm that men menstruate. The verse has been cited as evidence that it is not forbidden to enjoy a menstruating woman between the navel and the knee, and that only intercourse is forbidden. A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, was asked, as reported by Ibn Jarir: "What is permitted for a man from his wife when she is menstruating?" She said: "Everything except intercourse." A group held that enjoying what lies between the navel and the knee is forbidden, citing what Malik reported from Zayd ibn Aslam: "A man asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'What is permitted to me from my wife when she is menstruating?' He said to him: 'Let her tie her waist-wrap tightly, then do as you wish above it.'" This may be from the category of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i') in general. For this reason, what Imam Ahmad reported includes: "Abstaining from that is more virtuous." The command in the verse is for permission, on the pattern of ﴿And when you have left the state of ihram, then hunt﴾. So the verse permits intercourse, but it is restricted by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿from where Allah has commanded you﴾, that is, from the place which Allah, exalted is He, commanded you to avoid because of the harm, which is the vagina, and not to go beyond it. This was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Rabi'. Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is from the directions in which it is permitted to approach the woman, and do not approach them from where it is not permitted, as when they are fasting, in ihram, or in i'tikaf. It is supported by the argument that if it meant the vagina, the wording would have been (fi) rather than (min), because the verb (ityan), used in the sense of intercourse, is usually followed by (fi) and not by (min). Perhaps this is in the category of prohibition according to the proponents of the first view.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who are constantly repentant﴾, for what might occasionally be committed by them of some sins, such as intercourse during menstruation, which, as reported in a hadith, causes leprosy in the child, and what calls for the punishment of Allah, exalted is He. Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i reported from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Whoever has intercourse with a menstruating woman has disbelieved in what was revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ)." This is in the mode of warning (tarhib), so it does not contradict what al-Tabarani reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I had intercourse with my wife while she was menstruating.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded him to free a slave (nasamah)." The value of a slave at that time was one dinar. This applies if the intercourse occurred at the beginning of menstruation and the blood was red. But if it occurred at its end and the blood was yellow, then he should give half a dinar in charity, as the reports indicate.

﴿And He loves those who purify themselves﴾, that is, those who keep themselves far from indecencies and filth, such as intercourse with a menstruating woman and approaching her in a manner not commanded by Allah, exalted is He. Interpreting purification as keeping oneself free from these is what eloquence (balaghah) requires. It is a metaphor, according to al-Asas and Shams al-Ulum. It is related from Ata' that it is to be understood as purification with water. The two clauses form a concluding statement (tadhyil), independent of what preceded.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 223:

﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾. Al-Bukhari and a group of scholars narrated from Jabir, who said: "The Jews used to say that if a man approached his wife from behind, in her front passage, the child would be born squint-eyed (aḥwal). So this verse was revealed." The word ḥarth (tilth) means casting seed into the earth, and it is other than planting (zar'), since planting is causing it to grow. The saying of Allah, Exalted, ﴿Have you considered what you sow? ... Is it you who make it grow, or are We the growers?﴾ points you to this. Al-Jawhari said: ḥarth is planting (zar'), and ḥārith is the planter. In any case, this is a predicate about what precedes it, either by omitting a modifier, meaning "places of tilth," or by a figurative and eloquent comparison, meaning "like places of tilth." Their being compared to those places is based on comparing the sperm to seeds, since each of them is the material for what results from it and cannot be good without it. So it is a comparison which is alluded to by another comparison. ﴿So go to your tilth﴾ means: to that which is like tilth, so there is an explicit metaphor (isti'ara taṣrīḥiyya). It is possible that ḥarth remains in its literal sense, and the statement is a simile (tamthīl): it likens the state of their coming to women in the place of intercourse to the state of their coming to fields, in that there is no restriction to one direction rather than another. Then the term for the thing compared to was applied to the thing compared. The first (the metaphor) is more apparent and more fitting to the consequence of the command to come (to the wife) being derived from the eloquent comparison of them to tilth. This sentence explains the saying of Allah, Exalted, ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾, because of the generality in its object. The fa' is a conditional (jazā'iyya), and what precedes it is the cause of what follows it. It was placed before it out of concern for the matter of the cause, and so that the ruling would come with its reason, making it more effective. It is possible that the whole is like an explanation of what came before, and the fa' is for conjunction (ʿaṭf), and conjoining an imperative to a declarative is permissible with a conjunction other than waw.

﴿Come to them as you wish﴾. Qatada and al-Rabi' said: "From wherever you wish." Mujahid said: "How you wish." al-Dahhak said: "When you wish." The use of anna to mean "where," "how," and "when" is something that the great majority have affirmed. On the first (meaning "from where") the particle man (from) is required, either apparent or implied, and it is a conditional whose answer has been omitted because the preceding sentence indicates it. Some of the verifiers (muḥaqqiqūn) chose that it here is entirely in the sense of "from where," meaning: "from whatever direction," so that the statement about the occasion of revelation is included. The claim that the verse is then evidence for permissibility of coming from the rear arises from failing to reflect that man is required in that case. The meaning becomes "from whatever place," not "in whatever place." So what is derived then may be the generalization of directions: front, back, above, below, right and left, not the generalization of places of intercourse. There is therefore no proof in the verse for one who permits intercourse with a woman through her anus, like Ibn Umar. The reports from him on that are sound and well known, while the narrations from him to the contrary are contrary to them. Likewise (there is no proof in it for) Ibn Abi Mulayka and Abdullah ibn al-Qasim, to the point that he said in what al-Tahawi narrated from him: "I did not meet anyone whom I would take as a guide in my religion who doubted that it is permitted." And likewise Malik ibn Anas, to the point that al-Khatib narrated from Abu Sulayman al-Jawzajani that he asked him about that, and he said to him: "Just now I washed the head of my penis from it." Likewise (there is no proof in it for) some of the Imamiyya (Twelver Shi'a), not all of them, as some people think who have no knowledge of their school. And likewise (there is no proof in it for) Sahnun, from the Malikis. The rest of the companions of Malik deny the transmission of permissibility from him and do not hold it. Alas, how can the verse be used as proof of permissibility given what we have mentioned about it, and given that the possibility (of another meaning) remains? How can the argument stand, especially since it has been established before the obligation to withdraw during menstruation? He gave the reason that it is a filthy harm from which sound natures recoil, and this requires the obligation to withdraw from intercourse by the back passage, because the cause is shared. The filth that is in the lower passages cannot be compared with the blood of istiḥāḍa (irregular bleeding). Whoever makes the comparison has erred, his anus being in the pit, because the disgust is evident: the aversion from what is in the lower passages is greater than the blood of istiḥāḍa, which is blood from the bursting of a vein, like the blood of a wound. Even if it is granted that anna indicates the generalization of places of intercourse, as is common, it is answered that restricting it to places of tilth removes that. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Said ibn Jubayr, who said: "While I and Mujahid were sitting with Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, a man came to him and said: 'Will you not relieve me concerning the verse about menstruation?' He said: 'Yes.' So he recited ﴿They ask you about menstruation﴾ up to ﴿So come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾. Ibn Abbas said: 'From where the blood comes, from there you were commanded to come.' He said: 'What about the verse ﴿Your women are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth as you wish﴾?' He said: 'Woe to you! Is the back passage a tilth?! If what you say were true, the menstruation prohibition would have been abrogated (mansūkh) when someone is occupied from here, you come from here. But (it means) as you wish, by night and by day.'" As for what is said: that if the verse specified the front passage as the place of tilth, it would necessitate the prohibition of intercourse between the thighs and in the folds of the body, because these are not places of tilth like the lower passages, this is answered: the rubbing (the sexual contact) in other than the two thighs is not considered in custom to be coitus or penetration. Allah, Exalted, has prohibited penetration and coitus in other than the place of tilth, but not masturbation ( istimnā'). So the prohibition of masturbation between the thighs and in the folds of the body is not known from the verse, unless that is considered "coming to" and "intercourse" and it is "come to them." I do not think you doubt this. By this one knows the flaw in the debate between Imam al-Shafi'i and Imam Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. al-Hakim narrated from Abd al-Hakam that al-Shafi'i debated Muhammad on this question, and Ibn al-Hasan argued against him that tilth is only in the vagina. He said to him: "Would what is other than the vagina be prohibited, so that I should commit to it?" He said: "Tell me: if he penetrated her between her thighs or in the folds of her body, is that tilth?" He said: "No." He said: "Then is it prohibited?" He said: "No." He said: "Then how do you argue with what you do not hold?" It seems that from here al-Shafi'i said, as al-Tahawi, al-Hakim and al-Khatib related from him, when he was asked about that: "Nothing has been authenticated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in its permission or prohibition, and by analogy it is permitted." This is contrary to what we know of al-Shafi'i's school, for the report of his prohibition is well known. Perhaps he said that in his earlier (qadīm) view and retracted it in his later (jadīd) view, because what was authenticated to him of the reports, or what appeared to him from the verse, ﴿And send ahead for yourselves﴾, was something suitable for sending ahead of righteous deeds, including mentioning the name of Allah at intercourse and seeking a righteous child. Al-Shaykhan and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "If one of you, when he comes to his wife, says: 'In the name of Allah. O Allah, keep Satan away from us and keep Satan away from what You grant us,' then if a child is decreed from that union, Satan will never harm him." And it is authentically reported from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: "When a person dies, his deeds are cut off except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge from which people benefit, and a righteous child who prays for him." And it is reported from Ata': the specifying of the object of the (mentioning the name of Allah) by "mentioning the name." And from Mujahid: by supplication at intercourse. And from some of them: by seeking a child. And from others: by marrying chaste women. The generalization is preferable.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding what He has commanded you and forbidden you.

﴿And know that you will meet Him﴾ through resurrection, so He will recompense you for your deeds, so provide for yourselves what will benefit you. The pronoun in the genitive refers to Allah, Exalted, with an omitted modifier or without it. Its return to "what you have sent ahead" or to the recompense understood from it is remote. The commands are conjoined to His saying, Exalted, ﴿So go to your tilth﴾, and their benefit is general guidance after particular guidance. That the preceding sentence is a ground (mabniyya) does not require that the sentence conjoined to it be so.

﴿And give good news to the believers﴾ who received what they were addressed with acceptance and compliance, with honor and bliss that no expression can encompass. Some scholars understood "the believers" to mean those who are perfect in faith, on the basis that the earlier address was to believers in general. So if this good news were for them, the apparent form would have been "and give them good news." But when the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, it was known that the intended ones are other than those previously addressed, namely the perfect believers. It is not hidden that the shift to the apparent noun may be to indicate causation and because it is a closing rhyme (fāṣila), so what he mentioned is not complete. The waw is for conjunction. "Give good news" is conjoined to the previously mentioned "say" (qul), or to an implied "say" before "send ahead," which is conjoined to the mentioned one.

From the allusive (ishārī) approach: "They ask you about wine and gambling": wine of desire and love of the world, and gambling of the soul's scheming by means of its arrows, which are its ten senses deposited in the body's lute, to obtain some of the camel-meat of pleasures and appetites. "Say: In both is great sin": the sin of veiling and distance from the Presence, "and some benefit for people" in worldly livelihood and attaining bodily pleasure and joy through forgetting faults, troubling thoughts, and distressing cares. Their sin is greater than their benefit, because the loss of union in the gardens of beauty cannot be compensated by anything, and nothing can stand in its place (the union of Su'da or Mayy). There is indeed a difference, among the righteous, between intoxication from the Giver of drink (al-mudīr) and intoxication from the Dwelling (al-mudār). "A cup of arrival made the people drunk, and he was intoxicated from the Giver." This is lawful intoxication, but it is above the realm of obligation, and beyond this dense world, and it is the intoxication of spirits, not forms, and the intoxication of good pleasure, not the fever of jugs. "Its cup-bearer never tired, nor did a drinker tire of the wine of glances whose cup makes the intellect drunk."

﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾, which is whatever is other than the Truth of the two worlds. ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs﴾ revealed from the heaven of spirits, ﴿so that you may reflect﴾ on this world and the Hereafter, and cross their two valleys with the wings of journeying and wayfaring toward the King of kings. ﴿They ask you about menstruation﴾, which is the overpowering of the impulses of human attributes and human needs. ﴿Say: it is harm﴾ from which pure hearts recoil. So withdraw with your hearts from the women of the souls during the menstruation of the overpowering of passions, until they are purified and have finished meeting the necessary needs. When they purify themselves with the water of turning back (in repentance) and return to the Presence seeking nearness, then ﴿come to them from where Allah has commanded you﴾, that is, at the appearance of the signs of the Truth, by the vanishing of the falsehood of the soul and the dissolution of its desire. ﴿Indeed Allah loves those who turn often﴾ from the attributes of existence, and He loves those who purify themselves by the light of knowledge from the dust of created things. Or: He loves those who turn often from their questions. ﴿And He loves those who purify themselves﴾ from their desire for their women, who are the souls that became a garment for you, and you became a garment for them. (This is) the place of your tilth for the Hereafter. ﴿So go to your tilth﴾ whenever you wish the cultivation for your return. ﴿And send ahead for yourselves﴾ what benefits them and perfects their growth. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ from looking at what is other than Him. ﴿And know that you will meet Him﴾ by annihilation in Him if you fear Him. ﴿And give good news to the believers﴾ with what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not occurred to the heart of any human being.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 224:

﴿Do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths﴾. Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Jurayj: "It was revealed concerning al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may Allah be pleased with him, when he swore that he would not spend on Mistah ibn Uthathah, his maternal cousin, who was one of the poor Emigrants, because of what had occurred in the slander against 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her." Al-Kalbi said: "It was revealed concerning Abdullah ibn Rawahah when he swore concerning his brother-in-law Bashir ibn al-Nu'man that he would never enter upon him, never speak to him, and never reconcile between him and his wife, after he had divorced her and wished to take her back and be reconciled with her." The word ʿurḍah (obstacle, object of frequent appeal) is a noun of the pattern fuʿlah in the sense of the passive participle, like qabḍah and ghurfah. Here it derives either from ʿaraḍa al-shay' (in the pattern naṣara or ḍaraba), meaning he made it an obstacle (mu'tarid), or from ʿaraḍahu li-l-bay' (in the pattern ḍaraba), meaning he presented it for sale, when he put it forward for that purpose and set it up for it.

According to the first meaning: Do not make Allah a barrier against what you have sworn to and then abandoned of kinds of good. Thus "oaths" means the matters sworn about, and it is expressed by "oaths" because of their connection to them. Or because the oath (yamin) means the swearing (ḥalif), as you say "I swore an oath" (ḥalaftu yaminan) just as you say "I swore a swearing" (ḥalaftu ḥalifan), so the object is named by the verbal noun, as in the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in what Muslim and others reported: "Whoever swears an oath and then sees something else as better than it, let him make expiation for his oath and let him do that which is better." It has been said that "ʿalā" in the hadith is redundant, to imply the meaning of elevation (isti'lā').

As for His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿that you act righteously, fear Allah and make peace among people﴾, it is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "your oaths." This is common in non-proper nouns, and it is more frequent in them (i.e., in proper nouns). It has been said that it is a substitute (badal), but this was deemed weak, because the substituted-for element is not intended in relation to the substitute; rather it is a preparation and introduction for the substitute, and here this is not the case. The lam is connected to ʿurḍah, and it carries the sense of obstruction; or it is connected to tajʿalū. The first is preferable, although the outcome is one. It is also permitted that the oaths be taken in their literal sense, the lam be causal, and "an tabarrū" be understood as "because" (li-anna), and it would be connected either to the verb or to ʿurḍah. The meaning would be: Do not make Allah, may He be exalted, a barrier, for the sake of your oath by Him, against righteousness, God-consciousness and reconciliation.

According to the second meaning: ﴿And do not make Allah a target for your oaths﴾, so that you would wear Him out by frequently swearing by Him in every truth and falsehood, because in that there is a kind of audacity toward Allah, may He be exalted. This is the interpretation transmitted from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, and al-Jubba'i and Abu Muslim held it, and the Imamiyya transmitted it from the pure Imams. Here "an tabarrū" is the cause of the prohibition, in the sense: I forbid you from it, seeking your righteousness, your God-consciousness and your reconciliation. For the one who swears much is bold toward Allah, may He be exalted, and the one toward whom one is bold is far removed from being characterized by those qualities. It returns to: Do not swear by Allah frequently, so that you may be righteous and God-conscious, and so that people rely upon you and you reconcile between them. The supposition of "seeking" or the like is necessary if "an tabarrū" is in the accusative position, so that the condition for deleting the lam is fulfilled, which is concomitance, because what is concomitant with the prohibition is not righteousness, God-consciousness and reconciliation themselves, but seeking them. If it is in the genitive position, based on the view that deleting the genitive particle from "an" and "in" is analogical, then it is not necessary; they supposed it only to clarify the meaning. What is intended is the seeking of Allah, may He be exalted, not the seeking of the servant. If that is intended, it is the cause of the restraint derived from the prohibition, as if it was said: Restrain yourselves from making Him, glorified be He, a target. The seeking of the servant is suitable for restraint.

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of your statements and your oaths, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ [224] of your conditions and your intentions, so safeguard what you have been charged with.

The connection of the verse to what precedes it: when He, may He be exalted, commanded them to be God-conscious, He forbade them from profaning His name, which contradicts it, or He forbade them from making His mighty name a barrier to it and a preventer from it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 225:**

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle (*laghw*) oaths in your oaths.﴾ *Laghw* is what is dropped and not counted, whether in speech or otherwise. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, the *laghw* of an oath is what the tongue has merely uttered, and what is similar to it, in which no oath was intended, such as the Arabs' saying "No, by Allah" or "No, by God," for mere emphasis. This is what is reported from A'ishah, Ibn Umar and others in most of the narrations. The meaning is: Allah will not hold you accountable at all for what you did not intend as an oath.

﴿But He will hold you accountable for what your hearts have earned.﴾ That is, for the oaths you intended, when your hearts agreed with your tongues. This verse is not contradicted by the verse in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the idle oaths in your oaths, but He will hold you accountable for the oaths you have bound (*'aqqadtum*); its expiation is feeding ten needy persons﴾ and so on. This is on the basis that the accountability in this verse concerns the *ghamus* (the perjurious oath), since it is among what the heart earns, while the verse of al-Ma'idah requires its absence, because the *laghw* there is the opposite of the *mun'aqidah* (the binding oath), which is an oath sworn to do something in the future that is then not done. The *ghamus* is included in the phrase ﴿what you have bound﴾, which stands in contrast to it. The *ghamus* is an oath about a past matter in which one deliberately lies. Its being *laghw* is because the righteousness that is the purpose of a lawful oath is not realized in it. This is because al-Shafi'i interpreted ﴿what you have bound﴾ as what the heart earns, from the phrase "I bound myself to such-and-such" (*'aqadtu 'ala kadha*), meaning "I resolved upon it," and he did not reverse this. This is because *'aqd* is ambiguous (*mujmal*), as it may mean the binding of the heart or the tying of one thing to another, whereas *kasb* (earning) is explicit (*mufassar*). Among the principles is that the ambiguous is interpreted in light of the explicit. When it is interpreted this way, it includes the *ghamus*, and the *laghw* becomes what has no intention behind it, not the *mun'aqidah*, since the *mun'aqidah* is not included. Thus the two verses agree on accountability for the *ghamus* and non-accountability for the *laghw*. However, if the negated verb has a general scope, then in the two verses there is the negation of accountability by punishment and expiation for what has no intention behind it, and the affirmation of accountability in general, by both or by one of them, for what has intention behind it. If it does not have general scope, then the general sense of the unrestricted "accountability" in this verse is taken to mean the accountability restricted to expiation in the verse of al-Ma'idah, on the basis that the event and the ruling are one and the same, and the context of the verse is to explain expiation. So there is no repetition. The general scope is supported by what Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hasan, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) passed by a people who were shooting arrows, and with him was one of his companions. A man from the people shot and said: 'By Allah, I hit it! By Allah, I missed it!' The companion who was with him said: 'The man has broken his oath, O Messenger of Allah!' He said: 'Not so. The oaths of archers are *laghw*; there is no expiation for them and no punishment.'"

Imam Abu Hanifa held that the *laghw* here is what has no intention to lie, either because there is no intention at all or because the speaker believes it to be true. The accountability is interpreted as accountability in the Hereafter, on the basis that the abode of accountability is the Hereafter, and that the unrestricted term is understood in its complete sense. This accountability is linked to earning, since intention or its absence has no bearing on the obligation of the expiations, which are worldly accountabilities. There is no doubt that by the mere oath without breaking it, the accountability of the Hereafter in the *mun'aqidah* is not realized. Therefore it is not possible to apply "what the hearts have earned" in its general sense, and it must be restricted to the *ghamus*. From this verse, then, arises accountability in the Hereafter for the *ghamus* but not the worldly accountability which is the expiation. In this there is disagreement with al-Shafi'i. There is also no accountability in the Hereafter for anything else in which there is intention with belief in its truth, and for what has no intention at all, on which there is agreement with al-Shafi'i. The accountability in the verse of al-Ma'idah is taken to be worldly, by the indication of His words in it, ﴿so its expiation﴾ and so on, and His words ﴿what you have bound﴾ concerning the *mun'aqidah*, since what is understood from *'aqd* (binding) is tying one thing to another, which is clearly the *mun'aqidah*. Thus the *laghw* in that verse means what is other than it, including the *ghamus* and other things. From it arises the non-accountability of worldly expiation for what is not the *mun'aqidah*, which is the *ghamus*, and accountability for it in the Hereafter, as known from the verse of al-Baqarah. And the oath without intention, or with it while believing it true, is not held against one in the Hereafter, as also known from it. The worldly accountability for the *mun'aqidah*, whose ruling in the Hereafter is not known from the two verses, is evident from the order of worldly accountability placed upon it. So there is no contradiction between the two verses in his view either, because the requirement of the first is the realization of Hereafter accountability in the *ghamus*, and the requirement of the second is the absence of worldly accountability in it.

From this it is known that what is in *al-Hidayah* and has become widespread in the books of the Companions (of Abu Hanifa) from the Imam, where he said that oaths are of three kinds: the oath of *ghamus*, the binding oath, and the idle oath, and he explained the ruling of each, and the last is defined as swearing about a past matter while thinking it to be so, as he said, and the matter being otherwise, is not correct. It is also established in some narrations from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, and others, "it is nothing" (*laysa bishay'*). This is if what is meant by the explanation is restriction (*al-hasr*) and not illustration of the *laghw*. This is because it is fitting for the structure of the verse that "what the hearts have earned" should stand in contrast to the *laghw* without any intermediary between them. But if restriction is intended, then there remains an oath with no intention between them, whose name and mark are unknown, and this is something that scarcely exists, as is not hidden from the fair-minded. So let this be considered carefully, for many people have overlooked it.

Masruq held that the *laghw* is swearing to sins, and fulfilling it is abandoning that act, with no expiation. It is reported from Ibn Abbas and Tawus that it is an oath made in a state of anger, and there is no expiation for it.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The *laghw* of an oath is that you forbid what Allah the Exalted has made lawful for you, by saying, for example: 'My property is forbidden to me if I do such-and-such.'" Malik adopted this view, except regarding a wife. Ibn Jarir reported from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "It is like a man's saying: 'May Allah blind my sight if I do not do such-and-such,' or his saying: 'He is a polytheist, he is a disbeliever, if he does not do such-and-such.' He is not held accountable for it unless it is from his heart." It has also been said that the *laghw* of an oath is the oath of one who is compelled. This was related by Ibn al-Faras, but it has not been seen with a chain of transmission.

Here, the words of the Exalted, ﴿Allah will not hold you accountable﴾ and so on, are not joined to what precedes them, because they differ in being a statement of information and a statement of command, even though each of them is an explanation of the ruling on oaths.

﴿And Allah is Forgiving﴾ in that He did not hold you accountable for the *laghw*, ﴿Forbearing (*halim*)﴾ in that He did not make accountability for the oath of seriousness. The sentence serves as a concluding summary (*tadhyil*) of the two preceding sentences, and its purpose is to confer favour upon the believers and to show that His benevolence encompasses them. *Halim* (Forbearing) comes from *haluma* (with a *damma* vowel), *yahlumu*, meaning to grant respite by delaying punishment. The root meaning of *hilm* is patience (*ana'ah*). As for *hilm al-adim* (of hides), with a *kasra*, *yahlamu* with a *fatha*, it means it has spoiled. As for *halama*, meaning he saw in his sleep, it is with a *fatha*. The verbal noun of the first is *hilm* with a *kasra*, the verbal noun of the second is *halm* with a *fath* on the *lam*, and the verbal noun of the third is *hulum* with a *damma* on the *ha'* and with the *lam* either vocalized or unvocalized.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 226:

﴿لِلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِن نِسائِهِمْ﴾ Al-īlā' (an oath of abstention from one's wife, a vow to stay away from her), as al-Raghib said, is an oath that implies a shortcoming in the matter sworn about, from His saying: ﴿لا يَأْلُونَكم خَبالا﴾ (they will not spare you corruption), meaning: falsehood. And ﴿ولا يَأْتَلِ أُولُو الفَضْلِ مِنكُمْ﴾ (and let not those of virtue among you swear). In the Law it became a term for an oath that prevents intercourse with a woman. So ﴿يُؤْلُونَ﴾ means: they swear. ﴿مِن نِسائِهِمْ﴾ is with an omitted noun (i.e., "from the sexual relations with their wives"), or it is the substitution of the object for the intended verb, for emphasis. The oath concerning intercourse is construed with ﴿مِن﴾ because it implies the meaning of distance, so it is as if it were said: they keep themselves away from their wives by swearing. It was also said that this verb takes ﴿مِن﴾ and ﴿عَلى﴾. Abu al-Baqa' reported from some lexicographers that it takes ﴿مِن﴾, and it was said that ﴿مِن﴾ here means ﴿عَلى﴾, and it was said that it means ﴿فِي﴾, and it was said that it is extra (ziyadah). It is also permissible to make the preposition phrase a stationary adverbial complement, i.e., "there is established for them, concerning their wives, ﴿تَرَبُّصُ أرْبَعَةِ أشْهُرٍ﴾ (a waiting of four months)." It was read as (ألْوًا مِن نِسائِهِمْ), and in the codex of Ubayy it is (لِلَّذِينِ يُقْسِمُونَ), and this is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. Al-tarabbus means waiting and pausing. It is idafah to the adverb of time by way of extension (ittisa'), treating the adverbial object as if it were a direct object, while the meaning remains adverbial. The phrase before it is either its subject (mubtada') whose predicate is ﴿لِلَّذِينَ﴾, or the subject of the adverb, according to al-Akhfash, who permitted its operation even without a preceding base. The sentence, on both interpretations, stands in the position of an exception from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿ولَكِنْ يُؤاخِذُكم بِما كَسَبَتْ قُلُوبُكُمْ﴾ (but He will hold you to account for what your hearts have earned). For the īlā', since one of the two matters is necessarily entailed by it, expiation (kaffarah) is due if the oath is broken, without sin, while divorce, if the oath is kept, differs from the other binding oaths, in which "accountability" (mu'akhadhah) is specified with both or with one of them according to al-Shafi'i, and the accountability is in the Hereafter according to Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him. So it is as if it were said: except the īlā', for its ruling is other than what was mentioned. For this reason this sentence is not conjoined to what precedes it. After He, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned: (إنَّ لِلْمُوَلِينَ مِن نِسائِهِمْ تَرَبُّصَ أرْبَعَةِ أشْهُرٍ) (For those who swear abstention from their wives is a waiting of four months), He explained its ruling with His saying, majestic is His glory: ﴿فَإنْ فاءُوا﴾ (then if they return), meaning: they go back within the period, ﴿فَإنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ 226﴾ (then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful), for what arose from them of the oath of wrongdoing and the resolve of the heart upon that breaking of the oath, or because of the return (fay'ah) and the expiation. This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: (فَإنْ فاءُوا فِيهِنَّ) (then if they return to them).

**[p. 130 of the source]** ﴿And if they resolve on divorce﴾: that is, they firmly intend it, by not returning (to the wife) and persisting in the ila' (oath of abstention from intercourse). ﴿Then indeed Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of their ila', which becomes an irrevocable divorce (talaq ba'in) from them upon the expiry of the 'iddah (waiting period). ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of their purpose in this ila', so He will recompense them according to their intentions. This is what the Hanafiyyah (followers of Abu Hanifa) took this verse to mean. They said: ila' from the husband is for him to say, "By Allah, I will not approach you" for four months or more, whether restricted to months or unrestricted. It does not apply to less than that according to the four Imams. Most scholars disagree with this, including the Zahiriyyah (literalists), al-Nakha'i, Qatada, Hammad, Ibn Abi Hammad and Ishaq, for in their view the husband becomes a mu'li (one who has made an ila') for a short or long period alike. Its ruling is that if he returns to his wife within the period, by intercourse if possible, or by words if he is unable to do so, the return (fay') is valid. If he is able but breaks the oath, he is liable for the expiation of an oath (kaffarat al-yamin), while the one who is unable has no expiation. If the four months pass, she becomes irrevocably divorced by a single pronouncement, without the wife needing to demand that the husband pronounce it or that a judge do so.
The Shafi'iyyah said: there is no ila' except for more than four months. So if he says, "By Allah, I will not approach you" for four months, it is not an ila' in the sacred law according to them, and its ruling does not apply to it. Rather, it is an oath like other oaths: if he breaks it, he makes expiation, and if he keeps it, there is nothing upon him. The mu'li may delay during this period, so he is not required to return or to divorce. If he returns by breaking the oath, ﴿then indeed Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ to the mu'li for the sin of breaking his oath, provided he makes expiation, as in the al-Jadid (the New opinion of al-Shafi'i). Or (He is Forgiving) for what he intended by the ila' of harming the wife and the like, through the return (fay'ah), which is like repentance. And if they resolve on divorce, then indeed Allah is All-Hearing of his divorce and All-Knowing of his intention. When the period passes without his returning or divorcing, he is required to do one of the two, and if he refuses both, the judge (al-hakim) divorces her on his behalf. The Shafi'iyyah's view that the period is more than four months is supported by the fact that the particle fa' (then) in the verse indicates sequence, so it shows that the ruling of the ila' (return or divorce) follows it after four months have passed. Therefore, the ila' within this period is not a legal ila', since its ruling does not apply. They used this argument against the Hanafiyyah. They also objected to them that if divorce were not needed after the period passed, it would mean that divorce occurs without one who pronounces it, and that the text indicates it is heard (masmu'), so if she became irrevocably divorced without a divorce, there would be nothing heard here. They answered the first objection by saying that fa' indicates sequence in mention, and the second by saying that what is heard is what accompanies that abandonment of intercourse of argument, dispute and self-talk about it, just as one hears the whisperings of Satan upon them through the injustice or the ila' they persisted in, which became an irrevocable divorce upon the passing of the period. This is more appropriate to His saying, Glorified and Exalted is He: ﴿And if they resolve on divorce﴾, since He suffices with mere resolve. This is unlike what the Shafi'iyyah said, that it requires divorce after the period passes, which needs an added supposition, or requires taking "resolve on divorce" as a metaphor for it. So what is said, that the verse in its plain wording agrees with al-Shafi'i, is not correct. Abu Hanifa and many of the Imamiyyah (Twelver Shi'is) also held the view that he held.
Abd ibn Humayd related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, who said: "Ila' is of two kinds: ila' in anger and ila' in contentment. As for ila' in anger, when four months pass he is irrevocably separated from her. As for what is made in contentment, he is not held to account for it." Abd al-Razzaq related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: A man came to Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and said: "I swore that I would not go to my wife for two years." He said: "I do not see you as having made ila' then." He said: "I only swore because she is nursing my child." He said: "Then no." It is related from Ibrahim: "I know of no ila' except in anger, because of His saying, ﴿then if they return﴾, and returning is only from anger." This was also related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. The generality of the verse has been used as evidence for the validity of ila' from a disbeliever, and by any oath whatever, and without having consummated the marriage, and from a young girl, and from a eunuch. It is also argued that a slave is given the four months as a free man is. And the restriction of this ruling to the mu'li has been used as evidence that one who abandons intercourse out of harm without an oath is not liable for anything. What is related from A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said while admonishing Khalid ibn Sa'id al-Makhzumi, having heard that he had shunned his wife: "Beware, O Khalid, of prolonged shunning, for you have heard what Allah has made the term for the mu'li" is to be understood as intended for kindness, and as a warning against resembling the ila'.

[p. 131]

﴿Wal-mutallaqat﴾ means: those women who are divorced, who are of the ones with *qur'* (menstrual periods, or the intervening period of purity between them), from free women who have been consummated with (*al-madkhul bihinna*). This is because the Qur'an and the reports have made clear that there is no *'idda* (the prescribed waiting period) for one who has not been consummated with; that the *'idda* of one who does not menstruate, whether due to youth, old age, or pregnancy, is by months, and for a pregnant woman it is by delivery; and that the *'idda* of a slave woman is two *qur'* or two months. The *alif-lam* (*al*) in *al-mutallaqat* is not for comprehensiveness (*istighraq*), since that is impossible here for the reasons explained. It is therefore taken to denote the category (*jins*), as in "I will not marry women," and what is intended by it is what has been mentioned, by the indication of the ruling. This is the position of our masters the Hanafis, because an independent statement that is not connected (*mawsul*) to the general text is, in their view, abrogating (*nasikh*) for the general text. Abrogation is valid only if the general scope of the previous ruling is established, and there is no general scope here.

The Shafi'is said: "*al-mutallaqat*" is general, and some of it has been specified by an independent statement that is not connected. The Imam objected to this, saying that specification is only appropriate when what remains under the general term is greater in number, and here that is not the case. This is not correct, because it is a claim without any supporting evidence. What is mentioned in the books of usul al-fiqh is that a general term may be specified to the extent that what remains under it still merits the meaning of plurality, so that the form of the expression is not nullified. Understand this.

﴿Yatarabbasna﴾ means: they shall wait. It is a statement (*khabar*) whose intended meaning is a command, by way of metaphor (*kinaya*). Therefore, for its occurrence as a predicate of a subject, it does not need interpretation (*ta'wil*) according to the opinion of those who do not permit an imperative (*insha'*) to occur as a predicate without interpretation. It has also been said that the nominal sentence is declarative in meaning but imperative in sense, i.e., "let the divorced women wait." It is not hidden that this is not needed. The change of expression is for emphasis, because it indicates certainty. The original state of a statement is that it may be true or false, the falsehood being a rational possibility. The implication is that this is something that must be hastened in carrying out, since the wording that signifies occurrence is used in place of the wording that signifies a demand. Placing the verb after the subject adds emphasis, because it conveys the meaning of piety (*taqwa*) according to one of the two ways reported from Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir and al-Sakkaki.

The waiting (*tarabbus*) is restricted here by the words ﴿by themselves﴾ (*bi-anfusihinna*), and it is left unrestricted in the words of the Exalted ﴿a waiting of four months﴾, in order to urge the women to wait. This is because the *ba'* (the "bi") is for transitivity, so what is commanded is that they should restrain themselves and compel themselves to wait. This implies that they incline toward men, which they find repugnant. So when they hear this, they wait. This is different from the previous verse, where those commanded to wait are the husbands. Although they yearn for women, they do not find it repugnant, so mentioning "selves" there does not serve to urge them to wait.

﴿Thalathata qurū'﴾ is in the accusative as an adverb of time, since it denotes a period. The object is omitted, because *tarabbus* is transitive. The Exalted said: ﴿And we wait for you, that God may afflict you﴾. That is, they wait for marriage. Omitting the object implies that they abstain from marriage during this period to the extent that they do not even utter it. It is also permitted that it be in the objective case with an omitted genitive construction, i.e., they wait for its passing.

*Qurū'* is the plural of *qur'*, pronounced with either a fatha or a damma, the first being more eloquent. It is used for menstruation, as in what al-Nasa'i, Abu Dawud and al-Daraqutni narrated: "Fatima bint Abi Hubaysh said: 'O Messenger of God, I am a woman who suffers from istihada (irregular bleeding), so I do not become pure. Shall I leave off prayer?' The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'No. Leave off prayer during the days of your *aqra'* (menstrual periods).'" It is also used for the period of purity between two menstrual periods, as in the apparent meaning of the words of al-A'sha:

*Are you every year a raider of a raid, making your resolve firm for its farthest end,*
*Gaining wealth, yet among the tribe there is honor, for what was lost in it of the qurū' of your women.*

That is, their periods of purity, because that is the time of enjoyment, and there was no intercourse during menstruation in the pre-Islamic period either. The root meaning is transition (*al-intiqal*) from purity to menstruation, since this entails each of them. The evidence for this, as al-Raghib said, is that a woman who is pure and has not seen blood is not called *dhat qur'*, and a menstruating woman whose bleeding has continued is also not called that.

According to al-Shafi'i, the meaning of *qur'* in the verse is the transition from purity to menstruation, in one of his strong opinions, or the purity from which one transitions, as in the well-known view. This is what is related from 'A'isha, Ibn 'Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit, and a great many others, and not menstruation. They relied on rational and transmitted evidence. As for the rational: the purpose of the *'idda* is the cleansing of the womb from the water of the previous husband. What indicates the cleansing of the womb is the transition to menstruation, because it indicates the opening of the mouth of the womb, so there is no conception in it, whereas conception usually requires the closing of the mouth of the womb, not menstruation. The transition from menstruation to purity indicates the closing of the mouth of the womb, which is the likely place of conception. So when menstruation comes after it, it is known that the womb has not closed.

As for the second, it is the Exalted's words: ﴿So divorce them for their *'idda*﴾. The *lam* is for specifying a time and restricting to a time, so it indicates that what follows it is a time for what precedes it, as in His words: ﴿And we will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection﴾ and ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾. So it indicates that the *'idda* is the time of divorce, and divorce during menstruation is not lawful. This is because al-Shaykhan (Bukhari and Muslim) narrated that Ibn 'Umar (may God be pleased with them both) divorced his wife while she was menstruating, so 'Umar mentioned it to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who became angry and said: "Command him to take her back, then let him keep her until she becomes pure, then she menstruates and becomes pure again. Then if he wishes, he may keep her, and if he wishes, he may divorce her before he touches her. That is the *'idda* by which God the Exalted commanded that women be divorced." This is also one of the proofs that the *'idda* is by the periods of purity.

Our masters the Hanafis, however, held that the meaning of *qur'* is menstruation. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, 'Amr ibn Dinar, and a great multitude. The claim that the transition from purity to menstruation is what indicates cleansing, if accepted, is opposed by the argument that the flow of blood is the cause of the intended cleansing. We do not accept that considering the indicator is better than considering the cause. This is not obstinacy at all. Moreover, what is important in such discussions is the transmitted evidence, and in what they have cited from it there is a problem. This is because the *lam* of time does not require that what follows it be a container for what precedes it. In al-Radi it is said that the *lam* in phrases like "I came to you at the appearance of such-and-such" is for specification, which is its original meaning. The specification here takes three forms. Either the act is specified to the time by occurring within it, as in "I wrote it at the appearance of such-and-such"; or it is specified to the time by occurring after it, as in "for a night I was lost"; or it is specified to the time by occurring before it, as in "for a night I remained." With no qualifier, the specification is for occurrence within it; with a qualifier like "I was lost," it is for occurrence after it; and with a qualifier like "I remained," it is for occurrence before it. End of quotation. In our case there is a qualifier indicating that it is before it, because divorce occurs before the *'idda*, not concurrently with it. This is supported by the reading of the Prophet (ﷺ): "*fi qubuli 'iddatihinna*" (at the beginning of their *'idda*).

In al-Sihah: *al-qabl* and *al-qabul* are the opposite of *al-dabr* and *al-dubur*. It is said that the arrow struck the front and the back of the target, and his shirt was torn from the front and back, i.e., from its front and rear. It is also said: "Descend at the *qubul* of this mountain," i.e., at its foot. So the meaning of "*fi qabli 'iddatihinna*" is at the front of their *'idda* and before it, as the apparent examples require. What he mentioned, that the front of a thing is its first part, returns to this meaning as well. And even if it did not return to it, the front would return to the first by prevalence of usage and frequency of use, and the support gained from this degree is sufficient.

As for the hadith narrated by the two Shaykhs (Bukhari and Muslim), it cannot be accepted as evidence that the *'idda* is the periods of purity, because that depends on taking the demonstrative (*al-ishara*) to refer to the state of purity, and no evidence supports that. The *lam* in "*yutallaqu laha al-nisa'*" (for which women are divorced) is like the *lam* in "*li-'iddatihinna*," and it can mean "during" (*fi*) or "before" (*qabl*). So the referent may be menstruation. The demonstrative is feminine in agreement with the predicate, as a pronoun between a masculine antecedent and a feminine predicate is treated, since most scholars hold that agreement with the predicate is preferable, for what has passed is gone. The meaning is: "Those menstrual periods are the *'idda* before which women are to be divorced, not that women are to be divorced during them," as Ibn 'Umar understood, and so he divorced during it. The statement of al-Khattabi, that the *qur'* by which a divorced woman observes her *'idda* are the periods of purity, because he mentioned "that *'idda* is after purity," is answered by the argument that mentioning purity after it does not require that the demonstrative refers to it. The mention of purity may serve to indicate that a menstrual period surrounded by purity constitutes an *'idda*. In that case, mentioning the second purity requires no further reason, which is this: if he takes her back during the first purity by intercourse, her divorce during that purity is not in accordance with the Sunna, so he needs the second purity in order for a lawful (*sunni*) divorce to be valid then. Also, the reconciliation should not be solely for the purpose of divorce, but should be like repentance from sin by changing one's state, and he should prolong his stay with her, perhaps he will have intercourse with her, and what is in her soul regarding the cause of divorce will be removed, and so he keeps her. This is what goes back to repelling the matter.

As for the proof that *qur'* means menstruation, it is what Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, and al-Daraqutni narrated from 'A'isha that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The divorce of a slave woman is two pronouncements, and her *'idda* is two menstrual periods." He explicitly stated that the *'idda* of a slave woman is two menstrual periods. It is known that the difference between a free woman and a slave woman is in the quantity of the *'idda*, not in its kind. Therefore the words of the Exalted ﴿three *qurū'*﴾ are joined as a clarification (*bayan*) of the generality that arises from the homonymy (*ishtirak*). That this cannot be countered is shown by what [Abu Dawud] narrated—

[p. 133]

[Page 134]

The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) [did not include it] in the story of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, because of its weakness. Its chain contains a narrator named Mudhahir, and no one else is known to have related from him. This is open to discussion. First, as you have learned, that hadith is not explicit evidence for the claim being argued. Second, the reason given for weakening Mudhahir is not clearly valid. Ibn 'Adi related another hadith from him, and Ibn Hibban declared him trustworthy (thiqah). Al-Hakim said: "Mudhahir is a shaykh from the people of Basra, and none of our earlier shaykhs mentioned him as having any defect (jarh)." So if the hadith is not sahih, it is at least hasan. What strengthens the hadith is the practice of the scholars in accordance with it. Al-Tirmidhi, right after narrating it, said: "It is a gharib hadith, and the scholars among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and others act upon it." In the Daraqutni it is said: al-Qasim and Salim said, "And the Muslims acted upon it." Malik said: "The fame of a hadith makes its chain unnecessary." This is related in Fath al-Bari.

Among our (Hanafi) companions, some argued that if al-Qur' meant tuhr (the state of purity), it would necessarily invalidate the explicit wording of the particular ruling, namely the word "three" (thalathah), because then the waiting period would be two purities plus part of a third, in the commonly known divorce. It is not hidden that this kind of argument in this context arises from insufficient reflection on what Imam al-Shafi'i (may Allah be pleased with him) said. That is why they objected to him with it. He only made al-Qur' the transition from purity to menstruation, or the purity from which one transitions, not the purity that separates the two bloods. The aforesaid transition, or the purity from which one transitions, is complete. That "three" is the name for a complete number is not conceded. The correct view on this is that when one has begun the third (unit), it is permissible to use the term. Do you not see that they say: "He is the son of three years," even if the third year is not yet complete? This is because the excess is treated as a fraction (fard) metaphorically, and then the name of a complete number is applied to the whole.

Among the Shafi'is, some made al-Qur' the name for the menstruation that is surrounded by two bloods. Its application to part of the purity or to all of it is like the application of the word "water" or "honey." They said: "The derivation (ishtiqaq) points to the meaning of gathering and collecting, and this purity involves the gathering of blood in the womb; part of it and all of it are equal in indicating this." They extended the discussion on this at length. The Imamiyyah agreed with them on this, and they supported it with reports from their Imams. The report from 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) on this matter varies. In sum, the argument of the Shafi'is in this context is strong, as will not be hidden from one who has grasped the various aspects of their discourse, surveyed what they have said, and reflected on how they answered the evidence of their opponents. In the Kashf there is some disclosure, but what is in the Kashshaf does not satisfy our aim. This amount suffices as an example.

Furthermore, the analogical expectation was to mention al-Qur' in the form of paucity, which is al-aqra' (the plural of paucity). However, they use the two patterns interchangeably. Perhaps the reason that favours choosing it here is that the intended meaning of "the divorced women" here is all free women who have menstrual cycles, and all of them exceed ten. So it is used in the place of the plural of abundance. Each of them has three cycles, so abundance is achieved in the cycles. Hence it was fitting to use the plural of abundance in specifying the three, as an indication of this. This is like the use of anfusahunna (their selves) in place of nufusihinna (their souls), to indicate that divorce should be in the paucity.

﴿And it is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs﴾. Ibn 'Umar said: "It is the pregnancy and the menstruation." That is: it is not lawful for her, if she is pregnant, to conceal her pregnancy, nor, if she is menstruating, to conceal her menstruation, so that she says while menstruating, "I have become pure." They (the women of the Jahiliyyah) used to do the first, so that the divorce would not have to await her delivery, and so that the man would not feel compassion for the child and abandon releasing her. They did the second, hastening the completion of the waiting period and nullifying the right of return (raj'ah). This statement is what is related from al-Sadiq, al-Hasan, Mujahid and others. The view that menstruation is not created in the womb, but rather exits from it, so that the word "ma" (what) cannot be taken in its general sense and must be restricted to the child, is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. It is rebutted by the fact that the blood itself, though not created in the womb, acquires the attribute of being menstruation only within it. As for the claim that the discussion concerns divorced women with menstrual cycles, and therefore does not admit the creation of a child in their wombs, so that "what" must be restricted to menstruation, as is related from 'Ikrimah, this too is rebutted: the specification of a general term and its restriction by an external proof does not require that such specification or restriction be taken into account in the referent.

The verse has been used as evidence that their (women's) word is accepted regarding what Allah, exalted is He, has created in their wombs, since if that were not accepted, there would be no benefit in forbidding them to conceal it. Ibn al-Faras said: "In my view, the verse is general in all that pertains to the private parts: virginity, non-virginity (thayyubah), and defect. For all of that is among what Allah, exalted is He, has created in their wombs, so they must be truthful regarding it." There is room for reflection in this.

﴿If they believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾. This is a condition for His saying "it is not lawful." However, its purpose is not restriction, so that if they did not believe, like the women of the People of the Book, concealment would be permitted for them. Rather, it is to show the incompatibility of concealment with faith and to magnify its gravity in their hearts. This is a familiar method; one says: "If you are a believer, do not harm your father." It was also said that its consequent is omitted, i.e., "then let them not conceal," and His statement, glorified is He, "it is not lawful," is a reason for it that has taken its place. The construction of the sentence is: "If they believe in Allah and the Last Day, let them not conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, for it is not lawful for them." In this there is: "that they should not conceal the presumed"; if it is a prohibition, it entails explaining a thing by itself, and if it is a negation, the meaning of the sentence becomes making the non-occurrence of concealment in the future conditional upon their oaths in the past time. And this, as you see, is far-fetched.

﴿And their husbands (bu'ulatuhunna)﴾. That is, the husbands of the divorced women. It is the plural of ba'l, like 'amm and 'umumah, and fahl and fuhulah. The ha' is an extra letter emphasizing the feminine form of the plural. The patterns are learned by hearing and not by analogy, and one does not say ka'b and ku'ubah. This was said by al-Zajjaj. In the Qamus: al-ba'l is the husband; the female is ba'l and ba'lah; and also the lord, the master, the owner, and the palm tree which is not watered or is watered by rain. Al-Raghib said: al-ba'l is the palm tree that drinks through its roots; the word was used to refer to the husband because he remains with the wife for the specific meaning. It was also said: ba'alaha meant he had intercourse with her; and ba'ula al-rajul means when a man is astonished and remains standing, as if he were the palm tree that does not move. So in choosing the word "bu'ulah" (husbandhood) there is an indication that the origin of return (raj'ah) is through intercourse. It is also permissible that "bu'ulah" be a verbal noun described by it, from your saying: "a husband of good bu'ulah," i.e., good living with the wife; or it may stand in place of an omitted genitive, i.e., "and the people of their husbandhood."

﴿have more right to take them back﴾ to the marriage bond and to returning to them. This applies when the divorce is revocable (raj'i), because of the verse that follows it. Thus the pronoun, after taking the condition into account, is more specific than the referent to which it refers, and there is no impossibility in this, as when the apparent noun is repeated. It was also said: the husbands of divorced women have more right to take them back, and this is restricted to the revocable divorce. Here "ahaqq" (more entitled) means "haqq" (right), and was expressed with the comparative form for emphasis, as if it were said: "For the husbands there is a right of return," i.e., a right beloved to Allah, exalted is He, in contrast to divorce, which is hated. This is why it is related, to discourage it: "The most hated of lawful things to Allah, exalted is He, is divorce." It did not retain its meaning of sharing and excess, since the wife has no right of return, as is not hidden. Ubayy read: "bi-riddatihinna" (with their return).

﴿in that (period)﴾, that is, the time of waiting. It is connected either to "ahaqq" or to "biraddihinna."

﴿if they desire reconciliation﴾. That is: if the husbands desire, by the return, reconciliation between themselves and them, and they do not intend harm by prolonging the waiting period over them, for example. The conditioning does not mean that permissibility of return is conditional upon the intent of reconciliation, such that if their intention were not that, return would not be permitted; there is consensus on its permissibility absolutely. Rather, the purpose is to encourage them to intend reconciliation, since it is made as though the right depends on it, ceasing when it ceases.

﴿And they (the women) have rights similar to those which they have, according to what is reasonable﴾.
