In this there is the figure of speech called "ihtibak" (interlacing), and its subtlety in the relationship between husband and wife is not hidden. In the first part, the second is omitted by its indication, and in the second part, the first is omitted by its indication, as if it were said: "And they have over them a right similar to what the men have over them." The meaning of "similarity" is similarity in obligation, not in the kind of action. So it is not obligatory upon him, if she washes his garments or bakes for him, that he do the same for her; rather he repays her with what is fitting for men. At-Tirmidhi related it and graded it sahih, as did al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, from 'Amr ibn al-Ahwas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed you have a right over your wives, and your wives have a right over you. As for your right over your wives, it is that they should not let anyone you dislike tread upon your bed, nor admit into your houses anyone you dislike. Indeed their right over you is that you should be kind to them in their clothing and their food."

[Page 135]

Wakī' and a group related from Anas, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Indeed I love to adorn myself for the woman as I love that the woman adorn herself for me, because Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And they have rights...﴾ (the verse)." They also included among what is due to them: not hastening when having intercourse, until she has fulfilled her need. The final genitive phrase is connected to what the predicate is connected to. It was also said: it is an adjective of "mithl" (similar), which is not made definite by the genitive construction.

﴿But the men have a degree over them﴾. This is an addition to the right, because their rights are in the women themselves. It has been reported that marriage is like slavery, or it is a noble excellence, because they are the managers (qawwam) over them and their guardians. They share with them the purpose of marriage, namely enjoyment and the regulation of the interests of livelihood, and they are singled out with a nobility that accrues to them for the sake of looking after and providing for them. The "darajah" (degree) is originally a rung of a ladder. It is also pronounced "durajah" as in "humazah." Al-Raghib said: the darajah is like the manzilah (station), but it is used when considered in terms of ascent, not spreading over a plain, like the step of a roof or a ladder. It is used to express a lofty station, and the verse is an example of this. So according to both interpretations, it is figurative. In the Kashf: the original root of this word conveys the sense of gradualness and approaching slowly, from "daraja al-sabiyy" (the child crawled) when he crawled; similarly the old man and the one in fetters, because their steps approach one another. The darajah is the step on which one climbs, because ascent is not as easy as descent or walking on level ground, so there must be gradualness. The "daraj" are the places over which the flood passes little by little; and from this comes gradualness in affairs, and "istidraj" from Allah. The "darakah" is the very same as darajah, but in descent. "Al-rijal" is the plural of rajul (man), and the root of the matter is strength and dominance. He used the explicit noun in place of the pronoun to emphasize the manhood by which the superiority of men over women became apparent.

﴿And Allah is Mighty﴾, dominant, whom none can prevent from exacting retribution from those who oppose the rulings. ﴿Wise﴾ (228), knowing the outcomes of affairs and the interests for which He legislated what He legislated. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for both warning and encouragement.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 229 (part 1 of 3):

﴿The divorce is twice﴾ is an indication of the divorce understood from His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and their husbands have more right to take them back in that case﴾, namely the revocable (raj'i) divorce. It has the meaning of the act of pronouncing divorce (taṭlīq), which is the act of the man, like salām in the sense of taslīm (greeting), because it is the one described by unity and plurality, not what is a description of the woman. This is supported by the mention of what is also an act of the man in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿then either retain [them] in kindness﴾, meaning by taking back and good companionship, ﴿or release [them] with good treatment﴾, meaning a release accompanied by consoling the heart and fulfilling rights. This is either by not taking her back until she becomes separated (bāʾin), or by pronouncing the third divorce, which is what is related from the Prophet. Abu Dawud and a group related from Abu Razin al-Asadi that a man said: "O Messenger of Allah, I hear Allah, exalted is He, saying: ﴿The divorce is twice﴾, so where is the third?" He said: "Releasing with good treatment is the third." This indicates that the meaning of (twice) is two. The (fa') in the first part, as in the "ʿahd" (the specific reference), supports this, for its apparent sense is immediate succession without delay, and the ruling of a thing follows it without separation. This is what the Shafiʿis have adopted as the interpretation of the verse, and it is perhaps more fitting to the composition (naẓm), since he has completed the mention of the oath (yamīn) to the mention of the ila' (vow of abstention), which is a divorce; then he moved from that to the mention of the ruling on the divorced women (muṭallaqāt) regarding the waiting period (ʿidda) and the return (raj'a); then he moved from that to the mention of the rulings of divorce that follows the return; then he moved from that to explaining the khul' (divorce by ransom) and the third divorce. It is also more suitable regarding the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul). Mālik, al-Shafiʿi, al-Tirmidhi, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others related from ʿUrwa who said: "When a man divorced his wife and then took her back before her waiting period ended, that was permitted for him, even if he had divorced her a thousand times. A man deliberately divorced his wife, and when she was about to finish her waiting period he took her back, then divorced her again; then he said: 'By Allah, I will never give you shelter with me, nor will you ever be free.' So Allah, exalted is He, revealed the verse."

What led them to this is their statement that combining the three divorces is not forbidden, and that there is no sunnah in separating them, as in their Tuhfa. They used as evidence that "ʿUwaymir al-ʿAjlani, when he performed li'an with his wife, divorced her three times before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ informed him of her prohibition upon him," related by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim). Had it been forbidden, he would have forbidden him from it, since he pronounced it believing the marriage still continued. With the belief in its continuance, combining is forbidden according to the opponent. With prohibition, it is obligatory to denounce the knowledgeable and teach the ignorant, and neither occurred. This indicates there is no prohibition. Also, a group of the Companions did it and others issued fatwas permitting it.

Our masters the Hanafis said: combining two divorces or three is an innovation (bidʿa), and the sunnah is only separation, because of what is narrated in the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: "The sunnah is that you await a pure period (ṭuhr) and divorce her with one divorce for each menstrual cycle (qurʾ)." The Prophet ﷺ did not intend by "sunnah" that it entails reward, since it is a permissible matter in itself and not recommended, but rather that it is of the path followed in the religion, meaning what does not merit punishment. He, upon him blessings and peace, restricted it to separation, so it is known that other than it, namely combining and divorcing during menstruation, is an innovation, meaning what necessitates deserving punishment. With this, what is said is refuted: that the hadith only indicates that combining two divorces or several divorces in one purity is not a sunnah, but as for it being an innovation, that does not follow, due to the existence of an intermediate category according to the opponent. The basis of the refutation is clear, as is not hidden.

In al-Hidaya: al-Shafiʿi said: all divorce is permissible, because it is a legislated disposition (taṣarruf mashrūʿ) through which the ruling is established, and legislation (mashrūʿiyya) does not combine with prohibition. This differs from divorce during menstruation, because what is forbidden is prolonging the waiting period upon her, not the divorce itself. Our argument is that the basic principle of divorce is prohibition, because it involves severing the marriage, in which the religious and worldly interests are tied, and permission is for the need of release. There is no need for combining the three, and they are established in separation over the purities by consideration of their evidence, and the need itself remains, so it is possible to depict the evidence for it. The legislation in its essence, insofar as it is the removal of bondage, does not contradict prohibition for a reason external to it, which is what we have mentioned. End of quote. From this it is known that the opponent is generalizing, not dividing. And if we say he is a divider, based on what is in the books of some of his school, then the most that proves is that combining is contrary to the better course than separation over the menstrual cycles or the months. You have known that the division of Abu al-Qasim, upon him blessings and peace, is other than his division.

As for what is in the report of ʿUwaymir, it is answered that it is an event of a specific state, so perhaps it is among the exceptions, since the situation of li'an is constricted, so something like that is excused in it, and the jealous person is excused in it. Applying both pieces of evidence is better than neglecting one of them.

They interpreted the verse as meaning the legislated divorce is one pronouncement after another, separated; because it is the function of the Lawgiver to clarify legislative matters, and the lam is not explicit in the "ʿahd" (specific reference), rather its apparent meaning is the genus (jins). Also, restricting divorce to the revocable one leaves the mention of return by His statement, glorified is He: ﴿then retain [them] in kindness﴾ as a repetition, unless it is said that what is sought here is the ruling that is undecided between retaining and releasing. Also, the ruling on a single divorce is not known in that way except by the indication of the text (dalālat al-naṣṣ). This interpretation, along with being further from the suspicion of repetition and its indicating the ruling on a single divorce by expression (ʿibāra), gives an additional ruling, which is separation. The verse's indication, then, for what they went to is evident, if the meaning of (twice) is merely indefinite plurality (tanakkur), they return the dual form to the sense of His statement: ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾, meaning one return after another, not two returns. Except that it necessitates removing the dual from its apparent meaning, and likewise removing the (fa') too, and making what follows it a new ruling and an absolute option right after their being taught how to divorce, and not ordered upon the first, by necessity, because absolute separation is not followed by either of the two matters, since if it is with three it is not permitted after it to retain or release. The (fa') is then taken to indicate sequence in mention; that is, if you know how to divorce, then know that its ruling is retention or release,
page 137
so retention in the revocable and release in other than it. If the meaning of (twice) is separation together with duality, as the muhaqqiqun (verifiers) said, based on the view that it is literal in the second sense and apparent in the first, since one does not say of someone who gave another two dirhams at once that he gave him twice until they are separated, and likewise for one who divorced his wife two at once, that he divorced twice, then the objection of departing from the apparent sense in the dual is removed, as is clear, and in what follows also, for the validity of the sequence. The prohibition of combining the two divorces is derived from (twice), which indicates separation and duality, and the prohibition of combining the third is derived from His statement, glorified is He: ﴿or release﴾, where it is ordered after what precedes it by the (fa'). It is said that it is derived from the indication of the text. Then whoever made separation obligatory held that if he divorced without separating, his divorce takes effect, and he is sinful. The Imamiyya and some of the People of the Sunna disagreed with this, such as Shaykh Ahmad ibn Taymiyya and those who followed him. They said: if he divorces three times with one word, only one takes effect, arguing by this verse, and by analogy with the testimonies of li'an and the throwing of the pebbles, for if he gives the four with one word, they are not counted as four by consensus, and likewise if he throws seven pebbles at once, it does not suffice by consensus. Similar to that is if he swears he will send blessings upon the Prophet ﷺ a thousand times, and he says: "Allah bless the Prophet, may Allah bless him a thousand times," he is not fulfilling his oath unless he gives the individual units of the thousand. They also relied on what Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The triple divorce was in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr and two years of ʿUmar's caliphate as one divorce. ʿUmar said: 'Indeed the people have hastened in a matter in which they had leisure, so if we enforce it upon them,' and he enforced it."

Some of them held that the same applies if he divorces three times in one session, for only one takes effect as well. This is because al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "Rukana divorced his wife three times in one session, and he grieved over her greatly. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked him: 'How did you divorce her?' He said: 'I divorced her three times.' He said: 'In one session?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Then that is only one, so take her back if you wish, and take her back.'"

What the People of Truth hold today is contrary to all of that.

The answer to the argument from the verse is that, as you know, it is not explicit regarding the intended matter. As for the hadith, a group has answered it. Al-Subki said: "The best of the answers is that it concerns one who knows the wording. They were at first believed when they intended emphasis, because of their religiosity. When mixtures increased among them, the public interest required not believing them and imposing the three." Al-Allama Ibn Hajar objected to this, saying: "It is strange, for the clear position of our school is to believe the one who intends emphasis, on its condition, however deep in wickedness he may be." He then quoted from some verifiers: "The best of them is that they used to make it one pronouncement, then in the time of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, they hastened and began to pronounce it three, so he dealt with them according to their case and enforced the three upon them. So it is a report about the difference in people's custom, not about a change of ruling in a matter." He was objected to by the fact that it does not conform to the apparent meaning that is understood from the words of ʿUmar, especially with the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The three etc.," so it is a distant interpretation, not a good answer, let alone the best. Then he said: "The best in my view is to answer that when ʿUmar consulted the people, he knew in it an abrogating (nasikh) matter for what occurred before, so he acted upon its case, and that abrogator is either a report that reached him or a consensus, and consensus is only based on a text. For this reason the scholars of the Ummah agreed upon it. Ibn ʿAbbas's report was to explain that the abrogator was only known after a period had passed from the death of the Prophet ﷺ." End of quote.

I say: the triple divorce in the words of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, may be with one word, and in that case the argument with it for the claim is clear. What apparently supports this possibility is what Abu Dawud related from him: "If a man says to his wife: 'You are divorced three times with one mouth,' it is one." In that case it is answered by abrogation. It may also be with three words in one session, such as "You are divorced, you are divorced, you are divorced," and what Abu Dawud related is understood in this way, by

page 138

The verb "yakūna" (it is) is connected to "qāla" (he said), and "thalāthan" (three) is not an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "a divorce, three." It is also not a specifier (tamyīz, a noun that clarifies an ambiguity) of the ambiguity in the sentence before it. "Bi-famin wāḥidatin" means "in one utterance," i.e., successively. In this case the report outwardly agrees with the last opinion. It is answered that this applies to divorce before consummation, for in that case, as Imam Abu Hanifa (may Allah be pleased with him) held, only one divorce takes effect, because the separation (baynūna) occurred with the first pronouncement, so the second met a woman who was already separated. This is supported by what Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Tawus, that a man called Abu al-Sahba', who often questioned Ibn Abbas, said: "Do you not know that when a man divorced his wife three times before consummating the marriage, they counted it as one during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and the early part of the caliphate of Umar?" Ibn Abbas said: "Yes. When a man divorced his wife three times before consummation, they counted it as one during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), Abu Bakr, and the early part of the caliphate of Umar. When he saw that people had hastened into it, he said: 'Enforce them upon them.'" This is a matter of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), which existed during the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and it is not transmitted in the Sahih that it was brought to him and he gave a ruling on it. Perhaps it occurred in remote places near the end of his life (ﷺ), and whoever was given knowledge exercised ijtihad in it and counted it as one. There is no explicit statement in the words of Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) that the one who counted it as one was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Rather, in his saying "they counted it as one" there is an allusion to what we have said. Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), after some days of his caliphate, came to see by ijtihad that it was better to hold that three divorces take effect. However, this contradicts our school, and it is the view of many of the Companions, including Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them). Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Dawud and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Mu'awiya ibn Abi 'Ayyash that he was sitting with Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr and Asim ibn Umar when Muhammad ibn Abi Iyas ibn al-Bukayr came to them and said: "A man from the desert people divorced his wife three times before consummating the marriage. What do you two think?" Ibn al-Zubayr said: "We have no opinion on this matter. Go to Ibn Abbas and Abu Hurayra, for I left them with 'A'isha. Ask them." He went and asked them. Ibn Abbas said to Abu Hurayra: "Give him a fatwa, O Abu Hurayra, for a difficult problem has come to you." Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "One divorce separates her, and three make her unlawful until she marries another husband." Ibn Abbas said the same. If the three in this report is taken to mean three pronounced in a single formula, in order not to contradict the Imam's school, then according to him, if a man divorces his unconsummated wife three times with one formula, they take effect in full, because what takes effect is a verbal noun omitted, meaning a divorce that is irrevocable (bā'in). So "you are divorced" is not a separate pronouncement, and they take effect all together. This report would then conflict with what Muslim narrated, supporting abrogation (naskh), like the report that al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Suwayd ibn Ghafla, who said: "'A'isha al-Khath'amiyya was married to al-Hasan ibn Ali (may Allah be pleased with both of them), and he said to her: 'Ali (may Allah ennoble his face) has been killed.' She said: 'May the caliphate bring you joy.' He said: 'Ali is killed and you show gloating? Go, for you are divorced three times.' She wrapped herself in her clothes and sat until she completed her waiting period (iddah). He sent to her the remainder of her dowry that was still due to her, and ten thousand as charity. When the messenger came to her she said: 'A small provision from a beloved who is parting.' When this reached him, he wept, then said: 'Had I not heard my grandfather, or my father told me, that he heard my grandfather say: "Any man who divorces his wife three times at the (menstrual) periods, or three in an unspecified manner, she is not lawful to him until she marries another husband, and I would have taken her back."'" And what Ibn Majah narrated from al-Sha'bi, who said: "I said to Fatima bint Qays: 'Tell me about your divorce.' She said: 'My husband divorced me three times while he was going to Yemen, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approved that.'" As for the hadith of Rukana, it has been transmitted in several forms. The one that is authentic is what al-Shafi'i, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated: "'Rukana divorced his wife with the word al-battah (final). He informed the Prophet (ﷺ) of that and said: "By Allah, I intended only one." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "By Allah, you intended only one?" Rukana said: "By Allah, I intended only one." He said: "It is what you intended," and he returned her to him.'" This cannot serve as evidence for that claim, because divorce in this case is by an implicit expression (kinaya), in which intention and the number are taken into account. It may be used as evidence for the validity of three taking effect with one formula, since it shows that if he had intended more than one it would have taken effect, otherwise there would be no point in the oath. The analogy with the testimonies of li'an (mutual imprecation) and the throwing of the pebbles (ramy al-jamarat) is an analogy in the wrong place. Do you not see that it is impossible to suffice with part of those in any way, whereas in divorce one may suffice with part of the units of three, and separation is achieved by the completion of the waiting period, and the purpose is accomplished by consensus? And because the matter of li'an is grave, it was not sufficient except by bringing the testimonies one by one, reinforced by oaths, the fifth of which is joined with a curse on the man's side if he were lying, and with wrath on the woman's side if he were truthful. Perhaps retraction or confession occurs in between, so concealment is achieved or the prescribed punishment is applied and the sin is expiated. Also, the four testimonies of the husband stand in place of the four witnesses required in the accusation of chaste women, with an additional element, as His saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, lash them﴾, together with His saying after it: ﴿And those who accuse their wives and have no witnesses except themselves, then the testimony of one of them is four testimonies﴾, etc. Just as the testimony of witnesses is multiple and cannot be fulfilled by a single utterance, so too what stands in its place. The throwing of the pebbles and their being seven is an act of worship (ta'abbudi), its wisdom is hidden, so caution is taken regarding it, and the transmitted practice is followed exactly as it was. The chapter of divorce is not like these two chapters. Moreover, it is part of caution in it that we make it take effect as three with one formula and one session, and we do not nullify the formula of three, when he intended by it nothing but its taking effect in its fullest and most complete manner. As for what is mentioned in the case of the oath not to pray a thousand times, that he is not fulfilling it until he performs each of the thousand, that is a matter required by intention and custom, and that is beyond what we are discussing, as is not hidden. For this reason, reports from the People of the House (Ahl al-Bayt) were transmitted that support the school of Ahl al-Sunna. Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Bassam al-Sayrafi, who said: "I heard Ja'far ibn Muhammad say: 'Whoever divorces his wife three times out of ignorance or knowledge, she is freed (from him).'" And from Maslama ibn Ja'far al-Ahmasi, who said: "I said to Ja'far ibn Muhammad (may Allah be pleased with both of them): 'They claim that whoever divorces three times out of ignorance is returned to the Sunna, and they count it as one, narrating it from you?' He said: 'Allah forbid. This is not our saying. Whoever divorces three times, it is as he said.'" You have heard what we have narrated from al-Hasan. As for what the Imamiyya adopted, narrating it from Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), it has no established authority, and the matter is contrary to it. A sheikh in Kufa fabricated it upon Ali (may Allah ennoble his face), and he confessed to the fabrication in the presence of al-A'mash (may Allah have mercy on him). So let him remember what we have recited, for I do not think you will find it written in a book.

﴿And it is not lawful for you to take﴾ in exchange for the divorce ﴿from what you have given them﴾, that is, from the dowries (sadaqat), for that is contrary to kindness (ihsan). The same ruling applies to the rest of their property, except that the specification is either for the sake of custom or to point out that the impermissibility of taking from what is other than that is a fortiori (min bab al-awla). The prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa al-majrur) may be connected to what is before it, or be a circumstantial state (hal) of "shay'an," because if it were placed after it, it would be an adjective of it. The tanwin (nunation) of "shay'an" is for diminution (tahqir). The address is to the rulers (hukkam), and the attribution of taking and giving to them is because they are the ones who command both at the time of litigation. It was also said that the address is to the husbands. But it is objected that this causes disorder in the noble structure, because His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿except that they both fear﴾, meaning the spouses both or one of them, ﴿that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ by failing to fulfill the obligations of marriage, does not fit with it, since what is spoken of in the address is the husbands only, while in the third person (ghayba) it is the husbands and wives. It cannot be interpreted as a shift in grammatical person (iltifat), since one of its conditions is that the one spoken of must be the same in both modes, and where is this condition? Yes, there is a valid aspect to this view, but it neither nourishes nor satisfies, namely that the exception, since it follows the completion of the address, is one of the most general states or times, or an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), so that the meaning is: "for any reason except out of fear," and it is permissible to shift from address to third person for a rhetorical purpose, which is that a believer should not be addressed with the fear of failing to keep Allah's limits. It is also read as ﴿takhafa﴾ and ﴿tuqima﴾ with the second-person ta' (taa' al-khitab), and with this reading the matter is easier, for then it entails the prevalence of the addressed men over the absent wives, and the dual expression is according to the two groups. Hamza and Ya'qub read ﴿yukhafa﴾ in the passive form, with "an" replacing its complement from the pronoun-alif, as a substitution of part (badal ishtimal), like your saying: "Zayd was feared to be abandoned." ("hudud Allah" is the subject.) This is supported by the reading of Abdullah: ﴿except that they fear﴾ [with ﴿yakhafu﴾]. Ibn Atiyya said: "Khafa" (to fear) takes two objects: one is made the subject of the verb, and the other is implied with an omitted preposition, so the position of "an" is in the genitive by the implied preposition, or in the accusative according to the two differing opinions. Abu Hayyan refuted him in al-Bahr by saying that the grammarians did not mention it when they counted what transitively takes two objects, and the origin of one of them is with a preposition. In the reading of Ubayy: ﴿except that they suspect﴾ (yazunna), which supports interpreting "zann" (suspicion) as "khawf" (fear). ﴿So if you fear﴾ is an address to the rulers only, so that a change of style before the completion of the sentence is not required, ﴿that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾, which He has set for them.

﴿فَلا جُناحَ عَلَيْهِما﴾ That is, the two spouses. This clause stands in place of the apodosis, meaning: "So command them, for there is no blame." ﴿فِيما افْتَدَتْ بِهِ﴾ "in what she ransoms with" (her own self) by khul' (divorce initiated by the wife in return for compensation). It is not a matter of blame on the husband for taking it, nor on her for giving it to him. Ibn Jarir reported on the authority of Ikrimah that he was asked, "Did khul' have any precedent?" He said: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, used to say: "The first khul' in Islam was in the case of the sister of Abdullah ibn Ubayy, the wife of Thabit ibn Qays, that she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, nothing will ever bring my head and his together. I lifted the side of the tent and saw him coming with a group of people, and he is the darkest of them, the shortest of them in stature, and the ugliest of them in face.' Her husband said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I gave her my best property, a garden of mine. If she returns my garden to me—' He (ﷺ) said: 'What do you say?' She said: 'Yes, and if he wishes, I will add to it.' He said: 'So he separated them.'" In the narration of al-Bukhari, it is: "that the woman's name was Jamilah, and that she was the daughter of Abdullah the hypocrite." This is what the hadith scholars (huffaz) preferred. That her name was Zaynab came through the route of al-Daraqutni. The hafiz Ibn Hajar said: "Perhaps she had two names, or one of them is a laqab (epithet); otherwise Jamilah is more sound." It has also occurred in another hadith, reported by Malik, al-Shafi'i and Abu Dawud, that the name of Thabit's wife was Habibah bint Sahl. The hafiz said: "What appears is that these are two separate incidents that occurred to him with two women, because of the fame of the two hadiths, the soundness of the two chains, and the difference of the two contexts."

﴿تِلْكَ حُدُودُ اللَّهِ﴾ "These are the limits of Allah." This is a reference to the rulings that were set out from His saying, ﴿الطَّلاقُ مَرَّتانِ﴾ "Divorce is twice," up to this point. The sentence is a fadhlaka (concluding summary) of that, and it is introduced in order to make the prohibition that follows consequent upon it.

﴿فَلا تَعْتَدُوها﴾ "So do not transgress them," by opposing them or rejecting them. ﴿ومَن يَتَعَدَّ حُدُودَ اللَّهِ فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الظّالِمُونَ﴾ "And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah, it is those who are the wrongdoers" (229). This is a ta'dhil (concluding phrase) for the sake of exaggerating the warning, and the waw is for i'tiraD (parenthetical insertion). In placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, there is what is not hidden of bringing in awe and cultivating reverence.

The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that khul' is not permissible without dislike and discord, because the negation of permissibility, which is the ruling of the contract in all circumstances except the state of discord, indicates the invalidity of the contract and its impermissibility outwardly, unless some evidence indicates otherwise. It also indicates that it is not permissible for it to be with all that the husband has given her, let alone with the surplus, because (مَن) in ﴿مِمّا آتَيْتُمُوهُنَّ﴾ "of what you have given them" is partitive (tab'idiyyah). So the import of the exception is the permissibility of taking some portion of what you have given them at the time of fear. As for the word (ما) in His saying, ﴿فِيما افْتَدَتْ﴾ "in what she ransomed with," it is not apparent in generality such that it would contradict the apparent meaning of the verse concerning the stated ruling. Rather, the fa' of explanation (fa'u al-tafsir) in ﴿فَإنْ خِفْتُمْ﴾ "if you fear" indicates outwardly that it is an explanation of the ruling understood by way of mukhalafah (opposite implication) from the exception. Its benefit is the explicit statement of the ruling and the negation of blame in this contract, for the establishment of permissibility derived from the exception may coexist with blame, such as when it is accompanied by dislike. Yes, it admits generality, so it is not an explicit text on the impermissibility of khul' with all that is given.

For this reason, Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Divorce her even for her earring." And what supports the first is what Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it hasan) and al-Hakim (who graded it sahih) reported from Thawban, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Any woman who asks her husband for divorce without any harm, the fragrance of Paradise is forbidden to her," and he said: "The khul'at (women who seek khul') are the hypocrites." What supports the second is what was narrated in some routes, that he (ﷺ) said to Jamilah: "Will you return to him his garden?" She said: "I will return it and add to it." He (ﷺ) said: "As for the addition, no." And although this indicates the negation of an addition, not of the whole dowry, it is derived from it that (فِيما افْتَدَتْ بِهِ) is not on its generality. So the intended meaning is what is derived from the exception, which is a part.

Most of the jurists hold that khul' without discord and with all that was given is disliked (makruh), but it is valid (nafidh), because the pillars of the contract, namely offer and acceptance and the competence of the two contracting parties with mutual consent, are fulfilled, and the prohibition is due to an accompanying matter, like a sale at the time of the call to prayer (Friday), and that does not negate permissibility. It is also held that it is valid with the wording of mufadah (ransoming), because Allah, exalted is He, named khul' as iftida' (ransoming).

It is disputed whether, if it takes place without the word of divorce, it is a fasakh (annulment) or a talaq (divorce). Whoever holds it to be a fasakh argues with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿فَإنْ طَلَّقَها﴾ "then if he divorces her." For its following the khul' after the mention of the two divorces requires that it be a fourth divorce if khul' were a divorce. The more apparent view is that it is a divorce, and our companions (the Hanafis) went to this, and it is one opinion of the Shafi'is, because it is a separation by the choice of the husband, so it is like divorce for compensation. Thereupon it would be...

[Page 141]

﴿فَإنْ طَلَّقَها﴾ (*So if he divorces her*) is connected to His, may He be glorified, saying: ﴿The divorce is twice﴾, as an explanation of the Exalted's saying: ﴿or retain her with kindness﴾. It is not connected to the verse of khul' (*divorce initiated by the wife through compensation*), so as to impose the prohibited meaning. The mention of khul' is then a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraḍ*, an interjected phrase that does not grammatically complete the sentence) to show that divorce takes place sometimes without compensation and sometimes with compensation. The meaning is: if he divorces her after the two divorces, or after the divorce described earlier.

﴿فَلا تَحِلُّ لَهُ مِن بَعْدُ﴾ (*then she is not lawful to him thereafter*), that is, after that divorce, ﴿حَتّى تَنْكِحَ زَوْجًا غَيْرَهُ﴾ (*until she marries another husband*), that is, she marries another husband and he has intercourse with her. Mere contracting of the marriage is not sufficient, as Ibn al-Musayyib held, and his view was judged to be in error. This is because the contract is understood from *zawjan* (*a husband*), and the intercourse from *tankiha* (*marries*, in the sense of consummation). Even if this were not understood, and *nikah* were taken to mean the contract alone, the verse would be unrestricted, but the Sunnah has restricted it. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim and a group of others transmitted from A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The wife of Rifa'a al-Qurazi came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'I was with Rifa'a, and he divorced me, and his divorce was final. Then I married 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr, but he is like the hem of a garment (*i.e., impotent*).' The Prophet (ﷺ) smiled and said: 'Do you want to return to Rifa'a? No, until you taste his honey (*sexual intercourse*) and he tastes yours.'" And from Ikrima: "This verse was revealed concerning this woman, whose name is A'isha bint 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Atik, and there was revealed concerning her: ﴿So if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter until she marries another husband﴾," so he has intercourse with her. If he divorces her after he has had intercourse with her, ﴿there is no blame upon them both to return to each other﴾. In this there is evidence that the second spouse must be a true husband. Therefore, if a slave woman were divorced irrevocably (*albatta*) and then her master had intercourse with her, she would not become lawful to the first husband. It also shows that if the husband bought her from her master, or her master gave her to him, after he had made the divorce final, it would not be lawful for him to have intercourse with her in either case by right of ownership (*milk al-yamin*), ﴿until she marries another husband﴾. It also shows that the guardian (*wali*) is not a condition of the marriage, because He attributed the contract to her. The wisdom in this ruling is to deter the husband from hastening to divorce, because when he knows that if he makes the divorce final she will not become lawful to him until another man has had intercourse with her, he may refrain from divorcing her irrevocably. Perhaps they (*i.e., the scholars*) considered that he would be restrained from divorcing her irrevocably, because although it is permissible under the Sharia, human nature recoils from it and the jealousy of men rejects it. A marriage with the condition of *tahlil* (*a marriage contracted to make a woman lawful again to her former husband, known as halala*) is invalid according to Malik, Ahmad, al-Thawri, the Zahiris and many others, and they cited as evidence what Ibn Majah, al-Hakim (who authenticated it) and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Shall I not tell you about the borrowed ram?' They said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'It is the *muhallil* (*the one who effects halala*). Allah has cursed the muhallil and the muhallal lahu (*the one for whom halala is effected*).'" And 'Abd al-Razzaq transmitted from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I will not be brought a muhallil or a muhallal lahu except that I will stone them both." And al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Sulayman ibn Yasar that 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, was brought a man who had married a woman in order to make her lawful for her husband, so he separated them and said: "She will not return to him except by a marriage of desire, not of deceit." Among us (*i.e., the Hanafis*) this is disliked (*makruh*). The hadith does not indicate the invalidity of the marriage, because prohibiting the contract does not indicate that it is invalid. Calling it *muhallil* implies its validity, because it is the cause of lawfulness. Some scholars interpreted the hadith as referring to one who makes it a means of livelihood, or to the case where the condition of *tahlil* is stated within the contract itself, not to one who conceals that intention in his heart, for that is not of that rank. Indeed, it was said that the doer of this is rewarded.

﴿فَإنْ طَلَّقَها﴾ (*If he divorces her*), the second husband, ﴿فَلا جُناحَ عَلَيْهِما﴾ (*then there is no blame upon them both*), that is, upon the first husband and the woman, ﴿أنْ يَتَراجَعا﴾ (*to return to each other*), that each of them return to the other by marriage after the lapse of the waiting period (*'idda*), ﴿إنْ ظَنّا أنْ يُقِيما حُدُودَ اللَّهِ﴾ (*if they both think that they will keep the limits of Allah*), that is, if in their assumption they will uphold the rights of marriage which Allah, the Exalted, has defined and legislated. Interpreting *zann* (*assumption*) as *'ilm* (*certain knowledge*) here has been said to be incorrect, both in meaning and in wording. In meaning, because one does not know the future with certainty in most cases. In wording, because the particle *an* (*that*), which is verbal-noun-forming (*al-maṣdariyya*), indicates expectation, and that contradicts knowledge. It was answered that the future may be known and certain in some matters, and that is sufficient for validity; and that Sibawayh, who is the authority of Arabic grammar, permitted *ma 'alimtu illa an yaquma Zaydun* (*I know only that Zayd will stand*), while the one who disagreed with him in this was Abu Ali al-Farisi. It is not hidden that the first objection is of no benefit in our case, because although the future may be known in some matters, what is here is not such, and return is not tied to knowledge; rather, assumption suffices for it.

﴿وتِلْكَ﴾ (*These*) refers to the rulings mentioned up to this point, ﴿حُدُودَ اللَّهِ﴾ (*are the limits of Allah*), that is, His specified rulings, protected from being violated by change or contravention. ﴿يُبَيِّنُها﴾ (*He makes them clear*) by this suitable explanation, or *sa-yubayyinuhā* (*He will make them clear*), on the basis that some of them will receive additional clarification in the Book and the Sunnah. The clause is a predicate (*khabar*) according to the view of those who permit that in such a case, or a circumstantial clause (*ḥal*) from *ḥudūd Allāh*, with the operative element being the sense of the demonstrative. It was read as *nubayyinuhā* (*We make them clear*) with the nun, as an *iltifat* (*a shift from the third person to the first person*). ﴿لِقَوْمٍ يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (*for a people who know*), that is, who understand and act according to the requirement of knowledge. So it is for encouraging action, as has been said, or because they are the ones who benefit from the explanation, or because what will be added to some of the limits is not understood except by those firmly grounded in knowledge, or in order to exclude those who are not accountable (*ghayr al-mukallafin*).

**[p. 143]**

﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term﴾: that is, the end of their waiting period (*'iddah*). This is a metaphor (*majaz*) of the type where the whole is used for a part, if we say that *ajal* (term) is literally (*haqiqah*) applied to the entire duration, as the wording of *al-Sihah* suggests, and this is the usage common in the speech of the jurists. However, al-Azhari's report from al-Layth indicates that it is literally applied to the final part. Both usages are attested in the Noble Book. If it belongs to *ishtirak* (homonymy), then that is the case; otherwise, the figurative extension from the whole to the final part is stronger than the reverse. (*Al-buluugh*, "reaching") originally means arrival, but it may also be used for drawing near to it, which is the meaning intended in the verse. This is either a metaphor of approaching (*mushara'ah*) or a *isti'arah* (metaphorical borrowing), treating what is close to occurring as though it has occurred, so that a ruling may be based upon it.

﴿then retain them honourably or release them honourably﴾: because there is no retention after the term has ended, since at that point she is no longer his wife nor within his waiting period, and so he has no authority over her. *Al-imsak* (retention) is a metaphor for taking her back (*muraja'ah*), since it is its cause. *Al-tasrih* (release) means letting go, and is a metaphor for leaving. The meaning is: take them back without harm (*dirar*), or let them go so that their waiting period ends without prolongation. This is a restatement of the ruling in the case of their reaching their term, out of concern for the matter and emphasis on the obligation to comply with it. Some people have understood "retain them honourably" as contracting the marriage anew with good companionship, and "release them honourably" as not preventing them from marrying another. In that case there is no need to posit a metaphor in *balaghna* (they reached), though its distance from the occasion of revelation is evident. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted from al-Suddi that a man of the Ansar called Thabit ibn Yasar divorced his wife, and when her waiting period was about to end, with only two or three days remaining, he took her back and then divorced her again. He did this with her until nine months had passed, harming her. Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed this verse: ﴿And do not retain them to harm them﴾, as an emphasis on the command ("retain them honourably") and an explanation of its meaning. It is more indicative of permanence and stability than the former, and more explicit in forbidding what they used to practise. *Dirar* (harm) is in the accusative, either as a causative (*'illiyyah*) or a circumstantial (*hal*) construction; that is, do not take them back for the purpose of harm, or as those who harm. The object of the prohibition is the restriction. The *lam* in His saying ﴿so that you transgress﴾ is connected to *dirar*; that is, to wrong them by compelling them to ransom themselves. It has been objected that *dirar* is wrongdoing and *i'tida'* (transgression) is similar to it, so that it would reduce to "do not retain them wrongfully in order that you may wrong them", and this is, as you see, weak. It has been answered that by *dirar* is meant prolonging the term, and by *i'tida'* compelling them, so that it is as though it were said: do not retain them through prolongation in order that you compel them to seek release (*ikhtila'*) and to wrongdoing. It is often intended that this should lead to another wrong. The common view is that this interpretation is required on the first reading of *dirar*, and that it is impossible for this to be the cause of what preceded it, since the object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*) cannot be multiplied except by conjunction or by apposition (*badal*), and the latter is impossible because the *i'rab* (grammatical case-endings) differ. It is permissible on the second reading. It has also been permitted for it to be connected to the verb absolutely if the *lam* is taken to indicate consequence (*al-'aqibah*). There is no harm in a verb extending to both a cause and a consequence, since they differ, and even if the *lam* is literal for both, according to one view.

﴿And whoever does that﴾: the mentioned act, and the distance expressed in the demonstrative is to signal how far he has descended in evil and corruption. ﴿has certainly wronged himself﴾ by exposing himself to punishment, or by depriving himself of the benefits of religion, namely the reward attained through good companionship, and the benefits of this world, namely women's lack of desire for him afterwards because of his notoriety for this disgraceful act.

﴿And do not take the signs of Allah in jest﴾: the signs that contain the rulings mentioned concerning women, or all His signs, of which this is one, ﴿a mockery﴾, being made fun of by neglecting them and being careless in preserving them, because of your indifference to women and your lack of concern for them. This is a prohibition whose real intent is the opposite command: be earnest in acting upon them and in doing what they contain, and guard them with due care.

Ibn Abi 'Umrah and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Abu al-Darda', who said: "A man would divorce and then say, 'I was joking,' and would manumit and then say, 'I was joking,' so this was revealed." Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi (who graded it *hasan*), Ibn Majah and al-Hakim (who graded it *sahih*) transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three things, whether serious or jest, are binding: marriage, divorce, and taking back (a wife)." And from Abu al-Darda': "Three things, the one who plays with them is as one who is serious: marriage, divorce, and manumission." And from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: "Four things are locked (binding): the vow, divorce, manumission, and marriage."

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾: that is, respond to it with gratitude and by fulfilling its rights. *Al-ni'mah* (favour) may be general, so that ﴿and what He revealed to you﴾ is coordinated with it as a specific upon the general. Or it may be restricted to Islam and the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and these two are singled out for mention to be appropriate to what preceded, and to indicate that the retention for harm which they practised belongs to the customs of the Jahiliyyah that oppose the religion. As if it were said: be earnest in acting upon the verses, by way of allusion, and then this is affirmed by saying that it is the thanks for the favour, so fulfil its due. The conjunction is then an emphasis upon an emphasis, because Islam and the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) include the sending down of the Book and the Sunnah. This is close to *'atf al-tafsir* (explanatory conjunction), and there is no harm in calling it *'atf al-taqrir* (confirmatory conjunction). It has been said that if the favour were generalised, its placement would not have this excellence. It is not hidden that this is open to dispute. The first adverbial phrase is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) of *ni'mah*, or as a description of it, according to the view of those who permit the omission of the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause. It may also be connected to the noun itself if it is intended as bestowal, since it is a verbal noun like *nabat* (growth) in *man anbat* (one who causes growth), and the feminine *ta'* (tha'marbutah) does not affect its operation, because it is built upon it, as in his saying:

*Were it not for hope of victory from you and fear of your punishment,*
*They would have been to us like watering-places.*

The second adverbial phrase is connected to what is before it, and it was introduced to alert the addressees and to honour them. *Ma* is a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun has been omitted from the relative clause. *Min* in His saying ﴿of the Book and the Wisdom﴾ is explicative. What is meant by them is the Qur'an, which comprises both designations, or the Qur'an and the Sunnah. Singling them out for mention after their inclusion in what was mentioned serves to show their excellence and to indicate that nobility has reached a level at which inclusion is no longer possible. This is of the type of:

*Though the people may be wealthy and you among them,*
*Musk is nonetheless but a part of the blood of the gazelle.*

﴿He admonishes you thereby﴾: that is, by what He revealed. It is a circumstantial clause of the subject of *anzala* or of its object, or of both together. It is permitted that *ma* be the subject, with this clause as its predicate, and "of the Book" as a circumstantial phrase of the omitted returning pronoun. It has been said that the clause is parenthetical, for encouragement and for giving the reason.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ in His commands and in fulfilling His rights, ﴿and know that Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ 231. Nothing is hidden from Him of what you do or leave undone, so let one beware of His recompense and punishment. Or: He is knowing of all things, so He commands only what contains wisdom and benefit, so do not oppose Him. In this conjunction there is something that emphasises the preceding commands and rulings. This is not the kind of emphasis that requires separation (*fasl*), because it is not a repetition of the concept of what is emphasised, nor is it identical with it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 232:**

﴿When you divorce women and they reach their term﴾, i.e., their ʿiddah (the waiting period after divorce) has ended, as the context indicates.

﴿do not prevent them from marrying their husbands﴾. I.e., do not prevent them from that. The root of ʿadl is confinement and constraint. From it comes ʿaddalati al-dajājatu (with the doubled consonant), said of a hen when its egg gets lodged and does not come out. The verb has three vowel variants for its middle radical. Scholars differed about who is addressed. One view, which al-Imam [Fakhr al-Din al-Razi] chose, is that the address is to the husbands who divorced, since they used to prevent their divorcées from remarrying after the ʿiddah had passed, and did not let them marry, through oppression and coercion, out of the zealotry of the Jahiliyya (the pre-Islamic period). This could happen by sending someone to those who proposed to them to frighten him, or by attributing to the women things that would repel a man from wanting them. On this reading, the husbands are the ones meant by the wives who wish to marry someone. The Arabs often name a thing by what it eventually becomes. Another view, which al-Qadi [al-Baydawi] chose, is that the address is to the guardians (awliya'). Al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Abu Dawud and a great many others have related, through various routes, from Maqil ibn Yasar, who said: "I had a sister, and my paternal cousin came to me and proposed, so I married her to him. She remained with him for as long as it was, then he divorced her with one divorce and did not take her back until her ʿiddah had ended. Then he loved her and she loved him. Then he proposed to her along with the other suitors. I said to him: 'You worthless fellow! I honoured you by giving her to you in marriage, and you divorced her, then you came proposing to her! By God, she will never return to you.' He was a man of no harm, and the woman wanted to return to him. God, exalted is He, knew his need for her and her need for her husband, so God, exalted is He, revealed this verse." He said: "So it was about me that it was revealed. I made expiation for my oath and married her to him." In another wording: when Maqil heard it he said, "I hear and obey my Lord," then he called him and said, "I will marry you to her and honour you." On this reading, the husbands are those who had been husbands, and the address of divorce is then either to the same addressees as this address, with the attribution of divorce to the guardians being by way of causation, as the act of standing in the way of remarriage indicates. Or it may remain in its apparent sense, addressing the divorcing husbands, with the scattering of pronouns tolerated because the meaning is clear. A third view, which al-Zamakhshari chose, is that the address is to all people, so that it covers the prevention by both husbands and guardians together. This avoids the scattering of the two address pronouns and the separation of the two predications, while agreeing with the occasion of revelation. It also conveys the gravity of prevention: guardians must not even come near it, and it is the duty of all people to help the one who is wronged. Some scholars made the preceding addresses [in the verses] also general, and mentioned that since direct action depends on rational and legal conditions, it is distributed according to them. For example, when a group, whether counted or uncounted, is told: "Pay the zakah, marry off the suitable partners, and restrain the oppressors," all are addressed, and the distribution is as already explained. Furthermore, in the verse, under whichever interpretation it is understood, there is no evidence that a woman may not marry herself, as has been thought. The prohibition on guardians from preventing marriage does not mean that the validity of the marriage depends on their consent; rather, it is to remove harm from them. For although women are able to marry themselves according to the law, they avoid doing so for fear of blame and estrangement, or fear of being harmed by them. The attribution of the marriage to them in the phrase suggests that it does not depend on or require anyone else, which is a metaphorical usage and contrary to the apparent sense. Two possibilities have been allowed for ﴿that they marry﴾ (an-yankiḥna). The first is that it is a badal ishtimal (comprehensive substitution apposition) for the object pronoun before it. The second is that it is in the sense of dropping the preposition, and its place is then either accusative or genitive according to the two opinions. ﴿when they agree among themselves﴾ (idha taraḍaw) is a temporal clause modifying (do not prevent, lā taʿḍulū). The masculine form is used by way of predominance (taghlīb), and the condition is attached to it because it is the customary situation, not to permit prevention before the agreement is complete. It has also been said that it is a temporal clause modifying (that they marry, an yankiḥna). The phrase ﴿among themselves﴾ (baynahum) is a temporal adverb for the agreement, indicating its firmness and solidity. ﴿in a fair manner﴾ (bil-maʿrūf), i.e., in a way that is not reprehensible by the law or by custom. The bāʾ is either attached to an omitted verb that serves as a circumstantial clause from the subject of (they agree, taraḍaw), or it is a qualifier of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: an agreement that is in accordance with what is fair. Or it is attached to (they agree) or to (they marry). The specification of this indicates that preventing marriage to someone who is not an equal (kufʾ), or for less than the proper bridal gift (mahr al-mithl), is not a case of prevention. ﴿That﴾ (dhālika) refers to what has been detailed. The second-person address is to the plural in terms of the group, or to each individual, or the kāf (the suffix of "that") indicates an address in which attention is cut off from the addressee in number, gender and other respects.

The purpose is to indicate the presence of what is pointed to in the mind of the one addressed, in contrast to something absent and past. Or it is addressed to the Messenger (ﷺ), so that it conforms to what is in Surah al-Talaq. It also signals that the thing referred to is something that hardly anyone can conceive of by themselves, and that conceiving of it requires support from God, exalted is He.

﴿With it is admonished whoever among you believes in God and the Last Day﴾. He singled them out for mention because they are the ones who hasten to comply, out of reverence for God, exalted is He, and fear of His punishment. The phrase ﴿among you﴾ (minkum) is either attached to (was, kāna) according to the view of those who hold that, or to an omitted element serving as a circumstantial clause from the subject of (believes, yu'minu).

﴿That﴾ (dhalikum), i.e., being admonished by it and acting on its requirement. ﴿is purer for you﴾ (azkā lakum), i.e., greater in blessing and benefit. ﴿and more purifying﴾ (waṭhhar), i.e., more cleansing from the filth of sins. The word ﴿for you﴾ (lakum) is omitted, being sufficient by what precedes it. It has also been said that the intended meaning is "purer for you and for them," because of the suspicion that may fall upon the spouses through the relationship between them. ﴿And God knows﴾ what benefit is in it, ﴿while you do not know﴾ that. So there is no opinion except to follow. It is also possible to generalise the object in both places, so that what is mentioned is included first and foremost. The purpose of the sentence is to urge compliance.

[Page 146]

﴿The mothers shall nurse their children﴾ is a command expressed in the form of a report, for emphasis. Its meaning is recommendation (nadb) or obligation (wujub), if it is restricted to cases where the child will nurse only from his mother, or no wet-nurse (zi'r) is available for him, or the father is unable to hire one. The expression of the mothers by the above title is to appeal to their compassion for their children. The ruling is general for divorced and non-divorced mothers, as the apparent meaning requires. Some scholars restricted it to divorced mothers. This is related from Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Zayd ibn Aslam. Two arguments are cited for this view. The first is that Allah, exalted is He, mentioned this verse immediately after the verses on divorce, so it is part of their completion. He completed them with this because, when separation occurs, enmity and hatred often arise, and this usually moves the woman to harm the child, out of spite toward the divorcing husband and to harm him. She may also desire to marry another man, and this often leads to neglecting the child's affairs and failing to attend to him. Therefore, He commanded them in the most emphatic way to look after the child and attend to his affair. The second argument is that the obligation of provision (rizq) and clothing for the nursing mothers afterward requires specification, since if the marriage were still in place, the husband would owe that because of the marriage and not because of nursing. Al-Wahidi said: "It is better to restrict it to mothers while the marriage continues, because a divorced woman is not entitled to clothing, but only to payment." It is not hidden that applying the verse in its general sense is better, and the purpose of the subsequent connection is not lost. The obligation of provision and clothing for nursing mothers does not require specification, because it is for some of them. Moreover, as has been said: there is nothing in the verse indicating that it is for nursing. Whoever says it is for nursing has made it a payment (ujrah) to them, except that he did not express it as such, but expressed it by its most common purpose, as an encouragement to give themselves for this or to give what they spend it on. So reflect.

﴿Two whole years﴾: that is, two years. The root (of the word) revolves around turning over (inqilab). It is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and ﴿whole﴾ is its adjective. It is described thus as an emphasis, to clarify that the determination is precise and not approximate, based on the customary leniency. ﴿For whoever wishes to complete the nursing﴾ is an explanation of the person to whom the ruling is addressed. The prepositional phrase in such a construction is a predicate of an omitted subject; that is: that (ruling) is for whoever wishes to complete the nursing. It is also permitted that it be connected to ﴿shall nurse﴾, because the father is obligated to arrange nursing, just as he is obligated to provide maintenance for the mother, and the mother nurses for him. That nursing is obligatory on the father does not contradict the command to the mothers, because the command is for recommendation, or because it is obligatory on them too in the previous cases. The verse is used as evidence that the maximum period of nursing is two years, and nursing after them is not counted, so its ruling is not applied, and that it is permissible for it to be less than them. It was read as ﴿to complete﴾ in the nominative (an yutimma, with raf'), and its interpretation is disputed. It has been said: the verbal particle "an" has been treated like its sister in non-operation (ihmal), just as its sister has been treated like it in operation (i'mal) in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "As you are, so will you be ruled over," according to one opinion. It has also been said: the reading is "an yutimmu" with a plural pronoun, in view of the meaning of "min" (whoever), and the waw was dropped in pronunciation because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, so the written form followed it.

﴿And upon the one to whom the child is born﴾: that is, the father, for the child is born to him and is attributed to him. He did not express it with this (the word father) even though it is shorter and clearer, in order to indicate the reason for the obligation, through the sense of attribution contained in it, which the preposition (lam) points to. This indication is called idmaj (embedding) by the rhetoricians (ahl al-badi'), and "indication of the text" (isharat al-nass) by us (the jurists). It has been said: he expressed it this way because the father may not be bound to provide maintenance, but rather the one to whom the child is born is, such as when a slave woman is under him and bears a child: then her child's maintenance is on the owner of the mother, because he is the one to whom the child is born, not the father. This is far-fetched, because "the one to whom the child is born" does not refer to the father and the master in one single sense, and the ruling on slaves is an extraneous matter in the context.

﴿Their provision and their clothing﴾: that is, delivering that to them, i.e. to the mothers, as payment for them. Hiring the mother is permissible according to al-Shafi'i, while according to us it is not permissible as long as she is in marriage or in the waiting period ('iddah). ﴿In a fair manner﴾: that is, without extravagance or stinginess, or according to what the judge sees fit and what his means can bear.

﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾: this is a reason for the obligation of provision "in a fair manner," or an explanation of "fair manner." For this there is a separate clause, and it indicates that Allah, exalted is He, does not burden the servant with what he cannot bear. It does not negate the possibility and the essential capacity (al-jawaz wal-imkan al-dhati), so it is not a valid proof for the Mu'tazilah. The accusative of ﴿its capacity﴾ is as a second object of ﴿burdened﴾. It was also read as ﴿is not burdened﴾ (wa-la tukallaf) with a fatha on the ta', and as ﴿We do not burden﴾ (la nukallif) with the nun.

﴿No mother shall be harmed because of her child, nor a father because of his child﴾: this is a detailed explanation of what is understood from the preceding, and a bringing of it closer to understanding, and this is what calls for the separate clause. The word for harm (mudarra) is a form of reciprocal action (mufa'alah) from harm (darar). The reciprocal form is either intended, with the object omitted; that is: a mother shall not harm her husband by means of her child, which is by scolding him over it, demanding from him what is not just of provision and clothing, preoccupying his heart with neglect of the child's affair, or saying to him, after the child has become attached to her, "Find a wet-nurse for him," for example. Nor shall a father harm the wife he is married to because of his child, by withholding from her anything of her provision and clothing that is due from him, or by taking the child from her while she wants to nurse him, or by compelling her to nurse. Or it is not intended, and the meaning is: neither of them shall harm the other because of the child. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read ﴿shall not be harmed﴾ (la tuddarru) with a damma, so the clause is in the position of a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal) for what precedes it. al-Hasan read ﴿harm﴾ (tudarri) with a kasra, and its original form is "tudarri" with a kasra on the ra' and in the active voice, and he permitted a fatha on it in the passive voice. What makes this clear is that it was read as ﴿shall not be harmed﴾ (tudarar) and ﴿shall not harm﴾ (tudarir) with jazm and a fatha or kasra on the first ra'. On the reading in the passive voice, the intended meaning is the prohibition against the mother being harmed by the husband, and against the husband being harmed by her because of the child. The ba' (because of) in every case is causal. You may also take the form (fa'ala) to mean (fa'ala) (i.e. the same as the simple form), and the ba' is "a sword that speaks eloquently" (sayf khatib), i.e., an effective instrument. The meaning would then be: a mother shall not harm her child by spoiling his nourishment and care, neglecting what is fitting for him, and handing him over to the father after he has become attached to her; and a father shall not harm his child by taking him from her hands or by falling short in his duty toward her, so that she then falls short in her duty toward him. Abu Ja'far read ﴿shall not be harmed﴾ with sukun and shadda, in intention of pausing. From al-A'raj: ﴿shall not be harmed﴾ with sukun and without shadda, from "darra, yudir." He intended the pause just as the first did, otherwise the analogical form would be deleting the alif. From the scribe of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): "la tudrir." The mention of the child in both places, and its attribution to her at one time and to him at another, is for appeal to compassion, and to indicate what is like the reason for the prohibition. For this reason the apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun. Among the strange interpretations is what the Imamiyyah narrated from the two sayyids, al-Sadiq and al-Baqir (may Allah be pleased with them both): that the meaning is: "a mother shall not be harmed" by abstaining from intercourse for fear of pregnancy for the sake of her nursing child, and "a father shall not be harmed" by preventing her from intercourse in the same way for the sake of his child. In that case the ba' is definitely causal, and both verbs must be in the passive voice. There is no subtle reason apparent for the mention of the child in both places, and the verse would depart from what the context requires. It is far from al-Baqir and al-Sadiq to adopt what this lying narrator claimed.

﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾: this is a conjunction with His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and upon the one to whom the child is born﴾, etc., and what lies between them is an intervening explanation or reason. The intended "heir" is the heir of the child, for it is obligatory on him to provide the like of what was obligatory on the father of provision and clothing in a fair manner, if the child has no property. This is the interpretation transmitted from 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid, 'Ata', Ibrahim, al-Sha'bi, 'Abdullah ibn 'Utbah and many others. It is supported by the fact that the definite article (al) serves as a substitute for the pronoun of the genitive, and the return of the pronoun to the nearest antecedent, which is the most common usage. Imam Abu Hanifah restricted this heir to the one who had a forbidden kinship (dhu rahim muharram) with the child, and Hammad also said this. It is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "And upon the heir who has a forbidden kinship, the like of that." It has also been said: his agnatic relatives ('asabah). Abu Zayd said this, and something supporting it is related from 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him). al-Shafi'i said: the intended meaning is the heir of the father, that is, the child, meaning: the child's maintenance is from his own property if the father dies. It has been objected that this interpretation is rejected, because it does not specify that the maintenance is from his property if the father dies. Rather, if he has property, the father is not obligated to pay the wage for nursing; instead he is obligated to provide maintenance for the child, and the wage for nursing is from the child's property by right of guardianship. But there is room for discussion in this. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the surviving one of the two parents, and "heir" has come in the sense of "survivor," as in the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Allah, let me enjoy my hearing and my sight, and make them the inheritor from me." It has been said: this agrees with the school of al-Shafi'i, since according to him there is no maintenance obligation except for children. There is no concealing the difficulty in this: if "min" (from) is for explanation (bayan), it results in repetition, awkwardness, or departure from the apparent meaning; and if it is for origin (ibtida'), the remaining meaning is other than the two parents, and it may be from the agnatic relatives or the kin-relatives (dhawu al-arham) whose kinship is not the kinship of parenthood. That this agrees with the school of al-Shafi'i is only possible if it is determined that the survivors are relatives by parenthood, and there is nothing in the wording that indicates this, as is not hidden.

﴿And if both of them wish﴾: that is, the two parents, ﴿weaning﴾ (fisal), that is, the weaning of the child before the two years. This is related from Mujahid, Qatadah and the People of the House. It has been said: before them or after them, and this is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both). According to the first view, this is an explanation of the purpose of ﴿for whoever wishes to complete﴾, and a clarification of the ruling for the case of wishing not to complete it. The indefinite form is to signal that this weaning is not customary. According to the second view, there is an expansion regarding increase and reduction in the period of nursing after it was limited, and the indefinite form is for generality. According to both views, it is permissible that it be for indicating its magnitude, considering the child, because of what it involves in leaving what is familiar. ﴿By mutual consent﴾ is connected to an omitted element that the mind naturally supplies, even if it is a specific verb: that is, issuing ﴿by mutual consent﴾. It is also permissible to connect it to "wish" as "from both of them," that is, the two parents, not from only one of them alone, because of the possibility that one of them would proceed to do what harms the child, such as the mother becoming weary or the father being stingy. ﴿And consultation﴾ regarding the child's affair and investigating his conditions. It is derived from "shawr," which is gathering honey, and likewise "mushawarah" and "mashurah." What is meant by this is the extraction of an opinion. Its indefiniteness is for magnification.

﴿So there is no blame upon them both﴾ in that. He took the mother's consent into account, although the guardian of the child is the father, and his fitness is tied to his judgment, out of regard for the child's welfare; for the mother, because of the completeness of her compassion for the infant, may see what is in his best interest. ﴿And if you wish﴾ is an address to the fathers, urging them to comply, on the assumption that there is no agreement to wean [the child]. ﴿To have your children nursed by wet-nurses﴾ — the first object is omitted as being understood; that is, you seek wet-nurses to nurse your children, from "arda'at al-mar'ah tiflan" (the woman nursed a child) and "istarda'tuha iyyahu" (I asked her to nurse it for him), like your saying: "Anjaha Allah ta'ala hajati wa istanjahtuha iyyahu" (God, exalted is He, granted my need and I asked her to grant it). Al-Imam al-Kirmani has explicitly stated that the verbal form "istif'al" has come to express seeking more (such as "istinja'" meaning seeking deliverance, "isti'tab" meaning seeking appeasement), and others have stated this as well. So there is no need to say that it derives from "rada'a" in the sense of "ardha'a"; and [al-Kirmani] did not take it as the first [meaning] of the matter, because it is not found in their speech, and that is far from verification. It has been said that "istarda'a" only takes a second object by means of a preposition: one says "istarda'at" the woman for the child, and the meaning is that you seek wet-nurses ﴿for your children﴾, so the preposition is omitted, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they measure for them﴾, that is, measure for them, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, that is, in that. He used the absolute wording as evidence that the husband may have the child nursed and prevent the wife from nursing, which is the position of the Shafi'is; but in our view the mother has more right to nurse her child, and the father may not have another nurse brought when she is willing to nurse him, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the mothers nurse their children﴾; and by this the absolute wording is restricted. The words of Ibn Shihab point to this. ﴿When you hand over﴾ to the wet-nurses ﴿what you have given﴾, that is: what you have guaranteed and undertaken, or intended to give, so that the result is not a case of obtaining what is already obtained. Ibn Kathir read "ataytum" from "ata ilayhi ihsanan" (he did him a kindness) when he does it; and Shayban on the authority of Asim read "uwitum" (what Allah, exalted is He, has given you and empowered you to pay of the wage). ﴿In accordance with what is fair﴾ is connected to "sallamtum" (you hand over); that is, in the customary manner that is judged good by the Shari'ah. It is also permitted that it be connected to "ataytum," and that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from its agent or from the agent of the verb preceding it. The response of the conditional is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. Handing over is not a condition for the removal of sin; rather it is the preferable and more beneficial course for the child. So he likened what is among the conditions of priority to what is among the conditions of validity, for the sake of giving it attention, and so borrowed its expression for it. It has been said: there is no need for this, because the negation of sin through the payment of the wage is absolute, not restricted to paying it in advance; that is: there is no blame upon you in having them nursed, provided you do not sin by exceeding in the wage and wronging the hired nurse. There is room for reflection in this, because if the wage has not been handed over afterward, the sin lies only in the transgression, and the nursing beforehand was free of anything that would entail sin. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ in regard to observing the rulings, ﴿and know that Allah, of what you do, is All-Seeing﴾ (233), nothing of your deeds is hidden from Him, so He will recompense you for them. In the explicit mention of the Glorious Name there is an inculcation of awe, and in the verse there is a threat that is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 234:**

﴿Those who﴾ is the subject (mubtada', the inchoative). ﴿die﴾ (yutawaffawna) means their souls are taken, since tawaffi is qabd (seizing, taking). It is said: "I took (tawaffaytu) my money from so-and-so, and I received it in full (istawfaytuhu) from him," meaning I seized it and took it. ʿAlī, may Allah honor his face, read (yatawaffawna) with a fatḥa on the yā' (yā'), as narrated by Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī from him and al-Mufaḍḍal from ʿĀṣim. The meaning is: they fulfill (yastawfūna) their terms (ājālahum). On this reading, the dead person is called mutawaffā, meaning one who has fulfilled his life.

This has been raised as an objection, based on what is reported: Abū al-Aswad was behind a funeral, and a man said to him: "Who is the mutawaffī?" with a kasra on the fā', and he said: "Allah, exalted is He."
