This was one of the reasons ʿAlī, may Allah honor his face, ordered the writing of a book of grammar (naḥw). Al-Sakkākī answered that the cause of the error was that the questioner was one who did not know the reason for its correctness, so he was not fit to be addressed with it.

﴿from among you﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl, a descriptive state) from the nominative subject of yutawaffawna. The word min may carry the sense of partitive (tab'īd) or of specifying the kind (bayān al-jins). The address is to all people, with a shift in the form of address (talwīn al-khiṭāb).

﴿and leave behind﴾ means they leave (yatrukūn). The imperative is used from it, but neither the active participle nor the passive participle is used. The past tense comes in an irregular form (shudhūdh). ﴿wives﴾ means women belonging to them.

﴿they shall wait, keeping themselves [in seclusion]﴾ (yatarabbaṣna bi-anfusihinna) is the predicate (khabar) of "those who," and the linking pronoun is omitted. That is: for them, or after them. The first view was preferred for the lesser use of omission (qillat al-iḍmār, the infrequency of the implied pronoun), and because of the allusion in the lām to the idea that the waiting period is the right of the deceased. It has also been said that the predicate is for an omitted subject: their wives shall wait, and the sentence is the predicate of "those who." Some of the Basrans supposed an omitted genitive (muḍāf) at the start of the sentence, meaning: the wives of those who, and they are their women. Against this, the Qur'anic phrase "leave behind wives" then gains no new benefit that counts. It is narrated from Sībawayh that "those who" is the subject and the predicate is omitted, meaning: in what is recited to you is the ruling of those who, and so on. In that case the clause "they shall wait" is an explanation of that ruling. This involves a great deal of omission. Some verifying scholars held that "those who" is the subject and "they shall wait" is its predicate, and the linking is achieved merely by the return of the pronoun to the wives, since the meaning is: the wives whom they left behind shall wait. Al-Akhfash and al-Kisā'ī permitted such a construction. Were it not that the majority forbid it, it would be quite good.

﴿four months and ten days﴾. Perhaps this number is for the secret that Allah alone knows it, or that He informs whom He wills of His servants. The view that the reason for this is that the fetus in most cases moves at three months if male and four if female, so the longer of the two periods was taken, and ten days were added as an extra precaution, since its movement may be weak at the beginning and not be felt, is contrary to the authentic ḥadīth: "Indeed, one of you is gathered in his mother's belly for forty days as a drop, then he is a clot like that, then he is a lump like that, then Allah, exalted is He, sends an angel with four words, and he writes his deed, his term, his provision, and whether he is wretched or happy. Then the spirit is breathed into him." This is because its apparent meaning is that the breathing of the spirit occurs absolutely after this period, and it neither quenches the thirst nor heals the sick.

As for the feminine form of "ten" (ʿashr), it is said: because the omitted specifier (tamyīz) is "nights" (layālī). Rabīʿa and Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd went to this view. It has also been said: rather, it is in consideration of the nights, because they are the front of the months (ghurar al-shuhūr). For this reason they do not use the masculine form in such a construction, going with the days. Indeed, as al-Farrā' related, they say: "We fasted ten (ʿashran) of the month of Ramadan," even though fasting occurs in days. This is supported by Allah's words: ﴿you did not remain except ten﴾ and then ﴿you did not remain except a day﴾. Abū Ḥayyān mentioned that the rule for the masculine and feminine forms of numbers applies when the counted noun is expressed; but when it is omitted, both forms are permitted absolutely. This is perhaps better than what has been said.

The verse has been used as evidence that the waiting period (ʿidda) is obligatory for a woman whose husband has died, whether or not she was consummated with. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with both of them, held that a second wife has no waiting period. This is refuted by the general wording of the verse, as you see. The verse includes the Muslim and the scripturist (kitābiyya), the woman with menstrual cycles (dhāt al-aqrā'), the woman with istiḥāḍa (persistent bleeding), the woman past menopause (āyisa), the young girl, the free woman and the slave woman, as al-Aṣamm said, and the pregnant woman and others. However, analogy (qiyās) required halving the period for the slave woman, and consensus (ijmā', the agreement of scholars) excluded the pregnant woman from this, based on Allah's words: ﴿and for those with child, their term is that they lay down their burden﴾.

It is narrated from ʿAlī, may Allah honor his face, and Ibn ʿAbbās, that she observes the longer of the two terms as a precaution. This does not contradict the consensus; rather, it contains acting in accordance with the requirement of both verses.

Some scholars used the verse as evidence that the waiting period begins from the death, since it is linked to it. So if news of the husband's death reaches her only after the waiting period has passed, she is judged to have completed it. This is the view of most scholars, and of al-Shāfiʿī in one of his two opinions. It is supported by the fact that the young girl who has no knowledge (of her husband's death) has her waiting period completed by this period. It has also been said: if she does not know of her husband's death, her waiting period is not completed by these days, based on what is reported: "The wife of the missing man remains his wife until clear proof of his death or his divorce comes to her."

﴿Then when they have reached their term﴾, that is, their waiting periods have ended, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, O you who have authority over them. It has been said that the address is to the guardians (awliyā'). It has also been said that it is to all Muslims ﴿for what they do with themselves﴾ of what was forbidden to them during the waiting period. The restriction (in the phrase) contains an indication of the cause of the prohibition. ﴿in a reasonable manner﴾ means in the way that the Sharia recognizes and does not reject. It was qualified by this to signal that if they do otherwise, then it is incumbent upon you to restrain them, and if you fall short, you are sinful. ﴿And Allah is Aware of what you do﴾ (verse 234). So do not do the opposite of what you were commanded. The apparent meaning is that the one addressed in this is the one addressed in the preceding part. It was permitted that it be an address to the capable among the guardians and the husbands, in which case there are two shifts: the address (shifting) to the third person, and the masculine (shifting) to the feminine. This contains a warning to both groups. It is also possible that it is a promise and a warning for both of them.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 235:**

﴿There is no blame upon you﴾, O men who seek to marry, ﴿for what you hint at of the proposal to women﴾, by one of you saying what Al-Bukhari and others narrated: "From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: 'I wish to marry, and I truly love a woman of such-and-such character and such-and-such matters, and it is in my nature to desire women. I would love for Allah, exalted is He, to ordain for me a righteous wife,'" or by mentioning to the woman his excellence and nobility. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "entered upon Umm Salamah, who had been married to her paternal cousin Abu Salamah, and he had died leaving her. He kept mentioning to her his station with Allah, exalted is He, while he leaned on his hand, until the mat left a mark on his hand from the heaviness of his leaning upon it. And that was an allusion (ta'ridh) to her." And ta'ridh (allusion) originally means turning speech away from its straight course towards one of its sides and flanks. It is used to mean that one mentions something intended in general by its literal, figurative or implicative (kinayah) wording, so that by that thing one indicates another thing not mentioned in the speech. For example, one mentions coming for a greeting (salam) in its literal wording, to indicate asking for a gift and seeking a donation. This is other than kinayah (implicature), because kinayah is to mention an intended meaning by another word that is coined for it. However, in ta'ridh the word is used for its original meaning, but not with the intention of that meaning; rather, to move from it to the intended thing. Thus, "long of the sash" (tawil al-nijad) is used in its meaning, but its meaning is not the intended affirmation; rather, one moves from it to tallness of stature. Some verifiers have determined that between them there is a general and specific relation from one aspect. So the saying of the one in need, "I came to greet you," is both kinayah and ta'ridh; and "Zayd is long of the sash" is kinayah and not ta'ridh; and your saying, regarding one who harms you, while the addressee is not the one who harmed you, "You have hurt me, so you will know," is ta'ridh threatening the one who causes harm, not kinayah. The well-known usage calls ta'ridh "talwih" (hinting), because what you intend gleams (yaluh) from it. Al-Sakkaki, by way of enmity (adwan), made its name for distant kinayah, due to the abundance of intermediary steps, such as "one with much ash" for "one who is hospitable," as a new technical term. In al-Kashf: "Sometimes an incidental matter arises which makes kinayah like what is stated explicitly, as in 'the istiwa' (settling) upon the Throne' and 'the outstretching of the hand.'" And it makes the shift (iltifat) in ta'ridh towards the one alluded to, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾. So it does not refute the original principle.

And al-khutbah, with a kasra on the kha', is said to be the mention by which one seeks to conclude a marriage contract, taken from al-khitab (address), which is directing speech for the purpose of making it understood. With a damma, it is the admonition which is coherently composed in a certain style. It is also said that both are names of a state, except that the one with the damma is specific to admonition, and the one with the kasra is specific to a woman's solicitation and seeking her marriage. The "al" in "al-nisa'" (the women) is for prior reference (al-'ahd), and the referents are the wives mentioned in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and they leave behind wives﴾. It is not possible to take it as generic (istighraq), because among women are those for whom it is forbidden to allude to a proposal during their waiting period (iddah), such as revocable divorcees and irrevocably divorced women according to one opinion. The more apparent view according to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, is that it is permissible during their waiting period, by analogy with widows in their waiting period. It cannot be said: "This verse should have been placed before the saying of the Exalted: ﴿So when they reach their term﴾, because what is in it concerns women before they reach the term." Because we do not accept that; rather, it concerns the rulings of men in relation to them. So the appropriate placement would have been after finishing the rulings about them before reaching the term and after it. Al-Kiya derived from the verse the negation of the prescribed punishment (hadd) for slander by allusion, because He, exalted is He, made its ruling different from the ruling for explicit accusation. This is supported by what is narrated: "Whoever alludes, we allude [to him]; and whoever walks upon the grass, we throw him into the river." It was also used as evidence for the permissibility of marrying a pregnant woman from fornication, since she has no waiting period. But what is in this is not hidden.

﴿Or you conceal in yourselves﴾, meaning: you keep secret in your hearts the desire to marry them after the end of their waiting period, and you do not declare that to them. ﴿Allah knows that you will remember them﴾, and that you will not be patient with silence about them and with not showing your desire for them. Therefore He granted you the concession He granted. And in this is a kind of rebuke.

﴿But do not make a promise to them in secret﴾. This is an exception (istidrak) from an omitted element indicated by ﴿you will remember them﴾, meaning: so remember them, ﴿but do not make a promise to them﴾ of marriage. Rather, suffice yourselves with what has been permitted to you. It is also possible that it is an exception from "there is no blame," for it has the sense of "allude to their proposal" or "conceal in yourselves, but ...", and so on. Taking it as an exception based on what precedes is not valid. The meaning of "secret" as "marriage" is through the meaning of "intercourse," since it has become common to use it for that, because it is done secretly. From this is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"Has Basbasah claimed today that I have grown old,
and that men like me do not know how to keep secrets?"

And the meaning of "contract" from that is due to the causal and resultant relation between them. It was not made from the beginning an expression for the contract, because there is no apparent connection between them. What is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, is that "secret" here means intercourse. The notion of a concession in that case concerning the forbidden matter, which is the explicit mention of "marriage," is something that hardly comes to mind. And from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid, and it is also narrated from al-Habr (the scholar, Ibn 'Abbas), that it is the covenant not to marry another. In all these views it is in the accusative as an object. It is also permitted that it be accusative as an adverb of place, meaning: ﴿do not make a promise to them﴾ in secret, with the understanding that the intended meaning is a promise with what is considered disgraceful.

﴿Except that you say a customary word﴾, which is the allusion whose permissibility is known. The excepted element is what the prohibition implies, meaning: ﴿do not make a promise to them﴾ of marriage, a promise of any kind, except a known promise, or except a promise with a customary word; or do not say, regarding a promise of intercourse or a request to refrain from others, anything except your saying ﴿a customary word﴾. The exception in all of this is connected (muttasil). In the first view, the speech explicitly states what was understood from "there is no blame," in a way that emphasizes that affirmation, and this is a kind of tard (the converse implication), and the reverse is good. In the last two views, it establishes a meaning which may be known by way of analogy, since they took the allusion in them to be an allusion by promising her or requesting from her, which is different from the previous allusion, because the previous one is by the proposal itself. If the fourth view, which is the last of the previous views, is intended, the exception may be connected or disconnected. Disconnection is more apparent in meaning, according to the meaning of ﴿do not make a promise to them﴾ with what is disgraceful; but make a promise to them with a customary word that one is not ashamed to say openly, such as good companionship and steadfastness if the marriage takes place. Some said this, except that they took the exception from "in secret," and it was deemed weak because it leads to the allusion being a promise. Making it from the type of ﴿except one who has been wronged﴾ refuses that it is an exception from it, but rather from the origin of the ruling itself.

﴿And do not resolve upon the tie of marriage﴾, meaning: do not intend with a firm intention to conclude the tie of the marriage contract. In the prohibition of the precursor of a thing, there is a prohibition of the thing itself in a more emphatic way. The prohibition may be connected to it, because it is one of the inner actions that fall under choice, and for this one is rewarded for the intention. And what is meant by it is the accompanying resolve, because whoever says, "Do not resolve to travel in Safar, for example," is not understood to forbid a resolve about a matter whose action is delayed until Rabi'. That is because firm intention rightly accompanies the act. The genitive construction is supposed for the connection to be valid, because it can only apply to an action, and "the tie" is not an action, because it is the place of the tying, which is what one ties upon. Some did not supposed this, and they made the genitive explanatory (bayaniyyah), so the "tie" is then the marriage itself, which is an action. It is possible that the speech is of the type of ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾. In any case, it is the object. It is permitted that it be an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq), on the basis that the meaning of "do not resolve" is "do not conclude," so it is like "I sat, a sitting," and that the genitive is the genitive of the verbal noun to its object. It is said that the meaning is: do not sever, and do not bring about the tie of marriage, so the prohibition is about the act itself, not about intending it as in the first, and by this it is lowered from it. Some people took resolve to mean cutting, the opposite of joining, and made the meaning: do not sever the tie of marriage of the deceased husband by a contract of another marriage. There is then no need at all to supposed any genitive. There is in this a discussion. Firstly, because the coming of "resolve" with the meaning of cutting, the opposite of joining, in the language is a matter of doubt. And the saying of al-Zamakhshari, "The reality of resolve is cutting, as evidenced by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'There is no fast for one who does not resolve the fast from the night,'" and it is narrated: "who has not spent the night (lam yubayyit)," is not explicit on that; rather, it is hardly correct to take it that way, since the evidence does not support it. There is no doubt that by the resolve to fast is not meant cutting in the sense of undoing, but rather firm determination and the cutting off of hesitation. Secondly, because there is no sense in prohibiting the severing of the tie of the first husband's marriage, so that it would be forbidden. The tie of marriage of the deceased is not severed by a second marriage contract, because the second is void. From here it was said that the meaning is: do not undo the tie of your marriage and do not sever it. Negating severing is an expression for negating procuring, since the procuring of fruit from the tree is by cutting. This, as you see, is something that the speech of the Exalted, the Mighty, should not be interpreted as. ﴿Until the decreed term reaches its end﴾, meaning, until what was prescribed and obligated of the waiting period comes to its conclusion. ﴿And know that Allah knows what is in your souls﴾ of resolve upon what is not permitted, or of the things of the breasts of which that is a part. ﴿So beware of Him﴾, and do not resolve upon it, or "beware of Him" by avoiding resolve from the start, or by abandoning it after it has been established. ﴿And know that Allah is Forgiving﴾, forgiving whoever abandons his resolve or sin out of fear of Him. ﴿Forbearing 235﴾, who does not hasten with punishment. Therefore it should not be supposed from the delay of punishment that what He has forbidden does not entail accountability. And the repetition of the agent is for emphasis on the matter of the ruling. And what is in the sentence, showing the vastness of His mercy, exalted is His name, is not hidden.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 236:

﴿There is no blame upon you﴾ — there is no liability for a dowry (mahr). This is the apparent meaning. It is also said: it means no sin (wizr), because there is no innovation (bid'ah) in divorce before consummation (al-masis), even if it occurs during menstruation. It is also said: the Prophet (ﷺ) frequently forbade divorce, so they thought there was a sin in it, and this verse negated that. ﴿If you divorce women while you have not touched them﴾ — meaning, without having touched them, or for the period in which there is no touching; this is a metaphor (kinayah) for intercourse (al-jima'). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (tamassuhunna), al-A'mash read (min qabli an tamassuhunna), and Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) read (min qabli an tujami'uhunna). ﴿Or you have appointed for them an obligatory portion (fari≈ah)﴾ — meaning: "until you appoint," or "unless you appoint," as stated in the commentaries on the Book. Fariḍah is on the pattern fa'ilah in the sense of maf'ul, put in the accusative as a direct object; the ta' marbuta transfers the word from adjectival to nominal usage, so it came to mean the mahr, and therefore it is not permissible [to read it otherwise]. It is permitted that it be in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), but this is not the better view. The meaning is: there is no liability upon the one who divorces for claiming the mahr at all, if the divorce occurs before consummation in every case, except in the case of appointing a portion, for then upon him is half of the stipulated amount, as will be stated explicitly; and in the case of there being no stipulation, upon him is the muta'ah, not half the mahr al-mithl. As for when the divorce occurs after consummation, then in the case of stipulation upon him is the full stipulated amount, and in the case of no stipulation the full mahr al-mithl. These are four cases for the divorced woman: the verse by its explicit wording negated the obligation in some of them, and its implicit meaning (mafhum) required the obligation in general in the others. It is said: here there is a strong difficulty, namely that what follows "aw" (or), when it has the sense of "hatta" (until) or "ila" (up to), marks the endpoint of the preceding verb. So your saying, "I will certainly cling to you or you pay me my right," means that the clinging ends at the giving. By analogy, the appointing of a portion would be the endpoint of not touching, not of the absence of blame, and that is not the intended meaning. It is answered that what follows it is coordinated with the verb, and it is connected to what precedes it, so its meaning is restricted by it. It is as if it were said: you, as long as you do not touch them, are without blame and liability, except when the portion is appointed, in which case there is blame; because a restricted element in meaning ends by the removal of its restriction. Reflect. Some people made the word "aw" coordinating what follows it with what precedes it of the jussive verb, and "lam" then negates one of the two matters indefinitely, and it is a indefinite noun in the context of negation, so it conveys generality; i.e., as long as there has been among you neither touching nor appointing, in the manner of ﴿And do not obey from among them one who is sinful or ungrateful﴾. Al-Qutb objected to this that it implies the supposition of the negative particle, so that it becomes "as long as you do not touch them" and "as long as you do not appoint," and then the condition would be one of the two negations, not the negation of one of the two matters; it would follow that the mahr is not obligatory when there is no touching and there is an appointing, or when there is no appointing and there is touching. It is not hidden that this is not a valid objection, and there is no need to say that "aw" means "wa" (and), as in His saying, ﴿or they increase﴾, according to one opinion.

﴿And provide for them﴾ — i.e., make them possessors of that by which they may enjoy themselves; that thing is called a muta'ah (provision). It is coordinated with what is in meaning the response to the condition, as if it were said: if you divorce women, there is no blame, and provide for them. The coordination of a command upon a declarative statement is, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, because the condition gathers the two as though they were single items; that is, the ruling is this and that. Or because the meaning is: "there is no blame, and obligatory is this," or "do not resolve upon that, and provide for them." It is permitted that it be coordinated upon the declarative sentence as a coordination of narrative upon narrative, and that it be an interjected clause introduced by "wa," serving to explain what is obligatory for the divorced women upon their husbands after divorce. Coordination upon an omitted element that the speech extends over, i.e., "so divorce them and provide for them," is rejected by sound taste, for there is no meaning to our saying: "If you divorce women, then divorce them," unless the intended meaning is the coordinated element. The wisdom in giving the muta'ah is to console the wounded feelings caused by divorce. The apparent indication is that there is no specification of amount, based on His saying: ﴿Upon the wealthy according to his means, and upon the straitened according to his means﴾; i.e., upon each of them is the amount he can bear and that suits him, whatever it may be. Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The highest form of the divorce provision is a servant; below that is silver; below that is clothing." And from Ibn Umar: "The least of the muta'ah is thirty dirhams." Imam Abu Hanifah said: it is a shirt, a veil, and a wrap according to the circumstance, except that if the mahr of her like is less than that, then she has the lesser of half the mahr of her like or the muta'ah, and it must not be less than five dirhams. The "muwsi'" (wealthy) is one who has abundance and riches, from awsa'a al-rajul when his wealth increased and his condition became broad; and the "muqtir" (straitened) is one who is in narrow circumstances, from aqtara when he became poor and what is in his hand became little, and the root of the matter is scarcity. The sentence is a new independent clause with no grammatical position, explaining the measure of the muta'ah's state in relation to the state of the divorcer, in wealth and in straitness. The majority hold that it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (matti'uhunna), with an omitted link, i.e., "from you." Whoever made the alif and lam a replacement for the omitted genitive, i.e., "upon your wealthy," etc., dispensed with the claim of omission.

Abu Ja'far and the people of Kufa, except Abu Bakr and Ibn Dhakwan, read (qadarahu) with a fathah on the dal; the rest read it with a sukun, and both are dialectal forms of it. It is also said: (al-qadr) with sukun means capacity, and with fathah means measure. It was also read (qadraha) with an accusative, and it was explained that it is an object by meaning, because the meaning of "provide for them" etc. is that each of you should render the measure of his capacity. Abu al-Baqa said: better than this is that the supposition be: "so make it obligatory upon the wealthy according to his measure." ﴿A provision﴾ — a noun of action placed in the position of the verbal noun, i.e., a provision (tamti'an) ﴿in a fair manner﴾ — i.e., accompanied by the manner that is considered good, and it is in the position of a qualifier
صفحة 154
of "mata'an," and "haqqan," i.e., established, is a second qualifier of it. It is permitted that it be an emphatic verbal noun, i.e., "this is a right." ﴿A right upon the doers of good﴾ — related to the verb governing the verbal noun, or to it, or to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier. By "the doers of good" is meant those whose nature is to do good, or those who do good to themselves by hastening to comply, or to the divorced women by providing for them. They were so named by consideration of their approaching that station, as encouragement and incitement.

Imam Malik said: the doers of good are the voluntary ones, and on this basis he derived evidence for the recommendation of the muta'ah, and made it a diverting indication turning the command toward recommendation. According to us, it is obligatory for the divorced women in the verse, and recommended for the rest of divorced women. According to al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, in one of his two opinions: it is obligatory for every divorced wife, provided the separation was from the husband's side, except the one for whom a dowry was stipulated and who was divorced before consummation. Since the implicit meaning of the verse did not support him, and the generality in His saying, ﴿And for the divorced women is a provision in a fair manner﴾ was not taken into account, because it makes the unrestricted (mutlaq) carry the restricted (muqayyad), he spoke by analogy, and placed it before the implicit meaning, because analogy is among the definitive proofs, unlike it. It is answered regarding what Malik said by rejecting the restriction of the doer of good to the voluntary, for it is more general than that, and includes one who fulfills obligations; so it does not contradict obligation, and therefore it is not a diverting indication turning the command away from it, together with what is joined by the word "haqqan."

[Page 155 of the printed edition is omitted here.]

﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, while you had already fixed a dowry for them﴾: this is an explanation of the ruling for the woman for whom a dowry was specified and who was divorced before intercourse (masis). The clause "wa-qad" (and while) and what follows is either a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "tallaqtumuhunna" (you divorced them) or to its object. The fixing itself (al-farid) may be in the active or passive form. Although it did not coincide with the moment of divorce, the attribute of the one who fixed the dowry being the one who fixed it before that time is undoubtedly concurrent with the divorce. Likewise, the condition of the divorced woman being one for whom a dowry was fixed holds true for what came before. ﴿Then half of what you fixed﴾, i.e., then for them is half of what you determined and specified for them as dowry, or else it is obligatory upon you to pay that. This is explicit that what is negated in the earlier case is only the liability for the dowry. It has been read as "fa-nisfa" (in the accusative), meaning "then pay half." Perhaps the postponement of the ruling on specifying the dowry, although it is the basic element in the contract and the most common in occurrence, is due to the gradual arrangement of rulings and to mentioning the more difficult case before the more difficult. The claim that this verse was revealed because of "an Ansari who married a woman from Banu Hanifa, who had delegated the dowry (mufawwadah), and he divorced her before consummating the marriage, so they brought their dispute to the Messenger of God, and he (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Did you provide for her?' He said: 'I had nothing.' He said: 'Provide for her with your cap'" is, in my view, not something that merits consideration. Moreover, this report has been subject to criticism, to the extent that the hafiz Waliyy al-Din al-Iraqi said: "I have not found it."

﴿Unless they forgo﴾: this is a detached exception (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of states. That is: for them is half of the fixed amount, determined in every state, except the state in which they forgo it, i.e., the divorced women mentioned, for then that obligation falls away after having become due. The form itself is open to both masculine and feminine reading, and the distinction is by consideration: the "waw" in the first reading is a pronoun and the "nun" is the sign of the nominative case; in the second, the "waw" is the verb's radical and the "nun" is a pronoun, and the verb is indeclinable (mabni). For this reason, "an" here did not affect it, even though it is a governing particle (nasibah) and not a lightened one (mukhaffafah), as evidenced by the coordination of the accusative with it in God's words ﴿or that he forgo﴾. al-Hasan read it with a sukun on the waw, so it is in accordance with the line: "God refused that I should be exalted through a mother or a father."

﴿He in whose hand is the knot of marriage﴾: this is the husband who holds control over the contract of marriage and its dissolution. This is the interpretation transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), as reported by Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and al-Bayhaqi with a good chain, from Ibn Umar in a marfu' report, and it was held by a group of the Companions (may God be pleased with them). The meaning of his forgoing is that he leaves out of generosity what returns to him of half the dowry which he had given in full, according to what is customary, or that he gives the full fixed dowry after the divorce, as Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) explained. Calling that "forgoing" is figurative correspondence (mushakalah). It may also be interpreted as increase and excess, as in God's words ﴿They ask you what they should spend; say: the excess﴾, and in Zuhayr's line:

Resolve and righteousness toward God, and a disposition that overlooks the manners of the wrongdoer who corrupts.

Thus the exception then refers to prohibiting an increase in the amount stated, just as in the first case it refers to prohibiting a decrease in it. That is: for them is this amount without increase or decrease in all states, except in the state of their forgoing, for then they do not have the stated amount, rather it is cancelled or reduced; or in the state of the husband's forgoing, for then the increase is theirs. This applies on the first interpretation, where in "fa-nisf" the obligation is not considered. As for the second interpretation, it is necessary to affirm that the exception is disconnected (munqati'), because in the case of the husband's forgoing, obligation upon him is not conceivable. So it has been said, and let it be considered.

Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with them both), in one of the reports from him, as well as Aisha, Tawus, Mujahid, Ata', al-Hasan, Alqama, al-Zuhri, and al-Shafi'i (may God be pleased with him) in his earlier opinion, held that the one in whose hand is the knot of marriage is the guardian (wali) without whose permission a woman may not be married. For him is the right to forgo the dowry if the wife is a minor, according to some, and absolutely, even if she refuses, according to others. What is relied upon is the transmitted report, and it is the more fitting with God's words ﴿and that you forgo is nearer to piety﴾, for relinquishing the right of another has no part in piety. This address is to men and women alike, and the masculine is predominant because of its nobility; likewise in what follows. The "lam" is for transitivity. Among their rules, which few people master, is that the comparative form (af'al al-tafdil) and likewise the form of wonder (fi'l al-ta'ajjub) take the preposition that their verb takes: such as "azhadu fihi min kadha" (I am more abstinent regarding it than such-and-such). Even if it is from a verb that is transitive in origin, if the verb is understood as knowledge or ignorance it takes "bi," such as "a'lamu bil-fiqh" (more knowledgeable in jurisprudence) and "ajhalu bil-nahw" (more ignorant in grammar). If that is not understood, it takes "li," such as "anta adraba li-'Amr" (you are more apt to strike for 'Amr), except in the domain of love and hatred, where it takes "fi" to introduce the object, such as "huwa ahabbu fi Bakr" (he loves Bakr more), and "ab'adu fi 'Amr" (he hates 'Amr more), and "ila" to introduce the notional agent, such as "Zayd ahabbu ila Khalid min Bishr" (Zayd is more beloved to Khalid than Bishr), or "ab'adu ilayhi minhu" (more hateful to him than him). It was read "wa-an ya'fu" with "ya" (they forgo). ﴿And do not forget graciousness between you﴾ is coordinated with the nominal clause, whose purpose is the command in the most emphatic form; that is: do not leave off that some of you show graciousness to others, as a forgotten thing. The adverbial phrase ("bayna-kum") is either attached to "tansaw" (forget) or to an omitted element that stands as a circumstantial clause for "al-fadl" (graciousness). Taking "al-fadl" to mean increase is an allusion to God's earlier words ﴿and men have a degree over them﴾, in the lowest rank of weakness. It has been said that the adverbial phrase is attached to an omitted element standing as a qualifier of "al-fadl," according to the view of those who permit deleting the relative pronoun together with part of its relative clause; and "al-fadl" here means goodness, that is: do not forget the goodness that existed between you before, and let each of you keep it in mind, so that each is encouraged to forgo in return for the other's goodness toward him. This view is not sound, because according to it, it would be objected that generally there is no goodness between a woman and her husband before consummation. Ali (may God honour his face) read "wa-la tanasaw" and some read "wa-la tansu" with a sukun on the waw.

﴿Indeed God is seeing of what you do﴾: so He does not let what you have done be lost.

[p. 156]

﴿Be steadfast in the prayers﴾, meaning: persist in performing them at their appointed times without neglect, as the form of the verb (al-mufa'alah, which implies intensity) indicates. Perhaps the command to them comes right after the exhortation to pardon and the prohibition of abandoning grace, because prayer prepares the soul for excellent qualities, being that which forbids indecency and wrongdoing. Or it is so that reverence for the command of God Most High and compassion for His creatures are combined. It has been said that it was commanded in the course of explaining the interconnected legal rulings concerning spouses and children, as a notice that prayer deserves the utmost care and perseverance in it, without being distracted from it by those matters. It is as if it were said: let not your attachment to women and their affairs occupy you; turn to your Lord by guarding that which is the pillar of the religion and the ladder of the believers. ﴿And the middle prayer﴾, i.e., the one in between them, or the most excellent of them. On the first meaning, the verse is cited as evidence that the prayers are five, with no addition; on the second, it is not. Concerning its identification, there are several views:

First: it is the Dhuhr, because it is performed in the middle of the day.

Second: it is the 'Asr, because it falls between the daytime prayers and the nighttime prayers. This is what is related from Ali, al-Hasan, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, and a great many others, and the Shafi'is hold this view.

Third: it is the Maghrib, and Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb held this view, because it is intermediate in length and shortness.

Fourth: it is the 'Isha', because it lies between two prayers that are not shortened.

Fifth: it is the Fajr, because it lies between the nighttime and daytime prayers, and because it is a prayer that is not combined with any other, so it stands alone between two combined groups. This is what is related from Mu'adh, Jabir, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah, and Mujahid, and al-Shafi'i himself, may Allah be pleased with him, chose it.

It has also been said: the intended meaning is the Witr prayer; it has been said: the Duha (forenoon) prayer; it has been said: the 'Eid al-Fitr prayer; it has been said: the 'Eid al-Adha prayer; it has been said: the night prayer; it has been said: the Friday prayer; it has been said: congregational prayer; it has been said: the prayer of fear; and it has been said, and it has been said...

Most scholars have affirmed that it is the 'Asr prayer, on the basis of what Muslim transmitted from the hadith of Ali, may Allah honour his face, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said on the day of the Confederates: "They kept us busy from the middle prayer, the prayer of 'Asr. May Allah fill their houses with fire." It was singled out for mention because it falls at a time when people are preoccupied, especially the Arabs.

Some of the verifying scholars (muhaqqiqun) said: what the evidence requires among these views is that it is the Dhuhr, and this has been attributed to the Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him. The explanation of this is that all the other views have no basis on which a reasoner could rely, except the view that it is the 'Asr prayer. The narrations stating that it is the 'Asr are of two kinds: raised (marfu') and halted (mawquf). The halted ones are not used as evidence, because they are the sayings of Companions which were contradicted by other Companions who said it was something else, and the saying of a Companion is certainly not used as evidence when another Companion's saying contradicts it; the dispute over using it arises only when there is no contradiction. As for the raised narrations, most of them have chains of narration that are open to some criticism. The sound one free of criticism is of two kinds: a concise one containing only the phrase "the middle prayer, the prayer of 'Asr," and a longer one containing a story in which this phrase occurs. The concise one is taken from the longer one; some narrators abridged it and erred in the abridgement, as you will hear. Longer narrations are all open to some possibility of doubt, so they cannot validly be used as evidence.

So the words in Muslim's narration, "They kept us busy from the middle prayer, the prayer of 'Asr," admit two possibilities:

The first: that the phrase "the prayer of 'Asr" is not part of the raised speech, but was inserted into the hadith by one of the narrators as his own explanation, as happened often in hadiths. This is supported by what Muslim transmitted by another route from Ali, may Allah honour his face, with the wording: "They detained us from the middle prayer until the sun set," meaning the 'Asr.

The second: supposing it is not inserted, it may be a conjunction of coordination with the conjunction dropped, neither explanation nor apposition, and the sense would be: "They kept us busy from the middle prayer and the prayer of 'Asr." This is supported by the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) was not kept busy on the day of the Confederates from the 'Asr prayer alone, but was kept busy from both the Dhuhr and the 'Asr, as reported by another route. So he apparently meant by "the middle prayer" the Dhuhr, and joined the 'Asr to it.

With these two possibilities, the hadith cannot be validly used as evidence. The first possibility is stronger, given the narration referred to, and it is supported from outside by the fact that if it had been established from the Prophet as an explanation that it is the 'Asr, the Companions would have stopped at it and not disagreed. Ibn Jarir transmitted from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that he said: "The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) differed about the middle prayer like this," and he interlaced his fingers.

Then, supposing neither possibility holds, the hadith is in conflict with the raised hadith stating that it is the Dhuhr. When two hadiths conflict and reconciling them is not possible, one must seek preference (tarjih). The jurists of usul (usuliyyun) have stated that among the criteria of preference is that the occasion of revelation is mentioned in a narration. The hadith stating that it is the Dhuhr has the occasion of revelation explained in it, and it is cited directly for the purpose of mention, unlike the hadith "They kept us busy..." etc. So it is obligatory to turn to it. It is what Ahmad and Abu Dawud transmitted with a good chain from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray the Dhuhr at the time of intense heat, and no prayer was harder on the Companions than it. So there was revealed: ﴿Be steadfast in the prayers and the middle prayer﴾."

Ahmad also transmitted by another route, from Zayd as well: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to pray the Dhuhr at the time of intense heat, so that behind him there would be only one row or two rows, while people were at their midday rest and their trade. So Allah Most High revealed: ﴿Be steadfast in the prayers﴾, etc. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Men must desist, or I will burn their houses.'"

That it is other than the 'Asr is further confirmed by what Muslim and others transmitted by several routes: "From Abu Yunus, the freedman of 'A'isha, who said: 'A'isha ordered me to write for her a copy of the Qur'an, and she dictated to me: ﴿Be steadfast in the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ and the prayer of 'Asr. And she said: I heard it from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).'" The conjunction requires difference.

Malik and others also transmitted by several routes, from 'Amr ibn Rafi', who said: "I was writing a copy of the Qur'an for Hafsa, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), and she dictated to me: ﴿Be steadfast in the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ and the prayer of 'Asr."

Ibn Abi Dawud transmitted in his book on the codices (al-masahif) from 'Abdullah ibn Rafi' that he wrote a copy for Umm Salama, and she dictated to him the same as 'A'isha and Hafsa dictated. Ibn Abi Dawud also transmitted from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he recited it likewise. He also transmitted from Abu Rafi', freedman of Hafsa, who said: "I wrote a copy of the Qur'an for Hafsa, and she said: Write ﴿Be steadfast in the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ and the prayer of 'Asr. Then I met Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and he said: It is as she said. Is it not that we are most preoccupied at the time of the Dhuhr prayer with our work and our camels?" This indicates that the Companions understood from this reading that the middle prayer is the Dhuhr.

Here it should be noted that it was related from al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham and Abu Bakr al-Warraq that it is one of the five prayers, and Allah Most High did not specify it, but concealed it among the obligatory prayers, so that they would be steadfast in all of them, just as He concealed the Night of Power among the nights of the month of Ramadan, His Greatest Name among all the names, and the hour of acceptance among the hours of Friday.

'Abdullah and Ali recited: (al-salat al-wusta) in the accusative. It is related from 'A'isha that she read the word as an accusative (al-salata) as an expression of praise and specification. Nafi' recited al-Wusta with the letter sad (al-Wusta).

﴿And stand before Allah﴾, i.e., in prayer, ﴿devoutly obedient (qanitin)﴾, i.e., submissive, as is the original meaning of qunut according to some, and this is what is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both; or remembering Him Most High while standing, on the basis that qunut is the remembrance (dhikr) within it. It has been said: humble (khashi'in). It has been said: completing the act of obedience and perfecting it in the best manner, without neglecting anything that should be in it. This is supported by what Ibn Jarir transmitted from Mujahid, who said: "Among qunut is the lengthening of the bowing, lowering the gaze, humility, not turning around, not moving pebbles, not playing with anything, and not occupying the self with any matter of worldly affairs."

Al-Bukhari, in his Sahih, interpreted it as "silent (samitin)," because of what he and Muslim, Abu Dawud, and a group transmitted from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "We used to speak during prayer in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); a man among us would speak to his companion who was beside him in prayer, until there was revealed: ﴿And stand before Allah devoutly obedient﴾. So we were commanded to be silent, and forbidden to speak."

It is not hidden that this is not explicit in the intended meaning. Perhaps clearer than it is what Ibn Jarir transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was praying, and I gave him the greeting of peace, but he did not return it to me. When he had finished the prayer, he said: 'Nothing prevented me from returning your greeting except that we have been commanded to stand devoutly obedient, not to speak during prayer.'"

Ibn al-Musayyib said: what is meant by it is the qunut in the Subh (dawn) prayer, and this is a narration from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.

The prepositional phrase (al-jar wa-al-majrur) is connected either to what precedes it or to what follows it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 239:

﴿Then if you fear﴾ from an enemy or otherwise, ﴿on foot or riding﴾: these are two circumstantial qualifiers (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in the response of the condition; that is, pray on foot or riding. The first is the plural of rājil, meaning one who walks on his feet; rajul, with fatḥa then ḍamma or with fatḥa then kasra, has the same meaning. It has also been said: the rājil is one who is on his feet, standing or walking. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, took as evidence the apparent meaning of the verse for the obligation of prayer during close combat (al-musāyafa) even if standing is not possible. Our Imam (Abu Hanifa) held that walking, and likewise fighting, invalidates the prayer, and when the matter leads to that, one postpones it and then prays it in safety. Al-Shafi'i transmitted with a sound chain, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "We were detained on the day of the Trench until a portion of the night had passed, until we were relieved of fighting. That is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting﴾. So the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, called Bilal, and he commanded him, and he called the iqama for Dhuhr, and he prayed it as he used to pray it. Then he called the iqama for 'Asr and prayed it likewise, then he called the iqama for Maghrib and prayed it likewise, then he called the iqama for 'Isha and prayed it likewise." In another wording: "He prayed each prayer as he used to pray it at its time."

The prayer of fear was legislated before that, for it was revealed at Dhat al-Riqa', which was before the Trench, as Ibn Ishaq and other historians of the biographies (siyar) said. It is answered that it is not granted that the prayer of fear in general, even if severe, was legislated before the Trench, so that the postponement that occurred there could be used as evidence and made to abrogate what is in the verse, as has been said. What was legislated at Dhat al-Riqa' before the prayer of fear was the prayer of fear that is not severe, and it is the one in which was revealed ﴿And when you are among them and lead them in prayer﴾, not the prayer of severe fear explained by this verse, and the dispute is only concerning it. It was not legislated before the Trench but after it, and at the Trench the fear was severe, so the postponement does no harm. Some of the Hanafis have answered that we grant all of that, except that this verse is not an explicit text permitting prayer while walking or in close combat, since it is possible that "rājil" here means "one standing on his feet," especially since it is contrasted with "riding." It is known from external evidence that the prayer must not be disrupted, and this is a complete disruption that cannot be tolerated in it, since it removes it entirely from its reality. If you are fair, you know that the apparent meaning of the verse is explicitly on the side of the Shafi'is, because of the preceding ﴿and stand﴾, and because ﴿religion is ease, not hardship﴾, and because circumstances differ, and the possible part is not dropped because of the impossible part, and what cannot be fully attained is not wholly abandoned. So understand this.

It was also read: rujālan, with a ḍamma on the rā' with lightening, and with a ḍamma with shadda, and it was read: farajulan as well. ﴿Then when you are secure﴾, and your fear has passed. It is related from Mujahid: when you have left the abode of travel for the abode of residence, and perhaps this is by way of example. ﴿Then remember Allah﴾, that is, pray the prayer of security, as Ibn Zayd said, and he expressed it by remembrance (dhikr) because it is the greatest of its pillars. It has also been said: the intended meaning is give thanks to Him for security. Some made it obligatory to repeat (the prayer), and explained this as "repeat the prayer," which is far-fetched. ﴿As He taught you﴾, that is, a remembrance like what He taught you of the laws and the manner of prayer in the states of security and fear, or a thanks corresponding to that. The ma is verbal-masdar (maṣdariyya), and it was permitted that it be relative (mawṣūla), but this is remote. ﴿What you did not used to know﴾ is the object of ʿallamakum, and the verb "kuntum taʿlamūn" was added to convey the structure (naẓm). It occurs in another place without it, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He taught man what he did not know﴾. It was said: the benefit of mentioning the object here, though man knows only what he did not know, is to make explicit the state of ignorance from which he was moved, for it is clearer in expressing favor. In the first conditional, the use of what indicates the uncertainty and rarity of the occurrence of fear, and the opening of the second with "idha," which signals the certainty and frequency of the occurrence of security, together with brevity in the answer to the first and elaboration in the answer to the second, are both based on treating the situation of the occurrence of the commanded act in each as the situation of the occurrence of the command, a treatment that calls for applying the requirement of the first situation in each of them in the manner of the requirement of the second, in grandeur and consideration, as has been said. In that is a lesson for those with insight.

[Page 159]

﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind﴾ returns to explaining the remaining detailed rulings mentioned earlier. In ﴿yutawaffawna﴾ (are caused to die) there is *majāz al-mashāriqa* (a figurative usage). ﴿A bequest for their wives﴾: Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and Ḥamzah, on the authority of ʿĀṣim, read *waṣiyyatan* in the accusative, either as a verbal noun (*maṣdariyya*, a noun of the verbal action) or as an object. The implied sense is: "let them make a bequest," or "Allah the Exalted has prescribed for them," or "a bequest has been imposed on them." This is supported by the reading of ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd): "Allah has prescribed for you the bequest for your wives," in place of ﴿those who…﴾ etc. ﴿Provision until the year's end﴾ The other readers read it in the nominative, as a predicate (*khabar*), with an implied element so that the predication is sound: "and the bequest of those who die is…," or "their ruling is a bequest," or "those who die are the people of a bequest." It is also permitted that it be the deputy subject (*nāʾib fāʿil*) of an omitted verb, or the subject (*mubtadaʾ*) of a predicate omitted and placed before it: i.e., "it has been prescribed for them," or "for them is a bequest." Ubayy read *matāʿun li-azwājihim* (provision is for their wives), and it is related from him *fa-matāʿun* with a *fāʾ*.

﴿Provision until the year's end﴾ is governed by *yūṣūna* (they bequeath), if you take it as implied, and this would be from the category of *ḥadhf wa-īṣāl* (omission and transitive extension of the verb). Otherwise it is governed by *bi-l-waṣiyya* (by the bequest), because it carries the meaning of *al-tawṣiya* (the act of bequeathing); and by *matāʿin* (provision) on the reading of Ubayy, because it carries the meaning of *al-tamattuʿ* (enjoyment). ﴿Without expulsion﴾ is a substitute (*badal*) for it: a *badal al-ishtimāl* (substitute of inclusion) if the necessary connection is considered between enjoyment until the year's end and non-expulsion; and a *badal al-kull* (substitute of the whole) in terms of the essence, since the two are one in essence and differ in attribute. Some have said that on the reading of substitution there must be an implied noun governing it, different from the one implied, so that: ﴿provision until the year's end﴾ = provision, ﴿without expulsion﴾, otherwise it is not sound, because ﴿provision﴾ is explained as maintenance, while ﴿without expulsion﴾ is an expression for lodging, and its signified meaning is not the signified meaning of the first, nor a part of it, nor associated with it, so it would be a *badal al-ghalaṭ* (substitute by error), and that is not valid in the noble speech. Therefore the implied noun is required, and then it is the substitution of the specific for the general, which is of the kind of substituting the whole for a part, like "I saw the moon, its orb," and it is a *badal al-ishtimāl*, as the author of *al-Miftāḥ* (al-Sakkākī) stated explicitly. It was answered: we do not concede that ﴿provision﴾ is explained as maintenance only; rather, provision is general, comprising both maintenance and lodging together, so ﴿without expulsion﴾ is an expression for lodging, which is a part of ﴿provision﴾; thus it is a substitute of a part from the whole. It is also permitted that it be an emphatic verbal noun, because the bequest that they be provided for a year indicates that they do not leave; so it is as if it were said: "they do not leave, without leaving," and it serves as emphasis for the negation of expulsion indicated by "they do not leave," so it reverts to your saying: "they do not leave, they do not leave." It is also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from ﴿their wives﴾. Most scholars hold that it is an emphatic circumstance (*ḥāl muʾakkada*), since there is no sense in restricting the bequest to the concept of this state; and that it is a specifying circumstance (*ḥāl muqaddara*) is not right, because the meaning of negating expulsion until the year's end is not concurrent with the bequest; and there is room for reflection in this. It is also permitted that it be an attribute of *matāʿ* (provision), or an accusative by removal of the preposition. The meaning is: it is obligatory upon those who die to bequeath, before they are near death, for their wives, that they be provided for after them for a year, with maintenance and lodging. This was, according to the sound opinion, at the beginning of Islam. Then the duration was abrogated (*nusikhat*) by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿four months and ten days﴾. And although this verse precedes in recitation, it is later in revelation. Likewise maintenance was abrogated by their inheritance of a quarter or an eighth. There is disagreement on whether the right of lodging falls away or not. What our masters the Ḥanafīs hold is the first (that it falls away), and their argument is that the husband's property became an inheritance for the heirs, and his ownership ended by death. The Shāfiʿīs went to the second, based on His saying (ﷺ): "Remain in your house until the Book reaches its term." It was objected that there is no indication in it that she has lodging from the husband's property, and that is the point in question. ﴿But if they leave﴾ after the year and the passing of the waiting period (*ʿidda*); and it was said: during the period, by their own choice. ﴿Then there is no blame upon you﴾, O guardians of the deceased, or O rulers.

[Page 160]

﴿In what they do with themselves of what is reasonable﴾, that which the Sharīʿa does not deny, such as perfuming, adorning, abandoning mourning, and presenting themselves to suitors; or in not preventing them from leaving, or in cutting off maintenance from them. So there is no explicit text in the verse that it was not obligatory upon them to remain in the husband's dwelling and to mourn for him; rather they were given the choice between remaining and taking maintenance, and between leaving and forgoing it. ﴿And Allah is Mighty﴾, overpowering in His command, who takes vengeance on whoever opposes His command concerning the bequest, its execution, and other matters. ﴿Wise﴾, who considers in His rulings the interests of His servants; so His command and prohibition ought to be obeyed.

For the divorced women there is a provision (mata') in kindness, whether they have been touched or not. ﴿Mata'un﴾ means the general provision (mut'ah), both the obligatory and the recommended kind. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Zuhri held it to be obligatory for all of them. It is also said that what is meant by mata' is the maintenance during the waiting period ('iddah).

The definite article in ﴿al-mutallaqat﴾ may be for specific reference (lil-'ahd), meaning the divorced women mentioned in the preceding verse, who are those not yet touched and for whom no dowry was fixed. The repetition serves for emphasis and to state explicitly what is more evident in obligation. This is the more agreeable view according to our school (madhhab). It is supported by what Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd, who said: When the words of God Most High were revealed, ﴿a provision in kindness, a duty upon the doers of good﴾, a man said: "If I am good, I will do it, and if I do not wish to, I will not do it." So God revealed this verse. There is then no need, in that case, to say that the former verse is particularised by the implication (mafhum) of this general statement (manṭuq), according to the view of those who hold that position, nor to say that this verse was abrogated (naskh), as Ibn al-Musayyib held, which is one of the two opinions of the Imamiyyah.

﴿In kindness, a duty upon the God-conscious (muttaqin)﴾, that is, those who guard themselves against disbelief and sins.

﴿Thus﴾, that is, in the same manner as this clear explanation of the preceding rulings, ﴿God makes clear to you His signs﴾, which indicate what you need in your worldly life (ma'ash) and in the Hereafter (ma'ad), ﴿so that you may understand﴾, that is, so that your intellects may be perfected, or so that you may direct your intellects toward them, or so that you may comprehend what is intended by them.

For the divorced women there is a provision (mata') in kindness, whether they have been touched or not. ﴿Mata'un﴾ means the general provision (mut'ah), both the obligatory and the recommended kind. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Zuhri held it to be obligatory for all of them. It is also said that what is meant by mata' is the maintenance during the waiting period ('iddah).

The definite article in ﴿al-mutallaqat﴾ may be for specific reference (lil-'ahd), meaning the divorced women mentioned in the preceding verse, who are those not yet touched and for whom no dowry was fixed. The repetition serves for emphasis and to state explicitly what is more evident in obligation. This is the more agreeable view according to our school (madhhab). It is supported by what Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Zayd, who said: When the words of God Most High were revealed, ﴿a provision in kindness, a duty upon the doers of good﴾, a man said: "If I am good, I will do it, and if I do not wish to, I will not do it." So God revealed this verse. There is then no need, in that case, to say that the former verse is particularised by the implication (mafhum) of this general statement (manṭuq), according to the view of those who hold that position, nor to say that this verse was abrogated (naskh), as Ibn al-Musayyib held, which is one of the two opinions of the Imamiyyah.

﴿In kindness, a duty upon the God-conscious (muttaqin)﴾, that is, those who guard themselves against disbelief and sins.

﴿Thus﴾, that is, in the same manner as this clear explanation of the preceding rulings, ﴿God makes clear to you His signs﴾, which indicate what you need in your worldly life (ma'ash) and in the Hereafter (ma'ad), ﴿so that you may understand﴾, that is, so that your intellects may be perfected, or so that you may direct your intellects toward them, or so that you may comprehend what is intended by them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 243:

﴿Have you not considered﴾ This expression is sometimes used for someone whose knowledge is already established, and then it serves for wonder (ta'ajjub), affirmation (taqrir) and reminder for one who knows what is to come, such as the rabbis (ahbar) and the people of histories. It is also sometimes used for someone who is not like that, and then it serves to make him know and to make him wonder. This usage has become so well known that it has become like a proverb in this regard, in that the state of one who has not seen a thing is likened to the state of one who has seen it, in that it should not be hidden from him, and that he should be amazed by it. Then the speech is addressed to him as it is addressed to one who has seen it, intending to emphasize the fame and the eminence of the matter in wonder. The "seeing" (ru'yah) is either in the sense of sight (ibsar), used metaphorically for looking (nazar). The benefit of the figurative usage is to urge reflection (i'tibar), because looking is voluntary, unlike the perception that follows it. Or it is in the sense of inner perception (idrak qalbi), including the meaning of reaching and arriving at; for this reason it takes "ila" (to) in His words, ﴿to those who﴾, as many have said. Al-Raghib said: the verb is one that takes its object directly, but when it was borrowed for the meaning of "did you not look (talnzur)," it was given the construction with "ila." The benefit of this borrowing is that looking may be transferred from seeing, so when one intends to urge a look that necessarily results in seeing, it is borrowed for that. This is rarely used except for affirmation, so one does not say "ra'aytu ila kadha" (I saw to such-and-such). End of quotation. The word may also take its object directly with this meaning, though few have pointed this out, as in the words of Imru' al-Qays:

Did you not see me, whenever I came at night seeking her,
I found in her a fragrance, though you had not perfumed yourself?

The one referred to by the relative clause is the people of a village called Dawardan, near Wasit. ﴿They went out from their homes﴾ fleeing from the plague, or from jihad, to which they had been called. ﴿While they were thousands, fearing death﴾. They were more than ten thousand according to what most have inferred, on the basis that one does not say "ashara alf" (ten thousand) or "tis'a alf" (nine thousand) and so on, but only says "alf" in the plural (alaf). So the statement of Ata al-Khurasani, that they were three thousand, and Ibn Abbas in one of the reports from him, that they were four thousand, and Muqatil and al-Kalbi, that they were eight thousand, and Abu Salih, that they were nine thousand, and Abu Ra'uf, that they were ten thousand, is not supported by this usage. Those who hold that they were more than that disagreed: it was said that they were some thirty-odd thousand, and this is reported from al-Suddi. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that they were forty thousand. Ata ibn Abi Rabah said they were seventy thousand. I do not see any fruit in this disagreement after the statement of multitude, and the speech of al-Dahhak inclines towards this. It is reported from Ibn Zayd that the intended meaning is that they went out united in hearts and did not go out out of mutual hatred, so he made it the plural of "alif" (companion), like qa'id and qu'ud, and shahid and shuhud. This is contrary to the apparent meaning and there is not much consideration in it, since the arrival of death happens all at once, as His words indicate, ﴿So Allah said to them: "Die"﴾, upon a great multitude, which is more eloquent in reflection. As for its befalling a people among whom there is affection, it is like its befalling others. A similar statement is that the intended meaning is their affection and love for their homes or for their worldly life. The meaning of His words, ﴿Allah said﴾, is either its apparent sense, or a figurative usage for the connection of His will to their death all at once. It was also said: it is an image (tamthil) of His causing them to die a single death, in the nearest and shortest time, the swiftest and most rapid moment, by a command obeyed, to one who obeys. It was also said: an angel called out to them with this. It is reported from al-Suddi that the caller was two angels. The matter was ascribed to Him, may He be exalted, to instill fear and awe. ﴿Then He gave them life﴾ is a coordination (atf) upon an implied element demanded by the context; that is: they died, then He gave them life. It was said: it was omitted to indicate that its mention is unnecessary, because it is impossible for His will to be separated from His cosmic will (iradah kawniyyah). It was also permitted that it be coordinated upon "said," since it is an expression for causing death. The well-known report is that they remained dead for a period until their bones were scattered. Then Hizqil, known as Ibn al-Ajuz, the successor of Kaleb ibn Yufuna, the successor of Yusha' ibn Nun, passed by them. It was also said: Shim'un. This is reported from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. Wahb said: he was Shamu'il, who is Dhu al-Kifl. It was also said: Yusha' himself. He stood, amazed at the multitude he saw of them. So Allah, may He be exalted, revealed to him: call out, O bones, that Allah commands you to gather. They gathered until some of them clung to others, and they became bodies of bones, without flesh or blood. Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed to him: call out, O bodies, that Allah commands you to clothe yourselves with flesh. They clothed themselves with flesh. Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed to him: call out that Allah commands you to rise. So they were raised as living beings, saying: "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You; there is no god but You." The reports on this subject are many.

The apparent meaning is that they did not see in this death such terrors and states that would make their knowledge necessary, and that would prevent the validity of obligation (taklif) after the return to life, as in the Hereafter. It is possible to say that they saw what the dead see, but they forgot it after returning. The One who is able to cause death and give life is able to cause forgetfulness, and Glory be to Him Whom nothing can overpower. On both assumptions, the death of these people twice in this world does not conflict with His words, ﴿They do not taste death therein﴾ and the verse, because that was not at the completion of terms (ajal), as Mujahid said, but was a death of punishment, so it is as if it were not death. Also, it is one of the extraordinary events of custom (kharq al-'adat), so it does not constitute a counterexample. Some people have said: this was not a death like the death that is followed by life for the resurrection; it is only a kind of severing of the soul's connection to the body, such that decay and corruption befall it, and it is beyond a heart attack (sakta) and severe fainting, so that a skilled observer who saw it would not doubt that the connection had been completely severed, and would not know that some connection still remained, though it did not reach the degree of life known to us. Perhaps this view ultimately returns to a division of death, or to the view that the application of the term "death" to what is mentioned is figurative. Both matters leave something, indeed many things, in the heart.

Ibn al-Rawandi held a similar view concerning all the dead. He said: souls never leave bodies at all. Rather, afflictions and diseases occur in bodies, causing their parts to disperse, as happens to lepers. The soul remains lodged in the scattered parts wherever they may be, being devoid of sensation and perception. This is a doctrine that necessity judges to be false; may Allah, may He be exalted, protect us and the Muslims from believing in its like.

﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind﴾ all of them. As for those, He gave them life so that they might reflect and thus win felicity. As for those who heard, He guided them to reflection. This is like an explanation (ta'lil) for what was mentioned before. ﴿But most of mankind are not grateful﴾ is an exception (istidrak) to what the preceding statement contained; the implied meaning is: "so it is obligatory upon them to be grateful for His bounty, but..." It was also permitted that by gratitude is meant insight and reflection, but this is far-fetched. The use of an explicit noun in place of a pronoun is for greater reproach. The connection of this to what precedes it is that He, glorified be He, when He mentioned several rulings of obligation that included mention of some rulings concerning the dead, followed that with this wondrous story, as an alert to His great power, and that He is the One able to give life and to resurrect for recompense, and as an incitement of resolve to work for the hereafter, to fulfill rights, and to be patient in hardships.

It was also said: the connection is that when He, glorified be He, mentioned ﴿Thus Allah makes clear His signs to you, that you may understand﴾, He mentioned this story, because it is among His great signs and the marvels of His power. It was also said: Allah, may He be exalted, made this story for what it contains of encouragement of the Muslims to jihad, to seek martyrdom, to urge reliance upon Allah, and to submit to decree, as a preparation for His words, may He be exalted:

[Page 161]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 244:

﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾. It is connected in meaning to ﴿Have you not considered?﴾, because the latter carries the sense of "look and reflect." The noble surah, being the pinnacle (sanam) of the Qur'an, mentions in it the universal principles of the religious rulings (ahkam): fasting, pilgrimage, prayer and jihad, in a wondrous manner, digressing at times (mustatriden) for the sake of showing concern for these matters, returning to them whenever an occasion arises, and at other times pursuing them as a main subject (maqsudan), to indicate that the sincere believer should not allow one state to preoccupy him away from another, and that worldly interests are means (dharai') to being free for the otherworldly concerns. Since jihad is the summit of the peak of the religion, and is among the most arduous of obligations, He urged them to it by various means, beginning with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah﴾, and ending at this noble statement, concluding with the mention of spending in His way for the sake of completion (lil-tatmim), as said in al-Kashshaf. Several other possibilities have been permitted regarding the connection:

First: it is a connection to something implied (muqaddar), determined by what precedes it, as if it were said: "So thank His bounty by taking heed from what has been related to you, and fight in His way, for you know that flight does not save from death, and that what is decreed cannot be erased. If the term has come, then death in the way of Allah, may He be exalted, is the best path; otherwise, there is victory and reward."

Second: it is a connection to what is understood from the story; i.e., "Stand firm and do not flee as those fled, and fight."

Third: it is a connection to ﴿Guard the prayers﴾ up to ﴿And if you fear﴾, the verse; because there is in it an indication of meeting the enemy, and what came between came as an interjection (kal-i'tiraD).

Fourth: it is a connection to (He said to them, Allah), and the address is to those whom Allah gave life, and this, as you see, is [weak].

﴿And know that Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of what the one who lags behind from jihad says, of discouraging others from it, and of what the one who hastens to it says, of encouraging toward it. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of what this and that conceal, of the aims and motives, so He will recompense each according to his deed and intention.

[p. 163 begins]

﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah﴾. (مَنِ) is an interrogative (istifhamiyyah) and is in the nominative case (marfu' al-mahall) as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'). (ذا) is its predicate (khabar), and (الَّذِي) is either an adjective (sifah) for it or a substitute (badal) from it. It is not permissible for (مَن ذا) to function as a single word, like (ما تكون) and (ماذا كذلك), as Abu al-Baqa' explicitly stated, because (ما) is more indefinite (ashaddu ibhaman) than (مَن). The lending to Allah, exalted is He, is a metaphor for advancing good deeds in this world in pursuit of the reward in the Hereafter. What is meant here is either jihad, which involves giving up one's self and wealth, or good deeds in general, in which case jihad is included primarily. On both interpretations, the connection of this sentence with what precedes it is clear.

﴿a goodly loan﴾: (قرضًا) is either a verbal noun (masdar) in the sense of (إقراضًا), in which case it is in the accusative as a masdar, or it is in the sense of the passive object (maf'ul), in which case it is in the accusative as a direct object (maf'ul bih). His words, glorified is He, ﴿goodly﴾ (حسنًا) is an adjective (sifah) for it in both cases. The aspect of goodness, according to the first, is sincerity (al-khulus) for example, and according to the second, is lawfulness and purity (al-hill wa al-tayyib). Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that the goodly loan is striving (al-mujahadah) and spending in the way of Allah, exalted is He. According to this, the structure of the verse fits together in the most complete fitting.

﴿then He will multiply it﴾ for him, that is, the loan (al-qard). Making it multiplied is a metaphor, because it is the cause of the multiplication. It is also permissible to assume an omitted genitive (mudaf) so that the meaning is: He will multiply its reward. The form of mufa'alah is not on its usual pattern, since there is no sharing (mushārakah), and it was chosen for emphasis (al-mubalaghah), indicated by the sense of overpowering (al-mughalabah).

Asim recited (فيُضاعِفَهُ) with the accusative (فيُضاعِفَه) and on it there are two aspects. One: it is conjoined (ma'tuf) with the verbal noun (masdar) of (يُقرِضُ) in meaning; that is, "who is it from whom there is a loan, so there is a multiplication from Allah, exalted is He." Two: it is an answer (jawab) to an interrogation that is also in meaning, because the one being asked about, although the lender in the wording, is in meaning the act of lending; so it is as if it had been said: "Will anyone lend to Allah, exalted is He, so that He multiplies it?" This is what Abu al-Baqa' preferred, but he did not permit it to be an answer to the interrogation in wording, because what is asked about in it is the lender, not the loan. Nor did he permit conjoining it with the masdar which is (قرضًا), as a verb is conjoined with a masdar by an implied (أن), for two reasons, as it is said. The first: that (قرضًا) here is an emphatic masdar, and it is not to be construed with (أن) and a verb. The second: conjoining it to it would require that it be governed by (يُقرِض), and this is not valid, because the multiplication is not something lent; rather it is an act from Allah, exalted is He. In this there is room for reflection.

Ibn Kathir recited (يُضَعِّفُهُ) with a nominative (رفع) and emphatic doubling (تشديد). Ya'qub and Ibn Amir recited (يُضْعِفَهُ) with the accusative.
