(أضعافًا) is the plural of (ضِعف), which is the like of a thing in quantity when it is added to it. It is therefore not a masdar. The masdar is (الإضعاف) or (المضاعفة). On this basis it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun (ه) in (يُضاعِفَهُ), and it is permissible for it to be a second object (maf'ul thani) in meaning, in that the multiplication includes the sense of making/transforming (al-tasyir). It is also permitted to regard it as occupying the position of the masdar, so that it is in the accusative as a masdar at that point. It is plural, although masdars are not dualized or pluralized, because they are established for the reality (al-haqiqah) considered in itself, for the purpose of the different kinds. Its meaning here too is the reality, but it is intended in terms of its existence within its kinds that fall under it.

﴿many﴾: none knows its amount except Allah, exalted is He. Imam Ahmad, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi, who said: "It reached me from Abu Hurayrah that he said: 'Allah, exalted is He, indeed writes for His believing servant, for one good deed, a thousand thousand good deeds.' So I performed Hajj that year, and I had not intended to perform Hajj except to meet him for this hadith. I met Abu Hurayrah and told him, and he said: 'This is not what I said, and the one who related it to you did not memorize it. What I said is: Allah, exalted is He, gives the believing servant for one good deed two thousand thousand good deeds.' Then Abu Hurayrah said: 'Do you not find this in the Book of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan, then He will multiply it for him manifold many times﴾? So the many with Him, exalted is He, is more than two thousand thousand and two thousand thousand. By the One in whose hand is my soul, I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed Allah, exalted is He, multiplies the good deed two thousand thousand times two thousand thousand good deeds."'"

﴿And Allah withholds and extends﴾. That is, He restricts (yuqtir) for some and widens (yuwassi') for others, or He restricts at one time and widens at another, according to what wisdom requires, whose secret is subtle and whose worth is great. When you know that He is the One who withholds and extends, and that what you have is only from His extension and giving, then do not be stingy toward Him. So lend to Him and spend from what He has widened for you, in exchange for His widening and giving, and do not reverse this by being stingy instead of that; for then He would deal with you in the same way as you dealt with Him in the reversal, by withholding and restricting for you after He has widened for you and empowered you to spend. It is also reported from Qatadah, al-Asamm and al-Zajjaj that the meaning is: He withholds the charities and extends the reward for them. The statement is then like an emphasis and confirmation of what came before. The reason for placing extension after withholding is clear; the reason for placing it after withholding in the first interpretation is an indication that it follows withholding in existence, as consolation for the poor. It is also recited as (يَبْصُطُ).

﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾, so He will reward you according to what you have sent forward.

* * *

From the door of allusion (al-isharah): the prayers are five. The prayer of the innermost (al-sirr) is by witnessing His station of the unseen (maqam al-ghayb); the prayer of the self (al-nafs) is by its quieting from the callings of doubt; the prayer of the heart (al-qalb) is by its watching the lights of unveiling (anwar al-kashf); the prayer of the spirit (al-ruh) is by beholding the union (al-wasl); and the prayer of the body is by guarding the senses and upholding the limits. The meaning is: guard these five prayers, and the middle prayer, which is the prayer of the heart, whose condition is purity from inclination toward other than Him, and whose reality is turning toward the Master. For this reason it is nullified by passing thoughts and by deviation from the Ka'bah of the Essence.

﴿And stand before Allah﴾ by turning toward Him in devotion (qanitin), that is, obedient to Him outwardly and inwardly, by repelling the thoughts.

﴿And if you fear﴾ the collisions of majesty (sadamat al-jalal) during your journey to Allah, exalted is He, then pray on foot in the desert of the path, walking upon the feet of truthfulness, or riding upon the mounts of resolve, and let fear not turn you away from that.

﴿And when you are secure﴾ after returning from that journey to the original homeland by the unveiling of the veil, ﴿then remember Allah﴾, that is, pray to Him with your whole being until you pass away in Him; or, when you are secure by returning to subsistence after annihilation, then remember Allah, exalted is He, because distinction after unity then occurs. Before that there is no remembrance, since there is then no distinction and no preference. It has been said to the madman: "Do you love Layla?" He said: "And who is Layla? I am Layla." And one of them said:

"I am the one I love, and the one I love is I;
we are two spirits that have dwelt in one body.
So when you see me, you see Him,
and when you see Him, you see us."

﴿Have you not considered those who went out from their homes﴾: that is, their familiar homelands, the settled places of their souls, their stations and ranks from the world, and what they inclined to by the calls of desire. They were a people, many thousands, or loving one another and united in Allah, exalted is He, fearing the death of ignorance, the cutting off from true life, and falling into the natural abysses. ﴿Then Allah said to them: Die﴾, that is, He commanded them to a chosen death, or He caused them to die to their selves through the essential manifestation, until they passed away in Him. ﴿Then He gave them life﴾ with the true knowing life, or through Him with the existence of the Real, and subsistence after annihilation. ﴿Indeed Allah is full of bounty﴾ over all people, by preparing the means of their guidance. ﴿But most people do not give thanks﴾ because of their great heedlessness of what is intended for them.

﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾, the self and the devil. ﴿And know that Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of the whisperings of the souls of those who fight in His way, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of what is in their hearts. ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah﴾ and give up himself to Him with pure giving, free of association. ﴿So He will multiply it for him manifold many times﴾ by the manifestation within it of the attributes of His beauty and majesty. ﴿And Allah withholds﴾ the spirits of the monotheists with His compelling grasp in the light of pre-eternity, ﴿and extends﴾ the secrets of the knowers from the grasp of greatness, and spreads them in the witnessing of the praise of eternity. It is said: contraction is their secret, and expansion is their unveiling. It is also said: contraction is for the seekers, and expansion is for those who are sought; or the first is for the longing, and the second for the knowers. What is well known is that contraction and expansion are two states that follow the servant's ascent beyond the state of fear and hope. Contraction for the knower is like fear for one who is secure. The difference between them is that fear and hope relate to a future matter, disliked or loved, while contraction and expansion relate to a matter present in the moment that overpowers the heart of the knower from an unseen inspiration. The first is from the traces of majesty, and the second is from the traces of beauty.

[p. 164 ends]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 246:

﴿Have you not considered the eminent men of the Children of Israel?﴾ Al-mala' (the eminent) of a people are their faces and their nobles. It is a collective noun with no singular from its own form. The root sense is gathering around something that admits of no addition. The nobles are so called either because their awe fills hearts (yamla'u al-sudur), or because they "tama'alu," that is, they cooperate in what leaves nothing more to be added. The particle min (from) here is partitive (li-al-tab'id). The prepositional phrase is attached to an omitted verb and stands as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of al-mala'. ﴿From after Musa﴾ means from after his death, peace be upon him. Here min expresses the starting point (li-al-ibtida'), and it is linked to the same thing that the preceding min is linked to. The identity of the two particles in form does no harm, since they differ in meaning. ﴿When they said to a prophet of theirs﴾ Abu Ubayda said: he is Ashmawil ibn Hanna ibn al-'Aqir, and most scholars agree with this. From al-Suddi: he is Shim'un. Qatada said: he is Yusha' ibn Nun, because of the closeness of the time that preceded. This is apparent in terms of continuity. It is refuted by the claim that this Yusha' was the young servant (fata) of Musa, peace be upon them both, and that between him and Dawud there were many generations. Continuity is not necessary. The word idh (when) is linked to an implied element demanded by the context, meaning: "Have you not considered" the story of the nobles or their account, when they said: ﴿Raise up for us a king﴾, that is, establish for us a commander. The root sense of al-ba'th is sending the one sent from the place where he is, but it varies with its object. It is said: ba'atha al-ba'ir min mabrakihi (the camel was roused from its resting place) when it is stirred up; ba'athtahu fi al-sayr (I urged him on) when one agitates him in travel; Allah the Exalted ba'atha al-mayyit (raised the dead) when He gives him life; and dhuriba al-ba'th 'ala al-jund (the sending was imposed upon the army) when they are ordered to set out. [p. 165] ﴿We will fight in the way of Allah﴾ is jussed by the imperative. It was also read in the nominative, as a presumed circumstantial clause (hal muqaddara), meaning: "Raise him up for us, [while] we determine to fight," or as an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), as if it were said: "What then will you do with the king?" and the answer was: "We will fight." It was also read as yuqatil, with the yaa', jussed and nominative, as a response to the imperative and as a description of malikan (a king). The reason for their request, according to some reports, was that when Musa died he was succeeded by Yusha', so that he might uphold the command of Allah the Exalted among them and judge by the Torah. Then Kalib succeeded him in the same way, then Hizqil in the same way, then Ilyas in the same way, then al-Yasa' in the same way. Then an enemy appeared to them, namely the 'Amaliqa, the people of Jalut. They were dwellers of the Roman sea between Egypt and Palestine. They prevailed over them, overcame much of their lands, took captive four hundred and forty of the sons of their kings, imposed the jizya upon them, and seized their Torah. At that time they had no prophet to manage their affairs. The tribe of prophethood had perished except for a pregnant woman, who gave birth to a boy and named him Ashmawil, meaning Isma'il. It was also said: Shim'un. When he grew up she handed him the Torah, and he learned it in Bayt al-Maqdis. A shaykh of their scholars cared for him. When he grew up, Allah the Exalted made him a prophet and sent him to them. They said: "If you are truthful, then raise up for us a king," and so on in the verse. The stability of the affairs of the Children of Israel depended on gathering behind kings and obeying their prophets. The king was the one who led the armies, and the prophet was the one who upheld his command, guided him, and advised him. ﴿He said: Is it likely that if fighting is prescribed for you you will not fight?﴾ 'Asa (perhaps/it is likely) is among the nawasikh (the abrogating verbs that alter the structure of the nominal sentence), and its predicate is "an la tuqatilu" (that you will not fight). The conditional clause separates them, for the sake of emphasis on it. The meaning is: "Have you come close to not fighting, as I expect of you?" The purpose is to affirm that the expected thing is occurring and to establish it, as has been said. It was objected that 'asaytum an la tuqatilu means the expectation of not fighting, and that hal (is it?) is used only to question what it enters upon, so the question would be about the expectation and not about the expected thing. Affirming the question does not require that the expected thing be established, but only that the expectation exists, and how is this like that? It is answered that the interrogative entered upon a sentence containing an expectation and an expected thing. There is no way to the first, because a man is not questioned about his expectation, so it must be about the expected thing. Since the interrogative is in the manner of affirmation, what is meant is that the expected thing exists. It was also said: since 'asa is for the initiation of an expectation and does not leave it, the affirmative interrogative was directed at the expected thing, which is the predicate, the locus of benefit. So he affirmed it and established it. That the questioned element follows the hamza is not an absolute rule. It was also said: 'asa is not among the nawasikh, and it has included the meaning of qaraba (to draw near), and an and what follows it is its object. This is the meaning of the statement of some of them: it is a predicate, not an imperative. It was supported by the entry of the interrogative upon it and its occurrence as a predicate in the line:

Do not overdo it, for I have indeed become fasting.

Its meaning is not hidden. What was mentioned in the context of the condition is the prescription of fighting, not what they had asked for, even though what they asked for was more closely connected to their words. This is an exaggeration in showing their failure to comply with it. For if they did not fight when fighting was prescribed upon them by the command of Allah the Exalted, then not fighting when it was not prescribed is more fitting. Also, what they mentioned might give the impression that the cause of their failure was the one sent, not fighting itself. It is possible that he placed this in the position of that, as a hint that this sending, upon which fighting is consequent, when it occurs, occurs only in a way that makes it obligatory. It was also read as 'asitum with a kasra on the sin, which is a rare dialect. ﴿They said: And what is it with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah?﴾ That is: what motive do we have for not fighting, that is, for abandoning fighting? The prepositional phrase is linked to what is linked to lana (for us), or to itself, and it is the predicate of ma (what). The waw was included to indicate the connection of this speech with what precedes it. Had it been omitted, it would have been permissible for it to be disconnected from it. Abu al-Baqa said this. It was also permitted that it be a conjunction onto an omitted element, as if they had said: "Not fighting is not expected from us, and what is with us that we should not fight?" They did not state this explicitly, out of reluctance to address their prophet directly with what clearly rejects his words. The common usage in this kind of construction is: ma lana nafalu aw la nafalu (what is it with us that we do or do not do such and such), with the clause being a circumstantial qualifier. Since the verbal noun (masdariyya) is incompatible here, it is prevented from it, so what was required there was required. Al-Akhfash claimed the addition of an (that), and that governing does not negate it, and the clause is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier, as in the common usage. It was also said that it is by dropping the waw, and it reverts to: "What is with us and that we do not fight," as in your saying: iyyaka wa an tatakallama (beware of speaking), and it may be said: iyyaka an tatakallama. The meaning is according to the waw. It was also said that ma here is negative, meaning: it is not for us to abandon fighting. ﴿And we have been driven out from our homes and our sons﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier, and the governing element is nuqatila (we fight). The purpose is to inform that they will certainly fight, since there has befallen them what strongly necessitates fighting, namely expulsion from the homelands and estrangement from family and children. The singling out of the sons for mention is for greater reinforcement of the causes of fighting. It is conjoined to the homelands. According to Abu al-Baqa there is an omitted modifier in it, meaning: "and from among our sons." It was also said: there is no omission, and the conjunction is in the manner of the saying:

I fed her straw and cold water.

In the speech there is the attribution of what belongs to some to all, since those who were expelled are some of them, not all of them.

﴿So when fighting was prescribed for them﴾ after the prophet's question and the sending of the king, ﴿they turned away﴾ meaning they withdrew and neglected the command of Allah the Exalted. But not at the beginning of the matter; rather after witnessing the multitude of the enemy and its might, as will come. The outcome of their affair is mentioned here in summary, to display the contradiction and disparity between their words and their deeds. ﴿Except a few of them﴾ — they are the ones who crossed the river, and they were three hundred and thirteen, the number of the people of Badr, according to what al-Bukhari reported from al-Bara', may Allah be pleased with him. The "few" is relative, so there is no objection to describing this number at times as a great multitude. ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾. Among them are those who did wrong by turning away from fighting and abandoning jihad, and whose words and deeds were contradictory. The sentence is a concluding statement (tadhyil), intended as a warning upon that.

﴿And their Prophet said to them﴾ begins the detail after the summary. That is, he spoke after what had been revealed to them had been revealed. ﴿Indeed, Allah has raised up Talut as a king for you﴾ to manage your affairs, and you shall act upon his opinion in fighting. As for *Talut* (Ṭālūt), there are two views. The more apparent is that it is a non-Arabic proper name of Hebrew origin, like Dawud (David), and for this reason it is not declined (*lam yanṣarif*, i.e. it does not take nunation). It was also said that it is Arabic, from *al-ṭūl* (height), and that its original form was *ṭawalūt*, like *rahabūt* and *raḥamūt*. The waw was then changed to an alif because it was vowelled and the letter before it was open. Its declension is prevented in this case by its being a proper noun (*'alamiyya*) and by its resemblance to foreign words (*shibh al-'ujma*), since it does not follow the morphological patterns (*abniya*) of the Arabs. As for the claim that it is a modification (*'adl*) from *ṭawīl* and the view that it is Hebrew which happens to agree with the Arabic, that is far-fetched (*takalluf*). The word *malikan* (king) is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) of *Ṭālūt*.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Suddi that when their prophet asked his Lord to make a king over them, He brought him a staff by which the one to be made king over them would be measured, and none matched it except Talut. Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Jarir related from Wahb ibn Munabbih that when he called upon Allah, He said to him: "Look at the horn that has oil in your house. When a man enters upon you and bubbles up the oil in it, he is the king of the Children of Israel. Anoint his head with it and make him king over them." So he remained waiting for when that man would enter upon him. Talut was a tanner who worked with leather (*al-adam*); it was also said that he was a water-carrier. He was of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Jacob (peace be upon him), and there was neither prophethood nor kingship among them. Talut set out seeking a riding animal of his that had gone astray, and with him was a young servant. They passed by the house of the Prophet, and Talut's servant said to him: "If only you would enter with us upon this prophet, we could ask him about the matter of our animal, so that he might guide us and pray for us for good concerning it." Talut said: "There is no harm in what you have said." So they both entered upon him. While they were with him, mentioning to him the affair of their animal and asking him to pray for it, the oil in the horn bubbled up. The Prophet stood up, took it, and then said to Talut: "Bring your head close." So he brought it close, and he anointed him with the oil. Then he said: "You are the king of the Children of Israel whom Allah the Exalted has commanded me to make king over them." So he sat with him, and the people said: "Talut has been made king." The eminent men of the Children of Israel came to their prophet, astonished at this, since he was not from the house of prophethood or kingship.

﴿They said: "How can he have kingship over us?"﴾ That is: from where would it come to him, or how could it be his? The interrogation is either genuine or expresses wonder, not a denial of their prophet or a rejection of his judgment according to one opinion. Its place is in the accusative as a circumstantial (*ḥāl*) of *al-mulk* (kingship). The verb *yakūnu* may be the incomplete verb (*nāqiṣa*), in which case the predicate is *lahu*, and *'alaynā* is a circumstantial phrase of *al-mulk*; or the predicate is *'alaynā* and *lahu* is the circumstantial phrase. It may also be the complete verb (*tāmma*), in which case *lahu* is attached to it, and *'alaynā* is a circumstantial phrase. ﴿And we have more right to kingship than him, and he has not been given abundance of wealth﴾: the first *wāw* is circumstantial (*ḥāliyya*), and the second is conjunctive (*'āṭifa jāmi'a*), joining the two clauses. That is: how can he rule over us when the situation is that he does not deserve to rule, because there are those more worthy than him, and because he lacks the wealth on which kingship depends, or the thing that would compensate for his deficiency if he had it, and which by custom would place him among the nobles? The original form of *sa'a* (abundance) is *us'a* with a *wāw*, and it was deleted because it was deleted from *yasa'u*. The verb ought to have a kasra on its *sīn* so that the deletion could take place, as in *ya'idu*. The fatha was adopted only because of a guttural letter, so it is incidental; therefore the rule of the kasra is applied to it. Because of that fatha, the *sīn* is vowelled with fatha in the verbal noun, and it is not vowelled with kasra as the *'ayn* of *'idda* is.

﴿He said: "Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and increased him broadly in knowledge and physique, and Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing."﴾ He answered them in the most eloquent and complete manner, as if it were said: Do not consider it unlikely that he should be made king over you because of his poverty and the lowliness of his lineage compared to yours. First, the basis of the matter is the choice of Allah the Exalted, and He has chosen him and preferred him, and He, glory be to Him, knows best what is in your interest. Second, the essential matter is abundance of knowledge, by which one is enabled to recognise political affairs, and bulk of body, so that he is more awe-inspiring in hearts and stronger in confronting enemies and enduring wars, not what you have mentioned. Allah the Exalted has granted him a generous share of both. Third, He, the Exalted, is the owner of kingship absolutely, and the owner may empower whom he wills to dispose of his kingdom by his permission. Fourth, He, glory be to Him, is of vast bounty, who enriches the poor by making him wealthy, and He is All-Knowing of what befits kingship in terms of lineage and other qualities. The placing of "breadth in knowledge" before "breadth in body" implies that the psychological virtues are higher and more noble than the physical virtues, indeed there is almost no comparison between them, especially the massiveness of the body. For this reason some have interpreted the "breadth" here as beauty or strength, not as quantity such as tallness of stature, as it is said that a standing man would stretch out his hand and reach his head. If that were a perfection, the one most deserving of it would be the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, although "he, peace and blessings be upon him, was of medium height among men." Perhaps the mention of this, on that assumption, is because it is a quality that adds beauty to the king needed to fight the Amalekites, since they were massive and possessed breadth in their bodies, and their king Jalut's shadow was a mile long according to some reports. It is not that these are among the matters that are essential for kings as such, as is not hidden from one who understands that a person is by his two smaller parts (i.e. his heart and tongue), not by the size of his body or the length of his cloak.

In the choice of *All-Encompassing* and *All-Knowing* as the description of Allah the Exalted here, there is a fine appropriateness to the breadth of body and abundance of knowledge that stirs the minds, especially in view of the breadth of body that is immediately suggested, and the priority of the first description, even though what corresponds to it apparently comes later. This is because it has a semantic correspondence to the first statement, since choosing is also a matter of vast bounty. Also, *'Alīm* (All-Knowing) fits better with the rhyme (*fawāṣil*), and the display of the noble Name serves to instil awe.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 248:**

﴿Their prophet said to them﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the similar clause that precedes it. The preceding material was placed between them to indicate that the two are not directly connected, and that a statement from the addressees intervenes. That statement branches off from what came before and leads to what follows. The storytellers' narrations agree that they said to their prophet: "What is the sign of his kingship and his being chosen over us?" He said: ﴿Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the chest will come to you﴾. Since their saying did not appear explicitly, so that this would function as an explicit answer to it, the subject was repeated in order to differ from what was already clearly understood to be an answer. The reason it was not arranged in such a way as to mention their statement and make this an answer to it, relying on the pronoun as it did initially, is to hint that this question came after they had believed him and after he had explained to them what they were asking about. Such a question should not be answered, because it then bears a full resemblance to obstinacy, even if it is counted as a question for strengthening knowledge.

This is based on the premise that the people were believers. Some narrations, however, imply that they had not yet believed in him at that time. On the authority of al-Suddi: this prophet had been placed in the care of a shaykh from among the scholars of the Children of Israel. When God the Exalted wished to send him as a prophet, Jibril came to him while he was a young boy sleeping beside the shaykh, who trusted no one else with him. Jibril called him in the voice (lahn) of the shaykh. The boy got up in alarm and went to the shaykh, saying: "O father, did you call me?" The shaykh disliked saying "no" lest the boy be frightened, so he said: "O my son, go back and sleep." He went back and slept. Jibril called him a second time, and the boy came again, saying: "Did you call me?" He said: "Go back and sleep. If I call you a third time, do not answer me." When the third time came, Jibril appeared to him and said: "Go to your people and convey to them the message of your Lord, for God the Exalted has sent you among them as a prophet." When he came to them, they denied him and said: "You have hastened to prophethood before its time has come." They also said: "If you are truthful, raise up a king for us." Then what happened happened, and he said: ﴿Indeed, God has raised up Talut as king for you﴾. They said: "You have never been more false than you are right now." They objected, and were answered. Then they said: "If you are truthful, bring us a sign that this is a king." He said what God the Exalted has related.

In that case, it is not far-fetched that the explicit question in the verse, and likewise the demand alluded to in it, came from denial and lack of certainty. The reason for omitting mention of their question at that point, if the purpose is to indicate that it is the nature of prophets to bring signs even when they are not requested of them, is to make things clear to the wanderer and to restrict the one who comes to it, and ﴿so that those who believe may increase in guidance﴾.

The tābūt (chest) is a box. It is of the form faʿūl from al-tawb, which means "return," because what comes out of it continually returns to it, and its owner returns to it for what he needs of his deposits. Its tāʾ is an added letter, like the tāʾ in malakūt. Its original form was tawbūt, and the waw was changed to an alif. It is not fāʿūl from al-tabt, because roots whose first and third radicals are of the same kind are rare, as in salis and qalaq. It has also been read as tābūh with a hāʾ, which is the dialect of the Ansar, while the preferred form is the dialect of Quraysh, which is the one that ʿUthman (may God be pleased with him) ordered to be written in the Imam (the standard codex), when Zayd and Aban (may God be pleased with them both) disputed about it. Its measure at that point, according to al-Zamakhshari's preference, is fāʿūl, because the suspicion of derivation does not outweigh the addition of the hāʾ and the absence of a parallel. As for making the hāʾ a substitute for the tāʾ, because they share the quality of hams (breathiness) and both are among the letters of addition, this is weak, because substitution outside the feminine tāʾ is not established. Al-Jawhari held that the tāʾ in it is the feminine marker, and that its original form was, in his view, tābūah, like tarquwah. When the waw became sukūn (quiescent), the feminine hāʾ changed into a tāʾ. The chest is meant here as the box that the Children of Israel used to seek blessing from, and which was lost from them. There is disagreement about its identity.

The people of reports said: it is a box that God the Exalted sent down to Adam (peace be upon him), in which were the images of all the prophets. It was made of shimshad wood, about three cubits by two cubits. It kept passing from noble hand to noble hand until it reached Yaʿqub, then to his sons, and then to others, until the Children of Israel became corrupt and disobeyed after Musa (peace be upon him). God the Exalted then gave the Amalekites power over them, and they took it from them and placed it in a place of urine and excrement. When God the Exalted wished to make Talut king, He sent affliction upon them, so that whoever defecated near it was struck with hemorrhoids, and five cities of their land were destroyed. They realized that this was because of their contempt for it. So they brought it out and placed it on two bulls, which set off walking, and God the Exalted had assigned four angels to drive them, until they reached the dwelling of Talut.

It was also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with him and his father) that it was the box of the Torah. God had raised it to heaven as a sign of wrath against the Children of Israel when they disobeyed after the death of Musa (peace be upon him). When the sign was requested, it came down from heaven while the angels guarded it, and the Children of Israel watched it, until they lodged it in the house of Talut. It was also reported from Abu Jaʿfar (may God be pleased with him) that it was the chest in which Musa's mother had been given revelation, when she placed him in it and cast it into the sea. It remained with the Children of Israel, who sought blessing from it, until they became corrupt. Then they began to treat it with contempt, and God the Exalted raised it up, until what happened happened. Other reports have been transmitted, which would take too long to mention.

The closest of the views I have seen is that it is the box of the Torah, which the Amalekites overcame until God returned it. The most remote is that it is a box that came down from heaven to Adam (peace be upon him), and that people used to have their disputes judged by it after Musa (peace be upon him). It would rule between them and speak with them until they became corrupt, and then the Amalekites seized it. I have not found any sound, attributed (marfuʿ) hadith on which one can rely that opens the lock of this box, nor any such reasoning.

﴿In it is tranquility from your Lord﴾: that is, in its coming there is calm and reassurance for you. In this case, sakīnah is a verbal noun. Or it means that in it itself is that in which you find rest, namely the Torah. It was also said, and this is not correct as al-Raghib has stated, that it was a figure made of chrysolite or ruby, having a head and tail like the head and tail of a cat, and two wings. It would hum, and the chest would be sent toward the enemy while they advanced with it. When it settled, they stood firm, became calm, and victory descended. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl). The preposition min is either for the beginning of the limit (ibtidāʾ al-ghāyah) or partitive, meaning: from the tranquilities of your Lord.

﴿And a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun left behind﴾: this is the fragments of the tablets, the garments of Musa, the turban of Harun, and a golden basin in which the hearts of the prophets were washed. The words of relief were: "There is no god but God, the Forbearing, the Generous; glory be to God, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the mighty Throne; and praise be to God, Lord of the worlds." The "family" (āl) of them both are their followers, or themselves, or the prophets of the Children of Israel, since they are the sons of their paternal uncle. ﴿Carried by the angels﴾ is a circumstantial phrase relating to the chest. The carrying is either literal or figurative, as in the expression: "Zayd carried my goods to Makkah."

﴿Indeed, in that﴾ refers to what has been mentioned about the coming of the chest. In that case, it is part of the Prophet's speech to his people. Or it refers to the narration of the story and its recounting, in which case it is a new address from Him, the Exalted, to the Prophet (ﷺ) and those believers with him. It was placed before the story is completed, to show complete concern. The singular form of the address particle, despite the plurality of addressees under both interpretations, is according to the understanding of "group" and the like. ﴿A sign﴾, that is, a great sign existing for you, indicating the appointment of Talut as king over you, or indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), since he reported what he reported without hearing it from a human being or taking it from a book. ﴿If you are believers﴾: that is, if you are affirmers of his being made king over you, or of any of the signs. The "if" (in) is conditional, and its apodosis is omitted, relying on what precedes it. The intended meaning is not literal conditionality when the addressee is one whose faith is certain. It has also been said that it means "when" (idh).

﴿فَلَمّا فَصَلَ طالُوتُ بِالجُنُودِ﴾ *"So when Talut set out with the troops."* That is, he departed from Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) accompanying them to fight the Amalekites. Its original form is *faṣala nafsahu ʿanhu* (he separated himself from it). When its subject and object are one and the same, its use with the object omitted became common, until it took the place of an intransitive verb, like *infaṣala* (he separated). It is also said that *faṣṣala* means he made distinctions. It is also permitted that it is a primary root verb, distinguished from the transitive by its verbal noun, as in *waqafa wuqūfan* and *waqqafahu waqfan* (he made him stop), and *ṣadda ʿanhu ṣudūdan* or *ṣaddahu ṣaddan* (he turned him away). This is a well-known pattern. *Al-junūd* (the troops) means the helpers and supporters, the plural of *jund*, and it carries the sense of a collective. It is narrated that he said to his people: "No man who has built a house and not finished it should go out with me, nor a merchant occupied with trade, nor a man who has married a woman and not consummated the marriage. I only want the young, energetic and unoccupied." So there gathered to him, from those he had chosen, eighty thousand men. It is also said seventy thousand. The time was the height of summer, so they took a desert route and asked for a river.

﴿قالَ إنَّ اللَّهَ مُبْتَلِيكُمْ﴾ *"He said: Indeed God will test you."* That is, He will deal with you as one who wishes to examine you, so that the truthful among you and the liar may become visible to sight.

﴿بِنَهَرٍ﴾ *"with a river."* With the *ha'* vowelled with a fatḥah. It was also read with a sukūn, and that is a dialectal variant of the word. This river was the river of Palestine, as narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with them both) and from Qatadah and al-Rabiʿ, that it was a river between Palestine and the Jordan.

﴿فَمَن شَرِبَ مِنهُ﴾ *"Whoever drinks from it."* That is, he begins drinking from it out of excessive thirst, by bending down to the water itself (*kara'a*, drinking directly with the mouth from the water), since drinking from it in the literal sense is this. This is often what a thirsty man on the brink of death does. It is also said that the statement is elliptical, with an omitted *muḍāf* (a genitive construction), meaning: whoever drinks from its water in any manner.

﴿فَلَيْسَ مِنِّي﴾ *"then he is not of me."* That is, not of my followers, or he is not connected to me and not united with me. The *min* here is the *min* of connection, which according to some is different from the *min* of partitive, and according to others is an explanatory *min*. Others have specified it.

﴿ومَن لَمْ يَطْعَمْهُ فَإنَّهُ مِنِّي﴾ *"But whoever does not taste it, he is indeed of me."* That is, whoever does not taste it. From *ṭaʿima al-shayʾ* (he tasted the thing): when he tastes it, whether it is food or drink. This is related by al-Azhari from al-Layth. Al-Jawhari mentions that *al-ṭaʿm* is what tasting conveys, and is not the same as tasting itself. So whoever interprets it as tasting on this basis has taken a broad sense. On both views, the use of *ṭaʿima al-māʾ* in the sense of *dhāqa ṭaʿmahu* (he tasted its taste) is widespread and not objectionable in the usage of the pure Arabs. The following verse attests to it: "If you wish, I will forbid women other than you, and if you wish, I will not taste the sweet water or the cold." As for its use in the sense of drinking it or taking it as food, that is disliked, except where the context requires it, as in the hadith about Zamzam: *"It is food of nourishment and a cure for sickness."* For this indicates that it nourishes, unlike other waters. This is not undermined by what is related: that Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Qasri said from the pulpit of Kufa, when al-Mughirah ibn Saʿid had revolted against him: "Feed me water!" The Arabs found fault with him for this and mocked him for it, attributing it to the severity of his distress. And it was said about him:

*"Rather, the pulpits, from fear and dread,*
*and he asked for water to eat when he fled in haste."*

*"And the most ignorant of people is every person in general,*
*and he was fond of showing off with speeches."*

This is because it was criticized of him only because it proceeded from distress, so it was liable to suspicion and not intending the correct meaning. Otherwise, the occurrence of such a usage in their speech is not something to doubt.

Talut knew that whoever drank from it was disobeying him, and whoever did not taste it was obeying him, through revelation to the prophet of the Children of Israel. The prophet himself did not inform them of this, but conveyed it to Talut, who reported it as if from his own initiative, so that it would have an effect on their hearts. It is also permitted that this was by revelation to him, on the basis that he was made a prophet after being made king. But this is an opinion without proof, and the view that it may have been by insight and inspiration is far-fetched.

﴿إلا مَنِ اغْتَرَفَ غُرْفَةً بِيَدِهِ﴾ *"Except one who scoops a handful with his hand."* This is an exception (*istithnāʾ*) from the first relative clause (*mawṣūl*), or from its pronoun in the predicate. If drinking is understood as drinking by bending down to the water directly, the exception is disconnected (*munqaṭiʿ*); otherwise it is connected (*muttaṣil*). The purpose of placing the second sentence first is to signal that it is part of the first, and that its purpose is to confirm and complete it, by prohibiting bending down to drink in every way, and to convey that the one who scoops is not a taster in judgment. Thus it confirms the permission for scooping. If it were delayed, these benefits would not be conveyed, and the composition would be disturbed, since the exception would then indicate that the one who scoops is united with him, and the second sentence would indicate by its implication that he is not united with him. It is not sound for the exception to be from one of the two pronouns referring to the relative clauses within the *ṣilah* (the clause that completes the relative pronoun), because this would separate the parts of the *ṣilah* by the predicate. Its meaning, in the first case, would lead to the conclusion that the one who drinks with a single handful is not connected to him or united with him, since the sense would be: "Those who drank all of it, except the one who scooped, are not of me." Nor is it correct that it is from the second relative clause, or from the pronoun referring to it in the predicate, contrary to some scholars, since that would lead to the same conclusion, namely that the excepted person is excluded from the ruling of unity with him. The sense would be: "Those who did not taste it, all of them, except the one who scooped from them, are connected to me and united with me." This is not intended at all. *Al-ghurfa* is what is scooped. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and the people of Medina read *gharfatan* with a fatḥah on the *ghayn*, considering it a verbal noun. It is also said that *al-ghurfa* and *al-gharfa* are both verbal nouns, and the *ḍamma* and the *fatḥa* are two dialects. The *bāʾ* is connected to *ightaraf* (scooped), or to *ghurfa* according to one view, or to an omitted element that functions as a qualifier of it.

﴿فَشَرِبُوا مِنهُ﴾ *"Then they drank from it."* This is coordinated with an implied element required by the context, meaning: they were tested by it, and so they drank. What is meant is either that they bent down to the water, which is the more obvious meaning, and this is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with them both); or that they exceeded in drinking, except a few among them who did not bend down; or that they did not exceed in drinking, but were content with a handful by hand, which sufficed them for drinking and for their water-skins. This is what Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas (may God be pleased with them both). He also related from him that whoever drank did not increase except in thirst. In another narration: those who drank had their lips blackened and thirst overcame them. This was a miracle of that prophet. Ubayy and al-Aʿmash read *illā qalīlun* with a *ḍamma* (nominative), and they took it as an inclination towards the sense: for the statement "then they drank from it" is in effect the same as saying "so they did not obey him," so the excepted element should properly be in the nominative. This is like the verse of al-Farazdaq:

*"And the bite of time, O son of Marwan, has left*
*of wealth nothing but the stripped or the cut."*

Here his statement "has left" is in the sense of "has not remained." Abu Hayyan maintained that no interpretation is needed, and he permitted two ways of reading the affirmative (positive) exception: the accusative, which is the more eloquent, and following what precedes it as an adjective or an appositive. He cited as evidence the verse: "Every brother who parts from his brother, by the life of your father, except the two stars (al-Farqadan)." The problem with this is not hidden.

﴿فَلَمّا جاوَزَهُ﴾ *"Then when he had crossed it."* That is, the river, and passed beyond it. ﴿هُوَ﴾ *"he"*, that is Talut. ﴿والَّذِينَ آمَنُوا﴾ *"and those who believed"*: coordinated with the attached pronoun, which was emphasized by the detached pronoun. What is meant by them is the few. The reference to them in this way is to honour their rank, and to hint that those other than them are far from faith. ﴿مَعَهُ﴾ *"with him"*: this is connected to *jāwazahu* (crossed it), not to *āmanū* (believed). It is also permitted that it is the predicate of *alladhīna* (those who), on the basis that the *wāw* is for a circumstantial clause, as if it were said: "when he had crossed it, while those who believed were with him."

﴿قالُوا لا طاقَةَ لَنا اليَوْمَ بِجالُوتَ وجُنُودِهِ﴾ *"They said: We have no power today against Jalut and his troops."* That is, we have no capacity to fight them and resist them, let alone to overcome them. Jalut is like Talut in form. The speakers were some of the believers, speaking to others. This was a manifestation of weakness, not a retreat, when they witnessed from the enemy what they witnessed of numbers and ferocity. It is said there were one hundred thousand fully armed fighters. It is also said three hundred thousand.

﴿قالَ﴾ *"Said"*: as encouragement for that group. This is a resumptive explanatory sentence (*istināf bayānī*). ﴿الَّذِينَ يَظُنُّونَ﴾ *"those who are certain"*, that is, those who are certain (*yataya qanūn*), ﴿أنَّهم مُلاقُو اللَّهِ﴾ *"that they will meet God"*, by resurrection and return to what He has. They are the sincere among them, and the foremost in faith. Describing them with this does not contradict the faith of the rest, since the degrees of believers in this are varied. It is also possible to keep *ẓann* (supposition) in its literal meaning, and then the sense is: they suppose that they will soon be martyred and meet God Most High. It is also said that the relative clause refers to all believers, and the pronoun in *qālū* (they said) refers to those who withdrew from them, as if they said this in excuse for their staying behind, with the river between them. But this is far-fetched, since the apparent meaning is that they spoke this statement at the encounter with the enemy, and those who withdrew were not with them at that time. Moreover, what need is there to offer an excuse for staying behind, when Talut had already stated that those who drank are not of him at all? Had they not withdrawn, they would have been prevented from going with him.

﴿كَمْ مِن فِئَةٍ﴾ *"How many a company"*: that is, a portion of people and a group. It derives either from *fa'atta ra'sahu* (I split his head) if you cut it, or from *fā'a ilayhi* (he returned to it) if he came back. Its original form according to the first is *fiyawah*, so its final radical was dropped, and its pattern is *fi'ah*. Its original form according to the second is *fiy'ah*, so its middle radical was dropped, and its pattern is *fi'ah*... (the word's root and pattern are as given by the commentator). *Kam* here is declarative (*khabariyya*), and its meaning is "many." The *min* is redundant, and *fiʾatin* is a specifier (*tamyīz*). Abu al-Baqa' permitted that *min fiʾatin* be in the nominative position as a qualifier of *kam*, as you say: "I have a hundred from dirhams and dinars." Some permitted that *kam* be interrogative, but this is probably not its real sense. It is reported from al-Radi that *min* does not come after interrogative *kam*, so the view that it is declarative is preferable. ﴿قَلِيلَةٍ﴾ *"few"*: an adjective of *fiʾatin*, agreeing with its wording. ﴿غَلَبَتْ﴾ *"overcame"*: that is, subdued, in the battle. ﴿فِئَةً كَثِيرَةً﴾ *"a numerous company"*: relative to it.

﴿بِإذْنِ اللَّهِ﴾ *"by the permission of God"*: that is, by His command and facilitation. They did not say "it was able to," as occurred in the speech of their companions, out of exaggeration in encouraging them and calming their hearts. When the tanwīn (nunation) in the first *fiʾatin* is taken as diminutive, and in the second *fiʾatan* as magnifying, it is more eloquent for encouragement and more complete for reassurance. Something similar occurs in the verse:

*"He has a chamberlain against every matter that disgraces him,*
*and for the seeker of kindness he has no chamberlain."*

This, as you see, arises from the perfection of their faith in God and the Last Day, and their affirmation that He, glorified be He, is not incapable of bringing the dead to life, just as He is not incapable of causing the living to die, let alone of supporting the weak. There is no doubt that what is in the *ṣilah* (relative clause) has perfect suitability to the ruling given about the relative pronoun, especially since it takes in the permission and command of God. One who does not believe in meeting God Most High will hardly come close to this condition by a hair's breadth. Thereby is refuted what our master, the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, said: that this answer, as you see, arises from the perfection of their trust in the victory and success of God Most High, and that there is no bearing of the belief in meeting God by resurrection, nor of the expectation of His reward, glorified is His rank. There is no doubt that what is mentioned in the *ṣilah* should be the basis of the ruling given about the relative pronoun, or at least a suitable attribute for it. For the suitability, as this poor intellect has produced, has been attained in the most complete and perfect manner, so there is no need to achieve it through what he mentioned afterwards, may God Most High have mercy on him: namely, removing the word from its common apparent meaning, which is used for the Day of meeting Him, and reading the meeting with Him, glorified be He, as the meeting with His help and support, and making the expression with this a hyperbole. For this is far from its use in the whole of the Glorious Book. It is not of the same kind as His saying, Most High: ﴿وَاللَّهُ مَعَ الصّابِرِينَ﴾ *"And God is with those who are patient"*, where what is meant is companionship through support and kindness; for that is customary in the rest of the Qur'an in such contexts, as is not hidden. It is possible that this is from the speech of the foremost believers, brought in to complete the encouragement and to encourage patience, by alluding to what it contains. It is also possible that it is the beginning of speech from God Most High, brought to confirm their statement and as an invocation to the listeners to be like the condition of these people, whom their speech points to.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 250:**

﴿When they came out (bāraza)﴾, i.e., Talut and those with him appeared and found themselves in open ground (barāz), which is the part of the earth that is uncovered and level, ﴿before Jalut and his armies﴾, i.e., to fight and battle them. ﴿They said﴾, all together, after the hearts of the weak had been strengthened, humbly beseeching Allah the Exalted and disclaiming any power or strength of their own:

﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾, i.e., pour that upon us and grant us success in it. What is meant by it is restraining the self for fighting. ﴿And make firm our feet﴾, i.e., grant us complete strength and steadiness at the moment of the clash, such that we do not waver. The intended meaning of making the feet firm is not merely their being fixed in one place, since that would be of little benefit. ﴿And help us against the disbelieving people﴾, i.e., aid us against them by subduing and defeating them. The phrase ﴿the disbelievers﴾ is used in place of the pronoun referring to Jalut and his armies, to indicate the reason for victory over them. In this supplication there is much subtlety, fine style and rhetorical beauty that is not hidden. First, it contains an appeal through the attribute of lordship (rubūbiyya), which indicates bringing [the servant] to perfection. Second, it contains the verb "pour" (ifrāgh), which indicates abundance, and it makes patience like water poured over them, to calm their hearts and to suffice them in place of the water from which they had been prevented. Third, it contains the use of "upon" (ʿalā), which indicates making that like a container and them like things contained. Fourth, it contains the indefinite form of "patience" (ṣabran), which expresses magnitude. Fifth, the second request, which is making the feet firm, supports the idea of making patience like water in the first request, since the places where water is poured are slippery, and so they need firmness there. Sixth, it contains good ordering: they first asked for patience to be poured upon their hearts at the encounter, then for steadfastness of the foot and strength in confronting the enemy, since patience may be found in one who has no capacity to resist, and thirdly the principal aim of fighting, which is victory over the adversary, since courage without victory is a path whose goal is outside benefit. It has been said that they asked first for the pouring of patience because it is the foundation of the matter, second for firmness because it branches from it, and third for victory because it is the ultimate goal. This was objected to on the grounds that it would then require the use of the particle "fa" (then), since it is the one that indicates sequence. It was answered that "wa" (and) is more eloquent, because it relies for sequence on the mind, which is the most just witness, as al-Sakkaki mentioned.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 251:

﴿So they routed them﴾, that is, they broke them and overcame them. The *fa'* here is *fasiha* (the "eloquent" *fa'*, which signals an unstated intermediate step). The meaning is: God answered their supplication, so they were patient, were made firm, and were given victory, and so they routed them ﴿by God's permission﴾, that is, by His will to rout them. It is interpreted as referring to His aid and support. The *ba'* may be for seeking help and causation (*istiʿana* and *sababiyya*), or for accompaniment (*musahaba*). ﴿And Dawud killed Jalut﴾. He is the son of Ayshа. ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: When Talut came out against Jalut, Jalut said: "Send out to me whoever will fight me. If he kills me, then my kingdom is yours, and if I kill him, then your kingdom is mine." Dawud was brought to Talut, and he bargained with him that if he killed him, he would marry him to his daughter and give him authority over his wealth. Talut armed him, but Dawud disliked fighting him with weapons and said: "If God does not grant me victory over him, the weapons will avail nothing." So he went out to him with a sling and a pouch containing stones. Then he came forward, and Jalut said to him: "Are you fighting me?" Dawud said: "Yes." He said: "Woe to you! You have come out only as one comes out to a dog with a sling and stones. I will tear your flesh apart and feed it today to the birds and beasts of prey." Dawud said to him: "Rather, you are the enemy of God, worse than a dog." Dawud took a stone and slung it, and it struck him between his eyes until it lodged in his brain. Jalut cried out, those with him fled, and he was beheaded. ﴿And God gave him the kingdom﴾ among the Children of Israel after he killed Jalut and Talut died. This happened because Talut, as is related in some reports, when he returned, fulfilled the condition: he married Dawud to his daughter and set his ring over his kingdom. The people inclined toward Dawud and loved him. When Talut saw this, he was envious and resentful, and he intended to kill him. Dawud learned of this, so he laid a skin of wine on his bed. Talut entered Dawud's sleeping place while Dawud had fled, and he struck the skin a blow and split it, and the wine poured out. He said: "May God have mercy on Dawud; how much wine he drank!" Then Dawud came to him the next night in his house while he was asleep, and he placed two arrows at his head and at his feet, and two arrows on his right and on his left. When Talut awoke, he saw the arrows and recognized them, and he said: "May God have mercy on Dawud. He is better than I am. I had the upper hand over him and killed him, but when he had the upper hand over me he spared me." Then one day he rode out and found him walking in the desert, while Talut was on a horse. He said: "Today I will kill Dawud." Dawud, whenever he was frightened, could not be caught. Talut galloped after him, and Dawud was frightened and ran until he entered a cave. God inspired the spider, and it spun a web over the entrance. When Talut reached the cave and saw the spider's construction, he said: "Had he entered here, he would have torn the spider's web," and he turned back. The scholars and the devout began to reproach him for what he had done to Dawud. He began killing the scholars and everyone who forbade him from killing Dawud, until he had killed many people. Then afterwards he regretted it and gave up the kingdom. He had ten sons; he took them and went out fighting in the way of God, as expiation for what he had done, until he and his sons were killed in the way of God. The Children of Israel then gathered around Dawud and made him their ruler. This is the granting of the kingdom. ﴿And the wisdom﴾: what is meant by it is prophethood. Kingship and prophethood had not been combined in anyone before him, rather prophethood was in one tribe and kingship in another. This was after the death of that prophet, and his death had been before Talut. The mention of wisdom after kingship is either because it came after it in time, or it is for ascending from the lower to the higher mention. ﴿And He taught him of what He willed﴾, such as the craft of making coats of mail, the speech of birds, and the language of animals. The hidden pronoun refers to God. Its reference to Dawud, as al-Samin said, is weak, because most of what God taught him is something that scarcely occurs to the mind or enters the imagination of a human, so that he might be able to seek it and to will it. ﴿And had God not repelled some people by means of others﴾, who are the people of corruption in this world or in religion, or in both together, ﴿by means of others﴾ of them, who restrain them from what they are doing by means of killing as ordained by God, as in the story related here, or otherwise.
[Page 174]
Nafi' read here and in al-Hajj: *difa'* (with the form of contention, *mughalaba*), so that the form of intensity is for emphasis. ﴿The earth would have been corrupted﴾, and its benefits would have ceased, and its interests would have been disrupted, from cultivation and reproduction and everything else that sets the earth right and makes it flourish. It has also been said that this is a metaphor for the corruption of its inhabitants and the prevalence of evil among them. In this there is an indication of the excellence of kingship, and that without it the affairs of the world would not be stable. For this reason it has been said: religion and kingship are twins; when one is lifted, the other is lifted with it, because religion is the foundation and kingship is the guardian, and whatever has no foundation is destroyed, and whatever has no guardian is lost.

﴿But God is full of bounty﴾, whose extent cannot be measured, ﴿to the worlds﴾ in their entirety. This is an indication of an *istithnai* syllogism (a conditional syllogism in which the antecedent is negated), composed by positing the negation of the antecedent, which produces the negation of the consequent. Except that what is placed in its position is something that follows from it and requires it, namely His being full of bounty to the worlds, as an announcement that He bestows this grace in that repelling without it being obligatory upon Him, and that His bounty is not confined to it, but it is one instance of His great bounty. It is as if it were said: "But He repels the corruption of some by means of others, so the earth is not corrupted, and the interests of the world are ordered by it, and the conditions of nations are set right." This was said by our master, the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, may God sanctify his secret.

It has been objected that this contradicts the statement of the logicians that from a conditional (*muttasila*) proposition, the affirmation of its antecedent produces the affirmation of its consequent, because the existence of the implicans necessitates the existence of the implied; and the negation of its consequent produces the negation of its antecedent, because the non-existence of the implied necessitates the non-existence of the implicans. But it does not convert, so the affirmation of the consequent does not produce the affirmation of the antecedent, nor does the negation of the antecedent produce the negation of the consequent, because it is possible that the consequent is more general than the antecedent, so the existence of the implied does not necessitate the existence of the implicans, nor does the non-existence of the implicans necessitate the non-existence of the implied. It was answered that this holds only with respect to the form (*hay'a*), but it may necessitate it through the specific nature of the matter of equivalence. Ibn Sina has stated explicitly in *al-Fusul* that when the implication is from both sides, as between cause and effect, the affirmation of either the antecedent or the consequent produces the affirmation of the other, and the negation of one produces the negation of the other. The reasoning of the people also contains an indication of this, where they said that it is possible for the implied to be more general. It seems that the words of our master also indicate that the implication in a conditional runs from both sides, since he said "produces" (*muntij*) and did not say "it produces" (*yuntiju*).

Some have answered that their statement is not a universal rule. Rather, when the negation of the antecedent is more general than the negation of the consequent, then [it does not produce]. But when its negation is the reverse of this, as in this noble verse and similar ones, then it produces the consequent. This is because the mentioned repelling, since it necessitates the non-corruption of the earth, the implication between them is established, because the existence of the implicans necessitates the existence of the implied, as has been explained in its place. The claim that the implication runs from both sides here, as the first answerer supposed, is nothing, but rather the implied here is more general than the implicans, as is not hidden from one who reflects. And that the words of our master indicate that the implication from both sides is in the realm of denial, and what he mentioned does not indicate that, as is not hidden. So understand and reflect, for the view of our master is subtle.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 252:

﴿These are the signs of Allah﴾ refers to what preceded of the account of the thousands and their death and revival, the granting of kingship to Talut (Saul), his manifestation through a sign, and the destruction of the tyrants at the hand of a youth, along with the distance (of the demonstrative) indicating the exalted rank of what is pointed to. It has also been said that it refers to what passed from the beginning of the surah up to here, but this is weak. The sentence, under both interpretations, is resumptive (mustanaf'ah). His statement, exalted is He, ﴿We recite them to you﴾, means: through the agency of Jibril (Gabriel), peace be upon him. It is either a circumstantial clause (hal) from "the signs," with the governing element being the sense of the demonstrative, or a resumptive sentence with no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis). ﴿With truth﴾ is in the accusative position, as a circumstantial clause from the object of "natluha" (We recite them). That is: enveloped in the certainty about which none of the People of the Book or the authors of histories has any doubt, since they find it in agreement with what they possess; or it should not be doubted. Or it is from its subject: that is, We recite them to you as those clothed in truth and rightness, and He is with us. Or it is from the pronoun in the genitive: that is, clothed with truth, and He is with you.
Page 175
﴿And indeed you are among the messengers﴾, in that you report those signs and the stories of past generations and their reports as they truly were, without having studied any book and without meeting anyone who informs you of that. The connection of this story to what precedes it is evident. When Allah commanded the believers to fight in His way, and He had previously mentioned the story of those who left their homes fearing death, whether by plague or by battle, in order to encourage and strengthen the believers and to inform them that caution does not save from decree, He followed this with the fact that fighting had been required and legislated in earlier nations. Therefore it is not among the rulings特 specific to you; for what is shared is more readily accepted by the soul than an obligation that is borne alone.

* * *

Here, among the allusions (ishara) in these verses: (﴿Have you not considered﴾) the assembly of the faculties (malaʾ al-quwa) (﴿of the Children of Israel﴾) the body (﴿after Musa﴾) the heart (﴿when they said to a prophet﴾) their intellects: (﴿Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah﴾) and the path of reaching Him through His command and guidance (﴿He said: Is it likely that if fighting is prescribed for you, you will not fight?﴾) That is: I expect from you that you will not fight, because you are immersed in the conditions of nature (﴿They said: And why should we not fight in the way of Allah﴾) on the path of journeying to Allah, exalted is He, (﴿while we have been expelled﴾) from the homelands of our original preparedness, which we have not ceased to long for, and we have become estranged from the sons of our perfections, over whom we have not ceased to weep excessively (﴿So when fighting was prescribed for them﴾) against their enemy who caused their estrangement and brought upon them the marvelous wonder; (﴿they turned away﴾) and turned from fighting him, and joined the ranks of his partisans, (﴿except a few of them﴾) namely the preparing faculties (﴿And Allah is All-Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾) who diminished their own portions. (﴿And their prophet said to them: Indeed Allah has sent Talut to you﴾) the human spirit (﴿as king﴾) crowned with the crown of divine lights, seated upon the throne of eternal governances; (﴿They said﴾) because they were veiled by the veil of selfhood and heedless of the true sciences: How can he have kingship over us when his rank is low, having descended to the world of density from his original world, and there is no resemblance to us in him? (﴿while we have more right to kingship than he﴾), because we share in our world and resemble one another, and the likeness of a thing inclines toward it and is quick to follow it.

And every thing has a blight of its own kind.

(﴿And he has not been given abundance﴾) of the wealth of disposal, since one disposes only through an intermediary? He said: Indeed Allah has chosen him over you, because of his simplicity and your composition, and has increased him in breadth of divine knowledge and strength in the luminous essence. (﴿And Allah gives His kingship to whom He wills﴾), so He governs it by His permission. (﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾) by the breadth of absoluteness, (﴿All-Knowing﴾) of the wisdoms that require manifestation and self-disclosure through the loci of the names. (﴿And their prophet said to them: Indeed the sign of His kingship﴾) over you and His vicegerency from the Lord among you (﴿is that there comes to you﴾) the ark of the breast, (﴿in it is tranquility﴾) that is, serenity (﴿from your Lord﴾), which is serenity through faith and intimacy with Allah, exalted is He, (﴿and a remnant of what the family of Musa left﴾) the heart, (﴿and the family of Harun﴾) the inner secret, and it is from monotheism, and the staff of "there is no god but Allah," which swallows the great magic of the attributes of the self, and the basin of the manifestation of lights, in which the hearts of the prophets are washed, and a portion of the Torah of inspirations, carried by the angels of preparedness to Talut the spirit. At that moment the vicegerency is delivered to him, and all the tribes of human attributes submit to him. (﴿So when Talut departed with his soldiers﴾) from the minister of the intellect, the adviser of the heart, the manager of understandings, and the order of the senses; (﴿he said: Indeed Allah is going to test you with a river﴾) of physical nature, filled with the waters of desires, (﴿so whoever drinks from it﴾) and gulps it down, excessive in quenching thirst, then he is not of my followers who belong to the world of spirituality and the people of the unveilings of the attributes. (﴿And whoever does not taste it﴾) and does not drink from it, then he is among the dwellers of the enclosures of holiness and the attendants of the display of the brides of the dais of intimacy. (﴿except one who takes a handful with his hand﴾) and is content with it to the measure of necessity, out of need and without greed or immersion (﴿and they drank from it﴾) and gulped it down and became immersed in it (﴿except a few of them﴾), namely those who are pure of natural filth, sanctified from its garments, stripped of its coverings, and few indeed they are. Then when Talut the spirit crossed the river of nature and passed over it (﴿he and those who believed﴾) from the heart, the intellect, the kingship, and others, following the spirit with him, (﴿some of them said, namely the weak who had not reached the station of establishment﴾): (﴿We have no strength today﴾) against Jalut (Goliath) of the self and his helpers, because of their experience in deceptions and intrigues. (﴿But those who﴾) are certain (﴿that they will meet Allah﴾) by returning to Him (﴿said: How many a small company has overcome a large company﴾) and subdued it, until it removed its multitude (﴿by the permission of Allah﴾) and facilitation, (﴿and Allah is with the patient﴾) through His special manifestation to them. (Then when they went out) to fight Jalut and his soldiers, they disclaimed all power and strength and said: (﴿Our Lord, pour upon us patience﴾) and steadfastness, (﴿and make firm our feet﴾) in the battlefields of struggle, so that we do not retreat afterward, (﴿and help us against﴾) our enemies who concealed the truth, namely the commanding self and its attributes, (﴿so they defeated them﴾) and broke them (﴿by the permission of Allah. And Dawud﴾) the heart (﴿killed Jalut﴾) the self, and they all reached the station of establishment, so they fear no return or apostasy. He had struck him with the stone of submission, in the sling of contentment, by the hand of abandoning attention to other than Him, and it struck the brain of his desire, so he fell prostrate. Then Allah, exalted is He, gave Dawud the kingship of vicegerency and the wisdom of inspirations, (﴿and taught him of what He willed﴾) the craft of making coats of mail for wars, the speech of the birds of arrivals, and the glorification of the mountains of bodies. (﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others﴾) such as the seekers (﴿by means of others﴾) such as the accomplished shaykhs who have arrived, (﴿the earth would have been corrupted﴾) the land of their preparednesses, created in the best of stature, when Jalut the self gained dominance. (﴿But Allah is full of bounty toward the worlds﴾), and of His bounty is the setting in motion of the chain of the seeking of the seekers, the inspiring in their secrets the will for the perfect shaykhs, and the granting them success to hold fast to the hem of their training and cling to the fringes of their way. Glory be to Him, the Generous who does not withhold, and the Bestower upon those who ask and those who do not ask.

[Page 2]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Those messengers﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) that implies ascent in rank, as if it were said: "You are indeed among the messengers, and among the most excellent of them in merit." The demonstrative refers to the group of messengers, among whom is the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The sense of distance in it, as has been said, is to signal the high level of their rank and the remoteness of their station. The lam is for comprehensiveness (istighraq). It may also be for the group known to him (ﷺ), or for those whose stories are mentioned in the surah, in which case the lam is for reference (al-'ahd). The choice of the broken plural (jam' al-taksir) is due to its closeness to the sound plural (jam' al-taslim).

﴿We preferred some of them over others﴾ by singling out some of them with a distinction that is not held by the others. It has been said that what is meant is preference by the sacred laws (shara'i'), so some of them legislated and some did not legislate. It has been said that it is preference by degrees in the Hereafter. Each of these views has its difficulties. The first is supported by His words: ﴿Among them are those to whom God spoke﴾, for this is a detailing of the preference mentioned in general terms. The clause has no place in terms of i'rab (grammatical position). It has been said that it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿We preferred﴾. The relative pronoun refers either to Moses (peace be upon him), in which case the definiteness is referential ('ahdi), or to everyone to whom God spoke directly and with approval. These are Adam, as established in the sound hadiths; Moses, who is famous for this; and our Prophet (ﷺ), who is singled out with the station of "two bow-lengths" (qab qawsayn) and who attained the brides of address (ʿarāʾis al-khiṭāb), which address had only alluded to.

The verb is read as ﴿kallama Allāha﴾ with the accusative (naṣb), so that God is the object. Al-Yamani read ﴿kālama Allāhu﴾, from mukalama (conversation). It has been said that the use of the august Name through the shift of grammatical person (iltifat) serves to cultivate awe and signals the difference between speaking and raising, and between the general preference mentioned earlier and the bestowal of clear signs and support with the Holy Spirit that follows.

﴿And He raised some of them in degrees﴾: that is, among them is one whom God raised above the other messengers by widely separated ranks and in many respects. The change of style serves to instruct about the differences in their states in degrees of nobility. The word "some" here refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), as indicated by the announcement that he is among them, for he has been singled out with excellences at which wishes stand back weary. He was distinguished by special qualities of knowledge and practice that the tongue of time cannot enumerate. He ascended the banners of excellence, which were raised over his shoulders, and the crests of the battlements of nobility lowered their heads to him, so they kissed his feet. He is the one sent as a mercy to the worlds, the one described with a great character among the messengers, and the one upon whom was revealed the glorious Qur'an: ﴿No falsehood comes to it from before it or behind it; a revelation from One Wise, Praiseworthy﴾. He is the one whose religion was confirmed and made everlasting by manifest and enduring miracles, and who attained the praised station and the great intercession in the Hereafter. The vagueness (ibham) is for magnifying his status and to signal that he is the unique individual who needs no specification.

It has been said that the meaning is Abraham, since God singled him out with the station of intimacy (khullah), which is the highest of the ranks. What this entails is not hidden. It has been said that it is Idris, based on God's words: ﴿And We raised him to a lofty place﴾. It has been said that it is the Ulu al-'Azm among the messengers. Regarding this, as in al-Kashshaf, it does not at all suit the taste of the context in which the discussion stands. The same is my view concerning the preceding view, since the elevation over him is literal, while the context requires metaphor, as is not hidden.

[Page 3]

"Darajat" has been said to be a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from "ba'dahum," in the sense of "possessing degrees." It has been said that it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar), since "daraja" means "rif'a" (elevation), so it is as if it said: "and We raised some of them with elevations." It has been said that the implied preposition is "ʿalā," "ilā," or "fī" ("over," "to," or "in" degrees), and when the preposition was dropped the verb connected to its object directly. It has been said that it is a second object of "rafaʿa," taken as implying "balagha" (reached). It has been said that it is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal), but this is not correct.

﴿And We gave Jesus son of Mary the clear signs﴾: that is, the manifest signs and clear miracles, such as healing the blind and the leper, reviving the dead, and informing them of what they eat and store. Or it means the Gospel, or everything that indicates his prophethood. Mentioning these in the context of preference is an indication that they were the cause of it. This entails the superiority of our Prophet (ﷺ) over all the prophets, since he holds the first and foremost share of that, as in the drawing of arrows.

﴿And We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾: its explanation has already been given. The singling out of him (peace be upon him) with what has been mentioned is to refute what the people of the two Scriptures said about him, with excess and deficiency. The verse indicates that the prophets differ in rank, so it is permissible to prefer some of them over others, but this must be by definitive evidence, since conjecture in matters of belief does not avail against the truth at all.

﴿Had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another﴾: that is, those who came after each messenger, as the meaning requires, not after all the messengers as the apparent wording suggests, from the differing nations. That is, had God willed their not fighting, they would not have fought, by making them agreed upon the truth and on following the messengers who brought it. The object of the will is omitted because it is implied by the consequent of the conditional, according to the known rule. Whoever estimated, "Had God willed, He would have guided all people, and they would not have fought," and departed from what the rule requires, supposing that this non-occurrence needs no will and decree but suffices with the non-attachment of will to existence, has not achieved anything.

﴿After the clear signs had come to them﴾ from those messengers.
