It has been said that the pronoun refers to those before them, namely the messengers, and the prepositional phrase is connected to "fought." It has been said that it is a substitute for its counterpart mentioned before. ﴿The clear signs﴾: the manifest miracles and evident signs indicating the truth of what is true, which obligate following and restrain from turning away, which leads to fighting.

﴿But they differed﴾: this is a corrective (istidrak) to the conditional. By it is indicated an exceptive syllogism (istithnai) composed of positing the negation of its antecedent, which yields the negation of its consequent. However, "differed" has been placed where the negation of the antecedent would have stood, to indicate that the fighting arose from them and from their poor choice, not from Him directly at the outset. It is as if it were said: "But He did not will their not fighting, because they differed with a gross difference."

﴿So among them are those who believed﴾: that is, in what those messengers brought, and who remained steadfast in their faith and acted in accordance with it. This is an explanation of the differing, so the clause has no place in terms of i'rab. ﴿And among them are those who disbelieved﴾ with a disbelief from which they did not refrain. Wisdom therefore required that He not will their not fighting, so they fought in accordance with what their states required.

﴿Had God willed﴾ their not fighting after this stage of differing, which usually entails fighting, ﴿they would not have fought﴾ and would not have lifted the head of arrogance and hostility, since all things are in the hand of His dominion. So the repetition is not for emphasis, as some have thought, but to alert that their differing does not necessitate His not willing their not fighting, as might be understood from its placement in the corrective clause. Rather He, glory be to Him, is free in this: even if He willed, after that, their not fighting, they would not have fought. This is what the corrective clause expresses in His words: ﴿But God does what He wills﴾ [253], as He wills, without any obligation upon Him from anyone or any preventer restraining Him.

This was established by Mawla Abu al-Su'ud, may his secret be sanctified, and it is of excellent standing. However, 'Allama 'Abd al-Baqi al-Baghdadi objected to it in his tafsir, with something similar to what preceded regarding this same syllogism, and he mentioned that it is contrary to the usage of (law, "lau") among the grammarians and the specialists in reasoning.

[Page 4]

The answer to this is probably the answer to that, with slight modification, so do not be heedless. What he mentioned concerning the justification for the repetition is something unique to him, as far as I know. Most scholars hold that it is for emphasis. However, behind it there is a secret which was singled out, as mentioned by the author of al-Intisaf, namely: whenever the Arabs build the beginning of their speech upon one purpose, then another purpose intervenes, and they wish to return to the first, they intend to mention it either with that same expression or with something close to it. This is among them a well-known path of eloquence and an accepted method. In the Book of God there are instances of this, among them His words: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief, except one who is compelled while his heart is at rest with faith, but whoever opens his breast to disbelief...﴾. This verse is of this pattern: since the speech began by saying that their fighting was in accordance with the will, then the speech lengthened, and it was desired to explain that God's will, as it prevailed in this particular matter, namely the fighting of these people, also prevails in every event that occurs. This is what is expressed in His words: ﴿But God does what He wills﴾. The mention of the attachment of the will to the fighting arose because of its nearness to the general attachment of the will, so that the speech is harmonious and each element is joined to its like. This is a secret whose explanation opens the breast and gladdens the heart. It may be better than saying that the first (attachment) is without intermediary and the second is through the mediation of the believers, or vice versa.

In the verse there is evidence that events follow the will of God, whether they are good or evil, faith or disbelief.

[Page 5]

It has been said: he meant by it obligatory spending, such as zakah, and not voluntary spending, because the command is literally for obligation (wujub), and because a threat is attached to it. This is what is related from al-Hasan. It has also been said: it includes both obligatory and voluntary spending. This is what is related from Ibn Jurayj, and al-Balkhi chose it. He took the command to mean general request, and what follows is nothing but an informing about the terrors and hardships of the Day of Resurrection, as an encouragement to spend. There is no threat in it for abandoning it, so that obligation would be fixed. Al-Asamm said: what is meant is spending in jihad. The evidence for this is that it is mentioned after the command to jihad in meaning. By this the verse is connected to what precedes it. But it is not hidden that this evidence is not something that should be listened to, because the connection, on the assumption of generality, is also achieved by the entry of the spending mentioned into it as a first entry. Likewise on the assumption that obligatory spending is meant, because spending in jihad may be obligatory when the obligation depends on it. The word "ma" (what) is a relative pronoun whose returning pronoun has been omitted. The mention of its coming from Him, exalted is He, is for urging spending and encouraging it.

﴿Before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor friendship﴾, that is, no affection and no companionship, ﴿nor intercession﴾, that is, for anyone, except after the Most Merciful has given permission to whom He wills and is pleased with. He meant by this the Day of Resurrection. The purpose of describing it with what was mentioned is to indicate that no one has any power on that Day to obtain anything by which he may benefit in any way. This is because whoever has a debt upon him, for example, either takes by sale what he can pay with, or his friends help him, or he seeks refuge with one who will intercede for him to have it reduced, and all of these are negated. No help is sought except from Allah, mighty and majestic. The word "min" (from) is connected to what its sister particle is connected to, and there is no harm in the difference of their meanings, since the first is partitive and this one is for the beginning of the limit. The three negated nouns were given the nominative ending, although the context requires generality, and what suits it is the fatha ending. This is because the statement, on the assumption of the question "is there trade in it, or friendship, or intercession," and "trade" and its two companions are in the nominative there, so it was appropriate to give them the nominative in the answer, although generality is achieved in general, even if it is not equal to the generality achieved on the assumption of the fatha. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with fatha, following the original form in mentioning what is explicit in generality. So they say. But perhaps the more likely view is that the nominative is because generality is weak in most of them, namely friendship and intercession, due to the exception occurring in some verses, and the defeated follows the ruling of the dominant. As for what they said, it is refuted by the fact that what follows "day" is a clause that comes after an indefinite noun, so it is a non-detached qualifier, and it is not to be estimated that there is a separation between the qualifier and the qualified when there is no cutting off by a question, cutting off decisively. And considering that the indefinite noun is qualified by what the tanwin conveys of magnification, so that the clause is estimated as a detached qualifier in order to realize that and affirm it, then the estimation of the question at that point becomes something that a sound mind can hardly accept.

﴿And the disbelievers, they are the wrongdoers﴾ [254]. That is, they deserve to be described with this description because of the extremity of their wrongdoing. The sentence is coordinated with an omitted element, that is: so the believers who fear Allah are fulfillers, and the disbelievers, etc. What is meant by them are those who entirely abandon spending. He expressed the one who abandons it as a disbeliever in severe censure, since he made his act, which is abandoning spending, like disbelief, or considered him to be on the verge of it, or expressed the necessary by the thing it necessitates. So it is either a subsequent metaphor (isti'ara tab'iyya), or a metaphor of approaching (majaz mushara'a), or a sent metaphor (majaz mursal), or a metonymy (kinaya). Similar to this is the placing of "whoever disbelieves" (man kafara) in the place of "whoever does not perform Hajj" at the end of the verse about Hajj. Some did not use the word disbelief figuratively and said: it is an expression for disbelief in Allah, exalted is He, in its literal sense. The benefit of the informing in that case is to indicate that the negation of those things applies to them, and that this is not counted by Us as wronging them, because they are the wrongdoers against themselves, the ones who bring that upon themselves.

[Page 6]

﴿Allah, there is no god but Him.﴾ It is a subject (*mubtada'*, the inchoative subject of a nominal sentence) and a predicate (*khabar*), and what is meant is that He alone deserves worship, and no other. It is said that scholars differ over the case of the detached pronoun, and likewise over the Noble Name when it takes its place, in five views. Two of them are considered valid, and three are not relied upon. The two valid views are: first, that it is in the nominative as a substitute (*badal*); second, that it is in the nominative as a predicate. The first is the one commonly adopted by grammarians, and it is the view of Ibn Malik. On this view, it is either to be assumed that something is understood for the second term or not. Those who hold that something is to be supplied have differed. Some supply a general matter, such as existence or possibility, while others supply a specific matter, such as "for us" or "for creation."

The supplying of a general matter is objected to on the ground that it entails one of two undesirable results: either the existence of Allah, exalted is His majesty, is not affirmed in actuality, or His glorified self is not declared free from the possibility of having a partner. Likewise, the supplying of a specific matter is objected to on the ground that there is no evidence for it, or that it is obscure. The objection can be answered by choosing to supply it as a general matter, with no undesirable consequence. As for the supposition of existence, the negation of existence entails the negation of possibility, for if another being were characterized by necessary existence, it would necessarily be found. Since it is not found, it is known that it is not characterized by that. And what is not characterized by necessary existence cannot be characterized by it, because of the impossibility of a reversal. As for the supposition of possibility, we say that it has become clear that the possibility of a thing being characterized by necessary existence necessarily entails its actually being so characterized. So when its possibility is established, its existence is established as well, for whenever it is not found, it is impossible that it be a necessarily existent being. Moreover, more than one scholar has stated that the negation of the existence of any god other than Him, exalted is He, may be a level of monotheism (*tawhid*) by which Islam is established, and which is sufficient for most of the common people, even if they do not know the negation of its possibility, especially with heedlessness and lack of awareness of it. So the failure of the phrase to indicate it does no harm. Indeed, some have said: the affirmative negation came while the deities other than Allah, exalted is He, still existed, and their worship had been firmly established, and the polytheists were devoted to them in all regions. So people were commanded to negate their existence insofar as they are true deities. And had there been, at that time, people who said that a true god other than Him, exalted is He, was possible but did not actually exist at all, they would have been commanded to negate that possibility. But it is not hidden that this is not of great strength. The objection can be answered by choosing to supply it as a specific matter, namely that this specific one deserves worship, and the context is a clear indication of it. It has been objected that it does not indicate the negation of plurality, neither in possibility nor in actuality, since there may exist a god other than Him, glorified is He, who does not deserve worship. And it has been objected that one may say: what is meant is either the negation of another being, other than Him, exalted is He, that deserves worship in actuality, or the negation of possibility. The first does not negate possibility, and the second does not indicate that He, exalted is He, deserves worship in actuality. It is answered that it is known that necessary existence is the source of all perfections, so there is no doubt that it entails deserving reverence and veneration, and there is no meaning to deserving worship other than this. So if no other than He, exalted is He, deserves worship, then no other than He, exalted is He, exists, for otherwise it would certainly deserve worship. And if it does not exist, it is not possible either, as has been indicated. Thus it is established that the negation of deserving entails the negation of plurality absolutely.

[Page 6, continued]

As for those who hold that the predicate should not be supplied, most of them hold that this *la* (there is no) has no predicate. It is objected that this entails the negation of the judgment and the contract, which is certainly false, since monotheism necessarily requires that judgment. It is answered that the view that no predicate is needed does not remove the compound of *la* and its noun from the contract, because its meaning is that this genus is negated apart from this individual, and otherwise, according to these scholars, it is in the sense of something not following the position of the noun of *la*, and the case-ending is manifest in what follows it. There is no room for making it an exception, for if it were, the statement would not convey monotheism, because its sum would then be that this genus, if this individual is not included in it, is negated. So it is understood from it that what is not excluded from it is not negated, and that is far from monotheism, as is not hidden.

The substitution is objected to from two directions. The first: it is a partial substitute, and there is no pronoun referring back to what is substituted, which is a condition for it. The second: there is a contradiction between them, for the substitute is affirmative while the thing substituted is negative. It is answered regarding the first: that *illa* (except) suffices in place of the pronoun, because it conveys partiality. And regarding the second: that it is a substitute for the first in the governing of the governor, and their difference in affirmation and negation does not prevent substitution. Moreover, if it were said that the substitute in an exception is separate, it would not be far-fetched.

The second of the two valid views, which is the view of the predicate after *illa*, was held by a group, and it has been deemed weak on the ground that it entails that *la* governs definite nouns, which it does not, and that its noun is general while what follows *illa* is specific, so how can it be a predicate? And they have said: the impossibility of "the animal being a human." It is answered regarding the first: that *la* has no governing effect on the predicate according to the view of Sibawayh, and that when it is introduced, the predicate is in the nominative by what was in the nominative before, so it does not entail that it governs a definite noun. And this is as you see. Regarding the second: we do not grant that in the construction a specific thing is predicated of a general thing, since generality is negated and the statement is directed to the generality, and specification by one of the individuals covered by the general term is what is meant. And in this there is what there is.

As for the three views that are not relied upon, the first of them: that *illa* is not a particle of exception, but is in the sense of "other than," and it, together with its noun, the Exalted Name, is a qualifier and not the noun of *la* in terms of its position. The supposition is: there is no god other than Allah, exalted is His majesty, in existence. The second of them: it has been attributed to al-Zamakhshari that *la ilaha* is in the position of the predicate, while *illa* and what follows it are in the position of the subject, and the original is: "Or is Allah a god?" So when the restriction of the attribute to the subject was intended, the predicate was placed first and the subject was joined with *illa*, for what is restricted is the one that comes after *illa*, and what is restricted is the term occurring in the context of negation. And when a subject is joined with *illa*, the predicate must precede it, as has been established in its proper place. The third of them: that what follows *illa* is in the nominative by *ilah* (god), as is the case with a subject when it is a descriptive, because *ilah* means "one who is worshipped," so it stands in place of the agent and takes the place of the predicate, as in "the one struck, the building" (*ma madrubu al-'umran*). The first of these is objected to on the ground that it contains a flaw in meaning, because what is intended from the phrase are two matters: the negation of divinity from other than Him, exalted is He, and its affirmation for Him, glorified is He. This can only be complete if *illa* in it is for exception, since then negation and affirmation are understood by the explicit meaning. But if it is in the sense of "other than," the statement conveys by its explicit meaning only the negation of divinity from other than Him, exalted is He. As for its affirmation for Him, exalted is His name, it is not understood from the construction, and its being understood from the implied meaning (*mafhum*) is hardly acceptable. For if it is an implied meaning of a title (*laqab*), it carries no weight even according to those who hold to implied meaning, since none holds it except al-Daqqaq and some of the Hanbalis. And if it is an implied meaning of a qualifier (*sifah*), it is clear that it is not agreed upon. The second is objected to on the ground that, despite what it contains of artificiality, it entails that the predicate is indeclinable with *la*, whereas only the subject is indeclinable with it. Moreover, if the matter were as stated, there would be no reason for the accusative of the noun that comes after *illa* in this kind of construction, and a group has permitted that. The third is objected to on the ground that we do not grant that *ilah* is a qualifier, for otherwise it would have to be declined and carry tanwin, and no one holds that.

Now, if Allah, exalted is He, wills, I shall return again and again to what is in this good word of speech.

In the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿the Ever-Living (al-Hayy)﴾, there are seven aspects of grammatical parsing (i'rab). The first: that it is a second predicate for the Name of Majesty. The second: that it is a predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "He is the Ever-Living." The third: that it is a substitute for His saying, glorified is He: ﴿there is no god but He﴾. The fourth: that it is a substitute for "He" alone. The fifth: that it is a subject whose predicate is ﴿neither slumber nor sleep seizes Him﴾. The sixth: that it is a substitute for "Allah." The seventh: that it is a qualifier of Him, and the recitation with the accusative in praise supports it, since it is specific to the description.

As for its root, there are two views. The first: that its root is *hayyiy*, with two yā's, from *hayya*, *yahayy*. The second: that it is *hayiwa*, so the final waw preceded by a kasra was changed into a yā', and for this reason they wrote *al-hayah* (life) with a waw in the orthography of the Mushaf, as a reminder of this root. And *al-hayawan* (animal) supports it, because this root is evident in it. As for its pattern, it has been said: *fa'il*, and it has been said: *fay'il*, which was lightened, like *mayt* for *mayyit*.

Life, according to the natural philosophers (*tabi'iyyun*), is the power that follows the specific equilibrium (of the body), from which all the animal powers emanate; or it is the power of nutrition; or it is the power of sensation; or a power that requires sensation and movement. All of these are things whose attribution to Allah, exalted is He, is impossible, because they are attributes of corporeal things. So, in His case, glorified is He, it is an existent, real attribute, subsisting in His essence, whose true nature no one can grasp and whose reality is not known, like the rest of His attributes, exalted is His majesty. It is additional to the sum of knowledge and power, and it is not truly the essence itself, nor is it established as existent or non-existent, as has been said of each. So the Ever-Living is an essence in which that attribute subsists. And some of the theologians (*mutakallimun*, practitioners of *kalam*, scholastic theology) defined it as: "He who is such that he can know and can be powerful." Al-Imam objected to this, saying: this measure is found in all animals, so how is it fitting for Allah, exalted is He, to praise Himself with an attribute that the most base of animals shares with Him? Then he said: "What I hold in this matter is that *al-Hayy* in the original language is not an expression for this soundness itself; rather, everything that is complete in its kind is called living. Do you not see that the cultivation of a ruined land is called the reviving of the dead? And the attribute called life in the terminology of the theologians was named so because it is the perfection of the body that it be described by that attribute. Therefore that attribute was called life. And the perfection of the state of trees is that they be leafy and green, so this state was called life. So the original meaning of *al-Hayy* is that He is characterized by His most perfect states and attributes. And when this is so, the problem is resolved, because what is understood from *al-Hayy* is the complete, and since that is not restricted, it indicates that He is complete absolutely. And the complete in this sense is one who is not susceptible to non-existence, neither in His essence, nor in His real attributes, nor in His negative and relational attributes." End.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 255 (part 2 of 4):

It is not hidden that this is a smooth palace built of glass. First: the statement that al-Hayy means "the one who can know and have power," which is something shared by all animals, is in the utmost degeneracy, so it is not fitting for God Most High to praise Himself with it. For if one means sharing in the application of the word, then al-Hayy alone is not like that; rather al-Sami' (the All-Hearing) and al-Basir (the All-Seeing) are likewise applied in the same way to the lowest of animals, and God Most High has praised Himself with both, and the People of the Sunna did not find this problematic. And if one means sharing in the reality, then God Most High forbid that, for sharing in reality is impossible between dust and the Lord of lords, and between the Eternal and the perishable. And whenever you say that sharing in the application of the word necessitates sharing in reality, and there is no escape from it except by interpreting it as a metaphor, then you are bound to the same in all the other attributes, and no one among the People of the Sunna holds this. Second: that life in the language means perfection has not been established in any of the books of language at all; what is established in them is something other than that, and the description of inanimate things with it is only in the manner of metaphor, not reality, as he supposed. If he says that it is a metaphor for God Most High also in that sense, the problem returns through the sharing in perfection with inanimate things, let alone animals. If he says: the perfection of everything is relative to what befits it, we say: the life of every living thing is real relative to what befits it, and "there is nothing like unto Him" (Qur'an 42:11). I see you understand from my words an inclination toward the school of the Salaf in such places, so let that be the understanding of the people, all of them.

"How delightful is Hind, and the land in which is Hind."

Al-Zamakhshari explained al-Hayy as "the Remaining One against whom there is no path to death and annihilation," and they considered that an explanation of it in accordance with what is customary in Arabic speech. I find that there is something troubling about it in my heart, and perhaps I am in the position of withholding from it. Indeed, it is narrated from Qatada that it is "the One who does not die," but this is not an explicit text for the claim.

﴿al-Qayyum﴾ is an intensive form (sigha mubalagha) from al-qiyam (standing/maintaining), and its origin is qayyum on the pattern fay'ul. The waw and the ya' came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed into a ya' and they were assimilated. It cannot be fa'ul, for otherwise it would be qawum, since it is from a waw-root. It may also be qayyam and qayyim, and both were read; the first of them is narrated from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. It was also read as al-qa'im and al-qayyum in the accusative, and its meaning, as Dahhak and Ibn Jubayr said, is "the one whose existence is everlasting." It was also said: the one who stands by His own essence. It was said: the one who stands in managing His creation, through originating them from the beginning and delivering their provisions to them, and this is what is narrated from Qatada. It was said: he is the knower of affairs, from the saying "so-and-so stands by the book," meaning he knows what is in it. Some said: he is the ever-lasting, the one who constantly manages and preserves creation. al-Raghib mentioned that it is said: "qama kadha" means "dama" (it lasted), and "qama bikadha" means "hafizahu" (he preserved it), and al-Qayyum is the one who stands, the preserver of everything and the giver to it of what sustains it. The apparent meaning of it is that qiyam means duration, and then with transitivity it comes to mean causing to endure, which is preservation. It was objected to this that intensiveness is not among the causes of transitivity, so when al-qayyum is stripped of its particle it has the meaning of an intransitive verb, and therefore it is not correct to explain it as "preserver." Moreover, how does intensiveness in preservation convey giving what sustains it? Perhaps this is because independence in preservation is only realized by this, as is not hidden. And it was objected to explaining it as "standing by His own essence" that the meaning of "Qayyum of the heavens and the earth," which occurs in the transmitted supplications, would be "the Necessary Existent of the heavens and the earth," and that, as you see, is not so. So the apparent meaning is that it has another meaning there that is fitting, since that is not correct except through some strained interpretation.

A group held that al-Qayyum is the Greatest Name of God Most High, and these explained it as the one who stands by His own essence and the one who sustains others. They explained standing by essence as necessary existence, which entails all perfections and transcendence above all aspects of deficiency, and they made sustaining others include all the active attributes, so the saying was valid for them. The strangest of the sayings is that it is a Syriac word, meaning in Syriac "the One who does not sleep," but its remoteness is not hidden, because then it would be repeated in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep seizes Him﴾. Drowsiness (al-sina), with its first letter kasra, is a languor that precedes sleep and is not sleep, according to the saying of Adi ibn al-Riqa':
"A man overcome by drowsiness, so drowsiness (sina) settled in his eye, yet he is not asleep."
Sleep is a matter whose conception is self-evident; it befalls the animal from the relaxation of the nerves of the brain due to moisture from rising vapours, to the extent that the outer senses stop perceiving altogether. al-Suyuti claimed in some of his treatises that its cause is the smell of a wind that blows from beneath the Throne, but perhaps he meant the rising of vapours from the stomach beneath the heart, which is the throne of the spirit; otherwise I do not understand it. The placing of drowsiness before sleep, while the analogy of intensiveness would require the reverse out of regard for the existential order, is because drowsiness precedes sleep in reality, so it was placed before it in wording. It was also said that it is in the manner of tatmim (completion), and this is more eloquent because of the emphasis in it, since negating drowsiness entails negating sleep implicitly, so when it is negated a second time it is more eloquent. This was refuted by saying that it is only in the manner of comprehensiveness and enumeration, which requires regard for the existential order and beginning from the lighter to the heavier, as in His saying: ﴿It leaves nothing small or great﴾. For this reason the particle "la" was placed in the middle, to make explicit the comprehensiveness and that the negation includes each of them. It was also said that sleep was delayed for the sake of the verse endings (fawasil). It is not hidden that this stems from narrowness of perspective. Some verifiers said: all of this is only needed if "akhdh" is taken to mean befalling and attack. But if it is taken to mean subduing and overpowering, as al-Raghib and other lexicographers mentioned, and as in His saying: ﴿in the seat of a mighty King, omnipotent﴾ (Qur'an 54:55), then the order is according to the apparent meaning, since the meaning becomes: neither drowsiness nor sleep overcomes Him, and sleep is more overpowering than it.

The sentence is a negation of likeness and an affirmation of God Most High's transcendence that He should have any like among living beings, for these cannot be free of that, so how could they resemble Him? And in it is an emphasis on His being the Living, the Self-Subsisting, because sleep is a defect that contradicts the permanence and continuance of life, and His attributes are eternal without cessation. And because whoever is overtaken by sleep and overpowering does not have necessary existence that is everlasting, nor knowledge that is continuously sustained, nor a strong preservation. Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that "the Children of Israel said: O Musa, does your Lord sleep? He said: Fear Allah. So his Lord called to him: O Musa, they asked you whether your Lord sleeps, so take two glass bottles in your hands and stand in prayer through the night. Musa did so, and when a third of the night had passed he dozed, and fell onto his knees; then he recovered and steadied them. When it was the last part of the night he dozed, and the two bottles fell and broke. He said: O Musa, if I were to sleep, the heavens and the earth would fall and perish as the two bottles perished in your hands." And because of the emphasis in it, like the sentence after it, the conjunction is omitted; it is either a resumptive sentence with no place in terms of i'rab, or an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in al-Qayyum. It is also permitted that it be a predicate of al-Hayy or of the Glorious Name.

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth﴾ is an affirmation of His Exalted Qayyumiyya and an argument for His singularity in divinity. What is meant by "whatever is in them" is what is more general than their parts that enter into them and the matters outside them that are settled within them, among rational beings and others. Thus it is known from the verse that the sun, the moon, the rest of the stars, the angels, the idols, and the tyrants are not gods deserving worship.

﴿Who is it that intercedes with Him except by His permission?﴾ is a rhetorical question of denial, and for this reason "illa" enters. Its purpose is to show the greatness of His exalted station and that no one equals Him or approaches Him, such that anyone could independently repel what He wills in the manner of intercession, humility and submission, let alone independently repel it out of stubbornness, hostility, or enmity. In this is a dispelling of hope for the disbelievers, who claimed that their gods are intercessors for them before God Most High. ﴿He knows what is before them﴾, i.e., the affair of this world, ﴿and what is behind them﴾, i.e., the affair of the Hereafter, as said by Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and others. It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and from Qatada, the reverse of this. It was said: He knows what was before them and what came after them. It was said: what is before them of good or evil and what is behind them of what they did, likewise. It was said: what they perceive and what they do not perceive, or what they sense and comprehend, and all of these are possible. The generality of application here is evident. The plural pronoun returns to what is in "whatever is in the heavens" etc., except that the rational were given precedence over others. It was also said that the rational are implied within it, so there is no precedence. It is also permitted that it refers to what is indicated by "Who is it" among the angels and prophets; and it was said: the prophets specifically. Knowledge of what is before them and what is behind them is a metaphor for the comprehensiveness of His, Glorified is He, knowledge. The sentence is either a resumption, or an informative statement about what came before, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "intercedes" or from the pronoun in "by His permission."

﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾, i.e., of what He knows, like their saying: "O Allah, forgive us Your knowledge of us." To encompass a thing in knowledge is to know it as it truly is. The meaning is that none of these knows the reality of any of the things known to God Most High ﴿except what He wills﴾ to know. It is also permitted that "of His knowledge" means His specific known, which is everything in the unseen. ﴿So He does not reveal His unseen to anyone﴾ ﴿except one whom He has chosen from among the messengers﴾. This sentence is joined to what precedes it because of its difference from it: the former indicates that He, Glorified is He, knows everything, while this indicates that no one else knows it. Together they indicate His singularity in essential knowledge, which is among the fundamental attributes of perfection that the God Most High must be described by in actuality.

﴿His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth﴾. The Kursi is a body before the Throne that encompasses the seven heavens. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: "If the seven heavens and the seven earths were spread out and then joined to one another, they would be, in the vastness of the Kursi, no more than a ring in a desert." The Kursi is other than the Throne, as is shown by what Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Dharr that "he asked the Prophet ﷺ about the Kursi, and he said: 'O Abu Dharr, the seven heavens and the seven earths, compared to the Kursi, are no more than a ring thrown down in a desert land, and the excess of the Throne over the Kursi is like the excess of the desert over that ring.'" And in the narration of al-Daraqutni and al-Khatib from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, he said: "The Prophet ﷺ was asked about His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿His Kursi encompasses﴾ etc., and he said: 'His Kursi is the place of His two feet, and the Throne—its measure cannot be estimated.'" It was also said: it is the Throne itself, and this is attributed to al-Hasan. It was said: it is the power of God Most High. It was said: it is His management. It was said: it is one of His angels. It was said: it is a metaphor for knowledge, by naming a thing after its place, because the Kursi is the place of the world in which knowledge exists, so it is a place for knowledge by way of dependence, since an accident follows its substrate in being located in space; to the extent that they held that this is the meaning of an accident subsisting in a substrate, and this is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It was said: it is a metaphor for sovereignty, taking it from "kursi al-mulk" (the seat of kingship). It was said: the origin of kursi is that on which one sits, and it does not exceed the seat of the one who sits.

The discourse is presented as a figurative expression (*tamthil*) to convey the greatness of His majesty, the vastness of His dominion, and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all things. The verse therefore contains a figurative metaphor (*istiʿarah tamthiliyyah*), and there is no actual chair (*kursi*), sitter (*qaʿid*), or sitting (*quʿud*). This is the view adopted by the great majority of later scholars (*khalaf*), out of fear of falling into the notion of anthropomorphism (*tajsim*). They interpreted the traditions whose apparent meaning is that the Chair carries or encompasses a body in the same way, especially those traditions that mention its being ancient, as we have mentioned earlier. Likewise, they interpreted the tradition narrated by al-Bayhaqi and others from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari: "The Kursi is the place of the two feet, and it has a creaking (*ati*) like the creaking of a saddle." There is also a report from ʿUmar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "It has a creaking like the creaking of a new saddle when a heavy rider mounts it, with four fingers' breadth left over." You know that this and similar reports are not a strong basis for denying the Kursi altogether. The truth is that it exists, as the authentic reports affirm. The fear of anthropomorphism is not to be heeded; otherwise it would necessitate denying many of the attributes, and that is far from following the Lawgiver and submitting to him. Most of the pious predecessors (*salaf al-salih*) classed this among the ambiguous verses (*mutashabih*), whose knowledge no one can fully encompass, and they entrusted its meaning to God, Exalted is He, while affirming the utmost transcendence and sanctity of God.

As for the proponents of manifestations (*al-qa'ilun bil-maza-hir*) among our Sufi masters, may God sanctify their secrets, nothing of such things was problematic for them. Some of the knowers (*ʿarifin*) among them have stated that the Kursi is an expression for the manifestation of all the active attributes (*al-sifat al-fiʿliyyah*). It is thus a divine locus of manifestation (*mazhar ilahi*) and the place where the command, prohibition, bringing into existence, and annihilation take effect, which are expressed by the two feet. It has "encompassed the heavens and the earth" in the extent of My existence (*wus'a wujudi ʿayni*) and the extent of My judgment (*wus'a hukmi*), because their restricted existence is among the effects of the active attributes of which it is the locus of manifestation. The "two feet" in the traditions are not an expression for the two feet of a body or the place of sandals. Exalted is God, glorified be He, far above that by a great exaltation. Nor is the "creaking" (*al-atit*) an expression of what you hear and understand in the visible world. Rather, unless you entrust its knowledge to the All-Knowing, All-Aware, it is an indication of the emergence of opposing things, or their conjunction, in that locus of manifestation, which is the origin of differentiation and ambiguity, the place of bringing into being and annihilation, and the center of harm and benefit, separation and union. The meaning of "with four fingers' breadth left over" is clear if the pronoun refers to the saddle. If it refers to the Kursi, it indicates the existence of presences (*hadarat*) which are manifestations of certain Names that have not appeared in the world of sense perception, and which none can see except one who has been born twice. The four fingers are not what you know of yourself. The knowers have another discourse on this station, and we may point to some of it, God willing, Exalted is He.

Then, it is well known that the *ya'* in *al-kursi* is not a relative ending (*ya' al-nisbah*). Its derivation is from *al-kirs*, meaning gathering, from which comes *al-kurrasah*, for pages that gather knowledge. It has been said that it is as if it were attributed to *al-karas* (with a kasra), meaning felt or matted material. Its plural is *karasi*, like *bukhti* and *bakhati*. It has two dialect forms: the vowel on its *kaf* is dammah, which is the well-known form, and its kasrah is for assimilation (*itba'*). The majority read the *waw* and the *ʿayn* with fatha, and the *sin* with kasra in ﴿*wasiʿa*﴾ (He encompassed), taking it as a *fa'ila* form with *al-kursi* as its subject. It was also read with a sukun on the *sin*, with kasra on the *waw*, like *ʿilm* in *ʿalima*. It was also read with fatha on the *waw*, sukun on the *sin*, and damma on the *ʿayn*, with the genitive on *kursiyyihi* and the nominative on *al-samawat*. In that case, it is a subject (*mubtada'*) annexed to what follows it, and "the heavens and the earth" is its predicate (*khabar*).

﴿*Wa la yaʾuduhu*﴾ means: it does not burden Him, as Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said. It is derived from *al-awd*, meaning crookedness, because a heavy thing causes what is beneath it to bend. Its past tense is *ada*. The pronoun refers to God, Exalted is He. It has also been said that it refers to the Kursi.

﴿*Hifzuhuma*﴾ (their preservation), that is, of the heavens and the earth. The verse did not mention what is in them because preserving them entails preserving what is in them. It singled out the two for mention, not the Kursi, because their preservation is what is observed and perceived. The claim that this is a case of *istikhdam* (a device where one word bears two meanings), so that the Kursi, the Throne, and other things unknown to anyone but God are included, is far-fetched. ﴿*Wa Huwa al-ʿAliyy*﴾ means: the Exalted above likenesses, equals, peers, opposites, signs of deficiency, and indications of createdness. It has been said that it is from exaltation in the sense of power, authority, kingship, the loftiness of rank, subjugation, elevation, majesty, and grandeur. ﴿*Al-ʿAzim*﴾ [255] means: the Possessor of greatness, in comparison with whom everything is insignificant.

When the noble verse has displayed on its dais the brides of divine questions, and when the lights of the sublime attributes have shone upon its pages, because it gathers the fundamental attributes: divinity, unity, life, knowledge, dominion, power, and will, and because it contains seventeen positions in which the Name of God appears in some and is implied in others, it speaks of Him, glorified be He, as the existent who is singular in His divinity, living, necessary of existence in Himself, the bringer into existence of other than Himself, transcendent above locality and indwelling, free from change and languor, having no resemblance to forms, and to whose sacred presence nothing that befalls souls and spirits can descend. He is the owner of dominion and the kingdom of the unseen, the originator of roots and branches, possessor of severe might, the sole knower of the manifest and the hidden, the universal and the particular, of vast dominion and power over all that can be possessed and empowered. No difficulty is burdensome to Him, and nothing is heavy in His presence. He is exalted above all that does not befit His threshold, great, such that the bird of thought cannot soar in the wilderness of His attributes. These attributes, which subsist in Him, are distinguished by necklaces of excellence that the necks of the other noble ones are empty of, and by jewels of special favor that are displayed among their peers, but not in the manner in which Lubna and Su'ad display themselves.

Muslim, Ahmad, and others narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, the greatest verse in the Qur'an is the Verse of the Throne." Al-Bayhaqi narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet: "Whoever recites the Verse of the Throne after every obligatory prayer, he will be protected until the next prayer, and none will maintain it except a prophet, a truthful one, or a martyr." Al-Daylami narrated from ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, that he said: "If you knew what is in it, you would never abandon it in any state. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'I have been given the Verse of the Throne from a treasure beneath the Throne, which no prophet before me was given.'" The reports about its virtue are many and well known. However, some of them have no basis, like the report: "Whoever recites it, God sends an angel who writes down his good deeds and erases his bad deeds until the same hour of the next day." Some are extremely rejected (*munkar jiddan*), like the report: "God revealed to Moses, peace be upon him, to recite the Verse of the Throne after every obligatory prayer, for whoever recites it after every obligatory prayer, I shall give him the heart of the grateful, the tongue of those who remember, the reward of those who turn in repentance, and the deeds of the truthful."

It is not hidden that most of the traditions on this subject are a proof for those who say that some parts of the Qur'an may be preferred over others. There is disagreement on this. Some scholars prohibited it, such as al-Ash'ari, al-Baqillani, and others, because it implies a deficiency in what is lesser, and the speech of God has no deficiency. They interpreted "greater" as "great" and "more excellent" as "excellent." Ishaq ibn Rahawayh and many scholars and theologians permitted it, and this is the preferred view. It returns to the great reward of its reciter. God may specify whomever He wills with whatever He wills for whatever He wills.

The connection of this noble verse to what precedes it is that when He, glorified be He, mentioned that the disbelievers are the wrongdoers, it was fitting that He alert them, majestic is His glory, to the correct creed, which is pure monotheism, the creed upon which the messengers walked despite their differing ranks and varying levels, with what its gardens have ripened from it, its springs have flowed, its nightingale has sung, and its preacher has proclaimed from the pulpits of eloquence. So all praise is due to God for clarifying the proof and removing the dust from the face of the path.

* * *

Furthermore, from the mode of allusion (*al-ishara*) in the verses: ﴿*Tilka ayat Allah*﴾ (These are the signs of God), that is, His secrets, His lights, His symbols, and His allusions. ﴿*Natluha*﴾ (We recite them) through the tongue of revelation ﴿*ʿalayka*﴾ (to you), in conformity with the established truth that does not admit of change. ﴿*Wa innaka lamina al-mursalin*﴾ (And indeed you are among the messengers), who have crossed these stations
[page 12]
and for whom the purity of times has been sound. ﴿*Tilka al-rusul faddalna baʿdahum ʿala baʿd*﴾ (Those messengers: We preferred some of them over others), according to the requirement of the ascendancy of the lights of their readiness. ﴿*Minhum man kallama Allah*﴾ (Among them is one to whom God spoke), at the time of His manifestation upon the mountain of his heart and in the valley of his secret. ﴿*Wa rafaʿa baʿdahum darajat*﴾ (And He raised some of them in rank), by his annihilation from the darkness of existence entirely, his subsistence in the presence of the divine lights, his reaching the station of "two bow-lengths or nearer," and his attainment of a treasure, so He revealed to His servant what He revealed of the secrets of both worlds, until he became the light of lights and the greatest manifestation in the eyes of those who see. ﴿*Wa atayna ʿIsa ibn Maryam al-bayyinat*﴾ (And We gave ʿIsa son of Maryam the clear proofs), and the dazzling signs of reviving the dead hearts and reports of what is stored in the treasuries of secrets of the unseen. ﴿*Wa ayyadnahu bi-ruh al-qudus*﴾ (And We supported him with the Holy Spirit), which is the Spirit of spirits, transcendent above natural deficiencies and sanctified from natural attributes. ﴿*Wa law shaʾ Allah ma iqtatala alladhina*﴾ (Had God willed, those who came) ﴿*min baʿdihim*﴾ (after them) ﴿*min baʿdi ma jaʾathumu*﴾ (after the clear proofs had come to them) from the lights of the natural disposition and the guidance of the messengers, would not have fought one another, with the swords of desire and arrows of error. ﴿*Wa lakin ikhtalafu*﴾ (But they differed), according to what their eternal readiness required. ﴿*Faminhum man amana*﴾ (Among them are those who believed) in what revelation brought, ﴿*wa minhum man kafara*﴾ (and among them are those who disbelieved). ﴿*Wa law shaʾ Allah ma iqtatalu*﴾ (Had God willed, they would not have fought) with disagreement, by their readiness being uniform. ﴿*Wa lakinna Allah yafʿalu ma yurid*﴾ (But God does what He wills), and He wills only what is in His knowledge, and nothing other than this difference is in it. ﴿*Ya ayyuha alladhina amanu anfiqu mimma razaqnakum*﴾ (O you who believe, spend from what We have provided you) by giving up souls and guiding the servants, ﴿*min qabli an yaʾtiya yawm*﴾ (before there comes a Day) of the Great Resurrection ﴿*la bayʿ fihi*﴾ (in which there is no trade), and no attribute is exchanged for another attribute, so the perfection of the creation is not achieved. ﴿*Wa la khullah*﴾ (nor friendship), due to the manifestation of realities. ﴿*Wa la shafaʿah*﴾ (nor intercession), due to the majestic manifestation.

﴿*Wa al-kafirun hum*﴾ (And the disbelievers are they) who wronged themselves by diminishing their portions. "We did not wrong them" in that We did not decree upon them anything except what their readiness, which is not created, required. ﴿*Allahu la ilaha*﴾ (God, there is no god) in the knowing existence ﴿*illa Huwa al-Hayy*﴾ (except Him, the Living), whose life is the very essence of His Self, and whatever is living has not lived except by His life. ﴿*Al-Qayyum*﴾ (the Self-Subsisting), who subsists by Himself and sustains everything that subsists by Him. It has also been said: "The Living" is the One who clothed the secrets of the monotheists with His life, so they affirmed His unity through Him. "The Self-Subsisting" is the One who nurtured the spirits of the knowers through the manifestation of the attributes and the unveiling of the Essence, so they passed away in His Essence and were burned by the light of His majesty.

The commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 255 (part 4 of 4):

﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him.﴾ This explains His self-subsistence (qayyumiyya), and it points to the fact that His life is identical with His essence. ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ That is, the heavens of spirits and the earth of bodies. Nothing moves, nothing rests, and no thought arises, on land or at sea, whether secret or public, except by His power, His will, His knowledge, and His decree. ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ For all of them belong to Him, come from Him, return to Him, and subsist through Him. ﴿He knows what is before them﴾ of the passing thoughts, ﴿and what is behind them﴾ of the slips. Or, what is before them is their stations and what is behind them is their states. Or, He knows of them what preceded their coming into being, namely the measure of their capacity (isti'dad), and what follows their creation, namely the working out of what that capacity requires. ﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge﴾ of His known things, which are the manifestations of His names, ﴿except what He wills.﴾ Just as the people of the hearts (ahl al-qulub) attain, through direct witnessing, some of the secrets of the unseen. If intellects fall short of encompassing any part of His known things, then what hope do they have of encompassing His essence? Far, far off! How can a bat's understanding open its eye to the sun of that essence?

﴿His Throne (kursiyy) encompasses the heavens and the earth.﴾ The Throne here is the heart of the gnostic ('arif), because it is the source of divine sciences and of the knowledge granted directly by God (al-'ilm al-ladunni), which has no end and no limit. For this reason Abu Yazid al-Bistami said: "If the world, together with all that is in it, were to fall a thousand thousand times into one corner of the heart of the gnostic, he would not feel it." It has also been said that His Throne is the world of the malakut (the unseen dominion), and it is the place of circling for the spirits of the gnostics before the majesty of the jabarut (the realm of sovereign power).

﴿And their preservation does not weary Him﴾ nor burden Him, ﴿for they do not exist without Him.﴾ ﴿He is the Most High﴾ in rank, whom the cosmos cannot confine, ﴿the Most Great﴾ whose greatness has no bound, and whose essence cannot be conceived in its reality, because He is absolute, even beyond the bond of absoluteness.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 256:**

﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ It has been said that this (up to His words, exalted is He, ﴿eternal therein﴾) is part of the Verse of the Throne. The truth, however, is that it is not part of it. Rather, it is a separate, independent sentence, placed after the proofs of tawhid (monotheism) to indicate that compulsion in religion is inconceivable, because compulsion is in reality forcing another person to do something in which he sees no good that would motivate him to do it, whereas religion is entirely good. On this view, the sentence is a statement (khabar) in terms of the reality and the actual state of affairs. As for what appears to be otherwise, it is not genuine compulsion. He (al-Alusi) also allowed that it may be an informative statement with the meaning of a prohibition, i.e., "Do not compel people in religion and do not force them into it." In that case, it is either general and abrogated (mansukh) by His saying: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾. This is the view reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Zayd and Sulayman ibn Musa. Or it is specific to the People of the Book who accepted the jizyah (poll tax). This is the view reported from al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Dahhak. The occasion of revelation supports this, for Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that: "A man from the Ansar, from the Banu Salim ibn Awf, called al-Husayn, had two Christian sons, while he himself was a Muslim man. He said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Shall I not compel them, since they have refused anything but Christianity?' So Allah revealed concerning him that." The definite article in (al-din) ("the religion") is for previous reference (al-'ahd). It has also been said that it is a substitute for the genitive construction, meaning "the religion of Allah," which is the religion of Islam. Whatever the interpretation, the one who would compel is someone other than Allah, exalted is He. Some people have said that the meaning is: there is no compulsion in religion from Allah, exalted is He, and no coercion. Rather, the matter rests on empowerment and free choice. Otherwise, testing would not occur and examination would be void. The verse is thus similar to His saying: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾. This is the view taken by al-Qaffal.

﴿The right course has become distinct from error.﴾ This is a justification (ta'lil) introduced with the particle of confirmation (qad) to reinforce the assertion of its content. That is, it has been distinguished by what was mentioned of His attributes, which make it impossible to suppose that anything else shares in any of them: faith from disbelief, and correctness from error. The word (al-rushd) ("the right course"), with a damma on the ra' and a sukun on the shin, is according to the well-known reading the verbal noun of rashada (with a fatha on the shin), yarshudu (with a damma). It is also read with a fatha on both the ra' and the shin. Its verb is rashida, yarshadu, like 'alima, ya'lamu. It is the opposite of al-ghayy ("error"), and its original sense is following the path of destruction. Al-Raghib said: "It is like ignorance (jahl), except that jahl is used with reference to belief, while ghayy is used with reference to actions. For this reason it has been said: the removal of ignorance is by knowledge, and the removal of error is by right guidance." It is said of one who is correct: he has been rightly guided (rashida), and of one who errs: he has gone astray (ghawa). It is also said of one who fails: ghawa as well. From this is His saying (in poetry):

"Whoever meets good, people praise his affair; and whoever goes astray will not lack a blamer for his error."

﴿So whoever disbelieves in the Taghut﴾, that is, in the Shaytan (Satan). This is what is related from Umar ibn al-Khattab and al-Husayn ibn Ali (may Allah be pleased with them). Mujahid and Qatadah also said so. It is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah that it refers to the soothsayer (kahin). From Abu al-'Aliyah that it refers to the sorcerer. From Malik ibn Anas: everything that is worshipped besides Allah, exalted is He. From some of them: the idols. The better view is that it should be understood in its generality, as everything that transgresses (ma yatgha), and that restricting it to some of these in those statements is by way of example. The word (al-taghut) is an intensive form (bina' mubalagha), like al-jabarut and al-malakut. Scholars differed about it. It has been said that it is originally a verbal noun (masdar), and for this reason it is used in the singular and masculine, like the other verbal nouns applied to concrete things. This is the view of al-Fârisi. It has been said that it is a singular collective noun (ism jins mufrad), and for this reason it is obligatorily singular and masculine. This is the view of Sibawayh. It has also been said that it is a plural, which is the view of al-Mubarrad. Its pronoun may be feminine, as in His saying: ﴿Those who avoid the Taghut, not worshipping it﴾. This feminine is a notional feminine (ta'nith i'tibari). Its derivation is from taghā, yatghā, or taghā, yatghū. The verbal noun of the first is al-tughyan, and of the second al-tughwan. Its original form according to the first is taghyut, and according to the second taghwut. The lam was then moved before the 'ayn, so the weak letter became vowelled and the letter before it was opened, so it was changed to an alif. Its weight was formerly fa'lut, and now fal'ut. He placed the mention of disbelief in the Taghut before the mention of belief in Allah, exalted is He, to emphasise the necessity of clearing the way first (al-takhliyah), or in observance of the actual order, or for the connection with the word al-ghayy ("error").

﴿and believes in Allah﴾, that is, affirms Him in accordance with what His messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, brought. ﴿Then he has grasped﴾, that is, he has pursued grasping to the utmost, as if, while holding it, he were seeking from himself increase in it and steadfastness upon it. ﴿the firmest handhold﴾. This is faith, according to Mujahid. Or it is the Qur'an, according to Anas ibn Malik. Or it is the word of sincerity (kalimat al-ikhlas), according to Ibn Abbas. Or it is the correct belief, or the means that leads to the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, or the covenant. In every case, it is permissible that there be a clear metaphor (isti'arah tasrihiyyah) in (al-'urwah) ("the handhold"), and (istamsaka) ("has grasped") is a supporting element (tarshih) for it. Or it is another, subsequent metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah). It is also permissible to take the statement as an allegorical image (tamthil) built on the comparison of the mental state drawn from clinging to a truth that admits no contradiction in any respect, because it is established by clear and certain proofs, with the sensory state drawn from grasping a firm rope whose breaking is safe. This was chosen by some verifiers (muhaqqiqun), and it is not without beauty. However, taking (al-'urwah) to be a metaphor for sound reflection that leads to correct belief, as has been said, is not good, because that is not mentioned at all within the scope of the condition.

﴿there is no breaking of it﴾, that is, there is no severance for it. (al-infisam) and (al-inqisam) are two dialects, and with the letter fa' is more eloquent, as al-Farra' said. Some distinguished between them: the first is breaking without separation, and the second is breaking with separation. In that case, the negation of the second is known from the negation of the first by a stronger inference. The sentence is either a new, independent sentence confirming what precedes it regarding the solidity of the handhold, or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) for (al-'urwah), with (istamsaka) as the operating verb, or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun concealed in (al-wuthqa), because it is the comparative feminine of al-awthaq ("the most firm"). And (lahā) ("for it") is in the position of the predicate.

﴿Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of statements, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ [256] of resolutions and beliefs. The sentence is a concluding summary (tadhyil) that compels belief and deters disbelief and hypocrisy, because of the promise and warning it contains. It has been said that it also indicates that faith necessarily requires both belief in the heart and affirmation by the tongue.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 2, verse 257:**

﴿Allah is the Walī (Protector and Ally) of those who believe.﴾ That is, His helper, or His lover, or the one who manages their affairs. By "those who believe" is meant whoever intends faith, or whose faith is fixed in His knowledge, may He be exalted, or who has actually believed. ﴿He brings them out﴾ by His guidance and His enabling success. This is an explanation of "walāya" (guardianship, protection), or a second predicate according to those who permit it to be a sentence or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿Walī﴾. ﴿From the darknesses﴾ that belong to disbelief, or the darknesses of sins, or of doubts, however they may be. ﴿To the light﴾ that is, the light of faith, or the light of acts of obedience, or the light of certainty in its degrees.

It is related from al-Ḥasan that he explained "al-ikhrāj" (bringing out) here as "al-man‘" (preventing). The meaning then is that He prevents them from entering any of the darknesses. Al-Wāqidī, in explaining the darknesses and the light, limited himself to mentioning disbelief and faith, and he applied everything in the Qur'an to that meaning except what is in al-An‘ām [1], in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and He made the darknesses and the light﴾, since what is meant there is the night and the day. The better view is that "the darknesses" be taken in the sense that encompasses all of its kinds, and that "the light" also be taken in the sense that encompasses all of its kinds. For every darkness there is set in opposition an exit from it into a light that one is brought out to. Indeed He, glorified is He, brings out whomever He wills from the darkness of the night into the light of direct vision, and from the darkness of loneliness into the light of union, and from the darkness of the world of forms into the light of the world of spirits, and to other things "of what is not, nor..." Using the singular "the light" indicates the unity of the Truth, just as the plural "the darknesses" indicates the multiplicity of the kinds of error. Or else the singular is a hint at scarcity, and the plural a hint at abundance.

﴿And those who disbelieve﴾ that is, who intend disbelief, or whose disbelief is fixed in His knowledge, glorified is He, or who have actually disbelieved. ﴿Their protectors﴾ in reality, or in their own estimation, are ﴿the Ṭāghūt﴾ (false objects of worship, tyrants, or transgressors), that is, the devils, or the idols, or all those who lead astray from the paths of truth. The relative pronoun is the first subject, "their protectors" is the second subject, and "al-Ṭāghūt" is its predicate. The whole sentence is the predicate of the first, and the resulting sentence is conjoined to what precedes it. It has been said: perhaps the change of construction is to avoid placing the Ṭāghūt in opposition to the glorious Name, and to intend emphasis by repeating the predication, together with a hint at the complete contrast between the two groups in every respect, even in the manner of expression. It is also read as "al-ṭawāghīt" (plural), and its plural is valid on the view that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), since it has become a name for whatever is worshipped besides Allah, may He be exalted.

﴿They bring them out﴾ by whisperings and by casting doubts, or by being in a condition that led their believers to attribute to them benefit and harm, and that they bring them near to Allah, may He be exalted, in nearness. The expression for them with the pronoun of rational beings is either because they are among them in reality, or by claim. The attribution of bringing out to them is a metaphor (majāz) of the kind of attributing an act to its cause, so it does not contradict the connection of His power and will, may He be exalted, to that. ﴿From the light﴾ that is, the natural light (al-fiṭrah) upon which all people are created, or the light of the successive clear proofs which they witness, by a descent that enables them to be illuminated by them as if they were themselves light. So it is not objected that when they were in light, how could they come out from it? It has been said: the expression with this is for the sake of contrast. It has also been said: bringing out may mean preventing, and that does not require that entering had preceded. It is related from Mujāhid that the verse was revealed concerning a people who apostatized. Then there is no doubt that at that time they were brought out from the light in which they had been, which is the light of faith. ﴿To the darknesses﴾, which are the darknesses of disbelief and of immersion in error, and of not desisting and not being guided by the signs that come successively and are recited. The clause is an explanation of the guardianship of the Ṭāghūt, so the separation is due to the perfection of the connection. It may also be a second predicate, as has passed.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to the relative pronoun in terms of its being characterized by what is in the sphere of the relative clause and what follows that of ugly qualities. It has been permitted that it refers to the disbelievers and their protectors, but this is remote. ﴿The companions of the Fire﴾, that is, those who are associated with it and bound to it, because of the greatness of what they are upon. ﴿They are therein abiding forever﴾ [257], remaining eternally. In this there is a promise and a warning for the disbelievers. Perhaps the absence of its being set in contrast with a promise for the believers, as has been said, is to indicate their exaltedness, and that their matter does not need explanation, and that their state is higher than being set against these; or that what has been prepared for them cannot be expressed in words. It has been said: His saying, may He be exalted, "Walī al-Mu’minīn" (the Protector of the believers) indicates the promise, and that suffices.

[Page 15]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 258 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ This is an illustration of the support given to the believers, since He (may He be exalted) is their Guardian (waliyy), and of the abandonment of others. For this reason the verse is not joined by a conjunction, and attention is paid to explaining it, because those who deny that God is the Guardian of the believers are many. It has also been said that it is an illustration (istishhad) of what was mentioned, namely that the disbelievers have the Taghut as their guardians, and a confirmation of that. Just as what follows it is an illustration of God's guardianship of the believers and a confirmation of it. It begins with this verse in order to maintain the connection between it and its subject matter, and because it stands on its own as a remarkable matter, worthy of being introduced by the statement, namely his audacity in disputing about God, Mighty and Majestic, and the greatness he displayed in the course of it, which proclaims his complete foolishness. Also, what follows it contains enumeration and detail, and placing this verse first gives the discourse a wide scope. Moreover, it has been indicated within it that He (may He be exalted) also guided through Abraham (peace be upon him), since what is related from him concerning calling to the truth and refuting the argument of the disbelievers is among the effects of God's guardianship. The implications of this are not hidden. The interrogative hamza here serves to deny a negation and to affirm what is negated. Most scholars hold that the sentence carries the sense of wonder, meaning: "Have you not looked?" Or: "Has your knowledge not reached the story of this disbeliever, of whom I am not a guardian, how he presumed to dispute with the one whom you were made responsible to support, and you were informed that I am the Guardian of him and of whoever is among his followers?" That is, the vision of this remarkable story has been realised and established, on the basis that the matter is so manifest that it is hardly hidden from anyone who has a share of understanding. Therefore, let your awareness be at its utmost degree of certainty regarding what I have mentioned to you, namely that I am the Guardian of the believers and not of the disbelievers. Let your soul be content, O beloved, and rejoice in victory, for I supported the Friend (al-Khalil). And where is the station of the Friend compared with the Beloved? I also humiliated the chief of the tyrants, so how much more the lowly tails?

The relative pronoun refers to Namrud ibn Kan'an ibn Sanjarib, who was the first to become a tyrant and claim lordship, as stated by Mujahid and others. The term "argument" (muhajjah) is applied to what occurred, although it was a dispute based on falsehood, because it was placed in its proper context. Scholars have differed about its time. It has been said that it was at the breaking of the idols and before he was thrown into the fire, as narrated from Muqatil. It has also been said that it was after he was thrown into the fire and God made it cool and safe for him, as narrated from Ja'far al-Sadiq (may God be pleased with him). In mentioning the title of lordship (rububiyyah) together with its attribution to his (peace be upon him) pronoun, there is an honour for him and an indication from the very beginning of his Guardian's support for him in the argument, since upbringing (tarbiyah) is a kind of guardianship.

﴿Because God had given him kingship﴾: that is, because God the Exalted had given him that. The sentence is therefore based on the omission of the preposition "li" (for/because), which is regular with "an" and "in." There is no object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) here in the accusative, because the subject is not the same. The causation here is of two kinds. Either the giving of kingship led him to do this, because it produced in him pride and insolence, and the argument arose from these two; or it is of the reverse type in speech, meaning that he placed the argument where gratitude should have been, since it was his duty to thank God for that. According to the first, the causation is real; according to the second, it is sarcastic, as you would say: "So-and-so opposed me because I did him a kindness." It has also been permitted that ﴿he had been given﴾ etc. functions as an adverbial of time without a supplement, or with a supplement understood, meaning: he argued at the time when God gave him. An objection to this is that the argument did not occur at the time of the giving of kingship, rather the giving came before it. Another objection is that the grammarians have stated that only a pure verbal noun in its own form may stand in the place of a time adverb, as in "I came at the twinkling of the star and the crowing of the rooster," and it is not permitted to say "when it twinkled" or "when it crowed."

It has been answered that time is regarded as extended, and that the text is contradicted by the fact that they stated that the verbal "ma" (ma al-masdariyyah) takes the place of time, though it is not a pure verbal noun. The one who permitted this was Ibn Jinni and al-Saffar in their commentary on the Book. The truth is that causation, where it is possible, and which is agreed upon, free from what may be objected to, should not be abandoned, especially since taking a supplement together with the view of extension and adopting the view of Ibn Jinni and al-Saffar, which opposes the words of the majority, is in the extreme of artificiality.

The verse is a proof against those who prevent God from giving kingship to a disbeliever. Those who interpret it as God giving him what he overpowered with, and what made him dominant in wealth, servants, and followers, or as God giving him kingship as a test for His servants, as the one who holds that it is obligatory to observe what is most beneficial (ri'ayat al-aslah) did, are mistaken. This is not worth anything, for whoever has a particle of fairness knows that there is no meaning to giving kingship and authority except giving the causes (of it). Even if this were granted, the question would still apply to the giving of causes. And even if that were granted, there is no ugly act for which a sound purpose cannot be imagined, such as a trial. Because of the strength of this objection, some have insisted on making the pronoun in ﴿he had given him﴾ refer to Abraham (peace be upon him), since He (may He be exalted) said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾, and He (glory be to Him) said: ﴿We had already given the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom﴾. This is what is related from Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi. It is not hidden that this is contrary to what comes to the mind directly and contrary to the transmitted exegesis of the pious predecessors (al-salaf al-salih). Reality also refutes it, since at that time Abraham (peace be upon him) had no kingship, no authority, and no effective command.

Some of the Imamiyya (Twelver Shi'a) went so far as to hold that the kingship which God does not give to a disbeliever is that which consists of the transfer of command and prohibition, and the imposition of obedience upon the creatures. As for what is by domination, wide wealth, and the force of word by compulsion, like the kingship of Namrud, this is among matters over which two rams should not butt heads, or in which there should be two words. The claim that this rebel was given kingship in the first sense is outside fairness. Rather, the one who was truly given that was Abraham (peace be upon him), except that his kingship was contested and overcome, according to what God had bestowed upon him, until God decreed what He decreed and whoever passed away passed away, and falsehood has its circuit and then vanishes. This is a statement that comes as close to the truth as possible, but I smell from it the scent of error, and it appears to me to be an allusion to the Companions. God knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal. In shifting from the implicit pronoun to the explicit noun in this context, there is what is not hidden.

﴿When Abraham said﴾: this is an adverbial clause (zarf) modifying ḥājja (argued). It has also been permitted that it be a substitute (badal) for ﴿he had given him﴾, according to the view you have learned. Abu Hayyan objected to this, saying that the two adverbial phrases differ, since the time of his being given kingship is not the time of Abraham (peace be upon him). ﴿My Lord is He who gives life and causes death﴾: for it is related that he said this after he was imprisoned for breaking the idols, and following the statement of Namrud to him, when he had already been given kingship before, namely: "Who is your Lord to whom you call?" Al-Safaqsi answered by saying that ﴿he had given him﴾ is used figuratively, and that what is intended is not the beginning of the giving from Namrud, but rather the period of kingship, which is extended and can accommodate two statements or even several. Abu al-Baqa' also objected that the verbal noun is other than the adverb, so if it were a substitute it would be an error, unless (idh) is taken to mean "that" (an) in the verbal sense, and this has indeed occurred. Al-Halabi said that this objection is based on the view that "inna" (that) is an object of purpose and not functioning as an adverb. But if it does function as an adverb, it is not a substitute of error, but a substitute of whole for whole. The discussion before applies to this. It has also been said that it may be a substitute for ﴿he had given him﴾ as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal). Some have found difficulty in all of this concerning the position of His statement: ﴿He said, "I give life and cause death"﴾, unless it is made a new sentence in answer to a question. Making it a dependent of what precedes is rejected by that. From here it has been said that the adverb is connected to His statement (glory be to Him): ﴿He said, "I..."﴾ etc., and a question is supposed before ﴿when he said﴾, as if it were said: "How did Abraham argue?" So he was answered with what was answered. But it is not hidden that the refusal is the same refusal, so the better course from the outset is to say that this statement explains His statement ﴿argued﴾. ﴿Rabbi﴾ (My Lord) is with a fathah on the ya', and it is also read with the ya' omitted. Abraham (peace be upon him) meant by ﴿gives life and causes death﴾ that He creates life and death in bodies, while the accursed one meant something else. It is related of him that two men were brought to him, he killed one and spared the other, and he said what he said. Since this was far from the intended purpose, and its falsity was so clear and manifest that it is hidden from no one, and since refuting such a thing is a kind of striving to obtain what is already obtained, the Friend (peace be upon him) turned away from refuting it and brought another proof, clearer than the sun.
