﴿Abraham said, "Indeed, God brings up the sun from the east, so bring it up from the west"﴾. In this there is evidence for the permissibility of a disputant moving from one argument to another that is clearer. This is a matter in which there is disagreement. Understanding it in this way is one of the two well-known approaches to the verse. The second is that the transition is only within the example, as if he said: "My Lord is He who brings existent things into being and annihilates them," and he brought in giving life and causing death as an example. When he was objected to, he brought a clearer example to repel the confusion. The Imam said: "The difficulty with both of these is in several respects. The first: when the one who raises a doubt has voiced the doubt, and that doubt has reached the ears, it is obligatory upon the one who is right and capable of replying to give the answer immediately, to remove deception and ignorance from minds. So when the rebel challenged the first proof or the first example with that doubt, it became an obligatory and urgent duty to occupy oneself with removing it. How then is it fitting for the infallible to leave that and move on to something else? The second: when the falsifier raised that question, the rightly-guided person's refraining from speaking about it and from pointing out its weakness would cause the Messenger's standing to fall and his status to be belittled, and that is not permitted.

"The third: even though it is permissible to move from one proof to another, or from one example to another, it is necessary that what one moves to be clearer and closer. Here the matter is not so, for the genus of life is beyond the power of created beings, whereas the genus of moving bodies is within their power. So it is not far-fetched in reason that there exists a king of enormous body who moves the heavens. Given this, proof by giving life and causing death is clearer and stronger than proof by the rising of the sun. How then is it fitting for the infallible Prophet to move from the clearer proof to the hidden proof?

"The fourth: since the rebel was not ashamed to oppose the giving of life and death, which proceed from God the Exalted, with killing and releasing, how can one be safe from him, when one moves to the rising of the sun, that he will say: 'Rather, the rising of the sun from the east is from me. If you have a god, tell him to bring it up from the west.' At that point, the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) held that if he had raised this question, it would have been obligatory to bring it up from the west. It is known that occupying oneself with showing the corruption of his question about life and death is far easier than accepting this rising. Furthermore, supposing the sun did rise from the west, the proof of the existence of the Creator would be this rising and not the first rising, and then that would be lost just as the first was lost. Also, what led the Friend (peace be upon him) to abandon answering the feeble question and to rely on a proof that cannot be carried through except by accepting that the sun rises from the west? And supposing that, the second proof would be lost just as the first was lost. It is known that accepting these prohibited consequences is not fitting even for the least learned of people, let alone for the best of scholars and the most knowledgeable of the virtuous."

The truth is that this is not another proof or an illustration; rather, it is a continuation of the first proof. For when Abraham, peace be upon him, argued from giving life and causing death, the opponent raised an objection: if you claim that giving life and causing death happen without an intermediary, you cannot find a way to establish that; and if you claim that they occur through the movements of the celestial spheres (al-aflak), then something similar to it, or close to it, is found among humans. The Friend (Khalil), peace be upon him, replied that although giving life and causing death occur through the movements of the celestial spheres, those movements themselves came about from God, Exalted; and that does not detract from giving life and causing death being from Him. This is unlike creation, for they have no power to move the spheres, and therefore giving life and causing death do not issue from them. When the verse is understood in this way, none of the prohibited consequences follows from it. End of quotation.

Nothing is hidden in what this contains. First: when a doubt is at the utmost of baselessness and the extreme of falsehood, such that its condition is hardly concealed and no one from among the people would take it as a god, turning away from it to what is far from deception is not impermissible, in order to repel confusion and attain the intended aim without much toil. This does not entail any loss of standing or diminishment of the matter. And what confusion does this doubt create for minds, such that dealing with its removal would be an obligatory and urgent duty, so that neglecting it would harm the one who is protected from error? Moreover, it is reported that he did not depart until he had made clear to the rebel (al-marid) the corruption of his statement when he said to him: "You have given life to the living, and you have not given life to the dead." And it is related from al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him, that he said to him: "Bring to life the one you have killed, if you are truthful." But God, Exalted, did not relate that rebuke against us in the Book, being content with the manifest corruption of it.

Second: it is clear that the destination (al-muntaqal ilayhi) is more evident in the intended meaning than the starting point (al-muntaqal anhu), and to hold the opposite almost amounts to obstinacy. What he mentioned in the course of argument is not free from problems.

Third: what he mentioned fourthly is also refuted regarding the aspect he chose, for one cannot be secure from the rebel saying: "If the movements of the spheres are from your Lord, then ask Him to bring the sun from the west." Here the answer would be the same answer. They have responded to the fact that the accursed one did not say this by saying that the debate took place after his escape from the fire, so it was known that whoever was able to do that was able to bring the sun from its west, and so he fell silent. Or they have said that God, Exalted, caused him to forget this in support of His prophet, peace be upon him, but this is weak. Rather, the answer is that he, peace be upon him, argued that a particular motion and what moves with it necessarily require a mover, because the need of the moving thing for a mover in motion is self-evident. And it is self-evident that he is not Nimrod. So he said: "My Lord is He who..." Then: if you claim that you are the one who does it, then bring it from the west. This objection cannot be directed at him in any way. For if he claimed that motion in itself, although it is preceded by something else, even if by individual motions, then the self-evident would be denied. And if he claimed that he is the agent, while its impossibility is manifest, he would be compelled to change from that state. Thus one must acknowledge an agent who brings it from the east, and the claimant that this agent is the Lord.

Fourth: what he chose is not indicated by the noble verse in any way. There is nothing in the disbeliever's speech except his claim to give life and cause death, and there was no sense from it of any inquiry into the intermediacy of the movements of the spheres, nor was any trace of it established for him, so that it could be answered that those movements too are from God, Exalted, and so their intermediacy does not detract from giving life and causing death being from Him, Exalted in glory. I do not suppose you have any doubt about this.

Perhaps the more apparent view is that held by the Imam, which some of the verifying scholars have mentioned: since the rebel permitted the plurality of gods, he did not claim to be the god of the world. Had he claimed it, he would have been deemed mad, in some manner akin to the doctrine of the Sabians, that God, Exalted, delegated to the stars the management and the acts, including origination and other things, attributed to them. So he permitted that there might also be on earth one to whom such delegation is made, either by way of incarnation (hulul) or by acquiring celestial properties or otherwise. Abraham, peace be upon him, wished to draw attention to his deficiency from this rank and to the corruption of his opinion, from the standpoint of his necessary knowledge that he is a created being, brought into existence after he was not. And that whoever has no existence in himself cannot possibly have the origination, which is the outpouring of existence, since he is in need of an originator both at the beginning and in continuance. This is sufficient to refute the claim of the accursed one. Thus he did not generalize the claim regarding God's sole divinity. Moreover, he alluded to it in that there is no difference between origination and annihilation, the two kinds being giving life and causing death. The one able to originate and annihilate every contingent being must necessarily be outside the contingents and one in every respect, for plurality entails contingency and dependence, as has been demonstrated in its proper place. So the accursed one countered him with what gave the appearance that a contingent being may, by its independence from an agent in continuance, be delegated after its origination to something that can independently originate and manage others, as in the view of some deficient theologians. This has remained hidden from the intelligent, let alone the dull. And he said: "I give life and cause death, and I bring forth," thereby indicating that continuance has the ruling of beginning in the matter of giving life. In that he contradicts himself without realizing it, for if it were so, management would not have been delegated to anyone other than the Creator, and it would not be independent of the originator for an instant. Otherwise, pardon is not giving life, if one grants that killing is causing death. So Abraham, peace be upon him, obliged him by saying that for the Capable, continuance and beginning are not different in relation to Him, for God, Exalted, brings the sun from the east; so bring it from the west yourself, pointing out the aforementioned contradiction and explicitly stating that he had erred by attributing to something in continuance an action that is attributed to Another in beginning, making manifest to the listeners what might have been hidden from some of them. This is speech directed at persuasion (khitabah), while the demonstrative proof is received by the one addressed, willingly or unwillingly, with submission; there is no room in it for objection, free from defect. On this basis the whole is one proof, and it is not a shift to another proof, because of the talk and dispute that would involve; nor is it a turning to a clearer illustration, so that it would be said: as if it were said, "My Lord is He who brings contingent beings into existence," and He mentioned giving life and causing death as an illustration; then when he objected, He brought another clearer one to repel the confusion. For although it contains what the first contains, it is refuted by the fact that the speech was not framed in this manner, as is not hidden. And God, Exalted, knows best the realities of His glorious Book, so reflect.

As for the phrase "in the second clause He used the noble Name and did not use the title of Lordship as He did in the first clause," saying "My Lord" to correspond with "I" in that statement, together with what it indicates of His Exalted Lordship over him, peace be upon him, and over that rebel, may the curse be upon him: this contains an ascent beyond what is in that clause, like the ascent from earth to heaven. In this context, the use of "inna" for emphasis is fine. The imperative is for incapacitation (al-ta'jiz). The first "fa" indicates the dependence of what follows on what precedes. The meaning is: if you claim giving life and causing death for God, Exalted, and you err in understanding, or you deceive, then the one who relieves the mind and removes the confusion and perplexity is: "Indeed God brings the sun..." etc.

The "bi" is for transitivity (ta'diyah), and "min" in both places is for the starting point of the end (ibtida' al-ghayah), connected to the verb preceding it. It has been said that it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning "subjugated" or "compliant."

﴿So the one who disbelieved was bewildered﴾: that is, he was overcome, became bewildered, cut off from speech, perplexed, because the proof had overwhelmed him. It was read as "bahuta" with a fatha on the ba' and a damma on the ha', and as "bahita" with a fatha on the first and a kasra on the second; both are dialects, and the verb in both is intransitive. And "bahata" with fatha on both may be intransitive too, with "alladhi" as its subject, or transitive, with the pronoun of Abraham as subject and "alladhi" as its object, meaning: Abraham overcame the disbeliever and silenced him. Mentioning disbelief within the relative clause indicates the cause of the ruling. Al-Kiya said: the verse is evidence for the permissibility of debate in religion, even though the debate of this disbeliever was itself disbelief.

﴿And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ [258]: that is, to the paths of truth, as He guided His friends. It has been said: He does not guide them to the path of Paradise on the Day of Resurrection.

[Page 20]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 1 of 3):

﴿Or like one who passed by a town﴾. It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with what precedes it. The kaf (the particle "like") is either a noun meaning "like" (mithl), governing *ara'ayta* (did you see), which is elided: that is, "Or did you see someone like the one who passed by?" This is the view of al-Kisa'i, al-Farra', Abu ʿAli, and most of the grammarians. The verb of seeing is omitted because *alam tara* (have you not seen) indicates it. It is said that in this type of construction the verb of seeing is often omitted, as in the verse:

*He said to her, "Hurry, her dogs, like today, sought and not seeking."*

This kaf was brought to draw attention to the multiplicity of examples and that they are not limited to what has been mentioned, as in your saying "the past-tense verb, like: *nasara* (he helped)." The singling out of this case for this purpose, it is said, is because those who deny resurrection are many, and those who are ignorant of its manner are more than can be counted, unlike the claimant to lordship. It is also said that the kaf is extra (zaʾidah), and this is the view of al-Akhfash. Meaning: "Have you not seen the one who argued with Ibrahim, or the one who passed by, etc.?" It is also said that it is a coordination carried over to the meaning, as if it were said: "Have you not seen like the one who argued, or like the one who passed by?" It is also said that it is part of the speech of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who mentioned it as a reply to the opposition of that disbeliever, and its implied sense is: "If you give life, then give life like the giving of life by the one who passed by." Its weakness is not hidden, because of the intervening separation and the great number of elisions. The kaf was not made original (asliyyah) with the coordination on *alladhi* (the one who) itself in the previous verse, because that would require the entry of *ila* (to) upon the kaf, and this has a difficulty: if the kaf is a particle, it is obvious; and if it is a noun, then, because it is assimilated to a particle in not being inflected, only those particles that are established in their speech may enter upon it, and that is *ʿan* (from), and even that is rare.

Some of them said: each of the expressions *alam tara* and *ara'ayta* is used for the purpose of wonder (taʿajjub), except that the first is connected to the thing wondered at, so one says: "Have you not seen the one who did such-and-such?" meaning: look at him and wonder at his condition. And the second is connected to the like of the thing wondered at, so one says: "Did you see someone like the one who did such-and-such?" meaning that it is so strange that no like of it is seen. It is not correct to say *alam tara ila mathalih* (have you not seen his like), because the meaning would be: look at the like and wonder at the one who did it. For this reason your coordination of "the one who passed by" upon "the one who argued" is not correct, and it requires interpretation: either in the coordinated element, by making it connected to an elided thing, i.e., "Did you see like the one who passed by?", so that it is coordination of a sentence; or in the element coordinated upon, considering that it has the meaning of "Did you see like the one who argued?", so the coordination upon it is correct. From this it is known that the incorrectness is not merely due to the impossibility of entering *ila* upon the kaf. Rather, even if you say "Have you not seen the one who argued, or like the one who passed by?", the incorrectness remains as it is for one who knows the methods of speech. This is not from the extra use of the kaf at all; rather, in wonder with the expression *ara'ayta*, there must be the affirmation of a kaf or what has its meaning. This is not hidden, that it is very strange, for *alam tara* is used for wonder together with comparison in the speech of the Arabs, as the words of Sibawayh indicate, while *ara'ayta* is often used without the kaf or what has its meaning, and it is frequent in the Qur'an. How can one distinguish between them by saying that the first is connected to the thing wondered at, and in the second to its like? The likeness only comes from the mention of the kaf; if it had been mentioned in the first, it would be like it with no difference. So this is begging the question (muṣādarah ʿala al-maṭlub). There is nothing but what was mentioned first, except that estimating *ara'ayta* with the kaf is preferable, because its use with it is more frequent. So reflect.

And *aw* (or) is for choice (takhyir) or for detailing (tafsil). The passer-by was ʿUzayr ibn Sharkhiya, as al-Hakim transmitted from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, and Ishaq ibn Bishr from Ibn ʿAbbas, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam. This is the view of Qatadah, ʿIkrimah, al-Rabiʿ, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and a great many others. It is said: he was Irmiya ibn Khalqiya of the tribe of Harun (peace be upon him), and this is what is narrated from Abu Jaʿfar (may Allah be pleased with him), and this is the view of Wahb. It is said: he was al-Khadir (peace be upon him), and this is related from Ibn Ishaq. Some claimed that these two views are one, and that Irmiya is al-Khadir himself. It is said: Shiʿya. It is said: the boy of Lut (peace be upon him). Mujahid said: the passer-by was a disbelieving man in resurrection, and this is supported by his being placed in the same string with Nimrod, since the speech was brought for the purpose of wonder at the condition of both of them. It is also supported by the fact that the expression of astonishment in this context indicates denial, apparently, and it is not like its use in *anna yakunu li ghulam* (how can I have a boy) and *anna yakunu li walad* (how can I have a child). This is opposed by the great distance in meaningful correspondence between his story and the story of Ibrahim that comes later, for both of them asked to witness the giving of life, while what happened to him in the story is such that it is unlikely to happen with a disbeliever. And if one adds to that his seeking the outward in avoiding lying in the statement issued before the clarification, which would have required his faith according to the claim of those who assert his disbelief, this strengthens the opposing view greatly. And if we say that the indication of being placed in the string of Nimrod is more deserving of faith, so that it fits the detail presented in *Allah is the Guardian of those who believe* (2:257) and so on, as we indicated in the earlier discussion, then the view of disbelief would hardly be imagined, as is not hidden.

As for the town (*qaryah*), Ibn Zayd said: it is the one from which thousands came out. Al-Kalbi said: it is the monastery of Sabirabad. Al-Suddi said: the monastery of Salma Bad. It is said: the monastery of Heraclius. It is said: the overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikah). It is said: the town of grapes, two farsakhs from Jerusalem. ʿIkrimah, al-Rabiʿ, and Wahb said: it is Jerusalem, which Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar) had destroyed, and this is the most famous view. Its derivation is from *al-qura* (gatherings), which means collecting.

﴿And it was fallen upon its roofs﴾: that is, fallen down upon its ceilings, in that the roof fell first and then the walls collapsed upon it. It is said: the meaning is "empty of its people, standing upon its roofs," that is, its houses are still standing. On the first meaning, the prepositional phrase is connected to *khawiyah* (fallen); on the second, it is connected to an elided item which occurs as a predicate after the predicate of *la-hiya* (indeed it is). The sentence is said to be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun hidden in *marra* (passed by); it is said to be from *qaryah* (town), and a circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun occurs rarely; it is said to be in the position of a qualifier for it, but the intervening *waw* distances this. Some of them permitted that *ʿala ʿurushiha* (upon its roofs) be a substitute for *qaryah* (town), with repetition of the preposition, and that it be a qualifier for it. The sentence *wa-hiya khawiyah* is either a circumstantial clause from *ʿurush* (roofs), or from *qaryah*, or from *ha* (it), with the operating element being the meaning of the annexation. All of these are things that it is not fitting to impose upon the revelation.

(He) said, within himself or with his tongue: ﴿How will Allah give life to this after its death?﴾ The referent of "this" is either the town itself without any supposition, as is apparent; so the giving of life and causing death are metaphors for building and ruin. Or by supposing a possessed noun, that is, "the people of this town," in which case giving life and causing death are literal. Or the referent is the bones of the town, decayed, and its scattered corpses; the context indicates this, and giving life and causing death remain as they are. On the view of metaphor, this statement would be an expression of longing and yearning for the rebuilding of that town, but with a sense of despair regarding it, in the most eloquent and emphatic manner. For this reason Allah showed him the more remote of the two matters, first in himself and then in others. Then He showed him what he had regarded as remote, explicitly, as an exaggeration in removing whatever might stir in his mind. On the second view, it is an acknowledgment of inability to know the way of giving life, and an exalting of the power of the Giver of life, if we say that the speaker was a believer; and a denial of the power to do that if he was a disbeliever. The first of the three possibilities regarding the referent was preferred, on the ground that intending the giving of life to people or to their bones is precluded by the mention of the condition of the town without any mention of a condition for it, and by the restriction to mentioning their death rather than their becoming dust or decayed bones, even though that is more emphatic in the sense of remoteness, due to its sharp contrast with life. And the furthest extent of its distance from accepting life is that the will of Allah the Exalted had not been directed at giving them life, as His will had been directed at rebuilding it, and at the passer-by's seeing it, as you will hear. The placing of the object before the subject is for the sake of concern with it, because the sense of remoteness arises from its side and not from the side of the agent. *Anna* (how) is in the accusative as an adverb of place if it means *mata* (when), and in the accusative as a circumstantial clause of this if it means *kayfa* (how), and the operating element for it, in any case, is ﴿yuhyi﴾ (gives life).

﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years﴾: that is, He caused him to remain dead for a hundred years. It is necessary to consider this implicit meaning (tadmin), because causing death, meaning the departure of the soul and the removal of life, is not something that extends over time. *Al-ʿam* (year) is the period of a year, from *al-awm*, which is swimming, and it was so named because the sun swims through all its zodiac signs. ﴿Then He raised him﴾: that is, He gave him life, from "I raised the she-camel," when I made her stand from her place. Perhaps the reason he chose this over "gave him life" is to indicate its speed and the ease of its accomplishment for the Creator, the Mighty of Name, and to announce that he rose in the same state as the day he died, intelligent, understanding, prepared to reflect and to reason. This happened after the rebuilding of the town. In *al-Bahr* it is said that when seventy years had passed since his death, and Allah had protected him from beasts and birds and prevented eyes from seeing him, He sent an angel to a great king of the kings of Persia, called Kawsak, who said: "Allah the Exalted commands you to mobilize your people and rebuild the House of Jerusalem, and Ilya and its land, until it returns better than it was." The king took up the task with three thousand stewards, each steward with a thousand workers, and they began to rebuild it. Allah the Exalted destroyed Bukhtanassar with a gnat that entered his brain, and Allah the Exalted saved those of the Children of Israel who remained and returned them to Jerusalem, and they rebuilt it for thirty years, and they multiplied until they were as good as they had been. At that point Allah the Exalted gave him life.

(He) said: a resumption (istinaf) based on a question, as if it were said: "Then what did He say to him?" and it was said: he said, ﴿How long did you remain?﴾ so that his inability to comprehend the affairs of Allah the Exalted would become manifest in the most complete way, and so that the source of his remoteness-judgment would be cut off entirely. *Kam* (how many) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and its specifier is elided, its implied sense being "how many times." The operating element for it is ﴿remained﴾. The apparent view is that the speaker is Allah the Exalted. It is said: it was a voice from heaven. It is said: it was Gabriel. It is said: a prophet. It is said: a believing man who witnessed him on the day he died and lived until the time of his revival. In that case the attribution to Allah the Exalted is metaphorical.

﴿He said: I remained a day or part of a day﴾: he said this on the basis of approximation and estimation, or as an underestimation of the duration of his stay. It is said: he died in the forenoon and was raised after the hundred years, before sunset, so he said, before looking at the sun, "a day," then he turned and saw a remnant of it, so he said, "or part of a day," as a correction (idrab). It was objected that there is no basis for asserting that a full day had passed, even if calculated from sunset, because the deficiency at its beginning is certain.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 2 of 3):

﴿He said: Rather, you have remained a hundred years.﴾ This is an conjunction (ʿaṭf) on an implied clause, meaning: you did not remain that length of time, but rather this amount. ﴿So look at your food and your drink.﴾ It was said: his food was grapes or figs, and his drink was juice or milk. ﴿It has not spoiled (lam yatasannah)⁠﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿—﻿﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿﻿—﻿﻿—﻿—﻿﻿﻿﻿.﴾ That is, it has not changed over this lengthy period. Its derivation is from sanah (year), and there is a difference regarding its final radical. It was said that it is a hāʾ, as evidenced by sānahtu fulānan; so it is jussive (majzūm) by the sukūn of the hāʾ. It was also said that it is a wāw, as evidenced by the plural sanawāt; so it is jussive by the deletion of the last letter, and the hāʾ is the hāʾ of pause (hāʾ al-sakt), which is retained in pausal and continuous speech, treating it as if it were so. It is also possible that tasannuh is an expression for the passing of years, as is the original sense, and that non-tasannuh is a metonymy for its remaining in its state, fresh and tender, without becoming rancid. It was also said that its original form was lam yatasannan, and from it comes al-ḥamaʾ al-masnun, meaning changed clay. When three similar letters come together, one of them is converted into a weak letter (ḥarf ʿillah), as they said in tazannantu: tazannaytu, and in taqaḍḍaḍtu: taqaḍḍaytu. Here, in one view, the final nūn has been converted into a yāʾ, then the yāʾ into an alif, then it was deleted for the jussive. The negated clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and similar examples occur without a wāw, contrary to those who hesitated about it, such as the verse ﴿No harm touched them﴾ and ﴿or he said, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing had been revealed to him﴾. Its referent (ṣāḥib al-ḥāl) is either the food and drink, and the singular pronoun is used because they are treated as a single thing, like sustenance; or it is the latter (the drink) alone, and its state is taken as indicating the state of the former. This is supported by the reading of ʿAbd Allah: (and this is your drink, it has not spoiled). Ubayy read lam yassannah, with the tāʾ assimilated into the sīn. The dependence of ﴿So look﴾ on the remaining of a hundred years by means of the fāʾ has been questioned, since it implies change. It has been answered that what is made dependent is not the remaining of a hundred years, but the remaining of a hundred years without any change in his body, so that he thought it a short time; so there was made dependent on it what is more evident, namely the non-change of food and drink and the survival of the living being without nourishment. It was also said: the meaning is, if you have no assurance regarding the matter of resurrection, then look at your food and drink, which change quickly, until you know that One who does not change them is able to resurrect.

There is a consideration in this, because, apart from being contrary to the apparent sense, it is contradicted by His words: ﴿And look at your donkey﴾, how its bones were crumbled and its joints scattered; and this
صفحة 23
is the apparent sense, because it is more indicative of the state and more fitting to what follows. The view that what is meant is "look at it whole in its place, as you tied it, We preserved it without water or fodder, just as We preserved the food and drink," is nothing, and the transmitted reports do not support it. ﴿And that We may make you﴾ is connected to an implied element: that is, "and We did that so that We may make you"; some have made it postponed. It was also said that it is connected to what precedes, with the wāw being extra; and on this view it is conjoined to ﴿you have remained﴾, or to an implied element by way of resumption, meaning: We did that so that you may witness what you deemed unlikely, or so that you may be guided, and that We may make you. It was also said that it is conjoined to (he said), so there is an iltifāt (shift of address). (A sign) means a lesson or a guide ﴿for the people﴾, that is, their kind, or those of his people who remained, or those present in this age, in that they may see you, though you are one of the people of the bygone centuries, and take from you what has been hidden from them for ages of Torah knowledge. In this there is evidence for the lengthy sleep mentioned, and for this reason it is linked with the command to look at his donkey.

﴿And look at the bones﴾, that is, the bones of the donkey, as said by al-Suddi. The command is repeated because what was commanded first is looking at them with regard to the indication of a lengthy stay, and second is looking at them with regard to life coming upon them and its beginnings. It was also said: the bones of the dead people of the town. It is reported from Qatadah, al-Ḍaḥḥak and al-Rabiʿ: the bones of his own self; they said: the first thing God the Exalted revived in him was his eyes, while the rest of his body was dead and his bones were decayed, so he was commanded to look at them. It was also said: his bones and the bones of his donkey; and all of these are not to be relied upon.

﴿How We raise them﴾ with the dotted zāy, from inshāz, which is raising; that is, how We lift them from the earth and return them to their places in the body. al-Kisāʾi said: We soften them and magnify them. Ubayy read (nunshiʾuha), and Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr and Yaʿqub read (nunshiruha), from anshara God the Exalted the dead, meaning He revived them. Perhaps the intended meaning of reviving is what preceded, not its literal sense, given His words: ﴿Then We clothe them with flesh﴾, that is, We cover them with it as we cover the body with clothing. Abān from ʿAsim read (nanshuruha), with a fatḥah on the nūn and ḍammah on the shīn and rāʾ; and then it is from nashr, the opposite of folding, as al-Farrāʾ said; so the meaning is, how We spread them out. The clause is said to be either a circumstantial clause from the bones, meaning: and look at them assembled and clothed with flesh; or a substitute of inclusion, meaning: and look at the bones, how they were raised and how the flesh was spread over them. The circumstantial reading was objected to on the grounds that the clause is interrogative, and an interrogative cannot be a circumstantial clause; it was answered that the interrogative is not its true meaning, so what prevents its being circumstantial? Perhaps the non-mention of the manner of breathing in the spirit, as has been said, is because wisdom does not require its explanation. In some reports, an angel called out to the bones, and they responded and came from every direction; then He clothed them with sinews and tendons, then covered them with flesh, then made skin and hair grow over them, then breathed the spirit into it, and the donkey stood up, raising its head and ears to the sky, braying.

﴿So when it became clear to him﴾, that is, became completely clear to him what the command indicated regarding the manner of revival with its beginnings. The fāʾ is for conjunction to an implied element that the command mentioned requires; and it was omitted to signal that its occurrence is evident and needs no mention, and to indicate the swiftness of its occurrence, as if it were said: so God the Exalted revived it and clothed it with flesh, and he looked at it, and its manner became clear to him. When that became so, ﴿he said: I know that God is over all things﴾, and among all things is what was witnessed, ﴿Capable﴾ [259]. It was also said: the subject of (became clear) is an implied pronoun explained by the object of (I know), so the sentence is of the type of tanāzuʿ (contention of verbs) according to the Basran school. This is objected to on the grounds that the condition for tanāzuʿ, as the grammarians state, is that the two verbs share the same governed element by coordination or similar, so that they are linked; thus one cannot say "he hit me, I insulted Zayd." It was said: this is nothing, because only Ibn ʿUsfur stipulated it, and others of the same discipline, such as Abu ʿAli and others, expressed the opposite; moreover it is not restricted to coordination, since it occurs in His words: ﴿Here, read my book﴾. And (lammā, "when") is a linking particle for the two clauses, so a similar thing suffices for the linking even if they did not state it explicitly. Some people found it good to place it among cases where the intended meaning of the verb is the very occurrence of the act, not the agent's being engaged in it; so its meaning would be: when the becoming clear occurred to him, he said, "I know," etc. This is supported by the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, ﴿So when it was made clear to him﴾ in the passive. The choice of the present form signals that his knowledge of this is continuous, given that the original state had not changed, rather only its attribute was replaced through direct observation; and in it is an indication that he spoke as he did on the basis of the ordinary sense of improbability and magnification of the matter. Ibn Masʿud read (It was said: "Know!") in the imperative. Saʿid ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he used to read ﴿He said: I know﴾ and would say: he was no more excellent than Abraham, peace be upon him, to whom God the Exalted said: ﴿And know that God﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i also read thus. The commander is God the Exalted, or the Prophet, or the angel; and it is possible that the addressee is himself, by way of self-address, rebuking himself and reproaching him for that improbability that had overtaken him.

It is related that after this statement he rose, mounted his donkey, and went until he reached his neighborhood. The people did not recognize him, nor he them, nor did he recognize their dwellings. He set off, as a guess on their part, until he reached his house, and there he found an old blind woman, paralyzed, who had reached one hundred and twenty years of age; she had been his maidservant, and ʿUzayr had left when she was twenty years old. He said to her: "O woman, is this the house of ʿUzayr?" She said: "Yes," and wept, and said: "I have not seen anyone for such and such years mention ʿUzayr, and people have forgotten him." He said: "Then I am ʿUzayr." She said: "Glory be to God! ʿUzayr we lost a hundred years ago, and no mention of him has been heard." He said: "I am ʿUzayr; God the Exalted made me die for a hundred years, then raised me." She said: "ʿUzayr was a man whose supplication was answered; he would pray for the sick and the afflicted for health and cure. So call upon God the Exalted to return my sight to me, so that I may see you; if you are ʿUzayr, I will recognize you." He prayed to his Lord, and passed his hand over her eyes, and they were healed; he took her by the hand and said: "Rise, by God's permission." God the Exalted released her legs, and she stood up healthy, as if she had been loosed from a shackle. She looked and said: "I bear witness that you are ʿUzayr." She set off to the quarter of the Children of Israel, to their gatherings and assemblies. ʿUzayr's son was an old man of a hundred and eighteen years, and his sons' sons were elders in the assembly. She called out to them and said: "This is ʿUzayr; he has come to you." They denied her, so she said: "I am so-and-so, your freedwoman. He called to his Lord, and He returned my sight to me and released my legs, and he claimed that God the Exalted had made him die for a hundred years and then raised him." The people rose, came to him, and looked at him. His son said: "My father had a black birthmark between his shoulders." He uncovered his shoulders, and there it was: he was ʿUzayr. The Children of Israel said: "There was no one among us who memorized the Torah, as far as we have been told, except ʿUzayr. Bukhtnassar burned the Torah, and nothing of it remained except what men had memorized. So write it down for us." His father had buried the Torah in the time of Bukhtnassar in a place that no one but ʿUzayr knew. He set off with them to that place, dug it up, and extracted the Torah; the paper had rotted and the book had decayed. He sat in the shade of a tree while the Children of Israel were around him, and two meteors descended from heaven until they entered his body, and he recalled the Torah and renewed it for the Children of Israel. In another report, he recited it to them when they asked him for it, from memory, without omitting a single letter. A man from the descendants of those captives who returned to Jerusalem after the death of Bukhtnassar said: "My father told me on the authority of my grandfather that the Torah was buried on the day of our captivity in a jar in a vineyard; if you show me my grandfather's vineyard, I will bring it out for you." They went to his grandfather's vineyard, searched it, and found it. They compared it with what ʿUzayr had dictated to them from memory, and they did not differ in a single letter. At that point they said: ﴿"ʿUzayr is the son of God"﴾; God is exalted far above that, a great exaltation.

* * *

Among the allusive and esoteric interpretations of the verses: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾, because in reality it is the guidance derived from the inner light that is inherent in the primordial nature, and compulsion has no place in it. ﴿The right course has become distinct﴾ and clear, which is the path of Unity, and has been distinguished ﴿from error﴾, which is looking at other than God. ﴿Whoever disbelieves in the false deities﴾, which is everything other than God the Exalted, ﴿and believes in God﴾ with a true, witnessing faith, ﴿has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾, which is the essential Unity, ﴿that has no breaking﴾ in itself.

Because it is the one that agrees with what is in reality, and all possibilities and matters fall within its scope without being cut off from it. ﴿And God is All-Hearing﴾, who hears the words of everyone who holds a religion, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of their intentions. ﴿God is the Ally of those who believe﴾; there is no ally besides Him, and no helper or supporter for them other than Him. ﴿He brings them out from﴾ the darkness of the self (nafs), the doubts of imagination and illusion, into the light of certainty, guidance, and the expanse of the world of spirits. ﴿As for those who disbelieve﴾, by inclining toward other than Him, ﴿their allies are the false deities (taghut)﴾, which stand between them and God Exalted, so they do not turn toward Him. ﴿They bring them out from﴾ the light of readiness (isti'dad) and innate guidance (fitra) into the darknesses of the attributes of the self, doubts, and misgivings. ﴿Those﴾ are the ones who are distanced from the Presence, ﴿the companions of the Fire﴾ of nature, ﴿therein they abide forever﴾.

﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord?﴾ He is Nimrod: the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammara), disputing with Abraham, who is the holy spirit (al-ruh al-qudsiyya), which was thrown into the fire of nature, and it became for it "cool and safe." Or he is Nimrod the tyrant, and Abraham the Friend of God, peace be upon him. ﴿When God had given him the kingdom﴾, which is the world of bodily powers and the rule of this lowly world. ﴿When Abraham said﴾, the spirit, or Abraham the Friend of God, ﴿"My Lord"﴾, that is, the One by whose illumination I have been nourished, or by whose bringing into being and guidance I have been nourished, ﴿"is the One who gives life"﴾ to whoever turns toward Him, ﴿"and causes death"﴾ to whoever turns away from Him. Or: He gives life and causes death through the known kinds of life and death. ﴿He﴾, Nimrod, the commanding self or the tyrant, said: ﴿"I give life"﴾ to some of the powers by directing them into the fields of pleasures and inhaling the scent of desires, ﴿"and I cause death"﴾ to some of them by suspending them from that for a time. Or: I give life by pardon and cause death by killing. ﴿Abraham said﴾, the spirit or the Friend, ﴿"Indeed God brings the sun from the east"﴾, the sun of gnosis (irfan), from its rising place, which is the side of the overflowing origin, ﴿"so bring it from the west"﴾; that is, make it appear after its setting, when the land of existence stands as a barrier between you and it. Or: God brings the sun of the spirit from its rising place, which is its original source, so its lights shine upon the surfaces of the body. "So bring it" after it has set, that is, return it to the one you killed and caused to die. On this reading, it is a continuation of the first part. ﴿Thus was confounded﴾ and overcome ﴿the one who disbelieved﴾, who is the commanding self claiming lordship over the throne of the body, or the accursed Nimrod. ﴿Or like the one who passed by﴾, who is the human intellect, ﴿a town﴾, which is the heart, the Holy House; or he is Uzair the Prophet, who had come to Bayt al-Maqdis before the manifestation of the divine Name "the Giver of Life." ﴿It was in ruins﴾, empty of beneficial manifestations, ﴿standing upon its roofs﴾, its forms; or fallen and collapsed, because the foundation of readiness was weak, upon the roofs of resolutions. He said, ﴿in his bewilderment﴾, from his heedlessness of looking at realities, ﴿"How will God bring this to life﴾ (the town), ﴿the One who combines the attributes of beauty and majesty, ﴿"after its death"﴾ by the disease of ignorance and turning toward other than Him? ﴿So God caused him to die﴾, that is, He left him ignorant, ﴿for a hundred years﴾, that is, a long period. It has also been said that it originally refers to eight years and four months, or twenty-five years. ﴿Then He raised him﴾ with real life, and asked him to determine the length of his stay. He did not think it was more than a day or part of a day, belittling the period of his stay in the death of ignorance, which ends in comparison to eternal life. Or He caused him to die by voluntary death during one of the aforementioned periods, so the period is the time of his discipline, his spiritual journey, and his striving in the way of God Exalted. Or He caused him to die a natural death, then raised him with life. He said: "Rather, you have remained in truth a hundred years."

﴿Look at your food﴾, which was figs or grapes. The first is an indication of the universal perceptions, since it is entirely pith, and the particulars are in it potentially, like the seeds in the fig. The second is an indication of the particulars, because the material accompaniments remain with them in perception, like the skin and the pits. ﴿And your drink﴾, which was date-juice or milk. The first is an indication of love, will, and the sciences of realities and truths; the second is an indication of beneficial knowledge, such as the sacred laws. ﴿It has not spoiled﴾, that is, it has not changed from what it was originally, according to the natural dispositions deposited in you. For the sciences are stored in every soul according to its readiness, and people are like mines of gold and silver, even if they are covered by materials and hidden for a period through wandering in the intermediate realms (barzakh) and their darknesses. They do not perish or change from their state, until the veil is lifted and they appear as they were. ﴿And look at your donkey﴾, which is the body carrying the heart, or the outward meaning. ﴿And so that We may make you a sign﴾, that is, a proof, ﴿for the people﴾, by Our raising you. ﴿And look at the bones﴾ of the powers, ﴿how We raise them﴾ and lift them from the earth of nature, ﴿then We clothe them with flesh﴾, which is gnosis, serving as a garment for them. He expressed it as flesh because of its growth and increase, whenever the spirit is nourished with the foods of witnessing and the drinks of union. The outward meaning is evident. ﴿So when it became clear﴾ and manifest to him, ﴿he said: I know﴾ with continuous knowledge ﴿that God is over all things﴾, and among them what was, ﴿Omnipotent﴾, nothing is beyond Him and nothing can frustrate Him.

[Page 26]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 260 (part 1 of 3):

﴿And when Abraham said﴾ is an explanation of strengthening the believers after a previous explanation, and of its difference from what preceded it, as we will point out, God willing. The word is in a different style. The adverbial phrase (ẓarf) is in the accusative, either governed by an implied verb, which is expressed by something similar in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and remember when He made you successors﴾. The mention of the time requires the mention of what is in it, by way of demonstrative proof. Or it is governed by "qāla" (said), which comes next, and the verification of this has already been discussed.

"Rabb" (My Lord) is a word of entreaty, whose mention is placed before the supplication in order to intensify the request for an answer. ﴿Show me﴾ is from the visual seeing (ru'ya baṣariyya), which is transitive with the causative hamza (hamzat al-naql) to two objects. So the "bā'" (the particle "bi"/"bā'") is its first object, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿how You give life to the dead﴾ is in the position of its second object, which is suspended (mu'allaq) from it. Most grammarians went to this view. It was objected that the visual seeing does not suspend, and it was answered that this was mentioned only by some grammarians, and Ibn Hisham rejected it, saying that it has been heard to suspend. In "Sharh al-Tawdih" it is said that it may be cognitive (ʿilmiyya). Some people did not make what is here a suspension at all, and made the word "how" (kayfa) etc. in the sense of a verbal noun, which is the object, as Ibn Malik said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it became clear to you how We dealt with them﴾.

Then, the interrogative with "how" is only a question about something whose existence is established for both the questioner and the one questioned. So the interrogation here is about the manner of giving life, which is established for the questioner; that is, show me the modality of Your giving life to the dead. He, peace be upon him, asked in order to move from the rank of knowledge of certainty (ʿilm al-yaqīn) to the vision of certainty (ʿayn al-yaqīn). In a report: "Hearsay is not like seeing with one's own eyes." This was when he saw a carcass being torn apart by the beasts of land, sea, and air. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and Qatada, and it is what is related from the People of the House (ahl al-bayt). It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Suddi, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr that the angel gave him the good news, peace be upon him, that God, exalted is He, had taken him as a friend (khalīl), and that He answers his call and gives life to the dead by his supplication, so he asked for that. It is related from Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn Yasar that the cause of the question was a dispute with Nimrod over giving life, when he (Nimrod) claimed that pardon is giving life, and he (Abraham) refuted him, and Nimrod threatened him with death unless God, exalted is He, gives life to the dead in a way that he could witness. So he then prayed.

"[He] said" is a resumed statement built upon the question, and the pronoun refers to the Lord. ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ is conjoined to an implied clause, that is: Do you not know, and have you not believed, that I am capable of giving life in whatever manner I will, so that you ask me about it, or that I have taken you as a friend, or that the Compeller does not kill you? "[He] said" — that is, Abraham — "Yes" — I believed in that. ﴿But﴾ I asked ﴿so that my heart may be at rest﴾, that is, be calmed, ﴿my heart﴾, by joining the seen realities to faith and certainty that You are capable of that. Or: so that my heart may be at rest through friendship, or that the Compeller does not kill me. In every case, no deficiency returns to Abraham from this question, and it does not contradict the station of prophethood at all.

People have a fondness for asking about this verse, and what has been mentioned is the well-known view concerning it. I am pleased with what some verifying scholars have written on this point, and expanded upon in defending the Friend (al-Khalil), peace be upon him, in speech: that the question was not about doubt in a religious matter, God forbid, but a question about the modality of giving life, in order to encompass knowledge of it. The modality of giving life does not require faith to include knowledge of its form. So the Friend, peace be upon him, sought knowledge of what faith does not depend upon knowing. This is indicated by the question coming in the form of "how," whose subject is asking about the state. A parallel to this is that a speaker says: How does Zayd judge among people? He does not doubt that he judges among them, but he asked about the manner of his known judgment whose existence is established. Had he been asking about its existence, he would have said: Does Zayd judge among people? Since illusion may toy with some thoughts so that they are attributed to Abraham, and God forbid that doubt be attributed to him from this verse, the Prophet ﷺ cut off the root of this illusion by saying, as a matter of humility: "We are more deserving of doubt than Abraham" — that is, we have not doubted, so Abraham is even less likely to doubt. It was said: the speech with "more" (afʿal) came here to negate the meaning from the Beloved and the Friend, peace be upon them both — that is, there is no doubt with us all. From this category is ﴿Are they better, or the people of Tubba'?﴾ — that is, there is no good in either group. The affirmation came afterward because that form, although it is used apparently in asking about the manner, as you know, may also be used in declaring incapacity, as when a claimant claims that he can carry a load of burdens, while you are certain of his inability to carry it, so you say to him: Show me how you carry this, meaning that you are incapable of carrying it. So when He, glorified is He, knew the innocence of the Friend from circling around the sanctuary of this meaning, He wished to make him utter in the answer what would repel that verbal possibility in the first expression, so that his faith would be sincere with an expression that explicitly states it, understood by everyone who hears it without any doubt occurring to them. The meaning of tranquility then is the calm of the heart from wandering among the possible modes of giving life, through the appearance of the witnessed picture. Not having attained this tranquility before does not contradict the attainment of faith in the power to give life in its most perfect forms. I do not see that seeing the modality added anything to his faith that was required of him, peace be upon him; it only conveyed something that faith does not require. From here you know that ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, did not claim for himself a rank in faith higher than the Friend's rank in it, by his saying: "Had the veil been lifted for me, I would not have increased in certainty," as the ignorant among the Shi'a supposed.

Many of our companions, since they did not come upon what we have verified, have strained to repel what might be imagined from the words of the Friend and the Commander (al-Amir) concerning the superiority of the second over the first. Some repelled it by saying that certainty can be imagined to be subject to denial, as in His saying: ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were certain of them﴾, while tranquility cannot be imagined to be subject to that. This is attributed to the Proof of Islam al-Ghazali, and there is something in the heart about it. Others determined in repelling it that the station of prophethood differs from the station of truthfulness (ṣiddīqiyya). The station of prophethood has its tranquility and its lack of tranquility according to it, and the station of truthfulness has its tranquility and its lack of tranquility according to it too. The tranquility of the station of prophethood was for the Seal of the Prophets ﷺ, as he revealed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you not seen how your Lord extended the shadow?﴾ according to what the people of taste understand from the verse. The preparedness of Abraham, and likewise of Moses, peace be upon them both, was directed toward seeking that tranquility, as they expressed about themselves with ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ and ﴿My Lord, show me, that I may look at You﴾. The tranquility of the station of truthfulness belonged to the truthful (ṣiddīqīn) of the community of Muhammad ﷺ, as the Imam of the truthful, may God ennoble his face, revealed about himself with his saying: "Had the veil been lifted…" etc. The preparedness of the truthful of the rest of the prophets was directed toward seeking that tranquility. So the superiority was established for Muhammad ﷺ over all his brother prophets, and truthfulness over all the truthful of their communities. The truthful did not gain superiority over the prophets by finding their tranquility when the prophets lost theirs, because what they lost of tranquility is other than what the truthful found of it. The prophets lose only the tranquility appropriate to the station of prophethood, and the truthful did not find the like of that tranquility; they found only a tranquility appropriate to the station of the truthful. Had the prophets been content with its like, it would have been theirs, and more exalted than that by several degrees. The greatest truthful, may God be pleased with him, acknowledged this divergence when it reached him from the Messenger of God ﷺ that he said: "Indeed I forget," and he said: "Would that I were the forgetting of Muhammad ﷺ," for he knew that what the Messenger of God ﷺ counted as forgetfulness from his noble self was above the highest vigilance of the truthful, since the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of the near ones, and the good deeds of the near ones are the sins of the prophets. This is better than what preceded.

Some of the Sufis, like the ignorant among the Shi'a, adhered to the apparent meaning of each of the two statements and claimed that the saints (awliyā') and truthful of this community are higher in rank than the prophets, even if they attained the station of truthfulness, citing what is related from the Divine Imam, my master and my support, ʿAbd al-Qadir al-Kilani, may his secret be sanctified, that he said: "O company of prophets, the difference between us and you is in titles, and we were given what you were not given." And with some expressions of the Greatest Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, who speaks to that effect. You know that adhering to that and saying it breaches the consensus of the Muslims and collides with the definitive proofs of the superiority of the prophets over all creation. It is near that saying it is disbelief; indeed it has been said. As for what is related from Shaykh ʿAbd al-Qadir, may his secret be sanctified, it is among what has not been established as transmitted from him in a book relied upon. As for what is ascribed to the Greatest Shaykh, may his secret be sanctified, it is contradicted by other expressions of his, such as his saying, may his secret be sanctified — and he is the one whose biography is known as written by himself, and who counted himself among the greatest truthful, indeed the Seal of the Special Guardianship and the Muhammadan station: "There was opened for me the measure of the eye of a needle from the station of prophethood as a manifestation, not as entrance, and I nearly burned." Even granting the transmission of what was reported from those who reported it, and the assertion that the opposing claim lacks strength, we say: if that saying issued from its speaker in his annihilation in the Muhammadan Reality and the Ahmadi Essence, then the tongue at that time is its tongue and the speech is its speech, and that did not issue from him when seeing himself and standing at his rank. This is other than what the Shi'a went to, and far removed from it by stages. Perhaps the occasion will lead to verifying it more completely than this, God willing. The treasuries of thought, praise be to God, are full, and for every station there is a discourse.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that what is meant by tranquility here is knowledge in which there is no room for doubt, which is necessary knowledge (ʿilm al-ḍarūra), contrary to knowledge by inference (ʿilm al-istidlāl), in which such doubt is permissible. It was objected that knowledge that depends on a cause cannot be imagined to admit doubt as long as its cause is mentioned in the mind of the knower. What accepts doubt absolutely is belief, even if it is correct, while its cause remains in mind; by this, correct belief falls short of knowledge. It was answered that this is based on defining knowledge as a quality that produces a distinction that does not admit the opposite in any way, as Ibn al-Hajib mentioned in his "Mukhtasar"; and what has been said against it has been said, so reflect.

The lam in "li-yaṭma'inna" is the lam of purpose (lam kay), and the verb after it is in the subjunctive by an implied "an." It is not indeclinable, as al-Samin slipped into saying. The governed element of the lam is omitted, as we pointed out: what the exception ("istidrak") concerns has been omitted. It was said: the governed element is "arini," but I do not see it as anything. The past tense of the verb iṭma'anna is on the pattern of iqsha'arra. It has been disputed whether it is metathesized (maqlūb) or not. Sibawayh's view is that it is metathesized from iṭ'amanna: the ṭā' is the first radical, the hamza is its middle radical, and the mīm is its last radical; the last radical, which is the mīm, was moved before the middle, which is the hamza, so its pattern is iflaʿalla. Al-Jarmi's view is that it is not metathesized, and it seems he says that iṭ'amanna and iṭma'anna are two independent roots. Its verbal noun is al-ṭuma'nina, with the mīm sukun and the hamza fatha. It was said: ṭumānīna with the hamza lightened, and this is a regular analogy according to the Kufans, though it is against the analogy of verbal nouns according to all, since the analogy of iṭma'anna is that its verbal noun should be al-iṭmi'nān. And it was read "arnī" with sukun on the rā'.

[Page 29]

﴿He said﴾: i.e., the Lord. ﴿Then take﴾: the fa' (ف) here answers an implied conditional clause, meaning: if you wish that, then take. ﴿Four birds from among the birds﴾: It is well known that *tayr* (طير) is a collective noun (*ism jam'*), like *rakb* (ركب, riders) and *sifr* (سفر, travellers). It has also been said that it is the plural of *ta'ir* (طائر), like *tajir* (تاجر) and *tijr* (تجر), and this view was adopted by Abu al-Hasan. It has also been said that it is a lightened form of *tayyir* (طَيِّر) with shaddah. Abu al-Baqa' said: it is originally the verbal noun of *tara yatiru* (طار يطير), and then this category was named by it, and the *ta'* (ة) was added to its numeral because it is treated as masculine; the noun of genus for non-rational things may be masculine or feminine. The prepositional phrase (*jarr*) is connected to an omitted element that functions as a descriptive qualifier of what precedes it, or it is connected to *khudh* (take). It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are the *ghurnuq* (crane), the peacock, the rooster and the dove. It is narrated from Mujahid that instead of the *ghurnuq* it is the crow, and in another narration instead of the dove it is a duck, and in another narration a vulture. The specification of birds for this purpose is because they are the closest of creatures to humans in terms of seeking livelihood and dwelling. For this reason, the following hadith is reported: "If you were to rely upon Allah with the reliance due to Him, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds: they go out hungry in the morning and return full at evening." Also, birds combine the most distinctive features of animals, and it is easy to carry out on them processes of dividing and separating, and because they have more parts of feathers, so in bringing them back to life there is greater manifestation of power. [Page 30]

And because whoever is characterised by flying in the sky, and because it was in the aspiration of Abraham, peace be upon him, to incline toward the direction of height and to reach the malakut (the unseen realm), his miracle was fitting to his aspiration.

﴿Then cut them﴾ (*fa-surhunna*): Hamza and Ya'qub read it with a kasrah on the *sad* (صِ), while the rest read it with a dammah on the *sad* (صُ) with lightening (*takhfif*). Both are dialect forms of *sarahu yasuruhu* (صارَه يَصُوره) and *sarahu yasirahu* (صارَه يَصِيره) meaning "to cut" or "to incline," since it is common to both meanings, as Abu Ali mentioned. Al-Farra' said: the dammah is common to both meanings, while the kasrah means only cutting. It has also been said: the kasrah means cutting and the dammah means inclining. It is also reported from al-Farra' that *sarahu* (صاره) is an inversion of *saraahu 'an kadha* (صراه عن كذا), meaning to cut it. The correct view is that it is Arabic. It is reported from Ikrimah that it is Nabataean, from Qatadah that it is Abyssinian, and from Wahb that it is Greek (Rumi). If the intended meaning is "incline them," then the words ﴿to you﴾ are connected to it; if the intended meaning is "cut them," then it is connected to *khudh* (take) by way of its being construed as implying the meaning of inclining. Abu al-Baqa' preferred that it be a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of the implied object, meaning: then cut them, bringing them near and inclined to you. Ibn Hisham, following others, claimed that it is not valid to connect the prepositional phrase to *surhunna* (صرهن) in any case unless a genitive noun (*mudaf*) is assumed, i.e., "to yourself," arguing that a non-cognitive verb governing an attached pronoun cannot extend to a detached pronoun. This was refuted by saying that this is prohibited only when the verb is transitive by itself, but a verb transitive by means of a preposition is permissible, as the scholars of Arabic grammar have explicitly stated.

Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read (*fa-surrahunna*) with a shaddah on the *ra'* (رّ) together with a dammah or kasrah on the *sad*, from *surrahu* (صرّه), meaning to gather it. The *ra'* is either dammah for harmonisation (*ittiba'*), or fathah for lightening, or kasrah due to the meeting of two unvocalised letters. He also read (*fa-sarrihinna*) from *tasriyah* (التصرية), with a fathah on the *sad* and a kasrah on the shaddah *ra'*, whose original form is *tasrirah* (تصررة), and one of the doubled letters was replaced with a *ya'*. Originally it is from *sarayta al-shah* (صَرَيْتَ الشاةَ), meaning when you do not milk a sheep for days until the milk gathers in its udder; then it was used with the simple meaning of gathering: i.e., gather them and bring them together to you, so that you may contemplate them and know their condition in detail, so that after the revival you will know that not even a single part of them had moved from its original place at all.

﴿Then place﴾: i.e., throw, or make, after slaughtering them and mixing their flesh, feathers and blood, as Qatadah said ﴿upon every mountain﴾: wherever you are able to place them on it. He did not specify which mountain, as was reported from Mujahid and al-Dahhak. It is reported from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah that the mountains were four; from Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi that they were seven; and from Abu Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with him, that they were ten. ﴿A part of them﴾: i.e., a piece and a portion, a quarter, or a seventh, or a tenth, or otherwise. It is read (*juz'an*) with two dammahs, and (*juzzan*) with its hamza dropped for lightening, then with shaddah when pausing, then making the connected form like the pause form. It is the object of *ij'al* (اجعل), and the two prepositional phrases before it are connected to the verb. It is permissible for ﴿upon every﴾ to be a second object if it means *sayyir* (make). ﴿Of them﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of ﴿a part﴾, because originally it was an adjective of the indefinite noun but it was placed before it.

﴿Then call them﴾: i.e., summon them. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Hasan that he said: he, peace be upon him, called out: "O bones that have been scattered, O flesh that has been dispersed, O veins that have been severed, come together!" Allah would return their spirits into them, so the bone leapt to the bone, the feather flew to the feather, and the blood flowed to the blood, until each bird returned with its blood, flesh and feathers. Then Allah revealed to Abraham: "You asked Me how I give life to the dead, and I created the earth and placed in it four winds: the north wind, the east wind, the south wind and the west wind. When the Day of Resurrection comes, a trumpeter will blow into the Trumpet, and whoever is on the earth of the slain and dead will gather, just as four birds gathered from four mountains." Then he recited: ﴿Your creation and your resurrection are only like that of a single soul﴾. It is also narrated from Mujahid that he called them by the name of the God of Abraham, "Come, be swift." This raised the problem that calling inanimate things is not meaningful, and it was answered that it is of the type of calling for creation (*du'a' al-takwin*). It has also been said that there is an omission in the verse, as if it were said: "Then cut them, then place upon every mountain from each one of them a part, and Allah will give them life, and when He has revived them, then call them." ﴿They will come to you running﴾: thus the calling occurred after the revival. It is not hidden that the reports, along with what they contain of artificiality, do not support this; and more corrupt than that is what has been said: that he placed upon every mountain one of them as a living bird, then called it, and it came. This is an invalidating of the purpose of the request and contradicts the authentic reports, most of which state that he called them dead and scattered in parts; and in some, that their heads were in his hand, and when he called them, each part came to its companion until they became bodies, then they came to their heads, and each body joined its head, so each one returned to the form it had been in. ﴿Running﴾ (*sa'yan*) is a circumstantial qualifier of the subject of ﴿they will come to you﴾, meaning: hastening, swiftly, by flying or walking. It has also been said that applying *sa'y* (running) to flying is a metaphor. It is permissible for it to be in the accusative as a verbal noun, like *qa'adtu julusan* (I sat sitting).

Among the strange things is what is reported from al-Nadr ibn Shumayl, who said: I asked al-Khalil ibn Ahmad about the verse ﴿they will come to you running﴾: does one say that a bird, when it flies, runs? He said: no. I said: then what is its meaning? He said: its meaning is: they will come to you while you are running, running. This is among the unnecessary artificialities. Allah, glorified is He, only mentioned the narration of His commands, exalted is His majesty, without referring to the compliance of His friend, peace be upon him, nor to what resulted from it of the signs of His power, of which you have known a little, to indicate that the consequence of those matters from these majestic commands, and the impossibility of their failing to follow them, is so clear and manifest that there is no need to mention it at all. Some claimed that the Friend, peace be upon him, did not do anything of what the apparent meaning of the speech requires, and that the commands in it are like your saying to someone who does not know how to make ink: take such and such, pound them, place such and such upon them, put that in the sun for some days, then use it and you will find it good ink. This does not require compliance, since the purpose is mere instruction.

The seeing here is cognitive knowledge, as is reported from the *Sharh al-Tawdih*. Abraham had complete knowledge merely by the description of the manner, and his heart was at rest and his mind was calm. For this reason Allah did not mention what resulted from these commands of those matters, nor did He refer to compliance, nor did He pay attention to any allusion to it by statement or state. Abu Muslim inclined to this view and also denied the story, saying: when Abraham, peace be upon him, asked his Lord to revive the dead and He showed him a tangible example, the matter became easy for him. The meaning of ﴿incline them﴾ is: accustom them and train them to respond, meaning: train the four birds so that when you call them, they respond to you while alive. The purpose of this is to mention a tangible example of the return of spirits to bodies in an easy manner. It is not hidden that this contradicts the consensus (*ijma'*) of Muslims, and is a kind of nonsense upon which the people of religion do not rely, and a deviation from what the apparent meaning of the verse requires, which is supported by authentic reports and sound transmissions, toward what hearing rejects and no caller calls to. Therefore, the truth is to follow the community, and the hand of Allah is with them.

In the verse there is evidence for the one who holds that the revival of the dead on the Day of Resurrection is by gathering the scattered parts and sending the spirit back into them after their reassembly, and it is not of the category of re-creating something entirely non-existent, because Allah, glorified is He, explained the manner by separation, then gathering, and the return of the spirit, and He did not annihilate anything there except the formal part and the compositional structure, not the material parts. Some also used it as evidence that the structure is not a condition for life, because He, exalted is He, made each one of those parts and fragments a living being capable of running and moving swiftly.

Al-Qadi said: the verse indicates that structure is necessary, since cutting up caused the nullification of life. It was answered that the occurrence of concomitance does not indicate that concomitance is obligatory, and the separation in some states indicates that concomitance, wherever it occurs, was not obligatory. And since the verse indicates that those parts understood the calling, it is a decisive proof that structure is not a condition for life. But there is scrutiny in this.

It is well known that it is a proof against the one who holds that faith does not increase [Page 31] nor decrease. It is evident that it increases in quality, even if it does not increase in quantity. But what is obligated is the certainty acquired through reflection and inference, which some call *ilm al-yaqin* (knowledge of certainty), not the certainty that arises from direct observation, called *ayn al-yaqin* (eye of certainty), because obligating that would be a hardship in religion. You know that the verse's indication of the increase and decrease of faith, on the basis of the aspect we pointed out as preferred, is uncertain, as is not hidden. Also in it is evidence of the excellence of the Friend, peace be upon him, and the blessing of humble supplication in prayer, and the goodness of manners in asking, since Allah, glorified is He, showed him in the present moment what he asked for in the easiest way possible, and He showed Uzair, peace be upon him, what He showed him after causing him to die for a hundred years.

﴿And know that Allah is Mighty﴾: overpowering in His command, ﴿Wise﴾ [260]: possessing perfect wisdom in His acts. Therefore, the structuring of His acts is not based upon ordinary causes out of incapacity to break customs, but because it contains wisdoms and benefits. It is related that when Allah, glorified is He, fulfilled to Abraham, peace be upon him, what he asked for, He said to him: "O Abraham, We showed you how We give life to the dead; now show Us how you cause the living to die," alluding to what He would command him regarding slaughtering his son, peace be upon him. This is from the category of intimacy with the Friend, and the circle of friendship is wide. However, the memorisers of the hadith scholars have not mentioned this report, and it has no transmission at all in the books of hadith.

* * *

From the allusive (*ishara*) dimension of this story: ﴿And when Abraham said: My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾: i.e., the dead of hearts through the disease of ignorance. ﴿He said: Have you not believed?﴾: i.e., do you not know this with certain knowledge? ﴿He said: Yes﴾: I know that.

But for direct witnessing there is a subtle meaning, for which the Friend asked for observation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 260 (part 3 of 3):

It is the one indicated by His, glory be to Him, saying: ﴿that my heart may be at rest﴾, which is Your throne. ﴿He said, "Take four of the birds"﴾, as an allusion to the inner birds that are in the cage of the body. They are four: the birds of the unseen, of the intellect, of the heart, of the soul (nafs), and of the spirit (ruh). ﴿Then draw them to you﴾, that is, gather them and slaughter them. So slaughter the bird of the intellect with the knife of love (mahabba) at the gate of the malakut (the realm of dominion), slaughter the bird of the heart with the knife of longing (shawq) at the gate of the jabarut (the realm of power), slaughter the bird of the soul with the knife of passionate love (ishq) in the fields of singleness (fardaniyya), and slaughter the bird of the spirit with the knife of helplessness in the bewilderment of the majesty of the secrets of lordship (rabbaniyya). ﴿Then place a portion of them on every mountain﴾. So place the intellect on the mountain of greatness, until the lights of the sovereignty of lordship (rububiyya) accumulate upon it and it becomes characterized by them, so that it may perceive Me through Me after its annihilation in Me. Place the heart on the mountain of pride, until I clothe it in a holy radiance, and it wanders in the wilderness of contemplation, described by the turning of the light of love. Place the soul on the mountain of might, until I clothe it in the light of greatness, so that it becomes tranquil when My lordship passes over it. Then it does not contend with Me in servanthood, nor seek the attributes of lordship. Place the spirit on the mountain of the beauty of eternity, until I clothe it in the light of lights, the might of might, and the holiness of holiness, so that it is expanded in intoxication (sukr), tranquil in sobriety (sahw), loving in expansion (inbisat), and firm in the manifestations (tajalliyyat).

﴿Then call them﴾, and summon them with the voice of the secret of love, ﴿and they will come to you in haste﴾ to pure servanthood, by the beauty of oneness (ahadiyya). ﴿And know that Allah is Mighty﴾, who honors you by your knowledge of these meanings and your awareness of His ancient attributes, ﴿Wise﴾ in His manifestation through the wondrous manifestations (tajalli) to the secrets of your inner self.

It may also be said: by the four birds, He, glory be to Him, has indicated the four powers that prevent the servant from the station of direct vision and witnessing the true life. It has been reported in a narration that they were a peacock, a rooster, a crow, and a dove. Perhaps the peacock is an allusion to vanity, the rooster to lust, the crow to greed, and the dove to love of the world, because of its attachment to its nest and tower. In another narration, the dove is replaced by a duck, and in another by a vulture. The first set is an allusion to overpowering greed, and the second to long hope. The meaning of ﴿so draw them to you﴾ in this case is: gather them, and incline them to you by restraining them and preventing them from going out in pursuit of their pleasures and yearning for what they are accustomed to.
