It is reported that he, upon him be blessings and peace, was commanded to slaughter them, pluck their feathers, mix their flesh and blood by pounding, and keep their heads with him, that is, to restrain them from their actions, remove their forms from the soul, suppress their impulses, natures, and habits through discipline, [Page 32] and keep their roots within it. Then he was commanded to place a portion of them on each of the mountains in his presence, which are the four elements that are the pillars of his body. It seems that he, upon him be blessings and peace, was commanded to subdue and extinguish them, until only their roots remain, fixed in existence, and the materials prepared in the natures of the elements that are within him. In another narration, the mountains were seven, and so by them He may indicate the seven limbs that are the parts of the body. In yet another, they were ten, and on this basis they may be an allusion to the outer and inner senses. By His command to call them, glory be to Him, He indicates that when those attributes are alive with their life, they are unsubmissive, wild, and resistant to accepting command. When they are slain, they live with the true life, the imagined life after passing away and effacement, which is the life of the servant. At that point they are obedient and submissive: whenever they are called, they come in haste and comply willingly. That is the great triumph.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 2, Verse 261**

﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾: that is, in the various channels of good, which include jihad and other things. It is said that what is meant is spending in jihad, because it is that which is multiplied in this manner. As for spending in other than it, it is not multiplied in the same way; rather, ﴿a good deed is rewarded tenfold﴾ only. ﴿is like a grain﴾: this is the predicate (khabar, the predicate of a nominal sentence) referring back to the subject (mubtada', the topic) before it. It is necessary to supply a genitive-construct noun (mudaf) at one of the two ends, that is: the likeness of the spending of those who [spend] is like a grain, or their likeness is like the likeness of a sower of a grain. Without that, the comparison would not be valid. The word ḥabbah is the singular of ḥabb, which is what is sown for sustenance, and its most common application is to wheat. The seed of what is not eaten as sustenance from herbs is called ḥibbah with a kasra. ﴿It produced seven spikes﴾: that is, that grain sent forth a stalk from which seven branches sprouted, each one bearing an ear.

﴿In every spike is a hundred grains﴾, as we see in many grains in fertile lands, and even more than that. The word sunbulah is on the pattern fun'ulah, so the nun is an augment, based on their saying asbala al-zar' meaning sanbala, when the ear appeared in it. It is also said that its pattern is fu'lulah, so the nun is original; but the first is the well-known view. Attributing the producing to the grain is a metaphor (majāz), because it is the cause of the growth, while the one who truly causes growth is Allah, exalted is He. This comparison is a depiction of the multiplication, as if it were present before the eyes of the beholder; so it is from the figure of speech that likens the intelligible to the perceptible (tashbīh al-ma'qūl bi al-maḥsūs).

﴿And Allah multiplies﴾ this multiplication or more than it, up to whatever Allah wills. Some have restricted it to the first, and some to the second, and generality is more complete in benefit. ﴿for whomever He wills﴾ of His servants who spend, according to their condition in sincerity, hardship, and placing the spending in its best positions. Ibn Majah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ali, may Allah honor his face, and Abu al-Darda', Abu Hurayrah, Imran ibn Husayn, Abu Umamah, Abdullah ibn Umar, and Jabir ibn Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them all, who related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "Whoever sends out a provision in the way of Allah and remains in his house, for him is seven hundred dirhams for every dirham; and whoever fights himself in the way of Allah, the Exalted, and spends in that cause, for him is seven hundred thousand dirhams for every dirham on the Day of Resurrection." Then he recited this verse. And from Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "Indeed, Allah has stored up for those who fight and spend from the treasuries of His mercy what the knowledge of the servants cannot encompass."

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing﴾: nothing is constrained for Him by what He bestows of increase [261]. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the intention of the spender and all his other conditions.

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that when Allah mentioned the story of the one who passed by the town and the story of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and these two were among the strongest proofs of the Resurrection, He mentioned what benefits a person on the Day of Resurrection and what finds its reward there, which is spending in the way of Allah, exalted is He. Just as He followed the story of ﴿those who went out from their homes, being thousands, fearing death﴾ with His saying, Mighty is His affair: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan?﴾ And just as He followed the killing of Dawud of Jalut and His saying: ﴿Had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another﴾ with His saying, glorified is He: ﴿O you who believe, spend of what We have provided you﴾, etc.

Page 33

In His mention of the grain in this comparison, there is also an indication of the Resurrection and the greatness of power: for whoever is capable of bringing forth from one grain in the earth seven hundred grains is capable of bringing the dead out of their graves, by a common factor they share, which is nourishment and growth.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 262:**

﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that begins a fresh clause), brought to explain the manner of spending whose excellence was described.

﴿Then they do not follow up what they have spent﴾, that is, their spending, or what they have spent, ﴿with reminders﴾ (*mann*) of favour to the one they spent upon, ﴿nor with injury﴾, that is, to him. *Mann* is the cutting off of kindness, and in its original sense it means "cutting." From it comes the saying (of the poet): "a weak rope (*habl matin*)," meaning a weak one. It may also be applied to a favour, because the benefactor cuts off a portion of his wealth for the one he benefits. *Adha* is boasting and vaunting over the one spent upon because of one's spending. *Mann* is mentioned first because it occurs more frequently. The particle *la* ("not") is placed in the middle so that the negation covers the following of each of the two. *Thumma* ("then") indicates the difference in rank between spending and abandoning reminders and injury, and the distance between them in degree. It has been borrowed from its original meaning, which is the distance of times, and this is the well-known usage in such contexts.

In *al-Intisaf* another interpretation of this is mentioned: ((It indicates the continuance of the verb it conjoins, and the extension of its duration. On this basis it does not leave the implication of distance in time. But its original meaning is the delay in the time of the occurrence and happening of the act, and its borrowed meaning is the continuance of the existence of the act and the delay in the time of its persistence. On this basis is interpreted the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿then they remained upright﴾, that is, they persisted in uprightness with a lasting persistence, extended in its duration. That uprightness is the one that is regarded, not what is cut off by turning aside to its opposite, such as deviation toward desire and appetites. Likewise ﴿then they do not follow up﴾ etc., that is, they persist in forgetting the favour, in leaving aside any reckoning of it and any reminding of it, and they are not those who abandon it at certain times and then return to injury and to the practice of reminders. Because of this, a similar usage occurs with *sin* (the future particle) as in ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾, since the delay of guidance has no meaning, so it is interpreted as the continuance of the guidance granted to him, the delay of its duration, and the extension of its period.)) This is a good statement, and perhaps it is preferable to what they have mentioned, because it preserves the literal meaning more fully and is closer to the proper usage in the best manner.

As al-Wahidi reported from al-Kalbi, and the responsibility for it rests upon him, the verse was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. As for Abd al-Rahman, he "came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with four thousand dirhams as charity, and said: I had eight thousand dirhams, so I kept four thousand for myself and my dependants, and I lend four thousand to my Lord." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "May Allah bless you in what you kept and in what you gave." As for Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, he said: "The equipment of one who has no equipment is upon me in the expedition to Tabuk," so he equipped the Muslims with a thousand camels with their saddles and their coverings, and he gave in charity the well of Rumah, which had been his, to the Muslims. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raising his hands, supplicating for Uthman and saying: 'O Lord, Uthman ibn Affan, I am pleased with him, so be pleased with him,' and he continued raising his hands until dawn broke." Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed concerning him ﴿Those who spend﴾, etc.

﴿For them is their reward﴾, as He promised them, in the illustrative part (*damir al-tamthil*), and it is a nominal sentence of subject and predicate that has come as a predicate concerning the relative pronoun. In the repetition of the predication and in restricting the reward by His saying, exalted is He, "for them" ﴿with their Lord﴾, there is emphasis and honour that is not hidden. The apparent requirement would have been to introduce the particle *fa* ("so") into the scope of the relative clause, because it includes the meaning of a condition, as in your saying: "Whoever comes to me, for him is a dirham." However, it departed from that in order to convey that these spenders deserve the reward for their own selves, and for the intention of good that was established in their souls, and not because of the attribute of spending; for deserving by it is a descriptive deserving. In this there is a subtle encouragement that is not reached except by divine success. It has also been permitted that the omission of *fa*, which indicates that what precedes it is the cause of what follows, is intended to signal that the arrangement of the reward upon the mentioned spending and the abandoning of following reminders and injury is a clear matter that does not need explicit statement of causation.

﴿And no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ [262]. The intent is to state the continuance of the negation of these two, not to state the negation of their continuance. The discussion of a similar instance has already passed.

[p. 34]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 263:

﴿A kind word﴾, that is, a beautiful speech with which the beggar is answered, such as "May Allah have mercy on you," "May Allah provide for you," "If Allah wills, I will give you after this." ﴿And forgiveness﴾, that is, concealment of what the beggar has done of urgent insistence in asking and other things that burden the one being asked, and pardoning him for it, ﴿is better﴾ for the beggar ﴿than a charity﴾ given to him ﴿followed by injury﴾ from the giver ﴿to him﴾, because it is tainted by the harm that follows it, while the first two are free of harm. It was said: it is possible that by forgiveness is meant Allah's forgiveness of the one being asked, because of his bearing what he dislikes from the beggar; or the beggar's forgiveness of what is difficult for him from the refusal of the one being asked. "Better for the one being asked than that charity" — and in this there is a point: the more fitting reading is that the one preferred and the one preferred over in this context are both attributes of one person, and on these two aspects this is not the case. Moreover, considering the comparison of goodness in both leads to the implication that in the described affair there is some good relative to him, although it is entirely void. And making the statement of the type "a thing is better than nothing, which is not a thing" is possible. The sentence is a resumed clause confirming the consideration of abandoning following charity with reminders and injury. The reason reminder is not mentioned is that injury includes it and other things; mentioning it earlier is out of concern for it because of how often it occurs from those who give charity and the difficulty they have in guarding against it. The beginning with an indefinite noun in the first is valid because it is specified by the description; in the second, by the conjunction or by the implied attribute. It may be said that the conjoined element is a follower and does not require a justifying factor.

﴿And Allah is Free of need﴾ from the charities of the servants, and He only commanded them to give for a benefit that returns to them, or free of need from charity accompanied by reminder and injury, so He does not accept it; or He is Free of need, who does not cause the poor to bear the burden of reminder and injury, and provides for them from another source. ﴿Forbearing﴾ [263], so He does not hasten punishment for reminder and injury; not that they do not deserve it because of them. The sentence is a concluding remark for what precedes it, containing promise and threat, confirming the consideration of goodness relative to the beggar with certainty.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 264:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ He turned to them with direct address after explaining, by way of the emphatic third person, what makes the obligation to act in accordance with the prohibition binding; therefore He called them by the attribute of faith. ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reminders [of favor] and injury﴾, meaning, with each one of these two separately, because negation is more deserving of generality and more indicative of it. The intended "reminder" (al-mann) is reminding the poor person of one's favor, as was mentioned earlier, and this is the well-known view. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, reported that it refers to reminding Allah of one's favor, and "injury" (al-adha) refers to injuring the poor person. Ibn 'Atiyyah raised an objection to this verse: its apparent meaning requires that the reward of charity be nullified by either of these two matters, and it is not possible for nullification to be directed at the charity itself, because it has already come into existence in reality, so its nullification cannot be conceived. It is part of the creed that bad deeds do not nullify good deeds, contrary to the Mu'tazilah, and this verse is one of their proof-texts. It was answered that charity which Allah, glorified is He, knows its giver to be one who reminds and injures is not accepted, to the point that it was said: He, glorified is He, makes a sign for the angel so that he does not record it. The nullification in dispute concerns only a valid act that has come to stand, in Allah's sight, within the realm of acceptance, and what is here is not such. Thus the meaning of ﴿do not nullify﴾ then is: do not perform this act as something void. So they said, and it is not hidden that this is contrary to the apparent meaning; however, the statement of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿like the one who spends his wealth to be seen by people﴾ contains a kind of support for it, based on the view that ﴿like the one who﴾ is in the accusative position, either as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: do not nullify them with a nullification like the nullification of the one who etc., or as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of ﴿do not nullify﴾, meaning: do not nullify them while resembling the one who spends, that is, the one who nullifies his spending by showing off. The point of support is that the show-off, by consensus, has not performed the act as accepted and valid, but has performed it as void and rejected, and the comparison has occurred in the clear sense, so reflect.

The accusative of (riya') is either because it is a reason for (yunfiqu), meaning for the sake of their showing off; or because it is a circumstantial clause from its subject, meaning he spends his wealth showing off. He took it as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, meaning spending for the show of people is nothing. Close to this is making the prepositional phrase a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the supposed verbal noun, because this works only according to the view of Sibawayh. The origin of riya' is ri'a', so the first hamza is the root letter of the word and the second is a substitute for a ya' which is the lam, because it occurred final after an extra alif. It is permissible to lighten the first hamza by converting it into a ya', to flee from the heaviness of a hamza after a kasra, and al-Khuza'i, al-Shumuni and others read it thus. The reciprocal form in its verb, according to al-Samin, is on its proper pattern, because the show-off makes people see his deeds and people make him see praise of him and exaltation of him. The intended meaning of the relative clause includes both the believer and the disbeliever, as has been said, but most exegetes hold that it refers to the hypocrite, due to His statement: ﴿and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, until he hopes for reward or fears punishment.

﴿So his example﴾, that is, the show-off in spending, and the fa' links what follows to what precedes, ﴿is like the example of a smooth rock﴾, that is, a large smooth stone; it is the plural of safwanah, or safa', or a collective noun, and it was preferred by the return of the pronoun to it in the singular in His statement: ﴿upon which is dust﴾, that is, a small amount of it, ﴿and then a heavy rain strikes it﴾, that is, rain of strong impact; the pronoun refers to the smooth rock, and it was said it refers to the dust.

﴿and leaves it bare﴾, that is, smooth, with no dust on it at all. This comparison may be taken as divided: the hypocrite is like the rock in non-benefit, and his spending is like the dust, since benefit is hoped for from both through reward and growth; and his show-off is like the heavy rain that quickly washes it away, harming him from where he thinks benefit lies. If it were taken as a single composite comparison it would also be valid, and it was said that this is the better view, while the first is not worthless.

﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾, that is, they do not find the reward of anything of what they spent in show-off, nor do they benefit from it at all. The sentence either explains the aspect of resemblance or is a resumptive sentence built on a question, as if it were said: what, then, will their condition be at that time? So it was said: they have no power. Making it a circumstantial clause from (alladhi), as al-Samin said, is weak, as is not hidden. The pronoun returns to the relative clause according to its meaning after its wording has been observed, since it is an attribute of a word singular in form but plural in meaning, like the collective and the group; or it is used for the plural, as in His statement: ﴿and you plunged as those plunged﴾ according to one opinion, and in the verse:

Indeed, those whose blood was spilled at Falj, they are the people, all the people, O Umm Khalid.

It was said that man and alladhi alternate, so it was treated here in their manner, but its remoteness is not hidden. The return of the pronoun to (those who have believed) because of a shift of address is among things not to be turned to.

﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ [264] to what would benefit them. The sentence is a concluding statement confirming the content of what precedes, and in it is an implicit indication that each of show-off, reminder and injury upon spending is a characteristic of disbelievers, and the believers must avoid them.

[p. 36]

﴿And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God﴾: that is, seeking His good pleasure, or seeking it for Him. ﴿And for firming up from their own souls﴾: that is, for the firming up of, or firming up some part of, their own souls in faith. Here *min* is partitive (*tab'idiyyah*), as in the saying of the Arabs: "He shook *min* his shoulders (*'atfayhi*)" and "he stirred *min* his vigour (*nashatihi*)." The soul has faculties, one of which is the impulse to give wealth and another the impulse to give life. Whoever harnesses the faculty of giving wealth for the sake of God, Exalted, has firmed up part of his soul, and whoever harnesses both the faculty of giving wealth and the faculty of giving life has firmed up his whole soul. It may also be said that the object of *tathbitan* (firming up) is omitted, meaning: a firming up of Islam and a confirming of the reward, from the root of their souls and hearts. In that case *min* is initial (*ibtida'iyyah*), as in the words of God, Exalted: ﴿out of envy from their own souls﴾. It is also possible that the meaning is: a firming up from their souls in the eyes of the believers, that they are true in faith and sincere in it. This is supported by the reading of Mujahid, "*wa-tabyinan min anfusihim*" (and a clarifying from their souls). It is also permitted that *min* carries the sense of *li* (for), so that the meaning is "a settling of their souls upon obedience to God, Exalted." This is the view taken by Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i, and it is not far-fetched. In this there is an indication that the wisdom of spending for the spender is the purification of the soul from miserliness and love of wealth, which is the incurable disease and the head of every sin.

﴿Like the likeness of a garden on a height﴾: that is, an orchard on a raised piece of ground. The intended meaning is the comparison of the expenditure of these people in its increase (*zaka'*) with this garden. Its being on a height is considered because the trees of elevated places are finer in appearance and more abundant in fruit, owing to the lightness of their air and its lack of density through stagnation. Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read *birabwatin* with a *fatha*, the rest with a *damma*, and Ibn 'Abbas with a *kasra*; it is also read *rubawatin*. All of these are dialectal forms. It is also read *ka-mathali habbatin* (like the likeness of a grain) with *ha'* and *ba'*. ﴿Which a heavy rain has struck﴾: a violent downpour. ﴿So it yielded﴾: that is, it gave its produce to its owner or to people. Attributing the giving to it is figurative (*majaz*). ﴿Its fruit﴾: with a *damma* on the *hamza*, *ukul* means the thing eaten, and what is meant is its fruit. It is attributed to it because it is its place or its cause. Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and Nafi' read *ukuluha* with a sukun on the *kaf* for lightness. ﴿Twofold﴾: that is, doubled after doubling, so the dual is for abundance; or twice what it used to yield at other times because of what the heavy rain struck it with; or four times that, based on the disagreement over whether *di'f* means a like or two likes. It was also said that what is meant is that it yields its fruit twice in a single year, as was said regarding the words of God, Exalted: ﴿giving its fruit every season﴾. Its accusative is as a circumstantial state (*hal*) of *ukuluha*, meaning multiplied. ﴿And if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain﴾: that is, then it is struck by light rain; or the one that strikes it is a light rain; or a light rain suffices for it. What is meant is that its goodness does not fail in any state, owing to its quality, the nobility of its soil, and the lightness of its air. *Tall* is the fine drizzle of rain, which is its gentle kind.

The essential meaning of this comparison is that the expenditures of these people are growing (*zakiyah*) with God, Exalted, and are never lost in any state, even if they vary according to the variation in what accompanies them of sincerity, toil, love of wealth, delivering them to the most needy and pious, and other things. Thus there is a comparison of the state of the growing expenditure, sought for the pleasure of God, Exalted, pure from defilements, because it is for firming up, arising from the spring of truth and sincerity, to the state of a garden growing and pure by means of the height, one of the two rains being the heavy and the other the light, and the common element being growth joined with purity in the most complete manner. This is a compound rational analogy (*tashbih murakkab 'aqli*). You may also consider the comparison of the state of those people with God, Exalted, to the garden on a height, and their expenditure, whether little or much, to the heavy and light rain. Just as each of the two rains doubles the produce of that garden, so their expenditure, whether great or small, after it is sought for the face of God, Exalted, grows and increases their nearness and the goodness of their state with their Lord, may He be glorified. Thus it has been said, and this is possible, that the comparison in this case is an analogy of separate parts (*mufarraq*). It is also possible that it is a compound analogy, and the discourse is directed toward guiding to the deriving of the aspect of resemblance and the method of composition. The difference in that case is that the state refers to the expenditure in the first and to the spender in the second.

The summary is that their state in producing little or much, multiplied for their rewards, is like the state of the garden in producing, from the heavy and light rains reaching it, a doubling of its fruits. Some of the scholars preferred the first, and others rejected the second, so understand.

﴿And God is Seeing of what you do﴾ [265]: so He recompenses each of the sincere and the show-off with what He knows best about him. Thus in general there is encouragement for the first and warning for the second, together with an indication of disparaging the latter, in that he directed his deed toward being seen by one whose seeing avails him nothing, and abandoned the countenance of the True Seer, whose seeing enriches and impoverishes, may His glory be exalted.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on Surah 2, Verse 266:**

﴿Would any one of you wish﴾ means: would any one of you love (*yuhibbu*). 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) read it this way in one narration from him. The *hamza* in it (*al-hamza*, the interrogative particle) is for denial (*al-inkar*, rebuke): ﴿that there should be for him a garden﴾. It is also read as *jannat* (gardens). ﴿of date-palms and grapevines﴾ means: consisting of these two precious kinds, on the understanding that they are its pillar and its foundation, not that it contains nothing else. *Al-nakhil* (date-palms) is said to be an *ism jam'* (collective noun, a noun that denotes a plural without being its regular plural form), and it is also said to be the plural of *nakhl*, which is an *ism jins jam'i* (a collective generic noun). *A'nab* (grapevines) is the plural of *inabah*, and it is said *'anba'*, so it is not declined (*la yanṣarif*) because of the extended feminine ending (*alif al-ta'nith al-mamduda*). Wherever the Qur'an mentions these two things, it specifies the palm tree rather than its fruit, and the grapevine's fruit rather than the vine itself. Perhaps this is because the whole palm tree is beneficial, and "how excellent are its uses": its root is firm and its branch is in the sky, ﴿yielding its produce every season by the permission of its Lord﴾. The greatest benefit of the grapevine is its fruit, rather than the rest of it. In some reports, which I have not found in any book relied upon, Allah the Exalted says: "Do you disbelieve in Me while I am the Creator of the grape?" *Al-jannah* (garden) is applied to densely intertwined trees, and also to the land that contains them. The first meaning is more fitting with His words ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾, for on the second meaning one needs to supply an omitted noun, namely "beneath their trees." Likewise, on the second meaning one needs to take the attribution of the burning to it (in what follows) as figurative (*majazi*, metaphorical). The clause is in the position of a raised (*raf'*) description of *jannah*, or in the position of a *ḥal* (circumstantial clause, a state of the noun) with respect to it, because it has already been described by the prepositional phrase preceding it.

﴿For him therein are of all the fruits﴾. The first adverbial phrase (*al-zarf al-awwal*, "for him therein") is in the position of a raised predicate placed before its subject. The second is a *ḥal* from the concealed pronoun in the predicate. The third is an adjective (*na't*) for an omitted subject, meaning: provision or fruit existing from all the fruits. It is permitted to take *min* as an extra particle (*ziyadat min*), according to the view of al-Akhfash, and in that case there is no need to say the subject is omitted. On both interpretations, the intended meaning of "the fruits" is not totality but abundance. Some people permitted that the intended meaning of "fruits" is benefits, and this makes the mention of those two kinds because the garden does not contain anything other than them. Among them is one who said this is an instance of mentioning the general after the specific for the sake of completeness (*al-ta'mim*), but this is nothing.

﴿And old age has struck him﴾: that is, there has come upon him the effect of advanced age and decrepitude. *Al-kibar* is more emphatic than *kibar* (with a different vowelling, meaning the state of being old). The *waw* is for the circumstantial state (*li'l-ḥal*), and the clause, with *qad* implied, is in the position of an accusative circumstantial state from the subject of *yawaddu*, meaning: would any one of you wish that in this state, which is the context of the greatest need for the benefits of that garden and the burden of being unable to make up for the means of livelihood? It is also said that the *waw* is for conjunction (*al-'atf*), and that the past tense is placed in the position of the present, as al-Farra' said, or that the present is interpreted as past, meaning: if he had a garden and old age had struck him. Abu Hayyan objected to this, on the grounds that it entails that the striking of old age falls within the scope of wishing, whereas no one wishes for old age. The answer is that this is not valid, since the interrogative is for denial, so it denies the combination of the two; yet what is in it is not hidden.

﴿And he has offspring, weak﴾: this is in the position of a circumstantial state from the pronoun in *asabahu* ("struck him"), meaning: old age has struck him, while he has small children who are weak, unable to earn or to arrange their livelihood and his. *Al-du'afa'* is the plural of *da'if*, like *shuraka'* is the plural of *sharik*. Leaving aside the expression "young children" (*ṣighar*) while contrasting it with "old age" is because it is more fitting, as is not hidden. It is also read as *di'af*.

﴿Then there struck it a whirlwind﴾: that is, a wind that turns upon itself and is like a minaret. It is called a *zawba'a* (whirlwind). It may be descending and it may be ascending, contrary to what the apparent sense of some speakers' words suggests in restricting it to the second type. The cause of the first type is that when a wind separates from a cloud and intends to descend, a piece of cloud obstructs it in its path of descent, strikes it from below, and the other winds push it from above. The two opposing pushes, one from above and one from below, remain, so the wind turns around as a result of the two opposing pushes. Sometimes the twisting of the passages increases the rotation, just as hair curls because of the twisting of its pores. The cause of the second type is that when the windy mass reaches the earth and strikes it with violent force, and then is firmly fixed, and another wind from its direction overturns it, it twists and turns. It may also arise from the meeting of two strong winds. Sometimes its strength reaches the point where it uproots trees and snatches ships from the sea. The sign of a descending one is that its coils ascend and descend together, like a dancer. The sign of an ascending one is that nothing is seen of its coils except ascent. Either of them may occur by the mere power of Allah the Exalted, without any apparent intermediary cause. Sometimes the rotation of the whirlwind includes a strong burning vapour, so it becomes fire that also rotates. Because this type is specified, the *i'sar* is described by His words, glorified is He, ﴿in it is fire﴾. The pronoun is masculine in agreement with the masculine notion in it. The wind was called *i'sar* because it coils the way a squeezed garment coils. It is also said that it is so called because it squeezes the clouds, or squeezes the bodies that pass by it. The tanwin in *nar* (fire) is for magnification (*al-ta'zim*). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that *al-i'sar* is a strong wind in general, and that the intended meaning of "fire" is the *samum* (scorching wind). He, glorified is He, mentioned the *i'sar* and described it with what was mentioned, and did not restrict himself to mentioning fire, as one might say "then fire struck it," because of the eloquence contained in that sentence for one who examines it carefully. ﴿So it was burned﴾: the verb joined by *fa'* is coordinated with *asabaha* ("struck it"). It is also said that it is coordinated with an omitted antecedent, meaning: so He burned it, and so it was burned. This, as is reported from al-Suddi, is an image of the state of one who spends and adds to his spending what nullifies it, in regret and grief, when the Day of Resurrection comes and his need for it intensifies, and he finds it as scattered dust, in the state of one whose condition is like this.

Abd ibn Humayd reported from 'Ata' that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "A verse from the Book of Allah, I have not found anyone who can satisfy me concerning it: His words, 'Would any one of you wish (that there be for him a garden)...' etc." Then Ibn 'Abbas said: "O Commander of the Faithful, I find something in myself concerning it." 'Umar said to him: "Then why do you belittle yourself?!" He said: "O Commander of the Faithful, this is a parable which Allah has set forth. He said: 'Would any one of you wish that his life be spent doing the deeds of the people of goodness and the people of happiness, until his age advances and his death draws near and his bones grow frail, and he is most in need of concluding his deeds with the best deed, yet he works with the deeds of the people of wretchedness, and so corrupts his deeds and burns them?'" He said: "So it fell upon the heart of 'Umar, and pleased him."

In a narration of al-Bukhari, al-Hakim, Ibn Jarir and a group from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them), he said: 'Umar said one day to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Concerning what do you think this verse was revealed: ﴿Would any one of you wish...﴾ etc.?" They said: "Allah knows best." Then 'Umar became angry and said: "Say, 'We know' or 'We do not know.'" Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is something in my self concerning it, O Commander of the Faithful." 'Umar said: "O son of my brother, speak and do not belittle yourself." Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with both of them) said: "It was struck as a parable for a rich man who worked in the obedience of Allah the Exalted, then Allah sent Satan to him, and he worked in acts of disobedience until he drowned his deeds." It is said: "This is better than that it be an image of one who nullifies his charity by reminding of it, harming, and showing off." It was separated from what precedes it because it is connected to what is mentioned after it, also because that one has no deed. It is answered that he has a deed for which he is rewarded according to the apparent state of his circumstances and his assumption, and this suffices for the stated parable. You know that this does not refute that the former is better, especially since it was said by the Interpreter of the Qur'an, and the Commander of the Faithful, the transmitter of hadith (may Allah be pleased with him), approved it.

﴿Thus﴾: that is, like that clear explanation which runs in manifestness like evident matters. ﴿Allah makes clear to you the signs, that you may reflect﴾ [266]: that is, so that you may reflect upon them, take heed from what they contain of lessons, and act according to their requirement. Or: that you may direct your thoughts toward what perishes and vanishes of the world, and toward what remains for you in the Hereafter, so that you renounce the world, spend from what Allah the Exalted has given you of it, desire the Hereafter, and do not do what would grieve you therein.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 267:

﴿O you who have believed, spend from the good things⦆ i.e., the choice ones or the lawful ones
Page 39
﴿of what you have earned⦆ i.e., what you have earned, or your earnings, i.e., what you have acquired of cash, merchandise (ʿurud al-tijarah) and livestock. Ibn Jarir related from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said regarding ﴿good things of what you have earned﴾: from gold and silver. And regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and from what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾, he meant: from grain, dates, and everything upon which zakah is due. The clause is to explain the state of what is spent from, after explaining the basis of spending and its manner. He repeated "min" (from) in the conjoined phrase because each of the two conjoined items is an independent category, or for emphasis, and the latter is probably the better view. The omission of mention of "the good things" is because it is known from what precedes it; it was also said: because it is known from what follows it. Some have made "ma" (what) a reference to that.

﴿And do not intend⦆ i.e., do not aim at. Its origin is "tatayammamu" with two taʾs, one of which was dropped for lightness, either the first or the second, according to the difference of opinion. ʿAbdullah read "wa la tayammamu" and Ibn ʿAbbas read "tuyammamu" with a ḍammah on the taʾ; all of them have the same meaning. ﴿the bad⦆ i.e., the inferior. It is like "the good" among descriptive terms that are dominant and whose described nouns are not mentioned. ﴿from it you spend⦆ The pronoun in the genitive refers to "the bad," and it is connected to "you spend." The fronting is for restriction, and the clause is a presumed circumstantial clause (ḥal muqaddarah) from the subject of "tayammamu," i.e., do not aim at the bad while restricting your spending to it, or "from the bad," i.e., spending is specifically from it. Whichever is the case, it is not objected that this implies the prohibition concerns only the spending of the bad, while the mixed is likewise, because the restriction is for rebuking them for what they used to do, namely spending the bad specifically. From ʿUbaydah al-Salmani, who said: I asked ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, about this verse, and he said: It was revealed concerning obligatory zakah. A man would go to the dates, cut them, set aside the good in one place, and when the one entitled to charity came, he would give him from the inferior. So Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and do not intend the bad from it you spend﴾. It was also said: it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause from "the bad," and the pronoun refers to the wealth contained within the two categories, or to "what We brought forth"; its specification by that is because inferiority and prohibition are more prevalent in it, given the variety of its kinds and sources. And ﴿you spend⦆ is a circumstantial clause from the mentioned subject, i.e., do not aim at the bad, whether it is from wealth or from what We brought forth for you, while you are spending it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while you would not take it⦆ is a circumstantial clause in every state from the pronoun in ﴿you spend﴾, i.e., while you would not take it at any time or in any manner ﴿except that you overlook in it⦆ except at the time of your overlooking, or except by your overlooking in it. "Ighmad" (overlooking) is like "ghamḍ," meaning the closing of the eyelid due to sleep; it has been used here, as al-Raghib said, for neglect and leniency. It was also said that it is a metaphor for that, and it is not free of leniency and neglect. Abu al-Baqa mentioned that it is used transitively, which is the more common, and intransitively, like "aghḍa ʿan kadha." The verse admits both. On the first, the object is omitted, i.e., your eyes. The majority read with a ḍammah on the taʾ, sukun on the ʿayn, and a kasrah on the mim.

al-Zuhri read "tughammiḍu" with a shaddah on the mim, and also from him "taghmuḍu" with a ḍammah and kasrah on the mim with a fatḥah on the taʾ. Qatadah read "tughmaḍu" in the passive, i.e., you be made to overlook, i.e., you be found overlooking. Both meanings are among what the memorizers have established, and whoever memorized is a proof against whoever did not. The "an" with the verb is, on every reading, in the genitive position as we have indicated. Abu al-Baqa allowed that it may be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. Sibawayh does not allow "an" and what is in its scope to be a circumstantial clause. Al-Farra claimed that "an" here is conditional, because its meaning is "if you overlook, you take." It should be that the eye of acceptance closes to it. Among the far-fetched views on the verse is what has been said: that the speech was complete at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not intend the bad﴾, then it was resumed, and it was said in the manner of rebuke and reproach: ﴿from it you spend﴾ while you would not take it except if you overlook in it, and its implication is the rejecting interrogative, as if it were said: "Is it from it that you spend, etc.?" And this, despite its remoteness, is contrary to the interpretations transmitted from the pious predecessors, may Allah be pleased with them.

﴿And know that Allah is Rich⦆ independent of your expenditures; He only commanded you to spend for your own benefit. In commanding them to know this, despite their evident knowledge of it, there is a rebuke for them for what they do of giving the bad, and an indication that this results from ignorance of His matter and His due. ﴿Praiseworthy⦆ [267] i.e., deserving of praise for His blessings. Among the praise befitting His majesty is seeking to spend the good from what He has bestowed. It was also said: He is thankful, by accepting the good and rewarding for it.

The verse has been cited as evidence for the obligation of zakah on both the little and the much of what the earth produces, even herbs. It has also been used as evidence that whoever plants in land he has rented, the zakah is upon him and not upon the landowner, because "We brought forth for you" requires that it be upon the planter. And that the rightful owner is not compelled to accept a defective item, but he has the right to return it and take a sound substitute for it.

The Shaytan threatens you with poverty ﴿الشَّيْطانُ يَعِدُكُمُ الفَقْرَ﴾. This is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) explaining the reason for choosing the base (*al-khabith*) in spending and belittling his standing. The word *wa'd* (promise) in its original linguistic usage is common for both good and evil. In common usage, however, *wa'd* is used for good and *i'ad* (threat) for evil, so that anything contrary to this is interpreted as metaphor (*majaz*) or mockery (*tahakkum*). Here it is used for evil, in keeping with the original usage, because poverty is something a person sees as evil. For this reason Satan frightens those who give charity, saying to them: "Do not spend the good of your wealth, and the outcome of your spending will be that you become poor." Calling this a *wa'd* although it involves informing about what will happen, the one informing being Satan, does not attribute the coming of poverty to his side. This is to indicate the accursed one's exaggeration in asserting that its coming is certain, as if he had made it, in the certainty of its occurrence, like his actions that take place according to his will. Or it is because it stands in opposition to the promise of the Exalted, by way of parallelism (*mushakalah*). Some people claim that the use of *wa'd* here is for good, according to common usage, and that the meaning is that what he frightens you with is a promise of good, because poverty is the greatest good for spending. But it is not hidden that this is far removed from the taste of the revelation. The word *al-faqr* is read with a *damma* and with a *sukun*, and with two *fatha*s and two *damma*s; all of these are dialectal forms for *al-faqr*, whose original meaning is the breaking of the spine (*fiqar al-zahr*).

﴿ويَأْمُرُكم بِالفَحْشاءِ﴾ And he orders you to immorality. That is, the immoral trait, which is stinginess and abandoning charity. The Arabs call a miser *fahish*. Ka'b said:

My brother, O my brother, (not immoral) at his house,
nor cowardly, timid at meeting.

The meaning of the command here is incitement and urging toward it, so in the sentence there is an explicit, subordinate metaphor (*isti'arah musarrahah tab'iyyah*). It has also been said: the meaning of *al-fahshā'* is all sins, and interpreting it as fornication (we seek refuge with Allah from it) is possible. It is also permissible that it means a shameful word, so this sentence would be like an emphasis of the first. The promise of Satan is mentioned before his command because through the promise tranquility toward him is attained; when one is at ease with him and fears poverty, he gains dominance over him through the command, since there is superiority over the one commanded in it.

﴿واللَّهُ يَعِدُكُمْ﴾ And Allah promises you, in spending, through the tongue of your Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿مَغْفِرَةً﴾ forgiveness for your sins; and from Qatadah: for your immoralities. The *tanwin* on it is for magnification, and likewise its description by His saying (*minhu*, "from Him"), which emphasizes its greatness. In this there is an explicit statement of what was known implicitly from the promise, as you have learned, for exaggeration in belittling the matter of Satan. ﴿وفَضْلا﴾ and bounty, that is, provision and a replacement. This is what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. So forgiveness is an indication of the benefits of the Hereafter, and this (bounty) is an indication of the benefits of this world. In a hadith: "There is no day on which the servants rise in the morning but two angels descend, one of them saying: 'O Allah, give the one who spends a replacement,' and the other saying: 'O Allah, give the one who withholds destruction.'" He mentioned the benefits of the Hereafter first because they are more important to the one who believes in them. It has also been said: forgiveness and bounty are both in the Hereafter, and the mention of the first then is because clearing away (*takhliyah*) precedes adornment (*tahliyah*), and because removing harms is more important than attaining benefits. In the verse: ﴿فَمَن زُحْزِحَ عَنِ النّارِ وأُدْخِلَ الجَنَّةَ فَقَدْ فازَ﴾ "Whoever is distanced from the Fire and admitted to Paradise has triumphed." The description of the second was omitted because what is mentioned indicates it.

﴿واللَّهُ واسِعٌ﴾ And Allah is All-Encompassing in mercy and bounty, ﴿عَلِيمٌ﴾ [268] All-Knowing of what you spend, so He will reward you for it. The sentence is a concluding clause (*tadhyil*) confirming the content of what precedes it, and its like is in His saying, may He be exalted:

[Page 41]

﴿He gives wisdom﴾ Ibn Jarir and others related from Ibn Abbas that it is knowledge of the Qur'an: its abrogating (*nasikh*, the verse that abrogates) and abrogated (*mansukh*, the verse that is abrogated) verses, its ambiguous (*mutashabih*) and clear (*muhkam*) verses, its earlier and later verses, its lawful and unlawful matters, and its parables. In another report from him, it is understanding (*fiqh*) of the Qur'an. Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and a great many others said the same. What Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Abbas, that it is prophethood, can be understood in this sense, because al-Bayhaqi related from Abu Umamah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever recites a third of the Qur'an is given a third of prophethood; whoever recites half of the Qur'an is given half of prophethood; whoever recites two-thirds of it is given two-thirds of prophethood; and whoever recites the whole Qur'an is given all of prophethood. On the Day of Resurrection it will be said to him: Recite and ascend, one degree for every verse, until you finish what you have of the Qur'an. Then it will be said to him: Grasp. He will grasp, and it will be said to him: Do you know what is in your two hands? Then in his right hand is eternity, and in the other is bliss." The recitation meant in this report is not mere recitation, for that is something both the righteous and the wicked share. Rather, what is meant is recitation with understanding (*fiqh*). This is supported by what Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu al-Darda: "Wisdom is the recitation of the Qur'an and reflection upon it." And from Mujahid: it is correctness in speech and action. In another report from him, it is the Qur'an, knowledge, and understanding; in yet another, it is knowledge whose benefit is great and whose usefulness is noble. From Ata: it is knowledge of Allah, exalted is He. Abu Uthman said: it is a light by which one distinguishes between whispering (*waswas*) and inspiration (*ilham*). Other views have been given. In *al-Bahr* it is stated that there are twenty-nine opinions of scholars on it, some close to others. Some of them counted most of these as technical usages, limited to what the speaker saw as an important aspect of wisdom. Otherwise, in origin it is a verbal noun from *ihkam*, which means perfecting something in knowledge, action, speech, or all of these. From Muqatil: wisdom is explained in the Qur'an in four ways: sometimes as the admonitions of the Qur'an, at other times as the wondrous secrets it contains, at other times as knowledge and understanding, and at other times as prophethood. It has been said: the most fitting meaning for the context is what includes the rulings expressed within the noble verse, from one of the first two aspects. Giving it (*ita'uha*) means clarifying it and granting success in acting upon it, that is, clarifying it and granting success in knowledge and in acting upon it.

﴿to whomever He wills﴾ from among His servants, that He grants it to him, by the requirement of the vastness of His bounty and the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, just as He has given you what He has made clear within the verses of wise rulings, on which the sphere of your benefits revolves. So seize them and hasten to act upon them. ﴿And whoever is given wisdom﴾ is in the passive form, either because the aim is to show the excellence of whoever attains wisdom regardless of the agent, or to specify the agent. The use of the noun in place of the pronoun is to give attention to the matter of this manifestation, and for this reason it was placed before the first object. It also indicates the reason for the ruling. Ya'qub read *yu'ti* in the active form and made *man* (the conditional particle) the fronted object or the subject, with the returning pronoun omitted. The second possibility is supported by al-A'mash's reading: *wa man yu'tahu al-hikmah*.

﴿then he has indeed been given much good﴾, great and abundant, for the good of both abodes has been gathered for him. Al-Tabarani related from Abu Umamah who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Luqman said to his son: O my son, keep company with the scholars and listen to the words of the wise, for Allah gives life to the dead heart with the light of wisdom, as He gives life to dead earth with heavy rain." Al-Bukhari and Muslim related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no envy except in two: a man whom Allah has given wealth and empowered him to spend it in the right way, and a man whom Allah has given wisdom, so he judges by it and teaches it." Al-Tabarani related from Abu Musa who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "On the Day of Resurrection Allah will raise the servants, then He will single out the scholars and say: O assembly of scholars, I did not place My knowledge in you to punish you. Go, for I have forgiven you." In another report from Tha'labah ibn al-Hakam, that He, glorified is He, says: "I have not placed My knowledge and My judgment among you except that I wish to forgive you for what you have done, and I do not mind." This applies to the bearers of the sacred knowledge brought by the wisest of the prophets and the sage of the wise, the presence of the seal of the messengers, the one who defined the boundaries of justice and bravery (ﷺ), not to what Galen, Democritus, Plato, Aristotle, and those who walk in their footsteps and dwell in the portico of their thoughts have taught. Ignorance is far better than what they held, and safer by many degrees than what they relied upon. So much so that many scholars forbade looking into their books, and they argued for this with what Imam Ahmad and Abu Ya'la related from the hadith of Jabir: that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for permission to write down comprehensive passages from the Torah so that he could read them and gain more knowledge added to his own. He became angry and did not grant him permission, and said: "Even if Musa were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me." In another report: "The Book of Allah is sufficient for you." The point of the argument is that he (ﷺ) did not permit the use of the Book that Musa brought as guidance and light at a time when the lights of prophethood were shining and the clouds of doubts and suspicions had dispersed by returning to it. How then can it be permitted to occupy oneself with what the bewildered philosophers of Greece produced as falsehood and fabrication, at a time when suspicions multiplied, illusions grew great, and Islam had become strange? In the Book of Allah, exalted is He, there is sufficiency beyond all else, as is not hidden from one who distinguishes the husk from the kernel and the error from the truth.

﴿And none will be mindful except the people of understanding﴾ [269]. That is: none takes admonition or reflects upon the verses except those with pure intellects, free from the impurities of illusion and the wrong of following desire. These are the ones who have been given wisdom. To show attention to praising them with this attribute, the apparent noun has been used in place of the pronoun. The clause is either a circumstantial clause (*hal*) or a concluding parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD tadhyili*).

* * *

Among the allusive meanings (*isharah*) in these verses: they include three ranked kinds of spending. The first is spending in the way of Allah, exalted is He, which is spending in the realm of dominion (*mulk*) from the station of the manifestation of the Acts. To this He, glorified is He, alluded with His words: ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah are like a grain﴾ etc. The second is spending from the station of witnessing the Attributes, which is spending to seek the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He. To this He alluded with His words: ﴿Those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾. From His representing it by a garden, one can learn the measure of its excellence over the first, which is represented by a grain. Perhaps the excellence of one over the other is like the excellence of the garden over the grain. What further increases the difference is that the garden, while giving its fruit, remains in its condition, unlike the grain. To emphasize the elevation of this kind of spending above the first, He mentioned a *rabwah*, which is a high piece of land. The third is spending by means of Allah, exalted is He, which is from the station of witnessing the Essence. It is the spending of the self after it has been purified. To this He alluded with His words: ﴿O you who believe, spend from the good things you have earned﴾. In this sense the self is acquired (*muktasibah*). The reward of the first spending is multiplication up to seven hundred, and more, for the hand of bounty is long. The reward of the second is the Attributive Garden, which yields multiplication. The reward of the third is the wisdom that necessarily accompanies the bestowed existence after giving, and it is the great, abundant good, because it is among the most specific of His attributes. The one who spends in this way continually spends from the divine wisdoms and the innate sciences, because of the removal of separation and the witnessing of the eye. In the course of this, He, glorified is He, has alerted that spending is nullified by reminding (*man*) and harm (*adha*). This is because it is praiseworthy only in three respects: that it accords with the command, which is its state in relation to Him, exalted is He; that it removes the base vices of stinginess, which is its state in relation to the spender himself; and that it is beneficial and brings relief, which is its state in relation to the deserving recipient. So when its giver reminds and harms, he has opposed the command of Allah, exalted is He, and has done what contradicts the comfort and benefit of the deserving recipient. His self appears in self-exaltation, conceit, self-admiration, and veiling itself by its act, seeing the blessing as coming from itself rather than from Allah, exalted is He. All of these are vices worse than stinginess. For this reason, a kind word is better than charity followed by harm, indeed there is no comparison.

[Page 43]

**"And whatever expenditure you spend,"** whether small or large, secretly or openly, in a right cause or a wrong one. The verse is therefore a statement of a general ruling that covers all individual instances of expenditure, or what is similar to them, following the statement of the ruling on what was spent in the way of Allah, the Exalted. **"Or whatever vow you vow,"** whether it is connected to wealth or to actions, conditionally or unconditionally, in obedience or in disobedience. A *nadhr* (vow) is the heart's resolve to do something and its binding of itself to that thing in a specific manner. It has been said that its root meaning is fear, because the person binds himself by it out of fear of falling short or fear of the occurrence of a grave matter. From this comes *nadhr al-dam* (the vow of blood), which is the resolve to shed it out of fear of harm to its owner. ʿAmr ibn Maʿdi Karib said:

*Hum (yandhurūna damī) wa-an dhur, in laqītu bi-an ashuddā*

Its verb is conjugated like *ḍaraba* and *naṣara*. On the authority of Yunus, as reported by al-Akhfash, the Arabs say: *nadhara ʿalā nafsihi nadhran* ("he vowed upon himself a vow") and *nadhartu mālī fa-anā anduruhu nadhran* ("I vowed my wealth, so I vow it"). **"Indeed Allah knows it,"** a metaphor for His recompense for it, the Glorified, since otherwise it is already known. The *fa'* (then) enters the response if *mā* is conditional, and it is a connective in the predicate if *mā* is relative. The singular pronoun is used, although the object of knowledge is plural, because the referent is unified, on the basis that the conjunction is with *aw* (or), which is for one of two things. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the singularity is in view of what was mentioned, and it seems he did not consider the referent in view of the mentioned expenditure and vow, but the two verbal nouns understood from their two verbs, which are the items joined by *aw*, or neither of them. Even granting that the joining of the two verbs entails the joining of the two (nouns), it is not appropriate to consider both, because the pronoun is definitely masculine, while the two are masculine and feminine, and considering one of them to the exclusion of the other is preference without a preferring factor. This is not hidden in its problem. Such a pronoun may be considered in terms of the state of the preceding item, out of regard for priority, as in His saying, the Exalted: *"And when they saw a trade or amusement, they dispersed toward it"* (62:11). It may also be considered in terms of the state of the following item, out of regard for proximity, as in His saying, the Exalted: *"And whoever earns a sin or wrong and then throws it upon an innocent"* (4:112). Each of these is permissible and common in eloquent usage, and what we are discussing is of the second type if the mentioned is considered explicitly. Insisting on interpretation in all that has come is an unnecessary strain, as is not hidden. Yes, it has been permitted to return the pronoun to *mā*, but on the assumption that it is relative, as stated by more than one scholar.

**"And for the wrongdoers,"** i.e., those who place things in other than their proper places, where they ought to be placed. This includes those who spend for show, with reminders and harm, those who seek out the wicked in spending, those who spend in falsehood, those who vow in disobedience, those who refrain from fulfilling what they vowed in a right cause, and those who withhold charity from what Allah, the Exalted, has given them of His bounty. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi restricted them to those who spend with reminders, harm and show, and to those who squander in disobedience. Muqatil restricted them to the polytheists. Perhaps generality is preferable. **"Of helpers"** [270], i.e., assistants who would help them against the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, with neither intercession nor defense. It is the plural of *naṣīr* as in *ḥabīb* and *aḥbāb*, or of *nāṣir* as in *shāhid* and *ashhād*. Its being stated in the plural is in the manner of antithesis, so it is not objected that negating helpers does not negate a single helper, which is what is intended.

It was said that this would only be needed if *min* were considered superfluous, but you may consider it partitive, meaning "some of the helpers are not anything," as is not hidden. The sentence is a resumptive statement confirming the threat contained in the content of what precedes it. The negation that a wrongdoer has any helper, according to Muqatil's view, is absolutely evident. As for the assumption that *maẓālim* (wrongs) is taken generally or specifically in the sense stated by Abu Sulayman, then it is necessary to say that the verse is given in the mode of warning, because the sinner who is not a polytheist, whatever his disobedience, may have a helper who intercedes for him with his Lord.

The verse has been cited as evidence for the legitimacy of vows and the fulfilment of them, so long as they are not disobedience; otherwise there is no fulfilment. Al-Nasa'i reported from ʿImran ibn al-Husayn, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The vow is of two kinds. Whatever vow is in obedience to Allah, the Exalted, that belongs to Allah, the Exalted, and in it is fulfilment. Whatever vow is in disobedience to Allah, the Exalted, that belongs to Satan, and there is no fulfilment in it, and its expiation is what expiates an oath." The detailed discussion of vows will come later, God willing, the Exalted.

[Page 44]

﴿If you disclose your charities, how excellent they are﴾: that is, if you make their giving apparent. Al-Kalbi said: "When the verse ﴿And whatever you spend of any expenditure﴾ was revealed, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), is the charity given in secret better, or the charity given openly?' Then this was revealed." The clause is a kind of detailing of something left general in the conditional sentence, and an explanation of it. For this reason the conjunction (waw al-'atf) was omitted between them. According to the view of the majority of exegetes (mufassirun), the "charities" (sadaqat) here are voluntary charities. It has also been said that they are obligatory charities, and it has been said that the word is general. ﴿Then how excellent they are﴾: the fa' is the answer to the condition. Ni'ma is a past-tense verb. The word "ma," as Ibn Jinni said, is an indefinite complete noun (nakirah tammah) in the accusative, functioning as a specification (tamyiz). It is the subject (mubtada') that refers back to "the charities," with an elided noun (that is, "their disclosure") or with no elision. The clause is the predicate (khabar) of "hiya" (they), and the link (rabit) is the generality of the term. Ibn Kathir, Warsh and Hafs read it with a kasra on the nun and the ayn, for the sake of harmonization (li-l-ittiba'), and this is the dialect of Hudhayl. It has been said that it may be that the vowel was originally a sukun, then a kasra was added because of the meeting of two sukuns. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatha on the nun and a kasra on the ayn, according to the original form, like 'alima. Abu 'Amr, Qalun and Abu Bakr read it with a kasra on the nun and a concealed (ikhfa') vowel on the ayn. It is also narrated from them that it is read with a sukun, and Abu 'Ubayda chose this and related it as a dialect. The majority prefer the "ikhtilas" (rapid, partial vowelling) over the sukun, to the extent that some considered the sukun a mistake of the transmitters. Among those who rejected it were al-Mubarrad, al-Zajjaj and al-Farisi, because it involves joining two sukuns in a way that is not permitted.

﴿And if you conceal them﴾: that is, if you keep them secret. The pronoun in the accusative is either for "the charities" in general, or refers to them verbally but not in meaning, based on the view that the "disclosed charities" are the obligatory ones and the "concealed charities" are the voluntary ones. This is then like the expression "I have a dirham and half of it," meaning half of another dirham. In the combination of disclosure and concealment there is, among the types of rhetorical embellishment (badi'), the verbal antithesis (tibaq lafzi). In His words, ﴿and give them to the poor﴾, there is also the semantic antithesis (tibaq ma'nawi), since only the rich give charities. It has been said that perhaps the explicit mention of giving them to the poor, although it is also necessary in the case of disclosure, is because concealment is liable to confusion and uncertainty. The rich person may claim poverty and accept charity in secret, which he would not do in front of people. The poor are singled out for mention out of concern for their condition. It has also been said that since the disclosed charity is zakah, the poor were not mentioned in connection with it, because its disbursement is not restricted to them, whereas the concealed charity, being voluntary, specifies that its recipients are the poor only. This is not valid, because even granting that the disclosed charity is zakah and the concealed is voluntary, we do not accept that the recipients of the second are only the poor, and this is not established except by an overwhelming proof. It seems that for this reason some interpreted "the poor" as referring to the categories of recipients.

﴿That is better for you﴾: that is, concealment ﴿is better for you﴾ than disclosure. "Better for you" is one of the goods in general. The first meaning is what the reports and hadiths indicate regarding the superiority of concealment, and they are more than can be counted.

Imam Ahmad related from Abu Umamah that "Abu Dharr said: 'O Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which charity is best?' He said: 'A secret charity to a poor person, or the effort of one of modest means,' then he recited the verse." Al-Tabarani related it as a raised hadith: "Indeed, secret charity extinguishes the anger of the Lord." Al-Bukhari related: "Seven will be shaded by Allah, the Exalted, in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His shade," until he said: "and a man who gives a charity and conceals it, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand spends." Most scholars hold that this superiority applies when both the secret and the open charity are voluntary, and when the giver is not known to be wealthy. Otherwise, disclosing an obligatory charity is better, to remove suspicion, and likewise disclosure is better for one who is followed as an example, provided he is safe from harm. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both): "A secret voluntary charity is superior to its open form by seventy times, and an open obligatory charity is superior to its secret form by twenty-five times." The same applies to all obligatory and voluntary acts in all matters.

﴿And will remove from you some of your misdeeds﴾: that is, and Allah removes [them], or concealment does. The attribution is metaphorical (majazi). The "min" is partitive, because charities do not remove all misdeeds. It has been said that it is extra (mazidah) according to the opinion of al-Akhfash. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim in the transmission of Ibn 'Ayyash, and Ya'qub read "nukaffiru" with a nun, in the nominative, as a new independent clause (jumlah mubtada'ah), or a nominal clause coordinated with what follows the fa'. That is, "and We remove." It has been said that there is no need to posit an elided subject; the verb itself is coordinated with the position (mahall) of "ma" after the fa', since by itself it is in the nominative, because the linking fa' prevents its being in the jussive, lest the link be doubled. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "nukaffir" with a nun in the jussive, coordinated with the position of the fa' together with what follows it, because it is the answer to the condition. This was said by more than one scholar. Badr al-Damamini raised an objection to this, saying that it is clear that the fa' and "ma" entering upon it place it in a jussive position. It has been established that a clause does not have a position in i'rab unless it stands in the position of a single word, and this is not one of the positions of a single word, so that the clause could have a position in i'rab. This is because the answer to the condition is by nature a clause and cannot be a single word. The position therefore belongs to the clause essentially. He claimed that the jussive of the verb is not due to coordination with the position of the clause, but is because it is a present-tense verb that occurred at the beginning of a clause coordinated with the answer of the jussive conditional, and if that clause had begun with a present-tense verb, it would have been jussive. So the coordinated clause was given the ruling of the clause it is coordinated with, namely that its initial present-tense verb is jussive. This can be answered by careful consideration, so reflect. It has also been read "wa-tukaffiru" with a ta', in the nominative and jussive, according to what is known, and the verb refers to the charities.

﴿And Allah is well-acquainted with what you do﴾: in your charities, of disclosure and concealment, ﴿Acquainted﴾: knowing, nothing is hidden from Him, and He will reward you for all of that. In general, the verse encourages both public and private giving, even if they differ in superiority. It is also possible that the speech is directed toward encouraging the second, because of its proximity, and because awareness of disclosure does not contain much praise.

[Page 45]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 272:**

﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾: that is, O Messenger, it is not obligatory upon you to make these people, who are commanded to do these good deeds and forbidden from these vices, guided to comply and to refrain. ﴿You are only a bringer of good news and a warner﴾; ﴿upon you is only the clear conveyance﴾. ﴿But Allah guides﴾ by His special guidance, which leads without doubt to the desired goal, ﴿whom He wills﴾ of them. The sentence is parenthetical (mu'taridah), brought in as a shift of address (talwin al-khitab) and a turning of the address toward the master of those addressed, ﷺ, together with a turn to the third person (al-ghaybah) between the addresses concerning those who are obligated, for the sake of emphasis in urging them to comply. This meaning was held by al-Hasan and Abu Ali al-Jubba'i. It is based on the pronoun in ﴿their guidance﴾ referring to those addressed in the preceding verses. What the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) requires is that it refers to the disbelievers. Ibn Abi Hatim and others narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that: "The Prophet ﷺ used to order us not to give charity except to the people of Islam, until this verse was revealed." Ibn Jarir narrated from him that he said: "There were some people among the Ansar who had relatives and kin, and they avoided giving charity to them and wanted them to embrace Islam, so this was revealed." Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Do not give charity except to the people of your religion." So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾. That is: it is not upon you to guide those who oppose you, so that you withhold charity from them in order to make them enter Islam. In that case there is no turning of address (iltifat); there is only a shift of address (talwin al-khitab). The verse is also an exhortation to charity, but in another way. The connection is evident under both interpretations. Linking it to His saying, ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾, as a reference to another category of people who were not given it, is not valid.

﴿And whatever you spend﴾ in the ways of righteousness ﴿of good﴾, that is, wealth, ﴿it is for yourselves﴾, that is, it is for your own benefit; no one else among you will benefit from it in the Hereafter. So do not aim for the bad (al-khabith) and do not nullify it through reminding of favors, harm, and showing off to people. Or: do not withhold it from the poor, however they may be, for your benefit from it is religious, while the benefit to a disbelieving one among them is worldly. The word ﴿مَا﴾ (ma) is a conditional particle (shartiyyah) that governs the jussive ﴿تُنْفِقُوا﴾ (tunfiqu), and it is in the accusative as its object. The ﴿مِن﴾ (min) is partitive (tab'idiyyah), related to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier of the conditional noun, specifying and particularizing it.

﴿And you do not spend except seeking the Face of Allah﴾.
This is an exception from the most general causes and the most general states. That is: you do not spend for any reason except this reason, or in any state except this state. The sentence is either a circumstantial clause (hal) or conjoined to what precedes it, meaning: "And whatever you spend of good, it will be for you and not against you, when your condition is that you spend only seeking the Face of Allah the Exalted, or only seeking His Face, the Glorified, not harming, not reminding of favors, not showing off, and not intending the bad." Or the meaning is: "Your spending is only for such-and-such or in such-and-such a state, so why do you remind of it, and spend the bad, or withhold it from the poor among the polytheists, from the People of the Book and others?" It has also been said that this is a negation with the meaning of a prohibition, that is: "Do not spend except in such a way." The insertion of ﴿Face﴾ is for glorification and for removing association (daf' al-shirkah), because when you say "I did it for the face of Zayd," it is more honorable than saying "I did it for him," since the face of a thing is the noblest part of it. The word then became common until it was used to express nobility in general. Also, the saying of the speaker "I did this deed for so-and-so" may imply partnership, that he did it for him and for others. But when he says "I did it for his face," the thread of partnership is cut off by convention. Many of the linguists (ahl al-lughah) took "face" here to mean the essence (al-dhat). Some interpreted it here as "good pleasure" (al-ridha) and took the verse in the sense of the phrase "seeking the good pleasure of Allah the Exalted." The early generation (al-salaf), after declaring Allah free of all imperfection, committed the meaning to Allah (fawwadu), as is their custom regarding the ambiguous (al-mutashabih).

﴿And whatever you spend of good will be paid back to you in full﴾: that is, you will be given its reward in full and complete, as the form of the verb (taf'il) indicates, in the Hereafter, according to what the preceding verses have included. This is what was narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both. The intended meaning is the negation that they have any excuse for opposing the command mentioned concerning spending. So the sentence is an emphasis of the preceding conditional, but not a mere emphasis; otherwise it would have been separated. Rather, it includes that meaning because its context is to argue for the ugliness of abandoning that command. It is as if it was said: "How could he bestow favors or fall short in what returns its benefit to him? Or how could he do that when there is a return and an increase?" With this consideration it is an independent matter. It has also been said that the meaning is: "He will provide for you its substitute in this world, and nothing will be decreased from your wealth by it," in response to his saying ﷺ: "O Allah, give the one who spends a substitute, and the one who withholds destruction." Tawfiyah (full payment) is the completion of a thing. The phrase ﴿to you﴾ is good with it because it includes the meaning of "delivering" (al-ta'diyah). Its attribution to ﴿ما﴾ (ma) is metaphorical (majazi), and its literal sense is what you have heard.

Based on the occasion of revelation, the verse is evidence for the permissibility of giving charity to a disbeliever. This is an established matter for non-obligatory charity. As for obligatory charity that the Imam is entitled to collect, such as zakat, it is not permissible. As for other than it, such as the charity of fitr, vows, and expiation (kaffarah), there is disagreement about it. Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, permits it. The apparent meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they give food, despite love for it, to the needy, the orphan, and the captive﴾ supports this, since a captive in the land of Islam is none other than a polytheist.

﴿And you will not be wronged﴾ [272]: that is, you will not be deprived of anything of what you were promised. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿to you﴾, and the governing element is ﴿will be paid back﴾ (yuwaff).

[p. 47]

The phrase ﴿لِلْفُقَراءِ﴾ ("for the poor") is connected to an implied verb that the sentence leads to, and for this reason it has been omitted. The meaning is: "Commit (your charity) to the poor," or "Make what you spend for the poor," or "Your charity is for the poor." The sentence is a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence) built on a question.
