It is also permissible for the prepositional phrase to be connected to the words of God, Exalted be He: ﴿، وما تُنْفِقُوا﴾ ("and whatever you spend"), and His words, glorified be He: ﴿وأنْتُمْ لا تُظْلَمُونَ﴾ ("and you will not be wronged") form a parenthetical clause. That is, "And whatever you spend for the poor."

﴿الَّذِينَ أُحْصِرُوا في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ ("those who have been confined in the way of God"): that is, they have been held back by jihad or by work in pursuit of God's good pleasure. "Your reward will be repaid to you" is a connection whose remoteness is not hidden. ﴿لا يَسْتَطِيعُونَ﴾ ("they are not able") because they are occupied with that. ﴿ضَرْبًا في الأرْضِ﴾ ("to strike about in the land"): that is, walking about in it and going forth to earn a livelihood and trade. They are the People of the Suffa (Ahl al-Suffa, the people of the veranda), may God be pleased with them. Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: they were about three hundred, more or less, from among the poor emigrants (muhajirun). They lived in the shelter of the mosque, spending their times in learning and jihad, and they would go out on every sariyya (military detachment) that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: they are a people whom wounds sustained in the way of God had struck, so that they became disabled, and so provision was made for them from the wealth of the Muslims, as a right. Probably the intent of both reports is to indicate some individuals of this concept, and its inclusion in it at that time was a primary inclusion, not a restriction, since this ruling remains in force until the Day of Judgment.

﴿يَحْسَبُهُمُ﴾ ("he thinks them"), that is, supposes them, ﴿الجاهِلُ﴾ ("the ignorant one"), who has no knowledge of their condition, ﴿أغْنِياءَ مِنَ التَّعَفُّفِ﴾ ("rich because of their restraint"): that is, because of their abstaining from asking. Here "min" indicates cause, and it has been used because one of the conditions for the accusative (naṣb) is missing, which is the unity of the agent (ittiḥad al-fa'il). It has also been said that it indicates the starting point (ibtida' al-ghaya), and the meaning is that the ignorant person's supposition of their wealth arises from their restraint. Ta'affuf is leaving a thing and turning away from it while having the ability to engage in it. Its object is omitted for brevity, as we have pointed out. The status (ḥal) of this clause is like that of the preceding one.

﴿تَعْرِفُهم بِسِيماهُمْ﴾ ("you recognize them by their mark"): that is, you recognize their poverty and need by the apparent sign upon them, such as humility, exhaustion, and shabbiness of condition. Abu Nu'aym narrated from Fadala ibn 'Ubayd who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) led the people in prayer, men would fall down from their standing in their prayer because of the hardship that was upon them, and they were the People of the Suffa, until the Bedouins would say, 'These are madmen.'" And he also narrated from Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, who said: "Among the People of the Suffa there were seventy men, none of whom had a cloak." The address is to the Messenger (ﷺ), or to everyone who has a share of address, as an emphasis in clarifying the evidence of their poverty. The pattern of sima is fi'la, because it derives from the wasm, meaning the mark; the fa' was moved to the position of the 'ayn and turned into a ya' because it came after a kasra.

﴿لا يَسْألُونَ النّاسَ إلْحافًا﴾ ("they do not ask people insistently"): that is, with persistence, which is that one keeps company with the one asked until he gives. From their saying, "He covered me (alhafani) with the surplus of his blanket (lihafihi)," meaning he gave me from the surplus of what he had. It has also been said that persistence is named so because it covers the heart as a blanket covers the one beneath it. Its accusative is as an infinitive (maṣdar), since it is a kind of asking, or as a status: "insistently." The meaning is that they do not ask at all, and this is what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj and most of the scholars of meanings (ma'ani) went to this view. According to it the negation applies to two matters, in the manner of the saying of al-A'sha:

"He does not stumble from fatigue or ailment,
nor choke on the cartilage of his ribs in childhood."

It has been objected that this is only good when the restriction is necessary to the restricted, or as necessary, so that from its negation one follows by demonstrative means, and what is here is not like that, since insistence is not necessary to asking nor as necessary to it. It is answered that this is accepted if there is nothing in the speech that requires it, and here it is so, because restraint to the point that they are thought rich requires the absence of asking altogether. Also, ﴿تَعْرِفُهم بِسِيماهُمْ﴾ ("you recognize them by their mark") supports this, for if they had asked you would have recognized them by the asking, and recognition by the mark would have been unnecessary. It has also been said that the intent is that they do not ask, and if they ask out of necessity they do not persist. Some people made the accusative an absolute object (maf'ul muṭlaq) of the negation, that is, they abandon asking insistently, being insistent in abandoning it. But this, as you see, is weak.

﴿وما تُنْفِقُوا مِن خَيْرٍ فَإنَّ اللَّهَ بِهِ عَلِيمٌ﴾ ("And whatever good you spend, indeed God is Knowing of it") [273]: so He will repay you for it. This is an exhortation to spending, especially upon these people. Al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated from Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'The poor man is not the one who is turned away by a date or two dates, or a morsel or two morsels. Rather, the poor man is the one who refrains (yata'affaf). Recite, if you wish: ﴿لا يَسْألُونَ النّاسَ إلْحافًا﴾.'" The placing of the adverbial phrase first is for the sake of observing the rhyme (fawasil), or as an indication of emphasis.

﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾. That is, they make all times and states a time for good and charity. So "by night and by day" means all times, just as what follows it means all states. He placed "by night" before "by day" and "secretly" before "openly" to indicate the superiority of concealment over disclosure. The accusative of "secretly and openly" is either because both are verbal nouns (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "concealing and disclosing." Or they are two circumstantial clauses from the pronoun of the spending, according to the view of Sibawayh (Sibawayh). Or they are two adjectives of an omitted verbal noun, meaning "spending secretly." The "ba'" here means "in."

There is disagreement about who the verse was revealed concerning. Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that it was revealed concerning Ali, may Allah honour his face. He had four dirhams and spent one dirham by night, one by day, one secretly, and one openly. In the narration of al-Kalbi: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'What moved you to this?' He said: 'What moved me is that I deserve from Allah, the Exalted, what He promised me.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: 'Indeed, that is for you.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn al-Musayyib that the entire verse was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf regarding their spending in the Army of Hardship (Jaysh al-'Usra, the army of the expedition to Tabuk). Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Wahidi narrated through the chain of Hasan ibn Abd Allah al-San'ani that he heard Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, say concerning this verse: "﴿Those who spend﴾ etc. are those who provide fodder for horses in the way of Allah, the Exalted." This is also the view of Abu Umama, Abu al-Darda', Makhul, al-Awza'i and Rabah ibn Yazid. The mention of "secretly and openly" does not contradict this, as is clear.

Some said that it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, who gave in charity forty thousand dinars: ten by night, ten by day, ten secretly and ten openly. Al-Suyuti (al-Suyuti) responded to this, saying that the narration of his giving forty thousand dinars was reported by Ibn Asakir in his "Tarikh" from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, but a report that the verse was revealed concerning him I have not found. It seems that whoever claimed this understood it from what Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Ishaq, who said: "When Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, died and Umar was appointed as successor, he addressed the people, praised Allah, the Exalted, and extolled Him with what is fitting for Him. Then he said: 'O people, indeed some greed is poverty, and some despair is wealth. You gather wealth that you eat, and you hope for what you will not attain. Know that some stinginess is a branch of hypocrisy. So spend for your own souls. Where are the people of this verse?' And he recited the noble verse." You know that there is no indication in it for the claim.

﴿Then their reward is with their Lord﴾, which is hidden for them in the treasuries of bounty. The "fa" (then) is within the scope of the relative clause to indicate that what precedes it is the cause. It was also said that it is for coordination, and the predicate is omitted, meaning "and among them are those who..." etc. For this reason, it was permitted to stop at "openly."

﴿And no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾ [274]. Its explanation has already passed, and the indication in the verses is evident.

[Page 48]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 275 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Those who consume interest (al-riba)﴾ meaning: those who take it, so that it covers all kinds of benefiting from it. The expression "consume" is used because consuming is the main purpose for which it is sought. Al-riba (interest, usury) linguistically means increase, from the saying "al-shay' yarbu" when it increases. In the Sharia it is an expression for an excess of wealth that is not matched by a counter-value in an exchange of wealth for wealth. It is written with a waw, like al-salat (the prayer), for emphasis, according to the dialect of those who pronounce it with emphasis (tafkhim). An alif was added after it, by analogy with the waw of the plural, so the word conforms to its meaning in that each of them contains an unmerited increase. Thus the word riba took the extra letter, namely the alif, because of the word that resembles it, namely the waw of the plural, in which an alif is added, just as the meaning of the word riba takes on the meaning of the word bay' (sale) through resemblance, since both meanings involve the exchange of wealth for wealth by mutual consent, even if one of the two counter-values is greater. It was said: it is written with both the waw and the alif, because the word has a share of both; and the salat and the zakat were not written with both for fear that it would be liable to confusion with the plural. Al-Farra' said: they learned the script from the people of al-Hira, who were Nabateans, whose dialect was "rabu" with a quiescent waw, so it was written thus. This is the view of the Basrans. The Kufans permitted writing it (with an alif) and likewise its dual with a ya', because of the kasra at its beginning. Abu al-Baqa' said: this is an error in our view.

﴿They do not rise﴾ meaning: on the Day of Resurrection, and it was read thus, as in al-Durr al-Manthur.

Page 49

﴿except as one rises whom Satan has driven to madness by touch﴾ meaning: except a rising like the rising of the one who is staggering and struck down in this world. Takhabbut is a form of tafa''ul with the meaning of fa'l, and its origin is repeated striking in various manners; then it was used figuratively for every ungracious blow. The rising of the usurer on the Day of Resurrection is similarly what the traditions have reported. Al-Tabarani related from Awf ibn Malik, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of the sins that are not forgiven: misappropriation (ghulul); whoever misappropriates something will bring it on the Day of Resurrection; and consuming interest: whoever consumes interest will be raised on the Day of Resurrection insane, staggering," then he recited the verse. This is not something the intellect rules out or prevents, and perhaps Allah the Exalted made that a sign for him by which he is recognised on the Day of the Great Gathering, as a punishment for him, just as He made for some obedient ones a sign befitting them by which they are recognised, as an honour for them. What bears witness to this is that this community will be raised on the Day of Resurrection with shining faces and limbs marked by the traces of ablution. To this view went Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah, and al-Zajjaj chose it. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: what is meant is the comparison of the usurer in his greed and his agitation in acquiring in this world to the one struck down and staggering, as one says of someone who moves quickly with varied movements: "he has gone mad." It is not hidden that this contradicts what the early community of the Ummah held, and it has been related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), with no motive except the improbability that is not considered in such matters.

﴿by touch﴾ meaning: madness. It is said: "masa al-rajul" (the man was touched) and he is "mamsus" when he has gone mad. Its origin is touching with the hand, and it was so named because Satan may touch a man while his humours are prepared for corruption, so they become corrupt and madness arises. This does not contradict what the physicians mention, that it comes from the predominance of black bile, because what they mentioned is a near cause, while what the verse points to is a remote cause. Nor is it consistent or reciprocal: touch may occur without madness, as when the temperament is strong; and madness may occur without touch, as when the temperament is corrupted without any external agent. Madness caused by touch does sometimes occur, and the expert practitioners have signs by which they recognise it. Sometimes a corrupt wind enters some bodies in certain conditions, and an evil spirit that is suited to it becomes attached to it, so madness arises too in its complete form. Perhaps that vapour overpowers the senses and disables them, and that evil spirit becomes independent in control, so it speaks, strikes and moves with the instruments of that person in whom it has settled, without the person having any awareness of any of that at all. This is like what is observed and sensed, to the point that one who denies it is almost counted as a stubborn denier of what is plainly seen.

The Mu'tazilah and al-Qaffal of the Shafi'is said: the claim that epilepsy and madness are from Satan is false, because he has no power to do that, as He said, relating his words: "And I had no authority over you" (14:22). The "ma" here is directed at what the Arabs claim and believe, that Satan strikes a man and he falls, and that the jinn touches him and his intellect is confused. There is no reality to that and it is nothing; rather it is one of Satan's delusions upon its speaker, one of his baseless claims refuted by definitive texts of the Sharia. It has been transmitted: "No child is born but Satan touches it, and so it cries out screaming," and in some chains: "except that Satan pricks it in its side." From this comes "it cries out screaming, except Mary and her son," because of the words of her mother: "And I seek refuge for her and her offspring with You from the accursed Satan" (3:36). And his saying (ﷺ): "Keep your children inside at the beginning of the night, for it is the time when the devils spread out." It has also been related in the report of the lost man whom the devils seized and then returned, in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that something happened to him with them; he said: "Then a bird came to me, as if it were a huge camel, and it carried me upon one of its feathers." And other traditions besides these. In Luqat al-Marjan fi Ahkam al-Jann there is much of this. The belief of the early community and the People of the Sunnah is that what these indicate are real, actual matters, as the Sharia has reported them. To insist on interpreting all of them entails a long confusion, to which none incline except the Mu'tazilah and those who follow their path, and by such things and the like they departed from the upright rules of the Sharia. So beware of them; may Allah fight them, how are they turned away! The verse they cited as evidence for their claim does not show it, for the authority negated in it is only compulsion and forcing one to follow him, not attacking to harm and undertaking what leads to destruction.

Whoever traces the prophetic reports finds many of them definitively affirming that this can occur from Satan, indeed that it does occur in fact. The report "Plague is a stabbing from your enemies, the jinn" is explicit in this. Some of our later shaykhs interpreted it in a manner like what we interpreted in the matter of takhabbut and touch, saying: when the air putrefies with a particular putrefaction, prepared for mixing and formation, there separate from it and gather poisonous parts that remain in their airy nature, or are converted into fiery burning parts. A wicked spirit suited to them in sparkling attaches to them, and that is a kind of jinn, for they, as is known in speech, are living bodies that are not seen, whose predominant nature is either airy or fiery. They have kinds, rational and non-rational, which multiply and form. When one of them descends upon a person, by nature or by will, or penetrates his passages, or strikes and stabs himself with it, there occurs in him, according to the poisonous power in that evil and what the person has of readiness to be affected by it, as is the requirement of ordinary causes in their effects, a severe pain, usually fatal, which manifests as boils and pustules in most cases, because it corrupts the prepared temperament. By this the various statements on this subject are reconciled. This is a good verification that we did not find in anyone else, just as we did not find what we verified concerning the matter of touch with anyone besides ourselves, so let it be remembered.

The prepositional phrase is connected to what precedes it, namely the negated verb, on the basis that what comes before "illa" operates on what follows it when it is an adverbial complement, as in al-Durr al-Masun: that is, they do not rise because of the touch that is on them due to their consuming interest, or with "yaqumu" (rise), or with "yatakhabbatuhu" (strike).

﴿That﴾ refers to the consuming or to the punishment that befell them. ﴿Because they said: "Trade is only like interest."﴾ They intended to put them in one line, because both lead to profit. Wherever a sale of something worth one dirham for two dirhams is permitted, the sale of one dirham for two dirhams is permitted too. But they made interest the basis of permissibility and likened sale to it, reversing the comparison for emphasis, as in the verse:

"Its dust-laden plains, its ground dark as its sky" (the verse is reversed to make the ground seem like the sky).

It was also said: the comparison may be not reversed, on the basis of their understanding that sale is permitted for the sake of gain and profit, and that is certain in interest, but only supposed in other cases.

﴿And Allah has permitted trade and forbidden interest.﴾ This is a resumed sentence from Allah, the Exalted, refuting them and rejecting their equating the two. Its sum is that what you mention is a faulty analogy in its basis, because it contradicts the explicit text, so it is from the work of Satan. Moreover there is a difference between the two cases: whoever sells a garment worth one dirham for two dirhams has made the garment counter-valued by two dirhams, so no part of either is except that it is counter-valued by a part of the garment. But when he sells a dirham for two dirhams, he has taken the extra dirham without any counter-value, and it is not possible to make the delay a counter-value, since delay is not wealth so as to be opposite wealth. It was also said: the difference between them is that one of the two dirhams in the second case is necessarily lost, while in the first it is compensated by the pressing need for the commodity or by expectation of its circulation. It is permissible that the sentence be part of the speech of the disbelievers, rejecting the Sharia and denying it, meaning: such a distinction between like things is not with Allah, the Exalted; then it is circumstantial, and there is a deleted qad in it. It is not hidden that this is very far-fetched. The apparent meaning is that "sale" and "interest" are general, covering every sale and every interest, except what the evidence has specified, such as the prohibition of some sales and the permission of some interest. It was said: both are general terms that are ambiguous, so one may not permit any sale or forbid any interest except with an explanation. This is supported by what Imam Ahmad, Ibn Majah and Ibn Jarir related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Among the last things revealed was the verse on interest, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died before he explained it to us, so leave interest and whatever is doubtful."

﴿So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord﴾ meaning: whoever receives an exhortation and warning, such as the prohibition of interest and its permissibility. "Whoever" is conditional or relative. ﴿Admonition﴾ is the subject of "jaa" (came), and the feminine marker was dropped because of the separation and because the feminine here is metaphorical, together with the sense of masculinity in "admonition." Ubayy and al-Hasan read "jaatahu" with the feminine marker. ﴿From his Lord﴾ is connected to "jaahu" or to a deleted element that serves as an attribute of "admonition." On both readings there is glorification of its importance, and mention of the Lord contains reassurance toward accepting the admonition, since it implies the caring of the Lord for His servant. "From" indicates the starting point or partitive, and a noun was deleted. ﴿And desists﴾ is coordinated with "jaahu," meaning: he takes heed without delay and follows the prohibition. ﴿He keeps what has passed﴾ meaning: what he took before the prohibition is not reclaimed from him. This is what is reported from al-Baqir and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It was also said: what is meant is that there is no blame upon him in this world or in the next for what he had taken of interest before. The "fa" is either for the response or an addition in the predicate. The "ma" is in the position of the nominative, governed by the adverb if "man" is taken as a relative, or by the inchoative if it is taken as a conditional, according to the view of one who requires the dependence; and if the nominal subject is a verbal noun, while one who does not require these two conditions permits it to be the agent of the adverb. ﴿And his affair is with Allah﴾ meaning: the matter of the one who desists after the prohibition. If He wills, He preserves him from interest so he does not do it, and if He wills, He does not. It was also said: what is meant is that He will reward him for his desisting if it was from acceptance of the admonition and sincerity of intention, or He will judge his case on the Day of Resurrection as He wills, and there is no objection from you against Him. Some people made the pronoun in the genitive refer to "what has passed" or to "interest," and both are contrary to the apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 275 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And whoever returns﴾ meaning: returns to what was mentioned before, namely the practice of riba (usury), holding it to be permissible, and arguing for it by analogy with sale. ﴿Then those﴾ is a reference to whoever returns, and the plural is used in consideration of meaning. ﴿Are the companions of the Fire﴾ meaning: those who are constant in it. ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾ [275] meaning: they will remain eternally because of their disbelief. The sentence confirms what precedes it. Al-Zamakhshari, however, took the object of "returns" to be riba, and so the verse was used as evidence for the eternal punishment of one who commits a major sin. On his reading, and on the transmitted explanation we have mentioned, there is no room left for using the verse as such evidence. It has been objected that if eternity were made the recompense for regarding the act as lawful, then the recompense for the one who commits the act without regarding it as lawful would remain unmentioned in the speech at all, neither explicitly nor by allusion, even though it is the most important intended matter. By contrast, if that were made the recompense for the act itself, the intended matter would be stated explicitly, and it would also convey the recompense for regarding it as lawful, which is something beyond eternity. It has been answered that what makes one who regards such a thing as lawful a disbeliever can only be among the major prohibitions, and their recompense is known, which is why it was not pointed out, being evident. Some of the verifying scholars said in reply: if the reference in "that" is to eating, then the recompense is the rising mentioned from the graves to the place of standing, and that is sufficient as a deterrent. Then He informed that what drove them to eating was this statement. The description therefore first indicated that the threat applies to it, then He mentioned the cause of their audacity, which shows that it is the threat for every eater, whether or not that statement is what drove him to it.

As for His, glorified be He, saying: ﴿So whoever receives an admonition from his Lord and desists﴾, and His, exalted be He, saying: ﴿And whoever returns﴾, it refers to the speaker who holds the belief. And if it is taken as a reference to the mentioned rising, then the recompense is what is understood from joining the act to the statement, for if it had no part in the punishment it would not be fitting in the context of a threat. The view that the object of "returns" is riba, and that the verse is to be understood as an intensification of the warning, goes against the apparent meaning. So reflect.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on Surah 2, verse 276:

﴿Allah destroys usury (*riba*, unlawful interest)﴾. That is, He removes its blessing and destroys the wealth into which it enters. Aḥmad, Ibn Mājah, Ibn Jurayj and al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn Masʿūd, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Indeed, usury, however much it increases, its outcome becomes a decrease." ʿAbd al-Razzāq related from Maʿmar, who said: "We have heard that no period of forty years passes over the one who practises usury before it is destroyed. Perhaps this is the general pattern." From al-Ḍaḥḥāk: this destruction is in the Hereafter, by the nullifying of whatever comes from it that is expected to benefit, so that nothing of it remains for its people. ﴿And He causes charities to grow﴾: He increases them, multiplies their reward, and increases the wealth from which the charity is given. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim related from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever gives in charity the equivalent of a date from lawful earnings, and Allah accepts only what is good, Allah receives it with His right hand, then nurtures it for its giver just as one of you nurtures his foal, until it becomes like a mountain." Al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad related the like of this. The point of the verse is that the one who practises usury seeks an increase in wealth, while the one who withholds charity withholds it in pursuit of an increase in wealth. Thus Allah, glorified is He, made clear that usury is a cause of loss and not of growth, and that charity is a cause of growth and not of loss. This is what has been said, and they regarded it as the reason the verses on spending were followed by the verse on usury.

﴿And Allah does not love﴾, does not approve of, ﴿every ungrateful sinner﴾: one who holds fast to disbelief, persists in it, and is accustomed to it. ﴿Sinner﴾ [276]: one who is wholly immersed in committing it. The verse expresses the universality of the negation, not the negation of universality, since there is no difference between one individual and another. The choice of the intensive form (*kaffār*, *athīm*) serves to alert to the enormity of the one who consumes usury and of the one who deems it lawful. Concerning usury alone what has been reported has been reported; so what is his state if he deems it lawful? May Allah, exalted is He, protect us from that. Al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bayhaqī related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "A single dirham of usury is more grievous before Allah, exalted is He, than thirty-six acts of adultery." He also said: "Whoever has flesh grown from what is unlawful, the Fire is more fitting for him." Ibn Mājah and others related from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, usury has seventy gates, the least of which is like a man lying with his mother. And the most grievous usury is a man's disparagement of his brother's honour." Jamīl ibn Darrāj related from the Imāmiyya, from Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Ḥusayn, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "A single dirham of usury is greater before Allah, exalted is He, than seventy acts of adultery, all of them with a woman forbidden in marriage within the Sacred House of Allah." ʿAbd al-Razzāq and others related from ʿAlī, may Allah honour his face, that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed five parties in regard to usury: the one who consumes it, the one who pays it, its two witnesses, and its scribe."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 277:

﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾ in what belief in it is obligatory, ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ (al-a'mal al-salihat), in the manner they were commanded, ﴿and establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾. Their being singled out for mention, despite their being included among the deeds, is to draw attention to the great excellence of these two: the first (prayer) is the greatest of the physical acts of worship, and the second (zakah) is the most excellent of the financial acts. ﴿For them is their reward﴾ that was promised to them, in the state of being ﴿with their Lord﴾. Expressing it in this way carries additional kindness and honor. ﴿No fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve﴾ [277] because of the abundance of their share.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 278:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ outwardly. ﴿Fear Allah﴾, i.e., protect yourselves from His punishment. ﴿And give up﴾, i.e., leave ﴿what remains of interest﴾ owed to you by people. ﴿If you are believers﴾ [278], from the depths of the heart. Its evidence is carrying out what you have been commanded. This is a conditional clause (shart) whose answer has been omitted, relying on what precedes it. The (min) in ﴿ما بَقِيَ مِنَ الرِّبا﴾ is partitive (tab'idiyyah). It is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of (baqiya). It was also said that it is connected to (baqiya). Al-Hasan read (baqa), converting the (ya) into an alif, according to the dialect of Tayy'. The verse, as al-Suddi said, was revealed concerning al-Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, the son of Abd al-Muttalib, and a man from Banu al-Mughirah, who were partners in the pre-Islamic period. They used to lend at interest to some people from Thaqif, from Banu Amrah, who are Banu Amr ibn Umayr. When Islam came, they had great sums of interest owed to them, and they gave them up when this verse was revealed.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muqatil, who said: "This verse was revealed concerning Banu Amr ibn Umayr ibn Awf al-Thaqafi, Mas'ud ibn Amr ibn Abd Yalil ibn Amr, Rabi'ah ibn Amr, and Habib ibn Umayr. They were all brothers, and they were the creditors and the debtors, namely Banu al-Mughirah from Banu Makhzum. In the pre-Islamic period, they used to lend to Banu al-Mughirah at interest. The Prophet ﷺ had made a treaty with Thaqif, and they demanded their interest from Banu al-Mughirah, which was a great amount. Banu al-Mughirah said: 'By Allah, we will not pay interest in Islam, for Allah and His Messenger have abolished it for the Muslims.' They informed Mu'adh ibn Jabal, and it is said Itab ibn Usayd, of their situation. He wrote to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that Banu Amr ibn Umayr were demanding their interest from Banu al-Mughirah. Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who have believed﴾, etc. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote to Mu'adh ibn Jabal to present this verse to them. If they comply, they shall have their principal sums; but if they refuse, then announce to them war from Allah and His Messenger." This is the meaning of His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But if you do not do so﴾."

[Page 53]

﴿If you do not do it﴾, that is, what you were commanded of fearing God and leaving off what remains (of interest), whether while denying its prohibition or while acknowledging it, ﴿then be informed﴾, that is, then be certain. Thus did al-Hasan read it, and this is the transmitted explanation from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: ﴿of a war from God and His Messenger﴾. It is like the war against apostates according to the first case, and like the war against rebels (bughat) according to the second. It has been said: there is no actual war, but it is only a threat and intimidation. However, the majority of the exegetes hold the first view. Hamzah and 'Asim, in the transmission of Ibn 'Ayyash, read (fa-ādhanū) with a long vowel, meaning: then inform yourselves of it, or inform one another, or inform others. This implies their knowledge of the war in the most complete way. The indefiniteness of "war" (harb) is for magnification, and for this reason it was not said "the war of God" in the construct form. Abu Ya'la transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that when this verse was revealed, the Thaqif said: "We have no power against war from God and His Messenger ﷺ."

﴿But if you repent﴾ of what necessitates war, ﴿then you shall have your principal sums﴾, which you may take and nothing more. ﴿You shall not wrong﴾ your debtors by taking the excess, ﴿nor shall you be wronged﴾ [279] by them through diminishing the principal, or by both that and procrastination in payment and the like. Al-Mufaddal transmitted from 'Asim the reading "lā tazlimūna" with the first verb in the passive and the second in the active, the reverse of the first reading. The clause is either independent (mustaʾnafah), which is the apparent meaning, or it is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in (lakum), with the governing element being the sense of stability contained in the prepositional phrase because it occurs as a predicate; this is the view of al-Akhfash. Since this ruling is conditioned on their repentance, it follows that it does not hold when they do not repent. If their not repenting is coupled with denial of the prohibition, then they are apostates, and what they earned in the state of apostasy is spoils (fay') for the Muslims according to Imam Abu Hanifa, may God be pleased with him; and likewise all their other property according to al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him. According to us, it goes to their heirs, and they have nothing in any case. If their not repenting is coupled with acknowledgment, then if they have strength, they are on the verge of being killed, and their principal sums will hardly be safe for them, let alone their capital. Otherwise, the same applies according to Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both. Ibn Jarir transmitted from him that he said: "Whoever persists in usury and does not desist from it, it is incumbent upon the ruler of the Muslims to ask him to repent; if he desists, well and good, otherwise his neck is struck." Similar is reported from al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him. As for according to others, they are imprisoned until their repentance becomes evident, and they are not permitted to conduct any transactions at all. So as long as they do not repent, nothing of their property is handed over to them; rather, it is handed over only upon their death to their heirs. Mawla Abu al-Su'ud and others said: The verse has been cited as evidence that one who refuses to pay a debt while able to pay is a wrongdoer who is punished by imprisonment and other means, and the jurists have detailed this in the most thorough manner.

[Page 54]

*Ruh al-Ma'ani* of al-Alusi, on Surah 2, verse 280:

﴿And if the debtor is in hardship﴾: that is, if the one owed is in a state of straitened means, lacking wealth. Here *kana* (was/is) is a complete verb (*tammah*, meaning it needs no predicate). Some of the Kufans (*al-Kufiyyun*, the grammarians of Kufa) permitted that it be incomplete (*naqisah*, needing a predicate), with *dhu* as its subject and the predicate omitted, meaning: "And if there is a debtor who has a claim against you, or a creditor, or one of your creditors." 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, read *dha 'usrah* (with *dha* in the accusative), and it was also read *wa-man kana dha 'usrah* ("and whoever is..."). In both readings *kana* is incomplete, and its subject is a hidden pronoun within it referring to the creditor, even though he is not mentioned. The verse was revealed, as al-Kalbi said, when the Banu al-Mughirah said to the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Umayr: "We today are people of hardship, so defer us until the fruit ripens," and they refused to defer them.

[Page 54]

﴿then let there be respite﴾: the *fa'* is the answer to the conditional particle. *Nazrah* (respite) is a subject (*mubtada'*) whose predicate is omitted, meaning: "then for you there is a respite." Or it is the object of an implied verb, meaning: "then respite is obligatory." It was also said that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "then the matter is..." or "then what is required is respite." *Nazrah* is like *nazrah* (with the vowel on the *zay* dropped), meaning waiting; the intended meaning is granting time and delay. 'Ata' read *fa-nazirahu* (in the form of *fa-natiruhu*), with the noun *nazir* (one who waits) in the genitive, joined to the pronoun of ﴿dhu 'usrah﴾, meaning: "then the one entitled to it is his waiter, that is, the one who waits for him and grants him time, and the holder of his respite," in the manner of *Ibn wa-Tamir* (the same pattern as "possessor of milk and dates"). It was also reported from him that he read *fa-nazirhu* as an imperative of the form *mufa'alah*, meaning: "then be lenient with him by granting respite." ﴿until a time of ease﴾: that is, until a time or the existence of wealth. Hamzah and Nafi' read *maysurah* with a *damma* on the *sin*, and both forms are dialects, like *mushriqah* and *mushruqah*. It was also read with both forms in the construct state (*mudafan*), with the *ta'* dropped and the *idafah* standing in its place. The objection raised against this reading, that *maf'al* with a *damma* does not exist, or is rare, is answered: its basic form is *maf'alah*, not *maf'al*. It was also answered that it is absent in singular nouns, and this is the plural of *maysurah*, as it is said of *makram* being the plural of *makrumah*. It was also said that the original form is *maysurah* (with the *waw*), which was lightened by dropping the *waw*, the *damma* indicating it.

﴿And that you give charity﴾: one of the two *ta'*s is dropped. It was also read with the *sad* doubled, on the basis that the original is *tatasaddaqu*, the second *ta'* being changed into a *sad* and assimilated. Meaning: your giving of charity to your insolvent debtors, by remitting the principal, either entirely or in part, ﴿is better for you﴾: that is, more rewarding than granting respite, or better than what you take, because that is finite and this is lasting.

Ibn al-Mundhir related from al-Dahhak that he said: "Respite is obligatory, and the best of Allah's reward is charity over respite." It was also said that the meaning of *tasaddaq* (charity) is granting respite, for what Ahmad related from 'Imran ibn al-Husayn, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever is owed a right by a man and grants him an extension, for him there is a charity for each day." The Imam weakened this, both because it contradicts what is transmitted, and because the obligation of respite was established by the first verse, so this verse must be understood as having an additional benefit; and because His saying, glory be to Him, ﴿is better for you﴾ is not fitting for what is obligatory but for what is recommended.

Those who hold that it is obligatory to grant respite to the insolvent debtor in every case, whether the debt is a debt of *riba* (usury, unlawful interest) or not, based their argument on the unrestricted wording of the verse. This is the view taken by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt. Shurayh, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, in one narration from him, held that it is obligatory only in the case of a debt of *riba* specifically, and they interpreted the verse accordingly.

﴿if you know﴾: the answer to *in* (if) is omitted, meaning: "if you know that it is better for you, then do it." This contains an exhortation to act.

﴿And fear a Day﴾, which is the Day of Resurrection or the Day of Death. Its indefiniteness is for magnification, just as attaching fear of it is for emphasis in warning against its severities, which make the young grow old. ﴿In which you will be returned﴾ is in the passive voice from the verb *raja'a* (to return). It has also been read in the active voice, from *ruju'* (to return). The passive is more appropriate, as has been said, for conveying awe. It has also been read as *yurja'una* (they will be returned), in the grammatical shift known as *iltifat* (a change of grammatical person). Ubayy read *tusayyarun* (you will be made to go), and Abd Allah read *turaddun* (you will be sent back). ﴿To Allah﴾, that is, to His judgment and His decision. ﴿Then every soul shall be paid in full﴾, that is, be given in complete measure, ﴿what it earned﴾, whether good or bad. Its recompense, if good, is good, and if bad, is bad. *Al-kasb* (acquisition, earning) means action in whatever form it takes, as the language has affirmed and the reports have indicated. The *kasb* of al-Ash'ari (the theory of acquisition) is understood only by the Ash'aris (the followers of al-Ash'ari).

﴿And they will not be wronged﴾ [281]. This is a circumstantial clause (*jumla haliyya*) referring back to ﴿every soul﴾. The pronoun is plural because the sense is plural. He first returned the pronoun in the singular, taking account of the wording, and gave priority to consideration of the wording because it is the original basis, and because consideration of the sense came at the end of a verse-ending (*fasila*), so placing it later was better. You may also say that the plural is more fitting for what occurs on that Day, just as the singular is preferable in what precedes it.

Many narrators, through more than one chain, related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the verse ﴿And fear a Day﴾ etc. was the last of what was revealed of the Qur'an. There has been disagreement about how long he (ﷺ) lived after it: it was said nine nights, it was said seven days, it was said three hours, it was said twenty-one days, and it was said eighty-one days. Then he died. Upon him be blessings and peace, he was alive and dead (ﷺ).

It is reported that he (ﷺ) said: "Place it between the verse of usury (*riba*) and the verse of debt." In another report, he (ﷺ) said: "Gabriel came to me and said: Place it at the two hundred and eightieth verse of al-Baqara." There is no conflict between this and the report from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that this was the last verse revealed, as recorded by al-Bukhari, Abu Ubayd, Ibn Jarir and al-Bayhaqi through the chain of al-Sha'bi from him, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The last verse that Allah the Exalted revealed to His Messenger (ﷺ) was the verse of usury." Similar to this is what al-Bayhaqi recorded through the chain of Ibn al-Musayyib from Umar ibn al-Khattab. As Muhammad ibn Maslama said, as transmitted from him by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Kirbasi, the meaning of this is that the last of the verses revealed concerning sales was the verse of usury, or that it means this was among the last revealed, as Imam Ahmad's report explicitly states.

When He, glory be to Him, commanded granting respite to the debtor who is in hardship and deferring the payment, He followed it with an explanation of the rulings on deferred rights and contracts of debt, so the Mighty One, the Lord of all, said:

[Page 55]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 1 of 3):

﴿O you who have believed⦆ — in God, the Exalted, and in what came from Him — ﴿when you contract a debt⦆, i.e., when you deal with one another, and one of you lends to another, ﴿with a debt⦆. The benefit of mentioning it is to specify what is shared and to remove ambiguity, in support of the view that (tadayantum, "you contract a debt") comes with the meaning "you deal in debt" and also with the meaning "you reciprocate." This is not refuted by the claim that the context rules it out, because the discussion concerns the explicit wording, and the context may be noticed only by the discerning. It was also said: it was mentioned so that the pronoun may refer back to it, for otherwise it would have said: "then write the debt," and the composition would not have had that beauty in the judgment of one of refined taste who knows the styles of speech. It was objected that "contracting debt" already implies it, so it would be of the type of ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety⦆. It was answered that "debt" is not meant as a verbal noun but as one of the two counter-items, and "contracting" implies it only through the context, which is not sufficient in a setting of explanation, especially as it is ambiguous. It was also said: it was mentioned because it is clearer, distinguishing debt into deferred and immediate, since indefiniteness carries generality and partiality; when it is restricted by the time limit, and had it not been mentioned, it might have been understood that debt is only of that kind. ﴿For a specified term⦆, i.e., a period of time. It is connected to (tadayantum), and it may be an attribute of "debt," i.e., deferred or postponed until a term. ﴿Specified⦆ by days, months, or their equivalents, which convey knowledge and remove ignorance, not by something like the harvest, lest it return to its subject with invalidity. ﴿Then write it⦆, i.e., the debt with its term, because that is gentler and more secure. The majority hold it to be recommended, based on His words: ﴿But if one of you trusts another⦆. According to some, the verse clearly indicates that every debt has this ruling. Ibn 'Abbas restricted the debt to the salam (advance sale), for al-Bukhari narrated from him that he said: "I testify that the salaf (advance payment) guaranteed for a specified term — God has made it deferred and permitted it," then he recited the verse. Imam Malik used it as evidence for the permissibility of deferring a loan.

﴿And let a scribe write between you with justice⦆. This explains the manner of writing commanded and specifies who should undertake it, right after the general command. The object of "write" is omitted, being understood, or for the purpose of focusing on the act itself. Restricting with the adverbial phrase indicates that none of the two contracting parties should be the sole one handling it, to avert suspicion. The prepositional phrase is connected to an omitted element functioning as an attribute of "scribe," i.e., the scribe should be one whose nature is to be even-handed and not lean toward either side by addition or subtraction. It may also be an adverbial complement connected to "scribe" or to its verb. The meaning is that the contracting parties are commanded, by way of metonymy, to have the debt written by a just jurist of religion, so that what he writes is trusted and agreed upon among the people of knowledge. Thus, as al-Tibi said, the speech is directed to one meaning, and another is embedded in it by the indication of the text, namely the condition that the scribe be a jurist, because one cannot be even-handed in weighty matters except one who is learned. For this reason some have used the verse as evidence that no one should write documents except one who knows them, is just, and trustworthy; and whoever is not such, the ruler or his deputy must prevent him, lest corruption occur and disputes multiply. ﴿And God does not love corrupters⦆.

﴿And let not a scribe refuse⦆, i.e., let none of the scribes described by what was mentioned refuse ﴿to write⦆ the debt document between the contracting parties ﴿as God has taught him⦆, i.e., because of what God, the Exalted, has taught him of writing documents and bestowed upon him. It is connected to "write." The sentence is in the manner of ﴿And do good as God has done good to you⦆. ﴿As God has done good to you⦆, i.e., let him not refuse to bestow it on people, since God, the Exalted, has favored him and distinguished him. The particle "ka" may be connected to "to write," as an attribute of an omitted verbal noun, or as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun of the verbal noun according to the view of Sibawayh. The estimate is: to write a writing like what God, the Exalted, taught him; or to write it, i.e., the documents, like what God, the Exalted, taught him, and He explained it to him by His words: ﴿with justice⦆. It was also permitted that it be connected to His words, the Exalted: ﴿so let him write⦆, and the "fa" does not prevent this, as in ﴿and your Lord, so magnify⦆, since it is a connective in meaning. The command to write after the prohibition of refusal is, on the first reading, for emphasis, and it was needed because a prohibition of something is not explicitly a command to its opposite, according to the most correct view; so it was emphasized by stating it explicitly, out of concern for the matter of writing. From this, some went to the view that the command is obligatory and a communal obligation (fard kifaya). But since the command is for us and not against us, it was turned away from that, lest what preceded regarding the ambiguity of the term return. As for the second reading, there is no emphasis: it is a command to write the restricted kind after a prohibition of refusing the absolute kind, and this does not indicate emphasis, because a prohibition of refusing the absolute does not imply a command to the restricted to make its mention afterward an emphasis. Some have asserted this, because if refusing absolute writing is forbidden, then refusing lawful writing is forbidden all the more, and a prohibition of refusing lawful writing is a command to it; so the command to lawful writing is explicit for emphasis. Also, when an absolute and a restricted expression come concerning one event, the absolute is understood in light of the restricted, whether the absolute came first or later. Just as the command to write in absolute form in the first reading was understood as restricted writing for emphasis, why was the prohibition of refusing absolute writing not understood as restricted writing for emphasis? Is the distinction between the two commands anything but a pure arbitrary judgment, as is not hidden? As for (ma): it was said to be either a verbal (masdariyya) particle or a restricting particle, and it was permitted that it be a relative or a qualifying particle; in both cases the pronoun refers to it, and in the first two cases it refers to the scribe. Some estimated in every case that the second object is the knowledge of writing documents, so understand.

﴿And let the one upon whom the truth is due dictate⦆, i.e., from dictation, meaning casting onto the scribe what he writes; its verb is "amlaltu," and one of the doubled letters may be changed to a "y," followed by the verbal noun, and it may be changed to a hamza because it is final after an added alif, so it is said "imla'," which with "imlal" has the same meaning. That is: let what is dictated to the scribe of the debt he writes be ﴿that which is upon him, the truth⦆, and he is the one sought, because he is the one witnessed against, so he must be the acknowledger and no other. Exclusivity is understood from attaching the ruling to the attribute, for the placing of a ruling upon an attribute indicates causation, and the default is that there is no other cause. ﴿And let him fear God, his Lord⦆, i.e., the one upon whom the truth is due; he combined the august name with the beautiful attribute, for emphasis in urging piety by mentioning what conveys majesty and beauty. ﴿And let him not diminish⦆, i.e., let him not reduce (from it), i.e., from the truth that he dictates to the scribe, ﴿anything⦆, even if it is small. It was read "shay'an" with the hamza dropped, and "shayyan" with doubling.

This is the interpretation transmitted from Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It was said: the pronoun of "let him fear" may refer to the scribe, but this is not right, because the pronoun of "let him not diminish" is for the one upon whom the truth is due, since he is the one from whom diminishing is expected specifically; as for the scribe, increase is expected from him as much as reduction, so if his prohibition were intended, it would have forbidden both, and it has done so in commanding justice and returning each to each; a separation not indicated by any evidence. The strictness in obligating the dictator was because he combined in it the command of God-consciousness and the prohibition of diminishing, for there are motives within him toward what is forbidden, since man is naturally inclined to repel harm as far as possible.

Regarding (minhu, "from it") there are two possibilities: first, that it is connected to "let him not diminish," with "min" denoting the starting point; second, that it is connected to an omitted element, since originally it was an attribute of the indefinite noun, and when it was placed before it, it became a circumstantial clause. "Anything" is either a direct object or a verbal noun.

﴿But if the one upon whom the truth is due⦆ — he stated this explicitly in a place where a pronoun would have served, for greater clarity, not because the command and prohibition are for someone else. "Upon him" is connected to an omitted element, meaning "is obligated," and "the truth" is the subject. It was permitted that "upon him" be a predicate preceding and "the truth" a delayed subject, so the sentence is nominal; in either estimate it has no place in grammatical analysis, since it is the relative clause. ﴿Is a fool⦆, i.e., incapable and foolish, as said by Ibn Zayd; or ignorant of dictation, as said by Mujahid; or wasteful of his wealth and corrupting his religion, as said by al-Shafi'i. ﴿Or weak⦆, i.e., a child, or a senile old man. ﴿Or is unable himself to dictate⦆: this is a clause conjoined to a singular noun which is the predicate of "kana," since it is treated as a singular; i.e., or is unable to dictate by himself due to muteness, as was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both; or for what is more general than that, including ignorance of the language and all other preventing conditions. The explicit pronoun is an emphasis for the hidden pronoun in "yumilla," and the benefit of emphasizing with it is removing the metaphor that the attribution of the verb to the pronoun might bear, and the explicit statement that he is unable by himself. It was said that the pronoun is the subject of "yumilla," and the change of style is for attention to the matter of negation. The goodness of assimilation here, and of disjunction in what preceded, is not hidden. Similar to it is disjunction in His words: ﴿so let his guardian dictate⦆, i.e., the one who manages his affairs, even if he is not specifically the legal guardian, so it includes the appraiser, the agent, and the interpreter. Acknowledgment on behalf of another in such a case is accepted, and there is a difference between it and acknowledgment against another, so understand this. ﴿With justice⦆ between the rights-holder and the one under guardianship, so he neither adds nor subtracts. He was not obligated with the same thing he was obligated with regarding the truth, because increase is expected from him just as diminishing is expected.

Some used the verse as evidence that a guardian (wasi) may not be a dhimmi or a fasiq, and that he may be a slave or a woman, since no condition for guardians was stipulated except justice; this was mentioned by Ibn al-Faras, but it is not right, as is not hidden.

Some people used His words, ﴿so let him write⦆ and ﴿and let him not refuse⦆, as evidence for the obligation of writing. To this went al-Sha'bi, al-Jubba'i, and al-Rummani, except that they said it is obligatory as a communal duty. Al-Hasan's words incline to this. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: it is obligatory on him to write when he is commanded. It was said: it is recommended. It was narrated from al-Dahhak that it was obligatory and then abrogated.

﴿And call upon two witnesses⦆, i.e., seek them out so that they may bear witness to what passed between you. It was permitted that the sin and ta' be extra, i.e., "bear witness." In choosing the intensive form there is a hint toward seeking one who has repeatedly borne witness, so he knows its place and is capable of discharging it; and there seems to be an allusion to justice, because such repetition does not occur from a person before judges except that he is accepted by them. Perhaps that is why it did not say "two men." The command is for recommendation or obligation, according to the disagreement on this. ﴿From your men⦆: connected to "call upon," with "min" denoting the starting point, or to an omitted element as an attribute of "two witnesses," with "min" partitive. The address is to the believers with whom the verse begins. The mention of "men" as a plural attributed to the pronoun of the addressees indicates the requirement of Islam, puberty, and maleness in the two witnesses, and freedom, since "men" conventionally means full adults, while slaves are like cattle; moreover, the speeches of the Law do not include slaves by way of direct expression, as explained in its proper place. The Imamis went to the view that freedom is not a condition for accepting testimony, and that...

The condition for this, according to them, is Islam and justice (ʿadalah). This is the view of Shurayh, Ibn Sirin, Abu Thawr and ʿUthman al-Battiy. It contradicts what is narrated from ʿAli, may Allah ennoble his face, for he did not permit the testimony of a slave in anything. The verse does not address the testimony of disbelievers against one another. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, permitted it by analogy, even if their religious communities differ.

﴿فَإنْ لَمْ يَكُونا﴾ (“But if they are not”), that is, the two witnesses, ﴿رَجُلَيْنِ﴾ (“two men”). That is, their being called as witnesses was not intended, even if they were present. The ruling belongs to the category of negating the generality, not the generality of negation. Otherwise the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿فَرَجُلٌ وامْرَأتانِ﴾ (“then a man and two women”), would not be valid. That is: if there are not two men gathered together, then let a man and two women testify; or, “a man and two women shall testify or abstain”; or, “the witness is a man and two women”; or, “let a man and two women be called as witnesses”; or, “let a man and two women be witnesses.” If the verb *yakun* is taken as complete (*tammah*), then there is no need to supply the word “witnesses.” The sufficiency of one man and two women as testimony applies, according to us, in matters other than the hudud (prescribed punishments) and qisas (retaliation). According to al-Shafiʿi, it applies only to property, not to other matters such as the contract of marriage. Malik said: the testimony of those [a man and two women] is not valid in hudud, nor in qisas, nor in walaʾ (the right of patronage), nor in ihsan (the status of marital chastity). It is valid in agency (*wikalah*) and bequest (*wasiyyah*) if there is no manumission in them. As for the acceptance of the testimony of women alone, they have said it is valid concerning childbirth, virginity, the crying out of a newborn (*istihlal*), and what is similar to these, as explained in the books of jurisprudence (*fiqh*). The word ﴿وامْرَأتانِ﴾ has also been read with a silent hamzah, and perhaps that is due to the accumulation of moving letters.

﴿مِمَّنْ تَرْضَوْنَ﴾ (“of those whom you accept”) is connected to an omitted element that stands as a qualifier (*sifah*) of ﴿رَجُلٌ وامْرَأتانِ﴾, meaning: they are of those whom you accept. The explicit mention of this here, although its consideration applies to every witness, is due to the rarity of women being described by it. Therefore, what is stated in *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit* of Abu Hayyan) is not an objection: that making it a qualifier of the mentioned (party) implies the negation of this attribute from the two witnesses. It has also been said that it is a qualifier of the two witnesses, but this is judged weak because of the intervening separation between them. It has also been said that it is a substitute (*badal*) for ﴿رِجالِكم﴾ (“your men”) by repeating the governing verb, but this is also judged weak because of the separation. Abu Hayyan preferred connecting it to ﴿اسْتَشْهِدُوا﴾ (“call to witness”), so that it is a restriction on the whole, but that entails separation between the condition regarding the two women and its justification, and this, as you see, is weak. The address is to the believers. It has been said that the address is to the judges. He did not say “from among those who are approved” because that implies the requirement that they be such in reality, and we have no way to know it, for we have only the outward appearance, while Allah the Exalted takes charge of the inner states.

﴿مِنَ الشُّهَداءِ﴾ (“from among the witnesses”) is connected to an omitted element, as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the omitted returning pronoun. That is: of those whom you accept, in the state of being some of the witnesses, because of your knowledge of their justice. The inclusion of women within the plural is by way of predominance (*taghlib*).

﴿أنْ تَضِلَّ إحْداهُما فَتُذَكِّرَ إحْداهُما الأُخْرى﴾ (“that if one of them errs, the other reminds her”) is an explanation of the wisdom behind the legislation of the ruling and the requirement of the number regarding women. That is: this was legislated with the intention that one of them reminds the other if one of them errs, because forgetfulness predominates in the nature of women due to the abundance of moisture in their temperaments. The intention (*irādah*) is taken as implied because the restrictive element of the command must be an act of the one commanding and a motive for it, and here there is nothing but the will of Allah the Exalted, for it is certain that the error and the reminding after it are not the motive for the command; rather, the intention is that. It has been objected that forgetting and failing to be guided to the testimony should not be what Allah the Exalted intends by the legislative will, especially since He has commanded the calling of witnesses. It is answered that the will has not been directed to the error itself, meaning the failure to be guided to the testimony, but to the error that results in the reminder. Among their principles is that the restrictive element is the target of the purpose, so it is as if He linked the will to the reminding that is caused by and follows from the error, and so the justification returns to what we have mentioned. This is better than what some have held in the answer, that the intended meaning of “error” is the reminding, because error is a cause of reminding, so the cause is mentioned and the effect is intended. This is because it is evident that it cannot remain on its outward meaning in view of the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿فَتُذَكِّرَ﴾ (“so she reminds”). It has been said: the point in choosing ﴿أنْ تَضِلَّ﴾ etc. over “that if she forgets she reminds” is an indication of the intensity of concern with the matter of reminding, to the extent that what is disliked becomes as if it were sought for its sake, insofar as it leads to it. The second ﴿إحْداهُما﴾ (“one of them”) may be the subject (*fāʿil*) of ﴿تُذَكِّرَ﴾, and this is not a case of putting an explicit noun in place of a pronoun, since the one who reminds is not the one who forgets. It may also be the object (*maf'ūl*) of ﴿تُذَكِّرَ﴾, with the other being the subject. This is not of the type of “Musa struck ʿIsa,” as it has been wrongly supposed, so that the first would be determined. Rather, it is of the type of “the younger nursed the elder,” because the earlier mention of one of them with the attribution of error removes the error. The reason for placing the object before the subject is to draw attention to the concern with reminding the one who has erred. For this reason, as has been said, the explicit noun was used instead of the pronoun, because placing it first in that case would not signal concern as the placement of the explicit object does, for if it were postponed nothing would follow except that it was put in its original place.

Many have mentioned that the shift from ﴿فَتُذَكِّرُها الأُخْرى﴾ (“so she reminds the other one of them”), which is the reading of Ibn Masʿud as narrated by al-Aʿmash, to what is in the noble text is for emphasizing the ambiguity and for the great care in guarding against the supposition that the error is specific to one particular one of them and the reminding to the other. Al-Husayn ibn ʿAli al-Maghribi went far astray in this context, making the pronoun of the first ﴿إحْداهُما﴾ refer to the two testimonies, and the pronoun of the second ﴿إحْداهُما﴾ refer to the two women. The meaning, according to him, is: that one of the two testimonies errs, that is, is lost through forgetting, so one of the two women reminds the other of them. Al-Tabarsi supported this by saying that one who forgets a testimony is not called “erring”; rather it is said “the testimony erred” when it is lost, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿ضَلُّوا عَنّا﴾ (“they have strayed from us”), meaning they were lost to us. On this view the speech is free of any suspicion of the substitution of the pronoun for the explicit noun. But this is not valid, because then there would be no “other” of one of them in the speech, along with the disjointedness and lack of coherence. What was cited in support indicates little familiarity with the language, for in *Nihayat Ibn al-Athir* and others, “erring” is applied to the forgetful one. This was narrated concerning the verse from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak, al-Rabiʿ, al-Suddi and others. Close to this in strangeness is what has been said, that it is among the innovations of tafsir (*bidaʿ al-tafsir*), namely what is related from Ibn ʿUyaynah: that the meaning of ﴿فَتُذَكِّرَ﴾ etc. is “so that one of them makes the other a male,” meaning that when the two are together they are in the position of a male. This has a deficiency in both meaning and wording, for reminding as opposed to forgetting is a clear meaning and an evident purpose, and the preservation of the number is because women are the seat of forgetfulness in this way. Also, making her a male is a metaphor for placing her in the position of a male, and then there is a second metaphor because the two are those standing in his place, so one of them is not made to stand in his place (after the metaphor, it is not on its outward meaning), because the need for the presence of a male with them is absolutely necessary.

The words of the Glorified, ﴿فَإنْ لَمْ يَكُونا رَجُلَيْنِ﴾ (“But if they are not two men”), indicate their deficiency in that respect as well, and the obligation to justify the like of that. Presenting it for acceptance is not considered a virtue; rather, to people of taste it is pure superfluity. I have seen in *Tiraz al-Majalis* that al-Khafaji asked the Chief Judge Shihab al-Din al-Ghaznawi about the secret of the repetition of ﴿إحدى﴾ (“one of”), alluding to what al-Maghribi had mentioned, and he said:

O head of the scholars, the noble lords, and the one whose generosity has spread over all creation,
what is the secret of repeating “one of” without “reminding her” in a verse about the witnesses in al-Baqarah?
The apparent situation is the brevity of the pronoun instead of repeating “one of them,” if he had mentioned it.
Taking “one of” to refer to the testimony itself in the first is not acceptable to the skilled.
So plunge with your thought to extract its pearl from the sea of your knowledge, then send us pearls.

The judge answered:

O you whose benefits are spread abroad by knowledge, and whose virtues are famed in the universe,
O you who alone unveiled the sciences—your question has come while the secrets are still hidden.
(“One of them errs”): the saying is open to both of them, so it needs clarification to be made manifest.
Had he used a pronoun, it would have implied the specification of one particular party for the ruling, which is worth considering.
And the one to whom you referred the solution, as you have indicated, is not acceptable to anyone who examines it.
This is what the dull mind allowed me to offer, and Allah knows best what is meant in the content of what he mentioned.

It has been read ﴿أنْ تَضِلَّ﴾ with the passive voice and feminine form. It has been read (*fatudhākira*), and Ibn Kathir, Yaʿqub, Abu ʿAmr and al-Hasan read (*fatudhkir*) with a sukun on the dhal and a kasrah on the kaf. Hamzah read (*in taḍilla*) as a conditional, with *fatudhakkir* in the nominative. On this reading the verb is jussive (*majzum*), and the fathah is due to the meeting of two sukuns. The fa’ in the response (*jaza’*) has been said to be due to an omitted subject (*mubtada’*), which is the pronoun of the matter or of the testimony. It has been said there is no omission, because when the response is a affirmative present verb it is permissible to have the fa’ or omit it. It has been said: the best view is that the omitted subject is the pronoun of the one who reminds, and *ihdahuma* (“one of them”) is a substitute for it or for the pronoun in *tudhakkira*. Some scholars said: the best view in all of this is to posit a dual pronoun, that is, “they two: one of them reminds the other.” Much of the grammarians’ discussion follows this. Those who differed on this were moved because they saw al-Zamakhshari’s comparison of the nominative reading with the words of Allah the Exalted, ﴿ومَن عادَ فَيَنْتَقِمُ اللَّهُ مِنهُ﴾ (“and whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him”), and they did not perceive that this is only because of the postulation of a pronoun after the fa’ according to what the context requires, not because of the specific pronoun in singular or dual. And Allah the Exalted is the one who inspires right guidance. So reflect.

﴿ولا يَأْبَ الشُّهَداءُ إذا ما دُعُوا﴾ (“And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called”) means: to give testimony or to bear it. This is what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them. Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr restricted it to the first, which is the apparent meaning, since it does not require resorting to figurative usage. However, what is narrated from al-Rabiʿ is that the verse was revealed when a man would go around among a large group of people calling them to testify, and none of them would follow him. Its apparent meaning requires the view of a figurative usage of approaching (*mushārafah*). Here ﴿ما﴾ (“ma”) is a superfluous particle (*silah*), a regular and consistent usage after *idhā*.

﴿ولا تَسْأمُوا﴾ (“And do not be weary”) means: do not become bored or impatient. From this is the saying of Zuhayr:

I have grown weary of the burdens of life, and whoever lives eighty years, O your father, becomes weary.

﴿أنْ تَكْتُبُوهُ﴾ (“of writing it”) means the debt, or “the right,” or the written document implied by the verb. The clause formed with *an* is the direct object of *tasʾamū*, which takes its object directly. It has been said that it takes it with a preposition which is omitted because it is known. It has been said that by weariness is meant laziness, but it was expressed by it because it occurs in the Qur’an as a description of the hypocrites, as in His words: ﴿وإذا قامُوا إلى الصَّلاةِ قامُوا كُسالى﴾ (“And when they stand up for prayer, they stand up lazily”). For this reason a hadith says: “A believer should not say ‘I am lazy (*kasiltu*),’ but he should say ‘I am weighed down (*thaqiltu*).’” It has been read (*wa-lā yasʾamū an yaktubūhu*) with the *ya’* in both places.

﴿صَغِيرًا أوْ كَبِيرًا﴾ (“small or large”) are two circumstantial accusatives (*ḥāl*) of the pronoun, meaning: in every state, whether little or much, summarized or detailed. It has been said they are accusatives as predicates of an omitted *kāna* (“was”). The small is mentioned before the large out of concern for it and progression from the lower to the higher.

﴿إلى أجَلِهِ﴾ (“to its term”) is a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in *taktubūhu*, meaning: remaining in the debtor’s obligation until the time of its falling due, which he acknowledged. It is not connected to *taktubūhu*, because the writing does not continue up to the term, since writing is something that ends in a short time.

﴿ذَلِكُمْ﴾ (“That”) refers to the writing, which is the nearer reference, or to the calling of witnesses, which is the more distant, or to all that has been mentioned, which is the best. The address is to the believers. ﴿أقْسَطُ﴾ (“more just”) means more equitable ﴿عِنْدَ اللَّهِ﴾ (“with Allah”), that is, in His judgment, glorified is He. ﴿وأقْوَمُ لِلشَّهادَةِ﴾ (“and more upright for testimony”) means more firm for it and more helpful for establishing and giving it. Both forms are derived from *aqsaṭa* and *aqāma* according to the view of Sibawayh, for he permits forming the comparative (*afʿal*) from verbs without irregularity. It has been said that they are from *qāsiṭ*, in the sense of “one possessing justice” and “straight.” Abu Hayyan said: *qasaṭa* can mean “to act unjustly” and “to act justly,” and *aqsaṭa*

[Page 59]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 3 of 3):

It is in the sense of ʿadala (to be just), and nothing else; this is related by Ibn al-Qattaʿ, and based on it there is no need for the opinion of Sibawayh regarding aqsaṭ. It was also said: it is from qasuṭa, on the pattern of karuma, meaning "to become possessed of qist," i.e., ʿadl (justice). The waw in aqwam remained sound, and one did not say aqama, because it is not changed in the elative exclamation form, as in mā aqwamahu, due to its being rigid (jumūd), since it does not undergo conjugation (tasarruf). The comparative form (afʿal al-tafḍīl) is appropriate to this meaning, so it was analogized to it. ﴿And it is nearer that you will not doubt﴾: i.e., closer to the absence of your doubt and uncertainty regarding the kind of debt, its amount, its term, and the like. It was said: this is the wisdom behind the creation of the Preserved Tablet and the Noble Scribes, even though He is the Self-Sufficient, Complete, Free of need of everything, as a teaching for the servants and a guidance for the rulers. The preposition (ḥarf al-jarr) here is implied, and it is (ilā), as you have heard. It was said it is (al-lām), it was said (min), and it was said (fī); each has its own direction.

﴿Except that it be a present trade that you conduct among yourselves﴾: this is an exceptive (istithnāʾ) disjunct (munqaṭiʿ) from the command to write. Thus His saying, ﴿And let a scribe write it down between you justly﴾ up to here, is a parenthetical clause (jumla iʿtirāḍiyya) between the exception and what is excepted from. That is: but at the time when your indebtedness or your trade is a present trade, with both exchanged on the spot, which you conduct among yourselves by handling it hand to hand. So it was said. In al-Durr al-Masun it is permissible that it be a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil) from the call to witness, so that one is commanded to witness in every situation except in the situation of the presence of trade. It was also said: it is an exception from this and that, and it is disjunct as well; meaning: but a present trade does not require witnessing or writing. Something other than this was also said, and perhaps the first is preferable.

ʿĀṣim read (tijāratan) in the accusative, as the predicate of (takūna), and its subject is a pronoun concealed in it referring to the trade, as al-Farrāʾ said. The return of a pronoun in such a case to something later in both wording and rank is common in eloquent speech. Some said: it refers to the indebtedness and the transaction understood from the discourse; and according to this, tijāra is a verbal noun, so that it does not entail predicating a thing of its own essence. The rest read it in the nominative, taking it as the subject of (takūna), with the predicate being the clause ﴿you conduct it﴾. It is also permissible for (takūna) to be complete, in which case the clause ﴿you conduct it﴾ is a qualifier.

﴿Then there is no blame upon you that you do not write it﴾: i.e., there is no harm upon you, or no sin, in your not writing it, because such a thing is far from dispute and forgetfulness, or because imposing writing upon you at that time would be very burdensome. The introduction of the fāʾ indicates the connection of what follows to what precedes.

﴿And take witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾: i.e., this mentioned sale, or generally. ﴿And let no harm befall a scribe or a witness﴾: a prohibition against harm. The verb admits of being read in the active voice and in the passive voice. The evidence for this is the reading of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him (wa-lā yuḍārir) with fak and kasr, and the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, with fak and fatḥ. The meaning according to the first: the scribe and the witness are forbidden from refusing to respond to what is requested of them, and from distortion, addition, and omission. According to the second: the prohibition is against harming them by causing them to be hurried away from something important, or by not giving the scribe his due wage, or by making the witness bear the burden of coming from a town. This meaning is supported by what Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Rabiʿ, who said: When this verse was revealed, ﴿and let no scribe refuse﴾, etc., one of them would come to the scribe and say: "Write for me." He would say: "I am busy, or I have a need, so go to someone else." He would insist and say: "You have been commanded to write for me," and he would not leave him alone and would harm him by that, while he could find someone else.
