So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And let no harm befall a scribe or a witness.﴾ Some combined the form to both meanings, and that is not correct, as is not hidden. Al-Hasan read (yuḍārri) with kasr. It was also read with raf (nominative), on the basis that it is a negation in the sense of a prohibition.

﴿And if you do﴾ what you have been forbidden of harm, or of it and of other than it, and its occurrence from you is far-fetched: ﴿then indeed it is a transgression in you﴾: i.e., a departure from obedience that is attached to you. It is permissible that the bāʾ be for location (ẓarfiyya). It was said: this is more eloquent, since they were made a locus for transgression.

﴿And fear Allah﴾ regarding what He has commanded you and forbidden you from. ﴿And Allah teaches you﴾ His rulings which include your interests. ﴿And Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ [282]: so your condition is not hidden from Him, and He will recompense you for it. If it is asked: how did He, glorified be He, repeat the Mighty Name in the three clauses, when they have found fault with the like of His saying:

Ah, what for the date-pit? Crushed is the date-pit...

until it was said: Did Allah the Exalted set upon him a sheep that eats his date-pit? It is answered: repetition is of two kinds, praiseworthy and blameworthy. The praiseworthy is every repetition that occurs in the manner of magnification or belittlement, in successive clauses each of which is independent in itself. The blameworthy is that the repetition be in a single clause, or in clauses with one meaning, without magnification or belittlement. What is in the verse belongs to the second kind, because "judhdha al-nawa, quṭiʿa al-nawa" has one meaning. What is in the verse is the jewel of the crown of the first kind, because "fear Allah" is an exhortation to the fear of Allah the Exalted; ﴿and Allah teaches you﴾ is a promise of His bounty, glorified be He; ﴿and Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ is a magnification of His majesty, exalted be His majesty. From here you know the reason for the conjunction in them, despite their difference outwardly in being declarative and imperative. Some people permitted that the middle clause be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "fear," meaning: fear Allah, with the teaching guaranteed for you. It is also permissible that it be a future circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara). The first, which we mentioned, is preferable, because the affirmative present verb occurring as a circumstantial clause with a waw is rare.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 283:**

﴿And if you are on a journey﴾, that is, travelling. Here there is a *isti'ara tab'iyya* (a derivative or contextual metaphor, *isti'ara tab'iyya*), in that He likened their being firmly established in the journey to the rider's being firmly settled upon his mount. ﴿And you find no scribe﴾ who writes for you as has been explained before. The clause is coordinated with the conditional verb (*fi'l al-shart*) or is a circumstantial clause (*hal*). Abu al-'Aliya read *kutuban* (كُتُبًا), and al-Hasan and Ibn 'Abbas read *kuttaban* (كُتّابًا), the plural of *katib*. ﴿Then a pledge taken into possession﴾: that is, what is used for securing the debt, or "then upon you," or "then let it be taken," or "then the prescribed course is a pledge" (*rihan*). It is the plural of *rahn*, which originally is a verbal noun (*masdar*), then it was applied to the thing pledged, by way of applying the verbal noun to the object (*ism al-maf'ul*). This conditional is not meant to make the journey and the absence of a scribe a condition for the legitimacy of pledging, because the Prophet (ﷺ) "pawned his armour in Madina to a Jew for thirty *sa'* of barley," as is in al-Bukhari. Rather, it is to establish that securing the debt by a pledge takes the place of securing it by writing during a journey, which is the situation where scribes are likely to be scarce. Mujahid took the apparent meaning of the verse and held that pledging is permissible only during a journey. Likewise al-Dahhak held that it is not permissible during a journey except when a scribe is absent. The verse did not address the case of the witness because he is in the position of the scribe in securing and in scarcity. The majority hold that taking possession (*qabd*) is required for the completion of the pledge. Malik held that it is completed by offer and acceptance (*ijab* and *qabul*), and that the pledgor is bound by the contract to deliver it. He also holds that it must remain in the possession of the pledgee; so if it returns to the possession of the pledgor, for instance if the pledgee deposits it with him or returns it to him without restriction, then it has left the pledge. Thus if the creditors (*ghurama'*) came while it was in the hand of the pledgor under one of these two cases, for example, they would share in it equally. Apparently he held this view because of the requirement of continuance (*iqtida' al-dawam*) in the pledge. Abu 'Ali recited:

*Bread and meat are pledged to them,*
*and a wine whose strainer is pouring.*

The expression "taken into possession" (*maqbuda*) instead of "you take into possession" (*taqbidunaha*) hints that it is sufficient for the agent (*wakil*) to take possession, and it does not depend on the pledgee himself taking possession. It was also read *faruhunun* (فَرُهُنٌ), like *suqufun*, which is also the plural of *rahn*, and read with a sukun on the *ha'* for lightness.

﴿And if one of you trusts another﴾: that is, one of the creditors trusts one of the debtors through good opinion, whether during a journey or at home, so he does not secure the debt by writing, witnesses or pledge. Ubayy read *fa-in u'umina* (فَإنْ أُومِنَ), meaning people trusted him and described the debtor as trustworthy, faithful, and needing no security from one like him. On this reading *ba'dan* is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition, as has been said. ﴿Let him who was entrusted discharge it﴾, and he is the debtor. He was described with this title because it is the clearest way of informing, and because it compels him to pay. ﴿His trust﴾: that is, his debt. The pronoun refers either to the creditor or to the debtor, on the ground that the debt is upon him. *Amana* is a verbal noun applied to the debt which is in the liability (*dhimma*). It was called a trust (*amana*), although it is guaranteed, because of his being entrusted with it by abandoning the pledge for it.

Page 63

It was also read *alladhi tumina* (اَلَّذِيتُمِنَ) with the *hamza* changed to *ya'*. It is reported from 'Asim that he read *alladhi ttumina* (اَلَّذِتُّمِنَ) with the *ya'* assimilated into the *ta'*. It was said that this is an error, because what is changed from a *hamza* has the same ruling, so it is not assimilated. It was rebutted that this is attested in the speech of the Arabs, and Ibn Malik reported its permissibility, saying that it is restricted to what is heard. From it is the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, *utturnina* (اُتُّمِنَ). Al-Saghani reported that the view of its permissibility is the doctrine of the Kufans. A similar form occurs in the speech of the Mother of the Believers 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, and she is among the acknowledged eloquent speakers. In al-Bukhari it is reported from her: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to order me, so I would *atazzir*," (فَأتَّزِرُ). So the one who considers it an error is himself in error. ﴿And let him fear Allah, his Lord﴾ in betrayal and in denying the right. In combining the title of divinity with the attribute of lordship there is emphasis and warning that is not hidden. Allah, glorified is He, has commanded taqwa at the time of fulfilment just as He commanded it at the time of acknowledgement, to magnify the rights of the servants and to warn against what causes corruption to occur.

﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾: that is, do not hide it by refraining from giving it when you are called to it. This is addressed to the believing witnesses, as is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others. Others made it addressed to the debtors, meaning: do not conceal your testimony against yourselves by acknowledging the truth when dealing, or do not try to nullify the testimony of the witnesses against you by discrediting them or the like at litigation, contrary to the apparent meaning reported from the pious predecessors (*salaf al-salih*). It was also read *yaktumu* (يَكْتُمُوا) in the third person.

﴿And whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾. The pronoun in (*innahu*) refers back to (*man*), which is the apparent reading. It was said that it is the pronoun of the matter (*damir al-sha'n*), and the clause after it explains it. (*Athimun*) is the predicate of (*inna*), and (*qalbuhu*) is its subject, as it is dependent on the predicate. This does not apply on the view that the pronoun refers to the matter, because it is not explained except by a clause; an attribute with its subject is not a clause according to the Basrans, though the Kufans permit it. It was said that (*qalbuhu*) is a fronted predicate and (*athimun*) is a delayed subject, and the clause is the predicate of (*inna*). On this, the pronoun may be for the matter or for (*man*). It was also said that (*athimun*) is the predicate of (*inna*), and in it is a pronoun returning to what the pronoun of (*innahu*) returns to, and (*qalbuhu*) is an apposition from that pronoun, an apposition of part from whole. It was also said that (*athimun*) is the subject and (*qalbuhu*) is a subject-pronoun filling the place of the predicate, and the clause is the predicate of (*inna*). This is permissible according to al-Farra' among the Kufans and al-Akhfash among the Basrans, while most grammarians do not permit it. He attributed the sinfulness (*ithm*) to the heart, although if it had said "(*fa-innahu athimun*)" the meaning would have been complete with brevity. This is because the sinner by concealment is something that happens in the heart, and attributing the act to the organ by which one works is more emphatic. Do you not see that when you want to emphasise, you say: "This is something my eye has seen, and something my ear has heard, and something my heart has known"? Also, although sin is attributed to the whole person, the attribution to this specific part is regarded as a metaphor for the whole, because it is the noblest of the parts and its chief, and its act is greater than the acts of the other organs. So in the speech there is an alert that concealment is among the greatest sins. It was said: He attributed the sin to the heart so that it would not be thought that concealing testimony is among the sins connected only with the tongue, and so that it would be known that the heart is the origin of what is connected to it and the source of its commission. It was also said: it is to indicate that the effect of concealment appears in his heart, as in the report: "When a servant sins, a black spot is produced in his heart, and whenever he sins, that increases until it blackens entirely." Or it is to indicate that his heart is corrupted, so his whole body is corrupted, for it has been reported: "Indeed in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Verily it is the heart." All of this is nothing, as is not hidden. It was read *qalbahu* (قَلْبَهُ) in the accusative, by analogy to the object. (*Athimun*) is an attribute in the form of an adjective (*sifa mushabbaha*). Abu Hayyan permitted that it is an apposition from the subject of *inna*, an apposition of part from whole, and some permitted that it is a specification (*tamyiz*), but Abu al-Baqa' considered this remote. Ibn Abi 'Abla read *athimun qalbuhu*, meaning he made it sinful.

﴿And Allah, of what you do﴾, of concealing testimony and giving it correctly and otherwise, ﴿is All-Knowing﴾ [283]. So He will reward you for that: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

[Page 64]

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾: from the matters that are included in their reality and those that are external to them, in whatever manner they are. That is, all of them are the possession of Allah, the Exalted, and are specific to Him. So He may obligate whomever He wills among His creatures with whatever obligations He wills, and no one has the right to say, "The wealth is mine, I may dispose of it however I wish." Some scholars have made this sentence like a proof for what precedes it. ﴿And if you show﴾, that is, make apparent to the people, ﴿what is in your souls﴾, that is, what has come to be in them in an original manner, such that it necessitates their being characterized by it, such as the base dispositions and blameworthy traits: envy, arrogance, self-admiration, ingratitude, and concealing testimony; ﴿or conceal it﴾, by not making it apparent.

﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾, that is, He will recompense you for it on the Day of Resurrection. As for the mere imagining of sins and blameworthy traits, it is because it does not necessitate the soul's being characterized by it, so one is not punished for it unless it exists in actuality. The Prophet ﷺ alluded to this when he said: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my Ummah what its souls whisper to it, as long as they do not act upon it or speak of it." That is, Allah, the Exalted, does not punish my Ummah for the imagining of disobedience; He punishes only for acting upon it. So there is no contradiction between the hadith and the verse, contrary to those who imagined that and fell into confusion trying to resolve it. It is not objectionable in this regard that they said: when the imagining reaches the level of resolution and determination, one is held accountable for it, based on the Almighty's saying: ﴿But He will call you to account for what your hearts have earned﴾. This is because we say: the accountability in reality is for the determined resolve to commit the sin in actuality, and that is also among the psychological states that attach to the dispositions, unlike all the other things that arise in the soul. One of them versified this:

The degrees of intention are five, as they have mentioned: a passing thought, then a recollection, then the whisper of the soul, so listen.
Next is concern, then resolve; all of these are lifted, except the last, for in it accountability has occurred.

Thus the verse, according to what we have established, is muhkam (not abrogated). But some have claimed that it is mansukh (abrogated), citing what Ahmad and Muslim transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When the verse ﴿And if you show what is in your souls﴾ was revealed upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it weighed heavily upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and then knelt on their knees and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we have been charged with deeds we can bear: prayer, fasting, jihad, and charity, and Allah has revealed to you this verse which we cannot bear.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Do you want to say what the People of the Two Books before you said: We hear and we disobey? Rather say: We hear and we obey, [we seek] Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return.' When the people recited it and their tongues were smoothed over it, Allah, the Exalted, revealed after it: ﴿The Messenger believes﴾ until the end of the verse. When they did this, Allah, the Exalted, abrogated it, and He, glorified is He, revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾, etc." The like of this has been authentically reported from ʿAlī, may Allah ennoble his face, Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn Masʿūd, and ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with them. Al-Bukhari also transmitted from Marwan al-Asghar, from a man among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ [he said], "I think he was Ibn ʿUmar," regarding ﴿And if you show what is in your souls or conceal it﴾: "It was abrogated by the verse that follows it." On this basis, there is no need to reconcile the verse with that authentic hadith in any way, and the hadith becomes a report about what was the case after the abrogation.

It has been objected that abrogation applies only to injunctive (inshaʾ) statements and does not apply to informative (khabar) statements, and this verse is of the second type. For this reason al-Tabarsi said, and he erred, that the narrations on abrogation are all weak. It has been answered that abrogation did not apply to the content of the informative statement itself, whether we say it is something that changes, like the faith of Zayd and the disbelief of ʿAmr, or not, like the existence of the Creator and the createdness of the world. Rather, the prohibition understood from it, as indicated by the Companions' statement to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "We have been charged with deeds we can bear, and Allah has revealed to you this verse which we cannot bear," is explicit that they understood from the verse a obligation. The legal ruling understood from the informative statement may be abrogated by consensus, as the words of al-ʿAḍud and others indicate.

Some who claimed the verse is muhkam and hesitated to accept this answer went to the view that the meaning of naskh (abrogation) here is bayan (clarification) and elucidation of the intended meaning, figuratively, as was previously indicated at His saying: ﴿So pardon and overlook﴾. It is as if it were said: how can ﴿what is in your souls﴾ be understood to include the involuntary whisperings, when that would entail obligation with what is beyond capacity, while Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity? This was objected to: even if it is far-fetched, it entails that the Prophet ﷺ approved the Companions in what they understood, while that is far from the intent of Allah, the Exalted, and he did not clarify it to them, despite their agitation and anxiety, which caused them to kneel until the other verse was revealed. It may be answered, though far-fetched, that there is no objection to this implication, and one can commit to it as being of the same kind as his ﷺ approval of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, when he interpreted a dream in the presence of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and said: "Have I erred or been correct, O Messenger of Allah?" He ﷺ said to him: "You were right in part and wrong in part." He did not explain to him which part he got right and which he got wrong, for some reason. Perhaps the purpose here is their being tested and that what is in their breasts be purified. This, in general, is preferable to interpreting the naskh as takhsis (specification), because that would entail, along with what is objectionable in it, the imposition of obligation with what cannot be borne, as is not hidden.

It has also been said: the meaning of the verse is: whether you declare what is in your souls of evil, or do not declare it, by carrying it out secretly, Allah will punish you for it. This comes back to our statement: if you bring evil deeds into existence openly or secretly, Allah will call you to account for them. Or: if you make apparent what is in your souls of concealing testimony, by saying to the one who asks you for testimony: "We have testimony with us, but we will conceal it and not render it to you before the judges." Or conceal it, by saying to him: "We have no knowledge of the report you want us to testify to, and you are lying in that," Allah will call you to account for it. This is supported by what Saʿid ibn Manṣur, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through Mujahid from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, regarding the verse, that he said: "It was revealed concerning testimony." It has also been said: the verse is on its apparent meaning, and ﴿what is in your souls﴾ is on its generality, including all passing thoughts; but the meaning of ﴿He will call you to account﴾ is that Allah, the Exalted, will inform you of it on the Day of Resurrection. They have counted this among the meanings of al-Ḥasīb (the Reckoner), the All-Knowing. All these statements are not free from scrutiny, so reflect.

Return to your mind, for I do not think you will find above what we have mentioned, or its like, in any book.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the agent is for the sake of giving it attention. As for the fronting of disclosure (ibdāʾ) before concealment (ikhfāʾ), contrary to what is in His saying: ﴿Say: whether you conceal what is in your breasts or disclose it, Allah knows it﴾, it has been said: what is connected here to "what is in your souls" is the reckoning, and its basis is the outward deeds. As for knowledge, its relation to them is like its relation to hidden deeds, and the state does not differ for Him between manifest and latent things. Indeed, nothing is latent in relation to Him, glorified is He, except that the stage of concealment precedes the stage of disclosure, for nothing appears except that it, or its precursor, was previously hidden in the soul. So the connection of His knowledge to its first state precedes the connection of His knowledge to its second state.

﴿Then He forgives﴾ with the nominative (raf'), as a resumptive clause, meaning: so He forgives by His grace ﴿whom He wills﴾ of His servants to forgive, ﴿and punishes﴾ by His justice ﴿whom He wills﴾ of His servants to punish. The mention of forgiveness before punishment is because His mercy precedes His wrath. Other than Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, and Yaʿqūb read both verbs in the jussive, coordinated to the response of the conditional. Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, read them in the accusative, with the particle anna implied, so that it and what is in its scope form a verbal noun coordinated with the implied verbal noun from the preceding verb; the sense is: "Let there be a reckoning, then forgiveness and punishment." Among the established rules: if a verb comes after the response of a conditional, preceded by waw or fāʾ, it may be read in three ways, and Ibn Malik indicated this:

The verb after the response, if it is joined by fāʾ or waw, is worthy of three vocalizations.

The Companion Ibn Masʿūd read yaghfiru and yuʿadhdhibu in the jussive without fāʾ. Its justification for one who permits multiple responses, like the predicate, is clear. As for others, the jussive here is taken to make them a substitute (badal) for yuḥāsibkum: a partial substitute (badal al-baʿḍ min al-kull) or a substitute of inclusion (badal al-ishtimāl), for each of forgiveness and punishment is part of the reckoning indicated by "yuḥāsibkum," and the general notion of reckoning encompasses both. If its encompassing of them is considered as the whole including its parts, it is a partial substitute; if it is considered as universality includes its instances, it is a substitute of inclusion. So it is said. It has also been said: if by "yuḥāsibkum" its literal meaning is intended, the substitute is of inclusion, like "I love Zayd his knowledge"; if by it recompense is intended, the substitute is partial, like "I struck Zayd his head." It has been said: other than that. Abu Hayyan held that it is specifically inclusion, saying: its occurrence in verbs is sound, because the verb indicates a genus under which are species it includes; that is why, when negation falls upon it, all species of that genus are negated. As for partial substitution from the whole, it is not possible with verbs, since the verb does not admit division, so one does not say of it that it has a whole and part except by a distant figurative usage. Al-Halabi objected to this, saying: it is not evident, for wholeness and partness apply to a genus and its species; the genus is a whole and the species a part, so the correct view is that both species occur in verbs, and both have been said in this verse of poetry:

Whenever you come to us, you will visit us at our abodes, and you will find the best fire, and with it the best hearth.

They made visiting (ilmām) a substitute for coming (ityān): either a partial substitute, because it is a coming without stopping, so it is part of it, or an inclusive substitute, because it is a light descent. It is narrated from Abu ʿAmr that he assimilated rāʾ into lām. Al-Zamakhshari, in his habit of criticizing the seven readings when they do not conform to the rules of Arabic grammar, found fault with it. Among their rules is that rāʾ is assimilated only into rāʾ, because of the repetition in it which is lost by assimilating it into lām. This may be answered: the seven readings are mutawatir (transmitted through successive multiple chains), and transmission by mutawatir is certain knowledge, while the grammarians' statement is a probable negation. Even if the mutawatir status were denied, the least is that it is established as a language by the transmission of trustworthy narrators, and affirmation is preferred over negation. The assimilation of rāʾ into lām from Abu ʿAmr is so famous and clear that there is no denying it. Among those who transmitted it from him is Abu Muhammad al-Yazidi, who was an imam in grammar, an imam in readings, and an imam in languages. Its rationale, in terms of explanation, is the great closeness between them, to the extent that they are almost like two similar letters, as evidenced by the necessity of assimilating lām into rāʾ in the eloquent dialect. However, he noticed the repetition of rāʾ, so he did not make its assimilation into lām obligatory. Moreover, the prohibition of assimilating rāʾ into lām is the position of the Basrans, but the Kufans permitted it and related it as heard from the Arabs, including al-Kisai, al-Farra', and Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi. The Arabic language is not confined to what the Basrans alone transmitted, and the reciters from the Kufans are not inferior to the reciters of Basra; they permitted it on the authority of the Arabs, so it must be accepted and recourse made to their knowledge and transmission, for one who knows is a proof against one who does not know.

﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾ [284]: this is a concluding phrase (tadhyīl) confirming the content of what precedes it, for the perfection of His power over all things necessitates His power over what has been mentioned of reckoning, and what follows from it of forgiveness and punishment. In the verse there is evidence for the Ahl al-Sunnah in denying that punishment is obligatory, since it is linked to will (mashīʾa). The possibility that that will is obligatory, like one who wills the obligatory prayer, does not necessitate the absence of obligation, contrary to the apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 2, verse 285:

﴿The Messenger believes﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned in this glorious surah, whose proofs are manifest, the obligation of prayer (*salah*) and almsgiving (*zakah*), divorce, menstruation, *ila'* (a husband's oath to abstain from his wife), jihad, the stories of the prophets, peace be upon them, and debt and usury, He concluded it with this, glorifying His Prophet (ﷺ) and his followers, and as an affirmation and a summary (*fadhlakah*, a concluding recapitulation) of all that was mentioned before. Here, glorified and exalted is He, He has testified to those who were mentioned at the beginning of the surah for their perfect faith, their good obedience, and their actual embodiment of these qualities. His mention of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the third person (*ghaybah*), while he was addressed in the second person (*khitab*) there, is because the testimony that remains through the ages should not be addressed to the one it testifies for. He, glorified is He, did not here explain their success in attaining their aims, among which are the supplications He relates from them that follow, indicating that this is a settled matter, needing no explicit statement, especially after He had stated it in what preceded. Mentioning him (ﷺ) by the title of messengerhood, without referring to his noble name, is both a glorification of him and a preparation for what is mentioned after it.

Al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Anas, who said: «When this verse, ﴿The Messenger believes﴾, was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "It is fitting for him to believe."» In a narration of Abd ibn Humayd from Qatadah, which supports the hadith of Anas, [it reads]: «So its (the chain's) break is made good, and it is fitting for him to believe.»

﴿in what has been sent down to him from his Lord﴾: of the rulings mentioned in this surah and others. The intended meaning is that he believes in these in a detailed manner. He stated it in summary out of reverence for his station (ﷺ), and to signal that his faith (ﷺ) relates to the details of what was revealed to him, and that his comprehension of all that it contains, which its reality cannot be grasped and which thoughts cannot reach however high they soar, has reached such manifestness that it needs no mention and is sufficient without explanation. In placing the predicate (*intiha'*, the object of belief) before the subject (*ibtida'*), together with the mention of the title of lordship and its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ), there is evidently a glorification of his noble rank and a proclamation of the exaltedness of his lofty station.

﴿And the believers﴾: it is permissible that this be conjoined to "the Messenger" and be nominative as the subject (*fa'iliyyah*), so one stops at "the Messenger." This is supported by what Abu Dawud recorded in *al-Masahif* from Ali, may Allah honour his face, that he recited (*wa-amana al-mu'minun*, "and the believers believed"). In that case, the words of the Exalted, ﴿each believes﴾, form a resumptive clause consisting of a subject and predicate. The use of an indefinite noun as subject is permitted because it is in the sense of being in a construct relation (*idafah*). It is also permissible that it be a subject, with "each" (*kullun*) as a second subject and "believes" (*amana*) as its predicate, the clause being the predicate of the first, with a pronoun linking them understood. It is not permissible for "each" (*kullun*) to be an emphatic (*ta'kid*) term, because they have stated that it is not an emphasis for a definite noun unless it is lexically attached to a pronoun referring to it. The first option is preferred because it better serves the demands of eloquence and is more suitable for acceptance, since the Messenger (ﷺ) is then the principal in the ruling of faith in what Allah sent down, and the believers follow him, and it is a source of pride for them. It follows, on the second option, that the ruling for the believers is stronger than the ruling for the Messenger (ﷺ), because their clause is nominal and emphatic. This has been objected to: in the second option there is an indication of glorifying the Messenger (ﷺ) and an emphasis to signal the clear difference and manifest distinction between his faith (ﷺ), which is based on witnessing and direct observation, and the faith of the rest of the believers, which arises from proof and demonstration, to the point that they seem to be different in every respect, even in the structure of the composition. It follows on the first option that if each of the two beliefs is understood in a manner befitting his (ﷺ) station, in terms of his essence and of its relation, so that they are taken with respect to him as the faith of direct vision that relates to all the details, and with respect to the individual members of the community as faith acquired from his niche (ﷺ), and in the manner appropriate to their condition regarding generality and detail, then this is a clear forcing (*i'tisaf*) that the Revelation and the objection are free from. The objection that was thought to be a contradiction is answered by saying that the use of the nominal clause with repetition of the predication, which strengthens the judgment, is due to a kind of obscurity in the judgment of the faith of each of them in the manner that follows, which necessitates that. The singular pronoun in "amana" (believed), though referring to all the believers, is because the intent is to describe the faith of each individual one of them, without considering them collectively, as was considered in His saying: ﴿and each of them comes to Him humbled﴾. This is further from imitation (*taqlid*), which, if it does not wound, scratches; that is, each one of them individually is secure.

﴿in Allah﴾: that is, he affirmed Him and His attributes, and negated likeness from Him, and declared Him far above what is unbefitting His majesty, such as a partner in divinity and lordship, and other things. ﴿and His angels﴾: insofar as they are infallible and purified, they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded. It is their role to mediate between Him, exalted is He, and the messengers, through the sending down of Books and the casting of revelation. For this reason they were mentioned in the wording before His saying: ﴿and His books and His messengers﴾, meaning insofar as their coming is from Him, exalted is He, in a manner befitting the station of each of them. Detailed faith is required regarding what is known in detail of each of these, and general faith regarding what is known in general. The faith in the Last Day is not mentioned here as it is mentioned in His saying: ﴿but righteousness is in one who believes﴾, etc., because it is included in the faith in His books; and the subsequent items are often abbreviated.

Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, read (*wa-kitabihi*, "and His book") in the singular. This may mean the Qur'an, with the attribution taken as referring to a known [book], or it may mean the genus, in which case it is not restricted to it. The difference between it and the plural, according to what Imam al-Haramayn and al-Zamakhshari held, and what was narrated from the Imam Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, is that the generalization (*istighraq*) of the singular is more comprehensive than that of the plural, because the singular encompasses all individual units from the outset, so nothing of them is excluded, whether little or much; unlike the plural, which encompasses the collectives first and essentially, then extends to the individual units. This topic is among the difficult problems of the science of meanings (*'ilm al-ma'ani*), and it has been thoroughly examined there.

﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾: in the place of an accusative, governed by a hidden verb of saying attributed to the pronoun of "each" (*kull*), with consideration given to the wording, so it is singular, or to the meaning, so it is plural. The latter is perhaps preferable. The clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial (*hal*) clause from the pronoun of "believed," or in the nominative as another predicate of "each," meaning: they say, or he says, "We make no distinction between the messengers of Allah, exalted is He, by believing in some and disbelieving in others, as the People of the Two Books did, but we believe in them all and affirm the validity of the messengership of each one of them." They qualified their faith with this in order to establish the truth and to explicitly differentiate themselves from those distinguishers of both groups, by manifesting faith in what they disbelieved in. ﴿So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers.﴾

From here it is known that those who say this are only the individual believers, because it is unlikely that it would be attributed to him (ﷺ) to say, "I make no distinction between any of His messengers," while he intends to manifest his faith in the messengership of himself and his affirmation of its claim. Whoever considers the inclusion of the Messenger in "each" (*kull*) and finds this unlikely says that *taghlib* (predominance of one term over another) is at work here. Whoever does not find it unlikely, since he (ﷺ) would utter the testimony of faith as the rest of people do, or would replace the knowledge in it with the first-person pronoun, does not need to resort to *taghlib*. The omission of addressing the non-distinction between the Books is because the mentioned [statement regarding the messengers] implies it. It was not reversed, even though the implication is mutual, because the primary matter in the distinction of the distinguishers is the messengers, and their disbelief in the Books is a consequence of their disbelief in them. The choice of explicitly naming the messengers rather than using a pronoun, as occurs in His saying: ﴿and what was given to the prophets from their Lord; we make no distinction between any of them﴾, is either to guard against the presumption that the angels are included in the ruling, even remotely, which, though not objectionable, offers little benefit in addressing, since there is no apparent competitor; or to indicate the reason for not distinguishing; or to allude to the title, since what is considered is the non-distinction in respect of messengerhood, not other aspects.

Ya'qub and Abu Amr, in one narration from him, read (*la yufarriqu*, "he makes no distinction") in the third-person singular, in agreement with the wording of "each" (*kull*); and it was also read (*la yufarriquna*, "they make no distinction") in the plural, in agreement with its meaning. In that case the clause itself is a circumstantial clause or a predicate in the manner discussed in the hidden verb of saying above, but there is no need for it here. The discussion of "any" (*ahad*) and the placing of "between" (*bayn*) before it has already been covered in the explanation of His saying: ﴿We make no distinction between any of them﴾.

﴿And they say﴾: a conjunction to "believed," with the plural in consideration of meaning. It is a report of their compliance with the commands and prohibitions, following the report of their faith. ﴿We hear﴾: that is, we respond, which is the customary meaning of hearing. ﴿and we obey﴾: and we accept willingly what You call us to in the commands and prohibitions. It has been said: "We hear" means what truth came to us, and we are certain of its validity, and "we obey" means what commands and prohibitions it contains. ﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord﴾: that is, forgive us Your forgiveness of whatever diminishes our standing before You, or we ask You for Your forgiveness of that. Thus *ghufran* ("forgiveness") is a verbal noun, either an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) or a direct object. The first is probably preferable, because the second requires supplying a specific verb, which necessitates recourse to a contextual indicator. The mention of hearing before obedience is due to the precedence of the general over the specific, or because the legal obligation proceeds by hearing, and obedience follows it. Mentioning them before asking for forgiveness is because the precedence of the means over the one asked for is closer to being answered and accepted. The mention of the title of lordship has had its secret explained more than once.

﴿And to You is the final return﴾ [285]: that is, the return by death and resurrection. It is a mimi verbal noun. The clause is said to be conjoined to an implied clause, meaning: "So from You is the origin, and to You is the return." It is a concluding statement (*tadhyil*) to what precedes, confirming the need for forgiveness, and in it there is an affirmation of the Return, which had not been explicitly stated before.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 286 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity.﴾ This is a new independent sentence (*jumla musta'nafa*), given as information from Him, the Exalted, after they had received His obligations (*taklif*) with obedience and acceptance. Within the imposition of obligation there are fine effects of His bounty and mercy, given as a beginning and not in response to a question, as will come later. *Taklif* means imposing what involves hardship and difficulty. *Wus'* is what a person's power can contain, or what is easy for him of what lies within his capacity, that is, what falls short of the limit of his strength. The meaning is His, the Exalted's, practice (*sunna*): He does not impose upon any soul among souls except what it can bear, and what is less than that. As in what He has obligated us with, such as prayer and fasting for example: He obligated us to five prayers, while our capacity can bear six and more. He obligated us to fast Ramadan, while our capacity can bear Sha'ban along with it. He did this out of grace and mercy towards the servants, or out of honour and favour upon this community in particular.

Ibn Abi Ablah read *(wus'aha)* with a fatha on the sin. The verse, on both interpretations, indicates that obligation with the impossible does not occur, but it does not indicate that it is impossible. As for the first interpretation, this is evident. As for the second, it is by way of *a fortiori* (*bi-tariq al-awla*). It has been said that on the second interpretation it does not indicate this, because the address in that case is specific to this community. In any case there is no proof in it that obligation with the impossible is forbidden, as it has been wrongly supposed. Some of what relates to this topic has already passed before you, and perhaps what will benefit you in it will come to you, God willing, the Exalted.

﴿For it is what it has earned, and against it is what it has earned.﴾ Another new independent sentence, given for encouragement, for keeping to the duties of obligation, and for warning against neglecting them. It shows that the obligation of each soul, together with its accompaniment of the blessing of lightening and facilitation, entails in observing it a further benefit, and that this benefit returns to it and not to anything else. Neglecting it entails a harm that falls upon it and not upon anything else. For the fact that the benefit of an act belongs to its doer is among the strongest motives to bring it about, and the restriction of its harm to him is among the strongest deterrents from doing it. This was said by al-Mawla, the Mufti of the Ottoman lands, may his secret be sanctified, and it is what many have adopted. It has also been said: the two sentences may be placed within the scope of a saying, and this would be a report of the scattered statements, not joined to one another, of the believers, and it would be praise for them, in that they thanked God, the Exalted, for His obligation, seeing that it had not gone beyond their capacity, and that they see that God, the Exalted, does not benefit from their good deeds, rather it is for them, and is not harmed by their evil deeds, rather it is upon them. It is not hidden that this is distant in one respect and near in another. The pronoun in *(lah.a)* refers to the soul in general. The speech involves an elided noun, which is reward in the first and punishment in the second. The explanation of the first *(ma)* is "the good," because of the *lam* which indicates benefit to it. The explanation of the second *(ma)* is "the evil," because of the *ʿalā* which indicates harm to it. The use of *iktisab* (acquiring) in the latter position is because it contains additional meaning, namely *i'timal* (effort and exertion). Evil is what the soul craves and is drawn towards, so it is more keen to acquire it. Thus there is an allusion to what souls have been created upon. Since there is nothing like this in good, he used the form stripped of *i'timal*.

﴿Our Lord, do not take us to account if we forget or make mistakes.﴾ This begins the report of the rest of their supplications after explaining the secret of obligation. It has been said: it completes the report of the statements. In *al-Bahr* it is related from al-Hasan that this is on the assumption of a command, i.e., "Say this in your supplication." Thus it is instruction from Him, the Exalted, to His servants on how to supplicate and ask of Him. This is of the utmost generosity and the highest kindness: He teaches them to ask so that He may give them, and guides them to request so that He may reward them. For this reason it has been said, and it has been mentioned before:

*Had you not wished to grant what I hope for and seek from the overflow of your generosity, you would not have taught me to ask.*

*Mu'akhadha* means punishment. Here *fa'ala* is used in the sense of *fa'ala* (the verb form with the same meaning). It has been said that *mufa'ala* is in its proper sense, because God, the Exalted, takes the sinner to account by punishment, and the sinner seems to take his Lord to account by demanding pardon, since he finds no one other than Him to deliver him from His punishment. Therefore the servant, when afraid of Him, clings to Him for this reason. Thus each of the two is expressed by the word *mu'akhadha*. The corruption of this is not hidden except through strained effort.

They differed about what is meant by forgetting and error, in several ways. The first: the first is intended as abandonment, as in his saying:

*I was not, at the time of generosity, one who was disposed to generosity, nor was I, on the day of terror, forgetful of thrusting with the spear.*

The second is intended as disobedience, because sins are described as error, which is the opposite of correctness, even if their doer does it *(mutaʿammidan)*, deliberately. It is as if it were said: "Our Lord, do not punish us for abandoning obligations and committing forbidden acts." The second: what is meant by them is what they cause, namely negligence and heedlessness, since they rarely occur except as a result of a prior shortcoming. So the meaning is: do not take us to account for that shortcoming.

The third: what is meant by them is themselves, in terms of their consequences as mentioned, or in general, since there is no impossibility in being taken to account for them by reason. Sins are like poisons: just as taking them, even inadvertently or by mistake, leads to destruction, so likewise indulging in sins may not be far from leading to punishment, even if it was not done with resolve. But He, the Exalted, promised to overlook it out of mercy and grace. So it is permissible for a person to ask for this in order to continue and to count the blessing in it. This is supported by the implication of his saying (ﷺ) in what al-Tabarani transmitted, and al-Nawawi said it is a good hadith: "The error and forgetfulness of my community are lifted, and what they have been compelled to do." It was objected to this that it is not complete according to the view of the verifying scholars of the People of the Sunna and the Mu'tazila, that obligation with what is not within one's power is impossible by reason for Him, the Exalted. For then the omission of taking to account for error and forgetfulness would not be grace that continues, nor a blessing counted.

﴿Our Lord, do not lay upon us a burden (*isr*)....﴾ That is, a heavy load that holds its bearer in place, binding him. What is meant by it is severe obligations. It has been said: *al-isr* is a sin for which there is no repentance, so the meaning is "protect us from committing it." It was read *(aṣaran)* in the plural. Ubayy read *(wa-la tuḥammil)* with shadda, for emphasis. ﴿As You laid it upon those before us.﴾ This is in the accusative position, as an attribute of an elided verbal noun, i.e., a burden like Your laying it upon those before us. Or it is an attribute of *(isran)*, i.e., a burden like the burden that You laid upon those before us. This was what the Children of Israel were obligated with: killing oneself in repentance, or in retaliation, since no other option was permitted in their law; and cutting off the place of impurity from garments and the like, and it has been said from the body; and giving a quarter of one's wealth in zakat.

﴿Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear.﴾ This is a plea to be spared punishments that cannot be endured, after pleading to be spared what leads to them. The expression of sending that down as "burdening" is a metaphor, in view of what leads to it. It was also permitted that it be a request for something more general than the first, the restriction to it being by way of comparison, except that it depicts the burden in the form of what cannot be borne, for emphasis. It has been said: it is a plea to be spared obligation with what human power truly cannot fulfil. The verse would then be evidence for the permissibility of obligation with what cannot be borne, since otherwise there would be no reason to ask to be freed from it. But this is not strong. Intensification here is only for making the verb transitive to a second object, not for multiplicity.

﴿And pardon us.﴾ That is, wipe out the traces of our sins by abandoning punishment. ﴿And forgive us.﴾ By covering the ugly and displaying the beautiful. ﴿And have mercy upon us.﴾ And incline towards us with what calls for more. It has been said: ﴿and pardon us﴾ refers to deeds, ﴿and forgive us﴾ refers to words, and ﴿and have mercy upon us﴾ refers to the heaviness of the scale. It has been said: ﴿and pardon us﴾ in the agonies of death, ﴿and forgive us﴾ in the darkness of graves, and ﴿and have mercy upon us﴾ in the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. Abu Hayyan said: "In these three sentences the word *Rabbana* does not occur, because they are the results of the preceding sentences which began with it. So *(fa'fu 'anna)* corresponds to His saying, ﴿do not take us to account﴾; *(waghfir lana)* corresponds to His saying, ﴿do not lay upon us a burden﴾; and *(warhamna)* corresponds to His saying, ﴿do not burden us with what we have no strength to bear﴾. For among the effects of not being taken to account for forgetting and error is pardon; among the effects of not laying a burden upon them is forgiveness; and among the effects of not imposing what cannot be borne is mercy." The excellence of this order is not hidden.

﴿You are our Mawla.﴾ That is, our Owner and our Master. It was permitted that it mean "the one who manages affairs." Its origin is a verbal noun intended to mean the agent. When *al-mawla* and *al-sayyid* are both mentioned, usage requires placing *al-mawla* first, so one says *mawlana wa-sayyiduna* ("our Mawla and our Sayyid"), as in the words of al-Khansa':

*Indeed Sakhr is our Mawla and our Sayyid, and indeed Sakhr, when the winter comes, is a slaughterer.*

Those who said *sayyiduna wa-mawlana*, placing *al-sayyid* before *al-mawla*, were regarded as in error, as Ibn Aybak said; but I have some hesitation about this. It has been said: the sentence has the sense of a saying, i.e., "Say: You are our Mawla." ﴿So help us against the disbelieving people.﴾ [286] That is, against the enemies in religion who wage war against us, or against disbelievers in general. He used the *fa'* to indicate causation, because God, the Exalted, being their Mawla, Owner, and the Manager of their affairs, it followed that they asked Him to help them against their enemies. It is like your saying: "You are the generous one, so be generous to me; you are the champion, so protect the neighbour."

* * *

From the allusive (*ishari*) approach in these verses: ﴿To Allah belongs what is in the heavens﴾, that is, all the spiritual worlds, and what is hidden in the veils of His unseen and the treasuries of His knowledge, ﴿and what is in the earth﴾, that is, the corporeal world and the manifest appearances which are the loci of manifestation of the Names and Actions.

﴿And whether you show what is in your souls﴾ He witnesses it through His Names and manifest forms, and He will call you to account for it; ﴿or conceal it﴾ He witnesses it through His attributes and inner realities, and He will call you to account for it. ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾ for their monotheism, the strength of their certainty, the incidental nature of their bad deeds, and their not being firmly rooted in their essence. ﴿And He punishes whom He wills﴾ for the corruption of their belief and the existence of their doubt, or the firm rootedness of their bad deeds in their souls. ﴿And Allah is over all things capable﴾ because by Him every manifest thing becomes manifest and every hidden thing becomes hidden, so He is able to forgive and to punish.

﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord﴾, the perfect, most perfect one. That is, he affirmed it by accepting it and by being characterised by it. Indeed his character (ﷺ) was the Qur'an, and his ascent through its meanings and his realisation of it. ﴿And the believers, each believes in Allah﴾ alone, by witnessing, when they did not see anything else in existence, ﴿and His angels and His books and His messengers﴾, when they returned to witnessing them. Those multiplicities are manifestations of the Oneness. They say, ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ by rejecting some and accepting others, since they witness the Truth in them through the Truth. ﴿And they say: We hear﴾, that is, we respond to our Lord in His books, His messengers, and the descent of His angels, and we keep steady on our journey. ﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord﴾, that is, forgive our existences and our attributes, and cover that with Your existence and Your attributes, for from You is the origin. ﴿And to You is the return﴾ by annihilation in You. ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾, except what its capacity can contain, and its readiness for the manifestations of divine self-disclosure does not straiten its ability to bear. ﴿For it is what it has earned﴾ of good, perfections and unveilings, whether that was by effort or without effort. ﴿And against it is what it has earned﴾ and what it has directed itself to, by intention, of evil.

﴿Our Lord, do not take us to account if we forget﴾ Your covenant through our inclination towards the darkness of nature, ﴿or make mistakes﴾ by acting in a way other than what is fitting for Your presence. ﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden (*isr*)﴾, which is the weight of attributes and actions that hold hearts back from ﴿witnessing the unseen﴾ ﴿as You laid it upon those before us﴾, from those veiled by the outward forms of actions or the inward realities of attributes.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 2, verse 286 (part 2 of 2):

﴿Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear﴾: that is, the burden of separation and deprivation from Your union and from witnessing Your beauty, veiled by the veil of Your majesty. ﴿And pardon us﴾: the evil deeds of our actions and our attributes, for they are evils that veiled us from You and deprived us of the coolness of Your union and the delight of Your good pleasure. ﴿And forgive us﴾: the sins of our existence, for it is the greatest of the major sins. ﴿And have mercy on us﴾: with the existence bestowed after annihilation (fana'). ﴿You are our Mawla﴾: that is, our Master, and the one who manages our affairs, because we are Your manifestations and the traces of Your power. ﴿So give us victory over the disbelieving people﴾: from the powers of our commanding souls (nafs ammarah) and their attributes, and from the armies of the devils of our illusions, who are veiled from You and who veil us from You, because of their disbelief and darkness.

Furthermore, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "When this verse was revealed and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited it, it was said to him after every word, 'Indeed you have done it' (qad fa'altu)." Abu Sa'id and al-Bayhaqi related from al-Dahhak: "When Jibril came with this verse, along with whatever angels Allah willed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited it, he said to him after every word, 'That is yours' (laka dhalika), until he finished it." Abu 'Ubayd related from Abu Maysarah: "Jibril taught the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to say 'Amin' at the end of al-Baqarah." The six imams (al-a'immah al-sittah) related in their books from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever recites the last two verses of Surat al-Baqarah in a night, they will suffice him." al-Tabarani related with a good chain from Shaddad ibn Aws, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah wrote a book two thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth. From it He sent down two verses with which He concluded Surat al-Baqarah. They are not recited in a house for three nights, and a devil approaches it." Ibn 'Adi related from Ibn Mas'ud al-Ansari that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah sent down two verses from the treasures of Paradise, which the Most Merciful wrote with His own hand two thousand years before He created the creation. Whoever recites them after the late night prayer ('isha' al-akhirah), they will suffice him in place of the night prayer (qiyam al-layl)." al-Hakim related and authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, from Abu Dharr that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah concluded Surat al-Baqarah with two verses which He gave me from His treasure beneath the Throne. So learn them, and teach them to your women and children, for they are prayer (salah), Qur'an, and supplication (du'a')." In the narration of Abu 'Ubayd from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir: "They are Qur'an, they are supplication, they bring one into Paradise, and they please the Most Merciful." Musaddad related from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Darimi from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, both of whom said: "I did not see anyone of sound mind sleep until he recited these verses from the end of Surat al-Baqarah." The reports concerning its virtue are numerous, and what we have mentioned is sufficient for whomever Allah grants success.

O Allah, grant us the greatest share in the answering of these supplications, enable us to do righteous deeds and to speak what is correct, make the Qur'an the spring of our hearts, the polish of our hearing, and the delight of our spirits. Facilitate for us the completion of what we have intended, and do not place any obstacle before us in what we have wished for by Your success. And send blessings and peace upon Your greatest vicegerent and Your hidden treasure, and upon his family who stand upon the secrets of Your Book, and his companions who triumph through the judgment of Your address, for as long as a spirit finds rest and the one knocking at the door of Your generosity attains openings.

Surat Al 'Imran

It has two hundred verses. Ibn al-Darris, al-Nahhas and al-Bayhaqi related through several chains from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that it was revealed at Medina. Its name in the Torah, as Sa'id ibn Mansur related, is Taybah. In Sahih Muslim it is named, along with al-Baqarah, al-Zahrawan (the two bright ones). It is also called al-Aman (the security), al-Kanz (the treasure), al-Ma'niyyah, al-Mujadalah (the disputation), and Surat al-Istighfar (the surah of seeking forgiveness). The connection (munasabah) of this surah with that one is that many of the ambiguous matters in that surah are explained by what is in this surah, and that Surat al-Baqarah is in the position of establishing the proof, while this one is in the position of addressing doubts. For this reason, what relates to the intended purpose is repeated in it, which is the demonstration of the truth of the Book: from the sending down of the Book, its confirmation of the books before it, and guidance to the straight path. The verse ﴿Say: We believe in Allah and what has been sent down﴾ is repeated in full. For this reason, this surah mentions what follows from or is necessarily linked to what was mentioned in that one. There it mentions the creation of people, and here it mentions their formation in the wombs. There it mentions the origin of the creation of Adam, and here it mentions the origin of his offspring. More subtle than this is that al-Baqarah opened with the story of Adam and his creation from earth without a mother, while this surah mentions its counterpart in creation without a father, which is 'Isa. For this reason He struck the parable for him with Adam. Al-Baqarah was singled out with Adam because it is the first of the surahs, and he is the first in existence and the precursor. Also, because it is the origin, and this one is like its branch and completion, so it was singled out with the more wondrous. Also, because al-Baqarah was addressed to the Jews, who said about Maryam what they said, and denied the existence of a child without a father. So it began with the story of Adam so that it would be fixed in their minds, and thus the story of 'Isa would not come except after something of its kind had been mentioned to them that bears witness to it. Also, the story of 'Isa was analogized to the story of Adam, and the thing analogized to must necessarily be known so that the proof by analogy is complete. So the story of Adam and the surah in which it appears were worthy of precedence.

Some verifiers (muhaqqiqin) have mentioned, among the aspects of the connection between the two surahs, that in al-Baqarah, in describing the Fire, He said: ﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾, although it opened with mention of both the righteous (muttaqin) and the disbelievers together. And in the end of this surah He said: ﴿A Garden whose width is the heavens and the earth, prepared for the righteous﴾. So the two surahs are as if they were a single surah. What further strengthens the connection and linkage between them is that the ending of this surah corresponds to the opening of that one. The first opened with mention of the righteous and that they are the successful, and this one ends with His saying: ﴿And fear Allah that you may be successful﴾. The first opened with His saying: ﴿And those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾, and this one ends with His saying: ﴿And indeed among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and what has been sent down to you and what was sent down to them﴾. It has also been reported that the Jews said, when the verse ﴿Who is it that would loan Allah a goodly loan?﴾ was revealed: "O Muhammad, your Lord has become poor, asking His servants for a loan." So ﴿Allah has certainly heard the statement of those who said, 'Indeed Allah is poor and we are rich'﴾ was revealed. This also strengthens the connection. Similarly, in al-Baqarah there is the report of Ibrahim's words: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them a messenger from themselves﴾, the verse; and here: ﴿Allah has certainly conferred favor upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves﴾, the verse; and beyond that.
